parole.significato: Marks singular nouns, with a foundation in Greek or Latin, often implying femininity, especially when contrasted with w…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -a (nominative first declension neuter singular suffix)

parole.significato: Of, relating to, resembling or containing the thing suffixed
parole.testo: Suffixal construction from (1) Latin ‑āceus (“belonging to, of the nature of”) + -ous, from oblique stem of -āx, -ācis + -eus and (2) -acea + -ous. Also variant of -acious.

parole.significato: Denoting quality, state, condition.
parole.testo: From Latin -ācia or ultimately Latin -ātia. Also a suffixal construction from -ate + -cy.

parole.significato: toward
parole.testo: Derived from Latin ad (“at”), from Proto-Italic *ad, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd. Coined by British anatomist John Barclay.

parole.significato: pain, suffering
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin -algia. By surface analysis, alg- + -ia.

parole.significato: Appears in the names of Roman festivals.
parole.testo: From Latin -ālia.

parole.significato: walker, one who walks
parole.testo: From Latin ambulō (“to walk”).

parole.significato: A collection of things that relate to a specific place, person, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin -āna (neuter plural of -ānus).

parole.significato: Used in forming female given names.
parole.testo: From Latin -āna, feminine of -ānus (“of or pertaining to”).

parole.significato: Added to verbs and adjectives to form nouns conveying a condition or quality associated with the verb.
parole.testo: From Latin -antia, -entia, with influence from French -ance, French -ancie, Spanish -ancia, etc.

parole.significato: A suffix forming nouns denoting patients (i.e., recipients of actions), such as compiland.
parole.testo: From Latin gerundive termination -andus, -endus. More at -end.

parole.significato: Used to form an abstract noun from an adjective, to form the noun referring to the state, property, or quality of confo…
parole.testo: From Latin -āneitās, from -āneus + -tās. By surface analysis, -ane(ous) + -ity.

parole.significato: Found in adjectives from Latin.
parole.testo: From Latin -āneus, with influence from -ous (from Latin -ōsus) although the two suffixes are not etymologically related.

parole.significato: Of, near, or pertaining to; adjective suffix appended to various words, often nouns, to make an adjective form. Often a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -āris (“of, pertaining to”). Distant doublet of -al.

parole.significato: Ending of some nouns denoting occupations, chiefly inherited from Middle English nouns borrowed from Old French or Medi…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English -ar, -er, -arie, borrowed from Latin -ārius or Old French -aire. Doublet of -ary, -eer, -ier, and -yer.

parole.significato: leading, leader
parole.testo: From Late Latin -archa, from Latin -archēs, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule, government”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ergʰ- (“to begin, rule, command”).

parole.significato: A place associated with a specified thing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -ārium. Doublet of -ary.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to. Adjectival suffix appended to various words, often nouns, to produce an adjective form. Often adde…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English -arie, a back-formation from Latin and French-borrowed adjectives ending respectively in -ārius and -aire (more rarely from Latin adjectives in -āris: see exemplary and lapidary). Doublet of -ar, -eer, -ier, and -yer; see also the related -arian.

parole.significato: someone associated with something
parole.testo: From Latin -asta, from Ancient Greek -αστής (-astḗs), from -άζω (-ázō, verbal suffix) + -τής (-tḗs, agent-noun suffix).

parole.significato: Used to form diminutive and pejorative nouns, labeling someone pretending to be what they are not.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -aster (“little, petty, partial, incomplete”).

parole.significato: forms adjectives with meaning "having the specified thing"
parole.testo: First attested in the 15th century; borrowed from Latin -ātus, the perfect passive participle ending of first conjugation verbs, also used to form participial adjectives from nouns. Before -ate was introduced as a suffix in Middle English, Latin-borrowed participial adjectives were written with fina

parole.significato: derives or adapts verbs (mostly) from Latin stems
parole.testo: See Etymology 1. In Middle English, verbs were derived from Latin-borrowed participial adjectives (also used as their past participles) and formed their infinitives in -aten (see -en; Middle English desolaten for modern desolate). In the 15th century, the loss of most verbal morphology made verbs fo

parole.significato: forms nouns denoting a rank or office
parole.testo: From the Latin abstract-noun-forming suffix -ātus, -ātūs.

parole.significato: Changes a component into an adverb meaning "by that component."
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ātim.

parole.significato: Used to form agent nouns, usually from verbs that have the ending -ate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ātor or -ate + -or.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives of, relating to, or connected with the thing specified
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -atorius. By surface analysis, -ate + -ory.

parole.significato: Forms nouns that represent things or places where a specified activity takes place
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -atorium (neuter of -atorius). By surface analysis, -ate + -ory.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a tail-like structure.
parole.testo: From New Latin cercus, from Ancient Greek κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”).

parole.significato: Forms placenames, originally those settled by the Roman Empire in Great Britain.
parole.testo: From Old English ċeaster, from Latin castrum

parole.significato: shinned
parole.testo: From New Latin cnēmis, from Ancient Greek κνήμη (knḗmē, “shin”) + -ic.

parole.significato: any spherical microorganism
parole.testo: From New Latin coccus, from Latin coccum, from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos, “grain, seed”).

parole.significato: A cavity.
parole.testo: Via Latin, from Ancient Greek κοῖλος (koîlos, “hollow”).

parole.significato: Having a specified habitat.
parole.testo: From Latin -col(a) (“inhabitor”) + -ous. By surface analysis, -col(e) + -ous.

parole.significato: horn(s)
parole.testo: From Latin cornū (“horn”).

parole.significato: Used to form cell names and classifications for mature cells.
parole.testo: From Latin cyta, from Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos, “vessel, jar”). Compare cyte.

parole.significato: A linking vowel inserted between two morphemes, to ease pronunciation, without contributing to the meaning.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -e-.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives, usually from proper nouns.
parole.testo: From Latin -ānus, following Latin stems ending in -ae(us) (many from Ancient Greek -αῖος (-aîos)), -e(us) or -ē(us) (many from Ancient Greek -εῖος (-eîos)).

parole.significato: Forming abstract nouns denoting conditions, qualities, or states.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin -entia.

parole.significato: Forming nouns denoting patients or recipients of actions.
parole.testo: From Latin -endus, a gerundive ending, related to -andus.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives relating to places and nouns for their inhabitants.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ēnus, from Ancient Greek -ηνός (-ēnós), forming adjectives from place names.

parole.significato: Combining form denoting years.
parole.testo: From Latin -enniālis, from annus + -ium + -ālis.

parole.significato: Used to form verbs from nouns, following the pattern of verbs derived from Latin verbs ending in -esco
parole.testo: From Latin -ēscō (“to grow, become a certain way”, an inchoative suffix). Compare -ish (Etymology 2).

parole.significato: A process of becoming (growing or increasing in the trait specified by the prefixed stem).
parole.testo: From Latin -escens, form of -ēscō (“I become”). By surface analysis, -esce + -ence.

parole.significato: beginning to be; becoming
parole.testo: From Latin -ēscēns, present participle of -ēscō (“I become”). By surface analysis, -esce + -ent.

parole.significato: Used to form nouns denoting condition, action, or process.
parole.testo: From Latin -ēsis, from Ancient Greek -ησις (-ēsis), from -σις (-sis).

parole.significato: Noun suffix that denotes a condition, action, or process.
parole.testo: French form of -esis, from Late Latin -esia, from -ēsis, from Ancient Greek -ησις (-ēsis), from -σις (-sis).

parole.significato: Used to indicate qualities or states.
parole.testo: Cognate of -ity, ultimately from Latin -(i)tās. See more at -ity.

parole.significato: Noun-forming suffix found in words of Greek origin meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or per…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ēum, from Ancient Greek -εῖον (-eîon), originating in the substantivized neuter of -εῖος (-eîos, adjective suffix).

parole.significato: Used to construct company and product names that borrow meaning from the root word.
parole.testo: Imitative of the ending of Latin-derived words such as index and codex

parole.significato: Used to form nouns denoting the process of producing or making something.
parole.testo: Clipping of manufacture, ultimately from Latin factus (“done, made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (“to do, make”).

parole.significato: Holder or bearer of something.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin -fer (“bearer”).

parole.significato: Split, cleft
parole.testo: From Latin -fidus, a combining form of findō (“to split”).

parole.significato: Forming nouns denoting a morpheme used in word formation joined to a word in the specified way
parole.testo: The common element of prefix, suffix, and affix — all ultimately from Latin figere (“to fasten”).

parole.significato: Forms nouns related to flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -flōrus (adapted through -ous).

parole.significato: Having the shape or form of; looking like.
parole.testo: From Latin -fōrmis (“having the form of”), from fōrma (“a form, contour, figure, shape, appearance, looks”).

parole.significato: Related to formic acid in some way.
parole.testo: From formic, from Latin formīca (“ant”).

parole.significato: travelling out from
parole.testo: Formed from the stem of Latin fugiō (“flee”), with the suffix -al, from Latin -alis.

parole.significato: Used to signify a noun that dispels or removes.
parole.testo: From Latin -fugus.

parole.significato: origin
parole.testo: Via Latin, from Ancient Greek γένεσις (génesis). The simplex genesis is in use as a common noun (as opposed to Genesis, the name of the biblical book) since the late 16th century, as a suffix since the mid 17th century (attested in epigenesis and palingenesis). Influenced by French -génésie and Germ

parole.significato: Bearing or producing.
parole.testo: From Latin gerō (“to carry”) + English -ous.

parole.significato: Describes a specified way of walking or locomotion, especially according to the limbs or organs utilized.
parole.testo: From Latin gradus (“step, degree”) and gradior (“walk”).

parole.significato: Forms an alternative plural ending for various words borrowed from Latin that end in ⟨us⟩ in the singular.
parole.testo: From Latin -ī (nominative plural).

parole.significato: A vowel inserted interconsonantally between morphemes of Latinate origin in order to ease pronunciation (an anaptyxis,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -i-.

parole.significato: Used in forming placenames, especially of countries.
parole.testo: From Latin -ia and Ancient Greek -ία (-ía), -εια (-eia), which form abstract nouns of feminine gender.

parole.significato: Used in forming plurals of nouns in -ium and -ion.
parole.testo: From the endings of corresponding Latin and Ancient Greek plural nouns.

parole.significato: Used in forming female given names.
parole.testo: From Latin -ia, feminine of -ius, a suffix forming adjectives and the ending of most Classical Latin nomina gentilicia.

parole.significato: From, related to, or like.
parole.testo: From Latin -iānus, which forms adjectives of belonging or origin from a noun.

parole.significato: A pathological condition or process.
parole.testo: A Latin word-forming element meaning "process" or "morbid condition". Originally from Ancient Greek ἴασις (íasis). By surface analysis, -i- + -asis.

parole.significato: a collection of things that relate to a specific place, person, theme, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin -ica, neuter plural of -icus. Note that etymologically this is not -ic + -a (“(plural ending)”), as -ic is the English form, having dropped the -um, though adding an -a to an English word ending in -ic does produce a superficial etymologically.

parole.significato: Used to form diminutive nouns.
parole.testo: From Latin -culus (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Any of a group of related compounds - azide, polysaccharide, glycoside.
parole.testo: Generalized in the early 19th c. from oxide (which has its ending from French acide, itself from Latin -idus in acidus), and gradually displaced earlier -uret, both introduced in the English translation of de Morveau, Lavoisier et al.'s 1787 book Méthode de nomenclature chimique.

parole.significato: Creating or causing something.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -(i)ficus. By surface analysis, -ify + -ic.

parole.significato: Tending to, or capable of.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -ilis.

parole.significato: Suffix occurring in comparative adjectives borrowed from Latin.
parole.testo: From Latin -ior, the nominative masculine and feminine singular of the comparative suffix -iōr.

parole.significato: Forming adjectives, typically from a place ending in -polis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ītānus.

parole.significato: Forming verbs, typically implying intense or repetitive activity.
parole.testo: From Latin -itāt-, past participial stem of -itō. On the model of e.g. Classical Latin nōbilitō and found in borrowings e.g. premeditate, debilitate, agitate.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives.
parole.testo: From Latin past participles in -ītus, of verbs in -īre, -ĕre, -ēre, partly via Old French.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives denoting "pertaining to, characterized by, having the nature of, resembling, tending to."
parole.testo: From Latin -ītius or -īcius.

parole.significato: Denoting diseases characterized by inflammation, itself often caused by an infection.
parole.testo: From New Latin -itis, from Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis, “pertaining to”). This is the feminine form of adjectival suffix -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs). parole.significato: Used to form the names of metal elements, after the style of early-named elements, as well as the isotopes of hydrogen.
parole.testo: From Latin -um (neuter singular morphological suffix), based on Latin terms for metals such as ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: worship of
parole.testo: From Late Latin latria, from Ancient Greek λατρεία (latreía, “service; worship”).

parole.significato: speaking, speech
parole.testo: Extracted from Latin compounds such as soliloquium, vaniloquium.

parole.significato: Divination.
parole.testo: From Latin -mantīa, ultimately from Ancient Greek μᾰντείᾱ (mănteíā, “divination”).

parole.significato: Forms adjectives corresponding to nouns ending in -mancy.
parole.testo: From Latin ‑manticus, from -mantīa + -icus. Compare Ancient Greek ‑μάντικος (‑mántikos).

parole.significato: Used to form page and book sizes.
parole.testo: From Latin ending and apparent suffix of cardinal numbers.

parole.significato: Deadjectival suffix used to form an abstract noun usually from personal adjectives.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -mōnium, -mōnia.

parole.significato: A linking vowel inserted interconsonantally between two morphemes, to ease pronunciation, without contributing to the m…
parole.testo: Adopted from Latin -o-, originating ultimately from Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-). In English, the connective is found from the Middle English period in direct borrowings from Latin. Direct formations of English terms with the connective, always combining Greek or Latin roots, appear from the 16th or 17th

parole.significato: Resembling; having the likeness of (usually including the concept of not being the same despite the likeness, but count…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -oīdēs, from Ancient Greek -ο-ειδής (-o-eidḗs) (the ο being the last vowel of the stem to which the suffix is attached); from εἶδος (eîdos, “form, likeness”).

parole.significato: Indicating an oily substance
parole.testo: From Latin oleum (“oil, olive oil”), from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”).

parole.significato: Used to form the names of several commercial companies and products.
parole.testo: From Latin -ola, -ula, feminine form of -ulus, -lus (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Used to form words relating to oil or oiliness
parole.testo: From Latin oleum (“oil, olive oil”).

parole.significato: in the Hantzsch–Widman nomenclature for naming heterocycles, denotes an unsaturated five-membered ring system with nitr…
parole.testo: Partly arbitrary variant of -ol (now used to distinguish between specific cases) and partly from Latin oleum (“oil”).

parole.significato: Word.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek ὄνυμα (ónuma), Doric and Aeolic dialectal form of ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”); compare also -onymy § Etymology.

parole.significato: Used to form nouns of quality, state, or condition.
parole.testo: From Latin -or.

parole.significato: Forming nouns denoting a place for a particular function or thing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -ōrium. Doublet of -ory.

parole.significato: Added to nouns and verbs (often Latinate) to form adjectives meaning “of”, “pertaining to”, or “serving for”.
parole.testo: From Middle English -orie, from the Latin adjective suffix -tōrius. By surface analysis, -or + -y.

parole.significato: Added to nouns and verbs (often Latinate) to form nouns meaning “that which pertains to or serves for”.
parole.testo: From the Latin noun suffix -tōrium. By surface analysis, -or + -y.

parole.significato: a monoclonal antibody that targets bone
parole.testo: From Latin os (“bone”).

parole.significato: full of
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ōsus. Doublet of -ous in stressed position.

parole.significato: functional disease or condition such as hepatosis
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin -ōsis, from Ancient Greek -ωσις (-ōsis, “state, abnormal condition, or action”), from -όω (-óō) stem verbs + -σις (-sis).

parole.significato: parous; relating to parity (the number of times a woman has given birth).
parole.testo: From Latin -parus, from Latin pariō (“produce, bring forth, give birth”).

parole.significato: travelling towards
parole.testo: Formed from the stem of Latin petō, petere (“seek, aim”), with the suffix -al, from Latin -alis.

parole.significato: eater; something that eats, or consumes.
parole.testo: From Latin -phagus, from Ancient Greek φάγος (phágos, “glutton”), from φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”), aorist active infinitive of ἔφαγον (éphagon, “I ate, devoured”). parole.significato: Used to form adjectives meaning "eating" or "feeding on".
parole.testo: From Latin -phagus, from Ancient Greek -φάγος (-phágos, “-eating”), from φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”).

parole.significato: Denoting a condition of the phalange bones in the fingers and toes.
parole.testo: From Latin phalanx, with combining form phalang-.

parole.significato: Synonym of -phasia: forms names of speech disorders.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin -phēmia, from Ancient Greek φήμη (phḗmē, “voice”).

parole.significato: Forming nouns and adjectives meaning "loving", "friendly", or "friend".
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -phila, from Ancient Greek φίλος (phílos, “dear, beloved”).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns meaning fear of a specific thing.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin, from Ancient Greek -φοβία (-phobía), from φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives indicating a fear of a specific thing.
parole.testo: From -phobia (from Late Latin -phobia, from Koine Greek -φοβία (-phobía), from φόβος (phóbos, “fear”)) + -ic.

parole.significato: Bearer, carrier or conveyor.
parole.testo: From New Latin -phorus, from Ancient Greek -φόρος (-phóros, “bearing”), a derivative of φέρω (phérō, “to bear, to carry”). See phoresy.

parole.significato: Growth or formation
parole.testo: From New Latin -plasia, from Ancient Greek πλάσις (plásis, “molding, formation”).

parole.significato: A tuple containing the specified number of terms.
parole.testo: From Latin -plus (“more, in sum”).

parole.significato: Comprising a number of parts, as in duplex.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -plex (“fold”).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns that denote the making or creating of something.
parole.testo: From Latin -poeia, from Ancient Greek ποιέω (poiéō, “I make”).

parole.significato: Forms names of cities or kinds of cities.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -polis, from Ancient Greek πόλις (pólis, “city”).

parole.significato: Forms nouns indicating excessive discharge or haemorrhage from an organ.
parole.testo: From Latin -rrhagia, from Ancient Greek -ραγία (-ragía), from the stem of ῥήγνυμι (rhḗgnumi, “to break, burst”).

parole.significato: rupture
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ῥῆξις (rhêxis), from ῥήγνυμι (rhḗgnumi).

parole.significato: follow
parole.testo: Extracted from Latin compounds such as obsequium, exsequia.

parole.significato: Forming the names of different kinds of soil.
parole.testo: From Latin solum (“floor, ground”).

parole.significato: To look at, perceive, or observe.
parole.testo: From Latin specio.

parole.significato: Adjective suffix denoting "full of, prone to."
parole.testo: Rebracketed from words like fractious and presumptious, with the t from the base + -ious, ultimately from Latin ‑tiōsus, which is rebracketed from -t(us) + -i- + -ōsus.

parole.significato: Describes the cleavage of minerals.
parole.testo: From Latin -tomus, introduced by James Dwight Dana, from Ancient Greek τόμος (tómos, “slice, something cut”). Perhaps modelled on Ancient Greek ἀκρότομος (akrótomos, “cut off sharply”, adjective).

parole.significato: Tone, condition.
parole.testo: From New Latin -tonia, from Ancient Greek -τονία (-tonía) (in ἀτονία (atonía)), from τόνος (tónos) + -ία (-ía). Compare French -tonie, German -tonie.

parole.significato: place
parole.testo: From Latin topica, from Ancient Greek τοπικός (topikós, “pertaining to a place, local, pertaining to a common place, or topic, topical”), from τόπος (tópos, “a place”); equivalent to -topia + -ic.

parole.significato: Having a trema (hole or aperture) or tremata of the type, position or number specified by the prefix.
parole.testo: From New Latin trēma (“aperture”), from Ancient Greek τρῆμα (trêma), from Proto-Hellenic *trḗmə (“hole”), from Proto-Indo-European *tréh₁-mn̥ (“to drill”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to drill”).

parole.significato: Found on the end of words, chiefly female agent nouns.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -trīx, -trīcis.

parole.significato: something that turns, affects, changes, responds, moves.
parole.testo: From Latin tropus, from Ancient Greek τρόπος (trópos, “a turn, way, manner, style, a trope or figure of speech, a mode in music, a mode or mood in logic”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “turn; solstice; trope”). See trope.

parole.significato: movement, turning.
parole.testo: From Latin tropus (English trope) + -ism, from Ancient Greek τρόπος (trópos, “a turn, way, manner, style, a trope or figure of speech, a mode in music, a mode or mood in logic”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “turn; solstice; trope”). Early use in botany as geotropism and heliotropism.

parole.significato: A linking vowel inserted between two morphemes, to ease pronunciation, without contributing to the meaning.
parole.testo: From Latin -u-.

parole.significato: Forming diminutive nouns.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ula. Doublet of -ule.

parole.significato: Denotes singular grammatical number.
parole.testo: From the homographic case endings of the nominative, accusative, and vocative forms of numerous neuter Latin second declension nouns.

parole.significato: -ide.
parole.testo: Coined in 1788 by translator of de Morveau, Lavoisier et al.'s 1787 book Méthode de nomenclature chimique James St. John, from Modern Latin -uretum and French -ure.

parole.significato: urine; urination; presence in urine (of a substance denoted by a prefixed combining form); state or condition of the ur…
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, Latin -ūria, from Ancient Greek -ουρία (-ouría), from οὖρον (oûron, “urine”).

parole.significato: Used to refer to a person with a particular personality around other people.
parole.testo: From Latin vertere (“to turn”).

parole.significato: An organism, usually animal, identified by its kind of diet.
parole.testo: From Latin vorare (“to devour”).

parole.significato: forming adjectives with the sense of ‘habitually eating, feeding on’
parole.testo: From Latin -vorus, equivalent to -vore + -ous.

parole.significato: Village; settlement; hamlet; trading centre.
parole.testo: From Middle English wic, from Old English wīc (“abode, dwelling-place”), an early borrowing from Latin vīcus (“village”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ- (“village, household”). Latin cognate to Gothic 𐍅𐌴𐌹𐌷𐍃 (weihs), Old High German weihs (“village, settlement”), from Proto-Germanic *wīhsą (“village

parole.significato: Forming nouns indicating individual members of taxonomic groups whose names end in -zoa.
parole.testo: From Latin -zoon, from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).

parole.significato: Sixmo, sexto.
parole.testo: From Latin sexto.

parole.significato: Pound (unit of weight).
parole.testo: English lb English # Derived from the abbreviation lb for Latin libra (“pound”), via the medieval convention of indicating abbreviations with a bar, ℔.

parole.significato: Argued by means of force rather than logic.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ā baculō (literally “by means of the rod”), from ā (“of, from”) + baculō (“sceptre, rod”), ablative singular of baculum.

parole.parola: a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush
parole.significato: A sure thing is preferable to the mere chance at something more.
parole.termine_origine: plus valet in manibus avis unica quam dupla silvis

catena.termine: plus valet in manibus avis unica quam dupla silvis

parole.testo: Calque of Latin plus valet in manibus avis unica quam dupla silvis (“a single bird in the hands is worth more than two in the forest”), possibly deriving from sources as old as the ancient Middle East, with the 6th century BCE Proverbs of Ahiqar including "a sparrow in thy hand is better than a thou

parole.significato: With stronger or greater reason; as a corollary implied by a stronger claim; even more so; all the more so; so much the…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin ā fortiōrī.

parole.significato: That does not dissolve the marriage bond, but merely authorizes the husband and wife to live apart from each other.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin a mensa et thoro (“from board and bed”).

parole.significato: Describing a disposition of property granted by a party who has no title to it.
parole.testo: From Latin, literally "from the non-owner".

parole.significato: Involving induction of theories from facts.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā posteriōrī (“involving reasoning from effect to cause, from experience to theory”, literally “from what follows”). Popularized from the 19th century in reference to the work of Immanuel Kant.

parole.significato: from the stronger or more important; according to the majority
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin denominatio a potiori (“naming from the stronger”).

parole.significato: Self-evident, intuitively obvious.
parole.testo: First attested in 1610. Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā priōrī (“involving reasoning from cause to effect; from first principles”, literally “from the former”).
Learned borrowing from Latin a quō.

parole.significato: from behind
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin a tergo.

parole.significato: Describing an absolute divorce, after which the parties may remarry.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin a vinculo matrimonii (“from the bond of marriage”).

parole.significato: Away from.
parole.testo: From Latin ab (“of, off, from, away”).

parole.significato: In or for the meantime; temporarily.
parole.testo: From Latin a. i., an abbreviation of ad interim.

parole.significato: The leader of a group of thieves.
parole.testo: From Latin Aaron, from Ancient Greek Ἀαρών (Aarṓn), from Hebrew אַהֲרֹן (ʾAhărōn), of unknown meaning, possibly meaning “bearer of martyrs”, or perhaps also, or instead, related to the Ancient Egyptian ꜥḥꜣ rw (“warrior lion”), though it has been suggested to also mean “elevated”, “exalted” or “high

parole.significato: Synonym of Levite.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Aaronida under influence from French aaronide, from Koine Greek Αἀρωνίδης (Aarōnídēs) in the Septuagint. Equivalent to Aaron + -id.

parole.significato: From absurdity.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ab absurdō (literally “away from harsh”), from ab (“of, from, by, since”) + absurdō (“silly, stupid”), ablative masculine/neuter of absurdus.

parole.significato: From time immemorial; from an infinitely remote point in the past.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ab aeternō.

parole.significato: From outside.
parole.testo: First attested in the mid 17th century. Learned borrowing from Latin ab extra (literally “from outside”) From Late Latin ab (“from”) extra (“outside”).

parole.significato: From inconvenience or hardship.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ab inconvenientī.

parole.significato: From the time when a law, legal right or decree, contract, ownership interest, partnership (etc.) comes into force.
parole.testo: From Latin ab (“from”) + initiō, ablative singular of initium (“beginning”).

parole.significato: From an intestate (someone who dies with no legal will).
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: from inside; from within
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ab intrā (“from within”).

parole.significato: Against one's will; not of one's invitation.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: From the beginning.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ab ōvō (literally “from the egg”).

parole.significato: From utility.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ab utili (“from utility”)

parole.significato: From.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ab-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epo (“off, away”) (English off, of). Doublet of apo- and off-.

parole.significato: To blind by holding a red-hot metal rod or plate before the eyes
parole.testo: From Late Latin abacinātus, perfect passive participle of abacinō; possibly formed from ab (“off”) + bacīnum (“a basin”) or bacīnus. Probably cognate with modern Italian abbacinare (“to dazzle”).

parole.significato: One of the tiles or squares of a tessellated pavement; an abaculus.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀβακίσκος (abakískos, “a coloured stone for laying mosaic”), diminutive of ἄβαξ (ábax, “board”). See abacus.

parole.significato: One who uses an abacus in casting accounts; a calculator.
parole.testo: From Middle English abaciste, from Medieval Latin abacista, from abacus + -ista (“-ist”).

parole.significato: An inscribed stone square.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abacus.

parole.significato: Carrying away by force, especially of animals.
parole.testo: From Latin abāctiō.

parole.significato: One who steals and drives away cattle or beasts by herds or droves; a cattle rustler.
parole.testo: From Late Latin abactor (“cattle rustler”), from abigō (“drive away”); from ab (“from, away from”) + agō (“drive”).

parole.significato: A small tile of glass, marble, or other substance, of various colors, used in making ornamental patterns in mosaic pave…
parole.testo: From Latin abaculus, diminutive of abacus.

parole.significato: A table or tray scattered with sand which was used for calculating or drawing.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English abacus, abagus, agabus (“abacus; art of counting with an abacus”), from Latin abacus, abax (“sideboard or table with a slab at the top; slab at the top of a column; counting board, sand table; board for playing games”) (compare Late Latin abacus (“art of arithmetic”)), from

parole.significato: An informer; a criminal who informs on other criminals to the authorities.
parole.testo: UK C19. From Abaddon, from Middle English, from Late Latin, from Ancient Greek Ἀβαδδών (Abaddṓn, “Abaddon”), from Hebrew אבדון (ābaddōn, “destruction, abyss”), from אבד (ābad, “to be lost, to perish”).

parole.significato: To make another's that which was once yours; to transfer the title of from one to another; to alienate.
parole.testo: From Latin abaliēnātus, perfect passive participle of abaliēnō (“alienate; remove”); from ab- (“by, from; away”) + aliēnō (“alienate, estrange”); from aliēnus (“foreign, alien”), from alius (“other, another”). Equivalent to ab- + alienate.

parole.significato: The act of abalienating; alienation; estrangement; transferring a legal title.
parole.testo: From Latin abalienatio. Equivalent to abalienate + -ion.

parole.significato: A retaining wall; a wall erected to strengthen another wall.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin abamūrus.

parole.significato: Away from the joints; not articular.
parole.testo: From ab- + articular, from Latin ab- (“away from”) + articulus (“joint”).

parole.significato: An inability to walk due to a defect in muscular coordination.
parole.testo: From New Latin a- (“without”) + Ancient Greek βάσις (básis, “step”) + New Latin -ia (“pathological condition”).

parole.significato: Father, an honorific title given to God in the New Testament, especially used in prayers.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin abba, from Ancient Greek ἀββα (abba), from Aramaic אבא/ܐܒܐ (ʼabbāʼ, “father”).

parole.significato: Father; religious superior; in the Syriac, Coptic, and Ethiopic churches, a title given to the bishops, and by the bish…
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin, from Ancient Greek, from Aramaic אבא/ܐܒܐ (ʼaḇā, “father”); see abbot, Abraham for more.

parole.significato: The dignity, estate, term, or jurisdiction of an abbot or abbess.
parole.testo: From Middle English abbathie, from Late Latin abbātia, from abbās, abbātis (“abbot”). Doublet of abbey and Opatija.

parole.significato: A member of the dynasty of caliphs that ruled from Baghdad, from about 750 to 1250, claiming ancestry of Abbas.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Abbasidēs, from Abbas + -idēs (patronymic suffix). By surface analysis, Abbas + -id (dynastic suffix).

parole.significato: The superior or head of an abbey or monastery.
parole.testo: From Middle English abbot, abbod, abbed, from Old English abbat, abbad, abbod, from Latin abbās (“father”), from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”). Doublet of abba, abbé, and bwana.

parole.significato: An abbot who is exempt from diocesan control, and acts with papal authority.
parole.testo: Partly translated from New Latin abbas nullius, short for abbas nullius dioecesis (“abbot of no diocese”).

parole.significato: A person who abbreviates or shortens.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin abbreviātor. Compare French abbréviateur.

parole.significato: An abridgment; a compendium; an abstract.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin abbreviātūra, from Late Latin abbreviō (“shorten, abbreviate”). See also abbreviate.

parole.significato: An inhabitant or native of Abdera, in Thrace.
parole.testo: From Latin Abderita, Abderites, from Ancient Greek Ἀβδηρίτης (Abdērítēs).

parole.significato: To disclaim and expel from the family, as a father his child; to disown; to disinherit.
parole.testo: First attested in 1532; borrowed from Latin abdicātus (“renounced”), perfect passive participle of abdicō (“to renounce, reject, disclaim”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), formed from ab (“away”) + dicō (“proclaim, dedicate, declare”), akin to dīcō (“to say”). Compare Middle English abdicat (“fors

parole.significato: The act of disowning or disinheriting a child.
parole.testo: First attested in 1552. From Latin abdicātiō (“renunciation”), from abdicō. By surface analysis, abdicate + -ion.

parole.significato: A reasoning from the negative
parole.testo: From Latin abdicativus.

parole.significato: Having the quality of hiding
parole.testo: From Latin abditīvus (“removed or separated from”), from abdō (“hide, conceal”).

parole.significato: A concealed location used for storage or to hide items.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin abditorium, from abdō (“to hide”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the abdomen; ventral.
parole.testo: First attested in 1746. From New Latin abdōminālis, from Latin abdōmen. Equivalent to abdomin- + -al. Compare French abdominal.

parole.significato: A group of cirriped crustaceans having abdominal appendages.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: abdomen; abdominal.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Latin abdomen, which see.

parole.significato: Removal of the uterus via an incision made in the abdominal wall rather than via the vagina.
parole.testo: From Latin abdomino- + hysterectomy.

parole.significato: the cremaster muscle.
parole.testo: From Latin abdomen (“abdomen”) + New Latin scrotalis, from Latin scrotum; abdomino- + -scrotal.

parole.significato: Relating to the abdomen and the vagina
parole.testo: * From Latin abdomen (“abdomen”) + New Latin vaginalis, from Latin vagina (“scabbard, sheath”) * abdomino- + -vaginal

parole.significato: To draw; to conduct away; to take away; to withdraw; to draw to a different part; to move a limb out away from the cent…
parole.testo: (1530's) From Latin abdūcō (“lead away”), formed from ab (“from, away from”) + dūcō (“lead”). * See duke, and compare abduct.

parole.significato: Rectus lateralis muscle of the eye; muscle that moves the eye away from the center of the face.
parole.testo: Shortening of "abducens nerve", in turn from Latin nervus abducens, from abducent, abducens

parole.significato: Each of the sixth pair of cranial nerves that are the motor nerves supplying the lateral rectus in the eye.
parole.testo: From New Latin nervus abdūcēns (“nerve leading away”).

parole.significato: Musculus rectus lateralis bulbi.
parole.testo: From Latin abducō (“drawing away”) + Latin oculus (“eye”).

parole.significato: Drawing away from the median axis of the body, as a muscle; see etymology abducting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abducō (“to lead away”).

parole.significato: To take away by force; to carry away (a human being) wrongfully and usually with violence or deception; to kidnap.
parole.testo: From Latin abductus, perfect passive participle of abduco (“to lead away”), from ab (“away”) + duco (“to lead”). * (physiology): Back-formation from abduction.

parole.significato: A leading away; a carrying away.
parole.testo: From Latin abductiō(n) (“a robbing; an abduction”), from abdūcō (“to take or lead away”), from ab (“away”) + dūcō (“to lead”). By surface analysis, abduct + -ion or abduce + -tion. * (physiology): From French, from Latin abductus. * Compare French abduction.

parole.significato: One who abducts; a kidnapper.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abductor, By surface analysis, abduct + -or.

parole.significato: A muscle which serves to draw a part out, or from the median line of the body
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin abductor, from abdūcō + -tor.

parole.significato: A muscle that draws the eye outwards
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Relating to an abductor
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin abductōrius.

parole.significato: Someone who is learning the alphabet.
parole.testo: From Late Latin abecedarius (from the first four letters of the Latin alphabet + -arius). Equivalent to abecedary + -an. Compare abecedary.

parole.significato: A book used to teach the alphabet; alphabet book; primer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abecedārium. Doublet of abecedary.

parole.significato: An acrostic poem in which the lines begin with the letters of the alphabet in sequence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin abecedārius, from Late Latin. Doublet of abecedary.

parole.significato: The alphabet, written out in a teaching book, or carved on a wall; a primer; abecedarium.
parole.testo: From Middle English abscedary, from Medieval Latin abecedārium (“alphabet, ABC primer”), from Late Latin abecedārius (“of the alphabet”), formed from the first four letters of the Latin alphabet + -ārius. Doublet of abecedarium.

parole.significato: Referring to the alphabet; alphabetical; related to or resembling an abecedarius; abecedarian.
parole.testo: From Late Latin abecedārius. Doublet of abecedarius.

parole.significato: The edible and aromatic seed pods (properly, capsules) of the Abelmoschus moschatus.
parole.testo: From New Latin abelmoschus, from Arabic حَبّ الْمِسْك (ḥabb al-misk, “pills of musk”).

parole.significato: Relating to organs outside of the intestine.
parole.testo: From Latin ab- (“away from”) + Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Aberdeen.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Aberdonia (“Aberdeen”) + -an.

parole.significato: A typically malignant fatty tumor located on the trunk.
parole.testo: Named after John Abernethy, English surgeon, + New Latin, from Ancient Greek σάρκωμα (sárkōma, “fleshy growth”), from σαρκόω (sarkóō, “become fleshy”), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”).

parole.significato: To go astray; to err.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aberrō, from ab- (“from, away from”) + errō (“wander, stray”).

parole.significato: State of being aberrant; a wandering from the right way; deviation from truth, rectitude.
parole.testo: From aberr (“to stray”), from Latin aberrō (“to wander from the way”) + -ance.

parole.significato: Differing from the norm.
parole.testo: From Latin aberrāns, present active participle of aberrō (“go astray; err”), from ab (“from”) + errō (“to wander”). See aberr.

parole.significato: To go astray; to diverge; to deviate (from); deviate from.
parole.testo: From Latin aberrātus, perfect passive participle of aberrō (“wander, stray or deviate from”), formed from ab (“from, away from”) + errō (“stray”).

parole.significato: The secretion of milk from an abnormal location, not from the mammary glands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aberratio (“aberration”) + lactis (“milk”).

parole.significato: A testis that is descending to a wrong position after born, or not descending at all (cryptorchidism).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aberratio (“aberration”) + testis (“of a testis”), genitive of testis.

parole.significato: The act of wandering; deviation from truth, moral rectitude; abnormal; divergence from the straight, correct, proper, n…
parole.testo: A learned borrowing from Latin aberrātiō(n) (“relief, diversion”), first attested in 1594, from aberrō (“wander away, go astray”), from ab (“away”) + errō (“wander”). Compare French aberration. By surface analysis, aberrat(e) + -ion.

parole.significato: To eradicate; to pull up by the roots.
parole.testo: From Late Latin aberuncare, from Latin averruncare.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the grammatical case used in some languages to indicate absence.
parole.testo: From Latin abesse (“to be absent”), infinitive of absum, from ab- (“away”) + sum (“be”, verb). Compare English absent.

parole.significato: An abnormal evacuation.
parole.testo: From Latin ab (“from”) + evacuare (“evacuation”).

parole.significato: Inhuman; obsolete form of abominable.
parole.testo: From Latin abhominalis, from ab (“away from”) + hominis (“man”), but in practice from English abominable, which was erroneously folk-etymologized as this word, leading to this spelling and abhominable, which see for more.

parole.significato: Inconsistent with, or far removed from, something; strongly opposed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abhorrēns, abhorrēntis, present active participle of abhorreō (“abhor”). Equivalent to abhor + -ent.

parole.significato: Characterized by avoidance or withdrawal.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin abiens present participle of abeō (“to go away”), from ab (“from, away”) + eō (“to go”).

parole.significato: A volatile oil distilled from the resin or balsam of the nut pine (Pinus sabiniana).
parole.testo: From Abies, from Latin abiet- + -ene, oblique stem of abiēs (“silver fir”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or derived from fir trees
parole.testo: From Abies, from Latin abiet- + -ic, oblique stem of abiēs (“silver fir”).

parole.significato: A yellowish resin acid isolated from rosin and used in varnishes and esters for plasticizers; C₁₉H₂₉COOH.
parole.testo: From Latin abiet, abies (“silver fir”) + English -ic (“having the character of”), + acid.

parole.significato: A substance resembling mannite, found in the needles of the common silver fir of Europe (Abies alba).
parole.testo: From Abies, from Latin abiet- + -ite, oblique stem of abiēs (“silver fir”).

parole.significato: Theft of cattle by driving it away with the intention of feloniously appropriating it.
parole.testo: From Latin abigeatus, from the verb ab agō (“to drive”).

parole.significato: A thief who steals livestock in large quantities.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abigeus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Abila
parole.testo: From Latin Abilēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἀβιληνός (Abilēnós). By surface analysis, Abila + -ene.

parole.significato: Tending to make abject.
parole.testo: From abject + -ive. From Middle English abjecten, from the adjective abject, of Latin origin.

parole.significato: abjection; forlornness
parole.testo: From Latin abiectura.

parole.significato: To confiscate by judicial decision.
parole.testo: * ab- + judge, from Latin abiudicare. Doublet of abjudicate.

parole.significato: To reject by judicial sentence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abiūdicātus, perfect passive participle of abiūdicō (“deprive or take away by judicial sentence”), from ab (“from, away from”) + iūdicō (“pass judgement; determine, conclude”). Doublet of abjudge. See judge.

parole.significato: Rejection or confiscation by judicial sentence.
parole.testo: From abjudicate + -ion or from Latin abiūdicātiō. First attested in 1623.

parole.significato: To unyoke; set free; uncouple.
parole.testo: From Latin abiugātus, perfect passive participle of abiugō (“remove, separate from”); from ab- (“away from”) + iugō (“bind, connect”).

parole.significato: Exceptional, isolated, disconnected, separate,
parole.testo: From Latin abiūnctus, past participle of abiungō (“remove, separate”); from ab (“of, from, by”) + iungō (“join, connect, attach”).

parole.significato: A solemn recantation or renunciation on oath; as, an abjuration of heresy.
parole.testo: First attested around 1439. From Middle English abjuracioun, from Latin abiūrātiō (“forswearing, abjuration”), from ab (“from, away from”) + iūrō (“swear or take an oath”), from iūs (“law, right, duty”). Compare French abjuration.

parole.significato: To wean.
parole.testo: From Latin ablactātus, perfect passive participle of ablactō (“wean”), from ab + lactō (“suckle”), from lac (“milk”).

parole.significato: The weaning of a child from the breast, or of young animals from their dam.
parole.testo: From Middle English ablactacioun from Late Latin ablactatio, ablactō (“to wean”) from ab (“without”) + lacto (“suckle”), from lac (“milk”); equivalent to ab- + lactation.

parole.significato: To lay bare, as the roots of a tree, by loosening or removing soil.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ablaqueātus (“loosened, dug up”), past participle of ablaqueō (“to disentangle”), formed from ab- + laqueō (“noose”).

parole.significato: The act or process of laying bare the roots of trees to expose them to the air and water.
parole.testo: From Latin ablaqueātiō (“the process or act of digging or loosening the soil around the roots of a tree”), from ablaqueō (“disentangle”), from ab (“from, away from”) + laqueō (“entangle, ensnare”).

parole.significato: To remove or decrease something by cutting, erosion, melting, evaporation, or vaporization.
parole.testo: From Middle English ablat (“taken away”), from Latin ablātus, past participle of auferō (“to remove”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). First attested in the 1500s, it became obsolete by the early 1600s. Returned into use as a back-formation from ablation.

parole.significato: Synonym of ablation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ablātiō (“carrying away”). Doublet of ablation.

parole.significato: Synonym of placental abruption.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ablatio (“carrying away”) + placentae (“flat cake”).

parole.significato: Detachment of the retina.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ablatio (“carrying away”) + Middle English rethina, from Medieval Latin retina, from Latin rete (“net”).

parole.significato: A carrying or taking away; removal.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English ablacioun (“removal”), from Late Latin ablātiō (“a taking away”), from auferō (“to take away, carry off, withdraw, remove”) + -tiō (“-tion”, nominal suffix). Doublet of ablatio. Compare French ablation. By surface analysis, ablat(e) + -ion.

parole.significato: A construction in Latin and other sister languages in which an independent phrase with a noun in the ablative case has…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin ablativus absolutus.

parole.significato: Expulsion; banishment.
parole.testo: From Latin ablēgātio (“a sending away, banishment”).

parole.significato: To tie up, especially a body part.
parole.testo: From Latin ab- + ligātus, perfect passive participle of ligāre (“to tie”).

parole.significato: Prodigal expenditure on food.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₂epó Learned borrowing from Late Latin abligurrītiō, abligurītiō (“act of devouring; act of spending in feasting”), from abligurriō, abliguriō (“to lick away; to spend or waste indulgently, squander”) + -tiō (suffix forming abstract nouns from verbs); from ab- (“away; away from; from”) +

parole.significato: To be unlike; to differ.
parole.testo: From Latin ablūdō (“differ from”), from ab (“from”) + lūdō (“play; trick”).

parole.significato: Washing away; carrying off impurities; detergent.
parole.testo: From Latin abluēns, present active participle of abluō (“to wash off or away; cleanse, purify”), from ab (“from, away from”) + lavō (“to wash, cleanse”). See lave.

parole.significato: A person who fears bathing.
parole.testo: From Latin ablutio (“a washing”) + Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: A pathological fear of washing or bathing.
parole.testo: From Latin ablutio (“a washing”) + Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”) (equivalent to -phobia).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to or suffering from ablutophobia.
parole.testo: From Latin ablutio (“a washing”) + Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: That which is washed off.

parole.significato: To deny (oneself something); to renounce or give up (a right, a power, a claim, a privilege, a convenience).

parole.significato: A denial; a renunciation; denial of desire or self-interest.
parole.testo: First attested before 1398. From Middle English abnegacioun, borrowed from Latin abnegātiō, from abnegō (“refuse, deny”), from ab (“off”) + negō (“deny; refuse, say no”). Compare French abnégation.

parole.significato: Denying; renouncing; negative
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abnegativus.

parole.significato: One who abnegates, denies, or rejects.

parole.significato: Abnormal; irregular; misshapen.

parole.significato: Abominable; detested.

parole.significato: Bdelygmia.

parole.significato: One who abominates.

parole.significato: Abominable, detestable, execrable.
parole.testo: From Latin abominosus.

parole.significato: Away from the oral opening or mouth (compare with ventral)
parole.testo: From ab- (“away from”) + orad (“toward the mouth”), from Latin ōris (“mouth”).

parole.significato: The original people of a location; originally used of ancient Greek and Roman peoples.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aborīginēs.

parole.significato: Producing miscarriage.

parole.significato: The expulsion from the womb of a foetus or embryo before it is fully developed, with loss of the foetus.
parole.testo: From Latin abortiōnem (“miscarriage, abortion”), from aborior (“to miscarry”). Equivalent to abort + -ion. Displaced native Old English ǣwyrp (literally “throwing out, rejection”).

parole.significato: An abortion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin abortus (“miscarriage”). Doublet of abort.

parole.significato: A use of the mystical term ‘abracadabra’, supposed to work as part of a healing charm or a magical spell; any spell or…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin abracadabra.

parole.significato: To rub or wear off; erode.

parole.significato: Rubbed smooth or blank.

parole.significato: Either of the ratlike rodents that form the genus Abrocoma; rat chinchilla.

parole.significato: capable of being abrogated.

parole.significato: A bushy wormwood from Europe, sometimes used in the brewing of beer, southernwood, Artemisia abrotanum.

parole.significato: A colorless crystalline alkaloid obtained from abrotanum, C₂₁H₂₂N₂O.

parole.significato: Broken away (from restraint).

parole.significato: An abrupt pause or stop; an abruption.

parole.significato: A premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall.

parole.significato: A separating; a removal; a going away.

parole.significato: A logical process of elimination by eliminating successively all of the inapplicable cases.

parole.significato: Cavity; fossa.

parole.significato: Denoting the effect that irradiation of a tissue has on remote nonirradiated tissue.

parole.significato: Pertaining to absence.

parole.significato: The act of absenting oneself.

parole.significato: A momentary lapse of consciousness; a minor epileptic seizure.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to absence or to that which is absent.

parole.significato: To absterge; to cleanse; to purge away.
parole.testo: From Middle English absterse, from Latin abstersus, perfect passive participle of abstergeō (“wipe off, wipe away”); formed from abs- + tergeō (“wipe”).

parole.significato: Having an abstracting nature or tendency; tending to separate; tending to be withdrawn.

parole.significato: Something which is abstract or exists abstractly.

parole.significato: Of abstruse quality.

parole.significato: To consume gradually; to waste away.

parole.significato: Caution used to justify preemptive measures that are likely not strictly necessary.

parole.significato: Hell; the bottomless pit; primeval chaos; a confined subterranean ocean.

parole.significato: Belonging to, or resembling, an abyss; unfathomable.

parole.significato: Synonym of Abyssinian.
