parole.significato: Designating a line of verse having the required number of syllables in the last foot
parole.testo: From Late Latin acatalēcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκατάληκτος (akatálēktos, “leaving off”).

parole.significato: Incapable of being comprehended; incomprehensible; inconceivable.
parole.testo: From Latin acatalēpticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκατάληπτος (akatálēptos, “incomprehensible”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + καταλαμβάνω (katalambánō, “to seize”), from κατά (katá, “against”) + λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take”).

parole.significato: A member of a group of 4th century penitants who wore coarse clothing and used water for the Eucharist instead of wine.…
parole.testo: From a misreading of Saccaophori; from Latin saccus (“sack”) and Ancient Greek σᾰ́κκος (sắkkos, “sack, bag”) + φέρω (phérō, “bearer, carrier”).

parole.significato: To agree or assent [with to ‘a proposal, a request’]; to give way.
parole.testo: First attested in the early 15th century. From Middle English acceden, from Latin accēdō (“approach, accede”), formed from ad (“to, toward, at”) + cēdō (“move, yield”) (English cede). Compare French accéder. Unrelated to ascend, aside from the common ad prefix.

parole.significato: Acedia.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Latin acēdia. Doublet of accidie.

parole.significato: A nerve that speeds up the heartbeat by emitting noradrenaline.
parole.testo: From Latin accelerāns (“quickening”).

parole.significato: To cause to move faster; to quicken the motion of; to add to the speed of.
parole.testo: First attested in the 1520s. Either from Latin accelerātus, perfect passive participle of accelerō (“to accelerate, hasten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), formed from ad + celerō (“to hasten”), which is from celer (“quick”) (see celerity), or back-formation fr

parole.significato: The act of accelerating, or the state of being accelerated; increase of motion or action; as opposed to retardation or…
parole.testo: First attested in 1531. From French accélération or more likely directly from Latin accelerātiō (“a hastening, acceleration”). Equivalent to accelerate + -ion.

parole.significato: acceleration
parole.testo: From Latin accelerō.

parole.significato: To set on fire; to kindle.
parole.testo: From Middle English accenden, from Latin accendere (“to kindle”), formed from ad- + candere (“to shine”).

parole.significato: kindled, incited
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin accēnsus.

parole.significato: The act of kindling or the state of being kindled; ignition.
parole.testo: From Latin accensiōnem, from accendere.

parole.significato: One of the functionaries who light and trim the tapers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin accēnsor, from accendō (“light, kindle”) + -tor (agent noun suffix). Compare accend.

parole.significato: Any bird of the Eurasian genus Prunella, such as the dunnock.
parole.testo: From Latin accentor (“one who sings with another”), from ad + cantor (“singer”), from canō (“sing”). Superficially accent + -or.

parole.significato: To pronounce with an accent or vocal stress.
parole.testo: First attested in 1731; borrowed from Medieval Latin accentuātus, perfect passive participle of accentuō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin accentus. accent + -u- + -ate.

parole.significato: A more distinct or prominent form.
parole.testo: From Late Latin accentuatio. Compare French accentuation. Equivalent to accentuate + -ion.

parole.significato: The quality of being acceptable; acceptableness.
parole.testo: From Latin acceptābilitās. By surface analysis, accept + -ability.

parole.significato: Gratuitous discharge; a release from debt or obligation without payment; free remission.
parole.testo: From Latin acceptilatio (“entry of a debt collected, acquittance”), from past participle of accipere (compare accept) + latio (“a carrying”), from latus, past participle of ferre (“to carry”).

parole.significato: One who accepts.
parole.testo: From Middle English acceptour, from Latin acceptor, with the meanings from accept.

parole.significato: Someone who accedes to some act, now especially a crime; one who contributes as an assistant or instigator to the commi…
parole.testo: From Middle English accessarie, axcessary, excercary, from Medieval Latin accessārius.

parole.significato: Accompanying as a subordinate; additional; accessory; especially, uniting in, or contributing to, a crime, but not as c…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin accessārius.

parole.significato: The quality of being accessible, or of admitting approach; receptiveness.
parole.testo: From accessible + -ity, after Late Latin accessibilitas, from Latin accessibilis.

parole.significato: A coming to; the act of acceding and becoming joined.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin accessiō(n), from accēdō (English accede). Cognate to French accession. First attested in 1646.

parole.significato: An honorable mention in an academic contest.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin accessit (“he came near”), from accēdō (“approach”) + -it.

parole.significato: Having a secondary, supplementary or subordinate function by accompanying as a subordinate; aiding in a secondary way;…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin accessōrius, from Latin accessor (“helper, subordinate”), from accessus. Compare access, from same root.

parole.significato: Something that belongs to part of another main thing; something additional and subordinate, an attachment.
parole.testo: From Middle English accessorie, from Medieval Latin accessōrius, from Latin accessor (“helper, subordinate”), from accessus. Compare access, from same root.

parole.significato: In electing a pope, a method by which cardinals could change their most recent vote to accede to another candidate in a…
parole.testo: From Latin accessus. Doublet of access.

parole.significato: The inflection of words.
parole.testo: * First attested in the late 14th century. * (grammar): First attested in the mid 15th century. * From Middle English accidence, accidens, from Latin accidentia (“accidental matters”), from accidēns, present participle of accidere (“to happen”)

parole.significato: Synonym of accident (“a property, fact, or relation that is the result of chance or is nonessential or nonsubstantive”).
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: To prepare oneself for action.
parole.testo: From Latin accingō (“to gird”).

parole.significato: Someone who, or something which, accepts (willingly receives).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin accipiēns (“receiving”, stem: accipient-), the present active participle of accipiō (“to receive”), whence accept.

parole.significato: Any hawk of the genus Accipiter.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin accipiter (“hawk”).

parole.significato: The feigning of disinterest in something while actually desiring it.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin accismus, from Ancient Greek ακκισμός (akkismós, “prudery”).

parole.significato: To summon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin accitō (“summon”), from Classical Latin acciō (“call forth”), formed from ad + cieō (“summon, call”). The sense “excite, induce” is likely from or reinforced by conflation with excite.

parole.significato: To shout; to call out.
parole.testo: * First attested in the early 14th century. * (to applaud): First attested in the 1630s. * Borrowed from Latin acclāmō (“raise a cry at; applaud”), formed from ad- + clāmō (“cry out, shout”).

parole.significato: A shout of approbation, favor, or assent; eager expression of approval; loud applause.
parole.testo: * First attested in 1541. * Borrowed from Latin acclāmātiō, acclāmātiōnis (“calling, exclamation, shout of approval”), from acclamo (“shout approval or disapproval of, shout out at”), from ad (“toward”) + clamo (“cry out”) * Compare French acclamation.

parole.significato: Synonym of acclivous (“sloping upwards”).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin acclīvis.

parole.significato: A slope or inclination of the earth, as the side of a hill, considered as ascending, in opposition to declivity, or des…
parole.testo: First attested in 1614. From Latin acclīvitās, from acclīvis (“ascending”), from ad + clīvus (“slope”).

parole.significato: sloping upward; rising like a hillside.
parole.testo: Latin acclivis and acclivus.

parole.significato: A combining together.
parole.testo: From Latin; the first part is equivalent to ad; the second part to combination.

parole.significato: To render fit, suitable, or correspondent; to adapt.
parole.testo: First use appears c. the 1530s, borrowed from Latin accommodātus, perfect passive participle of accommodō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + commodō (“to provide, lend; to make fit, accommodate”), from con- + modus (“measure, proporti

parole.significato: Tending to accomplish.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin accompletivus.

parole.significato: Related to growth or increase by successive additions, particularly in size or volume, often through the gradual deposi…
parole.testo: From Latin accrēmentum (to increase or grow) + -al

parole.significato: To accrue.
parole.testo: From Latin accrescere. Doublet of accrease. See accrue.

parole.significato: Continuous growth; an accretion.
parole.testo: From Late Latin accrescentia. Compare Italian accrescente.

parole.significato: Growing; increasing.
parole.testo: From Latin accrescens, accrescentis, present participle of accrescere, from ad + crescere (“to grow”).

parole.significato: Increase by natural growth, especially the gradual increase of organic bodies by the internal addition of matter; organ…
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₂éd Learned borrowing from Latin accrētiō (“increase, increment”) + English -ion (suffix forming nouns denoting actions or processes, or their results). Accrētiō is derived from accrēscō (“to grow, increase”) + -tiō (suffix forming nouns denoting actions or processes, or their results);

parole.significato: The act or posture of reclining on a couch, as practiced by the ancients at meals.
parole.testo: From Latin accubatiō, accubitiō, from accubō (“to recline”), from ad- + cubō (“to lie down”).

parole.significato: To recline, as at table.
parole.testo: From Latin accumbō (“recline (at a table)”), from ad- + *cumbō (“lie down”).

parole.significato: Leaning or reclining, as the ancients did at their meals.
parole.testo: From Latin accumbō (“recline”), from ad- (“to”) + *cumbō (“recline”).

parole.significato: To heap up in a mass; to pile up; to collect or bring together (either literally or figuratively), often gradually and…
parole.testo: First attested c. 1487; from Middle English accumylaten, borrowed from Latin accumulātus, perfect passive participle of accumulō (“to amass, pile up”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), formed from ad (“to, towards, at”) + cumulō (“to heap”), from cumulus (“a heap”

parole.significato: A forceful summarisation of previously made points.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin accumulātiō (“the act of heaping up”). Doublet of accumulation.

parole.significato: One who, or that which, accumulates.
parole.testo: From Latin accumulātor, agent noun of accumulō (“pile up”), accumulate + -or.

parole.significato: Telling the truth or giving a true result; exact; not defective or faulty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin accūrātus, perfect passive participle of accūrō (“to take care of”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + cūrō (“care for”). First attested in 1610. Compare English cure.

parole.significato: Liable to be accused or censured; chargeable with a crime or breach; blamable
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin accūsābilis (“accusable”), corresponding to accuse + -able; compare French accusable.

parole.significato: An accuser.
parole.testo: From Latin accusans, present participle of accusare. Compare French accusant.

parole.significato: Categoria.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin. Doublet of accusation.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the accusative case.
parole.testo: Suffixation of the Latin accūsātīvum with the English -al.

parole.significato: an independent phrase in a sentence conveying additional circumstances in the accusative case; present:
parole.testo: Calque of Latin accūsātīvus absolūtus.

parole.significato: A syntactic construction, very common in Classical Latin, in which the subject of a subordinate clause is declined for…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin accūsātīvus cum īnfīnītīvō (literally “accusative [case] with infinitive [mood]”).

parole.significato: A female accusator.
parole.testo: From Latin accūsātrīx (“accuser (female)”). By surface analysis, accusator + -trix.

parole.significato: Spiritual or mental sloth and the feeling it provokes; apathy or indifference; a lack of care or interest and the resul…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin acēdia, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀκηδίᾱ (akēdíā), from ἀκηδής (akēdḗs, “careless”) + -ίᾱ (-íā). Doublet of accidie.

parole.significato: A group of individuals who didn't adhear to the condemnation of Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus (431 CE).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin acephalus, from Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos, “headless”), apparently referring to the various movements’ refusals to accept the decisions of church councils.

parole.significato: A radical Monophysite in the era after the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin acephalus + -ite, from Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos, “headless”), apparently referring to the movement’s refusal to accept the decisions of church councils.

parole.significato: a follower of an Acephali movement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin acephalus + -ite, from Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos, “headless”)

parole.significato: A fetus affected by acephaly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin acephalus.

parole.significato: An extinct rhinoceros of the genus †Aceratherium.
parole.testo: From New Latin †Aceratherium.

parole.significato: Sour, bitter, and harsh to the taste, such as unripe fruit.
parole.testo: From Latin acerbus, from Latin ācer (“sharp”): compare French acerbe. See acrid.

parole.significato: Embittered; having a sour disposition or nature.
parole.testo: From Latin acerbātus, perfect passive participle of acerbō (“make bitter”), from acerbus (“bitter”).

parole.significato: Tasting sour or bitter.
parole.testo: Attested since the 17th century, from Latin acerbus (“sour, bitter”).

parole.significato: Sourness and harshness; acerbity.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin acerbitudo, from acerbus (“bitter, severe”)

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or obtained from, the maple.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin acer (“maple”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Having the nature of chaff; chaffy.
parole.testo: From Latin acerōsus (“chaffy”), aceris + -ōsus, from root of acus (“chaff”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Rome, a small box for holding incense.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin acerra.

parole.significato: A person who does not cut their hair.
parole.testo: From Latin acersecomes.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a heap.
parole.testo: From Latin acervalis, from acervus (“heap”).

parole.significato: Heaped, or growing in heaps, or closely compacted clusters.
parole.testo: From Latin acervātus, perfect passive participle of acervō (“heap or pile up”), from acervus (“heap”).

parole.significato: Departing from the normal syntax of a series to increase its effect.
parole.testo: From Latin acervātiō (“heaping up”), from acervō (“heap up”) + -ātiō. Doublet of acervation.

parole.significato: A heaping up; accumulation
parole.testo: From Latin acervatio. Doublet of acervatio.

parole.significato: A small cluster, as of fungi appearing on bark or leaves.
parole.testo: From Latin acervulus.

parole.significato: Turning sour; readily becoming tart or acid; slightly sour.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin acēscēns, acēscentis, present participle of acēscēre (“to turn sour”), inchoative of acēre (“to be sour”): compare French acescent.

parole.significato: An ancient Roman measure, equivalent to about one eighth of a pint.
parole.testo: An Anglicisation of the Latin acetabulum.

parole.significato: Furnished with fleshy cups for adhering to bodies, as cuttlefish, etc.
parole.testo: Latin acetabuliferosa, from acetabulum (“little cup”) + -ferous

parole.significato: Shaped like a saucer or shallow cup.
parole.testo: From New Latin acetabuliformis, from acetabulum (“saucer”) + -form.

parole.significato: cup-shaped; acetabular.
parole.testo: From New Latin acetabulosus; by surface analysis, acetabulo- + -ous.

parole.significato: The bony cup of the hip bone which receives the head of the femur.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin acētābulum (“vinegar saucer, 1/48 congius”), from acētum (“vinegar”) + -bulum (“-bule: a vessel for”).

parole.significato: Used in salads or as salad
parole.testo: From Latin acētāria (“salad”, plural noun) + -ous, the former from acētum (“vinegar”), from aceō (“to be sour”).

parole.significato: A device wherein bacteria process a liquid containing alcohol with the help of oxygen into carboxylic acid.
parole.testo: From a theoretical Latin *acētātor from a acētāre (“to turn into acētum (“vinegar”)”).

parole.significato: To convert into acid or vinegar.
parole.testo: From Latin acetum (“vinegar”) + -fy or back-formation from acetification.

parole.significato: An instrument for estimating the amount of acetic acid in vinegar
parole.testo: From Latin acetum (“vinegar”) + -meter.

parole.significato: Containing a methyl group bonded to a carbonyl group (CH₃CO-); e.g., acetophenone
parole.testo: From Latin acētum (“vinegar”), because acetic acid is a constituent of vinegar.

parole.significato: The quality of being acetous; sourness.
parole.testo: acetous + -ity as -osity; from Late Latin acetositas.

parole.significato: Having a sour taste; sour; acid.
parole.testo: From Latin acētum (“vinegar”) + -ous, the former from aceō (“to be sour”).

parole.significato: In botanical medicine, a vinegar extract of herbs.
parole.testo: Blend of Latin acētum (“vinegar”) and extract.

parole.significato: Vinegar, sometimes medicated.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin acētum.

parole.significato: The univalent radical CH₃CO- derived from acetic acid.
parole.testo: aceto- + -yl. From Latin acētum (“vinegar”) + Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “substance”).

parole.significato: An inhabitant or resident of Achaea, especially a member of an ancient Hellenic tribe that inhabited the region of Acha…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin achaeus, from Ancient Greek Ἀχαιός (Akhaiós), + -an.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the dynasty which ruled the Persian empire c. 550–330 BCE (the Achaemenid Empire), founded by Achaeme…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Achaemenidēs, from Ancient Greek Ἀχαιμενίδης (Akhaimenídēs), from Ancient Greek Ἀχαιμένης (Akhaiménēs) + Ancient Greek -ίδης (-ídēs, patronymic suffix). By surface analysis, Achaemenes + -id.

parole.significato: Any dry indehiscent fruit.
parole.testo: From Latin achenium, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χαίνω (khaínō, “to gape”), + Ancient Greek καρπός (karpós, “fruit”).

parole.significato: The strong tendon formed of the united tendons of the large muscles in the calf of the leg, and inserted into the bone…
parole.testo: Calque of New Latin tendo Achillis, in reference to the mythological account of Achilles being held by the heel when dipped in the River Styx. Its coinage has been attributed to Dutch anatomist Philip Verheyden in 1693, but the term is first attested in 1684.

parole.significato: Deficiency or absence of bile.
parole.testo: From New Latin acholia, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χολή (kholḗ, “bile”).

parole.significato: dandruff (or similar condition)
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Synonym of acicula.
parole.testo: Latin acicula (“pin for a head-dress”)

parole.significato: One of the needlelike or bristlelike spines or prickles of some animals and plants; also, a needlelike crystal.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin acicula (“pin for a head-dress”)

parole.significato: Needle-shaped; slender like a needle or bristle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aciculāris.

parole.significato: Needle-shaped; acicular.
parole.testo: From Latin acicula (“needle”) + -iform.

parole.significato: A sulfide of bismuth, lead, and copper.
parole.testo: From Latin acicula, diminutive of acus (“needle”).

parole.significato: A needlelike spine or bristle, specially the seta of an annelid
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?]. Compare English acicula.

parole.significato: Containing or yielding an acid.
parole.testo: From Latin acidus (“sour, acid”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: To make something (more) acidic or sour; to convert into an acid.
parole.testo: From acid + -ify, from Latin acidus (“sour, acid”); compare French acidifier.

parole.significato: An instrument for ascertaining the strength of acids.
parole.testo: From acid + -i- + -meter, from Latin acidus (“sour, acid”).

parole.significato: The measurement of the strength of acids, especially by a chemical process based on the law of chemical combinations, o…
parole.testo: From acid + -metry, from Latin acidus (“sour, acid”).

parole.significato: Lactobacillus acidophilus, one of the bacteria commonly used in fermenting yogurt
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin acidophilus (“acid-loving”).

parole.significato: Both sour and sweet.
parole.testo: From Latin acidus (“sour”) + dulcis (“sweet”).

parole.significato: Slightly sour; subacid; sourish.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin acidulus (“sourish, acidulous”), diminutive of acidus (“sour, acid”). See acid. By surface analysis, acid + -ule + -ous.

parole.significato: (of bacteria) growing in acidic medium, but preferring an alkaline medium
parole.testo: From Latin acidum (“acid”) + dūrō (“endure”).

parole.significato: The full attention of one's sight, hearing or other senses, as directed towards a particular object.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aciēs (“edge, sharpness”).

parole.significato: Shaped like a needle.
parole.testo: From Latin acus (“needle”) + -form.

parole.significato: Containing seeds or stones of grapes, or grains like them.
parole.testo: Latin acinus (“a grape, grapestone”).

parole.significato: A short sword or saber.
parole.testo: From Latin acīnacēs, from Ancient Greek ἀκινάκης (akinákēs, “the short sabre of the Persians, Medes, and Scythians; a scimitar”).

parole.significato: Shaped like a scimitar.
parole.testo: From New Latin acīnacifōrmis, from acinaces (“short sword”) + -form.

parole.significato: Having the form of a cluster of grapes; clustered like grapes.
parole.testo: Latin acinus (“grape, grapestone”) + -form. Compare French aciniforme.

parole.significato: Consisting of acini, or minute granular concretions.
parole.testo: Latin acinosus, from acinus (“grapestone”).

parole.significato: One of the small grains or drupelets which make up some kinds of fruit, as the blackberry, raspberry, etc.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin acinus (“grape, grape-stone”); the histopathologic sense comes figuratively from the fancied resemblance (on microscopy) of acinic cells (acinar cells) to bunches of drupelets, berries, or grapes.

parole.significato: Meaningless activity engaged in just for show; deceptive nonsense.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, possibly coined by Damon Runyon.

parole.significato: A skin condition, usually of the face, that is common in adolescents. It is characterised by red pimples, and is caused…
parole.testo: From New Latin acnē, probably a corruption of Ancient Greek ἀκμή (akmḗ, “point, top”).

parole.significato: An uncommon and unusually severe form of acne characterized by burrowing and interconnecting abscesses and irregular sc…
parole.testo: From acne + Latin conglobata.

parole.significato: Synonym of rosacea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin acnē rosācea (literally “rose-colored acne”), from its resemblance to acne, which it is no longer considered as such.

parole.significato: An isolated point not upon a curve, but whose coordinates satisfy the equation of the curve so that it is considered as…
parole.testo: From Latin acus + nodus.

parole.significato: The poisonous herb aconite; also, an extract from it.
parole.testo: From Latin aconītum (“wolfsbane, monkshood”). See aconite.

parole.significato: Threadlike defensive organs, composed largely of nettling cells (cnidae), thrown out of the mouth or special pores of c…
parole.testo: From the plural of New Latin acontium, from Ancient Greek ἀκόντιον (akóntion, “little dart”).

parole.significato: Referring to a sound that has no visually identifiable cause.
parole.testo: From Latin acousmaticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκουσματικός (akousmatikós), from ἀκούω (akoúō, “to hear”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the sense of hearing, the organs of hearing, or the science of sounds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin acousticus, acūsticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκουστῐκός (akoustĭkós, “of or for hearing”), from ἀκούω (akoúō, “to hear”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Willing to acquiesce, accept or agree to something without objection, protest or resistance.
parole.testo: From Latin acquiescens (present participle of acquiēscō).

parole.significato: To quiet.
parole.testo: From Late Latin acquietare, from Latin ad + quies (“rest”). Equivalent to a- + quiet. Doublet of acquit. See also quiet and aquiesce.

parole.significato: acquired
parole.testo: From Latin acquisītus (“gained, acquired”), from Latin acquirere.

parole.significato: Acquired.
parole.testo: From an alteration of Latin acquisītus (“acquired, gained”), or possibly from acquisite + -ive.

parole.significato: Partial or total absence of the skull.
parole.testo: From New Latin acrania, from a- + crānium + -ia.

parole.significato: Lack of self-control; excess, intemperance; also, irregular or unruly behaviour.

parole.significato: Synonym of acrasia (“lack of self-control; intemperance, excess; also, irregular or unruly behaviour”); (countable) an…

parole.significato: Sharp and harsh, or bitter and not to the taste.

parole.significato: An oral discourse.
parole.testo: From Latin acroāsis, from Ancient Greek ἀκρόᾱσις (akróāsis, “a hearing or lecture”), from ἀκροάομαι (akroáomai, “listen”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Ceraunian Mountains.

parole.significato: A lack or defect of the pulse.

parole.significato: Any sea slug of the family Actaeonidae.

parole.significato: The use of voice and gestures in oratory; the style of delivery of a speech.

parole.significato: A female plaintiff.

parole.significato: Capable of being acted or actuated upon.

parole.significato: Registrar, clerk.

parole.significato: To activate, or to put into motion; to animate.

parole.significato: Very active.

parole.significato: impulsiveness

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or resembling the Biblical character Adam.

parole.significato: Additive; Increasing.

parole.significato: Pertaining to addition; that can be, or has been, added.

parole.significato: To yoke an animal to something
parole.testo: From Latin adjugatus.

parole.significato: Help; support; that which or one who helps or supports.
parole.testo: Latin adiūmentum, for adiuvāmentum, inflected form of adiuvō (“to help”), from ad- (“toward, to”) + iuvō (“to help”).

parole.significato: Connected in a subordinate function.
parole.testo: From Latin adiunctus, perfect passive participle of adiungō (“join to”), from ad + iungō (“join”). Doublet of adjoint.

parole.significato: The act of joining; the thing joined or added.
parole.testo: From Latin adjunctio, from adjungere: compare French adjonction, and see adjunct.

parole.significato: A grave warning.
parole.testo: From Latin adiuratio.

parole.significato: An adjutant; a helper or assistant.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin adiūtor (“helper, assistant”), from adiuvō (“help, assist”).

parole.significato: Serving to help or assist; helpful
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin adjutorius.

parole.significato: A female adjutor.
parole.testo: From Latin adiūtrīx, feminine of adiūtor. By surface analysis, adjutor + -trix.

parole.significato: Providing assistance or help; assistive, facilitative, helpful.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin adiuvant-, adjuvant- + English -ant (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘exhibiting a condition or process’; and forming agent nouns). parole.significato: To help; to further.
parole.testo: From Latin adiuvatum, variant of adiutus, perfect passive participle of adiuvo.

parole.significato: To choose or elect, especially to promote someone to higher office before they have served in a lower capacity.
parole.testo: From adlēct-, the perfect passive participial stem of the Latin adlegō, an alternative spelling of allegō (“to select, choose, recruit, or elect; to admit (to or into something)”).

parole.significato: A right formerly claimed by the states of the German Empire of joining their own ministers with those of the emperor in…
parole.testo: From Latin adlegatio, allegatio (“a sending away”), from adlegare, allegare (“to send away with a commission”), from ad (“in addition”) + legare (“to send as ambassador”). Compare allegation.

parole.significato: measurement, especially of area
parole.testo: From Latin admensuratio, from ad + mensurare (“to measure”). See mensuration.

parole.significato: Something that aids or supports.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adminiculum (“support pole”).

parole.significato: Supplying help; auxiliary; corroborative; explanatory.
parole.testo: From Latin adminiculō (“to prop up, support”) + -ar.

parole.significato: to administer
parole.testo: * archaic: Latin administrātus, past participle of administrō. * modern: Back-formation from administration (from Latin administrātiō, also from administrō) (The exact etymology is disputed, see note below.)

parole.significato: One who administers affairs; one who directs, manages, executes, or dispenses, whether in civil, judicial, political, o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin administrātor (literally “he that is near to attend”). Doublet of administrador.

parole.significato: A female administrator.
parole.testo: From New Latin administrātrīx. By surface analysis, administrator + -trix.

parole.significato: That quality which produces admiration or wonder
parole.testo: From Latin admīrābilitās. By surface analysis, admire + -ability.

parole.significato: The act or practice of admitting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin admissio, admissionis; compare French admission. See admit.

parole.significato: The certificate of admission formerly given in some American colleges, such as Harvard.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin admittātur (“let him be admitted”), the third-person singular present passive subjunctive form of admittō (“to let in; to admit”).

parole.significato: A mingling of different things; a mixture.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin admixtio.

parole.significato: An instance of admixing, a mixing in of something.
parole.testo: From Latin admixtūra, from admixtus, past participle of admisceō (“to mix in”), from misceō (“to mix”). Analyzable as ad- + mixture.

parole.significato: An admonisher; a monitor.
parole.testo: From Latin admonitor.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an admonition; serving to reprove, warn or advise.
parole.testo: From Latin admonitōrium (“admonition, reminder”).

parole.significato: A female admonitor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin admonitrīx. By surface analysis, admonitor + -trix.

parole.significato: In feudal law, the reducing of lands or tenements to mortmain.
parole.testo: From Latin admortizatio. Compare amortization.

parole.significato: To move toward.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin admoveō (“to move, bring, conduct, lead, or carry someone or something to or toward”).

parole.significato: Growing to or on something else.
parole.testo: From Latin adnascens, present participle of adnasci (“to be born, grow”).

parole.significato: Linked or fused to a structure of a type different from itself; for example, attachment of a stamen to a petal is adnat…
parole.testo: From Latin adnatus, past participle of variant form of agnascor (“born or growing at or upon”).

parole.significato: The appendages of an organ, such as the Fallopian tubes of the uterus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adnexa.

parole.significato: Narrowly attached to a stem or stipe.
parole.testo: From Latin adnexus (“annexed, attached”).

parole.significato: adoptive
parole.testo: From Latin adoptātus, perfect passive participle of adoptō (“adopt”).

parole.significato: Synonym of adore.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin adōrāt-, past participial stem of adōrō.

parole.significato: A room in a temple for the adoration of idols.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin adōrātōrium.

parole.significato: To make more beautiful and attractive; to decorate.
parole.testo: From Middle English adornen, adournen, from Latin adōrnāre; from ad- + ōrnō (“furnish, embellish”). See adore, ornate. Replaced earlier Middle English aournen (“to adorn”) borrowed from Old French aorner, from the same Latin source.

parole.significato: impregnation by external contact, without intromission
parole.testo: From Latin adosculari, adosculatum (“to kiss”). See osculate.

parole.significato: A work of adoxography.
parole.testo: From New Latin adoxus (“absurd, paradoxical”) from Ancient Greek ἄδοξος (ádoxos, “obscure, ignoble”) (from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + δόξα (dóxa, “expectation”)) + -graph.

parole.significato: Fine writing on a minor or trivial subject.
parole.testo: From New Latin adoxus (“absurd, paradoxical”) (from Ancient Greek ἄδοξος (ádoxos, “obscure, ignoble”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + δόξα (dóxa, “expectation”)) + -γραφίᾱ (-graphíā, “writing”).

parole.significato: An element that combines syntactically with a phrase and indicates how that phrase should be interpreted in the surroun…
parole.testo: From ad- + position, from Latin adpositio, from adpositum, past participle of adponere, an alternative form of apponere (“to put near”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the adrenal glands (suprarenal glands), their secretions, or the function derived therefrom.
parole.testo: From ad- (“near”) + renal (“pertaining to the kidneys”), from Latin rēn (“kidney”).

parole.significato: Relating to the adrenal gland.
parole.testo: From ad- (“near”) + ren(al) (“pertaining to the kidneys”) + -o-, from Latin rēn (“kidney”). By surface analysis, adren- + -o-.

parole.significato: Relating to the Adriatic Sea.
parole.testo: From Latin Hadrianus (“from the Roman harbor Hadria”) a place name ultimately from Etruscan 𐌇𐌀𐌕𐌓𐌉𐌀 (hatria). Doublet of Hadrian. See Adria.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Adrianople (modern-day Edirne).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Hadriānopolītānus.

parole.significato: A kind of adoption in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin adrogatio, arrogatio, from adrogare. See arrogate.

parole.testo: Coined by American author and neologist John Koenig in 2013, creator of The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, with reference to Latin andronitis, described by him as a "hallway connecting the front part of the house with a complex inner atrium" in Ancient Roman architecture. parole.significato: Derived or acquired from something extrinsic; not part of the real, inherent, or essential nature of a thing.
parole.testo: From Latin adscitus, from past participle of adscisco (“admit”).

parole.significato: A feudal serf or labourer who is attached to an estate and sold or transferred with it.
parole.testo: From Latin adscriptus, past participle of adscribere (“to enroll”). See ascribe.

parole.significato: Attached or annexed to the glebe or estate and transferable with it.
parole.testo: From Latin adscriptivus. See adscript.

parole.significato: To denote additionally.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin adsignificare (“to show”). By surface analysis, ad- + signify.

parole.significato: To improve something by augmentation or supplementation:
parole.testo: From Latin past participle stem astruct- (“erected”), from verb astruo, from ad (“towards”) + struo (“pile up, build”).

parole.significato: To flatter effusively.
parole.testo: A learned borrowing from Latin adūlor.

parole.significato: One who lavishes excessive praises or flattery; one who adulates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adūlātor.

parole.significato: Adulatory, flattering.
parole.testo: From Latin adūlātōrius.

parole.significato: Exhibiting adulation; overly flattering.
parole.testo: From Latin adulatorius.

parole.significato: An adulterer, especially a male one.
parole.testo: From Latin adulter.

parole.significato: To commit adultery.
parole.testo: From Latin adulterō.

parole.significato: Corrupted or made impure by being mixed with something else; adulterated.
parole.testo: From Latin adulterātus (“adulterate, adulterated, defiled, polluted, counterfeited”), perfect passive participle of adulterō (“to adulterate, defile, commit adultery (with), counterfeit”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ad- (“to, in the direction of”) + alter (“other”) + -ō (verb-forming

parole.significato: To corrupt, to debase (someone or something).
parole.testo: From Latin adulterātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Spurious; due to adulteration.
parole.testo: From Latin adulterīnus.

parole.significato: Giving a faint shadow, slight resemblance, or foreboding. By extension, faint or slight.
parole.testo: An adaptation of adumbrant-, the oblique stem of the Latin adumbrāns, the present active participle of adumbrō (“to cast a shadow upon”).

parole.significato: To foreshadow vaguely.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adumbrātus (“represented in outline”), from adumbrāre (“cast a shadow on”), from umbra (“shadow”).

parole.significato: The state of being in shadow or shade; (countable) a shadow.
parole.testo: From Latin adumbrātiō (“sketch; outline, silhouette; pretence, semblance”) + -ion (suffix indicating a condition or state). parole.significato: The act of uniting; union.
parole.testo: From Latin adūnātiō, from ad + ūnus (“one”).

parole.significato: Curved inward, hooked.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aduncus.

parole.significato: Crookedness, curvaceousness, hookedness.
parole.testo: From Latin aduncitās (“hookedness”), from aduncus + -itās. By surface analysis, adunc + -ity.

parole.significato: To burn, completely or slightly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adūrere.

parole.significato: The act of burning, or heating to dryness; the state of being thus heated or dried.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin adustiō.

parole.significato: The horizontal movement of a body of atmosphere (or other fluid) along with a concurrent transport of its temperature,…

parole.significato: Brought to a place from somewhere else; imported, foreign.
parole.testo: From Latin advectīcius + -ous.

parole.significato: To accede or to come to; to be superadded to, to be added to something or become a part of it, though inessential.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin advenire (“to come to, arrive at”), from ad (“to”) + venire (“to come”). Compare convene, intervene, supervene.

parole.significato: Caused by outside forces; coming from without; external, additional.
parole.testo: From the present participle of Latin advenīre.

parole.significato: Arrival; onset; a time when something first comes or appears; the time when it is approaching.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adventus (“arrival, approach”).

parole.significato: An external addition.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin advention (“addition”), ultimately from Latin adveniō (“to arrive”).

parole.significato: The outermost layer of epithelial tissue encasing a visceral organ.
parole.testo: From the Latin adventitius (“extraneous”).

parole.significato: From an external source; not innate or inherent, foreign.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin adventītius (“coming from abroad, extraneous”), a corruption of Latin adventīcius (“foreign, strange, accidental”), from adventus (“arrival, coming, approach, advent”) + -īcius (suffix forming adjectives), from adveniō (“to arrive”) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns).

parole.significato: Accidental.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adventīvus, from adveniō (“to come (to)”) + -īvus (verbal-adjective suffix).

parole.significato: Of or relating to an adverb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adverbiālis. By surface analysis, adverb + -ial.

parole.significato: Opposed; adverse.
parole.testo: From Latin adversus + -ant.

parole.significato: (treated as plural) A collection of miscellaneous notes, remarks, or fragments of writing, typically preserved in a not…
parole.testo: From Latin adversāri.

parole.significato: Expressing opposition or difference.
parole.testo: From Latin adversativus (“of conjunctions, expressing opposition”).

parole.significato: A tendency or wish to avoid someone or something.
parole.testo: From Latin adversiōnem, from adversiō.

parole.significato: Attentive.
parole.testo: Apparently a back-formation from inadvertent, or a learned borrowing from Latin advertent-, advertens, present participle of advertere, from the verb adverto (“to give or draw attention to”)

parole.significato: To draw towards evening.
parole.testo: From Latin ad- + vesper.

parole.significato: The approach of evening.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin advesperātiō. See advesperate.

parole.significato: Advocacy; the act of advocating or pleading.
parole.testo: From Latin advocātiō. Doublet of advowson

parole.significato: A female advocate, especially as a title of Mary, mother of Jesus.
parole.testo: From Latin advocātrīx, from advocāre (“advocate”) + -trīx (“-ess”, forming feminine agent nouns), from ad- (“to, toward, on behalf of”) + vocāre (“speak”). By surface analysis, advocate + -trix.

parole.significato: A medieval officeholder, particularly important in the Holy Roman Empire, who was delegated some of the powers and func…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin advocatus. Doublet of advocate and avocat.

parole.significato: To summon or call (to a higher tribunal).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin advocare, formed from ad + vocare (“to call”). Doublet of advocate, avouch, and avow.

parole.significato: A rolling toward something; goal orientation.
parole.testo: From Latin advolutum, past participle of advolvere (“to roll to”).

parole.significato: A form of hyperbole that uses exaggeration so magnified as to express impossibility; an instance of such hyperbole.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin adynaton (“impossibility; adynaton”), or directly from its etymon Ancient Greek ἀδύνατον (adúnaton, “an impossibility; impracticality”), substantivized neuter singular of ἀδύνατος (adúnatos, “unable; that cannot be done, impossible”) + -ον (-on, suffix forming nouns). parole.significato: The innermost sanctum of a temple, in which oracles are announced.
parole.testo: From Latin adytum.

parole.significato: The innermost sanctuary or shrine in a temple, from where oracles were given.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adytum, from Ancient Greek ἄδυτον (áduton, “innermost sanctuary; shrine”), inflected form of ἄδυτος (ádutos, “not to be entered”).

parole.testo: From New Latin aecium, from Ancient Greek αἰκίᾱ (aikíā, “injury, insult”). parole.significato: A copulatory organ of some male insects.
parole.testo: From New Latin aedeagus, derived from Ancient Greek αἰδοῖα (aidoîa, “private parts, pudenda”) + ἀγός (agós, “leader”), from ἄγω (ágō, “I lead”).

parole.significato: A painted framed niche giving the appearance of depth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aedicula.

parole.significato: A small house or room.
parole.testo: From Latin aedicula (“small house”), diminutive of aedēs (“a house”) + -culus.

parole.significato: An elected official who was responsible for the maintenance of public buildings, regulation of festivals, supervision o…
parole.testo: From Latin aedīlis (“commissioner or magistrate”), from aedēs + -īlis.

parole.significato: The office of an elected official responsible for festivals and the maintenance of public buildings.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aedīlitās, from Latin aedīlis (“commissioner or magistrate”), from aedēs + -īlis. By surface analysis, aedile + -ity.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Aegean Sea or the regions bordering it.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin aegaeus (from Ancient Greek Αἰγαῖος (Aigaîos, “Aegean”)) + English -an. The name might be connected to αἶγες (aîges, “waves”).

parole.significato: Absent and excused from one’s classes due to illness
parole.testo: From Latin aeger (“sick”).

parole.significato: An ulcer or fistula in the inner angle of the eye.
parole.testo: From Latin aegilōps, from Ancient Greek αἰγίλωψ (aigílōps, “haver-grass (Aegilops neglecta)”).

parole.significato: A goat-like creature resembling a satyr, sometimes portrayed as having a fish's tail.
parole.testo: From Latin Aegipān, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Αἰγίπαν (Aigípan), from αἴξ (aíx, “goat”) + Πάν (Pán, “Pan”).

parole.significato: A mythological shield associated with the Greek deities Zeus and Athena (and their Roman counterparts Jupiter and Miner…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aegis, from Ancient Greek αἰγίς (aigís, “goatskin; shield of Athena”), probably from αἴξ (aíx, “goat”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“goat”). The plural form aegides (/ˈiːd͡ʒɪdiːz/) is borrowed from Latin aegides, from Ancient Greek αἰγῐ́δες (aigĭ́des).

parole.significato: A certificate indicating that a student is ill, excusing attendance at lectures and examinations and allowing courses t…
parole.testo: UK 19th century. Latin aegrotat, literally “he/she is ill”, third-person singular present active indicative form of aegrōtō.

parole.significato: Bronze-colored.
parole.testo: From Latin aēneus (“made of copper or bronze”).

parole.significato: Of the Anatolian region Aeolis, Aeolia.
parole.testo: From Latin aeolicus, from Ancient Greek Αἰολικός (Aiolikós, “like the Aeolians”).

parole.significato: Commonwealth standard spelling of eon.
parole.testo: From Latin aeon, from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age, era”).

parole.significato: The case conveying an equality with another noun, equivalent to “like” or “as” in English. This case is used in some la…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aequālis (“equal”). Doublet of equal and egal.

parole.significato: Of or relating to that ancient people who resided in Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin Aequi + -ian.

parole.significato: marine; oceanic
parole.testo: From Latin aequoreus + -al.

parole.significato: The state treasury of Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin aerārium.

parole.significato: A spongy, airy tissue found especially in the roots of aquatic plants.
parole.testo: From Latin āēr (“air”) + -enchyma.

parole.significato: Resembling or consisting of air.
parole.testo: From Latin aer + -ous.

parole.significato: Of, or like copper or brass; brassy.
parole.testo: From Latin aerōsus (“full of copper”), from aes (“copper, brass”) + -ōsus.

parole.significato: Synonym of verdigrisy, of or related to copper carbonate, bluish green.

parole.significato: Metallic rust, particularly of brass or copper; verdigris; patina.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aerūgō, from aes (“copper, bronze, brass”).

parole.significato: Aerial; ethereal; incorporeal; visionary.
parole.testo: From Middle English aery, from Latin āerius.

parole.significato: Related to or concerning the Greek fabulist Aesop.
parole.testo: From Latin Aesopius (“Aesopian”), from Ancient Greek Αἴσωπος (Aísōpos, “the famous Greek fabulist Aesop”).

parole.significato: As the tide, turbulent; ebbing and flowing.
parole.testo: From Latin aestus (“heat, tide”) + -ferous (“bearing, bringing”).

parole.significato: A state of inactivity and metabolic depression during summer: the summer version of hibernation.

parole.significato: Of or relating to summer.
parole.testo: From Latin aestīvus (“related to summer”), from aestas (“summer”).

parole.significato: Relating to or happening in summer and autumn.

parole.significato: Full of passion; agitated.

parole.significato: Aged; at the age of.

parole.significato: Attributing a cause for a statement or claim made, often as a simple relative clause of explanation.

parole.significato: The establishment of a cause, origin, or reason for something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aetiologia. By surface analysis, aetio- + -logy. Doublet of aetiologia.

parole.significato: Any assumption of an age-based norm and particularly the assumption that adults and adult experiences are normative whi…
parole.testo: Coined in 2009 by Maria Nikolajeva, from Latin aetas (“age”) + normativity.

parole.significato: Synonym of eternity (“existence without end”).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aeviternus (“eternal, perpetual”) + English -ity (suffix forming nouns, especially abstract nouns), probably modelled after eternity. parole.significato: The temporal mode of existence between time and eternity, said to be experienced by angels, saints, and celestial bodie…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aevum (“temporal mode of existence between time and eternity”). Doublet of aeviternity and aye.

parole.significato: Executed in a workmanlike manner; ingeniously made.
parole.testo: From Latin affaber (“workmanlike”), from ad + faber.

parole.significato: To influence or alter.
