parole.significato: Lack of muscle tone.
parole.testo: From New Latin atonia, from Ancient Greek ἀτονία (atonía, “languor”).

parole.significato: Lack of muscle tone; flaccidity or atonia
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin atonia, from Ancient Greek ἀτονία (atonía, “languor”), from ἄτονος (átonos, “languid”), from ἀ- (a-, “privative”) + τόνος (tónos, “accent”), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”).

parole.significato: Characterized by melancholy or glum; atrabilarious; atrabilious.
parole.testo: From Latin ātra bīlis (“black bile”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to black bile.
parole.testo: From Latin ātrabīlārius.

parole.significato: Of or relating to black bile.
parole.testo: From Latin ātra bīlis (“black bile”) (āter (“dark, black”) + bīlis (“bile”)) + -ary.

parole.significato: Having an excess of black bile.
parole.testo: From Latin ātra bīlis (“black bile”) (āter (“dark, black”) + bīlis (“bile”)) + -ous (“full of”), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medicine associated with sadness and despondency.

parole.significato: Ink or an inklike substance.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English atrament, from Latin ātrāmentum, from ātrāre (“to blacken”), from āter (“black”). First attested in the 14th century.

parole.significato: Like ink; suitable for making ink.
parole.testo: From Latin ātrāmentārius (“pertaining to ink”), from ātrāmentārium (“inkstand”) + -ius. Compare French atramentaire.

parole.significato: Synonym of inky, black, inklike.
parole.testo: From Latin ātrāmentōsus, from ātrāmentum (“black liquid, ink”). Equivalent to atrament + -ous.

parole.significato: A condition in which a body orifice or passage in the body is abnormally closed or absent.
parole.testo: From Latin atresia, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not, without”) and τρῆσις (trêsis, “perforation”).

parole.significato: A central room or space in ancient Roman homes, open to the sky in the middle; a similar space in other buildings.
parole.testo: From Latin ātrium (“entry hall”), from Etruscan.

parole.significato: Frightful, evil, cruel, or monstrous.
parole.testo: From Latin atrōx (“cruel, fierce, frightful”) + -ious.

parole.significato: Synonym of Atropatian
parole.testo: From Latin Atropatēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἀτροπατηνός (Atropatēnós), from Ἀτροπάτης (Atropátēs, “Atropates”) + -ηνός (-ēnós). By surface analysis, Atropates + -ene.

parole.significato: Jet-black in color.
parole.testo: From Latin āter (“dark, black”) + -ous.

parole.significato: An endopeptidase enzyme, found in the venom of the diamondback rattlesnake Crotalus atrox, that catalyzes the cleavage…
parole.testo: From Latin atrox + -ase.

parole.significato: An ancient privilege granted to forest officers to take for their own any thorns, brushwood, and windfalls within their…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin attachiamenta de spinis et boscis.

parole.significato: A grey partridge (Perdix perdix) of Eurasia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin attagēn.

parole.significato: A state of being found guilty of an offence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin attinctūra, used to translate Old French ateint, from Vulgar Latin *attinctus (perfect passive participle of Latin attingō).

parole.significato: To be tedious to; to exhaust.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Late Latin attaediāre.

parole.significato: tempered; proportioned; properly adapted.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin attemperatus. Doublet of attemper.

parole.significato: Attentive, heedful; intent.
parole.testo: From Latin attentus.

parole.significato: Anything whatsoever, as a ruling, by the judge of a lower court in a matter pending an appeal.
parole.testo: A variant of attemptate assimilated to Latin attentātus and French attentat.

parole.significato: Mental focus.
parole.testo: From Middle English attencioun, borrowed from Latin attentio, attentionis, from attendere, past participle attentus (“to attend, give heed to”); see attend. Equivalent to attend + -tion.

parole.significato: archaic Making thin; diluting or thinning; rendering less dense and viscid.
parole.testo: From Latin attenuans, present participle of attenuare: compare French atténuant. See attenuate.

parole.significato: To reduce in size, force, value, amount, or degree.
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1530, the adjective in 1626; borrowed from Latin attenuātus, the perfect passive participle of attenuō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + tenuo (“to make thin”), itself from tenuis (“thin”) + -ō (verb-for

parole.significato: A gradual diminishing of strength.
parole.testo: From Middle English attenuacioun, a borrowing from Latin attenuātiō (“a diminishing”). Equivalent to attenuate + -ion.

parole.significato: Of or related to Attica, ancient Athens and its hinterland
parole.testo: From Latin Atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós), from some Pre-Greek demonym or toponym for Athens and its hinterland of Attica + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic: forming adjectives”). Equivalent to a modified and clipped Athens + -ic. Doublet of Atticus.

parole.significato: Pointed and delicate wit.
parole.testo: Attic + salt; a calque of Latin sāl Atticus or sāl Atticum. In classical times “salt” was a frequent metaphor for “wit”.

parole.significato: Epitympanic recess or the uppermost part of the middle ear cavity located above the tympanic membrane and containing th…
parole.testo: From Latin atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós) + -o-. By surface analysis, attic + -o-.

parole.significato: To touch lightly.
parole.testo: From Latin attingō (“to touch”). Doublet of attain and attainder.

parole.significato: The property of being attingent; adjacency.
parole.testo: From atting(ent) + -ence, ultimately from Latin attingēns (“touching”, passive participle), from Latin attingō (“to touch; to come into contact with”, verb).

parole.significato: touching; adjacent
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin attingēns (“touching”, passive participle), from Latin attingō (“to touch; to come into contact with”, verb). Further from Latin tangō (“to touch, to grasp”, verb), from Proto-Italic *tangō and Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g-, both verbs of the same meaning.

parole.significato: Expressive of or pertaining to attitude.
parole.testo: From Italian attitudine + -al, from Latin aptitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin aptitūdō, from aptus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, attitude + -al.

parole.significato: One who attitudinizes; one who postures or behaves in a stilted and pretentious manner.
parole.testo: From Italian attitudine + -arian, from Latin aptitūdin- + -arian, from oblique stem of Latin aptitūdō, from aptus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, attitude + -arian.

parole.significato: To cause (someone or something) to assume an attitude or pose; to pose, to posture.
parole.testo: From Italian attitudine + -ize, from Latin aptitūdin- + -ize, from oblique stem of Latin aptitūdō, from aptus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, attitude + -ize.

parole.significato: Having a bold and possibly unfriendly attitude; sassy.
parole.testo: From Italian attitudine + -ous, from Latin aptitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin aptitūdō, from aptus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, attitude + -ous.

parole.significato: Lifting up, raising (said of muscles, especially the levator palpebrae superioris ).
parole.testo: From Latin attollens, present participle of attollo; ad + tollo (“to lift”).

parole.significato: To pull toward without touching.
parole.testo: From Latin attractus, past participle of attrahere (“to draw to, attract”), from ad (“to”) + trahere (“to draw”).

parole.significato: That attracts; drawing, attracting.
parole.testo: From attrahent-, the stem of the Latin attrahēns (“drawing, pulling, or dragging to or toward with force”; “drawing”, “alluring”, “leading”, “bringing”, “moving”, “attracting”), the present active participle of attrahō (“to draw, pull, or drag to or toward with force”; “to draw, allure, lead, bring,

parole.significato: Frequent handling or touching; fingering.
parole.testo: From Latin attrectatio, from ad + tractare (“to handle”).

parole.significato: A characteristic or quality of a thing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin attributus.

parole.significato: One who attributes; an imputer.
parole.testo: From the Latin attribūtor.

parole.significato: To wear down through attrition, especially mechanical attrition.
parole.testo: From Latin attrītus, past participle of atterō. Said by multiple dictionaries to be a back-formation from attrition, but it is not a recent one, being centuries old.

parole.significato: Regretful of one's wrongdoing merely due to fear of punishment.
parole.testo: From Latin attrītus (“ground”).

parole.significato: material pulverized by attrition
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: abnormality in a cell (the state of being atypical)
parole.testo: From New Latin atypia, from a- + typus (English “type”) + -ia.

parole.significato: According to the Roman era, which reckons the number of years passed from the foundation of the city of Rome by Romulus…
parole.testo: From Latin AUC, (anno) ab urbe condita (“from the founding of the city”) or anno urbis conditae (“in the year of the city's having been founded”), both in reference to Rome's legendary establishment by Romulus. The era was not in common use by the Romans, who preferred dating by the years' consuls,

parole.significato: A public event where goods or property are sold to the highest bidder.
parole.testo: From Latin auctiō (“an increase, auction”), from augere (“to increase”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an auction.
parole.testo: Latin auctionarius.

parole.significato: A class of natural faculty.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin auctrīx.

parole.significato: To hunt, to seek with vigilance.
parole.testo: From Latin aucupātus.

parole.significato: Showing willingness to take bold risks; recklessly daring.
parole.testo: From Latin audacia (“boldness”) + -ious, from audax (“bold”), from audeō (“to be bold, to dare”).

parole.significato: Insolent boldness, especially when imprudent or unconventional.
parole.testo: From Middle English audacite, from Medieval Latin audācitās (whence -acity), from Latin audāx (“bold”), from audeō (“to be bold, to dare”).

parole.significato: A non-competitive long-distance (often over 200 km) cycling event.
parole.testo: From Latin audāx, via Italian.

parole.significato: "Hear both sides." A legal principle of fairness given to ensure that the accused has the chance to refute an accusatio…
parole.testo: From Latin audī (second-person singular present active imperative of audiō (“hear”)) + alteram (feminine accusative singular of alter (“the other”)) + partem (accusative singular of pars (“part, side”)).

parole.significato: The quality of being heard or understood; the degree to which a thing is audible.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin audibilitās.

parole.significato: Listening, paying attention.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin audientem, accusative singular of audiēns (“hearing, listening; attending, paying attention to”) (or directly from audiēns), the present active participle of audiō (“to hear, listen to; to attend, pay attention to”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewis (“clearly, manifestly”) (from

parole.significato: Audibly.
parole.testo: From Latin audient- + -ly. Compare later audient.

parole.significato: A person whose mental imagery consists of sounds.
parole.testo: Irregular formation from Latin audire + -ilis. By surface analysis, audio + -ile.

parole.significato: Sound.
parole.testo: From the root audi of Latin audiō (“to hear; to listen”) + -o-. Cognates include Proto-Germanic *awiz (“obvious”), Sanskrit आविस् (āvís, “manifestly, evidently”) and Ancient Greek αἰσθάνομαι (aisthánomai, “perceive, notice”) whence English aesthetic.

parole.significato: An early electronic amplifying tube consisting of a partially evacuated glass tube with three electrodes, a heated fila…
parole.testo: Neologism based on Latin audio (“to hear”).

parole.significato: A judicial examination.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin audītus, from audiō (“to hear”). The sense of examine is because examinations were originally presented orally, and the examiner listened.

parole.significato: A writ which lies for a party against whom judgment is recovered, but to whom good matter of discharge has subsequently…
parole.testo: Latin audita querela (“the complaint having been heard”).

parole.significato: A large room for public meetings or performances.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin audītōrium, from audītōrius (“pertaining to hearing”). Equivalent to auditory + -ium.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to hearing, or to the sense or organs of hearing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin audītōrius (“pertaining to a hearer or hearing”), from audiō (“to hear”) + -tōrius (“-tory”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of Augeas.
parole.testo: From Latin Augeas + -an. Augeas is a figure in Greek mythology whose stables were never cleaned until Hercules was given the task of cleaning them.

parole.significato: A quantity to which another is added.
parole.testo: From Latin augendum.

parole.significato: A variety of pyroxene, usually of a black or dark green color, occurring in igneous rocks, such as basalt.
parole.testo: From Latin augītēs.

parole.significato: A diviner who foretells events by the behaviour of birds or other animals, or by signs derived from celestial phenomena…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin augur, of uncertain origin; akin to augurō (“interpret omens”).

parole.significato: prophetic
parole.testo: From Latin augurālis. By surface analysis, augur + -al.

parole.significato: The position or office of an augur.
parole.testo: From Latin augurātus (“augurate”). By surface analysis, augur + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

parole.significato: To make or take auguries; to augur; to predict.
parole.testo: From Latin augurātus, perfect passive participle of augurō (“to predict, foretell”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, augur + -ate.

parole.significato: augury; divination
parole.testo: From Latin auguratio.

parole.significato: Relating to augurs or to augury.
parole.testo: Latin augurialis.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the times of the Roman emperor Augustus (63 B.C.E. - 14 C.E.).
parole.testo: From the Latin Augustānus, from Augustus, a Roman emperor who ruled a period of peace and prosperity known as the Pax Romana or Pax Augusta.

parole.significato: An Augustinian.
parole.testo: From Latin Augustīnus, derivative of Augustus. Doublet of Austin.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to St Augustine of Hippo or his doctrines, especially on predestination and grace.
parole.testo: From Middle English Augustinen, from Latin Augustīniānus, from Augustīnus + -iānus, after Augustine of Hippo. By surface analysis, Augustine + -ian.

parole.significato: A member of a supposed radical group of the early Reformation, who allegedly believed that humans would not enter Heave…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Augustīniānī pl, from Augustīnus + -iānus, after an unidentified person so named. By surface analysis, Augustine + -ian.

parole.significato: A court or hall.
parole.testo: From Latin aula (“forecourt”), from Ancient Greek αὐλά (aulá), the form of αὐλή (aulḗ, “forecourt”) in dialects other than Ionic and Attic.

parole.significato: A great hall or large classroom used for special occasions at a university.
parole.testo: From Latin aula (“hall”) magna (“great”).

parole.significato: A tail-like longitudinally differentiated appendage found in mitrates and cornutes, originally believed to be used for…
parole.testo: From Latin aulax (“furrow”) or its etymon Ancient Greek αὖλαξ (aûlax, “furrow”) + -phore (“bearer, carrier”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a large hall.
parole.testo: From stem of Late Latin aularis (from Latin aula (“a hall”), from Ancient Greek αὐλά (aulá)) + -ian.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a musical pipe or piper.
parole.testo: Latin auleticus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a royal court; courtly.
parole.testo: From Latin aulicus (“of a prince's court”), from aula (“royal court”), from Ancient Greek αὐλή (aulḗ, “courtyard”).

parole.significato: gold
parole.testo: First productive in the 1575 coinage auripotent: representing aur-, the stem of the Latin aurum (“gold”).

parole.significato: ear
parole.testo: First productive in the 1678 coinage aurist: representing aur-, the stem of the Latin auris (“ear”).

parole.significato: A subtle emanation or exhalation of any substance, such as an aroma or odour.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aura (“a breeze, a breath of air, the air”), from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breeze, soft wind”), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). Doublet of east, auster, air, and aria. Sense 4 originated in the early 2020s and was popularized on TikTok around May 2024.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the ear.
parole.testo: From Latin auralis, from auris (“ear”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an aura.
parole.testo: From Latin aura (“moving air, breeze, vital air”) + -al.

parole.significato: Having or resembling ears.
parole.testo: Coined based on Latin auris (“ear”).

parole.significato: Golden in color or shine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aureatus (“adorned or decorated with gold”). Equivalent to Latin aureus (“golden, gilded”) + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The enhancement of the seriousness of a topic by the use of elaborate circumlocutions or polysyllabic or Latinate words…
parole.testo: From aureate + -ion, from Latin aureatus (“decorated with gold”).

parole.significato: The particular property peculiar to gold; goldenness.
parole.testo: From Latin aureitās, with the suffix adapted to -ity.

parole.significato: Characteristic of the Roman emperor Aurelius
parole.testo: From Latin Aurelianus, derivative of the gens name Aurelius (“golden”).

parole.significato: Radiance of luminous cloud that surrounds the figure in a painting of a sacred personage.
parole.testo: From Latin aurea (“golden”) + -ola.

parole.significato: A yellow pigment used in painting, composed of potassium cobaltinitrite.
parole.testo: From Latin aureolus + suffix -in.

parole.significato: A gold coin, minted in the Roman Empire from approximately 100 B.C.E. to 309 C.E., equal to 25 denarii.
parole.testo: From Latin aureus (“golden; gold coin equivalent to 25 denarii”), noun use of adjective, from aurum (“gold”). Doublet of eyrir, öre, øre, and oyra.

parole.significato: Any appendage in the shape of an ear or earlobe.
parole.testo: From Latin auricula (“the external ear”), diminutive of auris (“the ear”). Doublet of auricula.

parole.significato: Having golden hair; yellow-haired.
parole.testo: From Latin auricomus (“golden-haired”), from aurum (“gold”) + coma (“hair of the head”). Compare English floricomous.

parole.significato: The external part of the ear.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin auricula (“external ear; ear”). Doublet of auricle.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the ear.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin auriculāris, from auricula (“the external ear; the ear”) + -āris (“-ar”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to auricle + -ar. Doublet of auricularis.

parole.significato: The larvae of the sea cucumber.
parole.testo: From Latin auriculāria (“ear-shaped things”).

parole.significato: Any of three muscles attaching the cartilage of the external ear to the skull.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin auriculāris, ellipsis of musculus auriculāris (“auricular muscle”). Doublet of auricular.

parole.significato: Containing or producing gold; gold-bearing.
parole.testo: From Latin aurifer (“gold-bearing”) + the English suffix -ous. The Latin term in turn derived from aurum (“gold”) + ferō (“to carry”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a chariot.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aurīgālis, from aurīga (“charioteer”).

parole.significato: The act of driving a chariot or a carriage.
parole.testo: From Latin aurigatio, from aurigare "to be a charioteer", from auriga.

parole.significato: The art of writing with or in gold.
parole.testo: From Latin aurum (“gold”) + -graphy.

parole.significato: A red colouring matter derived from phenol. Used as an indicator.
parole.testo: From Latin aurum (“gold”) + -in.

parole.significato: Embroidered or decorated with gold.
parole.testo: From Late Latin auriphrigiatus; Latin aurum (“gold”) + Late Latin phrygiare (“to adorn with Phrygian needlework, or with embroidery”); perhaps corrupted from some other word.

parole.significato: An earpick.
parole.testo: From Latin auris (“ear”) + scalpere (“to scrape”).

parole.significato: Auriscalpium, a genus of mushrooms.
parole.testo: The word is compounded of the Latin auris (“ear”) and scalpo (“to scratch”).

parole.significato: Gold-devouring.
parole.testo: From Latin aurum + -vorous.

parole.significato: An atmospheric phenomenon created by charged particles from the sun striking the upper atmosphere, creating coloured li…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aurōra (“dawn”). Doublet of Eos.

parole.significato: The aurora of the southern hemisphere
parole.testo: From New Latin aurōra austrālis, from Latin aurōra austrālis (literally “southern dawn”).

parole.significato: The aurora of the northern hemisphere.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin aurōra boreālis (literally “northern dawn”).

parole.significato: Belonging to the dawn, or resembling it in brilliant hue.
parole.testo: Either the Latin aurōre(us) + the English -an or formed from the two English elements auror(a) + -ean.

parole.significato: Gold in color.
parole.testo: From Latin aurulentus (“golden”).

parole.significato: Gold (used in the names of various substances, see "Derived terms").
parole.testo: From Latin aurum (“gold”). Doublet of or.

parole.significato: Diagnosis of disorders by listening to the sounds of the internal organs, usually using a stethoscope.
parole.testo: From Latin auscultātio (“act of listening”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to auscultation
parole.testo: Probably from Latin auscultātor (“listener, heeder”) + -y

parole.significato: Of ancient Ausonia or the Ausonians.
parole.testo: From Latin Ausonia (“Lower Italy”), extended poetically to “Italy”, from Ancient Greek Αὐσονία (Ausonía), from Αὔσων (Aúsōn), a son of Ulysses, who is said to have settled there.

parole.significato: To foreshow; to foretoken.
parole.testo: From Latin auspicatus, past participle of auspicari "to take auspices", from auspex "bird seer", "augur", a contraction of avispex; avis "bird" + specere, spicere, "to view".

parole.significato: Of good omen; indicating future success.
parole.testo: From auspice + -ious, from Latin auspicium (“augury”), from auspex (“augur”), possibly via French.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or coming from the south.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin australis (“southern”).

parole.significato: Southern.
parole.testo: From Latin australis (“southern”), from Latin auster (“south wind”).

parole.significato: A particular polyhydroxylated pyrrolizidine alkaloid.
parole.testo: From Latin australis + -ine. By surface analysis, austral- + -ine.

parole.significato: A prenylflavonoid found in Morus australis.
parole.testo: From Latin australis + -one.

parole.significato: Any of several extinct hominids, belonging to the genera Australopithecus and Paranthropus in the subtribe Australopith…
parole.testo: Originally in reference to a now-obsolete subfamily Australopithecinae, formed in New Latin, from Latin austrālis (“southern”) + Ancient Greek πίθηκος (píthēkos, “ape”).

parole.significato: Southern; southerly; austral.
parole.testo: From Latin austrinus, from auster (“south”).

parole.significato: Soothsaying or divination from observing the winds or clouds.
parole.testo: From Latin auster (“south wind”); austro- + -mancy.

parole.significato: A condition of absolute power.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin autarchia, from Koine Greek αὐταρχία (autarkhía, “absolute power, sovereignty, autocracy”), from αὔταρχος (aútarkhos, “autocratic”), from αὐτ- (aut-, “self”) + ἄρχω (árkhō, “to rule, govern”).

parole.significato: To render authentic; to give authority to, by the proof, attestation, or formalities required by law, or sufficient to…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin authenticō. By surface analysis, authentic + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A person’s own handwriting, especially the signature of a famous or admired person.
parole.testo: From Latin autographum, in turn from Ancient Greek αὐτόγραφον (autógraphon, “a writing in one’s own hand”). Equivalent to auto- + -graph.

parole.significato: Capable of operating without external control or intervention.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin automaticus, from Classical Latin automatum (“automaton”) + -icus (adjectival suffix), from Ancient Greek αὐτόματον (autómaton), neuter of αὐτόματος (autómatos, “self-moving, moving of oneself, self-acting, spontaneous”), from αὐτός (autós, “self, myself”) + μέμαα (mémaa, “to

parole.significato: Birds that are able to run about and obtain their own food as soon as they are hatched.
parole.testo: From auto- (“by oneself”) + Latin -phagus (“eater”, plural -phagī). The attested Ancient Greek αὐτοφάγος (autophágos) would have meant "self-devouring, autophagous".

parole.significato: A dissection performed on a cadaver to find possible cause(s) of death.
parole.testo: From New Latin autopsia, from Ancient Greek αὐτοψῐ́ᾱ (autopsĭ́ā, “seeing with one's own eyes”). By surface analysis, auto- + -opsy.

parole.significato: Of or relating to autumn.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin autumnāl(is). By surface analysis, autumn + -al.

parole.significato: auxiliary
parole.testo: From Latin auxiliaris.

parole.significato: Helping; giving assistance or support.
parole.testo: From Latin auxiliārius (“assistant, ally”), equiv. to auxiliāris (“helping, aiding”), from auxilium (“help, aid”), from augēre (“to increase”).

parole.significato: Growth or increase.
parole.testo: From Latin auxi, perfect stem of augeo (“enlarge”).

parole.significato: Avaricious.
parole.testo: Latin avarus

parole.significato: A salutation.
parole.testo: From Latin ave.

parole.significato: Hail Mary (Catholic prayer, part of the rosary)
parole.testo: From Middle English Ave Maria, Ave Marie, Ave Mary(e), from Latin Avē Marīa.

parole.significato: To pull away.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin āvellō.

parole.significato: Belonging to, or resembling, oats or the oat grasses.
parole.testo: Latin avena + -aceous

parole.significato: Having the appearance of oats.
parole.testo: From Latin avena (“oats”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the Aventine Hill, one of the seven hills on which Rome stood.
parole.testo: From Latin Aventinus.

parole.significato: To avert; to ward off.
parole.testo: From Latin āverruncāre (“to avert”), from āb (“off”) + verruncāre (“to turn”), but interpreted as being āb + ēruncāre (“to weed out”), and spelled accordingly.

parole.significato: Turned to show the back: said of a hand (or gauntlet).
parole.testo: From Latin āversantem, from āversāns.

parole.significato: Having a repugnance or opposition of mind.
parole.testo: From Latin aversus, past participle of avertere (“to avert”).

parole.significato: Apostrophe.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin āversiō. Doublet of aversion.

parole.significato: Opposition or repugnance of mind; fixed dislike often without any conscious reasoning.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin āversiō, āversiōnem. Doublet of aversio.

parole.significato: bird
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin avis (“bird”).

parole.significato: Characteristic of or pertaining to birds, or to bird-like or flying creatures.
parole.testo: From Latin avis (“bird”) + -ian.

parole.significato: A house, enclosure, large cage, or other place for keeping birds confined; a birdhouse.
parole.testo: From Latin aviārium, from avis (“bird”).

parole.significato: That is parasitic on birds
parole.testo: From Latin avis (“bird”) + -colous.

parole.significato: A tetrameric protein produced in the oviducts of birds, reptiles and amphibians and deposited in the whites of their eg…
parole.testo: From Latin avidus (“hungry”) + -in, based on its "hunger" for biotin.

parole.significato: The birds, or all the kinds of birds, inhabiting a region.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin avis (“bird”) + New Latin fauna (“animals”), from Latin Faunus (“god of herdsmen”).

parole.significato: Having the shape of a bird
parole.testo: From Latin avis (“bird”) + -form.

parole.significato: Characteristic of or pertaining to birds, or to bird-like or flying creatures.
parole.testo: From Latin avis (“bird”) + -ine.

parole.significato: Relating to a grandfather or ancestor.
parole.testo: From Latin avus (“grandfather”).

parole.significato: time for a judge to consider a case and reach a decision.
parole.testo: From Late Latin avizō (“consider”), from Latin a + vīsō (“look carefully”).

parole.significato: To call off or away; to withdraw; to transfer to another tribunal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin avoco, avocatus. Doublet of avoke.

parole.significato: A calling away; a diversion.
parole.testo: From Latin āvocātiō (“a distraction”), from āvocō (“to call off, distract”).

parole.significato: To call back again or revoke
parole.testo: Compare avocate. Ultimately from Latin āvōcō, āvōcāre.

parole.significato: To escape; to dissipate into the air.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin āvolō (“to fly away”).

parole.significato: Evaporation; dissipation into the air.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin āvolātiō (“flying away”), or formed directly from avolate + -ation.

parole.significato: To tear off forcibly.
parole.testo: From Latin avulsus, past participle of avello: ab- + vellō.

parole.significato: The loss or separation of a body part, either by surgery or due to trauma.
parole.testo: From Latin avulsio from a- + vellō.

parole.significato: In the manner of an uncle, pertaining to an uncle.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin avunculāris, from Classical Latin avunculus (“maternal uncle”) + -āris (“-ar”).

parole.significato: The killing of one's uncle.
parole.testo: From Latin avunculus (“maternal uncle”) + -icide.

parole.significato: Characterized by couples living with the husband's maternal uncle.
parole.testo: Latin avuncul(us) (“maternal uncle”) + -o- + local.

parole.significato: Relating to the axis
parole.testo: Clipping of axis, from Latin axis.

parole.significato: The angle or point of divergence between the upper side of a branch, leaf, or petiole, and the stem or branch from whic…
parole.testo: From Latin axilla. Doublet of axilla.

parole.significato: Divination by saws or axes.
parole.testo: Latin axinomantia, from Ancient Greek ἀξινομαντεία (axinomanteía), from ἀξίνη (axínē, “axe”) and μαντεία (manteía, “prophecy”)

parole.significato: An axiom.
parole.testo: From the Latin axiōma, from the Ancient Greek ἀξίωμα (axíōma): see axiom.

parole.significato: An imaginary line around which an object spins (an axis of rotation) or is symmetrically arranged (an axis of symmetry).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin axis (“axle, axis”) in the 16th century. Via Latin cognate with ala, aisle, atelier. Via Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- cognate with inherited English axle and borrowed axo-, axon.

parole.significato: A deer native to Asia, of species Axis axis.
parole.testo: From Latin, name of an Indian animal mentioned by the Roman senator Pliny.

parole.significato: The axis of Earth between the celestial poles, important in ancient geocentric coordinate systems.
parole.testo: From Latin axis mundi.

parole.significato: A tribe of Pannonia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Azalī.

parole.significato: sura (chapter of the Qurʾān)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin azoara.

parole.significato: Unleavened bread used in Jewish or Christian religious contexts.
parole.testo: From Late Latin azyma, from the adjective azymus (“unleavened”), from Ancient Greek ἄζυμος (ázumos).

parole.significato: One who administers the Eucharist with unleavened bread, in particular a member of the Latin Church or Roman Catholic C…
parole.testo: From Latin azȳmita, from Ancient Greek ἀζῡμίτης (azūmítēs), from ἄζῡμος (ázūmos) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs, suffix forming masculine nouns meaning being connected to or a member of something, or coming from a particular place). ἄζῡμος is derived from ᾰ̓- (ă-, the alpha privativum, a prefix forming words havi

parole.significato: unleavened, unfermented.
parole.testo: From Latin azymus (“unleavened, uncorrupted”).

parole.significato: A confused mixture of sounds and voices, especially in different languages.
parole.testo: From Latin Babel, from Biblical Hebrew בָּבֶל (bāḇel, “Babylon”), from Akkadian 𒆍𒀭𒊏𒆠 (Bābilim); in Genesis associated with the idea of confusion. Doublet of Babylon.

parole.significato: Any mammal in the genus Babyrousa in the pig family Suidae, in which the upper tusk grows upward.
parole.testo: From scientific Latin babyroussa (later as specific name), and its source, Malay babi rusa, from babi (“pig”) + rusa (“deer”).

parole.significato: A female baboon.
parole.testo: From New Latin, feminine of babuinus, from French babouin.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the city of Babylon, or the Babylonian Empire.
parole.testo: From Latin Babylōnius (“of Babylon, Babylonian”) (from Ancient Greek Βαβυλώνιος (Babulṓnios)) + -an. By surface analysis, Babylon + -ian. Piecewise doublet of Babelian.

parole.significato: Pertaining to Babylon, or made there.
parole.testo: From Latin Babylōnicus.

parole.significato: Stand back! give place!
parole.testo: back and Latin -āre. A cant word of the Elizabethan writers, probably in ridicule of some person who pretended to a knowledge of Latin which he did not possess.

parole.significato: Pulpy throughout, like a berry; said of fruits.
parole.testo: From Latin baccātus (“set or adorned with berries or pearls”), from bacca (“berry; pearl”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Relating to Bacchus or his festival.
parole.testo: From Latin Bacchānālis (“of or pertaining to Bacchus”). See Bacchanalia.

parole.significato: A priest of Bacchus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bacchantem, present active participle of bacchor (“to celebrate rites of Bacchus; to revel”), from Bacchus (“the god of wine”), from Ancient Greek Βάκχος (Bákkhos).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Bacchus.
parole.testo: From Latin Bacchicus.

parole.significato: Producing berries.
parole.testo: From Latin baccifer (“bearing berries”), bacca (“berry”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Having the form of a berry.
parole.testo: From Latin baca (“berry”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Eating, or having a diet based on, berries
parole.testo: Latin bāca (“berry”) + -vorous

parole.significato: Shaped like a rod or staff.
parole.testo: From Latin bacillum (“little staff”).

parole.significato: Any of various rod-shaped, spore-forming aerobic bacteria in the genus Bacillus, some of which cause disease.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bacillus (“little staff, wand”), diminutive of baculum (“stick, staff, walking stick”).

parole.significato: An oval bacterium, as distinguished from a spherical coccus or rod-shaped bacillus.
parole.testo: From New Latin bactēria, from Ancient Greek βακτηρίᾱ (baktēríā, “rod, stick”).

parole.significato: A single-celled organism with cell walls but no nucleus or organelles.
parole.testo: From New Latin bactērium, from Ancient Greek βακτήριον (baktḗrion, “small staff”), from βακτηρία (baktēría).

parole.significato: A rod-like element on the surface of some pollen.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin baculum.

parole.significato: Shaped like a bacillus; rod-shaped.
parole.testo: Latin baculum (“staff”) + -iform

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a rod or cane, or punishment with either of them.
parole.testo: Latin baculum (“staff”).

parole.significato: Any member of the genus †Baculites of extinct cephalopod heteromorph ammonites.
parole.testo: From Latin baculum (“stick”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Any large rod-shaped virus of the family Baculoviridae, including the granuloviruses and nucleopolyhedroviruses.
parole.testo: From baculo- + virus, from Latin baculum (“rod”).

parole.significato: A bone found in the penis of some placental mammals.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin baculum (“stick, staff, sceptre, cudgel”).

parole.significato: Chestnut-coloured.
parole.testo: From Latin badius (“reddish brown, chestnut colored”), with the suffix adapted to -ous.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a region of southern Spain, the mountain range that dominates it, and the language spoken there.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin baeticus.

parole.significato: A meteorite or similar-looking rough stone thought to be of divine origin and worshipped as sacred.
parole.testo: From Latin baetulus, from Ancient Greek βαίτυλος (baítulos, “a meteoric stone”).

parole.significato: Bearing or producing acorns.
parole.testo: From Latin balanus (“acorn”) + -ferous. By surface analysis, balan(us) + -i- + -fer + -ous.

parole.significato: Relating to the glans.
parole.testo: From Latin balanus, from Ancient Greek βάλανος (bálanos). By surface analysis, balan(us) + -o-.

parole.significato: The glans
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balanus, from Ancient Greek βάλανος (bálanos, “acorn”).

parole.significato: A buffoon; one who speaks a lot of nonsense and is characterized by self-indulgence.
parole.testo: From Latin balatrō (“jester, buffoon”). Cognate with Galician baladrón, Spanish baladrón, both meaning "braggart".

parole.significato: The red roselike flower of the pomegranate, having a bitter taste and sometimes used as an astringent in folk medicine.
parole.testo: Latin balaustinus

parole.significato: To stammer.
parole.testo: Latin balbutire, from balbus (“stammering”): compare French balbutier.

parole.significato: stammering
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balbūtiēs.

parole.significato: Meum athamanticum, an ornamental plant in the Apiaceae family.
parole.testo: Apparently a corruption of Latin valdē bona (“very good”) (a plant mentioned in Leonhart Fuchs's Great Herbal). Earliest forms seem to come from an intermediate, unattested French form baudemoine (modern French baudremoine) and by analogy to the plant name agrimony.

parole.significato: nonsensical
parole.testo: From Latin balducta (“the curds of milk”).

parole.significato: An ancient military engine, in the form of a crossbow, used for hurling large missiles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ballista, from Ancient Greek βαλλίστρα (ballístra), from βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”).

parole.significato: A crossbowman.
parole.testo: From Latin ballistārius.

parole.significato: Of or relating to ballistics.
parole.testo: From Latin ballista (“a military siege engine for throwing stones”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Synonym of bailey (“fortification”).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ballium.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to baths or to bathing
parole.testo: From Latin balneum (“bath, bathing place”) + -al.

parole.significato: A room for bathing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balnearium, from balneum (“bath”), from Ancient Greek βαλανεῖον (balaneîon).

parole.significato: The act of bathing.
parole.testo: From Latin balneum (“bath”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a bath
parole.testo: Latin balneatorius.

parole.significato: bath
parole.testo: From Latin balneum (“bath”).

parole.significato: A description or study of therapeutic baths.
parole.testo: From Latin balneum (“bath”) + -graphy.

parole.significato: The treatment of disease by bathing.
parole.testo: From Latin balneum (“bath”) + therapy.

parole.significato: A sweet-smelling oil or resin derived from various plants.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balsamum, from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon, “balsam”), of Semitic origin (Hebrew בושם (“spice, perfume”)); compare Old English balsam, balsamum (“balsam, balm”), Doublet of balm and desman. Not related to balsa.

parole.significato: A plant, the Impatiens balsamina, or garden balsam.
parole.testo: From Latin balsamina (“balsam plant”) (perhaps via French balsamine), from Ancient Greek βαλσαμίνη (balsamínē). The Latin name of the unrelated balsam plant must have been applied to Impatiens balsamina soon after it arrived in Europe- Leonhart Fuchs referred to it as balsamina as early as 1542.

parole.significato: An ethnic descendant of the Indo-European Baltic people, especially including ethnic Lithuanians, Latvians or Prussians…
parole.testo: Back-formation from Baltic and/or Medieval Latin and Late Latin Balthae; see Baltic for more.

parole.significato: The girdle of a biblical Jewish priest.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balteus (“belt, girdle”).

parole.significato: A very large wine bottle with the capacity of about 12 liters, equivalent to 16 standard bottles.
parole.testo: From Middle English Balthasar, from Latin Baltassar, from Ancient Greek Βαλτάσαρ (Baltásar), from Hebrew בֵּלְשַׁאצַּר (bēlšaṣṣar), attested in the Tanakh and the Old Testament (Daniel 5:1), from Akkadian 𒁹𒀭𒂗𒈗𒋀 (Bēl-šarra-uṣṣur, literally “May Bel protect the king”). Doublet of Belshazzar.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Baltic region or the Baltic Sea.
parole.testo: From Latin Balticus, from Latin Balthae (“dwellers near the Baltic sea”); equivalent to Balt + -ic. The ultimate origin of the ethnonym is unknown, but possibilities include: * Related to Lithuanian baltas (“white”) and Proto-Slavic *bolto (“swamp, bog, mud”), which are likely from Proto-Indo-Europe

parole.significato: Being or relating to a type of court involving a bench of judges, often an appeals court.
parole.testo: From in banco, from Latin in banco.

parole.significato: A permanent, publicly promulgated expulsion from the University of Oxford, whose public posting served to prevent the e…
parole.testo: Historically, from Medieval Latin bannimus (“we banish, we expel”), from bannō, bandō (“denounce, ban, banish, proclaim, proscribe”, verb), influenced in meaning by bannum (“ordinance, ban”), from Frankish *bannjan (“to proclaim, order or prohibit under penalty”), from Proto-Germanic *bannijaną (“to

parole.significato: The act of expulsion.
parole.testo: From Latin bannitio. See banish.

parole.significato: Synonym of ban (“gathering for war; mulct or penalty”).
parole.testo: From Latin bannum.

parole.significato: A tree, Adansonia digitata, native to tropical Africa, having a broad swollen trunk and edible gourd-like hanging fruit…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bahobab, from Arabic أَبُو حِبَاب (ʔabū ḥibāb, “father of many seeds”), from أَبُو (ʔabū, “father”) + حَبّ (ḥabb, “seed”).

parole.significato: A designated space within a church, or a separate room or building associated with a church, where a baptismal font is…
parole.testo: From Middle English baptistery, baptisterie, from Ecclesiastical Latin baptistērium, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστήριον (baptistḗrion); equivalent to baptism + -ry.

parole.significato: Baptism.
parole.testo: From Middle English baptizacion, from Latin baptizātiō. By surface analysis, baptize + -ation.

parole.significato: A pit, especially one at Athens into which criminals were thrown.
parole.testo: From Latin barathrum, from Ancient Greek βάραθρον (bárathron).

parole.significato: Relating to beards.
parole.testo: From Latin barba (“beard”) + -al.

parole.significato: Relating to people, countries, or customs perceived as uncivilized or inferior.
parole.testo: From Middle English barbarian, borrowed from Medieval Latin barbarinus (“Berber, pagan, foreigner”), from Latin barbaria (“foreign country”), from barbarus (“foreigner, savage”), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “foreign, non-Greek, strange”), possibly onomatopoeic (mimicking foreign languages

parole.significato: Rule by barbarians.
parole.testo: From Latin barbarus (“foreigner, savage”), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “foreign, strange”) + -cracy.

parole.significato: Not classical or pure.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Latin barbarus (“foreigner, savage”), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “foreign, strange”).

parole.significato: bearded; having long thin hairs
parole.testo: PIE word  *bʰardʰéh₂ Borrowed from Latin barbātus, from barba (“beard”) + -ātus (“-ate”). By surface analysis, barb + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Any of the thorny shrubs of genus Berberis, which bear yellow flowers and red or blue-black berries.
parole.testo: From Middle English berberie, from Medieval Latin berberis (on which see Arabic بَرْبَارِيس (barbārīs)), influenced by berie (“berry”). Doublet of berberis and related to Berber.

parole.significato: A tax, similar to murage, paid for the upkeep of a barbican.
parole.testo: From barbican + -age, or from Late Latin barbicanagium.

parole.significato: Having a beard; bearded; hairy.
parole.testo: From Latin barbiger from barba (“beard”) + gerō (“carry, wear”).

parole.significato: an ancient stringed musical instrument, apparently a type of lute or lyre
parole.testo: From Latin barbiton, from Ancient Greek βάρβιτον (bárbiton).

parole.significato: An ancient stringed musical instrument from Greece, apparently a type of lute or lyre.
parole.testo: From Latin barbitos, from Ancient Greek βάρβιτος (bárbitos).

parole.significato: A small barb or beard.
parole.testo: PIE word  *bʰardʰéh₂ Borrowed from Latin barbula (“little beard”).

parole.significato: A board fastened to the projecting gables of a roof to protect and hide other timbers.
parole.testo: Probably from Medieval Latin bargus (“a scaffold”).

parole.significato: Any of several compounds of barium, especially barium sulphate and barium hydroxide.
parole.testo: From New Latin baryta, from 18c. Latinization of French barote, 1782 coinage from Ancient Greek βαρύτης (barútēs, “heaviness”), from βαρύς (barús) + -της (-tēs).

parole.significato: Kiss.
parole.testo: From Latin bāsium (“kiss”).

parole.significato: A hard mafic igneous rock of varied mineral content; volcanic in origin, which makes up much of the Earth's oceanic cru…
parole.testo: From Late Latin basaltes, a misspelling of Latin basanites, from Ancient Greek βασανίτης (basanítēs), from βάσανος (básanos, “touchstone”), from Egyptian bḫn (“a hard stone”), b-x:n-O39

parole.significato: A basaltic extrusive rock, similar to chert.
parole.testo: From Latin basanites; more at basalt.

parole.significato: Positioned at the base; forming a base
parole.testo: From Latin basis.

parole.significato: Kissing.
parole.testo: From Latin bāsiātiō.

parole.significato: A Christian church building having a nave with a semicircular apse, side aisles, a narthex and a clerestory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βᾰσῐλῐκή (băsĭlĭkḗ), from βᾰσῐλῐκὴ στοά (băsĭlĭkḕ stoá, “royal hall”), ultimately from βασιλικός (basilikós, “royal”), from βασιλεύς (basileús, “king, chief”). Doublet of basoche.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Gnostic sect founded by Basilides of Alexandria in the 2nd century.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Basilidiānus, from Byzantine Greek Βασιλειδιανός (Basileidianós). By surface analysis, Basilides + -ian.

parole.significato: The middle of the anterior margin of the foramen magnum of the skull.
parole.testo: From New Latin, equivalent to basi- (“base”) + -ion (“cephalometric reference point”).

parole.significato: A physical base or foundation.
parole.testo: From Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷémtis, derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (whence also come). Doublet of base.

parole.significato: An overwhelming urge to be kissed.
parole.testo: From Latin bāsium (“kiss”) + -orexia. The term is not recorded in other major dictionaries and is likely a neologism. By surface analysis, bas- + -orexia.

parole.significato: An ancient Germanic tribe living in the region of Batavia around Nijmegen.
parole.testo: From Latin Batavi.

parole.significato: A variety of lettuce with broad flat leaves.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin Batavia, from Proto-Germanic *Batawjō. Doublet of Betawi and Passau.

parole.significato: A gelatinous substance found in mud dredged from the Atlantic and once supposed to be a free living protoplasm, later f…
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek. See bathy-. Coined by Thomas Henry Huxley.

parole.significato: Any frog (narrow sense) or toad.
parole.testo: From New Latin Batrachia, former name of the zoological order Anura, from Ancient Greek βατράχεια (batrákheia), neuter plural of adjective from βάτραχος (bátrakhos, “frog”).

parole.significato: A pale greenish-grey variety of montmorillonite.
parole.testo: From Latin batrachītēs, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Order of battle; disposition or arrangement of troops or of a naval force, ready for action.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia (“military exercises”), from Latin battuō (“to strike, beat”), from Gaulish. Doublet of battle.

parole.significato: A wild plant related to chives; ramsons, Allium ursinum.
parole.testo: Calque from Latin Allium ursinum.

parole.significato: Blessed, blissful, heavenly.
parole.testo: From Latin beātificus (“making happy or blessed”), from beātus (“blessed”) + -ficus (“making”).

parole.significato: To beatify.
parole.testo: From Latin beātificāt-, the perfect passive participial stem of beātificō (“to bless, to make happy”). Equivalent to beatific + -ate.

parole.significato: A person who has been beatified.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin beātus.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a beak or bill.
parole.testo: From Latin beccus (“beak”).

parole.significato: An administrative official at universities in several European countries, often with a policiary function at the time w…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pedellus, bedellus, bidellus, from Middle English bedel; cognate with beadle.

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter B/b.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Old English be, from Latin be (the name of the letter B).

parole.significato: To engage in the logical fallacy of begging the question (petitio principii).
parole.testo: Translating Latin petītiō prīncipiī, itself translating Ancient Greek τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ αἰτεῖσθαι (tò en arkhēî aiteîsthai, “to assume from the beginning”).

parole.significato: A great and mighty beast which God shows to Job in Job 40:15–24.
parole.testo: From Middle English behemoth, bemoth, from Late Latin behemoth, from Hebrew בְּהֵמוֹת (behemót). Most likely, the Hebrew word is an intensive plural of בְּהֵמָה (behemá, “beast”), from Proto-Semitic (compare Ge'ez ብህመ (bəhmä, “to be dumb, to be speechless”), Arabic ب ه م (b h m)). Some have instead

parole.significato: Any of various plants imported into Europe for the pharmaceutical trade in dried form, so of uncertain identity.
parole.testo: A Medieval Latin transcription of the Arabic بَهْمَن (bahman).

parole.significato: A group of tribes living in northern Gaul, between the English Channel and the west bank of the Rhine, from at least th…
parole.testo: From Latin Belgae, an Iron-Age European group of tribes located between the rivers Seine and Rhine.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Belgae, a Germanic tribe.
parole.testo: From Latin Belgicus, from Belgae (“the Belgians”).

parole.significato: A female warrior.
parole.testo: From Latin bellatrix, assumably through French.

parole.significato: An inclination to war; warlike policy or behaviour.
parole.testo: From Latin bellic(us) + -ism.

parole.significato: An adherent of bellicism; one who advocates war.
parole.testo: From Latin bellicus (“of or pertaining to war; warlike”), + -ist; possibly adapted from the French neologism belliciste (about Bismarck, 1871; in Émile Faguet, 1908).

parole.significato: Warlike or combative in nature; aggressively hostile.
parole.testo: From Middle English bellicose, from Latin bellicosus.

parole.significato: Engaged in warfare, warring.
parole.testo: From Latin belligerans (“waging war”), present active participle of belligerō (“to wage war”), from belliger (“waging war, warlike”), from bellum (“war”) + -ger (from gerō (“to lead, wage, carry on”)).

parole.significato: Strength in battle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin bellipotentia.

parole.significato: Mighty in war.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bellipotēns.

parole.significato: A woman of great spirit and vigour.
parole.testo: From Latin Bellōna, related to bellum.

parole.significato: Of, characteristic of, or pertaining to beasts; animal, bestial; brutal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin belluīnus, an alternative spelling of bēluīnus (“animal, bestial; brutal”) (whence the English beluine) + -ine (“suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’”). Bēluīnus is derived from bēlua (“(wild) beast; monster; brute”) + -īnus (“suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’”) (from Proto-In

parole.significato: To swear fealty or allegiance to another person.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin genūflectō. Popularized by its use on the television series Game of Thrones (2011-2019).

parole.significato: Good.
parole.testo: UK C16. Probably from Latin bene or Italian bene.

parole.significato: A canticle, the Latin version of which begins with the word benedīcite (“praise ye!”), which may be used in the order f…
parole.testo: From Latin benedīcite, a plural imperative of benedīcō (“to bless; to praise”, literally “to say well (of)”).

parole.significato: Having mild and salubrious qualities.
parole.testo: From Latin benedictus, past participle of benedicere (“to bless”). See benison. Doublet of bennet.

parole.significato: A short invocation for help, blessing and guidance from God, said on behalf of another person or persons (sometimes at…
parole.testo: From Middle English benediccion, from Ecclesiastical Latin benedictio, benedictionis, from benedictus (“blessed; well spoken of”). Doublet of benison.

parole.significato: The Gospel canticle of Zechariah (Luke 1:68–79), with the incipit Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel (“Blessed be the Lord…
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin benedictus (“blessed, praised”), from benedīcō (“to speak well (of)”).

parole.significato: Blessed; benedict.
parole.testo: From Middle English benedyght, benedight, from Latin benedictus. More at benedict, benediction.

parole.significato: An act of doing good; a benefit, a blessing.
parole.testo: From Latin benefactiōnem, from benefacere (“to benefit”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the linguistic form or case or the semantic role of the beneficiary of an action. Expressed in Engl…
parole.testo: From Latin benefactus (“benefited”) plus -ive. Attested since the twentieth century.

parole.significato: Somebody who gives a gift, often money to a charity.
parole.testo: From Middle English benefactor, borrowed from Medieval Latin benefactor (“he who bestows a favor”), from Latin benefaciō (“benefit someone”), from bene (“good”) + faciō (“do, make”).

parole.significato: A female benefactor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin benefactrīx. By surface analysis, benefactor + -trix.

parole.significato: An act of doing good; benefaction, beneficence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin benefactūrus, future active participle of benefaciō (“to do good, to benefit”) + -ure (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Favorable; beneficent.
parole.testo: From Latin beneficus. See benefice.

parole.significato: The practice of doing good, such as acts of philanthropy, kind deeds; or other acts which benefit someone else.
parole.testo: From Middle English beneficence, from Latin beneficentia.

parole.significato: Given to acts that are kind, charitable, philanthropic or beneficial.
parole.testo: From Latin *beneficens, *beneficent-, from bene (“well, good”) + -ficens, combining form from faciens, present participle of facere (“to make or do”). Compare English beneficence.

parole.significato: Helpful or good to something or someone.
parole.testo: From Late Latin beneficiālis (“beneficial”), from Latin beneficium (“benefit, favor, kindness”).

parole.significato: One who benefits or receives an advantage.
parole.testo: From Latin beneficiarius (“enjoying a favor, granted a privilege”) from beneficium (“benefit”), perhaps via or influenced by French bénéficiaire (“beneficiary”). parole.significato: Synonym of benefice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin beneficium.

parole.significato: kind; benevolent
parole.testo: Latin benevolus.

parole.significato: A $100 bill, which bears a portrait of Benjamin Franklin.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Benjamin, from Ancient Greek Βενιαμίν (Beniamín), from Biblical Hebrew בִּנְיָמִין (binyamīn, literally “son of the right/south or son of days”). Authorities differ on the meaning of the original Hebrew. Philo of Alexandria, the Samaritan Pentateuch The Testament of the Twelve Patria

parole.significato: Normal occlusion (alignment) of the teeth when the jaws are closed.
parole.testo: Probably coined by Simeon Hayden Guilford ante 1905: Latin ben(e) (“well, properly”) + occlusion (“alignment of the teeth in closed jaws”), after malocclusion (“misalignment of the upper and lower sets of teeth”).

parole.significato: A medieval English sheep farm.
parole.testo: From Latin bercaria (“sheepcote”).

parole.significato: A small, oval, transparent jellyfish, of genus Beroe (phylum Ctenophora).
parole.testo: Latin Beroe (“one of the Oceanidae”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Berytus (“the ancient city of Beirut”).
parole.testo: From Berytus + -ian (suffix meaning ‘from, related to, or like’; or ‘one from, belonging to, relating to, or like’). Berytus is derived from Latin Bērȳtus, from Ancient Greek Βηρῡτός (Bērūtós), from a Semitic source.

parole.significato: A bronze coin of the Roman Republic, worth two thirds of an as.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bes.

parole.significato: A medieval treatise of various real or imaginary animals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bēstiārium, from Latin bēstia (“beast, animal”). By surface analysis, beast + -ary.

parole.significato: A sweet, crystalline compound (not an alkaloid), trimethylammoniumacetate, found in sugar beet and similar plants, some…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin bēta (“beet”) + -ine.

parole.significato: A class of red and yellow indole-derived water-soluble pigments found in beets and other plants of the Caryophyllales a…
parole.testo: Coined to describe the pigments as derivatives from betalamic acid, from Latin bēta (“beet”), + -in.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Stachys.
parole.testo: From Middle English betayny, betanie, from Medieval Latin betōnia (possibly through Old French), from Latin betōnica or ve(t)tōnica, from Vettones, a people in Lusitania. Compare French bétoine.

parole.parola: better an egg today than a hen tomorrow
parole.significato: It is better to have a sure thing now than a possibility of more later.
parole.termine_origine: ad praesens ova cras pullis sunt meliora

catena.termine: ad praesens ova cras pullis sunt meliora

parole.testo: Calque of Latin ad praesens ova cras pullis sunt meliora, from Gargantua and Pantagruel by Rabelais.

parole.significato: A person's spouse or lover, most commonly a man's wife.
parole.testo: Ultimately from such Latin poetic phrases as animae dīmidium meae (“half of my soul”) (Horace writing about Virgil), when it instead referred to a close friend (compare soulmate). First written instance of it meaning “spouse” was in 1580 by Sir Philip Sidney.

parole.significato: It is better to do something late, than to never do it at all.
parole.testo: Perhaps a calque of Latin potius sero quam numquam from the 4th book of Ab Urbe condita (History of Rome) by Titus Livius, around 27 BC.

parole.significato: An enzyme that hydrolyzes the glucoside of methyl salicylate.
parole.testo: From Latin betula (“birch tree”) + -ase.

parole.significato: An organic compound with chemical formula C₃₆H₅₂O₁₆, obtained by adding betulin to nitric acid.
parole.testo: From betulin and Latin amārus (“bitter”).

parole.significato: One should not trust one's enemies.
parole.testo: Alludes to the ancient story of the Trojan horse, a gift for the Trojans which secretly contained Greeks. parole.significato: Two in number.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ Borrowed from Latin bi-, from Proto-Italic *dwi-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwi-. Doublet of twi- and di-.

parole.significato: Addicted to drinking alcohol; alcoholic
parole.testo: From Latin bibāx, bibācis, ultimately from bibō + -acious. See bib.

parole.significato: The practice or habit of drinking too much alcohol.
parole.testo: From Latin bibāx, bibācis, ultimately from bibō + -acity.

parole.significato: Drinking, act of drinking (especially alcohol), imbibing.
parole.testo: From Latin bibō (“I drink”) + -ation (“act of”).

parole.significato: penchant for drinking, love of liquids (not necessarily alcoholic), thirst.
parole.testo: Coined circa 1843, by Orson Squire Fowler, as variant of earlier aquativeness (1843), by analogy with earlier alimentiveness (1828). From Latin bibō (“I drink”) + -ative (“related to”) + -ness (“the quality of”); compare Latin bibāx (“tending to drink”).

parole.significato: A specific version, edition, translation, or copy of one of the above-mentioned texts.
parole.testo: From Middle English bible, from Medieval Latin biblia (“book”) (misinterpreted as a feminine from earlier Latin neuter plural biblia (“books”)), from Ancient Greek βιβλία (biblía, “books”), plural of βιβλίον (biblíon, “small book”), originally a diminutive of βίβλος (bíblos, “book”), from βύβλος (bú

parole.significato: A medieval Bible consisting of mainly pictures rather than text.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?] (literally “paupers' Bible”)

parole.significato: Biblical.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin biblicus, analyzable as bible + -ic.

parole.significato: Bookbinding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin bibliopegus (“bookbinder”) + -ism.

parole.significato: A bookseller.
parole.testo: From Latin bibliopōla, from Ancient Greek βιβλίον (biblíon, “paper, document, tablet”) + πωλέω (pōléō, “to barter, sell”) — (compare with the etymology of monopoly).

parole.significato: Bookselling.
parole.testo: From bibliopole (“bookseller”) + -poly (suffix denoting sellers in a market). parole.significato: A library.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bibliothēca, borrowed from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē, “library”). Equivalent to biblio- + -theca. Doublet of bibliotheque.

parole.significato: Belonging or pertaining to a library.
parole.testo: From Latin bibliothēcālis. See bibliotheque.

parole.significato: A librarian.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bibliothēcārius (“librarian”), from bibliothēca (“library”) + -ārius, from Ancient Greek βῐβλῐοθήκη (bĭblĭothḗkē, “library”), from βῐβλῐ́ον (bĭblĭ́on) + θήκη (thḗkē). Compare French bibliothécaire and Italian and Spanish bibliotecario. By surface analysis, bibliotheca +

parole.significato: Very absorbent.
parole.testo: From Latin bibulus from bibō (“drink”) + -ulus from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti, from root *peh₃- (“drink”); whence also imbibe and beverage via Old French beivre.

parole.significato: Having two tails
parole.testo: From bi- + caudal, from Latin cauda (“tail”).

parole.significato: Any muscle having two heads.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin biceps (“double-headed, two-peaked”), from bis (“twice”) + -ceps (“headed”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a biceps.
parole.testo: From Latin biceps (“double-headed”).

parole.significato: Having two colours
parole.testo: From Latin bicolor; also analyzable as bi- + colour.

parole.significato: A two-cornered hat, worn by European and American military and naval officers from the 1790s.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bicornis (“two-horned; two-pronged”). Compare French bicorne (“two-cornered hat; two-horned monster”) and Middle English bicorne (“two-horned anvil; two-pronged fork; fabulous (two-horned) beast”). Doublet of bicorne.

parole.significato: twice a day, two times per day
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bis in diē.

parole.significato: A form of spear having two prongs.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Latin bidentis (“two-toothed”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Rome, a place that had been struck by lightning and consecrated and enclosed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bidental.

parole.significato: Continuing for two days.
parole.testo: From Latin biduus.

parole.significato: Synonym of biennial: of or concerning a two-year period; lasting or occurring every two years.
parole.testo: From Latin biennium (“a two-year period”) + -ary (“forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Happening every two years.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bienni(um) (“two-year period”) [from bis, bi- (“twice”) + annus (“year”)] + -al (suffix forming adjectives). By surface analysis, bi- + -ennial.

parole.significato: A period of two years, particularly for purposes involving intercalation or fiscal calculations.
parole.testo: From Latin biennium, from biennis (“2-year”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns), from bi- (“two”) + annus (“year”), q.v.

parole.significato: twofold, double
parole.testo: From Latin bifārius (“twofold, double”), back-formed from the adverb bifāriam.

parole.significato: Cleft; divided into two principal or main parts, such as two lobes.
parole.testo: From Latin bifidus (“divided in two”), from bi- (“two”) + -fidus, combining form of findere (“to split”).

parole.significato: Bifid, divided into two main parts.
parole.testo: First attested in 1847; borrowed from Latin bifidātus, from bifidus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, bifid + -ate.

parole.significato: Bearing two flowers or blooms.
parole.testo: Latin bis twice + flos, floris (“flower”) + English -ous. By surface analysis, bi- + Latin flor- + -ous.

parole.significato: An oval sac or cell, found in the idioblasts of the leaves of certain araceous plants, with an opening at each end thro…
parole.testo: From Latin biforis, biforus (“having two doors”), from bis (“twice”) + foris (“door”).

parole.significato: Biforate.
parole.testo: From Latin biforis (“having two doors”), from bis (“twice, two”) + foris (“door”).

parole.significato: To divide or fork into two channels or branches.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin bifurcātus. Surface Analysis bi- + furcate.

parole.significato: Divided into two branches.
parole.testo: From verb bifurcate, from Medieval Latin bifurcatus, past participle of bifurcare, from Latin bifurcus (“two-pronged”), from bi- + furca (“fork”).

parole.significato: bifurcate
parole.testo: From Latin bifurcus, from bis (“twice”) + furca (“fork”).

parole.significato: A Roman racing chariot drawn by two horses abreast.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bīga.

parole.significato: A bigamist, or one who has married a widow.
parole.testo: From Latin bigamus (“twice married”): compare French bigame. See bigamy.

parole.significato: Bearing the figure of a bigae (pair of horses).
parole.testo: From Latin bīgātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Occurring in pairs; doubled or twinned
parole.testo: Latin bigeminus (“doubled”), from bi- (“two”) + geminus (“double”).

parole.significato: bijugate
parole.testo: From Latin bijugus (“yoked two together”), from bis (“twice”) + jugum (“yoke, pair”).

parole.significato: Bile.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Latin bīlis (“bile”).

parole.significato: A brownish-green pigment, derived from bilirubin, found in human gallstones and in old bile.
parole.testo: From Latin bilis (“bile”) + fuscus (“dark”) + -in.

parole.significato: Any of various biological pigments formed in many organisms as a metabolic product of certain porphyrins.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, and clearly reflecting New Latin, from Latin bīlis (“bile”). parole.significato: Having the ability to speak two languages fluently.
parole.testo: From Latin bilinguis + -al; equivalent to bi- + lingual.

parole.significato: Double-tongued, deceiving.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin bilinguis (“double-tongued”).

parole.significato: bilingual.
parole.testo: Latin bilinguis.

parole.significato: A dark green pigment found in small quantities in human gallstones.
parole.testo: From Latin bilis (“bile”) + prasinus (“green”).

parole.significato: Signifying that a presenter has furnished probable evidence, and is worthy of further consideration, presented to a par…
parole.testo: From the Latin, literally "the bill is true".

parole.significato: An alkylresorcinol and strong skin irritant found in Gingko biloba fruits.
parole.testo: From Latin biloba + -ol.

parole.significato: The ability to speak in two different voices, especially as a ventriloquist.
parole.testo: Probably coined by American novelist Charles Brockden Brown (1771-1810), from the Latin bi- (“two”) + loquor (“to speak”) + -ium.

parole.significato: Having two hands (rather than any other distal part of a forelimb).
parole.testo: From Latin bi (“two”) + manus (“hand”) + -ous.

parole.significato: Having two members.
parole.testo: From Latin bis (“twice”) + membrum (“member”).

parole.significato: The 2,000th anniversary of an event or happening.
parole.testo: From Latin bimillennialis, from bi- (“two”) mill- (“thousand”) + enni(us) (“yearly”). By surface analysis, bi- + millennial. Compare bicentennial.

parole.significato: To dispose of (something) by putting it into a bin, or as if putting it into a bin.
parole.testo: From Middle English bynne, from Old English binn (“crib, manger”), from Late Latin benna or a Celtic language, possibly Proto-Brythonic *benn (“cart, carriage”) (whence Middle Welsh benn, Old Breton benn (“caisson”), modern Welsh ben), from Proto-Celtic *bend(n)ā (whence Gaulish benna). Compare Germ

parole.significato: Being in one of two mutually exclusive states.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English binarie. By surface analysis, bin- + -ary.

parole.significato: To perform bination; to hold Mass twice on the same day.
parole.testo: From Latin bīnātus, past participle of bīnō (“to binate”), from bīnus (“two each, in pairs”). Equivalent to Latin bīnō + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A name having two parts.
parole.testo: Latin bis (“double, twice”) + nōmen (“name”).

parole.significato: Consisting of two terms, or parts.
parole.testo: Formed from Late Latin binōmium + -al. The derivation of binōmium is unclear. It was used by Gerard of Cremona in the 12th century. parole.significato: Consisting of two names.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin binōminis (“having two names”).

parole.significato: A person's life story, especially one published.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin biographia, from Ancient Greek βιογραφίᾱ (biographíā), from βίος (bíos, life) + -γραφία (-graphía, writing).

parole.significato: The study of all life or living matter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin biologia (1766), itself from Ancient Greek βίος (bíos, “bio-, life”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy, branch of study, to speak”). By surface analysis, bio- + -logy. In English, first attested in the modern meaning in the work of English physician Thomas Beddoes in 1799. The term is

parole.significato: A horizontally bedded stratum of fossilized remains of sedentary organisms
parole.testo: bio- (“life”) + Latin stroma (“coverlet”), from Ancient Greek στρῶμα (strôma, “bed, mattress”).

parole.significato: Synonym of life; Biota; all living things.
parole.testo: From New Latin biota, from Ancient Greek βιοτή (biotḗ), from βίος (bíos).

parole.significato: Dividing into two parts.
parole.testo: From Latin bis (“twice”) + partiens, present participle of partire (“to divide”).

parole.significato: Having two parts (two principal or main parts).
parole.testo: From Latin bipartītus (“bisected”), perfect passive participle of bipartiō (“to divide into two parts, bisect”). By surface analysis, bi- + part + -ite.

parole.significato: An animal, being, or construction that goes about on two feet (or two legs).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bipēs, bipedis. Alternatively analyzable as bi- + -ped.

parole.significato: An axe with an edge or blade on each side of the handle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bipennis (“two-winged”).

parole.significato: The larva of certain starfishes as developed in the free-swimming stage.
parole.testo: From Latin bis (“twice”) + pinna (“feather”).

parole.significato: Doubly pinnate; pinnate and having leaflets that are themselves pinnate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin bipinnātus or from bi + pinnate.

parole.significato: The state of being twice folded; reduplication.
parole.testo: From Latin bi- (“twice”). Bailey (1736) suggests borrowing from Latin biplicitas, but this is not well attested. Compare duplicity, from Latin duplicare (“double”).

parole.significato: Relating to books printed at Zweibrücken in Bavaria.
parole.testo: See bi- and Latin pōns (“bridge”). Zweibrücken means "two bridges".

parole.significato: a neume denoting either a single tone, either elongated or rearticulated.
parole.testo: From Latin bipunctum (“double point”).

parole.significato: An ancient galley having two banks of oars, one above the other.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin birēmis.

parole.significato: Two-wheeled.
parole.testo: From bi + rotate (“wheel-shaped”), ultimately from Latin rota (“wheel”).

parole.significato: A microsclere that has a straight shaft and umbrella-shaped ends
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin birota, feminine of birotus, from bi- (“two, double”) + rota (“wheel”) + -us.

parole.significato: A coarse kind of thick woollen cloak, worn by the poor in the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin birrus (“a kind of cloak”), from Gaulish *birros, from Proto-Celtic *birros (“short”).

parole.significato: Twice; showing that something is, or is to be, repeated, such as a passage of music, or an item in accounts.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bis (“twice”).

parole.significato: Something (e.g., payment, assistance, etc.) given promptly is much more valuable than if given after considerable delay.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bis dat qui cito dat.

parole.significato: Bisexual, hermaphroditic (having both male and female parts or functions).
parole.testo: From Latin bis (“twice”) + sexus (“sex”). Compare French bissexe.

parole.significato: The bissextile intercalary day.
parole.testo: From Middle English bisext, from Latin bisextus, bissextus.

parole.testo: From Latin bisextilis/bissextilis (annus) (“bissextile year”), from bisextus + -ilis, from bis- (“two; twice; doubled”) + sextus (“sixth”) + dies (“day”), from the Julian calendar's original reckoning of its quadrennial intercalary day as a 48-hour February 24, subsequently distinguished as the two

parole.significato: A member of the Bistons or Bistones
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Bistōn, from Ancient Greek Βίστων (Bístōn).

parole.significato: Any of several perennial herbs, classified in genera Bistorta, Persicaria, or Polygonum, having spikes of pink flowers.
parole.testo: From Latin bistorta, from bis (“twice”) and torta (“twisted”), in reference to its twisting roots.

parole.significato: bisulcate
parole.testo: From Latin bisulcus, from bis (“twice”) + sulcus (“furrow”).

parole.significato: A sticky, black, highly viscous liquid or semi-solid form of petroleum, burning with a bright flame. It occurs as an ab…
parole.testo: From Middle English bithumen, bitumen, from Latin bitūmen. Doublet of bitume.

parole.significato: To treat or impregnate with bitumen.
parole.testo: First attested in 1628; borrowed from Late Latin bitūminātus, perfect passive participle of bitūminō (“to bituminate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from bitūmen + verb-forming suffix.

parole.significato: Both two and one at the same time (for example, Jesus Christ as God the Son and the Son of Man).
parole.testo: From bi- + Latin unus (“one”).

parole.significato: Having, or leading, two ways.
parole.testo: From Latin bivius (“two-way, having two approaches”) + English -ous.

parole.significato: One side of an echinoderm, including a pair of ambulacra, in distinction from the opposite side (trivium), which includ…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bivium (“a place with two ways”).

parole.significato: One of the four humours of ancient and mediaeval physiology, that was believed to be secreted by the kidneys and spleen…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin ātra bīlis, itself a calque of Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía).

parole.significato: The metal lead.
parole.testo: In the sense of lead, calque of Latin plumbum nigrum (“lead”, literally “black lead”).

parole.significato: Cygnus atratus, a swan with black plumage and a red bill which is endemic to Australia.
parole.testo: From Middle English blak swan, calqued from a Latin quotation from Satire VI (written late 1st century – early 2nd century B.C.E.) of the Roman poet Juvenal: “Rara avis in terris, nigroque simillima cygno [a bird as rare upon the earth as a black swan]!”. Equivalent to black + swan. Sense 2.1 (“some

parole.significato: A small Old World warbler, Eurasian blackcap (Sylvia atricapilla), which is mainly grey with a black crown.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin ātricapillus (“blackcap; black-haired”), itself a calque of Ancient Greek μελαγκόρυφος (melankóruphos). By surface analysis, black + cap.

parole.significato: The extortion of money or favors by threats of public accusation, critique, or exposure.
parole.testo: From black + mail (“a piece of money”). Compare Middle English blak rente (“a type of blackmail levied by Irish chieftains”). parole.significato: Having a soothing effect; not irritating or stimulating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin blandus (“pleasant”).

parole.significato: flattery
parole.testo: Compare Latin blanditia, blandities, from blandus. See bland, blandishment.

parole.significato: Flattery.
parole.testo: From Latin blandus (“flattering”) + loquor (“speak”).

parole.significato: Speaking, or spoken, in a mild, flattering manner.
parole.testo: From Latin blandus (“flattering”) + loquēns (“speaking”).

parole.significato: Blandishment; flattery.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin blandīmentum (“blandishment, pleasure, remedy”).

parole.significato: Lacking piety or respect for the sacred; resembling blasphemy.
parole.testo: From Latin blasphēmus (“blaspheming”), from Ancient Greek βλάσφημος (blásphēmos, “uttering ill-omened words”), equivalent to blaspheme + -ous.

parole.significato: An early form in the development of an embryo, consisting of a spherical layer of cells filled with fluid; a blastosphe…
parole.testo: From New Latin blastula, diminutive of Ancient Greek βλαστός (blastós, “a germ, bud, sprout, shoot”), from βλαστάνω (blastánō, “to bud, sprout, grow, properly of plants, but also of animals”).

parole.significato: Blather; foolish talk.
parole.testo: From Latin blaterāre. Influenced by other expressive verbs ending in -er.

parole.significato: blather; foolish talk
parole.testo: Latin blateratio (“a babbling”).

parole.significato: A senseless babbler or boaster.
parole.testo: From Latin blatero + -onis.
