parole.significato: Excessive blennorrhea, or mucous discharge, especially as seen in gonorrhea.
parole.testo: From blenno- + -rrhagia, New Latin combining forms based on Ancient Greek roots.

parole.significato: An inordinate secretion and discharge of mucus.
parole.testo: From blenno- + -rrhea, New Latin combining forms based on Ancient Greek roots.

parole.significato: A true blenny, any of various marine fishes from the suborder Blennioidei or order Blenniiformes that are generally sma…
parole.testo: From Latin blennius, blendius, from Ancient Greek βλέννα (blénna, “mucus, slime”) (whence Modern Greek βλέννα (vlénna)), because of its slimy coating. From Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“soft”).

parole.significato: Eyelid.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek βλέφαρον (blépharon, “eyelid”).

parole.significato: The plant Amaranthus blitum, purple amaranth.
parole.testo: From Latin blitum.

parole.significato: Any of a group of large American snakes, of the genus Boa, subfamily Boinae, or family Boidae, including the boa constr…
parole.testo: From Middle English boa, from Latin boa (“large snake”), a species of serpent mentioned in Pliny's Naturalis Historia (Natural History). The scarf was named attributively, for its resemblance to the snake when worn.

parole.significato: Bellowing.
parole.testo: From Latin boātiō (“roaring”, “bellowing”), noun of action of boō (“to roar”, “to bellow”).

parole.significato: The collective body of a nation or state as politically organized.
parole.testo: From body + politic (postpositive adjective), calque of Latin corpus polīticum.

parole.significato: Any of a group of rotenoids present in spiderlings of the genus Boerhavia.
parole.testo: From Latin Boerhavia + -one.

parole.significato: A Gallic tribe of the later Iron Age.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Boiī.

parole.significato: A type of hornblendic gabbro.
parole.testo: From Latin Boiī + -ite, coined in 1898 by E. Weinschenk.

parole.significato: A boys' game where two or three children form a base, and others jump on them to make the base collapse.
parole.testo: From Afrikaans. Possibly Latin bucca bucca quot sunt hic. See Talk page.

parole.significato: A type of fruiting body produced by certain fungus species in the order Boletales, especially those of genus Boletus, m…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bōlētus (“edible mushroom”), from Ancient Greek βωλίτης (bōlítēs).

parole.significato: An edible mushroom of genus Boletus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bōlētus.

parole.significato: A bolide or fireball (type of meteor)
parole.testo: From Latin bolis, from Ancient Greek βολίς (bolís, “missile, arrow, javelin”). Doublet of bolide.

parole.significato: A round mass of something, especially of chewed food in the mouth or alimentary canal.
parole.testo: From Late Latin bōlus (“clod of earth, lump”), plural bōlī, from Ancient Greek βῶλος (bôlos, “clod, lump”). Doublet of bole.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Bombax of tropical trees in the mallow family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: An acid obtained from the silkworm, now found to be acetic acid.
parole.testo: Latin bombyx (“silk, silkworm”): compare French bombique.

parole.significato: To hum or buzz.
parole.testo: From Latin bombizātum, supine form of bombizō (“buzz, fart”).

parole.significato: to buzz or hum; to speak idly, vacuously, or to little effect.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin bombināre (“buzz, hum”), variant of Latin bombilō, from Ancient Greek βομβυλιάζειν (bombuliázein), from βόμβος (bómbos, “booming, humming”), of imitative origin.

parole.significato: A buzzing or humming.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bombus.

parole.significato: silken; made of silk
parole.testo: From Latin bombycinus. See bombazine.

parole.significato: Buzzing like a bumblebee.
parole.testo: From Latin bombyx (“bumblebee”) + English -ious.

parole.significato: In good faith; genuinely, sincerely.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin bonā fidē (“in good faith”).

parole.significato: Sincerity, good faith.
parole.testo: From Latin bona (nominative feminine singular of bonus (“good”)) + fidēs (“faith”).

parole.significato: perishable goods
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The principle that there is no unowned property, and that if there is no other owner then property vests in the Crown.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A bonnacon.
parole.testo: From Latin bonāsus, from Ancient Greek βόνᾱσος (bónāsos).

parole.significato: The state of being enslaved or the practice of slavery.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English bondage (“serfdom”), from British Medieval Latin bondagium (“an inferior tenure held by a bond or husbandman”), from Middle English bond (“tenant farmer, serf”), from Old English bonda (“householder, husband, head of a family”), of Old Norse origin. Sense development in

parole.significato: Naturally good-moraled.
parole.testo: From Latin bonus (“good”) + -form.

parole.significato: Something extra that is good; an added benefit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bonus (“good”). Doublet of bona.

parole.significato: A small wooden doll that is covered with a cape and made to vanish as part of a magic trick.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bonus genius (literally “good spirit”).

parole.significato: Relating to, or impregnated with borax.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin borax (genitive boracis), itself via Arabic بَوْرَق (bawraq), from Persian بوره (bura).

parole.significato: A member of the Borani
parole.testo: From Latin Boranus.

parole.significato: A rumbling sound made by the movement of gas in the intestines.
parole.testo: From New Latin borborygmus, from Ancient Greek βορβορυγμός (borborugmós), of onomatopoeic origin.

parole.significato: The low-level tenure by which a bordar held his cottage.
parole.testo: Latin bordagium.

parole.significato: A person ranking below villeins and above serfs in the social hierarchy of a manor, holding just enough land to feed a…
parole.testo: From Latin bordarius, of Teutonic origin. See board.

parole.significato: Synonym of bordar (“person ranking below villeins and above serfs”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bordarius, from Old French borde (“hut, cabin, small farm”) + -arius.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or coming from the north.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin boreālis (“northern”), from Boreās, from Ancient Greek Βορέᾱς (Boréās, “personification of the north wind”).

parole.significato: A strait or narrow sea between two seas, or a lake and a sea.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to botany.
parole.testo: From the Medieval Latin botanicus, perhaps via the French botanique, from the Ancient Greek βοτανικός (botanikós), from βοτάνη (botánē, “herb, pasture”).

parole.significato: Having the shape of a sausage
parole.testo: Latin botulus (“sausage”), + -iform.

parole.significato: An anaerobic soil bacterium, Clostridium botulinum, that secretes the toxin botulin
parole.testo: From Latin botulus (“sausage”) + -īnum.

parole.significato: botulinum toxin
parole.testo: Latin botulus (“sausage”) + toxin, because botulism was linked to sausage poisoning.

parole.significato: Synonym of oxgang.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin bovāta, from Latin bov-, bōs + -āta.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to cattle.
parole.testo: From Latin bovīnus, from bōs (“ox”). Cognate to beef.

parole.significato: The rearing and care of cattle.
parole.testo: From Latin bos (“cattle”) + cultura (“cultivation”); stem ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws which also gave Ancient Greek βοῦς (boûs), and English cow.

parole.significato: Shaped like an ox.
parole.testo: From Latin bos, bovis (“ox”) + -form.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or characteristic of cattle, buffaloes, or bison.
parole.testo: PIE word  *gʷṓws Borrowed from Late Latin bovīnus (“relating to cattle”), from Latin bōs (“ox”). Cognate to beef.

parole.significato: A Mediterranean food fish of the genus Boops, which is a variety of sea bream; a bogue or oxeye.
parole.testo: From Latin bōx, from Ancient Greek βῶξ (bôx, “box (marine fish)”), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye, view”), a reference to the large size of the fish's eyes relative to its body.

parole.significato: The box tree, Buxus sempervirens.
parole.testo: From box + wood; box from Latin buxus (“box-tree, object made of boxwood”), of uncertain origin; compare Ancient Greek πύξος (púxos).

parole.significato: Shapeless trousers of wool or skin tied at the waist and ankles by cords, worn chiefly by the ancient Gauls.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bracae, plural of braca, from Gaulish *brāca, of Celtic origin, cognate with Proto-Germanic *brōks; akin to Old High German bruoh (“a pair of breeches”) and to Dutch broek (“a pair of trousers”).

parole.significato: Pertaining or belonging to the arm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bracchialis, from bracchium (“arm”). Doublet of brachialis.

parole.significato: A muscle in the upper arm that flexes the elbow joint, in conjunction with the biceps brachii.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bracchialis, brachialis. Doublet of brachial.

parole.significato: Having decussate branches.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin brachiātus, from brachium (“arm, branch”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Arm.
parole.testo: From Latin bracchium.

parole.significato: The second stage of larval development in many sea stars, following the bipinnaria
parole.testo: From Latin brachiolum, diminutive of brachium (“arm”).

parole.significato: The upper arm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bracchium (“arm”). Doublet of braccio.

parole.significato: Having a head that is short from front to back (relative to its width from left to right); having a broad skull with a…
parole.testo: From brachy- + cephalic, literally “short-headed”, via New Latin brachycephalus, from Ancient Greek βραχυκέφαλος (brakhuképhalos), from βραχύς (brakhús, “short”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).

parole.significato: Concise speech; laconism.
parole.testo: From Late Latin brachylogia from Ancient Greek βραχυλογία (brakhulogía), from βραχύς (brakhús, “short”) + -λογία (-logía, “speech”), equivalent to brachy- + -logy; compare brachyology.

parole.significato: A figure of speech that is an abbreviated expression, for example, the omission of "good" from "good morning!" (resulti…
parole.testo: From Late Latin brachiologia, from Ancient Greek βραχύς (brakhús, “short”) + -λογία (-logía, “speech”); compare brachylogy.

parole.significato: brachyural
parole.testo: From Latin brachyūrus, from Ancient Greek βραχύουρος (brakhúouros, “short-tailed”), from βραχύς (brakhús, “short”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).

parole.significato: A leaf or leaf-like structure from the axil out of which a stalk of a flower or an inflorescence arises.
parole.testo: From Latin bractea (“a thin plate of metal; gold leaf”).

parole.significato: Having bracts.
parole.testo: From Latin bracteātus (“gold-plated, golden”), from bractea (“gold leaf, veneer, glitter”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix). By surface analysis, bract + -eate (second element from -ea + -ate).

parole.significato: A gill or other organ having the same function.
parole.testo: From Latin branchia, from Ancient Greek βράγχια (bránkhia, “gills”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling gills; of or pertaining to the embryonic branchial arches and clefts from which the gi…
parole.testo: From New Latin branchialis, from Latin branchiae.

parole.significato: Furnished with branchiae; gilled, having gills.
parole.testo: From New Latin branchiatus.

parole.significato: Having gills; branchiate.
parole.testo: From branchia + -ferous, or directly from New Latin branchiferus.

parole.significato: Gill-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin branchia, branchiae (“gills”) + -form.

parole.significato: Any of several wild geese, of the genus Branta, that breed in the Arctic, but especially the brent goose, Branta bernic…
parole.testo: From New Latin/Medieval Latin Branta, latinized form of Old Norse brandgás (“sheldrake”), literally "burnt (black) goose," from Proto-Germanic *brandaz (“burning”) + *gans (“goose”).

parole.significato: Any of many plants of the genus Brassica, including cabbage, mustard and rapes
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin brassica.

parole.significato: The triazole β-[(4-chlorophenyl)methyl]-α-methyl-α-phenyl-1H-1,2,4-triazole-1-ethanol that inhibits brassinosteroid bio…
parole.testo: From brassine + -azole, from Latin brassica.

parole.significato: The indole phytoalexin methyl (1H-indol-3-ylmethyl)carbamodithioate present in Chinese cabbage (Brassica campestris)
parole.testo: From brassin + -in, from Latin brassica.

parole.significato: A brassinosteroid that promotes cell elongation and division.
parole.testo: From brassin + -ol + -ide, from Latin brassica.

parole.significato: Any of a family of steroidal plant hormones produced by members of the genus Brassica; the brassins
parole.testo: By surface analysis, brassine + -o- + steroid, from Latin brassica.

parole.significato: Food and entertainment provided by the state, particularly if intended to placate the people.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin panem et circenses, a reference to Satire 10 of the Roman poet Juvenal’s Satires (early 2nd century C.E.). The relevant passage states: “… nam qui dabat olim imperium, fasces, legiones, omnia, nunc se continet atque duas tantum res anxius optat, panem et circenses” (“[F]or that sover

parole.significato: Short.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin brevis (“short”). Doublet of brie- (bri-).

parole.significato: A book containing prayers, hymns, and so on for everyday use at the canonical hours.
parole.testo: From Latin breviārium (“summary”) (compare abbreviation), ultimately from brevis (“short”). Doublet of brevier and brimborion.

parole.significato: A short account, brief statement; a summary, abridgement or precis
parole.testo: First attested in 1581; borrowed from Latin breviātum, from the perfect passive participle of breviō (“shorten, abridge”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To abbreviate, shorten.
parole.testo: First attested in the beginning of the 16ᵗʰ century; either borrowed from Latin breviātus, the perfect passive participle of breviō (“shorten, abridge”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)) or apheretic form of abbreviate.

parole.significato: A pertinent and terse style of speech; a style of speech exhibiting brevity.
parole.testo: Latin breviloquentia.

parole.significato: A brevipennate (short-winged) bird, in a former proposed classification, Brevipennes
parole.testo: From Latin brevis (“short”) + penna (“wing”). Compare French brévipenne.

parole.significato: short-winged; having short wings.
parole.testo: From Latin brevis (“short”) + pennate.

parole.significato: Having a short beak or bill
parole.testo: Latin brevis (“short”) + English rostral.

parole.significato: The situation where a short syllable at the end of a line can be counted as long.
parole.testo: From Latin brevis in longō (brevis (“short (syllable)”) + in (“in”) + longus (“long”)).

parole.significato: 23491Pa, a short-lived isotope of protactinium.
parole.testo: Latin brevis (“brief”) + -ium

parole.significato: Relating to, or resembling, Briareus, a giant fabled to have a hundred hands; many-handed.
parole.testo: From Latin Briareius, from Briareus (“a mythological hundred-handed giant”).

parole.significato: A scouring pad used for cleaning dishes, made from steel wool containing soap.
parole.testo: From a trademark, probably related to brilliant. The company has claimed that the name derives from a Latin word for bright, but there is no such fitting word in attested Latin; the ancestor of such verbs as Italian brillare (“to shine”) would be a hypothetical Vulgar Latin *b(e)rillāre.

parole.significato: An ancient Briton.
parole.testo: From Middle English brytayn, from Latin Britannus (adjective and noun, plural Britannī), apparently from Brythonic (compare Old Welsh Priten).

parole.significato: of or pertaining to Britain, Great Britain or the United Kingdom; British
parole.testo: From Latin britannicus.

parole.significato: A coward.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Bretany, Brytany, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin Britannia, applied to Brittany from at least the 6th century, and reinforced by Middle French Bretagne. See Britannia for more. Doublet of Britain and Britannia.

parole.significato: Any grass of the genus Bromus.
parole.testo: From the genus name, New Latin Bromus, from Ancient Greek βρόμος (brómos, “oat, wild oat”).

parole.significato: bronchus, relating to the trachea, or airways to the lungs.
parole.testo: From Latin bronchus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the bronchia, bronchi or bronchioles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bronchiālis. By surface analysis, bronchium + -al.

parole.significato: An inflammation of the bronchi of the lungs, that causes the cilia of the bronchial epithelial cells to stop functionin…
parole.testo: From Late Latin bronchus, from Ancient Greek βρόγχος (brónkhos, “windpipe”) + -itis.

parole.significato: A bronchial tube; a subdivision of the bronchus.
parole.testo: From New Latin bronchium, singular of Latin bronchia, from Ancient Greek βρογχία (bronkhía)

parole.significato: Either of two airways, which are primary branches of the trachea, leading directly into the lungs.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin bronchus, from Ancient Greek βρόγχος (brónkhos, “trachea, throat”).

parole.significato: Any member of the genus †Brontosaurus of herbivorous sauropod dinosaurs with whip-like tails, which lived in present-da…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek roots; by surface analysis, bronto- + -saurus (“thunder lizard”), according to the notion that its massive size must have made its footsteps shake the ground.

parole.significato: Any of various plants, of the genus Orobanche, that are parasitic on the roots of other plants.
parole.testo: From broom + rape, a partial calque of translingual Orobanche rapum-genistae, where Latin rapum means turnip and genista means broom. Orobanche rapum-genistae is parasitic on broom plants. Compare rapeseed. Cognates include Dutch bremraap.

parole.significato: A full brother: a brother born to the same mother and father, as distinguished from half brothers (uterine brothers), s…
parole.testo: From Middle English brother germain, equivalent to brother + german, after Anglo-Norman and Middle French frere germain and its etymon Classical Latin frāter germānus.

parole.significato: Any member of the Brotulidae.
parole.testo: From New Latin Brotula + -id, from Spanish brótula (“little bud”), from brotón (“bud, sprout”) + -ula (“diminutive suffix”), from brotar (“to bud, sprout”) + -ón (“augmentative suffix”).

parole.significato: Belonging to winter; winterlike; wintry.
parole.testo: From Latin brūmālis (“of or pertaining to the winter solstice; wintry”), from brūma (“the winter solstice; winter”), which is a contraction of *brevima (“the shortest (day)”).

parole.significato: A lethargic state that some ectothermic animals, such as many reptiles, assume during cold conditions. Partly analogous…
parole.testo: From Latin brūma (“winter solstice”) + -tiō, by analogy with hibernation.

parole.significato: Of a dark brown colour.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin brunneus (“brown”), derived from Proto-Germanic *brūnaz (“brown”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to John Brown (physician, born 1735), Scottish physician who taught that disease was caused by either ex…
parole.testo: From Bruno + -n- + -ian. From Latin Bruno (“Brown”), from Medieval Latin brunus (“brown”), from Old High German brun (“brown”).

parole.significato: Savagely violent, vicious, ruthless, or cruel, often in an unintelligent manner.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin brutalis (“savage, stupid”), from Latin brūtus (“dull, stupid”).

parole.significato: A judgement without effect.
parole.testo: From Latin brutum (“stupid”) + fulmen (“lightning”), derived from a 1680 pamphlet by Thomas Barlow of that title, originally from a passage of Pliny's Natural History: "hinc bruta fulmina et vana" ("these senseless and ineffectual thunder-claps", intended as a literal description of lightning).

parole.significato: A kind of wig.
parole.testo: From Latin Brutus.

parole.significato: A perennial herb of the genus Bryonia, especially the common wild subspecies Bryonia cretica dioica (syn. Bryonia dioic…
parole.testo: From Middle English brionie, from Latin bryōnia (“bryony”), from Ancient Greek βρυωνία (bruōnía, “bryony”), from βρύω (brúō).

parole.significato: Any of several North African antelopes of the genus Alcelaphus.
parole.testo: PIE word  *gʷṓws From Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos). Doublet of buffalo and buffle.

parole.significato: An inflamed swelling of a lymph node, especially in the armpit or groin, due to an infection such as bubonic plague, go…
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Medieval Latin būbō, from Ancient Greek βουβών (boubṓn, “groin, swelling”).

parole.significato: Synonym of cheek.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bucca (“the cheek”). Doublet of bocca and bouche.

parole.significato: A curved brass instrument used by the Ancient Roman army.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin būcina, buccina. Doublet of buisine and posaune.

parole.significato: Shaped or sounding like a trumpet.
parole.testo: Latin bucina (“a crooked horn or trumpet”).

parole.significato: A thin broad muscle forming the wall of the cheek.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin buccinātor (“trumpeter”), from buccinō (“blow the trumpet”) + -tor (“-ator, -er”).

parole.significato: buccal; related to the cheek.
parole.testo: From buccal, from Latin bucca (“mouth; cheek”). By surface analysis, bucc- + -o-.

parole.significato: A fold of fat beneath the chin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin buccula. By surface analysis, bucc(a) + -ula.

parole.significato: Possessing a wide mouth.
parole.testo: From Latin bucculentus.

parole.significato: A formation of escort troops used in the Roman Empire in Late Antiquity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Bucellarius (“biscuit-eater”), from buccellātum (“hardtack”) + -arius.

parole.significato: Any horse used for riding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Būcephalus, from Ancient Greek Βουκέφαλος, Βουκεφάλας (Bouképhalos, Boukephálas), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + κεφᾰλή (kephălḗ, “head”) + -ᾱς (-ās).

parole.significato: Any of several, often thorny shrubs or small trees, especially
parole.testo: Calque of Latin cervī spīna (“deer's thorny shrub”), cervi (“deer's”) being the genitive singular of cervus (“deer”), from Proto-Italic *kerwos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥h₂wós, from *ḱerh₂- (“horn”) + *-wós, spīna (“thorny shrub”) from Proto-Italic *speinā, from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“shar

parole.significato: Rustic, pastoral, country-styled.
parole.testo: PIE word  *gʷṓws Borrowed from Latin būcolicus, from Ancient Greek βουκολικός (boukolikós, “rustic, pastoral; meter used by pastoral poets”, literally “pertaining to cowherds”).

parole.significato: A pastoral poem.
parole.testo: From Latin būcolicum, neuter substantive of būcolicus.

parole.significato: The depiction of the head of an ox, as ornamental flourishes in architectural works.
parole.testo: From Latin būcrānium, from Ancient Greek βουκράνιον (boukránion).

parole.significato: A particular enzyme inhibitor derived from a toad toxin.
parole.testo: See Latin būfo (“toad”) and -genic, -in.

parole.significato: Resembling a toad.
parole.testo: From Latin būfō (“toad”).

parole.significato: A fossil consisting of the petrified teeth and palatal bones of fishes belonging to the family of pycnodonts, whose rem…
parole.testo: From Latin bufo (“toad”) + -ite. It was once believed to be formed in the head of a toad.

parole.significato: A liturgical candlestick held beside a Latin Catholic bishop or other prelate.
parole.testo: From New Latin bugia, from Medieval Latin candēla Bugiae, candēla dē Bugia (“candle from Bejaia (a seaport town in northeastern Algeria from which they were exported)”), a calque of Middle French chandelle de Bougie. Doublet of bougie.

parole.significato: A tubular glass or plastic bead sewn onto clothes as a decorative trim.
parole.testo: From Late Latin bugulus (“a woman's ornament”), probably from Latin būculus.

parole.significato: The bulb-shaped underground portion of a plant such as a tulip, consisting of a shortened stem and many fleshy scale le…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English bulb, bolbe, from Latin bulbus (“bulb, onion”), from Ancient Greek βολβός (bolbós, “plant with round swelling on underground stem”).

parole.significato: bulbous
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bulbāceus. See bulb.

parole.significato: Shaped like a bulb.
parole.testo: From Latin bulbus (“bulb”) + -form.

parole.significato: Having the shape of or resembling a bulb, bloated.
parole.testo: From bulb + -ous or alteration of Latin bulbosus.

parole.significato: A small bulb; a bulblet.
parole.testo: From Latin bulbulus, diminutive of bulbus. See bulb.

parole.significato: An erectile tissue structure on the penis of canid mammals and some pinnipeds, which swells up and locks inside the fem…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin bulbus glandis, from bulbus (“bulb”) + glandis (“acorn”).

parole.significato: A member of a migratory Turkic people from Central Asia who conquered Moesia in the 7th century and settled what is now…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Bulgarus, from Old Church Slavonic блъгаринъ (blŭgarinŭ), itself from the self designation of Turkic Bulgars, from Proto-Turkic *bulgar (“disturber, disturbing”), active noun/adjective of *bulga- (“to create a state of disorder; to stir, to disturb”). Displaced Old English Pulgar

parole.significato: An eating disorder characterized by a binge-and-purge cycle: extreme overeating followed by self-induced vomiting.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin būlīmia, from Ancient Greek βουλῑμῐ́ᾱ (boulīmĭ́ā, “ravenous hunger”), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + λῑμός (līmós, “hunger, famine”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, “-ia”), and Latin nervōsa (“nervous”).

parole.significato: A blister, vesicle, or other thin-walled cavity or lesion, as
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bulla (“bubble”). Doublet of bill and bull (“papal bull; bubble”).

parole.significato: Synonym of bullary (“a collection of papal bulls”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bullarium, from bulla (“seal; papal bull”) + -arium.

parole.significato: A collection of papal bulls.
parole.testo: From Late Latin bullarium: compare French bullairie.

parole.significato: Resembling a bulla or blister; inflated; blistered; bulliform.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin bullātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Having a blistered appearance; bullate.
parole.testo: Latin bulla (“any swollen round object”), + -iform

parole.significato: The action of boiling.
parole.testo: From Latin bullire, bullitum (“to boil”). See boil (verb) and ebullition.

parole.significato: Any of a number of jewel beetles of the family Buprestidae, usually with shiny metallic colours.
parole.testo: Latin buprestis, Ancient Greek a poisonous beetle, which, being eaten by cattle in the grass, caused them to swell up and die; ox, cow + to blow up, swell out.

parole.significato: The duty of a party in a legal proceeding to prove an assertion of fact; it includes both the burden of production and…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin onus probandi.

parole.significato: A pilgrim's staff.
parole.testo: From Latin burdonem.

parole.significato: A city or town.
parole.testo: The historical sense is from Late Latin burgus, from Frankish *burg, from Proto-Germanic *burgz (“borough, fortification”). Doublet of borough, Brough, burgh, burh, and bury. Also compare burgess. The modern sense may have been formed in part by analogy with the many North American city names that a

parole.significato: The governing body of a burgh or borough; burgage.
parole.testo: Probably from Latin burgāria. By surface analysis, burg + -ery.

parole.significato: A person who breaks in to premises with the intent of committing a crime, usually theft.
parole.testo: 16th century, from Medieval Latin burglātor, British byform of burgātor (“burglar”), derived from burgō (“to commit burglary”), from Late Latin burgus (“fortified town”), itself probably from Frankish *burg (“fortress”), from Proto-Germanic *burgz, *burgiją (“borough, watch-tower”). The -l- in burgl

parole.significato: The crime of unlawfully breaking into a vehicle, house, store, or other enclosure with the intent to steal.
parole.testo: From New Latin burglaria. By surface analysis, burglar + -y. Displaced native Old English hūsbryċe (literally “house-breach”).

parole.significato: A Germanic tribe dwelling near the territory of the Marcomanni
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Būrī.

parole.significato: Any of the many small fluid-filled sacs located at the point where a muscle or tendon slides across bone. These sacs se…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bursa (“purse”), from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa); compare purse and bourse, which are doublets.

parole.significato: The treasurer of a university, college or school.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bursārius, from bursa (“purse”) (English purse).

parole.significato: A monetary award to university students that allows them to continue their studies.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bursaria, from bursarius.

parole.significato: Shaped like a purse or bag.
parole.testo: From New Latin bursiformis, from Latin bursa (“purse”).

parole.significato: Any of a class of isoflav-3-enes found in the flowering plant Erythrina burttii.
parole.testo: From Latin burttii + -ol.

parole.significato: Any of the broad-winged soaring raptors of the genus Buteo.
parole.testo: From the genus name Buteo, from Latin būteō.

parole.significato: butyric substance.
parole.testo: Combining form of Latin būtȳrum (“butter”).

parole.significato: Invocation of the Roman god Jupiter.
parole.testo: From Latin pro Iovem. Ellipsis of a full oath of the form "I swear by Jove that…" Originally a literal oath; later a minced oath.

parole.significato: Invocation of the Roman god Jupiter.
parole.testo: From Latin pro Iuppiter. Ellipsis of a full oath of the form "I swear by Jupiter that…". Originally a literal oath; later a minced oath.

parole.significato: By divine will and benevolence.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin Deī grātiā. Doublet of Dei gratia.

parole.significato: A wallet.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Old English bīsæc, from Latin bisaccium.

parole.significato: Relating to, or possessing a byssus
parole.testo: From Latin byssus + -ate.

parole.significato: Made of, or resembling, silk; silken.
parole.testo: From Latin byssinus (“made of byssus”), from Ancient Greek βύσσινος (bússinos, “made of byssus”). See byssus.

parole.significato: A lung disease, caused by exposure to cotton dust in inadequately ventilated working environments.
parole.testo: From Late Latin byssinum (“linen cloth”) via Latin byssus + New Latin -osis.

parole.significato: The long fine silky filaments excreted by several mollusks (particularly Pinna nobilis) by which they attach themselves…
parole.testo: From Latin byssus, from Ancient Greek βύσσος (bússos, “flax; flax cotton”), from a Semitic source cognate to Hebrew בּוּץ (būṣ, “byssus”) and Aramaic בּוּצָא (būṣā, “byssus”)

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Byzantium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin bȳzantīnus, from Bȳzantium, from Ancient Greek Βυζάντιον (Buzántion). The figurative senses evoke the reputation for palace intrigue of the Byzantine imperial court.

parole.significato: A dark shade of purple, close to Tyrian purple and palatinate purple.
parole.testo: From Latin Bȳzantium, from Ancient Greek Βῡζᾰ́ντῐον (Būzắntĭon), named after its legendary founder, Byzas.

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to, a horse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caballīnus (“horse-related”).

parole.significato: Having cachexia; wasting away from a disease or chronic illness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cachecticus.

parole.significato: A systemic wasting of muscle tissue, with or without loss of fat mass, that accompanies a chronic disease.
parole.testo: From Late Latin cachexia or French cachexie, from Ancient Greek καχεξία (kakhexía), from κακός (kakós, “bad; injurious”) + ἕξῐς (héxĭs, “act of having; habit or state of body”) (ultimately from ἔχω (ékhō, “to have”)) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă, suffix added to adjectives to form abstract nouns).

parole.significato: To laugh immoderately, loudly, or too often.
parole.testo: From Latin cachinnō (“laugh aloud”), of onomatopoeic origin.

parole.significato: To defecate.
parole.testo: From Middle English cakken, from Old English *cacian, from Old English cac (“dung; excrement”), from Latin cacāre (“excrete feces”). Cognate with English caca. Compare Dutch kakken (“to defecate”), German kacken (“to relieve oneself; defecate”), Latin cacō (“defecate”) (see there for more); compare

parole.significato: Compulsion; mania.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cacoēthes, from Ancient Greek κακοήθης (kakoḗthēs, “ill-disposed”) from κακός (kakós, “bad”) + ἦθος (êthos, “disposition, nature”).

parole.significato: Ill-conditioned, malignant; cacoethical.
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek κακοήθης (kakoḗthēs, “ill-disposed”) (κακός (kakós, “bad”) + ἦθος (êthos, “disposition, nature”)) + -ic

parole.significato: dysphemism
parole.testo: From Latin cacophemia + -ism.

parole.significato: A stylistic affectation of diction, such as throwing in foreign words to appear learned.
parole.testo: From Latin cacozēlia (“a bad, faulty, awkward imitation”), from Ancient Greek κᾰκοζηλία (kăkozēlía, “unhappy imitation, affectation”).

parole.significato: The smallest possible piece of matter, making up part of an atom.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cacūmen.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a point, top, or crown.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin cacūmen, cacūminis (“extremity, point, peak”) + -al.

parole.significato: To make sharp or pointed.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin cacūmen, cacūminis (“extremity, point, peak”) + -al, ultimately from Latin cacūminātus, past participle of cacūminō, from cacūmen.

parole.significato: Having a pyramidal top.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin cacūmen, cacūminis (“extremity, point, peak”) + -ous.

parole.significato: A dead body; especially the corpse of a human to be dissected.
parole.testo: From Middle English cadaver, from Latin cadāver.

parole.significato: Corpselike; hinting of death; imitating a cadaver.
parole.testo: From Latin cadāverōsus; compare Middle English cadaverous (“gangrenous, mortified”).

parole.significato: An ornate capital letter used in calligraphy, consisting of interlaced pen strokes. See :Commons:Cadel letters.
parole.testo: From Latin capitellum, diminuitive of Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *kauput- (English head), itself from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Doublet of captain. Cognate with French cadeau. Doublet of caddie, cadet, capital, capitellum, and caudillo.

parole.significato: Falling.
parole.testo: From the Latin cadens (“falling”), present active participle of cado (“to fall”).

parole.significato: Synonym of calamine, a pink form of zinc oxide.
parole.testo: From Latin cadmia, ultimately from Ancient Greek Καδμεία (Kadmeía), from Κάδμος (Kádmos, “Cadmus”) + -εια (-eia, “-ia: forming related substances”). Doublet of calamine, calaminaris, and lapis calaminaris.

parole.significato: caduceus.
parole.testo: From Latin cādūceus, cādūceum.

parole.significato: The official wand carried by a herald in ancient Greece and Rome, specifically the one carried in mythology by Hermes,…
parole.testo: Via Latin cādūceus, cādūceum, adaptation of Doric Ancient Greek καρύκειον (karúkeion, “herald’s wand or staff”). This and Attic Greek κηρύκειον (kērúkeion) are derived from κῆρυξ (kêrux, “herald, public messenger”). Related to κηρύσσω (kērússō, “to announce”).

parole.significato: With temporary gills; applied to those amphibians (most amphibians do this) in which the gills do not remain in adult l…
parole.testo: From Latin caducus (“falling”) (from cadere (“to fall”)) + English branchiate.

parole.significato: Having deciduous horns or antlers.
parole.testo: From Latin caducus (“falling”) + -corn.

parole.significato: Having deciduous leaves
parole.testo: From Latin caducus (“that easily falls”) + folium (“leaf”).

parole.significato: Of a part of an organism, disappearing in the normal course of development.
parole.testo: Latin cadūcus (“falling; transitory”).

parole.significato: Any of a group of burrowing amphibians of the order Gymnophiona that resemble earthworms or snakes.
parole.testo: From Latin caecilia + -an, feminine form of Caecilius, from Caeculus + -ius, from caecus + -ulus.

parole.significato: A cavity open at one end (such as the blind end of a duct), especially a blind pouch connected to the large intestine b…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caecum (“invisible, hidden”), clipping of intestīnum caecum (“blind gut”), translation of Ancient Greek τῠφλὸν ἔντερον (tŭphlòn énteron).

parole.significato: An aecium of some rust fungi that has no peridium or outer membrane.
parole.testo: New Latin caeoma, from Ancient Greek καίειν (kaíein, “to burn”) + -ωμα (-ōma). Attested from 1832.

parole.significato: An official in charge of religious ceremonies.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A follower of Julius Caesar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Caesariānus, from Caesar + -iānus. By surface analysis, Caesar + -ian. Piecewise doublet of tsarian. For the sense “Caesarean section”, see also "Caesarean section § Etymology" on Wikipedia.

parole.significato: The combination of state (originally imperial) power with religious authority; state authority over ecclesiastical matt…
parole.testo: From caesar + -o- + papism, probably modelled after New Latin caesaro-papia, coined by the German ecclesiastical jurist Justus Henning Böhmer (1674–1749) in his work Jus ecclesiasticum Protestantium (Ecclesiastical Law of the Protestants, 1714–1736).

parole.significato: Having a blue color very low in chroma.
parole.testo: Latin caesius (“bluish-grey”); probably akin to Latin caelum (“sky”); see celestial.

parole.significato: The chemical element (symbol Cs) with an atomic number of 55. It is a soft, gold-colored, highly reactive alkali metal.
parole.testo: From Latin caesius (“sky-blue”), in reference to the radiation spectra, + -ium.

parole.significato: A pause or interruption in a poem, music, building, or other work of art.
parole.testo: Latin caesūra (“cutting, hewing”), from caesus, perfect passive participle of caedō (“to cut down, hew”).

parole.significato: A short Spanish shield.
parole.testo: From Latin caetra.

parole.significato: Synonym of star apple.
parole.testo: From Latin cainito, from Spanish caimito, from Lokono.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Cairo, the capital of Egypt.
parole.testo: From Latin Cairenus, from Cairo + -nus (“-ene: forming related nouns”). Equivalent to Cairo + -ene.

parole.significato: A mythical bird that had healing powers.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin caladrius, from Byzantine Greek χαλαδριός (khaladriós), from Ancient Greek χαραδριός (kharadriós).

parole.significato: A squid.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin calamārius, from calamus (“a reed pen”), because of the ink emitted by squids.

parole.significato: Having or producing reeds.
parole.testo: From Latin calamus (“reed”) + -iferous. Compare New Latin calamifer, used in Botanical Latin and taxonomic names.

parole.significato: To curl (the hair).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calamistrātus, perfect passive participle of calamistrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: curled or frizzed
parole.testo: Latin calamistratus (“curled with a curling iron”), from calamistrum (“curling iron”).

parole.significato: A comb-like structure on the metatarsus of the hind legs of cribellate spiders (Ciniflonidae), used to comb out fine ba…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calamistrum (“a curling-iron”).

parole.significato: Rod-shaped; long and thin.
parole.testo: From Latin calamus (“a reed”).

parole.significato: Sweet flag (Acorus calamus).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin calamus (“reed, cane”). Doublet of culm, haulm, helm (Etymology 4, stalk), qalam, and shawm.

parole.significato: Basket-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin calathus (“wicker basket”) + -iform.

parole.significato: A vase-shaped basket made from reeds or twigs, used in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin calathus, from Ancient Greek κάλαθος (kálathos).

parole.significato: The calcaneus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calcāneum, from Latin calx, calcis (“heel”).

parole.significato: The large bone making up the heel of the human foot, the heel bone.
parole.testo: From Latin calcāneus (“heel”), rare form of calx (“heel”).

parole.significato: A spur-like projection.
parole.testo: From the Latin calcar (“spur”).

parole.significato: Having a spur; spurred.
parole.testo: From Latin calcarātus (“spurred”).

parole.significato: Resembling, containing, or composed of calcium carbonate or limestone; chalky.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin calcārius (“of or pertaining to lime”), derived from calx (“lime”). Similar to calcium.

parole.significato: Synonym of trample: to crush or stomp underfoot.
parole.testo: From Latin calcātus, the past participle of calcāre (“to trample”), parsed via English -ate (verb-forming suffix), from calx (“heel”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of calque.

parole.significato: Synonym of trampling, the act of trampling someone or something, an instance of trampling.
parole.testo: From calcate (“to trample”) + -ion (“forming abstract nouns”), from Latin calcatus (“trampled”), the past participle of calcāre (“to trample”) parsed via English -ate (“forming verbs”), from calx (“heel”) + -āre (“forming verbs”). Doublet of calque.

parole.significato: Synonym of winepress, particularly a location where grapes are crushed underfoot to produce juice or wine.
parole.testo: From Latin calcātōrium, from calcāre (“to trample”) + -tōrium (“-ory: forming locations”), from calx (“heel”) + -āre (“forming verbs”). Equivalent to calcate + -ory.

parole.significato: A red silk embroidered sandal forming part of the insignia of the Holy Roman Empire.
parole.testo: From Latin calceamentum.

parole.significato: Synonym of shod: wearing shoes, particularly (Christianity) as opposed to the barefoot mendicant orders.
parole.testo: From Latin calceātus, participle of calceāre (“to shoe, to provide with shoes”), from calceus (“calceus, shoe”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), from calx (“heel”) + -eus (“-y”, adjective-forming suffix). Equivalent to Latin calceus + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Synonym of shod: wearing shoes, particularly (Christianity) as distinguished from the barefoot mendicant orders.
parole.testo: From Latin calceātus + English -ed under influence from English -ate (verb-forming suffix), past participle of calceāre (“to shoe, to provide with shoes”), from calceus (“calceus, shoe”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), from calx (“heel”) + -eus (“-y”, adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of calcated.

parole.significato: Synonym of shod, wearing shoes, particularly (Christianity) religious orders that do not eschew normal footwear.
parole.testo: A back-formation from discalced, with reference to Latin calceus (“calceus, footwear”).

parole.significato: Shoe-shaped, shaped like a shoe.
parole.testo: From Latin calceus (“calceus, footwear”) + English -form (“-shaped”) after the model of French calcéiforme.

parole.significato: A kind of low leather Roman boot or hightop shoe.
parole.testo: From Latin calceus, substantive use of calx (“heel”) + -eus (“-y: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Synonym of calcifugal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin calcifugus (“limestone-phobic”). By surface analysis, calci- + -fugous.

parole.significato: Containing lime.
parole.testo: From Latin calcis (“genitive singular of calx (chalk, limestone)”) + -gerous (“bearing”); compare calciferous.

parole.significato: A form of whitewash (inexpensive white paint) made from calcium carbonate, glue and water, used to coat wooden or plast…
parole.testo: Alteration of kalsomine, after Latin calcis, genitive of calx (“lime”).

parole.significato: A very widely distributed crystalline form of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, found as limestone, chalk and marble.
parole.testo: From Latin calx + -ite.

parole.significato: stubborn; refractory
parole.testo: From Latin calcitrans, present participle of calcitrare (“to kick”), from calx (“heel”), calcis (“heel”).

parole.significato: To kick.
parole.testo: From Latin calcitratus, past participle of calcitrare.

parole.significato: The chemical element (symbol Ca) with atomic number 20: a soft, silvery-white alkaline earth metal which occurs natural…
parole.testo: Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1808, from Latin calx (“lime, limestone”) because it occurs in limestone. By surface analysis, calc- + -ium.

parole.significato: drawing with chalk
parole.testo: From Latin calx (“chalk”) + English -graphy (“written”).

parole.significato: An equation, ratio, or other quantitative problem designated for calculation; “that which is to be calculated”.
parole.testo: A substantivisation in English of the Latin calculandum (the nominative neuter singular form of calculandus, “which is to be calculated”, “which is to be computed”, the future passive participle (gerundive) of calculō, “I calculate”, “I compute”), on the pattern of analysandum, cogitandum, explicand

parole.significato: To determine the value of something or the solution to something by a mathematical process.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calculātus, perfect passive participle of calculō (“to reckon, compute, calculate”, originally by means of pebbles) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from calculus (“a pebble”), further from calx (“limestone”, calc- in compounds) + -ulus (forms diminutives).

parole.significato: The act or process of calculating.
parole.testo: From Middle English calculation, borrowed from Latin calculatio, calculationis. Morphologically calculate + -ion.

parole.significato: A mechanical or electronic device that performs mathematical calculations; (now usually) an electronic one specifically.
parole.testo: In the sense of a person, from Middle English calkelatour (“a mathematician, an astrologer”), borrowed from Latin calculātor, equivalent to calculate + -or. The other meanings arose in Modern English.

parole.significato: Having the shape of a pebble
parole.testo: Latin calculus (“little stone”) + -iform

parole.significato: Calculation; computation.
parole.testo: * Borrowed from Latin calculus (“a pebble or stone used as reckoning counters in abacus”), diminutive of calx (“limestone”) + -ulus. * Mathematical topic is from differential calculus.

parole.significato: In Roman baths, the hottest room, with a plunge-pool. It preceded the tepidarium and frigidarium.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin caldārium (“room containing warm water for bathing”), substantive of caldārius (“of, pertaining to or suitable for bathing”), from caldus (“warm, hot”) + -ārius, alternative form of calidus, from caleō (“to be warm or hot; glow”).

parole.significato: The act of warming or heating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calefactiō, calefactiōnem.

parole.significato: warming
parole.testo: * Borrowed from Latin calefactorius.

parole.significato: The room or building in a monastery holding its communal fire, kept warm and used as a sitting room.
parole.testo: * Borrowed from Medieval Latin calefactorium.

parole.significato: A calendar or timeline or events.
parole.testo: From Latin calendārium. Doublet of calendar.

parole.significato: Often with initial capital: the first day of a month.
parole.testo: From Middle English calendes, calendas, calendis, kalandes, kalendas, kalendes, kalendez, kalendis, kalendus (also in the singular forms calende, kalend, kalende), from Latin kalendās, accusative plural of kalendae (“first day of a Roman month”), an archaic variant of calandae, from calandus (“which

parole.significato: To undergo calescence; to become or grow warm; to heat up; to warm; to glow with heat.
parole.testo: From Latin calescere.

parole.significato: Cup, cup-like.
parole.testo: From Latin calicis, genitive of calix. See also calyx.

parole.significato: Having the shape of a cup or calyx.
parole.testo: Latin calyx (“calyx”) + -iform. By surface analysis, calic- + -i- + -form.

parole.significato: Any cup-shaped depression.
parole.testo: From Latin caliculus, diminutive of calix. By surface analysis, calic- + -le.

parole.significato: Warm, hot.
parole.testo: From Latin calidus (“hot”), from caleō (“to be warm or hot; glow”) + -idus, from Proto-Italic *kalēō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelh₁-. Cognate with Italian calido (“hot”), French chaud (“warm, hot”), Portuguese cálido (“warm”), and Spanish cálido (“warm”).

parole.significato: Synonym of caldarium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calidārium.

parole.significato: Heat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caliditās, whence the Italian calidità. Compare calid.

parole.significato: A pipe or duct used, especially in ancient times, to convey hot air or steam for heating purposes.
parole.testo: Coined in 1624. From Latin calidus (“warm”) + -duct.

parole.significato: a type of water heater
parole.testo: Genericized trademark from Latin cali(dus) (“warm”) + font.

parole.significato: A heavy ancient Roman military sandal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caliga.

parole.significato: Wearing caligae or military boots.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caligātus (“wearing soldiers’ boots, booted”), from caliga (“a Roman military leathern boot”) + -ātus (“-ed, -ate”, suffix forming adjectives), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: dimness; cloudiness
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caligatio, from caligare (“to emit vapour, to be dark”), from caligo (“mist, darkness”).

parole.significato: darkness; obscurity.
parole.testo: From Latin cālīginōsus (“misty, dark”), from cālīgō (“fog; darkness”).

parole.significato: dimness or obscurity of sight, caused by a speck on the cornea
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cālīgō (“darkness”). Doublet of garua.

parole.significato: Monarchical government based on a claim of succession to the Islamic State of Muhammad, ruled by a caliph.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin calīphātus, equivalent to caliph + -ate.

parole.significato: A Utraquist.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin calix (“chalice”); so called from their demanding the cup as well as the bread for the laity.

parole.significato: cunning or shrewd; crafty.
parole.testo: From Latin callidus, from callere (“to be thick-skinned, to be hardened”), from callum, callus (“callous skin, callosity, callousness”).

parole.significato: craftiness, cunning
parole.testo: Latin calliditas.

parole.significato: Bearing or producing calluses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin callifer, equivalent to callus + -i- + -ferous.

parole.significato: painless vivisection
parole.testo: From Latin callere (“to be insensible”) + English section.

parole.significato: An African primate.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin callithrix. First attested in 1572.

parole.significato: A green monkey.
parole.testo: From Latin callithrix.

parole.significato: Emotionally hardened; unfeeling and indifferent to the suffering/feelings of others.
parole.testo: From Latin callōsus (“hard-skinned”), from callum (“hardened skin”) + -ōsus.

parole.significato: A hardened area of the skin (especially on the foot or hand) caused by repeated friction, wear or use.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin callum (“hard skin”). Displaced Old English wearr.

parole.significato: The study of heat flow and heat transfer.
parole.testo: From calorie + -ics. From Latin calor (“heat”).

parole.significato: An apparatus for measuring the heat generated or absorbed by either a chemical reaction, change of phase or some other…
parole.testo: From Latin calor (“warmth, heat”) + -meter.

parole.significato: The science of measuring the heat absorbed or evolved during the course of a chemical reaction or change of state.
parole.testo: From Latin calor (“warmth, heat”) + -metry.

parole.significato: A voltaic battery, from the 19th century, with a large surface of plate, producing (by the then standards) powerful hea…
parole.testo: Latin calor (“heat”) + English motor.

parole.significato: To form a protective surface on (a ferrous metal) by coating with aluminum powder and then heating.
parole.testo: From Latin calor (“heat”) + -ize.

parole.significato: In mathematical physics, a finite temperature instanton.
parole.testo: From Latin calor (“heat”) + -on.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Caltha; a marsh marigold.
parole.testo: From the genus name (Latin caltha).

parole.significato: Any secondary calcareous deposit, created by the action of water outside the natural cave environment. They are typical…
parole.testo: From Latin calx (“lime”) + Latin < Ancient Greek θέμα (théma, “what is laid down”), (also Mediaeval Latin thema, "deposit") and the Latin -īta < Ancient Greek -ίτης (-ítēs) – used as a suffix indicating a rock or mineral.

parole.significato: A metal object, usually small, with spikes arranged so that, when thrown onto the ground, one always faces up as a thre…
parole.testo: From Middle English calketrappe, from Old English calcatrippe, from Medieval Latin calcatrippa (“thistle”), from Latin calx or calcare (“to tread”) + trappa (“trap”).

parole.significato: To make hurtful untrue comments about.
parole.testo: First attested in 1554; borrowed from Latin calumniātus, perfect passive participle of calumnior (“to blame, cavil at; to accuse falsely”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A person who calumniates (slanders, or makes personal attacks upon, others).
parole.testo: From Latin calumniātor.

parole.significato: Possessing the traits of calumny.
parole.testo: From Late Latin calumniōsus.

parole.significato: The calvaria; the dome or roof of the skull.
parole.testo: From Latin calva (“the scalp”).

parole.significato: The dome or roof of the skull, the skullcap.
parole.testo: From Latin calvāria (“skull”). Doublet of calvarium, calavera, and calvary.

parole.significato: The upper, domelike portion of the skull (without the lower jaw).
parole.testo: From Latin calvāria (“skull”), from calva, from calvus (“bald”).

parole.significato: A life-size representation of the crucifixion of Jesus Christ on a piece of raised ground.
parole.testo: From Late Latin calvāria (“skull”). Doublet of calavera and calvaria.

parole.significato: Baldness, the condition of being bald.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calvitiēs (“baldness”).

parole.significato: Baldness.
parole.testo: From Latin calvitium (“baldness”), from calvus (“bald”).

parole.significato: Lacking most or all of one's hair; bald, hairless.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calvus (“bald, hairless”) (of unclear origin, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥h₂wós or *kalw- (“bald; naked”), from a root *kl̥H- + *-wós (suffix forming adjectives from verb stems)) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, denoting possession or presence of a quality).

parole.significato: The substance which remains after a metal or mineral has been thoroughly burnt, once seen as being the essential substa…
parole.testo: From Latin calx (“lime”). Doublet of cauk and chalk.

parole.significato: Calyx, bud, or cup of a flower or nut.
parole.testo: From Latin calycis, genitive of calyx, from Ancient Greek κάλυξ (kálux, “case of a bud, husk”). By surface analysis, calyc- + -i-.

parole.significato: Having the petals and stamens adnate to the calyx.
parole.testo: Latin calyx (“calyx”), calycis (“calyx”) + flos (“flower”), floris (“flower”). By surface analysis, calyc- + -i- + flor + -al.

parole.significato: calyculus
parole.testo: From Latin calyculus (“small flower bud, calyx”), diminutive of calyx. See calyx and compare calicle. By surface analysis, calyc- + -le.

parole.significato: Any cup-shaped structure.
parole.testo: From Latin calyculus (“small flower bud, calyx”), diminutive of calyx. By surface analysis, calyc- + -ulus.

parole.significato: A bulbous bog orchid of the genus Calypso, Calypso bulbosa
parole.testo: From Latin, itself from Ancient Greek Καλυψώ (Kalupsṓ, “name of a sea nymph”)

parole.significato: Either of two rounded lobes at the posterior base of the wing in many true flies.
parole.testo: From New Latin calyptra, from Ancient Greek κᾰλύπτρα (kălúptra, “hood”), from κᾰλύπτω (kălúptō, “I cover”).

parole.significato: The outermost whorl of flower parts, comprising the sepals, which covers and protects the petals as they develop.
parole.testo: From Latin calyx, from Ancient Greek κάλυξ (kálux, “case of a bud, husk”). Doublet of chalice and kelch.

parole.significato: That contains either of two or more different metal atoms
parole.testo: From Latin cambialis.

parole.significato: The half-demon offspring of either an incubus and a female human or a succubus and a male human.
parole.testo: From Late Latin cambio (“I exchange”). Doublet of change.

parole.significato: A layer of cells between the xylem and the phloem that is responsible for the secondary growth of roots and stems.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin cambium (“a change”), from Gaulish. Doublet of change.

parole.significato: A 12th-century English game somewhat similar to golf in that it was played with a wooden ball similar to a golf ball.
parole.testo: From Middle English camboke, from Late Latin cambuca (“hooked rod or stick”) referring to the 'club' used to play the game. Compare cammock.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to camels.
parole.testo: From Latin camelinus.

parole.significato: Synonym of giraffe.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin camēlopardus, variant of camēlopardalis, from Ancient Greek καμηλοπάρδαλις (kamēlopárdalis, “giraffe”).

parole.significato: A group of prophetic goddesses associated with childbirth, wells, and fountains.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Camēnae.

parole.significato: A device for taking still or moving pictures or photographs.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin camera (“chamber or bedchamber”), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “anything with an arched cover, a covered carriage or boat, a vaulted chamber, a vault”), of Old Iranian origin, from Proto-Iranian *kamarā- (“something curved”), from *kamárati, from Proto-Indo-Iranian

parole.significato: An instrument that uses a shaped prism or mirrors to cause an apparent image of external objects to appear as if projec…
parole.testo: Latin camera lucida

parole.significato: A darkened chamber in which the image of an outside object is projected and focused onto a surface.
parole.testo: From New Latin camera obscūra (literally “dark chamber”); compare camera.

parole.significato: Relating to a chamber, especially to a judicial or legislative one
parole.testo: Formed from the root of Latin camera (“room; chamber”), with the suffix -al, perhaps corresponding to a Late Latin, Medieval Latin cameralis.

parole.significato: To build in the form of a vault; to arch over.
parole.testo: From Latin camerātus, perfect passive participle of camerō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A vaulting or arching over.
parole.testo: Latin cameratio.

parole.significato: Dressed with a shirt over the other garments.
parole.testo: From Latin camisia.

parole.significato: An ancient kind of shirt or nightgown.
parole.testo: From Latin camisia.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Luís de Camões.
parole.testo: From New Latin Camoniānus [from Camonius + -ānus] or directly from Portuguese Camon- (stem of Camões) + -ian.

parole.significato: A Roman military boot.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin campagus.

parole.significato: A smallish suspended bell used in medieval monastic cloisters.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin campānella, from campāna (“steeple bell”) + -ella (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: In the shape of a bell.
parole.testo: Latin campana (“bell”) + -form

parole.significato: Shaped like a bell.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin campānulātus, from campānula (“litte bell”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A phytosterol, found in many vegetable oils, related to sitosterol
parole.testo: From Latin campester + -ol, campestris, from campus + -estris.

parole.significato: Relating to open fields or uncultivated land.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin campester (“of a field”), from campus (“field”), with the suffix -al.

parole.significato: A device used to measure a person's field of vision
parole.testo: From Latin campus (“field, scope”) + -meter.

parole.significato: A chicken of a breed originating from the aforementioned region.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Campania

parole.significato: The grounds or property of a school, college, university, business, church, or hospital, often understood to include bu…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin campus (“field”). Doublet of camp and champ. First used in its current sense in reference to Princeton University in the 1770s.

parole.significato: Channeled lengthwise; grooved.
parole.testo: From Latin canāliculātus (“channelled”).

parole.significato: canaliculus.
parole.testo: From Latin canaliculus.

parole.significato: Any of many small canals or ducts in the body, such as in the bone, or in some plants.
parole.testo: From Latin canāliculus (“small channel, pipe or gutter”), diminutive of canālis (“channel; pipe, gutter”), from canna (“cane, reed”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”).

parole.significato: Consisting of a network of veins, without intermediate parenchyma; lattice-like.
parole.testo: From Latin cancellatus, past participle of cancellare.

parole.significato: The act, process, or result of cancelling; as, the cancellation of certain words in a contract, or of the contract itse…
parole.testo: From Latin cancellātiō, from cancellō + -tiō.

parole.significato: Having low density and strength but high surface area, of the kind that fills the inner cavity of long bones.
parole.testo: From Latin cancellus (“lattice”).

parole.significato: A barrier, balustrade or railing, or screen, dividing the main body of a church from the chancel.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin cancellus (“little crab”). Doublet of chancel.

parole.significato: Someone with a Cancer star sign.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cancer (“crab”), calque of Ancient Greek Καρκίνος (Karkínos, “crab”), calque of Akkadian 𒀀𒇻𒌅 (allutu, “crab”), from Sumerian 𒀯𒀠𒈜 (ᵐᵘˡAL.LUL, “crab; name of constellation”).

parole.significato: A disease in which the cells of a tissue undergo uncontrolled (often rapid) proliferation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cancer (“crab”), a calque of Ancient Greek καρκίνος (karkínos, “crab; ulcer; cancer”), possibly cognate, applied to cancerous tumors because of a supposed resemblence between their enlarged veins and the legs of a crab. Doublet of canker and chancre.

parole.significato: To grow into a cancer; to become cancerous.
parole.testo: From Latin cancerātus (“eaten by a cancer”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the astrological sign of Cancer.
parole.testo: From Cancer + -ian; from Latin Cancriana, from Cancer + -iana.

parole.significato: Relating to or affected with cancer.
parole.testo: From Middle English cancerous, from Latin cancerōsus, from cancer (“crab; tumor, cancer”) + -ōsus (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, cancer + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to crabs.
parole.testo: From Latin cancer (“crab”) + -īnus, as if from *cancrīnus. The poetry sense comes from the fact that most species of crab can walk sideways, either left or right.

parole.significato: That feeds on crabs and other crustaceans
parole.testo: From Latin cancer (“crab”) + -vorous.

parole.significato: A type of canon in which the imitating voice repeats the notes of the theme in reverse order
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin, present participle of cancrizāre (“to go backwards”), from Latin cancr-, cancer (“crab”) + Late Latin -izāre (“-ize”).

parole.significato: noma, a gangrenous disease of the face
parole.testo: From Latin cancrum ōris, from cancrum (“canker”) and ōris (“of the mouth, face”), genitive singular of ōs (“mouth, face”). The Latin phrase itself is first attested in a source that gives it as a translation of an English common name "mouth canker" or "canker of the mouth".

parole.significato: In the International System of Units, the base unit of luminous intensity; the luminous intensity, in a given direction…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin candēla (“candle”). Doublet of candle and chandelle.

parole.significato: A candle holder with branches to hold more than one candle.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin candēlābrum (“candlestick”), from candēla. Doublet of chandelier. Displaced native Old English candeltrēow (literally “candle tree”).

parole.significato: Glowing as a result of its high temperature; incandescent, glowing with heat.
parole.testo: From Latin candentem, from candere.

parole.significato: Glowing with heat; white-hot, incandescent.
parole.testo: From Latin candēscēns, present participle of candēscō (“to brighten, radiate, become red hot”).

parole.significato: Somewhat white, or turning white.
parole.testo: From Latin candicans, present participle of candicare (“to be whitish”).

parole.significato: Impartial and free from prejudice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin candidus (“white”).

parole.significato: A person who seeks to be elected or appointed to a position or privilege.
parole.testo: From Latin candidātus (“a person who is standing for public office”, noun), from candidus (“dazzling white, shining, clear”) + -ātus, -āta, -ātum (participial adjective-forming suffix), in reference to Roman candidates wearing bleached white togas as a symbol of purity at a public forum. By surface

parole.significato: To make white; to whitewash.
parole.testo: From Latin candidātus (“dressed in white”, adjective); see Etymology 1 for further derivations. By surface analysis, candid + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A light source consisting of a wick embedded in a solid, flammable substance such as wax, tallow, or paraffin.
parole.testo: From Middle English candel, from Old English candel (“candle”), borrowed from Latin candēla (“candle”), from Latin candeō (“be white, bright, shining”, verb); see candid. Doublet of candela and chandelle.

parole.significato: The state of being sincere and open in speech; honesty in expression.
parole.testo: From Latin candor (“brightness, whiteness”), from candeō (“to shine”).

parole.significato: Turning white or gray.
parole.testo: From Latin canescens, present participle of canescere (“to become gray or white”).

parole.significato: The killing of a dog.
parole.testo: From Latin canis (“dog”) + -cide.

parole.significato: Synonym of Sothic: of or related to the star Sirius.
parole.testo: From Latin canīculāris (“of or related to a puppy; Sothic”), from Canīcula (“puppy; Sirius”) + -aris (“forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Synonym of dog days.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin diēs caniculārēs (literally “puppy days”), from Canīcula (“the Puppy”), a semantic loan of Ancient Greek Κῠ́ων (Kŭ́ōn, “the Dog”) in reference to Sirius, which appears in Epic Greek as κῠ́ων Ὠρίωνος (kŭ́ōn Ōríōnos, literally “Orion’s dog”) in its elided accusative form κύν’ Ὠρίωνος (

parole.significato: Characteristic of, or relating to the Caniformia.
parole.testo: From Latin canis (“dog”) + -form.

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to, a dog or dogs.
parole.testo: From Latin canīnus (“of dogs, doglike, dogtooth”), from canis (“dog”). Compare French canin.

parole.significato: Synonym of cuspid, one of the pointed teeth behind the incisors and in front of the premolars.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin dens canīnus (“doglike tooth”), from canis (“dog”), from their prominence in dogs and wolves. Compare dogtooth.

parole.significato: The caninus muscle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caninus, from canis + -inus.

parole.significato: A cylindrical or rectangular container usually of lightweight metal, plastic, or laminated pasteboard used for holding…
parole.testo: From Middle English canustyr (“basket”), a borrowing from Latin canistrum. Doublet of canaster and knaster. * (metal receptacle): Through influence of unrelated can. * (projectile): Short for canister shot, so called for its casing.

parole.significato: The condition of having gray hair.
parole.testo: From Latin cānitiēs (“gray hair, old age”).

parole.significato: A plant disease marked by gradual decay.
parole.testo: From Middle English canker, cancre, from Old English cancer (“cancer; crab”), akin to Dutch kanker, Old High German chanchar. Ultimately from Latin cancer (“a cancer”). Doublet of cancer, a later borrowing from Latin, and chancre, which came through French.

parole.significato: Relating to hemp; hempen.
parole.testo: Latin cannabinus.

parole.significato: A tall annual dioecious plant (Cannabis, especially Cannabis sativa), native to central Asia and having alternate, palm…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cannabis (“hemp”), borrowed from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). See there for more. Further reading at Etymology of cannabis on Wikipedia. Doublet of canvas and hemp.

parole.significato: A tube inserted into the body to drain or inject fluid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin cannula, canula (“tubular surgical instrument”), from Latin cannula (“reed; small reed- or tube-shaped object”), from canna (“cane; reed; object made from or shaped like a cane or reed”) + -ula (feminine form of -ulus (diminutive suffix). Canna is derived from Ancient Greek

parole.significato: A woman who holds a canonry in a conventual chapter.
parole.testo: From canon + -ess. Compare Latin canonissa.

parole.significato: canonical
parole.testo: From Late Latin canonicus (“canonic”).

parole.significato: Present in a canon, religious or otherwise.
parole.testo: From Middle English canonycal, from Medieval Latin canōnicālis. By surface analysis, canon + -ical.

parole.significato: The office of a canon; a canonry.
parole.testo: From Latin canonucatus canonical: compare French canonicat.

parole.significato: From or relating to the ancient city of Canopus in northern Egypt.
parole.testo: From Latin Canōpicus.

parole.significato: An Egyptian pottery container in which the entrails of a mummy have been placed.
parole.testo: From Latin Canōpicus, from Canopus + -icus.

parole.significato: A canopic jar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Canōpus.

parole.significato: melodious
parole.testo: From Latin canōrus.

parole.significato: An argot, the jargon of a particular class or subgroup.
parole.testo: From Latin cantō, probably via Old Northern French canter (“sing, tell”). Doublet of chant.

parole.significato: A graduate of the University of Cambridge.
parole.testo: Clipping of Cantabrigian, from Latin Cantabrigia (“Cambridge”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to or characteristic of Cambridge or its university
parole.testo: From Latin Cantabrigia (“Cambridge”) + -n.

parole.significato: A singing.
parole.testo: Latin cantatio.

parole.significato: Spanish fly, Lytta vesicatoria (syn. Cantharis vesicatoria).
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Latin cantharides, plural of cantharis.

parole.significato: A large drinking cup with two handles.
parole.testo: From Latin cantharus, from Ancient Greek κάνθαρος (kántharos).

parole.significato: Canthus, corner of the eye where the upper and lower lids meet.
parole.testo: From canthus, from Latin canthus (“corner of the eye”), from Ancient Greek κανθός (kanthós, “corner of the eye”). By surface analysis, canth- + -o-.

parole.significato: Either corner of the eye, where the eyelids meet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin canthus (“corner of the eye”), from Ancient Greek κανθός (kanthós, “corner of the eye”).

parole.significato: A chant, hymn or song, especially a nonmetrical one, with words from a biblical text.
parole.testo: From Latin canticulum, diminutive of cantus (“song”).

parole.significato: A canticle.
parole.testo: From Latin canticum (“chant, song”).

parole.significato: To chant, or to recite musically (especially in a synagogue).
parole.testo: First attested in 1864; borrowed from Latin cantillō (“to sing”), from cantillātus + -ō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A song, poem or incantation.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cantiō, from canere (“to sing”). Doublet of chanson and canzone. By surface analysis, Latin cant- + -ion.

parole.significato: A singer, especially someone who takes a special role of singing or song leading at a ceremony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cantor, agent noun from canere (“to sing”) + -tor (agent suffix). Doublet of chanter.

parole.significato: Of the side of the chancel, apse, altar or choir on which the cantor's (later precentor's) stall is placed (the left ha…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cantōris (“of the cantor”).

parole.significato: A female singer.
parole.testo: From Latin cantrīx.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Canterbury, England.
parole.testo: From Latin Cantuaria.

parole.significato: Synonym of superius.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cantus (literally “song, chant”).

parole.significato: A preexisting melody forming the basis of a polyphonic composition.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin cantus firmus (literally “fixed chant”).

parole.significato: To qualify, to allow.
parole.testo: From Latin capax, capacis (“capacious”) + -fy.

parole.significato: grandorder.
parole.testo: From Latin capax (“large, spacious”) + order.

parole.significato: The pungent grayish green flower bud of the European and Oriental caper (Capparis spinosa), which is pickled and eaten.
parole.testo: From Latin capparis, from Ancient Greek κάππαρις (kápparis).

parole.significato: An arrest warrant; a writ commanding officers to take a specified person or persons into custody.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin capiās (“you should seize, you are to seize”), from capiō (“to seize”).

parole.significato: An instrument for removing foreign bodies from a cavity, such as placental remnants from the uterus.
parole.testo: From Latin capiat (“let it take”).

parole.significato: A filament.
parole.testo: From Latin capillamentum, from capillus (“hair”). Compare French capillament.

parole.significato: Resembling or pertaining to hair, especially in slenderness or fineness.
parole.testo: From Latin capillāris (“pertaining to the hair”), from capillus (“the hair, properly of the head”), from caput (“head”).

parole.significato: A capillary (blood vessel).
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?] (“hair”).

parole.significato: A bush of hair; frizzing of the hair.
parole.testo: Latin capillatura.

parole.significato: Having the form of a hair
parole.testo: From Latin capillus (“hair”) + -iform.

parole.significato: A mass of sterile fibers within a fruiting body interspersed among spores.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin, “hair (collectively)”, from capillus.

parole.significato: Hooded, cowled.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin capistrātus, participial adjective from capistrō (“to halter”), from capistrum (“halter”) + -ō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Synonym of phorbeia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin capistrum. Doublet of capstan.

parole.significato: person
parole.testo: From the Latin capita, plural of caput.

parole.significato: In writing or editing, to write (something: either an entire word or text, or just the initial letter(s) thereof) in ca…
parole.testo: From capital + -ize, the first element ultimately from Latin capitālis (“of the head”).

parole.significato: Having a distinct globular tip.
parole.testo: From Latin capitātus (“having a head”), from caput (“head”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix). The noun comes from the clipping of capitate bone.

parole.significato: per head
parole.testo: From Latin capitatim, from caput + -atim.

parole.significato: Performing a headcount; the counting of people.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin capitātiōnem, from caput (“head”).

parole.significato: An ancient English tenure, abolished in 1660, by which either person or land was held immediately of the king, or of hi…
parole.testo: From Latin caput (“head”).

parole.significato: Having a very small knob-like termination, or collected into minute capitula.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin capitellātus, from capitellum + -ātus, diminutive of caput (“head”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Synonym of capitulum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin capitellum, diminuitive of Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *kauput- (English head), itself from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Doublet of caddie, cadel, cadet, capital, and caudillo.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Capitoline Hill in Rome or (historical) the various temples there in antiquity.
parole.testo: From Latin Capitolīnus (adj. & n.), from Capitolium (“Capitoline Hill”) + -inus (“-ine: forming adjectives”), from the oblique stem of caput (“head”) + -ō (“forming nouns”) or -ōlus (“-ole: forming diminutives”) + -ium (“forming location names”).

parole.significato: Synonym of capitol, similar citadels in ancient Italian and Roman towns.
parole.testo: From Latin Capitōlium (“Capitoline Hill, its temples; similar citadels”), from the oblique stem of caput (“head”) + -ō (noun-forming suffix) or -ōlus (“-ole”, diminutive suffix) + -ium (suffix forming place names). Doublet of capitol and capitoul.

parole.significato: An act passed in a chapter.
parole.testo: From Late Latin capitulāre, capitulārium, capitulārius, from Latin capitulum (“a small head, a chapter”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a capitulum.
parole.testo: From Middle English capituler, from Medieval Latin capitulāris, from Latin capitulum (“a small head, a chapter”).

parole.significato: To surrender on stipulated terms, end all resistance, give up, go along with or comply.
