parole.significato: A summary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin capitulum (“chapter”) (diminutive of Latin caput (“head”)).

parole.significato: A densely clustered inflorescence composed of a large number of individual florets arising from a platform-like base.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin capitulum. Doublet of chapiter and chapter.

parole.significato: The thick wall on the proximal side of the corpus of a pollen grain.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin cappa. Doublet of capa and cape.

parole.significato: A voluminous mantle worn by clergymen: in the Roman Catholic church, bishops wear violet, cardinals wear red.
parole.testo: From Latin cappa (“cape”) + magna (“great”).

parole.significato: Having a tendril or tendrils.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin capreolātus, from capreolus (“wild goat, tendril”) + -ātus, from caper (“goat”); see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Compare French capréolé.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the subfamily Capreolinae.
parole.testo: From Latin capreolus (“wild goat”), from caper (“goat”).

parole.significato: Goat.
parole.testo: From Latin caper (“male goat”) (genitive caprī). By surface analysis, capr- + -i-.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or derived from capric acid
parole.testo: From Latin caper (“goat”), after its smell + -ic. By surface analysis, capr- + -ic.

parole.significato: Someone with a Capricorn star sign.
parole.testo: From Latin Capricornus. By surface analysis, capri- + corn (“horn”).

parole.significato: A process for ripening, or pollinating, figs by means of their being punctured artificially, in a manner designed to re…
parole.testo: From Latin caprifīcātiōnem, ultimately from Latin caprifīcus (“wild fig tree”).

parole.significato: A hermaphrodite fruit, inedible to humans, of certain usually uncultivated species of Ficus, which is the source of the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caprifīcus.

parole.significato: The woodbine or honeysuckle.
parole.testo: From Latin caper (“goat”) + folium (“leaf”).

parole.significato: Having the form of a goat
parole.testo: From Latin capra (“she-goat”) + -form.

parole.significato: To pollinate (figs) by caprification.
parole.testo: From Latin caprifīcus + -ify. By surface analysis, capri- + -fy.

parole.significato: Resembling or originating from goats.
parole.testo: From Latin capra or caper (“goat”), + -genous.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Caprinae (goats, sheep, and certain wild relatives).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caprīnus. The taxonomic sense is a semantic loan from translingual Caprinae.

parole.significato: Having or relating to feet like those of a goat.
parole.testo: From Latin capriped-, capripēs.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or derived from caproic acid
parole.testo: From Latin caper (“goat”), after its smell + -oic. By surface analysis, capr- + -oic.

parole.significato: A liquid fatty acid, CH₃(CH₂)₄COOH, obtained from animal fats, and used in the manufacture of pharmaceuticals and flavo…
parole.testo: From Latin caper (“goat”) because of its smell. From capr- + -oic and acid.

parole.significato: Any of various tropical American plants, of the genus Capsicum, principally the species Capsicum annuum and Capsicum fr…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin capsicum, from Ancient Greek καψικός (kapsikós, “like a box”), from Latin capsa (“box”).

parole.significato: A form of mead made with chili peppers.
parole.testo: capsicum + Latin mel (“honey”).

parole.significato: A courting of favor or applause, by flattery or address; a captivating quality; an attraction
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin captatio, captationis, from capto. Compare French captation.

parole.significato: The descriptive heading or title, of a document or part thereof.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin captiō (“deception, fraud”), from the past participle of capiō (“to take, to seize”) (English capture). Compare Middle English capcioun (“seizure, capture”).

parole.significato: To make (a person, an animal, etc.) a captive; to take prisoner; to capture, to subdue.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin captīvātus, the perfect passive participle of captīvō (“to capture”), from Latin captīvus (“captive, prisoner”) (ultimately from capiō (“to capture, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to hold; to seize”)) + -ō (suffix forming first-conjugation verbs). parole.significato: A female captivator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin captīvātrīx. By surface analysis, captivate + -trix.

parole.significato: One who has been captured or is otherwise confined.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English captif; derived from Latin captīvus, probably through a borrowing from a Middle French intermediate. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“seize, hold”). Doublet of caitiff.

parole.significato: The state of being captive.
parole.testo: From Middle English captivite, from Latin captīvitās. By surface analysis, captive + -ity. Entered into the English lexicon around the 14th century.

parole.significato: One who is holding a captive or captives.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin captor, from Latin capiō. English usage began around 1688.

parole.significato: Worthless residue of sublimation or distillation.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin caput mortuum (literally “dead head”).

parole.significato: A neonatal condition involving a serosanguinous, subcutaneous, extraperiosteal fluid collection with poorly defined mar…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin caput succēdāneum.

parole.significato: An ancient small boat made of wickerwork covered with a hide or leather.
parole.testo: From Latin carabus. The entomological sense is borrowed from translingual Carabus, from the same Latin source.

parole.significato: A mark or sign.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin character.

parole.significato: A biennial plant of species Carum carvi, native to Europe and Asia, mainly grown for its seed to be used as a culinary…

parole.significato: Accumulation of wasteful elements of carbon or mere carbon inside blood.
parole.testo: From carbo- + -hæmia, conjunction: Latin carbo (“charcol”) and Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).

parole.significato: An excessive amount of carbon, particularity carbon dioxide, in the blood.
parole.testo: From carbon + -aemia, conjunction: Latin carbo (“charcol”) and Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling a carbuncle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin carbunculāris. By surface analysis, carbuncle + -ar.

parole.significato: The blasting of something, by excessive heat or cold.
parole.testo: Latin carbunculatio.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to imprisonment or a prison.
parole.testo: From Late Latin carcerālis (“carceral”), from Latin carcer (“jail, prison”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn, in the sense of an enclosure”)) + -ālis (suffix forming relational adjectives).

parole.significato: An invasive malignant tumour derived from epithelial tissue that tends to metastasize to other areas of the body.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin carcinōma (“tumour; ulcer; carcinoma”), from Ancient Greek κᾰρκῐ́νωμᾰ (kărkĭ́nōmă, “sore, ulcer; cancer”), from καρκινόω (karkinóō, “to make (something) resemble a crab”, in the mediopassive "to become cancerous; to suffer from cancer") + -μᾰ (-mă, action noun suffix). parole.significato: The dignity and ecclesiastic office of Roman Catholic cardinal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin cardinālātus, from cardinālis (“cardinal”) + -ātus, itself the noun use of an adjective derived from cardō (“hinge, main point”) + -ālis (“-al”). By surface analysis, cardinal + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

parole.significato: A piece of body armour—originally a metal breastplate or pair of plates—worn in classical antiquity to protect the regi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cardiophylax, derived from Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía) + φύλαξ (phúlax).

parole.significato: inflammation of the heart (any or all parts of it).

parole.significato: The basal joint of the maxilla in insects
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cardō (“hinge”). Doublet of kern.

parole.significato: An oily yellow phenolic compound C₂₁H₃₀O₃ extracted from the shell of the cashew nut and one of the primary components…

parole.significato: Synonym of carenum (“reduction of must or sweet wine in ancient European cuisine”).
parole.testo: From Latin carēnum or caroenum, from Ancient Greek κάροινον (károinon), q.v.

parole.significato: A 40-day fast or period of similar abstinence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin carēna (“40-day fast; remission of such a fast”), from Late Latin quadragēna (“40-day period, Lent”) or quarantena (“40-day period”), from Latin quadrāgēnus (“40 each”), from quadrāgintā (“four tens, forty”). Doublet of quadragene.

parole.significato: A reduction of must or sweet wine produced by boiling it in large kettles until it was reduced by half or two-thirds in…
parole.testo: From Latin carēnum or caroenum, from Ancient Greek κάροινον (károinon), q.v.

parole.significato: A mark ⟨ ‸ ⟩ used by writers and proofreaders to indicate that something is to be inserted at that point.
parole.testo: From the Latin caret (“it lacks”), the third-person singular present active indicative form of careō (“to lack”).

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Carex of sedges.
parole.testo: From Latin carex.

parole.significato: A junction of four roads.
parole.testo: From Middle English carfukes, an Anglicisation of Latin quadrifurcus (“four-pronged, four-forked”). Doublet of carfour.

parole.significato: Shaped like a fig.
parole.testo: Latin carica (“a kind of dry fig”) + -ous.

parole.significato: figs, especially those from Caria
parole.testo: From Latin carica.

parole.significato: A longitudinal ridge or projection like the keel of a boat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin carīna (“keel”). Doublet of careen and carene.

parole.significato: Shaped like a boat's keel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin carīnātus, from carīna (“keel”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). The noun comes from a substantivization of the adjective, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Synonym of scaphoid abdomen.
parole.testo: From Latin carinatus, from carina (“keel”), + Middle French abdomen, from Latin abdomen, possibly from abdō (“conceal”), from ab (“away”) + dere (“to put, place”).

parole.significato: charitable
parole.testo: From Latin cāritās.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the caritive case.
parole.testo: From Latin careo (“I lack, am without”).

parole.significato: Either of two amino acid toxins produced by the sea anemone species, Actinia cari.

parole.significato: A visual poem in the shape of an object.

parole.significato: The state of being carnal.
parole.testo: From Middle English carnalitee, carnalyte, carnalite, from Latin carnālitās, equivalent to carnal + -ity. Compare Old French charnalité.

parole.significato: A crypt, a charnel house.
parole.testo: From Latin carnarium, from caro, carnis (“flesh”).

parole.significato: Embodied in, or having, flesh (as opposed to just a spirit etc.).
parole.testo: From Late Latin carnātus (“fleshy”), from oblique stem of Latin carō, carnis (“meat, flesh”) + -ātus (whence -ate).

parole.significato: Carnelian.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin carneolus (“carnelian”), diminutive of Latin carneus (“fleshy”).

parole.significato: A pale pink or beige color; peach or flesh-tone.
parole.testo: Latin carneus.

parole.significato: An executioner.
parole.testo: From Latin carnifex (“butcher”).

parole.significato: To form flesh; to become like flesh.
parole.testo: From Latin carnificare, from Latin carnis (“flesh”) + facere (“to make”). Compare French carnifier.

parole.significato: Carnivorans.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin carnivora.

parole.significato: greedy appetite for meat
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin caro, carnis (“flesh, meat”) + -i- + voracity.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to carnivores, or the taxonomic order Carnivora.
parole.testo: From Latin carnivorus (“flesh-eating”).

parole.significato: Any writing, films, images, or other material that contains gratuitous amounts of bloodshed or violence.
parole.testo: From Latin carnis (“meat”) and Ancient Greek γραφή (graphḗ, “writing”), by analogy to pornography. Although it is often taken to be a blend carnage and pornography, this is not the case.

parole.significato: A strong fear or dislike of meat.
parole.testo: From Latin carnis (“meat”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: Fleshy.
parole.testo: From Latin carnosus.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a person named Charles or its variants and cognates; or places, things, or eras so named.
parole.testo: From Latin Carolus (“Charles”) + -ean. May be decomposed as Carol (“Charles”) + -ean.

parole.significato: A former gold coin of Germany
parole.testo: Latin Carolus (“Charles”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Carolean (“relating to the time of Kings Charles I and II of England or Charles III of the United Kingdom, o…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin carolīnus.

parole.significato: A descendant of Charles Martel; a Carolingian.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Carolingus, from a Frankish patronymic ultimately composed of Proto-West Germanic *karil + *-ing. By surface analysis, Carolus + -ing.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Carolings, the members of a Frankish dynasty, descended from Charles Martel, which arose from t…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Carolingī (“Carolings (descendants of Charles Martel)”) [plural of Carolingus, from a Frankish patronymic ultimately composed of Proto-West Germanic *karil + *-ing] + -ian. Reshaping of earlier Carlovingian, from Middle French Carlovingien, itself a misconstruction of Carlingien.

parole.significato: An old English gold coin, worth 20 (or later 23) shillings.
parole.testo: From Carolus, Latin for Charles. Doublet of Charles.

parole.significato: A Spanish-American peso or piece of eight issued by Charles III (1759–88) and Charles IV (1788–1808) of Spain.

parole.significato: Any of the eight bones of the wrist (carpus).

parole.significato: A carpal, especially one of the series articulating with the metacarpals.

parole.significato: Enjoy the present, make the most of today, (common mistranslation) seize the day.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin carpe diem (“enjoy the day”, literally “pluck (or harvest) the day”).

parole.significato: Synonym of carpel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin carpellum. See carpel for more.

parole.significato: The group of bones that make up the wrist.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin carpus, from Ancient Greek καρπός (karpós, “wrist”).

parole.significato: A heavy wheeled turnplough that was used during the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin carrūca.

parole.significato: A load: various English units of weight or volume based upon standardized cartloads of certain commodities.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin carrus (“load”). Doublet of car and horse.

parole.significato: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see carry, over.
parole.testo: Attested since the 17th century; listed for instance in Elisha Coles' 1676 dictionary as a translation of transfer, thereby possibly a calque of Latin transfero; compare Dutch overdragen, German übertragen.

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to, Descartes, his mathematical methods, or his philosophy, especially with regard to its emphasis on…
parole.testo: From the New Latin Cartesiānus, from Cartesius (“René Descartes”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Carthage.
parole.testo: Latin carthāginiānus, from Carthāgō + -iānus.

parole.significato: A member of a Christian contemplative order of monks founded by Bruno of Cologne (St Bruno) in 1084.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Carthusianus, from Cart(h)usia, Latinization of Old French Chartrouse, a region near Grenoble where the order was founded, now Chartreuse; from Late Latin Catorissium, Cantourisa, Caturissium, Chatrousse, probably ultimately from Gaulish *Katurīx (literally “battle-king”). parole.significato: The formation of cartilage.
parole.testo: From Latin cartilago, cartilaginis (“cartilage”) + facere (“to make”).

parole.significato: Comprising soft cartilage rather than bone.

parole.significato: A medieval manuscript register containing full or excerpted transcriptions of important documents, especially of origin…
parole.testo: From Middle English cartulari, borrowed from Medieval Latin chartulārium. Doublet of khaltura.

parole.significato: A form of land taxation that replaced Danegeld in twelfth-century England.
parole.testo: From Late Latin carrucagium, from carruca (“plough”); compare tillage.

parole.significato: The notional area of land able to be farmed in a year by a team of 8 oxen pulling a carruca plow, usually reckoned at 1…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin carūcāta (“ploughland”), from Latin carūca (“chariot; coach; carruca”). Compare French charrue (“plough”).

parole.significato: Synonym of caruncle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caruncula (“a little piece of flesh”). Doublet of caruncle.

parole.significato: An exoenzyme that hydrolyzes casein.
parole.testo: From Latin cāseus (“cheese”) + -ase.

parole.significato: To make or become cheeselike.
parole.testo: From Latin cāseus (“cheese”), + -fy.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling cheese.
parole.testo: Compare French caséique, from Latin caseus (“cheese”). Doublet of cheesy. By surface analysis, Latin case(us) + -ic

parole.significato: Casein.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caseum (“cheese”).

parole.significato: To render void; to undo or annul.
parole.testo: From Late Latin cassare. See cass.

parole.significato: An American bird (Psarocolius decumanus, syn. Cassicus cristatus), allied to the starlings and orioles, remarkable for…

parole.significato: An ellagitannin found in oak and chestnut wood.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Castalia, a mythical fountain of inspiration on Mount Parnassus, sacred to the Muses.

parole.significato: Having the colour of a chestnut; chestnut-coloured.

parole.significato: The office of a castellan, the lordship of a castle.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin castellania, from Latin castellānus. Doublet of chatellany.

parole.significato: castle-like: built or shaped like a castle.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin castellātus (“fortified” “made into a castle”), from castellum (“little fortification, castle”) + -ātus (forming participial adjectives). By surface analysis, Latin castellum + -ate (adjective-forming suffix) or castle + -ate.

parole.significato: The district of a castle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin castellātus. By surface analysis, castle + -ate (forming nouns denoting a rank or office, the concrete charge of this office).

parole.significato: Castle-like: built or shaped like a castle; usually, specifically, having castellations (crenellations).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin castellātus (“fortified, castellate”) + -ed (forming past participles). Equivalent to the past participle of castellate but attested earlier than other uses of the verb.

parole.significato: Synonym of enclosed, when used for fountains, cisterns, &c.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin castellum (“cistern”).

parole.significato: The study of castles.

parole.significato: A small Roman detached fort or fortlet used as a watch tower or signal station.

parole.significato: One who is castigated.

parole.significato: To punish or reprimand someone severely.

Doublet of chastise

parole.significato: The bitter exudate of the castor sacs of mature beavers, used as a scent mark, and as a tincture in some perfumes.

parole.significato: An extract from the glands of a beaver, reputed to have medicinal value.

parole.significato: Planning and construction of a military camp.

parole.significato: A castrated man; a eunuch.

parole.significato: To remove the testicles of a person or animal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin castrātus, perfect passive participle of Latin castrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Displaced native geld in its broader sense.

parole.significato: A female who castrates (either literally or metaphorically).

parole.significato: Belonging to a (military) camp.

parole.significato: castrensial
parole.testo: From Latin castrēnsis + -i- + -an, from castra (“camp”).

parole.significato: Among the Ancient Romans, a building or plot of land used as a military defensive position.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin castrum. Doublet of Caister, Chester, ksar, and qasr.

parole.significato: Synonym of casuistry, particularly in its neutral sense.
parole.testo: From casuistic + -s, equivalent to Latin casus + -istics, in the medical sense under the influence of English case. Also by surface analysis, casu(al) + -istics or by surface analysis, casu(al) + -ist + -ics or by surface analysis, casuist + -ics.

parole.significato: A chasuble.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin casula.

parole.significato: An act seen as justifying or causing a war; an act of war.

parole.significato: Either of two types of misuse of a word or misapplication of a concept.

parole.testo: From the Latin form of the Ancient Greek κατακόσμησις (katakósmēsis, “arrangement”).

parole.significato: (said of a line with incomplete meter) lacking a syllable at the end or ending with an incomplete foot.

parole.significato: The female menstrual discharge.

parole.significato: A boy or younger man in a homoerotic relationship with an older man.

parole.significato: Semicoma.

parole.significato: A Roman catapult (weapon for launching projectiles).

parole.significato: A platform for exhibiting slaves for sale.

parole.significato: Religious instruction given orally to catechumens.

parole.significato: Religious teaching, especially that given to children before confirmation.

parole.significato: A book, in question and answer form, summarizing the basic principles of Christianity.

parole.significato: To give oral instruction, especially of religion; (specifically) by the formal question-and-answer method; in the Churc…

parole.significato: Exposure of an opponent's secret wickedness, especially in the opponent's presence.

parole.significato: Purgative; inducing mental or physical catharsis.

parole.significato: The chair or throne of a bishop.

parole.significato: promulgated ex cathedra; authoritative.

parole.significato: The jurisdiction of an Armenian catholicos.

parole.significato: The jurisdiction of a catholicos.

parole.significato: The property of having a caudate extension or tail.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the tail, or anything tail-shaped.

parole.significato: The degree to which something, such as a plant or neuron, has a well-formed main stem.

parole.significato: Relating to an advocate (lawyer), or to the maintenance and defence of lawsuits.

parole.significato: Capable of burning, corroding or destroying organic tissue.

parole.significato: A small cell.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cellula (“a small apartment”), diminutive of cella.

parole.significato: An inflammation of subcutaneous or connective tissue caused by a bacterial infection.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin cellulitis. By surface analysis, cellule + -itis. Doublet of cellulite. First attested in the 1840s.

parole.significato: A member of one of the ancient peoples of Western Europe called Celtae by the Romans.
parole.testo: From Latin Celtae (singular Celta) from Ancient Greek Κελτοί (Keltoí). English Celts is from the 17th century. Until the mid 19th century, /sɛlt/ is the only recorded pronunciation. A consciously archaizing pronunciation /kɛlt/ was advocated during Irish and Welsh nationalism beginning in the 1850s.

parole.significato: A prehistoric chisel-bladed tool.
parole.testo: From Latin celtis (“chisel”), very probably a ghost word originating from a copyist's error in the Vulgate Bible, but taken as genuine and subsequently used in Medieval Latin.

parole.significato: The Swiss pine, Pinus cembra.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin cembra.

parole.significato: A bony substance that covers the root of a tooth; cement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caementum. Doublet of cement.

parole.significato: Of or relating to dinner (the evening meal) or supper.
parole.testo: From Latin cenatorius, from cenare (“to dine, sup”), from cena, coena (“dinner, supper”).

parole.significato: The leader of a cenobium: an abbot, a guru.
parole.testo: Simplification of coenobiarch, from Latin coenobiarcha (“abbot”), from Koine Greek κοινοβιάρχης (koinobiárkhēs, “abbot”), from κοινόβιον (koinóbion, “cenobium, monastery”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”) + -ης (-ēs).

parole.significato: (of an elective franchise, especially in the nineteenth century) dependent on or proportional to a poll tax (cense) or…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin censitarius, from Latin censere (“assess (for tax)”). Compare French censitaire, Spanish and Italian censitario.

parole.significato: One of the two magistrates who originally administered the census of citizens, and by Classical times (between the 8th…
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Latin cēnsor (“magistrate; critic”), from cēnseō (“to give an opinion, judge; to assess, reckon; to decree, determine”) + -sor (variant of -tor (suffix forming masculine agent nouns)). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱens- (“to announce, proclaim; to put in order”). Th

parole.significato: A censor of morals.
parole.testo: From Latin censor morum, a censor (critic) of morals.

parole.significato: Addicted to censure and scolding; apt to blame or condemn; severe in making remarks on others, or on their writings or…
parole.testo: From Latin cēnsōrius (“of or pertaining to a censor; severe”). In sense 3 ("tending to engage in or support censorship"), reanalyzed as censor + -ious.

parole.significato: Relating to, or containing, a census.
parole.testo: From Latin censualis, from census.

parole.significato: An official count or enumeration of members of a population (not necessarily human), usually residents or citizens in a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cēnsus, from cēnseō. See censor.

parole.significato: Rate by the hundred; percentage.
parole.testo: From Latin centum (“hundred”) + -age (forming nouns indicating a rate). Compare later percentage.

parole.significato: A weight of one hundred avoirdupois pounds.
parole.testo: From Latin centum (“a hundred”) + -al, perhaps modeled after quintal.

parole.significato: A mythical beast having a horse's body with a man's head and torso in place of the head and neck of the horse.
parole.testo: From Latin centaurus, from Ancient Greek κένταυρος (kéntauros), from Κένταυρος (Kéntauros, “a member of a savage race from Thessaly”).

parole.significato: Any of the plants in the genus Centaurea.
parole.testo: From the genus name, Centaurea, from Latin centaurēa. Doublet of centaury.

parole.significato: Any of the flowering plants in or formerly in the genus Centaurium.
parole.testo: From Middle English centaure, from Old English centaurie, from Medieval Latin centaurēa, centauria, from Latin centaurēum, centaurion, from Ancient Greek κενταύρειον (kentaúreion, “several plants related to Centaurea”), from κένταυρος (kéntauros, “centaur”) (due to the mythological discovery of its

parole.significato: Of or related to the number one hundred, particularly
parole.testo: From Latin centēnārius (“containing 100; local official overseeing a hundred”), either directly or through French centenaire from centēnī (“100 each”) + -ārius (-ary), from centum (“hundred”). Doublet of centner, kantar, and quintal.

parole.significato: Synonym of century: A period of 100 years.
parole.testo: From Late Latin centennium (“period of 100 years”), from centennis (“100-year”) + -ium (“forming abstract nouns”). Cognate with centennial.

parole.significato: Divided into a hundred parts.
parole.testo: From Latin centēsimus + -al.

parole.significato: To select one person in every hundred for a punishment.
parole.testo: First attested in 1753; borrowed from Latin centēsimātus, perfect passive participle of the Latin centēsimō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from centēsimus (“hundredth”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); compare tertiate, quintate, sextate, septimate, decimate, and duodecimate.

parole.significato: The selection by lot of every hundredth man (of an army or group of prisoners or mutineers) for execution.
parole.testo: From the Latin centēsimātiō, from centēsimō, from centēsimus (“hundredth”); compare quintation, septimation, decimation, vicesimation, and tricesimation.

parole.significato: One hundredth part; one percent.
parole.testo: Latin centesima.

parole.significato: Divided into a hundred parts.
parole.testo: From Latin centifidus, from centi- (“hundred”) + -fidus, from findere (“to split”). Equivalent to centi- + fid + -ous.

parole.significato: Having more leaves than can be easily counted.
parole.testo: From Latin centifolius, from centum (“hundred”) + folium (“leaf”).

parole.significato: A treatise consisting of a hundred astrological aphorisms.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin centiloquium.

parole.significato: A work divided into a hundred parts.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin centiloquium. By surface analysis, centi- + -loquy.

parole.significato: Synonym of Hecatoncheires.
parole.testo: From Latin centimanus, a calque of Ancient Greek Ἑκατόγχειρες (Hekatónkheires, “the Hundred-Handed”) from centi- (“100”) + manus (“hand”).

parole.significato: A hotchpotch, a mixture; especially a piece made up of quotations from other authors, or a poem containing individual l…
parole.testo: From Latin cento (“patchwork garment”).

parole.significato: Being in the centre.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin centrālis, from centrum (“centre”), from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron); by surface analysis, centre + -al.

parole.significato: The central, or one of the central, bones of the carpus or tarsus in most vertebrates. In the human tarsus it is repres…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin centrāle.

parole.significato: The middle part of the head; the part of the head situated between the occiput and sinciput.
parole.testo: From centri- + Latin -ciput, from oblique stem of caput (“head”).

parole.significato: Tending, or causing, to recede from the center.
parole.testo: From New Latin centrifugālis, coined by Christiaan Huygens from Latin centrum (“center”) + fugiō (“to flee”) + -al.

parole.significato: A barrel-shaped microtubule structure found in most animal cells, important in the process of mitosis (nuclear division…

parole.significato: Directed or moving towards a centre.
parole.testo: From New Latin centripetālis coined by Sir Isaac Newton, from Latin centrum (“center”) + petō (“to seek, aim”) + -al. Analysable as centri- + -petal.

parole.significato: central, especially of mass nouns
parole.testo: From centre + -o-, from from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron).

parole.significato: Having line converging to a centre.
parole.testo: From Latin centrum + linea (“line”).

parole.significato: A centre.
parole.testo: From Middle English centrum, from Latin centrum. Doublet of centre/center.

parole.significato: Referring to an Indo-European language that did not produce sibilants from a series of Proto-Indo-European palatovelar…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin centum (“hundred”), attested at least since 1890s. Its use in linguistics is due to it being a canonical example of a word retaining an original velar stop, as opposed to Avestan 𐬯𐬀𐬙𐬆𐬨 (satəm). Doublet of hundred and satem.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the centumviri
parole.testo: From Latin centumvirālis.

parole.significato: A group of one hundred people, especially (politics) a council of about 100 men who share power or rule, particularly (…
parole.testo: From Latin centumvirātus, from centumvirī (“centumvirs, centumviri”) + ātus (abstract noun-forming suffix). Equivalent to centumvir + -ate (forms nouns denoting a rank or office, here the group of people performing it).

parole.significato: To make a hundredfold; to repeat or multiply a hundred times.
parole.testo: Latin centuplicare. See centuple.

parole.significato: Divided into hundreds.
parole.testo: First attested in 1540; borrowed from Latin centuriātus, perfect passive participle of centuriō (“to divide into groups of one hundred”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A method of land measurement used in Ancient Rome, characterised by the regular layout of a square grid traced using su…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin centuriātiō.

parole.significato: An officer of the ancient Roman army, in command of a century of soldiers.
parole.testo: From Middle English centurioun, from Latin centuriō, centuriōnis (“a commander of a hundred, centurion”), from Latin centum (“a hundred”). Displaced native English hundreder and hundredman, from Middle English hundredman, from Old English hundredmann (“centurion”).

parole.significato: An organic compound with antiasthma properties, found in onions.
parole.testo: From Latin cepa (“onion”) + -ene.

parole.significato: Relating to, or affected with, headache.
parole.testo: Latin cephalalgicus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A Cepheid variable.
parole.testo: From Latin Cephei + -id, from Latin Cepheus, from Ancient Greek Κηφεύς (Kēpheús).

parole.significato: A radially pulsating (expanding and contracting) variable star with a regular period and known relationship between per…
parole.testo: From Latin Delta Cephei, the first such star identified. From Cepheus, the name of the constellation in which such stars were first discovered. From being a star with variable brightness.

parole.significato: Waxy.

parole.significato: A white amorphous substance, the insoluble part of cherry gum; meta-arabinic acid.

parole.significato: Covered with wax.

parole.significato: An orchid (Eria compressa).

parole.significato: The parasitic larva of trematodes that infect the final host generally.
parole.testo: From New Latin cercāria, from Ancient Greek κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”) + -āria.

parole.significato: Waxy.

parole.significato: The act of cerebrating; reflection, thinking, thought.

parole.significato: Cloth coated with wax so that it is waterproof, used for covering the dead.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, consisting of, or used in a ceremony.
parole.testo: From Middle English cerymonial, from Latin caerimōniālis. Morphologically ceremony + -al or -ial.

parole.significato: A ritual, with religious or cultural significance.
parole.testo: From Middle English cerymonye, from Latin caerimonia or caeremonia, later often cerimonia (“sacredness, reverence, a sacred rite”).

parole.significato: waxen; waxy; like wax
parole.testo: From Latin cēreus, from cēra (“wax”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Roman goddess Ceres
parole.testo: From Latin Cereris, genitive case of Cerēs.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Roman goddess Ceres.

parole.significato: Inclining or nodding downward; pendulous; drooping.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Turkey oak.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to certitude.
parole.testo: From Latin certitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin certitūdō, from certus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, certitude + -al.

parole.significato: Characterised by certitude.
parole.testo: From Latin certitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin certitūdō, from certus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, certitude + -ous.

parole.significato: Cerulean.
parole.testo: From Latin caerulus.

parole.significato: The act of becoming blue; bluing
parole.testo: From Latin caerulescens, from caeruleus (“cerulean”), from caelum + -uleus, equivalent to cerulean + -escence. By surface analysis, cerule + -escence.

parole.significato: A greenish-blue pigment consisting essentially of cobalt stannate.
parole.testo: From Latin ceruleum (“dark blue, dark green”).

parole.significato: A blue metalloprotein that contains copper; it acts as a ferroxidase in association with transferrin.

parole.significato: Earwax.

parole.significato: A mineral form of lead carbonate, PbCO₃, that is an ore of lead.
parole.testo: From Latin cērussa (“white lead”) + -ite.

parole.significato: neck pain

parole.significato: The killing of deer.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the cervix.
parole.testo: From Latin cervīcis, genitive of cervīx. By surface analysis, cervic- + -o-.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of deer (in the broad sense).
parole.testo: By anglicisation from Latin cervīnus; by surface analysis, Latin cerv(us) (“deer”) + -ine.

parole.significato: The neck.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cervīx (“neck”), see below.

parole.significato: A radical, C₂₇H₅₅, supposed to exist in several compounds obtained from waxes.

parole.significato: An oil obtained by distillation of peat, containing various members of the pyridine series.

parole.significato: tufty; growing in tufts.

parole.significato: Dormant, inactive.
parole.testo: From Latin cessans, present participle of cessare. See cease.

parole.significato: Of the air, yielding.
parole.testo: From Latin cess-, past participle stem of cedere (“cede”).

parole.significato: The person who receives transfer or cession of a personal obligation from the cedent.

parole.significato: A parasitic flatworm of the class Cestoda; a tapeworm.
parole.testo: From New Latin Cestoda, from cestus (“girdle, belt”), from Ancient Greek κεστός (kestós, “of Aphrodite’s charmed girdle”).

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to a boxer's gloves
parole.testo: Latin cestus (“boxing glove”)

parole.significato: A leather fighting glove, frequently weighted with metal.

parole.significato: A girdle, especially that of Aphrodite (or Venus) which gave the wearer the power to excite love.

parole.significato: The aliphatic hydrocarbon C₁₆H₃₄ (hexadecane) used as a standard for diesel fuel.
parole.testo: From Latin cetus (“whale”) + -ane.

parole.significato: All things being equal; with all other things or factors remaining the same; other things held constant; all else uncha…
parole.testo: From Latin cēterīs, the ablative plural of cēterus (“the other, the rest”), + paribus, the ablative case plural of pār (“equal”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to cetoleic acid or its derivatives
parole.testo: From Latin cetus + oleic.

parole.significato: Compare; compare to; compare with.
parole.testo: From Latin cf., abbreviation of cōnfer (“compare”), imperative of cōnferō (“to compare”).

parole.significato: A cyst in the eyelid, caused by inflammation of a blocked meibomian gland.

parole.significato: A form of fine-grained quartz that is nearly transparent or has a milky translucence; it fractures conchoidally.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin chalcēdōnius, from Ancient Greek χαλκηδόνιος (khalkēdónios), from Ancient Greek χαλκηδών (khalkēdṓn), cognate to Arabic كَرْكَنْد (karkand).

parole.significato: Synonym of Chalcidian
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Chalcidicus, from Ancient Greek Χαλκιδικός (Khalkidikós).

parole.significato: In ancient Roman architecture, the vestibule or portico of a public building opening on to the forum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin chalcidicum, from Chalcidicum, neuter singular of Chalcidicus (“Chalcidian”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Chaldea.

parole.significato: An idiom or peculiarity in Biblical Aramaic.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Chaldea specifically, or ancient Babylonia in general.

parole.significato: Filled with chaos.

parole.significato: A chapel within the jurisdiction of a church; a subordinate ecclesiastical foundation.
parole.testo: Compare English chapellenie, Latin capellania. See chaplain.

parole.significato: To depict someone or something a particular way (often negative).

parole.significato: Resembling paper or parchment; papery.
parole.testo: From Latin chartaceus. See charta.

parole.significato: A small piece of paper for the storage of one dose of a medicinal powder.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin chartula (“little paper”). Doublet of charter.

parole.significato: A deep, steep-sided rift, gap or fissure; a gorge or abyss.
parole.testo: From Latin chasma, from Ancient Greek χάσμα (khásma, “abyss, cleft”). Doublet of chasma. Compare schism. Displaced native Old English swelh and Old English elh.

parole.significato: Synonym of jungle cat (Felis chaus)
parole.testo: From New Latin chaus, from a native, probably Turkic, name; compare Nogai кавыс (kavıs).

parole.significato: The corner of the mouth (as used in cephalometry)

parole.significato: The typical pentadactyloid limb of the higher vertebrates.
parole.testo: From New Latin cheiropterygium, from Ancient Greek χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + πτερύγιον (pterúgion, “wing, fin”).

parole.significato: A pincer-like claw of a crustacean or arachnid.

parole.significato: Either of the prehensile claws found on the proboscis of chelicerates (horseshoe crabs, sea spiders and arachnids).
parole.testo: From New Latin chēlicera, from Ancient Greek χηλή (khēlḗ, “jawbone”) + κέρας (kéras, “horn”).

parole.significato: pseudoscorpion
parole.testo: From Latin chēlē (“claw”) (from Ancient Greek χηλή (khēlḗ, “claw”)) + -fer.

parole.significato: Practising chemistry (or, earlier, alchemy); pertaining to these sciences.
parole.testo: From New Latin chemicus, chimicus, chymicus.

From chemist, chymist, from Latin alchimista, from Arabic اَلْكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ), from article اَل (al-) + Ancient Greek χυμεία (khumeía, “art of alloying metals”), from χύμα (khúma, “fluid”), from χυμός (khumós, “juice”), from χέω (khéō, “to pour”).

parole.significato: Relating to or using chemicals or chemistry.
parole.testo: Back-formation from compounds built on New Latin chēmicus (“pertaining to alchemy or chemistry”) and chēmia (“chemistry”), ultimately of Ancient Greek origin.

parole.significato: to chemisorb
parole.testo: Blend of chemo- (“chemical”) + adsorb, from Latin sorbere (“to suck”)

parole.significato: alchemy, chemistry (prior to their being properly distinguished)
parole.testo: From the post-Classical Latin chemia, chymia, chimia. Doublet of Kimiya.

parole.significato: A hyrax.
parole.testo: From Latin choerogryllus, from Ancient Greek χοιρογρύλλιος (khoirogrúllios), a compound of χοῖρος (khoîros) and γρῦλος (grûlos), both meaning “pig”. The Greek word was used in the Septuagint to render Hebrew שפן (“hyrax”).

parole.significato: A peninsula.
parole.testo: From Latin Chersonēsus, from Ancient Greek χερσόνησος (khersónēsos, “originally, the Gallipoli peninsula; later, any peninsula”), from χέρσος (khérsos, “dry land”) + νῆσος (nêsos, “island”).

parole.significato: A winged creature attending God and guarding his throne described as a being with four faces (man, lion, ox, and eagle)…

parole.significato: A cherub.
parole.testo: From Middle English cherubin, cherubine, cherubym, cherubyn, cherybin, gerubin, jerubin, from Old English cerubin, cerubim, ceruphin, cherubin, from Latin cherūbīn, cherūbīm, from Ancient Greek χερουβίν (kheroubín), χερουβείν (kheroubeín), χερουβίμ (kheroubím), from Hebrew כְּרוּבִים (k'ruvím), from

parole.significato: The twenty-second letter of the Classical and Modern Greek alphabets.
parole.testo: From Latin chī, from Ancient Greek χεῖ (kheî).

parole.significato: A crossing of two nerves, ligaments etc.
parole.testo: From New Latin chiasma, from Ancient Greek χῑ́ασμα (khī́asma), from χῑάζω (khīázō, “to mark with an X”).

parole.significato: An inversion of the relationship between the elements of phrases.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin chiasmus, borrowed from Ancient Greek χιασμός (khiasmós), from χῑᾰ́ζω (khīắzō, “to mark with an X”) + -μός (-mós).

parole.significato: thousand; thousandfold.
parole.testo: From Latin chilias, itself from Ancient Greek χίλιοι (khílioi, “thousand”). Doublet of kilo-.

parole.significato: A group of 1000 things, particularly
parole.testo: From Latin chilias (“the number 1000, a group of 1000 things”), possibly via French chiliade, from Ancient Greek χιλιάς (khiliás, “the number 1000, any large amount, a millennium”), from χῑ́λιοι (khī́lioi, “1000”) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs, “-ad: forming collective nouns”). Equivalent to chilia- + -ad.

parole.significato: A regiment of 1000 soldiers, typically commanded by a chiliarch.
parole.testo: From Latin chiliarchia, from Ancient Greek χιλιαρχία (khiliarkhía), from χῑ́λιοι (khī́lioi, “1000”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “-archy: rule by”). Equivalent to chilia- + -archy.

parole.significato: Synonym of millenarian: a person who believes the Second Coming of Jesus Christ will involve his physical rule on Earth…
parole.testo: From Latin chiliasta, possibly via French chiliaste, from Ancient Greek χιλιαστής (khiliastḗs), from χῑ́λιοι (khī́lioi, “thousand”) + -αστής (-astḗs, “-ast, -ist: forming agent nouns”). Equivalent to chilia- + -ast.

parole.significato: Producing chyle.
parole.testo: From Latin chilus, chylus (“chyle”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a chimera.
parole.testo: From chimera, from Latin chimaera, from Ancient Greek χίμαιρα (khímaira, “she-goat”). This term entered English in or around 1638.

parole.significato: A Chinese pink (Dianthus chinensis).
parole.testo: From New Latin chinensis + -y.

parole.significato: snow
parole.testo: From New Latin chion- (“snow”), chio, German chio, from Ancient Greek χιών (khiṓn, “snow”), χιόνι (khióni, “snow”), akin to Ancient Greek χειμών (kheimṓn, “winter”).

parole.significato: inflammation of the eyes caused by exposure to ultraviolet light
parole.testo: From New Latin chionablepsia. By surface analysis, chion- (“snow”) + ablepsia (“blindness”).

parole.significato: Gout in the hand.
parole.testo: From Latin chīragra, from Ancient Greek χειράγρα (kheirágra).

parole.significato: massage as a form of therapy
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek χειραψίᾱ (kheirapsíā, “massage”), from χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + ἅψις (hápsis, “contact, touching”), from ἅπτω (háptō, “to touch”).

parole.significato: hand
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin chiro-.

parole.significato: Chironomy.
parole.testo: From Latin chīronomia, from Ancient Greek χειρονομία (kheironomía, “gesticulation”).

parole.significato: Any of various rock-clinging marine molluscs of the class Polyplacophora, including the genus Chiton.
parole.testo: ] From New Latin chiton. See above.

parole.significato: Any of several common, often asymptomatic, sexually transmitted diseases caused by the microorganism Chlamydia trachoma…
parole.testo: From New Latin chlamydia, from Ancient Greek χλαμύδιον (khlamúdion, “small cloak”), from χλαμύς (khlamús, “cloak”).

parole.significato: A funnel; a funnel-shaped opening.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin choana, from Ancient Greek χοᾰ́νη (khoắnē, “funnel”), from χέω (khéō, “to pour”) + -ᾰ́νη (-ắnē, suffix for utensil names).

parole.significato: A form of oriental ruby, carbuncle or possibly jasper
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin chodchod, a transliteration of Hebrew כַּדְכֹּד.
