parole.testo: From Latin compos (“in control, having mastery”) + mentis (“of mind”).

parole.significato: A payment of amends or to acquire a certain privilege, (universities) a tuition fee.
parole.testo: Originally from an obsolete sense of composition, “payment to settle an obligation”, from Medieval Latin compositiō (“payment made in amends or settlement”), see citations; compare legal sense of compound, “settle with a smaller payment than the claim”. Later reanalysed in some cases as meaning “agg

parole.significato: Having the quality of entering into composition; compounded.
parole.testo: Latin compositivus, from com- (“together”) + positus (“placed”).

parole.significato: Given a field extension F/K and subextensions A and B, the smallest subextension that contains both A and B.
parole.testo: From Latin compositum.

parole.significato: The social act of drinking together.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin compōtātiō. Equivalent to com- + potation.

parole.significato: The act of praying together.
parole.testo: From Latin comprecatio, from comprecari (“to pray to”). See precarious.

parole.significato: To understand or grasp fully and thoroughly; to plumb.
parole.testo: From Middle English comprehenden, from Latin comprehendere (“to grasp”), from the prefix com- + prehendere (“to seize”). Doublet of comprend.

parole.significato: Able to be comprehended.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin comprehēnsibilis.

parole.significato: A device that produces pressure, such as a gas compressor that produces pressurized gas.
parole.testo: From compress + -or, or from New Latin compressor.

parole.significato: To agree; to concur.
parole.testo: First attested in 1523; borrowed from Latin comprobātus, perfect passive participle of comprobō (“to approve wholly”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: joint attestation; proof
parole.testo: Latin comprobatio.

parole.significato: To compromise.
parole.testo: From Latin compromittere.

parole.significato: Neat; spruce.
parole.testo: From Latin comptus, past participle of comere (“to care for, comb, arrange, adorn”).

parole.significato: Compulsatory; employing force or constraint.
parole.testo: From Late Latin compulsāt-, participial stem of compulsāre, intensitive form of Latin compellere (“to compel”).

parole.significato: Enforced by or resulting from compulsion; employing force or constraint; compulsory.
parole.testo: Latin compulsāt- (perfect passive participial stem of the Latin compulsō) + English -ory

parole.significato: Required; obligatory; mandatory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin compulsorius, from Latin compulsus. Displaced native Old English ġenīedelīċ.

parole.significato: Affected with compunction; regretful, remorseful.
parole.testo: Latin compunctus, past participle.

parole.significato: Acquitting someone from a formal charge or accusation following the sworn oaths of a number of other people; vindicatio…
parole.testo: From Latin compurgātiōnem, from compurgāre (“to purify”).

parole.significato: Someone who vouches for another person's innocence, trustworthiness etc.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin compurgator or Middle French compurgateur, from Latin compurgō (“to purify”).

parole.significato: Female compurgator.
parole.testo: From Latin compurgatrix, equivalent to compurgator (“someone who vouches for another person's innocence”) + -trix (female agent noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The calculation of the date of Easter in the Christian calendar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin computus. Doublet of conto and count.

parole.significato: A disadvantage of something, especially when contrasted with its advantages (pros).
parole.testo: Abbreviation of Latin contrā (“against”).

parole.significato: The power or act which directs or impels to effort of any kind, whether muscular or psychical.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cōnātiō (“an act of attempting”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a striving action.
parole.testo: From Latin conatio (“an act of attempting”).

parole.significato: An effort, an endeavour, a striving.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnātus.

parole.significato: To arch over; to vault.
parole.testo: From Latin concameratus, past participle of concamero (“to arch over”), from con- + camera (“chamber, vault”). See camber.

parole.significato: An arch or vault, especially a system of interconnecting vaults
parole.testo: Latin concameratio.

parole.significato: To join or link together, as though in a chain.
parole.testo: From the perfect passive participle stem of Latin concatēnāre (“to link or chain together”), from con- (“with”) + catēnō (“chain, bind”), from catēna (“a chain”).

parole.significato: A series of links united; a series or order of things depending on each other, as if linked together; a chain, a succes…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin concatēnātiō. By surface analysis, concatenate + -ion. Related to chain.

parole.significato: concave
parole.testo: Latin concavus.

parole.significato: harmony
parole.testo: From Latin concentus, from concinō (“to sing together”).

parole.significato: concentrated
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin/New Latin concentrātus, perfect passive participle of concentrō (“concentate”). See Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: The act, process or ability of concentrating; the process of becoming concentrated, or the state of being concentrated.
parole.testo: From New Latin concentrātiō (“(1550) action or an act of coming together at a single place; (1659) extraction or separation of one or more of the metals present in an alloy”). Compare French concentration, Spanish concentración, Italian concentrazione (last quarter of 16th century). Equivalent to co

parole.significato: To come together at a common centre.
parole.testo: (late 16th century) From a Romance language, see French concentrer, Italian concentràre, Spanish concentrar; alternatively from Medieval Latin/New Latin concentrō. By surface analysis, con- + centre. Doublet of concentrate.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to concepts or mental conception.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin conceptuālis, from Latin conceptus, perfect passive participle of concipiō (“take hold of; conceive”); see concept and -al.

parole.significato: The fetus or embryo, including all the surrounding tissues protecting and nourishing it during pregnancy.
parole.testo: From Latin cōncipiō (“to take hold of, to receive”), from Latin capiō (“to capture”).

parole.significato: A form of dialogue and co-decision, implying the mutual exchange of information, open discussion and knowledge sharing,…
parole.testo: Latin concertatio.

parole.significato: Related to concertation, especially in the context of tripartism.
parole.testo: The "quarrelsome" sense is from Latin concertativus. The concertation sense is a back-formation from concertation, replacing the -ation suffix with -ative.

parole.significato: The rhetorical device of conceding or admitting something but pardoning it.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin concessiō. Doublet of concession.

parole.significato: A marine gastropod of the family Strombidae which lives in its own spiral shell.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin concha, borrowed from Ancient Greek κόγχη (kónkhē, “a mussel or cockle; a shell-like cavity”). Doublet of concha.

parole.significato: Shaped like a conch.
parole.testo: Latin: conch + -form

parole.significato: Any of a family of curves defined as the locus of points p, such that each p is on a line that passes through a given f…
parole.testo: From Latin concha (“mussel”) (from Ancient Greek κόγχη (kónkhē)) + -oid or directly from Ancient Greek κογχοειδής (konkhoeidḗs), referring to the curved outline of a mussel shell or anything in this form. By surface analysis, conch + -oid.

parole.significato: Of a purple colour, distinguished by Pliny from Tyrian purple and amethystine.
parole.testo: Latin conchȳliātus

parole.significato: Capable of being conciliated or reconciled.
parole.testo: From Latin conciliō + -ābilis.

parole.significato: A small or private assembly, especially of an ecclesiastical nature.
parole.testo: From Latin conciliābulum.

parole.significato: An obscure ecclesiastical council; a conciliable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin conciliābulum.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a council, especially an ecclesiastical council.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin conciliāris.

parole.significato: To acquire, to procure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin conciliātus, perfect passive participle of conciliō (“to unite”), from concilium (“council, meeting”).

parole.significato: A person who conciliates.
parole.testo: From Latin conciliātor. By surface analysis, conciliate + -or.

parole.significato: A female conciliator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin conciliātrīx. By surface analysis, conciliator + -trix.

parole.significato: To place fitly together; to adapt; to clear.
parole.testo: From Latin concinnatus, past participle of concinnare (“to concinnate”). See concinnity.

parole.significato: The harmonious reinforcement of the various parts of a work of art.
parole.testo: Coined 1531 by Sir Thomas Elyot in his treatise, The Boke Named The Governor, from Latin concinnitās (“skillfully put together”).

parole.significato: Characterized by concinnity, or (archaic, figurative) neat; elegant.
parole.testo: Latin concinnus.

parole.significato: A haranguer of the people; a preacher.
parole.testo: From Latin concionator.

parole.significato: Brief, yet including all important information.
parole.testo: From Latin concīsus (“cut short”), from concīdere (“cut to pieces”), from caedēre (“to cut, to strike down”).

parole.significato: Rousing, stirring up; excitement, agitation.
parole.testo: From Latin concitātiōnem, from concitāre. Compare concitate.

parole.significato: An outcry or shout of many together.
parole.testo: From Latin conclamatio.

parole.significato: To end; to come to an end.
parole.testo: From Middle English concluden, borrowed from Latin conclūdere (“to shut up, close, end”).

parole.significato: To prepare something by mixing various ingredients, especially to prepare food for cooking.
parole.testo: From Latin concoquō (“boil, prepare, digest”) (influenced by the participle concoctus), from con- (“together”) + coquō (“cook”).

parole.significato: Digested or affected by heat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin concoctus, perfect passive participle of Latin concoquō (compare Etymology 1).

parole.significato: The preparing of a medicine, food or other substance out of many ingredients.
parole.testo: From Latin concoctiō.

parole.significato: Of the same colour; of uniform colour.
parole.testo: From Latin concolor.

parole.significato: Capable of according; agreeing; harmonious
parole.testo: Latin concordabilis

parole.significato: agreement
parole.testo: Either concordance + -y or Borrowed from Late Latin concordāntia

parole.significato: A set of plotted points, appearing as a curve on a concordia diagram or isochron diagram, representing sample data from…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin concordia.

parole.significato: correlated to grammatical concord
parole.testo: From Late Latin concordialis.

parole.significato: union of things or entities in one mass or body
parole.testo: From Latin concorporatio.

parole.significato: To create at the same time.
parole.testo: From Latin concreātus, past participle of concreō. By surface analysis, con- + create.

parole.significato: The act of burning different things together, especially in Hinduism, along with a widow.
parole.testo: From Latin concrematio, from concremare. See cremate.

parole.significato: concretion
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin concrēmentum.

parole.significato: The growing together and merging of similar or dissimilar parts.
parole.testo: From Latin concrescentia.

parole.significato: Capable of growing together.
parole.testo: From Latin concrēscō + -ible.

parole.significato: Real, actual, tangible.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin concrētus, past participle of concrescō (to curdle) from con- (with, together) + crescō (to grow, rise).

parole.significato: Specifics; concrete details.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin concrētus. Compare terms like Bulgarian конкре́тика (konkrétika, “specifics”), which are vastly more common, suggesting this word may be derived from use by foreign speakers.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a concubine or concubinage.
parole.testo: Latin concubinalis.

parole.significato: A concubinage.
parole.testo: Latin concubinatus.

parole.significato: A type of non-marital monogamous union in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin concubinatus.

parole.significato: To tread or trample underfoot.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin conculcatus, past participle of conculcare (“to conculcate”).

parole.significato: An ardent desire, especially sexual desire; lust.
parole.testo: From Latin concupīscentia, from concupīscō (“to desire strongly, to desire eagerly; to covet”).

parole.significato: Amorous; lustful.
parole.testo: From Latin concupiscens (stem concupiscent-), present participle of concupīscō (“long for, covet”), inchoative of concupiō (“long for”), from con- + cupiō (“desire, wish for”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to concupiscence; lustful.
parole.testo: From Latin concupiscentialis.

parole.significato: Relating to the nature of concupiscence or lust; concupiscible.
parole.testo: From Latin concupīt(us) (“coveted”) + -ive, perfect passive participle Latin concupīscō (“desire very much, covet strongly, long for greatly”), from concupiō (“covet, long for”), from cupiō (“desire, long for”).

parole.significato: To agree (in action or opinion); to have a common opinion; to coincide; to correspond.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin concurro (“to run together, agree”).

parole.significato: To injure the brain of, usually temporarily, by violent impact.
parole.testo: From Latin concussus, the perfect passive participle of concutiō (“shake violently”), from con- + quatiō (“shake, hit”).

parole.significato: A violent collision or shock.
parole.testo: From Latin concussiō. Equivalent to concuss + -ion.

parole.significato: To condemn.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin condemnātus, perfect passive participle of condemnō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of condemn.

parole.significato: The act of condemning or pronouncing to be wrong.
parole.testo: From Middle English condempnacioun, from Latin condemnātiō, condemnātiōnem.

parole.significato: Serving to condemn or censure.
parole.testo: From Latin condemnāt-, past participle stem of condemnāre + -ory.

parole.significato: To condense.
parole.testo: First attested circa 1550; borrowed from Latin condēnsātus, perfect passive participle of condēnsō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act or process of condensing or of being condensed.
parole.testo: From condense + -ation, borrowed from Latin condēnsātiō, condēnsātiōnem.

parole.significato: The act of condescending; a manner of behaving in an outwardly polite way that nevertheless implies superiority to anot…
parole.testo: From Latin condēscēnsiō.

parole.significato: A claim for restitution of a payment
parole.testo: From Latin condictio.

parole.significato: To pickle; to preserve.
parole.testo: From Latin condītus, past participle of condīre (“to preserve, pickle, season”). Related to condiment. See also recondite.

parole.significato: Subject to conditions.
parole.testo: From Late Latin conditionatus.

parole.significato: A repository for holding things; a hiding place or relicary.
parole.testo: From Latin conditorium, from condere (“to hide”). See recondite and reconditory. The cake shop is from German Konditorei

parole.significato: Followed by with: to express condolence to, or sympathetic sorrow with, someone; to lament in sympathy with someone.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱóm Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin condolēre, the present active infinitive of condoleō (“to feel severe pain, suffer greatly; to suffer with or feel another’s pain, condole”), from Latin con- (prefix denoting a being or bringing together of several things) + doleō (“to suffe

parole.significato: Joint sovereignty over a territory by two or more countries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin condominium.

parole.significato: The condoning of an offence.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin condōnātiō, condōnātiōnem. Equivalent to condone + -ation.

parole.significato: To forgive, excuse or overlook (something that is considered morally wrong, offensive, or generally disliked).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin condōnāre (“to forgive”).

parole.significato: To cause (something) to occur; to bring about.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱóm From Late Middle English conducen (“to guide, lead; (surgery) to draw together (edges of a wound, or parts of a torn sinew); to set (a broken bone)”), borrowed from Latin condūcere, the present active infinitive of condūcō (“to bring, draw, or lead together, assemble, collect; to cont

parole.significato: conducive; tending
parole.testo: From Latin conducens.

parole.significato: conducive; tending; contributing
parole.testo: From Latin condūcibilis.

parole.significato: Tending to contribute to, encourage, or bring about some result.
parole.testo: From conduce + -ive, 1640s, from Latin condūcere, patterned after forms like conductive.

parole.significato: The act or method of controlling or directing.
parole.testo: From Late Latin conductus (“defense, escort”), from Latin conductus, perfect passive participle of condūcō (“bring together”); see also conduce. Displaced native Old English þēaw. Doublet of conduit.

parole.significato: The conveying of heat or electricity through material.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin conductio, conductionem (“a bringing together”); equivalent to conduct + -ion.

parole.significato: hired, employed (for wages)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin conductīcius.

parole.significato: A female conductor; a woman who conducts.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin conductrīx. By surface analysis, conduct + -trix.

parole.significato: A wartlike growth on the skin or a mucous membrane, caused by certain types of HPV viruses, usually occurring in the ge…
parole.testo: From Latin condylōma, from Ancient Greek κονδύλωμα (kondúlōma, “wart”), from κόνδυλος (kóndulos).

parole.significato: A surface of revolution formed by rotating a segment of a line around another line that intersects the first line.
parole.testo: From Middle English cone (“corner, angle”) and conoun (“cone”), from Medieval Latin cōnus, cōnon (“cone, wedge, peak”), from Ancient Greek κῶνος (kônos, “cone, spinning top, pine cone”). Reinforced by Middle French cone, from the same Graeco-Latin source.

parole.significato: To speak casually with; to chat.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin cōnfābulātus, perfect active participle of cōnfābulor, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A casual conversation; a chat.
parole.testo: From Middle English confabulacion (“conversation”), from Latin confābulātiōnem, from cōnfābulārī + -tiōnem.

parole.significato: To make up, prepare, or compound; to produce by combining ingredients or materials; to concoct.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnfectus, past participle of cōnficere, from com- (“together”) + facere (“to make”).

parole.significato: A rich, sweet, food item made of flavored sugar and often combined with fruit or nuts; a confection, comfit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnfectum. Doublet of comfit, confetto, confit, and konfyt.

parole.significato: Relating to, or of the nature of confections or their production.
parole.testo: From Late Latin cōnfectiōnārius (“one who prepares things by means of ingredients”), from Latin cōnfectiō (“preparing, producing”). See confection. By surface analysis, confection + -ary.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or united in a confederacy
parole.testo: First attested in 1387, in Middle english; inherited from Middle English confederat(e) (“confederated, allied, associated in a plot; united or bound, as in friendship or troth”), borrowed from Late Latin cōnfoederātus perfect passive participle of cōnfoederō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and

parole.significato: To unite persons or states in a league, confederacy or conspiracy; to ally, league.
parole.testo: First attested in 1531; borrowed from Late Latin cōnfoederātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more. Doublet of (obsolete) confeder.

parole.significato: Pleasure in another person's happiness.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin con- (“with”) + fēlīcitās (“happiness”)

parole.significato: To unite into a solid mass
parole.testo: First attested in 1826; borrowed from Latin conferrūminātus, perfect passive participle of conferrūminō (“to cement”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from con- + ferrūminō, from ferrūmen (“cement”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Any of a number of unbranched slender green freshwater algae, formerly in the genus Conferva, now mostly in genera Clad…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnferva. See comfrey.

parole.significato: One who makes a confession.
parole.testo: Latin confessarius.

parole.significato: A confession; a defense of one's faith, or a confession of guilt.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnfessiō. Doublet of confession.

parole.significato: A lover’s confession.
parole.testo: Latin: cōnfessiō (“confession”) + amantis (“of loving”, the genitive singular of amāns, “loving”, the present active participle of amō, “I love”)

parole.significato: A manual or guide to making confession.
parole.testo: From Late Latin confessionarium.

parole.significato: Self-assurance.
parole.testo: From Middle English confidence, from Latin cōnfīdentia (possibly via Old French confidence), from cōnfīdō (“believe, confide in”) from con- (“with”) + fīdō (“trust”). By surface analysis, confide + ence.

parole.significato: To configure; to arrange or shape.
parole.testo: First attested in 1566; borrowed from Latin cōnfigūrātus, perfect passive participle of cōnfigūrō (“to form or alter”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of configure.

parole.significato: A candidate for confirmation or affirmation of baptism.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnfirmandus.

parole.significato: # Someone or something that confirms; a confirmer.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: To use one's authority to lay claim to and separate a possession from its holder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnfiscātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin cōnfiscō (“to seize for the public treasury (fiscus)”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act or process of confiscating.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnfiscātiō. By surface analysis, confiscate + -ion.

parole.significato: A person who confesses; a confessor or penitent
parole.testo: Latin confitens, p.pr.

parole.significato: A prayer, typically beginning “I confess to Almighty God…” in English, in which public confession of sins is made.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnfiteor (“to confess”), the first word of the prayer and used as its title in Ecclesiastical Latin. Doublet of confess.

parole.significato: An affix consisting of a prefix and suffix attached simultaneously to the root.
parole.testo: From Latin configo or con- + fix.

parole.significato: Brilliantly burning; of or resembling a conflagration; intensely blazing.
parole.testo: From the Latin cōnflagrāns (oblique stem: cōnflagrant-), present active participle of cōnflagrō.

parole.significato: To catch fire.
parole.testo: First attested in 1657; borrowed from Latin cōnflāgrātus, perfect passive participial of cōnflāgrō (“to be consumed by fire; (rare) to set aflame”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To combine or mix together.
parole.testo: Attested since 1541: from Latin cōnflātus, past passive participle of cōnflō (“fuse, kindle, blow together”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A blowing or fusing together, as of many instruments in a concert, or of many fires in a foundry.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin cōnflātiō, from Latin cōnflātus. By surface analysis, conflate + -ion.

parole.significato: A clash or disagreement, often violent, between two or more opposing groups or individuals.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnflīctus, from com- + flīctus, past participle of conflīgō (“to strike together”), from com- + flīgō (“strike”) (whence con-).

parole.significato: A conflicting condition; conflict.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin conflictiō (“collision; conflict”), from Latin cōnflictus, from cōnfligō (“clash; collide”, verb).

parole.significato: to flow together into one stream, to converge
parole.testo: From con- + flow. Calque of Latin cōnfluō, apparently coined by Philemon Holland in his translations of Suetonius and Ammianus Marcellinus.

parole.significato: The act of combining that occurs where two rivers meet.
parole.testo: From late Middle English confluence, from Late Latin cōnfluentia (“a flowing together, conflux”), from cōnfluēns (present participle of cōnfluō (“to flow or run together”)) + -ia (nominal suffix).

parole.significato: The percentage of the surface of a culture dish that is covered by adherent cells
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cōnfluentia. Doublet of confluence.

parole.significato: Converging, merging or flowing together into one.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnfluēns, present participle of cōnfluō.

parole.significato: Synonym of confluence (“convergence or combination”).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cōnfluvium. First attested in 1670.

parole.significato: A merger of rivers, or the place where rivers merge.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnflūxus.

parole.significato: Of the same court or marketplace.
parole.testo: From Latin conforāneus (“using the same forum”), from con- (“with”, “together”) + forum (“marketplace”) + -āneus.

parole.significato: Having the same shape or form; very similar.
parole.testo: Latin conformabilis

parole.significato: The act of conforming; the act of producing conformity.
parole.testo: From Latin confōrmātiō. By surface analysis, conform + -ation.

parole.significato: The act or process of confuting; refutation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnfūtātiō (“refutation”, feminine noun). By surface analysis, confute + -ation.

parole.significato: A collection or aggregation of disparate items.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin congeriēs (“a heap, mass, pile”), from congerō (“to carry together, heap”).

parole.significato: A present of corn, wine, oil, etc. or later of money, made by a Roman emperor to the soldiers or the common people.
parole.testo: From Latin congiarium, from congius (“a liquid measure”).

parole.significato: To turn to ice; to freeze.
parole.testo: From Latin conglaciatus, past participle of conglaciare.

parole.significato: Shaped like or formed into a ball.
parole.testo: First attested in 1635; borrowed from Latin conglobātus, perfect passive participial of conglobō (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from con- (“together”) + globus (“ball”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix)

parole.significato: To express one’s sympathetic pleasure or joy to the person(s) it is felt for

parole.significato: To agree.

parole.significato: A formal gathering or assembly of persons; a conference held to discuss or decide on a specific question.

parole.significato: The act of coming together; congress.

parole.significato: To agree; to be suitable.

parole.significato: The quality of agreeing or corresponding; being suitable and appropriate.
parole.testo: From Middle English congruence, from Latin congruentia (“agreement”), from congruēns, present active participle of congruō (“meet together, agree”).

parole.significato: Corresponding in character; congruous.
parole.testo: From Middle English congruent, from Latin congruēns, present active participle of congruō (“meet together, agree”).

parole.significato: Corresponding in character.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Latin congruus, from congruō (“to coincide with; to agree”).

parole.significato: A plant belonging to the order Coniferales; a cone-bearing seed plant with vascular tissue, usually a tree.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnifer (“bearing cones”), by surface analysis, Latin cōnus (“cone”) + -fer.

parole.significato: Bearing cones, as the pine and cypress.
parole.testo: From Latin. By surface analysis, cone + -i- + -ferous (“bearing”), or conifer + -ous (“pertaining to”), as reflected in the meanings.

parole.significato: To conjecture.
parole.testo: From Latin conjectus.

parole.significato: One who guesses or conjectures.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?]

parole.significato: To inflect (a verb) for each person, in order, for one or more tenses; to list or recite its principal parts.
parole.testo: The adjective (as “combined, united”) and noun are first attested in 1471, in Middle English, the verb in 1530; partly from Middle English conjugat(e) (“combined, united”), partly directly borrowed from New Latin coniugātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin coniugō (“to yoke together, combine

parole.significato: The coming together of things; a union.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin coniugātiō (“combining, connecting; conjugation”), from coniugō (“join, unite together”). Equivalent to conjugate + -ion.

parole.significato: Either term of a conjunction.
parole.testo: From Latin conjunctus, the perfect past participle of conjungō. Doublet of conjoint. See conjoin.

parole.significato: A clear mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid and the exposed surface of the eyeball or sclera.
parole.testo: From 1540s late Middle English, borrowing from Medieval Latin conjūnctīva (“serving to connect, connective”, feminine), ellipsis of membrāna conjūnctīva (“conjunctive membrane”).

parole.significato: Connective: tending to join, unite, connect.
parole.testo: From Latin coniunctivus (“serving to connect”), from coniunctus, past participle of coniungere; compare conjoin. From late 15th c; grammatical sense from 1660s.

parole.significato: Of the same or a similar nature; proceeding from the same stock or root.
parole.testo: First attested in 1641; borrowed from Latin connātus, perfect active participle of connāscor (“to be born together (with)”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from con- + nāscor. Doublet of cognate.

parole.significato: To join (to another object): to attach, or to be intended to attach or capable of attaching, to another object.
parole.testo: From Latin connectere (“fasten together”), from con- (“together”) + nectere (“bind”), which is cognate with English knot and English knit.

parole.significato: Serving or tending to connect; connecting.
parole.testo: For connexive, borrowed from Latin connexīvus. Displacement of x by ct in Latin loanwords is very common. Compare connect, connectivum, connection.

parole.significato: To connect; to fasten together.
parole.testo: Latin connexus, p.p. See connect.

parole.significato: Dated spelling of connection.
parole.testo: From Middle English connexioun, from Latin connexiō (“a conclusion, binding together”), from connectō.

parole.significato: A fit of anger or panic; conniption fit.
parole.testo: Since 1833, from American English. Unknown origin, possibly a fanciful alteration of corruption, or maybe related to captious. Alternatively an arbitrary pseudo-Latinism coinage.

parole.significato: The process of conniving or conspiring.
parole.testo: From early 18th c., replaced earlier form connivence (late 16th c.), from Latin connīventia, from connīvēns (“winking”).

parole.significato: Forbearing to see; intentionally inattentive.
parole.testo: From Latin connīvēns.

parole.significato: A large, smothering, and destructive blizzard.
parole.testo: Humorous alteration of conflagration, the -flagr- having been substituted with Latin nix (“snow”).

parole.significato: To connote; to suggest or designate (something) as additional or representative; to imply.
parole.testo: First attested in 1596; borrowed from Medieval Latin connotātus, perfect passive participle of connotō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix). Doublet of connote.

parole.significato: A meaning of a word or phrase that is suggested or implied, as opposed to a denotation, or literal meaning. A character…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin connotātiō, from connotō (“to mark in addition”), from Latin con- (“together, with”) + notō (“to note”); equivalent to connote + -ation.

parole.significato: To signify beyond its literal or principal meaning.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin connotō (“signify beyond literal meaning”), from com- (“together”), + notō (“mark”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the state of being married.
parole.testo: 1650s, from Latin connūbiālis, from connūbium (“marriage, wedlock”) (variants of cōnūbiālis (“pertaining to wedlock”), from cōnūbium (“marriage, wedlock”)) from com- (“together”) (English com-) + nūbō (“marry, to take as husband”) (from which nubile) from Proto-Indo-European *snewbʰ- (“to marry, to

parole.significato: A reckoning or counting together.
parole.testo: From Latin connumeratio, from Latin connumerare, connumeratum (“to number with”).

parole.significato: A thin flap of silica on the external valve face of a diatom
parole.testo: From Latin cōnōpēum. Doublet of canapé and canopy.

parole.significato: To shake; to agitate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin conquassātus, perfect passive participle of conquassō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Consensual adult romantic and/or sexual love between family members; consensual adult incest.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnsanguineus (“consanguineous”) + amor (“love”) + English -y. Coined by activist Cristina Shy.

parole.significato: A patching together; patchwork.
parole.testo: From Latin consarcinare, consarcinatum (“to patch together”).

parole.significato: conscious; aware
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin consciens, conscientis, present participle.

parole.significato: Alert, awake; with one's mental faculties active.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1573 in the sense of "aware of wrongdoing".https://web.archive.org/web/20220714064352/https://www.lexico.com/definition/conscious From Latin cōnscius (“conscious, conscious of guilt”), itself from con- (a form of com- (“together”)) + scīre (“to know”) + -us.

parole.significato: To enroll; to enlist.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnscrībere. See conscript. By surface analysis, con- + scribe.

parole.significato: One who is compulsorily enrolled, often into a military service; a draftee.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnscriptus, perfect passive participle of cōnscrībō (“write together; enroll”).

parole.significato: A senator of Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin patrēs cōnscrīptī; see there for more.

parole.significato: To declare something holy, or make it holy by some procedure.
parole.testo: First attested in the late 14ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English consecraten (“to dedicate, consecrate (an altar, church); to ordain (a bishop), anoint (a king, a pope); to devote one to religious life”), from consecrat(e) (“consecrated”, used as the past participle of conse

parole.significato: The act or ceremony of consecrating; the state of being consecrated; dedication.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnsecrātiō, cōnsecrātiōnem.

parole.significato: Following as a matter of course.
parole.testo: Latin consectaneus.

parole.significato: That which follows by consequence or is logically deducible.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnsectārius.

parole.significato: To follow closely; to endeavour to overtake; to pursue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin consequor, consecutus.

parole.significato: A set of grammatical rules of a particular language, governing the agreement between the tenses of verbs in related cla…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnsecūtiō temporum (“sequence of tenses”).

parole.significato: A following, or sequel; actual or logical dependence.
parole.testo: From Middle English consecucioun (“attainment”), from Latin cōnsecūtiō (“effect, proper sequence, attainment”), from past participle of cōnsequor (“to follow, result, reach”).

parole.significato: Agreement; accord.
parole.testo: Latin consensio.

parole.significato: A process of decision-making that seeks widespread agreement among group members.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnsēnsus (“agreement, accordance, unanimity”), from cōnsentiō (“feel together; agree”); see consent.

parole.significato: Agreement about the terms and subject matter of a contract between all involved parties.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin consensus ad idem (“agreement to the same thing”). In English, first attested in 1864.

parole.significato: Done or made by general consent; widely agreed or approved.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin consentaneus + English -aneous. Consentaneus is derived from consentire (“to agree”).

parole.significato: Capable of being preserved from decay or injury.
parole.testo: Latin conservabilis.

parole.significato: Having the power or quality of conservation; conserving.

parole.significato: A political philosophy that advocates traditional values.
parole.testo: Either irregularly from conservative + -ism or from conservate + -ism; ultimately from Latin cōnservāre (“to conserve; to keep, guard, observe”).

parole.significato: Synonym of music school.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnservātōrium, from cōnservātus (“conserved, preserved”) + -ōrium (“-ory: forming related nouns”).

parole.significato: Having the quality of preserving from loss, decay, or injury.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cōnservātōrius directly and via French conservatoire, from cōnservāre (“to conserve, to preserve”) + -torius (“-atory: forming related adjectives”) and/or conservator (“conservator, preserver, protector”) + -ius (“-y: forming related adjectives”).

parole.significato: A medicine, especially a magical preservative.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cōnservātōrium directly and via French conservatoire and Italian conservatorio, from cōnservātus (“conserved, preserved”) + -ōrium (“-ory: forming related nouns”).

parole.significato: A female conservator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cōnservātrīx. By surface analysis, conservator + -trix.

parole.significato: An assembly or congregation of people, especially in religious contexts.
parole.testo: From Latin consessus.

parole.significato: An act of considering; consideration.

parole.significato: The act of consigning.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnsignātiō (“written proof, document”).

parole.significato: The concurrence of multiple inductions drawn from different data sets.

parole.significato: Of academic disciplines, displaying consilience.

parole.significato: A traditional form of expulsion from an organization or school.

parole.significato: Having similarities in common
parole.testo: From Latin cōnsimilis.

parole.significato: Of a regularly occurring, dependable nature.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a consistory.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cōnsistōriālis.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a cousin.
parole.testo: From Latin consobrin(us) + -al.

parole.significato: An associate; an accomplice.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnsociātus, past participle of cōnsociō (“to associate, unite”).

parole.significato: Comforted, consoled.
parole.testo: First attested in 1477, in Middle English; borrowed from Latin cōnsōlātus, perfect active participle of cōnsōlor, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of console.

parole.significato: A ceremonial oratory used to comfort mourners at funerals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin consolatio. Doublet of consolation.

parole.significato: One who consoles or comforts.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnsōlātor.

parole.significato: Which consoles.
parole.testo: From Middle English consolatory, from Latin cōnsōlātōrius.

parole.significato: A female consoler.
parole.testo: From Latin consōlātrix, from cōnsōlor (“to console”) + -trīx. Alternatively from cōnsōlō.

parole.significato: A substance applied to a material, such as rotten wood, to give it solidity and strength.
parole.testo: Latin consolidans, present participle of consolido (“to make firm”): compare French consolidant.

parole.significato: To combine into a single unit; to group together or join.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin consolidātus, from the verb consolidō, from solidus (“solid”). By surface analysis, con- + solid + -ate.

parole.significato: The act or process of consolidating, making firm, or uniting; the state of being consolidated.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnsolidātiō, cōnsolidātiōnem, from cōnsolidō.

parole.significato: Congruity; consistency.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnsonantia. Doublet of consonance.

parole.significato: concordant in sound; harmonious
parole.testo: From Latin consonus. See consonant.

parole.significato: To lull to sleep, to quieten, or to dull.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnsōpītus.

parole.significato: joining; association, or companionship
parole.testo: Latin consortio.

parole.significato: An association or combination of businesses, financial institutions, or investors, for the purpose of engaging in a joi…

parole.significato: Observation with understanding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnspectiō, from cōnspiciō (“to notice, gaze at”).

parole.significato: A detailed survey or overview of a subject.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnspectus (“survey”).

parole.significato: The act of sprinkling.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnspersiō, from cōnspergō (“to sprinkle”).

parole.significato: Obvious or easy to notice.
parole.testo: From Latin conspicuus (“visible, striking”), from cōnspicere (“to notice”), from con- (“with, together”) + specere (“to look at”).

parole.significato: A thickening or making viscous; thickness
parole.testo: From Latin conspissatio, from inspissare (“to make thick”).

parole.significato: To pollute; to defile.
parole.testo: From Latin conspurcatus, past participle of conspurcare.

parole.significato: defilement
parole.testo: From Latin conspurcare (“to defile”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to constables.
parole.testo: From mediaeval Latin conestabularia, a noun use of the feminine version of conestabularius, from Latin constabulus, from comes stabuli, literally ‘master of the stables’.

parole.significato: The quality of being constant; steadiness or faithfulness in action, affections, purpose, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnstantia.

parole.significato: A kind of wine, either white or red, from Constantia in Cape Colony.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Cōnstantia. Doublet of Constance.

parole.significato: Relating to Constantinople (modern-day Istanbul).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Cōnstantīnopolītānus.

parole.significato: It is clearly evident; It is certain, without a doubt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnstat.

parole.significato: To combine as a cluster.
parole.testo: From Latin constēllātus (“starred”), past participle of constēllō. Equivalent to Latin constēllō + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To cause constipation in, render costive.

parole.significato: A state of the bowels in which the evacuations are infrequent and difficult, or the intestines become filled with harde…
parole.testo: First attested in the beginning of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English constipacioun, borrowed from Medieval Latin constīpātiō or its Old French equivalent, from cōnstīpō + -tiō. By surface analysis, constipate + -ion.

parole.significato: Being a part or component of a whole.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnstituēns, present participle of cōnstituō (“to establish”), from com- (“together”) + statuō (“to set, place, establish”).

parole.significato: To set up; to establish; to enact.
parole.testo: From Middle English constituten, from Latin cōnstitūtum, neuter of cōnstitūtus, past participle of Latin cōnstituō (“to put in place; set up; establish”), from con- (“with”) + statuō (“to put up; establish”).

parole.significato: To narrow, especially by application of pressure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnstrictus (“compressed, contracted”), past participle of cōnstringō (“to draw or bind together; to compress”). Doublet of constrain.

parole.significato: The act of constricting, the state of being constricted, or something that constricts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin constrictio, constrictionis, from Latin constringo.

parole.significato: To constrict; to tighten.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnstringere. See constrain.

parole.significato: contracting, binding, or compressing.
parole.testo: From Latin constringens.

parole.significato: Something constructed from parts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnstrūctus, from cōnstruō (“to heap together”), from com- (“together”) + struō (“to heap up, pile”). Doublet of construe.

parole.significato: A grammatical construction in which a word’s inflection is determined by the semantics of the word or words with which…
parole.testo: From modern Latin cōnstrūctiō (“[grammatical] construction”) + ad (“toward, [according] to”) + sēnsum (accusative singular of sēnsus, abstractly “sense”, “notion”, “signification”): "grammatical construction according to [the] sense".

parole.significato: Relating to or causing construction.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnstrūctīvus. By surface analysis, construct + -ive.

parole.significato: A person who, or thing that, constructs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnstrūctor, from Latin cōnstruō + Medieval Latin -or. By surface analysis, construct + -or.

parole.significato: A translation.
parole.testo: From Middle English construen, from Late Latin construo, construere (“to relate grammatically”), from Latin construo (“pile together”); doublet of construct.

parole.significato: To act together in a foolish or stupid manner, to become as great a fool as those around, to behave as much in a foolis…
parole.testo: From Latin con- (“together”) + stultus (“foolish; fool”).

parole.significato: To rape, violate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin constuprātus, perfect passive participle of constuprō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from con- + stuprum (“dishonor, shame”) + -ō.

parole.significato: Of the same substance or essence.
parole.testo: From Latin consubstāntiālis, from con- + substāntia (“substance”), translating Ancient Greek ὁμοούσιον (homooúsion).

parole.significato: According to custom; customary; usual.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnsuētūdō (oblique stem cōnsuētūdin-) + -al, from cōnsuēscō + -tūdō, from con- + suēscō. By surface analysis, consuetude + -al.

parole.significato: A ritual book containing the forms and ceremonies used in the services of a particular monastery, cathedral or religiou…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cōnsuetudinārius, from cōnsuētūdō (oblique stem cōnsuētūdin-) + -ārius, from cōnsuēscō + -tūdō, from con- + suēscō. By surface analysis, consuetude + -ary.

parole.significato: Either of the two heads of government and state of the Roman Republic or the equivalent nominal post under the Roman an…
parole.testo: From Middle English consul, from Old English consul, from Latin cōnsul.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a consul, or the office thereof.
parole.testo: From Middle English consular, from Latin cōnsulāris. By surface analysis, consul + -ar.

parole.significato: Rule by consuls, as during most periods of the Roman Republic or in France between 1799 and 1804.
parole.testo: From Middle English consulat, consulate, from Latin consulātus, from consul + -ātus. In some senses, via French consulat. By surface analysis, consul + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

parole.significato: That gives advice or consultation; advisory.
parole.testo: From Latin-type *cōnsultātīvus (probably used in Medieval Latin), from cōnsultāt-, past participial stem of cōnsultō, + -īvus. By surface analysis, consult + -ative.

parole.significato: One who gives counsel; an adviser, especially in the Catholic Church.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnsultor.

parole.significato: Complete in every detail, perfect, absolute.
parole.testo: First attested in the beginning of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English consummat(e) (“(past participle) fulfilled, completed; (adjective) perfect, consummate”), borrowed from Latin cōnsummātus, perfect passive participle of cōnsummō (“to sum up, finish, complete”) (see

parole.significato: The act of consummating, or the state of being consummated; the state of being completed; completion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnsummātiō.

parole.significato: One who consummates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōnsummātor, by surface analysis, consummate + -or.

parole.significato: Synonym of consumptive.
parole.testo: From Latin cōnsūmptus, past participle of cōnsūmō, + -uous.

parole.significato: Wasting away gradually.
parole.testo: From Latin contabescens.

parole.significato: To lay floorboards.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin contabulātus, perfect passive participle of contabulō (“to cover with boards”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of touching physically; being in close association.
parole.testo: From Latin contactus, from contingō (“to touch on all sides”), from tangō (“to touch”). Used in English since the 17th century.

parole.significato: contagion; contagious matter
parole.testo: From Latin contagium (“contagion”).

parole.significato: Capable of being contaminated.
parole.testo: From Latin contāminābilis.

parole.significato: To make something dangerous or toxic by introducing impurities or foreign matter.
parole.testo: First attested in the early 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; from Middle English contaminaten (“to defile; to infect with desease”), from contaminat(e) (“sullied, defiled; infected with desease”, also used as the past participle of contaminaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), from Latin contāminātus,

parole.significato: The act or process of contaminating.
parole.testo: From Latin contāminātiōnem.

parole.significato: To modify or temper; to allay; to qualify; to moderate or soften.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin contemperō, from con- + temperō (“to temper”). Compare contemperate.

parole.significato: Contemplatable
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin contemplabilis

parole.significato: Given to contemplation; meditative.
parole.testo: From Latin contemplans (“contemplating”), present participle of contemplor (“to contemplate”).

parole.significato: To look at on all sides or in all its aspects; to view or consider with continued attention; to regard with deliberate…
parole.testo: First attested in the 1590s; borrowed from Latin contemplātus, the perfect active participle of contemplor (“to observe, survey, gaze (at), contemplate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). See also template.

parole.significato: One who contemplates.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English contemplatoure. By surface analysis, contemplate + -or.

parole.significato: A female contemplator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin contemplātrīx. By surface analysis, contemplator + -trix.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the grammatical aspect which expresses that a secondary action occurs (and is completed) immediately…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin contemporālis.

parole.significato: Legal opinions set forth at the time a document was written.
parole.testo: From Latin contemporanea expositio (“that which was said at the time”). Part of the expression contemporanea expositio est optima et fortissima, in lege ("contemporaneous explanation is best and strongest in law").

parole.significato: Existing or created in the same period of time.
parole.testo: From Latin contemporāneus (“contemporary”), from con- (“with”) + tempus (“time”) + -aneus (“of or pertaining to”) (compare Late Latin temporāneus (“opportune, timely”)).

parole.significato: In a contemporaneous way: in the same period of time.
parole.testo: From contemporaneous + -ly, from Latin contemporāneus, from co- (“together”) + tempus (“time”).

parole.significato: From the same time period, coexistent in time; contemporaneous.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin contemporārius, from Latin con- (“with, together”) + temporārius, an adjective derived from tempus (“time”).

parole.significato: Deserving contempt.
parole.testo: From Middle English contemptible, from Latin contemptibilis. By surface analysis, contempt + -ible.

parole.significato: Synonym of contempt
parole.testo: From Latin contemptio.

parole.significato: Showing contempt; expressing disdain; showing a lack of respect.
parole.testo: From Latin contemptus (whence contempt) + -ous.

parole.significato: Contempt for worldly concerns or secular life.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin contemptus mundī (literally “contempt for the world”), as used in works such as Bernard of Cluny’s De contemptu mundi. First attested in the mid-19th century in English.

parole.significato: An antagonist, rival, or contestant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin contendens, contendentis, present participle of contendō.

parole.significato: Satisfied, pleased, contented.
parole.testo: From Middle English contenten (“to satisfy”), from Latin contentus (“contained; satisfied”), past participle of continēre (“to contain”).

parole.significato: Contained.
parole.testo: From Middle English content (plural contentes, contence), from Latin contentus, past participle of continēre (“to hold in, contain”), as Etymology 1, above. English apparently developed a substantive form of the adjective, which is not mirrored in Romance languages.

parole.significato: contentment; satisfaction
parole.testo: Latin contentatio.

parole.significato: Conterminous.
parole.testo: From Latin conterminus, from con- (“with”) + terminus (“border, end”) + -al.

parole.significato: Having the same bounds or extent; coterminous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin conterminātus, perfect passive participle of conterminō (“to border upon”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from conterminus (“conterminous”), from con- + terminus (“border”).

parole.significato: A harmonious union.
parole.testo: From Latin contesseratio (“to contract friendship”), from con- + tesserae (“square tablets; especially as friendship tokens”).

parole.significato: To weave together; to form by interweaving.
parole.testo: From Latin contexere.

parole.significato: The surroundings, circumstances, environment, background or settings that determine, specify, or clarify the meaning of…
parole.testo: From Latin context(us).

parole.significato: silent
parole.testo: From Latin conticens, present participle of conticeo (“to be silent”), from con- + taceo (“to be quiet”).

parole.significato: The act or process of framing or slotting together, or uniting, like beams in a fabric.
parole.testo: From Latin contignātiō, from contignō (“to join with beams”), from con- + tignum (“beam”).

parole.significato: Contiguous, touching.
parole.testo: Middle English contiguat(e), borrowed from Medieval Latin contiguātus, participial adjective from contiguor (“to be contiguous”), from contiguus; see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Connected; touching; abutting.
parole.testo: From Latin contiguus (“touching”) + -ous, from contingere (“to touch”); see contingent, contact, contagion.

parole.significato: One of the main contiguous landmasses, separated by water or geological features, on the surface of a planet, sometimes…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin continens, noun use of present participle of continēre (“to contain”).

parole.significato: Contact; touching.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin contingentia (whence con- + and -ence), from contingēns, present passive participle of contingō (“to make contact with, to be touching”).

parole.significato: The situation where a plaintiff recovered damages for several trespasses in the same action.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin continuandō.

parole.significato: To make continuous, to give continuity to.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English continuaten, from continuat(e) (“continuous”, also used as the past participle of continuaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin continuātus, perfect passive participle of continuō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of continue.

parole.significato: Without stopping; without a break, cessation, or interruption.
parole.testo: From Latin continuus, from contineō (“hold together”). Displaced native Old English singal.

parole.significato: A continuous series or whole, no part of which is noticeably different from its adjacent parts, although the ends or ex…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin continuum, neuter form of continuus, from contineō (“contain, enclose”).

parole.significato: To twist in a violent manner.

parole.significato: Plaited lengthwise and also twisted.
parole.testo: From Latin contortuplicatus, from contortus (“contorted”) + plicare (“to fold”).

parole.significato: Against; contrary or opposed to; in opposition or contrast to.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin contrā.

parole.testo: From Latin contra proferentem.

parole.significato: Against; in opposition to.

parole.significato: A person or company that builds or improves buildings or structures.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or enforced by a contract.

parole.significato: To deny the truth or validity of (a statement or statements).
parole.testo: Derived from Latin contrādictus (“contradicted”), the past participle of contrādīcō (“speak against”) (originally two words).

parole.significato: contradiction in terms
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: That contradicts something, such as an argument.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin contradictorius, from Latin contradico. Equivalent to contradict + -ory.

parole.significato: The substitution of one text for another without substantial change to the music.
parole.testo: From Latin. Piecewise doublet of counterfeit.

parole.significato: Generally, denoting an object inversed and transposed (to another).
parole.testo: Neologism based on Latin contra and gradi.

parole.significato: Entering into covenant; contracting.

parole.significato: Of or in counterpoint.

parole.significato: The initial stage of the sexual act involving manual contact and tumescence; sexual foreplay.

parole.significato: To give something that is or becomes part of a larger whole.

parole.significato: To make sorrowful; to sadden or grieve.
parole.testo: First attested in 1616; borrowed from Latin contrīstātus, perfect passive participle of contrīstō (“to sadden”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of contrist.

parole.significato: Facing opposite directions.
parole.testo: From Latin contrōversus + -al.

parole.significato: Arousing or likely to arouse controversy.
parole.testo: From Latin contrōversiālis, from contrōversia + -ālis. By surface analysis, controversy + -al.

parole.significato: To dispute, to argue about (something).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin contrōvertere, from Latin contrō- (“against”) + vertere (“to turn”).

parole.significato: to crowd or push together (in senses relating to teeth)

parole.significato: Living in close proximity (as though sharing a tent); intimate, familiar.

parole.significato: A type of quasi-marriage between slaves.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin contubernium.

parole.significato: Contemptuous of authority; willfully disobedient; rebellious.
parole.testo: From Latin contumāx (“stubborn, obstinate”) + -ious. By surface analysis, contum(ax) + -acious.

parole.significato: Disobedience, resistance to authority.
parole.testo: From Latin contumācia, from contumāx (“refusing to appear in a court of law in disobedience of a summons; insolent, obstinate, stiff-necked”).

parole.significato: To disturb or perturb greatly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin conturbo, conturbatus.

parole.significato: disorder, disturbance
parole.testo: From Latin conturbatio.

parole.significato: To injure without breaking the skin; to bruise.
parole.testo: From (the participle stem of) Latin contundere (“pound or beat small”), from com- + tundere (“beat, thump”).

parole.significato: A continuous aggregation of built-up urban communities created as a result of urban sprawl.

parole.significato: A cone.

parole.significato: The infundibulum of the heart.

parole.significato: The tapered lower end of the spinal cord.

parole.significato: To recover health and strength gradually after sickness or weakness.
parole.testo: From Latin convalēscere, from con- (intensive prefix) + valēscere (“to become strong”), inchoative of valēre (“to be strong”).

parole.significato: The process of conveying something.

parole.significato: To tear (tissue, a nerve, etc.), to convulse.
parole.testo: From Latin convellō. Doublet of convulse.

parole.significato: Tending to tear or pull.

parole.significato: To make convenient.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin convenientia, from conveniens (“suitable”), present participle of convenire (“to come together, suit”). Doublet of convenance.

parole.significato: Serving to reduce a difficulty, or accessible with minimum difficulty; expedient.
parole.testo: From Middle English convenient, from Latin conveniēns (“fit, suitable, convenient”), present participle of conveniō, convinīre (“to come together, suit”); see convene and compare covenant.

parole.significato: To call before a judge or judicature; to summon; to convene.
parole.testo: From Latin convenio (past participle conventus), whence also convene; so of the same ultimate origin as Etymology 1.

parole.significato: A secret, unauthorized or illegal religious meeting.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English conventicle, conventicule (“a gathering, meeting (especially a secret or unlawful one); (derogatory) a church”), from Latin conventiculum (“assembly; meeting (or the place involved); association”), from conventus (“assembled, convened”) + -culum (suffix forming noun diminuti

parole.significato: A short intensive immersion workshop where participants speak only Latin (or sometimes Ancient Greek) from morning to n…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin conventiculum, diminutive of conventus (“meeting; conjunction; agreement”)

parole.significato: Pertaining to a convent or convent life; cloistered, monastic.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin conventuālis, from Latin conventus (“convent”).

parole.significato: (said of two or more entities) To approach each other; to get closer and closer; to become a unified whole; to come to…
parole.testo: From Latin convergere, from con- (“together”) + vergere (“to bend”).

parole.significato: The act of moving toward union or uniformity.
parole.testo: From converge + -ence (after Latin convergentia).

parole.significato: Opposite; reversed in order or relation; reciprocal.
parole.testo: From Latin conversus (“turned around”), past participle of converto (“turn about”).

parole.significato: A lay brother.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin conversus.

parole.significato: Any proposition which is subject to the process of conversion; so called in its relation to itself as converted, after…
parole.testo: From Latin convertendus (“to be converted”). Compare subtrahend.

parole.significato: To make someone believe, or feel sure about something, especially by using logic, argument or evidence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin convincō (“to refute, prove”), from con- + vincō (“to conquer, vanquish”). Doublet of convict. Displaced native Old English oferreċċan.

parole.significato: Relating to a feast or festivity; convivial.
parole.testo: From Latin convivalis. See convive.

parole.significato: coexistence, cohabitation
parole.testo: From Latin convivere (“to carouse together”), con- (“together”) + vivere (“to live”).

parole.significato: To call together (people); to convoke.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin convocatus, past participle of convocare (“to convocate”). Doublet of convoke.

parole.significato: To make unnecessarily complex.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin convolūtum, past participle of convolvere (“to roll together”).

parole.significato: A twist or fold.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin convolutus (“to roll together”), past participle of convolvere, from con- + volvere (“to roll”), with the suffix -tion. Equivalent to convolute + -ion. The mathematical sense is a semantic calque from Faltung.

parole.significato: To roll together, or one part on another
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin convolvere (“roll together”), from con- (“together”) + volvō (“roll”); see voluble, volute, and compare involve, evolve, revolve.

parole.significato: Any of several plants, of the genus Convolvulus, found in temperate climates, having small trumpet-shaped flowers.
parole.testo: From Latin convolvulus (“bindweed; caterpillar”), from convolvō (“convolve”).

parole.significato: To suffer violent involuntary contractions of the muscles, causing one's body to contort.
parole.testo: From Latin convulsus, past participle of convellere (“to pluck up, dislocate, convulse”), from com- (“together”) + vellere (“to pluck, pull”). Doublet of convel.

parole.significato: An intense, paroxysmal, involuntary muscular contraction.

parole.significato: A person who prepares food.

Cognates Cognate with Cimbrian khoch (“cook”), Dutch kok (“cook”), German Koch (“cook”), Luxembourgish Kach (“cook”), Danish kok (“cook”), Icelandic kokku

parole.significato: To work or act together, especially for a common purpose or benefit.

parole.significato: To choose; to elect.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin cooptātus, perfect passive participle of cooptō (“to elect”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from co- + optō (“to choose”).

parole.significato: Of the same rank; equal.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin coōrdinātus, perfect passive participle of coōrdinō (“arrange together”), from co- + ōrdinō, equivalent to co- + ordinate. See -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more. See also ordain and ordinate.

parole.significato: To place in the same order or rank.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin coōrdinātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more. Compare French coordonner.

parole.significato: A long, loose cloak worn by a priest, deacon, or bishop when presiding over a ceremony other than the Mass.
parole.testo: From Middle English cope, from Medieval Latin cāpa (“cape”) Doublet of cap, cape, and chape.

parole.significato: Total deafness.

parole.significato: Vast in quantity or number, profuse, abundant; taking place on a large scale.
parole.testo: From Middle English copious, from Latin copiosus, from copia (“abundance”), equivalent to co- + ops (“wealth”) + -osus (“full of”). By surface analysis, copy + -ous.

parole.significato: Any of various metallic sulphates formed from the reaction of sulfur with iron, zinc, or copper, especially (alchemy) s…
parole.testo: From Middle English coperas, coperose (“any metallic sulfate”), from Medieval Latin cuprosa directly or via Old French coperose, from Medieval Latin aqua cuprosa (“cupreous water”), from Latin cuprum (“copper”) + -osa (“-ose: forming related adjectives”). parole.significato: A living organism that feeds on feces or fecal matter.

parole.significato: A word, usually a verb, used to link the subject of a sentence with a predicate (usually a subject complement or an adv…

parole.significato: One engaged in sexual union.
parole.testo: From Latin cōpulāns.

parole.significato: To engage in sexual intercourse.
parole.testo: From Latin cōpulātus, perfect passive participle of cōpulō (“to couple, join, connect”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French copuler.

parole.significato: Joined; associated; coupled.
parole.testo: From Latin cōpulātus, the perfect passive participle of cōpulō (“to couple, join, connect”). See -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to copulation.

parole.significato: Synonym of culinary.

parole.significato: Massive hypertrophy of the left ventricle of the heart due to volume overload.

parole.significato: coracoid process

parole.significato: A mixture of phenolic dyestuffs consisting mostly of aurin.

parole.significato: The skeleton of a coral. It can be calcareous or horny, simple or compound.

parole.significato: A two-masted merchant ship of Ancient Rome.

parole.significato: The central part of a seed, from which the new plant develops.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Corinth; Corinthian.
