parole.significato: The stem of a plant, especially of grass or sedge.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin culmus. Doublet of French calame, calamus, and haulm; further related to caramel, chalumeau and shawm.

parole.significato: Top; summit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin culmen (“apex, acme”).

parole.significato: Of a heavenly body, to be at the highest point, reach its greatest altitude.
parole.testo: First attested in 1647; borrowed from Medieval Latin culminātus, perfect passive participle of culminō (“to crown”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin culmen (“peak, highest point”, oblique stem culmin-) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), older form columen (“top, summit”), from Proto-Italic *kol

parole.significato: A horny piece on a bird's beak that envelopes the culmen in some bird species, such as mollymawks.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin culmen, culminis (“top, roof, summit, peak”) + -i- + -corn.

parole.significato: Negligence or fault, as distinguishable from dolus (deceit, fraud), which implies intent, culpa being imputable to defe…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin culpa.

parole.significato: Gross negligence.
parole.testo: From Latin culpa (“blame”) + lata, feminine form of latus (“extensive”).

parole.significato: A slight fault.
parole.testo: From Latin culpa (“blame”) + levis (“light”).

parole.significato: A plant that has been deliberately altered or selected by humans, that is it has resulted from artificial rather than n…
parole.testo: From culti(vated) + -gen, or from Latin cultus (“cultivated”) + gēns (“kind”). Coined by American botanist Liberty Hyde Bailey in 1918.

parole.significato: Having a bill shaped like the coulter of a plough, or like a knife.
parole.testo: From Latin culter (“knife”) + rōstrum (“beak”).

parole.significato: To grow plants, notably crops.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cultivātus, perfect passive participle of cultivō (“till, cultivate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from cultīvus (“tilled”), from Latin cultus, perfect passive participle of colō (“till, cultivate”), which comes from earlier *quelō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (

parole.significato: The art or act of cultivating (improvement of land for or by agriculture), as:
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cultivātus, perfect passive participle of cultivō, + -ion, or Middle French cultivation. By surface analysis, cultivate + -ion.

parole.significato: Sharp-edged and pointed; shaped like a pruning knife
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cultrātus (“knife-shaped”), from culter + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Shaped like a pruning knife; cultrate.
parole.testo: From Latin culter, cultri (“knife”) + -form.

parole.significato: Established or accepted religious rites or customs of worship; state of religious development.
parole.testo: From Latin cultus (“cultivation, culture”). See cult.

parole.significato: A dove or pigeon, now specifically of the species Columba palumbus.
parole.testo: From Middle English culver, from Old English culufre, culfre, culfer, possibly borrowed from Vulgar Latin *columbra, from Latin columbula (“little pigeon”), from Latin columba (“pigeon, dove”).

parole.significato: Used in indicating a thing or person which has two or more roles, functions, or natures, or which has changed from one…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cum.

parole.significato: With a grain of salt; with a bit of common sense and skepticism.
parole.testo: A New Latin coinage, derived from the phrase cum grānō salis (which was not used in Classical Latin).

parole.significato: The logical fallacy of assuming that two events that occur at the same time have a cause-and-effect relationship.
parole.testo: From Latin cum hoc ergo propter hoc (“with this, therefore because of this”).

parole.significato: With praise; an honor added to a diploma or degree for work that is above average.
parole.testo: From Latin cum (“with”) + laude (ablative of laus, "praise").

parole.significato: A member of a nomadic Turkic people of central Asia who ruled parts of Eurasia and Eastern Europe in the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Cumani, from Byzantine Greek Κουμάνοι (Koumánoi), perhaps ultimately from the name of the Kuma River.

parole.significato: Accumulated; agglomerated; amassed.
parole.testo: First attested in 1534; borrowed from Latin cumulātus, perfect passive participle of cumulō (“to pile up”), see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3). Sporadic use of the participle up until Early Modern English.

parole.significato: Having the shape of a cumulus cloud.
parole.testo: Latin cumulus (“heap”) + -iform

parole.significato: A cloud with a tall structure and flat base, often associated with thunderstorms.
parole.testo: From Latin cumulus (“heap”) + nimbus (“cloud”).

parole.significato: A heap or mound.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cumulus. Doublet of comble. Sense 2 (“type of cloud”) was coined by the British chemist and amateur meteorologist Luke Howard (1772–1864): see the 1803 quotation.

parole.significato: The earliest abode; original dwelling place; originals.
parole.testo: Latin cūnābula (“cradle”).

parole.significato: Delay, hesitation, procrastination.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cūnctātiō (“a delaying, tarrying”), from cūnctor (“linger, hesitate”).

parole.significato: Inclined to delay
parole.testo: From Latin cunctari (“to delay”), + -ive.

parole.significato: One who delays or lingers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cūnctātor (“delayer”); applied as a surname to Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus.

parole.significato: delaying; procrastinating
parole.testo: From Latin cunctor (“delay, impede”).

parole.significato: wedge-shaped.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cuneātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The superintendent of the engravers of dies for making coins.
parole.testo: From cuneātor, Medieval Latin equivalent of Old French coigneur (“coiner”).

parole.significato: A portion of the occipital lobe of the human brain, involved in visual processing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cuneus. Doublet of coign and coin.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of a rabbit.
parole.testo: From Latin cuniculus (“rabbit, burrow”). See cony.

parole.significato: A burrow or low underground passage, such as a rabbit warren, mine, or catacomb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cunīculus.

parole.significato: Someone who performs cunnilingus.
parole.testo: From Latin cunnilinctor (“cunt-licker”).

parole.significato: Performance of oral sex upon the vulva or vagina.
parole.testo: From Latin cunnilingus (literally “cuntlicker”). The meaning shift, not yet complete in the early twentieth century, perhaps derives from figurative uses where the name for a person stands for the name of a practice.

parole.significato: A concave vessel for drinking, usually made of opaque material (as opposed to a glass) and with a handle.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English cuppe, coppe, from the merger of Old English cuppe (“cup”) and Old English copp (“cup, vessel”). Old English cuppe is a borrowing from Late Latin cuppa, itself of obscure origin, but probably from earlier Latin cūpa (“tub, cask”), from Proto-Indo-European *kewp- (“a hol

parole.significato: Of or relating to Cupid.
parole.testo: From Latin Cupīdō, gen. Cupīdinis

parole.significato: Characterized by or related to cupidity (greed, desire for wealth).
parole.testo: From Latin *cupīdinōsus, from cupīdō, cupīdinis (“desire; greed”).

parole.significato: A reddish-brown color, like that of polished copper.
parole.testo: From Latin cupreus, from cuprum (“copper”).

parole.significato: Resembling a cypress tree
parole.testo: From Latin cupressus (“cypress”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, copper; containing copper.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin cuprum (“copper”). See -ic.

parole.significato: Containing or producing copper.
parole.testo: From Latin cuprum (“copper”) + -iferous.

parole.significato: Synonym of cupric (“pertaining to or derived from copper”).
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin cuprum (“copper”). See -ine.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to copper.
parole.testo: From Late Latin cuprum (“copper”) through its compound form in -o-.

parole.significato: Of, or of the nature of, copper.
parole.testo: From Latin cuprum (“copper”), + -ous.

parole.significato: A cup-shaped or dome-shaped object.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cūpula, from cūpa + -ula. Doublet of cupola. False cognate of English cupule in which English cup is descendant of Old English copp of Germanic origin.

parole.significato: An assistant rector or vicar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cūrātus (“one who has been curated, a curate”), a substantivation of the perfect passive participle of cūrō. Doublet of curato. Equivalent to cure + -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A person who manages, administers or organizes a collection, either independently or employed by a museum, library, arc…
parole.testo: From Latin cūrātor (“one who has care of a thing, a manager, guardian, trustee”), from cūrāre (“to take care of”), from cūra (“care, heed, attention, anxiety, grief”).

parole.significato: A female curator, guardian, or custodian
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cūrātrīx. By surface analysis, curator + -trix.

parole.significato: Any of the subdivisions of a tribe in ancient Rome
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin curia.

parole.significato: Any of various councils of advisers and administrators in medieval Europe that served kings.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?] (literally “royal council, king's court”)

parole.significato: Relating to a court.
parole.testo: From Latin cūriālis (“belonging to the imperial court”), from cūria rēgis (“counsellors and retinue of a king”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a curia.
parole.testo: From Latin cūriātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A possibly unimportant point of interest; a curiosity.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cūriōsum.

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Courland
parole.testo: From Latin Curonia (“Courland”, literally “land of the Curonians”), from an original name Kurš, which could mean "quickly moving (at sea)," from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”).

parole.significato: The quality of being current (generally circulated and accepted); currency, currentness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin currentia + -ence, from Latin currō (“to run”).

parole.significato: Money or other items used to facilitate transactions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin currentia. By surface analysis, current + -cy.

parole.significato: Without deliberation or hesitation: extempore, off-the-cuff.
parole.testo: From New Latin currente calamō (“with the pen running on”).

parole.significato: A light two-wheeled carriage large enough for the driver and a passenger and drawn by a carefully-matched pair.
parole.testo: From Latin curriculum (“racing chariot”). Doublet of curriculum.

parole.significato: The set of courses, coursework, and content offered at a school or university.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin curriculum (“course”), derived from currō (“run, move quickly”). Doublet of curricle.

parole.significato: A written account of one's life comprising one's education, accomplishments, work experience, publications, etc.; espec…
parole.testo: From Latin curriculum (“course”) + vītae, genitive of vīta (“life”).

parole.significato: A courier or runner.
parole.testo: From Latin runner; in the legal sense, from Latin cursitor, from the words de cursu, applied in the statute to ordinary writs.

parole.significato: A part of any of several scientific or measuring instruments that moves back and forth to indicate a position.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cursor (“runner”), from currō (“run”) + -or (agentive suffix). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European.

parole.significato: A course; a journey or progression.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cursus. Doublet of course and cour.

parole.significato: Brief or terse, especially to the point of being rude.
parole.testo: From the Latin curtus (“shortened”). Cognate with Dutch kort, German kurz, Galician curto, French court, Italian corto, Portuguese curto, and Spanish corto. Doublet of short.

parole.significato: A short sword used for ceremonial purposes
parole.testo: From Latin curtus (“short”).

parole.significato: Shortened, having been shortened.
parole.testo: First attested in 1676; borrowed from Latin curtātus, perfect passive participle of curtō (“to shorten”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The interval of a planet's orbit in which its curtate or shortened distance is less than the true distance.
parole.testo: First attested in 1584; borrowed from New Latin curtātiō, from curtō + -tiō.

parole.significato: Designating a kind of elaborate ceremonial seat inlaid with ivory, used by the highest magistrates in ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin curūlis (“of or pertaining to a chariot; curule chair”), from currus (“chariot”), from currō (“run”).

parole.significato: bent in a regular form ; curved.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English (y)curvat(e) (“bent; hunched, stooped”), borrowed from Latin curvātus (“curved”), perfect passive participle of curvō (“to curve”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from curvus + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of curving or bending, or the shape of the resulting curve; curvature.
parole.testo: From Latin curvatio, equivalent to curve + -ation.

parole.significato: The shape of something curved.
parole.testo: From Latin curvare, from Latin curvatura. See also curve. Displaced native Old English ġebīeġednes.

parole.significato: Bent without angles; crooked; curved.
parole.testo: Attested since the 1690s, from Latin curvus (“bent, curved”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, curve, turn”) + *-wós. Doublet of curb, shrink, carcer, and cancer.

parole.significato: Having a curved or crooked tail.
parole.testo: Latin curvus (“bent”) + English caudate.

parole.significato: Having bent ribs.
parole.testo: Latin curvus + English costate.

parole.significato: Having a curved shape.
parole.testo: From Latin curvus + -form.

parole.significato: Having the ribs or veins of the curved.
parole.testo: Latin curvus bent + English nerved.

parole.significato: Distributed in a curved line, as leaves along a stem.
parole.testo: Latin curvus bent + English serial.

parole.significato: The state of being curved; a bending in a regular form; crookedness.
parole.testo: From Latin curvitas, from curvus (“bent”). Compare French curvité.

parole.significato: An arcograph.
parole.testo: From Latin curvus (“bent”) + -graph.

parole.significato: Any arboreal marsupial of most genera of the family Phalangeridae, native to northern Australia, New Guinea, and Indone…
parole.testo: From New Latin Cuscus, former genus name, ultimately (probably via French and Dutch koeskoes) from a local word for the marsupials in a language of the Moluccas.

parole.significato: A sharp point or pointed end.
parole.testo: From Latin cuspis (“a point, spear, pointed end”); first used in astrology. Doublet of cuspid and cuspis.

parole.significato: A pointed tooth between the incisors and premolars in heterodont mammals.
parole.testo: From Latin cuspid-, stem of cuspis (“point, apex”). Doublet of cusp and cuspis.

parole.significato: Having a cusp
parole.testo: First attested in 1693; borrowed from Latin cuspidātus, from cuspis (“point, tip”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To sharpen, to whet to a point.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin cuspidātus, perfect passive participle of cuspidō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix)

parole.significato: A point; a sharp end.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cuspis. Doublet of cusp and cuspid.

parole.significato: A person entrusted with the custody or care of something or someone; a caretaker or keeper.
parole.testo: From a shortening of Latin custōdiānātus, from Latin custōdia (“a keeping, watch, guard, prison”), from custōs (“a keeper, watchman, guard”). By surface analysis, custody + -ian.

parole.significato: Protecting; guarding.
parole.testo: From Latin custōdiēns, nominative participle of custōdīre.

parole.significato: A custodian.
parole.testo: Compare Latin custodiarus.

parole.significato: The legal right to take care of something or somebody, especially children.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin custōdia (“a keeping, watch, guard, prison”), from custōs (“a keeper, watchman, guard”). Doublet of custode.

parole.significato: In accordance with, or established by, custom or common usage.
parole.testo: From Middle English custumary, from Medieval Latin custumarius. By surface analysis, custom + -ary.

parole.significato: A warden.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin custōs.

parole.significato: A kind of viceregal locum tenens appointed, either alone or jointly, to execute the political duties of a monarch durin…
parole.testo: First attested in the plural in October 1644 and in the singular in 1683; Latin: custōs (“guard”, “protector”; “guardian”; “keeper”, “custodian”) + rēgnī (“of royal power”; genitive singular of rēgnum, “royal power”, “kingdom”) = “custodian of royal power” ≈ “guardian of the realm”.

parole.significato: The main justice of the peace in a given county of England, Wales or Ireland.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin custos rotulorum, from Latin custōs (“custos, keeper”) + genitive plural of rotulus (“roll”).

parole.significato: A survey of a medieval English manor, listing each tenant and the customs under which the tenancy was held.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin custumale (adjective, neuter form of custumalis), used as an adjectival noun. Attested to 1576.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, existing on, or affecting the exterior skin, especially the cutis.
parole.testo: From New Latin cutaneus, from Latin cutis (“skin”).

parole.significato: The outermost layer of the skin of vertebrates.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cutīcula (“cuticle, skin”). Doublet of cuticula.

parole.significato: A tough protective covering outside the epidermis of many invertebrates and plants; cuticle.
parole.testo: From Latin cutīcula (“skin, cuticle”). Doublet of cuticle.

parole.significato: The formation of cuticles.
parole.testo: Related to cutis (“the true skin or dermis, underlying the epidermis”) or cuticle; The Oxford English Dictionary proposes a connection to hypothetical Latin *cutificāre.

parole.significato: To form skin.
parole.testo: From Latin cutis (“skin”) and faciō (“make”).

parole.significato: Containing skin.
parole.testo: From Latin cuticula (“membrane, skin”) + gerere (“to bear”) + English -al (“of or relating to”).

parole.significato: Any inflammation or other skin reaction to an irritant.
parole.testo: From Latin cuticula (“cuticle, skin”) + reaction.

parole.significato: The true skin, underlying the epidermis.
parole.testo: From Latin cutis (“living skin”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
parole.testo: Latin, "hyperelastic skin".

parole.significato: A group of rare connective tissue disorders in which the skin becomes inelastic and hangs loosely in folds.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Any of various instruments that measure physical properties of the skin (typically elasticity).
parole.testo: From Latin cutis (“skin”) + -ometer.

parole.significato: A variety of cellulose, occurring as a fine transparent membrane covering the aerial organs of plants, and forming an e…
parole.testo: From Latin cutis (“skin”) + -ose.

parole.significato: An ancient Roman unit of liquid measure reckoned as the volume of 1⅔ Roman ounce of wine and equivalent to about 45 mL…
parole.testo: From Latin cyathus, from Ancient Greek κύαθος (kúathos, “ladle”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of kyathos.

parole.significato: Any of various primulaceous flowering plants, of the genus Cyclamen, widely cultivated as a houseplant, having decorati…
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin cyclamen, from Latin cyclamīnos.

parole.significato: An interval of space or time in which one set of events or phenomena is completed.
parole.testo: From Middle English cicle (“fixed length period of years”), from Late Latin cyclus, from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”), from Proto-Hellenic *kúklos, *kʷókʷlos, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷékʷlos (“circle, wheel”). Doublet of chakra, chakram, charkha, chukker, cyclus, kike, and wheel (see t

parole.significato: A one-eyed giant from Greek and Roman mythology.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cyclōps, from Ancient Greek Κύκλωψ (Kúklōps, “Cyclops ['round eyes']”). The sense for copepods is a semantic loan from translingual Cyclops.

parole.significato: A cycle, or series of poems.
parole.testo: From Latin cyclus. Doublet of chakra, chakram, charkha, chukker, cycle, kike, and wheel.

parole.significato: curved like the neck of a swan
parole.testo: from Latin cycnēus, from Ancient Greek κύκνειος (kúkneios).

parole.significato: Being of the genus Cygnus (swans), within subfamily Anserinae of the family Anatidae, though sometimes considered a dis…
parole.testo: From Latin cygnus (“swan”), with English -ine. The alkaloid was named in reference to the Swan River in Western Australia, where the toxic plants were discovered.

parole.significato: Of or relating to cylinders; shaped like a cylinder.
parole.testo: From Latin cylindricus. By surface analysis, cylinder + -ic.

parole.significato: cylindrical
parole.testo: From Latin cylindrus + -iform.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Mount Cyllene in Arcadia.
parole.testo: From Latin Cyllēnius, from Ancient Greek Κυλλήνιος (Kullḗnios), from Κυλλήνη (Kullḗnē).

parole.significato: The wavelike, curved shape of a cymatium, consisting of a concave and a convex line; (loosely) the cymatium itself.
parole.testo: From New Latin cȳma (“young sprout or shoot of cabbage”) (whence the botanic usage of cyme), from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma, “swell, wave”, “cyma”, “sprout of a plant”), from κύω (kúō, “to conceive, to become pregnant”). For more information, click to expand this box. Most English coinages on this ro

parole.significato: Synonym of cyma reversa.
parole.testo: cyma + Latin inversa (“inverted”)

parole.significato: A cyma concave in its upper part, and convex in its lower part.
parole.testo: cyma + Latin rēcta (“straight”)

parole.significato: A cyma convex in its upper part, and concave in its lower part.
parole.testo: cyma + Latin reversa (“returned”)

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to cymatics.
parole.testo: First attested in 1828, from Latin cȳmat(is) (“sprout, swelling, hollow sphere”) + -ic, stem of cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῡ́μᾰτος (kū́mătos, “wave, billow, swell, sprout, fetus”), genitive of κῦμα (kûma). Compare the latter cymatics (1966) and the earlier Latin cȳmaticus (1753).

parole.significato: The study of visible effects of sound and vibration.
parole.testo: Coined by Hans Jenny from Latin cȳmat(is) (“sprout, swelling, hollow sphere”) + -ics, stem of cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῡ́μᾰτος (kū́mătos, “wave, billow, swell, sprout, fetus”), genitive of κῦμα (kûma).

parole.significato: A molding on the cornice, above the corona, often having a wavelike form (cyma).
parole.testo: From Latin cȳmatium (“ogee”), from the Ancient Greek κῡμάτιον (kūmátion), the diminutive form of κῦμα (kûma, “wave”). Equivalent to Latin cȳmat(is) (“sprout, swelling, hollow sphere”) + -ium, stem of cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῡ́μᾰτος (kū́mătos, “wave, billow, swell, sprout, fetus”), genitive of κῦμα

parole.significato: An instrument for compounding the resultant of two parallel, simple, harmonic waves.
parole.testo: From Latin cȳmat(is) (“sprout, swelling, hollow sphere”) + -o- + -graph, stem of cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῡ́μᾰτος (kū́mătos, “wave, billow, swell, sprout, fetus”), genitive of κῦμα (kûma). Compare cymograph.

parole.significato: Synonym of cymoscope.
parole.testo: From Latin cȳmat(is) (“sprout, swelling, hollow sphere”) + -o- + -scope, stem of cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῡ́μᾰτος (kū́mătos, “wave, billow, swell, sprout, fetus”), genitive of κῦμα (kûma).

parole.significato: Shaped like a boat.
parole.testo: Latin cymba (“boat”), + -iform.

parole.significato: The tarsus of the copulatory pedipalp in certain spiders.
parole.testo: Concocted from Latin cymbium, not used in such a meaning.

parole.significato: A detector of electromagnetic waves.
parole.testo: First attested as cymatoscope in 1903 and as cymoscope in 1905; formed as cȳm- (the short stem of the Latin cȳma, from the Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma), kūma, “wave”) + -o- + -scope. Cymatoscope is philologically prescribed in place of cymoscope because it preserves the long stem (κῡμᾰτ- (kūmăt-), kūma

parole.significato: having a cyme, a usually flat-topped flower cluster in which the main and branch stems each end in a flower that opens…
parole.testo: From the Latin cȳmōsus, from cȳma, whence the English cyma.

parole.significato: A small cyme, or one with very few flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cȳmula (“a tender sprout”), the diminutive form of cȳma, whence the English cyma and, ultimately, cyme.

parole.significato: Any disease of the tonsils, throat, or windpipe, typicalling with inflammation, swelling, and difficulty breathing and…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cy̆nanchē, from Ancient Greek κῠνᾰ́γχη (kŭnắnkhē, “a dog's collar, a bad kind of sore throat”). Doublet of quinsy.

parole.significato: A member of a sect of Ancient Greek philosophers who believed virtue to be the only good and self-control to be the onl…
parole.testo: First used in English around 1540–50. From Latin Cynicus (cynic philosopher), from Ancient Greek Κυνικός (Kunikós, from κύων (kúōn, “dog”, see Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ) + -ικός (-ikós), literally “doglike, currish”). parole.significato: Of or pertaining to dogs.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cyno-, from the combining form of Ancient Greek κύων (kúōn, “dog”) formed with -ο- (-o-). Cf. cynic. By surface analysis, cyn- + -o-. Piecewise doublet of cano-.

parole.significato: A creature with the head of a dog or jackal and the body of a human.
parole.testo: From Latin cynocephalus; by surface analysis, cyno- + translingual -cephalus.

parole.significato: An ancient punishment in which the criminal was smeared with honey and exposed to insects.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin cȳphōnismus, from Ancient Greek κῡφωνισμός (kūphōnismós), from κῡ́φων (kū́phōn, “wooden collar, bent yoke”) + -ισμός (-ismós, abstract noun suffix). parole.significato: A thin, translucent, usually black fabric, a kind of crape.
parole.testo: From Latin Cyprus, from Ancient Greek Κύπρος (Kúpros).

parole.significato: Like or belonging to the swifts (Cypselidae, now known as the Apodidae.)
parole.testo: Latin cypselus (“a kind of swallow”), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Of or related to Cyrenaicism, the philosophical school founded by Aristippus of Cyrene and codified by Aristippus the Y…
parole.testo: From Latin Cȳrēnaicus, from Ancient Greek Κῡρηνᾰῐ̈κός (Kūrēnăĭ̈kós), from Κυρήνη (Kurḗnē, “Cyrene”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”, adjective-forming suffix). Equivalent to Cyrene + -ic or a backformation from Cyrenaica.

parole.significato: Denoting an alphabet devised for writing the Old Church Slavonic liturgical language, and its adaptations used for seve…
parole.testo: From the name Cyril + -ic, from Medieval Latin Cȳrillus, from Ancient Greek Κῡ́ρῐλλος (Kū́rĭllos), denoting Saint Cyril, who devised a predecessor to the Cyrillic script, the Glagolitic alphabet, and whose students later devised the Cyrillic script itself.

parole.significato: A kind of mead made with apples.
parole.testo: From Middle English ciser (“alcoholic beverage of great strength and potency”), from Medieval Latin sīcera, from Ancient Greek σίκερα (síkera), from Hebrew שֵׁכָר (šēḵār). Doublet of cider.

parole.significato: A pouch or sac without opening, usually membranous and containing morbid matter, which develops in one of the natural c…
parole.testo: From Late Latin cystis, from Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis, “anatomical sac”).

parole.significato: A cyst.
parole.testo: From Late Latin; see cyst.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Cythera, an island now part of Greece, at which the goddess Aphrodite came ashore on a seashell…
parole.testo: From Latin Cytherēius [from Ancient Greek Κυθερήϊος (Kutherḗïos), from Κύθηρα (Kúthēra) + -ήϊος (-ḗïos)] + -an.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Cyzicus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Cȳzicēnus, from Ancient Greek Κυζικηνός (Kuzikēnós). By surface analysis, Cyzicus + -ene.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to, or being, a large north-facing hall with a prospect towards the gardens; the windows of this hall…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cyzicenus used by Vitruvius, from the former.

parole.significato: Cavity of an abdomen.
parole.testo: From Latin coelia, from Ancient Greek κοιλία (koilía, “hollow place”).

parole.significato: An ancient cemetery, churchyard, or burial ground.
parole.testo: An unadapted adoption of the Latin coemētērium. Doublet of cemetery.

parole.significato: With.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of Latin cum

parole.significato: A British penny; an old penny (the modern decimal penny being abbreviated p).
parole.testo: Abbreviations. * (British penny; old penny): abbreviation of Latin denarii, the name of the corresponding Roman coin. * (dice): abbreviation of dice d # Abbreviation of died or death. #: William Shakespeare, d 1616

parole.significato: Let it be divided into equal parts.
parole.testo: From Latin dīvidātur in partēs aequālēs (“let it be divided into equal parts”).

parole.significato: a member of an ancient Indo-European ethnic group of Dacia.
parole.testo: From Dacia + -an, from Latin Dacia (“Dacia”).

parole.significato: A metrical foot of three syllables of the shape | – ⏖ |
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dactylus, from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”), from the three bones of the finger corresponding to three syllables. Doublet of dactylus, date, and (possibly) digit.

parole.significato: Synonym of dactyl (“type of metrical foot”).
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin dactylus. Doublet of dactyl and date.

parole.significato: Skilful, ingenious, cunning.
parole.testo: From Latin daedalus, from Ancient Greek δαίδαλος (daídalos, “skillful”).

parole.significato: A bulbous plant of the genus Narcissus, with yellow flowers and a trumpet shaped corona, especially Narcissus pseudonar…
parole.testo: Variant of Middle English affodill (“ramson”), from Medieval Latin affodillus, from Latin asphodelus, from Ancient Greek ἀσφόδελος (asphódelos), of Pre-Greek origin. The initial d- is perhaps from merging of the article in Dutch de affodil, the Netherlands being a source for bulbs (compare adder, ap

parole.significato: A form of dagesh which originally indicated gemination of its consonant sound.
parole.testo: From dagesh + Latin forte (“strong”).

parole.significato: A small dot put in the middle of a consonant in Hebrew. It originally had the effect of transforming a fricative sound…
parole.testo: From dagesh + Latin lēne (“soft, weak”).

parole.significato: In the way of a daimon; befitting a demon; fiendish.
parole.testo: From daimon + -ic; from Latin demon (“spirit”), originally from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn, “a god, goddess, divine power, genius, guardian spirit”). Doublet of demonic.

parole.significato: Synonym of dalmatic.
parole.testo: From Latin dalmatica.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Damascus.
parole.testo: From Latin Damascēnus, from Ancient Greek Δαμασκηνός (Damaskēnós). By surface analysis, Damascus + -ene. The sense “pertaining to a sudden and complete change in one's beliefs” refers to the conversion of St Paul to Christianity on the road to Damascus.

parole.significato: An ornate silk fabric originating from Damascus.
parole.testo: From Middle English damaske, from Medieval Latin damascus, named after the city Damascus, where the fabric was originally made.

parole.significato: A form of ancient Roman capital punishment in which the condemned was killed by wild animals, usually lions.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?] (literally “condemnation to beasts”)

parole.significato: A posthumous punishment for traitors etc. by which they were effectively erased from history by having their works undo…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin damnātiō memoriae (literally “condemnation of memory”).

parole.significato: Synonym of damnatio memoriae.
parole.testo: Calque of New Latin damnātiō memoriae.

parole.significato: Containing a sentence of condemnation.
parole.testo: From Latin damnatorius, corresponding to damn + -atory.

parole.significato: Causing loss or harm; injurious.
parole.testo: From Latin damnificus, damnum (“damage, loss”) + facere (“to make”). See damn.

parole.significato: The act of causing injury or loss.
parole.testo: Latin damnificatio.

parole.significato: harm; detriment
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin damnum.

parole.significato: When one person causes damage or loss to another for which the latter has no remedy. (For example, opening a burger sta…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin damnum absque injuria (“loss without injury”).

parole.significato: A subspecies of plum tree, Prunus domestica subsp. insititia, native to Eurasia.
parole.testo: From Middle English damascene, damasyn, damacene, from Latin prūnum damascēnum (“Damascene plum, plum of Damascus”). Doublet of damascene.

parole.significato: Any one of the fifty daughters of Danaus.
parole.testo: From the stem of Latin Danais, from Ancient Greek Δαναΐς (Danaḯs), from Δαναός (Danaós, “Danaus”) + -ις (-is), literally “sprung of Danaus”. By surface analysis, Danaus + -id.

parole.significato: Synonym of Danish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dānicus.

parole.significato: Sumptuous in cheer.
parole.testo: From Latin dapaticus, from daps (“feast, banquet”).

parole.significato: The servant that brings the meat to the table at a meal.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dapifer, from Latin daps (“feast”) + -fer (“bearer”).

parole.significato: A thin layer of vascular contractile tissue that contains smooth muscle fibers but no fat and is situated directly bene…
parole.testo: From Latin dartos, from Ancient Greek δαρτός (dartós, “flayed”), from δέρω (dérō, “to skin, to flay”) + -τός (-tós, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Having downy leaves.
parole.testo: From New Latin dasyphyllus (from Ancient Greek δασύς (dasús, “hairy, shaggy; dense”) + φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”)) + -ous.

parole.significato: Part of the Roman Catholic Curia, abolished in 1967, from which were sent graces or favours such as appointments to ben…
parole.testo: From Late Latin, from Latin datum (“given”).

parole.significato: The act of giving, granting or conferring (e.g. an office) but not liberal as a donation or gift.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin datiōnem.

parole.significato: Denoting the case of a noun which expresses the remoter or indirect object, generally indicated in English by to or for…
parole.testo: From Latin datīvus (“appropriate for giving”), itself from datus (the past participle of dō (“to give”)) + -īvus (“-ive”).

parole.significato: an independent phrase in a sentence conveying additional circumstances in the dative case; present:
parole.testo: Calque of Latin dativus absolutus.

parole.significato: benefactive dative
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dativus commodī.

parole.significato: malefactive dative
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dativus incommodī.

parole.significato: To provide missing data points by using a mathematical model to extrapolate values that are outside the range of a meas…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin datum, a nominalization of datus, perfect passive participle of dō, from Proto-Italic *didō, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, reduplication of *deh₃-, or from *-ti. Doublet of die.

parole.significato: The dignity of a dauphin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin delphīnātus. By surface analysis, dauphin + -ate (forms nouns denoting a rank or office). Doublet of Delphinate, Dauphiny, and Dauphiné.

parole.significato: A person or group considered unlikely to prevail; an underdog.
parole.testo: From Middle English David, Davyd, Davyde, from Old English Dauid, David, from Late Latin Dāvīd, from Koine Greek Δαυῑ̈́δ (Dauī̈́d), from Biblical Hebrew דָּוִד (dāwiḏ, literally “beloved”).

parole.significato: Conditionally; provisionally; in anticipation of future need.
parole.testo: From Latin de (“on account of”) bene (“well”) esse (“to be”), "on account of well-being".

parole.significato: concerning assets remaining in an estate after the death or removal of the estate administrator; remaining assets as di…
parole.testo: From Latin, literally meaning "of goods not administered."

parole.significato: Taking the utterance in consideration, without having a particular referent in mind.
parole.testo: From Latin dē dictō (“of the word”).

parole.significato: From day to day.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dē diē ad diem.

parole.significato: From day to day.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dē diē in diem.

parole.significato: In actual use or existence, regardless of official or legal status.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin dē factō (literally “according to fact”), from dē (“according to”) + ablative of factum (“fact, deed, act”).

parole.significato: By right; in accordance with or as deemed by the statute of the law, particularly as opposed to actual practice.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin dē jūre (literally “according to law”).

parole.significato: A legal document inquiring about the sanity of an individual.
parole.testo: From Latin dē lūnāticō inquīrendō.

parole.significato: Concerning things that are so minor as to be negligible, trivial, or trifling. Often used to describe exemptions in gov…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin de minimīs, ablative of minimus (“smallest, least”); shortened form of the legal maxim de minimis non curat lex (literally “the law does not concern itself with trifling matters”).

parole.significato: The law does not concern itself with trifles; expression of the rule that the law will not remedy an injury that is min…
parole.testo: From Latin dē minimīs nōn cūrat lēx.

parole.significato: Anew, afresh, from the beginning; without consideration of previous instances, proceedings or determinations.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dē novō (adverb, literally “from the new”), from dē (“from”) + novō, ablative singular of novus (“new”).

parole.significato: From deep feelings of misery or despair.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin de profundis (“from the depths”), first words of Psalm 130.

parole.significato: Taking the thing of reference in consideration.
parole.testo: From Latin de (“about”) re (“thing”) (ablative of res).

parole.significato: reversal, undoing
parole.testo: From Latin dē-, from the preposition dē (“of”, “from”). For sense development, compare Old English æf-, which was a similar prefix.

parole.significato: A female deus ex machina; a providential intervention (in a story etc.) from a female force or character.
parole.testo: An alteration of Latin deus ex māchinā in English, substituting the masculine or epicene deus (“god”) with the feminine dea (“goddess”).

parole.significato: A designated minister of charity in the early Church (see Acts 6:1-6).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English deken, dekne, from Old English diacon, from Ecclesiastical Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διᾱ́κονος (diā́konos, “servant, minister”).

parole.significato: To admit to a performance without charge.
parole.testo: From dead + head.
