parole.significato: To change the status of (a forest) so that it is no longer legally regarded as forest land.
parole.testo: From Latin deafforestō. By surface analysis, de- + afforest.

parole.significato: To whiten.
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin dēalbātus, perfect passive participle of dēalbō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Likely doublet of daub.

parole.significato: To go out walking; to stroll.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin dēambulātus, perfect passive participle of dēambulō (“to walk, take a stroll”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + ambulō (“to walk”). The medical sense is likely a new denominal from deambulation or by translation from Romance languages such as F

parole.significato: A walking abroad; a promenading.
parole.testo: Latin deambulatio.

parole.significato: A covered place in which to walk; an ambulatory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin deambulātōrium.

parole.significato: To gild.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin deaurātus, perfect passive participle of deaurō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Gilded.
parole.testo: From Middle English deaurat, from Latin deaurātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The removal of gold from an organogold compound.
parole.testo: From de- + Latin aurum (“gold”) + -ation.

parole.significato: To rant as if drunk.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin dēbacchātus, perfect active participle of Latin dēbacchor, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: wild raving or debauchery, as if drunk.
parole.testo: Latin debacchatio.

parole.significato: To conquer (someone) in war; to subdue.
parole.testo: First attested in 1611; borrowed from Latin dēbellātus, perfect passive participle of dēbellō (“to subdue”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of debel.

parole.significato: Debellation, the annihilation of a sovereign state through complete destruction in a war.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin dēbellātiō.

parole.significato: The act of conquering or subjugation in war.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēbellātiō (“total defeat”), from dēbellō (“conquer, subjugate”).

parole.significato: A certificate that certifies an amount of money owed to someone; a certificate of indebtedness.
parole.testo: From earlier debentur, from Latin debentur (“they are owing”), supposedly the first word of such a document in early times. The ending was apparently influenced by words in -(t)ure.

parole.significato: A hereditary condition characterized by low intelligence in which one can understand words but not abstract concepts.
parole.testo: Compare Polish debilizm and Russian дебилизм (debilizm), ultimately from Latin debilis (“weak; disabled”). By surface analysis, debile + -ism.

parole.significato: To make feeble; to weaken.
parole.testo: From debilitatus, the past passive participle of Latin dēbilitō (“to weaken, debilitate”), from the adjective dēbilis (“weak”), itself from de- + habilis (“able”). Equivalent to Latin dēbilitō + -ate (verb-forming suffix; adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A debtor
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin debitor, equivalent to debit + -or. Doublet of debtor.

parole.significato: The action or process of lopping off the top of a tree.
parole.testo: From Latin dēcacūminātiō (“a lopping off the top of a tree”).

parole.significato: decaying
parole.testo: From Latin dēcadēscēns, from dēcadēscō (“to be decaying”), from dēcidō, dēcadō (“to decay, to fall away”). By surface analysis, decay + -escent.

parole.significato: One of a collection of 36 small constellations or zodiacal subdivisions that appear heliacally at intervals of 10 days…
parole.testo: From Late Latin decānus.

parole.significato: A group of parishes over which a dean presides; a deanery.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin decānātus, from Latin decānus. Equivalent to Latin decānus + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, here the concrete charge of it). Compare dean.

parole.significato: Of the side of the chancel, apse, altar or choir on which the dean's stall is placed (the right hand side to a person f…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin decānī (“of the dean”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Decapolis (a group of ten cities on the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire located in modern-da…
parole.testo: From Latin Decapolitānus, from Decapolis + -ītānus.

parole.significato: To withdraw.
parole.testo: From Latin dēcēdō (“to withdraw”).

parole.significato: A dead person.
parole.testo: From Latin decedens, present active participle of decedere (“to depart, die”).

parole.significato: Ten.
parole.testo: From Latin decem (“ten”).

parole.significato: Having ten points or teeth.
parole.testo: From New Latin decemdentātus. By surface analysis, decem- + dentate.

parole.significato: Cleft into ten parts
parole.testo: From Latin decemfidus, from decem (“ten”) + -fidus, from findere (“to split”).

parole.significato: Ten feet in length or height.
parole.testo: From Latin decem (“ten”) + pes (“foot”) + -al. By surface analysis, decem- + -pedal.

parole.significato: Having ten parts; decuple or tenfold.
parole.testo: From Latin decemplex.

parole.significato: The making of ten identical copies of something.
parole.testo: From New Latin decemplicātus. By surface analysis, decem- + plicate.

parole.significato: Any of two groups of 10 men selected in 451 and 450 B.C. to wield complete power over Rome and establish the laws of th…
parole.testo: From Latin decemvir.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the decemvirs of ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin decemvirālis. By surface analysis, decemvir + -al.

parole.significato: A group of ten people, especially (politics) a council of ten men sharing office or power and particularly (historical)…
parole.testo: From Latin decemvirātus, equivalent to decemvir + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

parole.significato: Of or related to the number ten, (particularly) as a base of numeration.
parole.testo: From Latin decenarius (“containing 10 items; related to the number 10”), from decem (“ten”) + -ārius (“-ary”) Doublet of decener.

parole.significato: Of or related to a tithing.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin decēnārius, from decēna (“a tithing”) + -ārius (“-ary”).

parole.significato: The quality of being decent; propriety.
parole.testo: From Latin decentia, from decens. Equivalent to decent + -cy. Compare French décence.

parole.significato: Synonym of decennial, of or related to a 10-year period.
parole.testo: From Latin decennālis (“decennial”), from decennis (“10-year”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjective-forming suffix), from decem (“ten”) + annus (“year”) + -is (suffix forming compound adjectives). Equivalent to decennium + -al.

parole.significato: The festival and religious rituals celebrating a Roman emperor's 10th year of rule.
parole.testo: From Latin decennālia, from decennium (“10-year period”) + -ālia (“-alia: forming the names of festivals”), from decennis (“10-year”) + -ium (“-ium: forming abstract nouns”). Equivalent to decennium + -alia.

parole.significato: Synonym of decennial, of or related to a ten-year period.
parole.testo: From Latin decennalis (“decennial”) + -ian, from decennium (“10-year period”) + -alis (“-al: forming adjectives”), from decem (“ten”) + annus (“year”).

parole.significato: Decennial: of or related to a ten-year period.
parole.testo: From Latin decennis (“decennial, of ten years”) + -ary.

parole.significato: Synonym of decade, a ten-year period.
parole.testo: From Latin decennialis, from decennium (“10-year period”) + -ālis, from decennis (“10-year”) + -ium (“-ium”, suffix forming abstract nouns), from decem (“ten”) + annus (“year”) + -is (suffix forming compound adjectives).

parole.significato: Synonym of decade: a ten year period.
parole.testo: From Latin decennium, from decennis (“10-year”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns), from deciēs (“ten times”) + annus (“year”) + -is (suffix forming compound adjectives). Equivalent to decennial + -ium.

parole.significato: Of or related to the number nineteen.
parole.testo: From Latin decennovālis, from decemnovem (“nineteen”) + -ālis (“-al”).

parole.significato: deceptive, tending to deceive.
parole.testo: From Latin deceptiosus.

parole.significato: deceptive
parole.testo: From Latin deceptorius, from decipere.

parole.significato: To pluck off, to pick out, extract or gather.
parole.testo: From Latin decerpere, from de- + carpere (“to pluck”).

parole.significato: contest for mastery; contention; strife
parole.testo: From Latin decertatio, from decertare, decertatum, from de- + certare (“to contend”).

parole.significato: departure; decrease
parole.testo: From Latin decessio, from decedere (“to depart”). See decease (noun).

parole.significato: A tenth part.
parole.testo: From Latin decimus (“tenth”).

parole.significato: A falling off or falling out: shedding.
parole.testo: Latin decidens (“falling off”).

parole.significato: A mucous membrane that lines the uterus and is shed during menstruation and modified during pregnancy.
parole.testo: From Latin dēciduus (“falling down or off”), from dēcidō (“fall down”).

parole.significato: Describing a part that falls off, or is shed, at a particular time or stage of development.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dēciduus (“falling down or off”), from dēcidō (“to fall down or off”) + -uus.

parole.significato: Any of the values in a series that divides the distribution of individuals in that series into ten groups of equal freq…
parole.testo: From Latin decilis, equivalent to dec- + -ile.

parole.significato: A tenth, (particularly) a tithe or tax of one-tenth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin decima (“a tenth”). Doublet of decima, decime, and dime.

parole.significato: A tenth, particularly
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin decima (“a tenth”), now particularly via Italian decima. Doublet of decim, decime, and dime.

parole.significato: Concerning numbers expressed in decimal or mathematical calculations performed using decimal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin, Medieval Latin decimalis, from Latin decimus, from decem (“ten”) + adjective suffix -alis.

parole.significato: To kill one-tenth of (a group), (historical, specifically) as a military punishment in the Roman army selected by lot,…
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1591, the noun in 1641; borrowed from Latin decimātus, perfect passive participle of decimō (“to kill one tenth; to tithe”) (see, from -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from decimus (“tenth”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). As a noun, via Latin dec

parole.significato: The killing or punishment of every tenth person, usually by lot.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin decimātiō, a punishment where every 10th man in a unit would be stoned to death by the men who were spared. Used by the Romans to keep order in their military. Compare septimation and vicesimation.

parole.significato: Synonym of tithing (a division of the hundreds of medieval England)
parole.testo: From Latin decima (“a tenth; a tithing”). By surface analysis, dec- + -ime. Doublet of decim, decima, and dime.

parole.significato: hallucination or deception.
parole.testo: From Latin decipiens, present participle of decipere. See deceive.

parole.significato: A rabbi who decides matters in Jewish religious law.
parole.testo: From Latin dēcīsor, from dēcīdō (past participial stem dēcīs-) + -or.

parole.significato: A declaimer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēclāmātor.

parole.significato: A private outward manifestation of intention which is directly aimed at bringing about a legal effect.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin dēclārātiō voluntātis, directly and indirectly from calques of it.

parole.significato: Bent downward or aside.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1820; borrowed from Latin dēclīnātus, perfect passive participle of dēclīnō (“to bend down”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Containing or involving a declination or refusal, as of submission to a charge or sentence.
parole.testo: From Latin declinatorius, from declinare: compare French déclinatoire.

parole.significato: Downward movement, fall.
parole.testo: From Middle English declinen, and ultimately Latin declīnō (“to bend, turn aside, deflect, inflect, decline”, from dē- (“down”) + clīnō (“to bend, to incline”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (English lean). The senses arrived from two separate pathways in Middle English: * The grammatical sense c

parole.significato: Descending gradually; sloping; downhill.
parole.testo: Latin declivus (“sloping down”), from de- (“down from”) + clivus (“slope”).

parole.significato: To make an infusion.
parole.testo: From Latin dēcoquō (“to boil down”), from dē- + coquō (“to cook”).

parole.significato: To behead.
parole.testo: First attested in 1599; borrowed from Latin dēcollātus, perfect passive participle of dēcollō (“to behead”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- (“of, from”) + collum (“neck”) + -ō.

parole.significato: Tapering to a blunt end.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin dēcollātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: The act of beheading someone.
parole.testo: From the Latin decollatus, from de + collum.

parole.significato: ornament
parole.testo: From Latin decoramentum. See decorate.

parole.significato: To furnish with decorations.
parole.testo: From Middle English decorat (“adorned”), from Latin decorātus, perfect passive participle of decorō (“to adorn, distinguish, honor”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from decus (“ornament, grace, dignity, honor”, decor- in compounds), akin to decor (“elegance, grace, beauty, ornament”), from decet

parole.significato: The act of adorning, embellishing, or honoring; ornamentation.
parole.testo: From Latin decoratio: compare French décoration. Morphologically decorate + -ion.

parole.significato: That serves to decorate
parole.testo: From Latin decorātus + -ive. Cognate with French décoratif.

parole.significato: A female decorator.
parole.testo: From Latin decoratrix, equivalent to decorate + -trix.

parole.significato: Marked by behaviour, manners, etc., regarded as proper, tasteful, and in accordance with accepted standards; becoming,…
parole.testo: From the following: * Latin decōrus (“becoming, fitting, proper, suitable”) + English -ous (suffix adjectives denoting presence of a quality in any degree, typically an abundance). Decōrus is derived from decor (“elegrance, grace; charm beauty”) + -us (suffix forming adjectives); and decor is from d

parole.significato: To peel or remove the bark, husk, or outer layer from something.
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1611, the adjective in 1872; borrowed from Latin dēcorticātus, perfect passive participle of dēcorticō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from dē- (“of, from”) + cortex (“bark”, oblique stem in cortic-) + -ō.

parole.significato: The removal of the surface layer, membrane, or fibrous cover of anything
parole.testo: From Latin dēcorticātiōn-, dēcorticātiō.

parole.significato: Appropriate social behavior.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin decōrum, neuter form of decōrus (“proper, decent”).

parole.significato: the official decree marking the legal end of a marriage, allowing the two people to remarry.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin dēcrētum absolūtum.

parole.significato: a decree issued on a first petition for divorce; it becomes absolute at some later date unless cause is shown why it sh…
parole.testo: See decree + Latin nisi (“unless”).

parole.significato: A small quantity removed or lost; one of a series of regular subtractions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin decrementum.

parole.significato: To roast (a salt or mineral) until it stops crackling in the fire.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēcrepitātus, perfect passive participle of dēcrepitō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin dē- + crepitō.

parole.significato: A student, or epert, of decretals or decrees.
parole.testo: From Latin decretista, from decretum. Compare French décrétiste. See decree (noun).

parole.significato: Pertaining to an authoritative decree or final judgement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin dēcrētōrius (“decisive”), from Latin dēcernō (“decide, determine”).

parole.significato: The removal of a crust (various senses).
parole.testo: Noun of action from the Latin dēcrustō (“to peel off [a crust or outer layer]”), from dē + crustō (“to crust”, from crusta, “crust”). Compare the Old French décrustation.

parole.significato: Large; chief; applied to an extraordinary billow, supposed by some to be every tenth in sequence.
parole.testo: From Latin decumānus (“of the tenth, and by metonymy, large”), from decem (“ten”).

parole.significato: Lying down; reclining on the ground.
parole.testo: From the present participle of Latin dēcumbō.

parole.significato: The fact of lying down, specifically of a person due to illness.
parole.testo: From Latin dēcumbo (“lie or fall down”).

parole.significato: An officer in charge of ten men in the ancient Roman army.
parole.testo: From Latin decuriō.

parole.significato: The position or office of a decurion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin decuriōnātus, from decuriō + -ātus. By surface analysis, decurion + -ate (making nouns denoting rank or office).

parole.significato: Of plant parts: extending downward, most often in the case of leaf blades that partly wrap or have wings around the ste…
parole.testo: From Latin decurrens — de (“down”) + curro (“to run”).

parole.significato: A flowing.
parole.testo: From Latin decursio, from decurrere. See decurrent.

parole.significato: To cut short; to truncate; to curtail.
parole.testo: From Latin decurtare, from de- + curtare.

parole.significato: Shortened, curtailed.
parole.testo: First attested around the beginning of the 16th century; borrowed from Latin dēcurtātus, perfect passive participle of dēcurtō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of decurt.

parole.significato: A group of ten men under the command of a decurion.
parole.testo: From Latin decuria, from decem (“ten”).

parole.significato: Crossed; intersected; resembling a letter X.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1825, the verb in 1658. Borrowed from Latin decussātus, perfect passive participle of decussō (“to divide crosswise, arrange crosswise or mark with a cross”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from decussis (“a coin worth ten asse

parole.significato: A crossing or intersection of lines etc. so as to form an X-shape.
parole.testo: From Latin decussationem, from decussare.

parole.significato: An instrument for depressing the dura after trephining.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: To bring to shame; to disgrace.
parole.testo: From Latin dedecoratus, past participle of dedecorare (“to disgrace”).

parole.significato: Disgrace; dishonour.
parole.testo: Latin dedecoratio.

parole.significato: disgraceful; unbecoming
parole.testo: From Latin dedecorus. See decorous.

parole.significato: The difference between the radius of the pitch circle of a gear and its root circle.
parole.testo: From Latin dedere.

parole.significato: To set apart for a deity or for religious purposes; consecrate.
parole.testo: From Middle English dedicaten (“to dedicate”), from dedicat(e) (“dedicated”, also used as the past participle of dedicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), from Latin dēdicātus, the perfect passive participle of dēdicō (“to dedicate, proclaim”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Dedicated; set apart; devoted; consecrated.
parole.testo: from Middle English dedicat(e) (“dedicated”, also used as the past participle of dedicaten), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more. The nouns is derived through substantivization from Latin dēdicātus, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: One who dedicates.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin dedicator, either directly to English from Latin or by way of a Romance cognate.

parole.significato: A writ to commission private persons to do some act in place of a judge, such as to examine a witness, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin dedimus (“we gave”), from do (“to give”). So called because the writ began "Dedimus potestatem […] ".

parole.significato: In medieval Europe, an act of ritualized submission and request for mercy, performed before a monarch or other feudal l…
parole.testo: From Latin dēditiō.

parole.significato: yielding, surrender.
parole.testo: From Latin deditio, from dedere (“to give away, surrender”), from de- + dare (“to give”).

parole.significato: A slicing wound made by a sharp instrument grazing the surface.
parole.testo: From Latin dēdolāre (“to hew away”).

parole.significato: Feeling no compunction; apathetic.
parole.testo: From Latin dedolens, present participle of dedolere (“to give over grieving”); de- + dolere (“to grieve”).

parole.significato: To reach (a conclusion) by applying rules of logic or other forms of reasoning to given premises or known facts.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English deducen (“to demonstrate, prove, show; to argue, infer; to bring, lead; to turn (something) to a use; to deduct”), borrowed from Latin dēdūcere, the present active infinitive of dēdūcō (“to lead or bring out or away; to accompany, conduct, escort; (figuratively) to derive, d

parole.significato: To take one thing from another; remove from; make smaller or less by some amount.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin deductus, perfect passive participle of verb deducere (“lead from”).

parole.significato: One who deducts something, particularly one who deducts tax from wages or deducts certain expenditures from payment of…
parole.testo: From deduct + -or under influence from Latin dēductor.

parole.significato: The formal patron of a Roman colony.
parole.testo: From Latin dēductor (“guide; founder”). See deduce.

parole.significato: Placed after a catalogue abbreviation to indicate that this particular work does not appear in it.
parole.testo: From Latin dēsum (“to be missing”).

parole.significato: To misappropriate funds; to embezzle.
parole.testo: First attested in the 1530s, in the sense “to lop off”; borrowed from Medieval Latin dēfalcātus, perfect passive participle of dēfalcō (“to cut or lop off”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin dē (“off”) + falx (“sickle, scythe, pruning hook”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of cancelling part of a claim by deducting a smaller claim which the claimant owes to the defendant.
parole.testo: Late 15th century, from Medieval Latin dēfalcātiōnem, accusative singular of dēfalcātiō (literally “cutting off, lopping off with a sickle”), nominalization of dēfalcō, from Latin dē (“off”) + falx (“sickle, scythe, pruning hook”), from which also English falcate (“sickle-shaped”). By surface analys

parole.significato: Easily tired or wearied; capable of being fatigued.
parole.testo: From Latin defatigatus, past participle of defatigare (“to tire or weary”).

parole.significato: Weary, fatigued, exhausted.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested circa 1480, in Middle english; borrowed from Latin dēfatīgātus, perfect passive participle of dēfatīgō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Fatigue; weariness.
parole.testo: Latin defatigatio.

parole.significato: To excrete feces from one's bowels.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēfaecātus, the perfect passive participle of dēfaecō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). See also faeces; cognate with French déféquer.

parole.significato: The act or process of voiding feces from the bowels.
parole.testo: 17th century, borrowed from Late Latin dēfaecātiō.

parole.significato: A fault or malfunction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin defectus (“a failure, lack”), from deficere (“to fail, lack, literally 'undo'”), from past participle defectus, from de- (“of, from”) + facere (“to do”).

parole.significato: An act or incidence of defecting.
parole.testo: From Latin dēfectiō (stem dēfectiōn-).

parole.significato: One who defects.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēfector.

parole.significato: The process of polluting or making filthy; pollution.
parole.testo: From Latin defoedatio, from Late Latin defoedare (“to defile”), from de- with foedare, present tense verb of foedo, from foedus (“foul”).

parole.significato: To eject or throw (someone or something) from or through a window.
parole.testo: First attested in 1904; back-formation from defenestration on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), from New Latin dē- (“out”) + fenestra (“window”) + -ātiō (“-ation”).

parole.significato: The act of throwing something or especially someone out of a window, especially lethally.
parole.testo: From New Latin defenestratio, from dē (“from; out”) + fenestra (“window”) + -atio (suffix indicating an action or process); compare Middle French défenestrer (modern French défenestrer), défenestration, Italian defenestrazione and German Fenstersturz. The verb defenestrate was formed later.

parole.significato: Serving to protect or defend; defensive
parole.testo: From Latin defensare, defensatum (“to defend diligently”), intensive of defendere. See defend.

parole.significato: one who defends; a defender
parole.testo: From Latin dēfēnsor.

parole.significato: Tending to defend; defensive.
parole.testo: From Latin defensorius.

parole.significato: Respectful and considerate; showing deference.
parole.testo: From deference (or its Latin type *dēferentia) + -al; compare essence, essential; prudence, prudential, etc. Coined by Scottish novelist, poet and playwright Walter Scott.

parole.significato: To experience an abatement or resolution of fever.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēfervēscere, from dē- (prefix denoting removal, reversal, or undoing) + fervēscō (“to grow hot, to begin to boil”), from ferveō (“to be hot; to boil; to burn; to be agitated or inflamed”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil; to brew”).

parole.significato: The departure or subsiding of a fever.
parole.testo: From Latin defervescere (“to grow cool”).

parole.significato: Deficiency.
parole.testo: From Late Latin dēficientia.

parole.significato: Lacking something essential; often construed with in.
parole.testo: From Latin deficiens, present participle of deficere (“to lack, fail, be wanting”); see defect.

parole.significato: The separation of a child from its parents.
parole.testo: From Latin de- + filius (“son”).

parole.significato: The term (word or phrase) defined in a definition (whether inside a sentence, as a dictionary entry, or otherwise).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēfīniendum, gerund of dēfīniō.

parole.significato: The word or phrase that defines the definiendum in a definition.
parole.testo: From Latin, substantive use of dēfīniēns (“[a] defining”), present active participle of dēfīniō.

parole.significato: Having distinct limits.
parole.testo: From Latin dēfīnītus, past participle of dēfīniō, whence also English define.

parole.significato: definiteness
parole.testo: From de- + finitude or de- + Latin fin(is) + -itude, ultimately from Renaissance Latin finitūdō (“signifying a noun of state”), from fīnis (“end, limit”) + -tūdō.

parole.significato: To fix, fasten, or establish.
parole.testo: From Latin defixus, past participle of defigere (“to fix”), from de- + figere (“to fix”).

parole.significato: To burn with intense light and heat.
parole.testo: First attested in 1727; borrowed from Latin dēflagrātus, perfect passive participle of Latin dēflagrō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + flagrō (“to burn”).

parole.significato: The act of deflagrating; an intense fire; a conflagration or explosion. Specifically, combustion that spreads subsonica…
parole.testo: From Latin dēflagrātiō, from dēflagrāre.

parole.significato: To make (something) deviate from its original path or position.
parole.testo: From Latin deflecto, from de- (“away”) + flecto (“to bend”).

parole.significato: The act of deflecting or something deflected.
parole.testo: From Latin dēflexiō, from dēflectere (“to deflect”; participle stem dēflex-) + -iō (suffix forming abstract nouns). The non-etymological spelling deflection is taken from the present stem dēflect-, associated with collection, dissection, etc. By surface analysis, deflect + -ion.

parole.significato: A bending or turning aside; deflection.
parole.testo: From Latin deflectere, deflexum. See deflect.

parole.significato: Flowing down; falling off.
parole.testo: From Latin defluus, from defluere (“to flow down”), from de- + fluere (“to flow”).

parole.significato: downward flow
parole.testo: From Latin defluxus, from defluere, defluxum.

parole.significato: A flowing down; a running down.
parole.testo: From Latin defluxio.

parole.significato: The act of defrauding; a taking by fraud.
parole.testo: From Latin defraudatio, from defraudo (“cheat, defraud, overreach”).

parole.significato: A reduction of must in Ancient Roman cuisine, made by boiling down grape juice or must in large kettles until reduced t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēfrutum.

parole.significato: No longer in use or active, nor expected to be again.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēfunctus, past participle of dēfungor (“to finish, discharge”).

parole.significato: Death.
parole.testo: from Latin dēfūnctiō (“execution, performance, death”), from dēfungor (“to finish, perform, die”).

parole.significato: funereal or deathly
parole.testo: From Latin defunctivus, from dēfūnctiō (“execution, performance, death”), from dēfungor (“to finish, perform, die”).

parole.significato: To defile, to pollute.
parole.testo: From Late Latin defoedare.

parole.significato: To degenerate.
parole.testo: From Latin dēgenerāre.

parole.significato: Having deteriorated, degraded or fallen from normal, coherent, balanced and desirable to undesirable and typically abno…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dēgenerātus. See -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: Degenerate; base.
parole.testo: From Latin degener, + -ous. See degenerate.

parole.significato: To be swallowed
parole.testo: Latin degluttiatur

parole.significato: To loosen or separate by dissolving the glue which unites; to unglue.
parole.testo: First attested in 1609; borrowed from Latin dēglūtinātus, perfect passive participle of dēglūtinō (“to unglue”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + glūtinō (“to glue”), from gluten (“glue”) + -ō.

parole.significato: Descent, the act of descending.
parole.testo: From Latin degressio, from degressus + -io (“forming abstract nouns from verbs”), past perfect participle of degredi (“to descend by steps”), from de- (“down”) + gradi (“to step, walk, go”).

parole.significato: To taste or eat.
parole.testo: First attested in 1599; borrowed from Latin dēgustātus, perfect passive participle of dēgustō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of degust.

parole.significato: To burst or split open at definite places, discharging seeds, pollen or similar content.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dehīscō (“to gape, open”), from hiō (“to be open”); related to hiatus.

parole.significato: Opening of an organ by its own means (such as an anther or a seed pod) to release its contents.
parole.testo: From New Latin dehiscentia (in Linnaeus), from Latin dehiscentem, present participle of dehiscō. By surface analysis, dehisce + -ence.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to dehiscence, i.e., a rupture, as with a surgical wound opening up, often with a flow of serous fluid.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dehīscentem, present participle of dehīscō (“to divide, split open, gape”), from hīscō (“to yawn, gape”).

parole.significato: To disparage.
parole.testo: First attested in 1663; borrowed from Latin dēhonestātus, perfect passive participle of dēhonestō (“to dishonour”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: An act of dishonouring or disgracing.
parole.testo: Latin dehonestatio.

parole.significato: To dissuade.
parole.testo: From Latin dehortārī, present active infinitive of dēhortor (“to deter, dissuade”), from dē- (prefix indicating reversal or undoing) + hortor (“to encourage, exhort, urge”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to yearn for”)).

parole.significato: Dissuasion.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Advice against something; dissuasion.
parole.testo: From Latin dehortatio (“dissuasion”).

parole.significato: designed to dehort (dissuade); dissuasive
parole.testo: Latin dehortatorius.

parole.significato: by the Grace of God.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Deī grātiā (“by the grace of God”).

parole.significato: The killing of a deity; godslaughter.
parole.testo: Merged from Medieval Latin deicīdium and Medieval Latin deicīda.

parole.significato: To deify.
parole.testo: Back-formation from deification. For its use by non-native speakers, compare Galician, Portuguese, and Spanish deificar and Italian deificare, from Latin deificō.

parole.significato: Godlike.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin deifōrmis (literally “godlike”).

parole.significato: To disintegrate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēintegrātus, perfect passive participle of dēintegrō (“to impair, diminish, lessen”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Giving birth to a god or goddess.
parole.testo: From Latin deus (“god”) + -parous, calque from Ancient Greek Θεοτόκος (Theotókos, “birth-giver of God”), a traditional title of the Virgin Mary.

parole.significato: any liquid or solid waste matter that is emanated, shed or discharged from the body. Dejecta include urine, faeces, spu…
parole.testo: From Latin dejecta (“things which have been cast away”), neuter plural of dejectus, past participle of dejicio (“to cast away”).

parole.significato: Having power, or tending, to cast down.
parole.testo: Latin dejector (“a dejecter”).

parole.significato: The act of swearing solemnly.
parole.testo: Latin deieratio.

parole.significato: An act of tearing into pieces.
parole.testo: From Latin delacerare, delaceratum (“to tear in pieces”). See lacerate.

parole.significato: The act of weaning.
parole.testo: From de- + Latin lactāre (“to suck milk”), lactātiō (see lactation), from lac (“milk”).

parole.significato: To pass down by inheritance; to lapse.
parole.testo: Latin dēlābor

parole.significato: To carry; to convey.
parole.testo: From Latin delātus, perfect passive participle of deferō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of defer (Etymology 2). See also infer, collate and confer, relate and refer, as well as prelate and prefer among others.

parole.significato: Conveyance.
parole.testo: From Latin dēlātiō.

parole.significato: A grammatical case of nouns used, chiefly in Hungarian, to express movement from the surface of something (like "moved…
parole.testo: From the Latin deferre (“to bear or bring away or down”).

parole.significato: An accuser; an informer.
parole.testo: From Middle English delatoures pl, from Latin dēlātor.

parole.significato: To delete.
parole.testo: From Latin dēlē, second person singular imperative of dēleo (“delete”). Alternatively, a clipping of deleatur.

parole.significato: dele (“mark signifying deletion”)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēleātur (“may it be deleted; may it be destroyed”).

parole.significato: To delight.
parole.testo: From Latin dēlectāre. Compare Middle English delect (“to ease the pain of (an ulcer)”). Doublet of delight.

parole.significato: To delight, to charm, to bring pleasure to.
parole.testo: First attested in 1647; borrowed from Latin dēlectātus, perfect passive participle of dēlectō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A feeling of extreme pleasure or satisfaction.
parole.testo: From Latin dēlectiō. By surface analysis, delect + -ion.

parole.significato: An elementary reader (collection of passages) for learners of a language
parole.testo: From Latin delectus (“selection”), from deligo (“to select”).

parole.significato: To commit tasks and responsibilities to others, especially subordinates.
parole.testo: From the above noun by metanalysis or directly borrowed from Latin dēlēgātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: An act of delegating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēlēgātiō, dēlēgātiōnis, from dēlēgō: compare French délégation.

parole.significato: Holding a delegated position.
parole.testo: Latin delegatorius (“pertaining to an assignment”).

parole.significato: Things to be deleted or removed.
parole.testo: From Latin dēlenda.

parole.significato: To remove, get rid of or erase, especially written or printed material, or data on a computer or other device.
parole.testo: From Latin dēlētus, past participle of dēlēre (“destroy, blot out, efface”), from dēlēvī, originally perf. tense of dēlinere (“to daub, erase by smudging”), from dē- (“from, away”) + linere (“to smear, wipe”). Original sense first appears c. 1495. In common use for ordering the absence of features o

parole.significato: destroyer.
parole.testo: From New Latin dēlētērius, from Ancient Greek δηλητήρῐος (dēlētḗrĭos). Doublet of deleterious.

parole.significato: An item that has been or will be deleted.
parole.testo: From Latin dēlētiōnem (“destruction, effacement”), from the past-participle stem of dēlēre (“to blot out, destroy, efface”). Equivalent to delete + -ion.

parole.significato: To taste; to take a sip of.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; Borrowed from Latin dēlibātus, perfect passive participle of dēlibō (“to take away from, to taste from”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + libō (“to taste; to consecrate a liquid”).

parole.significato: Act of tasting; a slight trial.
parole.testo: Latin delibatio: compare French délibation.

parole.significato: Done on purpose; intentional.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English deliberat(e), borrowed from Latin dēlīberātus, perfect passive participle of dēlīberō (“to consider, weigh well”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + *līberō / lībrō (“to weigh”)), from *libera / libra (“a balance”); see libr

parole.significato: That which can be deleted or erased.
parole.testo: From Latin dēlēbilis. See also -ible.

parole.significato: To strip off the bark; to peel.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin dēlibrātus, perfect passive participle of dēlibrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The quality of being delicate.
parole.testo: From Middle English delicacie, from Middle English delicat, from Latin delicatus. Equivalent to delic(ate) + -acy.

parole.significato: Easily damaged or requiring careful handling.
parole.testo: From Middle English delicat, from Latin dēlicātus (“giving pleasure, delightful, soft, luxurious, delicate, (in Medieval Latin also) fine, slender”), from dēlicia + -ātus (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), usually in plural dēliciae (“pleasure, delight, luxury”), from dēliciō (“to allure, entice

parole.significato: A wrongful act, analogous to a tort in common law.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēlīctum (“fault”), neuter of dēlīctus, past participle of delinquo (“to fail; to be lacking”), from dē- + linquō (“to leave, quit, forsake, depart from”).

parole.significato: transgressing morality
parole.testo: From Latin dēlīctum (“crime”), from neuter of dēlīctus, past participle of delinquo (“to be lacking; to fail; to transgress”).

parole.significato: To bind up; to bandage.
parole.testo: First attested in 1530; borrowed from Latin dēligātus, perfect passive participle of dēligō (“to bind up”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A form of polymorphism in the repeat units of DNA
parole.testo: From Latin dēligere (“to choose, select, pick out”) + -o- (“connecting vowel”) + type.

parole.significato: The identification and characterisation of deligotypes
parole.testo: From Latin dēligere (“to choose, select, pick out”) + -o- (“connecting vowel”) + typing.

parole.significato: To sketch out, draw or trace an outline.
parole.testo: First attested in 1559; borrowed from Latin dēlīneātus, perfect passive participle of dēlīneo (“to sketch out, to delineate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from dē- + līnea (“line”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Regular participial usage of the adjective up unti

parole.significato: A smearing.
parole.testo: From Latin delinere (“to smear”). See liniment.

parole.significato: Misconduct.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin dēlinquentia, derived from Latin dēlinquēns, present participle of dēlinquō (“to transgress, err”). By surface analysis, delinquent + -cy

parole.significato: to relinquish
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēlinquō (“to fail, err”) with the addition of -ish. Sense 1 was influenced by the similar verb relinquish.

parole.significato: To cause (something) to melt away; to consume, to dissolve.
parole.testo: First attested in 1617; borrowed from Latin dēliquātus, perfect passive participle of dēliquō (“to clarify, skim a liquid”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To melt by absorbing water and disappearing.
parole.testo: From Latin dēliquēscō, from dē- + liquēscō (“to liquefy”).

parole.significato: Seeming to melt away.
parole.testo: Latin deliquescens, present participle of deliquesco; de + liquesco (“to melt”): compare French déliquescent. By surface analysis, deliquesce + -ent

parole.significato: Liquefaction through absorption of moisture from the air.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin deliquium, from Latin delinquere (“to lack, to fail”).

parole.significato: A wandering of the mind; a crazy fancy.
parole.testo: From Latin deliramentum, from delirare. See delirium.

parole.significato: Delirious.
parole.testo: From Latin dēlīrantis, present participle of dēlīrō. See delirium.

parole.significato: To act, speak or reason in a manner thought insane, to be affected or characterized by delirium; to rave.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin dēlīrātus, perfect passive participle of dēlīrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French délirer.

parole.significato: aberration of the mind; delirium
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dēlīrātio.

parole.significato: Producing, or tending to produce, delirium.
parole.testo: From delirium + Latin faciens, facientis, present participle of facere (“to make”).

parole.significato: Being in the state of delirium.
parole.testo: From delirium + -ous; see also Latin delirus (“silly, doting, crazy”).

parole.significato: A temporary mental state with a sudden onset, usually reversible, including symptoms of confusion, inability to concent…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēlīrium (“derangement, madness”).

parole.significato: A severe, potentially life-threatening form of alcohol withdrawal characterized by the abrupt onset of global confusion…
parole.testo: From Latin dēlīrium tremēns (literally “trembling madness”), coined by Thomas Sutton in 1813.

parole.significato: Lying uncovered inside; latent.
parole.testo: From Latin delitescens, present participle of delitescere (“to hide away”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a dauphin
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin delphīnālis, from delphīnus + -ālis.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of dolphins.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin delphīnus.

parole.significato: Relating to dolphins; delphine.
parole.testo: From Latin delphīnus (“dolphin”), from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís, “dolphin”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A temple dedicated to Apollo Delphinios.
parole.testo: From Latin delphīnus (“dolphin”) + -ion, from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís, “dolphin”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or resembling, the dolphin
parole.testo: From Latin delphinus (“a dolphin”) + -oid.

parole.significato: The formation of a delta or deltas.
parole.testo: From delta + Latin facere (“to make”).

parole.significato: The triangular space under the beak of many brachiopod shells.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin deltidium. By surface analysis, delta + -idium.

parole.significato: The deltoid muscle, a triangular muscle on the human shoulder.
parole.testo: From Latin deltoideus, which was in turn from Ancient Greek adjective δελτοειδής (deltoeidḗs). See also: δέλτα (délta), the fourth letter of the Greek alphabet.

parole.significato: A temple or shrine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēlūbrum.

parole.significato: To deceive into believing something which is false; to lead into error; to dupe.
parole.testo: From Middle English deluden, borrowed from Latin dēlūdō (“mock, deceive”), from de + lūdō (“to make sport of, to mock”). See ludicrous.

parole.significato: An adamant belief in a falsehood despite incontestable evidence.
parole.testo: From Latin dēlūsiō.

parole.significato: Madness; dementia.
parole.testo: From Latin dēmentia, from dēmens (“out of one's mind”).

parole.significato: Demented.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dement, from Latin demens; verb from Vulgar Latin dementare (“to deceive; to drive mad”), also from Latin dēmēns (“demented, mad”).

parole.significato: To dement, to make crazy.
parole.testo: First attested in 1628; borrowed from Latin dēmentātus, perfect passive participle of dēmentō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of depriving of reason; madness.
parole.testo: From Latin dēmentātiō. By surface analysis, dement + -ation.

parole.significato: Insane; mentally ill.
parole.testo: Past participle of dement + -ed, from Latin dēmentāre.

parole.significato: A progressive decline in cognitive function due to damage or disease in the brain beyond what might be expected from no…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēmentia.

parole.significato: A progressive, usually fatal condition that occurs in some hemodialysis patients
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Childhood disintegrative disorder.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: A form of encephalopathy seen in long-term dialysis patients.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A neurodegenerative disease or dementia associated with repeated concussions, as in boxers.
parole.testo: From Latin dementia pugilistica (“boxer's madness”).

parole.significato: To plunge down into; to sink; to immerse.
parole.testo: Latin demergo (“to submerge”).

parole.significato: To deserve.
parole.testo: From Latin dēmerit-, the past partipicial stem of dēmereō. By surface analysis, de- + merit.

parole.significato: That lives near the bottom of a body of water.
parole.testo: From Latin demersus, past participle of dēmergō (“to sink”); compare demersed.

parole.significato: To immerse, to submerge (something).
parole.testo: From Latin dēmersus, past participle of dēmergere. See merge.

parole.significato: Situated or growing or constantly under water.
parole.testo: From Latin dēmersus, past participle of dēmergere. Botanical sense coined by botanist Thomas Martyn in the 1790s.

parole.significato: The act of plunging into a fluid; a drowning.
parole.testo: Latin demersio.

parole.significato: A half-god or hero; the offspring of a deity and a mortal.
parole.testo: From demi- + god. Calque of the Latin semideus (“half-god”), which is probably a coining by the Roman poet Ovid for less important gods such as dryads.

parole.significato: To emigrate.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin dēmīgrātus, perfect passive participle of dēmīgrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, de- + migrate.

parole.significato: emigration
parole.testo: From Latin demigratio.

parole.significato: Humble, lowly; abject.
parole.testo: From Latin dēmissus, past participle of dēmittō (“demit”).

parole.significato: To let fall; to depress; to yield.
parole.testo: From Latin dēmittō (“send or bring down, let fall”).

parole.significato: An evil supernatural being.
parole.testo: From Middle English demon, a borrowing from Medieval Latin dēmōn, daemōn (“lar, familiar spirit, guardian spirit”), from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn, “dispenser, god, protective spirit”). Displaced native Old English sċucca (“evil spirit”) and Old English þyrs (“ogre or monster”). Doublet of daimon

parole.significato: Pertaining to demons or evil spirits; demoniac.
parole.testo: From Latin daemonicus, from Ancient Greek δαιμονικός (daimonikós, “possessed by a demon, sent by a demon”), from δαίμων (daímōn), equivalent to demon + -ic. Doublet of daimonic.

parole.significato: To turn into a demon.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin daemonizō, from daemon + -izō. Compare Ancient Greek δαιμονίζομαι (daimonízomai, “to be possessed by a demon”), from δαίμων (daímōn, “demon”). By surface analysis, demon + -ize.

parole.significato: Demon.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Worship of demons.
parole.testo: From Latin daemonolatria. By surface analysis, demono- + -latry.

parole.significato: An unnatural fear of devils and Hell.
parole.testo: From Latin daemonomania; equivalent to demono- + -mania.

parole.significato: A participant in a demonstration.
parole.testo: From Latin dēmonstrant- (stem of dēmonstrāns).

parole.significato: To show how to use (something).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēmonstrātus, the perfect passive participle of dēmonstrō (“to show, point at”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French démontrer.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or characteristic of Demosthenes, a celebrated Athenian orator (384-322, B.C.), especially famous for his…
parole.testo: From Latin Demosthenicus, from Demosthenes, from Ancient Greek Δημοσθένης (Dēmosthénēs, “a celebrated orator”). The name means "strong with the people", from δῆμος (dêmos, “the people”) + σθένος (sthénos, “strength”).

parole.significato: To soothe, assuage, pacify or soften.
parole.testo: From Latin dēmulceō (“to soothe”); dē- + mulceō (“to stroke”).

parole.significato: Soothing or softening.
parole.testo: From Latin dēmulcēns, present active participle of dēmulceō (“to stroke caressingly; to soften, soothe, allure”), from dē- (“from; of”) + mulceō (“to move or touch gently or lightly, to stroke; to make pleasant or sweet; to soften, soothe, alleviate, relieve”).

parole.significato: A printing paper size, 17½ inches by 22½ inches.
parole.testo: * (scholarship): From Latin demi-socii (“half-fellows”); see socius.

parole.significato: A place of immoral behavior, often of a sexual type.
parole.testo: Unclear, but probably inspired by the “den of thieves” in the KJV Bible, which is a calque of Latin spēlunca latrōnum.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the number 10.
parole.testo: From Latin dēnārius (“of the number ten”), from dēnī (“ten each”), from decem (“ten”) + -an.

parole.significato: A small silver coin issued both during the Roman Republic and during the Roman Empire, equal to 10 asses or 4 sesterces…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēnārius. Doublet of denar, denier, dinar, diner, dinero, and dinheiro.

parole.significato: An ancient coin, the denarius.
parole.testo: From Middle English denarie, from the Latin dēnārius, used elliptically for dēnārius nummus (“denary coin, coin containing ten asses”). Piecewise doublet of etymology 2 below. Doublet of dinar, denar, and denier.

parole.significato: Containing ten parts.
parole.testo: First attested in 1577; from the Latin dēnārius (“containing ten”), from dēnī (“ten each, ten at a time”) + -ārius (whence the English suffix -ary).

parole.significato: An arborescent or dendritic agate.
parole.testo: From Latin dendrachates, from Ancient Greek δένδρον (déndron, “tree”) + ἀχάτης (akhátēs, “agate”). By surface analysis, dendr- + achate.

parole.significato: To deny, refuse or contradict.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēnegātus, perfect passive participle of dēnegō (“to deny”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + negō (“to say no”). Doublet of deny.

parole.significato: To criticize so as to besmirch; traduce, disparage or defame.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin dēnigrātus, the perfect passive participle of dēnigrō (“to blacken”) [see -ate (verb-forming suffix)], from dē- (“of; from”) + nigrō (“to blacken”) [from niger (“black”)]. Cognate with Middle English denigart(e) (“darkened, discolored”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the process of melting snow.
parole.testo: From Latin niveus (“snowy”).

parole.significato: To name; to designate.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₁nómn̥ Inherited from Middle English denominat(e) (“named, called”), borrowed from Latin dēnōminātus, perfect passive participle of dēnōminō, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3). By surface analysis, de- + nominate.

parole.significato: Being a name.
parole.testo: From Late Latin dēnōminātīvus, a calque of Ancient Greek παρώνυμος (parṓnumos, “derivative”). It originally had the meaning “derived”, but in its grammatical sense, it has developed the meaning “from a noun”, perhaps a reinterpretation of the Latin morphemes that it consists of: the preposition dē (

parole.significato: The number or expression written below the line in a fraction (such as 2 in ½).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēnōminātor (“that which names”).

parole.significato: To mark off; to denote.
parole.testo: First attested in 1597; either borrowed from Latin dēnotātus, perfect passive participle dēnotō (“to mark, observe”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)) or a back-formation from denotation. Doublet of denote.

parole.significato: The act of denoting, or something (such as a symbol) that denotes
parole.testo: From Late Latin dēnotātiō, from Latin dēnotāre (“to denote, mark out”) + -tiō (suffix forming nouns of action), from dē- (“completely”) + notāre (“to mark”); equivalent to denote + -ation.

parole.significato: Something that is denoted; a referent.
parole.testo: From Latin denotatum.

parole.significato: A toothlike process projecting from the anterior end of the centrum of the axis vertebra on which the atlas vertebra ro…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēns (“a tooth”). Doublet of dent and tooth.

parole.significato: A rare dental malformation where there is an infolding of enamel into dentine, producing a "tooth within a tooth".
parole.testo: From Latin dens invaginatus.

parole.significato: Having teeth or toothlike projections; serrated, toothed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dentātus, from dēns (“tooth”, oblique stem in dēnt-) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Synonym of dento-.
parole.testo: Combining form of Latin dens (“tooth”).

parole.significato: A small tooth.
parole.testo: From Latin denticulus, from dens (“tooth”). Doublet of denticule.

parole.significato: Finely dentate, as a leaf edge; bearing many small toothlike structures.
parole.testo: First attested in 1661; borrowed from Latin denticulātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Bearing teeth or tooth-like structures.
parole.testo: From Latin dens, dentis (“tooth”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Having the shape or structure of a tooth.
parole.testo: Latin dens (“tooth”) + -form

parole.significato: Toothpaste or any other substance, such as a powder or liquid, for cleaning the teeth.
parole.testo: From Middle English dentifricie, from Latin dentifricium (“powder for rubbing the teeth”), from dens (“tooth”) + fricāre (“to rub”). Compare French dentifrice.

parole.significato: Bearing teeth or tooth-like structures; of or pertaining to tissue from which teeth develop.
parole.testo: From Latin dentis (“genitive singular of dens”) + -gerous (“bearing”).

parole.significato: A wash for cleaning the teeth.
parole.testo: From Latin dens, dentis (“tooth”) + lavare (“to wash”). Originally a trademark.

parole.significato: A small tooth, like that of a saw.
parole.testo: From Latin dentillus, for Latin denticulus. See dentil.

parole.significato: An instrument which, placed against the teeth, conveys sound to the auditory nerve; an audiphone.
parole.testo: From Latin dens, dentis (“tooth”) + Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”).

parole.significato: A dentirostral bird
parole.testo: From denti- + Latin rostrum (“beak”).

parole.significato: A toothpick.
parole.testo: From Latin dentiscalpium (“toothpick”), from dens (“tooth”) + scalpere (“to scrape”).

parole.significato: The set of natural teeth of an individual.
parole.testo: From Latin dentītiō (“teething, dentition”).

parole.significato: To teethe.
parole.testo: From Latin dens, dentis (“tooth”).

parole.significato: tooth or teeth
parole.testo: Combining form of Latin dens (tooth) with -o-, after the pattern of Greek combining words.

parole.significato: Shaped like a tooth.
parole.testo: From Latin dens, dentis (“tooth”) + -oid.

parole.significato: Synonym of denticulated.
parole.testo: From Latin dens (tooth), -ule, -ate.

parole.significato: To denude.
parole.testo: From Latin denudatus, past participle of denudare. See denude.

parole.significato: To condemn openly.
parole.testo: First attested in 1593; borrowed from Latin dēnūntiātus, perfect passive participle of dēnūntiō (“to declare”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of denounce.

parole.significato: denunciatory
parole.testo: Latin denuntiativus. By surface analysis, denunciate + -ive.

parole.significato: Someone who denounces, threatens or accuses.
parole.testo: From Latin denuntiator. denunciate + -or.

parole.significato: God willing
parole.testo: From Latin Deō volente, an absolute ablative. See James 4:15: “If it is the Lord’s will, we will live and do this or that.” - a critique of those who are over-confident in their ability to determine their own future.

parole.significato: A gift or offering to, or from, God.
parole.testo: From Latin Deo (“to God”) (from Deus (“God”)) + datum (“thing given”).

parole.significato: Any agent acting to eliminate, reduce, mask, or control odor.
parole.testo: From Latin de- + odorans, present participle of odorare (“to smell”), from odor (“a smell”); see odor. By surface analysis, de- + odor + -ant.

parole.significato: Synonym of theonym.
parole.testo: From Latin deus (“god”) + -onym.

parole.significato: disorder; dissoluteness
parole.testo: Latin deordinatio (“depraved morality”).

parole.significato: In a downwards direction.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin deorsum (“downwards”)

parole.significato: Consuming.
parole.testo: From Latin dēpāscēre + -ent.

parole.significato: To withdraw, or cause to withdraw, from one's country; to banish or expatriate.
parole.testo: From de- + Latin patria (“fatherland”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix) or an altered borrowing from Medieval Latin dispatriō.

parole.significato: Having stunted growth
parole.testo: From Middle English depauperat (“impoverished”), from Medieval Latin depauperātus (“impoverished”), past participle of depauperō (“to impoverish”), itself from Latin de- + pauperō (“to impoverish”), from pauper (“poor”). Equivalent to de- + pauper + -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Cognate with Ital

parole.significato: robbery or embezzlement.
parole.testo: From Latin depeculari, past participle depeculatus (“to rob”). See peculate.

parole.significato: Things lost or destroyed.
parole.testo: Late Latin deperditum, from Latin deperditus, past participle of deperdere.

parole.significato: To render a representation of something, using words, sounds, images, or other means.
parole.testo: From Middle English depicten, from Latin dēpictus, from dēpingō.

parole.significato: To remove all hair from skin so as to make it smooth.
parole.testo: First attested in 1575; borrowed from Latin dēpilātus, perfect passive participle of dēpilō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: hairless
parole.testo: From de- + pilous. Compare Latin depilis.

parole.significato: Flattened; made level or even.
parole.testo: First attested in 1884; borrowed from Late Latin dēplanātus, perfect passive participle of dēplanō (“to make level”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To reduce the amount of; to remove (a substance from something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēplētus (“empty”), from depleō. First attested in 1716; originally a medical term.

parole.significato: The act of depleting, or the state of being depleted; exhaustion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin depletio, depletionem, from depleō.

parole.significato: An unfolding, unplaiting, or untwisting.
parole.testo: From Latin deplicare (“to unfold”), from de- + plicare (“to fold”).

parole.significato: deplorable
parole.testo: First attested in 1544; borrowed from Latin dēplōrātus, perfect passive participle of dēplōrō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To testify, especially in the form of a deposition.
parole.testo: From Latin dēpōnō (“lay down, deposit, entrust”).

parole.significato: Having an active meaning, but conjugating as though it were being used with a different voice (such as the passive).
parole.testo: From Latin dēpōnēns (“laying aside”), the present active participle of dēpōnō (“lay aside”), from dē- + pōnō (“put, place”). The name comes from the idea that such verbs were originally reflexive and then later "laid aside" their passive meanings.

parole.significato: Something that depopulates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēpopulāns.

parole.significato: To reduce the population of a region by disease, war, forced relocation etc.
parole.testo: First attested in 1531; borrowed from Latin dēpopulātus, perfect active participle of dēpopulor (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)). Compare depeople, French dépeupler, Italian spopolare, Spanish despoblar, Portuguese despovoar and Romanian despopora; by surface anal

parole.significato: The act of depopulating or condition of being depopulated; the destruction or expulsion of inhabitants.

parole.significato: A person who depopulates an area, especially one who forcibly removes people from an estate.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English depopulator, borrowed Latin dēpopulātor. By surface analysis, depopulate + -or.

parole.significato: Sediment or rock that is not native to its present location or is different from the surrounding material. Sometimes re…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin depositus, past participle of depono (“put down”). Doublet of depot.

parole.significato: Acting as the trusted recipient of a deposit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin dēpositārius.

parole.significato: A place where something is deposited, as for storage, safekeeping, or preservation.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dēpositōrium, from Latin dēpositum, past participle of dēpōnō. By surface analysis, deposit + -ory.

parole.significato: A deposit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēpositum. Doublet of depot.

parole.significato: That may or should be deprecated.
parole.testo: Latin deprecabilis (“exorable”).

parole.significato: To express disapproval of, protest or plead against.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēprecātus, perfect active participle of dēprecor (“to pray against (a present or impending evil) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), pray for, intercede for (that which is in danger), rarely imprecate”), from dē- (“off”) + precor (“to pray”).

parole.significato: Strongly disapproved of.
parole.testo: From Latin dēprecātus, past participle of dēprecor (“to pray against (a present or impending evil), pray for, intercede for (that which is in danger), rarely imprecate”), from de (“off”) + precor (“to pray”).

parole.significato: One who deprecates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēprecātor.

parole.significato: To lessen in price or estimated value; to lower the worth of.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English depreciaten, borrowed from Late Latin dēpretiātus / dēpreciātus, perfect passive participle of dēpretiō / dēpreciō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + pretium (“price”) + -ō.

parole.significato: To ransack or plunder; to prey upon.
parole.testo: Late Latin depraedari, depraedat-: Latin de- + praedari (“to plunder”).

parole.significato: To take unawares or by surprise; to catch or seize (a criminal etc.) in the act.
parole.testo: From Latin deprehendere, deprehensum, from de- + prehendere (“to lay hold of, seize”). See prehensile.

parole.significato: A catching in the act; discovery (of a misdeed)
parole.testo: From Latin deprehensio. See deprehend.

parole.significato: A small muscle of each side of the upper lip that is inserted into the nasal septum and wing of the nose on each side a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin dēpressor sēptī nāsī (“depressor of the septum of the nose”).

parole.significato: An eye muscle, usually considered to be part of the orbicularis oculi.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Serving to depress (force or push down).
parole.testo: From Latin dēprimēns, present participle of dēprimō. See depress.

parole.significato: To drive away.
parole.testo: From Latin depulsus, past participle of depellere (“to drive out”).

parole.significato: expulsion or repulsion.
parole.testo: Latin depulsio.

parole.significato: Driving or thrusting away; averting.
parole.testo: Latin depulsorius.

parole.significato: To remove impurities from; to purify.
parole.testo: From Late Latin depuratus, past participle of depurare (“to purify”).

parole.significato: Serving to purge; tending to cleanse or purify.
parole.testo: From Latin dēpurgō (“to cleanse, purify”) + -atory.

parole.significato: Mental activity directed away from reality and towards subjective ideas or conceptions; fantasizing.

parole.significato: Not in accordance with reality; subjective, founded in fantasy.
parole.testo: From Latin de re (“away from the thing”) + -istic.

parole.significato: Given up by the guardian or owner; abandoned, forsaken.

parole.significato: Willful neglect of one's duty.
parole.testo: From Latin dērelictiō (“neglect, abandonment”), from dērelinquō (“to neglect, abandon”), from dē- + re- + linquō (“to leave”).

parole.significato: to abandon or desert, to leave to itself
parole.testo: From de- + relinquish as a calque of Latin dērelinquere. See dereliction in Roman law for its particular use in Scotland.

parole.significato: To laugh at or mock (someone or something) harshly; to ridicule, to scorn.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dērīdēre, the present active infinitive of dērīdeō (“to laugh at, make fun of, mock, deride”), from dē- (prefix denoting putting down or subjecting to indignity) + rīdeō (“to laugh; to laugh at, mock, ridicule”) (further etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-Euro

parole.significato: Deserving derision (“treatment with disdain or contempt”).
parole.testo: From Latin *dērīsibilis (compare Italian derisibile, “deridable”), from dērīsus + -ibilis (whence English -ible), a variant of -bilis (adjective-forming suffix that denotes the capacity or worth of being acted upon). parole.significato: Expressing or characterized by derision; mocking; ridiculing.
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Latin dērīdeō (“to deride”) + -ive.

parole.significato: Derived; derivative.
parole.testo: From Latin dērīvātus. Equivalent to derive + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The inner layer of the skin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin derma, from Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”). Doublet of derm.

parole.significato: Inflammation of the skin.
parole.testo: From New Latin dermatītis, from δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”), from δέρω (dérō, “to skin, flay”). By surface analysis, dermato- + -itis.

parole.significato: The tissue of the skin underlying the epidermis.
parole.testo: From New Latin dermis, from Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”), from δέρω (dérō, “to skin, to flay”).

parole.significato: dermal: dermis, but also often, broadly, skin or epidermis.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin”); compare dermis § Etymology.

parole.significato: derogatory
parole.testo: From Latin derogans.

parole.significato: To partially repeal (a law etc.).
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Middle English derogaten, from derogat(e) (“annulled, abrogated”, used participially and later as the past participle of derogaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix) borrowed from Latin dērogātus, perfect passive participle of dērogō (“to annul, repeal part of a law, take away, detract

parole.significato: A detractor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dērogātor, from dērogō. By surface analysis, de- + Latin rog- + -ate + -or.

parole.significato: Disparaging.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin dērogātōrius, from Latin dērogō; corresponding to derogate + -ory.

parole.significato: A climbing leguminous plant of Southeast Asia and the southwest Pacific Islands, Derris elliptica, whose roots are a so…
parole.testo: From New Latin and translingual Derris, from Ancient Greek δέρρις (dérrhis, “leather, skin”), referring to the leathery pods, from δέρω (dérō, “I skin, I flay”).

parole.significato: to deprive of blood; to remove the blood from
parole.testo: From Late Latin desanguināre.

parole.significato: A vessel used in alchemy to extract and filter oils.

parole.significato: A generatrix.
parole.testo: Latin dēscrībēns, present participle of dēscrībō (“to describe”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or providing a description.
parole.testo: From Latin dēscriptīvus (“containing a full description”).

parole.significato: That which describes; a word, phrase, etc. serving as a description.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēscrīptōris. Compare describe.

parole.significato: That which is described; the subject of a description.
parole.testo: From Latin dēscrīptum.

parole.significato: To cut, as with a scythe; to mow.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Medieval Latin dēsecātus, a variant of dēsectus, the perfect passive participle of dēsecō (“to cut off”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A person who has physically removed him- or herself from the control or direction of a military or naval unit with the…

parole.significato: A substance (such as calcium oxide or silica gel) that is used as a drying agent because of its high affinity for water.

parole.significato: Having had moisture removed; dehydrated, desiccated.
parole.testo: From Latin dēsiccātus (“dried up”), the perfect passive participle of dēsiccō: see above. Equivalent to Latin dēsiccō + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Desirable.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dēsīderābilis.

parole.significato: To miss; to feel the absence of; to long for.
parole.testo: From Latin, from the participle stem of the verb dēsīderāre (“to desire”). The verb is a doublet of desire.

parole.significato: The act of desiderating.
parole.testo: Latin desideratio.

parole.significato: Having or indicating wish or desire.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēsīderātīvus.

parole.significato: Something that is wished for, or considered desirable, particularly when thought to be essential.

parole.significato: idle; lazy

parole.significato: Capable of being designated; designatable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēsignābilis, from dēsignō (“to indicate, designate”).

parole.significato: Designated; appointed; chosen.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēsignātus, perfect passive participle of designō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of design.

parole.significato: An act or instance of designating
parole.testo: From Middle English designacioun, from Latin dēsignātiō, and partly (especially in sense 5) from design + -ation. By surface analysis, designate + -ion.

parole.significato: Ending; forming an end; lowermost.

parole.significato: consisting of desinences or grammatical endings; terminal
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dēsinentia + -al. Compare French désinentiel.

parole.significato: silliness, folly
parole.testo: From Latin desipientia, from desipere (“to be foolish”).

parole.significato: foolish; silly
parole.testo: From Latin desipiens, present participle of desipere (“to be foolish”), from de- + sapere (“to be wise”).

parole.significato: To shut up, as in a desk; to treasure.

parole.significato: Contempt, derision.

parole.significato: Fit or deserving to be despised; contemptible; mean.
parole.testo: From Late Latin dēspicābilis, from Latin dēspicor, a variant of dēspiciō (“to despise”), from de (“down”) + speciō (“to look at, behold”). First attested in the 1550s. Equivalent to despise + -able.

parole.significato: The act of looking down on someone; despisal.
parole.testo: From Latin despicientia. See despise.

parole.significato: A stripping or plundering; spoliation.

parole.significato: To give up the will, courage, or spirit; to become dejected, lose heart.
parole.testo: From Latin dēspondeō (“give up, abandon”), from dē (“from”) + spondeō (“promise”).

parole.significato: The loss of hope or confidence; despair or dejection.
parole.testo: From Latin dēspondentia, from dēspondēns + -ia. Equivalent to despondent + -ency.

parole.significato: In low spirits from loss of hope or courage.
parole.testo: From Latin dēspondēns, from the verb despondere (“to give up, to abandon”).

parole.significato: Synonym of betrothal.
parole.testo: From the Latin desponsus.

parole.significato: To skim the froth or other impurities from a liquid, to clarify, purify.
parole.testo: First attested in 1651; borrowed from Latin dēspūmātus, perfect passive participle of dēspūmō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + spūmō (“to foam, froth”), spūma (“foam, froth, scum”) + -ō. Doublet of despume.

parole.significato: The act of giving off froth or scum.
parole.testo: From Latin despumatio: compare French despumation.

parole.significato: To remove the scales from, to scale; (less narrowly) to peel.
parole.testo: First attested in 1740; borrowed from Latin dēsquāmātus, perfect passive participle of dēsquāmō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- (“off”) + squāma (“a scale”) + -ō (“verb-forming suffix”).

parole.significato: The shedding of the outer layers of the skin.
parole.testo: From Latin desquamare (“to scrape the scales off a fish”), from squāma (“scale”).

parole.significato: To destine, to choose.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in the first part of the 15th century, the verb in 1490, both in Middle English; borrowed from Latin dēstinātus, perfect passive participle of dēstinō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix); doublet of destine. parole.significato: The place set for the end of a journey or to which something is sent; place or point aimed at.
parole.testo: From Latin dēstinātiō, from dēstinō (“to destine”).

parole.significato: Deficient; lacking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēstituēns (“abandoning”), present participle of dēstituō (“to forsake, to abandon”).

parole.significato: Lacking something; devoid.
parole.testo: From Middle English destitute, destitut, from Latin dēstitūtus.

parole.significato: A profuse or morbid sweating, often succeeded by a rash of small pimples.
parole.testo: From Latin desudatio, from desudare (“to sweat greatly”), from de + sudare (“to sweat”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to desuetude; of a law or statute, no longer observed, practiced or enforced.
parole.testo: From Latin dēsuētūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of dēsuētūdō, from dēsuēscō + -tūdō, from dē- + suēscō. By surface analysis, desue(te) + -tude + -ous.

parole.significato: A person skilled at leaping from one horse or chariot to another.
parole.testo: From Latin desultor.

parole.significato: Jumping, or passing, from one thing or subject to another, without order, planning, or rational connection; lacking log…

parole.significato: To borrow, extract, or select.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēsūmō, dēsūmere, from dē- + sūmere (“to take”).

parole.significato: To discover or notice, especially by careful search, examination, or probing.
parole.testo: From Latin detectus, perfect passive participle of detegere (“to uncover or disclose”), from de- + tegere (“to cover”); see tegument, tile, thatch. Sense "to work or solve cases as a detective" a back-formation from detective.

parole.significato: The act or process of detecting, uncovering, or finding out, the discovery of something new, hidden, or disguised.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dētēctiōnem. By surface analysis, detect + -ion.

parole.significato: A police officer tasked with collecting evidence and information in order to solve a crime; an investigator.
parole.testo: The adjective is from Classical Latin dētēct-, past participial stem of dētegō (“to detect”), + -ive. By surface analysis, detect + -ive.
