parole.significato: To prevent something from happening.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēterreō (“deter, discourage”), from de (“from”) + terreō (“to frighten”).

parole.significato: To make worse; to make inferior in quality or value; to impair.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēteriorātus, perfect passive participle of Late Latin dēteriorō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from Latin dēterior (“worse”). Cognate with French détériorer.

parole.significato: A worsening in quality or state; or inferiority.
parole.testo: From Latin deterior (“worse”). See deteriorate.

parole.significato: A modifier; a word that modifies another word.
parole.testo: From Latin dētermināns, present active participle of dēterminō (“fix the limits of something”), from dē + terminō (“bound, limit”).

parole.significato: Distinct, clearly defined.
parole.testo: From Middle English determinate, determynat, determinat, from Latin dēterminātus, perfect passive participle of dēterminō (“to limit, set bounds”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: A determining factor.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: The uncovering of anything buried or covered with earth; an unearthing.
parole.testo: From Latin de + terra (“earth”) + -ation. Compare French déterrer (“to unearth”).

parole.significato: Serving to deter, preventing something from happening.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dēterrēns, dēterrentem.

parole.significato: to turn from the original or plain meaning.
parole.testo: From Latin detorqueo.

parole.significato: That detracts from something; disparaging, depreciatory.
parole.testo: From Latin dētractōrius, from dētractor.

parole.significato: To refuse; to decline.
parole.testo: From Latin dētrectō, from dē + tractō, frequentative of trahō (“to draw”).

parole.significato: Drawing back; refusal; withdrawal.
parole.testo: From Latin dētrectātiō.

parole.significato: Causing damage or harm.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin *dētrīmentālis, from Latin dētrīmentum (“harm”), from dēterō (“to rub off, wear”), from dē- (“down, away”) + terō (“to rub or grab”).

parole.significato: Pieces of rock broken off by ice, glacier, or erosion.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dētrītus (“(that which is) rubbed away”), from dēterō (“rub away”).

parole.significato: To truncate (shorten by cutting, or lop off)
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin dētruncātus, perfect passive participle of dētruncō (“to cut off”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + truncō (“to maim, shorten, cut off”).

parole.significato: truncation (the act of lopping off, or shortening
parole.testo: From Latin detruncatio; compare French détroncation.

parole.significato: A downward out outward thrust.

parole.significato: A prize consisting of a book given to a meritorious sophomore student. The official name is the Detur Prize or Detur Bo…

parole.significato: To usurp or depose.
parole.testo: Latin deturbare.

parole.significato: To evict; to remove.
parole.testo: First attested in 1570; Borrowed from Latin dēturbātus, perfect passive participle of dēturbō (“to beat, throw down; to deprive of”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To defile; to disfigure.

parole.significato: Waste or misapplication of the assets of a deceased person by an executor or administrator; devastation.

parole.significato: Bending down, stooping or sloping.

parole.significato: Characterized by deviation from an expectation or a social standard.

parole.significato: A person with deviant behaviour; a deviant, degenerate or pervert.
parole.testo: From a substantivation of Late Latin dēviātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (noun-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: A plant of species Succisa pratensis, native to Europe.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin morsus diaboli.

parole.testo: 1590s, "out of the common or direct way," from Latin devius (“out of the way, remote, off the main road”), from de via, from de (“off”) (see de-) + via (“way, road”). Compare deviate. Originally in the Latin literal sense; the figurative sense of "deceitful" is first recorded 1630s. Related to devio

parole.significato: To deprive of virginity; to deflower.
parole.testo: First attested in 1583; borrowed from Latin dēvirginātus, perfect passive participle of dēvirginō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Deprived of virginity.
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1470, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English devirginat(e), borrowed from Latin dēvirginātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: avoidable.
parole.testo: From Latin devitare (“to avoid”), from de + vitare (“to shun, avoid”).

parole.significato: An avoiding or escaping.
parole.testo: Latin devitatio.

parole.significato: A calling off or away.
parole.testo: From Latin devocare (“to call off or away”), from de + vocare (“to call”).

parole.significato: To devolve.
parole.testo: From Latin devolutus.

parole.significato: To be inherited by someone else; to pass down upon the next person in a succession, especially through failure or loss…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēvolvō (“roll or tumble off or down”), from dē- + volvō (“roll”).

parole.significato: The act of devouring.
parole.testo: From Latin devoratio. See devour.

parole.significato: to give one's time, focus one's efforts, commit oneself, etc. entirely for, on, or to a certain matter; to consecrate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēvōtus, past participle of Latin dēvoveō (“dedicate by a vow, sacrifice oneself, promise solemnly”). Doublet of devow; see also devout. Displaced native Middle English ēstful, from Old English ēstful.

parole.significato: A worshipper; someone given to devotion.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dēvōtor.

parole.significato: One of a breed of small hardy cattle originating from the Kerry breed of Ireland, valuable for beef and milk. They are…
parole.testo: Variant of Dyster. Also partially from Latin dexter (“right (handed)”).

parole.significato: Right; on the right-hand side. (In heraldry, specifically the bearer's right, which is the viewer's left.)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dexter (“right”).

parole.significato: Right; on the right; toward the right.
parole.testo: From Latin dexter (“right”).

parole.significato: Growing in a pattern that spirals clockwise around a central support; turning to the right when growing taller.
parole.testo: From Latin dextrorsum, contracted from dextrovorsum, dextroversum (“toward the right side”), from dexter (“right”) + versus, vorsus, past participle of vertere, vortere (“to turn”).

parole.significato: Two.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *dwi- Proto-Hellenic *dwi- Ancient Greek δῐ- (dĭ-)bor. Latin di-bor. English di- Borrowed from Latin di-, from Ancient Greek δι- (di-, “two”).

parole.significato: Diabetes mellitus; any of a group of metabolic diseases whereby a person (or other animal) has high blood sugar due to…
parole.testo: From Latin diabētēs (“siphon”), from Ancient Greek διαβήτης (diabḗtēs), from Ancient Greek διαβαίνω (diabaínō, “to pass through”).

parole.significato: A disease characterized by excretion of large amounts of severely diluted urine, which cannot be reduced when fluid int…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin diabetes insipidus (“tasteless diabetes”), as opposed to diabetes mellitus (“sweet diabetes”) because of the absence of glucose in urine in the former.

parole.significato: A medical disorder commonly called diabetes, characterized by varying or persistent hyperglycemia (high blood sugar lev…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin diabetes mellitus (“diabetes of the sweet type”) (from the fact that in centuries past, physicians sometimes tasted a patient's urine to help diagnose the illness).

parole.significato: To ascribe diabolical qualities to; to change into, or represent as, a devil.
parole.testo: From Latin diabolus (“devil”) + -fy.

parole.significato: The study of the Devil in religion.
parole.testo: From Latin diabolus (“devil”) + -logy.

parole.significato: Synonym of tritone.
parole.testo: From Latin diabolus. Doublet of devil, diable, and diablo.

parole.significato: Synonym of tmesis.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin diacopē, from Ancient Greek διακοπή (diakopḗ, “gash, cleft, rupture”), from διά (diá, “through, across”) + κοπή (kopḗ, “cutting”)

parole.significato: A separation of one syllable (especially a vowel which is a diphthong, that is, beginning with one sound and ending wit…
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwís Unadapted borrowing from Late Latin diaeresis (“distribution; division of a diphthong into two syllables”), from Ancient Greek δῐαίρεσῐς (dĭaíresĭs, “distribution, division; division of a poetic line when the end of a word and a metrical foot coincide; division of a diphthong into tw

parole.significato: The process of, or an instance of, identification of the nature and cause of a medical condition or illness.
parole.testo: From Latin diagnōsis, from Ancient Greek διάγνωσις (diágnōsis), from διαγιγνώσκω (diagignṓskō, “to discern”), from διά (diá, “through”) + γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to know”).

parole.significato: Dialectical (of or relating to dialectic)
parole.testo: From Latin dialecticus, from Ancient Greek δῐᾰλεκτῐκός (dĭălektĭkós).

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which multiple arguments are brought to bear on a single point.
parole.testo: From New Latin diallagē, from Ancient Greek διαλλαγή (diallagḗ, “interchange”).

parole.significato: A method of separating molecules or particles of different sizes by differential diffusion through a semipermeable memb…
parole.testo: From Latin dialysis, from Ancient Greek διάλυσις (diálusis). By surface analysis, dia- + -lysis. First use appears c. 1550.

parole.significato: A Diana monkey.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin Diāna, short form of Latin Dīāna, derived by syncope from Old Latin Dīvāna, equivalent to dīvus + -āna; roughly akin to Proto-Italic *deiwā (“goddess”) + Proto-Indo-European *-néh₂. Originally an Old Italic divinity of light and the moon; later identified as the Roman counte

parole.significato: powdered aromatic herbs, sometimes made into little balls and strung together
parole.testo: From Latin diapasma, Ancient Greek διάπασμα (diápasma), ultimately from πάσσω (pássō); compare French diapasme.

parole.significato: The musical octave.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin diapason, from Ancient Greek διαπασῶν (diapasôn), that is διά (diá, “through”) + πασῶν (pasôn, “all”) (χορδῶν (khordôn, “notes”)), “through all (notes)”.

parole.significato: The migration of blood cells, especially leucocytes, through the intact walls of blood vessels into the surrounding tis…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek, from dia- + Ancient Greek πηδᾰ́ω (pēdắō, “I leap”).

parole.significato: The interval of the fifth or the harmonic ratio 3:2.
parole.testo: From Latin diapente, from Ancient Greek διά (diá, “through, across”) + πέντε (pénte, “five”).

parole.significato: transparency
parole.testo: From Latin diaphaneitas. By surface analysis, diaph(anous) + -aneity.

parole.significato: Transparent or translucent; allowing light to pass through; capable of being seen through.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin diaphanus, from Ancient Greek διαφανής (diaphanḗs), from δια- (dia-, “through”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, appear”).

parole.significato: The formation and excretion of sweat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin diaphorēsis, from Ancient Greek δῐᾰφόρησῐς (dĭăphórēsĭs, “evaporation, dissipation, perspiration”); by surface analysis, dia- (“through, across”) + -phoresis (“transmission”); also synchronically held to end in the suffix -esis.

parole.significato: Generating sweat or perspiration.
parole.testo: From Latin diaphorēticus, from Ancient Greek διαφορητικός (diaphorētikós); by surface analysis, diaphor(esis) + -etic.

parole.significato: A daily log of experiences, especially those of the writer.
parole.testo: From Latin diārium (“a daily allowance for soldiers, in Late Latin also ‘diary’”), neuter of *diārius, from diēs (“a day”) (whence also journal). Cognate with Spanish diario (“daily; diary”).

parole.significato: Lasting for one day.
parole.testo: From Latin diārius.

parole.significato: A separation between two parts, such as separation of a bone, without fracture.
parole.testo: From New Latin diastasis, from Ancient Greek διάστασις (diástasis, “separation, standing aloof”), from δια- (dia-) + στάσις (stásis, “standing”). Compare diastema.

parole.significato: Intervening space; interval.
parole.testo: From Latin diastema.

parole.significato: A gap or space between two adjacent teeth, especially the upper front incisors (in humans).
parole.testo: From Late Latin, from Ancient Greek διάστημα (diástēma, “interval, space between”). Compare diastasis.

parole.significato: The interval of a fourth or the harmonic ratio 4:3.
parole.testo: From Latin diatessarōn, from Ancient Greek διά (diá, “through, across”) + τεσσάρων (tessárōn) (genitive plural of τέσσαρες (téssares, “four”)).

parole.significato: A hereditary or constitutional predisposition to a disease or other disorder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin diathesis, from Ancient Greek διάθεσις (diáthesis, “state, condition”), from διατίθημι (diatíthēmi, “to arrange”).

parole.significato: Talkative; pert; saucy.
parole.testo: From Latin dicāx, from dīcō (“to say”) + -acious.

parole.significato: The condition of dicephalic conjoined twins.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A cymose inflorescence with all branches below the terminal flower in regular opposite pairs.
parole.testo: From New Latin dichasium, from di- + Ancient Greek χάσις (khásis, “chasm, separation”).

parole.significato: Dividing or branching into two mutually exclusive pieces.
parole.testo: From Late Latin dichotomos, from Ancient Greek διχότομος (dikhótomos, “cut in half”). By surface analysis, dichotomy + -ous.

parole.significato: To bargain, haggle or negotiate over a sale.
parole.testo: From Middle English diker (“measure of ten”), from Late Latin dacra (“a dicker”), from Latin decuria (“a ten of something”), from decem (“ten”).

parole.significato: A saying; a statement.
parole.testo: From Middle English dicte, from Latin dictum. Doublet of dictum.

parole.significato: A dictation or dictate.
parole.testo: From Latin dictāmen.

parole.significato: An order or command.
parole.testo: First attested in 1581; borrowed from Latin dictātum (“a thing said, something dictated”), substantivized from the nominative neuter singular of dictātus, the perfect passive participle of dictō (“pronounce or declare repeatedly; dictate”), frequentative of dīcō (“say, speak”). Doublet of diktat.

parole.significato: To order, command, control.
parole.testo: First attested in 1577; borrowed from Latin dictātus, perfect passive participle of dictō (“to pronounce or declare repeatedly; to dictate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), frequentative of dīcō (“say, speak”).

parole.significato: Dictating, the process of speaking for someone else to write down the words.
parole.testo: From Late Latin dictātiō, noun of action from dictātus, the perfect passive participle of dictō. By surface analysis, dictate + -ion.

parole.significato: Exessively strict.
parole.testo: From Classical Latin dictātōrius. By surface analysis, dictate + -ory.

parole.significato: A female dictator.
parole.testo: From Latin dictātrīx. By surface analysis, dictate + -trix.

parole.significato: A reference work listing words or names from one or more languages, usually ordered alphabetically, explaining each ter…
parole.testo: From Middle English dixionare, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin dictiōnārium, from Latin dictiōnārius, from dictiō (“a speaking”), from dictus, perfect past participle of dīcō (“to speak”) + -ārium (“room, place”). By surface analysis, diction + -ary.

parole.significato: An authoritative statement; a dogmatic saying; a maxim, an apothegm.
parole.testo: From Latin dictum (“proverb, maxim”), from dictus (“having been said”), perfect passive participle of dico (“to say”). Compare Spanish dicho (“saying”). Doublet of dict.

parole.significato: Any spider in the family Dictynidae.
parole.testo: Originally only capitalized, from New Latin Dictynidae (“taxonomic family”), as Dictyna + -id.

parole.significato: Of or relating to education or teaching; didactic.
parole.testo: From Latin didascalicus (“didactic”), from Ancient Greek διδασκαλικός (didaskalikós, “didactic”). See also διδασκαλία (didaskalía, “teaching, instruction”).

parole.significato: The act of drawing apart; separation.
parole.testo: From Latin diductio, from diducere, diductum (“to draw apart”), from di-, dis- + ducere (“to lead, draw”).

parole.significato: Twin, twinned; growing or occurring in pairs.
parole.testo: Modern Latin, from Ancient Greek δίδυμος (dídumos, “twin”).

parole.significato: per day
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin die (“[in a] day”), locative of Latin dies (“day”).

parole.significato: Having a 24-hour period regardless of day or night.
parole.testo: From Latin dies (“day”) + -al.

parole.significato: The region of the human brain, specifically the human forebrain, that includes the thalamus, the hypothalamus, the epit…
parole.testo: From New Latin diencephalon, from di-, prevocalic form of dia- + encephalon.

parole.significato: Unlucky day.
parole.testo: From Latin dies (“day”) infaustus (“unlucky”).

parole.significato: A court day, i.e. a day when a legal court is functioning.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?]

parole.significato: A day on which courts are not held.
parole.testo: Latin dies non juridicus.

parole.significato: A regulated diet that excludes or constrains certain types of food, especially for health reasons; also, a book or simi…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin diētārium (“book prescribing diet”), from Latin diaeta (“diet”).

parole.significato: Relating to diet.
parole.testo: From Latin diaeteticus, from Ancient Greek διαιτητικός (diaitētikós).

parole.significato: A form of divorce, among the Ancient Romans, in which a cake was used.
parole.testo: From Latin diffarreatio, from dif- + farreum (“a spelt cake”). See confarreation.

parole.significato: A distinguishing feature which marks a species off from other members of the same genus.
parole.testo: From Latin differentia. Doublet of difference.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a difference.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin differentiālis. By surface analysis, different + -ial.

parole.significato: An equation involving the derivatives of a function.
parole.testo: First appears c. 1704 in the publications of Charles Hayes. Calque of Latin aequatio differentialis, which was coined by Leibniz in 1676.

parole.significato: To modify so as to create a difference or distinction.
parole.testo: From New Latin differentiātus, perfect passive participle of differentiō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from Latin differentia (“difference”); see difference.

parole.significato: To render difficult; to difficilitate.
parole.testo: From Latin difficultāt-, past participial stem of difficultō. By surface analysis, difficult + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To be distrustful
parole.testo: Latin diffido (“to distrust”)

parole.significato: The state of being diffident, timid or shy; reticence or self-effacement.
parole.testo: From Latin diffīdentiam (“distrust”), from diffīdere (“to mistrust”), from dis- and fīdere (“to trust”). Attested since ∼1400. The original sense was antonymous with confidence, and the modern sense of ‘distrusting oneself’ dates from the 1650s.

parole.significato: Lacking confidence in others; distrustful.
parole.testo: From Latin diffīdentem, present participle of diffīdere (“to mistrust”). Doublet of defiant.

parole.significato: A blowing apart or away.
parole.testo: From Latin difflatio, from Latin difflare, difflatum (“to disperse by blowing”).

parole.significato: Flowing apart or off; dissolving; not fixed.
parole.testo: From Latin diffluens (“flowing away”), present participle of diffluo (“to flow away”).

parole.significato: To cause diffraction
parole.testo: From Latin diffractus (“past participle of diffringo (“to shatter, to break into pieces”)”).

parole.significato: The bending of a wave around an obstacle.
parole.testo: From New Latin diffrāctiō (in which coined by Francesco Maria Grimaldi), from Latin diffrāctus, past participle of Latin diffringo (“to shatter, to break into pieces”). Coined in Physico-mathesis de lumine (1665) by Francesco Maria Grimaldi.

parole.significato: Everywhere or throughout everything; not focused or concentrated.
parole.testo: From Middle English *diffuse (attested in adverb diffuseli), from Latin diffūsus.

parole.significato: The act of diffusing or dispersing something, or the property of being diffused or dispersed; dispersion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin diffūsiō, from diffundō; can be decomposed as diffuse + -ion.

parole.significato: That is spread or dispersed across a wide area or among a large number of people.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin diffusivus (“tending to spread; expansive”) (13th century), from participle stem of Latin diffundere (“diffuse, disperse”).

parole.significato: A second marriage (as after the death or divorce of a spouse)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin digamia (“twice married”), from Ancient Greek διγαμία (digamía, “bigamy”), δίγαμος (dígamos), from δίς (dís, “twice”) + γάμος (gámos, “marriage”). By surface analysis, di- + -gamy.

parole.significato: Having two bellies.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin digastricus, from di- (“twice, doubly”) + gastricus (“gastric”); equivalent to di- + gastric. Doublet of digastricus.

parole.significato: Synonym of digastric muscle.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin digastricus, ellipsis of mūsculus digastricus (“digastric muscle”). Doublet of digastric.

parole.significato: To distribute or arrange methodically; to work over and classify; to reduce to portions for ready use or application.
parole.testo: From Middle English digesten, from Latin dīgestus, past participle of dīgerō (“carry apart”), from dī- (for dis- (“apart”)) + gerō (“to carry”), influenced by Middle French digestion. Partly displaced native Old English meltan (intransitive) and mieltan (transitive), both “to melt, to digest,” whenc

parole.significato: That which is digested; especially, that which is worked over, classified, and arranged under proper heads or titles.
parole.testo: From Latin dīgesta, neuter plural of dīgestus, past participle of dīgerō (“separate”).

parole.significato: A position in a sequence of numerals representing a place value in a positional number system.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English digit, borrowed from Latin digitus. Doublet of digitus and dedo.

parole.significato: Having to do with digits (fingers or toes); especially, performed with a finger.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin digitālis, from digitus (“finger, toe”) + -alis (“-al”), equivalent to digit + -al. Doublet of digitalis.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Digitalis (herbaceous plants of the Plantaginaceae family, including the foxglove, Digitalis pur…
parole.testo: Modern Latin, from Latin digitālis (“of the fingers”) (named in reference to the German common name for the plant, Fingerhut (“thimble”)). Doublet of digital.

parole.significato: Having digits, fingers or things shaped like fingers; fingerlike
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1661, the verb in 1657; the adjective was borrowed from Latin digitātus (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), the verb from digitātus, perfect passive participle of digitō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)).

parole.significato: A small keyboard used by pianists for exercising the fingers, without producing any sound.
parole.testo: Latin digitus (“a finger”).

parole.significato: A little finger or toe, or something resembling one.
parole.testo: From Latin digitulus, diminutive of digitus.

parole.significato: An Ancient Roman unit of length, approximately 0.73 inches.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin digitus. Doublet of digit.

parole.significato: Synonym of little toe (Latin designation).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin digitus minimus pedis.

parole.significato: Synonym of big toe (Latin designation).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin digitus prīmus pedis.

parole.significato: Synonym of ring toe (Latin designation).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin digitus quārtus pedis.

parole.significato: Synonym of long toe (Latin designation).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin digitus secundus pedis.

parole.significato: Synonym of middle toe (Latin designation).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin digitus tertius pedis.

parole.significato: To fight like gladiators; to contend or dispute violently.
parole.testo: From Latin digladiari, from di-, dis- + gladius (“a sword”).

parole.significato: The coexistence in a given population of two closely related native languages or dialects, one of which is regarded as…
parole.testo: From Latin diglōssia. In linguistics introduced 1959 by Charles A. Ferguson, based on French diglossie, from Ancient Greek δίγλωσσος (díglōssos, “bilingual”) + -ία (-ía). Equivalent to di- + -glossia.

parole.significato: The act of thinking or treating as worthy; honour (especially of God).
parole.testo: From Latin dignātiō.

parole.significato: distinguishing mark; a diagnostic or dicernment
parole.testo: From Latin dignoscere (“to distinguish”), from di-, dis- + gnoscere, noscere (“to learn to know”).

parole.significato: To step or turn aside; to deviate; to swerve; especially, to turn aside from the main subject of attention, or course o…
parole.testo: From Latin digressum, past participle of digredi.

parole.significato: The twelve great gods of Roman mythology, namely Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Nep…
parole.testo: From Latin di maiores (literally “greater gods”).

parole.significato: One who dijudicates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dijudicans, present participle of dijudico (“to dijudicate”).

parole.significato: To make a judicial decision; to decide; to determine.
parole.testo: From Latin dijudico (“to dijudicate”); di- (a combining form of dis-) + judico (“to judge”).

parole.significato: The act of dijudicating; judgement.
parole.testo: Latin dijudicatio.

parole.significato: To rend in pieces; to tear.
parole.testo: First attested in 1535; Borrowed from Latin dīlāniātus, perfect passive participle of dīlāniō (“to dilacerate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dis- + lāniō (“to tear to pieces”).

parole.significato: dilapidated
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dīlapidātus, perfect passive participle of dilapidō (“squander, consume, throw away”), see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: One who dilapidates; a person causing dilapidation.
parole.testo: From Latin, from dilapidare (“to destroy with stones”), from dis (intensive) + lapidare (“to stone”) (from lapis (“stone”)) + -tor (“-er”).

parole.significato: Dilated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dīlātātus, perfect passive participle of dīlātō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of dilate.

parole.significato: A muscle that dilates any part; a dilator.
parole.testo: From Latin dīlātātor (“propagator”), from dīlātō (“to spread out”).

parole.significato: Carried in different ways, spread, abroad, dispersed, published.
parole.testo: First attested in 1471, in Middle English; borrowed from Latin dīlātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 2 for more.

parole.significato: love; loving kindness
parole.testo: From Latin dilectio (“dilection”). See diligent.

parole.significato: A circumstance in which a choice must be made between two or more alternatives that seem equally undesirable.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ First attested 1523, from Late Latin dilemma, from Ancient Greek δίλημμα (dílēmma, “ambiguous proposition”), from δι- (di-, “having two of”) + λῆμμα (lêmma, “premise, proposition”), equivalent to di- + lemma.

parole.significato: diligence; carefulness
parole.testo: From Latin dīligentia.

parole.significato: Ambiguous or equivocal speech or discourse.
parole.testo: From Latin dilogia, from Ancient Greek διλογία (dilogía, “repetition”), from δίς (dís, “twice”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy”).

parole.significato: clear or lucid
parole.testo: From Latin dilucidus, from dilucere (“to be light enough to tell objects apart”). See lucid.

parole.significato: The act of making clear; clarification or explanation.
parole.testo: Latin dilucidatio.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to dawn.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dīlūculum + -ar.

parole.significato: That which dilutes.
parole.testo: Latin diluens, from diluere. See dilute.

parole.significato: To make thinner by adding solvent to a solution, especially by adding water.
parole.testo: From Latin dīlūtus, from dīluere (“to wash away, dissolve, cause to melt, dilute”), from dī-, dis- (“away, apart”) + luere (“to wash”). See lave, and compare deluge.

parole.significato: Relating to or produced by a flood or deluge.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin dīluviālis.

parole.significato: To run as a flood.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dīluviātus, perfect passive participle of dīluviō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: An inundation or flood; a deluge.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dīluvium (“flood”), from lavō (“to wash”). Doublet of deluge.

parole.significato: A single aspect of a given thing.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin dīmēnsiō.

parole.significato: A fight, battle or contest.
parole.testo: From Latin dimicatio, from dimicare (“to fight”).

parole.significato: related to something coming forth in halves
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dīmidiālis (“related to the half”) from dīmidium.

parole.significato: Divided into two (equal) halves.
parole.testo: From Latin dīmidiātus, past participle of dīmidiāre (“to halve”).

parole.significato: The act of dividing into halves.
parole.testo: Continuing the Middle English dimydicion (circa 1425, in an arithmetical sense), from the Late Latin dīmidiātiō.

parole.significato: half and half (mixture of ale and porter, or similar)
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from reduplication of Latin dimidium (“half”) with -que (“and”) as a humorous English-to-Latin calque of half and half, once used by students.

parole.significato: lessening
parole.testo: From Latin diminuens, present participle of diminuere. See diminish.

parole.significato: Small; diminutive.
parole.testo: From Middle English diminute, from Latin dīminūtus and Old French diminut.

parole.significato: permission to depart, or a dismissal.
parole.testo: From Latin dimissio. See dimit, and compare dismission.

parole.significato: Granting permission to be ordained.
parole.testo: From Latin dimissorius. Compare dimit.

parole.significato: To dismiss, let go, or release.
parole.testo: From Latin dimittere (“to send away, let go”), from di-, dis- + mittere (“to send”). See dismiss and demit.

parole.significato: A light strong fabric with woven stripes or squares.
parole.testo: From earlier dimite, from Middle English demit, demyt, from Medieval Latin dimitum, from Byzantine Greek δίμιτον (dímiton), from Ancient Greek δίμιτος (dímitos, “of double thread”).

parole.significato: enumeration
parole.testo: From Latin dinumeratio, from di-, dis- + numerare (“to count”), from numerus (“number”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Roman emperor Diocletian.
parole.testo: From Latin Dioclētiānus, Latinate form of Ancient Greek Διοκλῆς (Dioklês). The Roman emperor was named so after his home town of Dioclea in Illyricum.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to Dionysus or to the Dionysia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Dionȳsiacus, from Ancient Greek Διονυσιακός (Dionusiakós), from Δῐόνῡσος (Dĭónūsos, “Dionysus”) + -ακός (-akós).

parole.significato: A unit of measure of the power of a lens or mirror, equal to the reciprocal of its focal length in meters. Myopia is di…
parole.testo: From Latin dioptra, from Ancient Greek διόπτρα (dióptra).

parole.significato: A vase or drinking cup with two handles.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek, “two-handled”.

parole.significato: double
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek διπλόος (diplóos), διπλοῦς (diploûs, “double”).

parole.significato: A document issued by an educational institution testifying that the recipient has earned a degree or has successfully c…
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Latin diplōma, from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma, “folded paper, license”), from διπλόω (diplóō, “to double, fold over”), from διπλόος (diplóos, “double”).

parole.significato: A noun which has only two cases.
parole.testo: From Latin diptōtum, from Ancient Greek δίπτωτος (díptōtos), from δί- (dí-) + πτῶσις (ptôsis, “case”).

parole.significato: A writing tablet consisting of two leaves of rigid material connected by hinges and shutting together so as to protect…
parole.testo: From Late Latin diptycha, plural, from Ancient Greek, neuter plural of δίπτυχος (díptukhos, “folded, doubled”), from δι- (di-) + πτυχή (ptukhḗ, “fold, layer”).

parole.significato: The emission and diffusion of rays of light.
parole.testo: From Latin dīradiō (“to arrange in rays”), from dis- + radius.

parole.significato: Warning of bad consequences: ill-boding; portentous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dīrus (“fearful, ominous”).

parole.significato: Proceeding without deviation or interruption.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dīrēctus, perfect passive participle of dīrigō (“straighten, direct”), from dis- (“asunder, in pieces, apart, in two”) + regō (“make straight, rule”). Compare dress. Doublet of derecho. For the meaning development compare with Russian напра́вить (naprávitʹ, “to direct, to turn, t

parole.significato: A title held by music directors especially at European universities or cathedrals; sometimes also at cathedral schools.
parole.testo: Direct loan from Latin ("music director")

parole.significato: In the later Middle Ages, a Catholic liturgical guide for praying the Divine Office and Holy Mass.
parole.testo: From Latin dīrēctōrium (literally “guide”). Doublet of directory.

parole.significato: A list of names, addresses etc, of specific classes of people or organizations, often in alphabetical order or in some…
parole.testo: From Middle English directorie, dyrectorye, from Medieval Latin dīrēctōrium. By surface analysis, direct + -ory. Doublet of directorium. The political sense is a semantic loan from French directoire.

parole.significato: Containing directions; instructing; directorial.
parole.testo: From Middle English directorye, from Latin dīrēctōrius. By surface analysis, direct + -ory.

parole.significato: Distinct; separate; secrete; divided.
parole.testo: From the Latin diremptus (“separated, divided”), the past participle of dirimō (“to separate, divide”), formed as dir- (prevocalic variant of dis- (“apart, asunder”)) + emō (“to take”); compare dirempt².

parole.significato: To separate; to divide; to break off.
parole.testo: From the Latin *diremptō, frequentative of dirimō.

parole.significato: A ripping apart; a forceful sundering.
parole.testo: From Latin dirēmptiō (“a separation”), from dirimō (“to separate”) + -iō (“abstract noun suffix”).

parole.significato: The act of despoiling, plundering, looting, or taking away.
parole.testo: From Latin dīreptio, from dīripiō (“tear asunder, plunder”), from dis- + rapiō (“seize, carry off”).

parole.significato: A mournful poem or piece of music composed or performed as a memorial to a deceased person.
parole.testo: From Middle English dirige, from Latin dirige (“steer, direct”), from the beginning of the first antiphon in matins for the dead, Dirige, Domine, deus meus, in conspectu tuo viam meam. Doublet of dirige.

parole.significato: A Roman Catholic service for the dead, being the first antiphon of matins for the dead, of which dirige is the first wo…
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin dīrige (“guide”, imperative), from the beginning of the first antiphon in matins for the dead: Dīrige, Domine, Deus meus, in cōnspectū tuō viam meam (“Guide, O Lord my God, my way by your sight”). Doublet of dirge.

parole.significato: Something that or someone who directs; a director or guide.
parole.testo: From Latin dīrigēns, present participle of dīrigō.

parole.significato: Mentioning a balancing or opposing fact to prevent the argument from being one-sided or unqualified.
parole.testo: From Latin dirimēns cōpulātiō (“separating connection”).

parole.significato: Serving to invalidate an attempted marriage.
parole.testo: From Latin dirimēns (“separating”).

parole.significato: disruption
parole.testo: From Latin diruptio, from dirumpere. See disrupt (adjective).

parole.significato: The change in the legal status of an area from forest to that of normal land, entailing the loss of forest laws.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin disafforestātiō (13th cent.), from the participial stem of Latin disafforestō. By surface analysis, disafforest + -ation.

parole.significato: To remove shoes or other footwear.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin discalceātus, perfect passive participle of and participial adjective from discalceō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of removing footwear.
parole.testo: From Latin discalceatus (“unshod”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a religious order that historically forswore the wearing of shoes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin discalceātus (“barefoot”) + -ed, rendering French déchaussé. By surface analysis, dis- + calced.

parole.significato: Stripped of flesh.
parole.testo: From Renaissance Latin discarnatus, alteration of Classical Latin dēcarnātus. Compare decarnate.

parole.significato: To yield, give up, depart or dissolve.
parole.testo: From Latin discedere, from dis- + cedere (“to yield”).

parole.significato: To debate; to discuss.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin disceptō.

parole.significato: Controversy; disputation; discussion.
parole.testo: Latin disceptātiō.

parole.significato: One who arbitrates or decides; a judge.
parole.testo: From Latin disceptātor.

parole.significato: To tear into pieces; to rend.
parole.testo: From Latin discerpō, from dis- + carpō (“to pluck”).

parole.significato: departure
parole.testo: Latin discessio, from discedere, discessum. See discede.

parole.significato: To cut apart; to cut into pieces.
parole.testo: From Latin discidere.

parole.significato: ungirded or loosely dressed
parole.testo: From Latin discinctus, past participle of discingere (“to ungird”), from dis- + cingere (“to gird”).

parole.significato: To divide or split (something).
parole.testo: From Latin discindo, from dis- + scindo (“to cut, split”).

parole.significato: A person who learns from another, especially one who then teaches others.
parole.testo: From Middle English disciple, discipul, from Old English discipul (“disciple, scholar”), from Latin discipulus (“pupil, learner”). Later influenced or superseded in Middle English by Old French deciple.

parole.significato: That can be instructed (by discipline); able to be taught.
parole.testo: From discipline + -able and from Latin disciplinabilis.

parole.significato: Having to do with discipline, or with the imposition of discipline.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin disciplinarius, from Latin disciplina (“instruction, teaching, field of study, habit”).

parole.significato: Synonym of discipline.
parole.testo: First attested in 1584; borrowed from Latin disciplīnātus, perfect passive participle of disciplīnō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To disclose, make known.
parole.testo: From Middle English discluden, from Latin disclūdō, disclūdere (“separate or keep apart”).

parole.significato: A shutting off; exclusion.
parole.testo: From Latin disclusio, from discludere, disclusum (“to separate”). See disclose.

parole.significato: To render unfit or unsuitable; to fail to treat well.
parole.testo: From Latin discommodatus, past participle of discommodare, from dis- + commodare (“to make fit, help”).

parole.significato: Cheerless, dreary.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin discōnsōlātus (“comfortless”), from dis- (“away”) + cōnsōlātus (“consoled”).

parole.significato: A lack of continuity, regularity or sequence; a break or gap.
parole.testo: From Late Latin discontinuitās, from discontinuus, equivalent to dis- + continuity.

parole.significato: Like a disk/disc
parole.testo: From Latin discus (“disk”). See disk.

parole.significato: An inconsistency between facts or sentiments.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin discrepantia, from discrepans, from discrepō, from crepō. By surface analysis, discrepant + -cy. See also discrepant.

parole.significato: Showing difference; inconsistent, dissimilar.
parole.testo: From Latin discrepāns, present participle of discrepō (“to differ in sound, differ, disagree”), from dis- (“apart”) + crepō (“to make a noise, crackle”).

parole.significato: Marking distinction or separation.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin discrētīvus. See discrete.

parole.significato: A visible dividing line where two structures come together.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin discrimen.

parole.significato: Involved in discrimination.
parole.testo: Latin discriminalis (“serving to divide”).

parole.significato: To make distinctions.
parole.testo: First attested in 1615; borrowed from Latin discrīminātus, perfect passive participle of discrīminō (“to divide, separate, distinguish”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from discrīmen (“a space between, division, separation, distinction”), from discernō (“to div

parole.significato: Discernment, the act of discriminating, discerning, distinguishing, noting or perceiving differences between things, wi…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin discrīminātiō, discrīminātiōnem, the action noun to discrīminō, discrīmināre (“distinguish”). Equivalent to discriminate + -ion. In English use from the 17th century.

parole.significato: hazardous; dangerous
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin discriminosus, from discrimen (“the dangerous, decisive moment”). See discriminate (adjective).

parole.significato: To torture (someone); to excruciate.
parole.testo: First attested in 1596; borrowed from Latin discruciātus, perfect passive participle of discruciō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: leaning; fitted for a reclining posture
parole.testo: From Latin discumbere, discubitum (“to lie down, recline at table”), from dis- + cumbere (“(in comparative) to lie down”).

parole.significato: To free from blame or the imputation of a fault; to exonerate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin disculpātus, perfect passive participle of disculpō (“to disculpate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dis- (“off”, denoting the ending of an action) + culpō (“to blame”), from culpa (“fault”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of disculp.

parole.significato: A reclining position at a meal table, as was apparently the manner in old times such as in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin discumbens, present participle of discumbere. See discubitory.

parole.significato: The action of hurriedly moving hither and thither.
parole.testo: From Latin discursiō, from discurrō (“to run to and fro”); compare the English discurre, discurrent, discursation, and discurse.

parole.significato: argumentation; ratiocination; discursive reasoning
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin discursus. Doublet of discourse.

parole.significato: A round plate-like object that is thrown for sport.
parole.testo: 1656. From Latin discus, from Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos, “disk, quoit, platter”). Doublet of dais, desk, disc, dish, disk, and diskos.

parole.significato: Serving to disperse morbid matter; discussive.
parole.testo: From Latin discutiens, the present participle of discutere. See discuss.

parole.significato: insanity; folly
parole.testo: From dis- + en- (from Latin in) + sanity.

parole.significato: Eloquent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin disertus or French disert.

parole.significato: To disperse; to scatter.
parole.testo: First attested in 1593; borrowed from Latin disgregātus, perfect passive participle of disgregō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Separation; scattering.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin disgregātiō, from dis- (“apart”) + grex (“flock”). The thermodynamics sense was introduced in 1862 by German physicist Rudolf Clausius in his formulation of what is now called the second law of thermodynamics.

parole.significato: To break apart; separate
parole.testo: From Latin disicio.

parole.significato: Scattered fragments, especially of written work.
parole.testo: Alteration of Horace’s Latin phrase disjecti membra poetae (“limbs of a dismembered poet”).

parole.significato: destruction; dispersion
parole.testo: From Latin disjicere, disjectum (“to throw asunder, disperse”), from dis- + jacere (“to throw”).

parole.significato: To discharge; to end the employment or service of.
parole.testo: Middle English, from Latin dimissus (“sent away, dismissed, banished”), perfect passive participle of dīmittō (“send away, dismiss”), from dis- + mittere (“to send”).

parole.significato: To spread out; to expand.
parole.testo: From Latin dispandere (“to spread out”), from dis- + pandere, pansum (“to spread out”).

parole.significato: To drive away or cause to vanish by scattering.
parole.testo: From Middle English dispelen, from Latin dispellere (“to disperse; to dispel”).

parole.significato: Granting dispensation.
parole.testo: Latin dispensativus, dispensatorius.

parole.significato: A distributor; someone who dispenses.
parole.testo: From Latin dispēnsātor.

parole.significato: Granting, or authorized to grant, dispensations.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dispēnsātōrius, and the noun dispēnsātōrium. Compare Latin dispēnsātor, dispēnsō and English dispense.

parole.significato: A female dispensator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dispēnsātrīx. By surface analysis, dispensator + -trix.

parole.significato: To sprinkle, scatter, or disperse.
parole.testo: From Latin dispergere. See disperse.

parole.significato: Lack of complacency or gratification; displeasure or dislike.
parole.testo: From Latin displacentia, for displicentia, from displicere (“to displease”), from dis- + placere (“to please”). See displease, and compare displeasance.

parole.significato: Discontent, dislike, dissatisfaction.
parole.testo: From Latin displicentia. See displacency.

parole.significato: To burst with a loud bang; to explode.
parole.testo: From Latin displōdō, from dis- + plaudō.

parole.significato: A double spondee; a metrical foot consisting of four long syllables.
parole.testo: Latin dispondeus, from Ancient Greek [Term?].

parole.significato: To deposit.
parole.testo: From Latin dispositus, past participle of dispōnō.

parole.significato: One of the five canons of classical rhetoric: the organization of arguments.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dispositio. Doublet of disposition.

parole.significato: A disposer.
parole.testo: From Latin dispositor. See disposition.

parole.significato: To expunge; to erase.
parole.testo: From Latin dispungere.

parole.significato: Of opinions, propositions or questions, subject to dispute; not settled.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin disputābilis. By surface analysis, dispute + -able.

parole.significato: Tending to dispute.
parole.testo: From Latin disputativus (“pertaining to a dispute”).

parole.significato: One who takes part in a dispute; a disputant or debater.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin disputātor.

parole.significato: To throw into confusion or disorder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin disruptus, from disrumpo, commonly dirumpo (“to break or burst asunder”), from dis-, di- (“apart, asunder”) + rumpo (“to break”).

parole.significato: An interruption to the regular flow or sequence of something.
parole.testo: From Latin disruptionem, from disrumpere. By surface analysis, disrupt + -ion.

parole.significato: To put (someone) down, or show disrespect by the use of insulting language or dismissive behaviour.
parole.testo: Originated in Jamaican English or African American Vernacular English, probably originally a clipping of disrespect or disparage, both from the prefix dis-, ultimately from Latin dis-.

parole.significato: To study an animal's anatomy by cutting it apart; to perform a necropsy or an autopsy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dissectus past participle of dissecare (“to cut asunder, cut up”), from dis- (“asunder”) + secare (“to cut”); see section.

parole.significato: The act of dissecting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dissectiōnem, perhaps via Middle French dissection. By surface analysis, dissect + -ion.

parole.significato: Capable of being disseminated.
parole.testo: From Latin dissēminābilis.

parole.significato: To sow and scatter principles, ideas, opinions, etc, or concrete things, for growth and propagation, like seeds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dissēminātus, the perfect passive participle of dissēminō (“to broadcast, disseminate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from dis- (“asunder, in all directions”) + sēminō (“to plant, sow”), from sēmen (“seed”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See also Middle English dissemina

parole.significato: The act of disseminating, or the state of being disseminated; diffusion for propagation and permanence; a scattering or…
parole.testo: From Latin dissēminātiō, from dissēmināre [from dis- (“in all directions”) + sēmināre (“to plant or propagate”) (itself from sēmen (“seed”))] + -tiō. By surface analysis, disseminate + -tion.

parole.significato: One who, or that which, disseminates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dissēminātor. By surface analysis, disseminate + -or.

parole.significato: Disagreement, especially when widespread.
parole.testo: From Latin dissēnsus (“disagreement, quarrel; dissension, conflict”); or a blend of dissent + consensus.

parole.significato: To disagree; to withhold assent. Construed with from (or, formerly, to).
parole.testo: From Middle English dissenten, from Latin dissentiō, dissentīre (“to differ in sentiments, disagree, be at odds, contradict, quarrel”), from dis- + sentiō, sentīre (see sense).

parole.significato: disagreeing; contrary; differing
parole.testo: From Latin dissentaneus. See dissent.

parole.significato: A dissenter.
parole.testo: From the Latin dissentiēns (“dissenting”).

parole.significato: partition (in an organ); septum
parole.testo: From Latin dissepimentum (“a partition”).

parole.significato: To discourse or dispute; to discuss.
parole.testo: From Latin dissertus, past participle of disserere, from dis- + serere (“to join, connect”). Compare French disserter. See series; doublet of dissertate.

parole.significato: To make a dissertation; to discourse.
parole.testo: First attested in 1766; borrowed from Latin dissertātus, perfect passive participle of dissertō (“to argue, discuss”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), frequentative of disserō. Doublet of dissert.

parole.significato: A formal exposition of a subject, especially a research paper that students write in order to complete the requirements…
parole.testo: From Latin dissertātiō, from dissertō.

parole.significato: Someone who writes or performs a dissertation or speech.
parole.testo: Latin: compare French dissertateur.

parole.significato: The state of being dissident; dissent
parole.testo: From Latin dissideō (“disagree”, literally “sit apart”), from dis- + sedeō (“sit”).

parole.significato: In a manner that disagrees; dissenting; discordant.
parole.testo: From Latin dissidēns, present participle of dissideō (“to sit apart; to disagree”), from dis- (“asunder, apart, in two”) + sedeō (“to sit”).

parole.significato: Forcefully breaking apart or bursting open (or primed to do so); dehiscing explosively.
parole.testo: From Latin dissiliens, dissilientis, present participle of dissilire (“to leap asunder”): dis- + salire (“to leap”).

parole.significato: To make dissimilar or unlike.
parole.testo: First attested in 1841; borrowed from Medieval Latin dissimilātus, perfect passive participle of dissimilō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), hypercorrected form of Classical Latin dissimulō, from dis- + simulō, from similis (“similar, the same as”); the vocalism was perhaps influenced by assimilate,

parole.significato: Comparison or illustration by contraries.
parole.testo: From Latin dissimile, neuter dissimilis (“unlike”).

parole.significato: The quality of being dissimilar or different; lack of resemblance.
parole.testo: From Middle English dissimilitude, from Latin dissimilitūdō, from dissimilis (“unlike”). By surface analysis, dissimilar + -itude or dis- + similitude.

parole.significato: Dissimulation; dissembling.
parole.testo: From Latin dissimulāntia.

parole.significato: To practise deception by concealment or omission, or by feigning a false appearance; to dissemble.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dissimulaten, dissimilaten, from Latin dissimulātus + -en (“verb-forming suffix”), perfect passive participle of dissimulō (“to conceal, to pretend, to neglect”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dissimilis (“unlike”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Compare the obsolet

parole.significato: One who dissimulates.
parole.testo: From Latin dissimulātor, from dissimulāre (“to conceal, to pretend, to neglect”) + -tor (“-er: forming agent nouns”), from dissimilis (“unlike”) + -āre (“forming verbs”). Equivalent to dissimulate + -or.

parole.significato: Capable of being dissipated or dispersed.
parole.testo: From Latin dissipābilis, from dissipāre, also written dissupare (“to scatter, disperse, demolish, destroy, squander, dissipate”), from dis- (“apart”) + supare (“to throw”).

parole.significato: To drive away, disperse.
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1425, in Middle English, the adjective from 1606 to 1765; from Middle English dissipaten, from Latin dissipātus, perfect passive participle of dissipō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), also written dissupō (“to scatter, disperse, demo

parole.significato: The act of dissipating or dispersing; a state of dispersion or separation; dispersion; waste.
parole.testo: From Middle English dissipacion, dissipacioun, from Late Latin dissipātiō. Morphologically dissipate + -ion.

parole.significato: Lying or situated apart.
parole.testo: From Latin dissitus.

parole.significato: Able to be dissociated, divided or separated.
parole.testo: From Latin dissociābilis, from dissociare: compare English dissociable. See dissociate.

parole.significato: Which can be dissolved or disintegrated.
parole.testo: From Latin dissolubilis, itself from dissolvere (“to dissolve”) (from dis- (“apart”) + solvere (“to solve”) + -bilis (“-able”).

parole.significato: Unrestrained by morality.
parole.testo: From Middle English dissolute, from Latin dissolutus.

parole.significato: To terminate a union of multiple members actively, as by disbanding.
parole.testo: Recorded since c. 1374 (displacing Old English toliesan) as Middle English dissolven, from Latin dissolvere (“to loosen up, break apart”) but with the sense from Anglo-Norman dissoldre (variant of Old French dissoudre), itself from dis- (“apart”) + solvere (“to loose, loosen”). By surface analysis,

parole.significato: Capable of dissolution into a fluid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dissolvēns.

parole.significato: Immoderate, excessive.
parole.testo: First attested in 1398, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English distemperat(e), borrowed from Medieval Latin distemperātus (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from dis- + temperātus, perfect passive participle of temperō (“to temperate oneself, show restraint”).

parole.significato: To extend or expand, as from internal pressure; to swell
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin distendō.

parole.significato: distended
parole.testo: From Latin distentus.

parole.significato: To banish or drive from a country.
parole.testo: From Latin dis- + terra (“earth, country”); compare Spanish and Portuguese desterrar.

parole.significato: separated, divided
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin disterminātus, perfect passive participle of disterminō (“to divide, separate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: separation by bounds
parole.testo: Latin disterminatio.

parole.significato: A couplet, a two-line stanza making complete sense.
parole.testo: From Latin distichon (“a poem of two verses, a distich consisting of a hexameter and a pentameter”), from Ancient Greek δίστιχον (dístikhon).

parole.significato: Distinguishing, used to or enabling the distinguishing of some thing.
parole.testo: From Latin distinctus, perfect passive participle of distinguere (to push apart, to divide; see distinct) + -ive (forming adjectives signifying relation or tendency to). Cognate with French distinctif and Medieval Latin distinctivus.

parole.significato: A distinction.
parole.testo: From Latin distinguō (“to distinguish”).

parole.significato: In mosquitoes, the distal segment of the gonopods.
parole.testo: From disti-, from Latin distare (“to stand apart”) + Ancient Greek στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”). By surface analysis, disti- + -style + Latin -us.

parole.significato: To bring something out of shape, to misshape.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin distortum, past participle of distorqueō (“to twist, torture, distort”).

parole.significato: An act of distorting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin distortio, distortionis, from distortus.

parole.significato: The zygomaticus minor muscle.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: To divert the attention of.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin distractus, from distrahō (“to pull apart”), from dis- + trahō (“to pull”).

parole.significato: To divide into portions and dispense.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Latin distributus, past participle of distribuere (“to divide, distribute”), from dis- (“apart”) + tribuere (“to give, impart”); see tribute.

parole.significato: Sudden display; flash; glitter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin districtio (“a stretching out”).

parole.significato: A writ commanding the sheriff to distrain a person by his goods or chattels, to compel a compliance with something requ…
parole.testo: Latin, that you distrain, from distringere. See distrain.

parole.significato: disturbance
parole.testo: Latin disturbatio.

parole.significato: The act of making rich; enrichment.
parole.testo: From Latin ditare (“to enrich”), from dis, ditis, same as dives (“rich”).

parole.testo: From Latin dithyrambus, from Ancient Greek δῑθύραμβος (dīthúrambos). According to the American Heritage Dictionary, it is of non-Indo-European origin (Pre-Greek substrate, Illyrian/Phrygian), related to θρίαμβος (thríambos) and ἴαμβος (íambos). parole.significato: Dominion; rule or power.
parole.testo: From Latin ditiō, diciō. Compare French dition.

parole.significato: A double trochee; a metrical foot made up of two trochees.
parole.testo: Latin ditrochaeus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Excessive production of urine; polyuria.
parole.testo: From New Latin diūrēsis, from Ancient Greek διουρέω (diouréō, “to urinate”) + -σις (-sis). Morphologically, δῐουρέω (dĭouréō) can be analysed as δι- (di-) + οὐρέω (ouréō).

parole.significato: Happening or occurring during daylight, or primarily active during that time.
parole.testo: From Latin diurnālis, from diēs (“day”). Doublet of journal.

parole.significato: durable, long-lasting
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin diūturnus, + -al.

parole.significato: Long duration; lastingness.
parole.testo: From Latin diuturnitatem.

parole.significato: To wander about.
parole.testo: First attested in 1599; borrowed from Latin dīvagātus, perfect active participle of dīvagor (“to wander here and there”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin dis- (“in different direction”) + vagor (“to wander”). Cognate with French divaguer.

parole.significato: Straying off from a course or way.
parole.testo: Nominalization of divagate (from the Latin verb divagare) + -ion (from the Latin suffix -io).

parole.significato: To spread apart; to (cause to) diverge or branch off.
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1623, the adjective in 1788; borrowed from Latin dīvāricātus, perfect passive participle of dīvāricō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from dis- + vāricō (“to straddle, to stretch (the legs) apart”), from vāricus (“straddling”).

parole.significato: A divergence of opinion.
parole.testo: Unattested Latin *dīvāricātiō, from the verb dīvāricō (“to spread out”), from di- + vāricō (“to spread apart”).

parole.significato: To rend apart.
parole.testo: From Latin dīvellere.

parole.significato: Causing to break up or separate
parole.testo: From Latin divellens.

parole.significato: To detach, rip apart.
parole.testo: First attested in 1638; borrowed from Latin dīvellicātus, perfect passive participle of dīvellicō (“to pluck asunder”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dis- + vellicō, from vellō (“to pluck”).

parole.significato: A proverb or set phrase.
parole.testo: Latin diverbium (“the colloquial part of a comedy, dialogue”).

parole.significato: To run apart; to separate; to tend into different directions.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dīvergō (“bend away from, go in a different direction”), from Latin dī- + vergō (“bend”).

parole.significato: Synonym of divergence.
parole.testo: From New Latin divergentia; by surface analysis, diverge + -ency.

parole.significato: Growing further apart; diverging.
parole.testo: From Latin dis- (“apart”) + vergere (“to turn”) + the adjectival suffix -ent.

parole.significato: The act, or the result, of diversifying.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin diversificatiō, from diversificātus, past participle of diversificō (“diversify”), from Latin diversus (“turned in different ways”) + faciō (“make, do”). By surface analysis, diverse + -ification.

parole.significato: Of different or varying forms.
parole.testo: From Latin diversus (“diverse”) + -form.

parole.significato: A tactic used to draw attention away from the real threat or action.
parole.testo: From Middle English diversion, dyversioun, from Medieval Latin diversiō, from Latin divertō (“to divert”); see divert.

parole.significato: Desiring difference or argument.
parole.testo: Latin diversus (“diverse, different”) + volent-, present participial stem of vōlō (“I wish”).

parole.significato: A wayside inn.
parole.testo: From Latin diversorium, deversorium (“an inn or lodging”).

parole.significato: A turning; a byway.
parole.testo: From Latin diverticulum, deverticulum (“a bypath”), from divertere (“to turn away”).

parole.significato: A small out-pouching of an organ wall such as the large intestine or urinary bladder.
parole.testo: From Latin dīverticulum, alternative form of dēverticulum (“byroad; deviation”), from dēvertō (“turn away, turn aside”).

parole.significato: A rich person who lives in luxury.
parole.testo: From Latin dives (“rich man”).

parole.significato: To split or separate (something) into two or more parts.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Middle English dividen, from Latin dīvidere (“to divide”). Displaced native Old English tōdǣlan related to English deal which formerly meant a “portion” or “part” of something.

parole.significato: In order to rule securely, do not allow alliances between your enemies.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin dīvide et imperā.

parole.significato: Synonym of divide and conquer.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin divide et impera.

parole.significato: Division.
parole.testo: From Latin dīvidēns, present participle of dīvidō (“to divide”). Perhaps modelled on Italian dividenza.

parole.significato: Separate, distinct.
parole.testo: From Latin dividuus.

parole.significato: divided; dividual
parole.testo: From Latin dividuus (“divisible, divided”), from dividere.

parole.significato: One who practices or claims to practice divination; a diviner.
parole.testo: From Latin dīvīnātor. See divination.

parole.significato: One who foretells the future.
parole.testo: From Middle English divinour, from Latin dīvīnātor (“diviner; fortune-teller; soothsayer”), from dīvīnāre (“to foresee, to foretell”). Doublet of divinator. Equivalent to divine + -er.

parole.significato: To render divine; to deify.
parole.testo: From Latin divinus (“divine”) + -fy.

parole.significato: Separately.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dīvīsim (“separately”).

parole.significato: A category in the classification of organisms, ranking below regnum and above classis.
parole.testo: From Latin dīvīsiō (“division”). Doublet of division.

parole.significato: Having a quality that divides or separates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dīvīsīvus.

parole.significato: The condition of being rich.
parole.testo: From Latin dives (“rich”) + -ism.

parole.significato: To divulge.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested circa 1440, in Middle English, the verb in 1530; inherited from Middle English divulgat(e) (“divulgated”, used participially), borrowed from Latin dīvulgātus, perfect passive participle of dīvulgāre, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of divulging or publishing; publication.
parole.testo: From Latin dīvulgātiō (“wide publication”). Compare French divulgation. By surface analysis, di- + vulgation.

parole.significato: To make public or known; to communicate to the public; to tell (information, especially a secret) so that it may become…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English divulgen, from Latin dīvulgō + -en (verb-forming suffix), from dī- (“widely”) + vulgō (“to make known, announce; to publish”).

parole.significato: To pull apart forcibly.
parole.testo: From Latin dīvulsus (“torn apart”), from Latin dīvellō (“to tear apart”).

parole.significato: An utterance signifying the end of a speech.
parole.testo: From Latin dixi (“I have spoken.”).

parole.significato: A syllable used in solfège to represent the first and eighth tonic of a major scale.
parole.testo: Coined by Italian musicologist Giovanni Battista Doni in 1635 as an easier-to-sing open-syllable revision to the solmization ut of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin Dominus (“The Lord”) (speculated by some to be an ulterior abbreviation of Giovanni Battista Doni) on the pattern of ot

parole.significato: To perform no actions which will be injurious or in any way unfavorable to another person, regardless of whether one do…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin prīmum nōn nocēre.

parole.significato: Instructive; that teaches.
parole.testo: From Latin docēns, present participle of doceō (“to teach”). In the meaning of a university grade, as used in some Central European countries, it is clipped version of private docent, privat-docent, from German Privatdozent, from German Dozent.

parole.significato: Of or related to docetism or docetists, believing that Jesus was fully divine and only appeared to be human and to suff…
parole.testo: From Docetae + -ic, from Late Latin Docetae, from Koine Greek Δοκηταί (Dokētaí), from Ancient Greek δοκεῖν (dokeîn, “to seem, to appear”).

parole.significato: In a docetic manner; in terms of docetism.
parole.testo: From docetic + -ally, from Late Latin Docetae + -ic, from Koine Greek Δοκηταί (Dokētaí), from Ancient Greek δοκεῖν (dokeîn, “to seem, to appear”).

parole.significato: The belief that Jesus was fully divine and only appeared or pretended to be human and to suffer.
parole.testo: From Docetae + -ism, from Late Latin Docetae, from Koine Greek Δοκηταί (Dokētaí) coined 197–203 CE by Serapion of Antioch, from Ancient Greek δοκεῖν (dokeîn, “to seem, to appear”). Related to latter component of synecdoche.

parole.significato: One who believes in docetism.
parole.testo: From Docetae + -ist, from Late Latin Docetae, from Koine Greek Δοκηταί (Dokētaí), from Ancient Greek δοκεῖν (dokeîn, “to seem, to appear”).

parole.significato: Synonym of docetic, of or related to docetism or docetists.
parole.testo: From docetist + -ic, from Late Latin Docetae + -ic, from Koine Greek Δοκηταί (Dokētaí), from Ancient Greek δοκεῖν (dokeîn, “to seem, to appear”). Equivalent to Docetae + -istic.

parole.significato: To explain or interpret docetically.
parole.testo: From Docetae + -ize, from Late Latin Docetae, from Koine Greek Δοκηταί (Dokētaí), from Ancient Greek δοκεῖν (dokeîn, “to seem, to appear”).

parole.significato: Easily taught, tamed or managed; teachable.

parole.significato: Docile, amenable to order.

parole.significato: Speaking learnedly.

parole.significato: A terminal research degree and one of the highest doctorates awarded by a university.

parole.significato: Relating to a doctorate.

parole.significato: A postgraduate aiming to receive a doctorate; a Ph.D. student.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin doctōrandus. Doublet of doctorandus.

parole.significato: The title of a female doctor, chiefly a physician.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin doctrīx (“a female teacher”), the female equivalent of doctor, by analogy with English Doctor.

parole.significato: A female doctor, chiefly a physician.
parole.testo: From Middle English doctrice, from Latin doctrīx (“a female teacher”), feminine form of doctor (“a teacher”). parole.significato: Something transposed from a thought to a document; the written account of an idea.
parole.testo: From document + -ation or Medieval Latin documentātio.

parole.significato: Of, from, or related to Dodona, a town and religious shrine of ancient Greece, or its modern counterpart Dodoni.
parole.testo: From Latin Dodonaeus + -an.

parole.significato: A bronze coin of the Roman Republic, worth three quarters of an as.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dōdrāns.

parole.significato: To treat something as dogma.
parole.testo: From Late Latin dogmatizō.

parole.significato: The unit of measurement for pain.

parole.significato: An ancient axe or hatchet.

parole.significato: Shaped like the head of an axe or hatchet.
parole.testo: From Latin dolabra (“mattock”) (from dolo (“hew”)) + -iform.

parole.significato: Shaped like a barrel or cask.
parole.testo: From Latin dolium (“large jar”) + -form.

parole.significato: Any member of the family Doliolidae of pelagic tunicates.
parole.testo: From the genus name Doliolum + -id, from Latin doliolum.

parole.significato: A doliolid tunicate.
parole.testo: From the genus name Doliolum, from Latin doliolum.

parole.significato: A large earthenware vessel used for the storage and transportation of goods (especially wine an olive oil) in the ancie…

parole.significato: Producing pain.
parole.testo: Latin dolōrifer, from dolor (“sorrow, pain”)

parole.significato: Grievous and sorrowful.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dolōrōsus (“painful, sorrowful”); compare doloroso and dolorous.

parole.significato: Deceitful, with hidden malice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dolosus; compare dolus.

parole.significato: Evil intent: malice or fraud.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dolus (“deceit, trickery”); akin to Ancient Greek δόλος (dólos, “bait, ruse”). Compare dolose, dolosity.

parole.significato: special intent of an offence
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin dolus speciālis (“specific (evil) intent”).

parole.significato: Capable of being tamed; tameable, domesticable.
parole.testo: From Late Latin domābilis (“tameable”), from domāre (“to tame”), present infinitive of domō (“to break in, to tame”), from Proto-Italic *domaō (“to tame”), from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂- (“to domesticate, to tame”); compare Old French domable.

parole.significato: Of or relating to an astrological house.
parole.testo: From Latin domus (“house”).

parole.significato: A chamber produced by a plant in which insects, mites, or fungi live.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin dōmatium, from Ancient Greek δωμάτιον (dōmátion, “chamber, bedroom”), diminutive of δῶμα (dôma, “house, dwelling place of animals”); akin to δόμος (dómos, “house”).

parole.significato: Domestic.
parole.testo: From Latin domesticus + -al.

parole.significato: An animal or plant that has been domesticated.
parole.testo: First attested in 1860; borrowed from Medieval Latin domesticātus (“domesticated”), see Etymology 1 and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The head of a nunnery.
parole.testo: From Latin domina (“mistress”). Doublet of dame and donna.

parole.significato: To govern, rule or control by superior authority or power.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dominātus, perfect active participle of dominor (“to rule, have dominion”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dominus (“lord, master”) + -or (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The late period of the Roman Empire, following the principate, during which the emperor's rule became more explicitly a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dominātus (“rule, command”), from dominus + -ātus, see -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, a regime handled by people of such rank).

parole.significato: A dominating woman; a female dominator.
parole.testo: From Latin dominātrīx. By surface analysis, dominate + -trix.

parole.significato: Lord; master.
parole.testo: From Latin dominus. Doublet of dom, dominie, dominus, and don.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Jesus Christ as Lord.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dominical (“(adjective) of or pertaining to the Lord’s day or Sunday; (noun) a book containing the liturgy for Sunday (?)”), borrowed from Medieval Latin dominicālis (“of or pertaining to Sunday, dominical”), from Latin dominicus (“of or belonging to a lord or master; (

parole.significato: A member of the religious order founded by Saint Dominic.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dominicānus. By surface analysis, Dominic + -an.

parole.significato: The ownership of a thing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dominium. Doublet of demesne and domain.

parole.significato: master; sir; a title of respect formerly applied to a knight or clergyman, and sometimes to the lord of a manor, castle…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dominus (“master”). Doublet of dan, dom, domine, dominie, and don.

parole.significato: of a domestic nature.
parole.testo: From Latin domum(?) and natura, therefore meaning 'of a domestic nature'.

parole.significato: Someone's house or home.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of domicile, ultimately from Latin domus (“house, home”).

parole.significato: Robotic technology for use in the home.
parole.testo: Contraction of domestic robotics. Alternatively, from Latin domus (“home”) and robotics.

parole.significato: A farmstead with its people, plants and animals, considered as a unit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin domus. Doublet of dome and duomo.

parole.significato: A university professor, particularly one at Oxford or Cambridge.
parole.testo: From Latin dominus (“lord, head of household”), akin to Italian don, Sicilian don, Spanish don; from domus (“house”). Doublet of dom, domine, dominie, and dominus.

parole.significato: Capable of being donated or given.
parole.testo: From Latin donabilis, from donare (“to donate”).

parole.significato: An object given or donated to a sacred use.
parole.testo: From Latin donarium, from donare.

parole.significato: To make a donation; to give away something of value to support or contribute towards a cause or for the benefit of anot…
parole.testo: Circa 1845, back-formation from donation on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), chiefly found in American English. Ultimately from Latin dōnāre (“to give”).

parole.significato: a lifetime gift, a present or future gift given during the donor's lifetime.
parole.testo: From Latin dōnātiō (“donation, gift”) + inter (“between”) + vīvōs (“living”). Literally a gift between the living.

parole.testo: From Latin dōnātiō (“donation, gift”) + mortis (“death”) + causā (“on account of”, postposition). Literally a gift on account of (one's) death.

parole.significato: One of a group of Christians in fourth-century North Africa who broke away as a group after opposing the appointment of…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Dōnātista, from Dōnātus, one of their leaders.

parole.significato: Being or relating to a donation.
parole.testo: From Latin dōnātīvum (“a gratuity”), from dōnō (“to give [a present]”), from dōnum (“gift”).

parole.significato: Donor, one who donates.
parole.testo: From Middle English donatour, from Latin dōnātor and Old French; equivalent to donate + -or.

parole.significato: Female donator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dōnātrix. By surface analysis, donate + -trix.

parole.significato: A canelike grass of southern Europe (Arundo donax), used for fishing rods, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin donax (“reed; also a marine fish”), from Ancient Greek δόναξ (dónax).

parole.significato: Bearing or yielding gifts.
parole.testo: See Latin donum (“gift”) + -fer (“bearing”).

parole.significato: A person with poor judgment and taste; a foolish or silly person.

parole.significato: Gazella dorcas, a gazelle native to northern Africa and western Asia.
parole.testo: From Latin dorcas from Ancient Greek δορκάς (dorkás) + gazelle.

parole.significato: A silly or foolish person; a dork.

parole.significato: A form of the letter e modified by the addition of a diacritical “tail”: ⟨ę⟩.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ē caudāta (literally “tailed e”).

parole.significato: "out of many, one" or "from many, one" (alternatively translated as "one out of many" or "one from many”)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ē plūribus ūnum.

parole.significato: Used to form terms with the sense of something being absent, being removed, or moving outward.
parole.testo: From Latin ē-.

parole.significato: For emergency purposes.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of emergency.

parole.significato: Used to prefix product names, to indicate an electrified or all-electric variant of the product, particularly cars.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of electric or electrical.

parole.significato: An initialism used to introduce an illustrative example or short list of examples: for the sake of an example; for exam…
parole.testo: The adverb is a terser form of ex. gr., both abbreviating Latin exemplī grātiā (“for the sake of an example”); e.g. was also used as an abbreviation in Latin. The noun is derived from the adverb.

parole.significato: A hard, dense, deep black wood from various subtropical and tropical trees, especially of the genus Diospyros.
parole.testo: From earlier heben, hebeny, from Middle English ebenif, hebenyf (influenced by Late Latin hebeninus), from Ecclesiastical Latin ebenius (“of ebony”), from Latin hebenus (“ebon tree”), from Ancient Greek ἔβενος (ébenos), from Egyptian hbnj, U13:n-Z4:M3

parole.significato: Having no bracts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ebracteatus.

parole.significato: Having no bracteoles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ebracteolatus.

parole.significato: Drunk; intoxicated.
parole.testo: From Latin ebrius (“drunk”).
