parole.significato: Having a tendency towards alcohol abuse.
parole.testo: From Latin ēbrius (“drunk”).

parole.significato: A boiling or bubbling up; an ebullition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēbullientem + English -ence (suffix meaning ‘having the state or condition of’). Ēbullientem is the accusative feminine or masculine singular of ēbulliēns (“boiling”), the present participle of ēbulliō (“to boil”) (from ē- (prefix meaning ‘out, away’) + bulliō (“to bubble; to boi

parole.significato: Enthusiastic; high-spirited.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Latin ēbulliēns, present participle of ēbulliō (“to boil”), from bulliō (“to bubble up”) (English boil). Compare bubbling, bubbly, and perky, which use a similar metaphor.

parole.significato: An instrument used to measure the boiling point of liquids
parole.testo: From Latin ēbullīre + -scope.

parole.significato: the measurement of the boiling point of liquids
parole.testo: From Latin ēbulliō + -scopy.

parole.significato: To undergo eburnation.
parole.testo: From Latin eburnus (“of ivory”), from ebur (“ivory”).

parole.significato: A degenerative process of bone, occurring at sites of articular cartilage erosion and commonly found in patients with o…
parole.testo: From Latin eburnus (“of ivory”), from ebur (“ivory”). By surface analysis, eburnate + -ion.

parole.significato: Made of ivory.
parole.testo: Latin eburneus

parole.significato: The conversion of certain substances, such as pulp or bone, into ivory-like substance.
parole.testo: From Latin eburnus (“of ivory”), from ebur (“ivory”), + -ification.

parole.significato: Like ivory.
parole.testo: From Latin eburnus.

parole.significato: A dental condition characterized by the increased density, hardening, and polishing of exposed dentin that represents a…
parole.testo: From Latin eburnus (“of ivory”), from ebur (“ivory”), + -itis.

parole.significato: an interjection used to draw attention to something or someone; behold!
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ecce.

parole.significato: A picture representing Jesus Christ wearing a crown of thorns, before his crucifixion.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ecce homō̆ (“behold the man!”). See John 19:5 in the Bible.

parole.significato: The quality of being eccentric or odd; any eccentric behaviour.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin eccentricitās. By surface analysis, eccentric + -ity.

parole.significato: A skin discoloration caused by bleeding underneath the skin, especially one that is remote from a site of trauma or cau…
parole.testo: From New Latin ecchymōsis, from Ancient Greek ἐκχύμωσις (ekkhúmōsis), from ἐκχέω (ekkhéō, “I pour out”), from ἐκ- (ek-, “out”) + χέω (khéō, “I pour”).

parole.significato: The public legislative assembly of the Athenians.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía). Doublet of Eccles.

parole.significato: An official of the Eastern Church, equivalent to a sacristan in the Western Church.
parole.testo: Latin ecclesiarcha, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A member of the Athenian ecclesia (public legislative assembly).
parole.testo: From Middle English ecclesiaste, from Latin ecclēsiastēs, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησιαστής (ekklēsiastḗs). By surface analysis, ecclesia + -ast.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the church; ecclesiastical.
parole.testo: From Middle English ecclesyastyke, from Late Latin ecclēsiasticus (“of the church”), from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησιαστικός (ekklēsiastikós). By surface analysis, ecclesiast + -ic. Doublet of Ecclesiasticus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the church.
parole.testo: From Middle English ecclesiasticall, ecclesiasticalle, from Latin ecclēsiasticus + -al. By surface analysis, ecclesiastic + -al or ecclesiast + -ical.

parole.significato: church
parole.testo: From Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía), + -o-.

parole.significato: Any of several plants, of genus Echinacea, having pinkish-purple flowers.
parole.testo: From scientific Latin Echinacea, from Ancient Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos, “hedgehog”, because of the soft "spines" in the centre of the flower) + translingual -acea.

parole.significato: prickly; bristly
parole.testo: From Latin echinātus.

parole.significato: Having small spines or similar projections
parole.testo: From Latin echinulus (“little hedgehog”).

parole.significato: Resembling small spines.
parole.testo: From Latin echinus (“hedgehog”), + -form.

parole.significato: A sea urchin.
parole.testo: From Latin echīnus (“hedgehog; sea urchin”), from Ancient Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos).

parole.significato: Of a sound or sound waves: to reflect off a surface and return; to reverberate or resound.
parole.testo: From Middle English eccho, ecco, echo, ekko, from Medieval Latin ēccō, from Latin ēchō, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ), from ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound”). Possibly from the same Proto-Indo-European root as sough.

parole.significato: A complication of pregnancy characterized by seizures and coma due to hypertension.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin eclampsia, from French éclampsie, from Ancient Greek ἔκλᾰμψῐς (éklămpsĭs, “sudden development, violent onset”, literally “brightness”), from ἐκλᾰ́μπω (eklắmpō, “to shine or beam forth; to burst forth violently”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, nominal suffix).

parole.significato: The great circle on the celestial sphere that is the mean apparent path of the sun as viewed from the earth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin eclīptica. So named because an eclipse can occur only when the Moon lies on this plane.

parole.significato: Relating to an eclipse or the ecliptic.
parole.testo: From Middle English ecliptik, from Latin eclīpticus, from Ancient Greek ἐκλειπτικός (ekleiptikós).

parole.significato: A pastoral poem, often in the form of a shepherd's monologue or a dialogue between shepherds.
parole.testo: From Middle English eclog, from Latin ecloga, from Ancient Greek ἐκλογή (eklogḗ, “selection”).

parole.significato: Having no ribs or nerves.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ecostatus, ecostata.

parole.significato: Not cribellate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ecribellatus, ecribellata; see cribellate.

parole.significato: A woman perceived to have a highly sensitive emotional state, or prone to quasi-mystical trances.
parole.testo: From New Latin ecstatica, from Ancient Greek ἐκστατικός (ekstatikós).

parole.significato: Loose, pigmented connective tissue that forms the outer layer of the choroid
parole.testo: From ecto- + Latin choroidea.

parole.significato: The condition where an organ or other body part has an abnormal position.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin ectopia, derived from Ancient Greek ἔκτοπος (éktopos, “away from a place”), from ἐκ- (ek-) + τόπος (tópos). By surface analysis, ec- + -topia.

parole.significato: The displacement or malposition of the eye's lens from its normal location.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Ecumenical.
parole.testo: From Latin oecūmenicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκουμενικός (oikoumenikós, “concerning ἡ οἰκουμένη (hē oikouménē, “the inhabited (earth)”)”, “the whole (known) world”). Cognate with French œcuménique. By surface analysis, ecumene + -ic.

parole.significato: A church council to which bishops from the entire world are invited, held by Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Christ…
parole.testo: Calque of Ecclesiastical Latin oecūmenicum concilium.

parole.significato: A non-contagious acute or chronic inflammation of the skin, characterized by redness, itching, and the outbreak of oozi…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin eczema, from Ancient Greek ἔκζεμᾰ (ékzemă, “cutaneous eruption”), from ἐκζέω (ekzéō, “to boil out, break out”) + -μᾰ (-mă, nominal suffix).

parole.significato: Having an insatiable appetite; voracious; ravenous; piggish.
parole.testo: From Latin edā(c) (“gluttonous, greedy”) (from edō (“to eat”)) + -ious (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: The state of being edacious; huge capacity for eating; greediness; voracity; rapacity.
parole.testo: From Latin edācitās (whence -acity), from edāx, from edō (“eat”).

parole.significato: Published by.
parole.testo: Short for Latin ediderunt (“they have published”).

parole.significato: An excessive accumulation of serum in tissue spaces or a body cavity.
parole.testo: From New Latin oedēma, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”), from οἰδέω (oidéō, “I swell”).

parole.significato: Lacking teeth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin edentatus.

parole.significato: The condition of lacking some or all teeth; toothlessness.
parole.testo: From Latin ēdentulus + -ism.

parole.significato: Toothless.
parole.testo: Latin edentulus, which is in turn derived from the prefix e-, meaning "without", and the word dens, meaning "tooth."

parole.significato: Of or from Edessa.
parole.testo: From Latin Edessēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἐδεσσηνός (Edessēnós). By surface analysis, Edessa + -ene.

parole.significato: Capable of being eaten without harm; suitable for consumption; innocuous to humans.
parole.testo: From Late Latin edibilis, from Latin edō (“eat”). Doublet of eatable.

parole.significato: A proclamation of law or other authoritative command.
parole.testo: From Middle English edycte, borrowed from Latin edictum; earlier form edit, from Old French edit, from the same Latin word.

parole.significato: building; constructing
parole.testo: From Latin aedificans, aedificantis, present participle of aedificare. See edify.

parole.significato: to build
parole.testo: From Latin aedifico.

parole.significato: Pertaining to an edifice; structural.
parole.testo: Latin aedificialis.

parole.significato: The first printed edition of a work previously only published in manuscript form.
parole.testo: From New Latin ēditiō prīnceps (“first edition”), 1800s.

parole.significato: A person who edits or makes changes to documents.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ēditor, from Late Latin ēditor, from ēditus, perfect passive participle of ēdō (“give out, put forth, publish”).

parole.significato: A female editor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ēditrīx. By surface analysis, edit + -trix.

parole.significato: A Thracian people who dwelt mostly between the Nestus and the Strymon rivers in southern Thrace, but also once dwelt we…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Ēdōnī, from Ancient Greek Ἠδωνοί (Ēdōnoí). Doublet of hedon.

parole.significato: Capable of being educated.
parole.testo: From New Latin educabilis, from Latin ēducō (“to educate”) + -ābilis; see educate.

parole.significato: Someone who is to be, or is being educated
parole.testo: From Latin educandus (“that which is to be educated”), future passive participle of educo (“educate”).

parole.significato: To instruct or train.
parole.testo: From Middle English educaten, from educat(e) (“educated”, also used as the past participle of educaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), from Latin ēducātus, the perfect passive participle of ēducō (“(of a child, physically or mentally) to bring up, train, nourish; (of a person in learning or art) to re

parole.significato: educated
parole.testo: From Middle English educat(e) (“educated”, also used as the past participle of educaten), borrowed from Latin ēducātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: The process of imparting knowledge, skill and judgment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French éducation, from Latin ēducātiō (“a breeding, bringing up, rearing”), from ēducō (“to educate, train”), from ēdūcō (“to lead forth, to take out; to raise up, to erect”). See educate. Morphologically educate + -ion.

parole.significato: A person distinguished for their educational work, a teacher.
parole.testo: From Latin ēducātor. By surface analysis, educate + -or.

parole.significato: To direct the course of (a flow, journey etc.); to lead in a particular direction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēdūcere (“lead out, raise up”); from ex- (“out, up”) + dūcō (“lead, pull”).

parole.significato: The act of educing, of deducing: deduction.
parole.testo: From Latin eductio. Equivalent to educe + -ion.

parole.significato: To sweeten.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ēdulcōrō. Compare French édulcorer.

parole.significato: A sweetening.
parole.testo: From Latin ēdulcoratiō (“making sweet”), from ex (“from, out of”) + dulcis (“sweet”). By surface analysis, edulcorate + -ion.

parole.significato: To put into words; to express.
parole.testo: Back-formation from ineffable, ultimately from Latin effor (“utter”).

parole.significato: The quality or state of being effable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin effābilitās.

parole.significato: Able to be spoken of; able to be expressed.
parole.testo: From Latin effābilis (effor (“to utter”) + -able).

parole.significato: To charm; to bewitch.
parole.testo: Latin effascinare.

parole.significato: A charm; bewitchment or delusion.
parole.testo: Latin effascinatio.

parole.significato: Creation; a doing.
parole.testo: Latin effectio: compare French effection.

parole.significato: One who or that which brings about an event or result, accomplishes a purpose, etc.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin effector. By surface analysis, effect + -or.

parole.significato: An efficient cause.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin effectrīx. First attested in 1583. By surface analysis, effect + -trix.

parole.significato: To cause, bring about (an event); to accomplish, to carry out (a wish, plan etc.).
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Renaissance Latin effectuare, or its source, Latin effectus (“effect”); probably after Middle French effectuer.

parole.significato: Of a boy or man, exhibiting behavior or mannerisms considered typical of a woman or unmasculine.
parole.testo: From Middle English effeminat, effemynat, from Latin effēminātus, past participle of effēminō, from fēmina (“woman”).

parole.significato: effeminacy; womanishness
parole.testo: From Latin effeminatio.

parole.significato: To excite into a passionate, angry, bestial state.
parole.testo: From Latin efferātus, perfect passive participle of efferō (“to make wild or savage, brutalize, barbarize; to make fierce, infuriate, madden”). By surface analysis, ef- + Latin fer- + -ate.

parole.significato: Carrying away from.
parole.testo: From Latin efferēns, present active participle of efferō (“bring or carry out”), from ē (“out of”), short form of ex, + ferō (“carry, bear”). By surface analysis, ef- + -fer + -ent.

parole.significato: wild like a beast; fierce or ferocious
parole.testo: From Latin efferus (“savage”), from ex (“intensifier”) + ferus (“wild”). By surface analysis, ef- + Latin fer- + -ous.

parole.significato: To emit small bubbles of dissolved gas; to froth or fizz.
parole.testo: From Latin effervescere (“to boil up”). By surface analysis, ef- + Latin ferv- + -esce.

parole.significato: Giving off bubbles; fizzy.
parole.testo: From Latin effervescentem, from effervescere, from ex- + fervescere, from fervere. By surface analysis, ef- + Latin ferv- + -escent.

parole.significato: exhausted, spent, worn-out.
parole.testo: From Latin effētus (“exhausted”, literally “that has given birth”), 1620s.

parole.significato: The extent to which a resource is used for the intended purpose.
parole.testo: From Latin efficientia, equivalent to efficient + -cy.

parole.significato: A verbal depiction of someone's body, often from head to toe.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin effictiō.

parole.significato: An expressing or a representing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin effictiōnem. First attested in 1656.

parole.significato: To form as an effigy or make a representation of; to illustrate or depict.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin effigiātus, past participle of effigiō (“to form”), from effigiēs. See effigy.

parole.significato: The act of forming a resemblance, or the an effigy itself
parole.testo: Compare Latin effigiatio.

parole.significato: Having a definite (lobed) shape; not effuse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin effiguratus; compare figurate (figuratus).

parole.significato: To demand something urgently
parole.testo: From Latin efflagitare.

parole.significato: An earnest request, an entreaty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin efflāgitātiō.

parole.significato: To fill with breath; to puff up.
parole.testo: From Latin efflatus, past participle of efflare (“to blow or breathe out”), from ex + flare (“to blow”).

parole.significato: A blowing, breathing or puffing out.
parole.testo: From Latin efflātiō (“exhalation”), from Latin efflō (“to exhale”), from ex- (“out, away”) + flō (“to blow”).

parole.significato: To burst into bloom; to flower.
parole.testo: From Latin efflōrēscere, present active infinitive of efflōrēscō (“to bloom, blossom; to flourish”) + -ere (suffix forming infinitives). Efflōrēscō is derived from ef- (variant of ex- (prefix meaning ‘away; out’)) + flōrēscō (“to blossom, flower; to begin to flourish or prosper”) (from flōreō (“to b

parole.significato: Bursting into flower.
parole.testo: From Latin efflōrēscēns. Compare French efflorescent. By surface analysis, effloresce + -ent.

parole.significato: A gaseous or vaporous emission, especially a foul-smelling one.
parole.testo: From Latin effluvium (“an outlet”), from effluō (“flow out or away”), from ex (“out of, from”) + fluō (“flow”).

parole.significato: The process of flowing out.
parole.testo: From Latin effluxus, from effluō (“flow out or away”), from ex (“out of, from”) + fluō (“flow”). See also effluxion.

parole.significato: The process of flowing out.
parole.testo: From efflux + -ion, from Latin effluxus, from effluō (“flow out or away”), from ex (“out of, from”) + fluō (“flow”).

parole.significato: To dig up.
parole.testo: From Latin effodiō, effodicō.

parole.significato: involving digging up.
parole.testo: From Latin effodiēns, present participle of effodiō (“to dig out”), from ex + fodiō (“to dig”).

parole.significato: To form or shape (literally, or figuratively).
parole.testo: Latin effōrmō, from ex- + fōrmō.

parole.significato: A digging out or up.
parole.testo: From Latin effossio. See effodient.

parole.significato: Unrestrained.
parole.testo: From Latin effrēnātus (“unbridled, let loose”), past participle of effrēnō (“unbridle, let loose”).

parole.significato: The state of being effrenate; unrestrainedness.
parole.testo: From Latin effrēnātiō (“unbridled impetuosity”).

parole.significato: to radiate, shine or beam
parole.testo: From Latin effulgere (“to shine forth”). By surface analysis, ef- + Latin fulge(re).

parole.significato: A state of being bright and radiant, splendor, brilliance.
parole.testo: From Latin ex- (“out of, from”) and fulgere (“to shine”). By surface analysis, ef- + Latin fulg(ere) + -ence.

parole.significato: Radiant, resplendent, shining.
parole.testo: From Latin effulgēns (“flashing, glittering”), present participle of effulgeō (“to shine or gleam forth, flash, glitter”), from ē- (variant of ex- (prefix meaning ‘out; away’)) + fulgeō (“to flash, gleam, glisten, glitter, shine”) (from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“shiny; white”)). By surface analys

parole.significato: To breathe or puff out.
parole.testo: From Latin effumare (“to emit smoke”), from ex + fumare (“to smoke”), from fumus (“smoke”).

parole.significato: To pour out.
parole.testo: From Latin effundō. See effuse.

parole.significato: Gushy; unrestrained, extravagant or excessive (in emotional expression).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin effūsīvus, 1660s.

parole.significato: Lukewarm, tepid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin egelidus.

parole.significato: The state of needing, or of suffering a natural want.
parole.testo: From Latin egens, egentis, present participle of egere (“to be needy, suffer want”).

parole.significato: need; neediness; poverty.
parole.testo: From Latin egentia from egere (“to need, to be in need”).

parole.significato: A patroness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Egeria.

parole.significato: To germinate.
parole.testo: From Latin ēgermināt-, perfect passive participial stem of Latin ēgerminō (“to sprout”). See Latin ē- (“out, away”), Latin germinō (“to sprout”), English germinate.

parole.significato: To eliminate undigested food or waste from the body (as feces).
parole.testo: From Latin ēgestus, the perfect passive participle of ēgerō (“to carry, bear, or bring out or away; to discharge”).

parole.significato: The waste which is carried out from a cell or an organism; the result of egestion; excrement
parole.testo: From Latin ēgesta (“discharged [matter etc.]”), plural of Latin ēgestum (“[that which is] discharged”), an adjectivization of the perfect passive participle of Latin to discharge; to carry out.

parole.significato: Without glands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin eglandulōsus; see glandulose.

parole.significato: To unwind, as a thread from a ball.
parole.testo: From Latin eglomero, eglomeratus, from e- + glomeratus.

parole.significato: The self, especially with a sense of self-importance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ego (“I”). Chosen by Freud’s translator as a translation of his use of German Ich as a noun for this concept from the pronoun ich (“I”). Doublet of I and Ich.

parole.significato: self; ego
parole.testo: From Latin ego (“I”).

parole.significato: A tendency to talk excessively about oneself.
parole.testo: From Latin ego (“I”) + -t- (perhaps modelled on dogmatism, despotism, idiotism) + -ism.

parole.significato: Conspicuous, exceptional, outstanding; usually in a negative sense.
parole.testo: From Latin ēgregius, from e- (“out of”), + grex (“flock”), + English adjective suffix -ous, from Latin suffix -osus (“full of”); reflecting the positive connotations of "standing out from the flock".

parole.significato: An exit or way out.
parole.testo: From Latin ēgressus, from ex- + gressus, literally “out-way”.

parole.significato: To exit or leave; to go or come out.
parole.testo: From Latin ēgressum, past participle of ēgredior.

parole.significato: The act of going; egress.
parole.testo: From Latin ēgressiō.

parole.significato: Someone who goes out; someone who egresses or leaves.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Distress or sorrow.
parole.testo: From Latin aegritudo (“illness, sorrow”).

parole.significato: That lacks guttules at each end of the spore.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin eguttulatus, eguttulata; see guttulate.

parole.significato: of or relating to Ancient Egypt, Egyptian
parole.testo: From the Late Latin aegyptiacus (“Egyptian”), from the Ancient Greek Αἰγῠπτῐᾰκός (Aigŭptĭăkós, “of or for the Egyptians”), from Αἰγῠ́πτῐος (Aigŭ́ptĭos, “Egyptian”) + -ᾰκός (-ăkós). Equivalent to Latin Aegyptius (“Egyptian”) + -acus.

parole.significato: To eject abruptly; to throw out suddenly and swiftly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēiaculātus, perfect active participle of ēiaculor (“to hurl, shoot out”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from ē (“out”) + iaculor (“throw, dart”), from iaculum (“a missile, a dart”), from iaciō (“to throw, to hurl”).

parole.significato: Premature ejaculation.
parole.testo: Modern Latin, from noun type formed from participle stem of Latin ējaculāri (“to eject”) + praecox (“early”).

parole.significato: an inferred object of someone else's consciousness
parole.testo: From Latin ēiectum (“(that which is) thrown out”), from ēiciō (“to throw out”) (see Etymology 1). Coined by W. K. Clifford by analogy with subject and object.

parole.significato: Material which has been ejected, especially from a volcano or an impact crater.
parole.testo: Neuter plural of Latin ējectus.

parole.significato: A wailing, crying or lamentation.
parole.testo: From Latin eiulātiō, from eiulō (“to wail, lament”).

parole.significato: Renouncement, rejection; resignation of one's position.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēiūrātiō, from ēiūrō (“to abjure, disown, resign”) + -tiō.

parole.significato: A canon of construction holding that when a general term follows a list of particular terms, the general term only appl…
parole.testo: From Latin ejusdem generis ("of the same kind").

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter L/l.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old English el, from Latin el (the name of the letter L).

parole.significato: Complex, detailed, or sophisticated.
parole.testo: 1575, from Late Latin ēlabōrātus (“worked out”), past participle of ēlabōrō (“to work out”), from ē- (“out, forth, fully”) + labor (“work, toil, exertion”). More at e-, labour.

parole.significato: To disentangle.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlaqueō.

parole.significato: elastic
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἐλᾰστός (elăstós, “ductile”).

parole.significato: To make joyful or proud.
parole.testo: From Middle English elat, elate, from Latin ēlātus (“exalted, lofty”), perfect passive participle of efferō (“bring forth or out; raise; exalt”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Extremely happy and excited; delighted; pleased, euphoric.
parole.testo: Latin elatus (“raised”).

parole.significato: Elasticity; especially the expansibility of a gas.
parole.testo: From New Latin elatēr, from Ancient Greek ἐλατήρ (elatḗr, “driver, that which drives away”).

parole.significato: The mineral wurtzilite.
parole.testo: From New Latin elatēr, from Ancient Greek ἐλατήρ (elatḗr, “driver, that which drives away”) + -ite.

parole.significato: In Semitic languages, the “adjective degree of superiority”. In some languages such as Arabic, the concepts of comparat…
parole.testo: From Latin ēlātus (“exalted, lofty, high”) + -ive. Possibly borrowed from German, which has produced a great deal of pioneering Semitist literature, and where Elativ is a common term for absolute superlative in all languages.

parole.significato: In Finno-Ugric languages, one of the locative cases, expressing “out of,” or “from” as in Finnish talosta, Hungarian há…
parole.testo: From Latin ēlātus, perfect past participle of efferō (“to carry out or away”)

parole.significato: Of or relating to a certain school in Elea of Ancient Greek philosophers who taught that reality is stable and unchangi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Eleāticus, from Ancient Greek ’Ελεατικός (’Eleatikós), from Ἐλέα (Eléa, “Elea, Velia”).

parole.significato: A tall Eurasian herb, Inula helenium, whose roots have been used medicinally.
parole.testo: From Middle English elena campana, from a confusion of Latin enula campana and helenium.

parole.significato: One chosen or set apart.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēlēctus, past participle of ēligō (“to pick out, choose, elect”), from ē- (“out”) + legō (“to pick out, pick, gather, collect, etc.”); see legend. Cognate to eclectic, which is via Ancient Greek rather than Latin, hence prefix ἐκ (ek), rather than e- (from ex).

parole.significato: Someone who has the power of choosing; an elector.
parole.testo: From Latin electans, present participle of electare.

parole.significato: electrum, amber (alloy of gold and silver)
parole.testo: Latin electrum. See electrum.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, produced by, operated with, or utilising electricity; electrical.
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1646 in a publication by Thomas Browne. From New Latin ēlectricus (“electrical; of amber”), from ēlectr(um) (“amber”) + -icus (“adjectival suffix”); from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron, “amber”); related to ἠλέκτωρ (ēléktōr, “shining sun”), of unknown origin (see which for mor

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to amber, especially in having the ability to generate static electricity.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlectrīn(us) (“of amber”). See electric.

parole.significato: The wife of a German elector, often used as a title.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ēlēctrīx. By surface analysis, elector + -trix.

parole.significato: Amber.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlectrum, from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron).

parole.significato: Any preparation of a medicine mixed with honey or other sweetener in order to make it more palatable to swallow.
parole.testo: From Middle English electuarie, eletuarie, electuary, from Latin electuarium, from Ancient Greek ἐκλείκτον (ekleíkton, “medicine which is licked away”), from ἐκλείχω (ekleíkhō, “to lick up”), from ἐκ (ek, “out, from”) + λείχω (leíkhō, “to lick”). Doublet of lekvar.

parole.significato: Relating to charity, alms, or almsgiving.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin eleēmosynārius (“alms dispenser”), from Late Latin eleēmosyna (“alms”), from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē, “alms”), from ἐλεήμων (eleḗmōn, “merciful”) + -σῠ́νη (-sŭ́nē, “suffix denoting an abstract noun”). Compare Italian elemosina.

parole.significato: Of a gift or donation: made as an act of charity or almsgiving; charitable.
parole.testo: From Latin eleēmosyna f (“alms”) + -ous.

parole.significato: A judicial writ ordering seizure of a debtor's property.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlēgit (“he has chosen”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or being an element (as opposed to a compound).
parole.testo: From Middle English elementall, from Medieval Latin elementālis; compare Old French elementel. By surface analysis, element + -al.

parole.significato: Relating to the basic, essential or fundamental part of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English elementare, from Latin elementārius (“elementary”), from elementum (“one of the four elements of antiquity; fundamentals”) + -ārius (adjective-forming suffix). Cognate with French élémentaire. By surface analysis, element + -ary.

parole.significato: That part of an argument on which its conclusiveness depends; that which convinces or refutes an antagonist; a refutati…
parole.testo: Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos, “refutation, scrutiny”); compare Old French elenche. Doublet of elenchus.

parole.significato: A technique of argument associated with Socrates wherein the arguer asks the interlocutor to agree with a series of pre…
parole.testo: From Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos, “refutation, scrutiny, control”). Doublet of elench.

parole.significato: A complication of chronic filariasis, in which nematode worms block the lymphatic vessels, usually in the legs or scrot…
parole.testo: From Latin elephantiasis or directly from Ancient Greek ἐλεφᾰντῐ́ᾱσῐς (elephăntĭ́āsĭs).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, resembling, or characteristic of elephants.
parole.testo: From Latin elephantīn(us). By surface analysis, elephant + -ine.

parole.significato: Pertaining to ancient Eleusis, in Attica, or the Eleusinian Mysteries of Demeter celebrated there.
parole.testo: From Latin eleusīnius + -an.

parole.significato: To raise (something) to a higher position.
parole.testo: From Middle English elevaten (“to raise up, erect; to elate, inflate (e.g. with pride); (alchemy) to vaporize; (of a bone, excressence, blood vessel) to protrude”), from elevat(e) (“(in physical elevation, in rank, in altitude above the horizon) high”, also used as the past participle of elevaten) +

parole.significato: To evoke, educe (emotions, feelings, responses, etc.); to generate, obtain, or provoke as a response or answer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin elicitus from eliciō (“draw forth”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to elicitation.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlicitīvus. By surface analysis, elicit + -ive.

parole.significato: To leave out or omit (something).
parole.testo: From Latin ēlīdō (“to knock, dash or strike out”), from ex- (“out, away”) + laedō (“to strike, collide, hurt”) (whence e- (“assimilated form of ex-”)).

parole.significato: To completely remove, get rid of, put an end to.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēlīminātus, perfect passive participle of ēlīminō (“to turn out of doors, banish”), from ē- + līmen (“a threshold”, līmin- in compounds) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), akin to Latin līmes (“a boundary”); see also English limit and l

parole.significato: The act of eliminating, expelling or throwing off.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēliminātiō, from eliminate + -ion.

parole.significato: A woman or girl who eliminates; a female eliminator.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlīminātrīx, modeled after eliminator. Compare the French éliminatrice. By surface analysis, eliminate + -trix.

parole.significato: The removal of the tongue.
parole.testo: From Late Latin elinguatio.

parole.significato: tongue-tied, dumb or speechless
parole.testo: From Latin elinguis (“deprived of a tongue, tongueless; speechless”), from e + lingua (“tongue”).

parole.significato: liquation.
parole.testo: From Latin eliquatio, from eliquare (“to clarify, strain”), from e + liquare (“to make liquid, melt”).

parole.significato: The deliberate omission of something.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlīsiō (“striking out, forcing out”) (whence -ion (“noun suffix denoting action, result, process, state, condition”)), from ēlīsus (“knocked out, forced out”), past participle of ēlīdō (“to knock, dash or strike out”) (whence elide), from ex- (“out, away”) + laedō (“to strike, collide, hu

parole.significato: To boil; to seethe.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlixātus, past participle of ēlixāre (“to seethe”), from ēlixus (“thoroughly boiled”), from ex + *lixus (“fluid, flowing”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *wleykʷ- (“moist, to wet”) and thus cognate with Latin lixa (“water; lye”) and liqueō (“to be liquid, fluid”).

parole.significato: Boiling, stewing.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlixāre.

parole.significato: A liquid which converts lead to gold.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin elixir (“philosopher's stone”), from Arabic اَلْإِكْسِير (al-ʔiksīr, “philosopher's stone”), from Ancient Greek ξηρίον (xēríon, “powder for drying wounds”), from ξηρός (xērós, “dry”).

parole.significato: elixir of life
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A member of a minor biblical tribe mentioned in Nahum 1:1.
parole.testo: First attested in 1568 in the Bishops' Bible translation (see quotations); earlier English Bible translations instead used “of Elkosh”. From Middle English Helcesei, borrowed from Vulgar Latin Helcesei, from Ancient Greek Έλκεσαίου (Élkesaíou), from Hebrew אֶלְקֹשִׁי. Analysable as Elkosh (“the unid

parole.significato: A mark consisting of multiple full stops (with or without spaces), used to indicate omitted, missing, or illegible word…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ellīpsis, from Ancient Greek ἔλλειψις (élleipsis, “omission”). Doublet of ellipse.

parole.significato: One of the five canons of classical rhetoric: the mastery of stylistic elements.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlocūtiō. Doublet of elocution.

parole.significato: The art of speaking, especially public speaking, with expert control of gesture and voice, diction (articulation and wo…
parole.testo: From Middle English elocucioun, ellocucioun, from Late Latin ēlocutiōnem. Doublet of elocutio.

parole.significato: a eulogy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēlogium (“short saying, inscription”), from Ancient Greek ἐλεγεῖον (elegeîon, “elegy”), from ἔλεγος (élegos, “song, melody”). Doublet of elogy.

parole.significato: Praise, eulogy; inscription on a tombstone, epitaph
parole.testo: From Latin ēlogium. Doublet of elogium.

parole.significato: Elongated, extended, lengthened; (especially biology) having a long and slender form.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English elongat, elongate (“kept away; different or remote in nature”, adjective), borrowed from Late Latin ēlongātus (“having been stretched out, elongated; prolonged, protracted; having been kept aloof, removed”) + Middle English -at (suffix forming participles). Ēlongātus is the

parole.significato: The act of lengthening.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin elongatio, elongationem.

parole.significato: Synonym of eloquence.
parole.testo: From Latin ēloquentia. Doublet of eloquence, via Old French.

parole.significato: To make (something) lucid (“bright, luminous; also, clear, transparent”).
parole.testo: From Late Latin ēlūcidātus, perfect passive participle of ēlūcidō (“to lighten, enlighten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ē(x)- (“out, from”) + lūcidus (“bright, clear, understandable”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), literally “to make light of (something)”, ultimately from P

parole.significato: Clear, understandable.
parole.testo: From Late Latin ēlūcidātus (“lightened, enlightened”), see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: Avoidable, escapable.
parole.testo: From Latin ēluctābilis (whence e- and -able), from ēluctor (“struggle out”) + -bilis.

parole.significato: A struggling out of any difficulty.
parole.testo: From Latin eluctatio.

parole.significato: To solve, write or compose by working studiously at night; to study.
parole.testo: From the past participle of Latin elucubrare (“compose by lamplight”).

parole.significato: The act of elucubrating.
parole.testo: From the past participle of Latin elucubrare (“compose by lamplight”).

parole.significato: To evade or escape from (someone or something), especially by using cunning or skill.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlūdō (“to evade, elude”), from ē- (“out of”, short form of ex-) + lūdō (“to play; to trick”).

parole.significato: In chromatography, a solvent used in order to effect separation by elution.
parole.testo: From elute; Latin eluent-, eluens (washing out), 1941.

parole.significato: weak or lame in the loins
parole.testo: From Latin ēlumbis, from ex- (“without”) + lumbus (“loin”).

parole.significato: The act of eluding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ēlūsiō.

parole.significato: Evading capture, comprehension or remembrance.
parole.testo: From Latin elusus, past participle of eludo (“to parry a blow, to deceive”).

parole.significato: To separate one substance from another by means of a solvent; to wash; to cleanse.
parole.testo: First attested in 1731. Borrowed from Latin ēlūtus, from the verb ēluō (“to wash away”).

parole.significato: To decant; to purify something by straining it.
parole.testo: From Latin elutriare (“wash out”), from e- + lutriare (“wash”).

parole.significato: Dislocated.
parole.testo: From eluxate (“dislocate”) (a rare, synonymous variant of luxate), from Latin eluxātus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Elysian or Elysium, the location.
parole.testo: From Latin Elysium (from Ancient Greek Ἠλύσιον (Ēlúsion, “Elysium; one of the Elysian Fields”)) + -an (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To make or become lean; to emaciate.
parole.testo: From Latin emaceratus (“emaciated”), from e + macerare (“to make soft”).

parole.significato: To make extremely thin or wasted.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēmaciātus, perfect passive participle of ēmaciō (“to make lean, to cause to waste away”), from ex- (“out”) + maciēs (“leanness”), from macer (“thin”).

parole.significato: Desire or fondness for buying
parole.testo: From Latin emacitas.

parole.significato: To clear from spots or stains, or from any imperfection.
parole.testo: From Latin emaculatus, past participle of emaculare (“to clear from spots”). See maculate.

parole.significato: Flowing forth; emanating or issuing from or as if from a source.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin present participle ēmānāns, ēmānantis, from verb ēmānō (“to flow out, arise”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + mānō.

parole.significato: Unrealistic pictorial elements emanating from a character, symbolizing something about that character, such as a sweatd…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēmānāre, "to flow out,". ēmānāre is the present active infinitive of ēmānō "flow out, ēmānō is derived from the Latin ex- (prefix meaning "out, away") + mānō (verb meaning "to give out; to flow").

parole.significato: To come from a source; issue from.
parole.testo: From Latin ēmānāre (“to flow out, spring out of, arise, proceed from”), from ē (“out”) + mānāre (“to flow”).

parole.significato: To set free (a person or group) from the oppression or restraint of another; to liberate.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ēmancipātus (“liberated, emancipated”) + English -ate (suffix forming verbs, and adjectives with the sense ‘characterized by the specified thing’). Ēmancipātus is the perfect passive participle of ēmancipō (“to declare (someone) free and independent of another’s power, e

parole.significato: A person who emancipates.
parole.testo: From Late Latin ēmancipātor, from Latin ēmancipō (“to emancipate”). By surface analysis, emancipate + -or.

parole.significato: A woman, girl, or any other entity treated as female who emancipates; a female emancipator.
parole.testo: From Latin ēmancipātrīx. By surface analysis, emancipate + -trix.

parole.significato: With the outline of the margin more or less concave in places, usually at the apex.
parole.testo: From Latin emarginare; e- (“out”) + marginare (“to furnish with a margin”), from margo (“margin”).

parole.significato: To deprive of virile or procreative power; to castrate, to geld.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ēmasculātus, perfect passive participle of ēmasculō (“to emasculate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ē(x)- (“out, from, apart”) + masculus (“male, masculine”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), further from mās (“a man, a male”) + -culus (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Deprived of virility or vigor; unmanned, weak.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ēmasculātus (more at Etymology 1), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: One who, or that which, emasculates.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: An inlaid ornament.
parole.testo: From Latin emblēma. Doublet of emblem.

parole.significato: The fruit of Emblica officinalis (now Phyllanthus emblica, the Indian gooseberry, once used as a remedy against dysente…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin emblicus, from Arabic أَمْلَج (ʔamlaj), from Sanskrit आमलक (āmalaka). Doublet of amla.

parole.significato: A mineral consisting of silver chloride and silver bromide; a variety of bromian chlorargyrite.
parole.testo: From Latin embolus (“piston”), from Ancient Greek ἔμβολος (émbolos, “peg, wedge, stopper”).

parole.significato: A narrow piece separating the costa and corium in certain insects of the suborder Heteroptera.
parole.testo: From New Latin embolium, from Ancient Greek ἐμβόλιον (embólion, “insertion”).

parole.significato: An obstruction causing an embolism: a blood clot, air bubble or other matter carried by the bloodstream and causing a b…
parole.testo: The term was coined in 1848 by Rudolf Virchow From Latin embolus (“piston”), from Ancient Greek ἔμβολος (émbolos, “peg, stopper”).

parole.significato: To rub (a diseased part) with a moistened or liquid substance, usually an oil, on a cloth or sponge.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin embrocatus, past participle of Late Latin embrocare, from embrocha, from Ancient Greek ἐμβροχή (embrokhḗ, “lotion, fomentation”).

parole.significato: In the reproductive cycle, the stage after the fertilization of the egg that precedes the development into a fetus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin embryō, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “fetus”), from ἐν (en, “in-”) + βρύω (brúō, “to grow, swell”).

parole.significato: Embryonic.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin embryon, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “newborn animal, embryo”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to an embryo.
parole.testo: From New Latin embryonicus.

parole.significato: The act of one embryo cannibalizing another for food in utero; at present only observed in some species of sharks.
parole.testo: From Latin embryo and the suffix -phagy (“to feed on”); 1948; created to describe the behavior of sandtiger shark embryos.

parole.significato: To correct and revise (text or a document).
parole.testo: From Middle English emenden, from Latin ēmendō (“to free from fault”), from ex- (“out”) + mendum (“fault, blemish”). Doublet of amend.

parole.significato: Capable of being emended, corrigible.
parole.testo: From Latin emendabilis.

parole.significato: Emended, corrected, restored.
parole.testo: From the Latin ēmendātus (“corrected”), the perfect passive participle of ēmendō (“to free from faults, correct”).

parole.significato: The act of altering for the better, or correcting what is erroneous or faulty; correction; improvement.
parole.testo: From Middle English emendatioun, from Latin ēmendātiō; equivalent to emend + -ation. Piecewise doublet of amendation.

parole.significato: Someone who emends.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēmendātor.

parole.significato: To beg.
parole.testo: From Latin emendicatus, past participle of emendicare (“to obtain by begging”). See mendicate.

parole.significato: A situation which poses an immediate risk and which requires urgent attention.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin emergentia, from Latin emergens, present participle of emergo (“to emerge, arise, come forth”), equivalent to emergent + -cy or emerge + -ency. Doublet of emergence.

parole.significato: Emerging; coming into view or into existence; nascent; new.
parole.testo: From Latin ēmergēns, present participle of ēmergō. The medical sense is a back-formation from emergency.

parole.significato: A female person who is retired from active service or an occupation, especially one who retains an honorific version of…
parole.testo: From the Latin ēmerita, the feminine singular form of ēmeritus.

parole.significato: A bounty awarded to a soldier upon the completion of his term of service.
parole.testo: From the Latin ēmeritum (“a thing earned upon completion of a term of service”), a substantive use of the neuter singular form of ēmeritus (“earned, merited, having been earned; served, having done one’s service”), the perfect passive participle of ēmereō (“to earn, to merit”).

parole.significato: Retired, but retaining an honorific version of a previous title.
parole.testo: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ēmeritus (“(having been) earned, (having been) merited; (having been) served, having done one’s service”), the perfect passive participle of ēmereō (“to earn, merit; to gain by service; (military) to complete one’s obligation to serve, to serve out one

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Emesa or its region.
parole.testo: From Latin Emesēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἐμεσηνός (Emesēnós).

parole.significato: shining forth or flashing.
parole.testo: From Latin ēmicāns, present participle of ēmicō. See emication.

parole.significato: A spark, flickering or scintillation.
parole.testo: From Latin emicatio, from emicare (“to spring out or forth”), from e (“out”) + micare (“to move quickly to and fro, to sparkle”).

parole.significato: Urination.
parole.testo: From Latin e (“out”) + mingere, mictum (“to make water”). Cognate with Middle English miȝen (“to urinate”), from Old English mīġan (“to urinate”).

parole.significato: Someone who leaves a country to settle in a new country.
parole.testo: From Classical Latin ēmigrāns, present participle of ēmigrāre (“to emigrate”).

parole.significato: To leave the country in which one lives, especially one's native country, in order to reside elsewhere.
parole.testo: From Latin emigratus, perfect passive participle of emigro (“to move away, remove, depart from a place”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + migro (“to move, remove, depart”).

parole.significato: The act of emigrating; movement of a person or persons out of a country or national region, for the purpose of permanen…
parole.testo: From Late Latin stem of emigratio, from e (“out”) + migrare (“to move, remove, depart”).

parole.significato: The right of a government over the private property within its jurisdiction. Usually invoked to compel land owners to s…
parole.testo: Calque of New Latin dominium ēminēns (literally “supreme ownership”).

parole.significato: A drain or outlet.
parole.testo: From Latin ēmissārium.

parole.significato: Looking, or narrowly examining; prying, nosy or meticulous.
parole.testo: From Latin emissitius, from emittere.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or having the capacity to emit radiation, matter, or sound; emitting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēmissīvus, from ēmittō (“to emit”).

parole.significato: To send out or give off.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēmittō.

parole.significato: Sending forth; emissive.
parole.testo: From Latin emittens, present participle of emittere.

parole.significato: That degree of softness in a body beginning to melt which alters its shape; the first or lowest degree of fusibility.
parole.testo: From Latin e (“out”) + mollescere, inchoate from mollere (“to be soft”), mollis (“soft”). By surface analysis, e- + Latin moll- + -escence.

parole.significato: Special weight or forcefulness given to something considered important.
parole.testo: From Latin emphasis, from Ancient Greek ἔμφασις (émphasis, “significance”), from ἐμφαίνω (emphaínō, “to present; to indicate”), from ἐν- (en-, “in”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to show”).

parole.significato: To stress, give emphasis or extra weight to (something).
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek – see emphasis. By surface analysis, emphasis + -ize.

parole.significato: Having the quality of closing the pores of the skin.
parole.testo: From Latin emphracticus, from Ancient Greek ἐμφρακτικός (emphraktikós), from ἐμφράσσω (emphrássō), from ἐν- (en-) + φράσσω (phrássō).

parole.significato: A right to enjoyment of property with a given stipulation that the property will be improved or maintained in an agreed…
parole.testo: From Latin emphyteusis, from Ancient Greek ἐμφύτευσις (emphúteusis, “tenure of a type of leasehold”).

parole.significato: Someone who holds land by way of emphyteusis.
parole.testo: Latin emphyteuticarius, adjective.

parole.significato: Empirical.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin empiricus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπειρῐκός (empeirĭkós, “experienced”), from ἐμπειρία (empeiría, “experience, mere experience or practice without knowledge, especially in medicine, empiricism”), from ἔμπειρος (émpeiros, “experienced or practised in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πεῖρα (pe

parole.significato: Grafting by inoculation; budding.
parole.testo: Latin emplastratio (“a budding”).

parole.significato: Relating to an emporium, or to merchandise.
parole.testo: Latin emporeticus.

parole.significato: A city or region which is a major trading centre; also, a place within a city for commerce and trading; a marketplace.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin emporium (“trading station; business district in a city; market town”), from Ancient Greek ἐμπόριον (empórion, “factory, trading station; market”), from ἔμπορος (émporos, “merchant, trader; traveller”) + -ιον (-ion, suffix forming nouns). ἔμπορος is derived from ἐμ- (em-) (varian

parole.significato: The act of buying; purchase.
parole.testo: From Latin emptio, from emere (“to buy”).

parole.significato: Buyer.
parole.testo: From Latin ēmptor.

parole.significato: A phantom; ghost; spectre.
parole.testo: Latin empusa, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the highest heaven or the empyrean.
parole.testo: From Latin empyreus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios, “fiery”), from ἐν (en, “en-”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) (English pyre).

parole.significato: The highest heaven, supposed by the ancients to be a region of pure light and fire or else composed of ether, and somet…
parole.testo: From Latin empȳreus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) (whence English pyre).

parole.significato: Containing the combustible principle of coal.
parole.testo: From Latin empyricus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios, “fiery”), from ἐν (en, “en-”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).

parole.significato: To attempt to equal or be the same as.
parole.testo: First attested in 1586; borrowed from Latin aemulātus, perfect active participle of Latin aemulor (“to rival, emulate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Having a tendency to emulate others; imitative.
parole.testo: First attested in 1593; borrowed from New Latin emulatīvus, by surface analysis, emulate + -ive.

parole.significato: A female who emulates.
parole.testo: From Latin aemulātrīx, equivalent to emulator + -trix.

parole.significato: To milk out; to drain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin emulgeo, emulsum; e (“out”) + mulgeo (“to milk”); akin to English milk. See milk.

parole.significato: Of a straining or purifying process.
parole.testo: From Latin emulgens, present participle of emulgere (“to milk out”); so called because the kidney was regarded by the ancients as straining out the serum, as if by milking, and so producing the urine.

parole.significato: Ambitious or competitive.
parole.testo: From Middle English emulous, from Latin aemulus (“striving to equal or excel, rivaling; in a bad sense, envious, jealous”) + -ous, from Ancient Greek ἁμιλλάομαι (hamilláomai, “strive, contend”), akin to Latin imitari (“to imitate”); see imitate.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the elimination of waste from the body.
parole.testo: From Latin ēmūnctus, past participle of ēmungō (“to blow one's nose”) + -ory.

parole.significato: Cleaning; disinfection.
parole.testo: Latin emundatio (“cleaning out”).

parole.significato: To wipe or cleanse, especially one's nose.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēmungō.

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter N/n.
parole.testo: The name of the letter comes from Latin en. The typographic sense dates to 1793.

parole.significato: Vivid, lively description.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin enargīa, from Ancient Greek ἐνάργεια (enárgeia, “sensory vividness”).

parole.significato: A detailed exposition; relation.
parole.testo: From the Latin ēnarrātiō, from ēnarrō (“to explain in detail”, “to expound”).

parole.significato: Just coming into being; nascent.
parole.testo: From e- (“out”) + Latin nāscor (“be born”) + -ent, from Latin ēnāscēns, present participle of ēnāscor (“spring up”), from ēx- (“out”) + nāscor (“be born”).

parole.significato: A relative whose relation is traced only through female members of the family.
parole.testo: From Latin ēnātus.

parole.significato: A small outgrowth on the surface of a plant organ.
parole.testo: From Latin enatus (ēnātus) (from ēnāscor (“spring forth”)) + English + -ion.

parole.significato: The eight days of celebration for the dedication of the church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.
parole.testo: From Latin encaenia, from Ancient Greek ἐγκαίνια (enkaínia, “a festival of renewal or dedication”).

parole.significato: A festival held to mark the anniversary of the dedication of a church or temple; (especially), of the Temple at Jerusal…
parole.testo: From Latin encaenia, from Ancient Greek (τὰ) ἐγκαίνια ((tà) enkaínia, “dedication festival”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + καινός (kainós, “new”).

parole.significato: An ornament on a frieze or capital, consisting of festoons of fruit, flowers, leaves, etc.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἔγκαρπος (énkarpos, “containing fruit”) (ἐν- (en-) + καρπός (karpós)).

parole.significato: A clitic that joins with the preceding word phonetically, graphically, or both.
parole.testo: From Late Latin encliticus, from Ancient Greek ἐγκλιτικός (enklitikós, “inclined towards”), from ἐγκλίνειν (enklínein, “lean on”), from ἐν (en, “upon”) + κλίνειν (klínein, “to lean, incline”).

parole.significato: Warm praise, especially a formal expression of such praise; a tribute.
parole.testo: From Latin encōmium (“praise, eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐγκώμιον (enkṓmion, “laudatory ode, praise”), from ἐγκώμιος (enkṓmios, “of or pertaining to the victor”), from κῶμος (kômos, “festival, revel, ode”).

parole.significato: One of an ascetic 2nd-century sect of Christians who forbade marriage and counselled abstinence from meat.
parole.testo: Latin Encratitae (plural) from Ancient Greek ἐγκρατής (enkratḗs, “self-disciplined”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κρᾰ́τος (krắtos, “strength”).

parole.significato: Commonwealth standard spelling of encyclopedia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin encyclopaedia; the English word is an etymologically restored spelling variant of earlier encyclopedia, q.v.

parole.significato: A comprehensive reference work (often spanning several printed volumes) with articles (usually arranged in alphabetical…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin encyclopēdīa, encyclopaedīa (“general education”), a univerbated form of Koine Greek ἐγκύκλιος παιδείᾱ (enkúklios paideíā, “education in the circle of arts and sciences”), from Ancient Greek ἐγκύκλιος (enkúklios, “circular”) + παιδείᾱ (paideíā, “childrearing; education”) (q.v

parole.significato: The mucous membrane that lines the uterus in mammals and in which fertilized eggs are implanted.
parole.testo: From endo- (“inner”) + Late Latin metrium (“womb”), from Ancient Greek μήτριον (mḗtrion, “of a mother”). Compare μήτρᾱ (mḗtrā, “womb”).

parole.significato: To express support or approval, especially officially or publicly; to give an endorsement.
parole.testo: Alteration influenced by Medieval Latin indorsare of Middle English endosse, from Old French endosser (“to put on the back”), from Latin dossum, alternative form of dorsum (“back”), from which also dorsal (“of the back”). That is, the ‘r’ was dropped in Latin dossum, which developed into Old French

parole.significato: A process of bone formation in which ossification takes place within the substance of the cartilage.
parole.testo: From New Latin endostosis. By surface analysis, endo- + ostosis.

parole.significato: Senses relating to covering or putting on.
parole.testo: From both of the following: * Chiefly sense 1: Late Middle English induen (“to clothe (someone); to assume or take on (an appearance)”), from Latin induere, the present active infinitive of induō (“to put on (clothes, etc.); to assume (a part)”), from indu- (an archaic variant of in- (prefix meaning

parole.significato: A fast or series of privations undertaken by the Cathars to purify the soul, often resulting in death.
parole.testo: From New Latin endūra, from Old Occitan endurar (“to fast, endure”).

parole.significato: To kill off; to destroy.
parole.testo: From Latin ēnecātus, past participle of ēnecāre; ē- (“out, utterly”) + necāre (“to kill”).

parole.significato: An injection of fluid into the large intestine by way of the rectum, usually for medical purposes.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin enema, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἔνεμα (énema, “injection”), from ἐνίημι (eníēmi, “to send in, inject”).

parole.significato: A political or class opponent of the subgroup in power within a larger group.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin hostis publicus (compare public enemy).

parole.significato: Possessing or pertaining to energy.
parole.testo: From New Latin energeticus (16th c.), or its source, Ancient Greek ἐνεργητικός (energētikós), from ἐνεργέω (energéō, “to be active”), from ἐνεργός (energós, “active”). By surface analysis, energy + -etic.

parole.significato: A person possessed by an evil ghost, spirit, or entity.
parole.testo: From Latin energumenus, from Ancient Greek ἐνεργούμενος (energoúmenos), from verb ἐνεργέω (energéō, “to influence”).

parole.significato: To reduce strength or energy; debilitate.
parole.testo: From Latin ēnervātus, past participle of ēnervō (“to weaken”).

parole.significato: Lacking nerve or force
parole.testo: From Latin enervis, enervus.

parole.significato: Describing two or more identical or almost identical notes that are written differently when in different keys. (Whethe…
parole.testo: From Latin enharmonicus, from Late Latin enarmonius, from Ancient Greek ἐναρμόνιος (enarmónios), from ἐν (en)+ἁρμονία (harmonía).

parole.significato: The state of the human nature of Jesus Christ being entirely dependent on, and not existing independently of, the divin…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin enhypostasia, from Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + ὑπόστασις (hupóstasis, “existence; essence; substance”) + -ία (-ía, suffix forming nouns). ὑπόστασις is in turn derived from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, “below, under”) + στάσις (stásis, “standing”). Compare Ancient Greek ἐνυπόστα

parole.significato: Pertaining to an enigma.
parole.testo: From Latin aenigmaticus and French énigmatique, from Ancient Greek αἰνιγματικός (ainigmatikós); equivalent to enigma + -tic.

parole.significato: An unknotting; the act or operation of clearing of knots, or untying.
parole.testo: From Latin enodatio (“explanation”), from enodare (“to free from knots”). See enode.

parole.significato: To clear of knots; to make clear.
parole.testo: From Latin enodare, from e (“out”) + nodare (“to fill with knots”), from nodus (“a knot”).

parole.significato: The commander of an enomoty.
parole.testo: From Latin enōmotarcha, from Ancient Greek ἐνωμοτάρχης (enōmotárkhēs).

parole.significato: Deviating from the norm; unusual, extraordinary.
parole.testo: From Latin ēnormis. An assimilated form of ex- (“out of”) + norma (“rule, norm”) + -ous.

parole.significato: An entity or being; an existing thing, as opposed to a quality or attribute.
parole.testo: From Late Latin ēns (“thing”), from esse (“to be”). See entity.

parole.significato: The ‘being of beings’; God.
parole.testo: From Latin ens (“being”) + entium (“of beings”). Compare ens.

parole.significato: real being
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: sword-shaped
parole.testo: From New Latin ensatus, from Latin ensis (“sword”).

parole.significato: A salamander native to western North America in the genus Ensatina.
parole.testo: From New Latin Ensatina.

parole.significato: A member of the genus Ensifer, of the bacteria family Rhizobiaceae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēnsifer (“sword-bearing”).

parole.significato: Any insect of the suborder Ensifera.
parole.testo: From translingual Ensifera + -an. Further from Latin ēnsifer (“swordbearing”).

parole.significato: shaped like a sword blade
parole.testo: From Latin ensis (“sword”) + -form.

parole.significato: A state of feeling positive about both oneself and the world.
parole.testo: From the Latin word meaning 'to touch within'.

parole.significato: A slight convex curvature introduced into the shaft of a column for aesthetic reasons, or to compensate for the illusio…
parole.testo: From Latin entasis, from Ancient Greek ἔντασις (éntasis, “tension, straining”), from ἐντείνω (enteínō, “to stretch or strain tight”).

parole.significato: The complete realisation and final form of some potential concept or function; the conditions under which a potential t…
parole.testo: From Late Latin entelechia, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia), coined by Aristotle from ἐντελής (entelḗs, “complete, finished, perfect”) (from τέλος (télos, “end, fruition, accomplishment”)) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have”).

parole.significato: A form of enteritis caused by Salmonella enterica
parole.testo: From Latin enterītidis.

parole.significato: relating to the intestines.
parole.testo: From New Latin entero-, combining form from Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”).

parole.significato: The gut, the whole intestine (alimentary) canal
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”).

parole.significato: Divinely inspired.
parole.testo: From Latin entheātus (“divinely inspired”), from Ancient Greek ἔνθεος (éntheos, “inspired, possessed by (a) god”) + -ātus.

parole.significato: That which has a distinct existence as an individual unit, often used for organizations which have no physical form.
parole.testo: From the Medieval Latin entitās, from ēns (“being”) (stem: ent-) + -tās (compare essentia), see there for more information.

parole.significato: To clear from mist, clouds, or obscurity.
parole.testo: From Latin ēnūbilātus, past participle of ēnūbilāre (“to enubilate”), from ē- (“out”) + nūbila (“clouds”), from nūbilis (“cloudy”), nūbēs (“cloud”). By surface analysis, e- + Latin nubil- + -ate.

parole.significato: To remove the nucleus from (a cell).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēnucleātus, from ēnucleō (“to remove the kernel from”), from ē- + nucleus (“kernel”).

parole.significato: The surgical removal of an intact organ, especially of the eye and of cysts and tumors.
parole.testo: From Latin ēnucleātus, perfect passive participle of ēnucleō (“to remove the kernel, stone, etc. from (a fruit, grape)”). Equivalent to enucleate + -ion.

parole.significato: To specify each member of a sequence individually in incrementing order.
parole.testo: First attested in 1600–1650; borrowed from Latin enumerātus, the perfect passive participle of enumerō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

parole.significato: To make a definite or systematic statement of.
parole.testo: From Latin ēnuntiātus, past participle of ēnuntiō (“to report, declare”), from ē- + nūntiō (“to report”). Doublet of enounce.

parole.significato: The act of enunciating, announcing, proclaiming, or making known; open attestation; declaration.
parole.testo: From Latin ēnuntiātiō. By surface analysis, enunciate + -ion.

parole.significato: Relating to, or containing, enunciation; declarative.
parole.testo: From Latin enuntiativus, enunciativus.

parole.significato: Someone who enunciates.
parole.testo: From Latin ēnūntiātor (“enunciator”).

parole.significato: Involuntary urination: urinary incontinence.
parole.testo: From Latin enuresis, from Ancient Greek ἐνούρησις (enoúrēsis); surface analysis parses uresis as a constituent.

parole.significato: To conceive or see something within one's mind. To imagine.
parole.testo: From en- + vision, from Latin visionem (“a thing or sight seen”).

parole.significato: Through or by that very act or quality; thereby.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin eo ipso, ablative form of id ipsum (“that (thing) itself”).

parole.significato: Under that name; that is called thus; explicitly.
parole.testo: From Latin eo nomine, ablative form of id nōmen, “that name”.

parole.significato: An extinct early Eocene mammal (Hyracotherium leporinum), ancestral to the modern horse.
parole.testo: Originally a genus name, Eohippus, formed in New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”). By surface analysis, eo- + Latin hippus.

parole.significato: Any effect of wind on land.
parole.testo: Likely from Eolus (“god of wind”), Aeolian (“relating to Eolus”), or aeolo- (“of woodwind instruments”), all via Latin Aeolus from Ancient Greek Αἴολος (Aíolos), plus -ation, a suffix denoting a process or the result of a process.

parole.significato: Of the wind; referring to the action or the power of wind.
parole.testo: From Latin Aeolicus, from Ancient Greek Αἴολος (Aíolos, “Aeolus, god of the winds”).

parole.significato: Eternity, the duration of the universe.
parole.testo: From Latin aeon, from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age, era”).

parole.significato: The adducing of particular examples so as to lead to a universal conclusion; the argument by induction.
parole.testo: From Latin epagōgē, from Ancient Greek ἐπᾰγωγή (epăgōgḗ, “a bringing in”). See epact.

parole.significato: A figure of speech by which the same word is used both at the beginning and at the end of a sentence.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epanadiplōsis, from Ancient Greek ἐπαναδίπλωσις (epanadíplōsis, “doubling, folding”).

parole.significato: The repetition of the same word or clause after intervening matter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epanalepsis, from Ancient Greek ἐπανάληψις (epanálēpsis), from ἐπαναλαμβάνω (epanalambánō), from ἐπί (epí) + ἀνά (aná) + λαμβάνω (lambánō).

parole.significato: anaphora
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek ἐπαναφορά (epanaphorá, “reference”).

parole.significato: A district of the Roman Empire at the third echelon
parole.testo: Via Late Latin eparchia from Koine Greek ἐπαρχία (eparkhía, “province; prefecture”), from Ancient Greek ἔπαρχος (éparkhos, “commander, governor; prefect, eparch”) from ἐπι- (epi-, “on, upon; over”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “ruler”); equivalent to epi- + -archy.

parole.significato: the hindbrain.
parole.testo: From New Latin epencephalon, from ep- + encephalon.

parole.significato: The insertion of a phoneme, letter, or syllable into a word, usually to satisfy the phonological constraints of a langu…
parole.testo: Middle of 16th century: via Late Latin, from Ancient Greek ἐπένθεσις (epénthesis), from ἐπεντίθημι (epentíthēmi, “to insert”), from ἐπί (epí) + ἐντίθημι (entíthēmi, “to put in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put, place”).

parole.significato: ampersand
parole.testo: From Latin et + per se + English and.

parole.significato: An 18- to 20-year-old man in ancient Greece undergoing military training.
parole.testo: Via Latin ephēbus, from Ancient Greek ἔφηβος (éphēbos, “adolescent”), from ἐπί (epí, “early”) + ἥβη (hḗbē, “manhood”), late 19th c.

parole.significato: Synonym of freckle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ephēlis, from Ancient Greek ἔφηλῐς (éphēlĭs, “a freckle”), from ἐπ- (ep-, “upon, over, epi-”) + ἥλῐος (hḗlĭos, “the sun”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, nominal suffix).

parole.significato: Lasting for a short period of time.
parole.testo: From New Latin ephemerus, from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros), the more common form of ἐφημέριος (ephēmérios, “of, for, or during the day, living or lasting but for a day, short-lived, temporary”), from ἐπί (epí, “on”) + ἡμέρα (hēméra, “day”).

parole.significato: A journal or diary.
parole.testo: From New Latin ephēmeris, from Ancient Greek ἐφημερίς (ephēmerís, “diary, calendar”), from ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros, “daily”).

parole.significato: A depression in the sphenoid bone; the pituitary fossa.
parole.testo: From Latin ephippium (“saddlecloth”), from Ancient Greek ἐφίππιον (ephíppion), from ἐπῐ́ (epĭ́) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”).

parole.significato: An allegiant of the Israelite tribal patriarch Ephraim, a member of the tribe purportedly descended from him, or an inh…
parole.testo: An adaptation of the Latin Ephraimītēs, Ephraimīta, from the Ancient Greek Ἐφραιμῑ́tης (Ephraimī́tēs), from Ἐφραίμ (Ephraím, “Ephraim”) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs, “one connected to, a member of”). Equivalent to Ephraim + -ite.

parole.significato: A brassinosteroid isolated from Aegle marmelos
parole.testo: From epi- + brassinolide. By surface analysis, epi- + brassin + -ol + -ide, from Latin brassica.

parole.significato: The layer of tissue between the pericardium and the heart.
parole.testo: New Latin, from Latin epi- (“over”) + Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía, “heart”). Attested in English from the 19th century.

parole.significato: An elegy; an ode to someone deceased.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epicēdīon, from Ancient Greek ἐπικήδειον (epikḗdeion), neuter singular form of ἐπικήδειος (epikḗdeios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + κῆδος (kêdos, “care”). Doublet of epicedium.

parole.significato: An epicede: a dirge, lament, elegy.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epicēdīum. Doublet of epicede.

parole.significato: A syllogism in which the proof of the major or minor premise, or both, is introduced with the premises themselves, and…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπιχείρημα (epikheírēma).

parole.significato: A projection, formed by a separate ossification, at the scapular end of the furcula of many birds
parole.testo: From New Latin, from epi- + Ancient Greek κλείς (kleís, “key, clavicle”) + -ium.

parole.significato: The pattern of cell wall thickening which forms the ornamentation on spores of certain types of mushroom (especially of…
parole.testo: From Latin cŏrĭum ("skin") with the Ancient Greek prefix ἐπί- ("on top of").

parole.significato: Synonym of Epicureanism.
parole.testo: From Latin Epicurismus, from Epicurus + -ismus (“-ism”). Equivalent to epicure + -ism.

parole.significato: A small circle whose centre is on the circumference of a larger circle; in Ptolemaic astronomy it was seen as the basis…
parole.testo: From Latin epicyclus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκυκλος (epíkuklos), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”). The ad hoc complication sense is a generalization from the archetype supplied by the Ptolemaic astronomy sense.

parole.significato: The outer, protective layer of the skin of vertebrates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epidermis, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδερμίς (epidermís), ἐπί (epí, “on top of”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”). Equivalent to epi- + dermis.

parole.significato: Serving to explain; demonstrative.
parole.testo: From Latin epidicticus. See epideictic.

parole.significato: A cartilaginous organ in the throat of terrestrial vertebrates covering the glottis when swallowing to prevent food and…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin epiglōttis, from Ancient Greek ἐπῐγλωττῐ́ς (epĭglōttĭ́s, “valve covering the larynx”), from ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “upon, over”) + γλωττῐ́ς (glōttĭ́s, “glottis, mouth of the windpipe”); equivalent to epi- (“upon; above”) + glottis.

parole.significato: having the characteristics of an epigram
parole.testo: From Late Latin epigrammaticus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an epigraph or to epigraphy.
parole.testo: From New Latin epigraphicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπῐγρᾰφῐκός (epĭgrăphĭkós). By surface analysis, epigraph + -ic.

parole.significato: To remove hair from the skin in such a way that removes or destroys the root, especially by plucking it out.
parole.testo: From e- + Latin pilus (“hair”) + -ate.

parole.significato: A brief concluding summary.
parole.testo: Latin epilogatio.

parole.significato: The connective tissue framework and sheath of a nerve which bind together the nerve bundles, each of which has its own…
parole.testo: From New Latin epineurium, from Ancient Greek ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) + νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”).

parole.significato: An activity, process, or state that is the result of another; a by-product, a consequence.
parole.testo: From epi- (prefix meaning ‘above, on, over; in addition to’) + phenomenon. Phenomenon is derived from Late Latin phaenomenon (“appearance”), from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing that appears in one’s view; appearance; phenomenon”), a noun use of the neuter singular form of φαινόμενος (

parole.significato: An exclamation or reflection used to summarise or round off an argument or discourse.
parole.testo: From Latin epiphonema, from Ancient Greek ἐπιφώνημα (epiphṓnēma), from ἐπιφωνείν (epiphōneín, “call to”).

parole.significato: A rhetorical device where a sequence of rhetorical questions is used to criticise or blame, or more generally, to elici…
parole.testo: From Latin epiplexis (“rebuke”), from Ancient Greek ἐπίπληξις (epíplēxis, “rebuke”), from ἐπιπλήσσω (epiplḗssō, “to chastise”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) (see epi-) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”).

parole.significato: A figure of speech by which one striking circumstance is added, in due gradation, to another; escalation to a climax.
parole.testo: From Latin epiplocē (“(rhetoric) connection”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιπλοκή (epiplokḗ, “plaiting together”), from ἐπιπλέκω (epiplékō, “to interweave”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) (see epi-) + πλέκω (plékō, “to plait”).

parole.significato: An inhabitant or descendant of Epirus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Ēpīrōtēs, from Koine Greek Ἠπειρώτης (Ēpeirṓtēs).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the affairs of a bishop in various Christian churches.
parole.testo: From Middle English episcopal, from Late Latin episcopālis, from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “watchman, overseer”).

parole.significato: Bishops seen as a group.
parole.testo: From Late Latin episcopatus, from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “watching over”).

parole.significato: Fear or hatred of bishops.
parole.testo: From Latin episcopus (“bishop”), Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “bishop”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: A literary composition in the form of a letter or series of letters, especially one in verse.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₁epi The noun is derived from Middle English epistel, epistole, pistel (“letter; literary work in letter form; written legend or story; spoken communication; (Christianity) one of the letters by an apostle in the New Testament; extract from such a letter read as part of the Mass”) [and o

parole.significato: Of or relating to letters, or the writing of letters.
parole.testo: 1627, from Latin epistolārius, from epistola (“letter”) (English epistle) + -ārius, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ) from ἐπιστέλλω (epistéllō, “to send a message”) from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to prepare, send”). For the noun, compare Middle English pistelarie and Old English pis

parole.significato: Relating to letters or epistles, or in the form or style of them
parole.testo: From Latin epistolicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολικός (epistolikós, “suited to or in the style of a letter”).

parole.significato: The study of letters and epistles.
parole.testo: From Latin epistola or its etymon Ancient Greek ἐπῐστολή (epĭstolḗ) + -ology.

parole.significato: The repetition of the same word or words at the end of successive phrases, clauses or sentences.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epistrophē, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπιστροφή (epistrophḗ).

parole.significato: A massive piece of stone or wood laid immediately on the abacus of the capital of a column or pillar; an architrave.
parole.testo: Latin epistylium, Ancient Greek: compare French épistyle.

parole.significato: A song or poem celebrating a marriage.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epithalamium, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπιθαλάμιον (epithalámion, “bridal song”), neuter form of ἐπιθαλάμιος (epithalámios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + θάλαμος (thálamos, “inner chamber, wedding chamber”).

parole.significato: A membranous tissue composed of one or more layers of cells which forms the covering of most internal and external surf…
parole.testo: From New Latin epithēlium. By surface analysis, epi- + thel- + -ium.

parole.significato: A horny excrescence on the top of the beak of some birds, notably the hornbill.
parole.testo: From New Latin epithema, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθεμα (epíthema, “lid, cover”).

parole.significato: An epithet, an attribute of a person or thing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epitheton. Doublet of epithet.

parole.significato: Synonym of epitomize (“make an epitome of”).
parole.testo: An adaptation of epitomāt-, the perfect passive participial stem of the Latin epitomō (“to abridge”).

parole.significato: Synonym of epitomizer, a writer of epitomes.
parole.testo: From Latin epitomator (“epitomizer”), from epitomātus (“epitomized”) + -or (“-er: forming agent nouns”). Equivalent to epitome + -ator or epitomate + -or.

parole.significato: a hurried accumulation or enumeration of several points.
parole.testo: From Late Latin epitrochasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτροχασμός (epitrokhasmós), from ἐπιτροχάζω (epitrokházō, “run swiftly over”).

parole.significato: A figure by which permission is either seriously or ironically granted to someone to do what he or she proposes to do,…
parole.testo: From Latin epitrope, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτροπή (epitropḗ, “reference, arbitration”), from ἐπιτρέπω (epitrépō).

parole.significato: A particular period of history, or of a person's life, especially one considered noteworthy or remarkable.
