parole.testo: From Medieval Latin epocha, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ, “a check, cessation, stop, pause, epoch of a star, i.e., the point at which it seems to halt after reaching the highest, and generally the place of a star; hence, a historical epoch”), from ἐπέχω (epékhō, “to hold in, check”), from ἐπι- (

parole.significato: Moment of theoretical suspension of all action.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epocha or German Epoche, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ). Doublet of epoch. This term was introduced by Husserl and other phenomenologists, although it also seems to be present in Aristotelian philosophy (as the concept did originate with Aristotle).

parole.significato: A person who gave or supposedly gave their name to a people, place, institution, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin eponymus, from Ancient Greek ἐπώνῠμος (epṓnŭmos), from ἐπί (epí, “upon, epi-”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”) + -ος (-os, suffix forming adjectives and nouns). Equivalent to epi- + -nym.

parole.significato: An epic.
parole.testo: From Latin epos, from Ancient Greek ἔπος (épos, “word, song, epic”).

parole.significato: A drinking up; a quaffing.
parole.testo: From Latin epotare, epotatum (“to drink”), from e (“out”) + potare (“to drink”).

parole.significato: A feast or banquet.
parole.testo: Latin epulatio.

parole.significato: A hard tumour or tumorous growth developed from the gums.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin epūlis.

parole.significato: Equal; balanced; identical.
parole.testo: From Latin aequus (“equal”).

parole.significato: The condition of being equable.
parole.testo: From Latin aequabilitas, from aequabilis.

parole.significato: Unvarying, calm and steady; constant and uniform.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aequābilis, from aequō (“make level”), from aequus (“even, level”).

parole.significato: The same in one or more respects.
parole.testo: From Middle English equal, from Latin aequālis. Doublet of aequalis and egal.

parole.significato: Calm and composed; of stable disposition.
parole.testo: From Latin aequ(us) (“calm”) + animus (“mind”). By surface analysis, equ- + animus.

parole.significato: To consider equal or equivalent (to or with).
parole.testo: From Middle English equaten, from Latin aequātus, perfect passive participle of aequō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: An imaginary great circle around Earth, equidistant from the two poles, and dividing earth's surface into the northern…
parole.testo: From Late Latin (circulus) aequator (diei et noctis).

parole.significato: A member of the equestrian order (Latin: ordo equester), the lower of the two aristocratic classes of Ancient Rome, ran…
parole.testo: From Latin eques (“horseman, knight; equestrian”).

parole.significato: Of horseback riding or horseback riders.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin equester (“of or pertaining to equestrians/cavalry”) + -ianus (“-ian, related to”, adjective marker), from equus (“horse”).

parole.significato: Equal, equally.
parole.testo: From Latin aequi-, from aequus. See also equ-.

parole.significato: Having legs of equal size; isosceles.
parole.testo: From Latin aequicrurus, + -al.

parole.significato: Having the same form; uniform, equiformal
parole.testo: From Latin aequiformis, from aequus (“equal”) + forma (“form”).

parole.significato: To balance, or bring into equilibrium.
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Late Latin *aequilībrō.

parole.significato: Synonym of equilibrium.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aequilībriō.

parole.significato: The state of being balanced; equality of weight; equilibrium.
parole.testo: From Latin aequilibritas (“equal distribution”).

parole.significato: The condition of a system in which competing influences are balanced, resulting in no net change.
parole.testo: From Latin aequilībrium, from equal + lībra (“balance”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or reminiscent of horses.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin equīnus (“of or pertaining to horses”).

parole.significato: A person who studies horses.
parole.testo: From Latin equīnus (“relating to horses; equine”) + -ologist.

parole.significato: Equal in number.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: comparable, equatable
parole.testo: From Latin aequiparābilis, from aequiparō (“put on a level with, compare”) + -bilis (“-able”), from aequus (“equal”) + parō (“place”).

parole.significato: To perform equiparation; to transfer attributes from one object or concept to another.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin aequiparātus, past participle of aequiparō (“put on a level with, compare”), from aequus (“equal”) + parō (“place”).

parole.significato: The transfer or imputation of attributes from one object or concept to another; the drawing of an equivalence between t…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin aequiparātiō, from aequiparō (“put on a level with, compare”) + -tiō (noun suffix), from aequus (“equal”) + parō (“place”). Equivalent to equiparate + -ion.

parole.significato: One who loves horses.
parole.testo: From Latin equus (“horse”) + -phile.

parole.significato: A line, drawn on a map, that connects places having the same amount of rainfall in a particular time period
parole.testo: From equi- and Latin pluvia (“rain”).

parole.significato: Of equal weight on both sides; balanced.
parole.testo: From Latin aequipondium (“an equal weight”), from aequus (“equal”) + pondus (“weight”).

parole.significato: A horsetail (plant of genus Equisetum)
parole.testo: From Latin equus (“horse”) + saeta (“bristle”).

parole.significato: An equisonant note.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aequisonus, from aequus (“equal”) in combination with sonus (“sounding”).

parole.significato: Groom, ostler, equerry, jockey.
parole.testo: From Latin equīsō (“stable-boy, equison”), from equus (“horse”).

parole.significato: Mounted on, or sitting upon, a horse; riding on horseback.
parole.testo: From Latin equitans, equitantis, present participle of equitō (“to ride on horseback”), from eques (“horseman”), from equus (“horse”).

parole.significato: An equivalent thing.
parole.testo: From Latin aequivalentia.

parole.significato: Similar or identical in value, meaning or effect; virtually equal.
parole.testo: From Latin aequivalentem, accusative singular of aequivalēns, present active participle of aequivaleō (“to be equivalent, have equal power”). By surface analysis, equi- + -valent. Mostly displaced native Middle English efenmete (See evenmete).

parole.significato: To speak using double meaning; to speak ambiguously, unclearly or doubtfully, with intent to deceive; to vacillate in o…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English equivocaten, from Medieval Latin aequivocātus, perfect passive participle of aequivocō (“to be called by the same name”), from Late Latin aequivocus (“ambiguous, equivocal”). Compare French équivoque.

parole.significato: Equivocal.
parole.testo: From Late Latin aequivocus (“ambiguous, equivocal”), from Latin aequus (“equal”) + vocō (“call”).

parole.significato: That eats horsemeat.
parole.testo: From Latin equus (“horse”) + vorare (“to eat greedily”).

parole.significato: An ancient torture device, possibly resembling a wooden horse, or possibly a rack.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin equuleus.

parole.significato: A time period of indeterminate length, generally more than one year.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin aera.

parole.significato: Capable of being eradicated.
parole.testo: From Latin ērādīcābilis, from ērādīcō (“uproot”), equivalent to eradicate + -able.

parole.significato: To pull up by the roots.
parole.testo: PIE word  *wréh₂ds From Middle English eradicaten (“to eradicate”), from eradicat(e) (“eradicated”, past participle of eradicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin ērādīcātus, the perfect passive participle of ērādīcō (“to uproot, root out; to anihilate, eradicate”), from ē- (“out”)

parole.significato: The act of plucking up by the roots; an uprooting or rooting out; extirpation; utter destruction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ērādīcātiō, from ērādīcō + -tiō, from ē- (“out”) + rādīx (“root”) + -ō. Equivalent to eradicate + -ion or e- (“without”) + radication.

parole.significato: To remove (markings or information).
parole.testo: From Latin ērāsus, past participle of ērādere (“to scrape, to abrade”), from ex- (“out of”) + radere (“to scrape”). Compare Middle English arasen, aracen (“to eradicate, erase”). Displaced native Old English dilegian.

parole.significato: The act of erasing; a rubbing out or obliteration; erasure.
parole.testo: From Latin ērādō (“to erase, to scrape”) + -siō, equivalent to erase + -ion.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Erasmus (Catholic priest and theologian).
parole.testo: From the Renaissance Latin Erasmiānus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Desiderius Erasmus’s Novum Instrumentum omne (his authoritative revision of the Bible’s New Testame…
parole.testo: From the Latin Erasmīnus, from Erasmus + -īnus; equivalent to Erasmus + -ine.

parole.significato: An exchange student taking part in an Erasmus Programme.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Erasmus. The EU student exchange programme is named after Erasmus of Rotterdam, and also a backronym for “European [Community] Action Scheme for the Mobility of University Students”.

parole.significato: The action of erasing; deletion; obliteration.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from ērādō (“to erase”) + -tūra (“abstract noun suffix”), equivalent to erase + -ure.

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Er) with atomic number 68: a silvery-white metal, in nature always found in combination with…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin erbium; itself from Swedish Ytterby (the name of the town where the element was discovered) + -ium. Coined by Swedish chemist and mineralogist Carl Gustaf Mosander in 1843. Doublet of terbium, ytterbium, and yttrium.

parole.significato: Upright; vertical or reaching broadly upwards.
parole.testo: From Middle English erect, a borrowing from Latin ērectus (“upright”), past participle of ērigō (“raise, set up”), from ē- (“out”) + regō (“to direct, keep straight, guide”).

parole.significato: The act of building or putting up or together of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ērectiō, ērectiōnis, noun of action from perfect passive participle ērectus, from verb erigō, from prefix ē- (“out of”) + regō, + action suffix -iō.

parole.significato: A person who, or a device which erects.
parole.testo: From Latin ērigō (“to raise up, elevate, lift”), equivalent to erect + -or.

parole.significato: The group of muscles of the back responsible for erect posture of the vertebral column.
parole.testo: From New Latin.

parole.significato: Homo erectus.
parole.testo: Ellipsis of taxonomic name Homo erectus; from Latin erectus (“upright”).

parole.significato: A gradual decay through slow combustion or oxidation, like that of old trees or dead animals.
parole.testo: From New Latin ēremacausis, from Ancient Greek ἠρέμα (ēréma, “quietly”) + καῦσις (kaûsis, “burning”).

parole.significato: A hermit; a religious recluse, someone who lives alone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin eremita, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs), from ἐρῆμος (erêmos, “uninhabited”) + -ίτης (-ítēs). Doublet of hermit.

parole.significato: In relation to everyone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin erga omnes.

parole.significato: Consequently, therefore, or thus.
parole.testo: From Middle English ergo, from Latin ergō.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the heath family (Ericaceae).
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin erīcāceus.

parole.significato: hedgehog
parole.testo: From Latin ēricius.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling a hedgehog.
parole.testo: From Latin ērināceus (“hedgehog”).

parole.significato: to lay out, deal out or give out
parole.testo: From Latin ērogātus, past participle of ērogō, from ex- (“out”) + rogō (“ask”). By surface analysis, e- + Latin rog- + -ate.

parole.significato: The act of giving out, or bestowing.
parole.testo: From Latin erogatio.

parole.significato: Doing the good that is required in a situation; meeting the moral obligations.
parole.testo: From Latin ērogō (“pay out, expend”), from ex (“out of, from”) + rogō (“ask; request”).

parole.significato: Interrogatory, proceeding by means of questions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin erōtēmaticus, from Koine Greek ἐρωτηματικός (erōtēmatikós, “interrogative; relating to questions”), from ἐρώτημα (erṓtēma, “question”) + -ικός (-ikós). Equivalent to obsolete erotema (“question”) + -tic.

parole.significato: A figure of speech whereby a question is asked in confident expectation of a negative answer.
parole.testo: From Late Latin erotesis, from Ancient Greek ἐρώτησις (erṓtēsis), from ἐρωτάω (erōtáō, “I question”).

parole.significato: Erotic literature, art, decoration, or other such work.
parole.testo: From neuter plural of Latin eroticus (“amatory”), from Ancient Greek ἐρωτικός (erōtikós). By surface analysis, erotic + -ica.

parole.significato: Erratic, prone to error.
parole.testo: Latin errabundus.

parole.significato: An added page in a printed work where errors which are discovered after printing and their corrections (corrigenda) are…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin errāta (“mistaken things, mistakes”), neuter plural of errātus (“mistaken”).

parole.significato: Wandering or straying.
parole.testo: From Latin errātiō (“wandering”).

parole.significato: A published notice reporting an error belatedly discovered in a previous publication.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin errātum, neuter of errātus (“mistaken”).

parole.significato: Causing an increase in mucus within the nose, and hence causing one to sneeze.
parole.testo: From Latin errhīnum, from Ancient Greek ἔρρινον (érrhinon), from ἐν (en, “in”) + ῥίς (rhís, “nostril”).

parole.significato: The act of becoming red; reddening.
parole.testo: Mid 18th century. From Latin erubescens, from erubesco, from ex- + rubesco. Compare French érubescence. By surface analysis, e- + Latin rub(eō) + -escence.

parole.significato: Red; reddish.
parole.testo: 18th century. From Latin erubescens, present participle of erubescere (“to grow red”); e (“out”) + rubescere. See rubescent. By surface analysis, e- + Latin rub(eō) + -escent.

parole.significato: Synonym of bornite.
parole.testo: From Latin ērubēscō (“to redden”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Caterpillar; larva.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin eruca, in its senses of "caterpillar" and "colewort" respectively. Cognate with arugula, rucola, rocket, roquette.

parole.significato: Shaped like a caterpillar; the term is loosely applied to some larvae with little resemblance to typical caterpillars.
parole.testo: From Latin eruca (“caterpillar”) + -form.

parole.significato: To burp or belch.
parole.testo: From Latin ēructō.

parole.significato: To belch, to burp.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ēructātus, from the verb ēructō.

parole.significato: The act of belching, of expelling gas from the stomach through the mouth.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ērūctātiōnem, accusative of ērūctātiō (“a belching forth, burp”), from ērūctāre (“to belch, burp”). Compare Middle English eructuacioun (“belching, burp”), borrowed from the same root.

parole.significato: Educated; learned; erudite.
parole.testo: Latin ērūdiō.

parole.significato: Learned, scholarly, with emphasis on knowledge gained from books.
parole.testo: From Latin ērudītus, participle of ērudiō (“educate, train”), from e- (“out of”) + rudis (“rude, unskilled”). Doublet of erudit.

parole.significato: To remove wrinkles from.
parole.testo: From Latin ērūgō, ērūgātus.

parole.significato: Hardship, trouble, calamity.
parole.testo: From Latin aerumna.

parole.significato: That emerges, or bursts through; breaking forth.
parole.testo: From Latin ērumpēns, present active participle of ērumpō (“break forth”).

parole.significato: To eject something violently (such as lava or water, as from a volcano or geyser).
parole.testo: From Latin eruptus, past participle of ērumpō (“to break out (of), to burst out (from)”), from e (“out”) + rumpō (“to break”).

parole.significato: bitter vetch, blister vetch (Vicia ervilia).
parole.testo: From Latin ervilia.

parole.significato: The root of sea holly, Eryngium maritimum, formerly candied and taken as confectionery and held to have aphrodisiac pro…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin ēryngion, from Ancient Greek ἠρύγγιον (ērúngion), from ἤρυγγος (ḗrungos).

parole.significato: An acute, sometimes recurrent febrile disease caused by infection of a hemolytic streptococcus, associated with intense…
parole.testo: From Middle English erisipila, borrowed from Latin erysipelas, from Ancient Greek ἐρῠσῐ́πελᾰς (erŭsĭ́pelăs), probably related to ἐρῠθρός (erŭthrós, “red”) and πέλμᾰ (pélmă, “the sole of a foot”).

parole.significato: Abnormal redness and inflammation of the skin, due to vasodilation.
parole.testo: From New Latin erythēma, from Ancient Greek ἐρύθημα (erúthēma, “a redness or flush on the skin”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”)..

parole.significato: An inflammatory condition characterised by inflammation of the fat cells under the skin, resulting in tender red nodule…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Erythrae
parole.testo: From Latin Erythraeus (from Ancient Greek Ἐρυθραῖος (Eruthraîos)) + -an.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Erythraean Sea
parole.testo: From Latin erythraeus (“reddish”) (as it was used in Erythraeum mare (“the Erythraean Sea”), from Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”)) + -an.

parole.significato: The fleshy growth from an anglerfish's head that acts as a lure for its prey.
parole.testo: From Latin ēsca (“bait”).

parole.significato: Anything that escalates.
parole.testo: By genericization from the former trademark Escalator, created by American inventor Charles Seeberger in 1900, from Latin ē- (“from, out of”) + scala (“ladder”) + -tor, which forms nouns of agency; see the appendix. Broader usage may be influenced by its derivative escalate, by surface analysis, esc

parole.significato: A licence formerly required for the making over a bill of exchange to another person overseas.
parole.testo: From Latin escambium, excambium. See excamb.

parole.significato: To draw outside of; designating a circle that touches one of the sides of a given triangle, and also the extensions of…
parole.testo: From Latin e (“out, out of”) + scribere (“to write”).

parole.significato: Suitable for eating; eatable, edible.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ēsculentus (“fit for eating, eatable, edible; good to eat, delicious; nourishing; full of food”) + English -ent (suffix forming adjectives with the sense of causing, doing, or promoting a certain action). Ēsculentus is derived from ēsca (“food; dish prepared for the tabl

parole.significato: An acid obtained from the horse chestnut
parole.testo: Latin aesculus, generic name of the horse-chestnut, from Latin aesculus a kind of oak.

parole.significato: A coumarin glucoside which exists in horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum), California buckeye (Aesculus californica)…
parole.testo: Related to Latin aesculus.

parole.significato: The full profits or products yielded by land, such as hay, pasturage, grain, rents, services, and the like.
parole.testo: From Latin expletia, Old French espleit. Compare exploit.

parole.significato: Not covered in scales or scale-like objects; having a smooth skin or outer covering.
parole.testo: From e- (prefix forming adjectives with the sense of lacking something) + squamulose; squamulose is derived from New Latin squāmulōsus (“squamulose”), from Latin squamula (“small scales”) (diminutive of squāma (“scale of a fish or reptile; item shaped like a scale, flake”)) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘

parole.significato: A rabbit.
parole.testo: Coined in a 1995 episode of the animated TV show The Simpsons named "Lisa's Wedding", in which a Renaissance fair sideshow falsely promotes a normal rabbit as "a horse with the head of a rabbit and the body of a rabbit". Possibly inspired by fanciful names for creatures from Medieval Latin (e.g. bas

parole.significato: Essence, essential nature.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin esse.

parole.significato: that which is; an entity, a being, an existent
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, coined by Ralph Manheim in his 1959 English translation of Martin Heidegger’s Einführung in die Metaphysik to render German Seiendes (as distinct from Sein) on the basis of *essens, a pseudo-Latin present participle of sum.

parole.significato: Necessary.
parole.testo: From Late Latin essentiālis, from Latin essentia (“being, essence”).

parole.significato: of, or relating to the grammatical case that in some languages indicates existence in a state or capacity.
parole.testo: From New Latin casus essīvus (from Latin esse), coined in New Latin by Rasmus Rask.

parole.significato: It is best to live with moderation; it is best to find a middle ground.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin est modus in rebus.

parole.significato: that which is being estimated.
parole.testo: Apparently of mid-20th century coinage from Latin aestimandum, gerundive of aestimō (“to value”, “to estimate”).

parole.significato: A rough calculation or assessment of the value, size, or cost of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English estimat, borrowed from Latin aestimātus (“valuing, estimate”, only used in the ablative singular: "aestimātū..." (in valuing...)), from aestimō + -tus (“action noun-forming suffix”).

parole.significato: To calculate roughly, often from imperfect data.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aestimātus, perfect passive participle of aestimō (“to estimate”) (see -ate), older form aestumō (“to value, rate, esteem”); from Old Latin *ais-temos (“one who cuts copper”), meaning one in the Roman Republic who mints money. Compare Middle English estymatt (“reputed”) / estimat

parole.significato: estimated
parole.testo: From Latin aestimātus (“estimated”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 2 for more. Originally used as the past participle of estimate; compare generate or communicate.

parole.significato: A person who estimates, especially one who estimates costs
parole.testo: From Latin aestimātor; equivalent to estimate + -or.

parole.significato: A coastal water body where ocean tides and river water merge, resulting in a brackish water zone.
parole.testo: From Latin aestuarium (“creek”, “estuary of a river”).

parole.significato: To swell up or rage; to be agitated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aestuātus, past participial of aestuō (“to be in violent motion, to boil up, burn”), from aestus (“boiling or undulating motion, fire, glow, heat”).

parole.significato: An agitation or commotion.
parole.testo: From Middle English estuacioun, estuation, from Latin aestuātiō. By surface analysis, estuate + -ion.

parole.significato: Very greedy or hungry; ravenous; (figuratively) avid, eager.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēsurient, ēsurientem, from ēsuriēns (“hungering”), present participle of ēsuriō (“to be hungry, to hunger for something”), a desiderative verb from edō (“to eat”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁édti (“to eat”)) + -turiō (suffix indicating a desire for an action).

parole.significato: And others; to complete a list, especially of persons, as authors of a published work.
parole.testo: From Latin, abbreviation of et aliī (“and others”) (English: et alii) and its forms and derivatives.

parole.significato: And elsewhere; to complete a list of places.
parole.testo: From Latin, abbreviation of and other places (English: et alibi).

parole.significato: And others; used of things; neuter plural
parole.testo: From Latin et (“and”) + alia (“others”).

parole.significato: And others; used of females; feminine plural.
parole.testo: From Latin et (“and”) + aliae (“others”).

parole.significato: and elsewhere; used to terminate lists of passages in a text
parole.testo: From Latin et (“and”) + alibi (“elsewhere”).

parole.significato: And others; used of males, or groups of mixed gender; masculine plural
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin et alii (“and others”).

parole.significato: And others; used of people, unless exclusively of female gender
parole.testo: From Latin et (“and”) + alios (“others”).

parole.significato: Something in addition, which can easily be understood.
parole.testo: From Middle English et cetera, from Latin et cētera (“and the other things; and the rest of the things”).

parole.significato: And all this kind.
parole.testo: From Latin et hoc genus omne.

parole.significato: And everything of that sort.
parole.testo: From Latin et id genus omne (“and all that sort”).

parole.significato: And what follows, and following, and in the following [pages, sections, &c.].
parole.testo: Borrowing of Latin et seq., an abbreviation variously of et (“and”) sequens (“the following item”), sequente (“in what follows”), sequentes and sequentia (“the following items”), or sequentibus (“in the following items”).

parole.significato: And other similar items; and the like; and so on.
parole.testo: From Latin et similia.

parole.significato: "You too, Brutus" or "even you, Brutus"; expressing a recognition of betrayal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin et tū, Brūte (literally “and you, Brutus”). Used figuratively from 1591 (sometimes jocularly) to express shock and sadness at the treachery of a good friend. Although apparently an Elizabethan invention, a “genuine antique reproduction”, it appears to have been well known in Engl

parole.significato: "and wife", or "and his wife"
parole.testo: From Latin et uxor (“and [the] wife”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a dry north wind which blows in the eastern Mediterranean.
parole.testo: From Latin etesius (“annual”), from Ancient Greek ἐτήσιος (etḗsios, “annual”), from ἔτος (étos, “year”).

parole.significato: The substance formerly supposed to fill the upper regions of the atmosphere above the clouds, in particular as a medium…
parole.testo: From Middle English ēther (“the caelum aetherum of ancient cosmology in which the planets orbit; a shining, fluid substance described as a form of air or fire; air”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman ether and Middle French ether, ethere, aether, from Old French aether (“highest and purest part of the atm

parole.significato: Pertaining to the presupposition of an invisible air-like element permeating all of space, or to the higher regions bey…
parole.testo: From Latin aetherius (“of or pertaining to the ether, the sky, Heaven or the air or upper air”), from Ancient Greek αἰθέριος (aithérios, “of or pertaining to the upper air”). By surface analysis, ether + -ial.

parole.significato: Formed of ether; ethereal.
parole.testo: Latin aethereus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Moral, relating to morals.
parole.testo: From Middle English etik, from Late Latin ēthicus, from Ancient Greek ἠθῐκός (ēthĭkós).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the study of ethics.
parole.testo: From ethic + -al, from Late Latin ethicus (“moral, ethical”), from Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Ethiopia.
parole.testo: From Latin Aethiops from Ancient Greek Αἰθίοψ (Aithíops, “charred complexion”).

parole.significato: Ethiopian
parole.testo: From Latin aethiopicus, from Ancient Greek Αἰθιοπικός (Aithiopikós). By surface analysis, Ethiop + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a group of people having common racial, ancestral, national, religious or cultural origins.
parole.testo: From Middle English ethnik, from Latin ethnicus ("pagan", "heathen"), from Ancient Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikós, “of or for a nation, heathen”), from ἔθνος (éthnos, “a company", later "a people or nation, heathens”). By surface analysis, ethno- + -ic.

parole.significato: Ethnic.
parole.testo: From Middle English ethnicalle, from Late Latin ethnicālis.

parole.significato: The scientific study of animalian behavior, especially that of nonhuman animals.
parole.testo: From the Latin ēthologia (“the art of depicting or imitating character”), from the Ancient Greek ἠθολογία (ēthología, “painting of character, especially by mimic gestures”), from ἠθολόγος (ēthológos, “painting character by mimic gestures”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, especially moral character”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to Etna, a volcano in Sicily.
parole.testo: From Latin Aetnaeus, from Ancient Greek Αἰτναῖος (Aitnaîos), from Αἴτνη (Aítnē) + -αῖος (-aîos), equivalent to Etna + -ean.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the region and culture of Etruria, a pre-Roman civilization in Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin Etruscus (which see for more) + -an.

parole.significato: A book of etymologies.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin etymologicon.

parole.significato: Synonym of Euboean.
parole.testo: From Latin Euboicus, from Ancient Greek Εὐβοϊκός (Euboïkós). By surface analysis, Euboea + -ic.

parole.significato: A member of the eudicots.
parole.testo: Probably a back-formation from eudicots, short for eudicotyledons, from the New Latin coinage eudicotylēdōn, from the Ancient Greek components εὐ- (eu-, “good, well”) + δι- (di-, “two”) + κοτυληδών (kotulēdṓn, “cup-shaped cavity”); equivalent to eu- (“true”) + dicot.

parole.significato: applause
parole.testo: From Latin euge, from Ancient Greek εὖγε (eûge).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Gubbio.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Eugubīnus.

parole.significato: The belief that legends and mythology arise from exaggerated descriptions of historical people and events.
parole.testo: From Euhemerus + -ism, ultimately from Latin Euhēmerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: Someone who practices or upholds euhemerism, a person who believes all or most myths and legends arose from historical…
parole.testo: From euhemerism + -ist, from Latin Euhemerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: Of or relating to euhemerism.
parole.testo: From euhemerist + -ic, from euhemerism, from Latin Euhemerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: The fanciful invention of plausible historical figures and events as an attempt to rationalize mythology and legends
parole.testo: From euhemerize + -ation, ultimately from Latin Euhēmerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: To invent a plausible but fanciful historical origin for something in order to rationalize mythology and legends.
parole.testo: From euhemerism + -ize, ultimately from Latin Euhēmerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: The practice of sending the consecrated Eucharist to those not present, or the Eucharist itself so sent.
parole.testo: From Latin eulogia, from Ancient Greek εὐλογῐ́ᾱ (eulogĭ́ā).

parole.significato: A eulogy.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin eulogium, apparently from a confusion between ēlogium and eulogia. Doublet of eulogy.

parole.significato: An oration to honor a deceased person, usually at a funeral.
parole.testo: From Latin eulogium, apparently from a confusion between ēlogium (whence English elogium, elogy) and eulogia (from Ancient Greek εὐλογία (eulogía, “praise”), whence English eulogia); equivalent to eu- + logia ("good words"). Doublet of eulogium.

parole.significato: A castrated man.
parole.testo: From Middle English eunuk, from Middle French eunuque, from Latin eunūchus, from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunoûkhos), from εὐνή (eunḗ, “bed”) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have, keep”). Originally probably used to refer to a bed chamber attendant.

parole.significato: To make a eunuch of; to castrate (a man).
parole.testo: Latin eunuchatus, perfect participle of eunucho.

parole.significato: The condition of being a eunuch.
parole.testo: Latin eunuchismus (“act of unmanning”), equivalent to eunuch + -ism.

parole.significato: In medieval music, a mnemonic for the Latin words saeculōrum and āmēn (from “ […] in saecula saeculōrum. Āmēn.” from th…
parole.testo: From the vowels in the last two words of the final phrase of the Gloria Patri doxology in Latin: “[…] in saecula saeculōrum. Āmēn.” (literally “[…] into ages of ages (for ever and ever). Amen.”). In liturgical works used in Gregorian chant, instead of repeating the words, the letters were printed un

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Euphorbia, the spurges.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin euphorbia by 1601, reinforced by taxonomic name Euphorbia after 1753. Variant form euforbia is attested in Middle English.

parole.significato: An acrid dull yellow or brown resin consisting of the concreted milky juice of several species of Euphorbia, formerly u…
parole.testo: From Latin euphorbium, from Ancient Greek εὐφόρβιον (euphórbion), from Εὔφορβος (Eúphorbos, “Euphorbus, physician to the Mauretanian king Juba II”) + -ιον (-ion, “related to”). The name is from εὔφορβος (eúphorbos, “well-fed”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + φορβή (phorbḗ, “food, fodder”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Euripides (an ancient Greek tragedian).
parole.testo: Latin Eurīpidēus (from the Ancient Greek Εὐρῑπῐ́δειος, from Εὐρῑπῐ́δης, whence Euripides) + English -an

parole.significato: A strait; a narrow tract of water, where the tide or a current flows and reflows with violence, like the ancient firth…
parole.testo: From Latin eurīpus, from Ancient Greek εὔριπος (eúripos); from εὖ (eû, “well”) + ῥιπή (rhipḗ, “rushing motion”).

parole.significato: The east wind.
parole.testo: From Middle English Eurus, ewrus, from Latin eurus, from Ancient Greek εὖρος (eûros).

parole.significato: One who is comparable to Eusebius of Caesarea; an ecclesiastic historian.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Eusebius, borrowed from Ancient Greek Εὐσέβιος (Eusébios), from εὐσεβής (eusebḗs) + -ῐος (-ĭos).

parole.significato: To leave or withdraw from; to quit; to retire from.
parole.testo: First attested in 1526; borrowed from Latin ēvacuātus, the perfect passive participle of ēvacuō (“to empty out, evacuate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To wander.
parole.testo: From Latin evagor.

parole.significato: To evert a bodily organ inside surface to outside.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēvāgīnātus, perfect passive participle of ēvāgīnō (“to unsheath”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Protruded, or grown out, as an evagination; turned inside out; unsheathed; evaginated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēvāgīnātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Alternatively, back-formation from evagination.

parole.significato: The act of evaginating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēvāginātiō. By surface analysis, evaginat(e) + -ion.

parole.significato: Relating to time or duration.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin aevum (“lifetime, age, eternity”) + -al.

parole.significato: To disappear into a mist or dissipate in vapor
parole.testo: From Latin evanescere (“to vanish”). Doublet of vanish.

parole.significato: The act or state of vanishing away; disappearance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ēvānēscentia.

parole.significato: The "good news" revealed by the Gospel; redemption.
parole.testo: From ecclesiastical Latin evangelium.

parole.significato: Liable to vanish; faint; weak; evanescent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēvānidus, from ēvānēscere. See evanesce.

parole.significato: To transition from a liquid state into a gaseous state.
parole.testo: First attested in 1545, borrowed from Latin ēvapōrātus, the perfect passive participle of ēvapōrō (“to evaporate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). See also Middle English evaporaten (“to draw off humors or "spirits" as "vapor"”) and evaporen (“to draw off bodily

parole.significato: An instrument for measuring evaporation; an atmometer.
parole.testo: From Latin evaporare (“to evaporate”) + -meter. Compare French évaporomètre.

parole.significato: Modification of the lunar orbit due to the gravitational effects of the Sun.
parole.testo: From Latin evectiōnem, from evectiō (“act of carrying”), from evect-, past participle stem of evehō (“to carry together”), combination of ex- and vehō.

parole.significato: To occur; to happen; to come to pass.
parole.testo: From Latin ēveniō (“happen, fall out, come out”), from ē (“out of, from”) (short form of ex) + veniō (“come”).

parole.significato: To winnow out; to fan.
parole.testo: From Latin ēventilātus, past participle of ēventilō (“to fan”). See ventilate.

parole.significato: to evert (overthrow, subvert, or turn inside out)
parole.testo: From Latin ēversus, past participle of ēvertere (“to turn out, overthrow”); ē- (“out”) + vertere (“to turn”). Compare evert.

parole.significato: Tending to evert or overthrow; subversive.
parole.testo: From Latin ēversīvus, from ēvertō.

parole.significato: To turn inside out (like a pocket being emptied) or outwards.
parole.testo: From Late Latin ēvertere (“to turn (an item of clothing) inside out”), Latin ēvertere, present active infinitive of ēvertō (“to turn upside down; to overturn; to reverse”), from ē- (variant of ex- (prefix meaning ‘out, away’)) + vertō (“to reverse; to revolve, turn; to turn around”) (ultimately from

parole.significato: To investigate.
parole.testo: From Latin evestigatus (“traced out”), from e (“out”) + vestigatus, past participle of vestigare. See vestigate.

parole.significato: To vibrate.
parole.testo: From Latin evibrare. See vibrate.

parole.significato: To expel (one or more people) from their property; to force (one or more people) to move out.
parole.testo: From Middle English evicten, evycten, borrowed from Latin ēvictus, past participle of ēvincō (“to vanquish completely”). Doublet of evince.

parole.significato: Of or providing evidence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ēvidentiālis, from Latin ēvidentia + -ālis.

parole.significato: A wicked look conveying dislike or envy that in many cultures is believed to be able to cause bad luck or injury; also,…
parole.testo: From Middle English ivel eie (“evil eye; envy”), from Old English eage yfel, a calque of Latin oculus malus, from oculus (“eye”) + malus (“bad, evil, wicked; destructive, hurtful, injurious; unfavourable, unlucky”).

parole.significato: To castrate.
parole.testo: From Latin ēvirātus, perfect passive participle of ēvirō (“to emasculate”), from ē (“out of”) + vir (“man”).

parole.significato: Emasculation; effeminacy.
parole.testo: Latin eviratio.

parole.significato: To disembowel; to remove the viscera.
parole.testo: From Latin ēviscerātus, past participle of ēviscerāre (“to disembowel”), from e- (“out”) + viscera (“bowels”), equivalent to e- (“out”) + viscera + -ate.

parole.significato: To shun; to avoid.
parole.testo: From Latin evitatus, past participle of evitare (“to shun”); e (“out”) + vitare (“to shun”).

parole.significato: An avoidance.
parole.testo: Latin evitatio.

parole.significato: grammatically expressing the notion that something is avoided or feared: a grammatical mood found in some Australian Ab…
parole.testo: From Latin ēvītāre (“to avoid”), from ē- (“out”) + vītāre (“to shun”).

parole.significato: eternal; everlasting
parole.testo: From Latin eviternus, aeternus, aeviternitas (“eviternity”) + -al. See eternal.

parole.significato: To evoke
parole.testo: From Latin ēvocāre.

parole.significato: That evokes (brings to mind) a memory, mood, idea, feeling, or image; redolent or reminiscent.
parole.testo: From Latin ēvocātīvus (“pertaining to summoning”). By surface analysis, evoke + -ative.

parole.significato: A female evocator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ēvocātrīx. By surface analysis, evocate + -trix.

parole.significato: A flying out or up, such as evaporation.
parole.testo: Latin evolatio.

parole.significato: A change of position.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēvolūtiō, ēvolūtiōnis (“the act of unrolling, unfolding or opening (of a book)”), from ēvolūtus, perfect passive participle of ēvolvō (“unroll, unfold”), from ex + volvō (“roll”). Compare typologically Czech vývoj, Serbo-Croatian развој, Russian разви́ть (razvítʹ), развива́ть (ra

parole.significato: To move (something) in regular procession through a system.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēvolvō (“unroll, unfold”), from ē- (“out of”) (short form of ex) + volvō (“roll”).

parole.significato: The involute of a curve.
parole.testo: Latin ēvolvēns, ēvolventis (“unrolling”), present participle of ēvolvō (“to unroll”).

parole.significato: To vomit.
parole.testo: From Latin ēvomitus, past participle of ēvomere (“to vomit forth”); ē- (“out”) + vomere.

parole.significato: To publish or divulge.
parole.testo: From Latin evulgatus, past participle of evulgare (“to publish”).

parole.significato: A divulging, or publication (act of publishing).
parole.testo: From Latin evulgatio.

parole.significato: To promulgate or spread abroad.
parole.testo: From Latin evulgo.

parole.significato: The action of forcibly pulling something out.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēvulsiōnem, from ēvellere.

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter X/x.
parole.testo: From Latin ex.

parole.significato: the place the train originated from or called at prior to the present location.
parole.testo: From Latin ex (“out of, from”); originated as a telegraphic abbreviation.

parole.significato: out of an abundance of caution.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ex abundante cautēlā.

parole.significato: predicted; forecast
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ex ante (“before the event”).

parole.significato: With authority based on one's rank or office.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ex cathedrā (“from the (teacher's) chair”).

parole.significato: Of a legal obligation: arising from a contractual relationship.
parole.testo: From Latin ex (“from”) + contractū (ablative singular of contractus (“contract”)).

parole.significato: Not during copulation; not in the copulative state.
parole.testo: From Latin ex cōpulā.

parole.significato: Of a legal obligation: arising from a delict or tort, or some other wrongful act.
parole.testo: From Latin ex dēlīctō (literally “from transgression”).

parole.significato: From the face or appearance.
parole.testo: From Latin ex facie (“out of the face”).

parole.significato: Given as a favour; given as a gift.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ex grātiā (literally “out of grace”).

parole.significato: Following from the hypothesis; in accordance with the hypothesis; by hypothesis; as a consequence of assumptions made;…
parole.testo: From Late Latin ex hypothesi (literally “from the hypothesis”), from hypothesis.

parole.significato: Outside of the jurisdiction of the court.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A bookplate that identifies the owner of the book into which it is pasted.
parole.testo: From Latin ex librīs (“from the books [of]”).

parole.significato: From the negative.
parole.testo: From the Latin ex negativo.

parole.significato: Out of nothing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin (creātiō) ex nihilō (“(creation) out of nothing”).

parole.significato: Nothing comes from nothing; out of nothing, nothing is produced.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ex nihilō nihil fit (literally “out of nothing is made nothing”), from De rerum natura by Lucretius.

parole.significato: “from now on”. Used to describe certain legal effects which are applicable solely from this point (in time) on and ther…
parole.testo: From Latin ex (“from”) + nunc (“now”).

parole.significato: By virtue of the office that originated it, or of the title held.
parole.testo: From Latin ex officio (“by right of office”, literally “from the office”).

parole.significato: From the work worked; referring to sacraments deriving their power from Christ's work rather than the role of humans, a…
parole.testo: From Latin ex opere operātō.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or characteristic of a proceeding where one of the involved parties is not present.
parole.testo: From Latin ex parte ("from [one] part").

parole.significato: A maxim of proportionality: one can extrapolate the size of a thing from the size of a part.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?] (literally “from his foot, [we can measure] Hercules”)

parole.significato: actual
parole.testo: From Latin ex post (“after the event”).

parole.significato: Retroactive.
parole.testo: From Latin ex (“from”) + post (“after”) + factō, ablative of factum (“deed”). In Latin, ex takes the ablative case, while post takes the accusative case. (See Wikipedia for a discussion of the grammatical form and usage of this phrase.)

parole.significato: Professedly; by profession.
parole.testo: From Latin ex professo (“by profession”).

parole.significato: Of one's own accord.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: of its own force or volition
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ex proprio vigore.

parole.significato: From the nature of things; from the nature of the case; from nature; applied to arguments based on observation or exper…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ex rērum nātūrā (“from the nature of things”).

parole.significato: Outside its original position or place.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ex + sitū, ablative singular of situs.

parole.significato: carried out with no preparation; impromptu
parole.testo: From Latin ex (“immediately after”) + tempore, ablative singular of tempus (“time", "opportunity", "occasion”).

parole.significato: from the beginning, from the outset. Used to describe certain legal effects that can affect situations prior to this po…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ex tunc.

parole.significato: by definition
parole.testo: From Latin, ēx (“out of”) + vī, ablative singular of vīs (“force”) + terminī, genitive singular of terminus (“word”).

parole.significato: Outside the living organism.
parole.testo: From Latin ex vivo.

parole.significato: An offering to a church in fulfillment of a vow.
parole.testo: From Latin ex (“out of, in accordance with”) + voto, ablative of votum (“a vow”).

parole.significato: To make worse (a problem, bad situation, negative feeling, etc.).
parole.testo: First attested in 1660; borrowed from Latin exacerbātus, perfect passive participle of Latin exacerbō (“to provoke”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out of; thoroughly”) + acerbō (“to embitter, harshen or worsen”).

parole.significato: An increase in the severity of something (such as a disease)
parole.testo: From Middle English exacerbacyoun, from Latin exacerbātiōnem, from exacerbāre (“to provoke, make harsh”). See exacerbate.

parole.significato: exacerbation (particularly of a fever or disease)
parole.testo: From Latin exacerbescens, exacerbescentis, present participle of exacerbescere, inchoate of exacerbare. See exacerbate.

parole.significato: The act of heaping up.
parole.testo: From Latin exacervō (“to heap up exceedingly”), from acervus. See ex-, and acervate.

parole.significato: Precisely agreeing with a standard, a fact, or the truth; perfectly conforming; neither exceeding nor falling short in…
parole.testo: From Latin exāctus (the verb via Middle English exact), perfect passive participle of exigō (“demand, claim as due; measure by a standard, weigh, test”), from ex (“out”) + agō (“drive”).

parole.significato: A bet in which the bettor must correctly pick the two runners who finish first and second, in the correct order.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin exactus (literally “precise, acccurate”).

parole.significato: Synonym of actinon (“radon-219”).
parole.testo: From Latin ex actīniō (“out of actinium”).

parole.significato: To hone, whet or sharpen.
parole.testo: From Latin exacure, from ex (“out (intensive)”) + acuere (“to make sharp”). See acuate, acute.

parole.significato: An operation involving the removal of a part or parts of the body; excision, ectomy.
parole.testo: From New Latin exaeresis, from Ancient Greek ἐξαίρεσῐς (exaíresĭs, “a taking out, an extraction”).

parole.significato: To overstate, to describe more than the fact.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exaggerātus, perfect passive participle of exaggerō (“to heap up, increase, enlarge, magnify, amplify, exaggerate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out, up”) + aggerō, aggerāre (“to heap up”), from agger (“a pile, heap, mound, dike

parole.significato: The act of heaping or piling up.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exaggerātiō.

parole.significato: To excite, stir up.
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Latin exagitāre.

parole.significato: agitation
parole.testo: Latin exagitatio: compare Old French exagitation.

parole.significato: examination; inquiry
parole.testo: From Latin exāmen (“the tongue of a balance, examination”), for exagmen, from exigere (“to weigh accurately, to treat”): compare French examen. See exact.

parole.significato: One who examines; an examiner.
parole.testo: From Latin examinantis (“examining”).

parole.significato: One who is subjected to examination.
parole.testo: From Latin examinatus, past participle of examinare. By surface analysis, examine + -ate.

parole.significato: An examiner.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin examinator. Compare French examinateur.

parole.significato: Lifeless, not or no longer living, dead.
parole.testo: From Latin exanimātus, perfect passive participle of exanimō (see ex-, -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from Latin ex- + animō, from anima (“soul, spirit, breath”); see anima. The verb derives from the adjective, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Deprivation of life or spirits.
parole.testo: Latin exanimatio.

parole.significato: lifeless; dead
parole.testo: From Latin exanimus, exanimis; ex (“out, without”) + anima (“life”).

parole.significato: A widespread rash usually occurring in children.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exanthema, from Ancient Greek ἐξάνθημα (exánthēma), from ἐξανθέω (exanthéō), from ἐξ (ex) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

parole.significato: A rash on the skin.
parole.testo: From New Latin exanthesis, from Ancient Greek ἐξάνθεσις (exánthesis). See exanthema.

parole.significato: To exhaust or wear out.
parole.testo: From Latin exantlatus, past participle of exantlare, exanclare (“to endure”).

parole.significato: To plough up.
parole.testo: From Latin exaratus, past participle of exarare (“to plough up, to write”); ex (“out”) + arare (“to plough”).

parole.significato: The act of writing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exarātiō.

parole.significato: In the Byzantine Empire, a governor of a distant province.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin exarchus.

parole.significato: To tax the patience of; irk, frustrate, vex, provoke, annoy; to make angry.
parole.testo: First attested in 1534; borrowed from Latin exasperātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin exasperō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex (“out of; thoroughly”) + asperō (“to make rough”), from asper (“rough”). Participial usage of the adjective up until

parole.significato: To annul the consecration of: to deconsecrate, secularize, profane, or otherwise unhallow (historical) particularly in…
parole.testo: From Latin exauguratus under the influence of English -ate, past participle of exaugurāre (“to deconsecrate, to profane”), from ex (“ex-: undo”) + augurāre (“to act as augur, to consecrate”), from augur + -āre (verb-forming suffix), q.v.

parole.significato: The act of exaugurating; desecration.
parole.testo: Latin exauguratio desecration.

parole.significato: To deprive of authority or power
parole.testo: From Latin exauctoratus, past participle of exauctorare (“to dismiss”), from ex (“out”) + auctorare (“to bind to something, to hire”), from auctor. See author.

parole.significato: Deprivation of authority or dignity; degradation.
parole.testo: From Latin exauctoratio.

parole.significato: The removal of the shoes.
parole.testo: From Latin excalceātus + -tion.

parole.significato: exchange or barter, especially of lands.
parole.testo: Late Latin excambium. See excamb.

parole.significato: Disenchantment by a countercharm.
parole.testo: Latin excantare (“to charm out”).

parole.significato: To strip (something or someone) of flesh, perhaps as a form of torture.
parole.testo: From Latin ex (“out”) + carnificatus, past participle carnificare (“to carnify”). Compare Latin excarnificare (“to tear to pieces, torment”). See carnify.

parole.significato: To make a hole in (something); to hollow.
parole.testo: First attested in 1599, from Latin excavātus (“hollowed out”), perfect passive participle of excavō (“to hollow out”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex (“out”) + cavō (“to hollow out, pierce”), from cavus (“cave, hole”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Particip

parole.significato: Any member of a major grouping of unicellular eukaryotes, of the clade Excavata.
parole.testo: From a substantivization of Latin excavātus through the associated taxon's name (Excavata), see -ate (noun-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: The act of excavating, or of making hollow, by cutting, scooping, or digging out a part of a solid mass.
parole.testo: From Latin excavātiō (“a hollowing out”), from excavō (“to hollow out”), from ex + cavō (“to hollow out”), from cavus (“hollow”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- (“vault, hole”). Equivalent to excavate + -ion.

parole.significato: A female that excavates; a female excavator.
parole.testo: Probably from the scientific Latin specific epithet excavatrix. By surface analysis, excavate + -trix.

parole.significato: To excavate.
parole.testo: From Latin excavare.

parole.significato: To blind.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin excaecātus, perfect passive participle of excaecō (“to blind”), from ex- (denoting privation) + caecō (“to blind”), from caecus (“blind”).

parole.significato: excess (of spending, people, goods, etc.)
parole.testo: From Latin excēdentis.

parole.significato: Synonym of excellence; the quality of being excellent.
parole.testo: From Middle English excellencie, from Latin excellentia.

parole.significato: Loftier, yet higher, more elevated; ever upward.
parole.testo: From Latin excelsior, comparative of excelsus (“high”). The name of the stuffing material was originally a trademark. As an exclamation, originating in Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's poem Excelsior (1841), based on the New York state motto. Popularized in the comic book fandom by Marvel Comics editor

parole.significato: An exception whereby a defendant can claim that the plaintiff has not paid the money to him and that therefore the obli…
parole.testo: Latin phrase. exceptio (“an exception”) + non (“not (having)”) + numero - atis ("to count") + pecunia (“money”).

parole.significato: The exceptio metus; an exception based on the fact that the underlying cause of action was based on duress or intimidat…
parole.testo: From Latin exceptio (“exception”) quod (“based on”) metus (“duress”) causa (“a cause (of action)”).

parole.significato: The rare occurrence of a counterexample to a rule, used to demonstrate that the rule exists.
parole.testo: Derived from the medieval Latin legal principle "exceptio probat regulam in casibus non exceptis" ("the exception tests the rule in the cases not excepted").

parole.significato: The act of removing a person's brains.
parole.testo: From Latin excerebratus (“deprived of brains”), from ex (“out”) + cerebrum (“brain”).

parole.significato: excrete; give off
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin excernō.

parole.significato: To pick out.
parole.testo: From Latin excerpere, excerptum, from ex (“out”) + carpere (“to pick, gather”). See harvest and compare scarce (adjective).

parole.significato: A clip, snippet, passage or extract from a larger work such as a news article, a film, or a literary composition.
parole.testo: From Latin excerptus, past participle of excerpere (“to pick out”), from ex (“out”) + carpere (“to pick, pluck”).

parole.significato: The act of excerpting or selecting.
parole.testo: Latin excerptio.

parole.significato: To cut off.
parole.testo: From Latin excidere, excisum; ex (“out”) + caedere (“to cut”). See concise, and compare excise (“to cut off”).

parole.significato: An ingredient that is intentionally added to a drug for purposes other than the therapeutic or diagnostic effect at the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin excipiēns, present participle of excipiō. See except.

parole.significato: The outer part of an apothecium of those ascomycete fungi which have that sort of fructification. Most lichens come int…
parole.testo: From Latin excipere.

parole.significato: One who excises, especially one who performs female genital cutting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin excīsor. By surface analysis, excise + -or.

parole.significato: To excite.
parole.testo: From Latin excitatus, past participle of excitare. See excite.

parole.significato: Resembling an exclamation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exclāmātōrius.

parole.significato: To bar (someone or something) from entering; to keep out.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exclūdō, from prefix ex- (“out”) + variant form of verb claudō (“close”).

parole.significato: Excluding items or members that do not meet certain conditions.
parole.testo: From Latin exclūsīvus, from excludere (“to shut out, exclude”), from ex- (“out”) + variant form of verb claudere (“to close, shut”).

parole.significato: The act of excocting or boiling out.
parole.testo: Latin excoctio.

parole.significato: To think over something carefully; to consider fully; cogitate.
parole.testo: From Latin excōgitāre, from ex- + cōgitāre (“think”).

parole.significato: Careful thought or consideration.
parole.testo: From Latin excogitatio.

parole.significato: To officially exclude someone from membership of a church or religious community.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin excommunicātus, perfect passive participle of excommunicō (“excommunicate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, ex- + communicate.

parole.significato: Excommunicated.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin excommunicātus, perfect passive participle of excommunicō (“put out of the community”). See -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more. Displaced native Old English āmǣnsumian.

parole.significato: The act of excommunicating, disfellowshipping or ejecting; especially an ecclesiastical censure whereby the person agai…
parole.testo: From Middle English excommunicacion, from Late Latin excommūnicātiō. By surface analysis, excommunicate + -ion. Displaced native Old English āmǣnsumung.

parole.significato: One who excommunicates.
parole.testo: Derived from Late Latin excommūnicātor, from Late Latin excommūnicātio + -tor.

parole.significato: To remove the skin and/or fur of, to flay, to skin.
parole.testo: First attested in the first part of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English *excoriaten (only attested in its past participle), borrowed from Late Latin excoriātus perfect passive participle of excoriō (“to take the skin or hide off, flay, skin”), from ex- (“out off, from”

parole.significato: To strip of bark, shell or skin.
parole.testo: From Latin ex (“out”), from cortex, corticis (“bark”).

parole.significato: To spit out; to discharge from the throat by hawking and spitting.
parole.testo: From Latin excreare, exscreare, from ex (“out”) + screare (“to hawk”).

parole.significato: The act of spitting out.
parole.testo: From Latin excreatio, exscreatio.

parole.significato: Human and non-human animal solid waste excreted from the bowels; feces.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin excrēmentum, from excernō (“to excrete”).

parole.significato: Something which grows out of the body; hair, nails, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin excrēmentum, from excrēscō (“to grow out”).

parole.significato: Something, usually abnormal, which grows out of something else.
parole.testo: From Middle English, early 15th century, in sense “(action of) growing out (of something else)”. Borrowed from Latin excrescentia (“abnormal growths”), from excrescentem, from excrēscere, from ex- (“out”) (English ex-) + crēscere (“to grow”) (English crescent). Sense of “abnormal growth” from 1570s,

parole.significato: A growing mutation, usually abnormal.
parole.testo: From Latin excrēscēns, present participle of excrēscō.

parole.significato: Bodily waste which is excreted from the body.
parole.testo: From Latin excrēta, neuter plural of excrētus, past participle of excernere.

parole.significato: To discharge material (including waste products) from a cell, body or system.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin excrētum, past participle of excernō, from ex- (“out”), and cernō (“separate”).

parole.significato: Liable to torment.
parole.testo: Latin excruciabilis (“deserving of torture”).

parole.significato: To inflict intense pain or mental distress on (someone); to torture.
parole.testo: From Latin excruciātus, past participle of excruciō, from ex- + cruciō, from the base of crux (“cross”).

parole.significato: Causing great pain or anguish, agonizing
parole.testo: Present participle of excruciate, from Latin excruciō, from ex- + cruciō (“to torment”).

parole.significato: A keeping watch; a vigil.
parole.testo: From Latin excubatio, from excubare (“to lie out on guard”), from ex (“out”) + cubare (“to lie down”).

parole.significato: A gallery in a church, used for all-night vigils.
parole.testo: From Latin excubitorium, from ex (“out”) + cubare, cubitum (“to lie”).

parole.significato: The act of exculpating from alleged fault or crime.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exculpātiō. By surface analysis, exculpate + -ion.

parole.significato: Tending to excuse or clear of wrongdoing.
parole.testo: From exculpate + -ory (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to, serving for’). parole.significato: To digress.
parole.testo: From Latin excurro.

parole.significato: To make a journey, especially an excursion; to travel.
parole.testo: Probably partly from Classical Latin excurs-, past participial stem of excurrō, and partly from the noun.

parole.significato: Synonym of excursus.
parole.testo: From Classical Latin excursus. Doublet of excursus. In the “excursus” sense, some later examples in plural may show errors for excursuses.

parole.significato: A brief recreational trip; a journey out of the usual way.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin excursiō (“a running out, an inroad, invasion, a setting out, beginning of a speech”), from excurrere (“to run out”), from ex (“out”) + currere (“to run”). By surface analysis, excurse + -ion. Compare excursus.

parole.significato: A fuller treatment (in a separate section) of a particular part of the text of a book, especially a classic.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin excursus (“excursion”). Doublet of excurse.

parole.significato: One who makes, or is authorized to make, an excuse; an apologist.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin excusator.

parole.significato: To shake off.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin excussus, past participle of excutere (“to shake off”).

parole.significato: The process or proceedings whereby a creditor must proceed against a principal debtor before proceeding against a suret…
parole.testo: Latin excussus, past participle of excutere (“to shake off”).

parole.significato: A license or permit for absence from a university or a religious house (such as a monastery).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exeat, third-person singular subjunctive of exeō (“depart”) used as an impersonal imperative, literally “let him go forth”.

parole.significato: To feel loathing for; to abhor.
parole.testo: From Latin exsecrārī, execrārī, from ex (“out”) + sacrāre (“to consecrate, declare accursed”).

parole.significato: An act or instance of cursing; a curse dictated by violent feelings of hatred; an imprecation; an expression of utter d…
parole.testo: From Latin execrātiō.

parole.significato: Of or relating to an executive (branch of government etc.).
parole.testo: Latin executorialis.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to administration or execution.
parole.testo: From Middle English executory, from Latin execūtōrius. By surface analysis, execute + -ory.

parole.significato: A female person who executes or carries out something.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English executrice, executrix (“female executor; administrator of the law; wielder of fate”), from Medieval Latin execūtrīx (possibly through Anglo-Norman *executrice) from execūtor, exsecūtor (“accomplisher, performer; prosecutor, revenger”), + Latin -trīx (suffix forming feminine

parole.significato: consuming; that eats away
parole.testo: From Latin exedēns, present participle of exedere. See exesion.

parole.significato: To release; to exempt.
parole.testo: From Latin eximĕre.

parole.significato: Deserving honour, respect and admiration.
parole.testo: From Middle English exemplarie, from Latin exemplāris (“exemplary; a copy, facsimile”), from exemplum (“an example; a sample; a copy or transcript”). By surface analysis, example + -ary. Doublet of exemplar. First use appears before 1450.

parole.significato: An example, or typical instance.
parole.testo: From Middle English exemplarie, from Latin exemplārium. By surface analysis, example + -ary. First use appears before 1425.

parole.significato: Serving as or providing a typical example.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exemplātīvus. Possibly attested once in Middle English, but re-borrowed as it is not attested again until the 19th century.

parole.significato: For the sake of an example.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exemplī grātiā.

parole.significato: To exemplify.
parole.testo: Back-formation from exemplification. For its use by non-native speakers, compare Catalan and Portuguese exemplificar, from Latin exemplificō.

parole.significato: Something serving as an example.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exemplificātor.

parole.significato: An example.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exemplum. Doublet of example and sample.

parole.significato: To disembowel; to eviscerate.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exenterātus, perfect passive participle of exenterō (“to disembowel”). First attested in 1607.

parole.significato: The surgical removal of all the contents of a body cavity such as the pelvis or the orbit.
parole.testo: From exenterate + -ion, possibly corresponding to a learned borrowing from Latin *exenterātiō, from exenterō (“to disembowel”).

parole.significato: An official authorization given by a government to a consul etc.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exequātur.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to funerals; funereal.
parole.testo: From Latin exequialis, exsequialis, from exsequiae (“exequies”).

parole.significato: Currently working; practising; professional
parole.testo: From Latin exercents, exercentis, present participle of exercere. See exercise.

parole.significato: The exercise or exertion of some power, responsibility, faculty etc.
parole.testo: From Latin exercitatio, from exercitare, intensive, from exercere (“to exercise”).

parole.significato: To make use of, to apply, especially of something nonmaterial; to bring to bear.
parole.testo: From Latin exsertus, past participle of exserō (“to stretch or thrust forth or out”), from ex- + serō (“to string together”).

parole.significato: The act of eating, or corroding, out or through.
parole.testo: From Latin exedere, exesum (“to eat up”), from ex (“out”) + edere (“to eat”).

parole.significato: To be agitated; to boil up; to effervesce.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exaestuātus, passive participle of exaestuō (“to boil up”). See estuate.

parole.significato: A boiling up or effervescence.
parole.testo: Latin exaestuatio.

parole.significato: A stage direction for more than one actor to leave the stage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exeunt (“they leave”), the third-person plural present active indicative of exeō (“leave”).

parole.significato: In plays, an instruction that all actors should leave the stage.
parole.testo: From Latin exeunt omnēs (“they all exit; exit all”).

parole.significato: To remove the leaves from a plant.
parole.testo: From Late Latin exfoliō (“to strip of leaves”), from ex- (“out of”) + folium (“leaf”); compare effoliate and French exfolier.

parole.significato: The scaling off of a bone, a rock, or a mineral, etc.; the state of being exfoliated.
parole.testo: From Latin exfoliare (to remove leaves).

parole.significato: The act or process of exhaling; breathing out
parole.testo: From Latin exhālātiō, from exhālō (“to breathe out, to exhale”), from hālō (“to breathe”). Equivalent to exhale + -ation.

parole.significato: To draw or let out wholly; to drain completely.
parole.testo: From Latin exhaustus, past participle of exhaurīre (“to draw out, drink up, empty, exhaust”), from ex (“out”) + haurīre (“to draw (especially water), drain”).

parole.significato: The point of complete depletion, of the state of being used up.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exhaustiō, from exhauriō. Surface analysis: exhaust + -ion.

parole.significato: Including every possible element: fully comprehensive.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exhaustīvus. By surface analysis, exhaust + -ive.

parole.significato: To disinherit.
parole.testo: From Latin exheredatus, past participle of exheredare (“to disinherit”), from ex (“out”) + heres, heredis (“heir”).

parole.significato: A disinheriting; disherison.
parole.testo: Latin exheredatio: compare French exhérédation.

parole.significato: A disinheriting; disherison.
parole.testo: From Latin exhereditare, exhereditatum (“disinherit”).

parole.significato: To display or show (something) for others to see, especially at an exhibition or contest.
parole.testo: From Latin exhibitus, perfect passive participle of exhibeō (“to hold forth, present, show, display”), from ex (“out of, from”) + habeō (“to have, hold”); see habit.

parole.significato: Someone who exhibits something.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exhibitor. First attested in 1654. By surface analysis, exhibit + -or.

parole.significato: exhibiting; publicly showing
parole.testo: Latin exhibitorius relating to giving up: compare French exhibitoire exhibiting.

parole.significato: Causing exhilaration or pleasure.
parole.testo: From Latin exhilarantis. See exhilarate. By surface analysis, ex- + Latin hilar(ō) + -ant.

parole.significato: To cheer, to cheer up, to gladden, to make happy, to elate.
parole.testo: From Latin exhilarō (“to delight, to gladden, to make merry”), from ex- (“out, away”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs (“out”)) + hilarō (“to cheer, to gladden”), from hilaris (“cheerful, light-hearted, lively”), from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful, merry”), from ἵλαος (hílaos, “gracious,

parole.significato: Appearing to exhort; in an urging manner.
parole.testo: From late Middle English exhortatyf, from Latin exhortātīvus, from exhortātus + -ivus. By surface analysis, exhort + -ative.

parole.significato: Serving to exhort.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Late Latin exhortātōrius. By surface analysis, exhort + -atory.

parole.significato: To dig out of the ground; to take out of a place of burial; to disinter.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin exhumō, from Latin ex- + humō (“to bury”).

parole.significato: Urgent; pressing; needing immediate action.
parole.testo: From Latin exigēns, present active participle of exigō (“demand, require”). Doublet of exigeant.

parole.significato: Scanty; meager.
parole.testo: From Latin exiguus (“strict, exact”), from exigere (“to measure against a standard”).

parole.significato: The act of suddenly jumping up or out.
parole.testo: From Latin exilīo (“leap up, bound”) + -ion.

parole.significato: Thinness, smallness; a shrunken or meagre condition.
parole.testo: From Latin exilitatem, from exilis (“small, thin, narrow”).

parole.significato: Pre-eminent, outstanding.
parole.testo: From Latin eximius (“set apart, select”), from eximō (“take out or away; deliver, free”), from ex (“out of, from”) + emō (“buy; acquire, take”).

parole.significato: To make (something) weak and ineffective; to enervate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exinānīt-, exinānīre (“to empty the contents of; to drain or pour out”).

parole.significato: An emptying; an evacuation; an enfeebling; exhaustion; humiliation.
parole.testo: From Latin exinānitiō, from exināniō, from ex- (“out”) and ināniō (“to empty”).

parole.significato: existing; having life or being, current; occurring now
parole.testo: From Latin existens, from existere. By surface analysis, exist + -ent.

parole.significato: Of or relating to existence.
parole.testo: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Late Latin existentiālis, exsistentiālis (“coming into or relating to existence”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives; and forming nouns of verbal action). Existentiālis, exsistentiālis are derived from Late Latin existenti

parole.significato: Opinion, esteem or judgment.
parole.testo: From Latin existimatio.

parole.significato: An act of going out or going away, or leaving; a departure.
parole.testo: From Middle English exit, from Latin exitus (“departure, going out; way by which one may go out, egress; (figuratively) conclusion, termination; (figuratively) death; income, revenue”), from exeō (“to depart, exit; to avoid, evade; (figuratively) to escape; of time: to expire, run out”) + -tus (suff

parole.significato: Used as a stage direction for an actor: to leave the scene or stage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exit, the third-person singular present active indicative of exeō (“to depart, exit; to avoid, evade; (figuratively) to escape; of time: to expire, run out”); see further at etymology 1 above.

parole.significato: destructive; fatal
parole.testo: From Latin exitialis, exitious, from exitium (“a going out”).

parole.significato: Harmful, destructive, deadly, pernicious.
parole.testo: From Latin exitiosus.

parole.significato: death
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exitus. Doublet of ejido and exit.

parole.significato: An outlaw.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exlēx.

parole.significato: To bring into existence from nothing.
parole.testo: Based on Latin; compare annihilate and ex nihilo.

parole.significato: The act of bringing into existence from nothing.
parole.testo: From Latin ex (“from”) + nihil (“nothing”). Compare annihilation.

parole.significato: To deprive of eyes; blind.
parole.testo: From Latin exoculātus, perfect passive participle of exoculō (“to remove the eyes”).

parole.significato: departure; exodus, especially the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt
parole.testo: From Latin exodium, from Ancient Greek ἐξόδιον (exódion).

parole.significato: Synonym of exode (“a comic performance after a tragedy”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exodium.

parole.significato: A sudden departure of a large number of people.
parole.testo: From Latin exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos, “expedition, procession, departure”). Doublet of exodos. From late Old English only as a proper noun, Exodus, the biblical book; use as a common noun is from the early 17th century.

parole.significato: That has gone out of use; disused, obsolete.
parole.testo: From the Latin exolētus, the perfect passive participle of exolescō, from ex + olēscō (from oleō + -ēscō).

parole.significato: To relieve (someone or something) of a load; to unburden (a load).
parole.testo: From Middle English exoneraten (attested in past participle exonerated), from Latin exonerātus, past perfect participle of exonerō (“to discharge, unload; to exonerate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Exonerō is from ex- (“out, from”) + onerō (“to burden, lade; to load”) further from onus (oner-)

parole.significato: Freed from an obligation; freed from accusation or blame; acquitted, exonerated.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exonerātus (more at etymology 1), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: An act of disburdening, discharging, or freeing morally from a charge or imputation.
parole.testo: From Latin exonerātiō. By surface analysis, exonerate + -ion.

parole.significato: One who exonerates.
parole.testo: From Latin exonerātor. By surface analysis, exonerate + -or.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Exeter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Exonia, the Latin name for Exeter which appears in the Liber Exoniensis (1086), + -an. See its adjectival form Exoniensis.

parole.significato: Highly desirable.
parole.testo: Latin exoptabilis.

parole.significato: An earnest wishing or desire.
parole.testo: From Latin exoptatio.

parole.significato: Capable of being moved or persuaded.
parole.testo: From Latin exorabilis.

parole.significato: entreaty
parole.testo: From Latin exōrātiōnem (“petition, prayer”) (whence ex- + and -ation), from exōrō (“persuade, win over, beg, plead, entreat”), from ōrō (“orate, plead, beg, pray, entreat”).

parole.significato: To go off track or orbit; to deviate.
parole.testo: From Latin exorbitatus, passive participle of exorbitare. See exorbitant.

parole.significato: The act of leaving the usual path or course; deviation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exorbitatio, from exorbitō (“to go off the track, deviate”) + -tio.

parole.significato: To drive out (an evil spirit) from a person, place or thing, especially by an incantation or prayer.
parole.testo: From Middle English exorcisen, exorzisen, from Medieval Latin exorcizō, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō, “to banish an evil spirit; bind by oath”), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos). Compare Old French exorciser.

parole.significato: The minor order of exorcists.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exorcistātus.

parole.significato: A preface or prefatory passage.
parole.testo: From Latin exordium.

parole.significato: of or relating to an exordium, beginning or introduction
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exordiri.

parole.significato: A beginning.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exordium (“beginning, commencement”), from exōrdior (“to begin, commence”), from ex (“out of, from”) + ōrdior (“to begin”).

parole.significato: To embellish, adorn, decorate.
parole.testo: From Latin exōrnātus.

parole.significato: ornament; decoration; embellishment (physically, or relating to prose)
parole.testo: From Latin exornatio, from exornare. See ornate.
