parole.significato: Of a doctrine, information, etc.: suitable to be imparted to the public without secrecy or other reservations.
parole.testo: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Late Latin exōtericus + English -ic (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’). Exōtericus is borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξωτερῐκός (exōterĭkós, “exterior, external, outside”, adjective), from ἐξωτέρω (exōtérō, “more exterior”) (the co

parole.significato: A wide stretch, usually of sea, sky, or land.
parole.testo: From Latin expansum, from expandō.

parole.significato: Comprehensive in scope or extent.
parole.testo: From Latin expāns-, past-participle stem of expandere (“to spread out”; see expand) + -ive.

parole.significato: To write or speak at length; to be copious in argument or discussion.
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Latin expatior, from ex- + spatior (“walk about”).

parole.significato: Living outside of one's own country.
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1787, the adjective and noun in 1812; borrowed from Medieval Latin expatriātus, perfect passive participle of expatriō (“to banish”) (see -ate (etymology 1,2 and 3)), from Latin ex- (“out of”) + patria (“native land”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); possibly after French ex

parole.significato: To predict or believe that something will happen
parole.testo: From Latin expectāre, infinitive form of exspectō (“look out for, await, expect”), from ex (“out”) + spectō (“look at”), frequentative of speciō (“see”).

parole.significato: To cough up fluid from the lungs.
parole.testo: From Latin expectorātus, past participle of expectorō (“(only figurative) banish from the mind; (post-classical) expel from the breast)”), from ex (“out of”) + pectus (“the breast”).

parole.significato: To injure (a dog) by cutting away the pads of the forefeet, thereby preventing it from hunting.
parole.testo: From Latin (ex-, pes, pedis (“foot”)); compare excoriate.

parole.significato: To deprive of the claws or the balls of the forefeet.
parole.testo: From Latin expeditatus, past participle of expeditare (“to expeditate”), from ex (“out”) + ped- (“foot”).

parole.significato: To accelerate the progress of.
parole.testo: From Latin expedītus (“unimpeded, unfettered”), perfect passive participle of expediō (“bring forward, set right”).

parole.significato: Fast, prompt, speedy.
parole.testo: From Middle English expedycius (“useful, fitting”), from Latin expedītus (“disengaged, ready, convenient, prompt; unfettered, unencumbered”), past participle of expediō.

parole.significato: To eject.
parole.testo: Late Middle English: from Latin expellere, from ex- (“out”) + pellere (“to drive”).

parole.significato: To consume, exhaust (some resource).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin expendō (“to weigh; to pay out”). Doublet of spend.

parole.significato: Act of expending or paying out.
parole.testo: From stem of Medieval Latin expenditus, irregular perfect passive participle of expendō (“to weigh, to pay out”), + -ure (“process or result”).

parole.significato: Having a high price or cost.
parole.testo: From Latin *expēnsīvus, from expendō (“to weigh out (money), to pay out”) (whence English expend). By surface analysis, expense + -ive. In the sense of "high-priced" has largely displaced dear.

parole.significato: An awakening.
parole.testo: From Latin expergefactiō, from expergefaciō.

parole.significato: Lessons learned from experience are the most lasting.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin ūsus magister est optimus, from Prō Rabīriō Postumō by Cicerō about Gāius Rabīrius Postumus.

parole.significato: A person who experiences something.
parole.testo: From Latin experiēns.

parole.significato: Of, related to, encountered in, or derived from experience.
parole.testo: From Latin experientiālis, from experientia + -ālis.

parole.significato: An experimenter.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Worthy of being wished for; desirable or sought after
parole.testo: Latin, expetibilis, from expeto (“I wish for, I aspire to”), from ex (“out”) + peto (“I seek”)

parole.significato: To atone or make reparation for.
parole.testo: From Latin expiātus, past participle of expiō (“atone for”).

parole.significato: One who makes expiation or atonement.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin expiātor.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to expiation.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin expiātōrius.

parole.significato: One who plunders or pillages.
parole.testo: From Latin expīlātor, from expīlō.

parole.significato: An act, process, or instance of expiring.
parole.testo: From Middle English expiracioun, exspiracioun (“vapor, breath”), from Latin expīrātiōnem, exspīrātiōnem, accusative singular of expīrātiō, exspīrātiō. By surface analysis, expire + -ation.

parole.significato: To fish out; to find out by skill or laborious investigation; to search out or rummage (for information)
parole.testo: From Latin expiscatus, past participle of expiscari (“to fish out”), from ex (“out”) + piscari (“to fish”), piscis (“fish”). By surface analysis, ex- + Latin pisc- + -ate.

parole.significato: Able to be explained or understood
parole.testo: From explain + -able from Latin explanō (“to flatten, spread out, make plain or clear, explain”).

parole.significato: That which is to be explained (cf. explanans).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin explanandum.

parole.significato: A collection of propositions that, taken together, explain another proposition (the explanandum).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin explānāns.

parole.significato: Flat; flattened.
parole.testo: From Latin explanatus (“flattened”).

parole.significato: The act or process of explaining.
parole.testo: From Latin explanatio (“an explanation, interpretation”), from explanare (“explain”); see explain. Morphologically explain + -ation. Displaced native Old English racu.

parole.significato: One who explains.
parole.testo: From Latin explānātor, from explānō (“to flatten out, make plain, explain”).

parole.significato: Intended to serve as an explanation.
parole.testo: From Late Latin explānātōrius, from Latin explānāt-, past-participle stem of explānāre (“to explain”). Displaced Old English ġereclīċ.

parole.significato: The remainder of subtracting an angle from a full circle.
parole.testo: From Latin explēmentum, from expleō (“to fill up”).

parole.significato: Complete, perfect
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin expletus (“completed”).

parole.significato: accomplishment; fulfillment
parole.testo: From Latin expletio (“a satisfying”). See expletive.

parole.significato: Serving to fill up, merely for effect, otherwise redundant.
parole.testo: From Late Latin explētīvus (“serving to fill out”), from Latin explētus, the perfect passive participle of expleō (“fill out”), itself from ex (“out, completely”) + *pleō (“fill”).

parole.significato: That which is to be explained or explicated
parole.testo: From Latin explico.

parole.significato: The underlying meaning of an explicandum.
parole.testo: From Latin explicāns.

parole.significato: To explain meticulously or in great detail.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin explicāre (“unfold, explain”).

parole.significato: Explanatory; serving to explain logically or in detail.
parole.testo: From Latin explicātīvus, from explicō (“to unfold, open out”).

parole.significato: Explanatory; serving to explain logically or in detail.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin explicātōrius, from Latin explicō (“to unfold, open out”). By surface analysis, explicate + -ory.

parole.significato: Used at the conclusion of a book to indicate the end.
parole.testo: Abbreviated from Latin explicitus est liber (“the book is set in order, ended”).

parole.significato: To fly apart with sudden violent force; to blow up, to burst, to detonate, to go off.
parole.testo: First recorded around 1538, from the Latin verb explōdere (“drive out or off by clapping”). The meaning was originally theatrical, "to drive an actor off the stage by making noise," hence meaning to "to drive out" or "to reject". From ex- (“out”) + plaudere (“to clap; to applaud”). In English it use

parole.significato: To explore.
parole.testo: From Latin explorare, exploratum.

parole.significato: Able to, or likely to, explode.
parole.testo: From Latin explōs-, stem of the perfect passive participle of explōdō + the suffix -ive.

parole.significato: To polish thoroughly.
parole.testo: Compare Latin expolire. See polish.

parole.significato: To expound; to explain.
parole.testo: From Middle English exponen, from Latin expōnō. Doublet of expose and expound.

parole.significato: One who expounds, represents or advocates.
parole.testo: From Latin expōnēns, present participle of expōnō (“to expose; to exhibit, display, set out; to explain”), from ex- (“out, away”) + pōnō (“to lay, place, put”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to exportation or exports.
parole.testo: From Latin exportare.

parole.significato: The act of reasoning earnestly in order to dissuade or remonstrate.
parole.testo: From Latin expostulātiōnem, accusative singular of expostulātiō (“complaint, expostulation”), from expostulō (“demand, expostulate”), from ex (“out of, from”) + postulō (“demand or claim”). See expostulate.

parole.significato: A canon of construction holding that, when a legal document includes a list, anything not in that list is assumed to be…
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Expressly; explicitly.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin expressis verbis (“pronounced with words”).

parole.significato: To reproach or upbraid
parole.testo: From Latin exprōbrātus (“reproached”) (whence -ate, past participle of exprōbrō (“to reproach, upbraid or reprove”), from ex- + probrum (“disgrace, shame”) (whence ex-).

parole.significato: Reproachful accusation; upbraiding.
parole.testo: From Latin exprōbrātiō (whence -ion), from exprōbrō (“to reproach, upbraid or reprove”), from ex- + probrum (“disgrace, shame”) (whence ex-). Compare French exprobration. By surface analysis, exprobrate + -ion.

parole.significato: Expressing, or relating to, exprobration.
parole.testo: From Latin exprōbrātus (“reproached”) + -ory, past participle of exprōbrō (“to reproach, upbraid or reprove”), from ex- + probrum (“disgrace, shame”) (whence ex-).

parole.significato: To deprive a person of (their private property) for public use.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin expropriātus.

parole.significato: Able to be overcome, conquered or taken by storm.
parole.testo: Latin expugnabilis.

parole.significato: The act of taking by assault; conquest.
parole.testo: Latin expugnatio.

parole.significato: To expel, usually by means of violence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin expulsō.

parole.significato: Tending to expel or resulting in expulsion.
parole.testo: From Latin expulsīvus. By surface analysis, expulse + -ive.

parole.significato: Synonym of expulsive.
parole.testo: From Latin expulsorius. By surface analysis, expulse + -ory.

parole.significato: The act of expunging or erasing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin expunctiō, expunctiōnem.

parole.significato: To erase or strike out.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin expungere.

parole.significato: To edit out (incorrect, offensive, or otherwise undesirable information) from a book or other publication; to cleanse;…
parole.testo: From Latin expurgātus, perfect passive participle of expurgō (“purge, cleanse, purify”).

parole.significato: To search into or out.
parole.testo: From Latin exquīrere. See exquisite.

parole.significato: Especially or extraordinarily fine or pleasing; exceptional.
parole.testo: From Latin exquīsītus (“to be outsought”), perfect passive participle of exquīrō (“to outseek”).

parole.significato: An inquiry, research.
parole.testo: From Latin exquisitio.

parole.significato: To drain (a living or dead body, or (medicine, surgery) a body part) of blood.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₁ésh₂r̥ Learned borrowing from New Latin exsanguinātus (“depleted of blood, exsanguinated; lacking blood, bloodless”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Exsanguinātus is a participial adjective formed on ex- (“out, from”) + sanguī̆s (sanguin-) (“blood”) + -ātus.

parole.significato: Destitute of blood; bloodless.
parole.testo: From Latin exsanguis, from ex (“out”) + sanguis, sanguinis (“blood”). Compare exsanguineous.

parole.significato: To cut out.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exscindō (“demolish, destroy”), originally in the sense “to destroy utterly”.

parole.significato: To copy down onto paper; to transcribe.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin excribere; ex (“out, from”) + scribere (“to write”).

parole.significato: A copy; a transcript.
parole.testo: From Latin exscriptus, past participle of exscribere.

parole.significato: To cut out or away; to remove by exsection.
parole.testo: From Latin exseco.

parole.significato: A cutting out or away.
parole.testo: From Latin exsectiō.

parole.significato: To thrust out; to cause to protrude.
parole.testo: From Latin exsertus, past participle of exserō (“to stretch out or forth”). See exert.

parole.significato: Having the quality of drying up; causing a drying up.
parole.testo: From Latin exsiccans, present participle of exsiccare. See exsiccate.

parole.significato: To dry, to desiccate, to dehydrate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exsicco, exsiccatus, from ex- + siccus (“dry”).

parole.significato: The act of operation of drying; evaporation or expulsion of moisture.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin exsiccatio, exsiccationis, from Latin exsicco: compare French exsiccation.

parole.significato: A dried specimen such as that in a herbarium.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exsiccātum.

parole.significato: To separate from one another at a critical point in temperature.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exsolvere. Doublet of exolve.

parole.significato: Spoliation.
parole.testo: From Latin exspoliatio, from exspoliare (“to spoil, to plunder”), from ex (“out”) + spoliare. See spoliate.

parole.significato: The act of spitting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Without juice or sap; completely dry.
parole.testo: Latin exsuccus, from ex- + succus ‘juice’.

parole.significato: The act of sucking out.
parole.testo: From Latin ex(s)ugō, ex(s)uctum (“to suck out”), from ex (“out”) + sugō (“to suck”). Equivalent to ex- + suction.

parole.significato: To exorcise or renounce by blowing.
parole.testo: From Latin exsufflare (“to blow at or upon”); ex (“out”) + sufflare. See sufflate.

parole.significato: empty and inflated; frivolous
parole.testo: From Latin ex + sufflāre.

parole.significato: To rouse; to excite.
parole.testo: From Latin exsuscitatus, past participle of exsuscitare; ex (“out”) + suscitare. See suscitate.

parole.significato: A stirring up; a rousing.
parole.testo: From Latin exsuscitatio.

parole.significato: Emergence.
parole.testo: From Latin extantia, exstantia (“a standing out”), from exstans, present participle. See extant.

parole.significato: The state of rising above others, or a projection.
parole.testo: From Latin extantia, exstantia.

parole.significato: Still in existence; not having disappeared.
parole.testo: First attested in 1545, from Latin extantem, extāns, present participle of extō (“to stand out, exist, be extant”), from ex- (“out”) + stō (“stand”).

parole.significato: Extemporaneous.
parole.testo: From Latin extemporāl(is) (“extemporary, unrehearsed”).

parole.significato: That which is extemporaneous; something effortless but transient or superficial.
parole.testo: From Latin extemporānea, neuter plural of extemporāneus (“extemporaneous”).

parole.significato: With inadequate preparation or without advance thought; offhand.
parole.testo: From Late Latin extemporāneus, from Latin ex tempore (“impromptu”).

parole.significato: extent; expanse
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin extensus.

parole.significato: Capable of being extended.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin extēnsibilis, from extendō (“to extend”).

parole.significato: Having a great extent; covering a large area; vast.
parole.testo: From late Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin extensīvus, from Latin extensus.

parole.significato: A muscle in the human forearm that acts to extend and abduct the radiocarpal joint.
parole.testo: Latin. Cognate with French muscle court extenseur radial du carpe.

parole.significato: Of a person: emaciated, wasted, weakened; of the body or part of it: atrophied, shrunken, withered.
parole.testo: From Middle English extenuat (“(medicine) made thin, emaciated”), from Latin extenuātus (“diminished, reduced, thinned”), perfect passive participle of extenuō (“to diminish, reduce, thin”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out-, thoroughly”) + tenuō (“to enfeeble, weaken, wear down;

parole.significato: To make (something) less dense, or thinner; also, to lower the viscosity of (something).
parole.testo: From Latin extenuātus (“diminished, reduced, thinned”) (more at etymology 1), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: That attenuates or lessens the seriousness of something, e.g. by providing a mitigating excuse for it.
parole.testo: From Latin ex (“to delete, to cross out”) and tenuatus, past participle of tenuare (“to make thin”) + Middle English -ing. By surface analysis, ex- + tenuate + -ing.

parole.significato: The action of extenuating; extenuated condition.
parole.testo: An adaptation of extenuātiōn-, the oblique stem of the Latin extenuātiō (“a thinning or diminishing”, “rarefaction”; rhetoric “a lessening”, “diminution”, “extenuation”), noun of action from extenuō (“to thin, reduce, or diminish”). Equivalent to extenuate + -ion. Compare the French exténuation.

parole.significato: Tending to extenuate or palliate.
parole.testo: Compare Latin extenuātōrius (“attenuating”).

parole.significato: Relating to the outside parts or surface of something.
parole.testo: From Latin exterior.

parole.significato: Capable of being exterminated.
parole.testo: From Latin exterminabilis (“that may be destroyed”).

parole.significato: To kill or otherwise permanently eliminate all of (a population, often of pests or undesirables), usually intentionally.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exterminātus, perfect passive participle of exterminō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ex- (“thoroughly”) + terminō (“to finish, close, end”), from terminus (“limit, end”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Someone or something that exterminates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exterminātor. By surface analysis, exterminate + -or.

parole.significato: A woman who exterminates.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exterminātrīx. By surface analysis, exterminate + -trix.

parole.significato: Outside of something; on the exterior.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English, from Medieval Latin externus (“outward, external”), from exter/exterus (“on the outside, outward”).

parole.significato: foreign; belonging to, or coming from, abroad or outside
parole.testo: From Latin exterraneus, from ex (“out”) + terra (“land”).

parole.significato: The act of wiping or rubbing out.
parole.testo: From Latin extergere, extersum (“to wipe out”), from ex (“out”) + tergere (“to wipe or rub off”).

parole.significato: Synonym of thoron (“radon-220”).
parole.testo: From Latin ex (“out of”) + thōriō (“thorium”).

parole.significato: To drop or distill.
parole.testo: From Latin extillare, exstillare, from ex (“out”) + stillare (“to drop”), stilla (“drop”).

parole.significato: To stimulate.
parole.testo: From Latin extimulatus, exstimulatus, past participle of extimulare, exstimulare (“to goad”). See stimulate.

parole.significato: Of fire, etc.: no longer alight; of a light, etc.: no longer shining; extinguished, quenched.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English extinct (“eliminated, eradicated, extinguished”), from Latin extīnctus, exstīnctus (“extinguished, quenched; destroyed, killed; made extinct”), the perfect passive participles of extinguō, exstinguō (“to extinguish, put out, quench; (figurative) to abolish; to destroy, kill”

parole.significato: Synonym of extinction (“the action of becoming or making extinct; annihilation”).
parole.testo: Either: * from Latin extīnctus, exstīnctus, a noun use of the perfect passive participle of extinguō, exstinguō (see etymology 1); or * from the verb (see etymology 2).

parole.significato: The action of making or becoming extinct; annihilation.
parole.testo: From late Middle English, borrowed from Latin extinctio (“extinction, annihilation”), from extinguere, past participle extinctus (“to extinguish”); see extinguish.

parole.significato: exine
parole.testo: From Latin ext- (in extimus (“most outward”)) + -ine. Compare intine.

parole.significato: To end (something).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin extinguo (“to put out (what is burning), quench, extinguish, deprive of life, destroy, abolish”), from ex (“out”) + stinguere (“to put out, quench, extinguish”). Doublet of extinct.

parole.significato: To clear an area of roots and stumps.
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1538, the adjective in 1541; borrowed from Latin exstirpātus perfect passive participle of exstirpō (“to uproot”), from ex- (“out of”) + stirps (“the lower part of the trunk of a tree, including the roots; the stem, stalk”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix) (see -ate (verb-for

parole.significato: The act of extirpating or uprooting.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exstirpātiō.

parole.significato: Somebody who predicts the future using entrails
parole.testo: From Latin extispex.

parole.significato: Pertaining to divination by examining entrails.
parole.testo: From Latin extispicium + -ous.

parole.significato: Synonym of haruspicy: the study and divination by use of animal entrails, usually the victims of sacrifice.
parole.testo: From Latin extispicium, from extispex (“diviner of entrails”) + -ium (forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: To praise; to make high.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin extollō (“elevate, raise high”).

parole.significato: To take or seize from an unwilling person by physical force, menace, duress, torture, or any undue or illegal exercise…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin extortus, past participle of extorquere (“to twist or wrench out, to extort”); from ex (“out”) + -tort, from torqueō (“twist, turn”).

parole.significato: The practice of extorting money or other property by the use of force or threats.
parole.testo: From Middle English extorcion, from Anglo-Norman extorcion, extorcioun, extorsioun, from Late Latin extortiō, from extorqueō. By surface analysis, extort + -ion.

parole.significato: Not deriving from the linguistic expression used; for a reason other than of ambiguity, division, et cetera.
parole.testo: From Latin extra dictionem, translation of Ancient Greek ἔξω τῆς λέξεως (éxō tês léxeōs), which appears in chapter 4 of Aristotle’s Sophistical Refutations.

parole.significato: Outside of, beyond.
parole.testo: From Latin extra (“outside, except, beyond”, adverb and preposition), from exter (“being on the outside”).

parole.significato: Supernatural.
parole.testo: Latin extranaturalis (“unnatural”)

parole.significato: Outside of wartime; during peacetime.
parole.testo: From extra- + Latin bellum.

parole.significato: Something that is extracted or drawn out.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin extractum, neuter perfect passive participle of extrahō, from ex- (“out of”) + trahō (“to drag”).

parole.significato: Outdoor.
parole.testo: From extra- + Latin foris (“door”) + -aneous.

parole.significato: Belonging to another race, type or kind.
parole.testo: From extra- + Latin genus (“race”).

parole.significato: Emission.
parole.testo: From Latin extra mittere.

parole.significato: Taking place outside the walls of an institution, especially a school or university or prison.
parole.testo: From Latin extramuralis, from extra (“outside”) + muralis (“of a wall”).

parole.significato: Not belonging to, or dependent upon, a thing; without or beyond a thing; foreign.
parole.testo: From Latin extrāneus (“from without, strange”). Doublet of strange. Cognate with estrange (verb), Spanish extraño.

parole.significato: Out of the ordinary; exceptional; unusual.
parole.testo: From Latin extrāōrdinārius, from extrā ōrdinem (“outside the order”). By surface analysis, extra- + ordinary. Doublet of extraordinaire.

parole.significato: Within the canon law of the Roman Catholic Church, those papal decretals not contained in certain canonical collections…
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: To rove.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin extrāvagāt- + English -ate (suffix forming verbs). Extrāvagāt- is the participial stem of extrāvagārī, from Latin extrā (“beyond, outside of”, preposition) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs (“out”)) + vagārī (the present active infinitive of vagor (“t

parole.significato: That has been let out of the veins.
parole.testo: From extra- + Latin vena (“vein”).

parole.significato: A point, or value that is a maximum or a minimum.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin extrēmum, neuter form of extrēmus (“extreme in degree”). Doublet of extreme.

parole.significato: To free, disengage, loosen, or untangle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin extrīcātus, past participle of extrīcō. Compare intricate.

parole.significato: outward, outwards.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, based upon Latin extra- (“outside, beyond”) under the influence of the distinction between Latin intro- (“inwards”) and intra- (“inside, within”). Formations in English are mostly limited to words formed as antonyms of terms formed with intro-.

parole.significato: Seeking or going out after external objects.
parole.testo: From Latin extra (“on the outside”) + ire, itum (“to go”).

parole.significato: To construct.
parole.testo: From Latin extructus, exstructus, past participle of extruere, exstruere (“to build up”), from ex (“out”) + struere (“to build”).

parole.significato: A building up; a construction.
parole.testo: Latin exstructio.

parole.significato: To push or thrust out.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin extrūdere.

parole.significato: A manufacturing process where a billet of material is pushed and/or drawn through a die to create a shaped rod, rail or…
parole.testo: Mid-16th century from Latin extrūdere, from ex- (“out”) + trūdere (“to thrust”).

parole.significato: swelling or sticking out; protuberant
parole.testo: Latin extuberare.

parole.significato: To swell out.
parole.testo: From Latin extuberatus, present participle of extuberare (“to swell”), from ex (“out”) + tuber (“a swelling”).

parole.significato: protuberance
parole.testo: Latin extuberatio.

parole.significato: A swelling or rising.
parole.testo: From Latin ex + tumescens, present participle of tumescere, inchoate from tumere (“to swell”). Compare French extumescence.

parole.significato: To abound; to be in great abundance.
parole.testo: From Latin exuberatus, past participle of exuberare. See exuberant (“adjective”).

parole.significato: To discharge through pores or incisions, as moisture or other liquid matter; to give out.
parole.testo: Latin exudāre, exsudāre (“to sweat out”), from ex- (“out, out of”) + sudāre (“to sweat”), from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-.

parole.significato: Very sore; ulcerated.
parole.testo: From Latin exulcerātus, perfect passive participle of exulcerō.

parole.significato: ulceration
parole.testo: Latin exulceratio: compare French exulcération.

parole.significato: exultance, exultation
parole.testo: From Latin exsultantia.

parole.significato: Very happy, especially at someone else's defeat or failure.
parole.testo: From Latin exsultāns, present participle of exsultō (“rejoice; boast”). See also exult.

parole.significato: To overflow; to inundate.
parole.testo: From Latin exundatus, past participle of exundare (“to overflow”), from ex (“out”) + undare. See undated (“waved”).

parole.significato: An overflow, flooding or overflowing abundance.
parole.testo: From Latin exundatio.

parole.significato: To pare off (nails, the hoof, flowers etc.).
parole.testo: From Latin exungulare (“to lose the hoof”), from ex (“out”) + ungula. See ungula.

parole.significato: superiority; superfluity
parole.testo: From Latin exuperantia, exsuperantia.

parole.significato: excessive or superfluous
parole.testo: From Latin exuperans, exsuperans, present participle.

parole.significato: To defeat, surmount, or overcome
parole.testo: From Latin exuperatus, exsuperatus, past participle of exuperare, exsuperare (“to excel”); ex (“out”) + superare (“to go over”), super (“above, over”).

parole.significato: Arising or emergent.
parole.testo: From Latin exurgens, exsurgens, present participle of exurgere, exsurgere (“to rise up”); ex (“out”) + surgere (“to rise”).

parole.significato: The act or operation of burning up.
parole.testo: From Latin exustio, from exurere, exustum (“to burn up”), from ex (“out”) + urere (“to burn”).

parole.significato: The coverings of an animal that have been shed or cast off, particularly the molted exoskeletons of arthropods.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exuviae, from exuō (“cast off, undress”).

parole.significato: Related to something sloughed off or stripped away.
parole.testo: From Latin exuviae (“what is stripped”), from exuo (“shed, strip”).

parole.significato: To shed or cast off a covering, especially a skin; to slough; to molt (moult).
parole.testo: From Latin exuviae (“what is shed”), from exuō (“cast off, strip”).

parole.significato: Synonym of exuviae.
parole.testo: Perhaps from Latin exuvium, or perhaps an independent back-formation from exuvia, under the impression that exuvia is the plural of a Latin second-declension neuter noun exuvium, whereas exuvia is in reality the regularised first-declension singular of Latin exuviae.

parole.significato: Having the nature of a bean; like a bean.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fabaceus, from faba (“bean”). By surface analysis, Latin fab(a) + -aceous.

parole.significato: One of the small sesamoid bones situated behind the condyles of the femur, in some mammals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin fābella, diminutive of Latin faba (“bean”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to or reminiscent of Roman general Fabius Maximus, whose tactics against Hannibal during the Second Punic Wa…
parole.testo: From Latin Fabiānus (“belonging to Fabius”), derived from Fabius + -ānus.

parole.significato: Shaped like a bean
parole.testo: From Latin faba (“bean”) + -iform.

parole.significato: the process or act of creating or developing, as of a work of art
parole.testo: From Latin fabrēfacĕre.

parole.significato: A workshop in an ancient Roman fort.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fabrica. Doublet of fabric and forge.

parole.significato: Able to be shaped into a finished product.
parole.testo: From late Latin fabricabilis.

parole.significato: To form into a whole by uniting its parts; to construct; to build.
parole.testo: From Middle English fabricaten (“to fashion, make”), from Latin fabricātus, perfect active participle of fabricor (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fabrica (“a fabric, building”) + -or (verb-forming suffix); see fabric and forge. Cognate with French fabriquer.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a factory, or to stonework, metalwork, woodwork, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin fabrilis, from faber (“workman”). See forge.

parole.significato: A series of events forming the basis of a story or narrative.
parole.testo: From Latin fabula (“story”). Doublet of fable.

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to, fables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fābulāris. By surface analysis, fable + -ar, or, by surface analysis, fabula + -ar. Compare tabular and fabulist.

parole.significato: To tell invented stories, often those that involve fantasy, such as fables.
parole.testo: From Latin fābulātus, perfect active participle of fābulor (“to tell stories, chat”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fābula (“fable”).

parole.significato: Fabulousness; the quality of being fabulous; fictitiousness; mythical character.
parole.testo: From Latin fabulositas.

parole.significato: Of or relating to fable, myth or legend.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English fabulous, fabulose, from Latin fābulōsus (“celebrated in fable”); Equivalent to fable + -ous.

parole.significato: Facetious.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin facētus; perhaps via Italian faceto.

parole.significato: Of or affecting the face.
parole.testo: Early 17th century, borrowed from Medieval Latin faciālis (“face-to-face, direct, open”), from faciēs (“form, configuration, figure; face, visage, countenance”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: The multiplicand.
parole.testo: From neuter of Latin faciendus, gerundive of facere (“to do”).

parole.significato: Something that must be done.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin faciendum, from facere (“to do”).

parole.significato: One who does something; a doer; an agent.
parole.testo: From Latin faciens, facientis, present participle of facere (“do, make”).

parole.significato: General appearance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin faciēs (“form, configuration, figure; face, visage, countenance”). Doublet of face.

parole.significato: The pallid or shrunken face of someone about to die.
parole.testo: Latin; so called because the effect was described by Hippocrates.

parole.significato: Extremely wicked.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin facinorōsus, from facinus (“deed, bad deed”), from faciō (“to make, to do”).

parole.significato: A copy or reproduction.
parole.testo: From Latin fac simile (“make like”), from fac (“make”) (imperative of facere (“make”)) + simile (neuter of similis (“like, similar”)).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or caused by factions.
parole.testo: From Latin factiosus (“divisive; inclined to separate”); derivative of factio.

parole.significato: Created by humans; artificial.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin factītius (“artificial”), alternative form of factīcius, from faciō (“to make, do”). Doublet of fetish.

parole.significato: Taking a complement that expresses a result along with a direct object, or inherently implying a complement; or synonym…
parole.testo: From Latin factitāre, from factus, perfect passive participle of facere + -itāre.

parole.significato: Making; creative.
parole.testo: From New Latin factīvus, from Latin facere (“to make”).

parole.significato: A building or other place where manufacturing takes place.
parole.testo: Probably from factor + -y, although in noun sense 1 (“a place where manufacturing takes place”) apparently influenced strongly by association with Classical Latin fact-, the past participial stem of faciō (“to make”); compare manufactory and Latin factōrium (“an oil press”). In noun sense 8 (“a trad

parole.significato: A person employed to perform all sorts of duties.
parole.testo: Ellipsis of domine fac totum, dominus fac totum /dominus factotum (“absolute ruler; head servant”), from Medieval Latin domine fac tōtum (“O Lord, do everything”), also with substition of nominative dominus for vocative domine.

parole.significato: A female factor (agent or representative).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin factrīx. By surface analysis, factor + -trix.

parole.significato: Somebody's own act and deed.
parole.testo: From Latin factum. See fact.

parole.significato: A bright spot or patch between sunspots.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin facula (“little torch”).

parole.significato: eloquent; wordy
parole.testo: Latin facundiosus.

parole.significato: eloquence; loquaciousness
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin facunditas.

parole.significato: Shaped like a sickle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin falcātus (“curved, sickle-shaped”), from falx (“sickle”, oblique stem in falc-) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Synonym of falcate.
parole.testo: Latin falcatus (“sickle-shaped”)

parole.significato: One of the mandibles of a spider.
parole.testo: From Latin falx, falcis (“a sickle”). By surface analysis, Latin falc- + -er (“agent suffix”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Publius Falcidius, a Roman tribune.
parole.testo: From Latin Falcidius.

parole.significato: A seta that has a curved tip.
parole.testo: From Latin falc- (“sickle, scythe”) + -i- + Latin -ger (“carrier, bearer”), from gerere (“bear, carry”).

parole.significato: The parasitic protozoan Plasmodium falciparum that causes falciparum malaria
parole.testo: From Latin falc- (“sickle, scythe”) + -i- + Latin -parum (“-parous”), from Latin parere (“bring forth, bear”).

parole.significato: In reference to ribs on shells, in the shape of a wave but initially straight, spoon shaped.
parole.testo: Latin falx (“sickle”) + -oid (“like”).

parole.significato: A privilege of setting up, and moving about, sheepfolds, in any fields within manors, in order to manure them or to kee…
parole.testo: From Latin faldagium, from Old English fald (whence English fold). Compare foldage.

parole.significato: A movable seat place in the chancel, where the bishop sat.
parole.testo: From Latin faldistōrium, faldestōrium, from Old High German faldstuol, faldan, faltan (“to fold”) (German falten) + stuol (“stool”), so called because it could be folded or laid together. See fold and stool. Doublet of faldstool, fauteuil, and foldstool.

parole.significato: A member of an ancient Italic people who lived in southern Etruria
parole.testo: From Latin Faliscus + -an; see Falisci.

parole.significato: The Faliscan people.
parole.testo: From Latin Falisci.

parole.significato: cavillation; petty criticism
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fallāx (“deceptive”).

parole.significato: An exception (to a rule).
parole.testo: From Latin fallentia, fallens, present participle of fallere. Doublet of failance.

parole.significato: Capable of making mistakes or being wrong.
parole.testo: From Middle English fallible, from Medieval Latin fallibilis (“liable to err, also deceitful”), from Latin fallere (“to deceive”).

parole.significato: A falsifier of evidence.
parole.testo: From Latin falsarius, from falsus. See false.

parole.significato: Untrue, not factual, factually incorrect.
parole.testo: From Middle English false, fals, from Old English fals (“false; counterfeit; fraudulent; wrong; mistaken”), from Latin falsus (“counterfeit, false; falsehood”), perfect passive participle of fallō (“deceive”). Reinforced in Middle English by Anglo-Norman and Old French fals, faus. Compare Scots fals

parole.significato: Having a false basis.
parole.testo: From Latin falsidicus (“speaking falsehood”), from falsi- (“false”) + dicus (“speaker”).

parole.significato: An arbitrary contradiction, denoted ⊥.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin falsum.

parole.significato: A short Dacian sword resembling a sickle.
parole.testo: From Latin falx (“sickle”). Doublet of dalk.

parole.significato: A fold of the dura mater that divides the hemispheres of the cerebellum.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The larger of the two folds of dura mater separating the hemispheres of the brain that lies between the cerebral hemisp…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin falx cerebrī (“the sickle of the brain”).

parole.significato: Any notorious rumour ascribing immoral conduct to a minister or office-bearer in a church.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: To report or carry news from abroad.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fāmigerātus.

parole.significato: A household or religious community under one head, regarded as a unit.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin familia (“family”). Doublet of family.

parole.significato: Known to one, or generally known; commonplace.
parole.testo: From Middle English familiar, familier, from Latin familiāris (“pertaining to servants; pertaining to the household”). By surface analysis, family + -ar. Piecewise doublet of familial. Displaced native Old English hīwcūþ.

parole.significato: The beliefs or practice of the Family of Love religious sect, active in sixteenth century England.
parole.testo: From Latin familia + -ism.

parole.significato: A group of people who are closely related to one another (by blood, marriage or adoption); kin; in particular, a set of…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English famylye, from Latin familia (“a household”). Displaced native Old English hīred and hād. Doublet of familia.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being famous.
parole.testo: From Latin famositas (“infamy”). Compare French famosité. See famous.

parole.significato: A close attendant or assistant, especially of a magician or occult scholar.
parole.testo: From Latin famulus (“servant”).

parole.significato: A hand-held device consisting of concertinaed material, or slats of material, gathered together at one end, that may be…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English fan, inherited from Old English fann (“a winnowing, fan”), derived from Latin vannus (“fan for winnowing grain”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”). Cognates * Latin ventus (“wind”) * Dutch wan (“winnowing basket”) * German Wanne (“winnowing basket”)

parole.significato: Fanatical.
parole.testo: First attested in 1525. Learned borrowing from Latin fānāticus (“of a temple, divinely inspired, frenzied”), from fānum (“temple”). Influenced by French fanatique.

parole.significato: A temple or sacred place.
parole.testo: From Middle English fane (“temple”), from Latin fānum (“temple, place dedicated to a deity”). Doublet of fanum.

parole.significato: The site of an Ancient Roman temple or shrine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fānum (“shrine”). Doublet of fane.

parole.significato: Emmer (a type of wheat), especially in the context of Roman use of it.
parole.testo: From Latin far. Doublet of farro.

parole.significato: A disclaimer stating that something should not come to pass, or that a person would never do or think a certain thing.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin absit ("may it be away"), found in the Latin Vulgate translation of the Bible as part of the phrase absit hoc a me ("may this [thing] be away from me") at 1 Samuel 2:30, 1 Samuel 22:15 and 2 Samuel 20:20. Wyclif translated the phrase "Fer be this fro me"; the King James Version at 2

parole.significato: Pudding stone.
parole.testo: From farcical + -lite, in the Latin sense of the word farce which means to stuff or to season, because the composite mineral is "stuffed" with quartz nodules. See puddingstone.

parole.significato: A fine flour or meal made from cereal grains or from the starch or fecula of vegetables, extracted by various processes…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin farīna (“flour, meal”), from far (“kind of grain”).

parole.significato: Made from, or rich in, starch or flour.
parole.testo: From Latin farinaceus (“relating to, or made from, flour”), derived from Latin farīna (“flour, meal”). By surface analysis, farin(a) + -aceous.

parole.significato: A recording made with a farinograph.
parole.testo: From Latin farīna (“flour”) + -gram.

parole.significato: A device for measuring properties of flour mixed with water, such as its shear and viscosity.
parole.testo: From Latin farīna (“flour”) + -graph.

parole.significato: Yielding or related to farina
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin farīnōsus, from Latin farīna. By surface analysis, farin(a) + -ose.

parole.significato: The brown trout
parole.testo: From Latin fario (“salmon trout”), possibly from late Proto-Indo-European *sr̥Hyón-, akin to English sturgeon.

parole.significato: Random, miscellaneous, indiscriminate.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Latin farrago + -ous.

parole.significato: A collection containing a confused variety of miscellaneous things.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin farrāgō (“mixed fodder; mixture, hodgepodge”), from far (“emmer (a kind of wheat), coarse meal, grits”). Doublet of farro.

parole.significato: A vernacular paraphrase inserted into Latin liturgy.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin farsa. Doublet of farce.

parole.parola: fas est et ab hoste doceri
parole.significato: One should be open to lessons from other people, even from one's enemies.
parole.termine_origine: fas est et ab hoste doceri

catena.termine: fas est et ab hoste doceri

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fas est et ab hoste doceri (literally “it is right to be taught even by [one's] enemy”).

parole.significato: A Roman symbol of judicial authority consisting of a bundle of wooden sticks, with an axe blade embedded in the centre;…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fascēs (plural of fascis).

parole.significato: A wide band of material covering the ends of roof rafters, sometimes supporting a gutter in steep-slope roofing, but ty…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fascia (“a band, bandage, swathe”). Related to fascēs (“bundle of rods containing an axe with the blade projecting”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰask- (“bundle, band”). Cognate with fajita, fess, and fascism.

parole.significato: An intercellular junction that transmits contractile forces in cardiac muscles
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A thin membrane that envelops the eyeball from the optic nerve to the limbus, separating it from the orbital fat and fo…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: To bind.
parole.testo: From Latin fasciātus, perfect passive participle of fasciō (“to swathe or bind”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Bound with a fillet, sash, or bandage.
parole.testo: From Latin fasciātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A bundle or cluster.
parole.testo: From Latin fasciculus, a diminutive of fascis (“bundle”); see also fasces. Doublet of fasciculus.

parole.significato: A small bundle of nerve, muscle or tendon fibers.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin fasciculus. Doublet of fascicle.

parole.significato: An actin-bundling protein.
parole.testo: From Latin fascis (“bundle”) + -in.

parole.significato: To evoke an intense interest or attraction in someone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fascinātus, perfect passive participle of fascinō (“to enchant, bewitch, fascinate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fascinum (“a phallus-shaped amulet worn around the neck in Ancient Rome; witchcraft”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), itself of obscure origin.

parole.significato: The act of bewitching, or enchanting
parole.testo: From Latin fascinare ("to bewitch"), possibly from Ancient Greek βασκαίνιεν (baskaínien, “to speak ill of; to curse”). Morphologically fascinate + -ion.

parole.significato: Caused or acting by witchcraft.
parole.testo: From Latin fascinum (“witchcraft”), akin to fascinare. See fascinate.

parole.significato: An ivory phallus used in certain ancient erotic rites.
parole.testo: From the Latin fascinum.

parole.significato: A band of grey matter bordering the fimbria in the brain; the dentate convolution.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fasciola.

parole.significato: A band of minute tubercles, bearing modified spines, found on the shells of spatangoid sea urchins.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fasciola (“a little bandage”). See fascia.

parole.significato: The calendar, which gave the days for festivals, courts, etc., corresponding to a modern almanac. They were generally e…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fāstī.

parole.significato: Excessively particular, demanding, or fussy about details, especially about tidiness and cleanliness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fastīdiōsus (“passive: that feels disgust, disdainful, scornful, fastidious; active: that causes disgust, disgusting, loathsome”), from fastīdium (“a loathing, aversion, disgust, niceness of taste, daintiness, etc.”), perhaps for *fastutidium, from fastus (“disdain, haughtiness,

parole.significato: repugnance toward food; unwillingness to eat
parole.testo: From Latin fastīdium (“loathing, disgust”).

parole.significato: Erect and parallel.
parole.testo: From New Latin fastīgiātus (“peaked”) (from fastīgium), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: An apex or summit; culmination.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fastigium.

parole.significato: proud; haughty; disdainful
parole.testo: From Latin fastuōsus, from fastus (“haughtiness, pride”). Compare French fastueux and Spanish fastuoso.

parole.significato: To foreordain or predetermine, to make inevitable.
parole.testo: From Middle English fate, from Latin fāta (“prediction”), plural of fātum, from fātus (“spoken”), from for (“to speak”). In this sense, displaced native Old English wyrd, whence Modern English weird.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to prophecy; prophetic.
parole.testo: From Latin fātidicus, from fātum (“fate”) + dico (“to speak”). Via Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- cognate with the synonymous English prophetic.

parole.significato: Having power to foretell future events; prophetic; fatiloquent.
parole.testo: From Latin fātidicus, from fātum (“fate”) + dīcō (“to say, tell”).

parole.significato: Fate-bringing; deadly; destructive.
parole.testo: From Latin fatifer, from fatum (“fate”) + ferre (“to bear, bring”).

parole.significato: To weary; to tire; to fatigue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fatīgātus, perfect passive participle of fatīgō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: prophetic; speaking of fate.
parole.testo: From Latin fatiloquus, from fatum (“fate”) + ultimately loqui (“speak”) (modeled on eloquent and other such words).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Fatsia of Asian evergreen shrubs.
parole.testo: From the genus name, New Latin Fatsia.

parole.significato: Obnoxiously stupid; vacantly silly; content in one's foolishness.
parole.testo: From Latin fatuus (“foolish, silly, simple”).

parole.significato: Relating to the fauces, or opening of the throat; faucial.
parole.testo: Latin fauces (“throat”).

parole.significato: The narrow passage from the mouth to the pharynx, situated between the soft palate and the base of the tongue.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Latin faucēs (“the upper part of a throat”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the fauces; pharyngeal.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Latin faucēs + -al.

parole.significato: A woodland creature with pointed ears, legs, and short horns of a goat and a fondness for unrestrained revelry.
parole.testo: From Middle English fawn, from Latin faunus.

parole.significato: Animals considered as a group; especially those of a particular country, region, time, biological group, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin fauna, from Latin Fauna, sister of Faunus (“god of forests and herdsmen”); akin to Ancient Greek θαῦνον (thaûnon, “wild animal, beast”), θώς (thṓs, “jackal, wild dog; panther”), Phrygian δάος (dáos, “wolf”).

parole.significato: Patron, protector.
parole.testo: From Latin fautor.

parole.significato: A patroness.
parole.testo: From Latin fautrix: compare French fautrice.

parole.significato: A patroness.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fautrīx. By surface analysis, fautor + -trix.

parole.significato: Resembling a honeycomb; cellular.
parole.testo: Obscure formation from Latin favus (“honeycomb”). Compare deluginous (where the -in- is also unexpected); most -ginous terms derive from Latin words ending in g being suffixed with -īnus (“-inous”).

parole.significato: Having cavities or cells like those of a honeycomb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin faveolātus, from faveolus + -ātus, a diminutive of favus (“honeycomb”) modelled on alveolus; see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to ashes.
parole.testo: From Latin favilla (“sparkling or glowing ashes”) + -ous.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the west wind.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin favōniānus, from Favōnius (“the West Wind”), which heralded the beginning of spring.

parole.significato: To favor especially or unduly.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin favorizare.

parole.significato: Honeycombed.
parole.testo: From Latin favus (“honeycomb”) + -ose.

parole.significato: A severe, chronic infection of ringworm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin favus (“honeycomb”).

parole.significato: Feverish.
parole.testo: From Latin febrīcitāns, from febrīcitō.

parole.significato: A mild fever of short duration, of indefinite origin, and without any distinctive pathology.
parole.testo: From Latin febrīcula.

parole.significato: Somewhat feverish.
parole.testo: From Latin febrīculōsus.

parole.significato: Causing fever.
parole.testo: From Latin febris (“fever”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: That causes, or is associated with fever
parole.testo: From febri- + -genic, from Latin febris (“fever”).

parole.significato: Feverish, or having a high temperature.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin febrīlis, from Latin febris (“fever”). By surface analysis, Latin febr- + -ile.

parole.significato: Purification, rejuvenation, or renewal, especially ritual or ceremonial.
parole.testo: From Latin februatio, from februare (“purify”).

parole.significato: Digested waste material (typically solid or semi-solid) discharged from a human or other mammal's stomach to the intest…
parole.testo: From Latin faecēs, nominative plural of faex (“residue, dregs”), further origin unknown; possibly borrowed from a substrate language.

parole.significato: Starchy sediment extracted from plants, especially those which are used as food.
parole.testo: From Latin faecula, diminutive of faex (“residue, dregs”).

parole.significato: Synonym of fertilizable
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fecundābilis, from fēcundō + -ābilis.

parole.significato: To make fertile.
parole.testo: From Latin fecundātus, perfect passive participle of fecundō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, fecund + -ate. Compare French féconder.

parole.significato: Ability to produce offspring.
parole.testo: From Latin fēcunditās (“fruitfulness, fertility”), from fēcundus, equivalent to fecund + -ity.

parole.significato: Treaty-breaking.
parole.testo: From Latin foedifragus (“perfidious, league-breaking”).

parole.significato: Turpitude or vileness.
parole.testo: From Latin foeditas.

parole.significato: A South American evergreen shrub, Acca sellowiana (syn. Feijoa sellowiana).
parole.testo: From the New Latin former genus name Feijoa, which was named after Portuguese botanist João da Silva Feijó by the German botanist Otto Karl Berg.

parole.significato: The killing of a cat.
parole.testo: From Latin fēlis (“cat”) + -cide.

parole.significato: To congratulate.
parole.testo: From Latin fēlicitātus, perfect passive participle of fēlīcitō (“to felicitate”) (from fēlīx (“happy”)), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French féliciter.

parole.significato: Made very happy.
parole.testo: From Latin fēlicitātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: Resembling a cat; applied to member of the Feliformia, a suborder within the order Carnivora consisting of cat-like car…
parole.testo: From Latin feles, felis (“cat”) + -form.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to cats.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fēlīnus, from fēlēs (“wildcat, marten”).

parole.significato: A cat: member of the cat family Felidae.
parole.testo: Substantive use of the adjective feline, from Latin fēlīnus.

parole.significato: A series of miserable events that will eventually lead to a happier outcome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fēlīx culpa (“blessed fault”), via Roman Catholic theology, first used in Latin in the 4th century CE.

parole.significato: Anger; gall; melancholy.
parole.testo: Perhaps from Latin fel (“gall, poison, bitterness”), or more probably from the adjective above.

parole.significato: To stimulate the penis or scrotum using the mouth.
parole.testo: Back-formation from fellatio on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), from Latin fellō (“suck”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck, to suckle”).

parole.significato: Performance of oral sex upon the penis.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fellātiō, from fellātus, perfect participle of fellō (“to suck, to fellate”). The word started to appear in medical literature in the 19th century but it was still treated as Latin. In 1919, the California Supreme Court struck down a law criminalizing fellatio because th

parole.significato: One who performs fellatio.
parole.testo: From Latin fēllātor. By surface analysis, fellate + -or.

parole.significato: Pertaining to fellatio.
parole.testo: From the past participle stem of Latin fellāre + -ory.

parole.significato: A woman who performs fellatio.
parole.testo: From Latin fēllātrīx. By surface analysis, fellate + -trix.

parole.significato: Flowing with bile or gall.
parole.testo: From Latin fellifluus, from fel (“gall”) + fluere (“to flow”).

parole.significato: An acid apparently obtained by treating bilin with hydrochloric acid.
parole.testo: From Latin fel, fell- (“bile”).

parole.significato: A crime committed against oneself, in particular suicide.
parole.testo: From Latin felō (“felon”) dē (“of”) sē (“himself”).

parole.significato: Relating to the Feloidea.
parole.testo: From feline + -oid. From Latin felis.

parole.significato: The killing of a woman or girl, originally (figurative) with reference to loss of virtue but now usually (law) specific…
parole.testo: From fem- + -icide, ultimately derived from Latin fēmina (“woman”), after the model of homicide, genocide, etc.

parole.significato: A wing feather from a female ostrich.
parole.testo: From Latin fēmina (“woman”), perhaps via Italian femmina. Doublet of feme, femme, and hembra.

parole.significato: Feminine; (also) effeminate, womanish.
parole.testo: First attested circa 1533; borrowed from Latin fēminātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Relating to or in accordance with feminism.
parole.testo: First attested in 1852. Ultimately from Latin fēminīnus, from fēmina (“woman”). See also feminine, feminism.

parole.significato: Pertaining to feminism or to women generally.
parole.testo: Latin femina (“woman”) with -o-.

parole.significato: Synonym of women's studies.
parole.testo: From Latin fēmina + -ology.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or near the femur or thigh.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin femorālis, from Latin root femor-, from femur (genitive femoris). Equivalent to femur + -al.

parole.significato: A thighbone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin femur (“thigh”).

parole.significato: Capable of being defended
parole.testo: Latin defendere (“to defend”).

parole.significato: Lending money at interest; usury.
parole.testo: From Latin faenerationem, from faenerare.

parole.significato: A niche on the south side of an altar, containing the piscina and sometimes the credence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fenestella.

parole.significato: An opening in a body, sometimes with a membrane.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin fenestra. Existed in Middle English as fenestre, fenester, from Old English fenester (“window”).

parole.significato: Any hydrocarbon consisting of a central carbon atom connected with single bonds to four other carbon atoms each of whic…
parole.testo: From Latin fenestra (“window”) + -ane, from the apparent similarity of the structure to a windowpane.

parole.significato: fenestrated
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fenestrātus, perfect passive participle of fenestrō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from fenestra (“window”).

parole.significato: Having windows.
parole.testo: Latin fenestro, from the noun fenestra (“window”).

parole.significato: The arrangement of windows and similar openings in a building.
parole.testo: Latin fenestratio

parole.significato: One of the openings in a fenestrated structure.
parole.testo: From Latin fenestrula (“a little window”), diminutive of fenestra (“a window”).

parole.significato: A transparent form of marble or alabaster, formerly sometimes used for windows.
parole.testo: Like phengite from Latin phengites, from Ancient Greek φέγγος (phéngos). Superficially contains -ite.

parole.significato: An ancient people of northeastern Europe first described by Cornelius Tacitus in Germania in AD 98. It is unclear wheth…
parole.testo: From Latin Fennī; compare Ancient Greek Φίννος (Phínnos). The name as used by Tacitus is unclear about whom it actually describes, but it may nevertheless be from Old Norse Finnr (“a Sami”). More at Fenni.

parole.significato: Producing in abundance; fertile, fruitful
parole.testo: From Latin ferax, from ferre (“to bear”) + -acious.

parole.significato: The state of being feracious, or fruitful.
parole.testo: From Latin ferācitās, from ferre (“to bear”) + -acity.

parole.significato: Undomesticated animals; wild beasts.
parole.testo: From Latin ferus and natura, therefore meaning 'of a wild nature'.

parole.significato: Deadly, fatal.
parole.testo: From Latin fērālis (“funereal”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁s (“god, sacred place”).

parole.significato: Of a penalty, only coming into force after it is imposed by an authority, and not by the fact of the law being broken.
parole.testo: From Latin ferendae sententiae (“of a sentence to be passed”).

parole.significato: A kind of medieval reliquary or shrine containing the sacred effigies and relics of a saint.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin feretrum, from Ancient Greek φέρετρον (phéretron). Doublet of feretory.

parole.significato: A weekday on a Church calendar on which no feast is observed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin fēria.

parole.significato: Pertaining to an ordinary weekday, rather than a festival or fast.
parole.testo: From Middle English ferial, from Medieval Latin fēriālis, from Latin fēria (“weekday”) (whence the first sense), fēriae (“holidays”) (whence the second).

parole.significato: A holiday or break from work or effort.
parole.testo: From Latin ferior (“to keep holiday”), from feriae (“holidays”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to wild, menacing animals; feral.
parole.testo: From Latin ferīnus, from fera (“wild animal”). The zoological sense was coined by William Whewell in 1840.

parole.significato: The quality or fact of being wild or in a wild state.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin feritas, from ferus (“wild”). By surface analysis, Latin fer- + -ity.

parole.significato: To cause to ferment
parole.testo: From Latin fermentātus, past participle of fermentō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Alternatively, back-formation from fermentation.

parole.significato: Any of many anaerobic biochemical reactions in which an enzyme (or several enzymes produced by a microorganism) catalys…
parole.testo: From Middle English fermentacioun, from Latin fermentātiō, fermentātiōnem. By surface analysis, ferment + -ation.

parole.significato: Marked by extreme and violent energy.
parole.testo: Taken from Latin ferōx (“wild, bold, savage, fierce”) + -ous.

parole.significato: wild; savage; feral
parole.testo: From Latin ferus. See fierce and feral. By surface analysis, Latin fer- + -ous.

parole.significato: The art of ironworking.
parole.testo: From Latin ferraria (“iron works”). See ferreous.

parole.significato: Synonym of ferrous, of or related to iron.
parole.testo: From ferro- + -eous after the model of Latin ferreus, from ferrum (“iron”) + -eus (“-eous: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to, derived from, or containing iron.
parole.testo: From Latin ferricus, from ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: The interstitial solid solution of carbon in body-centered cubic iron.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin ferrum (“iron”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Any of a family of iron-carrying globular protein complexes consisting of 24 protein subunits; the key protein of intra…
parole.testo: From Latin ferrātus (“iron-bearing”) and -in; compare also ferri- and ferro-.

parole.significato: ferrous
parole.testo: Latin ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: An orthorhombic-dipyramidal mineral containing aluminum, hydrogen, iron, magnesium, manganese, oxygen, silicon, and tit…
parole.testo: From ferro- + carpholite, from Latin ferrum (“iron”), for being the ferrous analog of carpholite.

parole.significato: A student of ferroequinology; a person who studies trains as a hobby.
parole.testo: From Latin ferrum (“iron”) + Latin equus (“horse”) + English -logist (“one who studies”).

parole.significato: The study of railways in general, but especially locomotives.
parole.testo: Latin ferrum (“iron”) + Latin equus (“horse”) + English -logy; from iron horse

parole.significato: Of or containing iron.
parole.testo: From ferro- + -ous, from Latin ferreus directly or via French ferreux, from ferrum (“iron”) + -eus (“-ous: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Synonym of ferrous, of or related to iron.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ferrūgineus, from ferrūgo (“rust”).

parole.significato: rust (plant disease).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ferrūgō (“iron rust”), from ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: A band or cap (usually metal) placed around a shaft to reinforce it or to prevent splitting.
parole.testo: From Middle English verel, virel, virole (“ferrule; metal pivot on the end of an axle”), altered under the influence of Latin ferrum (“iron”), from Old French virole (“ferrule”), from Latin viriola (“little bracelet”), diminutive of viria (“bracelet worn by men”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *we

parole.significato: Any of various remedies made from iron-containing compounds.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ferrum.

parole.significato: To solder, fuse together, merge or unite, as if metals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ferrūminātus, perfect passive participle of ferrūminō (“to cement, solder”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ferrūmen (“cement”).

parole.significato: The soldering or uniting of metals.
parole.testo: Latin ferruminatio: compare French ferrumination.

parole.significato: A ferule.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ferula (“giant fennel”), whose stalks were once used in punishing schoolboys. Doublet of ferule.

parole.significato: Pertaining to reeds and canes.
parole.testo: From Latin ferulaceus, from ferula (“rod”). Compare French férulacé.

parole.significato: Growing hotter.
parole.testo: From Latin fervescens, present participle of fervescere (“to become boiling hot, inchoate”), from fervere. See fervent. By surface analysis, Latin ferv- + -escent.

parole.significato: Intensely hot; radiating with energy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fervidus, from ferveō. By surface analysis, Latin ferv- + id.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the ancient Etruscan town of Fescennia
parole.testo: From the Latin Fescennīnus.

parole.significato: Obscene or scurrilous.
parole.testo: From Latin Fescennīnus, from the name of the ancient Etruscan town of Fescennia, noted for the "Fescennine Verses", a tradition of scurrilous songs performed on special occasions.

parole.significato: To become involuntarily quicker, such as when walking or speaking, due to certain disorders.
parole.testo: First attested in 1556; Borrowed from Latin festīnātus, perfect passive participle of festīnō (“to hurry”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Of a straw colour; greenish-yellow.
parole.testo: From Latin festula (“stalk, straw”). Compare fescue. The chemical is called "festucine" because it is found in Festuca.

parole.significato: Formed of, consisting of, or similar to, straw.
parole.testo: From Latin festūcōsus, from festūca.

parole.significato: A member of the Roman college of priests who acted as representatives in disputes with foreign nations.
parole.testo: From Latin fētiālis (“priest who sanctioned treaties and demanded satisfaction from enemies before formal declarations of war”). The root of the Latin word is thought to be Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, place, put”), also the source of the verb Latin faciō (“to do; to build, construct; to app

parole.significato: A fetial.
parole.testo: From Latin fētiālis.

parole.significato: Foul-smelling, stinking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fētidus (“having offensive odour”), originally fēteō (“to stink”).

parole.significato: Producing young; fruitful, productive.
parole.testo: From Latin fētifer (“causing fruitfulness”) + -ous, from fētus (“pregnant, fruitful”) + -fer (“bearing, carrying, bringing”).

parole.significato: An unpleasant smell.
parole.testo: From Latin fētor.

parole.significato: An unborn or unhatched vertebrate showing signs of the mature animal.
parole.testo: A learned borrowing from Latin fētus (“offspring”). Doublet of fawn.

parole.significato: Used to call for or reference the act of getting an abortion (hence destroying the fetus).
parole.testo: From fetus + rhyming alteration of delete with Latin -us after fetus. Compare Latin dēlētus (“deleted”).

parole.significato: A fetus growing inside the body of another fetus, either from an unsuccessful twin pregnancy, or as a tumorlike growth.
parole.testo: From Latin fētus in fētū.

parole.significato: An estate granted to a vassal by a feudal lord in exchange for service.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin feudum. Doublet of fee, fief, and feoff.

parole.significato: Held by, or relating to, feudal tenure.
parole.testo: Late Latin feudarius.

parole.significato: Relating to feudalism, feudal.
parole.testo: From the Latin feudātōrius, from the Mediaeval Latin feudāre (“to enfeoff”), from feudum, feodum.

parole.significato: and the following (pages, paragraphs etc.)
parole.testo: Abbreviation of Latin foliō (“on the (next) page”), ablative of folium (“leaf, page”).

parole.significato: An arbitrary or authoritative command or order to do something; an effectual decree.
parole.testo: From Latin fīat (“let it be done”).

parole.significato: Let there be light, especially in the context of light being a metaphor for wisdom.
parole.testo: From Latin fīat lūx (“let there be light”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Fibonacci sequence.
parole.testo: From Latin filius (“son”) + Italian Bonacci, a diminutive of Bono, from Latin bonum, ultimately meaning literally, "son of the (little) good man."

parole.significato: A fine fibre or filament.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fibrilla, diminutive of Latin fibra. Doublet of fibrilla. Compare fibre.

parole.significato: Synonym of fibril (“a fine fibre or filament”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fibrilla, diminutive of Latin fibra + -illa. Doublet of fibril. Compare fibre. By surface analysis, fibre + Latin -illa.

parole.significato: A very rare, disabling genetic disorder of the connective tissue in which fibrous tissue (including ligaments, muscles,…
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₃ésth₁ From English fibrodysplasia, and borrowed from New Latin ossificans + Latin prōgressīvā, literally “abnormal development of fibrous tissue with ossification that is progressive”: * Fibrodysplasia is derived from fibro- (prefix meaning ‘fibre; fibrous’) (from Latin fibra (“fibre; f

parole.significato: An ancient kind of brooch used to hold clothing together, similar in function to the modern safety pin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fībula (“buckle, clasp, pin”). The bone is so named because the shape it makes with the tibia resembles a clasp, the fibula being the pin.

parole.significato: Synonym of peroneus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin fībulāris, clipping of mūsculus fībulāris (“fibular muscle”).

parole.significato: Synonym of peroneus brevis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin fībulāris brevis, clipping of mūsculus fībulāris brevis (“short fibular muscle”).

parole.significato: Synonym of peroneus longus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin fībulāris longus, clipping of mūsculus fībulāris longus (“long fibular muscle”).

parole.significato: Synonym of peroneus tertius.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin fībulāris tertius, clipping of mūsculus fībulāris tertius (“third fibular muscle”).

parole.significato: Any of a family of calcium-binding glycoproteins found in the extracellular matrix and in plasma.
parole.testo: From Latin fibula (“clasp, buckle”) + -in.

parole.significato: Fig-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin ficus (“fig”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Capable of being molded into the shape of an artifact or art work
parole.testo: Latin fictilus, from fictus (from fingere (“to shape, form, devise”)) + -ilis

parole.significato: Fictitious.
parole.testo: From ficti(on) + -ous, as if Latin *fictiōsus, from fictiō.

parole.significato: Invented; contrived.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fictīcius.

parole.significato: An artist who models or forms statues and reliefs in any malleable material.
parole.testo: From Latin fictor, from fingo (“to shape, to sculpt”).

parole.significato: Worthless.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fīculneus (“of the fig or fig tree”).

parole.significato: Any plant belonging to the genus Ficus, including the rubber plant, of species Ficus elastica.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fīcus (“fig”).

parole.significato: A benefit bequeathed to a beneficiary who inherits the benefit, subject to the obligation of bequeathing it to another.
parole.testo: Latin fidei (“trust”) (genitive) + commissum, from committō (“give, entrust”), from con- + mittō (“to send”).

parole.significato: suretyship.
parole.testo: From Latin fideiussiōnem (with -ion), from fidēiussus, from fideiubeō, from fidēs (“faith”) + iubēre (“order”). Compare French fidéjussion.

parole.significato: A surety or guarantor.
parole.testo: From Latin fīdēiussor (with -or (“agent suffix”)), from fidēiussus, from fideiubeō, from fidēs (“faith”) + iubēre (“order”). Compare French fidéjusseur.

parole.significato: One who pledges himself as security for another; bail, surety
parole.testo: From Latin fidēprōmissor (“guarantor, surety”), from fidēprōmittō (“make a promise on behalf of another person, stand as guarantor or surety”) + -tor, from fidē (“in faith”) + prōmittō (“promise”) + -or (“agent suffix”).

parole.significato: A piece of paper used for lighting a pipe, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fidibus.

parole.significato: stringed (of or pertaining to a stringed instrument).
parole.testo: From Latin fidicen, fidicinis (“lute player”) + -al.

parole.significato: Accepted as a fixed basis of reference.
parole.testo: From Late Latin fīdūciālis, from fīdūcia (“trust, reliance”) + -ālis, from fīdō (“to trust”).

parole.significato: Relating to an entity that owes to another good faith, accountability and trust, often in the context of trusts and tru…
parole.testo: From Latin fīdūciārius (“held in trust”), from fīdūcia (“trust”).

parole.significato: designating a durative and dynamic action performed by the subject
parole.testo: From Latin fīēns (“becoming; happening”, present active participle of fīō (“to become; to happen”)), on the pattern of words such as stative, durative, iterative, causative etc.

parole.significato: Any of certain fishes of the genus Carapus.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Provençal fielat-fèr, fierasfèr, from fielat, fieras (“net, moray”) (from Old Provençal filat, from fil (“thread”), from Latin fīlum) + fèr (“fierce, wild”), from Latin ferus.

parole.significato: In English law, a writ of execution issued after judgment obtained in a legal action for debt or damages.
parole.testo: From Middle English fieri facias, from Medieval Latin fierī faciās (“thou shouldst cause it to be done”), which is not a normal Classical Latin construction but a calque from Romance causatives from faciō and infinitive (attested since Late Latin).

parole.significato: A fabrication, fantasy, invention; something fictitious.
parole.testo: From Late Latin figmentum (“anything made, a fiction”), from fingō (“make, form, feign”); see fiction, feign, feint.

parole.significato: Made of potter's clay.
parole.testo: From Latin figulātus, perfect passive participle of figulō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Any of the non-signifying constituents of signifiers.
parole.testo: From Latin figūra. Coined by Louis Hjelmslev.

parole.significato: Composed of threads, stringy.
parole.testo: Latin fīlum (“thread”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: A fine thread or wire.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin fīlāmentum, from Late Latin fīlō (“to spin, draw out in a long line”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”).

parole.significato: Having a thread across the field of view.
parole.testo: From Latin filum (“a thread”).

parole.significato: A machine for forming threads.
parole.testo: From Latin filatorium (“place for spinning”), from filare (“to spin”), from filum (“a thread”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to or befitting a son or daughter.
parole.testo: From Middle English filial, from Latin fīliālis, from fīlius (“son”) / fīlia (“daughter”) + -al.

parole.significato: Derived from ferns
parole.testo: From Latin filix (“a fern”) + -icis.

parole.significato: The killing of one's own child.
parole.testo: From Latin fīlius (“son”), fīlia (“daughter”) + -cide.

parole.significato: Shaped like a fern or like the parts of a fern leaf.
parole.testo: From Latin filix (“fern”) + Latin -icis + English -form. Compare French filiciforme.

parole.significato: Any fern-like plant.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin filix (“fern”) + English -oid.

parole.significato: The botanical study of ferns.
parole.testo: From Latin filic- (stem of filix (“fern”)) + English -ology (a variant of -logy (suffix denoting the study of a particular subject)). Filix is probably derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“henbane”) + Latin -ix (a variant of -ex (suffix found in plant names such as cārex (“sedge”) and rumex (“s

parole.significato: The relation of a son to a father; sonship
parole.testo: From Late Latin filietatem, from filius (“son”).

parole.significato: Producing or constituting threads.
parole.testo: From Latin filum (“a thread”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Shaped like or resembling a thread or filament; filamentous.
parole.testo: Latin filum (“filament”), + -iform.

parole.significato: The use of the Latin word filioque (“and from the son”) in the Western form of the Nicene Creed, to indicate that the H…
parole.testo: From Latin filioque, from filiō (“from the son”, ablative) + -que (“and”).

parole.significato: The philosopher's stone.
parole.testo: Latin filius philosophorum (literally “philosophers' child”)

parole.significato: A hair-like feather; a feather with a slender scape and without a web in most or all of its length.
parole.testo: From Latin filum (“a thread”) + pluma (“a soft feather”).

parole.significato: Terminating in a thread-like process, or threadlike
parole.testo: From Latin filum (“a thread”).

parole.significato: A device which separates a suspended, dissolved, or particulate matter from a fluid, solution, or other substance; any…
parole.testo: From Middle English filtre, from Medieval Latin filtrum (compare also Old French feutre (“felt; filter”)), from Frankish *filtir, from Proto-West Germanic *felt. See felt. Doublet of phin.

parole.significato: The liquid or solution that has passed through a filter, and which has been separated from other fractions of the origi…
parole.testo: From the substantivation of New Latin filtrātus (“filtered”) past perfect participle of filtrō (“to filter”). Equivalent to filter (the verb) + -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: a filamentous anatomical structure
parole.testo: From Latin fīlum (“thread”). Doublet of file.

parole.significato: A series of threads or other projections resembling a fringe.
