parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin fimbria (“a border, fringe”), from Latin fimbriae (“fibers, threads, fringe”). Doublet of fringe.

parole.significato: To fringe; to hem.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fimbriātus (“fibrous, fringed”), participial adjective formed on fimbriae (“fibers, threads, fringe”) + -ātus (participial adjective-forming suffix). See -ate (verb-forming suffix), -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Growing on dung.
parole.testo: From Latin fimēta + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to dung
parole.testo: From Latin fimētum (“dunghill”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Inhabiting dung.
parole.testo: An adaptation of the Latin fimicolus (“dung-dwelling”).

parole.significato: Given to fashioning or molding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fingēns (“shaping, fashioning”).

parole.significato: The final pilot-in-command, pilot-flying flight of a pilot during a stage of life, such as on a particular aircraft, ai…
parole.testo: fini + flight. Ultimately from Latin finis (“ending”). See also Middle English finis (“the end”) and Romance latin derivations of Latin finis (French finis (“fini”), French fin; Spanish fine (“fini”), Spanish fin)

parole.significato: Of a book or other work: the end.
parole.testo: From Middle English finis, from Latin fīnis (“end; limit”). Doublet of fin, fine, and finish.

parole.significato: Having an end or limit; (of a quantity) constrained by bounds; (of a set) whose number of elements is a natural number.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Middle English fynyte, finit, from Latin fīnītus, perfect passive participle of fīniō (“to finish; to terminate”), from fīnis (“boundary”). The word displaced Old English ġeendodlīċ. The noun is derived from the adjective.

parole.significato: The state or characteristic of being finite; limitedness.
parole.testo: From Latin fin(is) + -itude or directly from Renaissance Latin finitūdō (“signifying a noun of state”), from fīnis (“end, limit”) + -tūdō.

parole.significato: Synonym of alchemist.
parole.testo: A calque of Latin philosophus per ignem (“philosopher by fire”).

parole.significato: strength; stability
parole.testo: From Latin firmitudo. See firm.

parole.significato: strength; firmness; stability
parole.testo: Latin firmitas.

parole.significato: A person or position that is formally of equal rank to others in a group, but nonetheless takes a leading role within t…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin primus inter pares.

parole.significato: Forms of pronouns or verbs used for the speaker or writer of the sentence in which they occur.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin prīma persōna, itself a calque of Ancient Greek πρῶτον πρόσωπον (prôton prósōpon). Displaced native Old English forma had, literally, "form hade".

parole.significato: All matters concerning taxation
parole.testo: Recorded since 1854, cognate with Dutch fiscaliteit and (derived from?) older French fiscalité, all from Latin fiscalis (“fiscal”), itself from fiscus (“imperial treasury”) + -alis (“-al”). By surface analysis, fiscal + -ity.

parole.significato: A government treasury.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fiscus (“treasury”).

parole.significato: cleft, split, cloven
parole.testo: Combining form of Latin fissus (“cleft”), past participle of Latin findere (“to cleave, split”).

parole.significato: Able to be split.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fissilis.

parole.significato: Having a forked tongue.
parole.testo: From Latin fissus (p.p. of findere (“to split”)) + lingual.

parole.significato: The process whereby one item splits to become two.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fissiōnem, accusative singular of fissiō (“the act of breaking up”), from findō (“split, divide”).

parole.significato: Factious, tending to break into pieces.
parole.testo: An adaptation of New Latin fissiparus, from fissus (“split, cleft”) + pariō (“to bring forth”) by analogy with vīviparus.

parole.significato: Having the toes separated from each other.
parole.testo: From Latin fissiped-, fissipēs.

parole.significato: Being or relating to a fissiped.
parole.testo: From Latin fissus (“split”) + pedis (“foot”).

parole.significato: A small, connective tissue-filled cleft in the temporal bone, located just anterior to the oval window in the inner ear…
parole.testo: From Latin fissula (“small cleft, slit”), from Latin fissum + -ula + Latin ante (“in front of, before”) + Latin fenestram (“window”), accusative of fenestra.

parole.significato: A kind of pile driver.
parole.testo: From Latin fistūca.

parole.significato: An abnormal connection or passageway between organs or vessels that normally do not connect.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fistula (“pipe, ulcer, catheter”). Doublet of fester.

parole.significato: Resembling the genus Fistularia (cornetfishes); having a long, tubular body.
parole.testo: From Fistulari(a) (“genus of cornetfishes”) + -oid (“resembling”), from Latin fistula (“pipe, tube”) and Ancient Greek εἶδος (eîdos, “form, likeness”). By surface analysis, fistule + -arioid.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a fistula.
parole.testo: From Latin fistula (“pipe, tube”) + -ary.

parole.significato: Fistula.
parole.testo: From Latin fistula (“pipe, tube”) + -o-.

parole.significato: An operation to create a surgical connection between a fistula and the intestine.
parole.testo: From fistulo- (“fistula”) + entero- (“intestine”) + -stomy (“mouth, surgical connection”), from Latin fistula (“pipe, tube”), Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”), and Ancient Greek στόμα (stóma, “mouth”).

parole.significato: Formed like a fistula; hollow; reed-like.
parole.testo: Latin fistulosus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a fistula.
parole.testo: Possibly from Latin fistulōsus (“pipe-shaped, hole-filled, fistulous”), or an English medical pseudo-Latinism via fistula + -ous.

parole.significato: A seizure or convulsion.
parole.testo: Unknown. From Middle English fit (“hardship, danger”), possibly from Old English fitt (“conflict”)—a word only attested once. Compare Cornish fit (“game match, bout”); or else, maybe cognate with Italian fitta (“sudden and stabbing pain”) (see further at Latin fīgere).

parole.significato: Cinquefoil.
parole.testo: From Middle English fivelefe, fyflef; from Old English fīflēaf, a calque of Latin quīnquefolium. By surface analysis, five + leaf.

parole.significato: Fixed position; stable condition; firmness.
parole.testo: From Latin fixura (“a fastening”), from figere (“to fix”). See fix, and compare fixture.

parole.significato: A fan or flabellum.
parole.testo: From Latin flabellum (“a fan”), diminutive of flabrum (“a breeze”), from flare (“to blow”).

parole.significato: Fan-shaped; having parts or segments that are flattened and lengthened on one side, such that they are long and narrow.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin flābellātus (“fanlike”). By surface analysis, flabell(um) (“fan-shaped structure”) + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of keeping cool by use of a fan or fan-like instrument.
parole.testo: From Latin flabella (“fan”) + -ation.

parole.significato: Having many nerves diverging radiately from the base.
parole.testo: Latin flabellum a fan + English nerve.

parole.significato: A large fan used for religious ceremonies.
parole.testo: From Latin flabellum (“fan”).

parole.significato: Liable to be blown about; pertaining to wind or breath.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin flabilis.

parole.significato: Flabby; lacking firmness or muscle tone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin flaccid(us).

parole.significato: a person who whips themselves or others either as part of a religious penance or for sexual gratification.
parole.testo: From Latin flagellāns, present participle of flagellāre (“to whip”).

parole.significato: To whip or scourge.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin flagellātus perfect passive participle of flagellō (“to whip, flog”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The formation by plants of flagella, or their arrangement
parole.testo: From flagellum (“elongated filiform appendage”), itself a diminutive of Latin flagrum (“whip”), closely related to etymology 1.

parole.significato: shaped like a whip
parole.testo: Latin flagellum (“whip”) + -form

parole.significato: One who administers punishment by whipping.
parole.testo: From Latin flagellum (“whip”) + -ist.

parole.significato: A penchant for whipping, or being whipped.
parole.testo: From Latin flagellō (“to whip, flog”) + -mania.

parole.significato: In protists, a long, whiplike membrane-enclosed organelle used for locomotion or feeding.
parole.testo: From Latin flagellum (“whip”), diminutive of flagrum.

parole.significato: To importune; to demand fiercely or with passion.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin flāgitātus, perfect passive participle of flāgitō (“to demand, ask urgingly”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: begging; passionate asking
parole.testo: Latin flagitatio.

parole.significato: To burn.
parole.testo: First attested in 1756; borrowed from Latin flagrātus, perfect passive participle of flagrō (“to burn”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A priest devoted to the service of a particular god, from whom he received a distinguishing epithet. The most honored w…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin flāmen (“ancient Roman priest devoted exclusively to one deity”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a flamen.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin flāmen, flāminis (“priest”) + -ic + -al.

parole.significato: A dense cumuliform cloud associated with fire or volcanic eruptions.
parole.testo: From Latin flamma (“flame”) + genitus (“begotten”), past participle of gignō.

parole.significato: Pertaining to, consisting of, or resembling fire; fiery.
parole.testo: From Latin flammeus (“fiery”), derivative of flamma (“a flame”).

parole.significato: Producing flame; blazing.
parole.testo: From Latin flammifer, from flamma (“flame”) + ferre (“to bear”). Compare Italian fiammifero.

parole.significato: Throwing up flames, as a volcano does.
parole.testo: From Latin flammivomus, from flamma (“flame”) + vomō, vomere (“vomit”, verb).

parole.significato: A little flame or flame-like pattern.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin flammula, from flamma (“flame”) + -ula (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Flathe; flan.
parole.testo: From Middle English flathon, probably representing Medieval Latin fladon-, stem form of flado (“a flat-cake”), from Frankish *flaþō (“flat-cake”). Cognate with Middle English flathe (“a flat-cake, flat fish”). More at flathe.

parole.significato: Producing farts; flatulent.
parole.testo: From the Latin flātīvus, from flō (“to blow”).

parole.significato: Gas generated in the digestive tract.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin flātus (“blowing, wind, fart”). First attested in the 1660s–1670s.

parole.significato: A synthetic yellow dyestuff, C₁₆H₁₄N₂, a complex derivative of aniline and quinoline.
parole.testo: Latin flavus yellow + English aniline.

parole.significato: The exocarp in citruses.
parole.testo: From New Latin flāvēdō (“yellowness, sallowness, yellow color”), derived from Latin flāvus (“yellow, golden”).

parole.significato: A phytoplasma disease of grapevines.
parole.testo: From Latin flavescens, present active participle of flāvēscō (“to become yellow”). By surface analysis, Latin flāv(us) + -escence.

parole.significato: yellowish in colour, or turning yellow
parole.testo: 19th century. From Latin flavescens. By surface analysis, Latin flāv(us) + -escent.

parole.significato: of or pertaining to the Flavian Dynasty, between the years 69 and 96 AD
parole.testo: From the Latin Flaviānus, from Flavius + -ianus.

parole.significato: yellow
parole.testo: From Latin flāvidus, ultimately from flāvus.

parole.significato: A flavonoid obtained from anthraquinone.
parole.testo: From Latin flavus (“yellow”) + -ol.

parole.significato: Any of a class of tricyclic aromatic heterocyclic ketones, especially the naturally occurring flavonoids.
parole.testo: From Latin flāvus (“yellow”) + -one, as many are yellow in nature.

parole.significato: Any of many compounds that are plant metabolites, being formally derived from flavone; they have antioxidant properties…
parole.testo: From flavone + -oid, from Latin flāvus (“yellow”). Not related to flavor.

parole.significato: yellow
parole.testo: Latin flavus.

parole.significato: Producing tears.
parole.testo: From Latin fletifer, from fletus (“a weeping”) (from flere, fletum (“to weep”)) + ferre (“to bear”).

parole.significato: Flexibility, pliancy.
parole.testo: From Latin flexus, past participle of flecto (“to bend”).

parole.significato: Flexible; capable of being repeatedly flexed without breaking.
parole.testo: From Latin flexil(em).

parole.significato: The act of bending a joint, especially a bone joint; the counteraction of extension.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin flexiō, from flectō (“to bend, curve”) + -tiō, possibly via French. By surface analysis, flex + -ion.

parole.significato: A muscle whose contraction acts to bend a joint or limb.
parole.testo: From New Latin flexor, agent noun of flectō (“to bend”).

parole.significato: A muscle in the anterior compartment of the human forearm which flexes the radiocarpal joint.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A muscle in the anterior compartment of the human forearm.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A muscle in the intermediate layer of the anterior compartment of the human forearm.
parole.testo: From flexor (muscle that bends) + Latin digitorum (genitive singular; literally "finger") + Latin superficialis (relating to the surface), in all, "surface bending finger muscle".

parole.significato: winding from side to side; sinuous
parole.testo: From Latin flexuosus, from flexus (“bend”), from flectere (“bend”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin floccosus.

parole.significato: Plants considered as a group, especially those of a particular country, region, time, etc.

parole.significato: The time, or the condition, of budding or flowering.

parole.significato: Flowering or budding.
parole.testo: From Latin florescens, present active participle of floresco (“I flower”).

parole.significato: A garden where flowers are grown for research purposes.

parole.significato: Relating to flowers.

parole.significato: florescence.

parole.significato: Shaped like a flower.

parole.significato: A collection of flowers.

parole.significato: Communication through the use of flowers, with different types of flowers having particular symbolic meanings.

parole.significato: Flowery; blossoming.
parole.testo: Latin florulentus, from flos (“flower”).

parole.significato: A variety of aragonite occurring in delicate white coralloidal forms, common in beds of iron ore.

parole.significato: Any of the rotifers of the genus Floscularia.
parole.testo: From Latin flosculus (“a floweret”).

parole.significato: A floret.
parole.testo: From Latin flōsculus, diminutive of flōs (“flower, blossom”). Compare French floscule.

parole.significato: That fluctuates or causes fluctuation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fluctuans, fluctuantem.

parole.significato: To vary irregularly; to swing.
parole.testo: First attested in 1630; borrowed from Latin flūctuātus, perfect passive participle of flūctuō (“(of the sea) to surge, swell; (of man) to waver, fluctuate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A motion like that of waves; a moving in this and that direction; an irregular rising and falling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fluctuatiōnem, accusative singular of fluctuatiō, from fluctuō, from fluctus. Morphologically fluctuate + -ion.

parole.significato: fluctuating
parole.testo: From Latin flūctuōsus. By surface analysis, fluct(us) + -uous.

parole.significato: An area covered by outflow from a volcano.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fluctus.

parole.significato: The quality of smoothness of flow.

parole.significato: That flows; flowing, liquid.
parole.testo: From Latin fluens (“flowing”), present active participle of fluō (“to flow”).

parole.significato: In planetary geology, any of the river-like features on Saturn's moon Titan.

parole.significato: flowing, fluent (of rivers)

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, inhabiting, or produced by the action of a river or stream.

parole.significato: Belonging to rivers or streams; fluviatile.
parole.testo: From Latin fluviaticus. See fluvial.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or produced by rivers; fluvial.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fluviatilis.

parole.significato: Deposition of silt etc. by the action of a river or stream.
parole.testo: From Latin fluviātiō, from fluviātus (“fluviated”) + -iō (“-tion: forming abstract nouns”), from fluvius (“river”) + -ātus (“-ate: forming adjectives”) as if from a verb fluviō. Equivalent to fluviated + -ion.

parole.significato: river
parole.testo: Latin fluvius (“river”).

parole.significato: A genetically young kind of soil found in alluvial deposits.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fluvius (“river”) + -sol.

parole.significato: fluxible
parole.testo: From Latin fluxilis (“fluid”).

parole.significato: The quality of being fluid; fluidity.
parole.testo: From Latin flūxūra (“a flowing”).

parole.significato: Belonging to, concerning, or located at a focus (definite location).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin focālis. By surface analysis, focus + -al.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin focus (“hearth, fireplace”); see there for more. Related to fuel. parole.significato: A trace fossil formed by deposit feeders as they excavate the sediment in search of food.

parole.significato: A confederate. One of the tribes bound by treaty, who were neither Roman colonies nor had they been granted Roman citiz…

parole.significato: Foliage; leafage.
parole.testo: Latin foliatura (“foliage”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to foliage; pteroylglutamic, as in folic acid.

parole.significato: A polycyclic heterocyclic carboxylic acid, one of the vitamin B complex, essential for cell growth and reproduction

parole.significato: Producing leaves.

parole.significato: One of the distinct parts of a compound leaf; a leaflet.

parole.significato: The eating of leaves.

parole.significato: Like a leaf; thin; insubstantial.

parole.significato: A leaf.
parole.testo: From Latin folium (“leaf”). Doublet of foil and folio, distantly also with phyllo and phyllon.

parole.significato: A herbivore that eats mostly foliage.
parole.testo: From Latin folium (“a leaf”) + -vore, Latin vorō (“to devour”).

parole.significato: A small cavity or sac, such as a hair follicle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin folliculus.

parole.significato: The process of growing and developing for an ovarian follicle in the ovary.
parole.testo: From Latin folliculus + -o- + genesis.

parole.significato: Follicular; having or producing follicles.

parole.significato: Morbid matter created by a disease.

parole.significato: The source and origin.

parole.significato: Only used in vicar forane and vicariate forane.

parole.significato: An instrument used in surgery or medical procedures for grasping and holding objects, similar to tongs or pincers.

parole.significato: A runner at the front or ahead.

parole.significato: The ability, or the due use of one's ability, to foresee or prepare wisely for the future.
parole.testo: From Middle English forsight, forsyght, forsichte (since 14th c.), a calque of Latin providentia. By surface analysis, fore- + sight. Compare Scots foresicht, Saterland Frisian Foarsicht, archaic Dutch voorzicht (now voorzichtigheid), German Vorsicht (all “caution, foresight”).

parole.significato: To take precedence or superiority over; to preside over.
parole.testo: From fore- (“before”) + sit, sometimes as a calque of Latin praesideō or Old English foresittan.

parole.significato: To remove the foreskin.
parole.testo: From fore- + skin, a loose calque of Latin praepūtium. Compare German Vorhaut, etc. First attested in c. 1535.

parole.significato: A pair of shears.

parole.significato: Synonym of form (“the component of a thing that determines its kind”).

parole.significato: A formative faculty.

parole.significato: An ant colony, a pile of earth built by ants in which they nest.

parole.significato: An unmarried person who engages in sexual intercourse, especially when considered to be of an illicit or illegal nature.
parole.testo: From Middle English fornicatour, from Medieval Latin fornicātor.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to fornication.

parole.significato: An archlike or vaulted structure or fold:

parole.significato: A small fortress.

parole.significato: To lead forth.

parole.significato: A little fort; a blockhouse.

parole.significato: Relatively strongly articulated, hence voiceless and possibly aspirated; especially as compared to the others of a grou…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fortis (“strong”). Doublet of fort and forte.

parole.significato: Having fortitude; courageous.

parole.significato: The state of being fortuitous.

parole.significato: fork-shaped
parole.testo: From Latin furca (“fork”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Having a forked tail
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin furcātus (“forked, branched”), from Latin furca (“fork”) + -cercous.

parole.significato: A forked process or structure, generally two-pronged.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin furcula.

parole.significato: furcula (wishbone of birds)
parole.testo: From Latin furculum, diminutive of furca (“fork”).

parole.significato: a particle of dandruff
parole.testo: From Latin furfur (“bran”), reduplication of *fur, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰur-, metathesis of *gʰrus- (compare Lithuanian grū́sti (“to grind (barley)”), Ancient Greek χρώς (khrṓs, “skin, husk”)).

parole.significato: Made of bran.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin furfur (“bran”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: The falling of dandruff from the head.
parole.testo: Latin furfur bran, scurf, + -ation.

parole.significato: Made of, or resembling, bran
parole.testo: From Latin furfurōsus.

parole.significato: Full of rage.
parole.testo: From Latin furibundus, from furere (“to rage”).

parole.significato: A boil or infected, inflamed, pus-filled sore.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin fūrunculus (“a petty thief, pilferer; a pointed burning sore, boil”), diminutive of fūr (“a thief”).

parole.significato: A thief.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fur (“thief”).

parole.significato: A darkening; obscurity; obfuscation.
parole.testo: From Latin fuscare, fuscatum (“to make dark”), from fuscus (“dark”).

parole.significato: A brown nitrogenous pigment contained in the retinal epithelium; a variety of melanin.
parole.testo: From Latin fuscus (“dark-colored, tawny”) + -in.

parole.significato: Of a dark, brownish-grey color; dark-hued, dusky, swarthy.
parole.testo: From Latin fusc(us) (“dark, dusky”) + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to fusidic acid or its derivatives.
parole.testo: From the generic name Fusidium (from the Latin fūsus, “spindle”) + the English -ic, so named because fusidic acid was originally isolated from a strain of the fungus Fusidium coccineum.

parole.significato: Shaped like a spindle with yarn spun on it; having round or roundish cross-section and tapering at each end.
parole.testo: From Latin fusus (“spindle”) + -iform.

parole.significato: That can be melted; meltable
parole.testo: From Latin fūsilis, from the participle stem of fundere (“to pour”).

parole.significato: Synonym of fusiform.
parole.testo: From Latin fusus (“spindle”) + -oid.

parole.significato: A coin melter.
parole.testo: From Latin fūsor, from fundō + -tor. By surface analysis, fuse + -or. The astronomical sense was coined by Gibor Basri, Professor of Astronomy at the University of California, Berkeley, at the 2003 IAU conference.

parole.significato: To hit someone with a club.
parole.testo: First attested in 1656; borrowed from Latin fūstīgātus, perfect passive participle of fūstīgō (“to cudgel to death”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fūstis (“a cudgel”) + -igō.

parole.significato: Act of fusing; fusion.
parole.testo: From Latin fusura, from fundere, fusum. See fuse (transitive verb).

parole.significato: The quality of being futile or useless.
parole.testo: From Latin fūtilitās (“worthlessness, futility”). By surface analysis, futile + -ity.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the ancient city of Gadara (near modern-day Umm Qais, in Jordan).
parole.testo: From the Late Latin Gadarēnus, from the Ancient Greek Γαδαρηνός (Gadarēnós, “inhabitant of Gadara”), from Γάδαρα (Gádara, “Gadara”, now “Umm Qais”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Cadiz in Spain.
parole.testo: From Latin Gaditanus (“of Cadiz”).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city of Cádiz, Andalusia, Spain.
parole.testo: From Latin Gādītānus, from Gādēs (“Cadiz”), + -ian.

parole.significato: The rare earth gadolinium oxide
parole.testo: From New Latin gadolinia. See gadolinite.

parole.significato: An ancient Berber tribe inhabiting Gaetulia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Gaetūlī, from Ancient Greek Γαίτουλοι (Gaítouloi).

parole.significato: Agate.
parole.testo: From Latin gagātēs. Doublet of jet.

parole.significato: Used to form medical and biochemical terms related to galactose
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek stem γάλακτ- (gálakt-) of γάλα (gála, “milk, milky sap, the Milky Way”).

parole.significato: An acidic galectin from Bothrops atrox snake venom
parole.testo: galectin + Latin atrox

parole.significato: A bitter, aromatic resin or gum, extracted from plants of the genus Ferula, that resembles assafoetida and has been use…
parole.testo: From Latin galbanum (“galbanum”), from Ancient Greek χαλβάνη (khalbánē, “galbanum”).

parole.significato: A fleshy seed-producing cone of junipers and cypresses
parole.testo: Latin galbulus (“cypress cone”).

parole.significato: A Roman helmet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin galea.

parole.significato: Any of the extinct class †Galeaspida of jawless fish.
parole.testo: From Latin galea (“helmet”) + aspis (from Ancient Greek ἀσπίς (aspís, “round shield”)); compare translingual †Galeaspida.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a galea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin galeātus (“helmeted”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A guinea fowl.
parole.testo: From Latin gallīna (“hen”).

parole.significato: A physician.
parole.testo: From Middle English Galen, from Latin Galēnus, from Ancient Greek Γαληνός (Galēnós), from γαλήνη (galḗnē, “calm, tranquillity”).

parole.significato: A mineral, lead sulphide (PbS), mined as an ore for lead.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin galēna (“dross from smelting lead”).

parole.significato: A guinea fowl.
parole.testo: From Latin gallīna (“hen”).

parole.significato: A cretaceous fossil sea urchin of the genus †Galerites.
parole.testo: Latin galerum a hat, cap: compare French galérite. See -ite.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Geoffrey of Monmouth (c.1100–c.1155), cleric and one of the major figures in the development of Briti…
parole.testo: From his Latin name, Galfridus Monemutensis, + -ian.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Galilee, or a native or inhabitant thereof.
parole.testo: Originated 1605–15 from Latin Galilaeus [from Ancient Greek Γαλιλαῖος (Galilaîos)] + -an.

parole.significato: An alloy of gallium, indium and tin which is liquid at room temperature.
parole.testo: Trade name, from gallium, indium, and Latin stannum (“tin”).

parole.significato: A verse consisting of four Ionics a minore, with variations and substitutions.
parole.testo: From Latin Galli + iambus. Used by the Galli, priests of the Phrygian goddess Cybele. The first element, Ancient Greek γάλλος (gállos), was said by Ovid to be named after a Phrygian river.

parole.significato: Of or related to Gaul or the Gauls.
parole.testo: From Latin Gallicus (“of or related to Gaul”), from Gallia (“Gaul”) + -icus (“-ic: forming adj.”), used archaically in New Latin and English in reference to modern France.

parole.significato: Relating to Gaul or France; Gallic; French.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Gallicānus (“pertaining to Gaul or France; Gallican”), from Gallicus (“Gaulish, French”) (from Gallia (“Gaul”)) + -ānus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’).

parole.significato: Synonym of frenchify, to make French or more French-like.
parole.testo: From Gallic + -ize, from Latin Gallicus (“of or relating to Gaul”) and used archaically in English in reference to modern France.

parole.significato: Affecting chickens; applied to certain alphaherpesviruses.
parole.testo: From Latin gallus (“cock, rooster”) + -id.

parole.significato: Synonym of Gallophilia.
parole.testo: From Latin gallicus + -mania.

parole.significato: Related to the genus Gallus, poultry; notably said of the order Galliformes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gallīnāceus, from gallīna (“hen”), itself from gallus (“cock”).

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Ga) with an atomic number of 31; a soft bluish metal.
parole.testo: Named by its discoverer Lecoq, after Latin Gallia (“Gaul”). It was claimed that Lecoq had named the element after himself, since gallus is the Latin translation of the French le coq, but Lecoq denied this in an article of 1877.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Galloway, Scotland.
parole.testo: From Latin Gallovidia (“Galloway”), from Cumbric/Welsh Gallgwyddel.

parole.significato: The metacarpus or metatarsus of ruminants, etc.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gamba (“leg”); compare gambol. Doublet of gam, gamb, jamb, and jambe.

parole.significato: Any of several species of trees of the genus Garcinia found in South and Southeastern Asia, especially Garcinia xanthoc…
parole.testo: From New Latin gambogium, cambogium (“resin from trees used to make yellow dye”), from New Latin Gambogia, Cambogia (“Cambodia”). The Latin word was first attested in English as a colour in 1634. Doublet of Cambodia and Kampuchea.

parole.significato: A (normally) complete range.
parole.testo: 1520s, original sense “lowest note of musical scale”, contraction of Medieval Latin gamma ut, from gamma (“Greek letter, corresponding to the musical note G”) + ut (“first solfège syllable, now replaced by do”). In modern terms, “G do” – the first note of the G scale. Meaning later extended to mean

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the river Ganges.
parole.testo: From Latin Gangēticus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Γαγγητικός (Gangētikós), from Γάγγης (Gángēs, “(River) Ganges”).

parole.significato: Any of several dock plants of the genus Rumex, especially Rumex patientia.
parole.testo: From garden and a corruption of Low Vulgar Latin lapathium.

parole.significato: a gargle; a liquid used to gargle with.
parole.testo: From Latin gargarisma, from Ancient Greek γαργάρισμα (gargárisma).

parole.significato: To gargle (rinse or wash mouth and throat).
parole.testo: From Latin gargarizo, from Ancient Greek γαργαρίζω (gargarízō).

parole.significato: A fermented fish sauce popular as a condiment in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin garum, from Ancient Greek γάρον (gáron, “the fish whose intestines were originally used in the condiment's production”).

parole.significato: A highly esteemed variety of garum from Cartagena and Gades in Hispania Baetica.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?] (literally “garum of the allies”)

parole.significato: Related to, or from, the region of the river Garonne.
parole.testo: From Latin Garumna.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the stomach.
parole.testo: From New Latin gastricus, from Ancient Greek γαστήρ, γαστρός (gastḗr, gastrós, “stomach”). By surface analysis, gastr- + -ic; Doublet of gastrique.

parole.significato: The muscle at the back of the calf, whose insertion is the Achilles tendon at the heel.
parole.testo: 1670s, borrowed from New Latin gastrocnēmius, from Ancient Greek γαστροκνημία (gastroknēmía, “calf of the leg”), from γαστήρ (gastḗr, “paunch, belly”) + κνήμη (knḗmē, “leg”).

parole.significato: omnium-gatherum
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from gather + Latin -um.

parole.significato: A students' merrymaking.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gaudeamus (“may we rejoice”)

parole.significato: A reunion held by one of the colleges of the University of Oxford for alumni, normally during the long vacation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gaudium (“joy”). Doublet of joy and jo.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of the historical region of Gaul, or poetically the modern nation of France.
parole.testo: From Middle English Gall, from Latin Gallus. The change in spelling is due to the influence of the place-name Gaul, which is thought to be etymologically unrelated (see above).

parole.significato: Capable of being congealed, or converted into jelly.
parole.testo: From Latin gelare (“to congeal”). Compare French gelable. See geal.

parole.significato: The formation of a solid by cooling; freezing.
parole.testo: From Latin gelātiō (“freezing”), from gelātus (“frozen”), past participle of gelō (“to freeze”).

parole.significato: Young and weakly developed soils that form in very cold climates where permafrost is present near the surface and that…
parole.testo: From Latin gelāre (“freeze”) + (inc)ept(isol).

parole.significato: Very cold; icy or frosty; frigid.
parole.testo: First attested in 1630. From Latin gelidus (“cold”), from gelu (“frost”).

parole.significato: A kind of soil found in cold climates, containing permafrost near the surface.
parole.testo: Latin gelāre (“freeze”) + + -sol

parole.significato: A tribe of Scythia settled near the river Borysthenes
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Gelōnī, from Ancient Greek Γελωνοί (Gelōnoí).

parole.significato: A person who studies humour and laughter
parole.testo: From Latin zelus (“laughter”).

parole.significato: Producing twins
parole.testo: From Latin gemellipara f, from gemellus (“twin”) + parere (“to bear, produce”).

parole.significato: Describing identical atoms or groups attached to the same atom in a molecule
parole.testo: From Latin geminālis, from geminī (“twins”).

parole.significato: Forming a pair.
parole.testo: First attested in 1589; borrowed from Latin geminātus, perfect passive participle of geminō (“to double”), see -ate (etymology 1,2 and 3).

parole.significato: The process of indicating that a vowel is pronounced long by writing it twice, especially as was sometimes done in Lati…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin geminatio vocalium (“doubling of vowels”).

parole.significato: A doubling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin geminātiō, geminātiōnis (“a doubling”).

parole.significato: Someone who has the Gemini star sign.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin geminī, plural of geminus (“twin”), calque of Ancient Greek Δίδυμοι (Dídumoi), calque of Akkadian 𒀯𒈠𒀸 (māšu), calque of Sumerian 𒀯𒈦𒋰𒁀 (ᵐᵘˡMAŠ.TAB.BA, “the Divine Twins, in Mesopotamia identified as Lugal-irra and Meslamta-ea; name of constellation”). See Lugal-irra and Meslamta-e

parole.significato: Having the flowers arranged in pairs.
parole.testo: From Latin geminus (“twin”) + flos, floris (“flower”).

parole.significato: Having a structure consisting of two identical parts.
parole.testo: From Latin geminī (“twins”) + -form.

parole.significato: The study of twins; gemellology.
parole.testo: From Latin gemini (“twins”) + -logy.

parole.significato: double; appearing or growing in pairs
parole.testo: Latin geminus.

parole.significato: An asexual reproductive structure, as found in animals such as hydra (genus Hydra) and plants such as liverworts (divis…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gemma (“bud on a plant”). Doublet of gem and Gemma.

parole.significato: Relating to, or containing, gemmae.
parole.testo: From Latin gemma + -aceous.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to gems.
parole.testo: From Late Latin gemmarius.

parole.significato: Having buds; reproducing by buds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gemmātus, perfect passive participle of gemmō (“to put forth buds”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from gemma (“a bud”).

parole.significato: Resembling or relating to gems.
parole.testo: From Latin gemmeus. See gem.

parole.significato: Producing gemmae or buds.
parole.testo: From Latin gemma (“bud”) + -ferous. Compare French gemmifère.

parole.significato: The production of a bud or gem.
parole.testo: From Latin gemma (“bud”) + -ficare (“in comparative) to make”). See -fy.

parole.significato: The branch of mineralogy that studies mineral gems and petrified gemstones.
parole.testo: From Latin gemma (“gem”) + -logy (“science”).

parole.significato: The use of remedies made from the embryonic tissue of various trees and shrubs, or other meristematic parts
parole.testo: From Latin gemma (“bud”) + therapy.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Gemonian Stairs, a flight of steps used as a place of execution in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin gemoniae (“of laments”) (from gemō) + -an, referring to the scalae gemoniae ("stairway of laments") where the bodies of executed people were exposed.

parole.significato: new genus and species
parole.testo: From Latin genus et species novus.

parole.significato: The cheek; the feathered side of the under mandible of a bird.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gena (“cheek”). Doublet of chin.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the cheeks
parole.testo: From Latin gena (“cheek”) + -al.

parole.significato: generalities; general terms
parole.testo: Neuter plural, from Latin generalis.

parole.significato: The quality of being general.
parole.testo: From Middle English generalite, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French generalité (modern French généralité), from general + -ité; also influenced by Latin generālitās. By surface analysis, general + -ity.

parole.significato: generative; producing
parole.testo: From Latin generans.

parole.significato: Generated, not self-existent.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin generātus, perfect passive participle of generō (“beget, procreate, produce”). See Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: One who, or that which, generates, begets, causes, or produces.
parole.testo: From Latin, from past participle of genero (“beget, father”), equivalent to generate + -or.

parole.significato: A curve that, when rotated about an axis, produces a solid figure.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin generātrīx. By surface analysis, generator + -trix.

parole.significato: The process of making generic; the conversion to use generics.
parole.testo: From Latin genus (“kind, class”). See -fy.

parole.significato: The trait of being willing to donate money, resources, or time.
parole.testo: From Middle English generosite, from Latin generōsitās, equivalent to generous + -ity.

parole.significato: The origin, start, or point at which something comes into being.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin genesis (“generation, nativity”), from Ancient Greek γένεσις (génesis, “origin, source, beginning”). Related to Ancient Greek γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to be produced, become, be”). Doublet of kind, gens, and jati.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the casting of horoscopes at a person's birth
parole.testo: From Latin genethliacus, from Ancient Greek γενεθλιακός (genethliakós, “belonging to a birthday”).

parole.significato: A birthday ode.
parole.testo: Via Latin genethliacon from Ancient Greek γενεθλιακόν (genethliakón, “of or related to a birthday”, neuter sg.).

parole.significato: The quality of being genial; friendly cheerfulness; warmth of disposition and manners.
parole.testo: From Latin geniālitās, and perhaps also partly formed within English as genial + -ity.

parole.significato: Bent abruptly, with the structure of a knee.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ǵónu Learned borrowing from Latin geniculātus (“with bended knee”), from geniculum (“little knee”) + -ātus (participial adjective-forming suffix), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To form joints or knots on.
parole.testo: From Latin geniculātus (more at etymology 1), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of kneeling.
parole.testo: Latin geniculatio a kneeling.

parole.significato: Of the structure of a knee.
parole.testo: From Latin geniculātus (“with bended knee”) + -o-, from geniculum (“little knee”) + -ātus (participial adjective-forming suffix), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A small genu, or angular knee-like structure, especially (anatomy) a sharp knee-like bend in a small structure or organ.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin geniculum.

parole.significato: A flat, fan-shaped muscle that originates from the superior mental spine and inserts onto the undersurface of the tongu…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin genīoglōssus, clipping of musculus genīoglōssus (“genioglossal muscle”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the chin and hyoid bone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin genīohyoīdeus, clipping of musculus genīohyoīdeus; from Ancient Greek γένειον (géneion, “the chin”) + Latin hyoīdēs (“U-shaped”) + Latin -eus (adjectival suffix); equivalent to genio- (“relating to the chin”) + hyoid.

parole.significato: Of or relating to biological reproduction.
parole.testo: From Middle English genital, from Latin genitalis (“of or belonging to generation”), from genitus, past participle of gignō (“to beget, generate”); see genus.

parole.significato: External sex organs.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin (membra) genitālia, substantive use of neuter plural of genitālis (“pertaining to generation or birth”). First attested in 1651.

parole.significato: an independent phrase in a sentence conveying additional circumstances in the genitive case; present in many Indo-Europ…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin genitīvus absolūtus.

parole.significato: The biological mother of a child.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin genitrīx. By surface analysis, genitor + -trix.

parole.significato: Someone possessing extraordinary intelligence or skill; especially somebody who has demonstrated this by a creative or…
parole.testo: From Latin genius (“inborn nature; a tutelary deity of a person or place; wit, brilliance”), from gignō (“to beget, produce”), Old Latin genō, from the Proto-Indo-European root *ǵenh₁-. Doublet of genio. See also genus and genie.

parole.significato: A spirit presiding over or guarding a family or household.
parole.testo: From Latin genius (“lar”) + familiae (“of (a) person”), genitive singular form of familia (“family”, “household”) = “(guardian) spirit of a family”.

parole.significato: The tutelary deity or spirit watching over a particular person.
parole.testo: A borrowing of Latin genius hominis (“tutelary deity of a person”), from the nominative possessive form of homo (“person”).

parole.significato: The minor deity or spirit watching over a particular place.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin genius loci (“tutelary deity of a/the place”), from the singular genitive form of locus (“place”).

parole.significato: A single spirit or minor deity (genius) which watches over several places, rather than only one.
parole.testo: A borrowing of Latin genius locorum (“tutelary spirit of the places”), employing the genitive plural of locus (“place”).

parole.significato: A legally defined unit of Roman society, being a collection of people related through a common ancestor by birth, marri…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gēns (“gens; people, tribe”), from Proto-Italic *gentis, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tis (“birth; production”), from *ǵenh₁- (“to beget; to give birth; to produce”) + *-tis (suffix forming abstract or action nouns from verb roots). Doublet of kind, genesis, and jati. See also

parole.significato: Any of various herbs of the family Gentianaceae found in temperate and mountainous regions with violet or blue flowers.
parole.testo: Via Middle English from Latin gentiāna, which, according to Pliny the Elder, was named after Gentius (Ancient Greek Γένθιος (Génthios)), the last king of Illyria, who supposedly discovered the plant's medicinal benefits. This has been dismissed as folk etymology but the word may still ultimately be

parole.significato: The killing of a race or nation of people; the slaughter of an ethnic group; a genocide.
parole.testo: From the Latin gēns (“a race, nation, people; a clan, family”, oblique stem: gent-) + -cide (“a killing of”). The combination represents a hypothetical Latin etymon of the form *genticīdium, regularly formed from gēns + -cīdium. Compare genericide and genocide.

parole.significato: Tribal or national.
parole.testo: From Latin gentilis (“of a clan or gens”) + English suffix -ic.

parole.significato: Synonym of gentilicial.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gentīlicius.

parole.significato: The knee.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ǵónu Borrowed from Latin genu (“knee”).

parole.significato: The condition in which the knees are abnormally close together and the ankles far apart.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin genū valgum (“knockkneed”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a genu or to the knee.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ǵónu From New Latin genuālis, from Latin genū (“knee”). By surface analysis, Latin genū + -al.

parole.significato: To bend the knee, as in servitude.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ǵónu From around 1620–1630 from Medieval Latin genūflectō (“to bend the knee”) equivalent to the Latin genū (“knee”) + flectō (“to bend”).

parole.significato: The act of genuflecting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin genuflexio, though with standardized spelling. By surface analysis, genuflect (“to bend the knee”) + -ion (Latinate abstract-noun suffix).

parole.significato: Belonging to, or proceeding from the original stock; native.
parole.testo: From Latin genuīnus (“innate, native, natural”).

parole.significato: The placement of someone's penis between another person's knees.
parole.testo: Macaronic from Late Latin genu (“knee”) + phallus (“penis”) + -ation.

parole.significato: A category in the classification of organisms, ranking below family (Lat. familia) and above species.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin genus (“birth, origin, a race, sort, kind”) from the root gen- in Latin gignō (“to beget, produce”). Doublet of gender and genre, further related to kin.

parole.significato: Pertaining to geography (or to geographics).
parole.testo: From Latin geōgraphicus; see French géographique. By surface analysis, geography + -ic.

parole.significato: The science that studies the structure of the Earth (or other planets), together with its origin and development, espec…
parole.testo: From geo- + -logy, partly after Renaissance Latin geōlogia, from Ancient Greek γεω- (geō-, “earth”) + Latin -logia (“the study of”), from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía).

parole.significato: A method of divination using earth or the ground, such as interpreting markings on the ground or how handfuls of dirt l…
parole.testo: From Middle English geomancie, from Medieval Latin geomantia from late Ancient Greek γεωμαντεία (geōmanteía). Equivalent to geo- + -mancy.

parole.significato: Of or relating to geomancy.
parole.testo: From Latin geōmanticus. By surface analysis, geo- + -mantic.

parole.significato: A mathematician who specializes in geometry.
parole.testo: From Middle English gemeter, geometer, ultimately from Late Latin geōmetrēs, from Ancient Greek γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) + μετρέω (metréō, “to measure”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to geometry.
parole.testo: From Latin geōmetricus, from Ancient Greek γεωμετρικός (geōmetrikós), from γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs). By surface analysis, geometer + -ic or geo- + -metric.

parole.significato: A unit of measure used in the 16th century, defined as "five feet" or "five geometrical feet".
parole.testo: Calque of Latin passus geometricus or French pas géometrique.

parole.significato: radiotelephony clear-code word for the letter G.
parole.testo: Name of an early saint, from Middle English George, from Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργῐος (Geṓrgĭos), from γεωργός (geōrgós, “farmer, earth worker”), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) (combining form γεω- (geō-)) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”) Doublet of Jorge and Geevarghese. The aircraft autopilot sense i

parole.significato: A British citizen during the reign of a king named George.
parole.testo: From George + -ian, possibly with influence from its Latin equivalent (as other regnal adjectives and nouns so derived), Geōrgius.

parole.significato: A rural poem; a poetical composition on husbandry, containing rules for cultivating land, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin georgicum, georgicus, from Ancient Greek γεωργός (geōrgós, “farmer, earth worker”), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) (combining form γεω- (geō-)) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

parole.significato: A member of an East Germanic people related to the Goths.
parole.testo: From Latin Gepidae.

parole.significato: The Gepids, an East Germanic people.
parole.testo: From Latin Gepidae, from Gothic *𐌲𐌹𐌱𐌹𐌳𐍉𐍃 (*gibidōs), from Proto-Germanic *gibidōz (which see for more).

parole.significato: Any flowering plant of the genus Geranium, of family Geraniaceae.
parole.testo: From Latin geranium, from Ancient Greek γερᾰ́νῐον (gerắnĭon), from γέρᾰνος (gérănos, “crane”) + -ῐον (-ĭon, diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Gerasa
parole.testo: From the Late Latin Gerasēnus, Gergesēnus, from the Ancient Greek Γερασηνός (Gerasēnós), Γεργεσηνός (Gergesēnós), from Γέρασα (Gérasa), Γέργεσα (Gérgesa). By surface analysis, Gerasa + -ene.

parole.significato: A manager.
parole.testo: From Latin gerēns, present participle of gerō.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the nation of Germany.
parole.testo: From Latin Germānus, Germānī (“the peoples of Germānia”), as distinct from Gauls (in the writings of Caesar and Tacitus), and of uncertain ultimate origin (possibly Celtic/Gaulish). Not related to german (“closely related”) or germane (from the Latin adjective germānus, through Old French). Attested

parole.significato: Relating to the Germanic peoples (such as Germans, Scandinavians or Anglo-Saxons).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin germānicus, equivalent to German + -ic.

parole.significato: The basic form of an organism; the seed or germ.
parole.testo: From Latin germen (“germ, seed”). Doublet of germ.

parole.significato: Relating to spring
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin germen, germinis (“seed”) + -al.

parole.significato: Of a seed, to begin to grow, to sprout roots and leaves.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”) + -ate, from germinātus (“sprouted, budded, grown”), past participle of germinō (“to sprout, bud, grow”), from germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”).

parole.significato: The process of germinating; the beginning of vegetation or growth from a seed or spore; the first development of germs,…
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”) + -ation, from Latin germinātiō, germinātiōnem (“sprouting, budding, growing”), from germinātus (“sprouted, budded, grown”), past participle of germinō (“to sprout, bud, grow”), from germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”). By surfac

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to germination
parole.testo: From germinate + -ive. From oblique stem of Latin germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”) + -ate, from germinātus (“sprouted, budded, grown”), past participle of germinō (“to sprout, bud, grow”), from germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”).

parole.significato: magistrates in Sparta who, with the kings, constituted the Gerousia
parole.testo: From New Latin Gerontes, from Ancient Greek γέροντες (gérontes, literally “elders”).

parole.significato: A verbal form that functions as a verbal noun.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gerundium, from gerendus (“which is to be carried out”), future passive participle (gerundive) of gerō (“carry, bear”).

parole.significato: A verbal adjective that describes obligation or necessity, equivalent in form to the future passive participle.
parole.testo: From Middle English gerundif, gerundyf, gerundyfe, gerundyffe, gerundyve, from Latin gerundīvum (“gerundive”), from gerundium (“gerund”), from gerundus (“which is to be carried out”), future passive participle (gerundive) of gerō (“carry, bear”). By surface analysis, gerund + -ive.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or behaving like a gerund.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gerundīvus. By surface analysis, gerund + -ive.

parole.significato: Having within; laden; burdened; or pregnant, gestating.
parole.testo: From Latin gestāns, present participle of gestō.

parole.significato: The period of time during which an animal or human offspring physically develops inside the mother's body until it is b…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gestātiō.

parole.significato: A sedan chair used as a portable throne by popes.
parole.testo: A calque of Latin and Italian sedia gestatoria (“carrying chair”).

parole.significato: gestational (pertaining to gestation or pregnancy)
parole.testo: From Latin gestatorius (“that serves for carrying”). Compare French gestatoire.

parole.significato: To make gestures or motions, as in speaking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gesticulātus, perfect active participle of gesticulor (“to gesticulate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from gesticulus (“a mimic gesture”), diminutive of gestus (“gesture”), from gerō (“to bear, carry, perform”).

parole.significato: The act of gesticulating, or making gestures to aid expression of thoughts, sentiments or passion.
parole.testo: From Middle English gesticulation, from Latin gesticulatio.

parole.significato: One who gesticulates
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gesticulātor.

parole.significato: A manager of another's affairs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gestor.

parole.significato: A motion of the limbs or body, especially one made to emphasize speech.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin gestūra (“a mode of action”), from Latin gerō (“to bear; (reflexive) bear oneself, behave, act”), past participle gestus. By surface analysis, Latin gest- + -ure.

parole.significato: Do not tempt or torment me; I reject you, your statements, or your beliefs.
parole.testo: Originally uttered by Christ in the King James Bible, Matthew 16:23: “get thee behind me, Satan”; Latin vāde retrō, Satanā; Ancient Greek ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου, Σατανᾶ (húpage opísō mou, Satanâ).

parole.significato: A Dacian tribe inhabiting the regions of the lower Danube.
parole.testo: From Latin Getae, from Ancient Greek Γέται (Gétai).

parole.significato: humped; protuberant; having one or more large elevations
parole.testo: From Latin gibbosus, from gibbus, gibba (“hunch, hump”). Compare gibbous.

parole.significato: Curved or bulged outward.
parole.testo: From Middle English gibbous, from Latin gibbus (“humped, hunched”), probably cognate with cubō (“bend oneself, lie down”), Italian gobba (“humpback”), Ancient Greek κῡφός (kūphós, “humpback, bent”), κύβος (kúbos, “cube, vertebra”), Spanish giboso (“humped”). Also ultimately compare dialectal Norwegi

parole.significato: giant-like; gigantic, mighty.
parole.testo: From Latin giganteus. See giant.

parole.significato: The killing of a giant.
parole.testo: From Latin gigāns, gigantis + -cide.

parole.significato: The gizzard of some birds.
parole.testo: Latin gigeria (“(plural) the cooked entrails of poultry”).

parole.significato: The internal flesh of a mushroom gill.
parole.testo: A macaronic blend of gill + Latin trāma (“woof”)

parole.significato: The gum, consisting of the tissue surrounding the roots of the teeth and covering the jawbone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gingīva (“gums”).

parole.significato: Relating to the gums.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin gingīvālis.

parole.significato: A hinge joint.
parole.testo: From Late Latin, from Ancient Greek γίγγλυμος (gínglumos, “hinge”).

parole.significato: A member of a certain group of descendants of Canaan who inhabited the land of Canaan.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin Gergeseum, from Ancient Greek Γεργεσαῖον (Gergesaîon), from Biblical Hebrew גִּרְגָּשִׁי (girgāšî). Further etymology is unknown.

parole.significato: to distribute or circulate something
parole.testo: (to surround): Calque of Latin circumdō (“to surround”), which is formed from circum- (“around, about”) + dō (“give”).

parole.significato: The space between the eyebrows and above the nose.
parole.testo: From Latin glaber (“smooth, hairless, bald”).

parole.significato: smoothness or baldness.
parole.testo: Latin glabritas.

parole.significato: Bald, hairless; smooth.
parole.testo: From Latin glaber (“smooth; bald, hairless”) + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives, denoting possession or presence of a quality in any degree, commonly in abundance). Glaber is ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʰleh₂dʰ- (“smooth; bright, shining”), possibly from *ǵʰelh₂- (“to shine”

parole.significato: To cover with ice or a glacier.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin glaciātus, perfect passive participle of glaciō (“to freeze”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To become icy; to freeze into ice or ice crystals.
parole.testo: From Latin glaciēs (“ice”) + -ify.

parole.significato: The study of ice and its effect on the landscape, especially the study of glaciers.
parole.testo: From Latin glaciēs (“ice”) + -ology (“study of a particular subject”).

parole.significato: Sword grass.
parole.testo: From Old English glaedene from Latin gladiolus (“little sword; sword lily”).

parole.significato: A person (professional or slave) who entertained the public by engaging in mortal combat with another, or with a wild a…
parole.testo: From Latin gladiātor, from gladius (“sword”). See also English gladius.

parole.significato: gladiatorial
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gladiatorius.

parole.significato: gladiator (female)
parole.testo: From Latin gladiātrīx (“gladiator (female)”). By surface analysis, gladiator + -trix.

parole.significato: swordplay; gladiatorial contest
parole.testo: From Latin gladiatura.

parole.significato: gladiolus (flowering plant)
parole.testo: From Middle English gladiol, from Latin gladiolus.

parole.significato: The center part of the sternum.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gladiolus (“little sword, sword lily”), diminutive of gladius (“sword”). Compare Middle English gladiol, whence gladiole.

parole.significato: A Roman sword roughly two feet long.
parole.testo: From Latin gladius (“Roman short sword, gladius”). Doublet of glaive.

parole.significato: Any structure, in soil, whose morphology is different from the surrounding matrix
parole.testo: From Latin glaebula. By surface analysis, Latin glaeb(a) + -ule.

parole.significato: Of or written with the Glagolitic alphabet.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin glagoliticus, from Old Church Slavonic глаголица (glagolica), from глаголъ (glagolŭ, “word, speech”), Glagolitic spelling ⰳⰾⰰⰳⱁⰾⰻⱌⰰ (glagolica).

parole.significato: Bearing acorns or other similar nuts.
parole.testo: From Latin glandifer, from glans, glandis (“acorn”) + ferre (“to bear”). Compare French glandifère.

parole.significato: A small gland or secreting vessel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin glandula, from glans + -ulus. Doublet of glanders.

parole.significato: Bearing glandules.
parole.testo: From Latin glandula (“gland”) + -ferous. Compare French glandulifère.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or composed of glands; glandular, glandulose.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin glandulōsus, from Latin glandula. By surface analysis, glandule + -ous.

parole.significato: The clitoral glans
parole.testo: Directly from Latin glans clitoridis (“glans of the clitoris”), clitoridis being a genitive.

parole.significato: A conical vascularized body forming the extremity of the penis.
parole.testo: From New Latin glāns pēnis (“glans of the penis”), pēnis being a genitive.

parole.significato: The quality of being glaucescent, the state of being a bluish-green color.
parole.testo: By surface analysis, glaucescent + -ence, though Merriam-Webster presumes a New Latin *glaucēscentia, from New Latin glaucēscēns (“glaucescent”). However, the Missouri Botanical Garden's A Grammatical Dictionary of Botanical Latin holds no examples attesting this, instead attesting Latin glaucēdō. B

parole.significato: Of a pale grey or bluish-green, especially when covered with a powdery residue.
parole.testo: From Latin glaucus, from Ancient Greek γλαυκός (glaukós, “blue-green, blue-grey”), 1670s. See Irish glas.

parole.significato: The fleshy, spore-bearing inner mass of certain fungi.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin glēba (“lump, mass”). Doublet of glebe.

parole.significato: Relating to or resembling animals of the clade Glires.
parole.testo: From translingual Glires + -an, from Latin glīrēs (“dormice”).

parole.significato: A terracotta pot used in Roman times to breed dormice for consumption as food.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin glirarium.

parole.significato: Relating to or resembling animals of the clade Gliriformes.
parole.testo: From Latin glis (“dormouse”).

parole.significato: Relating to animals the Linnaean order Glires.
parole.testo: From Latin glis (“dormouse”).

parole.significato: Having the form of a globe; spherical.
parole.testo: From Latin globatus, past participle of globare (“to make into a ball”), from globus (“ball”).

parole.significato: Having a globular form.
parole.testo: From Latin globosus (“round as a ball, spherical, globular”).

parole.significato: A spherical or globose shape.
parole.testo: Latin globositas: compare French globosité.

parole.significato: Bearing, containing, or generating globules.
parole.testo: From globule + -iferous, after New Latin globulifera.

parole.significato: The nucleus globosus.
parole.testo: From Latin globulus.

parole.significato: A globe topped by a cross, used as a symbol of royal power.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin globus cruciger (“globe bearing a cross”).

parole.significato: Globus (lump in the throat) when believed (by the speaker or writer) to be psychosomatic (hysterical).
parole.testo: Scientific Latin, from Latin globus (“globe”) + hystericus (“hysteric”).

parole.significato: The inner part of the lenticular nucleus of the brain.
parole.testo: From Latin globus pallidus (“pale body”).

parole.significato: One of the two prominences at the posterior extremity of the frog of a horse's foot.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin glomus (“a ball”). Compare globe.

parole.significato: A depside with the molecular formula C₂₅H₃₀O₈.
parole.testo: From translingual Glomellifer(a) + -ic, from Latin *glomella + -fer + -a, from glomus (“ball-shaped mass”).

parole.significato: To gather or curl into a ball; to collect (threads, etc.) into a spherical form or mass.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin glomerātus, perfect passive participle of glomero (“to glomerate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of forming or gathering into a ball or round mass
parole.testo: Latin glomeratio.

parole.significato: Gathered or formed into a ball or round mass.
parole.testo: From Latin glomerosus, from glomus. See glome.

parole.significato: A head or dense cluster of flowers, formed by condensation of a cyme, as in the flowering dogwood.
parole.testo: Diminutive of Latin glomus ball.

parole.significato: glomerulus
parole.testo: From glomerulus, from New Latin glomerulus, from glomus (“ball-shaped mass”) (stem glomer-) + -ulus (diminutive suffix). By surface analysis, glomerul- + -o-.

parole.significato: A small intertwined group of capillaries within nephrons of the kidney that filter the blood to make urine
parole.testo: From the diminutive of the Latin glomus (gen. glomeris) meaning "ball of yarn" or "ball-shaped mass".

parole.significato: Grammar, particularly medieval Latin grammar.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin glomeria (“grammar”).

parole.significato: Having small clusters of minutely branched coral-like excrescences.
parole.testo: From Latin glomus (“a ball”) + -iferous.

parole.significato: A fold of the mesothelium arising near the base of the mesentery in the pronephron, and containing a ball of blood vess…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin glomus (“ball-shaped mass”).

parole.significato: A lightweight fabric used for umbrellas and dresses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gloria. Doublet of glory.

parole.significato: A boast; a triumphing.
parole.testo: From Latin gloriatio, from gloriari (“to glory, boast”), from gloria (“glory”). See glory (noun).

parole.significato: To glorify.
parole.testo: Back-formation from glorification. For its use by non-native speakers, compare Occitan, Portuguese, and Spanish glorificar and Italian glorificare, from Latin glōrificō.

parole.significato: halo
parole.testo: From Latin gloriola.

parole.significato: Synonym of gloss and glossary, particularly (historical) in medieval contexts.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin glōssārium. Doublet of glossary.

parole.significato: A list of difficult words or specialized terms used in a particular book or document, or in a particular domain of know…
parole.testo: From Middle English glosarie, from Latin glossārium, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). Doublet of glossarium.

parole.significato: One who writes glosses.
parole.testo: From Middle English glosatour, from Medieval Latin glōsātor, glossātor, from glōsāre, glōssāre (“to gloss”) + Latin -tor (agent suffix).

parole.significato: A specifically female glossator.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin glossātrīx, equivalent to glossator + -trix.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the glottis; glottal.
parole.testo: An irregular formation from Latin glōttid-, stem of glōttis + -ean.

parole.significato: The opening between the true vocal cords which is located in the larynx and affects voice modulation through expansion…
parole.testo: Late 16th century borrowing from New Latin glōttis, from Ancient Greek γλωττῐ́ς (glōttĭ́s, “mouth of the windpipe”), from γλῶττᾰ (glôttă, “tongue”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, feminine noun suffix). Cognates include Latin gula.

parole.significato: beryllium.
parole.testo: From New Latin glucina, from French glucine, from Ancient Greek γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”) + -um, in reference to the sweet taste of some of its salts.

parole.significato: sweetness
parole.testo: From the New Latin combining form from Ancient Greek γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”).

parole.significato: A basal, membranous, outer sterile husk or bract in the flowers of grasses (Poaceae) and sedges (Cyperaceae).
parole.testo: From Latin gluma (“husk of grain”). The root can also be seen in glubere (“to peel”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or derived from glutamic acid
parole.testo: Latin gluten (“glue”) + -amic

parole.significato: The largest of the muscles of each buttock.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gluteus maximus.

parole.significato: Synonym of glutinous.
parole.testo: From Latin glūtin-, stem of glūten, + -aceous.

parole.significato: To unite with glue; to cement; to stick together.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin glūtinātus, perfect passive participle of glūtinō (“to glue”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from glūten (“glue”).

parole.significato: A gluing together; a joining together with, or as though with, glue.
parole.testo: From Latin glūtinō.

parole.significato: Having the quality of cementing or binding together; agglutinative
parole.testo: Latin glutinativus: compare French glutinatif.

parole.significato: Glue-like, sticky, viscid.
parole.testo: From Latin glūtinōsus. By surface analysis, gluten + -ous.

parole.significato: The act or process of swallowing.
parole.testo: From Latin gluttītiō, from gluttiō (“to swallow”). By surface analysis, Latin glut- + -ite + -ion.

parole.significato: Any legume (such as liquorice) of the genus Glycyrrhiza.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα (glukúrrhiza, “sweet root, licorice”). Doublet of licorice.

parole.significato: A member of the genus Glyptodon of extinct giant armadillos.
parole.testo: From the New Latin genus name Glyptodon (from Ancient Greek Ancient Greek γλυπτός (gluptós, “sculptured”) + -odon (“tooth”), 'grooved or carved tooth').

parole.significato: The ramus of the lower jaw of a bird as far as it is naked
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin gnathidium. By surface analysis, gnath- + -idium.

parole.significato: Inflammation of the cheek or upper jaw.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin gnathitis. By surface analysis, gnath- + -itis.

parole.significato: Deceitful and flattering; toadying.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Gnathōnicus, from Gnathō (genitive Gnathōnis), name of a parasitical character in the Eunuchus of Terence. Gnathō is from Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw”), used in the genitive γνάθου (gnáthou, “of a jaw”) to mean “greedy”; hence, a parasite in general.

parole.significato: Showing all great circles as straight lines, and thus preserving the shortest distances between any two locations.
parole.testo: From Latin gnōmonicus, Ancient Greek γνωμονικός (gnōmonikós, “judging by rule”). Compare French gnomonique. See gnomon.

parole.significato: Any of various small fish from the large family Gobiidae, in which the pelvic fins are fused to form a disc-shaped suck…
parole.testo: From Latin gobius (“gudgeon”), from Ancient Greek κωβιός (kōbiós), a type of small fish, of unknown ultimate origin. See also gudgeon.

parole.significato: witchcraft, demonic magic, necromancy.
parole.testo: From Latin goetia, from Ancient Greek γοητεία (goēteía, “witchcraft”), from γόης (góēs, “sorceror”).

parole.significato: A position of balance between excess and deficiency.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin aurea mediocritās.

parole.significato: A sex organ that produces gametes; specifically, a testicle or ovary.
parole.testo: From 1880 New Latin gonadēs, plural of New Latin gonas, coined from Ancient Greek γονή (gonḗ, “seed, begetting, birth, offspring”), from γίγνεσθαι (gígnesthai, “be born”).

parole.significato: An arched structure that is a principal feature of the male genitalia of some insects.
parole.testo: From gon- + Latin arcus (“arc, bow”).

parole.significato: One of the bluish-green granules that replace the more usual gonidia in certain lichens.
parole.testo: From New Latin gonimium, possibly from Ancient Greek γόνιμος (gónimos, “productive”).

parole.significato: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a species of bacteria (the gonococcus) that affects t…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Late Latin gonorrhoea, from Ancient Greek γονόρροια (gonórrhoia), from γόνος (gónos, “sperm, seed, offspring”) + ῥοία (rhoía, “flow”) (ca. 1526). By surface analysis, gono- + -rrhea.

parole.significato: Synonym of doofus.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from goof + Latin -us, possibly taking its ending from ignoramus.

parole.significato: A vicious female monster from Greek mythology with sharp fangs and hair of living, venomous snakes. One of the three si…
parole.testo: From Middle English gorgon, from Latin Gorgō, from Ancient Greek Γοργώ (Gorgṓ), from γοργός (gorgós, “terrible”).
