parole.significato: A circumscript mass of cells in the caudal and dorsal aspect of the dorsal thalamus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin habenula, diminutive of habena.

parole.significato: Qualified or entitled.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin habilitātus, past participle of habilitāre (“to enable”).

parole.significato: Equipment; qualification.
parole.testo: From Latin habilitatio, from Latin habilitāre.

parole.significato: An action performed on a regular basis.
parole.testo: From Middle English habit, from Latin habitus (“condition, bearing, state, appearance, dress, attire”), from habeō (“to have, hold, keep”). Distantly related to gift. Replaced Middle English abit, from Old French abit, itself from the same Latin source. Displaced native Old English þēaw, wuna, ġewun

parole.significato: Conditions suitable for an organism or population of organisms to live.
parole.testo: From Latin habitat (“it dwells, lives”), the 3rd person singular present active indicative form of habitō (“to live or dwell”). In Linnaeus and similar authors, the geographical ranges of species were customarily denoted in Latin by a sentence beginning with "Habitat", e.g. "Habitat in Europa" ("It

parole.significato: A dweller; an inhabitant.
parole.testo: From Latin habitātor.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a habit; established as a habit; performed over and over again; recurrent, recurring.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English habitual (“of one's inherent disposition”), from Medieval Latin habituālis (“customary; habitual”), from Latin habitus (“character; disposition; habit; physical or emotional condition; attire, dress”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationshi

parole.significato: To make accustomed; to accustom; to familiarize.
parole.testo: From Middle English habituat(e) (“physically established or present”) (borrowed from Late Latin habituātus, perfect passive participle of habituō (“to bring into a condition or habit of body”)). See -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of habituating, or accustoming; the state of being habituated.
parole.testo: From Middle English habituacioun, from Medieval Latin habituātio. By surface analysis, habituate + -ion.

parole.significato: Relating to habitus or habitude.
parole.testo: From Latin habitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin habitūdō, from habitus + -tūdō, past participle of habeō. By surface analysis, habitude + -al.

parole.significato: Habitude; mode of life; bearing.
parole.testo: From Latin habitus (“habit”), from habeō (“have; maintain”). The plural habiti is a misconstruction, as the Latin plural is in fact habitūs. habiti may have been influenced by Latin habitī, the plural of the participle habitus; however, it is not the etymon of the English term.

parole.significato: The essence of a particular thing; those qualities that define it and make it unique.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin haecceitās.

parole.significato: The essence of a particular thing that gives it its unique particularity; those qualities that make an individual this…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin haecceitas (“thisness”) coined by Duns Scotus (from haec (“this, these”)) + -ity.

parole.significato: Young goat, kid.
parole.testo: From Latin haedus.

parole.significato: Resembling in form or exhibiting the behaviour typical of a kid (i.e., a juvenile goat); compare caprine, hircine.
parole.testo: From the Latin haedīnus (“kidlike”), from haedus (“kid, young goat”); compare caprine, hircine. By surface analysis, haed- (“kid, young goat”) + -ine.

parole.significato: A magical plant mentioned by John Milton, said to be good against enchantments.
parole.testo: Coined by John Milton for the play Comus around 1634 (see quotation below). Various scholars suggest that the word comes from a classical source such as Latin Haemonia (“Thessaly”, a place associated with magic), Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”), or Ancient Greek αἵμων (haímōn, “skillful”).

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Hf) with an atomic number of 72: a lustrous, silvery-grey tetravalent transition metal.
parole.testo: From Latin Hafnia (“Copenhagen”) + -ium.

parole.significato: An (early) Arab Muslim.
parole.testo: From Middle English Agarene, from Medieval Latin Agarēnus. By surface analysis, Hagar + -ene. From the belief that Arabs are descendants of Hagar and Abraham.

parole.significato: A kingfisher whose nesting by the sea was said, in classical mythology, to cause the Gods to restrain the wind and wave…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Alceoun, from Latin halcyōn, alcyōn (“kingfisher”), from Ancient Greek ἀλκυών (alkuṓn).

parole.significato: A period of calm during the winter, when storms do not occur.
parole.testo: From halcyon, from Latin Alcyone, from Ancient Greek Ἀλκυόνη (Alkuónē), daughter of Aeolus and wife of Ceyx. When her husband died in a shipwreck, Alcyone threw herself into the sea whereupon the gods transformed them both into halcyon birds (kingfishers). When Alcyone made her nest on the beach, wa

parole.significato: The dugong.
parole.testo: From Late Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek ἅλς (háls, “sea”) + κόρη (kórē, “girl, maiden”).

parole.significato: A treatise upon fish or the art of fishing, especially in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin halieuticus ("halieutic, of or about fishing"), from Ancient Greek ἁλιευτικός (halieutikós) (alieutikós, "of or about fishermen"), from ἁλιεύς (halieús, “fisherman”). The Christianity definition comes from the fish being a symbol of the Christian faith.

parole.significato: The condition of having stale or foul-smelling breath.
parole.testo: Coined by doctor Joseph William Howe in 1874 and described as being derived from the Latin hālitus (literally “whiff, breath”) and the Ancient Greek νόσος (nósos, literally “disease”). It can be also understood as combination of the Latin hālitus and the English suffix -osis.

parole.significato: Produced by, or like, breath; vaporous.
parole.testo: From Latin halitus (“breath, vapor”), from halare (“to breathe”): compare French halitueux.

parole.significato: A vapour.
parole.testo: From Latin halitus.

parole.significato: To seem to perceive things (with one or more of one's senses) which are not really present; to have visions; to experie…
parole.testo: First attested in 1604; borrowed from Latin hallūcinātus, alternative form of alūcinātus, perfect active participle of alucinor (“to dream”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A sensory perception of something that does not exist, often arising from disorder of the nervous system, as in deliriu…
parole.testo: From hallucinate + -ion, from Latin hallucinatus. Compare French hallucination. The first known usage in the English language is from Sir Thomas Browne.

parole.significato: A big toe.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hallux, from Latin allus, hallus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Haloragaceae.
parole.testo: From translingual Haloragaceae + -ous, from New Latin Haloragis + -aceae, formed irregularly from Ancient Greek ἅλς (háls, “salt”) + ῥάξ (rháx, “berry”) (a Pre-Greek / Mediterranean loan).

parole.significato: A wood-nymph who was physically a part of her tree; she would die if her tree were felled.
parole.testo: From Latin Hamadryas, from Ancient Greek Ἁμαδρυάς (Hamadruás), from ἅμα (háma, “together”) + δρῦς (drûs, “tree”).

parole.significato: Any of the flowering plant genus Hamamelis, the witch hazels.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἁμαμηλίς (hamamēlís, “medlar”).

parole.significato: One of the eight bones of the wrist (carpals).
parole.testo: From Latin hāmātus (“hooked, crooked”).

parole.significato: The hamate bone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hamatum.

parole.significato: Curved at the extremity.
parole.testo: First attested in glossaries in 1842 and first used in 1870; either directly from the Latin hāmiformis (1651, 1806) or formed from the suffixation of its etymon, hāmus (“hook”), with the English -form.

parole.significato: A certain stone with spangles of gold color in it, known to Pliny, perhaps golden mica or yellow mica schist.
parole.testo: From Latin hammochrȳsos, (h)ammochrȳsus, from Ancient Greek ἀμμόχρῡσος (ammókhrūsos), from ἄμμος (ámmos, “sand”) + χρῡσός (khrūsós, “gold”).

parole.significato: Having the end hooked or curved.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hāmōsus, from hāmus (“hook”).

parole.significato: Hamose.
parole.testo: Latin hamus (“hook”), + -ous.

parole.significato: A little hook.
parole.testo: Latin hamulus

parole.significato: Bearing a small hook at the end
parole.testo: Latin hamulus, diminutive of hāmus (“hook”)

parole.significato: A hook, or hook-like process.
parole.testo: Latin hamulus (“a little hook”).

parole.significato: A hook- or barb-like structure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hāmus (“hook, barb”).

parole.significato: A kind of basket, usually of wickerwork, and adapted for the packing and carrying of articles; a hamper
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hanaperium (“a large vase”), extended from hanapus (“bowl, cup”). Doublet of hamper.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the German Hanse.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hanseaticus, from hansa, of Germanic origin, from Old High German hansa (“troop, company”), from Proto-West Germanic *hansu (“crowd, company”).

parole.significato: Any of the cichlid fishes of the tribe Haplochromini.
parole.testo: Shortening of New Latin Haplochromis.

parole.significato: Being or relating to a form of arthrodontous peristome:
parole.testo: From New Latin haplolepideus, from Ancient Greek ἁπλόος (haplóos, “two-fold, single”) + λεπίδιον (lepídion, “small plate used to close a tube”).

parole.significato: Any primate of the evolved clade (half of the order) which comprises all apes (including hominoids), monkeys and even (…
parole.testo: From Neo-Latin Haplorrhini, from Ancient Greek ἁπλόος (haplóos, “simple”) + ῥίς (rhís, “nose”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to harmony.
parole.testo: From Latin harmonicus, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονικός (harmonikós), from ἁρμονία (harmonía, “harmony”). By surface analysis, harmony + -ic. Doublet of armónico.

parole.significato: Synonym of corvus (“grappling hook in Ancient Roman naval warfare”).
parole.testo: From Latin harpagō.

parole.significato: A grappling hook.
parole.testo: Adapted from Latin harpagō, gen. harpagōnis, from Ancient Greek ἁρπάγη (harpágē, “hook”), from ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to snatch away, to carry off, to seize, to captivate”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of harpoon.

parole.significato: A pupil of Harrow School, England.
parole.testo: From New Latin Harrovia (“Harrow”) + -an.

parole.significato: A student of law or medicine at Cambridge who, being of the same standing as the students in arts in his year, is allow…
parole.testo: According to a 17th century chronicler, from Latin sophister Henricianus after King Henry VIII, but remodeled to fit a fanciful Ancient Greek *ἐρίσοφος (*erísophos, “very wise indeed”), from ἐρι- (eri-) + σοφός (sophós).

parole.significato: A soothsayer or priest in Ancient Rome (originally Etruscan) who practiced haruspicy, divination by inspecting entrails.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin haruspex.

parole.significato: Divination by use of animal entrails, usually the victims of sacrifice.
parole.testo: From Latin haruspicium, from haruspex (“diviner of entrails”) + -ium (forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the patriotic Jewish family to which the Maccabees belonged; Maccabean.
parole.testo: From Latin Asmonaeus (latinized name of the family's founder) + English -an, from (Hellenic) Ancient Greek Ἀσαμωναῖος (Asamōnaîos), from Hebrew חַשְׁמוֹנַאי (ḥašmōnay).

parole.significato: An artificially-produced transuranic chemical element (symbol Hs) with atomic number 108.
parole.testo: From Latin Hassia (“Hesse”), the location of the institute where the element was first synthesized, + -ium.

parole.significato: A spear carried by early Roman legionaries.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hasta.

parole.significato: Shaped similarly to a halberd, with pointed lobes pointed outward from the base.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English hastate, borrowed from Latin hastātus (“armed with a spear”), from hasta (“spear”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A medieval martial game.
parole.testo: From Latin hastiludum, from hasta (“spear”) and ludus (“sport, game”).

parole.significato: Of a fish, etc.: in a vertical orientation, with its head up (to chief) and tail down (to base).
parole.testo: From Latin hauriēns (“drawing (water, etc.); draining”), the present participle of hauriō (“to draw (water, etc.); to drain”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews- (“to draw water”).

parole.significato: A root of a parasitic plant modified to take nourishment from its host.
parole.testo: From Latin haustor (“drainer”) + -ium.

parole.significato: Any of the small pouches of the colon caused by sacculation, giving the colon its segmented appearance.
parole.testo: From Latin haustrum.

parole.significato: A group of seven.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hebdomada (“number seven; group of seven; seven days”), hebdomas (“number seven; seven days; seventh day”), from Ancient Greek ἑβδομάς (hebdomás, “group of seven, especially seven days or seven years”), from ἕβδομος (hébdomos, “seventh”) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs, suffix forming abstract nouns of

parole.significato: Lasting seven days.
parole.testo: From Latin hebdomadālis. According to The Poly-Olbion Project, coined by John Selden in 1612.

parole.significato: hebdomadal
parole.testo: From Late Latin hebdomadārius, from hebdomas (“week”).

parole.significato: Blunt, dull.
parole.testo: From Latin hebes (“blunt, dull, dim”).

parole.significato: Ebony.
parole.testo: From Middle English ebenif, hebenyf (influenced by Late Latin hebeninus), from Ecclesiastical Latin ebenius (“of ebony”), from Latin hebenus (“ebon tree”), from Ancient Greek ἔβενος (ébenos), from Egyptian hbnj, U13:n-Z4:M3

parole.significato: Causing lethargy.
parole.testo: From Latin hebetāns, present participle of hebetō (“to dull, deaden”).

parole.significato: Obtuse, dull.
parole.testo: First attested in 1574; borrowed from Latin hebetātus, perfect passive participle of hebetō (“to dull”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of making blunt, dull, or stupid.
parole.testo: Latin hebetatio: compare French hébétation.

parole.significato: unintelligent; stupid.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hebes, hebetis (“dull, stupid”), from hebere (“to be dull”).

parole.significato: Mental lethargy or dullness.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hebetūdō.

parole.significato: Displaying mental lethargy or dullness.
parole.testo: From Latin hebetūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin hebetūdō, from hebes + -tūdō, from hebeō. By surface analysis, hebetude + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Hebrew people, language, or culture.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Ebrayk, Hebrak, Hebrayke, a learned borrowing from Late Latin hebraicus, borrowed from Byzantine Greek Ἑβρᾰῐ̈κός (Hebrăĭ̈kós), from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos, “Hebrew”). By surface analysis, Hebra- + -ic.

parole.significato: Texts or artifacts containing Hebrew writing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin hebraica, neuter plural of hebraicus (“Hebrew”), from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos), from Hebrew עִבְרִי (ʿiḇrī, “Hebrew”) (likely through Aramaic עִבְרַי (ʿiḇray, “Hebrew”)), traditionally from עֵבֶר ('éver, “Eber”), the ancestor of the Israelites. By surface an

parole.significato: The traditional Hebrew and Aramaic text of the Jewish Bible, viewed as its original, correct, and authoritative text.
parole.testo: Composed of the Latin hebraica (“Hebrew”, feminine nominative singular of adjective hebraicus) + vēritās (“truth”).

parole.significato: A great public sacrifice to the gods, originally of a hundred oxen; also, a great number of animals reserved for such a…
parole.testo: The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin hecatombē (“great sacrifice of a hundred oxen, hecatomb”), from Ancient Greek ἑκατόμβη (hekatómbē, “great sacrifice of a hundred oxen, hecatomb; any animal sacrifice or large sacrifice”, from ἑκᾰτόν (hekătón, “hundred”) + βοῦς (boûs, “cattle, cow, ox”)). Th

parole.significato: A modified arm of any of several male cephalopods that functions as a reproductive organ by transferring sperm to the m…
parole.testo: From New Latin, corresponding to hecto- + Ancient Greek κότυλος (kótulos, “small cup”).

parole.significato: Sometimes in the form Hector: a blustering, noisy, turbulent fellow; a braggart, bully.
parole.testo: From Hector (“in Greek and Roman mythology, a character in Homer’s Iliad who is the greatest warrior of Troy”), from Late Middle English Hector (“warrior with the qualities of Hector”), from Latin Hectōr or Ancient Greek Ἕκτωρ (Héktōr), from ἕκτωρ (héktōr, “holding fast”), from ἔχειν (ékhein), prese

parole.significato: Any Old World ivy of the genus Hedera
parole.testo: From the genus name Hedera, in turn from Latin hedera (“ivy”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling ivy.
parole.testo: Latin hederaceus, from hedera (“ivy”).

parole.significato: Producing or bearing ivy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin hederifer.

parole.significato: ivy-shaped
parole.testo: From Latin hedera (“ivy”) + -iform.

parole.significato: methyl orange
parole.testo: Probably Latin helianthes (“sunflower”), alluding to its colour.

parole.significato: snail farming
parole.testo: From helici- + culture, from the genus of snails Helix, from helix, from Latin helix, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “something twisted”).

parole.significato: helix, spiral
parole.testo: From Latin helic- + -o-, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Helicon.
parole.testo: Latin Heliconius

parole.significato: A device that includes a plane mirror which turns so as to keep reflecting sunlight toward a predetermined target, comp…
parole.testo: First use appear c. 1747, from New Latin heliostata, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) + Latin status (“stationary”). By surface analysis, helio- + -stat.

parole.significato: The second-lightest chemical element (symbol He), with an atomic number of 2 and atomic weight of 4.002602, a colorless…
parole.testo: From New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) (because its presence was first theorised in the Sun's atmosphere) with the suffix + -ium. Probably coined by Norman Lockyer. This suffix is unusual, because it is usually used only for metallic elements. It is likely that Lockyer, bein

parole.significato: A curve on the surface of a cylinder or cone such that its angle to a plane perpendicular to the axis is constant; the…
parole.testo: From Latin helix, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “something twisted or spiral”).

parole.significato: A glutton, a gormandizer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin helluo (“glutton, squanderer”).

parole.significato: An insatiable and obsessive bookworm (“avid book reader”).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin helluō librōrum (“glutton of books”), from Latin helluō (“glutton; squanderer”) + librōrum (“of books”). Helluō is derived from helluārī + -ō (suffix forming masculine agent nouns, nicknames, and other designations); helluārī is the present active infinitive of hell

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Helvetii, the ancient inhabitants of the Alps, now Switzerland, or to the modern states and inh…
parole.testo: From Latin helveticus, from Helvetii (“the Helvetii”).

parole.significato: Helvite.
parole.testo: From Latin helvus (“of a light bay color”) + -ine.

parole.significato: A yellowish mineral consisting chiefly of silica, beryllium, manganese, iron, and sulfur. Its chemical formula is Mn₄Be…
parole.testo: From Latin helvus (“of a light bay color”) + -ite.

parole.significato: An antibiotic chemical compound found in Aspergillus.
parole.testo: Coined by Chain et al. in 1944, in reference to the mold Aspergillus fumigatus, mut. helvola Yuill. The epithet helvola is a feminine diminutive of Latin helvus (“honey-yellow”). By surface analysis, Latin helvus + -ole + -ic.

parole.significato: A variety of agate, sprinkled with spots of red jasper.
parole.testo: From Latin haemachātēs, from Ancient Greek *αἱμᾰχᾱ́της (*haimăkhā́tēs), from αἷμᾰ (haîmă, “blood”) + ᾰ̓χᾱ́της (ăkhā́tēs, “agate”).

parole.significato: The inability to see clearly in bright light; day blindness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin hēmeralōpia, from Ancient Greek ἡμεραλωπία (hēmeralōpía). From ἡμέρα (hēmérā, “day”), ἀλαός (alaos, “blind”), and ὄψ (ops, “eye”).

parole.significato: A headache affecting one side of the head.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hemicrania (“pain in one half of the head”), from Ancient Greek ἡμικρᾱνίᾰ (hēmikrāníă), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “hemi-, half”) + κρανίον (kraníon, “skull”) (from whence also cranium). Cognate to megrim and migraine, which also derive from the Latin.

parole.significato: A Roman unit of liquid measure reckoned as the volume of ⁵⁄₆ Roman pound of wine, equivalent to around 0.27 L.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hēmīna (“half-sextarius”), from Ancient Greek ἡμῑ́νᾱ (hēmī́nā).

parole.significato: Equus hemionus, the onager or kiang, a kind of wild ass of Tibet.
parole.testo: From New Latin hēmionus, from Ancient Greek ἡμῐ́ονος (hēmĭ́onos, “half ass, mule”).

parole.significato: Total or partial inability to move one side of the body.
parole.testo: From New Latin hemiplegia, from Ancient Greek ἡμιπλήξ (hēmiplḗx), also ἡμιπληγής (hēmiplēgḗs, “stricken on one side”), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”). By surface analysis, hemi- + -plegia.

parole.significato: To divide along the mesial plane or median plane.
parole.testo: From hemi- + Latin secare (“to cut”).

parole.significato: Half of the celestial sphere, as divided by either the ecliptic or the celestial equator .
parole.testo: From Latin hemisphaerium, from Ancient Greek ἡμισφαίριον (hēmisphaírion), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”). Equivalent to hemi- + sphere. Displaced native Old English healftrendel (literally “half-sphere”).

parole.significato: A semitone.
parole.testo: Latin hemitonium, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A heavy release of blood within or from the body.
parole.testo: From Latin haemorrhagia, from Ancient Greek αἱμορραγία (haimorrhagía, “a violent bleeding”), from αἱμορραγής (haimorrhagḗs, “bleeding violently”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + -ραγία (-ragía), from ῥηγνύναι (rhēgnúnai, “to break, burst”); see ῥήγνῡμῐ (rhḗgnūmĭ) for more.

parole.significato: Having eleven syllables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hendecasyllabus, from Ancient Greek ἑνδεκασύλλαβος (hendekasúllabos), from ἕνδεκα (héndeka, “eleven”) + συλλαβή (sullabḗ, “syllable”).

parole.significato: A line, verse, or word that comprises eleven syllables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hendecasyllabus, from Ancient Greek ἑνδεκασύλλαβος (hendekasúllabos); equivalent to hendeca- + syllable.

parole.significato: A figure of speech used for emphasis, where two words joined by and are used to express a single complex idea.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin, from Ancient Greek ἕν (hén), stem of εἷς (heîs, “one”) + διά (diá, “through”) + δύο (dúo, “two”), “one [idea] through two [words]”.

parole.significato: Relating to someone named Henry, especially a king or his reign; supporting or on the side of Henry.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Hēnrīciānus, from Hēnrīcus (“Henry”) + -iānus (“relating to”).

parole.significato: liver of sulphur; a substance of a liver-brown colour, sometimes used in medicine, formed by fusing sulphur with carbon…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hepar (“liver”). Cf. liver of antimony.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the liver.
parole.testo: From Middle English epatik, from Late Latin hepaticus, from Ancient Greek ἡπατικός (hēpatikós, “of the liver”), from ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”).

parole.significato: A variety of barite that emits a foetid odour when rubbed or heated.
parole.testo: From Latin hepatitis, an unknown precious stone, from Ancient Greek ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”); compare French hépatite.

parole.significato: Inflammation of the liver, sometimes caused by a viral infection.
parole.testo: From Latin hēpatītis, from hēpar (“liver”), from Ancient Greek ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”). By surface analysis, hepat- + -itis.

parole.significato: A valuable metal alloy in antiquity, thought to have been an alloy of copper with gold and silver, mixed and treated to…
parole.testo: From the Latin hēpatizon, from the Ancient Greek ἡπᾰτῐ́ζον (hēpătĭ́zon), from ἡπᾰτῐ́ζων (hēpătĭ́zōn, “liver-coloured”).

parole.significato: Any of a people who comprised a nomadic confederation in Central Asia during the 5th–6th centuries CE.
parole.testo: Hypercorrect respelling of Ephthalite, with unetymological initial h-, from Latin Ephthalītēs, from Ancient Greek Ἐφθαλίτης (Ephthalítēs), from Bactrian Ηβοδαλο (Ēbodalo) + Ancient Greek -ίτης (-ítēs).

parole.significato: A government of seven people.
parole.testo: From New Latin heptarchia, from Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá, “hepta-: seven”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “-archy: rule”). Equivalent to hepta- + -archy.

parole.significato: A messenger, especially one bringing important news.
parole.testo: From Latin heraldus, from Middle English herald, herauld, heraud, from Anglo-Norman heraud, from Old French heraut, hiraut (modern French héraut), from Frankish *heriwald, from Proto-Germanic *harjawaldaz, a compound consisting of Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“army”) + *h₂welh₁- (“to be strong”). Doub

parole.significato: The plant Logfia filaginoides.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Not woody, lacking lignified tissues.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin herbāceus (“grassy”). By surface analysis, herb + -aceous.

parole.significato: A collection of dried plants or parts of plants.
parole.testo: From Latin herbārium. Doublet of arbor.

parole.significato: Growing into herbs.
parole.testo: From Latin herbescens, present participle of herbescere.

parole.significato: Covered with herbs.
parole.testo: Latin herbidus.

parole.significato: Feeding chiefly on plants.
parole.testo: Adapted borrowing of New Latin herbivorus + -ous, from Latin herba (“grass”) and -vorus, from vorō (“to devour”).

parole.significato: Having an abundance of herbage; full of herbs.
parole.testo: From the Latin herbōsus (“grassy, full of grass or herbs”).

parole.significato: A Hercules beetle.
parole.testo: From Latin Herculēs, from Etruscan 𐌇𐌄𐌓𐌂𐌋𐌄 (hercle), from Ancient Greek Ἡρακλῆς (Hēraklês), apparently cognate of Ἥρα (Hḗra, “Hera”) and, according to Haudry, from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, season”) + κλέος (kléos, “glory”). Doublet of Heracles.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Hercynian Forest, an extensive forest in ancient Germany.
parole.testo: From Latin Hercynia silva, Hercynius saltus (“the Hercynian forest”).

parole.significato: A fanciful notation, commonly attributed to historical maps, held to indicate either the belief that unknown dangers ex…
parole.testo: Evidence of the use of this term as a notation on actual historical maps is lacking. parole.significato: A phrase written on gravestones followed by the buried person's name.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin hīc jacet (whence also English hic jacet, a direct borrowing).

parole.significato: Passed on as an inheritance, by last will or intestate.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English hereditarie, from Latin hērēditārius, from hērēditās (“inheritance”), from hērēs (“heir”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Rome, inheritance or hereditary succession.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?]

parole.significato: heretical
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin haeresiacus (“heretical”).

parole.significato: To denounce as heresy or a heretic.
parole.testo: First attested in 1629; borrowed from Medieval Latin haereticātus, perfect passive participle of haereticō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a master.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin erīlis, herīlis.

parole.significato: A rectangular pillar bearing a bust of Hermes, once used as a boundary marker and later as decoration.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Herma, a Latinization of Hermēs, from Ancient Greek Ἑρμῆς (Hermês).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the ancient Greek Olympian god Hermes.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hermeticus, irregular derivation of Hermes Trismegistus, the god and mythological alchemist, said to possess a magic ability to seal treasure chests so that nothing could access their contents.

parole.significato: A cell annexed to an abbey, for the use of a hermit.
parole.testo: Compare Latin hermitorium, eremitorium.

parole.significato: A type of root, probably from a plant of the genus Colchicum, as imported and used in Western medicine.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hermodactylus, from Ancient Greek ἑρμοδάκτυλος (hermodáktulos, “Hermes's finger”).

parole.significato: Protruded viscus, rupture.
parole.testo: From Latin hernia (“protruded viscus”).

parole.significato: A disorder in which a part of the body protrudes abnormally through a tear or opening in an adjacent part, especially o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hernia (“protruded viscus”). See also yarn and cord.

parole.significato: Heroic.
parole.testo: From Middle English heroicalle, from Latin hērōicus + -al. By surface analysis, hero + -ical.

parole.significato: A female hero.
parole.testo: From Latin hērōīna, from late Ancient Greek ἡρωΐνη (hērōḯnē) (2nd century), a feminine equivalent of ἥρως (hḗrōs, “hero, demigod”), equivalent to hero + -ine (suffix forming feminine nouns). * English from 1587. The sense of "female lead character" is from 1715.

parole.significato: A temple dedicated to a hero, often over his supposed tomb.
parole.testo: From Latin hērōon, from Ancient Greek ἡρῷον (hērōîon), from ἡρῷος (hērōîos, “of a hero”).

parole.significato: Seeking infamy.
parole.testo: From Herostratus + -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives from nouns). Herostratus is a learned borrowing from Latin Hērostratus, from Ancient Greek Ἡρόστρατος (Hēróstratos), from Ἥρᾱ (Hḗrā, “Greek goddess of marriage, women, and family”) + στρᾰτός (strătós, “army, military for

parole.significato: Fame (or infamy) won through crime, destruction, or some other misdeed.
parole.testo: Herostratic is derived from Herostratus (learned borrowing from Latin Hērostratus, from Ancient Greek Ἡρόστρατος (Hēróstratos) + -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives from nouns)). Herostratus (died c. 356 B.C.E.) was a Greek arsonist who sought fame by destroying the second T

parole.significato: A viral infection, caused by Human alphaherpesvirus 1 and Human alphaherpesvirus 2, marked by painful, watery blisters…
parole.testo: From Latin herpēs, from Ancient Greek ἕρπης (hérpēs, “herpes”, literally “a creeping”), from ἕρπειν (hérpein, “to creep”).

parole.significato: One of the most infectious of herpes-caused diseases, transmissible by skin-to-skin contact.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Synonym of Hesiodic (“relating to the ancient Greek poet Hesiod”).
parole.testo: Akin to Hesiod + -ean, from Latin Hēsiodēus, from Ancient Greek Ἡσιόδειος (Hēsiódeios).

parole.significato: Synonym of Hesiodic (“relating to the ancient Greek poet Hesiod”).
parole.testo: Akin to Hesiod + -ian, from Latin Hēsiodīus, from Ancient Greek Ἡσιόδειος (Hēsiódeios).

parole.significato: Relating to the Ancient Greek poet Hesiod, or characteristic of his didactic poetry style.
parole.testo: Akin to Hesiod + -ic, semi-learned borrowing from Latin Hēsiodicus.

parole.significato: The act or state of hesitating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin haesitantia.

parole.significato: A pausing or halting before beginning a task, often as a result of some fear or uncertainty about the outcome.
parole.testo: From Latin haesitantia. By surface analysis, hesitant + -cy.

parole.significato: Tending to hesitate, wait, or proceed with caution or reservation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin haesitans, present participle of haesitare (“to stick fast, to hesitate”).

parole.significato: To stop or pause respecting decision or action; to be in suspense or uncertainty as to a determination.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin haesitātus, perfect passive participle of haesitō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), intensive of haereō (“to hesitate, stick fast; to hang or hold fast”). Displaced native Old English wandian. Compare French hésiter.

parole.significato: An act of hesitating
parole.testo: From Latin haesitātiōnem, accusative singular of haesitātiō (“hesitating, stammering”), from haesitō (“hesitate”). Displaced native Old English ġewand.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the land where the sun sets; western
parole.testo: From Latin Hesperius + -ian.

parole.significato: A group of nymphs who tend a blissful garden filled with trees that grew golden apples in a far western corner of the w…
parole.testo: From Latin Hesperides, from Ancient Greek Ἑσπερίδες (Hesperídes).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to yesterday.
parole.testo: From Latin hesternus (“of or pertaining to yesterday; yesterday’s”) + English -al (suffix forming adjectives).

parole.significato: A monk of the Orthodox Catholic Church that engages in noetic prayer.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hesychasta, from ecclesiastical Greek ἡσυχαστής (hēsukhastḗs), from ἡσυχάζειν (hēsukházein, “to be quiet”), from ἥσυχος (hḗsukhos, “quiet”).

parole.significato: The condition of having two irises of different colors.
parole.testo: Latin.

parole.significato: Irregularly declined or inflected.
parole.testo: From Late Latin heteroclitus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερόκλιτος (heteróklitos), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + κλίνω (klínō, “lean, incline”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley-.

parole.significato: Diverse in kind or nature; composed of diverse parts.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin heterogeneus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερογενής (heterogenḗs, “of different kinds”), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + γένος (génos, “kind”). Compare hetero- and -ous.

parole.significato: A pyrrolizidine alkaloid found in Parsonsia heterophylla.
parole.testo: From Latin heterophylla + -ine.

parole.significato: Six.
parole.testo: From Latin hexa-, from Ancient Greek ἑξα- (hexa-), from ἕξ (héx, “six”). By surface analysis, hex- + -a-. Piecewise doublet of sexa-.

parole.significato: A polygon with six sides and six angles.
parole.testo: From Latin hexagōnum, from Ancient Greek ἑξάγωνον (hexágōnon). By surface analysis, hexa- + -gon. Piecewise doublet of sexagon.

parole.significato: A poem consisting of six verses or lines.
parole.testo: From Latin hexastichus (“of six rows, lines, or verses”).

parole.significato: To gape; to cause a hiatus.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hiō, hiāre, hiāvī, hiātum.

parole.significato: A gap in a series, making it incomplete.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hiātus (“opening”) (mid-16th century), from hiō (“stand open, yawn”).

parole.significato: A winter retreat; winter quarters.
parole.testo: From Latin hībernācula, plural of hībernāculum.

parole.significato: The place where a hibernating animal shelters for the winter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hībernāculum (“winter quarters”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to winter; brumal or hiemal
parole.testo: From Latin hībernālis (“wintry”), from hiems (“winter”).

parole.significato: To spend the winter in a dormant or inactive state of minimal activity, low body temperature, slow breathing and heart…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hībernātus, perfect passive participle of hībernō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from hībernus (“wintry”).

parole.significato: A state of minimum power consumption, inactivity and metabolic depression in some animals during winter.
parole.testo: From Latin hībernātus, from hībernō, from hībernus (“wintry, of or pertaining to winter”).

parole.significato: A flowering plant of the genus Hibiscus, especially Hibiscus syriacus, found in tropical to temperate regions, of some…
parole.testo: From Late Latin hibiscus, from Latin hibiscum, from Ancient Greek ἰβίσκος (ibískos, “marsh mallow”), probably ultimately from Gaulish.

parole.significato: Here and now, in the immediate present.
parole.testo: From Latin hic et nunc (“here and now”).

parole.significato: An epitaph (gravestone inscription).
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin hīc jacet (“here lies”).

parole.significato: Prove what you can do, here and now.
parole.testo: The phrase arises from the Latin form of Aesop's Fables (Gibbs 209; Perry 33; Chambry 51), as translated from Ancient Greek "Αὐτοῦ γὰρ καὶ Ῥόδος καὶ πήδημα" (literally) "Here is Rhodes, jump here!". In the fable, a boastful athlete brags that he once achieved a stupendous long jump in competition on

parole.significato: A juggler.
parole.testo: Corrupted from Latin hic est doctus (“this is a learned man”).

parole.significato: A chronic condition which causes inflamed, painful, swollen lumps to form under the skin.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: The formation and excretion of sweat.
parole.testo: From New Latin hīdrōsis, from Ancient Greek ῑ̔δρώς (hīdrṓs, “sweat”) + -ωσῐς (-ōsĭs); also synchronically held to end in the suffix -osis.

parole.significato: Relating to hidrosis.
parole.testo: From the Medieval Latin hidrōticus, from the Ancient Greek ἱδρωτικός (hidrōtikós), from ἱδρώς (hidrṓs, “sweat”, stem: ἱδρωτ-); by surface analysis, hidr(osis)- + -otic.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to winter, wintry.
parole.testo: From Latin hiemālis (“pertaining to winter”), from hiems (“winter”). More at hibernate.

parole.significato: Hibernation.
parole.testo: From Latin hiemātiō.

parole.significato: A warming cathartic medicine made from aloes and canella.
parole.testo: From New Latin hiera picra, from Ancient Greek ἱερᾱ́ πίκρᾱ (hierā́ píkrā, literally “sacred bitterness”).

parole.significato: One who has high and controlling authority in sacred things; the chief of a sacred order.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hierarcha, from Ancient Greek ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs) Derived from ἱερός (hierós, “holy”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “ruler”, “leader”). ἱερός from Proto-Hellenic *iherós, from Proto-Indo-European *ish₁ros. There are a number of candidate cognates with this word. Compare Sanskrit इषिर (iṣi

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to priests or other religious authorities, especially pharaonic priests of Ancient Egypt.
parole.testo: From Latin hieraticus, from Ancient Greek ἱερατικός (hieratikós), from ἱερατεία (hierateía, “priesthood”), from ἱερατεύω (hierateúō, “be a priest”), from ἱερεύς (hiereús, “priest”), from ἱερός (hierós, “sacred”). Use pertaining to the Egyptian writing system originates with the Greek phrase γράμματα

parole.significato: Of or relating to sacred writing.
parole.testo: From Latin hierographicus, Ancient Greek ἱερός (hierós, “sacred”) + γραφικός (graphikós, “of or pertaining to writing”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Jerusalem.
parole.testo: From Latin Hierosolymītānus.

parole.significato: Very funny; causing great merriment and laughter.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hilaris (“cheerful”) + -ious, from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful, merry”).

parole.significato: A great amount of amusement, usually accompanied by much laughter.
parole.testo: From Latin hilaritās (“cheerfulness”), from hilaris (“cheerful”), from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful”). By surface analysis, Latin hilar(ō) + -i- + -ty.

parole.significato: The second term of the legal year, running from January to March or April, during which the upper courts of England and…
parole.testo: Hilary + term. The name Hilary is from the Latin Hilarius (“Latin name of Saint Hilary of Poitiers”), hilarius (“more cheerful, more joyful”), from hilarē (“cheerful, joyful”), from hilaris (“cheerful, light-hearted, lively”), from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful, glad, happy, joyful, merry

parole.significato: The eye of a bean or other seed, or the center of that eye; the mark or scar at the point of attachment of an ovule or…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hīlum (“a trifle; a spot on a seed”).

parole.significato: A hilum.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hīlus.

parole.significato: A former Hebrew liquid measure of volume (about 3.8 L).
parole.testo: From Middle English hin, from Latin hin, from Hebrew הִין, from Egyptian h:n-nw-w-W22 (hnw, “jar, unit of liquid volume”).

parole.significato: The hybrid offspring of a stallion (male horse) and a she-ass (female donkey).
parole.testo: From Latin hinnus, from Ancient Greek ἴννος (ínnos), γίννος (gínnos). Possibly cognate with hinnire (“to whinny”).

parole.significato: A mythological creature with the front head and forelimbs of a horse and the rear of a fish.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hippocampus, from Ancient Greek ἱππόκαμπος (hippókampos, from ῐ̔́ππος (hĭ́ppos, “horse”) + κάμπος (kámpos, “sea-monster”)). The anatomy sense is so named from its resemblance to the seahorse. By surface analysis, hippo- + campus.

parole.significato: centaur
parole.testo: From Latin hippocentaurus, from Ancient Greek ῐ̔πποκένταυρος (hĭppokéntauros).

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or in accordance with the theories of, ancient Greek physician and philosopher Hippocrates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Hippocraticus, equivalent to Hippocrates + -ic.

parole.significato: Shaped like a horseshoe.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) + Ancient Greek κρηπίς (krēpís, “boot”) + -form (from Latin -formis).

parole.significato: An ancient love philter obtained from a mare or foal in heat.
parole.testo: From Latin hippomanes, from Ancient Greek ἱππομᾰνής (hippomănḗs); see hippo- and the related suffix -mania.

parole.significato: Eaters of horsemeat.
parole.testo: From the plural of New Latin hippophagus. See hippophagous.

parole.significato: A semi-aquatic, herbivorous, African hoofed mammal of the family Hippopotamidae.
parole.testo: From Latin and New Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos), from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) (English hippo-) + ποταμός (potamós, “river”). First attested in the 1560s. Displaced displaced English nicker (from native Old English nicor) and river horse.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to extremely long words.
parole.testo: An extension of sesquipedalian using a modified form of hippopotamus and Latin monstrum, with the extensions almost certainly chosen with the intention of making the new construct autological.

parole.significato: The fear of long words.
parole.testo: From hippopotomonstrosesquipedalian, in turn an extension of sesquipedalian with ad hoc combining forms of Latin monstrum (“monster”) and hippopotamus (intended to exaggerate the length of the word itself and the idea of the size of the words being feared), + -phobia.

parole.significato: A creature that is half bull and half horse.
parole.testo: From Latin hippotaurus, from Ancient Greek ἱππόταυρος (hippótauros), from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”, English hippo-) + ταῦρος (taûros, “bull”).

parole.significato: Buck, male goat.
parole.testo: From Latin hircus.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of goats.
parole.testo: First attested in its present form in 1650–1660: From Middle English hircyne, from Latin hircīnus (“of a goat”, “goat-scented”); equivalent to hircus (“a male goat”) + -īnus (“-ine”). Cognate with French hircin. By surface analysis, hirc- (“buck, male goat”) + -ine. Compare caprine, haedine.

parole.significato: A mythical creature, half goat, half stag.
parole.testo: From Latin hircus (“goat”) + cervus (“stag”).

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to goats; hircine
parole.testo: By surface analysis, hirc- (“buck, male goat”) + -ose. Ultimately related to Latin hircīnus (“of a goat”, “goat-scented”)

parole.significato: Having a strongly trilled sound, like that of a cat purring.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hirrient.

parole.significato: Covered in hair or bristles; hairy.
parole.testo: From Latin hirsūtus (“shaggy, hairy”).

parole.significato: hirsutism
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hī̆rsūtiēs.

parole.significato: The medical condition of having pearly penile papules.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hīrsūtiēs papillāris corōnae glandis (literally “papillary hirsutism of the corona of the glans”).

parole.significato: The medical condition of having pearly penile papules.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hīrsūtiēs papillāris genitālis (literally “genital papillary hirsutism”).

parole.significato: The medical condition of having pearly penile papules.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hīrsūtiēs papillāris pēnis (literally “papillary hirsutism of the penis”), pēnis being a genitive.

parole.significato: with minute hairs.
parole.testo: Diminutive from Latin hirtus (“hairy”), with -ous.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the leeches.
parole.testo: From Latin hirūdō (“leech”) + -ine.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a swallow (the bird); of or relating to the family Hirundinidae.
parole.testo: From Latin hirundo (“a swallow”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Spain.
parole.testo: From Latin hispānicus, from Hispānia (“Iberia”) + -icus.

parole.significato: Relating to Spain and Spanish culture.
parole.testo: Latin Hispānia

parole.significato: Covered in short, stiff hairs.
parole.testo: From Latin hispidus (“rough, hairy, bristly”).

parole.significato: An inferior historian.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from New Latin historiaster, from Latin historia (“history”) + -aster (suffix denoting incomplete or partial resemblance, and hence sometimes having a derogatory connotation). parole.significato: Very important; noteworthy: having importance or significance in history.
parole.testo: From Latin historicus (“historical”), from Ancient Greek ἱστορικός (historikós, “exact; historical”). Cognate with French historique. By surface analysis, history + -ic.

parole.significato: Synonym of historiaster (“an inferior historian”).
parole.testo: From Latin historicus (“historical”) + -aster (suffix denoting incomplete or partial resemblance, and hence sometimes having a derogatory connotation). Historicus is derived from historia (“history”) + -icus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives), and is modelled after Ancient Gre

parole.significato: A spell which invokes a mythical narrative, asking for the events it describes or similar ones to be enacted (as found…
parole.testo: From Latin historiola, from historia.

parole.significato: A stage actor.
parole.testo: From Latin histriō. Compare French histrion. See histrionic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to actors or acting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin histriōnicus (“pertaining to acting; scurrilous, shameful; wretched”), from Latin histriōnicus (“pertaining to acting and the theatre”), from histriō (“actor, player”) + -icus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’). By surface analysis, histrion + -ic.

parole.significato: To deceive (someone) by making them believe something that has been maliciously or mischievously fabricated.
parole.testo: Reportedly a form of hocus. Possibly from hocus-pocus or Latin iocus (“joke”). Compare hokey.

parole.significato: To play a trick on, to trick (someone); to hoax; to cheat.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from ellipsis of hocus-pocus. The verb is from the noun.

parole.significato: A phrase used (by a stage magician, etc.) as a magical incantation to bring about some change: abracadabra, hey presto.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism. The interjection and noun are derived from pseudo-Latin magical incantations used by conjurers (formerly called “jugglers”) such as “hocus pocus, tontus talontus, vade celeriter jubeo” (by a particular 17th-century conjurer who allegedly adopted the moniker Hocus Pocus) and “hax pax

parole.significato: Of this day; present-day.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hodiernus, from hodie (“today”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the present day or today; hodiern.
parole.testo: From hodiern (“of this day, present-day”) + -al (suffix forming adjectives). Hodiern is derived from Latin hodiernus (“of today, today’s; present, present-day; actual”), from hodiē (“today”) (from hōc (“this (thing)”) + diē (“day”) (ultimately Proto-Indo-European *dyew- (“to be bright; heaven, sky”)

parole.significato: A large merchantman ship in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin holcas, from Ancient Greek ὁλκάς (holkás). Compare hulk.

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Ho) with atomic number 67: a soft and malleable silvery-white metal, too reactive to be foun…
parole.testo: From Latin Holmia (“Stockholm”), the hometown of Per Teodor Cleve, one of the discoverers of holmium.

parole.significato: Synonym of sea cucumber.
parole.testo: Latin holothuria, plural, a sort of water polyp, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The plant Angelica archangelica.
parole.testo: From Middle English Holi Gost, from Old English Hāliġ Gāst, a calque of Latin Spīritus Sānctus, which in turn is a calque of Ancient Greek Πνεῦμα τὸ Ἅγιον (Pneûma tò Hágion), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “breath, vital force, soul”) + ἅγιος (hágios, “holy”)), a calque of Hebrew רוּחַ הָקֹדֶשׁ (rûaḥ hā-qōḏeš

parole.significato: Resembling or relating to the epic poetry of Homer.
parole.testo: From Latin homēricus (“of or pertaining to Homer; Homeric”), from Ancient Greek Ὁμηρικός (Homērikós), from Ὅμηρος (Hómēros, “Homer”) (possibly from ὅμηρος (hómēros, “hostage”), a nickname) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, suffix forming relational adjectives) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-kos (suffix formin

parole.significato: In human form.
parole.testo: From Latin homo (“man”) + -iform.

parole.significato: The process of becoming like a human.
parole.testo: From Latin homo (“human being”) + -ization.

parole.significato: Any anthropoid (including humans and apes) belonging to the superfamily Hominoidea.
parole.testo: From Latin homin- + -oid, after scientific Latin Hominoidea (superfamily name).

parole.significato: A human.
parole.testo: From Latin homō̆ (“a human being, man, person”), sometimes as a shortening of Homo sapiens. Doublet of gome, hombre, ombre, and omi.

parole.significato: A person with the characteristics and nature depicted in the comedies of the ancient Athenian playwright Aristophanes (…
parole.testo: PIE word  *dʰéǵʰōm Learned borrowing from Latin homō Aristophanēus (literally “Aristophanean man”), not attested in Latin works: homō (“human being, person”) + Aristophanēus (“of, pertaining to, or characteristic of Aristophanes or his works”), possibly influenced by French homo aristophaneus (1951)

parole.significato: The human being viewed as a tool maker and user, or having evolutionarily reached the stage of tool use.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin homō faber (“man the maker”, literally “ingenious man”).

parole.significato: Humans as a group, viewed as a foolish species.
parole.testo: A pseudotaxonomic name formed by analogy with Homo sapiens. From Latin homō + idiōticus, influenced by English idiotic.

parole.significato: Humans as a group, seen as a foolish species.
parole.testo: From Homo sapiens (“the human species”, literally “wise man”), replacing sapiēns (“wise”) with Latin īnsipiēns (“foolish”).

parole.significato: The human being viewed as primarily concerned with play, seeing it as an aim in itself.
parole.testo: Coined by Dutch cultural historian Johan Huizinga in Homo Ludens (1938), which introduces the concept, from Latin homō lūdēns (“playful man”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Roman law, a person who was banned and could be killed by anybody, but not sacrificed in a religious ritual.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A human being (Homo sapiens).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin homō sapiēns, from Latin homō (“human being”) + sapiēns (“wise, sensible, judicious”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the belief established in the fourth century as a middle ground between the homoousian and homoiousian po…
parole.testo: From Latin homoeus, from Ancient Greek ὅμοιος (hómoios, “like, similar”), + -an.

parole.significato: Of the same kind; alike, similar.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin homogeneus, from Ancient Greek ὁμογενής (homogenḗs, “of the same race, family or kind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + γένος (génos, “kind”). Compare homo- (“same”) and -ous (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: To confirm, ratify or approve, especially officially or legally.
parole.testo: From Latin homologō + -ate.

parole.significato: The books of the New Testament which were acknowledged as canonical by the early church, as opposed to Antilegomena.
parole.testo: From New Latin homologūmena, from Ancient Greek ὁμολογούμενα (homologoúmena, literally “things agreed upon”), neuter plural form of the present mediopassive participle of ὁμολογέω (homologéō, “to agree with”).

parole.significato: Showing a degree of correspondence or similarity.
parole.testo: From Late Latin homologus, from Ancient Greek ὁμόλογος (homólogos, “agreeing, of one mind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + λόγος (lógos, “reason, reckoning”). Compare homo- (“same”) and -ous (adjectival suffix). From 1655, in the mathematical sense. See also homolog, homologue.

parole.significato: The relationship of being homologous; a homologous relationship.
parole.testo: From Latin homologia, from Ancient Greek ὁμολογία (homología, “agreement, assent”); compare French homologie. By surface analysis, homo- + -logy. In topology, first used by French polymath Henri Poincaré, in the sense (close to what is now called a bordism) of a relation between manifolds mapped int

parole.significato: A word that sounds or is spelled the same as another word (but not necessarily both).
parole.testo: From Latin homōnymum, from Ancient Greek ὁμώνυμον (homṓnumon), nominalized from the neuter of ὁμώνῠμος (homṓnŭmos, “homonymous”). By surface analysis, hom- + -onym.

parole.significato: A pathological fear of mankind.
parole.testo: Latin homo (“man”) + -phobia (“fear”)

parole.significato: Of the same tenor or tone
parole.testo: Latin homotonus, from Ancient Greek [Term?].

parole.significato: A small, artificially created human or human-like being.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin homunculus, from homō (“man”) + -culus (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: One who receives an honor.
parole.testo: From Latin honōrandus, gerundive of honōrāre (“to honor”); equivalent to honor + -and.

parole.significato: Compensation for services that do not have a predetermined value.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin honōrārium (dōnum), from honōrārius. See honorary.

parole.significato: Given as an honor, with no duties attached, and without payment.
parole.testo: From honor + -ary, modelled after French honoraire, from Latin honōrārius.

parole.significato: An honorarium; a fee for services of no fixed value.
parole.testo: From Latin honōrārium.

parole.significato: The state of being able to achieve honours; honourableness.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin honōrificābilitūdinitātibus, the ablative and dative plural of honōrificābilitūdinitās (“the state of being able to achieve honours”).

parole.significato: The quality of being honourable; honourableness.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin honōrificābilitūdinitās.

parole.significato: honorary degree
parole.testo: From Latin honoris causa (“for the sake of the honor”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to an hour, or to hours.
parole.testo: From Latin horalis, from hora (“hour”). See hour.

parole.significato: The daily schedule of a religious house or seminary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hōrārium.

parole.significato: Pertaining to an hour or hours.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hōrārius, from Latin hōra (“hour”).

parole.significato: Any of a class of benzofuran glucopyranosides found in ungerminated barley
parole.testo: From Latin hordeum (“barley”) + ?

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to barley.
parole.testo: From Latin hordeum (“barley”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: An acid derived from barley (Hordeum spp.), possibly identical with lauric acid.
parole.testo: From Latin hordeum (“barley”).

parole.significato: Resembling the shape of barley grains.
parole.testo: From Latin hordeum (“barley”) + -iform.

parole.significato: A glycoprotein found in barley and some other cereals.
parole.testo: Latin hordeum (“barley”).

parole.significato: stye, sty. An infection of a sebaceous gland of the eyelid. This is distinguished from a chalazion, which is not infect…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hordeolus, diminutive from hordeum (“barley”) + -olus, referring to its resemblance to a grain of barley in appearance and size.

parole.significato: A cornucopia.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin cornūcōpia.

parole.significato: A yearling; a bird born in the current year.
parole.testo: From Latin hornotinus (“of this year”).

parole.significato: Synonym of chronometric, of or related to horologia or horology.
parole.testo: From Latin horologicus, from Ancient Greek. Equivalent to horo- + logic or horology + -ic.

parole.significato: Synonym of chronometer or clock, a timekeeping device.
parole.testo: From Latin horologium, from Ancient Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion). In reference to Eastern Orthodoxy, via its Byzantine Greek development. See menologium. Doublet of horologe.

parole.significato: The study or measurement of time
parole.testo: From Latin horologia, from horo- + -logia, equivalent to Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “period of time, hour”) + -λογία (-logía, “-ology: study or proper knowledge of”). Equivalent to horo- + -ology.

parole.significato: Extremely bad; awful; terrible.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin horrendus, future passive participle (gerundive) of horreō (“to dread”) + -ous.

parole.significato: Standing upright, like bristles; bristled; bristly.
parole.testo: From Latin horrens, present participle of horrere (“to bristle”). See horror.

parole.significato: Horrible to say; horribly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin horribile dictu (literally “horrible to say”).

parole.significato: Bristling, rough, rugged.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin horridus (“rough, bristly, savage, shaggy, rude”), from horrere (“to bristle”). See horrent, horror, ordure.

parole.significato: Causing horror; horrifying.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin horrificus, from horreō (“to be afraid”) + -ficō (“to make”).

parole.significato: To cause to feel extreme apprehension or unease; to cause to experience horror.
parole.testo: From horror + -ify, or borrowed from Latin horrificare (cf. French horrifier). 1791, in form horrifying.

parole.significato: Synonym of horripilating.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin horripilāns, the present participle of horripilō.

parole.significato: To bristle in fear or horror; to have goose bumps or goose pimples.
parole.testo: From Late Latin horripilātus, perfect passive participle of horripilō (“(of hairs) to bristle”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from horreō (“to bristle, shiver, dread”) + pilus (“hair”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰers- (“to bristle”).

parole.significato: A real or fancied bristling of the hair of the head or body, resulting from disease, terror, chilliness, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin horripilatio, horripilationem.

parole.significato: Having an unpleasant sound.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin horrisonus.

parole.significato: Sounding dreadfully; uttering a terrible sound.
parole.testo: From Latin horrisonus, from horrere (“to be horrible”) + sonus (“a sound”).

parole.significato: The Aristotelian principle that there are no vacuums in nature.
parole.testo: From Latin horror vacuī (“fear of empty space”), from horror (“horror, fear”) + vacuum (“vacuum”).

parole.significato: The act of exhorting, inciting, or giving advice; exhortation.
parole.testo: From Latin hortatio, from hortari (“to incite, exhort”), from hori (“to urge”).

parole.significato: Urging, exhorting, or encouraging.
parole.testo: From Latin hortātīvus, from hortor (“to exhort”).

parole.significato: hydrangea (Hydrangea spp.)
parole.testo: From the genus name, New Latin Hortensia, from hortēnsius (“of the garden”), from hortēnsis.

parole.significato: Fit for a garden.
parole.testo: From Latin hortensius, hortēnsis, from hortus (“garden”). Akin to English yard (“an enclosure”). By surface analysis, Latin hortēns(is) + -i- + -al.

parole.significato: Related to growing fruits, vegetables, flowers, or ornamental plants.
parole.testo: From Latin hortus (“garden”) + -i-.

parole.significato: One who cultivates a garden.
parole.testo: From Latin hortus (“garden”) + cultor (“a cultivator”), colere (“to cultivate”).

parole.significato: The art or science of cultivating gardens; gardening.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin *horticultūra. Attested since the late 1600s.

parole.significato: Belonging to a garden.
parole.testo: From Latin hortulanus, from hortus (“garden”). Doublet of ortolan.

parole.significato: An enclosed private garden, in medieval times usually divided into quadrants by four paths, with a well or fountain in…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hortus (“garden”) and Latin conclusus (“shut up, confined, restricted, enclosed”).

parole.significato: A collection of specimens of plants, dried and preserved and arranged systematically; a herbarium.
parole.testo: From Latin hortus (“garden”) + siccus (“dry”).

parole.significato: A cry of praise or adoration to God in liturgical use among the Jews, and said to have been shouted in recognition of t…
parole.testo: From Latin osanna, hosanna, from Ancient Greek ὡσαννά (hōsanná), from Aramaic אושענא/ܐܘܫܥܢܐ ('ōsha‘nā), from Biblical Hebrew הוֹשַׁע נָא (hōsha‘ nā, “please save”).

parole.significato: hospitality (lodging or putting someone up)
parole.testo: From Latin hospitagium, for Latin hospitium. See hospice.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a hostel or hospitallers.
parole.testo: From Latin hospitālārius.

parole.significato: To receive with hospitality; to provide lodging to a guest.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hospitātus, perfect passive participle of hospitō, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).

parole.significato: One who kills his guest or host.
parole.testo: From Latin hospiticīda or *hospiticīdium, from hospes (“host, guest”) + -cīda (“killer”); equivalent to + -cide.

parole.significato: An inn, lodging or hospice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hospitium. Doublet of hospice.

parole.significato: The act of killing an enemy.
parole.testo: From Latin hostis (“enemy”) + English -cide or Latin caedere (“to kill”).

parole.significato: A person who has committed a criminal act so grave – originally maritime piracy and slave-trading, and now torture as w…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hostis hūmānī generis (“enemy of the human race”): hostis (“enemy of the state”) + hūmānī, genitive singular neuter of hūmānus (“of man”) + generis, genitive singular of genus (“race”).

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Cynoglossum of small-flowered herbs and shrubs of the Old World.
parole.testo: From Middle English houndestonge, from Old English hundes tunge (“hound’s tongue (cynoglossum officinale)”), a calque of Latin cynoglossos, itself from Ancient Greek κυνόγλωσσον (kunóglōsson, literally “hound’s tongue”). Compare Dutch hondstong, German Hundszunge.

parole.significato: Imbued with humanity.
parole.testo: First attested in 1551; borrowed from Late Latin hūmanātus, from hūmanus + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Having the appearance or characteristics of a human; being anthropomorphic under some criteria (physical, mental, genet…
parole.testo: From human (from Latin hūmānus m (“of or belonging to a man, human, humane”, adjective)) + -oid.

parole.significato: Any substance that promotes the retention of water, especially one used to keep a food product moist.
parole.testo: From Latin ūmectāns, present participle of ūmectō (“to moisten”), from ūmectus (“moist”), from ūmeō (“to be moist”).

parole.significato: To moisten.
parole.testo: First attested in 1640; borrowed from Latin humectātus, perfect passive participle of humectō/ūmectō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from humectus/ūmectus (“moist”).

parole.significato: moistening.
parole.testo: Latin humectatio: compare French humectation.

parole.significato: The bone of the upper arm.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin humerus, from umerus. Cognate with Spanish hombro (“shoulder”).

parole.significato: The act or practice of lying on the ground.
parole.testo: From Latin humus (“the ground”) + cubare (“to lie down”).

parole.significato: The process of humifying; conversion into humus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin hūmificatiō. By surface analysis, humus + -ification, following humify.

parole.significato: Spread over the surface of the ground; procumbent
parole.testo: From Latin humus (“ground”) + fusus, past participle of fundere (“to spread”).

parole.significato: humiliating; humbling
parole.testo: From Latin humilians, present participle of humiliare.

parole.significato: To cause to be ashamed; to injure the dignity and self-respect of.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin humiliātus, perfect passive participle of humiliō (“to abase, humble”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin humilis (“lowly, humble”), from humus (“ground; earth, soil”); see humble.

parole.significato: One who humiliates.
parole.testo: From Latin humiliātor. By surface analysis, humiliate + -or.

parole.significato: A dominatrix who specialises in humiliation.
parole.testo: From Latin humiliātrīx or humiliate + -trix, compare humiliator and dominatrix.

parole.significato: A large group of natural organic compounds, found in the soil, formed from the chemical and biological decomposition of…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin humus.

parole.significato: A member of a nomadic tribe (the Huns) who invaded Europe in the fourth century from Central Asia.
parole.testo: From Old English Hūnas, Hūne (both plural), from Late Latin Hunni, from Koine Greek Οὗννοι (Hoûnnoi), borrowed through Middle Iranian. Cognate with Old Norse húnir, Old High German Hunni. See also etymology of Xiongnu. Compare Sogdian 𐼶𐼴𐼻 (xwn), Sanskrit हूण (hūṇa), and 匈奴 (OC *hoŋ-nâ) (c. 318 BCE)

parole.significato: A centipede.
parole.testo: A calque of Latin centipēs.

parole.significato: Of the colour of a hyacinth (either the gem or the flower); reddish-gold (chiefly with reference to hair).
parole.testo: From Latin hyacinthinus, from Ancient Greek ὑακίνθινος (huakínthinos), from ὑάκινθος (huákinthos); corresponding to hyacinth + -ine.

parole.significato: Glassy, transparent; amorphous.
parole.testo: From Latin hyalinus, from Koine Greek ὑάλινος (huálinos), from ὕαλος (húalos, “glass”).

parole.significato: Offspring resulting from cross-breeding different entities, e.g. two different species or two purebred parent strains.
parole.testo: From Latin hybrida, a variant of hibrida (“a mongrel; specifically, an offspring of a tame sow and a wild boar”). Attested since 1601, but rare before c. 1850.

parole.significato: Causing a discharge of water; expelling serum effused into any part of the body, as in dropsy.
parole.testo: From Latin hydragogus (“conveying off water”), from Ancient Greek ὑδραγωγός (hudragōgós, “to lead”). Compare French hydragogue.

parole.significato: Bearing or producing mercury
parole.testo: From Latin hydrargyrum (“mercury”) + -iferous.

parole.significato: Mercury (chemical element).
parole.testo: From New Latin hydrargyrum (“mercury”). By surface analysis, hydr- + argyr- + -um.

parole.significato: Synonym of water organ.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hydraulus.

parole.significato: The hollow stem of a hydrozoan
parole.testo: From New Latin hydrocaulus, from hydro- + Ancient Greek καυλός (kaulós, “stalk, stem”).

parole.significato: Mead, especially one of low alcohol content.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hydromel, hydromeli, from hydro- (from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”)) + mel (“honey”).

parole.significato: a denomination, sect, church, or other group which professes to be Christian but uses water to administer the Eucharist…
parole.testo: From Latin hydroparastatae from Ancient Greek ὑδρο- (hudro-, “water”) + παραστάτης (parastátēs, “defender”), from παρίστημι (parístēmi, “to stand by, defend”).

parole.significato: An aversion to water, as a symptom of rabies; the disease of rabies itself.
parole.testo: From Middle English idroforbia (“hydrophobia”), from Latin hydrophobia, from Ancient Greek ὑδροφοβία (hudrophobía), from ὑδρο- (hudro-), combining form of ῠ̔́δωρ (hŭ́dōr, “water”), + φοβία (phobía, “phobia”). The word is analysable as hydro- + -phobia.

parole.significato: Dropsical.
parole.testo: From Latin hydropicus + -al.

parole.significato: The passing of a winter in a particular place; a wintering.
parole.testo: Latin hiematio.

parole.significato: Synonym of matter, physical substance.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hyle, from Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “wood, matter”), particularly in Aristotle as πρώτη ὕλη (prṓtē húlē, “protomatter, fundamental undifferentiated matter”).

parole.significato: Synonym of physical, material, or base.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hylicus, from Ancient Greek ὑλικός (hulikós, “wooden, material”), from ῡ̔́λη (hū́lē, “wood, matter”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic, forming adjectives”). As a noun, a clipped calque of homo hylicus (“hylic man”).

parole.significato: Synonym of physical or material.
parole.testo: From hyle + -ical, originally translating Latin hylicus in notes on Irenaeus's Against Heretics after the manner of earlier psychical and pneumatical, from Ancient Greek ὑλικός (hulikós, “wooden, material”), from ῡ̔́λη (hū́lē, “wood, matter”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic, forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to marriage.
parole.testo: From Latin hymenaeus (from Ancient Greek ὑμεναῖος (humenaîos, “matrimonial”)) + -al. Compare hymen.

parole.significato: A collection of hymns; a hymn book.
parole.testo: From Middle English hymnale, from Medieval Latin hymnāle, noun use of neuter of hymnālis.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to hymns.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hymnālis.

parole.significato: A flat muscle on either side of the tongue, connecting it with the body and the thyrohyal of the hyoid bone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin hyoglōssus, clipping of musculus hyoglōssus (“hyoglossal muscle”).

parole.significato: Open-air, outdoor, exposed to the sky.
parole.testo: From Latin hypaethrus, from Ancient Greek ὕπαιθρος (húpaithros), from ὑπό (hupó) + αἰθήρ (aithḗr, “air, ether”).

parole.significato: The use of a grammatical modifier which syntactically modifies an item other than the one it belongs to semantically, g…
parole.testo: From Latin hypallagē, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπαλλαγή (hupallagḗ), from ὑπό (hupó, “hypo-”) + ἀλλάσσειν (allássein, “to exchange”).

parole.significato: In ancient musical theory, the lowest-pitched fixed note in the nearer tetrachord on a lyre, always pitched a perfect f…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin hypatē, from Ancient Greek ὑπάτη (hupátē, literally “highest/nearest [string]”). The hypate was the "highest" in the sense of being the string on a lyre nearest the player and physically above the remaining strings (compare a modern guitar, where the low E string is ne

parole.significato: An inversion of the usual or logical order of words or phrases, for emphasis or poetic effect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hyperbaton, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπερβατόν (huperbatón, “overstepping”), from ὑπερβαίνω (huperbaínō), from ὑπέρ (hupér) + βαίνω (baínō, “walk”).

parole.significato: A conic section formed by the intersection of a cone with a plane that intersects the base of the cone and is not tange…
parole.testo: From New Latin hyperbola, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (huperbolḗ). Doublet of hyperbole.

parole.significato: Deliberate overstatement, particularly extreme overstatement.
parole.testo: From Middle English iperbole, yperbole, from Latin hyperbolē, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (huperbolḗ, “excess, exaggeration”), from ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH-). Doublet of hyperbola.

parole.significato: Of or relating to hyperbole.
parole.testo: From Latin hyperbolic(us), from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολικός (huperbolikós). First attested in the 15th century. By surface analysis, hyperbol(e) + -ic.

parole.significato: One of a race of people living in the extreme north, beyond the north wind.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hyperboreanus, cognate with Classical Latin hyperboreus, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβόρεος (huperbóreos), composed of ὑπέρ (hupér, “over”) + βόρειος (bóreios, “northern”). By surface analysis, nearly hyper- + boreal. See also Ὑπερβόρεοι (Huperbóreoi).

parole.significato: Which has an extra syllable added to the last dipody (foot of a verse).
parole.testo: Recorded from circa 1700; from Latin hypercatalēcticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπερκατάληκτος (huperkatálēktos).

parole.significato: The addition of one or two syllables to the last foot of a verse
parole.testo: Coined in the late 1880s as a back-formation from hypercatalectic, from Latin hypercatalēcticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπερκαταληκτικός (huperkatalēktikós), from ὑπερ- (huper-, “over”) + καταληκτικός (katalēktikós, “incomplete”)

parole.significato: A level of veneration higher than dulia but less than latria, properly given to the Virgin Mary only.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hyperdūlīa, from hyper-, from Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”) + dūlīa, from Ancient Greek δουλείᾱ (douleíā, “slavery”), from δοῦλος (doûlos, “slave”).

parole.significato: A rare complication of pregnancy, similar to severe morning sickness, sometimes fatal if left untreated.
parole.testo: From hyperemesis + Latin gravidārum (“of pregnant women”).

parole.significato: Hypericum; St. John's wort.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hypericon.

parole.significato: The condition of having an abnormally high body temperature caused by a failure of the heat-regulating mechanisms of th…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “over”) + θέρμη (thérmē, “heat”) + -ία (-ía). By surface analysis, hyper- + -therm + -ia.

parole.significato: That part of the architrave which is over a door or window.
parole.testo: From Latin hyperthyrion, from Ancient Greek ὑπερθύριον (huperthúrion).

parole.significato: An abnormal increase in tightness of muscle tone, common in cerebral palsy.
parole.testo: From New Latin hypertonia, from hyper- + Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos) + -ia. By surface analysis, hyper- + -tonia.

parole.significato: Any of the long, threadlike filaments that form the mycelium of a fungus.
parole.testo: From New Latin hypha, from Ancient Greek ὑφή (huphḗ, “web”).

parole.significato: The symbol "‐", typically used to join two or more words to form a compound term, or to indicate that a word has been s…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin hyphen, from Ancient Greek ῠ̔φέν (hŭphén, “in one, as a single word”), univerbation of ῠ̔φ’ ἕν (hŭph’ hén, “under one”), from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, “under”) + ἕν (hén, “one”), neuter of εἷς (heîs, “one”).

parole.significato: legendary asp said to kill people by making them go in an endless sleep or by attacking them in their sleep.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ypnalis, ipnalis, from Ancient Greek ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”).

parole.significato: An underfloor space or flue through which heat from a furnace passes to heat the floor of a room or a bath.
parole.testo: From Latin hypocaustum, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκαυστον (hupókauston), from Ancient Greek ὑπό (hupó, “underneath”) + καυστόν (kaustón, “burnt offering”).

parole.significato: A formerly defined psychological disorder characterized by excessive preoccupation or worry about having a serious illn…
parole.testo: From New Latin hypochondria (the morbid condition so called, supposed to have its seat in the upper part of the abdomen), from hypochondrium (see English hypochondrium for more).

parole.significato: A mental disorder (in some classifications of such disorders, including ICD-11) characterized by a persistent preoccupa…
parole.testo: From New Latin; by surface analysis, hypochondr(ium) + -iasis. See also hypochondria, hypochondrium, and Wikipedia at hypochondriasis § Etymology.

parole.significato: The upper region of the abdomen, covering the upperribs, at each side of the epigastrium.
parole.testo: From New Latin hypochondrium, from Ancient Greek ὑποχόνδριον (hupokhóndrion, “the soft part of the body below the cartilage and above the navel”), from ὑπό (hupó, “below”) + χόνδρος (khóndros, “cartilage”). See also hypochondria, hypochondriac, and Wikipedia at hypochondriasis § Etymology.

parole.significato: A term of endearment, often a diminutive; a pet name.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin hypocorisma, a loan from Ancient Greek ὑποκόρισμα (hupokórisma), ὑποκορισμός (hupokorismós, “pet name”), from ὑποκορίζεσθαι (hupokorízesthai), ὑποκορίζομαι (hupokorízomai, “to use a pet name; to act in a childish manner”), from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, prefix indicating a small degree)

parole.significato: A mark ⟨⸒⟩ in late Classical and Byzantine Greek used as a form of interpunct to show two words should be read separate…
parole.testo: From Latin hypodiastolē, from Ancient Greek ὑποδιαστολή (hupodiastolḗ), from ὑπό (hupó, “under, lower”) + διαστολή (diastolḗ, “separation, distinction”), from διαστέλλω (diastéllō, “separate”), from διά (diá, “through, during”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “order, arrange”).

parole.significato: Existing or growing underground.
parole.testo: From Latin hypogaeus, hypogēus (from Ancient Greek ὑπόγειος (hupógeios)) + -an.

parole.significato: An underground room or cavern (also used figuratively).
parole.testo: From Latin hypogaeum, from Ancient Greek ὑπόγειον (hupógeion), a noun use of the neuter singular of ὑπόγειος (hupógeios, “underground”).

parole.significato: A lesser proposition or subsumption within a larger syllogism.
parole.testo: From Latin hypolēmma, from Ancient Greek ὑπόλημμᾰ (hupólēmmă, “supposition”), from ὑπο- (hupo-, “lesser”) + λῆμμα (lêmma, “assumption”).

parole.significato: An aftershaft.
parole.testo: From New Latin hypoptilum, from hypo- + Ancient Greek πτίλον (ptílon, “soft feathers, down”).

parole.significato: A sedimentary deposit, especially in urine.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin hypostasis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόστασις (hupóstasis, “sediment, foundation; substance, existence, essence”), from ὑπό (hupó, “under”) + στάσις (stásis, “standing”). Morphologically hypo- + -stasis.

parole.significato: Pertaining to hypostasis, especially with reference to hypostatic union.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hypostaticus, from Ancient Greek ὑποστατικός (hupostatikós), from ὑποστατός (hupostatós). Equivalent to hypostasis + -tic.

parole.significato: In Chalcedonian Christianity, the unity of the two natures of Jesus Christ, divine and human, in a single individual pe…
