parole.testo: Calque of Ecclesiastical Latin ūniō hypostatica, from Byzantine Greek ἕνωσις καθ’ ὑπόστασιν (hénōsis kath’ hupóstasin, literally “union according to the hypostasis”).

parole.significato: The side of a right triangle opposite the right angle.
parole.testo: From Latin hypotenusa, from Ancient Greek ὑποτείνουσα πλευρά (hupoteínousa pleurá, “side subtending [the right angle]”), from ὑποτείνουσα (hupoteínousa, “stretching, extending, subtending”), active participle of ὑποτείνω (hupoteínō, “subtend, stretch under”).

parole.significato: In Scotland, a landlord's right over the stocking (cattle, implements, etc.), and crops of his tenant, as security for…
parole.testo: From Latin hypothēca (“pledge, mortgage”), from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē, “warning, pledge”).

parole.significato: To pledge (something) as surety for a loan; to pawn, mortgage.
parole.testo: From Latin hypothecatus, past participle of hypotheco, hypothecare. This was in turn derived from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē, “pledge”), from the verb ὑποτίθημι (hupotíthēmi, “to pledge as surety”).

parole.significato: The use of property, or an existing mortgage, as security for a loan, etc.
parole.testo: From hypothecate + -ion. From Latin hypothecatio, from hypotheco (“to pledge as collateral”), from Greek.

parole.significato: Abnormally low body temperature; specifically, below 35 degrees Celsius for humans.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὑπο- (hupo-, “under”) + θέρμη (thérmē, “heat”) + -ία (-ía, “feminine suffix”) . By surface analysis, hypo- + therm- + -ia.

parole.significato: A state of reduced pressure of the intraocular fluid.
parole.testo: From New Latin hypotonia, from hypo- + Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos) + -ia. By surface analysis, hypo- + -tonia.

parole.significato: the portion of the capital of a column that is below the annulets, and above the end of the shaft
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hypotrachelium, from Ancient Greek ὑποτραχήλιον (hupotrakhḗlion), from ὑπό (hupó, “under”) + τράχηλος (trákhēlos, “neck”).

parole.significato: A vivid, picturesque description of scenes or events.
parole.testo: New Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The petrified remains of hyrax urine and feces produced by the rock hyrax (“Cape hyrax”), Procavia capensis (“P. apensi…
parole.testo: From New Latin hyraceum, from hyrax (stem form hyrac-) + -eus.

parole.significato: Any of several small, paenungulate herbivorous mammals of the family Procaviidae from the order Hyracoidea, with a bulk…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὕραξ (húrax, “shrewmouse”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Hyrcanian.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Hyrcānus, from Ancient Greek Ὑρκανός (Hurkanós).

parole.significato: Any of several aromatic bushy herbs, of the genus Hyssopus, native to Southern Europe and once used medicinally.
parole.testo: Via Latin hȳsōpum, from Ancient Greek ὕσσωπος (hússōpos), of Semitic origin.

parole.significato: Behavior exhibiting excessive or uncontrollable emotions, in a wide range from joy to panic but usually including anxie…
parole.testo: From New Latin hysteria, a back-formation from Latin hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós, “suffering in the uterus, hysterical”), from ὑστέρα (hustéra, “womb”). Compare French hystérie.

parole.significato: Hysterical; relating to hysteria.
parole.testo: From Latin hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós, “suffering in the uterus, hysterical”), from ὑστέρα (hustéra, “womb”).

parole.significato: Of, or arising from hysteria.
parole.testo: From hysteric + -al, from Latin hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós, “suffering in the womb, hysterical”), from ῠ̔στέρᾱ (hŭstérā, “womb”).

parole.significato: A plant or fungus that lives on dead or living organic matter.
parole.testo: From New Latin hysterophȳtum, from Ancient Greek ὑστέρα (hustéra, “womb, figuratively the earth”) + φῡτόν (phūtón, “plant”). By surface analysis, hystero- + -phyte.

parole.significato: Like or pertaining to porcupines.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hystrix (genitive hystricis), a kind of porcupine.

parole.significato: Any rodent in the Hystricomorpha, a suborder of the order Rodentia
parole.testo: From Latin hystrīx (“porcupine”) -o- + -morph.

parole.significato: The ninth letter of the English alphabet, called i and written in the Latin script.
parole.testo: From Latin i, minuscule of I.

parole.parola: I came, I saw, I conquered
parole.significato: I gained a total and swift victory.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin vēnī, vīdī, vīcī (“I came, I saw, I conquered”).

parole.significato: Synonym of long i (“tall variant of letter i”).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ī longa.

parole.significato: A form of the prefix in-, used before gn, as in ignoble, ignominy, and ignore.
parole.testo: From Latin i-, assimilated form of in- used before gn-.

parole.significato: That is, namely, in other words, that is to say.
parole.testo: From Latin i. e., an abbreviation of id est (“that is”).

parole.significato: the same as
parole.testo: From the Latin īdem (“same”) + quod the neuter nominative of quī (“what”).

parole.significato: A verse consisting of an iambic dimeter and half an elegiac pentameter.
parole.testo: From Latin iambelegus.

parole.significato: Synonym of iamb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ïambus (“a certain poetic meter”), from Ancient Greek ἴαμβος (íambos).

parole.significato: A member of an Olympian dynasty, the "house of Iamus", an extended family of seers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Iamidēs, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἰαμίδης (Iamídēs), from Ἴαμος (Íamos, “Iamus”) + -ίδης (-ídēs, “son of”, patronymic suffix).

parole.significato: Any of the family Epitoniidae (syn. Janthinidae) of violet snails.
parole.testo: Latin ianthinus (“violet”)

parole.significato: therapeutic inunction
parole.testo: From Latin iātraliptice.

parole.significato: A tribe of Sarmatia settled on the Danube.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Iazyges.

parole.significato: Synonym of Iberian.
parole.testo: From Latin Ibericus (“Iberian”). Attested since the 18th century as Iberick.

parole.significato: A type of wild mountain goat of the genus Capra, such as the species Capra ibex.
parole.testo: From Latin ībex (“chamois”), possibly from Iberian or Aquitanian; akin to Old Spanish bezerro (“bull”) (modern becerro (“yearling”)).

parole.significato: In the same place; indicates a reference to the same source as the previous one.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ibīdem (“in the same place”).

parole.significato: Any of various long-legged wading birds in the family Threskiornithidae, having long downcurved bills used to probe the…
parole.testo: Mentioned in the Wycliffe Bible (Lev. 11:17) as ybyn or ibin, as ibys from 16th century and ibis shortly after. From Latin ībis, from Ancient Greek ἶβις (îbis), from Egyptian h-b-G26 (hbj) (compare Coptic ϩⲓⲃⲱⲓ (hibōi) or ϩⲓⲡ (hip)).

parole.significato: An Egyptian mongoose (Herpestes ichneumon), found in Africa and southern Europe.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ichneumōn, from Ancient Greek ἰχνεύμων (ikhneúmōn, “tracker”), from ἴχνος (íkhnos, “track, footstep”).

parole.significato: The study of ichneumon wasps (Ichneumonidae).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ichneumōnologia. By surface analysis, ichneumon + -ology.

parole.significato: The liquid said to flow in place of blood in the veins of the gods.
parole.testo: Sense 1 (“liquid said to flow in place of blood in the veins of the gods”) is borrowed from Medieval Latin ichor, from Ancient Greek ῑ̓χώρ (īkhṓr, “fluid running through the veins of gods, ichor; watery part of blood, lymph, serum; watery part of milk, whey; gravy; pus; naphtha”); further etymology

parole.significato: Fish glue, isinglass; a glue prepared from the sounds (swimming bladders) of various fishes.
parole.testo: From Latin ichthyocolla, from Ancient Greek ἰχθυόκολλα (ikhthuókolla, “fish-glue”), from ἰχθύς (ikhthús, “fish”) + κόλλα (kólla, “glue”).

parole.significato: fish fin.
parole.testo: From New Latin ichthyopterygium, from Ancient Greek ἰχθύς (ikhthús, “fish”) + πτερύγιον (pterúgion, “fin”). By surface analysis, ichthyo- + pterygium.

parole.significato: Any of a group of genetic skin disorders characterized by dry, thickened, scaly skin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin ichthyōsis. By surface analysis, ichthyo- + -osis. First attested in 1815.

parole.significato: Lamellar ichthyosis.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: A genetic skin disorder causing dry, scaly skin.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: An image, symbol, picture, portrait, or other representation, usually as an object of religious devotion.
parole.testo: From Latin īcōn, from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “likeness, image, portrait”). Eastern Orthodox Church sense is attested from 1833. Computing sense first recorded in 1982.

parole.significato: Relating to, or having the characteristics of, an icon.
parole.testo: From Late Latin īconicus, from Ancient Greek εἰκονικός (eikonikós). By surface analysis, icon + -ic.

parole.significato: the state of being iconic (in all meanings)
parole.testo: From Latin iconicitas.

parole.significato: A collection of icons.
parole.testo: From Latin īconothēca from Ancient Greek εἰκονοθήκη (eikonothḗkē) from εἰκών (eikṓn) + θήκη (thḗkē).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a sudden physiologic attack such as a seizure, stroke or headache.
parole.testo: From ictus + -al, from Latin ictus (“a blow”).

parole.significato: Jaundiced (having icterus); having yellowing of the skin, mucous membranes of the sclerae of the eyes, or other parts o…
parole.testo: From icterus (“jaundice”) + -ic, or Latin ictericus.

parole.significato: An excess of bile pigments in the blood; jaundice.
parole.testo: From the Latin icterus, from the Ancient Greek ἴκτερος (íkteros, “jaundice”).

parole.significato: neonatal jaundice
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin icterus neonatorum (literally “icterus of newborns”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or caused by, a blow; sudden; abrupt.
parole.testo: Latin ictus (“a blow”).

parole.significato: The pulse.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ictus (“a blow”), from īco (“to hit, strike”).

parole.significato: The unconscious impulsive component of the personality in the Freudian psychoanalytic model.
parole.testo: From New Latin id (“it”), chosen by Freud’s translator as a translation of his use of German Es (“it”) as a noun for this concept from the pronoun es (“it”).

parole.significato: Synonym of i.e. or that is.
parole.testo: From Middle English id est, from Old English id est, from Latin id est.

parole.significato: Pertaining to Mount Ida, the name given to a mountain near ancient Troy, and to a mountain of Crete, sometimes held to…
parole.testo: From Latin Idaeus (from Ancient Greek Ἰδαῖος (Idaîos)) + -an.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Idalium, an ancient city of Cyprus where Aphrodite was worshipped.
parole.testo: From Latin Īdalius (“pertaining to Idalium”) (ultimately from Koine Greek Ιδάλιον (Idálion)) + -an.

parole.significato: An abstract archetype of a given thing, compared to which real-life examples are seen as imperfect approximations; pure…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin idea (“a (Platonic) idea; archetype”), from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know; see”). Cognate with French idée. Doublet of idée. Related to idol, idolum, and eidolon.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being ideal.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ideālitās (“ideality”), from Late Latin ideālis (“ideal”). By surface analysis, ideal + -ity.

parole.significato: The actual existence supposed to correspond with an idea; the correlate in real existence to the idea as a thought or e…
parole.testo: From Late Latin ideatum. See idea.

parole.significato: The same.
parole.testo: From Middle English idem, borrowed from Latin idem (“the same”).

parole.significato: Incorrectly spelled, but sufficiently correct to identify someone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin idem sonāns (“sounding the same”).

parole.significato: A quality of an action such that repetitions of the action have no further effect on the outcome; the state of being id…
parole.testo: Latin roots, idem (“same”) + potence (“the quality of having power”) – literally, “the quality of having the same power”. Coined by 19th century American mathematician Benjamin Peirce in context of algebra.

parole.significato: Idempotence.
parole.testo: From Latin roots, idem (“same”) + potency (“power”).

parole.significato: (said of a function) Such that, when performed multiple times on the same subject, it has no further effect on its subj…
parole.testo: From Latin roots idem (“same”) + potent (“having power”), thus “having the same power”. Coined in 1870 by American mathematician Benjamin Peirce in the context of algebra, later generalized to computer science.

parole.significato: The 15th of March in the Ancient Roman calendar, on which day Julius Caesar was assassinated.
parole.testo: From Latin idūs Martii.

parole.significato: The chief financial officer in Egypt when it was part of the Roman Empire.
parole.testo: From Latin idiologus.

parole.significato: A disease or condition arising spontaneously or having no known cause.
parole.testo: From Latin idiopathia, from Ancient Greek ἰδιοπάθεια (idiopátheia). By surface analysis, idio- + -pathy. First appears c. 1634, in the publications of Philiatreus (fl. 1630).

parole.significato: Idiom.
parole.testo: From Latin idiotismus.

parole.significato: Divination by idols, images or figures.
parole.testo: First element is from Late Latin idolum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”). Second element is from Latin -mantīa, ultimately from Ancient Greek μᾰντείᾱ (mănteíā). Equivalent to idol + -mancy.

parole.significato: An insubstantial image; a spectre or phantom.
parole.testo: From Latin īdōlum. Doublet of aidoru, eidolon, and idol and related to idea.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being idoneous.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin idōneitās.

parole.significato: appropriate; suitable
parole.testo: From Latin idōneus.

parole.significato: Any poem or short written piece composed in the style of Theocritus's short pastoral poems, the Idylls.
parole.testo: From Latin īdyllium, from Ancient Greek εἰδύλλιον (eidúllion), from diminutive of εἶδος (eîdos, “form, shape”).

parole.parola: if you want peace, prepare for war
parole.significato: Visibly preparing for a fight can deter one's enemies from opening hostilities, by not giving the appearance of an easy…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin sī vīs pācem, parā bellum, an adage adapted from a statement found in 4th century AD Roman author Vegetius's tract De re militari, in which the actual phrasing is igitur quī dēsīderat pācem, praeparet bellum (“therefore let him who desires peace prepare for war”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to or having the nature of fire; containing fire; resembling fire.
parole.testo: From Latin igneus (“fiery”). By surface analysis, Latin ign- + -eous.

parole.significato: Emitting sparks of fire when struck with steel; scintillating.
parole.testo: Latin ignescens, present participle of ignescere (“to become inflamed”), from ignis (“fire”): compare French ignescent. By surface analysis, Latin ign- + -escent.

parole.significato: Related to fire.
parole.testo: From Latin ignis (“fire”).

parole.significato: A worshiper of fire.
parole.testo: From igni- + Latin colere (“to worship”) + -ist.

parole.significato: Producing fire
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ignifer.

parole.significato: Flowing with fire.
parole.testo: From Latin ignifluus, from ignis (“fire”) + fluere (“to flow”). By surface analysis, igni- + Latin flu- + -ous.

parole.significato: igneous
parole.testo: From Latin ignigenus, from ignis (“fire”) + genere, ginere (“to beget, produce”). By surface analysis, igni- + -genous.

parole.significato: fiery, or having control over fire.
parole.testo: From Latin ignipotens, from ignis (“fire”) + potens (“powerful”). By surface analysis, igni- + potent.

parole.significato: A will o' the wisp.
parole.testo: From New Latin ignis fatuus (literally “foolish fire”).

parole.significato: To set fire to (something), to light (something)
parole.testo: From Latin ignītus, past participle of igniō, ignire (“to set on fire, ignite”), from Latin ignis (“fire”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥gʷnis, and thus related to Sanskrit अग्नि (agní), Lithuanian ugnis, and Russian ого́нь (ogónʹ).

parole.significato: A curfew bell.
parole.testo: From Latin ignitegium.

parole.significato: The act of igniting.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ignītiō. By surface analysis, ignite + -ion.

parole.significato: Throwing out fire, as a volcano does.
parole.testo: From Latin ignivomus.

parole.significato: The state or condition of being ignoble.
parole.testo: From Latin ignōbilitās. By surface analysis, ignoble + -ity.

parole.significato: A statement such that whether or not it is true can never be known.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A totally ignorant person—unknowledgeable, uneducated, or uninformed; a fool.
parole.testo: After the ignorant lawyer Ignoramus, the titular character in the 1615 play Ignoramus by the English playwright George Ruggle; from Latin ignōrāmus (“we do not know, we are unacquainted with, we are ignorant of”), the first-person plural present active indicative of ignōrō (“to not know, to be unacq

parole.significato: A grand jury's ruling on an indictment when the evidence is determined to be insufficient to send the case to trial.
parole.testo: Directly from Latin ignōrāmus (“we do not know”).

parole.significato: Ignorance of the law is not a valid excuse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ignōrantia factī excūsat, ignōrantia jūris nōn excūsat (“ignorance of fact excuses, ignorance of law does not excuse”).

parole.significato: The fallacy of presenting an argument that may or may not be logically valid, but fails to address the issue in questio…
parole.testo: From Latin ignōrātiō elenchī (“ignorance of the refutation”).

parole.significato: pardonable
parole.testo: From Latin ignoscibilis, from ignoscere (“to pardon; literally, not to wish to know”), from in- (“not”) + gnoscere, noscere (“to learn to know”).

parole.significato: unknown
parole.testo: From Latin ignotus; prefix in- (“not”) + gnotus, notus (“known”), past participle of gnocere, nocere (“to learn, to know”).

parole.significato: An attempt to explain something obscure in terms of something else which is even more obscure.
parole.testo: From Latin ignōtum per ignōtius, “[to explain] the unknown by the more unknown”.

parole.significato: not; a form of the prefix in-, used before l
parole.testo: From Latin il-, assimilated form of in- before l-.

parole.significato: The last, and usually the longest, division of the small intestine; the part between the jejunum and large intestine.
parole.testo: Via Medieval Latin from Latin ilia.

parole.significato: Disruption of the normal propulsive ability of the gastrointestinal tract, due to failure of peristalsis.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin īleus, from Ancient Greek εἰλεός (eileós, “intestinal obstruction”).

parole.significato: Holm oak (Quercus ilex).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ilex (“holm oak”).

parole.significato: Relating to ancient Ilium, or Troy.
parole.testo: Latin Iliacus.

parole.significato: A specific version, edition, translation, or copy of the above-mentioned Homeric text.
parole.testo: From Latin Iliadis, genitive of Ilias, from Ancient Greek Ἰλιάς (Iliás), the poem about Ἴλιον (Ílion, an alternative name for Troy). By surface analysis, Ili- + -ad.

parole.significato: An acid derived from various plants, such as the holly (Ilex).
parole.testo: From Latin ilex, ilicis (“holm oak”).

parole.significato: The upper and widest of the three bones that make up each side of the hipbone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īlium (“lower abdomen”), from īle (“flank”).

parole.significato: A gliding in; an immission or entrance of one thing into another.
parole.testo: From Latin illapsus (“a falling, gliding, or flowing in; an irruption”); from illābor (“to fall, to slide”) + -tus (“suffix forming action nouns from verbs”).

parole.significato: Capable of being ensnared or entrapped.
parole.testo: From Latin illaqueō (“to entrap”) + -able.

parole.significato: Trapping or entangling someone or something in a noose, snaring; hanging.
parole.testo: From Latin illaqueare + -ation.

parole.significato: The act of inferring or concluding, especially from a set of premises; a conclusion, a deduction.
parole.testo: From Latin illātiō (“logical inference, deduction, conclusion”), from illātus, perfect passive participle of inferō (“carry or bring into somewhere; conclude”), from in + ferō (“bear, carry; suffer”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to an illation.
parole.testo: From Late Latin illātīvus (“illative”), from Latin illātus, perfect passive participle of inferō (“carry or bring into somewhere; bury; conclude”), from in + ferō (“bear, carry; suffer”).

parole.significato: Not laudable; unpraiseworthy.
parole.testo: From Late Latin illaudabilis.

parole.significato: Tending to attract; enticing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin and Latin illecebrōsus (“attractive, enticing”) + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives denoting possession or presence of a quality, commonly in abundance). Illecebrōsus is derived from illecebra (“enticement, lure”) + -ōsus (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘full of’);

parole.significato: Not conforming to known principles, or established or accepted rules or standards.
parole.testo: First attested in 1536, from Latin illēgitimus, most likely an adapted borrowing of Middle French illegitime, equivalent to il- + legitimate, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).

parole.significato: The practice of (excessively) referring to oneself in the third person.
parole.testo: From Latin ille (“that man; he”) + -ism, modelled on egoism.

parole.significato: Someone who refers to themselves in the third person.
parole.testo: From Latin ille (“that man; he”) + -ist.

parole.significato: An external embodiment of the self.
parole.testo: From Latin ille (“that man; he”) + -ity.

parole.significato: Synonym of unfreedom.
parole.testo: From Latin illibertatem (“unfreedom”), equivalent to il- + liberty.

parole.significato: The modified dorsal fin on the head of anglerfish, acting as a lure.
parole.testo: Latin illiciō (“entice”)

parole.significato: The act of smearing or rubbing in or on.
parole.testo: From Latin illiniō (“to besmear”), from in- (“in, on”) + liniō (“to smear”).

parole.significato: The melting or dissolving of one thing into another.
parole.testo: From il- (“in”) + Latin liquare (“to melt”).

parole.significato: The act of dashing or striking against.
parole.testo: Latin illisio, from illidere, illisum, to strike against; prefix il- in + laedere to strike.

parole.significato: Unable to read and write.
parole.testo: First attested in 1425–1475, in Middle English; from Middle English illiterat(e) (“uneducated, ignorant of Latin”), borrowed from Latin illīterātus, illitterātus (“unlearned, ignorant”), itself from in- (“un-”) + līterātus, litterātus (“furnished with letters”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)),

parole.significato: The aim of a speaker in making an utterance as opposed to the meaning of the terms used.
parole.testo: From il- (“in”) (an assimilated version of in-) + locution (“speech”), from Latin loquor.

parole.significato: To give a false impression to.
parole.testo: From Latin illūdō.

parole.significato: To shine light on something.
parole.testo: From Middle English illuminaten, borrowed from Latin illūminātus, perfect passive participle of illūminō (“lighten, light up, show off”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from in + lūminō (“light up”), from lūmen (“light”). Cognate with Old English lȳman (“to glow, shine”). More at leam.

parole.significato: Enlightened, illuminated, made bright.
parole.testo: From Latin illūminātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more. For sense 3, see also Lumières.

parole.significato: A member of any of various societies, sects or other people claiming religious or intellectual enlightenment.
parole.testo: From Latin illūminātus.

parole.significato: Subject to or pertaining to an illusion, often used in the sense of an unrealistic expectation or an unreachable goal o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin illūsīvus.

parole.significato: Admired, distinguished, respected, or well-known.
parole.testo: From Latin illūstris (“bright, shining; distinguished, prominent, illustrious”) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, to denote possession or presence of a quality in any degree). Illūstris is derived from illūstrō (“to brighten, illuminate; to make famous or illustrious”), from in- (“in, in

parole.significato: The act of smearing the body with mud, especially with the sediment from mineral springs; a mud bath.
parole.testo: From il- (“in”) + Latin lutum (“mud”).

parole.significato: Expressing negation; not.
parole.testo: From Latin im-, assimilated form of in- used before b-/p-/m-.

parole.significato: Able to be imagined; conceivable.
parole.testo: From Middle English ymaginable, from Latin imāginābilis; equivalent to imagine + -able.

parole.significato: imagining; conceiving, or imaginative
parole.testo: From Latin imaginans, present participle of imaginari: compare French imaginant.

parole.significato: Existing only in the imagination.
parole.testo: From Middle English ymaginarie, ymagynary, from Latin imāginārius (“relating to images, fancied”), from imāgō, equivalent to imagine + -ary. The mathematical sense derives from René Descartes's use (of the French imaginaire) in 1637, La Geometrie, to ridicule the notion of regarding non-real roots o

parole.significato: One who imagines.
parole.testo: From Latin imāginātus (past participle of imāginārī) + English -or. Compare Middle English ymagynatourys (“?schemers or plotters”).

parole.significato: The final developmental stage of an insect after undergoing metamorphosis.
parole.testo: From Latin imāgō. Doublet of image. Compare typologically a Russian term for coordinate larva: личи́нка (ličínka) (akin to лик (lik)).

parole.significato: A depiction of a deceased or famous person on a round shield (clipeus), popular in the art, manuscripts and architectur…
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: The study of cultural stereotypes as presented in literature etc.
parole.testo: From Latin imago (“image”) + -logy.

parole.significato: A type of dry north wind which blows in the eastern Mediterranean.
parole.testo: A widespread word in the Mediterranean related to Latin battuo (“beat, strike”). Possibly directly from Ottoman Turkish ایمبات (imbat, “sea breeze; etesian”). Doublet of limbat.

parole.significato: Not warlike or martial.
parole.testo: From Latin imbellis, from im- = in- (“not”) + bellum (“war”). Compare Latin bellicus (“warlike”).

parole.significato: To drink (used frequently of alcoholic beverages).
parole.testo: From Middle English imbiben, from Latin imbibō, from im- + bibō (“to drink”) (whence also beverage), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃-, whence also potable, potion.

parole.significato: Lack of goodness.
parole.testo: From im- (“not”) + Latin bonitās (“goodness”).

parole.significato: A roof tile common in Ancient Greek and Roman architecture, used in an overlapping formation with the tegula.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin imbrex.

parole.significato: To overlap in a regular pattern.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin imbricātus (“tiled”).

parole.significato: To instill or inspire (someone) with a certain quality, feeling, or idea.
parole.testo: From Latin imbuō (“wet, moisten”). Compare imbibe.

parole.significato: To put into a purse; to save, to store up.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin imbursāre, Late Latin imbursāre, from Latin im- (variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside’ usually affixed to verbs)) + bursa (“animal skin, oxhide; purse (usually made of leather or skin); supply of money, funds”) (from Ancient Greek βῠ́ρσᾰ (bŭ́rsă, “animal skin; skin stripped

parole.significato: Tendency to imitation.
parole.testo: From Latin imitāns, present participle of imitō.

parole.significato: To follow as a model or a pattern; to make a copy, counterpart or semblance of.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin imitātus, perfect active participle of imitor (“to copy, portray, imitate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French imiter.

parole.significato: Imitating; copying; not original.
parole.testo: From Latin imitātīvus.

parole.significato: A female imitator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin imitātrīx. By surface analysis, imitate + -trix.

parole.significato: Having no blemish or stain; absolutely clean and tidy.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English immaculat, immaculate (“blameless; flawless, spotless; specifically of the Virgin Mary: pure, undefiled”), borrowed from Latin immaculātus (“unstained”), from im- (negative prefix) + maculātus (“stained, spotted; defiled, polluted; (figurative) dishonoured”), the perfect pas

parole.significato: A flowing or entering in.
parole.testo: From im- (“in”) + Latin manare (“to flow”). Compare mantio (“a flowing”).

parole.significato: Very large; huge; vast.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin immānis.

parole.significato: Great size; enormousness, hugeness.
parole.testo: From Latin immānitās.

parole.significato: Youth; the condition of being immature or not fully grown
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin immātūritātem.

parole.significato: Inability to pass through or to permit passage.
parole.testo: From im- (“not”) + Latin meabilis (“passable”), from meare (“to pass”).

parole.significato: That cannot be remembered or has been forgotten.
parole.testo: From Latin immemorabilis (“not memorable”).

parole.significato: undeserving
parole.testo: From Latin immeritus, from im- (“not”) + meritus, past participle of merere, mereri (“to deserve”).

parole.significato: To place within a fluid (generally a liquid, but also a gas).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin immersus, from immergō, from in + mergō.

parole.significato: The act of immersing or the condition of being immersed.
parole.testo: From late Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin immersiō, immersiōnem (“dipping”).

parole.significato: A non-native person who comes to a country from another country to permanently settle there.
parole.testo: From Latin immigrans, present active participle of immigrāre (“to migrate into”), from in- (“into”) + migrāre (“to migrate”).

parole.significato: To move into a foreign country to stay permanently.
parole.testo: From Latin immigratus, past participle of immigro (“remove, move into”).

parole.significato: The state or condition of being about to happen; imminent quality.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin imminentia.

parole.significato: About to happen, occur, or take place very soon, especially of something which won't last long.
parole.testo: From the present participle of Latin imminēre (“to overhang”), from mineō ("to project, overhang"), related to minae (English menace) and mons (English mount). Compare with eminent.

parole.significato: reduction; lessening; decrease.
parole.testo: From Latin imminutio, from imminuere, imminutum (“to lessen”), from im- (“in”) + minuere.

parole.significato: insertion of the penis (into a vagina or anus)
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: The act of immitting; injection or infusion.
parole.testo: From Latin immissiō.

parole.significato: To send in, put in, insert, inject or infuse
parole.testo: From Latin immitĕre, from in (“into”) and mittĕre, missum (“to send”).

parole.significato: Lack of moderation; excess.
parole.testo: Latin immoderantia.

parole.significato: Not moderate; excessive.
parole.testo: From Middle English inmoderat, immoderate, from Latin immoderātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To kill as a sacrifice by burning.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1534, the verb in 1548; borrowed from Latin immolātus, perfect passive participle of immolō (“to sacrifice”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: One who offers in sacrifice.
parole.testo: Latin immolator

parole.significato: Not susceptible to death; living forever; never dying.
parole.testo: From Latin immortālis, from prefix im- (“not”) (from in-) + mortālis (“mortal”) (from mors (“death”), combining form mort- + adjectival suffix -alis), equivalent to im- + mortal. Displaced native undeadly, from Old English undēadlīċ. The term referring to the Persian soldiers was a Calque of Ancient

parole.significato: unclean or impure
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin immundus.

parole.significato: Unable to be changed without exception.
parole.testo: From Middle English immutable, from Latin immūtābilis (“unchangeable”); im- + mutable.

parole.significato: unchanged
parole.testo: First attested in 1788; borrowed from Latin immūtātus, from in- (“not”) + mūtātus (“changed”), perfect passive participle of mūtō (“to change”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: change (alteration, mutation, modification)
parole.testo: From Latin immutatio, from immutare, immutatum (“to change”). See immute.

parole.significato: To change or alter.
parole.testo: From Latin immutare, immutatum, from im- (“in”) + mutare (“to change”). Compare Old French immuter. See mutable.

parole.significato: implacable (unable to be appeased)
parole.testo: From Latin im- (“not”) + pacare (“to quiet”). See pacate.

parole.significato: The striking of one body against another; collision.
parole.testo: Attested since the 17th century, from Latin impāctus.

parole.significato: A compression; the packing together of loose matter.
parole.testo: From Latin impingere (“to dash against, impinge”).

parole.significato: Any of several machines or devices in which a part impacts on another, or on a material.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin impāctor, from impingō + -tor.

parole.significato: A diseased state affecting the inhabitants of paludal, marshy areas.
parole.testo: Latin palus (“marsh”) + -ism

parole.significato: To embody in bread, especially in the bread of the Eucharist.
parole.testo: From Late Latin impānātus, past participle of impānō.

parole.significato: The actual, substantial presence of the body of Christ with the bread and wine of the sacrament of the Lord's Supper —…
parole.testo: From Latin impānātiō, impānātiōnis, from Latin impānātus, past participle of impānō (“to impanate”), + -tiō, from im- (“in”) + pānis (“bread”). By surface analysis, impanate + -ion.

parole.significato: One who holds the doctrine of impanation.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Having an odd number of fingers or toes.
parole.testo: From Latin impar (“unequal”) + digitus (“finger”).

parole.significato: pinnate with a single leaflet at the apex
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin impar (“unequal”) + English pinnate.

parole.significato: Not having the same number of syllables in all its inflections (especially of Greek or Latin nouns); for example, the L…
parole.testo: From Latin impar (“unequal”) + syllabic.

parole.significato: The state or condition of being impassible.
parole.testo: From impassible + -ability, from Latin impassibilitas.

parole.significato: Impatience.
parole.testo: From Latin impatientia + -ency.

parole.significato: fearless, undaunted
parole.testo: From Latin impavidus, itself from im- (“not”) + pavidus (“fearful”).

parole.significato: Lacking money.
parole.testo: From im- + pecunious, from Latin pecūniōsus, from pecūnia (“money”) + -ōsus (“full of”).

parole.significato: To get in the way of; to hinder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin impediō (“to shackle”), from pēs (“foot”) (compare pedestrian). First attested use as a verb was in William Shakespeare's Macbeth, see quotations.

parole.significato: Serving to make a marriage illicit but valid.
parole.testo: Latin impediēns (“hindering”).

parole.significato: A hindrance; that which impedes or obstructs progress; impedance.
parole.testo: From Middle English impediment, borrowed from Latin impedimentum.

parole.significato: Hindered; obstructed.
parole.testo: From Latin impeditus.

parole.significato: That which impedes; a hindrance.
parole.testo: From Latin impeditio.

parole.significato: To urge a person; to press on; to incite to action or motion via intrinsic motivation.
parole.testo: From Middle English impellen, borrowed from Latin impellō.

parole.significato: To hang or be suspended over (something); to overhang.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin impendere (“to hang over, to weigh out”), 1590s.

parole.significato: impending; threatening
parole.testo: From Latin impendēns.

parole.significato: the property of being impenitent, of lacking penitence, of not being regretful of wrongs done
parole.testo: From Late Latin impaenitentia.

parole.significato: Not penitent; specifically (Christianity), not repenting of one's sins; unrepentant.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English impenitent (“not penitent, unrepentant”), from Latin impaenitentem, the accusative feminine or masculine singular of impaenitēns (“unrepentant”), from im- (a variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + paenitēns (“contrite, penitent, regretting, repentin

parole.significato: commanding
parole.testo: From Latin imperans, present participle of imperare (“to command”).

parole.significato: To command.
parole.testo: First attested in 1543, as an adjective, as a verb in 1598; borrowed from Latin imperātus, perfect passive participle of imperō (“to command”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of mpret.

parole.significato: The action of governing or commanding; governance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin imperationem (accusative of imperatio).

parole.significato: Essential; crucial; extremely important.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin imperātīvus.

parole.significato: The reigning emperor; Male equivalent of Imperatrix
parole.testo: From Latin imperator (“emperor”).

parole.significato: An emperor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin imperātor. By surface analysis, imperate + -or. Doublet of emperor and mpret.

parole.significato: Commanding; authoritative.
parole.testo: Latin imperatorius.

parole.significato: Not destructible.
parole.testo: From im- (“not”) + Latin perdere (“to destroy”).

parole.significato: Domineering, arrogant, or overbearing.
parole.testo: From Latin imperiōsus (“mighty, powerful”), from imperium (“command, authority, power”).

parole.significato: Supreme power; dominion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin imperium (“power, command”), from imperō (“command, order”), from im- (form of in) + parō (“prepare, arrange; intend”). Doublet of empery and empire.

parole.significato: A state within a state, inclusive of deep states or other forces which operate with sovereign-like impunity within a po…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin imperium in imperio.

parole.significato: Not capable of being sought or understood; inscrutable.
parole.testo: Latin imperscrutabilis.

parole.significato: Not perspirable, not capable of sweating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin imperspīrābilis. By surface analysis, im- + perspirable.

parole.significato: impermeable
parole.testo: From Latin im- (“not”) + pertransire (“to go through”). See per- and transient.

parole.significato: Freedom from agitation of mind; calmness.
parole.testo: Latin imperturbatio.

parole.significato: Unaffected or unable to be affected by something.
parole.testo: From Latin impervius (“that cannot be passed through”), from in- (“not”) + pervius (“letting things through”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or suffering from, impetigo.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin impetīginōsus.

parole.significato: A contagious bacterial skin disease forming pustules and yellow crusty sores, chiefly on the face and hands. It is comm…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin impetīgō, from impetĕre (literally “to rush upon, assail, attack”).

parole.significato: Capable of being obtained or influenced by petition.
parole.testo: From Latin impetrabilis. Compare French impétrable. See impetrate.

parole.significato: To obtain by asking; to procure upon request.
parole.testo: First attested in 1528; borrowed from Latin impetrātus, perfect passive participle of impetrō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- + pātrō (“to achieve, make happen”).

parole.significato: The act of impetrating, or obtaining by petition or entreaty.
parole.testo: From Latin impetrātiō: compare French impétration.

parole.significato: Of the nature of impetration; getting, or tending to get, by entreaty.
parole.testo: Latin impetrativus (“obtained by entreaty”).

parole.significato: Anything that impels; a stimulating factor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin impetus (“a rushing upon, an attack, assault, onset”), from impetō (“to rush upon, attack”), from in- (“upon”) + petō (“to seek, fall upon”).

parole.significato: To pledge or pawn.
parole.testo: From Latin impignoratus, perfect passive participle of impignorare (“to pawn”). See pignoration.

parole.significato: The act of pawning or pledging; the state of being pawned.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin impignoratio: compare French impignoration.

parole.significato: To make a physical impact on.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin impingō (“dash against, impinge”). Compare impact, derived from the perfect passive participle of impingō.

parole.significato: Striking against or upon; impinging.
parole.testo: From Latin impingens.

parole.significato: To fatten; to make fat.
parole.testo: From Latin impinguatus, past participle of impinguare (“to fatten”); prefix im- (“in”) + pinguis (“fat”).

parole.significato: Not pious.
parole.testo: From Latin impius.

parole.significato: To bring about; to put into practice; to carry out.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin implēmentum (“a filling up”), from Latin impleō (“to fill up”).

parole.significato: An act of filling; the state of being full.
parole.testo: From Late Latin implētiō (past participle of Latin impleō (“to fill up”) + -iō); see also implement.

parole.significato: Intricate, involved, entangled, complicated, complex.
parole.testo: From Latin implexus.

parole.significato: The antecedent in the if-clause; the well-formed formula (wff).
parole.testo: From Latin implicans.

parole.significato: To show to be connected or involved in an unfavorable or criminal way.
parole.testo: First attested in the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English implicaten (poorly attested), from implicat(e) (“wrapped, entwined; involved, connected (with)”, possibly also used as the past participle of implicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin implicātus,

parole.significato: That which is implied.
parole.testo: Introduced by Paul Grice in 1975, from Latin.

parole.significato: Entreating, supplicatory.
parole.testo: From Latin implōrātus + English -atory (suffix forming adjectives of, relating to, or connected with [the specified thing]). Implōrātus is the perfect passive participle of implōrō (“to beseech, entreat, implore; to appeal to, pray to”): see further at implore.

parole.significato: A low basin in the center of a household atrium, into which rainwater flowed down from the roof through the compluvium.
parole.testo: Latin impluvium, from impluit (“rains upon”)

parole.significato: Not polite; discourteous; not of polished manners; wanting in good manners.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin impolītus. Equivalent to im- + polite.

parole.significato: To stake; to wager; to pledge.
parole.testo: From Latin imponere, impositum (“to place upon”); prefix im- (“in”) + ponere (“to place”). See imposition.

parole.significato: That imposes a rule.
parole.testo: From Latin impōnēns (“laying aside”), present active participle of impōnō (“to put upon”), from im- + pōnō (“put, place”).

parole.significato: Importance; significance.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin importantia.

parole.significato: Having relevant and crucial value; having import.
parole.testo: From Middle English important, from Medieval Latin important-, importāns. By surface analysis, import (“to be important”) + -ant. Displaced native Old English hēah and hefiġ.

parole.significato: Grievous, severe, exacting.
parole.testo: From Middle English importune, inportune, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French importun and its etymon Classical Latin importūnus.

parole.significato: Without a port or harbour.
parole.testo: From Latin importuosus, from im- (“not”) + portuosus (“abounding in harbours”), from portus (“harbour”).

parole.significato: A female impostor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin impostrīx. By surface analysis, impostor + -trix.

parole.significato: The inability of males to perform coition, often (but not necessarily) as a result of erectile dysfunction.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin impotentia coeundī (“incapacity to copulate”).

parole.significato: To call down by prayer, as something hurtful or calamitous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin imprecātus, perfect active participle of imprecor (“to invoke (good or evil) upon, pray to, call upon”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“upon”) + precor (“to pray”).

parole.significato: The act of imprecating, or invoking evil upon someone; a prayer that a curse or calamity may befall someone.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin imprecātiō (“calling down of curses”), from imprecor (“call down, invoke”).

parole.significato: To cause to become pregnant.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1540, the verb in 1605; borrowed from Medieval Latin impraegnātus, perfect passive participle of Latin impraegnō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of impregn; participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern Englis

parole.significato: Synonym of unprepared.
parole.testo: From Latin impraeparātus. Attested since the 17th century.

parole.significato: To affect (someone) strongly and often favourably; to inspire admiration from (someone).
parole.testo: From Middle English impressen, from Latin impressus, perfect passive participle of imprimere (“to press into or upon, stick, stamp, or dig into”), from in (“in, upon”) + premere (“to press”).

parole.significato: One who, or that which, impresses.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?] (“printer”).

parole.significato: An official license to publish or print something, especially when censorship applies.
parole.testo: From Latin imprimātur (“let it be printed”), third person singular present subjunctive passive form of imprimere (“to imprint”).

parole.significato: In the first place (used to introduce a list of items or considerations).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin imprimis (“firstly”).

parole.significato: Not likely to be true.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin improbābilis. By surface analysis, im- + probable.

parole.significato: To disallow, disqualify, or annul.
parole.testo: First attested in 1656; borrowed from Latin improbātus, perfect passive participle of improbō (“to disapprove”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“not”) + probō (“to approve”).

parole.significato: disapproval
parole.testo: Latin improbatio.

parole.significato: A lack of probity or integrity; dishonesty.
parole.testo: From im- + probity, from Latin improbitas.

parole.significato: Not prompt; delayed.
parole.testo: From Latin imprōmptus. By surface analysis, im- + prompt.

parole.significato: A reproach; an instance of upbraiding or contumely.
parole.testo: From Latin improperare.

parole.significato: A series of antiphons and responses expressing the remonstrance of Jesus Christ with his people, usually sung on Good F…
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?] (“reproaches”).

parole.significato: To appropriate for private use.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin impropriātus, past participle of impropriāre (“to take as one's own, appropriate”), from Latin in- + proprius (“one's own”).

parole.significato: Lack of prosperity.
parole.testo: From im- + prosperity, from Latin improsperitas.

parole.significato: Synonym of unprotected.
parole.testo: From Latin imprōtēctus. By surface analysis, im- + protected.

parole.significato: To disprove or make void; to refute.
parole.testo: From Latin improbō (“disapprove, reject”). Doublet of improbate.

parole.significato: failing to provide for the future; reckless
parole.testo: From the Latin improvidens, equivalent to in- + provident.

parole.significato: Not prepared beforehand; unpremeditated; extemporaneous.
parole.testo: From Latin improvisus (“unforeseen”); compare Italian improvviso.

parole.significato: The fact or quality of being imprudent; rashness.
parole.testo: From Latin imprūdēntia.

parole.significato: Immature; not having come to puberty.
parole.testo: From the stem of Latin impubes, from im- + pubes (“mature age, puberty”).

parole.significato: Impudence, insolence.
parole.testo: From Latin impudēntia.

parole.significato: Not showing due respect; bold-faced, impertinent.
parole.testo: From Middle English impudent, originally meaning immodest, shameless, from Latin impudēns (“shameless”), ultimately from in- + pudere (“to feel shame”).

parole.significato: One who or that which impels; an inciter, an instigator.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin impulsor.

parole.significato: Unpunished.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin impūnis.

parole.significato: The point where the ecliptic crosses the northern meridian, said to represent the deep subconscious.
parole.testo: From Latin imum coeli (“bottom of the sky”).

parole.significato: In summary; briefly or simply.
parole.testo: Calque of New Latin in nuce, derived from an anecdote in Pliny the Elder, who ascribes to Cicero the claim that the whole Iliad was once written on parchment and enclosed within a nutshell (Naturalis Historia 7.21.85). Compare typologically Czech stručný, stručně (< struk).

parole.significato: While not present; while absent
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin in absentia (“in absence”).

parole.significato: Between antae; where columns are set between two antae, forming the angles of the building.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in antis.

parole.significato: At the moment of death. (In law, especially canon, or church, law, this expression can mean that someone has been given…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in articulō mortis (literally “in the article of death”), from in (“during; at”, preposition governing the ablative) + articulō, ablative singular form of articulus (“a joint; figuratively: a point in time, a moment”) + mortis, genitive singular of mors (“death”).

parole.significato: In secret or in private (in an enclosed room, behind closed doors).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in camerā (“in the chamber”).

parole.significato: In abridged form; in summary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in compendio.

parole.significato: In a concrete sense; concretely.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in concreto.

parole.significato: During copulation; in the copulative state.
parole.testo: From Latin in cōpulā.

parole.significato: Deriving from the linguistic expression used; for reason of ambiguity, division, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin in dictione, translation of Ancient Greek παρὰ τὴν λέξιν (parà tḕn léxin), which appears in chapter 4 of Aristotle’s Sophistical Refutations.

parole.significato: Daily.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in dies.

parole.significato: In being, in actuality, having actual existence (contradistinguished by in posse; compare in potentia).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in (“in”) + esse (“be”).

parole.significato: To the highest degree; archetypal, quintessential.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin in excelsīs (“on high, in the highest”), as in the Gloria.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the actions made by those in positions of authority; in the exercise of executive power.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in executivis.

parole.significato: At full length; unabbreviated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in extenso.

parole.significato: At the point of death.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in extrēmīs.

parole.significato: Ultimately, in the end; in conclusion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in fīne.

parole.significato: In the act of committing a misdeed.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin in flagrante delicto (literally “while the crime is blazing”), from in + flāgrō (“burn”) + dēlictō, form of dēlīctum (“crime, misdeed”).

parole.significato: A request to have a court waive filing fees in a civil action because the plaintiff is indigent.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin in fōrma pauperis (literally “in the manner of a pauper”).

parole.significato: morally, but not necessarily legally.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in forō conscientiae (“in the court of conscience”).

parole.significato: In the form of goods and services rather than money.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin in specie.

parole.significato: At the beginning, as a preliminary matter; specifically, before a particular procedure or proceeding takes place.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin in līmine (literally “in the threshold”).

parole.significato: In the right, proper or natural place.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in loco.

parole.significato: Assuming the place or position of a parent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in locō parentis (“in place of a parent”).

parole.significato: in an unfavorable or evil manner
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in malam partem.

parole.significato: In the middle of a storyline.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in mediās rēs (literally “into the middle of things”).

parole.significato: In memory (of); as a memorial.
parole.testo: From Latin in memoriam (“into memory”).

parole.significato: Having a retroactive (ex post facto) effect that softens or mitigates a penalty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in mitius.

parole.significato: In default.
parole.testo: From Legal Latin in morā (“in delay”).

parole.significato: In a state of suspension; nebulous and unfulfilled.
parole.testo: Latin, meaning "in the clouds".

parole.significato: Dealing with the same matter or subject.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in pari materia.

parole.significato: Of a bishop or see: merely titular, without regular jurisdiction, and serving to assist some other bishop or to act as…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin in partibus īnfidēlium (literally “in the regions of the infidels”), so named because such bishops were assigned sees corresponding to territories that had passed under the control of other religions, and so did not imply a duty of residence or diocesan responsibil

parole.significato: In a lawsuit against a specific individual, a summons and complaint to give the court jurisdiction that is served to a…
parole.testo: From Latin in persōnam (literally “towards a person”).

parole.significato: In possibility, having a potential to exist, in potential but not in actuality, (contradistinguished by in esse)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in posse, from in (“in”) + posse (“to be able; can”).

parole.significato: Potentially; in posse but not in esse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in potentia, from in (“in”) + potentiā, ablative singular form of potentia (“force; power”).

parole.significato: By the person themselves; often used when a defendant is representing themselves in court without an attorney.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in propria persona.

parole.significato: In a purely natural state; naked.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in puris naturalibus.

parole.significato: In the matter of; with regard to.
parole.testo: From Latin in rē, literally meaning "in the matter [of]".

parole.significato: Against a thing (such as property) rather than a person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in rem (“against the thing”).

parole.significato: Sequentially, one after another.
parole.testo: By surface analysis, in + sequence. Possibly a confusion from Latin īnsequēns (“following, pursuing, next”, present active participle).

parole.significato: In computer simulation or in virtual reality.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from in and silicon (from Latin silex (“flint, pebble, stone; crag, rock”)) + Latin -ō, by analogy with English in vitro (“in glass, referring to an experiment conducted in a test tube”). The silico component refers to silicon chips which were used for computing at the time

parole.significato: In its original position or place.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in + sitū, ablative singular of situs.

parole.significato: In respect to kind
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in + specie, ablative singular form of species (“kind, form; type”).

parole.significato: Nascent; emerging but not yet fully formed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in statu nascendi, literally “in a state of being born”.

parole.significato: In the state of pupilage; subject to the rules of a college or university as they apply to junior members.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: In the former or same state.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin in statū quō (literally “in the state in which”). First attested in 1602.

parole.significato: As a warning or deterrent; in order to terrify or deter others.
parole.testo: From Latin in terrorem.

parole.significato: Asleep, sleeping.
parole.testo: In Ovid’s Metamorphoses, Morpheus is the god of dreams, and subsequently he was often referred to as the god of sleep. The name is borrowed from Latin Morpheus, from Ancient Greek Μορφεύς (Morpheús), from μορφή (morphḗ, “form, shape”) (alluding to the fact that Morpheus appeared in dreams in the for

parole.significato: At the point of death.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin in articulō mortis.

parole.parola: in the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king
parole.significato: Even someone with limited abilities or opportunities is dominant over, and considered special by, those who have even f…
parole.termine_origine: in regione caecorum rex est luscus

catena.termine: in regione caecorum rex est luscus

parole.testo: Calque of Latin in regione caecorum rex est luscus, popularized by Desiderius Erasmus’ Adagia (1500). For further origin compare Aramaic בשוק סמייא צווחין לעווירא סגי נהור (literally “in the street of the blind, the one-eyed man is called the guiding light”), found in the Genesis Rabbah (4th or 5th

parole.significato: In total.
parole.testo: From Latin in tōtō (“in all”).

parole.significato: in transit; during transportation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in transitu.

parole.significato: In use, in practice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in ure.

parole.significato: Occurring while a baby is within their mother's womb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in utero (“in the uterus”).

parole.significato: synonym of in utrumque partes
parole.testo: From Latin in utramque parte (“literally 'into both sides, to either part'”). A common variant of in utramque partem with the accusative singular partem misspelled or altered to parte (ablative singular), likely due to scribal error or conflation with the ablative case in late Latin.

parole.significato: Synonym of in utrumque partes
parole.testo: From Latin in utramque partem (“literally 'into both sides, to either part'”). Variant of in utrumque partes with feminine accusative singular utramque instead of neuter accusative plural utrumque, and singular partem instead of plural partes.

parole.significato: Arguing both sides of an issue; the practice of presenting arguments for and against a given proposition.
parole.testo: From Latin in utrumque partes (“literally 'into both sides, arguments for either part'”). From in + utrumque (accusative of uterque (“both”)) + partes (accusative plural of pars (“part, side”)). The phrase originates in rhetorical practice of arguing for and as a proponent against a proposition.

parole.significato: In a partial or full vacuum.
parole.testo: From Latin in vacuō (“in vacuum”).

parole.significato: Synonym of in wine, there is truth (one tells the truth under the influence of alcohol)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin in vīnō vēritās (literally “in wine there is truth”), from in (“in”) + vīnō, the ablative singular of vīnum (“wine”) + vēritās (“truth”). While various classical writers in both Greek and Latin make similar statements, the form in vino veritas is from the 16th-century humanis

parole.significato: In an artificial environment outside the living organism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in vitro, from vitrum (“glass”).

parole.significato: Within a living organism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin in vīvō.

parole.significato: Statements made or expressed under the influence of alcohol reveal true beliefs that are not expressed when sober.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin in vīnō vēritās.

parole.significato: in, into
parole.testo: From Middle English in-, borrowed (in words of Latinate origin) from Latin in-, from Latin in, from Proto-Indo-European *en (cognate to Germanic in-, above). Often borrowed from French in- (e.g. incise, incite, incline, indication), or as French en-, originally from Latin in.

parole.significato: Used with certain words to reverse their meaning.
parole.testo: PIE word  *né From Middle English in-, borrowed (in words of latinate origin) from Latin in- (“not”). Sometimes the Latin word has passed through French before reaching English (e.g. incapable, incertainty, inclement, incompatible). Doublet of un-.

parole.significato: consisting of goods or commodities (as opposed to money).
parole.testo: From in + kind, a calque of Latin in specie.

parole.significato: Not intentional; not on purpose; not conscious.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin inadvertēns.

parole.significato: Incapable of being lost.
parole.testo: From Latin inamissibilis.

parole.significato: enamoured; in love
parole.testo: First attested in 1602; borrowed from Latin inamōrātus, perfect passive participle of inamōrō (“to enamour”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + amor (“love”). Doublet of enamour and enamoured.

parole.significato: Lacking sense or meaning, often to the point of boredom or annoyance.
parole.testo: From Latin inānis (“empty, vain, useless”), of unknown origin.

parole.significato: Tending to speak inanely; loquacious; garrulous.
parole.testo: From Latin inānis (“empty, hollow, void; vain; worthless; foolish, inane”) + loquī (from loquor (“to say, speak, tell, talk”)); compare ināniloquium (“nonsense; vain talking”).

parole.significato: Lacking the quality or ability of motion; as an inanimate object.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English inanimat(e), from Late Latin inanimātus, from Latin in- + animātus (“animated”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, in- + animate. The noun was derived by substantivization from the adjective, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To animate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inanimātus, the perfect passive participle of inanimō (“to animate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in, into”) + animō (“to animate”); by surface analysis, in- + animate.

parole.significato: That cannot be apprehended; not apprehensible to or graspable by either body or mind.
parole.testo: Either from the Late Latin inapprehensibilis or formed in English as in- + apprehensible.

parole.significato: Embodied in, or changed into, water.
parole.testo: First attested in 1550; borrowed from Latin inaquātus, perfect passive participle of inaquō (“to turn into water”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + aqua (“water”) + -ō.

parole.significato: Not articulated in normal words.
parole.testo: From Latin inarticulatus and from in- + articulate. See -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Lacking in audacity; not audacious.
parole.testo: From Latin audacia (“boldness”), from audax (“bold”), from audeō (“to be bold, to dare”).

parole.significato: Inducted into a dignity or office with a formal ceremony or in a ceremonious manner; inaugurated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inaugurātus (“having been taken as an omen, divined; having been approved, consecrated, or inaugurated on the basis of omens; installed, having been installed”) (the perfect passive participle of inaugurō (verb): see etymology 1). See -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To cover with gold; to gild.
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1623, the adjective in 1826; borrowed from Latin inaurātus, perfect passive participle of inaurō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: inauspicious
parole.testo: From Latin inauspicatus; prefix in- (“not”) + auspicatus, past participle auspicari. Equivalent to in- + auspicate.

parole.significato: Becoming warmer; heating up; calescent.
parole.testo: From Latin incalēscēns, present participle of incalēscere, from in + calēscere (“to grow warm”).

parole.significato: hoary or grey; canescent.
parole.testo: From Latin incanescens, present participle incanescere (“to become gray”).

parole.significato: Hoary with a white pubescence.
parole.testo: From Latin incanus, from in- (“in”) + canus (“hoary”).

parole.significato: To state solemnly, to chant.
parole.testo: First attested in 1546; borrowed from Latin incantō. Doublet of enchant and incantate.

parole.significato: To sing or speak formulas and/or rhyming words, often during occult ceremonies, for the purpose of raising spirits, pro…
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin incantātus, perfect passive participle of incantō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of enchant and incant, cognate with French incantation.

parole.significato: To lock away; to imprison, especially for breaking the law.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1575; borrowed from Medieval Latin incarcerātus, perfect passive participle of incarcerō (“to imprison”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from Latin in- (“in”) + carcer (“a prison”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of confining, or the state of being confined; imprisonment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin incarcerātiō, equivalent to incarcerate + -ion.

parole.significato: Embodied in flesh; given a bodily, especially a human, form; personified.
parole.testo: First attested in 1395, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English incarnat(e) (“(of God or Christ) embodied in human form or flesh, incarnate; provided with new tissues, healed; (with devel, in curses) bloody”), borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātus, perfect passive participle of inca

parole.significato: To embody in flesh; to invest with a bodily, especially a human, form.
parole.testo: First attested in 1533; borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: Causing growth of new flesh i.e. healing or regenerative.
parole.testo: From Middle English incarnatif, incarnative, incarnatyf, incarnatyve, from Medieval Latin incarnātīvus.

parole.significato: To make into a castle.
parole.testo: First attested in 1552; borrowed from Medieval Latin incastellātus, perfect passive participle of incastellō (“to fortify, incastle, incastellate”) from in- (“in-: make into”) + castellum (“little fortification, castle; cistern”). Cognate with Italian incastellare.

parole.significato: To add castles to a place.
parole.testo: From Mediaeval Latin incastellāre (“to fortify, to incastle”), from in- (“in-: make into”) + castellum (“little fortification, castle”). Cognate with Italian incastellare and Old French encasteler.

parole.significato: The act of linking together; enchaining.
parole.testo: From Latin incatenatio, from Latin in- (“in”) + catena (“chain”). See enchain.

parole.significato: To officially invest into a position of authority.
parole.testo: First attested in 1635; borrowed from Medieval Latin incathedrātus, perfect passive participle of incathedrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: hollowed, bent round or in, or concave
parole.testo: From Latin incavatus, past participle of incavare (“to make hollow”), from in- (“in”) + cavare (“to hollow out”), from cavus (“hollow”).

parole.significato: Majestically.
parole.testo: From Latin incedere (“to walk majestically”) + English -ing + -ly.

parole.significato: To inflame; to excite.
parole.testo: From Latin incendere, incensum (“to kindle, burn”). See incense (“to inflame”).

parole.significato: Promoting faction or contention; seditious; inflammatory.
parole.testo: From Latin incendiosus (“burning, hot”). Compare incendiary.

parole.significato: The act of heating or burning
parole.testo: From Latin incensio. See incense (“to inflame”).

parole.significato: Synonym of censer (“religious ornamental container for burning incense”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin incēnsōrium. First attested in 1598. By surface analysis, incense + -ory.

parole.significato: Something that motivates, rouses, or encourages.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin incentīvus (“that strikes up or sets the tune”), from incinō (“to strike up”), from in- (“in, on”) + canō (“to sing”) + -ive. The formation appears to have been influenced by incendō (“to set on fire”).

parole.significato: To take in or ingest.
parole.testo: * Originally borrowed from Latin inceptus, past participle of incipio. The term is marked "obsolete" in the first edition of the OED (1905); newer usage is a back-formation from inception. * (put an idea into someone's mind): Inspired by the film Inception (2010).

parole.significato: The creation or beginning of something; the establishment.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin inceptiō, from inceptus, perfect passive participle of incipiō (“to begin”). The layering sense derives from the 2010 science fiction film Inception, in which a team of people infiltrate someone’s subconscious mind, proceeding through several layers of dreams

parole.significato: A kind of freely-draining soil that forms quickly through alteration of parent material and has no accumulation of clay…
parole.testo: From Latin inceptum + -i- + -sol

parole.significato: A beginner; one in the rudiments.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inceptor.

parole.significato: ceration.
parole.testo: From Latin incerare (“to smear with wax”), from in- (“in”) + cerare (“to wax”), from cera (“wax”). Compare French incération.

parole.significato: Cleaving or sticking like wax.
parole.testo: From Latin cera (“wax”).

parole.significato: Without pause or stop; not ending, especially to the point of annoyance.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English incessaunte, from Late Latin incessāns, incessantem, from Latin in- + cessāns.
From Latin incedere, incessum (“to walk”).

parole.significato: Intense and active.
parole.testo: From Latin incessus + -ive, from Latin incesso + -ive.

parole.significato: Sexual relations between close relatives, especially immediate family members and sometimes first cousins, usually cons…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin incestus. Displaced Old English mǣġhǣmed (literally “relative-sex”). Doublet of inchaste.

parole.significato: An English unit of length equal to 1/12 of a foot or 2.54 cm.
parole.testo: From Middle English ynche, enche, from Old English ynċe, borrowed from Latin ū̆ncia (“Roman inch, various similar units”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one”). Doublet of ounce, uncia, onça, onza, oka, ouguiya, and awqiyyah.

parole.significato: Recently started but not fully formed yet; just begun; only elementary or immature.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1534, the verb circa 1631; borrowed from Latin incohātus (“begun, unfinished”), perfect passive participle of incohō (“to begin”), see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3). Cognate with Spanish incoar (“to initiate, commence, begin”).

parole.significato: Initial; as yet unformed; inchoate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inchoātīvus, formed by metathesis from incohātīvus, from incohō (“to begin”). Compare French inchoatif.

parole.significato: Impossible to tame.
parole.testo: From Latin incicur (“not tame”), from in- (“not”) + cicur (“tame”), + -able.

parole.significato: To separate and remove (something); to cut.
parole.testo: From Latin incīdere; prefix in- (“in”) + caedere (“to cut”). See concise, and compare incise.

parole.significato: To destroy by burning.
parole.testo: From Latin incinerātus, perfect participle of incinerō (“to burn into ashes”), from cinis (“ashes”).

parole.significato: A beginning, or first stage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin incipientia.

parole.significato: In an initial stage; beginning, starting, coming into existence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin incipiēns, present participle of incipiō (“begin”).

parole.significato: The first few words of a text, especially its first line.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin incipit (“it begins”).

parole.significato: Intelligently analytical and concise. (of a person or mental process)
parole.testo: Late Middle English (in the sense “cutting, penetrating”), borrowed from Medieval Latin incīsīvus, from incīdō (“to cut in, cut through”) + -īvus (“-ive”, adjectival suffix). Compare Middle French incisif.

parole.significato: A narrow-edged tooth at the front of the mouth of mammals, between the canines and adapted for cutting; in humans there…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin incīsor, from Latin incīdō (“to cut into, cut through”) + -tor (“-er, -or”, agent noun suffix).

parole.significato: a notch or indent
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin incisura.

parole.significato: A notch or indent.
parole.testo: From Latin incisura.

parole.significato: Inciting; stimulating.
parole.testo: From Latin incitans.

parole.significato: exclamation; (loud) utterance
parole.testo: From Latin inclamatio. See in- + claim + -ation.

parole.significato: Set; fast; fixed.
parole.testo: From Latin inclavatus, from in- (“in”) + clavare (“to fasten with nails”), from clavus (“nail”).

parole.significato: The quality of being inclement; lack of clemency.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin inclēmentia. By surface analysis, inclemen(t) + -cy.

parole.significato: Stormy, of rough weather; not clement.
parole.testo: From Latin inclēmēns (“unmerciful, severe”), from in- (“not”) + clēmēns (“mild, placid”).

parole.significato: To bring into a group, class, set, or total as a (new) part or member.
parole.testo: From Middle English includen, borrowed from Latin inclūdere (“to shut in, enclose, insert”), from in- (“in”) + claudere (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂w- (“key, hook, nail”). Doublet of enclose. Displaced native Old English belūcan (“to include,” also “to shut in”).

parole.significato: An addition or annex to a group, set, or total.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inclūsiō, inclūsiōnis, from the verb Latin inclūdō (“to shut in, enclose, insert”), from in- (“in”) + claudō (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂w- (“key, hook, nail”). By surface analysis, include + -sion. Doublet of enclosure.

parole.significato: Not cogitable; inconceivable.
parole.testo: From Latin incogitabilis, from in- (“not”) + cogitabilis (“cogitable”).

parole.significato: A lack of thought or thinking.
parole.testo: From Latin incōgitantia (“thoughtlessness”), from incōgitāns, from in- + cogitāns, present active participle of cōgitō (“think”).

parole.significato: thoughtless; inconsiderate
parole.testo: From Latin incogitans, from in- (“not”) + cogitans, present participle of cogitare (“to think”). See cogitate.

parole.significato: An American mammoth or mastodon, especially when presumed extant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin incognitum (“unknown”). Coined by William Hunter.

parole.significato: safety; security
parole.testo: From Latin incolumitas, from incolumis (“uninjured, safe”), perhaps from in (“intensifier”) + (doubtful) columis (“safe”).

parole.significato: Not commiscible; not mixable.
parole.testo: From Latin incommiscibilis, from in- (“not”) + commiscibilis (“that can be mingled”).

parole.significato: To incommode, make uncomfortable.
parole.testo: First attested in 1575; borrowed from Latin incommodātus, perfect passive participle of incommodō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of incommode.

parole.significato: inconvenience; trouble; annoyance; disadvantage
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin incommoditās. Compare French incommodité. See incommodious.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being incommutable.
parole.testo: Latin incommutabilitas: compare French incommutabilité.

parole.significato: The condition of being incomparable.
parole.testo: From Latin incomparabilitas.

parole.significato: Not complete; not finished.
parole.testo: From Middle English incomplete, incompleet, from Late Latin incomplētus, from in- (“un-; not”) + complētus (“complete”), equivalent to in- (“not”) + complete.

parole.significato: Not composite; simple or single.
parole.testo: From Latin incompositus. By surface analysis, in- + composite.

parole.significato: Lack of harmony or suitability.
parole.testo: From Latin inconcinnitas.

parole.significato: Not concinnous; unsuitable; discordant.
parole.testo: Latin inconcinnus.

parole.significato: inconcocted
parole.testo: From Latin in- (“not”) + concoctus, past participle of concoquere. See concoct.

parole.significato: Not concrete.
parole.testo: Latin inconcretus (“incorporeal”).

parole.significato: Unshakable;
parole.testo: From in- (“not”) + Latin concussibilis (“that can be shaken”). See concussion.

parole.significato: Badly-arranged, ill-composed, disorderly (especially of artistic works).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inconditus.

parole.significato: Not congealable; incapable of being congealed.
parole.testo: From Latin incongelabilis. Compare Portuguese incongelável. See congeal.

parole.significato: Not similar or congruent; not matching or fitting in.
parole.testo: From Latin incongruus, from in- (“not”) + congruus (“congruent”), equivalent to in- + congruous.

parole.significato: Invisible.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin incōnspicuus. Equivalent to in- + conspicuous.

parole.significato: Not consummated; unfinished; incomplete.
parole.testo: First attested in 1641; borrowed from Latin incōnsummātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: inconsumable
parole.testo: From Latin inconsumptibilis.

parole.significato: Not contaminated; pure.
parole.testo: From Latin incontaminatus, from in- (“not”), and contaminate.

parole.significato: Synonym of incontinence.
parole.testo: From Middle English incontinency, from Latin incontinentia. Doublet of incontinence.

parole.significato: The condition of being inconvertible
parole.testo: From Latin inconvertibilitas.

parole.significato: To include (something) as a part.
