parole.significato: The middle pair of tail feathers, or middle rectrices.
parole.testo: Latin intermedius intermedial.

parole.significato: Being between two extremes, or in the middle of a range.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin intermediātus, perfect passive participle of intermediō (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), further from intermedius (“intermediate”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To mediate, to be an intermediate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin intermediātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: To menace; to threaten.
parole.testo: From Latin intermināt-, passive perfect participial stem of interminor (“to threaten, menace”).

parole.significato: A menace or threat.
parole.testo: Latin interminatio.

parole.significato: A break, especially between two performances or sessions, such as at a concert, play, seminar, or religious assembly.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin intermissiō, from intermittō (“interrupt, omit”) + -tiō.

parole.significato: To interrupt, to stop or cease temporarily or periodically; to suspend.
parole.testo: From Latin intermittere, from inter- + mittere.

parole.significato: A space between worlds.
parole.testo: From Latin intermundium, singular of intermundia.

parole.significato: Between walls; enclosed by walls.
parole.testo: From Latin intermūrālis. By surface analysis, inter- + mural.

parole.significato: Of or situated on the inside.
parole.testo: From Middle English internall, internalle, borrowing from New Latin internālis (“of or pertaining to the inner part”), from internus (“inward, internal”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, intern + -al.

parole.significato: Between pregnancies or births.
parole.testo: From inter- + Latin nātālis (“relating to birth”).

parole.significato: Between the buttocks; intergluteal.
parole.testo: From inter- + Latin natis (“rump”) + -al.

parole.significato: Mutually destructive; most often applied to warfare.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin internecīnus (“deadly”), from internecium (“a massacre, bloodbath; an eradication”) + -īnus. In Latin, the sememe 'between' was here not expressed by the prefix, it instead either had a somewhat emphatic meaning or meant "down, under", comparable to its use in other Latin terms r

parole.significato: destruction, massacre
parole.testo: From Latin interneciō.

parole.significato: internecine
parole.testo: From Latin internecīvus.

parole.significato: intimate connection
parole.testo: From Latin internectere (“to bind together”), from inter (“between”) + nectere (“to fasten”).

parole.significato: To interrupt, break in upon, or intercede with.
parole.testo: Latin interpello, from inter (“between”) + pellare, akin to pellere (“to drive”), compare French interpeller.

parole.significato: interrupting.
parole.testo: From Latin interpellans. See interpel.

parole.significato: To interrupt (someone) so as to inform or question (that person about something).
parole.testo: First attested in 1599; borrowed from Latin interpellātus, perfect passive participle of interpellō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French interpeller.

parole.significato: To introduce (something) between other things; especially to insert (possibly spurious) words into a text.
parole.testo: From Latin interpolātus, perfect passive participle of interpolō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French interpoler.

parole.significato: To interpose; to insert or place between.
parole.testo: From Latin interponere; inter (“between”) + ponere (“to place”). See position.

parole.significato: An intermediate depot or station between one commercial city or country and another.
parole.testo: From Latin interpositus, past participle of interponere. See interposition.

parole.significato: Capable of being interpreted or explained.
parole.testo: From the Late Latin interpretābilis, from interpretor; equivalent to interpret + -able; compare the obsolete French interpretable.

parole.significato: interpretation
parole.testo: From Latin interpretamentum.

parole.significato: The punctuation mark ⟨·⟩.
parole.testo: From Latin interpunctus, from inter- (“between, mid-”) + punctus (“point”).

parole.significato: punctuation (insertion of points between words or sentences)
parole.testo: From Latin interpunctio, from interpungere, interpunctum (“to interpoint”). See inter- and point.

parole.significato: A period of time between the end of one monarch's reign and the accession of their successor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin interrēgnum, from inter- (prefix meaning ‘between’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁entér (“between”)) + rēgnum (“reign; royal power”) (nominalized from the neuter of *rēgnus, from rēx (“king; ruler”, oblique stem rēg-) + -nus (suffix forming adjectives), ultimat

parole.significato: An official in Ancient Rome who acted as single head of state during the interregnum between two consulates.
parole.testo: From Latin inter- (“between”) + rex (“king”).

parole.significato: To question or quiz, especially in a thorough or aggressive manner.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin interrogātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin interrogō (“to inquire, interrogate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Asking or denoting a question.
parole.testo: From Late Latin interrogātīvus, equivalent to interrogate + -ive.

parole.significato: One who interrogates; a person who asks questions, especially one who is adversarial.
parole.testo: From Latin interrogātor. By surface analysis, interrogate + -or.

parole.significato: A formal question or set of questions submitted to opposing party to answer, generally governed by court rule.
parole.testo: From Late Latin; equivalent to interrogate + -ory (“pertaining to”), or more distantly inter- + rogatory.

parole.significato: A female interrogator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin interrogātrīx. By surface analysis, interrogator + -trix.

parole.significato: To disturb or halt (an ongoing process or action, or the person performing it) by interfering suddenly, especially by s…
parole.testo: From Middle English interrupten, derived from Latin interruptus, past participle of interrumpere (“to break apart/off, interrupt”), from inter (“between”) + rumpere (“to break”).

parole.significato: To write or draw between.
parole.testo: From Latin interscribere; inter (“between”) + scribere (“to write”). By surface analysis, inter + scribe.

parole.significato: Crossing, intersecting; (figuratively) clashing, conflicting.
parole.testo: From Latin intersecans, present participle of intersecare. See intersect.

parole.significato: To cut into or between; to cut or cross mutually; to divide into parts.
parole.testo: From Latin intersecare (“to cut between, cut off”), from inter (“between”) + secare (“to cut”).

parole.significato: To put in between other things; to insert.
parole.testo: From Latin intersertus, past participle of interserere (“to intersert”), from inter (“between”) + serere (“to join, weave”).

parole.significato: sounding between
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intersonāns.

parole.significato: A space or interval between two things; an interstice
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin interspatium. By surface analysis, inter- + space.

parole.significato: To mix two things irregularly, placing things of one kind among things of other.
parole.testo: From Latin interspergō, interspersus.

parole.significato: spiritual inspiration at separate times, or at intervals
parole.testo: From Latin interspiratio. See inter- and spirit.

parole.significato: a planetary-mass object which has either been ejected from its system or was never gravitationally bound to any star or…
parole.testo: Constructed from Latin: inter- + stellar + planet. The latter derives from Middle English planete, from Old English planēta (“planet, chasuble”), from Latin planeta, planetes, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs) variant of πλάνης (plánēs, “wanderer, planet”), from πλανάω (planáō, “wander about, s

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or situated in an interstice.
parole.testo: From Latin interstitiālis. By surface analysis, interstitium + -al.

parole.significato: An interstice or interstitium; an interstitial space.
parole.testo: From Latin interstitiō, or by confusion with interstitium.

parole.significato: An interstitial space within a tissue or organ.
parole.testo: From Latin interstitium, from inter (“between”) + sistō (“to stand, place”).

parole.significato: To intertwine; to weave or bind together.
parole.testo: From Latin intertexere, from inter (“between”) + texere (“to weave”).

parole.significato: Chafing or dermatitis occurring between two folds of skin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin intertrīgō.

parole.significato: An interval.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intervallum.

parole.significato: To become involved in a situation, so as to alter or prevent an action.
parole.testo: Back-formation from intervention, and/or from Latin interveniō (“come between”, verb).

parole.significato: Being only in between other more important things; secondary, incidental.
parole.testo: From the present participle stem of Latin intervenīre.

parole.significato: One who intervenes; a mediator, especially one designated by a church to reconcile parties and unite them in the choice…
parole.testo: From Latin interventor. Compare French interventeur.

parole.significato: Embezzlement.
parole.testo: From Late Latin interversiō.

parole.significato: To turn to another course or use.
parole.testo: From Latin interverto.

parole.significato: The state of being intervolved or coiled up; a convolution
parole.testo: From Latin inter (“between”), from volvere (“to roll”).

parole.significato: To involve one with another.
parole.testo: From Latin inter (“between”), from volvere (“to roll”).

parole.significato: Without a valid will indicating whom to leave one's estate to after death.
parole.testo: From Latin intestātus, from in- (“not”) + testātus (“testate”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Relating to the intestines.
parole.testo: From Latin intestīnālis. By surface analysis, intestine + -al.

parole.significato: The alimentary canal of an animal through which food passes after having passed all stomachs.
parole.testo: From Latin intestīnum, neuter of intestīnus (“internal”), as Etymology 2, below.

parole.significato: Domestic; taking place within a given country or region.
parole.testo: From Latin intestīnus (“internal”), from intus (“within”).

parole.significato: Placed upon a throne; enthroned.
parole.testo: From Late Latin int(h)ronizātus, perfect participle participle of int(h)ronizō (“to inthronize”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The innermost part of an anatomical structure, particularly a tubular one
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intima, feminine form of intimus (“innermost”).

parole.significato: Closely acquainted; familiar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intimātus, the perfect passive participle of intimō (“to put or bring into, to impress, to make familiar”) (see -ate (adjective forming suffix)), from intimus (“inmost, innermost, most intimate”), superlative of intus (“within”), from in (“in”); see interior.

parole.significato: To suggest or disclose (something) discreetly.
parole.testo: From Latin intimātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more. Cognate with French intimer.

parole.significato: inward; internal; intimate
parole.testo: From Latin intimus (“innermost”) perhaps via French intime. Compare intimate (adjective).

parole.significato: To make timid or afraid; to cause to feel fear or nervousness; to deter, especially by threats of violence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin intimidātus, perfect passive participle of Latin intimidō (“to intimidate, terrify”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + timidus (“afraid, timid”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); see timid.

parole.significato: The act of steeping or soaking the bread (or 'body' of Christ) in the wine (or 'blood' of Christ) so the communicant ma…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin intinctiō, from intingere (“to dip in”).

parole.significato: To entitle.
parole.testo: From Late Latin intitulātus, past participle of intitulāre, whence intitule and entitle (obsolete intitle).

parole.significato: The state of being intolerable; intolerableness.
parole.testo: From Latin intolerabilitas.

parole.significato: To intone or recite (words), especially emphatically or in a chanting manner.
parole.testo: First attested in 1795; borrowed from Medieval Latin intonātus, perfect passive participle of intonō (“to vocalize, chant”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (inchoative prefix) + tonus (“pitch, tone”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); doublet of intone. Cognate with French entonner, Italian into

parole.significato: To thunder or to utter in a sonorous or thunderous voice.
parole.testo: First attested in 1631; borrowed from Latin intonātus, perfect passive participle of intonō (“to thunder forth”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A winding, bending, or twisting.
parole.testo: From Latin intortio (“a curling, crisping”). Compare French intorsion. See intort, and compare intortion.

parole.significato: To twist in and out; to twine; to wreathe, wind, or wring.
parole.testo: Latin intortus, past participle of intoquere (“to twist”) equivalent to in- (“in-”) + torquereto (“twist”).

parole.significato: To stupefy by doping with chemical substances such as alcohol.
parole.testo: First attested in 1450, in Middle English; from Middle English intoxicaten, from intoxicat(e) (“(of a weapon or drug) smeared, anointed or filled with poison; (of a human being, animal) poisoned, intoxicated”, also used as the past participle of intoxicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed fro

parole.significato: within the legal power or authority of a person or body
parole.testo: Latin “within the power”

parole.significato: Within a single entity indicated by the root word:
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intrā (“within”).

parole.significato: Within the ear.
parole.testo: From intra- (“within”) + aural (“ear”), from Latin roots.

parole.significato: Within the walls; within one institution, particularly a school.
parole.testo: From Latin intramuralis, from intra (“within”) + muralis (“of a wall”).

parole.significato: Internal, that is within.
parole.testo: From Latin intrāneus (“from within”).

parole.significato: Incapable of being transgressed; not to be passed over or crossed.
parole.testo: From Latin intragressibilis (“that can not be crossed”). See in- (“not”) + transgress + -ible.

parole.significato: That enters or penetrates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intrans, present participle of intrare (“to enter”).

parole.significato: During parturition (childbirth; labor).
parole.testo: From intra- + Latin partum (“giving birth”).

parole.significato: A piece of music which serves as an introduction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intrata.

parole.significato: During the life of an organism.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Having a great deal of fine detail or complexity.
parole.testo: From Middle English intricat(e) (“entangled, intricate”), from Latin intrīcātus, perfect passive participle of intricō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To become enmeshed or entangled.
parole.testo: As for Etymology 1; from Latin intrīcātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: An introduction.
parole.testo: Clipping of introduction, from Latin intrōductiō (“lead-in, introduction”) – the abbreviation removes the second part of the compound; the first part ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁énteros (“inner, what is inside”). The demoscene sense comes from the fact that they were originally prepended

parole.significato: inward, inwards.
parole.testo: From Latin intro- (“inwards”), from intro (“inward, inwards”), q.v.

parole.significato: A depression or inward sinking of parts.
parole.testo: From Latin introcedere, introcessum (“to go in”), from intro (“within”) + cedere (“to go”).

parole.significato: Someone who introduces someone or something.
parole.testo: From Latin introductor.

parole.significato: Introducing; giving a preview, idea or foretaste of.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin intrōductōrius, from Latin intrōductus.

parole.significato: To infiltrate the genes of one species into the gene pool of another through repeated backcrossing of an interspecific…
parole.testo: From Latin introgredior (“to step in, enter”).

parole.significato: The prayers spoken by the priest at the foot of the altar at the start of a Tridentine Mass.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin introībō ad altāre Deī (“I shall go in towards the altar of God”), the first line spoken.

parole.significato: The entrance to a hollow organ or canal; often specifically the entrance to the vagina.
parole.testo: From Latin introitus.

parole.significato: The entrance to the vagina.
parole.testo: From Latin introitus vāgīnæ (“entrance of [a/the] vagina”).

parole.significato: The state of being allowed to enter; admittance
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin intrōmissiō, intrōmissiōn- (“introduction, admission; usurpation”), intro- (“into”) + missiō (“sending”), from Latin intrōmissus (“sent in, introduced, let in, admitted”), perfect passive participle of intrōmittō (“send in, let in”).

parole.significato: To intermeddle with the effects or goods of another.
parole.testo: From Latin intrōmittō.

parole.significato: Facing or turned inwards or towards an axis.
parole.testo: From Latin introrsus, introrsum (“toward the inside”, adverb), variant of introversus, from intrō + versus (“turned”).

parole.significato: To engage in introspection.
parole.testo: From Latin intrōspectus, past participle of intrōspiciō. By surface analysis, intro- + -spect.

parole.significato: Examining one's own perceptions and sensory experiences; contemplative or thoughtful about oneself.
parole.testo: From Latin intro "inward, within" (see intro-) + Latin specere "look at".

parole.significato: Coming in together; entering; commingling.
parole.testo: From Latin introveniens, present participle of introvenire (“to come in”), from intro (“within”) + venire (“to come”).

parole.significato: A turning inward, particularly
parole.testo: From New Latin intrōversio, from intrōvertere (“to turn within”), from Classical Latin intro (“within”) and vertere (“to turn”). Equivalent to introvert + -sion or intro- + -version.

parole.significato: An organ or other body part that is or can be turned inside out, especially an anterior portion of some annelid worms c…
parole.testo: From New Latin intrōvertere, from intro- (“within”) and vertere (“to turn”). Popularized as a psychological term by the German works of Carl Jung. By surface analysis, intro- + -vert.

parole.significato: To thrust oneself in; to come or enter without invitation, permission, or welcome; to encroach; to trespass.
parole.testo: From Latin intrudere, from in- + trudere (“to thrust”).

parole.significato: To know intuitively or by immediate perception.
parole.testo: A back-formation from intuition and intuitive; compare Latin intuitus (“observed; considered”), perfect participle of intueor (“to look at, upon or towards; to observe, regard; to consider, contemplate”), from in- (“in, inside”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”)) + tueor (“to look or

parole.significato: To swell or enlarge (abnormally)
parole.testo: From Latin intumēscō.

parole.significato: That becomes swollen, especially upon exposure to heat.
parole.testo: From Latin intumēscēns, present participle of intumescō (“rise, swell”), from tumescō (“become inflated”).

parole.significato: unburied
parole.testo: From Latin intumulātus. See in- (“not”) + tumulate + -ed.

parole.significato: A swelling (the act of swelling, or state of being swelled).
parole.testo: From Latin inturgescens, present participle of inturgescere (“to swell up”), equivalent to in- + turgescence. See turgescent.

parole.significato: A bruise; a contusion.
parole.testo: From Latin intundere (“to bruise”), from in- (“in”) + tundere, tusum (“to beat, bruise”).

parole.significato: The part that prolapses into another during an intussusception.
parole.testo: From New Latin, probably from neuter singular of assumed New Latin intussusceptus, the passive past participle of New Latin intussuscipiō (“to take in”). Compare intussuscipiens.

parole.significato: The part that receives the prolapsed part during an intussusception.
parole.testo: From New Latin, probably from present participle of assumed New Latin intussuscipiō (“to take in”). Compare intussusceptum.

parole.significato: Any of several plants of the genus Inula, such as elecampane.
parole.testo: From Latin inula. Compare elecampane.

parole.significato: To put in shadow; to darken.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin inumbrātus, perfect passive participle of inumbrō (“to shade”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To smear with ointment.
parole.testo: From Latin inunctus, perfect passive participle of inunguere (“to anoint”). Doublet of anoint.

parole.significato: The anointing or rubbing in of oil or balm.
parole.testo: From Latin inunctio, from inunctus, past participle of inungo (“anoint”), from in- + ungo (“anoint”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“anoint”).

parole.significato: overflowing
parole.testo: From Latin inundans, present participle of inundare.

parole.significato: To cover with large amounts of water; to flood.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin inundātus, the perfect passive participle of inundō (“to flood, overflow”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- + undō (“to overflow, wave”), from unda (“wave”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: uncivil; unpolished; rude
parole.testo: From Latin inurbānus. By surface analysis, in- + urbane.

parole.significato: Unusual.
parole.testo: From Latin inūsitātus (“unusual; new; unseen; different”). See use.

parole.significato: burnt in
parole.testo: From Latin inurere, inustus (“to burn in”), from in- (“in”) + urere (“to burn”).

parole.significato: Uselessness.
parole.testo: From in- + utility, from Latin inutilitas.

parole.significato: To move into.
parole.testo: From Latin invādō (“enter, invade”).

parole.significato: sheathed
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin invāgīnātus, past participle of Medieval Latin invāgīnāre, from in- + vāgīna (“sheath”).

parole.significato: strength; health
parole.testo: From Latin invalescens, present participle of invalescere (“to become strong”). See in- and convalesce.

parole.significato: To import or introduce.
parole.testo: From Latin invehō (“bring in, carry in”), from in- + vehō (“carry”).

parole.significato: Having a border consisting of semicircles with the convex part outwards (and the points inwards).
parole.testo: From Latin invectus.

parole.significato: An inveighing against; invective.
parole.testo: From Latin invectio. See inveigh.

parole.significato: To complain loudly, to give voice to one's censure or criticism
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin invehō (“bring in, carry in”), from in- + vehō (“carry”). Compare vehicle, invective.

parole.significato: Not vendible or saleable.
parole.testo: From Latin invendibilis. See in- (“not”) + vendible.

parole.significato: One of the five canons of classical rhetoric: the method used for the discovery of arguments.
parole.testo: From Latin inventiō. Doublet of invention.

parole.significato: One who invents, either as a hobby or as an occupation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inventor. By surface analysis, invent + -or.

parole.significato: The stock of an item on hand at a particular location or business.
parole.testo: From Middle English inventorie, from Medieval Latin inventōrium, alteration of Late Latin inventārium, from Latin inveniō (“to find out”).

parole.significato: A female that invents.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin inventrīx. By surface analysis, inventor + -trix.

parole.significato: Immodest; shameless.
parole.testo: From Latin inverecundus, from in- + verecundus (“modest”), from vereri (“to revere”).

parole.significato: To curve so as to extend into
parole.testo: From Latin invergo, from in- + vergō (“to incline, turn”).

parole.significato: Opposite in effect, nature or order.
parole.testo: Recorded since 1440, from Latin inversus, the past participle of invertere (“to invert”), itself from in- (“against, in”) + vertere (“to turn”).

parole.significato: The action of inverting.
parole.testo: From Latin inversiōnem.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, characterised by, or causing inversion.
parole.testo: From Latin invers-, the past participial stem of invertō, + -ive.

parole.significato: The inverted part of a composition.
parole.testo: From Latin inversus.

parole.significato: The condition of being invertible.
parole.testo: From invertible + -ity, from Latin invertibilitas.

parole.significato: Serving to cover or clothe.
parole.testo: From Latin investiens, present participle of investire.

parole.significato: Capable of being investigated or studied.
parole.testo: From Latin investigabilis.

parole.significato: To inquire into or study in order to ascertain facts or information.
parole.testo: Recorded since circa 1510, a back-formation from investigation on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), from Latin investīgātiō (“a searching into”), from investīgātus, the perfect passive participle of investīgō, equivalent to in- + vestigate. Displaced native Old English undersēċan (literally “

parole.significato: One who investigates.
parole.testo: Attested in the mid‐16th century; from Latin investigator, from investigare, equivalent to investigate + -or.

parole.significato: Firmly established from having been around for a long time; of long standing.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1574; borrowed from Latin inveterātus (“of long standing, chronic”), perfect passive participle of inveterō and participial adjective (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in, into”) + veterō (“to age”),

parole.significato: The act of making inveterate.
parole.testo: From Latin inveteratio.

parole.significato: Unconquered; unsubdued.
parole.testo: From Latin invictus.

parole.significato: Causing ill will, envy, or offense.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin invidiōsus, from invidia (“envy, ill will”), from in- (“upon”) + videō (“to see”); the meaning developed from “look back at” to “look askance at” to “envy.” Doublet of envious, from Old French.

parole.significato: To oversee a test or exam.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin invigilātus, past participle of invigilō (“to stay awake, watch over”).

parole.significato: A person who supervises students during an examination; a proctor
parole.testo: From invigilate + -or, from Latin invigilatus, past participle of invigilo.

parole.significato: To impart vigor, strength, or vitality to.
parole.testo: First attested in 1646; borrowed from New Latin invigōrātus, perfect passive participle of invigōrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, in- + vigor + -ate.

parole.significato: Not violated; free from violation or hurt of any kind; secure against violation or impairment.
parole.testo: From Middle English inviolat, inviolate, from Latin inviolātus. By surface analysis, in- (“not”) + violate (adjective).

parole.significato: untrodden
parole.testo: From Latin invius, from in- (“not”) + via (“way”).

parole.significato: To daub, catch, or entangle with glue or birdlime or other viscous matter.
parole.testo: From Latin inviscatus, past participle of inviscare (“to birdlime”), from in- (“in”) + viscum, viscus (“mistletoe, birdlime”).

parole.significato: Deep-seated; internal.
parole.testo: Latin invisceratus, past participle.

parole.significato: The act of inviting; solicitation; the requesting of a person's company.
parole.testo: From Middle English invitacioun, ynvytacioun, from Latin invītātio, reinforced by Middle French invitation. By surface analysis, invite + -ation. Displaced native Middle English lathinge from Old English laþung (see dialectal English lathing).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an invitation
parole.testo: From Latin invitatorius.

parole.significato: To implore or invoke.
parole.testo: First attested in 1530; borrowed from Latin invocātus, perfect passive participle of invocō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of invoke.

parole.significato: One who invocates the spirits of the dead.
parole.testo: From Late Latin invocātor. By surface analysis, invocate + -or.

parole.significato: Containing or characterized by invocation; invoking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin invocō (“I invoke”) + -ory. Compare French invocatoire.

parole.significato: An involucel.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A protein component of human skin.
parole.testo: From Latin involūcrum (“wrapper, covering”) + -in.

parole.significato: A sheath that covers or envelopes, especially one that forms around the sequestrum of new bone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin involūcrum. Doublet of involucre.

parole.significato: Without intention; unintentional.
parole.testo: From in- + voluntary, from Late Latin involontarius, from in + volontarius.

parole.significato: Difficult to understand; complicated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin involutus.

parole.significato: Entanglement; a spiralling inwards; intricacy.
parole.testo: From Latin involūtiō, from involvō.

parole.significato: Invulnerable or unscathed.
parole.testo: First attested in 1680; borrowed from Latin invulnerātus (“unwounded”), from in- (“not”) + vulnerātus see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A form of witchcraft: piercing a wax or clay image of a person in order to harm them.
parole.testo: From Latin invultare (“to stab the face of”), from vultus (“face”).

parole.significato: A type of moth, the io moth.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek Ἰώ (Iṓ, “Io”).

parole.significato: An exclamation of joy or triumph.
parole.testo: From Latin iō; compare Ancient Greek ἰώ (iṓ, “oh!”).

parole.significato: Solitary masturbation.
parole.testo: From Latin ipse (“self”).

parole.significato: Denoting a measure that forces a person to choose among multiple desirable options.
parole.testo: From Latin ipse (“of the self”).

parole.significato: A dogmatic and unproved proposition or dictum that is accepted solely on the authority of someone who is known to have…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ipse dīxit (“he himself said it”), calque of Ancient Greek αὐτὸς ἔφα (autòs épha). Originally used by the followers of Pythagoreanism, who claimed this or that proposition to be uttered by Pythagoras himself. Extended during the Middle Ages to the statements of Aristotle, and mor

parole.significato: An unfounded, false and dogmatic assertion; an ipse dixit.
parole.testo: From Latin ipse dīxit (“he himself said it”, used in the Middle Ages in reference to Aristotle) + -ism. Coined in the late 18th century by Jeremy Bentham.

parole.significato: selfhood; individual identity
parole.testo: From Latin ipse + -ity.

parole.significato: self
parole.testo: By alteration of Latin ipse (“self”).

parole.significato: The actual words (spoken or transcribed).
parole.testo: From Latin ipsissima verba (“the very words”).

parole.significato: By that very fact itself; actually.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ipsō factō (“by the fact itself”).

parole.significato: Of an intersex person: identifying with the sex they were medically assigned; having a gender which matches their assig…
parole.testo: Coined by C. G. Costello in 2014. Latin ipso means "at the very same" (gender as they were assigned), compare ipso facto or ipso substitution.

parole.significato: Used for expressing negation; not
parole.testo: From Latin ir-, assimilated form of in- used before r-.

parole.significato: Angry; irritable
parole.testo: From Latin iracundus.

parole.significato: The quality of being irascible; irritability of temper.
parole.testo: From Latin īrāscor (“to be angry, to be enraged”) + -ibility. See also irascible.

parole.significato: Extremely angry; wrathful; enraged.
parole.testo: From Latin īrātus (“angered, angry”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from īrāscor (“to be angry”), from īra (“anger, wrath”).

parole.significato: An officer in Ancient Greece having functions corresponding to those of a Justice of the Peace.
parole.testo: From Latin īrēnarcha, īrēnarchēs, from Ancient Greek εἰρηνάρχης (eirēnárkhēs), from εἰρήνη (eirḗnē, “peace”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a rainbow.
parole.testo: Formed from (the stem of) Latin īris, Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris) + -al.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Iris, common in the northern hemisphere, and generally having attractive blooms (See Iris (plant)…
parole.testo: From Middle English iris, from Latin īris, from Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris, “rainbow”). Presuming an earlier form *ϝῖρις (*wîris), possibly from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *w(e)ih₁-ro- (“a twist, thread, cord, wire”), from *weh₁y- (“to turn, twist, weave, plait”). If so, it would be cognate t

parole.significato: Characterized by or constituting (any kind of) irony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós). Compare Middle French, ironique, equivalent to irony + -ic.

parole.significato: Made brilliant or bright; irradiated, illuminated.
parole.testo: From Middle English irradiate (“illuminated, shining”), borrowed from Medieval Latin irradiātus, perfect passive participle of irradiō, from ir- (“against; into; on, upon”) + radiō (“to cause to radiate, irradiate; to emit beams, radiate”), from radius (“ray of light; rod, staff; spoke of a wheel”)

parole.significato: Archaic form of irrational.
parole.testo: From Latin irratiōnābilis, from ir- + ratiōnābilis.

parole.significato: Not rational; unfounded, nonsensical or wrong-headed.
parole.testo: From Latin irratiōnālis, from ir- + ratiōnālis.

parole.significato: Synonym of intangible, immaterial, not composed of things, having no concrete existence.
parole.testo: From Latin irrealis, from in- (“un-: not”) + reālis (“real, material, tangible, composed of physical things”), from res (“thing”) + -ālis (“-al: forming adjectives”). Doublet of irrealis.

parole.significato: Inflected to indicate that an act or state of being is not a fact.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin irreālis (“intangible, immaterial”), from Latin in- (“un-: not”) + reālis (“real, material, composed of physical things”), from res (“thing”) + -ālis (“-al: forming adjectives”). Doublet of irreal.

parole.significato: Which cannot be refuted; clearly right, incontrovertible, indisputable, irrefutable.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin irrefrāgābilis (“irrefragable”) + English -able (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘able or fit to be done’). parole.significato: undeniable; unable to be disproved or refuted
parole.testo: From Late Latin irrefūtābilis, from ir- (“not”) + refūtābilis (“refutable”), from refūtō (“to refute”) + -bilis (“-able”), equivalent to ir- + refutable.

parole.significato: Not regible; ungovernable, unmanageable, intractable.
parole.testo: From the post-Classical Latin irregibilis (“ungovernable”), from ir- (“un-”) + regibilis (“governable”, “tractable”); equivalent to the English ir- (“un-”) + regible (“governable”, “tractable”).

parole.significato: The quality of being irreligious.
parole.testo: From Latin irreligiōsitās.

parole.significato: Having no relation to religion.
parole.testo: From Latin irreligiōsus. By surface analysis, ir- + religious.

parole.significato: Admitting no return; from or by which one cannot return.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin irremeābilis, from in- (“not”) + remeābilis (“returning”), from remeō. Compare French irréméable. See remeant.

parole.significato: Unable to be remedied, cured, corrected or repaired; irreparable, incurable.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin irremediābilis. By surface analysis, ir- + remediable.

parole.significato: Not remunerable.
parole.testo: From Latin irremūnerābilis. Compare French irrémunérable. See remunerate.

parole.significato: not reprehensible, blameless, without blame; innocent
parole.testo: From Latin irreprehēnsibilis. Compare French irrépréhensible. See reprehensible.

parole.significato: A creeping in.
parole.testo: From Late Latin irrēptiō, from Latin irrēpō (“to creep in”) + -tiō (suffix forming action nouns).

parole.significato: surreptitious; spurious
parole.testo: From Latin irrēpō (“I creep into”); ir- (“in”) + rēpō (“I creep”).

parole.significato: The quality of being irresistible.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin irresistibilitās. By surface analysis, irresistible + -ity.

parole.significato: Impossible to resist.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin irresistibilis, equivalent to ir- + resistible.

parole.significato: Regardless of; without regard for; without considering.
parole.testo: Opposite of Medieval Latin respectivus, "having regard for", from Latin respectus.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being irreverent; want of proper reverence; disregard of the authority and character of a super…
parole.testo: From Middle English irreverence, from Latin irreverentia, from irreverēns (“irreverent”) + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns). By surface analysis, ir- + reverence.

parole.significato: Lacking respect; not having or not showing respect for or seriousness towards something that is usually treated with re…
parole.testo: From Latin irreverēns. By surface analysis, ir- + reverent.

parole.significato: To supply (farmland) with water, by building ditches, pipes, etc.
parole.testo: First attested in 1615; borrowed from Latin irrigātus, perfect passive participle of irrigō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). See also Middle English irrigat(e) (“watered, irrigated”).

parole.significato: Irrigated, well-watered.
parole.testo: From Latin irriguus, from in- + riguus (“watered”), from rigāre (“to wet”).

parole.significato: The act of laughing at another; derision.
parole.testo: From Latin irrīsiō, from irrīdēre (“to laugh at”); ir- (“in”) + rīdeō (“to laugh”): compare French irrision.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being irritable; quick excitability.
parole.testo: From Latin irritabilitās, equivalent to irritable + -ity.

parole.significato: To provoke impatience, anger, or displeasure in.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin irrītātus, perfect passive participle of irrītō (“excite, irritate, incite, stimulate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To render null and void.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin irritātus, perfect passive participle of irritō (“to invalidate, render void, annul”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from irritus (“invalid”), the equivalent of in- + ratus (“valid, established, fixed”).

parole.significato: To sprinkle or moisten with dew; to bedew.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin irrōrātus, perfect passive participle of irrōrō (“to bedew”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: rushing, moving quickly, especially inwards
parole.testo: From the present participle stem of Latin irruere.

parole.significato: To wrinkle.
parole.testo: First attested in 1566; borrowed from Latin irrūgātus, perfect passive participle of irrūgō (“to wrinkle”), from rūga (“a wrinkle”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To thrust the penis into the mouth; to practice irrumation.
parole.testo: First attested in 1887; borrowed from Latin irrumātus, perfect passive participle of irrumō (“to irrumate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of, or an instance of, thrusting the penis into the mouth; active penetration of a mouth.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin irrumātiō, from irrumō + -tiō.

parole.significato: To break into.
parole.testo: From Latin irruptus, past participle of irrumpō.

parole.significato: An introduction, especially (particularly capitalized) Porphyry's introduction to the works of Aristotle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īsagōgē, from Ancient Greek εἰσαγωγή (eisagōgḗ, “lead-in”), from εἰς (eis, “into”) + ἀγωγή (agōgḗ, “to lead”).

parole.significato: Local disturbance in blood circulation due to mechanical obstruction of the blood supply (for example, embolism, thromb…
parole.testo: From New Latin ischaemia, from Ancient Greek ἴσχαιμος (ískhaimos, “stoppage of blood flow”), from ῐ̓́σχω (ĭ́skhō, “to hold back, restrain; to stay, stop”) + αἷμᾰ (haîmă, “blood”). The plural form ischemiae is also from New Latin ischaemiae.

parole.significato: pain in the region of the ischium; sciatica
parole.testo: From New Latin ischialgia, from Latin ischion + -algia.

parole.significato: A muscle just below the surface of the perineum, used to flex the anus, stabilize the erect penis (in males), and tense…
parole.testo: From ischio- + Latin cavernōsus.

parole.significato: The lowest of the three bones that make up each side of the pelvis.
parole.testo: 17th century, from Latin ischium, from Ancient Greek ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip joint”).

parole.significato: The inability to empty the bladder
parole.testo: Latin ischuria, Ancient Greek ἰσχουρία (iskhouría, “retention of urine”), from ἴσχω (ískhō, “to keep back, restrain”) + οὖρον (oûron, “urine”).

parole.significato: A temple dedicated to the worship of the Egyptian goddess Isis.
parole.testo: From Latin Iseum, from Ancient Greek Ἴσειον (Íseion), from Ἶσις (Îsis, “Isis”). By surface analysis, Isis + Latin -eum.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the goddess Isis or her worship.
parole.testo: From Latin īsiacus, from Ancient Greek Ἰσιακός (Isiakós).

parole.significato: A function between metric spaces (or on a single metric space) having the property that the distance between two images…
parole.testo: From New Latin isometria, from Ancient Greek ἰσομετρία (isometría), from ἰσο- (iso-) + -μετρία (-metría), from ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) and μέτρον (métron, “measurement”) + -ια (-ia, “-y”). Equivalent to iso- + -metry.

parole.significato: Having (at least) two sides of equal length, used especially of a triangle or trapezoid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īsoscelēs, from Ancient Greek ἰσοσκελής (isoskelḗs, “equal-legged”), from ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) + σκέλος (skélos, “leg”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjective suffix). See also iso-.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of
parole.testo: From the Latin Isrāēlīta (“Israelite”), from the Ancient Greek Ἰσρᾱηλῑ́της (Isrāēlī́tēs, “Israelite”), from Ἰσρᾱήλ (Isrāḗl, “Israel”), from the Hebrew יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yiśrāʼēl, “Israel”); by surface analysis, Israel + -ite.

parole.significato: A narrow strip of land, bordered on both sides by water, and connecting two larger landmasses.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Latin isthmus (“a strip of land between two seas”), from Ancient Greek ῐ̓σθμός (ĭsthmós, “neck, narrow passage”), possibly from εἶμῐ (eîmĭ, “to go”). Cognate to Old Norse eið (“isthmus”).

parole.significato: I don't understand any of it; it makes no sense.
parole.testo: First quoted as it was Greek to me in Julius Caesar by Shakespeare, possibly translated from a sentence in Medieval Latin.

parole.significato: Pertaining to Italy.
parole.testo: From Middle English Italian, from Medieval Latin Italiānus, from Latin Italia (“Italy”). By surface analysis, Italia + -n.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Italian peninsula.
parole.testo: Via Latin ītalicus from Ancient Greek Ἰταλικός (Italikós), from Ἰταλία (Italía, “Italy”).

parole.significato: To make a note of.
parole.testo: From Middle English item, from Latin item (“also; in the same manner”). The present English meaning derives from a usage in lists, where the first entry would begin in primis (“firstly”) or imprimis, and the other entries with item (“also, moreover”). Later, the members of lists were referred to as

parole.significato: A passage, especially the passage between the third and fourth ventricles in the brain; the cerebral aqueduct.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iter (“passage”).

parole.significato: To perform or repeat an action on each item in a set.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1471, in Middle English, the verb in 1533, the noun in 1941; partly inherited from Middle English iterat(e) (adjective), partly borrowed from Latin iterātus, perfect passive participle of iterō (“to do something for a second time, repeat”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2

parole.significato: A recital or a second performance; a repetition.
parole.testo: From Latin iterātiō, from iterō. Morphologically iterate + -ion.

parole.significato: reproducing more than once in a lifetime
parole.testo: From Latin iterum (“again, a second time”) + pariō (“give birth, produce, bring forth”). Coined by Lamont Cole in 1954.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the erect phallus that was carried in bacchic processions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ithyphallicus, from Ancient Greek ἰθυφαλλικός (ithuphallikós), from ῑ̓θῠ́φαλλος (īthŭ́phallos, “phallus carried in festivals of Bacchus; ode sung in honour of the phallus; dance accompanying such an ode; dancer performing such a dance”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, suffix forming adjecti

parole.significato: A depiction of an erect penis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ithyphallus, from Ancient Greek ἰθύφαλλος (ithúphallos, “Bacchic phallus," literally "straight penis”).

parole.significato: Habitually travelling from place to place.
parole.testo: From Late Latin itinerantem, present active participle of itineror (“travel”), from itiner-. By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ant.

parole.significato: An Ancient Roman road map in the form of a listing of cities, villages and other stops, with the intervening distances.
parole.testo: From Latin itinerārium, from itiner- + -ārium.

parole.significato: A written schedule of activities for a vacation or road trip.
parole.testo: From Middle English itinerarie, from Latin itinerārium (“an account of a journey, a road-book”), from iter (“a way, journey”). By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ary.

parole.significato: A travelling around.
parole.testo: From itinerate + -ion, ultimately borrowed from Medieval Latin itinerātiō, from itineror (“travel”), from itiner-.

parole.significato: Synonym of andative.
parole.testo: From Latin itus (“gone”), perfect passive participle of eō (“to go”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ey- (“to go”) + -ive.

parole.significato: The principle that a judge should base their decision on the strength of the arguments rather than their quantity.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin iūdex nōn calculat (literally “a judge does not calculate”).

parole.significato: Parties to a legal dispute do not need to plead or prove the law that applies to their case.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iura novit curia. Literally, “the court knows the law”.

parole.significato: Relating to or caused by hard ticks.
parole.testo: From New Latin Ixodes (from Ancient Greek ἰξώδης (ixṓdēs)) + -ic.

parole.significato: The marmoset (Hapale vulgaris)
parole.testo: From Latin Iacchus (“Bacchus”).

parole.significato: Lying stretched out.
parole.testo: From Latin jacens, present participle of jacere (“to lie”): compare French jacent. Doublet of jessant.

parole.significato: A breed of multihorned sheep.
parole.testo: From Middle English Iacob, from Late Latin Iācōbus, from Ancient Greek Ἰάκωβος (Iákōbos), from Biblical Hebrew יַעֲקֹב (yaʿăqōḇ, literally “May He Heel”), from the third-person singular masculine imperfective form of the Semitic verb "to heel" (with various meanings), in turn from עָקֵב (ʿāqēḇ, “hee

parole.significato: boasting; bragging
parole.testo: From Latin jactantia, from jactans, present participle of jactare (“to throw, boast”), freq. from jacere (“to throw”). Compare French jactance.

parole.significato: To move about restlessly.
parole.testo: First attested in 1822; borrowed from Latin iactitātus, perfect passive participle of iactitō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Bragging or boasting, especially in a false manner to another's detriment.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin jactitio, from iactitō (“throw, fling; boast, brag; utter, mention”).

parole.significato: One who throws or casts.
parole.testo: Latin; see jaculate.

parole.significato: Darting, shooting or throwing out suddenly
parole.testo: Latin jaculatorius: compare French jaculatoire.

parole.significato: prickly; bearing spines
parole.testo: Latin jacula (“dart”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: conjoined twins whose heads are fused together but look in opposite directions
parole.testo: From Latin Iānus (“two-headed god”) + -ceps (“headed”).

parole.significato: Someone who looks after the maintenance and cleaning of a public building.
parole.testo: From Latin ianitor (“doorkeeper”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the supposed descendants of Japheth, one of the three sons of Noah in the Bible.
parole.testo: The English Japheth or the Latin Iapetus, + -ic. Coined in the first half of the 19th century alongside Semitic and Hamitic.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Japonic language family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin japonicus.

parole.significato: A species of camellia (Camellia japonica), a native flower of Japan, bearing beautiful red or white flowers.
parole.testo: From New Latin iaponicus (“Japanese”), from Iaponia.

parole.significato: Any of several plants originally native to Japan.
parole.testo: From New Latin japō̆nica, the species name.

parole.significato: jaspidean; made of jasper
parole.testo: From Latin iaspideus, from iaspis (“jasper”).

parole.significato: A form of onyx, part or all of whose layers consist of jasper.
parole.testo: Latin iasponyx

parole.significato: A pair of trousers made from denim cotton.
parole.testo: From Gene(s) (also spelled Jean(s)), an obsolete English name for the Italian city of Genoa. Compare French Gênes. parole.significato: Of or relating to the liver.
parole.testo: From Latin jecoris, from jecur (alternative form of iecur).

parole.significato: An azotized substance containing sulfur, found in the livers of young animals.
parole.testo: From Latin iecur, iecoris (“liver”) + -in.

parole.significato: fasting
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ieiūnātiō.

parole.significato: Not nutritious.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iēiūnus (“fasting”).

parole.significato: The central of the three divisions of the small intestine which lies between the duodenum and the ileum
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iēiūnum, neuter of iēiūnus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to breakfast; specifically, one taken early in the morning or immediately upon getting up.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin iēntāculum (“breakfast (particularly taken right after getting up)”) + English -ar (suffix meaning ‘of, near, or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). parole.significato: A person who is pessimistic about the present and foresees a calamitous future; a prophet of doom.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Jeremias, from Ancient Greek Ἰερεμίας (Ieremías), from Hebrew יִרְמְיָה (yirm'yá, “Jeremiah”, literally “Yahweh exalt”). Doublet of Jeremias.

parole.significato: A place of retirement or concealment.
parole.testo: From Middle English Iericho, from Old English Iericho, from Latin Ierīchō, from Ancient Greek Ἰερῑχώ (Ierīkhṓ), from Biblical Hebrew יְרִיחוֹ (yərīḥō), recorded early as Ugaritic 𐎊𐎗𐎃 (yrḫ). Regarding the "place of concealment" sense, see 2 Samuel 10:5.

parole.significato: A member of the Society of Jesus.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin Iēsūīta, from Latin Iēsūs + -īta.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Jesuits, or to their principles and methods.
parole.testo: From New Latin Iēsūīticus, from Iēsūīta + Latin -icus. By surface analysis, Jesuit + -ic.

parole.significato: The Christian savior.
parole.testo: From Middle English Jhesus, Iesus, from Latin Iēsūs, from Ancient Greek Ἰησοῦς (Iēsoûs), from Biblical Hebrew יֵשׁוּעַ (yēšū́aʿ), a contracted form of יְהוֹשֻׁעַ (yəhōšúaʿ, “Joshua”), meaning "the Lord saves". parole.significato: A savior; one who provides critical help or salvation to others in need.
parole.testo: From Middle English Jesu Crist, Jesus Crist, from Latin Iēsūs Chrīstus. By surface analysis, Jesus + Christ. N.b. that Christ is a title, and not a surname.

parole.significato: A kind of edible fungus (Auricularia auricula-judae), growing on tree-trunks, formerly used for medicinal purposes.
parole.testo: A mistranslation of mediaeval Latin auricula Judae (“Judas's ear”), from its shape, and its occurrence on the tree on which Judas Iscariot was supposed to have hanged himself.

parole.significato: asphalt, bitumen, pitch
parole.testo: Calque of Latin bitūmen iūdaicum.

parole.significato: A young woman; a sweetheart; like the variant spelling Gill it was also associated with various assertive uses of the t…
parole.testo: A variant of Gill, diminutive of Gillian, a medieval form of Juliana, ultimately from Latin.

parole.significato: A placeholder or conventional name for any woman, particularly a younger lower-class woman.
parole.testo: A clipped or hypochoristic form of Joanna, from Latin Joanna, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα (Iōánna), from Hebrew יוֹחָנָה (Yôḥānāh, literally “God is gracious”), the feminized form of יְהוֹחָנָן (Yəhōḥānān) which produced John and its many doublets. As a placeholder name, cf. similar use of John and Jack

parole.parola: Joan's as good as my lady in the dark
parole.significato: Synonym of all cats are grey in the dark: Sex is enjoyable regardless of the status, physical attractiveness, or social…
parole.testo: From or alongside the use of Joan as a sexually available member of the lower classes found in related expressions such as He is our Ladies Chaplaine, but serves Ione and Joan's as good as this French lady. parole.significato: A person who shows remarkable patience, especially in the face of great misfortune.
parole.testo: From Latin Iob, from Ancient Greek Ἰώβ (Iṓb), from Biblical Hebrew אִיּוֹב (ʾiyyōḇ), related to אָיַב (ʾāyaḇ, “to be an enemy”) and אוֹיֵב (ʾōyēḇ, “enemy”).

parole.significato: given to jesting; habitually jolly
parole.testo: From Latin iocōsus (“humorous”), from iocus (“jest, joke”).

parole.significato: Humorous, amusing or joking.
parole.testo: From Latin iocularis, from ioculus (“a little jest”), diminutive of iocus (“a jest”).

parole.significato: jocular; jocose; joking
parole.testo: From Latin jocularius. Compare jocular.

parole.significato: A jester; a joker.
parole.testo: From Latin joculātus. Doublet of juggler and jongleur.

parole.significato: funny; witty
parole.testo: Latin joculatorius.

parole.significato: A female joculator; a female jester, comedian or entertainer.
parole.testo: From Latin ioculātrīx. By surface analysis, joculator + -trix.

parole.significato: A former Portuguese gold coin.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Iōhannēs, variant of Latin Iōannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yôḥānān).

parole.significato: A harbinger or prophetic figure, often one initially ignored or rejected by others.
parole.testo: From Middle English Johan þe Babtis, calqued from Latin Iōannēs Baptista.

parole.significato: An amusing story.
parole.testo: From Latin iocus (“joke, jest, pastime”), from Proto-Italic *jokos (“word, (playful?) saying”), from Proto-Indo-European *yokos (“word, utterance”), from ultimate root Proto-Indo-European *yek- (“to speak, utter”) (of which distant cognates include Proto-Celtic *yextis (“language”) (Breton yezh (“la

parole.significato: A vessel resembling a retort bulb or Florence flask with a truncated neck and flared mouth, used by medieval doctors an…
parole.testo: From Middle English jordan, from Latin jurdanus, unattested outside of England and of uncertain etymology. parole.significato: Synonym of microspecies
parole.testo: New Latin, from Alexis Jordan †1897 French biologist + -on, on analogy with taxon.

parole.significato: The smallest letter or stroke of any writing; an iota.
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Latin iōta (“the letter iota of the Ancient Greek alphabet”), from Ancient Greek ἰῶτα (iôta, “ninth letter of the Ancient Greek alphabet; (figurative) very small part of writing, jot”), from Phoenician 𐤉 (y‬, “tenth letter of the Phoenician abjad, yodh”). Doublet of iota an

parole.significato: A chained iron collar once used in churches to expose sinners to public scorn.
parole.testo: From Latin iugum (“yoke”), possibly via French jougs.

parole.significato: An expression of surprise or amazement.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Joves, from Latin Iovis, genitive of Iuppiter, from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws. Doublet of Dyeus, Jupiter, and Zeus.

parole.significato: The separation between two different depth layers of the planet Jupiter, where the microwave emission characteristics o…
parole.testo: From Jove + -cline. From Latin Jovi (“Jupiter”) (Iove, Iuppiter) + clino (“incline”) (gradient). Coined in reference to thermocline and halocline.

parole.significato: To show elation or triumph; to rejoice.
parole.testo: Either a back-formation from jubilation, or borrowed from Latin iūbilātus, perfect passive participle of iubilō (“to shout for joy”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: the hundredth psalm (ninety-ninth in the Vulgate); the music to which it is set.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin jūbilāte (“rejoice!, shout ye!”), second-person plural present active imperative of jūbilō, the first word of the psalm in Latin.

parole.significato: Pleasant, agreeable.
parole.testo: From Latin iūcundus. Doublet of jocund.

parole.significato: Pleasantness or happiness.
parole.testo: From Latin iūcunditās, from iūcundus + -tās. By surface analysis, jucund + -ity. Doublet of jocundity.

parole.significato: Artifacts, or less commonly, matters pertaining to the Jews, their culture or their religion, particularly ritual objec…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iūdaica, neuter plural of iūdaicus (“Jewish”), from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yehuda, “Judah”). By surface analysis, Juda + -ica. Doublet of giudecca and Judecca.

parole.significato: Jesus! (an exclamation used to express shock or surprise at something negative)
parole.testo: From Middle English Iudas, from Latin Iudas, from Ancient Greek Ἰούδας (Ioúdas), from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (y'hudá). Doublet of Judah.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Judea.
parole.testo: From Latin iūdaeus [from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), from Ἰουδά (Ioudá, “Judah”) + -ιος (-ios)] + -an. By surface analysis, Judah + -ean.

parole.significato: Judean, Judaic, Jewish
parole.testo: From Latin iūdaeus (“Jewish”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yehûdâ, “Judah”).

parole.significato: Able to be judged; capable of being tried or decided upon, especially in a legal case.
parole.testo: From Latin iūdicābilis. See judge.

parole.significato: To judge; to adjudicate.
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1577; borrowed from Latin iūdicātus, perfect passive participle of iūdicō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)) and possibly partly a clipping of adjudicate. Doublet of judge.

parole.significato: The act of judging, judgment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iudicatio, iudicationis.

parole.significato: Pertaining to judgement, or to passing a sentence.
parole.testo: From Latin iūdicātōrius.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the administration of justice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iūdiciālis.

parole.significato: The collective body of judges, justices, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iudiciarius, judiciarius.

parole.significato: Detention (after-school student punishment).

parole.significato: Relating to a jugum.
parole.testo: From Latin jugum (“yoke”).

parole.significato: Side by side or joined.
parole.testo: Latin, neuter plural of iugatus (“joined”).

parole.significato: Forming a pair.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iugātus (“yoked together in pairs”), perfect passive participle of iugō (“to yoke”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A Roman unit of area, equivalent to rectangle with sides of 240×120 Roman feet (2 acti or about ¼ ha).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iūger, variant of iūgerum.

parole.significato: An extract of green walnut shells, formerly used in medicine and as a dye.
parole.testo: Latin juglans, + -in.

parole.significato: The walnut and similar trees of the genus Juglans
parole.testo: From Latin iūglāns (“walnut, walnut tree”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the zygomatic bone and the maxilla
parole.testo: From Latin jugum + maxillary.

parole.significato: Relating to, or located near, the neck or throat.
parole.testo: Late 16th century borrowing from Late Latin jugulāris, from jugulum (“the collarbone; the hollow part of the neck above the collarbone; the throat”) + -āris (“-ar, -ary”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to jugulum + -ar.

parole.significato: To cut the throat of.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin iugulātus, perfect passive participle of iugulō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Prevention of a disease from progressing.
parole.testo: From Latin iugulum (“neck”) + -ation.

parole.significato: The neck or throat.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin jugulum (“the collarbone; the hollow part of the neck above the collarbone; the throat”), diminutive of jugum (“a yoke, collar”).

parole.significato: A connecting ridge or projection, especially on a bone.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Latin jugum (“a yoke, collar; a pair of anything; the summit, ridge”). Doublet of yoke and yuga.

parole.significato: A device to compress the penis, used to prevent masturbation in Victorian times.
parole.testo: From New Latin iugum pēnis (“yoke/collar of the penis”), pēnis being a genitive.

parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The sweet and edible drupes (fruits) of several Mediterranean and African species of small trees.
parole.testo: From Middle English jujube, from Medieval Latin jujuba or Old French jujube, perhaps via Old Occitan from Classical Latin zīzyphum, zīzyphus, from Ancient Greek ζίζυφον (zízuphon)․ First attested in the 14th century.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Julius Caesar.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin Iūliānus.

parole.significato: Having the form of a catkin
parole.testo: From Latin iulus, + -form.

parole.significato: Full of rushes; resembling rushes; juncaceous.
parole.testo: Latin juncosus

parole.significato: The act of joining, or the state of being joined.
parole.testo: From Latin iūnctiō (“union, joining, uniting”), from iungō (“join, attach together”). Equivalent to join + -tion.

parole.significato: joint, juncture
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A place where things join, a junction.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English juncture, from Latin iūnctūra. Doublet of jointure.

parole.significato: Low in rank; having a subordinate role, job, or situation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin junior, a contraction of iuvenior (“younger”) which is the comparative of iuvenis (“young”); see juvenile.

parole.significato: Any shrub or tree of the genus Juniperus of the cypress family, which is characterized by pointed, needle-like leaves a…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English junyper, juniperus, from Latin iūniperus (“juniper-tree”).

parole.significato: To attend a junket; to feast.
parole.testo: From Middle English jonket (“basket made of rushes”), from Medieval Latin iuncta, possibly from Latin iuncus (“rush, reed”) and therefore a possible doublet of jonquil. parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, occurring in, or typifying any one or more of the editions of texts published by the Giunti family o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Juntīnus.

parole.significato: A common name for various plants:
parole.testo: Calque of Latin barba Iovis.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to law.
