parole.significato: A jury or inquest consisting half of aliens and half of natives.
parole.testo: Latin, literally "half tongue".

parole.significato: The middle part; half; moiety.
parole.testo: From the late Middle English medietee (“a half”), borrowed from the Classical Latin medietās. Doublet of moiety.

parole.significato: The adoption of Persian interests by a Greek, regarded as treachery.
parole.testo: From Latin mēdismus, from Ancient Greek μηδισμός (mēdismós). By surface analysis, Mede + -ism.

parole.significato: To contemplate; to keep the mind fixed upon something; to study.
parole.testo: First attested in 1560; borrowed from Latin meditātus, perfect active participle of meditor (“to think or reflect upon, consider, design, purpose, intend”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), morphologically as if frequentative of medeor (“to heal, to cure, to remed

parole.significato: Mediterranean.
parole.testo: From Latin mediterraneus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Mediterranean Sea and its surrounding region.
parole.testo: From Latin mediterrāneus (“inland”, from medius (“middle”) + terra (“earth, land”) + -āneus (adjectival suffix)) + -an.

parole.significato: A mostly enclosed sea that has limited exchange of deep water with outer oceans, and where the water circulation is dom…
parole.testo: PIE word  *médʰyos The word mediterranean is from Latin mediterrāneus (“inland, remote from the coast”) + English -an (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’). Mediterrāneus is derived from medius (“middle”) + terra (“dry land, ground”), modelled after Ancient Greek μεσόγαιος

parole.significato: The material of the surrounding environment, e.g. solid, liquid, gas, vacuum, or a specific substance such as a solvent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin medium, neuter of medius (“middle”), from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Compare middle. Doublet of mid, medio, media, and meson.

parole.significato: The middle finger.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin from Latin medius (“middle”). See medium. Doublet of minge and middle.

parole.significato: The soft inner part of something, especially the pith of a fruit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin medulla (“pith, marrow”), perhaps from medius (“middle”).

parole.significato: The lower portion of the brain stem.
parole.testo: From New Latin medulla (“inner part, marrow, pith”) and New Latin oblongata (“elongated, oblong”).

parole.significato: Spinal cord.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin medulla spīnālis.

parole.significato: Relating to a medulla.
parole.testo: From Classical Latin medullāris. By surface analysis, medulla + -ary.

parole.significato: Irish elk
parole.testo: New Latin, from Ancient Greek, meaning "great horn".

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or in honour of, Cybele.
parole.testo: Latin Megalesius, from Ancient Greek word for "the Great", a surname of Cybele, the Magna Mater.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or from the ancient city of Megalopolis (now Megalopoli) in Greece.
parole.testo: A variant of Megalopolitan; analysable as Megapolis + -itan. Megapolis is derived from Late Latin megapolis, from Ancient Greek μεγα- (mega-, “prefix meaning ‘large’”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”).

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to, Megara
parole.testo: Derived from Latin megaricus, from Ancient Greek Μεγαρικός (Megarikós). Also Megara + -ic.

parole.significato: A sporangium which produces only megaspores
parole.testo: From neo-Latin, from mega- (“major”) + sporangium. The prefix is from Ancient Greek μέγας (mégas, “great”), and the base from spora + Ancient Greek ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “vessel”).

parole.significato: Honey, when used as an ingredient in cosmetic products.
parole.testo: From Latin mel (“honey”). Doublet of mell.

parole.significato: A Scythian tribe which dwelt in Pontus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Melanchlaenī, from Ancient Greek Μελάγχλαινοι (Melánkhlainoi).

parole.significato: Deep sadness or gloom; melancholy
parole.testo: From Late Latin melancholia, which was in turn borrowed from the Ancient Greek medical term μελαγχολία (melankholía, “blackness of the bile”) (from μέλας (mélas), μελαν- (melan-, “black, dark, murky”) + χολή (kholḗ, “bile”)), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medici

parole.significato: Filled with or affected by melancholy—great sadness or depression, especially of a thoughtful or introspective nature.
parole.testo: From Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós, “atrabilious, impulsive, of atrabilious or melancholic temperament”), from μελαγχολία (melankholía, “melancholy”). By surface analysis, melancholy + -ic.

parole.significato: Any of a group of naturally occurring dark pigments, especially the pigment found in skin, hair, fur, and feathers.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek stem of μέλας (mélas, “black”) + -in; by surface analysis, melan(o)- + -in.

parole.significato: A tan or dark skin discoloration, particularly common in pregnant women, thought to be caused by the stimulation of mel…
parole.testo: From Latin melasma, from Ancient Greek μέλασμα (mélasma), from μελαίνειν (melaínein, “to blacken”) + -σμα (-sma), from μέλας (mélas, “black”).

parole.significato: A very large wine bottle (named after the King) with the capacity of about 18 liters, equivalent to 24 standard bottles.
parole.testo: From Latin Melchior, from Hebrew מלכיאור (“king of light”), from מלך (“king”) + אור (“light”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the genus Meleagris, including turkeys.
parole.testo: From Latin meleagris (“turkey”) + -ine.

parole.significato: The passage of dark, tarry stools containing blood, a result of upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
parole.testo: From New Latin melaena, based on Ancient Greek μέλαινα (mélaina, “black”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Greek lyric verse.
parole.testo: From Latin melicus, from Koine Greek μελικός (melikós), from Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “song, lyric”).

parole.significato: Consisting of or containing honeylike matter; said of certain encysted tumours.
parole.testo: From Latin meliceris (“a kind of tumor”), from Ancient Greek μελικηρίς (melikērís, “honeycomb”), from μέλι (méli, “honey”) + κηρός (kērós, “wax”).

parole.significato: Any of a number of birds in the genus Melidectes in the honeyeater family, endemic to New Guinea and New Britain.
parole.testo: From New Latin Melidectes, from Ancient Greek μέλι (méli, “honey”) + δέκτης (déktēs, “receiver”).

parole.significato: A fragrant plant of the genus Melilotus, often having small yellow or white flowers.
parole.testo: From Latin melilōtos, from Ancient Greek μελίλωτος (melílōtos), from μέλι (méli, “honey”) + λωτός (lōtós, “lotus”); later reinforced by Old French mellilote.

parole.significato: Having the qualities of or relating to a badger.
parole.testo: From Latin mēlīnus.

parole.significato: To make better; to improve; to solve a problem.
parole.testo: First attested in 1542; borrowed from Late Latin meliorātus, perfect passive participle of meliorō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from melior (“better”).

parole.significato: That meliorates; curative, improving, salutary.
parole.testo: From Late Latin meliōrō (“make better, improve”) + English -ative (“tending to”, suffix forming adjectives).

parole.significato: The view or doctrine that the world can be improved through human effort (often understood as an intermediate outlook b…
parole.testo: From Latin melior (“better”) + -ism. Reportedly coined by British author George Eliot in her letters, published in 1877.

parole.significato: A proponent of meliorism
parole.testo: From Latin melior (“better”) and English -ist. Reportedly coined by British author George Eliot in her letters, published in 1877.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being better; melioration.
parole.testo: From Latin melioritas, from melior. See meliorate.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Melissa, especially lemon balm (Melissa officinalis), often used medicinally.
parole.testo: From Late Latin melissa, from Ancient Greek μέλισσα (mélissa, “bee”), because the plant attracts bees.

parole.significato: A writ commanding a further enquiry into something.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: In 5th-century Syria and Egypt, a sobriquet applied to Chalcedonians by their opponents, denoting the Chalcedonians' fi…
parole.testo: From Latin Melchita, from Byzantine Greek Μελχίτης (Melkhítēs), from Classical Syriac ܡܠܟܝܐ (malkāyāʾ, “royal; royalist”) + Byzantine Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs). See these for more.

parole.significato: Honey.
parole.testo: From Middle English mel, mell, melle, from Latin mell-, mel. Doublet of mel.

parole.significato: Pertaining to honey.
parole.testo: From Latin melleus (“of, pertaining to or resembling honey”), from mel (“honey”).

parole.significato: Of a plant or its parts: bearing any substance (such as nectar or pollen) which is collected by bees to produce honey.
parole.testo: PIE word  *mélit Learned borrowing from Latin mellifer (“honey-bearing, honey-producing, melliferous”) + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives denoting the presence of a quality, typically in abundance). Mellifer is derived from mel (“honey”) (plural form mella; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European

parole.significato: Producing honey.
parole.testo: From Latin mel, mellis (“honey”) + -ficare (“to make”) (in comp.). See -fy.

parole.significato: The production of honey by honey bees.
parole.testo: From Latin mellificare (“to make honey”). Compare French mellification. See mellific.

parole.significato: Mellifluous.
parole.testo: From Latin mellifluēns.

parole.significato: Flowing like honey.
parole.testo: From Middle English mellifluous, mellyfluous, from Latin mellifluus (“flowing like honey”) + -ous, from mel (“honey”) + fluō (“flow”). Compare superfluous and fluid, from same root, and with dulcet (“sweet speech”), alternative Latinate term with a similar meaning.

parole.significato: To embalm in honey.
parole.testo: From Latin mellificāre (“to make honey”), or mel (“honey”) + -ify.

parole.significato: Having the qualities of honey.
parole.testo: From Latin mel, mellis + -genous.

parole.significato: honeydew (sweet sticky substance found on plants)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin melligo.

parole.significato: Speaking sweetly or harmoniously.
parole.testo: From Latin mel, mellis (“honey”) + loquens (“speaking”), present participle of loqui (“to speak”).

parole.significato: A mineral that is the aluminium salt of mellitic acid; honeystone.
parole.testo: From Latin mell-, stem of mel (“honey”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Synonym of hyenanchin.
parole.testo: Latin mel (“honey”), and English toxin.

parole.significato: Relating to a member, in various senses; especially, (anatomy, zoology) pertaining to a limb.
parole.testo: From Latin membrum + -al.

parole.significato: A membrane.
parole.testo: From Latin membrāna (“membrane, parchment”). Doublet of membrane.

parole.significato: Resembling or having properties of a membrane.
parole.testo: From Latin membrānāceus.

parole.significato: A flexible enclosing or separating tissue forming a plane or film and separating two environments.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin membrāna (“skin or membrane that covers parts of the body”), from membrum (“a limb or member of the body”) + -āna. Doublet of membrana.

parole.significato: A small membrane
parole.testo: Anglicized form of Latin membrānula.

parole.significato: The penis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin membrum virile.

parole.significato: A keepsake; an object kept as a reminder of a place or event.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mementō (“remember”), imperative form of meminī (“to remember”).

parole.significato: An emblematic object or personal ornament, such as a skull, used as a reminder of one's mortality.
parole.testo: From Latin mementō morī (literally “be mindful of dying”).

parole.significato: Objects that are connected to or remind their owner of past events.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin memorābilia (“things to be remembered”); its use as noun is after Ancient Greek ἀπομνημονεύματα (apomnēmoneúmata) of the neuter plural of memorābilis (“memorable”). Its English use is perhaps after the Latin title Memorabilia of Xenophon’s collection of Socratic dialogues.

parole.significato: Worthy to be remembered; very important or remarkable.
parole.testo: From Middle English memorable, memorrable, from Latin memorābilis, from memorō (“to bring to remembrance”), from memor (“mindful, remembering”). By surface analysis, memory + -able, see memory. Doublet of memorabile (singular of memorabilia).

parole.significato: A short note serving as a reminder.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin memorandum, neuter of memorandus (“to be remembered”).

parole.significato: an oral narrative from memory relating a personal experience, especially the precursor of a legend.
parole.testo: From Latin memorātus, past participle of memorāre (“to bring to remembrance, mention, recount”), from memor (“remembering”); see memory.

parole.significato: One of the five canons of classical rhetoric: the discipline of memory and recall.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin memoria, from memor (“mindful, remembering”). Doublet of memoir and memory.

parole.significato: Synonym of mnemotechny.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?]

parole.significato: Memory; recollection.
parole.testo: From Late Latin memoriale, neuter of memorialis. By surface analysis, memory + -ial.

parole.significato: By, or from, memory; by heart.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin memoriter.

parole.significato: Of, from or pertaining to Memphis, Egypt.
parole.testo: From Middle English Memphyte, from Classical Latin Memphītis. By surface analysis, Memphis + -ite.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Memphis, Egypt.
parole.testo: From Classical Latin Memphītēs, from Ancient Greek Μεμφῑ́της (Memphī́tēs).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Memphis or the Memphites.
parole.testo: From Middle English memphetik, from Latin Memphīticus. By surface analysis, Memphite + -ic.

parole.significato: The annual fixed liturgical cycle of services used in the Eastern Orthodox and Greek-Catholic Churches, containing a li…
parole.testo: From New Latin mēnaion, from Ancient Greek μηναῖος (mēnaîos, “lunar”).

parole.significato: The action of telling lies in an artful way
parole.testo: From Latin mendācitās (“falsehood”), and -loquence from Latin loquor (“to speak”).

parole.significato: Depending on alms for a living.
parole.testo: From Middle English mendicant, from Latin mendīcāns, present participle of mendīcō (“beg”). Compare French mendiant.

parole.significato: To beg.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mendīcātus, perfect passive participle of mendīcō (“to beg”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a Cambrian lithostratigraphic group in west Wales.
parole.testo: From Latin Menevia (“St Davids, a city in Wales”).

parole.significato: The three membranes that envelop the brain and spinal cord.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mēningēs, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μῆνιγξ (mêninx, “membrane”).

parole.significato: A membrane, especially one of the three membranes lining the skull and vertebral canal and enclosing the brain and spin…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin mēninx, from Ancient Greek μῆνῐγξ (mênĭnx, “membrane of the eye; membrane enclosing the brain; eardrum”).

parole.significato: A calendar of the days of the month or of all the days of the year divided by month, particularly as a table of informa…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mēnologium, from Ancient and Byzantine Greek μηνολόγιον (mēnológion), from μήν (mḗn, “month”) + λόγιον (lógion, “writing, record, announcement”), itself from λόγος (lógos, “writing, recording”). Doublet of menologion, menologe, and menology.

parole.significato: The study of months; the names and system of months within a given calendar.
parole.testo: Partially from meno- (“month-”) + -ology (“study, account”) and partially from anglicization of Medieval Latin mēnologium and Byzantine Greek μηνολόγιον (mēnológion), q.v. Doublet of menologion, menologium, and menologe.

parole.significato: A reactive mind, a conscious knowing by the individual that an act was committed, either by themselves or by another.
parole.testo: From Latin mēns + reus (literally “guilty mind”), from the English common law precept Actus non facit reum nisi mens rea sit ("The act does not make a person guilty unless the mind is also guilty").

parole.significato: In planetary geology, a large mesa-like area of raised land.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mēnsa (“table, altar”). Doublet of mesa.

parole.significato: Occurring once in a month; monthly.
parole.testo: From Latin mensis (“month”).

parole.significato: Belonging to the table; transacted at table.
parole.testo: Latin mensalis, from mensa (“table”).

parole.significato: The discharge of blood and cellular tissue that flows from the inner lining of the uterus out through the vagina, occur…
parole.testo: From Latin mēnsis (“month”), the plural being mēnsēs (“months”), corresponding to the approximately month-long span of the menstrual cycle. Compare month.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the menses.
parole.testo: From Middle English menstruall, from Latin mēnstruālis, from mēnstrua (“menses”), from neuter plural of mēnstruus (“of a month, monthly, of menstruation”), from mēnsis (“month”) + -ālis (“-al”); see moon.

parole.significato: The periodic discharging of the menses, the flow of blood and cells from the lining of the uterus in unfertilized femal…
parole.testo: From menstruum + -ation, modelled after Late Latin menstruatio. The word is a cognate with French menstruation, Spanish menstruación, which displaced Old English mōnaþblōd (literally “monthblood”).

parole.significato: The menses; menstrual discharge.
parole.testo: From Latin mēnstruum (“menstrual discharge”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a month.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mēnsuālis (“monthly”).

parole.significato: measurable
parole.testo: From Middle English mensurable, from Medieval Latin mensūrābilis. Doublet of measurable. See also -able.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to measure or measurement.
parole.testo: From Latin mēnsūrālis, from mēnsūra (“measure”) + -ālis.

parole.significato: To measure absolutely the height, latitude and longitude of a point on the earth.
parole.testo: First attested in 1653; borrowed from Latin mēnsūrātus, perfect passive participle of mēnsūrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of measure.

parole.significato: The act or process of measuring; measurement.
parole.testo: From Late Latin mensūrātiōnem (“a measuring”).

parole.significato: sycosis
parole.testo: From Latin mentāgra, from mentum (“chin”) + Ancient Greek ἄγρα (ágra, “a catching”).

parole.significato: A paired central muscle of the lower lip, situated at the tip of the chin; it originates in the incisive fossa of the m…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin mentālis, ellipsis of musculus mentālis (“the chin muscle”).

parole.significato: Any of the mint genus Mentha, mints and similar species.
parole.testo: From the genus name, Mentha, from Latin mentha (“mint”). Doublet of mint.

parole.significato: A cyclic monoterpene alcohol; the major component of the essential oil of peppermint; used in pharmaceutical preparatio…
parole.testo: From Latin mentha (“mint”) + -ol.

parole.significato: Brain-washing, conditioning people to abandon their beliefs.
parole.testo: From Latin mēns (“mind”) or mentālis (“mental”) + -cide (“killing”), from Latin -cīdium, by analogy to homicide, genocide, etc. Coined during the 1950s.

parole.significato: A female mentor.
parole.testo: From Latin mentrix or mentor + -trix.

parole.significato: A penis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mentula.

parole.significato: The chin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mentum (“the chin”). Doublet of menton.

parole.significato: As is my wont (custom, habit).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin meō mōre (“as is my custom”).

parole.significato: Foul-smelling or noxious, particularly of a gas or atmosphere.
parole.testo: From Latin mephīticus, from mephītis; compare French méphitique.

parole.significato: A poisonous or foul-smelling gas, especially as emitted from the earth; an unpleasant smell.
parole.testo: From Latin mefītis, mephītis, from the name of a Samnite goddess who personified the poisonous gases emitted from swamps and volcanoes.

parole.significato: Without mixture or adulteration; strong; racy.
parole.testo: From Latin meracus, from merus (“pure, inmixed”).

parole.significato: Capable of being bought or sold.
parole.testo: From Latin mercabilis, from mercari (“to trade, traffic, buy”). See merchant.

parole.significato: The univalent radical -SH
parole.testo: From mercaptan, from Latin mercurius captans (“mercury capturing”).

parole.significato: an organosulfur compound that contains a carbon-bonded sulfhydryl or sulphydryl
parole.testo: The term mercaptan was introduced in 1832 by the Danish chemist William Christopher Zeise and is derived from the Latin mercurium captāns (capturing mercury) because the thiolate group bonds very strongly with mercury compounds.

parole.significato: Market; trade.
parole.testo: From Latin mercātus. See market.

parole.significato: Synonym of Mercator projection.
parole.testo: From Gerardus Mercator, Latinized name of Gerard de Cremer (1512–1594), Flemish cartographer and mathematician, from Latin mercātor (“merchant”).

parole.significato: An orthomorphic map projection, in which meridians appear at right-angles to the equator, and lines of latitude are hor…
parole.testo: From Gerardus Mercator, Latinized name of Gerard de Cremer (1512–1594), Flemish cartographer and mathematician, from Latin mercātor (“merchant”).

parole.significato: The tendency of transnational commerce to operate outside any system of national laws, making use, instead, of a system…
parole.testo: From Latin mercator (“merchant, trader”) + -ism.

parole.significato: commerce; trade
parole.testo: From Latin mercatura (“commerce”).

parole.significato: One motivated by gain, especially monetary.
parole.testo: From Middle English mercenarye (“someone paid to work, hireling”), from Latin mercēnārius (“hired for money”), from mercēs (“reward, wages, price”).

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Mercius + -an, Latinized from Old English Mierċe.

parole.significato: A male given name from Latin.
parole.testo: From Latin Mercurius, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Quicksilver, mercury. (No longer capitalized, as the name of the metal is no longer recognized as that of the planet.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Mercurie, from Latin Mercurius.

parole.significato: Senses relating to the metal.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English mercurie (“metallic chemical element, quicksilver; a plant, probably goosefoot (genus Chenopodium); (possibly) dog’s mercury (Mercurialis perennis); etc.”), borrowed from Late Latin mercurius (“metallic chemical element, quicksilver”), Latin Mercurius (“Mercur

parole.significato: Dung-eating, coprophagous.
parole.testo: From Latin merda (“excrement”) + -vorous.

parole.significato: Tastelessly gaudy; superficially attractive but having in reality no value or substance; falsely alluring.
parole.testo: From Latin meretrīcius, from meretrīx (“harlot, prostitute”), from mereō (“earn, deserve, merit”) (English merit) + -trīx (“(female agent)”) (English -trix).

parole.significato: A prostitute in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin meretrīx.

parole.significato: Any of various diving ducks of the genera Mergus or Lophodytes, which feed on fish and have a sharply serrated bill.
parole.testo: From Late Latin merganser, from Latin mergus (“waterfowl, diver”), from mergō (“to dip, immerse”) + ānser (“goose”).

parole.significato: To combine into a whole.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mergō (“to dip; dip in; plunge; sink down into; immerse; overwhelm”).

parole.significato: In full celestial meridian: a great circle passing through the poles of the celestial sphere and the zenith for a parti…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English meridian, meridien (“midday, noon; position of the sun at noon; the south; longitude of a place; (astronomy) celestial meridian”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman meridien (“midday”), Middle French meridien (“midday; the south; terrestrial meridian; (

parole.significato: Midday, noon.
parole.testo: Back-formation from the phrases ante meridiem and post meridiem (more commonly a.m. and p.m.), from Latin merīdiem, accusative of merīdiēs (“midday, noon”).

parole.significato: An internode.
parole.testo: From New Latin merithallus, from Ancient Greek μερίς (merís, “part”) + θαλλός (thallós, “branch”).

parole.significato: Deserving of merit or commendation; deserving reward.
parole.testo: From Middle English meritorious, borrowed between 1375 and 1425 from Latin meritōrius (“earning money”), from meritus, past participle of mereō (“to earn”).

parole.significato: A worker ant that is deformed by parasitic nematodes.
parole.testo: From New Latin mermithergata, from Ancient Greek μέρμις (mérmis, “cord, string”) + ἐργάτης (ergátēs, “worker”).

parole.significato: (Of) one's own accord.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin motu mero (with transposition of elements), ablative of motus merus (“free impulse, volition”), from classical Latin mōtus (“motion, movement”).

parole.significato: A descendant of Merovech; a Merovingian.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Merovingus, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Mārīwīg [a male given name composed of *mārī (“famous”) + *wīg (“fight”)] + *-ing. By surface analysis, Merovech + -ing. Cognate with Old English Merewīoingas (a hapax legomenon in the genitive case).

parole.significato: A dinner; meal.
parole.testo: From Middle English mese, mes, mees (“dinner, dish”), from Old English mēse, mēose, mīse, mȳse (“table; that which is set on a table; dish; food, meal”), a vernacular loan from Latin/Late Latin mē(n)sa (“table; meal”). Cognate with Scots mes, mese (“a serving of food”), Old High German mias, meas (G

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek musical theory, the highest-pitched fixed note in the nearer tetrachord on a lyre, always pitched a pe…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin mesē, from Ancient Greek μέση (mésē, literally “middle [string]”).

parole.significato: The mesentery.
parole.testo: From Late Latin mesenterium and its source, Ancient Greek μεσεντέριον (mesentérion).

parole.significato: The membrane that attaches the intestines to the wall of the abdomen, maintaining their position in the abdominal cavit…
parole.testo: From Late Latin mesenterium, from Ancient Greek μεσεντέρῐον (mesentérĭon), from μέσος (mésos, “middle”) + ἔντερον (énteron, “gut”).

parole.significato: Mesenteric.
parole.testo: From Late Latin meseraicus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek μεσαραϊκός (mesaraïkós) (in Galen), from μεσάραιον (mesáraion, “mesaraeum”).

parole.significato: A supernumerary malformed, peg-like tooth occurring between the maxillary central incisors.
parole.testo: From mesio- + Latin dens (“tooth”).

parole.significato: The mesogastrium.
parole.testo: From New Latin mesogastrium, from Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos, “middle”) + γαστήρ (gastḗr, “belly”).

parole.significato: The part of the embryonic mesentery that includes the stomach
parole.testo: From meso- (“middle”) and Latin gaster (“belly”).

parole.significato: An ancient instrument for finding two mean proportionals between two given lines, required in solving the problem of th…
parole.testo: From Latin mesolabium, from Ancient Greek μεσόλαβος (mesólabos).

parole.significato: The dorsal portion of the mesothorax of insects.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek, meaning "middle of the back".

parole.significato: The middle portion of the foot in the gastropods and pteropods.
parole.testo: From New Latin mesopodium, from meso- + -podium.

parole.significato: The fold of peritoneum that attaches the testis to the dorsal wall of the body cavity or scrotum.
parole.testo: From New Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek [Term?], literally "between the testicles".

parole.significato: Any member of the flowering plant genus Mespilus (now Crataegus sect. Mespilus), of medlars.
parole.testo: From the genus name, from Latin mespilum.

parole.significato: Mass; a church service.
parole.testo: From Middle English mes, partly from Old English mēse, mēose (“table”), a vernacular loan from Latin/Late Latin mē(n)sa (“table; meal”); and partly from Old French mes, Late Latin missum, from mittō (“to put, place (e.g. on the table)”). See mission, and compare Mass (“religious service”).

parole.significato: The one who is ordained by God to lead the people of Israel, believed by Christians and Muslims to be Jesus Christ.
parole.testo: From Middle English Messyas, Messy, Messie, from Latin Messīās, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Μεσσίας (Messías), from Aramaic ܡܫܺܝܚܳܐ (məšīḥā), from Biblical Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšîaḥ, “anointed”). Doublet of Masih and Moshiach.

parole.significato: Boundary marker.
parole.testo: From Latin mēta.

parole.significato: A change from one subject to another.
parole.testo: From Late Latin metabasis, from Ancient Greek μετάβασις (metábasis, “a change, a transition”), from μεταβαίνω (metabaínō, “I cross”), from μετά (metá) and βαίνω (baínō, “I move”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem-.

parole.significato: A rhetorical device whereby one word is metonymically substituted for another word which is itself a metonym; more broa…
parole.testo: From Latin metalēpsis, from Ancient Greek μετάληψις (metálēpsis, “succession”), from Ancient Greek μετά (metá, “after”) and λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or characteristic of metal.
parole.testo: From Latin metallicus, from metallum (“metal”), from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon). Equivalent to metal + -ic.

parole.significato: Having the form or structure of a metal.
parole.testo: From Latin metallum (“metal”) + -form. Compare French métalliforme.

parole.significato: A transformation, such as one performed by magic.
parole.testo: First attested in 1533, from Latin metamorphōsis, from Ancient Greek μεταμόρφωσις (metamórphōsis), from μετά (metá, “change”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “form”). Analyzable as meta- + -morph + -osis

parole.significato: The dorsal portion of the metathorax of insects
parole.testo: From New Latin metanōtum, from Ancient Greek μετα- (meta-) + νῶτον (nôton).

parole.significato: Metaphysical.
parole.testo: From Latin metaphysicus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to metaphysics.
parole.testo: From Middle English metaphisicalle, methafisical, from Medieval Latin metaphysicālis. By surface analysis, meta- + physical.

parole.significato: Any change in a word made by altering its letters or sounds.
parole.testo: From Latin metaplasmus from Ancient Greek μεταπλασμός (metaplasmós).

parole.significato: The posterior division of the foot in the Gastropoda and Pteropoda.
parole.testo: From New Latin metapodium, from Ancient Greek μετα- (meta-) + πούς (poús). By surface analysis, meta- + -pode.

parole.significato: A change in nature, form, or quality.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin metastasis (“(rhetoric) rapid or sudden transition from one argument, point, or topic to another”), and from its etymons Koine Greek μετάστασις (metástasis, “(rhetoric) rapid or sudden transition from one argument, point, or topic to another”) and Ancient Greek μετά

parole.significato: Of a disease (especially cancer) or a tumour: to form a metastasis (“a secondary focus away from the primary site”) in…
parole.testo: From metastasis + -ize (suffix forming verbs meaning to do things denoted by the adjectives or nouns the suffix is attached to). Metastasis is a learned borrowing from Late Latin metastasis (“(rhetoric) rapid or sudden transition from one argument, point, or topic to another”), and from its etymons

parole.significato: The part of the foot between the toes and the ankle, especially its five bones.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin metatarsus.

parole.significato: The transposition of letters, syllables or sounds within a word.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin metathesis, from Ancient Greek μετάθεσις (metáthesis), from μετά (metá, “among”) + θέσις (thésis, “placement”).

parole.significato: Transmigration of the soul, especially its reincarnation after death.
parole.testo: From Late Latin metempsychosis, from Koine Greek μετεμψύχωσις (metempsúkhōsis).

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek city-states, a resident alien who did not have the rights of a citizen and who paid a tax for the righ…
parole.testo: From Late Latin metycus (also metoecus), from Ancient Greek μέτοικος (métoikos, “foreigner, metic”).

parole.significato: Characterized by very precise, conscientious attention to details.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin meticulōsus (“full of fear, timid, fearful, terrible, frightful”), from metus (“fear”) and -culōsus, extracted from perīculōsus (“perilous”). Sense of “characterized by very precise, conscientious attention to details” is a semantic loan from French méticuleux.

parole.significato: The use of a single characteristic or part of an object, concept or phenomenon to identify the entire object, concept,…
parole.testo: From Late Latin metonymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).

parole.significato: The architectural element between two triglyphs in a Doric frieze.
parole.testo: From Latin metopa and its source, Koine Greek μετόπη (metópē), from μετά (metá, “between”) + ὀπή (opḗ, “hole”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or situated at the forehead
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin metōpicus, from Ancient Greek μετωπικός (metōpikós).

parole.significato: The posterolateral ossification in the sternum of birds, or the part resulting from such ossification.
parole.testo: From New Latin metosteon, from Ancient Greek μετα- (meta-, “after”) + ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”).

parole.significato: A creative principle supposed to be responsible for changes in borderlines.
parole.testo: Coined by Bracha L. Ettinger. See Late Latin metrium (“womb”) and metamorphosis.

parole.significato: Rhythm or measure.
parole.testo: From Old English, from Latin metrum, from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, “measure, rule, length, size, poetic metre”).

parole.significato: Synonym of metri gratia.
parole.testo: From Latin metrī causā (literally “for the sake of poetic metre”).

parole.significato: for the sake of the meter.
parole.testo: From Latin metrī grātiā.

parole.significato: The basic unit of the underlying rhythm of verse.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin pēs metricus.

parole.significato: To make verse.
parole.testo: From Latin metrum (“meter”) + -fy. Compare French métrifier.

parole.significato: The mother (founding) polis (city state) of a colony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mētropolis, from Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis, “mother city”), from μήτηρ (mḗtēr, “mother”) + πόλις (pólis, “city (state)”). By surface analysis, metro- + -polis. Doublet of metropole.

parole.significato: A bishop empowered to oversee other bishops; an archbishop.
parole.testo: From Late Latin metropolitanus, from Ancient Greek μητροπολίτης (mētropolítēs).

parole.significato: A metropolitan (bishop).
parole.testo: Latin metropolita, from Ancient Greek μητροπολίτης (mētropolítēs).

parole.significato: denizen, sojourner, stranger, outlander.
parole.testo: From Latin metoecus, from Ancient Greek μέτοικος (métoikos, “alien, outsider, foreigner”), combination of μετά (metá) and οἶκος (oîkos, “residency”). Cognate with French métèque.

parole.significato: Meum athamanticum, a European herb.
parole.testo: From Latin mēum (“umbelliferous plant, Meum athamanticum”), from Ancient Greek μῆον (mêon), probably from μεῖον (meîon, “lesser”) for its small size. The English form came perhaps via Middle French meu, a word with a single isolated attestation from the 14th century which only began to appear consis

parole.significato: spignel, Meum athamanticum
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mēum (“Meum athamanticum”), from Ancient Greek μῆον (mêon), probably from μεῖον (meîon, “lesser”) for its small size.

parole.significato: What is mine and what is yours; owned property.
parole.testo: From Latin meum et tuum.

parole.significato: An ornamental shrub, Daphne mezereum, having purple flowers and bright red fruit.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mezereon, mezereum, from Arabic مَازَرْيُون (māzaryūn).

parole.significato: Any of a group of hydrous aluminosilicate minerals characterized by highly perfect cleavage, so that they readily separ…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mīca (“grain, crumb”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, consisting of, containing or resembling mica.
parole.testo: From mica + -aceous. From Latin mīca (“grain, crumb”). Often erroneously associated with Latin micō (“to twinkle, glitter”) and hence with English micacious.

parole.significato: Sparkling, glittering, twinkling
parole.testo: From Latin micō (“to twinkle, glitter”). Not from English mica; compare micaceous.

parole.significato: a colloidal aggregate, in a simple geometric form, of a specific number of amphipathic molecules which forms at a well-…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin mīcella, from mīca (“crumb”) + -ella.

parole.significato: The first term of the legal year, running from October to December, during which the upper courts of England and Wales,…
parole.testo: From Michaelmas + term; Michaelmas is from Michael (“the name of the biblical archangel”) + -mas (suffix indicating a holiday or sacred day), meaning the feast day of St Michael. Michael is derived from Late Latin Michahel, from Koine Greek Μιχαήλ (Mikhaḗl), from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָאֵל (mîḵāʾēl, “

parole.significato: Micronation.
parole.testo: Back-formation from micropatriology (“study of micronationalism”). Analysable as micro- + Latin patria (“country”), literally "microcountry".

parole.significato: Synonym of micropatriology.
parole.testo: From micro- (“very small”) + Latin patria (“country”) + -ology (“branch of learning; a study of a particular subject”), coined by the International Micropatrological Society in 1973. Perhaps a classical compound via translating micronation into Latin as micropatria (literally “microcountry”).

parole.significato: A member of the superseded taxonomic order Micropoda, which possess a diminutive foot or lack one, such as oysters.
parole.testo: From New Latin Micropoda, from micro- + -poda.

parole.significato: Urination.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mictiō.

parole.significato: To urinate.
parole.testo: First attested in 1842; irregular back-formation from micturition on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), from Latin micturiō (“to urinate”). Related to Old English mīgan (whence Early Middle English miȝen (“to urinate”) See also Mingere and meiere: urination.

parole.significato: Urination.
parole.testo: From Latin micturio (“to urinate”).

parole.significato: A very large champagne bottle (named after the King) with the capacity of about 30 liters, equivalent to 40 standard bo…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Midās, from Ancient Greek Μίδᾱς (Mídās), from Phrygian midas.

parole.significato: A muscle arising from the transverse processes of the lower six cervical vertebrae, inserting on the upper surface of t…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin musculus scalenus medius.

parole.significato: To relocate periodically from one region to another, usually according to the seasons.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin migrātus, perfect passive participle of migrō (“to migrate, change, transport”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Migrating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin migrātōrius or migrate + -ory.

parole.significato: The ambition to publish and name large numbers of taxa as a form of personal aggrandizement.
parole.testo: From Latin mihī̆, dative of egō̆ (“I”), + itch.

parole.significato: A standard character in ancient comedy and in modern comedy depicting ancient military figures: the bravado-filled, sel…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mīles (“soldier”) + glōriōsus (“glorious”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to Milesius or his people; Irish.
parole.testo: From Latin Milesius, Latinised form of Míl Espáine, a legendary Spanish king whose sons were reputed to have conquered Ireland around 1300 BC.

parole.significato: A large silver coin of Ancient Rome, introduced in the early 4th century.
parole.testo: From Late Latin mīliārense, neuter form of mīliārensis (“pertaining to a thousand”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to millet seeds.
parole.testo: From Latin miliārius, from milium.

parole.significato: To give force or effect toward; to influence.
parole.testo: First attested in 1598; borrowed from Latin mīlitātus, perfect passive participle from mīlitō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Semantically from its cognate, French militer.

parole.significato: An army of trained civilians, which may be an official reserve army, called upon in time of need, the entire able-bodie…
parole.testo: From Latin mīlitia (“army, military force/service”), from mīles (“soldier”). Doublet of militsia. The use of "militia" rather than "police" to refer to the police force (of Belarus and some other countries) originated in the USSR.

parole.significato: A keratin-filled cyst that can appear just under the epidermis or on the roof of the mouth.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin milium. Compare Middle English mile.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a thousand, especially to a thousand years.
parole.testo: From Latin mīllēnārius.

parole.significato: Often capitalized: a person from the generation born in the last two decades of the 20th century, from around the early…
parole.testo: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Late Latin mīllennium (“millennium”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives; and forming nouns). The English word may be analysed as millennium + -al or milli- (prefix meaning ‘thousand’) + -ennial (suffix meaning ‘years’). Ad

parole.significato: A period of time consisting of one thousand years.
parole.testo: From Late Latin mīllennium, from Latin mīllennis (“1000-year”) + -ium (forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: thousandth; consisting of or divided into thousandth parts
parole.testo: From Latin millesimus, from mille (“a thousand”).

parole.significato: A milestone.
parole.testo: From Latin mīlliārium.

parole.significato: thousandfold
parole.testo: Latin mille thousand + English -fold times.

parole.significato: Any of many elongated arthropods, of the class Diplopoda, with cylindrical bodies that have two pairs of legs for each…
parole.testo: From Latin mīllipeda (“wood louse”), from mīlle (“thousand”) + pēs, pedis (“foot”), equivalent to milli- + -pede.

parole.significato: Of or resembling birds of the kite kind.
parole.testo: From Latin milvus (“kite”).

parole.significato: A form of acting without words; pantomime.
parole.testo: Possibly from Middle English mime, from Old English mīma (“a buffoon, jester, mime”), from Latin mimus, from Ancient Greek μῖμος (mîmos, “imitator, actor”), but more likely re-borrowed in modern times from French mime (“mimic actor”), from the same source.

parole.significato: Exhibiting mimesis.
parole.testo: From Latin mīmēticus or its etymon Ancient Greek μῑμητικός (mīmētikós, “imitative”). By surface analysis, mime + -etic.

parole.significato: To imitate, especially in order to ridicule.
parole.testo: From Latin mīmicus, from Ancient Greek μῑμικός (mīmikós, “belonging to mimes”), from μῖμος (mîmos, “imitator, actor”); see mime.

parole.significato: A plant belonging to the genus Mimosa usually found in tropical climates, their leaves are usually prickly and sensitiv…
parole.testo: From New Latin mimosa, from Latin mimus (“mime, actor”), referring to Mimosa pudica and its habit of shrinking back when touched. The cocktail is named after the bright yellow, fragrant flowers of the mimosa Acacia dealbata.

parole.significato: A monetary unit of ancient Greece and the Middle East, originally equivalent to the weight of a mina of silver.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mina, from Ancient Greek μνᾶ (mnâ, “mna”). Compare maneh, from Biblical Hebrew מָנֶה (māne), as well as maund.

parole.significato: Menacing, threatening.
parole.testo: From Latin mināx (“threatening, menacing, projecting”) + -acious.

parole.significato: Synonym of threatening, in its various senses.
parole.testo: From Late Latin minacia (“threat”) + -ious, from Latin minax (“threatening”) + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns). Cf. Italian minaccioso, attested 1532.

parole.significato: Synonym of threateningly: in a minacious manner.
parole.testo: From minacious + -ly, from Late Latin minacia (“threat”), from Latin minax (“threatening”).

parole.significato: Synonym of threateningness: the quality of being minacious.
parole.testo: From minacious + -ness, from Late Latin minacia (“threat”), from Latin minax (“threatening”).

parole.significato: Synonym of menace: The action or process of threatening or the tendency to threaten.
parole.testo: From Late Latin minacitas, from Latin minax (“threatening”) + -itas (“-ity: forming abstract nouns”).

parole.significato: An alloy of (starting with the main component, and ending with the smallest) copper, nickel, tungsten, and aluminium, f…
parole.testo: Probably from aluminium and Latin argentum (“silver”).

parole.significato: The branch of petrology that studies minerals.
parole.testo: From New Latin minerālogia, from Medieval Latin minera (“mineral”) + Latin -logia (“study”). By surface analysis, mineral + -logy.

parole.significato: A gift given in gratitude by a student to a teacher; financial compensation paid to a teacher for their services.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Minervālis.

parole.significato: A mining business.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mineria, minaria, from Old French miniere.

parole.significato: Smaller version of an item than usual.
parole.testo: Shortened from miniature, ultimately from Latin minium (“red lead”). Influenced by similarity to minimum and minus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the colour of red lead or vermilion; painted with vermilion.
parole.testo: Partly borrowed from Latin miniātus (adjective), partly from miniātus, perfect passive participle of miniō (“to cover with vermilion”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Orange-red, the colour of red lead.
parole.testo: From Latin miniatus, suffixed with -ous.

parole.significato: The lowest limit.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin minimum, neuter form of minimus (“least, smallest”).

parole.significato: absolute minimum; the least of all minimums.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: In Aristotelian philosophy, the smallest part into which a homogeneous natural substance (such as bone or wood) could b…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A being of the smallest size.
parole.testo: From Latin minimus (“smallest”). See minim.

parole.significato: A non-noble (originally unfree) official or retainer under certain feudal systems, especially in the Holy Roman Empire,…
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin ministeriālis (“ministerial”). Doublet of ministerial and minstrel.

parole.significato: One who ministers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ministrāns.

parole.significato: A female minister.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ministrīx. By surface analysis, minister + -trix.

parole.significato: Cinnabar, especially when used as a pigment; vermilion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin minium.

parole.significato: Lesser, smaller in importance, size, degree, seriousness, or significance compared to another option, particularly
parole.testo: From Middle English minor, menor, menour, etc., from Latin minor (“lesser; young; young person”) both directly and via Norman and Middle French menor, menour, etc. Doublet of minus but not mini-. Cognate with minister, minify, Minorca, Menshevik, and possibly minnow. Compare Latin minimum and minuō,

parole.significato: To diminish.
parole.testo: First attested in 1534; Latin minōrātus, perfect passive participle of minōrō (“to diminish”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from minor (“lesser”).

parole.significato: Reduction; lessening.
parole.testo: From Late Latin minoratio, from the participle stem of Latin minōrāre.

parole.significato: A domestic chicken of a certain breed originating on the island of Menorca.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Minorca, Minorica, from Latin Balearis Minor. Compare Majorca.

parole.significato: Synonym of Poor Clare: a nun of the Order of Saint Clare.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin minorissa, from Latin minor (“little, lesser”) + -issa (“-ess”), under influence from Norman frere-menouresse and Middle French sereur meneuresse (“lesser sister”), from menour (“minor”) + -esse (“-ess”), after the model of Medieval Latin Fratres Minores (“Lesser Brothers”), chos

parole.significato: Synonym of Franciscan: a friar of the Order of Friars Minor.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Minorita, from Latin minor + -īta (“-ite”), from Ordo Fratres Minores (“Order of Friars Minor”), literally the "Order of the Lesser Brothers", chosen by St. Francis to inculcate humility in its members. Equivalent to minor + -ite. Doublet of minister.

parole.significato: A monastic church.
parole.testo: From Middle English mynster (see mynisterie), from Old English mynster, from Latin monastērium (“monastery”), from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, “monastery; solitary dwelling”). Doublet of monastery.

parole.significato: A number or quantity from which another is to be subtracted.
parole.testo: From Latin minuendus (“something to be diminished”), gerundive of minuō (“decrease, diminish”), by surface analysis, minus + -end.

parole.significato: Made less or reduced by (followed by an expression of number or quantity).
parole.testo: From Middle English mynus, from Latin minus, neuter form of minor, comparative form of parvus (“small, little”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *mey- (“few, small”).

parole.significato: Very small.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin minūtus (“small", "petty”), perfect passive participle of minuō (“make smaller”).

parole.significato: A minor detail, often of negligible importance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin minutia, from minūtus (“small, little”), from minuō (“make smaller”). By surface analysis, minute + -ia.

parole.significato: A member of a race said to be autochthonous to the Aegean area.
parole.testo: From Latin Minyes (from Ancient Greek Μινύες (Minúes)) + -an.

parole.significato: A precalculated, optimised collection of images accompanying a main texture, used to increase rendering speed and reduc…
parole.testo: From mip (an acronym of Latin multum in parvo (“much in little”), referring to many images in a small space) + map, modelled on bitmap.

parole.significato: Wonderfully, amazingly; remarkable to relate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mīrābile dictū (literally “able to astonish by the saying [of it]”).

parole.significato: Wonderful to behold.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mīrābile vīsū (literally “strange to see”).

parole.significato: Wonderful or extraordinary things; marvels.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin mīrābilia. Doublet of marvel.

parole.significato: Any of the plant genus Mirabilis; a four-o'clock.
parole.testo: From the genus name, from Latin mīrābilis. Doublet of mirable.

parole.significato: An evaporite, consisting of sodium sulfate, with the chemical formula Na₂SO₄·10H₂O.
parole.testo: From Latin mīrābilis (“miraculous”) + -ite. From the Latin term sal mirabilis (“wonderful salt”), which was used by German-Dutch alchemist Johann Rudolph Glauber (1604–1670) after he inadvertently synthesised the substance.

parole.significato: Marvellousness.
parole.testo: Probably from Latin mīrābilitās.

parole.significato: A set of tasks that fulfills a purpose or duty; an assignment set by an employer, or by oneself.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin missiō, missiōnem (“a sending, sending away, dispatching, discharging, release, remission, cessation”).

parole.significato: A written message; a letter, note or memo.

parole.significato: Tending to mitigate.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin monumentālis, from Latin monumentum; equivalent to monument + -al.
