parole.testo: Alteration of mode, from Latin modus, with specialized uses in grammar, music and logic.

parole.significato: A delay in bringing a claim.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mora (“duration of time, delay”).

parole.significato: Any tree of the genus Mora of large South American trees.
parole.testo: From New Latin from a botanical name, from Tupi moira-tinga and/or Arawak mora.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling the mulberry plants in the family Moraceae.
parole.testo: Latin morus (“mulberry tree”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: A delay.
parole.testo: Latin moratio.

parole.significato: An authorization to a debtor, permitting temporary suspension of payments.
parole.testo: New Latin from Late Latin morātōrium, noun use of the neuter of morātōrius (“moratory, delaying”), from Latin moror (“to delay”), from mora (“delay”), from Proto-Indo-European *mere (“to delay, hinder”). See also moratory.

parole.significato: Pertaining to delay of payment or fulfilment of an obligation.
parole.testo: Latin moratorius (“delaying”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or afflicted by disease.
parole.testo: From Latin morbidus (“diseased”), from morbus (“sickness”), itself from the root of morī (“to die”) or directly from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to rub, pound, wear away”).

parole.significato: measles, rubeola
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin morbillus, from Latin morbus (“disease”) + -illus (“diminutive suffix”).

parole.significato: Resembling the erythematous, maculopapular rash of measles.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin morbillus (“measles”) + -form. See morbilli for more.

parole.significato: Resembling or relating to measles.
parole.testo: Latin morbilli (“measles”), diminutive of Latin morbus (“disease”) + -ous: compare French morbilleux.

parole.significato: Proceeding from disease; morbid; unhealthy.
parole.testo: From Latin morbosus (“diseased”), from morbus (“disease”).

parole.significato: A diseased state; unhealthiness.
parole.testo: Latin morbositas.

parole.significato: Physical or mental illness or infirmity.
parole.testo: Perhaps from morbid, ultimately from Latin morbus (“malady (of body or mind), distress”).

parole.significato: A disease.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin morbus.

parole.significato: Dupuytren's contracture
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Biting, causing a physical bite or sting; corrosive
parole.testo: From Latin mordax (“given to biting, corrosive”) (from mordere (“to bite, sting”)) + -ious.

parole.significato: biting; acrid (normally talking about pain)
parole.testo: From Latin mordicans, p.pr. of mordicare (“to bite”), from mordere. Compare French mordicant.

parole.significato: The act of biting or corroding.
parole.testo: From Latin mordicatio.

parole.significato: Biting or corrosive.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mordicativus.

parole.significato: In his or her own manner.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Synonym of morello (“type of cherry”).
parole.testo: From Middle English morel, morell, from Anglo-Norman and Old French morel, morele, morelle and their etymon Medieval Latin maurella, morella, from Late Latin maurus, morus (“black”) + Latin -ella (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: A set of moral norms or customs derived from generally accepted practices rather than written laws.
parole.testo: From Latin mōrēs (“ways, character, morals”), the plural of mōs. Doublet of moeurs.

parole.significato: Designating a marriage (or the wife involved) between a man of higher rank and a woman of lower rank, often having vari…
parole.testo: From New Latin morganāticus, from the Medieval Latin phrase mātrimōnium ad morganāticum, from Proto-Germanic *murgnagebō (“morning gift”) (whence Old English morgenġiefu).

parole.significato: Approaching death; about to die; dying; expiring.
parole.testo: From Latin moribundus (“dying”).

parole.significato: The production of mulberry leaves to provide feed for silkworms.
parole.testo: From Latin morī, genetive of mōrus (“black mulberry tree”), + culture.

parole.significato: Dying, moribund.
parole.testo: From Latin moriēns.

parole.significato: Mulberry-like.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin morus (“mulberry”) + -form.

parole.significato: Servile acquiescence; unqualified sycophancy towards a bully or a tyrant.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mōrigerātiō. Compare Middle English morigeracioun (“character or nature”).

parole.significato: obedient; obsequious
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin morigerus, from mōs, mōris (“custom, manner”) + gerō (“to bear, conduct”).

parole.significato: A variety of tannic acid extracted as a yellow crystalline substance from fustic (Maclura tinctoria, formerly Morus tin…
parole.testo: From morin (“moric acid”) (from Latin morus (“fustic”)) + English tannic.

parole.significato: The act of lingering with pleasure on an impure thought.
parole.testo: Calque of Medieval Latin dēlectātiō mōrōsa, used by Thomas Aquinas in the Summa Theologiae.

parole.significato: An acid derived from the mulberry.
parole.testo: Latin morus (“mulberry tree”) + Ancient Greek ξύλον (xúlon, “wood”) + -ic + acid. Named by Martin Heinrich Klaproth

parole.significato: A blemish or mark on the skin, especially a blister caused by scurvy.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin morphea, perhaps from Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “form, shape”). Doublet of morphea.

parole.significato: The way in which an organism (or an organ) changes form during development.
parole.testo: From Late Latin morphosis, from Ancient Greek μόρφωσις (mórphōsis, “shaping”).

parole.significato: A lesion of the oral mucosa (the inside of the cheek) caused by friction, as in repetitive biting or chewing.
parole.testo: From the Latin morusus (“bite”).

parole.significato: A kind of mortar used by ancient Romans for grinding.
parole.testo: From Latin mortārium. Doublet of mortar.

parole.significato: The trail or trace left by a dying animal, especially as preserved in a fossil.
parole.testo: From Latin mors (“death, corpse”) + -ichnion, with influence from -ium.

parole.significato: An undertaker or funeral director; especially, one who is also the embalmer or cremator.
parole.testo: From Latin mort- (“death”) + -ician.

parole.significato: The energy of the death instinct.
parole.testo: From Latin mors (“death”), modeled after libido.

parole.significato: Causing spiritual death.
parole.testo: From Latin mortifer + -ous.

parole.significato: Rule or government based on death in some way.
parole.testo: Latin mors (“death”) + -cracy

parole.significato: Mosaic.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Mosaicus + -al.

parole.significato: Exuding a musk-like odour.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin moschātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The Church regarded as nourishing and protecting its members.
parole.testo: From an association of spiritual comfort and hierarchy with familial relationships, probably originally as a calque of similar expressions in other languages, especially 2nd-century Latin mater ecclesia (“mother church”) and 12th-century Old French mere eglise (“mother church”).

parole.significato: Said in supplication to Mary.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin Mater Dei and its descendants in other languages, from the Christian concept of the Trinity whereby Jesus as God the Son is identical to God the Father as the single divinity.

parole.significato: The hard pearly inner layer of certain mollusk shells; nacre.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin māter perlārum, with the first element perhaps connected in popular imagination with obsolete mother (“dregs”). Possibly referring to the fact that the nacre-lined shells are the belly (“mother”) in which pearls are produced.

parole.significato: Producing motion.
parole.testo: From Latin motus (“motion”) (from movere (“to move”)) + facere (“to make”).

parole.significato: In organisms: having the power to move spontaneously.
parole.testo: From Latin mōtus, perfect passive participle of moveō (“to move”, whence English move), + -ile.

parole.significato: The act of capturing a motion picture; filming.
parole.testo: Possibly from Latin mōto(r) (“mover”) + -graphy.

parole.significato: A machine or device that converts other energy forms into mechanical energy, or imparts motion.
parole.testo: From Middle English motour (“controller, prime mover; God”), from Latin mōtor (“mover; that which moves something”), from mōtō (“to set in motion”).

parole.significato: Causing or setting up motion.
parole.testo: From Latin motorius (“that has motion”). See motor (noun).

parole.significato: A female instigator or cause of something.
parole.testo: A post-classical Latin female form of classical Latin motor (“motor”). It is used as the feminine form of motor (“(he) that moves”) in neo-Latin, as in the original of Newton's Laws of Motion: proportionalem esse vi motrici impressae ‘is proportional to the motive force applied’ formed on the agenti

parole.significato: Of one’s own free will, of one’s own volition.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin motu proprio, from ablative form of classical Latin motus (“motion”) + proprius (“one’s own”).

parole.significato: A star's own motion, independent of the motion due to the displacement of the observer.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The process of shedding or losing a covering of fur, feathers or skin etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English mouten, from Old English *mutian (attested in bemutian, “to exchange for”), from Latin mūtō (“to (re)move, change, vary, mutate, exchange, abandon”). Doublet of mute and mutate. The unetymological ⟨l⟩ was introduced into the spelling by mistakenly assuming a French origin with -l

parole.significato: A hill or mountain.
parole.testo: From Middle English mount, munt, from Old English munt, from Latin mōns (“a hill, mountain”), from a root seen also in ēmineō (“to project, to protrude”) (English eminent). Doublet of mons. Not related to mound.

parole.significato: Musty; mouldy; slimy or mucous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mucidus, from Latin mucus (“mucus”). See mucus, and compare moist.

parole.significato: Inducing or stimulating the secretion of mucus; blennogenous.
parole.testo: From mucus + Latin -ficare (“to make”) (in comparative). See -fy.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to mucilage; of, pertaining to, or resembling mucus; slimy and viscous.
parole.testo: From New Latin mūcilāginōsus from Late Latin mūcus.

parole.significato: Secreting, or producing, mucus or mucin.
parole.testo: From mucus + Latin parere (“to produce”).

parole.significato: An insect that feeds on mucus, or the sap of plants, such as certain Diptera like aphids.
parole.testo: From Latin mucus (“slime, mucus”) + -vore.

parole.significato: mucus.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from mucus; more at mucus § Etymology.

parole.significato: The property of being mucid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mucor.

parole.significato: Pertaining to mucus.
parole.testo: Naturalized from Late Latin mūcōsus, from Latin mūcus. By surface analysis, muc(us) + -ous = muco- + -ous.

parole.significato: A pointed end, often sharp, abruptly terminating an organ, such as a projection at the tip of a leaf; the posterior tip…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mucro. From 17th century.

parole.significato: An apical attachment organelle present in archigregarines
parole.testo: From Latin mucro. Doublet of Doublet of mucro.

parole.significato: Terminating in a mucro (an abruptly tapering point or a sharp spine) such as at the end of a leaf.
parole.testo: From mucro(n) + -ate (adjective-forming suffix) or directly from Latin mūcrōnātus.

parole.significato: Having a sharp pointed end or mucro.
parole.testo: From Latin mūcrō, mūcrōnem (“a sharp point”) + -iform.

parole.significato: slimy; moist and unpleasantly viscous
parole.testo: From Latin mūculentus, from mūcus.

parole.significato: Lowing; bellowing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mūgiēns, present participle of mūgiō (“to bellow”).

parole.significato: Imposing a pecuniary penalty; consisting of, or paid as, a fine.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mulctuārius + English -ary (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining’ to forming adjectives). Mulctuārius is derived from mulcta (“fine”).

parole.significato: Womanly, feminine, relating to or in the manner of an adult woman.
parole.testo: From Latin muliebris (“womanly”) + -al.

parole.significato: The female genitals.
parole.testo: From Latin muliebria.

parole.significato: womanly; feminine
parole.testo: Latin muliebris + -ile, presumably after virile.

parole.significato: A fondness for women.
parole.testo: Latin mulierositas.

parole.significato: Wine or water boiled and mixed with honey.
parole.testo: Latin mulsum (vinum), from mulsus (“mixed with honey, honey-sweet”), past participle of mulcere (“sweeten, soften”).

parole.significato: A polygon.
parole.testo: From Renaissance Latin multangulum, use as noun of neuter of Classical Latin multangulus.

parole.significato: Having many minds or aspects; many-sided.
parole.testo: From multi- + Latin animus (“mind”).

parole.significato: manifoldness; multiplicity; the quality of being many.
parole.testo: From Latin multus (“much, many”).

parole.significato: More than one; pertaining to more than one thing.
parole.testo: From late Middle English multi-, from Latin multī, from multus.

parole.significato: Having many cavities.
parole.testo: From Latin multicavus, from multus (“much, many”) + cavum, cavus (“a cavity, hole”), from cavus (“hollow”).

parole.significato: Having many heads or stems from one crown or root
parole.testo: From multi- + Latin caput (“head”).

parole.significato: Having, resembling, or pertaining to many colors.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin multicolor, equivalent to multi- + color; see below.

parole.significato: Having great diversity or variety; of various kinds; made up of many differing parts.
parole.testo: From Latin multifārius.

parole.significato: Bearing or producing much or many; fruitful.
parole.testo: From Latin multifer, from multus (“much, many”) + ferre (“to bear”).

parole.significato: Cleft into many parts or lobes.
parole.testo: From Latin multifidus, from multi- (“many”) + -fidus, from findere (“to split”). Equivalent of multi- + -fid. Doublet of multifidus and multifidous.

parole.significato: A thin muscle consisting of a number of fleshy and tendinous fasciculi that fill up the groove on either side of the sp…
parole.testo: From Latin multifidus. Doublet of multifid and multifidous.

parole.significato: The hardy rose Rosa multiflora
parole.testo: From the New Latin multiflora (species epithet, literally “having many flowers”).

parole.significato: Having many flowers.
parole.testo: From Latin multiflorus, from multus (“much, many”) + flos, floris (“flower”). Compare French multiflore.

parole.significato: The quality of being multiform, or having many forms.
parole.testo: From Latin multiformitas.

parole.significato: Having many kinds.
parole.testo: From Latin multigenerus, from multus + genus.

parole.significato: Very talkative.
parole.testo: From Latin multiloquus, from multus (“much, many”) + loqui (“to speak”).

parole.significato: An excess of words or talk.
parole.testo: From Middle English multiloquye, from Latin multiloquium. By surface analysis, multi- + -loquy.

parole.significato: multinodate; having many knots or nodes
parole.testo: Latin multinodus.

parole.significato: Having many names or terms.
parole.testo: From multi- + oblique stem of Latin nōmen, nōminis + -ous.

parole.significato: Having two or more pregnancies resulting in viable offspring.
parole.testo: From Latin multiparus. By surface analysis, multi + parous.

parole.significato: Having many feet.
parole.testo: From Latin multipeda, multipēs; equivalent to multi- + -pede.

parole.significato: Comprising several interleaved parts.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin multiplex, from multi- + -plex.

parole.significato: Consisting of many, or of more than one; multiple; multifold.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin multiplicātus, perfect passive participle of multiplicō, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to multiplication.
parole.testo: From 6th-century Latin multiplicativus, from Classical Latin multiplicāre (“to multiply”).

parole.significato: The state of being made of multiple diverse elements.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin multiplicitas.

parole.significato: Having much or varied knowledge.
parole.testo: From Latin multiscius, from multus (“much”) + scius (“knowing”), from scire (“to know”).

parole.significato: Divided into many similar segments; said of an insect or myriapod
parole.testo: From multi- + Latin sectus, past participle of secare (“to cut”).

parole.significato: Having many sounds.
parole.testo: From Latin multisonus, from multus (“much, many”) + sonus (“sound”).

parole.significato: Giving birth to multiple young at one time; synonym of multiparous and polytocous.
parole.testo: From Latin multi- + Ancient Greek τόκος (tókos).

parole.significato: Multitudinous; very numerous.
parole.testo: From Latin multitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin multitūdō, from multus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, multitude + -al.

parole.significato: multitudinous
parole.testo: From Latin multitūdin- + -ary, from oblique stem of Latin multitūdō, from multus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, multitude + -ary.

parole.significato: The principle that the interests of the people generally are more important than those of individuals
parole.testo: From Latin multitūdin- + -ism, from oblique stem of Latin multitūdō, from multus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, multitude + -ism.

parole.significato: Relating to multitudinism
parole.testo: From Latin multitūdin- + -ist, from oblique stem of Latin multitūdō, from multus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, multitude + -ist.

parole.significato: Existing in multitudes or great numbers; very numerous; innumerable.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin multitūdin- (the oblique stem of multitūdō (“great number (of people), multitude”)) + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, denoting the presence of a quality in any degree (typically an abundance)). Multitūdō is derived from multus (“many; much”) (ultimate

parole.significato: wandering a lot
parole.testo: From Latin multivagus, from multus (“much”) + vagus (“wandering”). Compare vagans, present participle of vagari. See vagary.

parole.significato: Many and various
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin multivarius.

parole.significato: Turning into many shapes; assuming many forms; protean.
parole.testo: From multi- + Latin versans, present participle. See versant.

parole.significato: Having many different interpretations, meanings, or values.
parole.testo: From Late Latin multivocus (“expressed by many words”), from multi- + form of vocare (“to call”).

parole.significato: That writes a great deal.
parole.testo: From Latin multus (“much”) + English -o- + scribbling. The earliest recorded usage appears in the writings of poet Lord Byron in the 1820s.

parole.significato: Much in little; a lot in a small space.
parole.testo: From Latin multum n (“much, many”) + in + parvo (ablative of parvum, “small, little, puny”).

parole.significato: A medicinal preparation of mummified human flesh; mummy.
parole.testo: From Late Latin mummia, mumia.

parole.significato: A person who obstinately adheres to old ways in spite of clear evidence that they are wrong; an ignorant and bigoted op…
parole.testo: Malapropism of Latin sumpsimus, form of sūmō (“to take”), from a story of an old monk who misrecited the Eucharist with quod in ōre mumpsimus instead of quod in ōre sumpsimus “which we have taken into the mouth”, and stubbornly continued using the incorrect form even after being corrected. Attested

parole.significato: The act of cleaning.
parole.testo: From Latin mundātio (“cleaning”), from mundō (“to make clean”), from mundus (“clean, neat, elegant”), from Proto-Indo-European *mewH- (“to wash, wet”). Cognate with Dutch mooi (“nice, beautiful, sheen”).

parole.significato: Synonym of purificator (“napkin used during Holy Communion”).
parole.testo: Latin mundatorius.

parole.significato: Serving to cleanse and heal.
parole.testo: From Latin mundificans, p.pr. of mundificare (“to make clean”), from mundus (“clean”) + -ficare (“to make”) (in comparative). See -fy.

parole.significato: To cleanse.
parole.testo: From Middle English mundifien, borrowed from Latin mundificō.

parole.significato: Wandering across the world; globetrotting.
parole.testo: From Latin mundus (“world”) + vagans (“wandering”), present participle of vagari. See vagary.

parole.significato: Not immune; subject or vulnerable to (something).
parole.testo: Formed under the implication that the word immune was formed in modern English with the prefix im- and another word. The word immune was actually formed from a prefix in Latin immūnis (“exempt from public service”), from in- (“not”) + mūnus (“service”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to gifts; having the nature of a gift.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mūnerārius, from mūnus (“service; gift”).

parole.significato: To remunerate.
parole.testo: From Latin muneratus, past participle of munerare (“to give, bestow”).

parole.significato: An ancient Roman town or city.
parole.testo: From Latin municipium. Doublet of municipio.

parole.significato: Very liberal in giving or bestowing.
parole.testo: Back-formation from munificence, from Latin mūnificentia.

parole.significato: To fortify, strengthen.
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Latin mūnīre (“to wall round, fortify”), earlier moenīre, from moenia (“walls”).

parole.significato: Materials of war: armaments, weapons and ammunition.
parole.testo: From Latin mūnitiō (“a defence, fortification”) via French munition, from mūnīre (“fortify, defend (with a wall)”) + -tiō, from moenia (“city walls, defensive walls, or walls in general”). Equivalent to munite + -ion.

parole.significato: A crown or headpiece representing city walls or towers, used as a military decoration in Ancient Rome and later as a he…
parole.testo: Latin corona muralis

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to muramic acid or its derivatives
parole.testo: From Latin mūrus (“wall”) + -amic.

parole.significato: A secret killing, distinguished from simple homicide in that the victim and the killer are unknown.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Medieval Latin murdrum, a Germanic borrowing from Frankish *murþr, *morþr, from Proto-Germanic *murþrą (“murder”). More at murder.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Murex of marine gastropods.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin murex.

parole.significato: Pertaining to salt or brine.
parole.testo: From Latin muriāticus (“pickled”), from muria (“brine”).

parole.significato: covered with short rough points or studs
parole.testo: First attested in 1661; borrowed from Latin mūricātus (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from mūrex (“a pointed rock or stone”).

parole.significato: Mouse-killing (especially in rats).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mūricīdus (literally “mouse-killer”). By surface analysis, Latin mūs (“mouse”) + -icide (“killing; killer”).

parole.significato: Resembling or relating to the genus Murex or family Muricidae.
parole.testo: Classical Latin mūrex (stem: mūric-) + English -oid

parole.significato: bromine
parole.testo: From Latin muria (“brine”) (since it was obtained from seawater) + -ide.

parole.significato: Resembling a wall.
parole.testo: From Latin murus (“a wall”) + -form.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of a mouse.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mūrīnus (“mouselike”).

parole.significato: An act or instance of murmuring.
parole.testo: 1350–1400; Medieval Latin murmuratio (“murmuring, grumbling”), equivalent to murmur + -ation. The “flock of starlings” sense is probably derived from the sound of the very large groups that starlings form at dusk.

parole.significato: Any peptidoglycan associated with a cell wall.
parole.testo: From Latin murus (“wall”) + peptide.

parole.significato: Made of murra; applied to certain valuable vases of great beauty and delicacy used by the luxurious in Rome as wine cup…
parole.testo: From Latin murrhinus, from murrha. Compare French murrhin.

parole.significato: A wall, in the context of Ancient Rome. "Ubi vero moveri et adpropinquare muris viderunt, nova atque inusitata specie c…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mūrus (“wall”).

parole.significato: floater (threadlike speck in the visual field)
parole.testo: From a Latin phrase meaning "a fly (musca) flying around (volitans)".

parole.significato: An extremely poisonous alkaloid, obtained from fly agaric, that disrupts the action of acetylcholine neurotransmitter.
parole.testo: From the fungus Amanita muscaria, from Latin musca (“fly”).

parole.significato: Any substance that kills flies.
parole.testo: From Latin musca (“fly”) + -icide.

parole.significato: Having the appearance or form of a moss.
parole.testo: From Latin mūscus (“moss”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Something which repels or kills flies, typically a plant; a fly repellent. Also spelled "muscafuge" (1844) by Henry Ste…
parole.testo: From Latin musca (“fly”) + -fuge (“repellent”), compare medieval Latin muscifugium, a fly fan.

parole.significato: Any fly in the superfamily Muscoidea.
parole.testo: Latin musca (“fly”)

parole.significato: Synonym of bryology.
parole.testo: From Latin muscologia, from muscus (“moss”) + -o- + -logia.

parole.significato: mossiness
parole.testo: From Latin muscosus (“mossy”), from muscus (“moss”).

parole.significato: An inhabitant or native of Muscovy or Moscow.
parole.testo: 1535. From Latin Moscovita (“resident of Moscow or Muscovy, Russian”), also Muscovita, Moschovita, from Moscovia or Muscovia (“Muscovy”) + -ita.

parole.significato: pectinate muscles
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: syntonin
parole.testo: From Latin musculus (“a muscle”) + -in.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the radial nerve (also called the musculospiral nerve)
parole.testo: Latin musculus (“muscle”) + English spiral.

parole.significato: A muscle.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin mūsculus (“a little mouse; a muscle”), diminutive of mūs (“a mouse”).

parole.significato: Synonym of papillary muscle.
parole.testo: From Latin mūsculus papillāris.

parole.significato: One of the nine Ancient Greek deities of the arts.
parole.testo: From Middle English Muse, from Latin Musa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).

parole.significato: A building or institution dedicated to the acquisition, conservation, study, exhibition, and educational interpretation…
parole.testo: From Latin mūsēum (“library, study”), from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)). Doublet of mosaic.

parole.significato: The use of chromatically altered tones in the contrapuntal music of the 10th to the 16th centuries.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mūsica ficta (literally “fashioned music”).

parole.significato: Synonym of music of the spheres.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Synonym of mouflon (“wild sheep”).
parole.testo: From Latin musimo (“wild sheep”), related to Late Latin mufrō (“wild sheep”), both probably of pre-Latin origin. Compare mouflon; see also musmon.

parole.significato: A wild or domestic cat.
parole.testo: From Latin mus (“mouse”) + -ion (compare mouser).

parole.significato: Relating to mosaic art.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin musivus.

parole.significato: A kind of sheep, the mouflon.
parole.testo: From Latin musmo, musimo.

parole.significato: The fear of mice (and rats).
parole.testo: From Latin mūs (“mouse”) or Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “mouse”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: Speech conducted in a hushed manner, akin to a murmur or a whisper.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mussitātiō (“soft noise made by dogs, or (Late Latin) people”) + English -ion (suffix denoting a condition or state). Mussitātiō is derived from mussitātus (“kept quiet; having been kept quiet; murmured, muttered; having been muttered”) (see further at mussitate) + -iō (

parole.significato: Any of the carnivorous mammals of the genus Mustela.
parole.testo: From Latin mūstēla and translingual Mustela.

parole.significato: Like or relating to the family Mustelidae, or the weasels and martens.
parole.testo: From the Latin mūstēlīnus, from mūstēla (“weasel”), from mūs (“mouse”, “rat”).

parole.significato: Relating to mutation.
parole.testo: From mutation, itself from Latin mūtātiō, by analogy with other Graeco-Latin prefixes.

parole.significato: That which is to be changed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mutandum.

parole.significato: That which has mutated, with one or more new characteristics from a mutation.
parole.testo: From Latin mūtāns, present participle of mūtō. By surface analysis, muta- + -ant.

parole.significato: To undergo mutation.
parole.testo: First attested in 1796; back-formation from mutation on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), ultimately from Latin mūtō (“to exchange; to change, to vary”). Doublet of moult.

parole.significato: Any alteration or change.
parole.testo: Late 14th century as Middle English mutacioun, from Latin mūtātiō, both directly and via Old French mutacion.

parole.significato: With the necessary changes being made; with the necessary modifications; with such changes as are necessary to ensure c…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Late Latin mūtātīs mūtandīs (“with [the things] to be changed having been changed”).

parole.significato: To cast off; to moult.
parole.testo: From Latin mutare (“to change”).

parole.significato: Without a point or pointed end; blunt.
parole.testo: Latin muticus, for mutilus. See mutilate.

parole.significato: To physically harm as to impair use, notably by cutting off or otherwise disabling a vital part, such as a limb.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mutilātus, the perfect passive participle of mutilō (“to mutilate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), itself from mutilus (“maimed”).

parole.significato: The act of mutilating or the state of being mutilated.
parole.testo: Latin mutilatio; compare French mutilation.

parole.significato: deformity, defectivity
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mutilitās.

parole.significato: mutilated, defective, or imperfect
parole.testo: From Latin mutilus. See mutilate.

parole.significato: A motion-picture device of the late nineteenth century, to be viewed by one person at a time through a peephole.
parole.testo: Originally a trademark, from Latin mutare (“to change”), and -scope.

parole.significato: One who borrows personal chattels which are to be consumed by him, and which he is to return or repay in kind
parole.testo: From Latin mutuarius (“mutual”). See mutuation.

parole.significato: An act of borrowing or exchanging.
parole.testo: From Latin mutuatio, from mutuare, mutuari (“to borrow”), from mutuus. See mutual.

parole.significato: Any of the rectangular blocks under the soffit of the cornice of the Greek Doric temple, which are studded with guttae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mutulus.

parole.significato: A loan of a fungible thing to be restored by a similar thing of the same kind, quantity, and quality.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Latin mūtuum (“loan”), neuter substantive of mūtuus (“borrowed, lent”).

parole.significato: The vegetative part of any fungus, consisting of a mass of branching, threadlike hyphae, often underground.
parole.testo: From New Latin mycelium; synchronically, myc- + -el- + -ium, where the infix -el- is of unknown origin, perhaps introduced from a rebracketing of epithelium.

parole.significato: The condition of having abnormally large and dilated pupils due to illness or narcotics, particularly stimulants such a…
parole.testo: From Latin mydriasis, from Ancient Greek μυδρίᾱσις (mudríāsis, “undue enlargement of the pupil”), from μύδρος (múdros, “mass of red hot material in a forge”), possibly because the pupil is particularly bright or sparkling when dilated, or because of the red eye effect when exposed to a flash of ligh

parole.significato: megakaryocyte or osteoclast
parole.testo: From New Latin myeloplax, from Ancient Greek μυελός (muelós, “marrow”) + πλάξ (pláx, “plate”).

parole.significato: A shrew or ferret.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mygale (“field mouse”) (Vetus Latina), from Ancient Greek μυγαλέη (mugaléē, “shrew”) (used in the Septuagint to translate Hebrew אֲנָקָה, now generally thought to indicate a gecko or similar small reptile).

parole.significato: Relating to or in the region of the lower jaw and the hyoid apparatus, or the mylohyoid muscle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin mylohȳoīdēs, from Ancient Greek μῠ́λη (mŭ́lē, “a molar”) + Latin hȳoīdēs (“U-shaped”); equivalent to mylo- (“molar”) + hyoid.

parole.significato: The mylohyoid muscle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin mylohȳoīdeus, clipping of musculus mylohȳoīdeus (“mylohyoid muscle”).

parole.significato: The muscular substance of the heart; the middle of the three layers forming the outer wall of the human heart.
parole.testo: From New Latin myocardium, from Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “muscle”) + καρδίᾱ (kardíā, “heart”).

parole.significato: The smooth muscle forming the wall of the uterus.
parole.testo: From myo- + Late Latin metrium (“womb”), from Ancient Greek μήτριον (mḗtrion, “of a mother”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Myosotis, the forget-me-nots.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin myosōtis, from Koine Ancient Greek μυοσωτίς (muosōtís, literally “ears of a mouse”), from genitive of μῦς (mûs, “mouse”) and nominative plural of οὖς (oûs, “ear”).

parole.significato: A protein that acts as an inhibitor to the growth of muscle tissue.
parole.testo: Perhaps from myo- (“muscle”) + Latin statos, status, sto (“remain, stand, fix, set"”) or Ancient Greek στάσις (stásis, “inactivity, a freezing, state of motionlessness, arrest, a standing”). myo- + -statin?

parole.significato: A symptom of several muscular disorders characterized by the slow relaxation of the muscles after voluntary contraction…
parole.testo: From New Latin myotonia, from myo- + -tonia. By surface analysis, myo- + -tonia.

parole.significato: Synonym of eardrum.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, from Latin myrinx. parole.significato: One of a fierce tribe or troop who accompanied Achilles, their king, in the Trojan War.
parole.testo: From Latin Myrmidones, from Ancient Greek Μυρμιδόνες (Murmidónes), a tribe of warriors led by Achilles to the Trojan War. Folk etymology in Ovid's time derived the tribe's name from μυρμηδών (murmēdṓn, “ant-nest”), from μύρμηξ (múrmēx, “ant”)).

parole.significato: A soldier or a subordinate civil officer who executes orders of a superior without protest or pity (sometimes applied t…
parole.testo: From Myrmidon, from Latin Myrmidones, from Ancient Greek Μυρμιδόνες (Murmidónes).

parole.significato: A plum-like fruit from various trees of the genus Terminalia, formerly used in medicine and now in the dyeing industry;…
parole.testo: From Latin myrobalanum, myrobalanus (“ben nut”), from Ancient Greek μυροβάλανος (murobálanos), from μύρον (múron, “perfume”) + βάλανος (bálanos, “acorn”).

parole.significato: A red-brown resinous material, the dried sap of a tree of the genus Commiphora, especially Commiphora myrrha, used as p…
parole.testo: From Middle English mirre, from Old English myrre, from Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), from Semitic. Compare Arabic مُرّ (murr, “myrrh”, literally “bitterness”), Hebrew מור / מֹר (mōr, “myrrh”, literally “bitterness”). Compare מרור : maror.

parole.significato: A myrtle grove.
parole.testo: From Latin myrtētum.

parole.significato: A set of growth stages in the larvae of Decapoda after protozoea and prior to the juvenile stage, in which pereiopods a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek μῡ́ειν (mū́ein, “to close”, used of the lips or eyes).

parole.significato: A person who prepares an initiate for entry into a mystery cult, or who teaches mystical doctrines.
parole.testo: From Latin mystagōgus, Ancient Greek μυσταγωγός (mustagōgós). By surface analysis, mystic + -agogue.

parole.significato: A mystagogue.
parole.testo: From Latin mystagogus.

parole.significato: One who rules over mysteries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin mystēriarchēs (“one who presides over Christian sacraments”), from Ancient Greek μυστηριάρχης (mustēriárkhēs, “one who rules over religious mysteries”), from μυστήριον (mustḗrion) + -άρχης (-árkhēs), corresponding to mystery + -arch.

parole.significato: Any of various unknown elements thought to make up existing forms of matter, or a substance seen as an elemental or pur…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mystērium. Doublet of mystery.

parole.significato: An ancient Roman priest of the secret rites of divine worship.
parole.testo: From Latin mystēs.

parole.significato: Mythical; existing in myth.
parole.testo: 1660s; from Latin mȳthicus or Ancient Greek μυθικός (muthikós); equivalent to myth + -ic.

parole.significato: Anything transmitted by word of mouth, such as a fable, legend, narrative, story, or tale (especially a poetic tale).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mȳthos (“myth”), from Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “report, tale, story”). Doublet of myth. The plural form mythoi is from Ancient Greek μῦθοι (mûthoi), and the form mythoses from mythos + -es.

parole.significato: Synonym of mythos.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mythus, from Late Latin mȳthos (“myth”), from Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “report, tale, story”).

parole.significato: A tumor consisting of primitive connective tissue and mucous elements.
parole.testo: From New Latin myxōma. By surface analysis, myxo- (“mucus”) + -oma.

parole.significato: not applicable
parole.testo: From Latin non + applicabilis, from applicō (“join to, attach, apply”).

parole.significato: The ancient inhabitants of Nabataea, a region of Arabia inhabited by the Nabataeans that covers parts of northern Arabi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Nabataeus (“Nabataean”), which was borrowed from Ancient Greek Ναβαταῖος (Nabataîos, “Nabataean”), which was borrowed from Nabataean Aramaic 𐢕𐢃𐢋𐢈 (nbṭw, “Nabataean”). Possibly cognate with Arabic نَبَطِيّ (nabaṭiyy, “Nabataean, Nabaṭ”), Arabic أَنْبَاط (ʔanbāṭ), and Hebrew נבטים

parole.significato: A Hebrew stringed instrument.
parole.testo: From Latin nabla, from Ancient Greek νάβλα (nábla, “Phoenician harp”), from ancient Hebrew נֵבֶל (nḗḇel) or a Phoenician cognate. Doublet of nebel, which comes via the modern Hebrew נֵ֤בֶל.

parole.significato: The point of the celestial sphere, directly opposite the zenith; inferior pole of the horizon; point of the celestial s…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nadir, from Arabic نَظِير السَّمْت (naẓīr as-samt), composed of نَظِير (naẓīr, “counterpart, corresponding to”) and السَّمْت (as-samt, “the zenith”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Latin poet Gnaeus Naevius.
parole.testo: From the Latin Naeviānus.

parole.significato: A vascular birthmark or naevus, usually on the head and neck, consisting of an overgrowth of capillaries which produce…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A female deity (nymph) associated with water, especially a spring, stream, or other fresh water.
parole.testo: From Latin Nāïas, from Ancient Greek Νᾱϊάς (Nāïás, “naiad”), from νάω (náō, “to flow”).

parole.significato: In the International System of Units and other metric systems of units, multiplying the unit to which it is attached by…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nānus (“dwarf”), borrowed from Ancient Greek νᾶνος (nânos, “dwarf”).

parole.significato: A form of dwarfism characterized by a very short trunk
parole.testo: From nano- (“dwarf”) + Latin cormus, Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós, “trunk”).

parole.significato: The monkshood or wolfsbane (Aconitum napellus).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin napellus.

parole.significato: Naturally occurring liquid petroleum.
parole.testo: From Latin naphtha, from Ancient Greek νάφθα (náphtha, “naphtha”), from Old Persian *naftah, probably borrowed or assimilated from Akkadian 𒉌𒆳𒊏 (napṭu, “naphtha”) . The Greek mediation is reflected in the spelling – ‘ph’ and ‘th’ (from ‘φ’ and ‘θ’).

parole.significato: Shaped like a turnip; spherical at the top, but with a tapering bottom.
parole.testo: From Latin nāpus (“turnip”) + -form.

parole.significato: Narcissistic, loving oneself excessively.
parole.testo: From Latin narcissinus, from Ancient Greek ναρκίσσινος (narkíssinos), from νάρκισσος (nárkissos, “narcissus”).

parole.significato: The ointment nard.
parole.testo: From Latin nardus, from Ancient Greek νάρδος (nárdos).

parole.significato: Shaped like a nose
parole.testo: Latin nārifōrmis, from nāris (“nostril”).

parole.significato: a nostril
parole.testo: From Latin naris (“nostril”). Itself from Latin nāsus with rhotacism.

parole.significato: Capable of being narrated or told.
parole.testo: From Latin nārrābilis, from narrāre (“to narrate”). By surface analysis, Latin narr- + -able.

parole.significato: One who narrates or tells stories.
parole.testo: From narrate + -or, from Latin narrātor. By surface analysis, Latin narr- + -ate + -or.

parole.significato: A female narrator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin narrātrīx. By surface analysis, narrate + -trix.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the nose or to the nasion.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Medieval Latin nāsālis, from nāsus (“the nose”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of nasalis.

parole.significato: A small muscle on each side of the nose that constricts the nasal aperture by the action of a triangular transverse por…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin nāsālis, ellipsis of mūsculus nāsālis (“nasal muscle”). Doublet of nasal.

parole.significato: Birth.
parole.testo: Adapted borrowing of Latin nāscentia + -ence, from nāscentem (“arising young, immature”), present participle of nāscī (“to be born”) (Old Latin gnāscī; see genus). Doublet of nascency.

parole.significato: A state of incipiency; a quality of nascence.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nāscentia. Doublet of nascence.

parole.significato: Emerging; just coming into existence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nāscēns, nāscentis, present participle of nāscor (“to be born”). Doublet of naissant.

parole.significato: Synonym of cyrtos.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Latin nassa, or back-formed from New Latin Nassula

parole.significato: The popular name of any of the plants in the Tropaeolum genus of flowering plants native to south and central America.
parole.testo: From Middle English nasturcium, from Old English nasturcium (“watercress”), from Latin nasturtium.

parole.significato: A horn-like elongated rostrum on the head of soldier termites of the subfamily Nasutiterminae, capable of producing and…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nāsus (“the nose; the nozzle or spout”).

parole.significato: The visible part of the human nose.
parole.testo: Latin, meaning "external nose".

parole.significato: Having a long snout.
parole.testo: From Latin nāsūtus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to birth.
parole.testo: From Middle English natal, natale (“native, one’s own; inherited; presiding over birthdays or births”), from Classical Latin nātālis (“natal”), from nātus, perfect active participle of nāscor (“to be born”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁-. Doublet of nada, Natal, née, and Noel.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a birthday.
parole.testo: From Latin natalitius, from natalis. See natal.

parole.significato: Floating or swimming (in water).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin natāntem, accusative of natāns. Doublet of naiant.

parole.significato: The act or process of swimming
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin natātiō.

parole.significato: swimmer
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin natator.

parole.significato: A swimming pool, especially an indoor one; a building housing one or more swimming pools.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin natatorium, noun use of the neuter singular of Latin natātōrius (“for swimming”). Equivalent to natatory + -ium.

parole.significato: of, or relating to, swimming
parole.testo: From Latin natare.

parole.significato: The two anterior of the four lobes on the dorsal side of the midbrain of most mammals; the anterior optic lobes.
parole.testo: From Latin natēs, plural of natis.

parole.significato: A national standard variety of a language spoken in more than one region.
parole.testo: From natio(n) + -lect. The first component is from Latin nātiōn(em), with the second abbreviated from dialect, from Ancient Greek. Coined by Godelieve Laureys in 1997.

parole.significato: Synonym of sodium.
parole.testo: From New Latin natrium. See natron for more.

parole.significato: table salt
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The logarithm in base e: either the function that given x returns y such that eʸ = x, or the value of y given by the fu…
parole.testo: From New Latin logarithmus nātūrālis, coined in 1668 by Nicholas Mercator in his book Logarithmo-technica.

parole.significato: A shipmaster, a shipowner, a skipper
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nauclērus, from Ancient Greek ναύκληρος (naúklēros).

parole.significato: To wreck (something).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin naufragātus, perfect passive participle of naufragō (“to become shipwrecked”).

parole.significato: The recreation of a sea battle staged for entertainment.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin naumachia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ναυμαχία (naumakhía). Compare naumachy.

parole.significato: A crustacean larva that has three pairs of locomotive organs (corresponding to antennules, antennae, and mandibles), a…
parole.testo: ] Borrowed from New Latin Nauplius (former genus name) (coined by Danish naturalist Otto Friedrich Müller (1730–1784) who mistakenly thought the larvae were a separate genus of animal), from Latin nauplius (“argonaut, paper nautilus (genus Argonauta)”), from Ancient Greek ναύπλιος (naúplios, “type o

parole.significato: A feeling of illness or discomfort in the digestive system, usually characterized by a strong urge to vomit.
parole.testo: From Middle English nausea, a borrowing from Latin nausea, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, “sea-sickness”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂-. Displaced native Old English wlǣtta.

parole.significato: A substance that induces nausea.
parole.testo: Latin nauseans.

parole.significato: To cause nausea in.
parole.testo: From earlier nauseat, from Latin nauseātus (“nauseated”), perfect past participle of nauseō (“to feel sea sick, nauseate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)), from nausea, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía), from ναῦς (naûs), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂-. By surface analys

parole.significato: Causing nausea; sickening or disgusting.
parole.testo: From Latin nauseōsus (“causing nausea”), corresponding synchronically to nausea + -ous.

parole.significato: A marine mollusc, of the family Nautilidae native to the Pacific Ocean and Indian Ocean, which has tentacles and a spir…
parole.testo: From Latin nautilus, from Ancient Greek ναυτίλος (nautílos, “paper nautilus, sailor”).

parole.significato: The commander of a fleet.
parole.testo: From Latin navarchus, from Ancient Greek ναύαρχος (naúarkhos, “leader of the ships”), corresponding to navy + -arch.

parole.significato: The middle or body of a church, extending from the transepts to the principal entrances.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin nāvem, singular accusative of nāvis, possibly via a Romance source. Doublet of nef and nau.

parole.significato: A thurible in the shape of a boat.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nāvicula.

parole.significato: Shaped like a boat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin navis (“ship”) + -iform.

parole.significato: To plan, control and record the position and course of a vehicle, ship, aircraft, etc., on a journey; to follow a plann…
parole.testo: First attested in 1588; borrowed from Latin nāvigātus, the perfect passive participle of nāvigō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from nāvis (“ship”) + -igō, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us (“boat”).

parole.significato: A person who navigates, especially an officer with that responsibility on a ship or an aircrew member with that respons…
parole.testo: From Latin nāvigātor. By surface analysis, navigate + -or.

parole.significato: A female navigator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nāvigātrīx. By surface analysis, navigate + -trix.

parole.significato: The concept that no legal action can be instituted twice for the same cause.
parole.testo: Latin, meaning "not twice for the same".

parole.significato: A common law writ prohibiting the departure of a person or of property from the jurisdiction of a court.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nē exeat (literally “may he not go forth”), from nē (“not”) + exeat, third-person singular subjunctive of exeō (“depart”).

parole.significato: The highest, ultimate point of achievement which can be reached; perfection.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nē plūs ultrā.

parole.significato: Appearing younger than one's actual age.
parole.testo: Presumably from Latin neanias (“young man”) + -morphic.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city of Naples, capital and largest city of Campania, Italy, or the surrounding metropolita…
parole.testo: From Latin neāpolītānus, from Neāpolis, from Ancient Greek Νεάπολις (Neápolis, literally “new city”), a Greek city in modern Naples. Doublet of naporitan.

parole.significato: The skin of a fawn, as worn by Dionysus, and as worn in his honor by his male followers and female followers (maenads)…
parole.testo: From Latin nebris, from Ancient Greek νεβρίς (nebrís), earlier νεβρός (nebrós, “fawn”).

parole.significato: A cloud in outer space consisting of gas or dust (e.g. a cloud formed after a star explodes).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nebula (“little cloud, mist”). First attested in 1655. Akin to Ancient Greek νεφέλη (nephélē, “cloud”), German Nebel (“mist, nebula”), Old Norse nifl, Polish niebo (“sky, heaven”), Russian не́бо (nébo, “sky”).

parole.significato: A decorative wavy or curly pattern; moulding of an undulating or wavy form.
parole.testo: From Latin nebula (“little cloud, mist”), though the first sense ("a decorative wavy pattern", as a noun) is perhaps a misunderstanding of the adjective nebulé (“wavy”).

parole.significato: To convert liquid into a fine spray of aerosols, by using a nebulizer; to atomize
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nebula (“little cloud, mist”) + -ize.

parole.significato: The characteristic of being nebulous; cloudiness (measured in octas).
parole.testo: From Latin nebulōsitās.

parole.significato: a cloud species which consists of a veil of cloud, showing no distinct details. Associated with cirrostratus, and strat…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nebulosus.

parole.significato: Synonym of reredorter: a monastery's latrine, outhouse, or lavatory, typically located behind the dormitory.
parole.testo: From Latin necessarium (“reredorter; outhouse”), from necesse (“unavoidable or necessary [thing]”) + -ārium (“-arium, -ium: forming locations”).

parole.significato: Necessaries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin necessārius.

parole.significato: To make necessary; to behove; to require (something) to be brought about.
parole.testo: From earlier necessitat, from Medieval Latin necessitātus, perfect past participle of necessitō (“to make necessary”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)), from Classical Latin necessitās (“necessity, need”) + -ō. Necessitās is derived from necesse (“unavoidable”) (from ne- (“not”

parole.significato: The state or characteristic of being in need; neediness.
parole.testo: From Latin necessitūdō, from necesse + -tūdō, from ne- + cessus.

parole.significato: Characterized by or a result of necessity.
parole.testo: From Latin necessitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin necessitūdō, from necesse + -tūdō, from ne- + cessus, from cēdō. By surface analysis, necessitude + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or relating to necromancy: the resurrection of or communication with the dead, especially through the use of black m…
parole.testo: From Late Latin necromanticus.

parole.significato: The drink of the gods.
parole.testo: From Latin nectar, from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar, “nourishment of the gods”), from Proto-Indo-European *neḱ- (“perish, disappear”) + *-tr̥h₂ (“overcoming”), from *terh₂- (“to overcome, pass through, cross over”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to nectar; nectarous.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nectareus (“of nectar; sweet”), from Ancient Greek νεκτάρεος (nektáreos, “sweet as nectar, fragrant”), from νέκταρ (néktar, “nectar”).

parole.significato: The swede (rutabaga); turnip.
parole.testo: From Middle English neep, from Old English nǣp (“turnip, rape”), borrowed from Latin nāpus. Compare Icelandic næpa (“turnip”). Cognate with English turnip.

parole.significato: Unspeakable, appalling.
parole.testo: From Latin nefandus, from ne- (“not”) + fandus, gerundive of fārī (“to speak”).

parole.significato: Sinful, villainous, criminal, or wicked, especially when noteworthy or notorious for such characteristics.
parole.testo: From Latin nefārius (“execrable, abominable”), from nefās (“something contrary to divine law, an impious deed, sin, crime”), from ne- (“not”) + fās (“the dictates of religion, divine law”), which is related to Latin for (“to speak, to say”) and cognate to Ancient Greek φημί (phēmí, “to say”).

parole.significato: wicked
parole.testo: From Latin nefastus (“irreligious, inauspicious”).

parole.significato: In the calendar of Ancient Rome, those days on which business could not be transacted and assemblies and courts could n…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nefasti.

parole.significato: inauspicious, disastrous, ill-omened
parole.testo: From Latin nefastus.

parole.significato: To deny the existence, evidence, or truth of; to contradict.
parole.testo: From Latin negātus, perfect passive participle of negō (“to deny, refuse, decline”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: One who, or that which, negates.
parole.testo: From negate + -or, or directly from Latin negātor.

parole.significato: Negative; negating.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin negātōrius (possibly via Middle French negatoire), from Latin negātus.

parole.significato: To fail to care for or attend to something.
parole.testo: The verb is inherited from Middle English neglect, neclect, derived from Latin neglēctus, perfect passive participle of neglegō (“to make light of, disregard, not to pick up”), itself from nec (“not”) + legō (“to pick up, select”). The noun is from neglēctus (“neglect”). First attested in 1460, the

parole.significato: neglect
parole.testo: From Latin neglectiōnem, accusative singular of neglectiō (“neglect”), from neglectus, perfect passive participle of neglegō (“neglect”). Equivalent to neglect + -ion.

parole.significato: Able to be neglected, ignored or excluded from consideration; too small or unimportant to be of concern.
parole.testo: From negligence/negligent + -ible, as if from New Latin *negligibilis, from Latin neglegō (“to neglect”) + -ibilis (“-ible”).

parole.significato: To confer with others in order to come to terms or reach an agreement.
parole.testo: c. 1598; borrowed from Latin negōtiātus, perfect active participle of negōtior (“to do business, trade”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from negotium (“business”) + -or, from nec (“not”) + otium (“leisure, ease, inactivity”).

parole.significato: One who negotiates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin negōtiātor (“merchant, banker”), equivalent to negotiate + -or.

parole.significato: A female negotiator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin negōtiātrīx. By surface analysis, negotiate + -trix.

parole.significato: A quasi-contract imposing a duty to reimburse an intervenor (gestor) who has seen to, managed, or looked after the affa…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin negotiōrum gestiō (literally “management of business”).

parole.significato: The ability to negotiate many things at once.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin negōtiōsitās. By surface analysis, negotious + -ity.

parole.significato: Engaged in much business; busy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin negotiosus. See also negotiate and -ious.

parole.significato: Relating to a black ethnicity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish and Portuguese negro (“black”), from Latin nigrum (“shiny black”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *negʷ- (“bare; night”). Doublet of noir. Compare nigrescence.

parole.significato: Having the form of threads; fibrous.
parole.testo: Latin nema (“thread”).

parole.significato: Any of many worms of the phylum Nematomorpha.
parole.testo: Formed as nemato- + -morph after the scientific Latin Nēmatomorpha.

parole.significato: With nobody contradicting; by consensus; without dissent.
parole.testo: From Latin nemine contradicente (“with nobody contradicting”).

parole.significato: with nobody dissenting
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A clownfish
parole.testo: From Latin nemo. The "clownfish" meaning comes from the film Finding Nemo, where Nemo is a clownfish.

parole.significato: Pertaining to groves or woodland.
parole.testo: From Latin nemorālis, from nemus (“grove”).

parole.significato: Forested; full of trees, dark with shady groves.
parole.testo: From Latin nemus (“grove”).

parole.significato: A funeral song; an elegy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nēnia.

parole.significato: A water lily, especially the European white water lily (Nymphaea alba) or the yellow water lily (Nuphar lutea).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nenuphar, from Arabic نِلُوفَر (nilūfar), نِينُوفَر (nīnūfar), from Middle Persian nylw(k)pl (nīlōpal, “lotus, water-lily”), from Sanskrit नीलोत्पल (nīlotpala, “blue lotus”), from नील (nīla, “blue”) + उत्पल (utpala, “lotus, water-lily”). Compare French nénufar.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Lower Greensand.
parole.testo: From Latin Neocomum (“Neuchâtel”) + -ian.

parole.significato: The time of the new moon; the beginning of the month in the lunar calendar.
parole.testo: From Latin neomēnia.

parole.significato: A newborn infant; recently born baby.
parole.testo: From New Latin neonātus (“newborn”).

parole.significato: A beginner; a person who is new to a subject, skill, or belief.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin neophytus, from Ancient Greek νεόφυτος (neóphutos, “newly planted”), from νέος (néos, “new”) + φυτόν (phutón, “plant, child”). By surface analysis, neo- + -phyte.

parole.significato: Part of the lung of birds formed by the parabronchi from the laterodorsal and lateroventral bronchi
parole.testo: From neo- + Latin pulmō (“lung”).

parole.significato: Modern, new-fangled.
parole.testo: From Late Latin neotericus, from Hellenistic Greek νεωτερικός (neōterikós), from comparative of Ancient Greek νέος (néos, “new”).

parole.significato: Catmint, catnip; Nepeta cataria.
parole.testo: From Middle English neppe, nepe, nepte, nept, from Old English nepte, nefte, from Latin nepeta. Compare Dutch neppe, nippe (“catnip”). Doublet of nepeta.

parole.significato: A drug mentioned in Homer's Odyssey (c. 8th century B.C.E.) as bringing relief from anxiety or grief; hence, any drug o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nēpenthes (“a drug bringing relief from grief”), from Ancient Greek νηπενθές (nēpenthés), neuter of νηπενθής (nēpenthḗs, “sorrow-banishing”), from νη- (nē-, “not”) + πένθος (pénthos, “grief”) (from πάσχειν (páskhein), present active infinitive of πάσχω (páskhō, “to be ill or inju

parole.significato: A semi-precious stone, one of the two types of stone commonly referred to as jade (the other being jadeite).
parole.testo: From Latin lapis nephriticus, via Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos) νεφριτικός (nephritikós), meaning kidney stone, because jade was believed to have cured kidney stones.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or affected with nephritis or nephritic syndrome.
parole.testo: From Middle English neufretic, from Medieval Latin nefreticus; compare Classical Latin nephrīticus; equivalent to nephritis + -ic = nephr- (“kidney”) + itis (“inflammation”) + -ic (“related”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a nephew.
parole.testo: From Latin nepōtālis, from nepōs.

parole.significato: A government run by multiple members of the same family.
parole.testo: From Latin nepōs + -archia, coined by American journalist Richard Dudman in February of 1963. By surface analysis, nepotism + -archy.

parole.significato: prodigal, dissolute, or uproarious behavior
parole.testo: From Late Latin nepōtātiō.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to nepoticide.
parole.testo: From nepoticide + -al, from oblique stem of Latin nepōs, nepōtis (“nephew”) + -icidal.

parole.significato: The killing of one's own nephew.
parole.testo: From Latin nepōs, nepōtis (“nephew”) + -cide.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Neptune, the Roman god of fresh water and the sea, the counterpart of the Greek god Poseidon.
parole.testo: From Latin Neptūnius (“of or pertaining to the Roman god Neptune”), from Neptūnus (“the Roman god Neptune”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nebʰ- (“to become damp, cloudy”)) + -ius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns); analysable as Neptune + -ian. The English word is cognate with F

parole.significato: Any one of the fifty sea-nymphs who were daughters of the sea-god Nereus and attendants upon Poseidon (Neptune), and we…
parole.testo: From the stem of Latin Nērēis, from Ancient Greek Νηρηΐς (Nērēḯs), from Νηρεύς (Nēreús, “Nereus”) + -ις (-is), literally “sprung of Nereus”. By surface analysis, Nereus + -id.

parole.significato: oleander (Nerium oleander)
parole.testo: From Latin nerion.

parole.significato: Any cruel and wicked tyrant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Nerō.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Roman emperor Nero, notorious for debauchery and barbarous cruelty.
parole.testo: From Latin Nerōniānus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the ancient Roman emperor Nero.
parole.testo: From Latin Nerōn- (the stem of Nerō) + -ic.

parole.significato: Early Modern English spelling of nerve
parole.testo: Recorded since circa [1374] as Middle English nerve, from Medieval Latin nervus (“nerve”), from Latin nervus (“sinew”). Doublet of neuron and sinew.

parole.significato: A pattern of nerves, e.g. as seen on a leaf.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin nervus (“nerve, sinew”), perhaps via French nervation.

parole.significato: A bundle of neurons with their connective tissue sheaths, blood vessels and lymphatics.
parole.testo: Recorded since circa 1374 as Middle English nerve, from Medieval Latin nervus (“nerve”), from Latin nervus (“sinew”). Doublet of neuron and sinew. Verb sense 4 (“to get on (someone’s) nerves”) is chiefly a semantic loan from German nerven.

parole.significato: Having the quality of acting upon or affecting the nerves; quieting nervous excitement.
parole.testo: From Latin nervinus.

parole.significato: The state of being nervous; nervousness.
parole.testo: From Latin nervōsitās.

parole.significato: Of sinews and tendons.
parole.testo: From Middle English nervous (“composed of or incorporating nerves”), from Latin nervōsus (“nervous; sinewy; energetic, vigorous”), from nervus (“nerve; muscle; sinew, tendon; (figuratively) energy, power; nerve; force, strength, vigour”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snéh₁wr̥ (“sinew, tendon

parole.significato: The branch of the facial nerve that contains sensory and parasympathetic fibers and that supplies the anterior tongue a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin nervus intermedius (“intermediate nerve”).

parole.significato: The absence of knowledge, especially of orthodox beliefs.
parole.testo: From Latin nescientia, from the present participle of nescire.

parole.significato: An ignorant person.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin nesciēns (“ignorant, unknowing”), the present participle of nesciō (“to don’t know, to be ignorant of”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek musical theory, the highest-pitched fixed note in the farther tetrachord on a lyre, always pitched a p…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin nētē, from Ancient Greek νήτη (nḗtē, literally “lowest [string]”). It was "lowest" in the sense of being the farthest from the player and physically below the other strings, but was the highest in pitch. Compare the high E string in a modern guitar, which is farthest f

parole.significato: An acute, severe, intermittent pain that radiates along a nerve.
parole.testo: From New Latin neuralgia, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”). By surface analysis, neur- + -algia.

parole.significato: A nomad tribe of Scythia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Neurī, from Ancient Greek Νευροί (Neuroí).

parole.significato: Any of a class of transmembrane proteins that bind to neurexins
parole.testo: From neuro- + Latin ligō (“bind”) + -in.

parole.significato: The branch of medicine that deals with the disorders of nervous system including the brain and spinal cord of the centr…
parole.testo: From New Latin neurologia. By surface analysis, neuro- + -logy.

parole.significato: A cell of the nervous system, which conducts nerve impulses; consisting of an axon and several dendrites. Neurons are c…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”), doublet of nerve and sinew. By surface analysis, neuro- + -on.

parole.significato: The deep-seated parts of the vertebrate skeleton related to the nervous axis and locomotion.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin neūrosceletus. By surface analysis, neuro- + skeleton.

parole.significato: A puppet; a marionette
parole.testo: From Latin neurospaston, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: An embryo of vertebrates in the stage when the primitive band is first developed.
parole.testo: From New Latin neurula, diminutive in -ula of Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “sinew, tendon, cord”).

parole.significato: Neutral.
parole.testo: From Latin neutralis (“neuter”).

parole.significato: Any of a number of different, usually benign, pigmented, raised or otherwise abnormal lesions of the skin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin naevus.

parole.significato: A skin condition characterized by soft, yellowish papules or cerebriform plaques, usually of the buttock or thigh, with…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A contract in early Ancient Rome in which the debtor pledged his own person as collateral should he default on his loan…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nexum.

parole.significato: A form or state of connection.
parole.testo: From Latin nexus (“connection, nexus; act of binding, tying or fastening together; something which binds, binding, bond, fastening, joint; legal obligation”), from nectō (“to attach, bind, connect, fasten, tie; to interweave; to relate; to unite; to bind by obligation, make liable, oblige; to compos

parole.significato: Synonym of nickeline.
parole.testo: Latin niccolum (“nickel”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Nicaea.
parole.testo: Latin Nīcaenus

parole.significato: Nihil
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nichil, from nihil.

parole.significato: A Nicolaitan.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Nicolaita, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Νικολαΐτης (Nikolaḯtēs), from Νικόλαος (Nikólaos, “Nicolas”); Nicolas of Antioch was associated with the sect, although the word may have come from a different allegorical use of the name.

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Nicosia, the capital of Cyprus and Northern Cyprus.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Nicosianus, from Nicosia + -ānus. Equivalent to Nicosia + -an.

parole.significato: To wink or blink; (of certain animals) to close the nictating membrane.
parole.testo: First attested in 1755; borrowed from Latin nictātus, perfect passive participle of nictō (“to wink, blink”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: winking, blinking
parole.testo: From the past participle stem of Latin nictitō, frequentative form of nictō (“to wink”) (see English nictate).

parole.significato: Used to describe an internal organ, in some elasmobranchs and molluscs, that secretes egg cases or the gelatinous cover…
parole.testo: From Latin nidamentum (“materials for a nest”) + -al.

parole.significato: egg case
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nidamentum.

parole.significato: The implantation of the early embryo in the uterus.
parole.testo: From Latin nīdus (“nest”).

parole.significato: Tending to stay at the nest or birthplace for a long time after birth, due to dependence on the parents for feeding and…
parole.testo: From Latin nīdus (“nest”) + -colous.

parole.significato: To make or build a nest.
parole.testo: First attested in 1814; borrowed from Latin nīdificātus, perfect passive participle of nīdificō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from nīdus (“a nest, dwelling of animals”) + -ficō (“to make, build”). Doublet of nidify and cognate with French nidifier.

parole.significato: Shaped like a nest.
parole.testo: From the New Latin nīdifōrmis (1828).

parole.significato: That leaves the nest shortly after hatching.
parole.testo: From Latin nīdus (“nest”) and fugiō (“to flee, escape”) + -ous. By surface analysis, nidi- + -fugous.

parole.significato: To make a nest.
parole.testo: First attested in 1656; borrowed from Latin nīdificō (“to build a nest”), from nīdus (“nest”) + -ficō (“to make, build”). Doublet of nidificate and cognate with French nidifier.

parole.significato: a nest-like structure
parole.testo: Latin nidus (“nest”) + -o-

parole.significato: The study of nests.
parole.testo: From nido- (“nest”) + -logy (“study of”). From Latin nidus + French -logie (“from Latin -logia, from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía)”).

parole.significato: The smell of burning animals, especially of burning animal fat.
parole.testo: From Latin nidor.

parole.significato: Emitting a strong, unpleasant odor, especially one like that of cooking fat or similar greasy substances.
parole.testo: From nidor (“the unpleasant smell of some cooked animal substances”) + -ous, or from Medieval Latin nidorosus.

parole.significato: Nestling, as a bird in its nest.
parole.testo: Latin nidulans, compare French nidulant.

parole.significato: An aggregate of neurons.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nīdus (“nest”). Doublet of nye and nest.

parole.significato: Synonym of dweeb (“boring or socially inept person”).
parole.testo: English form of Latin Nigellus, from nigellus (“slightly black”), diminutive of niger (“black”), used in the Middle Ages to Latinize Norman Néel and Old Irish Níall, from which the former is derived via Old Norse Njáll. Compare Neil.

parole.significato: An Ethiopian herb (Guizotia abyssinica), grown for its seed and edible oil.
parole.testo: From the name of the Niger River, from Latin Nigris. See further etymology at Niger.

parole.significato: A polysaccharide found in black mold, Aspergillus niger.
parole.testo: From Latin niger (“black”).

parole.significato: A complex, nitrogenous, organic base and black dyestuff
parole.testo: Latin niger (“black”), and aniline.

parole.significato: A process of putrefaction or decomposition, one of the four major stages of the alchemical magnum opus.
parole.testo: From Latin nigrēdō (“blackness”).

parole.significato: The process of becoming black or dark; blackening.
parole.testo: Mid 19th century. From Latin nigrescens, present active participle of nigrescō. By surface analysis, Latin nigr(ēre) + -escence.

parole.significato: Approaching blackness; blackish, dark-coloured.
parole.testo: From Latin nigrescens, present participle of nigrescere (“to grow black”), from niger (“black”). By surface analysis, Latin nigr(ēre) + -escent. See negro.

parole.significato: The act or process of making black.
parole.testo: From Latin nigrificare (“to blacken”), from niger (“black”) + -ficare (“to make”, in comparative). See -fy.

parole.significato: A black ferruginous variety of rutile, or a compound of rutile and ilmenite.
parole.testo: Latin niger (“black”): compare French nigrine.

parole.significato: An insulating material consisting of the impure residuum obtained in the distillation of paraffin.
parole.testo: From Latin niger (“black”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Blackness; the state of being black.
parole.testo: From Latin nigritūdō, from niger (“black”).

parole.significato: Black in color.
parole.testo: From Latin nigritūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin nigritūdō, from niger + -tūdō. By surface analysis, nigritude + -ous.

parole.significato: A dark blue synthetic dyestuff of the induline group.
parole.testo: Latin niger (“black”), + -ine.

parole.significato: Black.
parole.testo: From Latin nigrum, + -ous.

parole.significato: A nihil dicit.
parole.testo: From Latin nihil, nil.

parole.significato: Synonym of zinc oxide, particularly white forms.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nihil album (“white nothing”), from late medieval confusion of German nichts (“nothing”) and nix with Latin nix (“snow, snow-white thing”), used for white forms of zinc oxide. Doublet of nill.

parole.significato: The general issue in certain actions of debt.
parole.testo: Latin, meaning "he owes nothing".

parole.significato: A declinature by the defendant to plead or answer.
parole.testo: Latin, meaning "he says nothing".

parole.significato: A declaration of no objection; (specifically) a declaration used by the Catholic Church to indicate a book, initiative,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nihil obstat, from nihil (“nothing”) + obstat (“hinders”).

parole.significato: To annul.
parole.testo: From Latin nihilō (“to reduce to nothing”).

parole.significato: The act of nihilating.
parole.testo: From Latin nihilō (“to reduce to nothing”).

parole.significato: A person who accepts or champions nihilism.
parole.testo: From Latin nihil (“nothing”) + -ist.

parole.significato: The state or fact of being nothing; nothingness, nullity; nonexistence.
parole.testo: From Renaissance Latin nihilitās, from Latin nihil (“nothing”).

parole.significato: Nothing; zero.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nīl, a contraction of nihil, nihilum (“nothing”). See nihilism, nihility.

parole.significato: Do not despair.
parole.testo: Latin nīl ‘nothing’, dēspērandum, gerund of dēspērāre ‘despair’, as used in Nil desperandum Teucro duce et auspice Teucro ‘no need to despair with Teucer as your leader and Teucer to protect you’, in Horace, Odes.

parole.significato: Nothing by mouth: Nothing may be eaten or drunk.
parole.testo: From Latin nīl (“nothing”) + per (“by means of”) + ōs (“mouth”), literally “nothing by mouth”.

parole.significato: Zero.
parole.testo: From Latin nil (“nothing”), shortened form of nihil.

parole.significato: Synonym of zinc oxide, particularly white forms used in medicine and cosmetics.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nil and nihil (“nothing”) to represent German nichts and nix (“nothing”), confused with Latin nix (“snow, snow-white thing”), used for white forms of zinc oxide. Doublet of nihil album.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Nile or the people who live on its banks.
parole.testo: From Latin Nīlōticus, from Ancient Greek Νειλώτης (Neilṓtēs, “on the Nile”). Analyzable as Nile + -otic.

parole.significato: Such that, for some positive integer n, xⁿ = 0.
parole.testo: From nil (“not any”) + potent (“having power”) with literal meaning “having zero power” - bearing Latin roots nil and potens. Coined in 1870, along with idempotent, by American mathematician Benjamin Peirce to describe elements of associative algebras.

parole.significato: A nimbus or halo.
parole.testo: From Latin nimbus. Doublet of nimbus.

parole.significato: Foreboding clouds or stormy weather.
parole.testo: From Latin nimbifer, from nimbus (“a cloud”) + ferre (“to bear”). By surface analysis, Latin nimb(us) + -iferous.

parole.significato: cloudy
parole.testo: From Latin nimbosus, from nimbus (“cloud”). By surface analysis, Latin nimb(us) + -ose.
