parole.testo: From Latin notātus + English -ive.

parole.significato: To notify.
parole.testo: Back-formation from notification. For its use by non-native speakers, compare Catalan, Portuguese, and Spanish notificar and Italian notificare, from Latin nōtificō.

parole.significato: Mental apprehension of whatever may be known, thought, or imagined; idea, concept.
parole.testo: From Latin nōtiō (“a becoming acquainted, a taking cognizance, an examination, an investigation, a conception, idea, notion”), from nōscō (“to know”). Compare French notion. See know.

parole.significato: A roll, list, or register: a catalogue of public functionaries, with their districts: a list of episcopal sees.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin notitia. Doublet of notice.

parole.significato: A notice conveyed to a prosecutor that a crime is alleged to have occurred.
parole.testo: From Latin nōtitia (“renown”) + crīminis, genitive of crīmen (“verdict”).

parole.significato: Senses with an unfavourable connotation.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English notoryous, from Medieval Latin nōtōrius (“evident, known; famous, well-known; infamous”), from Latin nōtus (“known, recognized; familiar, widely known; famous, well-known; infamous”) + -tōrius (suffix forming adjectives). Nōtus is the perfect passive participle of nōscō (“to

parole.significato: Pertaining to magical signs or symbols.
parole.testo: From Late Latin notorius, variant form of notarius (“notary”).

parole.significato: A small circular pit on an internal fossil mold of a trilobite marking the impression of an apodeme.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin notula.

parole.significato: A noun that represents a number
parole.testo: Calque of Latin nōmen numerāle.

parole.significato: A word that can be used to refer to a person, animal, place, thing, phenomenon, substance, quality, or idea; one of the…
parole.testo: From Middle English noun substantyf, a calque of Latin nōmen substantīvum.

parole.significato: A variety of chert, very rich in quartz, that has been used to make whetstones.
parole.testo: From Latin novācula (“dagger”) plus the suffix -ite.

parole.significato: To replace something with something new
parole.testo: First attested in 1611; borrowed from Latin novātus, perfect passive participle of novō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A follower of Novatianism.
parole.testo: From Latin Novatius (plausibly via French Novatien).

parole.significato: Replacement of a contract with one or more new contracts, in particular in financial markets the replacement of a contr…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin novātiō (“a renewing, rennovation”), from novō, from novus (“new”). Compare novel, novelty.

parole.significato: A new legal constitution.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin novella, feminine of novellus.

parole.significato: Synonym of novel (“a new legal constitution”)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin novella. Doublet of novel.

parole.significato: Novel thoughts or interpretations, usually associated with Jewish commentaries (see Chiddush); any novel interpretation…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin novellae.

parole.significato: Cleft into nine
parole.testo: From Latin novemfidus, from novem (“nine”) + -fidus, from findere (“to split”).

parole.significato: 10¹²⁰.
parole.testo: From Latin novem (“nine”) + trigintillion.

parole.significato: 10⁹⁰.
parole.testo: From Latin novem (“nine”) + vigintillion.

parole.significato: Any member of a group of nine officials.
parole.testo: From Latin novemvir.

parole.significato: A group of nine people, especially (politics) a council of nine men who share office or rule.
parole.testo: From Latin novemvirātus, from novemvir + -ātus. By surface analysis, novemvir + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, a group of people performing it)

parole.significato: A recitation of prayers and devotions for nine consecutive days, especially one to a saint to ask for their intercessio…
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin novēna, from Latin novēnus (“nine [each]”).

parole.significato: A group of nine.
parole.testo: From Latin novenarius, from novem (“nine”).

parole.significato: Lasting nine days, especially in relation to the period of mourning for a Pope.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin novendiālis.

parole.significato: Relating to, or dependent on, the number nine; novenary.
parole.testo: From Latin novenus (“nine each”).

parole.significato: A nine-year period.
parole.testo: From Late Latin novennium, from novennis (“9-year”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a stepmother.
parole.testo: From Latin novercalis, from noverca (“a stepmother”).

parole.significato: Fear or dislike of one's stepmother.
parole.testo: From Latin noverca + -phobia.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the new moon.
parole.testo: From Latin novus (“new”) + luna (“the moon”).

parole.significato: new; recent
parole.testo: From Latin novitius, novicius.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Newcastle upon Tyne or Newcastle, New South Wales.
parole.testo: From Latin novus (“new”) + castra (“castle, fort”).

parole.significato: In Scottish feudal land law, a fresh grant of lands to the grantee, usually to make some change in the incidents of ten…
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Any of several polymers derived from phenols and formaldehyde with low molecular weight and related to Bakelite but les…
parole.testo: From Latin novus (“new”) + Swedish lack (“lacquer”), because these materials were envisioned to replace natural lacquers such as copal resin.

parole.significato: A new feature, a novelty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin novum.

parole.significato: A doctrine of law that, in certain circumstances, an intervening event can break the chain of causation between a perso…
parole.testo: Latin, "new intervening act"

parole.significato: The period of darkness in each twenty-four hours; a night.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nox, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.

parole.significato: millilux (unit of illuminance)
parole.testo: From Latin nox (“night; darkness”), by analogy with lux from Latin lūx (“light; daylight, day”). Doublet of night.

parole.significato: Anything that exerts a harmful influence, such as trauma, poison, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin noxa (“harm, damage”).

parole.significato: Harmful; injurious.
parole.testo: From Latin noxius (“hurtful, injurious”), from noxa (“hurt, injury”), from nocere (“to hurt, injure”); see nocent.

parole.significato: A nebula; specifically, the Magellanic Clouds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūbēcula, diminutive of nūbēs (“cloud”).

parole.significato: Of or related to Nubia, its animals, or the Nubian people.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Nubianus directly and via French nubien, from Nubia + -anus (“-an: forming adjectives”), from Nubae (“ancient Nubians”) + -ia (“-ia: forming place names”), from Koine Greek Νοῦβαι (Noûbai), q.v. Equivalent to Nubia + -an or Nuba + -ian.

parole.significato: Bringing, or producing, clouds; cloudy.
parole.testo: From Latin nubifer, from nūbēs (“cloud”) + ferre (“to bear”). Compare French nubifère. By surface analysis, Latin nub- + -iferous.

parole.significato: cloud-shaped
parole.testo: From Latin nūbēs (“cloud”) + -iform.

parole.significato: To cloud or obscure
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūbilātus, perfect passive participle of nūbilō (“to cloud”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from nūbila (“clouds”). By surface analysis, Latin nubil- + -ate.

parole.significato: Cloudy, misty.
parole.testo: Latin nubilus (“cloudy”), from nubes (“cloud”).

parole.significato: Wandering in the clouds; moving through the air.
parole.testo: From Latin nubes (“cloud”) + vagant (“wandering”).

parole.significato: A catkin or amentum.
parole.testo: From Latin nucamenta (“fir cones”), from nux, nucis (“a nut”).

parole.significato: The spinal cord.
parole.testo: From Middle English nucha, nuche, nuca, nuka, nuke (“spinal cord”), borrowed from Medieval Latin nucha (“spinal cord; nape of the neck”). Doublet of nuque.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the back or nape of the neck.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin nuchālis, from nucha + -ālis, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ, “spinal cord”).

parole.significato: Bearing or producing nuts.
parole.testo: From Latin nux, nucis (“nut”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Shaped like a nut.
parole.testo: From Latin nux, nucis (“nut”) + -form.

parole.significato: juglone
parole.testo: From Latin nux, nucis (“a nut”) + -in.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the nucleus of an atom.
parole.testo: From Latin nū̆cleus, a contraction of the adjective nuculeus, masculine of feminine nuculea (“pertaining to a small nut”) from nucula + adjectival suffix -eus, -ea, -eum. The Latin nucula + -āris adds up to nuculāris, a term that in English becomes nucular; the Latin nuculea + -āris, becomes Latin n

parole.significato: Having the form of a kernel
parole.testo: From Latin nucleus (“kernel”) + -form.

parole.significato: Forming words pertaining to nuclei.
parole.testo: Formed from nucleus, from Latin nucleus (“kernel, core”), a diminutive of nux (“nut”).

parole.significato: The core, central part of something, around which other elements are assembled.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nucleus (“kernel, core”). The earliest uses refer to the head of a comet and the kernel of a seed, both recorded in Lexicon Technicum in 1704. The sense in atomic physics was coined by British scientist Michael Faraday in 1844 in a theoretical meaning.

parole.significato: A dopaminergic nucleus found near the most anterior portion of the caudate nucleus. It is connected to the ventral tegm…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A mass of grey matter between the fastigatum and the embolus in the cerebellum.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The gel-like centre of an intervertebral disc.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Synonym of red nucleus.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A section of a compound fruit; a nutlet; a small nut.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nucula (“little nut”).

parole.significato: The evangelical view that scripture is the only rule of faith, to the exclusion of all other sources.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?] (literally “bare scripture”).

parole.significato: The act of stripping, or making bare or naked.
parole.testo: From Latin nudatio, from nudare (“to make naked”), from nudus (“naked”). See nude.

parole.significato: Without clothing or other covering of the skin; without clothing on the genitals or female nipples.
parole.testo: Entered English 1493 as a legal term, meaning "unsupported, not formally attested," from Middle English nud, from Latin nūdus (“naked, bare”).

parole.significato: The act of making nude or bare.
parole.testo: From Latin nudus (“naked”) + -ficare (“to make”, in comparative). See -fy.

parole.significato: One who relies on faith alone without works for salvation.
parole.testo: From Latin nuda fides (naked faith).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the day before yesterday; very recent.
parole.testo: From Latin nū̆diū̆stertiānus (“taking place the day before yesterday”), from nudius tertius. Coined by Nathaniel Ward (1578–1652) in The Simple Cobler of Aggawam in America (1647).

parole.significato: In common law, a promise that is not legally enforceable due to lack of consideration.
parole.testo: From Latin nūdum, the neuter form of nūdus (“nude, bare”) + pāctum (“bargain, agreement”).

parole.significato: futility; trifling talk or behaviour; drollery
parole.testo: From Latin nūgācitās (“trifling”), from nūgāx, -itās. Further from nūgor, from nūgae.

parole.significato: The act or practice of trifling (focusing on the trivial or inconsequential.)
parole.testo: From Latin nugatio (“chatter”).

parole.significato: Trivial, trifling or of little importance.
parole.testo: From Latin nūgātōr (“jester”) + English -y (“adjectival suffix”). Borrowed from Latin nūgātōrius, from nūgātor m (“jester”) + -ius (“suffix forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Rendering trifling or futile; making silly.
parole.testo: From Latin nugae (“trifles”) + -fy + -ing.

parole.significato: No goods; used to indicate that a search has found no seizable property.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: The principle that a person shall receive no punishment unless he has committed an offence as explicitly defined in a l…
parole.testo: From Latin: nūlla (feminine form of nūllus, “not any”) + poena (“penalty”, “punishment”) + sine (“without”) + lēge (ablative singular form of lēx, “a law”) = “no punishment without a law”.

parole.significato: The property of being nowhere; non-existence.
parole.testo: From Latin nullibi + -iety.

parole.significato: One who denies that the soul exists in physical space.
parole.testo: From Latin nullibi + -ist.

parole.significato: The act of nullifying; a rendering void and of no effect, or no legal effect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin nullificatio, from nullifico, equivalent to null + -ification.

parole.significato: Synonym of atheist (“a person who does not believe in deities or gods”).
parole.testo: From nulli- (prefix meaning ‘null; no’) + Latin fidēs (“belief, faith”) + English -ian (suffix meaning ‘one belonging to, from, like, or relating to’, forming nouns; and ‘from, like, or related to’ forming adjectives) (compare Late Latin nullifidius (“infidel”)): * Nulli- is derived from Latin nūllu

parole.significato: A woman who has never carried a pregnancy beyond 20 weeks (one who has never given birth). It includes women who have e…
parole.testo: From Latin nūllipara.

parole.significato: That has never given birth.
parole.testo: From Latin nūlliparus. By surface analysis, null + parous.

parole.significato: Any of various algae which secrete calcium carbonate, such as those of the order Corallinales.
parole.testo: From Latin nullus (“none”) + porus (“pore”).

parole.significato: Describing an action which has no side effect. Queries are typically nullipotent: they return useful data, but do not c…
parole.testo: Latin roots, Latin nullus (“not any”) + potent (“having power”) – literally, “having no power”.

parole.significato: A child of unknown parentage; an orphan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin nullius filius (“nobody's son”), from Latin nullius + filius.

parole.significato: No one's property.
parole.testo: From Latin nūllīus (“of no one”) (genitive of nūllus) + in + bonīs (“goods, property”) (ablative of bōna).

parole.significato: A foundational principle dictating that a person cannot be prosecuted or punished for an act unless that specific condu…
parole.testo: Latin.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the ancient Celtiberian city of Numantia.
parole.testo: From Latin Numantīnus.

parole.significato: A divinity, especially a local or presiding god.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūmen.

parole.significato: Able to be counted; countable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin numerābilis.

parole.significato: Numerical skill.
parole.testo: From numerate + -cy, from Latin numerus; coined with numerate in 1959 by the UK Committee on Education, presided over by Sir Geoffrey Crowther.

parole.significato: A symbol that is not a word and represents a number, such as the Arabic numerals 1, 2, 3 or the Roman numerals I, V, X,…
parole.testo: As an adjective, from Middle English numeral, numerall, from Latin numerālis (“pertaining to a number”), from numerus (“a number”). As a noun, via Middle French numeral.

parole.significato: Relating to numbers or numbering.
parole.testo: From Latin numerarius, from numerus (“number”). Doublet of numéraire.

parole.significato: To count.
parole.testo: From Latin numerātus, perfect past participle of numerō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)). By surface analysis, Latin numerus + -ate.

parole.significato: Numbered; counted.
parole.testo: From Middle English numerat, numerate, from Latin numerātus, perfect past participle of numerō (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix, of participial origin)).

parole.significato: The act of counting or numbering; enumeration.
parole.testo: From Middle English numeracioun, from Latin numerātiō. By surface analysis, numerate + -ion.

parole.significato: The number or expression written above the line in a fraction (such as 1 in ½).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin numerātor.

parole.significato: The sign ⟨ № ⟩.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin numerō, the ablative singular form of numerus (“number”).

parole.significato: The combining form of number.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin numerus (“number”) + -o-.

parole.significato: The condition of being numerous.
parole.testo: From numerous + -ity, from Latin numerositas.

parole.significato: An indefinite large number of.
parole.testo: From Middle English numerous from Latin numerōsus (“numerous, abundant; harmonious”), from numerus (“number”). Doublet of numerose. Analyzeable as numero- + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to coins or money.
parole.testo: From Latin nummarius (“pertaining to money”), from nummus (“a coin, a piece of money”), akin to Ancient Greek νόμος (nómos, “a custom, law”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to coins or money.
parole.testo: From Latin nummulus (“(small amount of) money”) + English -ar (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of, pertaining to, or near’). Nummulus is the diminutive of nummus (“a coin; piece of money”) + -ulus (diminutive suffix); while nummus is from Doric Greek νοῦμμος (noûmmos), from Ancient Greek ν

parole.significato: The arrangement or aggregation of red blood cells into rouleaux, resembling piles of coins.
parole.testo: From Latin nummulus (“money”) + -ation. By surface analysis, numm(us) + -ule + -ate + -ion.

parole.significato: Any of a range of low-value copper coins issued by the Roman and Byzantine empires during Late Antiquity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nummus. Doublet of luma.

parole.significato: A member of a Christian religious community of women who live by certain vows and usually wear a habit, (Roman Catholic…
parole.testo: From Middle English nonne, nunne, from Old English nunne (“nun”), from Late Latin nonna (“nun, tutor”), originally (along with masculine form nonnus (“man”)) a term of address for elderly persons, perhaps from children's speech, reminiscent of nana, like papa etc. Doublet of nonna.

parole.significato: Performed so as to have the same legal force and effect as if it had been performed at an earlier time.
parole.testo: Latin "now for then"

parole.significato: Eternal existence as an attribute of God.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nunc (“now”) + stāns (“staying, remaining”).

parole.significato: The status or rank of a nuncio (diplomatic representative of the Roman Catholic Church).
parole.testo: From Latin nūnciāre, nūntiāre (“to announce, report”), from nūncius, nūntius (“messenger”). Compare French nonciature, Italian nunziatura.

parole.significato: A nuntius.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūncius, medieval form of nūntius (“messenger”).

parole.significato: To dedicate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nuncupātus, past participle of nuncupō (“pronounce, name as heir”), contraction of nōmen (“name”) and capiō (“take, seize”).

parole.significato: Nuncupative; oral rather than written.
parole.testo: From Latin nuncupāt-, past participial stem of nuncupō, + -ory. Compare Late Latin nuncupātōrius.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a nundine
parole.testo: From Latin nundinalis.

parole.significato: nundinal
parole.testo: From Latin nundinarius.

parole.significato: Traffic at fairs; buying and selling.
parole.testo: From Latin nundinatio.

parole.significato: A market or fair held every eight days, particularly (historical) in Roman contexts.
parole.testo: From Latin nundinae (“ninth-days”), a clipped form of nundinae feriae (“ninth-day festivals”), from its observance every eighth day (9 counting inclusively) and from the Latin practice of treating most recurring calendrical days as plurals.

parole.significato: A messenger.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūntius (“messenger”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to wedding and marriage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūptiālis (“pertaining to marriage”), from nūptiae (“wedding”), from nūbō (“to marry, to take as husband”).

parole.significato: A wedding ceremony.
parole.testo: From nuptial, borrowed from Latin nūptiālis (“pertaining to marriage”), from nūptiae (“wedding”) (also plural only), from nūpta, from nūbō (“to marry, to take as husband”), from Proto-Indo-European *sneubho-, *snewbʰ- (“to marry, wed”). Cognate with French noces and Italian nozze.

parole.significato: To rock or sway involuntarily.
parole.testo: First attested in 1880; back-formation from nutation (1610s) on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), from Latin nūtātiō (“a nodding”), from nūtō (“to nod”), from Proto-Indo-European *neu-. Compare mutate.

parole.significato: A bobbing motion that accompanies the precession of a spinning rigid body.
parole.testo: 1610s, from Latin nūtātiō (“nodding”), from nūtō (“to nod”). Compare mutation.

parole.significato: An evergreen tree (Myristica fragrans) cultivated in the East Indies for its spicy seeds.
parole.testo: From Middle English notemege, notemuge, a partial translation of Medieval Latin nux muga, a variant of Medieval Latin nux muscata (“musky nut”). Compare also Old French nois mugede. For the term used in various ball sports, see Wikipedia.

parole.significato: feeding or nourishment
parole.testo: From Latin nutricatio, from nutricare, nutricari (“to suckle, nourish”), from nutrix (“a nurse”).

parole.significato: Relating to a nurse.
parole.testo: From Latin nūtrīx + -al.

parole.significato: A source of nourishment, such as food, that can be metabolized by an organism to give energy and build tissue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūtriēns, present participle of nūtriō (“to suckle, nourish, foster”).

parole.significato: A source of nourishment; food.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English nutriment, from Latin nūtrīmentum.

parole.significato: Providing nutrients; healthy to eat or drink.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nūtrītius, from nūtrītus, from nūtrīre.

parole.significato: nutrition; nourishment
parole.testo: Latin nutritura.

parole.significato: A nurse, primarily a wet nurse or similar hired child carer.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nūtrīx.

parole.significato: A strychnine tree (Strychnos nux-vomica), an evergreen tree found in southeastern Asia.
parole.testo: From Latin nux (“nut”) and vomica (“vomiting”).

parole.significato: A nymph.
parole.testo: From Latin nympha, from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “bride, nymph”). Doublet of nymph.

parole.significato: the European white water lily.
parole.testo: From Latin nymphaea, from Ancient Greek νυμφαῖα (numphaîa), feminine singular form of νυμφαῖος (numphaîos, “sacred to the nymphs”), from νύμφη (númphē, “nymph”). Sense 2 is a semantic loan from translingual Nymphaea, from the same Latin and Greek.

parole.significato: A shrine consecrated to water nymphs, often with a fountain.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nymphaeum, from Ancient Greek νυμφαῖον (numphaîon), a substantivisation of νυμφαῖος (numphaîos, “sacred to the nymphs”), from νύμφη (númphē, “nymph”).

parole.significato: Excess of sexual behaviour or desire in women.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin, from Latin nympha + -mania. By surface analysis, nympho- + mania.

parole.significato: Rapid and excessive involuntary eye movement, usually lateral.
parole.testo: First attested in 1798. From New Latin nystagmus, from Ancient Greek νυσταγμός (nustagmós, “nodding, drowsiness”), from νυστάζω (nustázō, “nod, be sleepy”).

parole.significato: A form of the letter o modified by the addition of a diacritical “tail”: ⟨ǫ⟩, used in Old Norse.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin o caudāta (literally “tailed o”).

parole.significato: A spring of fresh water, surrounded by a fertile region of vegetation, in a desert.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Oasis, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian wḥꜣt (“oasis, cauldron”), G43-V28-G1-X1:N25 Compare Sahidic Coptic ⲟⲩⲁϩⲉ (ouahe) and Arabic وَاحَة (wāḥa).

parole.significato: a halfpenny
parole.testo: From Latin ob, abbreviation of obolus.

parole.significato: Against; facing; a combining prefix found in verbs of Latin origin.
parole.testo: From Latin ob-.

parole.significato: Synonym of died, particularly used with historical dating.
parole.testo: From Latin ob., abbreviating obiit (“he or she passed on”) or obiter (“incidentally”).

parole.significato: To walk about; to wander aimlessly.
parole.testo: First attested in 1614; borrowed from Latin obambulātus, perfect passive participle of obambulō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Wandering about; a casual outing.
parole.testo: From obambulate + -ion. From Latin obambulatio.

parole.significato: To cover.
parole.testo: From Latin obducere, obductum; ob (see ob-) + ducere (“to lead”).

parole.significato: The act of drawing or laying over, as a covering.
parole.testo: Latin obductio; see Latin ob, ductio.

parole.significato: Stubbornly persistent, generally in wrongdoing; refusing to reform or repent.

parole.significato: To rebuke or scold strongly.

parole.significato: To delight; to please greatly.

parole.significato: The act of pleasing highly, or state of being greatly pleased; delight.

parole.significato: To bind, compel, constrain, or oblige by a social, legal, or moral tie.

parole.significato: Requiring a (specified) way of life, habitat, etc.

parole.significato: Imposing obligation, legally, morally, or otherwise; binding; mandatory.

parole.significato: Lacking awareness; unmindful; unaware, unconscious of.

parole.significato: Oblivion.

parole.significato: Having a length and width that are different; not square or circular.

parole.significato: Extremely offensive or unpleasant; very annoying, contemptible, or odious.

parole.significato: The action of darkening or fact of being darkened, as with a cloud; obscuration.

parole.testo: From Latin occasivus, from occasus (“a going down, setting of the heavenly bodies”), from occidere (“to fall or down”). See occasion.

parole.significato: The act of making blind

parole.significato: The process of occluding, or something that occludes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin occlūsiō, occlūsiōnis (“occluding, obstruction”), from the Classical Latin occlūdō (“to shut up or close up; to restrain”), from ob + claudō (“to shut or close”).

parole.significato: That tends to occlude.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin occlūsīvus.

parole.significato: To cover or hide from view.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin occultus (“hidden, secret”).

parole.significato: An astronomical event that occurs when one celestial object is hidden by another celestial object that passes between i…
parole.testo: From Latin occultātiōnem, accusative singular of occultātiō (“concealment; insinuation”), from occultāre, present active infinitive of occultō (“to conceal, hide”); analysable as occult + -ation.

parole.significato: Synonym of occursion (“joining or striking together”).
parole.testo: From Latin occursus.

parole.significato: A meeting or striking together; a clash or collision.
parole.testo: From Latin occursio. See occur.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the ocean.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōceanicus. By surface analysis, ocean + -ic. Doublet of oceany.

parole.significato: Any of the daughters of Oceanus and Tethys; a sea-nymph.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Oceanis, from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανίς (Ōkeanís), from Ὠκεανός (Ōkeanós) + -ις (-is), literally “sprung of Oceanus”. By surface analysis, Oceanus + -id.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, resembling or having an ocellus.
parole.testo: Latin ocellatus, from ocellus (“a little eye”).

parole.significato: The development of eye-like markings, such as those on the wing of a butterfly or tail of a peacock.
parole.testo: From Latin ocellus (“little eye”), from oculus (“eye”) + -ation.

parole.significato: Relating to the ocellus and the occiput
parole.testo: From Latin ocellus + occipital.

parole.significato: A simple eye consisting of a single lens and a small number of sensory cells.
parole.testo: From Latin ocellus (“little eye”), from oculus (“eye”).

parole.significato: A sheath around a plant stem forming from the stipule of a leaf and extending above the point of insertion of the leaf.
parole.testo: From Latin ocrea (“greave, legging”).

parole.significato: A polygon with eight sides and eight angles.
parole.testo: From Latin octagōnon, octōgōnon (“octagon”), and from its etymon Ancient Greek ὀκτάγωνον (oktágōnon, “octagon”), probably from Koine Greek ὀκτάγωνος (oktágōnos, “having eight corners”) + -ον (-on, suffix forming nouns). ὀκτάγωνος is derived from ὀκτᾰ- (oktă-, prefix meaning ‘eight’) (from ὀκτώ (oktṓ

parole.significato: The eighth part of a circle; an arc of 45 degrees.
parole.testo: From Latin octāns. Doublet of Octans.

parole.significato: The pint (eighth of a gallon) in the apothecaries' system.
parole.testo: From New Latin octarius.

parole.significato: A collection of eight books; especially, the first eight books of the Old Testament.
parole.testo: From the Late Latin octateuchus, from the Byzantine Greek ὀκτάτευχος [βίβλος] (oktáteukhos [bíblos], “[a volume] containing [the first] eight books [of the Old Testament]”), from the Ancient Greek ὀκτα- (okta-, “eight”, combining variant of ὀκτώ) + τεῦχος (teûkhos, “book”).

parole.significato: An interval of twelve semitones spanning eight degrees of the diatonic scale, representing a doubling or halving in pit…
parole.testo: From Latin octavus (“eighth”). Doublet of octavo, ochava, and oitava.

parole.significato: A sheet of paper 7 to 10 inches (= 17.78 to 25.4 cm) high and 4.5 to 6 inches (= 11.43 to 15.24 cm) wide, the size vary…
parole.testo: From Latin octavo. Doublet of octave, oitava, and ochava.

parole.significato: An eight-year period.
parole.testo: From Late Latin octennium, from octennis (“8-year”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: Of the eighth degree or order.
parole.testo: From Latin octo (“eight”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A size of a sheet of paper resulting from folding and cutting a sheet of paper into eighteenths (3.5"–4.5" x 4.9"–5.9").
parole.testo: From Latin ablative of octusdecimus (“eighteenth”).

parole.significato: Cleft or separated into eight segments.
parole.testo: From Latin octofidus, from octus (“eight”) + -fidus, related to findere (“to split”).

parole.significato: 10²⁴³
parole.testo: From Latin octōgintā (“eighty”) + -illion.

parole.significato: A verse having eight metrical feet.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin octōnārius. Doublet of octonary.

parole.significato: Of eighth rank or order.
parole.testo: From the Latin octōnārius (“containing eight”), from octōnī (“eight at a time”, “by eights”, “eight each”) + -ārius (whence the English suffix -ary). Doublet of octonarius.

parole.significato: Any of several marine molluscs of the order Octopoda, having no internal or external protective shell or bone (unlike t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin octōpūs, from Ancient Greek ὀκτώπους (oktṓpous), from ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”) + πούς (poús, “foot”). Piecewise doublet of octopod and octopede.

parole.significato: Any member of a group of eight officials.
parole.testo: From Latin octōvir.

parole.significato: A group of eight people, especially (politics) a council of eight men who share office or rule.
parole.testo: From Latin octōvirātus, from octōvir + -ātus. By surface analysis, octovir + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, a group of people performing it).

parole.significato: A set of eight like or identical things.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin octuplicātus, perfect passive participle of octuplicō or formed by blend of octuple + duplicate, either way, see -ate (noun-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the eye, or the sense of sight
parole.testo: Derived from the Latin oculāris (“of the eye”), from oculus (“eye”).

parole.significato: A slit in a helmet through which the wearer could see.
parole.testo: From Latin oculārium.

parole.significato: Having a good sight, sharp-eyed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oculātus (“having eyes, seeing”), from oculus (“eye”) + -ātus; see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To set one's eyes upon, glaze at, behold.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin oculātus, perfect passive participle of oculō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Having the shape of an eye
parole.testo: From Latin oculus (“the eye”) + -form.

parole.significato: A paraphilia involving licking the eyeballs.
parole.testo: From Latin oculus (“eye”) + linctus (“licked”), past participle of lingo (“to lick”).

parole.significato: A window or other opening that has an oval or circular shape (as of an eye).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin oculus (“eye”). Doublet of occhio.

parole.significato: Fit to excite hatred; hateful, odious.
parole.testo: From Latin odibilis. See odium.

parole.significato: Hatred; dislike.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin odium, from Proto-Italic *odjom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed-.

parole.significato: Hatred for the human race.
parole.testo: From Latin odium (“hatred”) + generīs (“species”) + hūmānī (“of man”).

parole.significato: rancor generated by theological disputes
parole.testo: From Latin, meaning "theological hatred".

parole.significato: toothache
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὀδονταλγία (odontalgía, “toothache”). By surface analysis, odonto- + -algia.

parole.significato: Something which gives off a scent; an odoriferous substance.
parole.testo: From Latin odōrāmentum.

parole.significato: odorous
parole.testo: From Latin odoratus, past participle of odorare (“to perfume”), from odor (“odor”).

parole.significato: Having an odor or fragrance.
parole.testo: From Latin. By surface analysis, odor + -i- (“bearing, carrying”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: A device used to measure the intensity of a smell
parole.testo: From Latin odor + -meter.

parole.significato: Having a distinctive odor.
parole.testo: From Middle English odorous, from Medieval Latin odōrōsus, equivalent to odor + -ous.

parole.significato: The household common to the individuals of a compound organism.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

parole.significato: A married priest (chiefly Orthodox Christian and Uniate usage), as opposed to a hieromonk.
parole.testo: From Latin oeconomus, from Ancient Greek οἰκονόμος (oikonómos), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νόμος (nómos, “law, rule”).

parole.significato: An apartment, room, or hall in an ancient Roman dwelling house.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oecus, from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

parole.significato: A beverage made of wine and honey.
parole.testo: From oeno- + Latin mel (“honey”).

parole.significato: A biting insect; a gadfly or botfly.
parole.testo: From Latin oestrum, variant of oestrus.

parole.significato: A biting fly of the genus Oestrus; a botfly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oestrus (“gadfly, sting, frenzy”), from Ancient Greek οἶστρος (oîstros), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eys-, used to form words denoting passion; see also Latin īra (“anger”), Lithuanian aistra (“violent passion”), Avestan 𐬀𐬈𐬯𐬨𐬀 (aesma, “anger”).

parole.significato: Refuse from wool.
parole.testo: From Latin oesypum.

parole.significato: Honorific epithet used parenthetically to mark a beloved person as being deceased.
parole.testo: A calque of Latin beatae memoriae, possibly a calque of Hebrew זיכרונו לברכה (zikhronó/á/ám/án livrakhá, “memory-of-him/her/them to blessing”), ז״ל (Z.L.).

parole.significato: Describing a doctrine or proposition that is not heretical, but formulated improperly or ambiguously and hence liable t…
parole.testo: Calque of Ecclesiastical Latin piārum aurium offēnsīvus.

parole.significato: A prayer said or sung as an anthem while offerings of bread and wine are placed on the altar during the Roman Catholic…
parole.testo: From Late Latin offertorium, from the participle stem of offere (“to offer”).

parole.significato: offer; proposal
parole.testo: Latin offertūra (“an offering”).

parole.significato: A person who officiates at a religious ceremony (in Christianity, at any ceremony other than the Eucharist).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin officiāns, present participle of officiō, officiāre (“to perform a duty or service”) (not to be confused with Classical officiō, officere (“to obstruct, hinder”)), a denominal verb from officium (“duty, service”).

parole.significato: To perform the functions of some office.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin officiātus, perfect participle of Late Latin officior (“to perform a function”) and of Medieval Latin officiō (“to officiate, say mass (9th cent.); to serve a church (13th cent.); to serve (early 13th c., 14th in British sources); to discharge an office (14th c.)”), from Latin of

parole.significato: A monetary office that issues coins.
parole.testo: From Latin officīna. Doublet of oficina and usine.

parole.significato: Obliging, attentive, eager to please.
parole.testo: 15th century, from Middle English offycyous, from Latin officiōsus (“kindly”), from officium (“service”).

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter O/o.
parole.testo: From Middle English o, oo, from Old English ō, from Latin ō.

parole.significato: A fragile spore produced by some fungi.
parole.testo: From New Latin ōidium, equivalent to Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión, “egg”) + -idium.

parole.significato: Reminiscent of the content of the Old Testament, or of the behavior of God in it; especially dramatic, violent or venge…
parole.testo: From Middle English Olde Testament, calqued from Latin Vetus Testāmentum. Old refers to ancientness, not to obsolescence. Equivalent to a retronym, by comparison with the New Testament.

parole.significato: A soft ointment prepared from oil.
parole.testo: Probably from borrowed from Latin oleāmen (“ointment containing olive oil”), from oleum (“olive oil”) + -amen (“noun suffix”).

parole.significato: A plant in the family Elaeagnaceae,
parole.testo: From Middle English oliaster, olyaster, from Latin oleaster.

parole.significato: That produces oil
parole.testo: From Latin oleum (“oil”) + -iferous.

parole.significato: scented
parole.testo: From Latin olens, present participle of olere (“to smell”).

parole.significato: oil or oil-based materials
parole.testo: From Latin oleum (“oil”).

parole.significato: A proposed basic taste sensation triggered by fatty acids.
parole.testo: Coined in 2015 by researchers at Purdue University, Indiana, USA, from oleo- (“oil”) and Latin gustus (“taste”).

parole.significato: An oil-sugar; a preparation made by saturating thirty grains of sugar with one drop of volatile oil.
parole.testo: From Latin oleum (“oil”) + saccharum (“sugar”).

parole.significato: oily
parole.testo: From Latin oleōsus.

parole.significato: Relating to potherbs.
parole.testo: From Latin oleraceus, from olus, oleris (“garden or pot herbs, vegetables”).

parole.significato: A unit measuring the strength of an olfactory pollution source as detected by an average adult in typical conditions.
parole.testo: From Latin olfactus (“smelled”).

parole.significato: To smell.
parole.testo: From Latin olfactus, past participle of olfaciō (“smell”).

parole.significato: Having an odor; capable of being smelled.
parole.testo: From Latin olfacere (“to smell”) + -ible.

parole.significato: Referring to the olfactory senses or the sense of smell.
parole.testo: Noun of action from Latin olfacere (“to smell (trans.)”), from olere (“to emit a smell”) (see odor) + facere (“to make”) (see factitious).

parole.significato: smell
parole.testo: From Latin olfactus.

parole.significato: Concerning the sense of smell.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin olfactōrius.

parole.significato: A gum resin from trees of the genus Boswellia, formerly used as a medicine and now mainly as incense.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin olibanum, from Latin oleum libani, the first word meaning oil and the second from Ancient Greek λίβανος (líbanos, “frankincense (Boswellia sacra)”), from a Semitic source, compare Proto-Semitic *laban- (“white”). parole.significato: evil-smelling; fetid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin olidus from olēre (“to smell”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to oligarchy.
parole.testo: From Late Latin oligarchicus, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχικός (oligarkhikós). By surface analysis, oligarch + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a kitchen garden; used for culinary purposes.
parole.testo: From Latin olitōrius (“of or related to gardeners, produce, or vegetables”), from olitor (“gardener, seller of vegetables or herbs”), from olus + -itō (“forming frequentative verbs”) + -or (“-er: forming agent nouns”), variant of holus (“vegetable”), from Old Latin helus, believed to come from unatt

parole.significato: olivary body
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oliva (“olive”). Doublet of olive.

parole.significato: Shaped like an olive
parole.testo: From Latin olīvārius, from olīva (“olive”).

parole.significato: An umbelliferous plant, the common alexanders, found in Western Europe (Smyrnium olusatrum).
parole.testo: From Latin holusatrum, olusatrum, from olus (“garden herb”) + ater (“black”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Mount Olympus, the highest mountain in Greece; or (Greek mythology) the Greek gods and goddesses who…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English Olympyan, from Latin Olympius (“of or relating to Mount Olympus”) and its etymon Ancient Greek Ὀλῠ́μπῐος (Olŭ́mpĭos, “of or relating to Mount Olympus; living on Mount Olympus; Olympian”) + English -an (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, or forming agent

parole.significato: Of or relating to the town of Olympia in Elis, Greece; Olympic.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Olympianus (“Olympic”) + English -an (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, or forming agent nouns). parole.significato: The third compartment of the stomach of a ruminant; the lining of said compartment, regarded as a foodstuff.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin omāsum.

parole.significato: The omasum.
parole.testo: Misinterpretation of Latin omasum.

parole.significato: Something which portends or is perceived to portend either a good or evil event or circumstance in the future, or which…
parole.testo: From Latin ōmen (“foreboding, omen”).

parole.significato: Either of two folds of the peritoneum that support the viscera.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōmentum.

parole.significato: The 15th letter of the Classical and Modern Greek alphabets (16th in Ancient and Old Greek), used in ordering lists as…
parole.testo: From Latin omicron, from Koine Greek ὂ μῑκρόν (ò mīkrón, “little o”), named in contrast with omega (“big o”). The uncommon form omicra is similarly borrowed from Latin and Greek. The use for designating stars in a constellation—typically in order of apparent brightness—began with Johann Bayer's 1603

parole.significato: To be an omen for (something); to foreshow, to presage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ominātus, perfect active participle of ominor (“to presage”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from omen.

parole.significato: presage; omen.
parole.testo: Latin ominatio.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an omen or to omens; being or exhibiting an omen; significant.
parole.testo: From Latin ōminōsus (“full of foreboding”), from ōmen (“forbidden fruit, omen”), from Old Latin osmen, of uncertain origin, with many origins proposed (see ōmen).

parole.significato: Able to be omitted.
parole.testo: Latin omissum, supine of omitto + -ible. Compare omission.

parole.significato: To leave out or exclude.
parole.testo: At least by 1422, from late Middle English omitten, borrowed from Latin omittō (“to let go”), from ob- + mittō (“to send”), but also had the connotations “to fail to perform” and “to neglect”.

parole.significato: A compound eye, found on, for example, insects and crustaceans.
parole.testo: From New Latin ommateum, from Ancient Greek ὄμμα (ómma, “eye”).

parole.significato: all
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin omnis (“all”).

parole.significato: Of many or all forms, varieties, or kinds.
parole.testo: From Latin omnifarius.

parole.significato: That bears everything; producing all types.
parole.testo: From Latin omnifer, from omnis (“all”) + ferre (“to bear”).

parole.significato: Capable of making or doing anything; all-creating.
parole.testo: From omni- + Latin facere (“to make or do”), modelled on omnipotent etc.

parole.significato: all-creating, omnific.
parole.testo: From omni- + form of Latin faciens, a participle of facere (“to do”).

parole.significato: Having every form or shape.
parole.testo: From Latin omniformis, from omnis (“all”) + forma (“form”). Compare French omniforme.

parole.significato: Bisexual.
parole.testo: From omni- + Latin futuēns, present participle of futuō (“fuck”). Likely influenced by words like omnipotent.

parole.significato: omnium-gatherum
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from omni- + gather + Latin -um.

parole.significato: Consisting of all kinds.
parole.testo: From Latin omniqenus, from omnis (“all”) + genus (“kind”).

parole.significato: Producing or bringing forth all things.
parole.testo: From Latin omniparens (“all-producing”), from omnis (“all”) + parere (“to bring forth”).

parole.significato: Omnipotence.
parole.testo: From Late Latin omnipotentia.

parole.significato: Being everywhere simultaneously.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin omnipraesēns, equivalent to omni- + present.

parole.significato: The capacity to know everything.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin omniscientia (“all-knowledge”), from Latin omni- (“all”), and scient from the Latin scientia (“knowledge”).

parole.significato: Omniscience.
parole.testo: From Late Latin omniscientia, or from omniscient + -ency.

parole.significato: Having total knowledge.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin omnisciens (“all-knowing”), from Latin omnis (“all”) + sciens (“knowing”) (further analysable via scient).

parole.significato: Omniscient; all-knowing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin omniscius.

parole.significato: Beholding everything; all-seeing.
parole.testo: From omni- + Latin spectus, past participle of specere, spicere (“to view”).

parole.significato: Subjugating all others.
parole.testo: From omni- + Latin subiugāns.

parole.significato: The fact or condition of being all.
parole.testo: From New Latin omnitūdō (attested in the 18th century).

parole.significato: A multiple race event in track cycling. Historically the omnium has had a variety of formats. Currently it consists of…
parole.testo: From Latin omnium (literally “of all”), genitive plural of omnis (“all, every”).

parole.significato: A collection containing a variety of miscellaneous things.
parole.testo: Dog Latin, a reduplication derived from Latin omnium (“of all”) and gather + Latin -um, suggesting a collection of everything.

parole.significato: Free-roaming; travelling everywhere.
parole.testo: From omni- + Latin vagans, present participle of vagari (“to wander”).

parole.significato: An animal which is able to consume both plants (like a herbivore) and meat (like a carnivore).
parole.testo: From the Latin omnivorus. By surface analysis, omni- + -vore.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the shoulder and the hyoid bone.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin ōmohȳoīdēs, from Ancient Greek ὦμος (ômos, “shoulder”) + Latin hȳoīdēs (“U-shaped”); equivalent to omo- (“shoulder”) + hyoid. Doublet of omohyoideus.

parole.significato: Synonym of omohyoid muscle.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin ōmohȳoīdeus, ellipsis of mūsculus ōmohȳoīdeus (“omohyoid muscle”). Doublet of omohyoid. By surface analysis, omo- (“shoulder”) + hyoid + -eus.

parole.significato: The central part of the hilum of a seed, through which the nutrient vessels pass into the raphe or chalaza.
parole.testo: From the post-classical Latin omphalodium from Ancient Greek ὀμφαλοειδής (omphaloeidḗs, “navel-like”) itself from Ancient Greek ὀμφαλός (omphalós, “navel”).

parole.parola: on the horns of a dilemma
parole.significato: Facing a choice between two equally undesirable alternatives.
parole.testo: From horn (“alternative in an argument”), from Latin argūmentum cornūtum (“argument with alternatives”, literally “horned argument”), a reference to an alternative that one can metaphorically get caught on or injured by.

parole.significato: A disease caused by a worm of the genus Onchocerca, especially as transmitted to humans by flies and often causing blin…
parole.testo: From New Latin Onchocerca (a genus of parasitic worms), from Ancient Greek ὄγκος (ónkos, “barb”) + κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”) + -iasis.

parole.significato: Pertaining to tumors.
parole.testo: First attested 1857, from New Latin onco- (“tumor”). from Ancient Greek ὄγκος (ónkos, “lump, mass, bulk”).

parole.significato: Relating to osmotic pressure caused by the presence of colloids.
parole.testo: From New Latin onco- (“tumor”), from Ancient Greek ὄγκος (ónkos, “lump, mass, bulk”) + -tic.

parole.significato: The selfsame. Used to emphasize the identity or equivalence of two things.
parole.testo: Possibly a calque of Latin unus et idem.

parole.significato: The study of dreams and their interpretation.
parole.testo: From oneiro- + -logy, historically from Latin oneirologia from Ancient Greek ὄνειρος (óneiros, “dream”).

parole.significato: Fitted for, or carrying, a burden.
parole.testo: From Latin onerarius, from onus, oneris (“load, burden”). Compare French onéraire. See onus, onerous.

parole.significato: To load; to burden or bedeck.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin onerātus, perfect passive participle of onerō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Onerousness.
parole.testo: From onerous + -ity, from Latin onerositas.

parole.significato: Being the only child of one’s parent (especially one’s father)
parole.testo: From Middle English oonlybigeten, equivalent to only + begotten. Calque of Lat

parole.significato: A centaur with the body of an ass, instead of a prototypical horse.
parole.testo: Late Latin onocentaurus, from Ancient Greek ὀνοκένταυρος (onokéntauros, from ὄνος (ónos, “ass”) + κένταυρος (kéntauros, “centaur”)).

parole.significato: A white crystalline waxy triterpene extracted from the root of the leguminous plant spiny restharrow (Ononis spinosa).

parole.significato: a fish with a pointed snout
parole.testo: From New Latin oxyrhynchus, from Ancient Greek ὀξῠ́ρρῠγχος (oxŭ́rrhŭnkhos, “a kind of Egyptian fish”) (whence also the place name Ὀξῠ́ρρῠγχος (Oxŭ́rrhŭnkhos), from ὀξῠ́ς (oxŭ́s, “sharp”) + ῥῠ́γχος (rhŭ́nkhos, “snout”).

parole.significato: A broad and bifid P wave on an electrocardiogram, most commonly observed in lead II, usually caused by enlargement of t…
parole.testo: From P (“P wave”) + New Latin mitrāle, neuter singular of mitrālis (“relating to a mitre; mitral”), from mītra (“mitre”) + -ālis. So named because it often appears as a consequence of mitral valve disease.

parole.significato: A high, narrow and peaked P wave on an electrocardiogram, most commonly observed in leads II and III, usually caused by…
parole.testo: From P (“P wave”) + New Latin pulmōnāle, neuter singular of pulmōnālis (“relating to the lungs; pulmonary”), from pulmō (“lung”) + -ālis. So named because it often appears as a consequence of pulmonary disease.

parole.significato: The act of eating or feeding.
parole.testo: From pābulātiōn-, the stem of the Classical Latin pābulātiō (“action of collecting fodder or food; foraging”), from pābulor (“eat fodder, graze; collect fodder, forage”), from pābulum (“food, fodder”); compare the Middle French pabulation (“action of providing oneself with forage”).

parole.significato: nourishing
parole.testo: Latin pabulosus (“abounding in fodder”), from pabulum (“food or nourishment”).

parole.significato: Food or fodder, particularly that taken in by plants or animals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pābulum (“food, nourishment; fodder or pasture for animals; nourishment for the mind, food for thought”), from pā(scō) (“to nourish”) + -bulum (suffix denoting an instrument), or directly from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-dʰlom (*peh₂- (“to protect, shepherd”) + *-dʰlom, variant of

parole.significato: Able to be easily pacified.
parole.testo: From Latin pacare + -able.

parole.significato: peaceful, tranquil
parole.testo: From Latin pācātus, perfect passive participle of pācō (“to make peaceful, pacify”), from pāx (“peace”).

parole.significato: pacified, placated
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pācātus + -ed, By surface analysis, pacate + -d.

parole.significato: pacifying, placation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pacatio.

parole.significato: With all due respect to.
parole.testo: From Latin pāce (“in peace”), ablative form of pāx (“peace”).

parole.significato: A genus, Pachysandra, of four or five species of evergreen shrubs or subshrubs, belonging to the boxwood family, Buxace…
parole.testo: From the New Latin genus name, equivalent to English pachy-, from Ancient Greek παχύς (pakhús) [Term?].

parole.significato: A steam locomotive of the 4-6-2 wheel arrangement.
parole.testo: From Latin pācificus (“peace-making”), so called by Magellan because he sailed peacefully over it after weathering Cape Horn.

parole.significato: Synonym of pacify.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pācificāt-, the past participial stem of pācificō. Also sometimes an independent back-formation from pacification. For its use by non-native speakers, compare Portuguese and Spanish pacificar and Italian pacificare.

parole.significato: A peacemaker, a pacifier.
parole.testo: From Latin pācificātor.

parole.significato: Promoting peace; conciliatory.
parole.testo: From Latin pācificātōrius.

parole.significato: Something which is packed, a parcel, a box, an envelope.
parole.testo: Equivalent to pack + -age. Possibly influenced by Anglo-Latin paccagium or Old French pacquage.

parole.significato: A taxane antineoplastic drug C₄₇H₅₁NO₁₄ originally isolated from the bark of the Pacific yew, Taxus brevifolia, but now…
parole.testo: From Pac(ific yew) + Latin (brevifo)li(a) + -taxel (“alteration of taxol”).

parole.significato: Agreements must be kept.
parole.testo: Latin plural of pactum (“pact”) + sunt servanda (“must be kept”), after pacta et promissa semperne servanda sint (“whether agreements and promises should always be kept”) in Cicero, De Oficiis 3.92.

parole.significato: Settled by a pact or treaty; relating to pacts or treaties.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pactītius, pactīcius.

parole.significato: An agreement in which a creditor promises not to enforce a debt.
parole.testo: Latin: pactum (“agreement”) + dē (“concerning”, “about”) + nōn (“not”) + petendō (“which is to be sued for”, the ablative singular of the neuter substantive of the future passive participle of petō, “I demand or claim at law”, “I bring an action to recover”, “I sue for”) ≅ “agreement not to sue”.

parole.significato: An unlawful agreement.
parole.testo: From Latin pactum illicitum.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the river Po in Italy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Padānus, from Padus + -ānus. By surface analysis, Padus + -an.

parole.significato: A kind of woollen cloak or mantle used by Romans, worn on journeys and in rainy weather.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin paenula.

parole.significato: The rule of Classical Latin pronunciation which states that a word receives antepenultimate stress if its penult is a s…
parole.testo: First attested in 1892; Latin paenultima (“penult”) + English law.

parole.significato: Relating to, characteristic of religions that differ from main world religions.
parole.testo: From Middle English pagan (adjective and noun), from Latin pāgānus (“rural, rustic; civilian”), replaced Middle English payen from the same root. The meaning “not Christian” arose in Vulgar Latin, probably from the 4th century, owing to the Roman countryside being largely non-Christian, or potential

parole.significato: Any indigenous polytheistic religion.
parole.testo: From Latin pāgānismus (“heathenism”), from pāgānus (“peasant, rural, rustic”). The term was used pejoratively by local Orthodox Christian Demonyms to belittle what remained of alternative native ideas and ideals. By surface analysis, pagan + -ism.

parole.significato: To exhibit in show; to represent; to mimic.
parole.testo: Late 14th c. as Middle English pagent, from Medieval Latin pagina (“play in a cycle of mystery plays”), perhaps from Latin pāgina (“page of a book”).

parole.significato: The surface of a leaf or of a flattened thallus.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pāgina. Doublet of page.

parole.significato: To number the pages of (a book or other document); to foliate.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin paginare, from Latin pagina.

parole.significato: A country district with scattered hamlets.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pāgus.

parole.significato: Synonym of African hunting dog.
parole.testo: Calque of New Latin Lycaon pictus, its taxonomic name.

parole.significato: A part of an insect's leg that is spade-shaped and can be used as a scoop for feeding.
parole.testo: From Latin pāla. Doublet of peel.

parole.significato: Of a leaf: having a spade-like shape.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin palaceus (“spade-like”), from pāla (“spear”) + -āceus.

parole.significato: An old book printed between 1500 and 1550.
parole.testo: From New Latin palaeotypus (“which dates from the early days of printing; incunabulum, paleotype”), synchronically palaeo- + type.

parole.significato: A public area in ancient Greece and Rome dedicated to the teaching and practice of wrestling and other sports; a wrestl…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palaestra, from Ancient Greek παλαίστρα (palaístra, “wrestling school”).

parole.significato: The office or rank of a palatine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palātīnātus.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the Elector Palatine or the German Palatinate or its people.
parole.testo: From Latin Palātīnus, from Palātium.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the palate.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin palātum (“the palate”).

parole.significato: A small fleshy muscle, narrower in the middle than at either end, that arises from the soft palate on each side, contri…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin palātoglōssus, clipping of mūsculus palātoglōssus (“palatoglossal muscle”).

parole.significato: A long, fleshy longitudinal muscle, narrower in the middle than at either end, that arises from the soft palate, contri…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin palātopharyngeus, clipping of mūsculus palātopharyngeus (“palatopharyngeal muscle”). Doublet of palatopharyngeal.

parole.significato: The interior chaff or husk of grasses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palea (“chaff”).

parole.significato: chaffy; resembling or consisting of paleae, or chaff
parole.testo: From Latin palea (“chaff”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: A diminutive or secondary palea
parole.testo: Diminutive of Latin palea.

parole.significato: Part of the lung of birds formed by the parabronchi from the mediolateral and medioventral bronchi
parole.testo: From paleo- + Latin pulmō (“lung”).

parole.significato: chaffy; like chaff
parole.testo: From Latin palea (“chaff”) + -ous.

parole.significato: A Philistine.
parole.testo: From Latin Palaestinus, from Ancient Greek Παλαιστινὸς (Palaistinòs). Cognate with Middle French palestin, Palestin.

parole.significato: The act or practice of driving piles or posts into the ground to make it firm.
parole.testo: From Latin palus (“a stake”) + -ficare (“to make”, in comparative). Compare French palification. See -fy.

parole.significato: Emphatic repetition of a word or phrase.
parole.testo: From Late Latin palilogia (“palilogy”), from Ancient Greek παλιλογία (palilogía, “palilogy”), from πάλιν (pálin, “again”) + -λογία (-logía, “pertaining to speech, discourse”) or -λόγος (-lógos, “word, speech”).

parole.significato: A manuscript or document that has been erased or scraped clean, for reuse of the paper, parchment, vellum, or other med…
parole.testo: From Latin palimpsēstus, from Ancient Greek παλίμψηστος (palímpsēstos, “scraped again”).

parole.significato: Rebirth; regeneration.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin palingenesia (“rebirth; regeneration”), from Koine Greek παλιγγενεσία (palingenesía, “rebirth”), from Ancient Greek πᾰ́λῐν (pắlĭn, “again, anew, once more”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to turn (end-over-end); to revolve around; to dwell, sojourn”))

parole.significato: Rebirth; regeneration; (countable) an instance of this.
parole.testo: Probably a variant of palingenesia + -genesis (suffix meaning ‘origin; production’). Palingenesia is a learned borrowing from Late Latin palingenesia (“rebirth; regeneration”), from Koine Greek παλιγγενεσία (palingenesía, “rebirth”), from Ancient Greek πᾰ́λῐν (pắlĭn, “again, anew, once more”) (ultim

parole.significato: A rectangular piece of cloth worn by ladies in Ancient Rome and fastened with brooches.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin palla. Doublet of pall.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Pallas, an epithet of Athena, the goddess of wisdom, and potentially to other female Greek figures su…
parole.testo: From Latin Palladius (“of or relating to Pallas”) + -an (suffix forming adjectives from nouns). Palladius is derived from Pallas (from Ancient Greek Παλλάς (Pallás), genitive Παλλάδος (Palládos), an epithet of Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom) + -ius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns).

parole.significato: A safeguard.
parole.testo: The sense of "safeguard" comes from Latin Palladium (the image of Pallas that protected Troy), from Ancient Greek Παλλάδιον (Palládion), from Παλλάς (Pallás), an epithet used before Athena.

parole.significato: Growing or becoming pale.
parole.testo: From (the present participle stem of) Latin pallēscere (“to become pale”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or produced by a mantle, especially the mantle of mollusks.
parole.testo: Latin pallium (“a mantle”).

parole.significato: A dress; a robe.
parole.testo: Latin palliare (“to clothe”), from Latin pallium (“a mantle”). See pall, the garment.

parole.significato: Appearing weak, pale, or wan.
parole.testo: From Latin pallidus. Doublet of pale.

parole.significato: Pallidum (pale globe) in the basal ganglia of the brain.
parole.testo: From Latin pallidus (“pale yellow-green”).

parole.significato: Relating to the globus pallidus.
parole.testo: From Latin pallidus (“pale yellow-green”). By surface analysis, pallid- + -o-.

parole.significato: The globus pallidus.
parole.testo: From Latin pallidus (“pale yellow-green”).

parole.significato: A large cloak worn by Greek philosophers and teachers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pallium (“a cloak”). Doublet of pall.

parole.significato: Any of various evergreen trees from the family Palmae or Arecaceae, which are mainly found in the tropics.
parole.testo: From Middle English palme, from Old English palm, palma (“palm-tree, palm-branch”), from Latin palma (“palm-tree, palm-branch, palm of the hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂meh₂, *pl̥h₂emeh₂ (“palm of the hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Cognate with Dutch palm, German Palme,

parole.significato: Any castor oil plant of species Ricinus communis.
parole.testo: From Latin palma Christi, “palm of Christ.”

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the palm of the hand or comparable appendage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palmāris. By surface analysis, palm + ar.

parole.significato: Worthy of the palm; preeminent; superior.
parole.testo: From Latin palmarius, palmaris (“belonging to palms, deserving the palm or prize”). Cognate to Spanish palmario.

parole.significato: Having three or more lobes or veins arising from a common point.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin palmātus (“hand-shaped, palm-leaf shaped”), from palma (“palm, palm-tree”). Equivalent to palm + -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Compare French palmé.

parole.significato: Having digits connected by a thin membrane; webbed.
parole.testo: From Latin palmātus (“embroidered with palms”).

parole.significato: Synonym of palmatilobate; palmate lobed, with the divisions separated less than halfway to the common centre.
parole.testo: Latin palmatus (“palmate”) + English lobed.

parole.significato: Bearing palm trees.
parole.testo: From Latin palmifer, from palma (“a palm”) + ferre (“to bear”). Compare French palmifère.

parole.significato: A web-footed bird.
parole.testo: From Latin palmipes, palmipedis (“broad-footed”); palma (“the palm of the hand”) + pes (“a foot”). Compare French palmipède.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to ancient Palmyra or Palmyrena.
parole.testo: From Latin Palmȳrēnus, from Ancient Greek Παλμυρηνός (Palmurēnós). By surface analysis, Palmyra + -ene.

parole.significato: To examine or otherwise explore through touch, particularly (medicine) in reference to an area or organ of the human bo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palpātus, perfect passive participle of palpō (“touch softly”).

parole.significato: Someone who palpates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palpātor.

parole.significato: An eyelid.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Latin palpebra (“an eyelid”). Compare Middle English palpebre.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or located on or near the eyelids.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin palpebrālis (“of or on the eyelids”), from palpebra (“an eyelid”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix), equivalent to palpebra + -al.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the eyelids.
parole.testo: From New Latin palpebratus (“eyebrowed”), from Latin palpebra (“an eyelid”) + -atus.

parole.significato: To beat strongly or rapidly; said especially of the heart.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palpitō, palpitātus (“throb, pulsate, palpitate”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to marshes, marshy, palustral, (especially designating a plant's habitat).
parole.testo: From Latin palus (“marsh”).

parole.significato: Synonym of paludamentum.
parole.testo: From Latin palūdāmentum.

parole.significato: A military cloak worn by a general and his principal officers, fastened at one shoulder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palūdāmentum.

parole.significato: A tank or vivarium containing both aquatic and terrestrial elements.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin palūs, palūdis (“marsh, swamp”) + -arium.

parole.significato: Pertaining to marshes and swamps.
parole.testo: From Latin palūdem (palūs).

parole.significato: A member of any of various schools in Slough, Berkshire, England.
parole.testo: From Latin paludis (“of a slough or mire”).

parole.significato: Paludicolous; inhabiting marshes.
parole.testo: From Latin palūs (“marsh”) + -cole. Compare French paludicole.

parole.significato: That lives in swamps or marshes.
parole.testo: From Latin palūs (“marsh”) + -colous.

parole.significato: The productive use of wet peatland.
parole.testo: From Latin palus (“swamp”) + cultūra (“cultivation, agriculture”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a marsh.
parole.testo: From Latin palus, paludis (“a marsh”).

parole.significato: Paludinal: characteristic of or relating to marsh, swamp or fen.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin palūdīnōsus (“marshy, swampy”), ultimately from palūs. Sense 2 from translingual Paludina + -ous.

parole.significato: Growing or living in marshy places; marshy.
parole.testo: From Latin paludosus (“marshy”).

parole.significato: A vertical pillar along the inner septal margin of a coral.
parole.testo: From Latin pālus (“stake, post”). Doublet of pole, peel, and pale.

parole.significato: A small plain (compared to mare) on the surface of a planet or satellite.
parole.testo: From Latin palūs (“marsh, swamp”).

parole.significato: Any of the ranks in the hierarchy of gladiators.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?]

parole.significato: Pertaining to or located in marshes; marshy.
parole.testo: From Latin palustris, from palūs (“swamp”), -al.

parole.significato: In the form of tendrils.
parole.testo: From Latin pampinus (“a tendril”) + -form.

parole.significato: A remedy believed to cure all disease and prolong life that was originally sought by alchemists; a cure-all.
parole.testo: From Latin panacēa, from Ancient Greek πανάκεια (panákeia), from πανακής (panakḗs, “all-healing”), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) (equivalent to English pan-) + ἄκος (ákos, “cure”).

parole.significato: The purulent inflammation of a digit.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin panāritium.

parole.significato: A pantry or storehouse for bread.
parole.testo: From Latin pānārium (“pantry”). Doublet of pannier.

parole.significato: Relating to the making of bread.
parole.testo: From Latin pānārius.

parole.significato: Synonym of pankration.
parole.testo: From Latin pancratium, from Ancient Greek παγκράτιον (pankrátion, “a complete contest”). Doublet of pankration.

parole.significato: A gland near the stomach which secretes a fluid into the duodenum to assist with food digestion.
parole.testo: Existing in English since the sixteenth century: from Latin pancreas, from Ancient Greek πάγκρεας (pánkreas), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) (equivalent to English pan-) + κρέας (kréas, “flesh”).

parole.significato: Any of various palm-like plants in the genus Pandanus.
parole.testo: From New Latin pandanus, from Malay pandan.

parole.significato: A person who furthers the illicit love affairs of others; a pimp or procurer, especially when male.
parole.testo: From Chaucer’s character Pandare (in Troilus and Criseyde), from Italian Pandaro (found in Boccaccio), from Latin Pandarus, from Ancient Greek Πάνδαρος (Pándaros). (See also Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida.)

parole.significato: A yielding or warping.
parole.testo: From Latin pandare (“to bend”).

parole.significato: Usually in the plural form Pandects: a compendium or digest of writings on Roman law divided in 50 books, compiled in t…
parole.testo: Sense 3 (“comprehensive treatise”) is from Latin pandectēs (“book that contains everything, encyclopedia”), from Ancient Greek πανδέκτης (pandéktēs, “encyclopedia”, literally “all-receiver”), from παν- (pan-, prefix meaning ‘all’) (from πᾶς (pâs, “all”)) + δέκτης (déktēs, “receiver, recipient”) (fro

parole.significato: A high-quality white bread, baked from the finest sifted flour, suitable for the lord of the manor.
parole.testo: From Latin panis domini, lord's bread.

parole.significato: To fully stretch the torso and upper limbs, typically accompanied by yawning.
parole.testo: From Latin pandiculātus, perfect active participle of pandiculor (“stretch oneself”).

parole.significato: An Ancient Greek stringed instrument, a kind of lute with three strings that were stopped with a fingerboard to alter t…
parole.testo: From Late Latin pandura, from Ancient Greek πανδοῦρα (pandoûra), a Pre-Greek/substrate loan. Doublet of mandola.

parole.significato: Having a shape reminiscent of a fiddle; obovate with a pair of sinuous indentations near the base.
parole.testo: From Latin pandura (“a pandore”).

parole.significato: To strike on the palm of the hand with a strap as a school punishment.
parole.testo: From Latin pande (“hold out”), in schoolmaster commands pande manum "hold out [your] hand" or pande palmum "hold out [your] palm".

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Unknown; Possibly; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A paroxysm of extreme physical pain or anguish; a feeling of sudden and transitory agony; a throe.
parole.testo: The origin of the noun is uncertain; it is possibly derived from Middle English *pange, perhaps an altered form of prange, prōnge (“affliction, agony, pain; pointed instrument”) as in prongys of deth (“pangs of death, death throes”), from Anglo-Latin pronga, of unknown origin. Perhaps connected with

parole.significato: Any of several of the species of grass in the genus Panicum.
parole.testo: From Latin pānicum (“Italian millet”) + grass.

parole.significato: A compound raceme.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pānicula, diminutive of pānus (“ear of millet, literally 'thread wound on a bobbin'”), from Ancient Greek πῆνος (pênos, “web”), πηνίον (pēníon, “bobbin”). Doublet of panocha.

parole.significato: breadmaking
parole.testo: From Latin panis (“bread”) + -ficatiō (“-making”, noun-forming suffix). Compare French panification.

parole.significato: Eating bread.
parole.testo: From Latin panis (“bread”) + vorare (“to devour”).

parole.significato: The Hegelian doctrine that the universe is the act or realization of Logos, and therefore logic and ontology are the sa…
parole.testo: Coined by Johann Eduard Erdmann as New Latin Panlogismus in Die Entwicklung der deutschen Speculation seit Kant. Ultimately from Ancient Greek παν- (pan-) + λόγος (lógos) + -ισμός (-ismós), equivalent to pan- + Logos + -ism.

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to panmixia.
parole.testo: From New Latin panmicticus, from Ancient Greek παν- (pan-, “every, all”) + μίξις (míxis, “mixing, mingling”) + Latin -ia.

parole.significato: A situation in which an individual is just as likely to mate with a randomly chosen individual as any other in the popu…
parole.testo: From New Latin panmixia, from Ancient Greek παν- (pan-, “every, all”) + μίξις (míxis, “mixing, mingling”) + Latin -ia.

parole.significato: Panmixia.
parole.testo: From New Latin panmixis, from Ancient Greek παν- (pan-, “every, all”) + μίξις (míxis, “mixing, mingling”).

parole.significato: A dense layer of fatty tissue growth, consisting of subcutaneous fat in the lower abdominal area.
parole.testo: From Latin panniculus, diminutive of pannus (“cloth”).

parole.significato: Bread; food.
parole.testo: Compare Norwegian Rodi cant pannom/panum, meaning loaf; Swedish Månsing cant pan (“loaf”), and old jargon Dutch paen (“bread”). Having in mind the fact that Rodi and Månsing tend to have many Latin borrowings, it is likely that English pannum is also derived from Latin pānem, the accusative of pānis

parole.significato: A hanging flap of skin or other tissue, especially one covering the cornea (in trachoma) or cartilage (in rheumatoid ar…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pannus (“cloth”). Doublet of pagne and pane.

parole.significato: Uttering ominous or prophetic voices; divining.
parole.testo: From Latin panomphaeus, borrowed from Ancient Greek πανομφαῖος (panomphaîos).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Panormus
parole.testo: From Latin Panormitānus. By surface analysis, Panormus + -itan.

parole.significato: A Classical comic actor, especially one who works mainly through gesture and mime.
parole.testo: First appears c. 1606, from Latin pantomīmus, from Ancient Greek παντόμιμος (pantómimos), from πᾶς (pâs, “each, all”) + μιμέομαι (miméomai, “to mimic”). The verbal form first appears c. 1768.

parole.significato: A male pantomime performer in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin pantomīmus.

parole.significato: A lymphatic gland that is inflamed but not suppurating.
parole.testo: From Latin panus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the pope or the papacy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pāpa, from Ancient Greek πάππας (páppas).

parole.significato: The office of a pope.
