parole.testo: From Late Latin peiōrātus (“worsened”, past participle of peiōrāre (“worsen”), from Latin peior (“worse”)) + -ive. Compare French péjoratif (“depreciative, disparaging”). By surface analysis, pejorate + -ive.

parole.significato: One who believes that the world is getting worse.
parole.testo: From Latin peior (“worse”) + -ist.

parole.significato: pejoration; process of making or becoming worse
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin peiōritās.

parole.significato: Only used in Pelagian Islands
parole.testo: Calque of Latin Pelagiae as used in Īnsulae Pelagiae.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the open sea.
parole.testo: From Latin pelagius [from Ancient Greek πελάγιος (pelágios), from πέλαγος (pélagos) + -ιος (-ios)] + -an.

parole.significato: Living in the open sea rather than in coastal or inland waters.
parole.testo: From Latin pelagicus (and possibly pelagus); from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós), from πέλαγος (pélagos, “sea”). By surface analysis, -pelag + -ic.

parole.significato: Any of the extinct crocodile-like animals of genus †Pelagosaurus which lived during the Jurassic period.
parole.testo: From Latin pelagus from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós), from πέλαγος (pélagos, “sea”) + -saur.

parole.significato: Synonym of melicope: a plant of the genus Pelea.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin pelea, from Hawaiian Pele (Hawaiian fire goddess) + -ea. Equivalent to Pele + -a.

parole.significato: Any of various seabirds of the family Pelecanidae, having a long bill with a distendable pouch.
parole.testo: From Middle English pellican, pellicane, from Old English pellican (“pelican”), from Latin pelecānus, from Ancient Greek πελεκάν (pelekán), πέλεκυς (pélekus, “hatchet”).

parole.significato: A circumscribed, elevated, livid patch on the skin.
parole.testo: From Latin pelidnoma, from Ancient Greek πελίδνωμα (pelídnōma, “dark spot”).

parole.significato: A fur or hide.
parole.testo: From Latin pellis (“animal skin, pelt”), from Proto-Italic *pelnis, from Proto-Indo-European *pel-ni-. Distantly related to fell and film.

parole.significato: A thin skin or film.
parole.testo: From Latin pellicula, from pellis (“skin”). Doublet of pellicule.

parole.significato: A thin diaphanous fabric.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pellicula (“small skin or hide”), from Latin pellis (“a skin”) + Latin -cula. Cognate with French pellicule, Spanish película.

parole.significato: Allowing the passage of light; translucent or transparent.
parole.testo: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin pellūcidus, perlucidus (“transparent, pellucid; very bright; very understandable”), from per- (prefix meaning ‘through; throughout; completely, thoroughly’) + lūcidus (“clear; full of light, bright, shining; (figuratively) easily understood, clear, luc

parole.significato: Transparency; lucidity; clarity.
parole.testo: From pellucid + -ity, from Latin pelluciditas.

parole.significato: pilosity; hairiness
parole.testo: From Latin pilosus (“hairy”), from pilus (“hair”).

parole.significato: To bombard (someone or something) with missiles.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Late Middle English pelt, pelte; further origin uncertain, probably a variant of Late Middle English pilten (“to push, thrust; to strike; to cast down, humble; to incite, induce; to place, put; to extend, reach forward with”) [and other forms], possibly from Old English *pyl

parole.significato: A small shield, especially one of an approximately elliptical form, or crescent-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin pelta, from Ancient Greek πέλτη (péltē, “shield”).

parole.significato: A prodorsal shield in chelicerates
parole.testo: From Latin pelta (“shield”) + -idium.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Peltogaster.
parole.testo: From Latin Peltogaster.

parole.significato: Pelusian
parole.testo: Latin Pelusiacus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Pelusium, an ancient city in the eastern extremes of Egypt's Nile delta.
parole.testo: From Latin Pēlūsiānus. By surface analysis, Pelusium + -ian.

parole.significato: pelvis.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Latin pēlvis (“basin”). By surface analysis, pelv- + -i-.

parole.significato: The large compound bone structure at the base of the spine that supports the legs in hominids.
parole.testo: From Latin pēlvis (“basin”), from Old Latin pēluis (“basin”), further etymology uncertain.

parole.significato: Forming an almost complete ring, but with a break or opening.
parole.testo: From Latin paene (“almost”) + annular.

parole.significato: The household deities thought to watch over the houses and storerooms of ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin penātēs, from penus (“inner part of house”). Displaced native Old English cōfgod.

parole.significato: Pending a legal suit in court.
parole.testo: From Latin pendente līte (“awaiting the litigation”).

parole.significato: An appendage; something attached to something else.
parole.testo: From Middle English, probably from Medieval Latin pendiculum (“appendage”), from Late Latin pendiculus (“cord, noose”), from Latin pendere (“to weigh”).

parole.significato: Hanging from, or as if from, a support.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pendulus (“pendant”), from pendeō (“to hang”).

parole.significato: A body suspended from a fixed support so that it swings freely back and forth under the influence of gravity, commonly…
parole.testo: Borrowed from the neuter of Latin pendulus (“hanging”).

parole.significato: Almost the thing or quality expressed by the root, as peneplain (almost a plain), peninsula (almost an island), penulti…
parole.testo: From Latin paene (“almost”).

parole.significato: The innermost, secret or hidden parts; mysteries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin penetrālia.

parole.significato: To enter into; to make way into the interior of; to pierce.
parole.testo: From Latin penētrātus, perfect passive participle of penētrō (“to put, set, or place within, enter, pierce, penetrate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from penes (“within, with”) by analogy to intrō (“to go in, enter”). Compare French pénétrer.

parole.significato: That can or does physically penetrate something; piercing, penetrating.
parole.testo: From Middle English penetratyve, penetratif, from Medieval Latin penetrativus, from (the participle stem of) Latin penetrāre (“to penetrate”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; or from; nodo incerto nell'albero; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: Any of several flightless sea birds, of the family Spheniscidae within the order Sphenisciformes, found in the Southern…
parole.testo: Uncertain. First attested in the 16th century in reference to the auk of the Northern hemisphere; the word was later applied to the superficially similar birds of the Southern hemisphere (as was woggin). Possibly from Welsh pen (“head”) and gwyn (“white”), or from Latin pinguis (“fat”). See citation

parole.significato: A tent or pledget for wounds or ulcers.
parole.testo: From Latin penicillum, penicillus (“a painter's brush, a roll of lint, a tent for wounds”).

parole.significato: Falling in the position after initial position; second.
parole.testo: Blend of penultimate + initial, treating pen- (from Latin paene (“almost”)) as a prefix.

parole.significato: A piece of land projecting into water from a larger land mass.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin paenīnsula, from paene (“almost”), and īnsula (“island”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, resembling, or connected with a peninsula or peninsulas.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin paenīnsulāris. By surface analysis, peninsula + -ar. In the historical sense borrowed from Spanish peninsular.

parole.significato: The male erectile reproductive organ used for sexual intercourse that in the human male and other placental mammals is…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pēnis, from Proto-Italic *peznis, from Proto-Indo-European *pes-ni-s, from *pes- (“penis”). First attested in the late 17th century. Doublet of pencil. Displaced native English pintle, tarse, pillicock.

parole.significato: Pertaining to penance or penitence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin paenitentiālis, from Latin paenitentia (“repentance”). Attested since the 16th century.

parole.significato: A state or federal prison for convicted felons; (loosely) a prison.
parole.testo: From Middle English penitentiary, from Medieval Latin pēnitentiārius (“place of penitence”), from Latin paenitentia (“penitence”), term used by the Quakers in Pennsylvania during the 1790s, describing a place for penitents to dwell upon their sins.

parole.significato: a contour feather
parole.testo: From Latin penna (“feather”). Doublet of panne, pen, and pinna.

parole.significato: having the structure of a normal feather
parole.testo: From Latin penna (“feather”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: feathery covering; plumage
parole.testo: From penna + -age, from Latin penna, pinna (“wing, feather”). Perhaps analogous to French pennage, the same Latinate root and suffix elements having both entered at an earlier stage (cf. Middle English penne, -age).

parole.significato: Having a feather-like shape
parole.testo: From Latin pennātus.

parole.significato: Any of numerous species of Pennatula, Pteroides, and allied genera of Alcyonaria, having a feather-like form; a sea pen.
parole.testo: From Latin pennatulus, from pennātus + -ulus, from penna + -ātus.

parole.significato: A forelimb, found on various species of extinct and extant coelurosaur, that is not used in flight or gliding but still…
parole.testo: From Latin penna (“feather”) + brachium (“arm”). Coined by Sullivan et al. in 2010.

parole.significato: Bearing feathers or quills.
parole.testo: From Latin penniger, from penna (“feather”) + gerere (“to bear”), + -ous.

parole.significato: Strong of wing; strong on the wing.
parole.testo: From Latin pennipotens, from penna (“wing”) + potens (“strong”).

parole.significato: Study of the processes devised and adopted for the punishment and prevention of crime.
parole.testo: From Latin poena (“penalty, punishment”) + -ology.

parole.significato: Hanging down, suspended.
parole.testo: From classical Latin pēnsilis, from the past participle stem of pendere (“to hang”).

parole.significato: A task or imposition set as a school punishment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pensum. Doublet of peso.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Linnean class Pentandria; having five stamens.
parole.testo: From New Latin pentandrus, from penta- + -andrus (“-androus”).

parole.significato: A noun having five cases.
parole.testo: From Latin pentaptōtum, from Ancient Greek πεντάπτωτος (pentáptōtos).

parole.significato: Government by five persons.
parole.testo: From Late Latin pentarchia, from Ancient Greek πενταρχίᾱ (pentarkhíā), from πεντα- (penta-, “penta-, five”) + -αρχίᾱ (-arkhíā, “-archy, rule”), perhaps via Middle French pentarchie. Equivalent to pent- + -archy.

parole.significato: Having five syllables.
parole.testo: Late Latin pentasyllabos + English -ic

parole.significato: The commander of a platoon of fifty men.
parole.testo: From Latin pentēcontarchus, from Ancient Greek πεντηκόνταρχος (pentēkóntarkhos, literally “commander of fifty”).

parole.significato: A military unit commanded by a pentecontarch.
parole.testo: From Latin pentēcontarchia, from Ancient Greek πεντηκονταρχία (pentēkontarkhía). By surface analysis, pentecontarch + -y.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Mount Pentelicus (Penteliko Mountain), near Athens, famous for its fine white marble quarries.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Pentelicus, from Ancient Greek Πεντελικός (Pentelikós).

parole.significato: A white marble with a uniform, faint yellow tint, quarried on Mount Pentelicus near Athens.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin marmor Pentelicum.

parole.significato: A prosal group of two and a half feet.
parole.testo: From Latin penthēmimeris, from Ancient Greek πενθημιμερής (penthēmimerḗs, “having five half-feet”): πέντε (pénte, “five”) + ἡμι- (hēmi-) + μέρος (méros, “part, metrical foot”).

parole.significato: the next to last syllable in a word
parole.testo: From Latin, from pēnultimus, paenultimus (“the last but one”).

parole.significato: A partially shaded area around the edges of a shadow, especially an eclipse.
parole.testo: From New Latin pēnumbra, from Latin paene (“almost”) + umbra (“shadow”).

parole.significato: Miserly; excessively cheap.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pēnūriōsus. See penury from Latin penuria (“want”), related to paene (“scarcely”), c. 1400. Compare French pénurie.

parole.significato: Extreme need or want; destitution, poverty; (countable) an instance of this.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English penuri, penurie (“destitution, need, poverty; dearth, lack, scarcity”), borrowed from Latin pēnūria (“need, scarcity, want”) + Middle English -i, -ie (suffix forming abstract and collective nouns); further etymology uncertain, possibly related to paene (“almost, nearly; bare

parole.significato: A flowering plant of the genus Paeonia with large fragrant flowers.
parole.testo: From Old English peonie, peonia et al., from Latin paeōnia; later reinforced by Anglo-Norman peonie, Old French peone, pyoine (French pivoine), from Latin paeōnia, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek παιωνία (paiōnía), from Ancient Greek Παιών (Paiṓn, “Paeon, the physician of the gods”)/παιών (paiṓn, “a

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Peperomia, some of which are popular houseplants.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin peperomia, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”) + ὅμοιος (hómoios, “similar, like”).

parole.significato: A peplos, an Ancient Greek garment formed of a tubular piece of cloth folded back upon itself halfway down so that the…
parole.testo: From Latin peplum, from Ancient Greek πέπλον (péplon), accusative singular of πέπλος (péplos).

parole.significato: An upper garment worn by women in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A fruit of plants of the gourd family Cucurbitaceae, possessing a hard rind and producing many seeds in a single, centr…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pepō, from Ancient Greek πέπων (pépōn, “large melon”), from πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”), from πέπτω (péptō, “ripen”). Doublet of pumpion; compare pumpkin.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, capable of, or aiding digestion.
parole.testo: From Latin pepticus, from Ancient Greek πέψις (pépsis, “digestion”), a form of πέσσω (péssō).

parole.significato: For each.
parole.testo: From Latin per (“through, during”), from Proto-Indo-European *per. Doublet of par.

parole.significato: By chance; by reason of an accidental, incidental or non-essential circumstance; contingently; indirectly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin conversio per accidens, English from 1425.

parole.significato: By others; through others. Said of a proposition held to be true because it follows from other true propositions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per alia, from per (“by; through”) + alia (“others”).

parole.significato: In a year.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin per annum, English from the 16th century.

parole.significato: via the anus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per anum.

parole.significato: Per person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per capita (“per head”).

parole.significato: Percent.
parole.testo: Latin per + centum

parole.significato: in contrast, on the contrary
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per contra.

parole.significato: An opinion delivered by an entire court rather than a single judge.
parole.testo: Latin per (“by means of”) curiam (“the court”)

parole.significato: Per day; daily.
parole.testo: From Latin per + diem (“day”).

parole.significato: As is impossible.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per impossibile.

parole.significato: By letter; in a message to the author.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of Latin per litterās (“by letter”).

parole.significato: monthly; by the month
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: via the nose
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per nasum.

parole.significato: At night.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: by the agency of, especially when signing a letter in place of someone else
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per procurationem (“by the agency of/on the instruction of/by proxy”).

parole.significato: By or through the rectum, as (usually, more specifically) the rectal route of administration for drugs.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: At a single leap; all at once.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Without determination by or involvement of extraneous factors; by its very nature.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per sē (“by itself”), from per (“by, through”) and sē (“itself, himself, herself, themselves”).

parole.significato: A method of distributing an estate to the descendants or heirs of a deceased legatee in which the estate is divided equ…
parole.testo: From Latin per (“by, through”) and stirpēs (“rootstock”).

parole.significato: Through the vagina, as (usually, more specifically) by the vaginal route of administration.
parole.testo: Naturalized into medical English from neoclassical use of Latin in the professions. Exists in loanword form (retaining the Latin inflection, -am) and also in a further naturalized form with reanalysis in English morphology, per vagina = per + vagina, in parallel with other per + [English noun] const

parole.significato: To go through with, perform, or carry out
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin peractus, past participle of peragere.

parole.significato: Very sharp; very violent.
parole.testo: From Latin peracūtus.

parole.significato: To travel around or through.
parole.testo: From Latin peragratus (“wandered through”), past participle of peragro (“to wander”). See peregrine, peregrinate.

parole.significato: The act or state of travelling, or passing through any space.
parole.testo: From Latin peragratio: compare French peragration.

parole.significato: To walk around, roam, or stroll.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin perambulō, perambulātus. Equivalent to per- + ambulate.

parole.significato: For every hundred (used with preceding numeral to form a noun phrase expressing a proportion).
parole.testo: From New Latin per centum (“by the hundred”).

parole.significato: The amount, number or rate of something, regarded as part of a total of 100; a part of a whole.
parole.testo: From percent, from Latin per centum (“for every hundred”), + -age (suffix indicating a rate).

parole.significato: Something perceived; the object of perception.
parole.testo: A learned borrowing, after concept, from Classical Latin perceptum (“a proposition, principle, general idea”), from the neuter of perceptus (“perceived”), the past participle of percipiō (“to perceive”); see perceive. Coined by the Scottish metaphysician Sir William Hamilton, 9th Baronet (1788–1856)

parole.significato: Synonym of perceive.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin percept-, the past participial stem of percipiō (“to perceive”). In etymology 2 sense 2, perhaps independently from percept (“something perceived”).

parole.significato: Able to be perceived, sensed, or discerned.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin perceptibilis, from Latin percipio.

parole.significato: Having or showing keenness or sharpness of perception, insight, understanding, or intuition.
parole.testo: From Latin perceptīvus.

parole.significato: That which perceives.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin perceptor.

parole.significato: Resembling a perch (the fish).
parole.testo: From Latin perca (“perch”) + -ine.

parole.significato: perception
parole.testo: From percipient, itself from the Latin percipiens, the past participle of percipere (“to perceive”).

parole.significato: The faculty, act or power of perceiving; perception.
parole.testo: From percipient + -cy, from Latin percipiō (“perceive”)

parole.significato: That which is to be perceived.
parole.testo: From Latin percipiendum.

parole.significato: Having the ability to perceive, especially to perceive quickly.
parole.testo: From Latin percipiēns, present participle of percipiō (“to perceive”).

parole.significato: Of or belonging to Percoidea, a taxonomic superfamily in the order Perciformes.
parole.testo: From Latin perca (“perch”).

parole.significato: To pass a liquid through a porous substance; to filter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin percōlātus, perfect passive participle of percōlō (“to filter”), itself, from per (“through”) + cōlō (“to strain”) (from cōlum (“a strainer”), of unknown origin); see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The seepage or filtration of a liquid through a porous substance.
parole.testo: From Latin percōlātiō.

parole.significato: an enquiry
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin percontatiō (“inquiry, questioning”), from percontor (“to interrogate, investigate”) + -tiō.

parole.significato: That is, expressed in, or having the character of the grammatical mood (mode) of rhetorical questioning; percontatorial.
parole.testo: From the Latin percontativus.

parole.significato: Given to or characterised by the asking of questions, especially open-ended ones (percontations).
parole.testo: First attested in 1853; formed from Latin percontātōrius (from percontōr (“to inquire”)) + -al.

parole.significato: Indissolubly associated.
parole.testo: A humorous neologism and nonce word coined by Canadian sketch comedy troupe The Kids in the Hall for a 1991 episode of their eponymous Canadian sketch comedy. In principle, Latin per- (“throughout”) + *cumbō (“to lie down”).

parole.significato: Running through the entire length; running through from top to bottom, as the midrib of a dicotyledonous leaf, the nerv…
parole.testo: From Latin percurrens, present participle of percurrere (“to run or pass through”), from per (“through”) + currere (“to run”).

parole.significato: rushed, hasty or cursory.
parole.testo: From Latin percursor (“one who runs through”), from percurrere. See percurrent.

parole.significato: To strike; to hit; to knock; to give a blow to.
parole.testo: From Latin percussus, past participle of percutiō (“to strike, to beat”), from per (“through”) + quatiō (“to shake, to strike”).

parole.significato: Striking; having the power of striking or hitting.
parole.testo: From Latin percutiens. See percuss.

parole.significato: Any deciduous plant.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin perdere (“to lose”) + folium (“leaf”).

parole.significato: A woman who has fallen into prostitution.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin perdita (“lost woman”).

parole.significato: treason
parole.testo: Latin perduellio.

parole.significato: To travel from place to place, or from one country to another, especially on foot; hence, to sojourn in foreign countri…
parole.testo: From Latin peregrinari (“to live or travel abroad”). See also peregrine and pilgrim.

parole.significato: Peregrine; having travelled; exotic, foreign.
parole.testo: From Latin peregrinatus (“having travelled abroad”), past participle of peregrinari.

parole.significato: One who peregrinates; one who travels about.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin peregrīnātor.

parole.significato: The quality of being foreign or strange.
parole.testo: From peregrine + -ity, from Latin peregrīnitās. Compare French pérégrinité.

parole.significato: To destroy or defeat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin peremptum, past participle of perimere.

parole.significato: A quashing (of law, lawsuit, appeal etc.)
parole.testo: Latin peremptio: compare French péremption.

parole.significato: To procrastinate for a long time, especially two days.
parole.testo: From Latin perendinare (“to defer until the day after tomorrow”), from Latin perendie (“on the day after tomorrow”), from dies (“day”).

parole.significato: To survive from one growing season to the next
parole.testo: From Latin perennō.

parole.significato: Lasting or remaining active throughout the year, for multiple years, or all the time.
parole.testo: The adjective is borrowed from Latin perennis (“lasting through the whole year or for several years, perennial; continual, everlasting, perpetual”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Perennis is derived from per- (“completive or intensifying prefix with the sens

parole.significato: The quality of being perennial.
parole.testo: From perenn + -ity, from Latin perennitas.

parole.significato: A rambling or wandering through various places.
parole.testo: From Latin pererrare, pererratum (“to wander through”).

parole.significato: A number that is the sum of all of its divisors except itself.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin numerus perfectus, with this use of perfectus itself a semantic loan from Ancient Greek τέλειος (téleios).

parole.significato: the office of a perfectissimus
parole.testo: From Latin perfectissimatus.

parole.significato: Synonym of perfect (“leader of the Cathar movement”).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin perfectus. Doublet of parfait, perfect, and perfecto.

parole.significato: Extremely, excessively, or feverishly passionate; zealous.
parole.testo: From Late Latin perfervidus, from Latin per- + fervidus. By surface analysis, per- + fervid; compare pellucid.

parole.significato: A very ardent disposition.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?]; see perfervid.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or representing perfidy; disloyal to what should command one's fidelity or allegiance.
parole.testo: From Latin perfidiōsus (“treacherous”), from perfidia. By surface analysis, perfidy + -ous.

parole.significato: Capable of being blown through; permeable to air currents.
parole.testo: From Latin perflābilis. Compare perflate.

parole.significato: The act of perflating, or blowing through.
parole.testo: Latin perflatio.

parole.significato: Appearing to have the stem passing through the blade.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin perfoliāta, from Latin per- (“through”) + the feminine of Latin foliātus (“foliate”).

parole.significato: The long flexor muscle of the toes, or the deep flexor muscle of the fingers.
parole.testo: From Latin perforans.

parole.significato: The short flexor of the toes, or the superficial flexor of the fingers.
parole.testo: From Latin perforātus.

parole.significato: To rub over.
parole.testo: From Latin perfricatus, past participle of perfricare.

parole.significato: A thorough rubbing, as with an ointment or embrocation.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin perfricātiō, from perfricō.

parole.significato: A severe chill
parole.testo: From Latin perfrictio (“a chilling through”).

parole.significato: Done only or merely to conform to a minimal standard or to fulfill a protocol or presumptive duty.
parole.testo: From Late Latin perfunctōrius (“careless, negligent”), from the past participial stem of perfungor, perfunct- (“perform, carry through”), from per- + fungor.

parole.significato: To permeate or suffuse something, especially with a liquid or with light.
parole.testo: From 1520s, from Latin perfusus, past participle of perfundo (“to pour over, besprinkle”) from per- + fundo (“to pour”) (from nasalised form of PIE root *gheu- ("to pour")); compare diffuse, suffuse.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Pergamum.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Pergamēnus or its etymon Ancient Greek Περγαμηνός (Pergamēnós). By surface analysis, Pergam(um) + ene.

parole.significato: Reminiscent of parchment.
parole.testo: From the suffixation of post‑Classical Latin pergament(um) (“parchment”) with the suffix -aceous (“of the nature of”) (itself from the Latin compound adjectival suffix ‑āceus).

parole.significato: To shudder (at).
parole.testo: From Latin perhorrēscere.

parole.significato: The perianth.
parole.testo: From New Latin perianthium, from peri- + Ancient Greek ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”) + -ium. Doublet of perianth.

parole.significato: The involucre that surrounds the common receptacle in composite flowers.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek [Term?] "around" + "a bed".

parole.significato: To endanger.
parole.testo: From the past participle stem of Latin periclitari, from periculum (“experiment, risk”). Compare peril.

parole.significato: The state of being in peril.
parole.testo: From Latin periclitatio. Compare French périclitation.

parole.significato: Surrounding the locus coeruleus
parole.testo: From peri- + Latin coeruleus.

parole.significato: A section of text forming a coherent thought, suitable for use in a speech.
parole.testo: From Late Latin pericope, from Ancient Greek περικοπή (perikopḗ, “section”), from περι- (peri-, “across”) + κοπή (kopḗ, “cutting”), from κόπτω (kóptō, “I cut”).

parole.significato: The membrane (or periosteum) which covers the outer surface of the skull.

parole.significato: dangerous, hazardous, perilous
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin periculosus (“dangerous, hazardous, perilous”). Doublet of perilous.

parole.significato: accident or casus, as distinguished from dolus and culpa, and hence relieving one from the duty of performing an obliga…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin periculum. Doublet of peril.

parole.significato: The outer layer that covers the spore-bearing organ in many fungi.
parole.testo: A New Latin form of Ancient Greek πηρίδιον (pērídion, “little pouch”).

parole.significato: A specialized sheath-like bract that surrounds the ovary or fruit of some flowering plants, especially those in the fam…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin perigynium, from peri- + Ancient Greek γῠνή (gŭnḗ, “woman”) + -ium.

parole.significato: The point of an elliptical lunar orbit where the distance between the satellite and the Moon is at its minimum.
parole.testo: From peri- + Latin lūna (“moon”).

parole.significato: The sum of the distance of all the lengths of the sides of an object.
parole.testo: From Latin perimetros, Ancient Greek περίμετρος (perímetros). Equivalent to peri- + meter.

parole.significato: The outer serosa layer of the uterus.
parole.testo: From peri- + Late Latin metrium (“womb”), from Ancient Greek μήτριον (mḗtrion, “of a mother”).

parole.significato: The region between the genitalia and anus.

parole.significato: Someone living on the same latitude as someone else, but on a different or opposite side of the world; one's antithesis.
parole.testo: From Late Latin perioeci, from Ancient Greek περίοικοι (períoikoi), plural of περίοικος (períoikos, “neighbour”), from περι- (peri-, “peri-”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

parole.significato: That occurs around the time of labor and childbirth (parturition) (typically, within a few weeks before, intrapartum, o…
parole.testo: From peri- + Latin partum (“giving birth”), thus "around [the time of] birth".

parole.significato: A sudden reversal of fortune as a plot point in Classical tragedy.
parole.testo: From Late Latin peripetia, and its source Ancient Greek περιπέτεια (peripéteia), from περιπίπτω (peripíptō, “to change suddenly”), from περί (perí, “round, around, about”) + the stem of πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”).

parole.significato: The use of more words than are necessary to express the idea; a roundabout, or indirect, way of speaking; circumlocutio…

parole.significato: An account of a voyage, particularly those of Hanno and Arrian, recording ports and coastal landmarks.
parole.testo: From Latin periplūs (“account of a voyage”) and Ancient Greek περίπλους (períplous, “voyage, naval manouver, account of a voyage”), from περί (perí, “peri-: around”) + πλοῦς (ploûs, “voyage”), from πλεῖν (pleîn, “to sail”). Cf. French périple, Spanish periplo, & Italian periplo.

parole.significato: pneumonic (of or pertaining to pneumonia (an inflammation of the lungs))
parole.testo: Latin peripneumonicus, Ancient Greek: compare French péripneumonique. peripneumonia + -ic

parole.significato: Superfluity of words; verbosity; long-windedness.
parole.testo: From Latin perissologia, from Ancient Greek περισσός (perissós, “odd, uneven”) + Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía). By surface analysis, perisso- + logy or periss- + -ology.

parole.significato: The herb vervain (Verbena officinalis).
parole.testo: From Late Latin peristerion, from Ancient Greek περιστέριον (peristérion).

parole.significato: A peristyle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin peristylium.

parole.significato: A peristyle.

parole.significato: skilled

parole.significato: In mammals, the serous membrane lining the cavity of the abdomen and that is folded over the viscera.
parole.testo: From Latin peritonaeum, from Ancient Greek περιτόναιον (peritónaion), from περιτόναιος (peritónaios, “stretched or strained over”).

parole.significato: The wheel which, together with the axle, forms the axis in peritrochio.
parole.testo: From New Latin peritrochium, from Koine Greek περιτρόχιον (peritrókhion), from Ancient Greek περίτροχος (perítrokhos, “circular”).

parole.significato: A Roman Catholic theologian attending an ecumenical council to give advice.

parole.significato: Any of several evergreen plants of the genus Vinca with blue or white flowers.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to perjury.

parole.significato: The state or quality of permanence.

parole.significato: Capable of being mixed.

parole.significato: Synonym of chilblain.

parole.significato: To stay up all night; to pass the night (especially in prayer).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin peroneum.

parole.significato: Any of several muscles of the lateral side of the leg, which arise from the fibula and act to move the foot.

parole.significato: To be guilty of, or responsible for a crime etc; to commit.

parole.significato: One who perpetrates; especially, one who commits an offence or crime.

parole.significato: female perpetrator
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin perpetrātrīx. By surface analysis, perpetrate + -trix.

parole.significato: Condition or state of being perplexed; perplexity.
parole.testo: From Latin perplexionem, from perplexio, equivalent to perplex + -ion.

parole.significato: excessive drinking; boozing
parole.testo: From Latin perpotatio, from perpotate. See per- and potation.

parole.significato: Exactly.

parole.significato: Any monetary or other incidental benefit beyond salary.

parole.testo: From per- (“throughout, thoroughly”) + + Latin scōpātus, from scōpāre (“sweep”), from scōpa (“broom, bundle of sticks”) (classically only found as plural scōpae). By surface analysis, per- + scop(a) + -ate.

parole.significato: A thorough searching; a minute inquiry or scrutiny.

parole.significato: A female persecutor.

parole.significato: A descendant of Perseus.

parole.significato: lady's thumb

parole.significato: A person who is welcome or acceptable.

parole.significato: A nonspeaking role, a silent actor.

parole.significato: A person who is not welcome, especially a diplomat in a foreign country.

parole.significato: All the personal belongings, writings and information of an individual.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin persōnālia.

parole.significato: To fraudulently portray another person; to impersonate.

parole.significato: To celebrate loudly; to extol, to praise.

parole.significato: An instrument for drawing objects in perspective. They come in many shapes and sizes.
parole.testo: From Latin perspectus, past participle of perspicere (“to look through”) + -graph.

parole.significato: discernible
parole.testo: From Latin perspicabilis, from perspicere.

parole.significato: Of acute discernment; having keen insight; mentally perceptive.

parole.significato: The act of looking sharply; keen vision.
parole.testo: From Latin perspicientia, from perspiciens, past participle of perspicere. See perspective.

parole.significato: An optical glass; a telescope.
parole.testo: From Latin perspicilla, from perspicere (“to look through”).

parole.significato: Clarity, lucidity, especially in expression; the state or characteristic of being perspicuous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin perspicuitās (“evidentness”, “self-evidency”, literally “transparency”, “clarity”, “lucidity”), from Latin perspicuus (“clear”, “transparent”; “evident”); compare perspicacity and the French perspicuité. By surface analysis, perspicuous + -ity.

parole.significato: Clearly expressed, easy to understand; lucid.
parole.testo: From Latin perspicuus, in turn from perspiciō (“see through”).

parole.significato: Capable of being perspired.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin perspīrābilis. By surface analysis, perspire + -able.

parole.significato: Performing the act of perspiration or sweating; perspiratory.

parole.significato: To censure; criticize.

parole.significato: To successfully convince (someone) to agree to, accept, or do something, usually through reasoning and verbal influence.
parole.testo: From Latin persuādeō (“to persuade”). Cognate to for, sweet.

parole.significato: Persuasive.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being pertinent; pertinence.

parole.significato: Touching; having direct contact with.

parole.significato: Passing through; transient.

parole.significato: To perturb.

parole.significato: pierced or punched with holes

parole.significato: The act of punching or piercing with a pointed instrument.

parole.significato: A worst or lowest point.
parole.testo: From Latin pessimum.

parole.significato: A delicate bar of cartilage connecting the dorsal and ventral extremities of the first pair of bronchial cartilages in…

parole.significato: Containing organisms that cause contagious diseases.

parole.significato: Highly injurious or destructive to life: deadly.

parole.significato: Of or relating to pestilence or plague.

parole.significato: A petal.

parole.significato: A large broad-rimmed bell used for summoning monks.
parole.testo: From Latin petasius, from Ancient Greek πέτασος (pétasos, “petasus: a broad-brimmed hat”).

parole.significato: Any flying marsupial of the order Phalangeriformes, such as those in genera Petaurista, Phalanger, Acrobates.

parole.significato: A small spot, especially on an organ, caused by bleeding underneath the skin.

parole.significato: Characterized by, pertaining to, or resembling petechiae (small, nonraised haemorrhages on the skin).

parole.significato: radiotelephony clear-code word for the letter P.

parole.significato: The claimant or plaintiff in ancient legal systems.

parole.significato: Petrifying; converting into stone.

parole.significato: Rock-dwelling; living among or on rocks.

parole.significato: An object made of stone, especially one formed from petrifaction.
parole.testo: From Latin petra (“stone”) + (arte)fact.

parole.significato: Petrifying, turning into stone; petrifactive.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin petrificus (13th c.), from petra (“rock, stone”).

parole.significato: The quality of being comparable to or originating from Saint Peter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Petrīnitās. By surface analysis, Petrine + -ity.

parole.significato: stone

parole.significato: A flammable liquid ranging in color from clear to very dark brown and black, consisting mainly of hydrocarbons, occurri…

parole.significato: Doctor of Philosophy, a terminal research degree, the highest of academic degrees conferred by a college or university.

parole.significato: One of the filaments on the inner surface of the gastric cavity of certain jellyfishes.

parole.significato: The warthog.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Phacochoerus.

parole.significato: Spreading, obstinate ulceration.

parole.significato: Relating to phagedena.

parole.significato: An Ancient Roman javelin wrapped in tow and pitch that was set on fire before being fired

parole.significato: Any of three small wading birds in the genus Phalaropus, of the family Scolopacidae, that have lobed toes.

parole.significato: In Ancient Greece, a metal medallion worn by men or used to ornament the harness of a horse.

parole.significato: Phallic priest thought to have been a precursor of the Christian stylite.

parole.significato: The person who carries the phallus in a phallophoria
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phallophorus, from Ancient Greek φαλλοφόρος (phallophóros). By surface analysis, phallo- + -phorus.

parole.significato: A penis, especially when erect.

parole.significato: Phantasmal, incorporeal.

parole.significato: phantasmal

parole.significato: Drugs capable of producing hallucinatory experiences, now known as hallucinogens.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a pharaoh.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Pharisees.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Pharisees.

parole.significato: The doctrines and practices, or the character and spirit, of the Pharisees.

parole.significato: The study of lighthouses or other forms of light-signalling.

parole.significato: A distinguishable part of a sequence or cycle occurring over time.

parole.significato: The French bean, or kidney bean.

parole.significato: any of several domesticated beans, of the genus Phaseolus, native to the Americas
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phaseolus.

parole.significato: A phase (of the moon, a planet etc.).

parole.significato: An apparition; a phantom.

parole.significato: A phasmid.

parole.significato: Φ, the 21st letter of the Euclidean and modern Greek alphabet, usually romanized as "ph".

parole.significato: Any of the discourses of Demosthenes against Philip II of Macedon, defending the liberty of Athens.

parole.significato: Synonym of phillumeny.

parole.testo: From New Latin philodendron, from Ancient Greek φῐλόδενδρον (phĭlódendron), neuter of φῐλόδενδρος (phĭlódendros, “loving trees”). First known use: 1877.

parole.significato: A philologist.

parole.significato: The humanistic study of texts and their languages, especially ancient or classical languages.

parole.significato: The nightingale.

parole.significato: Any flowering plant of the genus Phlox.
parole.testo: From New Latin Phlox, from Ancient Greek φλόξ (phlóx, “flame”).

parole.significato: An irrational, abnormal, or obsessive fear (of something).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the ancient Greek region of Phocis.

parole.significato: Pertaining to true seals (also known as earless seals, as opposed to eared seals such as sea lions); seallike.
parole.testo: From Latin phōca (“seal”) (from Ancient Greek φώκη (phṓkē)) + -ine.

parole.significato: Relating to the sounds of spoken language.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phōnēticus, from Ancient Greek φωνητῐκός (phōnētĭkós). By surface analysis, phone + -etic.

parole.significato: Any of various compounds of transition metals or of rare earths that exhibit phosphorescence.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Photios I of Constantinople.

parole.significato: A member of the genus Physeter; a sperm whale.
parole.testo: From Latin physeter.

parole.significato: Relating to or concerning existent materials; physical.
parole.testo: From Middle English phisik, from Latin physicus, from Ancient Greek φῠσῐκός (phŭsĭkós, “natural; physical”), from φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth; nature, quality; form, shape; type, kind”), from φῠ́ω (phŭ́ō, “grow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to appear, become, rise up”).

parole.significato: The ring finger.
parole.testo: Calque of the Latin digitus medicus.

parole.significato: Of medicine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin physicālis, from Latin physica (“study of nature”), from Ancient Greek φυσική (phusikḗ), feminine singular of φυσικός (phusikós, “natural; physical”), from φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth; nature, quality; form, shape; type, kind”), from φῠ́ω (phŭ́ō, “grow”), ultimately from P

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to physiology.
parole.testo: Either from physio- + -logic or Latin physiologicus.

parole.significato: Feeding on plants; herbivorous.
parole.testo: From phyto- + Latin vorare (“to eat greedily”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Phytolacca of herbaceous plants; the poke or pokeweed.

parole.significato: A plant-like animal; a zoophyte.
parole.testo: From phyto- + zoon, from New Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The innermost of the meninges, the membranes that surround the brain and spinal cord.

parole.significato: A heinous offense that requires expiation.

parole.significato: The quality of being piacular, of requiring atonement.
parole.testo: From Latin piaculariter (“by way of atonement; sinfully”), piacularius (“atoning, expiatory”) from piaculo (“to appease or propitiate with an offering”). See pius (“dutiful”).

parole.significato: Piacular; atoning for sin or crime.
parole.testo: Coined a. 1920 by T.S. Eliot, from Latin piaculum (“propitiatory sacrifice”) + -ative.

parole.significato: An expiatory sacrifice.
parole.testo: From Latin piāculum. Doublet of piacle.

parole.significato: A member of the Order of Poor Clerics Regular of the Mother of God of the Pious Schools, a Catholic educational order f…
parole.testo: From Latin pius (“pious”), + -ist.

parole.significato: atonement or expiation.
parole.testo: From Latin piatio. See piacle.

parole.significato: A disorder characterized by appetite and craving for non-edible substances, such as chalk, clay, dirt, ice, or sand.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pīca (“jay; magpie”). Doublet of pie (“magpie”). * (pathology): From the idea that magpies will eat almost anything.

parole.significato: A size of type between small pica and English, now standardized as 12-point.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pica (“pica: a service book”), possibly from Latin pīca (“magpie”) after the piebald appearance of the typeset page (cf. pie (“disordered type”)). parole.significato: An oily liquid hydrocarbon extracted from the creosote of beechwood tar, and consisting essentially of certain derivati…
parole.testo: From Latin pix, picis (“pitch”) + amarus (“bitter”).

parole.significato: Money paid at fairs for permission to set up booths.
parole.testo: Latin piccadium, from French piquer (“to prick”).

parole.significato: A resident of ancient Picenum in Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin Picenum.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to pitch (“a sticky, dark brown substance obtained from distilling turpentine or wood tar, or crude oi…
parole.testo: From Latin piceus (“like pitch; pitch-black”) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives denoting possession or presence of a quality). Piceus is derived from pix (“pitch, tar”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peyH- (“fat; milk”)) + -eus (suffix forming adjectives indicating the sources of attributes).

parole.significato: The powder of aloes with canella, formerly officinal, employed as a cathartic.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin picra, from Ancient Greek πίκρα (píkra, “a kind of antidote”), from πικρός (pikrós, “sharp, bitter”).

parole.significato: A member of an ancient people of northern and central Scotland.
parole.testo: From Latin Pictus, probably rendering a Pictish autonym; see the Latin entry for details. Compare Old English Peohtas, which appears to show the effects of Grimm's law.

parole.significato: The picture or image component of something, such as an emblem or poem, that contains a combination of imagery and text…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pictūra (“a painting”). Doublet of picture.

parole.significato: A representation of anything (as a person, a landscape, a building) upon canvas, paper, or other surface, by drawing, p…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English picture, from Latin pictūra (“the art of painting, a painting”), from pingō (“to paint”). Doublet of pictura.

parole.significato: A raised platform built from the shore out over water, supported on piles; used to secure, or provide access to shippin…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pere (“bridge pillar, breakwater”), from either Anglo-Norman pere (“stone”, from Latin petra) or Old French *piere (Old Northern French pire, from either Late Latin *petricus or pēra "satchel"); compare Medieval Latin pira.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Pierides or Muses.
parole.testo: Latin Pierius, from Mount Pierus in Thessaly, sacred to the Muses.

parole.significato: Any color in plant or animal cells.
parole.testo: From Middle English pigment, from Latin pigmentum (“pigment”), itself from pingō (“to paint”) + -mentum; variants of this word may have been known in Old English (e.g. 12th century pyhmentum). Doublet of pimiento, pimento, and piment.

parole.significato: Being or relating to a probability that a rational person will assign to an option when required to make a decision.
parole.testo: Coined by Philippe Smets from Latin pignus (“a bet”) + -istic.

parole.significato: Synonym of pignoratitious.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pignoratus, variant of earlier Latin pignerātus (“pledged, guaranteed”).

parole.significato: to pledge or pawn
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pignoro, variant of earlier Latin pignerō (“to pledge, to guarantee”).

parole.significato: The act of pledging or pawning.
parole.testo: From Latin pignorātio, pignerātio, derivation of pignerāre (“to pledge”), derivation of pignus, genitive pignoris, pigneris (“a pledge, a pawn”). Compare French pignoration.

parole.significato: Of, like, or pertaining to pignoration.
parole.testo: Late Latin pigneraticius, pignoraticius, from Latin pigneratus, pignoratus + -icius (“-itious”).

parole.significato: A gift or keepsake that is symbolic of a love relationship; a love token.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pignus amōris.

parole.significato: Slothfulness, laziness.
parole.testo: From Latin pigritūdō.

parole.significato: A mortar.
parole.testo: From Latin pīla (“mortar”).

parole.significato: Relating to hair.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pilāris, from Latin pilus (“a hair”) + -ar.

parole.significato: A gown or case of skin, or one trimmed or lined with fur.
parole.testo: From Middle English pilche, from Old English pylċe, pyleċe, from Late Latin pellicia. A doublet of pelisse; also see pelt (“skin”).

parole.significato: The symbol ¶.
parole.testo: Probably an alteration of Middle English pylcrafte, modification of Late Latin paragraphus, itself from the Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos).

parole.significato: A hemorrhoid.
parole.testo: Apparently from Late Latin pilus. Doublet of pilus.

parole.significato: The uppermost layer of hyphae in the pileus of a fungal fruit body.
parole.testo: From New Latin pileus + pellis.

parole.significato: A ceremonial chariot or carriage, used by Roman noblewomen.
parole.testo: From Latin pilentum.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or consisting of hair.

parole.significato: Haemorrhoids.
parole.testo: From Latin pila (“ball”).

parole.significato: The top of a bird's head, from the base of the bill to the nape.

parole.significato: The cap of a mushroom.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pīleus, a form of pilleus (“a felt cap”).

parole.significato: A condition of the skin appendage, characterized by short and brittle hairs that appear flattened and twisted when view…

parole.significato: Containing or producing hair.

parole.significato: Resembling hair.

parole.significato: piliferous (covered in hair)

parole.significato: To peel; to remove the outer layer of hair, skin, or bark.
parole.testo: From Middle English pillen, pilen, from Old English pilian (“to peel”), from Latin pilō (“depilate”), from pilus (“hair”). Doublet of peel.

parole.significato: hair
parole.testo: From Latin pilus (“hair”).

parole.significato: Any cell with prominent external hair-like structures.
parole.testo: From Latin pilus + -cyte.

parole.significato: Having body hairs which have grown in a concentrated area on the skin and formed a cyst or abscess.
parole.testo: From Latin pilus (“hair”) and nidus (“nest”).

parole.significato: Covered with fine hair.
parole.testo: From Latin pilōsus, from pilus (“hair”).

parole.significato: A little pill.
parole.testo: From Latin pilula.

parole.significato: Resembling a pill or pilule.
parole.testo: From Latin pilula (“a pill”) + -ous.

parole.significato: A Roman military javelin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pilum. Doublet of pile.

parole.significato: A hair.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pilus (“hair”). Doublet of pile.

parole.significato: A colourless oily liquid related to the ketones, and obtained by the decomposition of pinacone.
parole.testo: From pinacone + Latin oleum (“oil”) + -in.

parole.significato: An art gallery, especially one exhibiting pictures.
parole.testo: From Latin pinacotheca, from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē).

parole.significato: The saturated bicyclic hydrocarbon 2,6,6-trimethyl-, (1a,2b,5a)-bicyclo[3.1.1]heptane made by the hydrogenation of pine…

parole.significato: The maritime pine (species Pinus pinaster), that grows in southern Europe.

parole.significato: A tablet or register.

parole.significato: Either of two isomeric bicyclic monoterpene hydrocarbons that are the principal components of pine resin.
parole.testo: From pine + -ene, from Latin pinus (“pine tree”).

parole.significato: An arboretum, or part of an arboretum or garden, devoted to growing conifers.

parole.significato: the process of growing obese

parole.significato: growing obese, fattening

parole.significato: Relating to fat.

parole.significato: Containing fat; fatty.

parole.significato: fatness; obesity

parole.significato: A dicarboxylic acid and recognized as an oxidation product of α-pinene, a common terpene found in pine resin.

parole.significato: Resembling a feather.
parole.testo: From Latin pinnātus (“feathered”), from pinna (“feather”).

parole.significato: Having lobes with incisions that extend almost, or up to midrib.
parole.testo: From New Latin pinnatisectus, from Latin pinnātus (“feathered”) + sectum, past participle of secō (“to cut”).

parole.significato: Shaped like a fin or feather.
parole.testo: From Latin pinna (“feather, fin”) + -form.

parole.significato: A marine mammal belonging to the parvorder Pinnipedia, comprising walruses, eared seals and earless seals, characterize…
parole.testo: From Latin pinna (“fin”) + pes (“foot”).

parole.significato: A small crab of the genus Pinnotheres, which live symbiotically in the shells of certain molluscs.
parole.testo: From Latin pīnotērēs, from Ancient Greek πινοτήρης (pinotḗrēs), from Ancient Greek πίνη (pínē, “pen shell”) + Ancient Greek τηρέω (tēréō, “to guard”).

parole.significato: A pinnule or subleaflet.

parole.significato: Any of the ultimate leaflets of a bipinnate or tripinnate leaf; a subleaflet.

parole.significato: Any gymnosperm (of the division Pinophyta)

parole.significato: An inscription indicating the identity of the one who created a painting.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to piety, exhibiting piety, devout, god-fearing.

parole.significato: An act of innocent deceit, technically using the methods of a fraudster but for an honest, honorable purpose.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin pia fraus.

parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin pirifōrmis, ellipsis of mūsculus pirifōrmis (“pear-shaped muscle”). Doublet of piriform.

parole.significato: Babesia, a genus of hematozoa that invades the red blood cells of humans and domesticated animals such as dogs and sheep
parole.testo: From Latin pirum (“pear”) + Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “image, formation”).

parole.significato: Synonym of calefactory: the room holding an abbey, convent, or monastery's communal fire.

parole.significato: fishery
parole.testo: From Latin piscarius (“relating to fishes or to fishing”), from piscis (“a fish”). By surface analysis, Latin pisc- + -ary.

parole.testo: From Latin piscatio, from piscari (“to fish”).

parole.significato: The study of fishing.

parole.significato: A fisherman; an angler.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to fishermen or fishing.

parole.significato: A female fishmonger in ancient times.

parole.significato: Someone with a Pisces astrological sign.

parole.significato: Related to fish.

parole.significato: Having the shape of a fish.

parole.significato: A drained basin near a church's altar for the disposal of water from liturgical ablutions.
parole.testo: From Latin piscīna (“fishpond; swimming pool”), from piscis (“fish”). Compare Middle English piscyne (“pool, pond”), from the same Latin word. By surface analysis, Latin pisc- + -ina.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of fish; ichthyic.
parole.testo: From Late Latin piscinus or from Latin piscis (“fish”) + -ine.

parole.significato: That feeds on fish; fish-eating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin piscivorus. By surface analysis, piscivore + -ous or pisci- + -vorous.

parole.significato: fishy.
parole.testo: From Latin piscōsus (“full of fish”).

parole.significato: Abundant with fish.
parole.testo: From Latin pisculentus (“fishy, full of fish”), from pisces (“fish”) + -ulentus (“full of, abounding in”) (whence -ule and -ent).

parole.significato: Resembling a pea or peas in size and shape
parole.testo: Latin pisum (“pea”) + -iform

parole.significato: A concretionary grain, typically of calcium carbonate, between a microid and a macroid in size.
parole.testo: From Latin pisum + -oid.

parole.significato: A sedimentary rock formed from pisoids
parole.testo: From Latin pisum + -lite.

parole.significato: A pisoid.
parole.testo: From Latin pisum + -lith.

parole.significato: A soft, black, tarry bitumen, intermediate between petroleum and asphalt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pissasphaltus, from Ancient Greek πισσάσφαλτος (pissásphaltos), from πίσσα (píssa, “pitch”) + ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt”).

parole.significato: Having faith; trusting
parole.testo: From Latin pisticus (“pure; genuine”), from Ancient Greek πιστικός (pistikós).

parole.significato: An archegonium.

parole.significato: A pistil.

parole.significato: Phlegm; mucus.
parole.testo: From Latin pītuīta (“mucus, phlegm”). Doublet of pip.

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pītuītārius (“mucous”), from pītuīta (“mucus, phlegm”). First attested in the 1610s. First attested as a noun by 1899. The term was adopted as the name for the gland, because it was believed that it channeled mucus to the nose.

parole.significato: Consisting of, or resembling, pituite or mucus.
parole.testo: From Latin pituitosus: compare French pituiteux.

parole.significato: Any of several varieties of skin diseases characterized by the shedding of flakes or scales, such as dandruff.
parole.testo: From New Latin pityriasis, from Koine Greek πιτυρίασις (pituríasis), from Ancient Greek πίτῡρον (pítūron, “bran”).

parole.significato: The quality of being placable or appeasable.
parole.testo: From Latin plācābilitās. Compare French placabilité.

parole.significato: Able to be easily pacified; quick to forgive.
parole.testo: From Latin plācābilis.

parole.significato: A process or act of placating; appeasement or an expression of appeasement.

parole.significato: A dummy medicine containing no active ingredients; an inert treatment.

parole.significato: A dessert cake originating in ancient Greece, consisting essentially of layered dough interwoven with cheese and honey.

parole.significato: A complication of pregnancy in which the placenta is inserted partially or completely in the lower segment of the uteru…

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the placenta.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin placentalis, corresponding to placenta + -al.

parole.significato: pleasing or pleasant
parole.testo: From Latin placentius, from placeō (“to please”).

parole.significato: A vote of assent, as of the governing body of a university, an ecclesiastical council, etc.

parole.significato: The state of being placid; peacefulness.

parole.significato: Designating a mode lying a perfect fourth below the authentic form.

parole.significato: The crime of literary theft; plagiarism.

parole.significato: abduction, especially of a child

parole.significato: Fond of flogging.

parole.significato: A form of monophonic chant in unison using the Gregorian scale, sung in various Christian churches.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a plane.

parole.significato: A lament or dirge, a popular literary form in the Middle Ages.

parole.significato: Of a surface: flat or level.

parole.significato: Membership of a particular planet or moon, by origin, birth, naturalization, ownership, allegiance or otherwise.
