parole.significato: A memory aid; a reminder or memorandum, especially a book or document serving this purpose.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pro memoria (literally “for memory”).

parole.significato: In part; used in nomenclature to denote that a taxon includes more than one currently recognized entity, and that only…

parole.significato: Of an allocation, in proportion to some factor that can be exactly calculated.

parole.significato: Dealing with something that arises unexpectedly or out of due course; for special business.

parole.significato: Representing oneself (in court); without an attorney.
parole.testo: From Latin pro se.

parole.significato: To that extent.
parole.testo: From Latin prō tantō (“so great/much”).

parole.significato: temporarily; for the time being.

parole.significato: temporarily; for the time being
parole.testo: From the Latin prō tempore (literally “for a time”).

parole.significato: agreeing with; supporting; favouring
parole.testo: Derived from Latin prō (“in favor of, on behalf of”).

parole.significato: forward movement
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin prō- (“forward direction, forward movement”).

parole.significato: One who holds, in opposition to the probabilists, the theory of probabiliorism.
parole.testo: From Latin probabilior, comparative of probabilis (“probable”), + -ist.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being likely to occur; likelihood, probability.
parole.testo: Latin probabilis, From probable + -ness, in existence since the 1600s.

parole.significato: An individual who presents with a genetic disorder or other specific characteristic, when this leads to the genetic inv…
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, from New Latin, from Latin probandus (“the one to be tested”) (denoting, in this application, the first one tested); By surface analysis, probe + -and.

parole.significato: To establish the legality of (a will).
parole.testo: From Middle English probate, from Latin probatus, past participle of probare (“to test, examine, judge of”); see probe, prove.

parole.significato: An examiner; an approver.
parole.testo: From Latin probātor.

parole.significato: Any of various medical instruments used to explore wounds, organs, etc.
parole.testo: For verb: borrowed from Latin probare (“to test, examine, prove”), from probus (“good”). Doublet of prove. parole.significato: Fossil specimens or elements that cannot be identified or assigned to a taxon.
parole.testo: From Latin problēmatica (“problematic things”).

parole.significato: An elongated tube from the head or connected to the mouth, of an animal.

parole.significato: Bold, forward, insolent.
parole.testo: From Latin procāx (“bold, impudent”), from procō (“ask, demand”), from procus (“suitor”).

parole.significato: A rhetorical exercise in which the speaker raises an objection to his own argument and then immediately answers it, in…
parole.testo: From Latin procatalepsis (“anticipating and answering an objection”), from Ancient Greek προκατάληψις (prokatálēpsis, “seizing in advance”).

parole.significato: A prerogative writ that sends a case from an appellate court to a lower court with an order to proceed to judgment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin procedendo.

parole.significato: A metrical foot consisting of four short syllables.
parole.testo: From Latin proceleusmaticus, from Ancient Greek προκελευσματικός (prokeleusmatikós), to rouse to action beforehand, to incite.

parole.significato: Any of a family of oceanic birds (Procellaridae) including the petrels, fulmars, and shearwaters.

parole.significato: stormy; tempestuous
parole.testo: From Latin procellosus, from procella (“a storm”).

parole.significato: Of high stature; tall.

parole.significato: tallness, height

parole.significato: tall
parole.testo: From Latin procerus (“tall”).

parole.significato: A roughly triangular facial muscle that arises from the fascia of the nasal bone and a cartilage in the side of the nos…

parole.significato: A process, or projecting part.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōcessus.

parole.significato: A rounded protuberance found on the posterior edge of the superior articular process of a lumbar vertebra.
parole.testo: Coined by the British surgeon G. M. Humphry; from Latin, because of its resemblance to a small breast.

parole.significato: A falling down; a prolapsus.
parole.testo: From Latin procidentia.

parole.significato: droopy
parole.testo: Latin prociduus.

parole.significato: Inclined, directed, or leaning forward, like the teeth of some mammals and the bristles on the frons of many insects.
parole.testo: From Latin prōclīnātus.

parole.significato: Of teeth, to lean forward.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōclīnō (“I bend or lean forward”).

parole.significato: Having a tendency by nature; prone
parole.testo: From Latin prōclīvis (“sloping, inclined”).

parole.significato: A predisposition or natural inclination, propensity, or a predilection; especially, a strong disposition or bent.
parole.testo: From Latin prōclīvitās, from prōclīvis (“prone to”).

parole.significato: inclined towards something; tending by nature
parole.testo: From Latin proclivus. See proclive.

parole.significato: A magistrate who served as a consul and then as the governor of a province.
parole.testo: From Latin prōcōnsul.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a proconsul, or the office thereof.
parole.testo: From Latin prōcōnsulāris.

parole.significato: The office of a proconsul.

parole.significato: To delay taking action; to wait until later.

parole.significato: A female who procrastinates.

parole.significato: That procreates.

parole.significato: To beget or conceive (offsprings).

parole.significato: Having the power to beget; generative.

parole.significato: A female procreator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin prōcreātrīx. By surface analysis, procreator + -trix.

parole.significato: The terminal segment of an insect's abdomen, containing the anus.

parole.significato: prone or prostrate

parole.significato: The office of a procurator.

parole.significato: Tending to, or authorizing, procuration.

parole.significato: A form of elision in which the latter word loses its first vowels.

parole.significato: wastefulness; profusion

parole.significato: An extraordinary occurrence or creature; an anomaly, especially a monster; a freak.
parole.testo: From Middle English prodige (“portent”), from Latin prōdigium (“omen, portent, prophetic sign”).

parole.significato: Disclosure.

parole.significato: A phobia that others are conspiring against one.

parole.significato: Treacherous, traitorous.

parole.significato: One who produces, or provides for inspection.

parole.significato: To produce.

parole.significato: Capable of producing something, especially in abundance; fertile.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a proem or proemium.

parole.significato: The addition of a leap day to the lunar calendar.

parole.significato: Profit.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or similar to a professor; professorial.

parole.significato: A female professor.

parole.significato: Good at something; skilled; fluent; practiced, especially in relation to a task or skill.
parole.testo: From Latin proficiens, present participle of proficere (“to go forward, advance, make progress, succeed, be profitable or useful”), from pro (“forth, forward”) + facere (“to make, do”); see fact.

parole.significato: Useful or profitable.

parole.significato: Onward flow; current.

parole.significato: Flowing smoothly as if in a stream.

parole.significato: A copious discharge of fluid, especially a bodily fluid.

parole.significato: Shining out; gleaming.

parole.significato: A deep-seated artery, as of the arm, neck, or leg.

parole.significato: Relating to the deep zone of an inland body of water where very little sunlight penetrates; located between the limneti…

parole.significato: To make profound; to make a concept unnecessarily complicated.

parole.significato: abundant or generous to the point of excess; copious; volubly expressed.

parole.significato: To beget; to generate; to produce.

parole.significato: The act of begetting; propagation, bearing children, or reproduction.

parole.significato: Deriving from or otherwise related to progeny or a progenitor or the anatomical region employed for progeneration.

parole.significato: A female progenitor, a foremother, any of a person's direct female ancestors (ancestresses).

parole.significato: A forecast of the future course or outcome of a situation based on what is presently known; a prediction.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to or characterized by prognosis or prediction.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prognosticus, from Ancient Greek προγνωστικός (prognōstikós, “foreknowing”), from πρό (pró) + γνωστικός (gnōstikós, “of or for knowing, good at knowing”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to learn to know, to perceive, to mark, to learn”).

parole.significato: To predict or forecast, especially through the application of skill.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prognosticare; see prognostic for more.

parole.significato: Same as programme.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Late Latin programma (“a proclamation, edict”).

parole.significato: Of the course of an illness, progressive.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: To forbid, disallow, or proscribe officially; to make illegal or illicit.
parole.testo: From Middle English prohibiten, from Latin prohibeō (“to fend off, prevent, prohibit”) (through past participle prohibitus).

parole.significato: Tending to prohibit, preclude, or disallow.
parole.testo: From Middle English prohibitif, prohibityve, from Medieval Latin prohibitīvus, from prohibit-, past-participle stem of Latin prohibēre. By surface analysis, prohibit + -ive.

parole.significato: A planned endeavor, usually with a specific goal and accomplished in several steps or stages.

parole.significato: An object intended to be or having been shot from a weapon.

parole.significato: Someone who devises or suggests a project; a proposer or planner of something.

parole.significato: Something that juts out beyond a surface; a projection.

parole.significato: Someone or something that launches a projectile.
parole.testo: From Latin prōiciō, from prō- (“from, in the place of; for”) + iaciō (“throw, hurl”).

parole.significato: To move out of place; especially for an internal organ to protrude beyond its normal position.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin prolapsus.

parole.significato: prolapse
parole.testo: From Latin prōlāpsiō.

parole.significato: Elongated at the poles.
parole.testo: From Latin prolatum, past participle of proferre (“to extend, lengthen”).

parole.significato: Speaking, utterance, the producing of words or speech.
parole.testo: From Latin prolationem, from the past participle stem of proferre (“bring forward, produce”).

parole.significato: uttered
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōlātīvus.

parole.significato: The deputy or substitute legate.
parole.testo: From Latin prolegatus, from pro (“for”) + legatus (“legate”).

parole.significato: The assignment of something to a period of time that precedes it.
parole.testo: From Latin prolepsis, from Ancient Greek πρόληψις (prólēpsis, “preconception, anticipation”), from προλαμβάνω (prolambánō, “take beforehand, anticipate”).

parole.significato: Having numerous offspring.
parole.testo: Latin proletaneus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the proletariat.
parole.testo: From Latin proletarius (“a man whose only wealth is his offspring, or whose sole service to the state is as father”), from proles (“offspring, posterity”).

parole.significato: A proletarian.
parole.testo: From Latin prōlētārius, from prōlēs.

parole.significato: The crime of destroying one's offspring, either in the womb or after birth.
parole.testo: From Latin prōlēs (“offspring”) + -cide.

parole.significato: Producing many offspring; prolific or proliferative.
parole.testo: From Latin prōlifer, from prōlēs (“offspring”) + -fer (“bearing”), + -ous.

parole.significato: Productive, generative; prolific.
parole.testo: From modern Latin proliger (from Latin proles + -ger) + -ous.

parole.significato: A spokesman, one who speaks on behalf of others.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English prolocutor, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin prōlocūtor.

parole.significato: Occurring in or serving as a prologue.
parole.testo: Probably either from the Latin prologēticus or formed in English as prologue + -etic, in both cases resembling a hypothetical Ancient Greek etymon of the form *προλογητικός (prologētikós), from πρόλογος (prólogos, “prologue”) + -ητικός (-ētikós, “-etic”), a formation akin to the extant words ἀναλογη

parole.significato: Synonym of prolong.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin prōlongāt-, the past participial stem of prōlongō.

parole.significato: A trial before the principal performance; a prelude.
parole.testo: From Latin prolusio, from proludere (“to prelude”).

parole.significato: Relating to prolusion; preliminary, introductory
parole.testo: From Latin proludo (“practice beforehand”), from pro- + ludo (“Latin - play”).

parole.significato: The act of flowing forth; emanation.
parole.testo: From pro- + Latin manatio (“a flowing”), from manare (“to flow”).

parole.significato: To oblige; to confer a favour on.
parole.testo: From Latin promeritus, past participle of promerere (“to deserve”), from pro (“before”) + merere (“to merit”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Prometheus, a demigod in Greek mythology who created mortals from clay and stole fire from Zeus to…
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Prometheus (“demigod in Greek mythology”) + -an (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives; and forming agent nouns). parole.significato: Made up of various disparate elements mixed together; of disorderly composition.
parole.testo: From Latin prōmiscuus (“mixed, not separated”), from prō (“forth”) + misceō (“mix”).

parole.significato: Containing or consisting of a promise.
parole.testo: From Middle English promissorye, from Medieval Latin prōmissōrius. By surface analysis, promise + -ory.

parole.significato: Synonym of promontory.
parole.testo: A borrowing of Latin promontorium.

parole.significato: A high point of land extending into a body of water, headland; cliff.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prōmontōrium, from prōmineō, from prō- + *mineō (“to project or jut”, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stand out”)) + -tōrium (“place”).

parole.significato: To raise (someone) to a more important, responsible, or remunerative job or rank.
parole.testo: From Latin prōmōtus, perfect passive participle of prōmoveō (“move forward, advance”).

parole.significato: A female promoter.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin prōmōtrīx. By surface analysis, promote + -trix.

parole.significato: The quality of being prompt; alacrity.
parole.testo: From Middle English promptitude, from Late Latin prōmptitūdō, from Classical Latin prōmptus. By surface analysis, prompt + -itude.

parole.significato: A magazine, repository, or handbook.
parole.testo: Latin promptuarium (“storehouse”).

parole.significato: To turn or rotate one’s hand and forearm so that the palm faces down if the forearm is horizontal, back if the arm is p…
parole.testo: From Latin prōnatus, past participle of prōnare (“to bend forward”). See prone.

parole.significato: A muscle in the distal ends of ulna and radius which serves to pronate the forearm and stabilise the distal radioulnar…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Lying face-down.
parole.testo: From Middle English prone, proone, proon, from Latin prōnus (“turned forward, bent or inclined”), from prō (“forward”).

parole.significato: Being the product of two consecutive integers.
parole.testo: Apparently from New Latin pronicus, a misspelling of Latin promicus, from Ancient Greek προμήκης (promḗkēs, “elongated, oblong”), but the spelling has been pronic from its earliest known occurrence in English (Leonhard Euler, Opera Omnia, series 1, volume 15).

parole.significato: Proneness to do something; propensity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōnitās.

parole.significato: Walking with the length of the body parallel to the ground.
parole.testo: From Latin pronus (“bent over”) + -grade (“means of walking”) (from Latin gradus). Compare prone.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, resembling, or functioning as a pronoun.
parole.testo: From Late Latin prōnōminālis, from Latin prōnōmen, prōnōminis. By surface analysis, pro- + nominal.

parole.significato: Promoting, or presiding over, marriage.
parole.testo: From Latin prōnuba.

parole.significato: Of or relating to pronunciation.
parole.testo: Latin pronunciativus.

parole.significato: Someone who pronounces; a pronouncer.
parole.testo: Latin pronunciator, from prōnūnciō (“to pronounce”).

parole.significato: One of the five canons of classical rhetoric: the discipline of delivering speeches.
parole.testo: From Latin prōnūntiātiō. Doublet of pronunciation.

parole.significato: Agitation, publicity, public communication aimed at influencing an audience and furthering an agenda.
parole.testo: From New Latin prōpāganda, short for Congregātiō dē Prōpāgandā Fidē (“a committee of cardinals established in 1622 by Gregory XV to supervise foreign missions”, literally “congregation for propagating the faith”), and properly the ablative feminine gerundive of Latin prōpāgō (“propagate”). Once the

parole.significato: An idea or topic spread with the goal of convincing or influencing large numbers of people, regardless of its actual va…
parole.testo: From Latin prōpāgandum, neuter of prōpāgandus (“which is to be propagated”). Reinterpretation of the form propaganda as a plural, by analogy with e.g. memorandum.

parole.significato: To cause to continue or multiply by generation, or successive production.
parole.testo: First attested in 1535; from Latin prōpāgātus, perfect passive participle of prōpāgō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Participial usage up until Early Modern English.

parole.significato: A female propagator
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin propāgātrīx. By surface analysis, propagate + -trix.

parole.significato: A layer or branch laid down to root.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōpāgō.

parole.significato: A runner terminated by a germinating bud.
parole.testo: From Late Latin. See propagate.

parole.significato: To provide an impetus for motion or physical action; to cause to move in a certain direction; to drive or push forward.
parole.testo: From Middle English propellen (“drive out, expel”), from Latin propellō, from pro- (“forward”) and pellō (“to push, to move”).

parole.significato: Capable of propelling.
parole.testo: From propel + -ent; originally from Latin prōpellēnt-, from prōpellēns, from prōpellō. Less common than propellant despite being more correct from an etymological viewpoint.

parole.significato: To incline or lean.
parole.testo: From Latin prōpendēre.

parole.significato: Inclining, hanging, or projecting forward or toward
parole.testo: From Latin propendens.

parole.significato: Leaning toward, in a moral sense; inclined; disposed; prone.
parole.testo: From Latin prōpensus, perfect passive participle of prōpendeō.

parole.significato: An inclination, disposition, tendency, preference, or attraction.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin prōpensitās. By surface analysis, propense (“inclined, disposed”) + -ity.

parole.significato: The direction which is to the left from an object's perspective, the direction 90 degrees counter-clockwise from the fr…
parole.testo: proper (in the sense of "its own") + left; from Latin proprius.

parole.significato: The change in apparent position of a celestial body due to that body's velocity relative to the Sun.
parole.testo: proper (in the sense of "its own") + motion; from Latin proprius.

parole.significato: The direction which is to the right from an object's perspective, the direction 90 degrees clockwise from the front.
parole.testo: proper (in the sense of "its own") + right; from Latin proprius.

parole.significato: To hasten or press forward.
parole.testo: From Latin properatus, past participle of properare (“to hasten”).

parole.significato: haste; hurrying.
parole.testo: Latin properatio.

parole.significato: A medicine which preserves or defends against disease; a preventive.
parole.testo: From Latin prophylacticus, from Ancient Greek προφυλακτικός (prophulaktikós, “prophylactic”).

parole.significato: The prevention of, or the protective treatment for, disease.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek πρό (pró, “before”) + φύλαξις (phúlaxis, “a watching, guarding”).

parole.significato: The right to distill spirits.
parole.testo: From Latin propinatio. See propine.

parole.significato: To pledge; to offer as a toast in the manner of drinking, that is, by drinking first and passing the cup.
parole.testo: From Latin propinō, from Ancient Greek προπῑ́νω (propī́nō, “to drink to someone's health”).

parole.significato: Capable of being propitiated.
parole.testo: Latin propitiabilis.

parole.significato: Synonym of propitiatory.
parole.testo: From Latin propitiāre (“to appease”) + -ary.

parole.significato: To conciliate, appease, or make peace with someone, particularly a god or spirit.
parole.testo: From Latin propitiāt-, the past participial stem of propitiāre (“make favourable”), from propitius (“favourable, gracious”).

parole.significato: One who propitiates or appeases.
parole.testo: From the Latin propitiātor.

parole.significato: Intended to propitiate, reconcile, expiate or appease; conciliatory.
parole.testo: From the Latin propitiātōrius (“atoning; reconciling, propitiating”).

parole.significato: An aromatic glue-like substance produced by honeybees from tree resin, waxes, and their own secretions, used in the con…
parole.testo: From Latin propolis, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πρόπολις (própolis, “suburb; propolis”) (apparently because the material was used by bees to extend their hives), from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-, “pro-”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”).

parole.significato: To propose or put forward for discussion or consideration.
parole.testo: From Latin prōpōnō (“place before; offer, propose”), via Scots [Term?].

parole.significato: One who supports something; an advocate.
parole.testo: From Latin prōpōnēns, present participle of prōpōnō (“to put forward; propose”).

parole.significato: the property of being proportional
parole.testo: From proportional + -ity, from Latin proportionalitas.

parole.significato: In proportion; proportional; commensurable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōportiōnātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, proportion + -ate.

parole.significato: The first identified male case of an inherited disease in a family; the proband or index case.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōpositus.

parole.significato: To put forward; to offer for discussion or debate.
parole.testo: From the Middle English proponen (“to put forward”), from Latin prōpōnere (“to put forward”), from prō- (“before”) + pōnere (“to put”). Doublet of propose. Compare expound.

parole.significato: A magistrate of ancient Rome who governed a province after serving as a praetor in Rome.
parole.testo: From the Latin prōpraetor.

parole.significato: Relating specifically to the spine, and especially to those structures that connect segments of the spine
parole.testo: From Latin proprius (“one's own”) + spinal.

parole.significato: A property that applies to all members of a species and only to them, serving to distinguish the species from other spe…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin proprium (“of one's own”).

parole.significato: shameful, infamous, disgraceful
parole.testo: From Latin prōpudiōsus (“shameful, disgraceful, infamous”), from propudium (“scandal, shameful act; shameful person, wretch”) + -ōsus (“-ose: full of, prone to”), from prō- (“for, to, towards”) + pudēre (“to be ashamed, to cause shame”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: means of defence; defence
parole.testo: Latin propugnatio.

parole.significato: A champion or defender.
parole.testo: From Latin prōpugnātor.

parole.significato: Serving to force the contents to move in a rapid outflow.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin propulsio (“term”), from Latin past participle of propello (“to drive forward, drive forth, drive away, drive out”).

parole.significato: The act of driving away or repelling; a keeping at a distance.
parole.testo: From Latin propulsatio. See propulse.

parole.significato: To repel; to drive off or away.
parole.testo: From Latin propulso.

parole.significato: The process of propelling, driving, or pushing, typically forward or onward; a propulsive force or impulse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin propulsio, propulsionis, from the past participle of Latin propello (“to drive forward, drive forth, drive away, drive out”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to propulsion
parole.testo: Formed from Latin prōpulsus with the suffix -ive.

parole.significato: A propellor enclosed in a short cylinder, that can typically be swivelled to change the angle of thrust.
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Latin prōpellō (“propel”) + -or.

parole.significato: A vestibule or entrance, (especially) to a temple.
parole.testo: From Latin propylaeum, from Ancient Greek προπύλαιον (propúlaion), from προ- (pro-, “before”, “in front of”) + πύλη (púlē, “gate”).

parole.significato: To divide proportionately, especially by day; to divide pro rata.
parole.testo: American English derivation from pro rata, from Latin pro (“according to”) + ratus (“calculated”).

parole.significato: The front part of a ship.
parole.testo: From Latin prora (“prow”). Doublet of prow.

parole.significato: viceroy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prorex.

parole.significato: Inclined forward.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin prōrsus + radiate.

parole.significato: The act or state of bursting forth; a bursting out.
parole.testo: From Latin proruptio, from prorumpere, proruptum (“to break forth”), from pro (“forth”) + rumpere (“to break”).

parole.significato: The advantages and disadvantages or positives and negatives regarding a specific choice or situation.
parole.testo: From Latin prō (“for, on behalf of”) and contrā (“against”).

parole.significato: The stage area between the curtain and the orchestra.
parole.testo: From Latin proscaenium (“in front of the scenery”), from Ancient Greek προσκήνιον (proskḗnion), from πρό (pró, “before”) + σκηνή (skēnḗ, “scene building”).

parole.significato: An early larval form of a trematode worm; a redia.
parole.testo: From New Latin proscōlēx, from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-) + σκώληξ (skṓlēx).

parole.significato: To forbid or prohibit.
parole.testo: From Middle English proscriben, from Latin prōscrībō (“to proclaim, forbid, banish”).

parole.significato: A prohibition.
parole.testo: From Middle English proscripcion, from Latin prōscrīptiō, from prōscrībō (originally "publish in writing"), from prō- and scrībō (“write”).

parole.significato: A person who prepares a body for dissection by students, or dissects them as demonstrations.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?] (“an anatomist”), from prosecare (“to cut up”).

parole.significato: To start criminal proceedings against.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōsecūtus, perfect participle of prōsequor. Doublet of pursue, from Old French. Compare also persecute.

parole.significato: A prosecuting attorney.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1542, from Medieval Latin prosecutor, from prōsequor (English prosecute). By surface analysis, prosecute + -or.

parole.significato: A female prosecutor
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin prōsecūtrīx. By surface analysis, prosecutor + -trix.
Latin prosilere (“to leap forth”)?

parole.significato: A poetic composition consisting of both prose and verse, usually in alternation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin prosimetrum.

parole.significato: A study of the individuals in a group of people within a specific context and their relationships.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting New Latin combining forms: prosopo- + -graphy; from the Latin prosōpographia (“description of a person’s appearance; description of an individual’s life”), from the Ancient Greek πρόσωπον (prósōpon, “face, person”) + -γρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (-grăphĭ́ā, “writing,

parole.significato: The region which the eye overlooks at one time; a view; a scene; an outlook.
parole.testo: From Middle English prospecte, from Latin prōspectus (“view, sight, prospect; panorama”), from prōspiciō (“to look forward”) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns), from pro (“before, forward”) + speciō, spiciō (“to look, to see”). By surface analysis, pro- + -spect. Doublet of prospectus and prospekt

parole.significato: To have or afford a view; to face or look out.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin prōspectō.

parole.significato: Able to be seen from far away; conspicuous.
parole.testo: From Latin prōspicuus.

parole.significato: The ventral sclerite (plate) of the prothorax of an insect.
parole.testo: From Latin. See pro- and sternum.

parole.significato: An artificial replacement for a body part, either internal or external.
parole.testo: Via Latin, from Ancient Greek πρόσθεσις (prósthesis, “addition”), from προστίθημι (prostíthēmi, “to add”), from πρός (prós, “towards”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to place”), from Proto-Indo-European *próti, *préti + *dʰédʰeh₁ti (“to be putting, to be placing”). By surface analysis, prosth- + -esis.

parole.significato: Artificial, acting as a substitute for part of the body; relating to prosthesis.
parole.testo: From New Latin prostheticus, from Ancient Greek προσθετικός (prosthetikós, “adding; repletive; giving additional power”), from πρόσθεσις (prósthesis, “addition”), from προστίθημι (prostíthēmi, “I add”), from πρός (prós, “towards”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “I place”). By surface analysis, prosth- + -etic.

parole.significato: A brothel.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin prostibulum.

parole.significato: Of or relating to prostitutes or prostitution; meretricious.
parole.testo: Latin prostibulum (“prostitute”), + -ous.

parole.significato: Debased, corrupt; seeking personal gain by dishonourable means.
parole.testo: From Latin prōstitūtus, past participle of prōstituō, from prō̆ (“for, before”) + statuō (“to set up, to erect”).

parole.significato: Engaging in sexual activity with another person for pay.
parole.testo: From Late Latin prostitutio. Equivalent to prostitute + -ion.

parole.significato: Lying flat, face-down.
parole.testo: From Middle English prostrat(e) (“prostrate”, also used as the past participle of prostraten), borrowed from Latin prōstrātus, perfect passive participle of prōsternō (“to prostrate”). Participial usage up until Early Modern English.

parole.significato: To lie flat or face-down.
parole.testo: From Middle English prostraten (“(reflexive) to prostrate; (with doun) to fall down in a state of humility or submission”), from prostrat(e) (“prostrate, prostrated”, also used as the past participle of prostraten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), from Latin prōstrātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) an

parole.significato: The first part of a play, in which the setting and characters are introduced.
parole.testo: From Late Latin protasis, from Ancient Greek πρότασις (prótasis), from προτείνω (proteínō, “put forward, tender, propose”), from πρό (pró) + τείνω (teínō, “stretch”).

parole.significato: To keep safe; to defend; to guard; to prevent harm coming to.
parole.testo: Attested in English since 1530, from Latin prōtēctus (“covered, protected”), past participle of prōtegō, prōtegere (“to cover the front, protect”) from prō, prō- (“before, in front of”) + tegō, tegere (“to cover”), see tegument. Largely displaced native Middle English shelden, from Old English sċild

parole.significato: Serving or intended to protect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōtēctīvus. By surface analysis, protect + -ive.

parole.significato: A female who protects.
parole.testo: From Middle English protectrice, protectrix, protectryse, from Latin prōtēctrīx. By surface analysis, protect + -trix.

parole.significato: To hold out; to stretch forth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin protendere, from pro (“before, forth”) + tendere (“to stretch”).

parole.significato: A drawing out, extension, or stretching; (alternatively) a duration (of time).
parole.testo: From Latin prōtēnsiō, from prōtendō (“draw out”).

parole.significato: Drawn out; extended.
parole.testo: From Latin prōtēnsīvus, from prōtendō (“draw out”).

parole.significato: wantonness; waywardness; petulance; peevishness
parole.testo: Latin protervitas, from protervus (“violent, wanton”).

parole.significato: A plant, usually a pteridophyte, in gametophyte stage in the metagenesis cycle.
parole.testo: From Latin pro (“forwards”) + Ancient Greek θᾰλλός (thăllós, “young branch, twig”).

parole.significato: The prepending of phonemes at the beginning of a word without changing its morphological structure, as in Spanish esfer…
parole.testo: From Late Latin prothesis, prosthesis, alteration (dropping the ‘s’) from Ancient Greek πρόσθεσις (prósthesis, “addition, augmentation”), (English prosthesis) from προστίθημι (prostíthēmi, “to add”), from πρός (prós, “towards”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to place”), from Proto-Indo-European *próti, *préti

parole.significato: A chief legal clerk or notary in Roman Byzantium, and (hence) in Rome.
parole.testo: From Middle English prothonotarie, from Medieval Latin protonotarius, from Byzantine Greek πρωτονοτάριος (prōtonotários), from Ancient Greek πρῶτος (prôtos) + Byzantine Greek νοτάριος (notários), from Latin notārius (“notary”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to protocol.
parole.testo: From the Medieval Latin prōtocollārius.

parole.significato: The original manuscript of a given text, from which all further copies derive.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin protographum.

parole.significato: To draw out; to extend, especially in duration.
parole.testo: From the past participle stem of Latin prōtrahō. By surface analysis, pro- + tract.

parole.significato: To cause (something) to extend above, beyond, or from a boundary or surface; to cause (something) to project or stick o…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin prōtrūdere, the present active infinitive of prōtrūdō (“to push or thrust forwards; to protrude”), from prō- (“prefix denoting a forward direction or movement”) (from Proto-Indo-European *pro- (“forward; toward”)) + trūdō (“to push, shove, thrust”) (ultimately from Proto

parole.significato: Swelling or bulging outward.
parole.testo: Latin protuberans, protuberantis, present participle of protuberare. See protuberate.

parole.significato: Relating to a protuberance.
parole.testo: From Latin prōtubērantiālis. By surface analysis, protuberance + -ial.

parole.significato: mature; advanced (in age)
parole.testo: From Latin provectus, past participle of provehere (“to carry forward”).

parole.significato: The carrying forward of a final consonant to a following word, as in "a nickname" from Middle English "an ekename".
parole.testo: From Latin prōvectiō (“an advancement”), from prōvect-, past participle stem of prōvehō (“to carry together”), combination of prō- and vehō. By surface analysis, provect + -ion.

parole.significato: Having been proved; having proved its value or truth.
parole.testo: From Scottish English, as past participle of preve, a Middle English variant of prove – compare woven (from weave) and cloven (from cleave), both of which feature -eve → -oven. Preve died out in England, but survived in Scotland, where proven developed, initially in a legal context, as in “The jury

parole.significato: source; findspot; origin
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōveniēns, present participle of prōvenīre (“to come up”); compare provene, provenient, and provenance.

parole.significato: The part of the avian stomach, between the crop and the gizzard, that secretes digestive enzymes.
parole.testo: From New Latin proventriculus (19th century), from pro- + ventriculus.

parole.significato: Of, resembling, or expressed as a proverb, cliché, fable, or fairy tale.
parole.testo: From Latin prōverbiālis, equivalent to proverb + -ial

parole.significato: Describing the tendency of a plane to roll in the same direction as yaw.
parole.testo: From Latin prōversus (“turned forwards”), perfect passive participle of prōvertō (“to turn forwards”), from prō- (“before, in front of”) + vertō (“to turn”). By surface analysis, pro- + -verse. Doublet of prose.

parole.significato: To make a living; earn money for necessities.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English providen, from Latin prōvidēre (“to foresee, act with foresight”). Doublet of purvey.

parole.significato: Possessing, exercising, or demonstrating great care and consideration for the future.
parole.testo: From Middle English provident, from Latin prōvidēns, prōvidentis, present participle of prōvideō (“to foresee; to be cautious; to provide”): compare French provident. By surface analysis, provide + -ent. Doublet of prudent.

parole.significato: A conditional provision to an agreement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin proviso (“it being provided”), ablative singular neuter of provisus, past participle of providere (“to provide”); see provide.

parole.significato: It being provided that.
parole.testo: From Latin proviso quod, from prōvīsō (ablative neuter singular past participle form of prōvidēre, “to provide”) + quod (neuter form of quī, “that”).

parole.significato: A deputy of a Roman Catholic bishop.
parole.testo: From Latin prōvīsor, agent noun of prōvideō (“provide”).

parole.significato: Temporary; pending something more permanent.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin provisorius, from provis- (supine stem of provideo) + -orius (“-ory”).

parole.significato: One who or that which provokes.
parole.testo: From Latin prōvocāns.

parole.significato: To provoke.
parole.testo: From Middle English provocaten, from Latin prōvocō, prōvocātus. Doublet of provoke.

parole.significato: provocative
parole.testo: From Late Latin provocatorius, from Latin provoco.

parole.significato: A female provocator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin prōvocātrīx. By surface analysis, provocator + -trix.

parole.significato: One placed in charge: a head, a chief
parole.testo: From Middle English, from late Old English prōfost, prāfost, from Late Latin prōpositus, variant of Latin praepositus (“[one] placed in command”). parole.significato: To publish, to make public; promulgate.
parole.testo: From Latin provulgo.

parole.significato: The act of publishing, making known, promulgation.
parole.testo: From Latin provulgatio, from provulgo.

parole.significato: To promulge; to promulgate.
parole.testo: From Latin prōvulgō. Doublet of promulgate and promulge.

parole.significato: A negotiator; a factor, especially one who negotiates marriages.
parole.testo: Latin proxeneta, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Closer to the point of attachment or observation.
parole.testo: From Latin proximus, superlative form of prope (“near, nigh”).

parole.significato: Close or closest; adjacent.
parole.testo: From Late Latin proximatus, past participle of proximare (“to draw near, approach”), from Latin proximus (“nearest”), superlative of prope (“near”).

parole.significato: Next; following; immediately preceding or following.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin proximus. See proximate; compare proximo.

parole.significato: Runner up or second place for an award.
parole.testo: From proxime (“next or immediately following”), accessit, from Latin for "she/he came very near".

parole.significato: Of next month.
parole.testo: From Latin proximō (“on the next”).

parole.significato: Prussian leather.
parole.testo: From Middle English Pruce (“Prussia”) (whence also spruce), from new Latin, from a Baltic language, probably Old Prussian; for more, see Prussia. Compare French Prusse.

parole.significato: Characterised by the use of prudence; arising from careful thought or deliberation.
parole.testo: From Latin prudentia + -al.

parole.significato: Having a very fine whitish powder (bloom) on a surface.
parole.testo: Latin pruīnōsus, from pruīna.

parole.significato: A member of the genus Prunella of herbaceous plants, the allheals.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin prunella, from brunus + -ella, perhaps because of the plant's brown sepals.

parole.significato: Any of various diseases characterised by inflammation of the mouth or throat.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin prunella, alternation of brunella (“infectious epidemic”), from brunus + -ella.

parole.significato: Bearing plums.
parole.testo: From Latin prunum (“a plum”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Shaped like a plum.
parole.testo: From Latin prūnifōrmis.

parole.significato: A type of traditional decoration on porcelain that depicts the leaves and branches of the Chinese plum, Prunus mume.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prūnus. Doublet of prune and plum.

parole.significato: Uneasy with desire; itching; especially, having a lascivious anxiety or propensity; lustful.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin prūriēns, present participle of prūriō (“itch”).

parole.significato: related to, affected by, or resembling, prurigo.
parole.testo: From Late Latin from Latin prurigo (“itching, itch”): compare French prurigineux.

parole.significato: A skin condition, characterized by itching of papules as the main symptom.
parole.testo: From Latin prūrīgō (“an itching, the itch”), from prūriō (“to itch”).

parole.significato: itching
parole.testo: From Latin prurire (“to itch”).

parole.significato: Itching; especially, severe itching of undamaged skin; caused by allergy, infection, lymphoma, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prūrītus (“an itch, an itching”), from prūriō (“to itch”).

parole.significato: derived from Prussian blue
parole.testo: From Latin prussicus (“Prussian”) or French prussique.

parole.significato: The town hall in an Ancient Greek city.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prytanēum, from Ancient Greek πρυτανεῖον (prutaneîon), from πρύτανις (prútanis, “prytanis”) + -εῖον (-eîon, noun-forming suffix meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or person”). By surface analysis, prytanis + -eum.

parole.significato: An official in ancient Athens
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prytanis, from Ancient Greek πρύτανις (prútanis).

parole.significato: The singing or the writing of psalms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin psalmōdia, from Koine Greek ψαλμῳδίᾱ (psalmōidíā), from Ancient Greek ψαλμός (psalmós, “psalm”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

parole.significato: A writer of psalms; a psalmist.
parole.testo: Latin psalmographus.

parole.significato: An omasum.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin psalterium, from Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion). Doublet of psalter, psalterion, and psaltery.

parole.significato: A Byzantine cantor.
parole.testo: Latin psaltēs

parole.significato: A psephism.
parole.testo: From Latin psēphisma, and its source, Ancient Greek ψήφισμα (psḗphisma).

parole.significato: Divination by drawing pebbles from a pile.
parole.testo: From New Latin psēphomantia, from Ancient Greek ψῆφος (psêphos, “pebble used for casting a vote”), + -mancy.

parole.significato: A false pregnancy: the appearance of signs and symptoms associated with pregnancy when the person or animal is not preg…
parole.testo: From pseudo- + cyesis, from Latin pseudo- + Ancient Greek κύησις (kúēsis).

parole.significato: False history.
parole.testo: From pseudo- + history, coined around 1815, after New Latin pseudo-historia (since 1654 or earlier according to OED).

parole.significato: compulsive lying (telling of falsehoods)
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A pathological liar
parole.testo: From Latin pseudologus (“liar”), from Ancient Greek ψευδολόγος (pseudológos, “speaking falsely, lying”). Equivalent to pseudo- + -logue.

parole.significato: One of the minute spindle-shaped embryos of gregarines and some other Protozoa.
parole.testo: From pseudo- + Latin nāvicula, diminutive of nāvis (“ship”). See navicular.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a pseudonym.
parole.testo: From Latin pseudōnymus, from Ancient Greek ψευδώνῠμος (pseudṓnŭmos). By surface analysis, pseudonym + -ous.

parole.significato: A disease characterised by increased intracranial pressure of idiopathic aetiology, commonly affecting middle-aged wome…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin.

parole.significato: The twenty-third letter of Classical and Modern Greek and the twenty-fifth letter of Old and Ancient Greek.
parole.testo: From Middle English psi, from Latin psī, from Ancient Greek ψεῖ (pseî), the name for the twenty-third letter of the alphabet (Ψ, ψ).

parole.significato: Parrot.
parole.testo: From Latin psittacus (“parrot”), from Ancient Greek ψιττακός (psittakós).

parole.significato: Mechanical, repetitive words used without understanding or consideration.
parole.testo: From Latin psittacus (“parrot”) + -ism. By surface analysis, psittac- + -ism.

parole.significato: An infection by Chlamydia bacteria, caught from infected birds, and characterised by fever, pneumonia and headaches.
parole.testo: From Latin psittacus (“parrot”) + -osis. By surface analysis, psittac- + -osis.

parole.significato: A cutaneous disease, especially psoriasis, scabies, or mange.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin psōra, from Ancient Greek ψώρα (psṓra).

parole.significato: A noncontagious disease whose main symptom is gray or silvery flaky patches on the skin which are red and inflamed unde…
parole.testo: From Late Latin psōriasis (“mange, scurvy, psoriasis”), from Koine Greek ψωρίασις (psōríasis), from Ancient Greek ψώρα (psṓra, “itch”) + -σις (-sis, “-sis: forming nouns of action & medical disorders”). Cognate with psora.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to psora.
parole.testo: Latin psoricus: compare French psorique.

parole.significato: The human soul, mind, or spirit.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin psychē, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”).

parole.significato: A spirit, deity, person, etc., who guides the souls of the dead to the afterlife.
parole.testo: From Latin psȳchopompus, from Ancient Greek ψῡχοπομπός (psūkhopompós), from ψῡχή (psūkhḗ, “soul”) + πομπός (pompós, “conductor”).

parole.significato: Any of several plants of Plantago subg. Psyllium.
parole.testo: From Latin psyllium, from Ancient Greek ψύλλιον (psúllion, “fleawort”), from ψύλλα (psúlla, “flea”) + -ιον (-ion, forming neuter diminutives).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to or lying in the region of the inferior part of the sphenoid bone of the vertebrate skull.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin pterygoīdēs, from Ancient Greek πτερῠγοειδής (pterŭgoeidḗs, “like a wing”), from πτέρῠξ (ptérŭx, “a wing”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like, -oid”).

parole.significato: A bladder-like pouch on the head of schizophoran flies that by expanding enables the fly to emerge from its puparium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ptilīnum, itself an adaptation of the French ptiline.

parole.significato: The appearance or study of feathers on a bird, including factors such as their texture or shape.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ptilōsis, from the Ancient Greek πτῐ́λωσῐς (ptĭ́lōsĭs).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Ptolemy dynasty of pharaohs, the Ptolemies, rulers of Hellenistic Egypt.
parole.testo: Via Latin Ptolemāicus from Koine Greek Πτολεμᾱϊκός (Ptolemāïkós) from Πτολεμαῖος (Ptolemaîos), a proper name derived from Epic Greek πτόλεμος (ptólemos), variant of Ancient Greek πόλεμος (pólemos, “battle, war”); equivalent to Ptolemy + -ic.

parole.significato: The way in which an individual leaf is folded in the bud.
parole.testo: From New Latin ptyxis, from Ancient Greek πτύξις (ptúxis, “a folding”).

parole.significato: Covered in soft, downy hairs.
parole.testo: From the Latin puberulentus, see puber (“downy, adult”), -ulentus (“abounding in”).

parole.significato: The pubic hair.
parole.testo: From Latin pubes (“the hair which appears on the body at the age of puberty, the genitals”), from pubes, puber (“grown up, of mature age; of plants, downy, pubescent”); see puberty.

parole.significato: The state of being in or reaching puberty.
parole.testo: From Latin pūbēscentia, from pūbēscō.

parole.significato: The pubic bone; the part of the hipbone forming the front arch of the pelvis.
parole.testo: Genitive of Latin pubes (“the pubic hair”, collective). The noun was generalized from medical Latin os pubis, the pubic bone.

parole.significato: To publish or make publicly known.
parole.testo: Cited from the mid 16th century and traced from Latin publicat (“to publish, to make publicly known”)

parole.significato: pubes
parole.testo: From Latin pūbēs + -o-.

parole.significato: Part of the levator ani muscle that loops around the vagina in women.
parole.testo: From pubo- + New Latin vaginalis.

parole.significato: Modesty.
parole.testo: From Latin pudentia, from Latin pudet (“it shames”).

parole.significato: Vagina; female genitals.
parole.testo: From Latin pudenda muliebria.

parole.significato: Relating to or near the pudendum.
parole.testo: From Latin pudendum (“external genitals, shaming”) + -al. By surface analysis, pudend- + -al.

parole.significato: External genitals.
parole.testo: From Latin pudendum (“external genitals, shaming”). By surface analysis, pudend- + -o-.

parole.significato: External genital organs in a human; especially a woman's vulva.
parole.testo: From Latin pudenda (“that whereof one ought to feel shame”), substantive use of the neuter plural gerundive of pudet (“it shames”); in Latin the usage in the plural form (to mean external genitalia), was far more common than the singular form, as is also the case in English.

parole.significato: A woman's pudendum; the vulva.
parole.testo: From Latin pudendum (“a thing to be ashamed of”) + muliebre, neuter form of muliebris (“of a woman”).

parole.significato: A part of the male pudenda; the principal male organ of intromission and micturition; the penis.
parole.testo: From Latin pudendum (“a thing to be ashamed of”) + virile, neuter form of virilis (“of a man”).

parole.significato: Shy, bashful; prudish.
parole.testo: From Latin pudibundus, from pudeō (“make ashamed, be ashamed”).

parole.significato: The Ancient Roman concept of sexual virtue, involving modesty and loyalty to one's partner.
parole.testo: From Latin pudīcitia.

parole.significato: An appropriate sense of modesty or shame.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pudor (“sense of modesty or shame”), from pudet (“it shames”), as is pudency (via pudentia).

parole.significato: A female puer aeternus.
parole.testo: From Latin puella aeterna (“eternal girl”), female form of puer aeternus (“eternal boy”) (in Ovid, Metamorphoses), after use in German by CG Jung.

parole.significato: A female prostitute.
parole.testo: Latin puella (“girl”) + pūblica, feminine of pūblicus (“public”)

parole.significato: Characteristic of, or pertaining to, a girl or girls.
parole.testo: From Latin puella (“female child, girl”) + English -ile (suffix meaning ‘capable of; tending to’ forming adjectives), modelled after puerile. Puella is derived from puellus (“male child, young boy”) + -a (feminine form of -us); puellus is a contraction of puerulus (“little boy; little slave”), from

parole.significato: Synonym of puellile (“characteristic of, or pertaining to, a girl or girls”).
parole.testo: From Latin puella (“female child, girl”) + English -ine (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Puella is derived from puellus (“male child, young boy”) + -a (feminine form of -us); puellus is a contraction of puerulus (“little boy; little slave”), from puer (“boy, lad; male page,

parole.significato: A child-god who is forever young.
parole.testo: From Latin puer aeternus (“eternal boy”) (in Ovid, Metamorphoses), after use in German by Carl Jung.

parole.significato: Childish; trifling; silly.
parole.testo: From Latin puerīlis (“childish”), from puer (“child, boy”). By surface analysis, puer + -ile.

parole.significato: A woman undergoing puerperium; a woman whose uterus is still enlarged from pregnancy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin puerpera (“woman in labor or childbed”), substantive of puerperus (“parturient, bringing forth children”), from puer (“child, boy”) + pariō (“to bring forth, bear”) + -us (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or associated with the puerperium (the first month of postpartum), or, sometimes also
parole.testo: From New Latin puerperālis, from Latin puerpera (“woman in childbirth”), from puer (“child”) + pariō (“to bear”).

parole.significato: The period of time lasting around a month immediately following childbirth, when the mother’s uterus shrinks back to it…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin puerperium (“childbed, childbirth”), from puerpera (“woman in labor or childbed”) + -ium (nominal suffix), from puerperus (“parturient, bringing forth children”), from puer (“child, boy”) + pariō (“to bring forth, bear”) + -us (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Bearing children.
parole.testo: From Latin puerpera + -ous.

parole.significato: As much as is taken up between the thumb and two first fingers; a pinch.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pugillus, pugillum (“a fistful”), akin to pugnus (“the fist”).

parole.significato: Fighting with fists.
parole.testo: From Latin pugil (“fist”) + -ism, related to pugnus (“fist”), from Proto-Indo-European roots. Compare contemporary pugilist (“boxer”), 1790.

parole.significato: One who fights with their fists, especially a professional prize fighter; a boxer.
parole.testo: From Latin pugil (“boxer”) + -ist, related to pugnus (“fist”), from Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”). Compare contemporary pugilism (“boxing”) (1791).

parole.significato: A kind of notebook or tablet used in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Latin pugillaris (“fist”), since they were hand-sized.

parole.significato: A dagger or poignard, especially the kind used by the Ancient Romans.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pūgiō.

parole.significato: Dagger-shaped.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin pugioniformis, from Latin pūgiō (“dagger”). By surface analysis, Latin pugion + -i- + form.

parole.significato: The act or characteristic of being aggressive or combative.
parole.testo: From Latin pugnacitas (whence -acity).

parole.significato: To fight
parole.testo: From Latin pugnāre.

parole.significato: Physical beauty.
parole.testo: From Middle English pulcritude, from Latin pulchritūdō, from pulcher (“beautiful”).

parole.significato: Having great physical beauty.
parole.testo: From Latin pulchritūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin pulchritūdō, from pulcher + -tūdō. By surface analysis, pulchritude + -ous.

parole.significato: beautiful
parole.testo: From Latin pulchrum (“beautiful”) + -ous.

parole.significato: Any insecticide that kills fleas
parole.testo: Latin pulex (“flea”) + -cide

parole.significato: of or pertaining to fleas.
parole.testo: From Latin pulex (“flea”).

parole.significato: flea-ridden
parole.testo: From Latin pulicosus, from pulex (“flea”).

parole.significato: A severe infectious disease of young poultry, caused by a form of the salmonella bacterium.
parole.testo: From Latin pullorum, originally as part of a specific name Bacterium pullorum, now as the name of a serovar.

parole.significato: To multiply rapidly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pullulātus, perfect passive participle of pullulō (“sprout forth”), from pullulus (“a young animal, a sprout”), diminutive of pullus.

parole.significato: A chick; a young bird in the downy stage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pullus.

parole.significato: Breathing by means of lung sacs.
parole.testo: From Latin pulmō (“lung”) + branchiate.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or connecting the lungs and the skin.
parole.testo: From Latin pulmo (“a lung”) + English cutaneous.

parole.significato: Swimming by means of jet propulsion.
parole.testo: From Latin pulmo (“a lung”) + -grade (“means of locomotion”).

parole.significato: A kind of historical spirometer.
parole.testo: From Latin pulmo (“a lung”) + -meter.

parole.significato: Pertaining to, having, or affecting the lungs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pulmōnārius (“of the lungs”), from pulmō (“lung”) + -ārius, from Proto-Indo-European *pléu-mon-. Cognate with Greek πλεμόνι (plemóni), French poumon, Lithuanian plaučiai, Polish płuco and Russian пла́вать (plávatʹ, “to swim”).

parole.significato: Having lungs or similar organs.
parole.testo: From New Latin pulmōnātus (“having lungs”), from pulmō (“lung”) + -ātus.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or produced by the lungs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pulmōnicus, from pulmō (“lung”).

parole.significato: Having lungs; pulmonate.
parole.testo: From Latin pulmo, pulmonis (“a lung”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: pneumonitis
parole.testo: From Latin pulmō (“lung”) + -itis.

parole.significato: An apparatus for producing artificial respiration by pumping oxygen and/or air into and out of the lungs, as of a perso…
parole.testo: From Latin pulmo (“a lung”) + English motor. Originally a brand name.

parole.significato: A soft, moist, shapeless mass or matter.
parole.testo: From Middle English pulpe, from Latin pulpa.

parole.significato: A preparation of food; an appetizer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pulpamentum.

parole.significato: A massive, often decorative screen of stone or timber that divides the choir from the nave and ambulatory in medieval c…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin pulpitum. Doublet of pulpit.

parole.significato: To expand and contract rhythmically; to throb or to beat, exhibit a pulse.
parole.testo: Perhaps formed within English as a back-formation from pulsation (attested from the early 15th century, in Middle English). A figurative derivation from New Latin pulsō, pulsātum (“(of an organ) to pulse, to emit a pulse”, intransitive) is also possible, itself a back-formation of New Latin pulsātiō

parole.significato: Pulsating; that pulses.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pulsātilis, Latin pulsō + -ilis.

parole.significato: Any pulsating astronomical object
parole.testo: From Latin pulsator.

parole.significato: To emit or impel (something) in pulses or waves.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English pulse, Middle English pulsen (“to pulse, throb”), from Latin pulsāre, the present active infinitive of pulsō (“to push; to beat, batter, hammer, strike; to knock on; (figuratively) to drive or urge on, impel; to move; to agitate, disquiet, disturb”), the frequentative of pel

parole.significato: A sign where, on palpation of the pulse, a double peak per cardiac cycle can be appreciated.
parole.testo: Latin pulsus (“stroke”) + bis (“twice”) + feriens (“striking”): "striking a stroke twice".

parole.significato: Macerated; softened; nearly fluid; gloopy
parole.testo: From Latin puls (“meal, porridge”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: Powder.
parole.testo: From Middle English pulver, from Latin pulver-, pulvis. Doublet of powder.

parole.significato: To pulverise; to make into powder.
parole.testo: From Middle English (participle pulvered), from the noun or Latin pulverō.

parole.significato: To beat or reduce to powder or dust; to pulverise.
parole.testo: From Latin pulveratus, past participle of pulverare (“to pulverize”). See pulverize. By surface analysis, pulver + -ate.

parole.significato: ashes of barilla
parole.testo: From Latin pulvis, pulveris (“dust, powder”). Compare French pulvérin.

parole.significato: To render into dust or powder.
parole.testo: From Middle English pulverizen, from Latin pulverizō, pulverizāre, from pulvis (“powder”). Compare French pulvériser. By surface analysis, pulver (“powder”) + -ise.

parole.significato: Resembling or consisting of dust or powder.
parole.testo: Compare Latin pulvereus, from pulvis, pulveris (“dust, powder”). By surface analysis, pulver + -ous.

parole.significato: Consisting of, covered with, or disintegrating into a fine powder; powdery; dusty.
parole.testo: From Latin pulverulentus, from pulvis (“dust”). By surface analysis, pulver + -ule + -ent.

parole.significato: One of the tiny cushions or pads on the feet of certain insects.
parole.testo: From Latin pulvillus (“a little cushion”).

parole.significato: A prominence on the posterior part of the thalamus of the human brain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pulvīnar (“a cushion”).

parole.significato: Curved convexly or swelled.
parole.testo: From Latin pulvinatus, from pulvinus (“a cushion, an elevation”).

parole.significato: An aromatic hydroxy-butenolide, derivatives of which occur naturally in certain fungi and moulds.
parole.testo: From pulvinic acid + -one. By surface analysis, pulvin- + -one, from anagram of vulpinic acid, from Latin vulpinus (“of a fox”), from vulpes.

parole.significato: A pulvillus
parole.testo: Latin, a little mound.

parole.significato: A joint on a plant leaf or petiole that may swell and cause movement of the leaf or leaflet.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pulvīnus (“cushion, pillow, bolster”). Doublet of pillow, polverine, pulvino, pulvillus, and pulvinulus, as well as others.

parole.significato: The powder contained in the spore-cases of certain fungi.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pulvisculus (“fine powder”).

parole.significato: To make smooth with pumice.
parole.testo: From Latin pumicatus, past participle of pumicare (“to pumicate”), from pumex. See pumice.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to pumice; resembling pumice.
parole.testo: Latin pumiceus.

parole.significato: Marked by spots, dots, points, or punctures.
parole.testo: From Latin punctum (“point”). See point and punctuate.

parole.significato: pointed; pointy
parole.testo: From Latin punctum (“point”) + -iform.

parole.significato: A puncture or pricking.
parole.testo: From Middle English punccioun, from Latin pūnctiō, pūnctiōn-. Doublet of puncheon.

parole.significato: Prompt; on time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnctuālis (“relating to a point”), from Late Latin pūnctus (“point”) + -ālis (adjective suffix).

parole.significato: To add punctuation to.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnctuātus, perfect passive participle of pūnctuō (“to mark with points”), from Medieval Latin pūnctus (“a point, dot”), from pungō (“to prick, punch”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of punch.

parole.significato: A set of symbols and marks which are used to clarify meaning in text by separating strings of words into clauses, phras…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin punctuātiō (“a marking with points, a writing, agreement”), from punctuō (“to mark with points, settle”). Morphologically, punctuate + -ion.

parole.significato: A little point or spot.
parole.testo: From Latin pūnctulum. By surface analysis, punct(us) + -ule.

parole.significato: A sharp tip of any part of the anatomy; a point or other small area.
parole.testo: From Latin pūnctum. Doublet of point, pointe, ponto, puncto, punt, and punto.

parole.significato: The blind spot in the eye.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A dot placed above a letter to indicate that it is a copying error and should be ignored.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin pūnctum dēlēns.

parole.significato: near point
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: far point
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The primordial heart in an embryo, appearing as a throbbing point.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin punctum saliēns (“leaping point”), attributed to Volcher Coiter or Ulysses Aldrovandi, after a Latin translation of Aristotle's History of Animals (book 6, part 3).

parole.significato: The static Ptolemaic universe
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Any small drop of blood seen as a spot in sections of the brain.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The fifth voice in addition to the superius, altus, tenor and bassus in a piece of vocal polyphony.

parole.significato: composed of bric-a-brac, miscellaneous
parole.testo: From Latin quisquilia (“bric-a-brac”).

parole.significato: Whoever, whosoever.

parole.significato: Hard to deal with; dubious; of people: having a character difficult to assess.

parole.significato: With respect to religious observance or worship, as opposed to temporal matters.

parole.significato: which was to be proved; which was to be demonstrated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin quod erat dēmōnstrandum (“that which was to be proved”), calqued from Ancient Greek ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι (hóper édei deîxai, “precisely what was required to be proved”).

parole.significato: Something that is not true.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin quod nōn.

parole.significato: A form of music with melodies in counterpoint.
parole.testo: From Latin quod libet (“that which is pleasing”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a quodlibet

parole.significato: each, every

parole.significato: The means, way, or method (of doing something).
parole.testo: From Latin quōmodo (“In what way?”).

parole.significato: Former; once; at one time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin quondam. Compare whilom.

parole.significato: There are as many opinions as there are people who hold them.
parole.testo: From Latin, echoing line 454 of Terence’s Phormio: quot (“how many”) + hominēs (“men”, “people”; nominative plural form of homō: “man”, “person”) + tot (“so many”) + sententiae (“opinions”, “thoughts”; nominative plural form of sententia: “opinion”, “thought”).

parole.significato: A proportional part or share; the share or proportion assigned to each in a division.
parole.testo: From Latin quota pars; see Latin quota.

parole.significato: A fragment of a human expression that is repeated by somebody else, for example from literature or a famous speech.

parole.significato: The number (either a fraction or an integer) resulting from the division of one number by another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin quotiēns, from quotiēs.

parole.significato: The relation of an object to number.
parole.testo: From Latin quotus (“of what number, how many”).

parole.significato: A part or proportion; a fraction; quota.
parole.testo: From the neuter of Latin quotus (“of what number”).

parole.significato: A curved form of the letter r, found in some medieval and fraktur scripts: ⟨ ꝛ ⟩.
parole.testo: From or representing Latin r rotunda (literally “round ‘r’”). parole.significato: Synonym of ruled or reigned, used in historical dating to distinguish regnal years from births and deaths.
parole.testo: Originally from Latin r., abbreviating Latin rexit or Latin rēgnāvit (“[he/she/it] ruled or reigned”). Now often parsed as an abbreviation of English ruled or reigned.

parole.significato: A Jewish scholar or teacher of halacha (Jewish law), capable of making halachic decisions.
parole.testo: From Middle English raby, from Ecclesiastical Latin rabbi, and its source Koine Greek ῥαββί (rhabbí), from (post-Tanakh) Hebrew רַבִּי (rabbi, “my master”), from רַב (rav, “master”) + ־ִי (-í, “my”). Compare late Old English rabbi. Doublet of rebbe and related to rav.

parole.significato: A rabbi.
parole.testo: From Latin rabbonī. From biblical sources Aramaic רַבָּן (“my master/teacher”) derived from Rabbi.

parole.significato: Affected with rabies.
parole.testo: From the Latin rabidus, from rabiō (“to rave”).

parole.significato: An infectious disease caused by species of Lyssavirus that causes acute encephalitis in warm-blooded animals and people…

parole.significato: raging; rabid
parole.testo: From Latin rabiōsus. By surface analysis, rabi(es) + -ous.

parole.significato: A cluster or bunch, as of grapes. Also used figuratively.

parole.significato: An indeterminate inflorescence in which the flowers are arranged along a single central axis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin racēmus (“cluster, bunch”). Doublet of raisin.

parole.significato: Bearing racemes.
parole.testo: From Latin racemifer (“bearing clusters”), from racemus (“cluster”) + ferre (“to bear”). Compare French racémifère.

parole.significato: Having flowers arranged along a single central axis, as in a raceme, spike, or catkin.
parole.testo: From Latin racēmōsus (“full of clusters”), from racēmus (“cluster, bunch”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Rachel sandwich.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin Rāchēl, from Ancient Greek Ῥαχήλ (Rhakhḗl), from Biblical Hebrew רָחֵל (rāḫēl, “ewe”). Doublet of Raquel.

parole.significato: The part of a spikelet, in grasses and sedges, that bears the florets
parole.testo: From Latin rachilla, diminutive of rachis.

parole.significato: The spinal column, or the vertebrae of the spine.
parole.testo: From New Latin rhachis/rachis, from Ancient Greek ῥάχις (rhákhis, “spine, ridge”).

parole.significato: Rickets.

parole.significato: A member of a sect of Socinians or Unitarians in Poland, with their headquarters in Raków
parole.testo: From the Latin Racōviānus, from Racōvia (“Raków”).

parole.significato: Arranged like rays that radiate from, or converge to, a common centre.

parole.significato: A radial muscle, artery, or nerve.
parole.testo: From Latin radius + -alis.

parole.significato: Radiating light and/or heat.
parole.testo: From Middle English radyant, from Latin radiāns, radiantis, present participle of radiāre (“to emit rays or beams”).

parole.significato: The Monterey pine. Pinus radiata.
parole.testo: From Latin radiata, from the specific epithet.

parole.significato: To extend, be sent or spread out from a center like radii.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin radiātus, perfect passive participle of radiō (“to radiate, furnish with spokes, give out rays, radiate, shine”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from radius (“a spoke, ray”).

parole.significato: Radiating from a center; having rays or parts diverging from a center; radiated.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin radiātus (see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the root of a plant.

parole.significato: The process of taking root, or state of being rooted.

parole.significato: A small branch of a root; a rootlet.

parole.significato: That lives in or on the roots of plants

parole.significato: Flowering from the root.

parole.significato: Having the nature or appearance of a root (radix).

parole.significato: That feeds on plant roots.

parole.significato: radiation, radioactive

parole.significato: The barbule of a feather

parole.significato: The long bone in the forearm, on the side of the thumb.

parole.significato: the root of couch grass, once used medicinally

parole.significato: The rasping tongue of snails and all other mollusks except bivalves.

parole.significato: rasplike

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to members of the Rallidae family (also referred to as rails).

parole.significato: A scraping; a shaving.

parole.significato: One of the thin brownish chaffy scales found on the epidermis of the leaves or young shoots of some ferns

parole.significato: ramal; relating to a branch or branching

parole.significato: A hernia, varicocele, or any scrotal tumor.

parole.significato: Having flowers on the branches.

parole.significato: Bearing branches; branched.

parole.significato: Having branches; branching

parole.significato: A small branch, or branchlet, of corals, hydroids, and similar organisms.

parole.significato: A small spray or twig.

parole.significato: A twig, a small branch.

parole.significato: Becoming rancid or sour.

parole.significato: Rank in taste or smell.

parole.significato: Shaped like a frog; resembling a frog.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or resembling a frog.

parole.significato: A frog-eater; a creature that eats frogs.

parole.significato: Voracious; avaricious.
parole.testo: Perhaps from rapacity + -ous, in any case ultimately from Latin rapāx (“grasping, greedy”) + -acious.

parole.significato: radish (especially the root of the plant)

parole.significato: Synonym of biastophilia.

parole.significato: A state of rapture.
parole.testo: From Latin raptus, from rapio (“seize”).

parole.significato: Extremely rare books, manuscripts, or prints.

parole.significato: The wrinkling and creases on the inner surface of the wrist.

parole.significato: A five-pointed writing implement used to draw parallel lines of a staff in sheet music.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rāstrum (“rake”).

parole.significato: confirmation or approbation, as of an act or contract

parole.significato: The legal principle or rationale on which a judicial decision is based.

parole.significato: the formal grounds for something; the essential attributes of matter as they appear in the mind or in a definition.

parole.significato: To use the powers of the mind logically and methodically; to reason.

parole.significato: Reasoning (typically with oneself) by asking questions.
parole.testo: From Latin ratiōcinātiō.

parole.significato: Synonym of rationality or reasonability.

parole.significato: Synonym of rational or reasonable.
parole.testo: From Middle English racionable, a learned borrowing from Classical Latin ratiōnābilis. Doublet of reasonable.

parole.significato: A number that can be expressed as the ratio of two integers.

parole.significato: An explanation of the basis or fundamental reasons for something.

parole.significato: A liturgical vestment worn by some Christian bishops of various denominations.
parole.testo: From Latin ratiōnāle.

parole.significato: By reason of time (for example, referring to the temporal scope of a law or of a court's jurisdiction).

parole.significato: A ratio very close to unity.

parole.significato: Hoarse, raucous.

parole.significato: Harshness of sound; rough utterance
parole.testo: From rauc(ous) + -ity, from Latin raucitas, from raucus (“hoarse”). Compare French raucité.

parole.significato: Harsh and rough-sounding.

parole.significato: Ravennate; of Ravenna.

parole.significato: About, regarding, with reference to; used especially in letters, documents, emails and case law.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rē, ablative of rēs (“thing, matter, topic”).

parole.significato: With the matter unfinished or incomplete.

parole.significato: To regain; to recover.
