parole.significato: A compound or mixture of compounds used to treat or test materials, samples, other compounds or reactants in a laborato…
parole.testo: Possibly from Latin reagō. Compare with Norwegian Bokmål reagens. The sequence of act → action → agent → agency shows morphologic and semantic parallel, and apparent cognate relation, with react → reaction → reagent → reagency.

parole.significato: A mineral, arsenic sulfide (AsS), often associated with orpiment and stibnite in lead, silver and gold ores.
parole.testo: From Middle English realgar, from Medieval Latin realgar, resalgar, from Arabic رَهْج اَلْغَار (rahj al-ḡār, literally “cave dust”).

parole.significato: Objects from real life or from the real world, as opposed to theoretical constructs or fabricated examples.
parole.testo: From Late Latin realia, neuter plural of realis (“real”).

parole.significato: A category of grammatical moods, the most common of which is the indicative mood, that indicate that something actually…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin reālis. Doublet of real.

parole.significato: To animate again.
parole.testo: From re- + animate (verb), probably after Medieval Latin reanimāre or French réanimer.

parole.significato: One who protested in the Rebecca Riots; a Rebeccaite.
parole.testo: The Vulgate (Latin) form of biblical Rebekah, from Hebrew רִבְקָה (Rivka, “enchantingly beautiful, captivating, snare”).

parole.significato: Of a place: to re-echo to or with a sound.
parole.testo: From re- + bellow, after Latin reboāre.

parole.significato: That reverberates or resounds loudly.
parole.testo: From Latin reboō (“bellow, resound”).

parole.significato: Reverberating.
parole.testo: From Latin reboāns, present participle of reboō (“bellow back; resound”).

parole.significato: A loud reverberation; the echo of a bellow or roar.
parole.testo: From Latin reboare; compare reboant.

parole.significato: The act of boiling up or effervescing.
parole.testo: From Latin rebullire (“to bubble up”).

parole.significato: An increase in temperature that occurs while cooling metal through a range of temperatures in which change in structure…
parole.testo: From Latin recalescere (“to grow warm again”), from re- + calēscere (“to grow warm”), inchoative of calēre (“to be warm”). In use since at least 1873 (Webster's Ninth New Collegiate Dictionary, published 1985). By surface analysis, re- + calescence, or, by surface analysis, recalesce + -ence.

parole.significato: To withdraw or repudiate a statement or opinion formerly expressed, especially formally and publicly.
parole.testo: First attested in 1535, from Latin recantare (“to sing back, reecho, sing again, repeat in singing, recant, recall, revoke, charm back or away”), from re- (“back”) + canto (“to chant, to sing”), frequentative of cano.

parole.significato: To summarize or repeat in concise form.
parole.testo: From Late Latin recapitulātus, past participle of recapitulāre (“to go over the main points of a thing again”), from re- (“again”) + capitulum (“head, main part, chapter”), from caput (“head”) + -ulum (diminutive suffix); see capitulate. By surface analysis, re- + capitulate.

parole.significato: The property of being recent; newness.
parole.testo: From Latin recentia, from recens, equivalent to recent + -cy. See recent.

parole.significato: To review; to revise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin recensere.

parole.significato: A census, an enumeration, a review, a survey.
parole.testo: From Latin recēnsiō (“enumeration; review; reassessment”), from recēnseō (“to count, reckon; to examine, review; to go over, revise”), from re- (“again”) (from Proto-Italic *wre- (“again”); further etymology uncertain) + cēnseō (“to give an opinion; to suppose, think; to assess”) (ultimately from Pr

parole.significato: Having happened a short while ago.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin recēns (genitive recentis).

parole.significato: An idea that is formed by the repetition of percepts.
parole.testo: From Latin receptum (“thing received”), neuter singular of receptus, perfect passive participle of recipiō (“take back; receive”). Doublet of receipt. Coined by G.J. Romanes in 1888.

parole.significato: A receptacle.
parole.testo: From Latin receptaculum. Doublet of receptacle.

parole.significato: receivable
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin receptibilis.

parole.significato: Capable of receiving something.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English receptive, receptyue (“capable of receiving something; acting as a receptacle”), borrowed from Medieval Latin receptivus (“capable of receiving something”), from Latin receptus (“retaken, having been retaken; received, having been received”) + -īvus (suffix added to the perf

parole.significato: A receptacle, a container .
parole.testo: From Middle English receptorie, from Medieval Latin receptorium (“a place of shelter”).

parole.significato: A depressed, hollow, or indented space; also, a hole or opening.
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Latin recessus (“act of going back, departure, receding, retiring; (figuratively) retreat, withdrawal; (metonymically) distant, secluded, or secret spot, corner, nook, retreat; recessed part, indentation”) (also Late Latin recessus (“decree or resolution of the Diet of the

parole.significato: The act or an instance of receding or withdrawing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin recessiō, from recēdō (“recede, retreat”), from re- (“back”) + cēdō (“to go”). By surface analysis, recess + -ion.

parole.significato: Going back; receding.
parole.testo: From Latin recēdō + -ive, or directly from New Latin recessīvus.

parole.significato: To relapse into a previous pattern of behavior, especially to commit new offenses after having been punished or sanctio…
parole.testo: Adapted borrowing of Medieval Latin recidīvātus + -ate (verb-forming suffix), past participle of recidīvō, from Latin recidīvus (“returning, recurring”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Compare French récidiver. By surface analysis, recidive + -ate

parole.significato: Relapse of a disease or a symptom.
parole.testo: From Middle English recidivacion, from Latin recidīvātiō. By surface analysis, recidivate + -ion or recidive + -ation.

parole.significato: Synonym of recidivous (“recurring”).
parole.testo: From Latin recidīvus; compare Middle French recidive. Doublet of recidivous.

parole.significato: Synonym of recidivate (“to fall back into prior habits”).
parole.testo: From Middle English resydiven, from Latin recidīvō, from recidīvus + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Of a feeling, action or such: mutual, uniformly felt or done by each party towards the other or others; two-way.
parole.testo: From Latin reciprocus, possibly from a phrase such as reque proque (“back and forth, to and fro”), from re- (“back”), prō (“forwards”) and -que (“and”).

parole.significato: A contravariant expressing a certain condition of tangency; a differential invariant.
parole.testo: From Latin reciprocus + -ant.

parole.significato: To exchange two things, with both parties giving one thing and taking another thing.
parole.testo: From Latin recīprocātus, perfect passive participle of recīprocō (“to move back and forth”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from reciprocus (“back an forth, reciprocal, alternating”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), itself possibly from a phrase such as reque proque (“back and forth”)

parole.significato: The act of cutting off.
parole.testo: From Latin recisio, from recidere, recisum (“to cut off”).

parole.significato: Bending or leaning backward.
parole.testo: From Latin reclinans. See recline.

parole.significato: bent downward, so that the point is lower than the base.
parole.testo: From Latin reclīnātus, past participle of reclīnāre (“to bend or lean back”).

parole.significato: To cause to lean back; to bend back.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin reclīnāre (“to bend back”). Compare decline, incline.

parole.significato: To open; to unblock.
parole.testo: From Latin reclūdere (“to open; to shut off”), from re- + claudere (“to close”).

parole.significato: The place someone uses as a recluse; a hermitage.
parole.testo: Latin reclosorium.

parole.significato: To boil or cook again.
parole.testo: From Latin recoctus, past participle of recoquere (“to cook or boil over again”). See re- and cook.

parole.significato: To think or ponder.
parole.testo: From Latin recōgitō.

parole.significato: Connected with recognition.
parole.testo: From Latin recognitus + English -ive (adjective suffix).

parole.significato: One of a jury impaneled on an assize.
parole.testo: From Latin recognitor, agent noun of recognosco.

parole.significato: To recognise.
parole.testo: From Latin recognoscere. See recognizance.

parole.significato: To recall; to collect one's thoughts again, especially about past events.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin recollectus (“remembered, composed”), from Latin recolligo (“gather again, recover”).

parole.significato: To compose or construct again.
parole.testo: From re + compose; semantically partly borrowed from Latin recompōnō.

parole.significato: To restore a friendly relationship; to bring back or return to harmony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin reconciliō.

parole.significato: That reconciles.
parole.testo: From Latin reconciliāt (third-person singular present active indicative of reconciliō) or reconciliātus (“reunited”) + -ory.

parole.significato: To put away; to set apart.
parole.testo: From Latin recondō (“to put back, to reestablish; to put away, to hide”), from re- (“again”) + condō (“to build, to form; to store; to conceal”).

parole.significato: A repository; a storehouse
parole.testo: Latin reconditorium

parole.significato: To give new life, energy or encouragement (to); to refresh, enliven.
parole.testo: From Middle English recreate, from the participle stem of Latin recreāre (“to restore”), from re- (“re-”) + creāre (“to create”).

parole.significato: To accuse in return, state an accusation in return, make a countercharge.
parole.testo: From Latin recrīminātus, past participle of recrīminō. By surface analysis, re- + criminate.

parole.significato: The condition or state being recrudescent; the condition of something (often undesirable) breaking out again, or re-eme…
parole.testo: From Late Latin recrūdēscentia, from Latin recrūdēscēns, present participle of recrūdēscere (“to recrudesce”), from recrūdēscō (“(of a wound) to break open again; (of a fight, sedition,...) to break out again, be rekindled”); from re- (“again”) + crūdēscō (“to grow harsh or violent; to become worse”

parole.significato: Breaking out again or reemerging after temporary abatement or suppression.
parole.testo: From Latin recrūdēscō (“to become raw again”); from re- + crūdēscō (“to become harsh or raw”).

parole.significato: “Right reason”, which regards virtue as desirable in itself.
parole.testo: First attested in an English text in 1677; borrowed from Latin rēcta ratiō (“right reason”), a calque of Ancient Greek ὀρθὸς λόγος (orthòs lógos). Cf. Cicero, De leg. I, 7, I, 2: “Recta ratio - quae cum sit lex, lege quoque consociati homines cum diis putandi sumus.” Term used in a letter to "Tom" b

parole.significato: Used parenthetically in a verbatim quotation to correct an error in the source (compare sic, which notes an error witho…
parole.testo: From Latin recte (“rightly, correctly”).

parole.significato: straight
parole.testo: Latin rectus (“straight”).

parole.significato: To rectify.
parole.testo: Back-formation from rectification. For its use by non-native speakers compare, Catalan and Spanish rectificar and Portuguese retificar, from Latin rēctificō.

parole.significato: In a straight line.
parole.testo: From post-Classical Latin; either from rectilīneāris or from rectilīneus (whence rectiline) + -ar, in both cases ultimately deriving from rectus (“straight”) + līnea (“line”).

parole.significato: regimen; government; the rules governing the syntax, rules of agreement of a language.
parole.testo: From Latin rectio, from regere (“to rule, to govern”).

parole.significato: Characterized by rectitude.
parole.testo: From Latin rēctitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin rēctitūdō, from rēctus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, rectitude + -al.

parole.significato: A person who has a high standard of rectitude
parole.testo: From Latin rēctitūdin- + -arian, from oblique stem of Latin rēctitūdō, from rēctus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, rectitude + -arian.

parole.significato: righteous or correct or upright
parole.testo: From Latin rēctitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin rēctitūdō, from rēctus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, rectitude + -ous.

parole.significato: The front side of a flat object which is to be examined visually, as for reading, such as a sheet, leaf, coin or medal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rēctō foliō (“on the right leaf, on the right page”), the ablative case of the Latin rēctus (“right”). Compare versus (“turned”).

parole.significato: The male head of a German university.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Synonym of rectorship.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin rēctōrātus.

parole.significato: A governess; a rectoress.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rēctrīx (“one who directs”). By surface analysis, rector + -trix.

parole.significato: The terminal part of the large intestine through which feces pass after exiting the colon, but before leaving the body…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin rectum, clipping of Latin rectum intestinum (literally “the straight intestine”), rectum, neuter of rectus (“straight”). See right.

parole.significato: A paired muscle running vertically on each side of the anterior wall of the abdomen in humans and some other mammals.
parole.testo: From New Latin rectus abdominis, from Latin rēctus + abdōminis.

parole.significato: A pair of segmented skeletal muscle on the ventral aspect of a person's abdomen.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin mūsculus rēctus abdōminis. Literally, “straight abdominal muscle”.

parole.significato: A fusiform muscle, one of the four quadriceps muscles, situated in the middle of the front of the thigh.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: A rectus, any of several straight muscles in the body.
parole.testo: From Latin musculus rectus (“straight muscle”).

parole.significato: recumbence; a state of lying down
parole.testo: From Latin recubare (“to lie upon the back”).

parole.significato: To lean; to recline; to repose.
parole.testo: From Latin recumbō, from re- (“back”) + *cumbō, akin to cubō (“to lie down”).

parole.significato: Lying down.
parole.testo: From Latin present participle recumbēns, from recumbō (“to recline”).

parole.significato: recoverable
parole.testo: From Middle English recuperable, from Medieval Latin recuperābilis and Old French recuperable. By surface analysis, recuperate + -able.

parole.significato: To recover, especially from an illness; to get better from an illness or from exhaustion (or sometimes from a financial…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin recuperāre, alternative form of reciperāre (“get again, regain, recover”). Doublet of recover. The pronunciation without /j/ may have been influenced by the semantically similar, but etymologically distinct verb recoup.

parole.significato: Gradual restoration to health.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin recuperātiō. By surface analysis, recuperate + -ion.

parole.significato: A person who recuperates, or regains their health.
parole.testo: Either borrowed from Latin recuperator (“a recoverer”) or coined directly in English as recuperate + -or.

parole.significato: Of or relating to recuperation; tending to recovery.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin recuperatorius.

parole.significato: Of an event, situation, etc.: to appear or happen again, especially repeatedly.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin recurrō (“to hurry or run back; to return, revert”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘back, backwards’) + currō (“to hasten, hurry; to move, travel; to run”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”)). cognates * Anglo-Norman recurre, recorre (“to have recourse to”

parole.significato: To cure, heal.
parole.testo: From Middle English recure, probably partly from Latin recūrāre, and partly from a reduced form of recover.

parole.significato: Return or reversion to a certain state.
parole.testo: From recurrent + -ence, cognate with Latin recurrentia, from recurrēns (“returning back, recurring”), form of recurrō (“to return, to recur”) (English recur).

parole.significato: Recurring; happening time after time.
parole.testo: From Latin recurrens, present participle of recurrere. Morphologically recur + -ent.

parole.significato: Having its back towards the observer.
parole.testo: From Latin recursans, recursantis, present participle of recursare (“to run back”), v. freq. of recurrere. See recur.

parole.significato: The act of recurring.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin recursiō (“the act of running back or again, return”), from recurrō (“run back; return”), from re- (“back, again”) + currō (“run”).

parole.significato: Drawing upon, invoking, or referring back to itself.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin recursīvus. Equivalent to recurse + -ive.

parole.significato: A type of knife blade shape that involves several curves including a concave curve on a portion of the edge, resulting…
parole.testo: Derived from Latin recurvō.

parole.significato: recurved
parole.testo: From Latin recurvus, from re- (“re”) + curvus (“curved”).

parole.significato: Someone refusing to attend Church of England services, between the 16th and early 19th centuries, whether a Protestant…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin recūsans, recūsāntis, from recūsō (“to refuse, decline; to object to; to protest”). See recuse.

parole.significato: The act of disqualifying a judge or jury in a specific case on the grounds of possible partiality or prejudice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin recusatio, recusationis. Compare French récusation.

parole.significato: Refusing; denying; rejecting of the norm.
parole.testo: From the Late Latin recūsātīvus (“prohibitory”).

parole.significato: A great quantity of blood.
parole.testo: From Middle English Red See, Reede See, Rede See, reade sea, from Old English Rēad Sǣ, a calque of Latin Mare Rubrum, itself a calque of Ancient Greek Ἐρυθρᾱ̀ θάλασσα (Eruthrā̀ thálassa); equivalent to red + sea.

parole.significato: The act of loving in return.
parole.testo: From the New Latin redamantia, from the Classical Latin redamō (“to requite love”, transitive verb).

parole.significato: To love in return.
parole.testo: From Latin redamō.

parole.significato: The act of redarguing; refutation.
parole.testo: From Latin redargutio.

parole.significato: A clause in a deed by which some new thing is reserved out of what had been granted before; the clause by which rent is…
parole.testo: Neuter of Latin reddendus (“that must be given back or yielded”), gerundive of reddere. See reddition.

parole.significato: restoration; restitution: surrender
parole.testo: From Latin redditio, from reddere (“to give back, to return”). Compare French reddition. See render and rendition.

parole.significato: Answering to an interrogative or inquiry; conveying a reply.
parole.testo: From Latin redditivus.

parole.significato: A word which answers an interrogative.
parole.testo: From Latin redditivum.

parole.significato: A female redeemer.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin redēmptrīx. By surface analysis, redemptor + -trix.

parole.significato: The annulling of a sale, and the return by the buyer of the article sold, on account of some defect.
parole.testo: Latin redhibitiō (“a taking back”), from redhibeō.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to redhibition (the annulling of a sale).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin redhibitōrius, from redhibeō. For sense 2, compare French rédhibitoire.

parole.significato: returning
parole.testo: From Latin rediēns, present participle of redīre (“to return”); prefix red- + īre (“to go”).

parole.significato: To renew, restore to wholeness.
parole.testo: From the Latin redintegrō (“to restore or renew; to refresh or revive”).

parole.significato: Restored to wholeness or a perfect state; renewed.
parole.testo: From the Latin redintegrātus (“restored or renewed”, “refreshed or revived”), the perfect passive participle of redintegrō.

parole.significato: Restoration to a whole or sound state.
parole.testo: From the Latin redintegrātiō (“renewal, restoration, repetition”).

parole.significato: The act of returning; a return.
parole.testo: From Latin reditio, from redire. See redient.

parole.significato: Living again; brought back to life.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin redivīvus.

parole.significato: A Gallic tribe dwelling in the eastern part of the Brittany peninsula during the Iron Age and subsequent Roman conquest…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Rēdonēs. Doublet of Rennes.

parole.significato: Tending to reduce.
parole.testo: From Latin reducens, present participle of reducere.

parole.significato: The method of disproving a statement by assuming the statement is true and, with that assumption, arriving at a blatant…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin reductiō ad absurdum.

parole.significato: Synonym of red-baiting.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from reductio ad absurdum by analogy with reductio ad Hitlerum.

parole.significato: Redundancy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin redundantia.

parole.significato: Superfluous; exceeding what is necessary (and therefore no longer needed because other things fulfill its task or purpo…
parole.testo: From Latin redundāns, present participle of redundō (“to overflow, redound”), from red- (“again, back”) + undō (“to surge, flood”), from unda (“a wave”).

parole.significato: doubled
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin reduplicātus, from reduplicāre, from re- with duplicāre.

parole.significato: Of a topic, redone, restored, brought back, or revisited.
parole.testo: From Latin redux (“that returns”), from redūcō (“to bring back”). The word may have re-entered popular usage in the United States with the publication of the novel Rabbit Redux (1971) by John Updike, although it had previously been used in medicine, literary titles, and product names.

parole.significato: A dining hall, especially in an institution such as a college or monastery.
parole.testo: Via Middle English refectori from Late Latin refectorium, from Latin reficere (“to remake, to rebuild”).

parole.significato: To refute, disprove (an argument); to confute (someone).
parole.testo: From Latin refellere, from re- + fallere (“to deceive”).

parole.significato: One to whose decision a cause is referred; a referee.
parole.testo: From Latin referendarius, from Latin referendus (“to be referred”), gerundive of referre. Compare French référendaire. See refer.

parole.significato: A direct popular vote on a proposed law or constitutional amendment.
parole.testo: From Latin referendum (“that which ought to be announced”), from refero (“to announce”).

parole.significato: referable
parole.testo: From Latin referō.

parole.significato: An automatic response to a simple stimulus which does not require mental processing.
parole.testo: From Late Latin reflexus, past participle of reflectere (“to bend back”), equivalent to re- + flex. Photography sense is from noun sense meaning “reflection”. Compare English reflect.

parole.significato: Referring back to the subject, or having an object equal to the subject.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin reflexīvus, from Latin reflexus, equivalent to reflex + -ive.

parole.significato: A new blossoming of a plant during the season.
parole.testo: From re- + florescence. Alternatively, directly from Latin reflōrēscēns, present active participle of reflōrēscō (“to flower anew”), from re- + flōrēscō (“to flower”).

parole.significato: That flowers again.
parole.testo: From re- + florescent. Alternatively, directly from Latin reflōrēscēns, present active participle of reflōrēscō (“to flower anew”), from re- + flōrēscō (“to flower”).

parole.significato: Flowing back.
parole.testo: From Latin refluens, present active participle of refluō (“to flow back”).

parole.significato: Flowing backwards; refluent.
parole.testo: Latin refluus.

parole.significato: To revive or refresh.
parole.testo: From the Latin refocillō, an alternative form of refocilō.

parole.significato: The restoration of strength by means of refreshment.
parole.testo: From the Latin refocillātiō.

parole.significato: That which is to be reformed.
parole.testo: From Latin refōrmandum.

parole.significato: Of a medium, substance, object, etc.: to deflect the course of (light rays), esp. when they enter the medium, etc., at…
parole.testo: From Latin refrāctum, neuter form of refrāctus, the past participle of refringō, itself from re- (“again”) + frangō (“to break”).

parole.significato: The turning or bending of any wave, such as a light or sound wave, when it passes from one medium into another of diffe…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin refrāctiō.

parole.significato: Obstinate and unruly; strongly opposed to something.
parole.testo: From Latin refractārius (“obstinate”), from refrāctus, past participle of refringere (“to break up”). Originally refractary, refractarie, but reanalysed after other adjectives in -ory.

parole.significato: Capable of being refuted; refutable.
parole.testo: Latin refragabilis, from Latin refragari (“to oppose”).

parole.significato: That may be refracted.
parole.testo: From Latin refrangibilis, from refrangō, refringō (“refract”).

parole.significato: A rubbing up afresh; a brightening.
parole.testo: Latin refricare to rub again.

parole.significato: A substance used in a heat cycle that undergoes a phase change between gas and liquid to allow the cooling, as in refri…
parole.testo: From Latin refrīgerāns, present participle of refrīgerō (“to cool, to refresh”).

parole.significato: To make (someone or something) cool; to cool down.
parole.testo: From participle stem of Latin refrigerō (“to make cold”), from re- + frigerō.

parole.significato: The process of transferring heat from an object in order to cool it.
parole.testo: From Latin refrigero. Morphologically refrigerate + -ion.

parole.significato: A household or commercial appliance used for keeping food fresh using refrigeration.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin refrīgerātor (“cooler”).

parole.significato: Cooling refreshment; refrigeration.
parole.testo: From Latin refrigerium.

parole.significato: refractive power; refraction
parole.testo: From refringe + -ence, from Latin refringere. Refract and derivatives come from the past participle of the same Latin verb.

parole.significato: Any local environment that has escaped regional ecological change and therefore provides a habitat for endangered speci…
parole.testo: From Latin refugium. Doublet of refuge.

parole.significato: To shine brightly; to be refulgent.
parole.testo: From Latin refulgēre.

parole.significato: the quality of being refulgent; refulgency
parole.testo: From Latin refulgentia. By surface analysis, re- + Latin fulg(ere) + -ence.

parole.significato: Resplendent, or shining brightly and radiantly.
parole.testo: From Latin refulgentem, accusative singular of refulgēns, present active participle of refulgeō, from re- (“back”) + fulgeō (“shine”). By surface analysis, re- + Latin fulg(ere) + -ent.

parole.significato: Able to be refuted, or shown to be false.
parole.testo: From Late Latin refūtābilis (“refutable”), equivalent to refute + -able.

parole.significato: Something that is to be refuted.
parole.testo: From Latin refūtandum, neuter of refūtandus.

parole.significato: Tending to refute.
parole.testo: Latin refutatorius: compare French réfutatoire.

parole.significato: To prove (something) to be false or incorrect.
parole.testo: From Latin refūtō (“refute, repudiate”).

parole.significato: Royal rights, prerogatives and privileges actually enjoyed by any sovereign, regardless of his title (emperor, grand du…
parole.testo: From Middle English regalie, from Medieval Latin rēgālia (“royal powers”), substantivisation of the neuter plural of rēgālis (“of a king”), from rēx (“king”). By surface analysis, regal + -ia.

parole.significato: Things that inherently belong to the sovereign and are inseparable from his or her person.
parole.testo: From Latin regalia majora.

parole.significato: Things that inherently belong to the sovereign but may be conveyed to a subject.
parole.testo: From Latin regalia minora.

parole.significato: A system of government that substitutes for the reign of a king or queen when that king or queen becomes unable to rule.
parole.testo: From Middle English regencie (cf. regente), from Medieval Latin regentia, from Latin regēns, present participle of regō. By surface analysis, regent + -cy; compare also + -ency (“abstract-noun suffix”).

parole.significato: To construct or create anew, especially in an improved manner.
parole.testo: From Latin regenerātus, perfect passive participle of regenerō, from re- + generō, from genus, generis (“descent, origin, birth”); -ō, equivalent to re- + generate.

parole.significato: Rebuilding or restructuring; large scale repair or renewal; revitalisation.
parole.testo: From re- + generation or regenerate + -ion, from Latin regenerātiō.

parole.significato: A female regenerator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin regenerātrīx. By surface analysis, regenerate + -trix.

parole.significato: Germination again or anew; the act of regerminating.
parole.testo: Latin regerminatio.

parole.significato: A register.
parole.testo: From Latin regesta, plural: compare Old French regestes, plural. See register.

parole.significato: A monarchist; a royalist.
parole.testo: Latin regius (“regal”).

parole.significato: That may be ruled; governable, tractable.
parole.testo: From the post-Classical Latin regibilis.

parole.significato: The killing of a king.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rēgicidium (“king-killing”)

parole.significato: One who kills a king.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rēgicida (“king-killer”).

parole.significato: One who kills a queen.
parole.testo: From Latin rēgīna (“queen”) + -cide.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or resembling a queen.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rēgīnālis, from rēgīna + -ālis.

parole.significato: Any large area of a planet or moon that is strongly differentiated from neighbouring areas by colour or albedo.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin regiō. Doublet of region.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an ecclesiastical region.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin regionarius, referring to a deacon in charge of one of the seven wards of Rome, from Latin regiō + -ārius. Equivalent to region + -ary. Doublet of regionarius.

parole.significato: To enter in a register; to enlist.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin registrum, from Late Latin regesta (“list, items recorded”), from Latin regerō (“to record, to carry back”), from re- + gerō (“to carry, bear”). Compare Latin registoria (“a treasurer”). Some senses influenced by association with unrelated Latin regō (“to rule”).

parole.significato: An official keeper or recorder of records.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin registrārius, from registrum (“register”) + -ārius (“agent of use”). See more at register. By surface analysis, register /registry (“a record”) + -ar.

parole.significato: registered, recorded
parole.testo: From the post-Classical Latin registrātus, the perfect passive participle of registrō (“to register”).

parole.significato: To register.
parole.testo: From registrāt-, the perfect passive participial stem of the post-Classical Latin registrō (“to register”).

parole.significato: A registrar or registrant, person or device which registers data
parole.testo: From Middle Latin, from registro (cognate with registrarius), from registrum 'register', an alteration of Late Latin regesta "list, matters recorded," from the neuter plural of regestus, the past participle of regerere "to record, literally to carry back", itself from re- "back" + gerere "carry, bea

parole.significato: A building in which things are registered or where registers are kept.
parole.testo: A variant of registery, from Middle English regestery (“?a record book; ?a bookmark”), partly from Medieval Latin regesterium, registerium and probably also partly formed with -ery. Equivalent to register + -y.

parole.significato: An annual grant of public money to Presbyterian and other nonconformist ministers in England, Scotland, and especially…
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Of or relating to a king; royal.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rēgius, from rēx, rēgis (“a king”). Doublet of regious.

parole.significato: A professor who holds a position created by or filled by a royal patron.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rēgius professor.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the reign of a monarch (or pope).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rēgnālis, from Latin rēgnum + -ālis.

parole.significato: A rank in the classification of organisms, below dominium and above divisio.
parole.testo: From Latin rēgnum (“kingdom”). Doublet of reign.

parole.significato: To go back; to retrograde, as the apsis of a planet's orbit.
parole.testo: From Latin regredi (“to go back”). Compare regrade, regress.

parole.significato: The act of passing back; passage back; return; retrogression.
parole.testo: (verb) From Latin regressus, past participle of regredior (“to go back”), from re- (“back”) + gradior (“to go”). Doublet of regressus.

parole.significato: An action of regressing, a return to a previous state.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin regressio. Equivalent to regress + -ion. The statistics sense comes from regression to the mean.

parole.significato: That tends to return, revert or regress.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin regressīvus, equivalent to regress + -ive.

parole.significato: The entitlement of a debtor to have a co-debtor pay their share.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin regressus. Doublet of regress.

parole.significato: A book of rules for a religious establishment.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rēgula (“rule”). Doublet of rail, regal, rigol, and rule.

parole.significato: To dictate policy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin regulatus, perfect passive participle of regulō (“to direct, rule, regulate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from regula (“rule”), from regō (“to keep straight, direct, govern, rule”). Compare regle, rail. Displaced native Old English metegian.

parole.significato: To make or become regular; regularize.
parole.testo: From Latin regulare (“to direct, rule, regulate”), from regula (“rule”), from regere (“to keep straight, direct, govern, rule”) + -ize.

parole.significato: An impure metal formed beneath slag during the smelting of ores.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin regulus.

parole.significato: To throw up or vomit; to eject what has previously been swallowed.
parole.testo: From Late Latin regurgitātus, past participle of regurgitāre, combined form of re- (“back”) + gurgitāre (“to engulf, flood”), from gurges (“whirlpool, gulf, sea, abyss”).

parole.significato: To restore (someone) to their former state, reputation, possessions, status etc.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rehabilitātus, perfect passive participle of Latin rehabilitō. See habilitate.

parole.significato: To flow in again.
parole.testo: From re- + Latin infundere (“to pour in”).

parole.significato: Something that has been reintegrated.
parole.testo: From the Latin reintegrāns (stem: reintegrant-).

parole.significato: A form of concretism stating that (i) every object is a body and (ii) no object is a state or relation, or property.
parole.testo: From Latin rēs (“thing”) + -ism.

parole.significato: To say or do (something) for a second time, such as for emphasis.
parole.testo: Early 15th century, from Late Latin reiteratus, past participle of reiterare (“to repeat”) from re- (“again”) + iterare (“to repeat”) from iterum (“again”).

parole.significato: To refuse to accept; to forswear.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English rejecten, from Latin reiectus, past participle of reicere (“to throw back”), from re- (“back”) + iacere (“to throw”). Displaced native Old English āweorpan (literally “to throw out”).

parole.significato: Things that are thrown away or rejected; items with little or no value waste, rubbish, garbage, refuse, ejecta
parole.testo: From Latin rēiciō (“throw back”).

parole.significato: rejectable or rejected.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin reiectāneus.

parole.significato: The process of rendering young again.
parole.testo: From rejuvenate + -ion, cf. Latin reiuvenatiō.

parole.significato: To fall back again; to slide or turn back into a former state or practice.
parole.testo: From Latin relapsus, past participle of relabi (“to slide back, fall back”), from re- (“back”) + labi (“to slip, slide, fall”).

parole.significato: To tell in a descriptive way.
parole.testo: From Latin relātus, perfect passive participle of referō (“carry back; report”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of refer. See also infer, collate and confer, delate and defer, as well as prefer and prelate among others.

parole.significato: One who relates, or tells; a narrator.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin relator.

parole.significato: A female relator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin relātrīx. By surface analysis, relator + -trix.

parole.significato: A term that is related to the referent.
parole.testo: From Latin relatum, neuter past participle of referre.

parole.significato: The act of relaxing or the state of being relaxed; the opposite of stress or tension; the aim of recreation and leisure…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin relaxatio, relaxationis; equivalent to relax + -ation.

parole.significato: Made slack or feeble; weak, soft.
parole.testo: From relax + -ed, originally after Latin relaxātus.

parole.significato: Exile, banish, remove, or send away.
parole.testo: First attested in 1561, borrowed from Latin relēgātus, the past participle of relēgō (“to dispatch, banish”).

parole.significato: A person who has been banished from proximity to Rome for a set time, but without losing his civil rights.
parole.testo: First attested circa 1550: from the Classical Latin relēgātus (“banished person, exile”), the nominative singular masculine substantive form of relēgātus, the past participle of relēgō (“to dispatch, banish”).

parole.significato: Relegated; exiled.
parole.testo: First attested circa 1425: from the Classical Latin relēgātus, the perfect passive participle of relēgō (“I dispatch”, “I banish”).

parole.significato: The act of being relegated
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin relēgātiō, relēgātiōnis.

parole.significato: Raise (a person’s) spirits or lighten (his) mood; relieve (someone of a mental or emotional burden).
parole.testo: From Latin relevātus, the perfect passive participle of relevō (“to raise, lighten, relieve, alleviate”); compare Middle French and Modern French relever, as well as English relevation. Doublet of relieve.

parole.significato: Left uncovered, as land by recession of water
parole.testo: Latin relictus, past participle.

parole.significato: To ligate again.
parole.testo: Partly from Latin religātus, the perfect passive participle of religō (“to bind back or behind”) and partly formed in English as re- + ligate.

parole.significato: A fear or hatred of religion, religious faith, religious people or religious organizations.
parole.testo: From Latin religiō (“moral obligation, worship”) and Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: The quality of being religious or pious, especially when zealous.
parole.testo: From religio(u)s + -ity, from Latin religiositas.

parole.significato: relinquishing
parole.testo: Latin relinquens.

parole.significato: Remains, especially of fossil organisms.
parole.testo: From Latin reliquiae.

parole.significato: shining with reflected light.
parole.testo: From Latin relūcent-, relūcēns, present participle of relucēre.

parole.significato: To be averse to.
parole.testo: From Latin reluctor.

parole.significato: Unwillingness to do something.
parole.testo: From reluct + -ance. From Latin relū̆ctor (“to struggle against, oppose, resist”) + -ance, from re- (“back”) + luctor (“to struggle”).

parole.significato: Resistance, opposition.
parole.testo: From reluct(ant) + -ancy, from Latin relū̆ctor (“to struggle against, oppose, resist”), from re- (“back”) + lū̆ctor (“to struggle”). Doublet of reluctance.

parole.significato: Not wanting to take some action; unwilling to do something.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin reluctāns (whence -ant), present participle of reluctor (“to struggle against, oppose, resist”), from re- (“back”) + luctor (“to struggle”) (whence re-.

parole.significato: Resistance, struggle.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Late Latin reluctatio, from the participle stem of Latin reluctārī.

parole.significato: A toothed ring or wheel that rotates past a variable reluctance sensor.
parole.testo: From re- + Latin luct(or) (“to struggle”) + -or.

parole.significato: The act of returning; reabsorption.
parole.testo: From Latin remanare (“to flow back”); compare emanate.

parole.significato: Remaining or persisting especially after an electrical or magnetic influence is removed.
parole.testo: From Latin remanens, present participle of remaneō (“to remain”).

parole.significato: A bill that has been postponed or deferred to another session.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin remanet (“it remains, it is left”).

parole.significato: Coming back; returning.
parole.testo: From Latin remeāns, present participle of remeō (“to go or come back”).

parole.significato: curative; providing a remedy
parole.testo: From Latin remediālis. By surface analysis, remedy + -al.

parole.significato: To correct or improve (a deficiency or problem).
parole.testo: From Latin remediare.

parole.significato: To remember or recall
parole.testo: From Latin rememoror.

parole.significato: A quill.
parole.testo: From Latin rēmex (“rower”).

parole.significato: A Belgic tribe dwelling in the Aisne, Vesle and Suippe river valleys during the Iron Age and the Roman period.
parole.testo: From Latin Rēmī.

parole.significato: Shaped like an oar or paddle.
parole.testo: From Latin remus (“oar”) + -form.

parole.significato: To recall the past in a private moment, often fondly or nostalgically.
parole.testo: Back-formation from reminiscence, from Latin reminīscēns, present participle of reminīscor (“to remember”).

parole.significato: An act of remembering long-past experiences, especially positive or pleasant ones, often fondly.
parole.testo: From Late Latin reminīscentiae (“remembrances”), from Latin reminīscēns, present active participle of reminīscor (“remember”); see reminiscent.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to reminiscence.
parole.testo: From Latin reminīscēns, present participle of reminīscor (“remember”), from re- (“again”) + min-, base of me-min-isse (“to remember, think over”), akin to mens (“mind”); see mental, mind, etc.

parole.significato: Of or relating to remembering; reminiscent.
parole.testo: From Late Latin reminiscentia + -al.

parole.significato: At fault; failing to fulfill responsibility, duty, or obligations.
parole.testo: From Middle English remisse, remysse, from Latin remissus (“languid, negligent”), perfect passive participle of remittō (“remit”).

parole.significato: Remitting; forgiving; abating.
parole.testo: From Latin remissivus. See remit.

parole.significato: To transmit or send (e.g. money in payment); to supply.
parole.testo: From Middle English remitten, from Latin remittere (“to send, send back”). Compare Old French remettre, remetre, remitter.

parole.significato: Alternately increasing and decreasing in severity or intensity.
parole.testo: From Latin remittent-, present participle of remittō.

parole.significato: The reduction by a judge of damages awarded by a jury.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Synonym of Sarabaite.
parole.testo: From Latin remoboth, a loan from Coptic ⲣⲙⲛⲟⲩⲱⲧ (rmnouōt), from ⲣⲱⲙⲉ (rōme) + ⲟⲩⲱⲧ (ouōt).

parole.significato: mollifying; softening; soft
parole.testo: From Latin remolliens, present participle of remollire (“to mollify”). Compare French rémollient. See mollient.

parole.significato: To object with in critical fashion; to express disapproval (with, against).
parole.testo: From (the participle stem of) Late Latin remōnstrō, from Latin re- + mōnstrō.

parole.significato: Earnest protest or objection, disapproving pleading, or an act thereof.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Medieval Latin remōnstrātiō.

parole.significato: Any of various elongate fish from the family Echeneidae, the dorsal fin of which is in the form of a suction disc that…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin remora (“delay, hindrance, passive resistance”), from the belief that the fish would attach themselves to ships and slow them down, from re- (prefix meaning ‘back, backwards’) + mora (“delay”) (from Proto-Indo-European *mere (“to delay, hinder”), from *(s)mer- (“to fall into thin

parole.significato: To hinder; to delay.
parole.testo: From Latin remoratus, past participle of remorari; prefix re- (“re-”) + morari (“to delay”).

parole.significato: Resounding, echoing.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Latin remugiens, present participle of remugire. See mugient.

parole.significato: To compensate; to pay.
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Latin remūnerō (“to reward”), from mūnus (“gift”). Unrelated to money.

parole.significato: Something given in exchange for goods or services rendered.
parole.testo: From Latin remūnerātiō.

parole.significato: A kidney.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rēn. Doublet of rein (“kidney”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the kidneys.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin renalis, from Latin rēnēs (“kidneys”).

parole.significato: Able to be reproduced.
parole.testo: From re- + Latin nāscor (“be born”) + -ible, from Latin renāscor.

parole.significato: Reborn or reincarnated.
parole.testo: From Latin renātus (“reborn”). Equivalent to Latin renāscor (“to reborn”, renā- in compounds) + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To break a promise or commitment; to go back on one's word.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin renegō, from negō (“to deny”). Possibly influenced by renegotiate. Doublet of renay. See also renegade.

parole.significato: One of the lobules of the kidney, especially in whales.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin reniculus.

parole.significato: Synonym of kidney-shaped (“having an approximately circular or elongated ovoid shape with an inward curve or indentatio…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rēnis (the genitive singular of rēn (“kidney”); see further at that entry) + English -form (suffix meaning ‘having the form or shape of’), modelled after New Latin rēnifōrmis (“of seeds: kidney-shaped”).

parole.significato: The state or quality of being renitent; resistance to physical pressure or constraint
parole.testo: From Latin renitens, present participle of reniteo. First known use: 1701. Compare French rénitence.

parole.significato: resistant to physical pressure; unyielding
parole.testo: From Latin renītēns, present participle of renītor (“resist, struggle”).

parole.significato: kidney.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rēn.

parole.significato: To renew; to revamp something to make it look new again.
parole.testo: The adjective first attested in 1440, the verb in 1535; from Middle English renovat(e) (“renewed”), from Latin renovātus, perfect passive participle of renovō (“to renew”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Participial usage up until Early Modern English.

parole.significato: A small kidney.
parole.testo: From Latin renulus, from ren (“kidney”).

parole.significato: A person who renounces something; especially, someone who renounces worldly life for spiritual reasons, or a person who…
parole.testo: From Latin renuntiāns, present participle of renuntiāre.

parole.significato: That renounces.
parole.testo: From Latin renuntiātus, past participle of Latin renūntiāre. Doublet of renounce.

parole.significato: The act of rejecting or renouncing something as invalid.
parole.testo: From Latin renūntiātiō. Compare renounce.

parole.significato: A modified abortive egg that may be used to protect the other eggs from predation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin repagulum (“bolt, bar, restraint”).

parole.significato: Having a slightly undulating margin.
parole.testo: From Latin repandus (“bent backward, turned up”), from re- (“re-”) + pandus (“bent, crooked”).

parole.significato: Restored to a state of good repair; returned to working order.
parole.testo: From Latin reparātus (“repaired”), perfect participle of reparō (“to renew, repair”).

parole.significato: A payment of time, effort or money to compensate for past transgression(s).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin reparātiō, reparātiōnis.

parole.significato: A person who has returned to their country of origin or whose original citizenship has been restored.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin repatriare, from re- + patria (“homeland”). Cognate to repair (“to return”).

parole.significato: Repulsive, inspiring aversion.
parole.testo: From Latin repellēns. Equivalent to repel + -ent.

parole.significato: Creeping along the ground.
parole.testo: From Latin rēpēns, present participle of rēpō (“to creep”).

parole.significato: unexpected
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin repentīnus.

parole.significato: To drive or beat back.
parole.testo: From Latin repercusus, past participle of repercutere (“to drive back”), from re- (“re-”) + percutere. See percussion.

parole.significato: Found by chance.
parole.testo: From Latin repertīcius (“newly found”), from repertus (“found, discovered, invented”), from reperīre (“to find, discover, invent”), from re- (“again, anew”) + parere (“to bear, to get”), + -īcius (“-itious”), under influence of English -ious, q.v. Cognate with repertible and repertor.

parole.significato: A discoverer.
parole.testo: From Latin repertor, from repertus (“found”), from reperīre (“to find”), from re- (“again, back”) + parere (“to bear, to get”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to bring forth”), + -or (“-er: forming agent nouns”). Influenced by Middle French repertour (“inventor, discoverer”). Cognate with repertib

parole.significato: A repertoire.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin repertōrium. Doublet of repertoire.

parole.significato: Let it be repeated.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of Latin repetātur.

parole.significato: Anaphora.
parole.testo: From Latin repetītiō. Doublet of repetition.

parole.significato: The act or an instance of repeating or being repeated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin repetitionem (accusative singular of repetitio; cf. French répétition). Doublet of repetitio. By surface analysis, repeat + -ition.

parole.significato: Happening many times in a similar way; containing repetition; repeating.
parole.testo: From Latin repetitus, with the suffix -ive.

parole.significato: replicative
parole.testo: From Latin replicāns, present participle of replicō. The science fiction sense was coined by David Peoples in the 1982 film Blade Runner.

parole.significato: To make a copy (replica) of.
parole.testo: From Latin replicātus, past participle of replicāre (“to fold or bend back; reply”), from re (“back”) + plicāre (“to fold”); see ply. Doublet of reply and replica.

parole.significato: The framework of some pods, such as the cress, which remains after the valves drop off
parole.testo: From Latin replum (“door frame”).

parole.significato: To replace.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin reponere; prefix re- (“re-”) + ponere (“to place”).

parole.significato: Senses relating to placing or positioning.
parole.testo: From Middle English reposen (“to put (something) back, replace”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘again; back, backwards’) + posen (“to place (something)”), modelled after Latin repōnō (“to put back; to restore; to store”). Posen is derived from Old French poser (“to place, put”) (modern French poser), fr

parole.significato: To cause to rest or stay in a certain place; to place, put, or deposit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin repositus, past participle of repōnō (“put back”), from re- + pōnō (“put”). See position.

parole.significato: A location for storage, often for safety or preservation.
parole.testo: From Middle English reposytorye, from Latin repositōrium. By surface analysis, reposit + -ory.
From reposit or its etymon Classical Latin reposit-, past participial stem of repōnō, + -ory. Compare Medieval Latin repositōrius (“used for storage”).

parole.significato: To criticize, to reprove.

parole.significato: Blameworthy, censurable, guilty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin reprehensibilis, from Latin reprehendo; equivalent to reprehend + -ible.

parole.significato: the act, or an expression, of criticism, censure or condemnation; reprimand
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin reprehensio, reprehensionis.

parole.significato: A representation; a thing serving to represent something.
parole.testo: From Latin repraesentāmen. See also represent.

parole.significato: To forcefully prevent an upheaval from developing further.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin repressus, the perfect passive participle of reprimō (“to repress”).

parole.significato: To take back or away.
parole.testo: re- + Latin privare (“to deprive”).

parole.significato: Rejected; cast off as worthless.
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1425, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English reprobat(e) (“condemned, damned”, also used as the past participle of reprobaten), borrowed from Latin reprobātus (“disapproved, rejected, condemned”), perfect passive participle of reprobō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffi

parole.significato: To have strong disapproval of something; to reprove; to condemn.
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1451, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English reprobaten, from reprobat(e) (“condemned, damned”, also used as the past participle of reprobaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin reprobātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more. Doublet

parole.significato: Creeping along the ground.
parole.testo: From Latin rēptō (“to creep”).

parole.significato: A creeping movement.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rēptātiō.

parole.significato: Crawling, creeping.
parole.testo: From reptatory (“crawling, creeping”) + -al (suffix forming adjectives). parole.significato: Synonym of reptile: creeping, crawling.
parole.testo: From Late Latin reptitius (“creeping”), corruption of Latin reperticius, from reptus (“crept, crawled”) + -īcius (“-itious”), from rēpere (“to creep, to crawl”), modified by English -ious, q.v. Cognate with repent, reptant, reptile, reptilious, surreptitious.

parole.significato: To reject the truth or validity of; to deny.
parole.testo: First attested in 1543; from Latin repudiātus, the perfect passive participle of repudiō (“to cast off, reject”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), from repudium (“rejection, repudiation, divorce”).

parole.significato: The act of refusing to accept; the act of repudiating.
parole.testo: From Latin repudiātiōnem, equivalent to repudiate + -ion.

parole.significato: To oppose or resist
parole.testo: Latin repugno.

parole.significato: The quality of being repugnant: offensiveness, repulsion.
parole.testo: From Middle English repugnancie, from Latin repugnantia. By surface analysis, repugnant + -cy. Doublet of repugnance.

parole.significato: To oppose; to fight against.
parole.testo: From Latin repugnare. See repugn.

parole.significato: Defensive or repulsive, particularly as applied to glands of certain invertebrates, with which they produce poisonous o…
parole.testo: From Latin repugnatorius.

parole.significato: To bud or sprout again.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin repullulō, repullulātum, from pullulō. See pullulate.

parole.significato: To repel or drive back.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English repulsen, a learned borrowing from Latin repulsus, from repellō. For spelling, as in pulse, the -e (on -lse) is so the end is pronounced /ls/, rather than /lz/ as in pulls, and does not change the vowel (‘u’). Compare else, false, convulse.

parole.significato: Repulsive; acting to repel; driving back.
parole.testo: Latin repulsorius.

parole.significato: A Mass (especially Catholic) to honor and remember a dead person.
parole.testo: From Middle English requiem, from Latin requiem, the first word of the introit for the traditional requiem mass, an alternative accusative case of Latin requiēs (“rest, repose”), from re- (“again”) + quiēs (“rest, quiet”).

parole.significato: May they rest in peace.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin requiēscant in pāce.

parole.significato: A prayer for the peaceful repose of the soul of a dead person
parole.testo: First word of the Latin phrase requiēscat in pāce (“may he/she rest in peace”). The Latin word requiēscat means "may he/she rest" and is a form of the Latin verb requiēscō (“to rest, repose”).

parole.significato: May he/she rest in peace.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin requiēscat in pāce.

parole.significato: Quiescence, repose, quiet.
parole.testo: From Latin requiescere + -ence.

parole.significato: Quiescent; quiet; at rest.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin requiēscēns (“resting, reposing, sleeping”), present participle of requiēscere, from re- + quiēscō (“rest, repose”).

parole.significato: A sepulchre.
parole.testo: From Latin requietorium, from requiescere, requietum (“to rest”). See re- and quiesce.

parole.significato: Essential, indispensable, required.
parole.testo: From Latin requīsītus, perfect passive participle of requīrō (“to require, seek, ask for”), from which English require.

parole.significato: Something that is asked for; the answer demanded by a problem.
parole.testo: From Latin requisitum.

parole.significato: The severe pressure of poverty.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A nonphysical substance of which minds are composed, separate from res extensa, according to Cartesian dualism and idea…
parole.testo: From Latin rēs cōgitāns.

parole.significato: The commons, or common heritage of mankind.
parole.testo: From Latin res communis.

parole.significato: In Cartesian ontology, corporeal substance, distinguished from the res cogitans from which the mind or soul is made.
parole.testo: From Latin rēs extēnsa.

parole.significato: The overall start-to-end sequence of a felony. Certain statements heard by witnesses during this period (e.g. "this is…
parole.testo: From Latin res gestae (“deeds”, literally “things done”).

parole.significato: A new point that has not previously been decided in law.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A thing done between others (such as a contract), which cannot adversely affect the rights of those who are not parties…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The import of a thing or situation is obvious.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin rēs ipsa loquitur (“the thing speaks for itself”, literally “the thing itself speaks”).

parole.significato: A legal claim that has already been decided in another lawsuit or proceeding, and therefore must be dismissed.
parole.testo: From Latin rēs (“thing, matter, affair”) and jūdicata, feminine nominative singular form of jūdicatus, past participle of jūdico (“judge”).

parole.significato: Something that has no owner and is not subject to the jurisdiction of any state, but is susceptible to national appropr…
parole.testo: From Latin rēs nūllīus (“nobody's thing”).

parole.significato: The common good, as identified with the wider state; the commonwealth, the body politic.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin rēs pūblica. Doublet of republic.

parole.significato: To greet in return.
parole.testo: From Latin resalutare; or formed from re- + salute.

parole.significato: To repeal, annul, or declare void; to take (something such as a rule or contract) out of effect.
parole.testo: From the Latin rescindō (“to cut back”), from re- (“back”) + scindō (“to cut”).

parole.significato: An act of rescinding: removing, taking away, or taking back.
parole.testo: 1651, Late Latin rescissio, from Latin rescindō (“to cut back”), from re- (“back”) + scindō (“to cut”).

parole.significato: Tending to rescind; pertaining to rescission.
parole.testo: Latin rescissorius.

parole.significato: To write back; to write in reply.
parole.testo: From Latin rescribere.

parole.significato: A copy, or act of rewriting something; a rewrite.
parole.testo: From Latin rescriptum (“written reply”).

parole.significato: The act of writing back; the answering of a letter.
parole.testo: From Latin rescriptio. Compare French rescription. See rescribe.

parole.significato: One who makes an unlawful rescue; a rescuer
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: To remove (some part of an organ or structure) by surgical means.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin resectus, past participle of resecare (“to cut off”), formed in turn from re- + secare (“to cut”).

parole.significato: The surgical removal of part or all of a tissue, organ, tumor, or body part.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin resectiō.

parole.significato: To unlock; to open.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin reserō, reserātus (“I unlock, open”).

parole.significato: A place in which things are reserved or kept.
parole.testo: From Latin reservatorium, from resservare. See reserve and compare reservoir.

parole.significato: residence; abode
parole.testo: Latin reseantia, Old French reseance.

parole.significato: Remaining; residual.
parole.testo: Latin residuus.

parole.significato: The residue, remainder or rest of something.
parole.testo: From Latin residuum. Doublet of residue.

parole.significato: To rebound; to bounce back.
parole.testo: From Latin resiliō (“leap or spring back; rebound”).

parole.significato: Returning quickly to original shape after force is applied; elastic. (of objects or substances)
parole.testo: From Latin resiliēns, resilientem (“rebounding”, present active participle of resiliō) (whence -ent), from saliō (“leap, jump”).

parole.significato: Having the quality of resin; yielding resin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rēsīnāceus; equivalent to resin + -aceous.

parole.significato: Synonym of resolvable.
parole.testo: From Late Latin resolubilis, from Latin resolvō.

parole.significato: Able to resolve (separate) the constituents of a mixture
parole.testo: From Latin resolvēns, present participle of resolvere: compare French résolvant. See resolve.

parole.significato: To vibrate or sound, especially in response to another vibration.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin resonō.

parole.significato: To absorb (something) again.
parole.testo: From Latin resorbere, from re- (“again”) + sorbere (“to suck in”).

parole.significato: swallowing up
parole.testo: From Latin resorbens, present participle of resorbere.

parole.significato: respect; regard
parole.testo: Compare Latin respectio.

parole.significato: Relating to particular persons or things, each to each; particular; own.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin respectivus, from Latin respectus. By surface analysis, respect + -ive.

parole.significato: To sprinkle; to scatter.
parole.testo: From Latin respersus, past participle of respergere; prefix re- (“re-”) + spargere (“to strew, sprinkle”).

parole.significato: The act of sprinkling or scattering.
parole.testo: Latin respersio.

parole.significato: look to the end; consider the final outcome
parole.testo: From Latin respice fīnem.

parole.significato: The process of inhaling and exhaling.
parole.testo: From Middle English respiracioun, borrowed from Latin respīrātiō, respīrātiōnem.

parole.significato: Relating to respiration or the organs of respiration; breathing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin respīrātōrius, equal to respire + -atory.

parole.significato: To shine radiantly; to be resplendent.
parole.testo: From Latin resplendere (“to shine brightly”).

parole.significato: The property of being, or that which causes something to be, resplendent.
parole.testo: From Middle English resplendence, from Latin resplendentia.

parole.significato: resplendence, radiant beauty
parole.testo: Latin, from resplendere (“to shine brightly”).

parole.significato: A legal doctrine which holds that an employer, officer, manager, supervisor, or other individual or group superior to a…

parole.significato: A loan upon goods laden on board a ship.

parole.significato: A body of written decisions and rulings given by legal scholars in response to questions addressed to them.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin respōnsa, plural of respōnsum (“answer”).

parole.significato: One who is answerable or responsible.
parole.testo: Compare Latin responsalis.

parole.significato: A receiver used in conjunction with an interrogator to receive and interpret signals from a transponder.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin respōnsor. First attested in the a. 1649. By surface analysis, clipping of responsory.

parole.significato: A chant or anthem recited after a reading in a church service; a respond.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English responsorie, from Late Latin respōnsōrium, from Latin respōnsus (“answered”), from the verb respondeō (“to answer”). Compare respond.

parole.significato: A blessing or expression of hope that a deceased person is at peace.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin requiescat in pace.

parole.significato: stagnant; motionless
parole.testo: Latin restagnans, present participle

parole.significato: To stagnate; to cease to flow.
parole.testo: Latin restagnare to overflow.

parole.significato: stagnation
parole.testo: Latin restagnatio (“an inundation”).

parole.significato: To restore
parole.testo: Either an alteration of restore, or borrowed from Latin restaurāre.

parole.significato: To restore.
parole.testo: From Latin restaurātus, past participle of restaurāre. See restore.

parole.significato: Formed like a rope; applied especially to several rope-like bundles or masses of fibres on the dorsal side of the medul…
parole.testo: From Latin restifōrmis. By surface analysis, Latin restis (“rope”) + -form.

parole.significato: To quench or extinguish.
parole.testo: From Latin restinguere, restinctum, from re- (“re-”) + stinguere (“to quench”).

parole.significato: Any of the restiform bodies on the dorsal side of the medulla oblongata.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin restis (“rope, cord”).

parole.significato: Synonym of restitutio ad integrum.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?]

parole.significato: The process of bringing an object back to its original state; the process of restoring something.

parole.significato: To confine; to contract; to stringe.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rēstringō (“to tighten, to restrain”).

parole.significato: astringent; styptic
parole.testo: From Latin restringens.

parole.significato: The act of sweating again.
parole.testo: From Latin resudare (“sweat again”); see sudation.

parole.significato: Following as a result or consequence of something; resulting.

parole.significato: The act of resuming or starting something again.

parole.significato: Having the appearance of being upside down.

parole.significato: Lying on the back; supine.
parole.testo: From Latin resupinus, from re- (“re-”) + supinus (“bent backward, supine”).

parole.significato: To rise again; to go through a period of renewed vigor or vitality.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin resurgō (“rise again”).

parole.significato: To raise from the dead; to bring life back to.

parole.significato: To restore consciousness, vigor, or life to.
parole.testo: From Latin resuscitātus, past participle of resuscitō (“to raise up again, revive”), from re- (“again”) + suscitō (“to raise up”), from sub- (“up, under”) + citō (“to summon, rouse”).

parole.significato: To do something harmful or negative to get revenge for some harm; to fight back or respond in kind to an injury or affr…
parole.testo: From Latin retāliātus, past participle of retāliō (“to requite, retaliate”).

parole.significato: That retards; delaying, impeditive.
parole.testo: From (the participle stem of) Latin retardāre + -ive.

parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rete mirabile (literally “wonderful net”) (14th century).

parole.significato: Disclosure or detection of something concealed.
parole.testo: From Latin retectio, retectionem (“discovery, uncovering”).

parole.significato: That which is retained.

parole.significato: The act of retaining or something retained.
parole.testo: From Middle English retencioun, borrowed from Latin retentiō, retentiōnis, from retentus, the perfect passive participle of retineō (“retain”) (from re- (“back, again”) + teneō (“hold, keep”)).

parole.significato: A muscle which holds a body part in place, notably in extended or retracted position
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin retentor, from retentare, from retinere (“retain, hold back”), from re- + tenere.

parole.significato: Any of several species of bryozoans of the genus Reteporella (syn. Retepora) or the family Reteporidae, that form delic…
parole.testo: Latin rete (“net”) + porus (“pore”)

parole.significato: A gladiator who uses a casting net (a rete or iaculum) as a weapon.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rētiārius.

parole.significato: Unwilling to communicate; keeping one's thoughts and opinions to oneself; reserved or restrained.
parole.testo: Latin reticēns, present participle of reticeō (“to keep silence”).

parole.significato: Having the structure of a net or a network; netlike.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin rēticulāris, from Latin rēticulum (“little net”).

parole.significato: Network-like in form or appearance.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rēticulātus (“reticulated, net-like”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rēticulum (“net”). Doublet of reticle, reticule, and Reticulum.

parole.significato: Having the form of a net; reticulate
parole.testo: From Latin rēticulum (“net”) + -form.

parole.significato: A connecting band.

parole.testo: Latin rete (“a net”) + English nerved.

parole.significato: Part of the eye of an invertebrate which corresponds in function with the retina of a vertebrate, hypothetical membrane…
parole.testo: From New Latin retineum, from Medieval Latin retina. By surface analysis, retin(a) + -eum.

parole.significato: One of the group of pigmented cells that surround the retinophorae of invertebrates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin rētinula, diminutive of Medieval Latin rētina. By surface analysis, retin(a) + -ula.

parole.significato: A sharp or witty reply, or one which turns an argument against its originator; a comeback.
parole.testo: From Middle English retorte, from Latin retortus, from retorquēre (“to be forced to twist back”).

parole.significato: To pull (something) back or back inside.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English retracten, retract (“to absorb, draw in”), from Latin retractus (“withdrawn”), the perfect passive participle of Latin retrahō (“to draw or pull back, withdraw; to bring back; to compel to turn back; to recall; to get back, recover; to hold back, restrain, withhold; to remov

parole.significato: An act of retracting or withdrawing (a mistake, a statement, etc.); a retraction.
parole.testo: Partly: * from retract (verb) (see etymology 1); and * from Late Latin retractus (“a pulling back, retreat; refuge”), from Latin retractus (“withdrawn”), the perfect passive participle of Latin retrahō (“to draw or pull back, withdraw; to bring back; to compel to turn back; to recall; to get back, r

parole.significato: To retract; to recant.
parole.testo: From Latin retractatus, past participle of retractare. See retract.

parole.significato: retraction (of something previously said)
parole.testo: Compare French rétractation, Latin retractatio (“a revision, reconsideration”).

parole.significato: A muscle that draws the ear backward.

parole.significato: A dismissal with prejudice based on a plaintiff's withdrawal of the suit.
parole.testo: From Latin retraxit (“[he] has withdrawn”), inflection of retraho (“[I] withdraw”).

parole.significato: To pay back; to give in return, as payment, reward, or punishment; to requite.
parole.testo: Latin retributus, past participle of retribuo (“to retribute”); prefix re- + tribuo (“to bestow, assign, pay”). See tribute.

parole.significato: Punishment inflicted in the spirit of moral outrage or personal vengeance.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Latin retribuere (“repay”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to retribution; of the nature of retribution; involving retribution or repayment.
parole.testo: Compare Latin retributorius (“worthy of retribution”).

parole.significato: refuse; dregs
parole.testo: Latin retrimentum.

parole.significato: Back or backward.
parole.testo: See retro.

parole.significato: To grant back.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin retrōcēdere, from retrō- (“back, backward”) + cēdere (“to go, go back, give, return, etc.”). Equivalent to retro- + cede.

parole.significato: To employ retroduction
parole.testo: From Latin retro (“backward”) + Latin ducere (“to lead”).

parole.significato: Synonym of abduction.
parole.testo: From Latin retroducere, retroductum (“to lead or bring back”), from retro (“backward”) + ducere (“to lead”).

parole.significato: Bent or curved backwards.
parole.testo: From Latin rētrōflexus, the perfect participle of rētrōflectō (“bend, turn”), from flectō (“bend, turn”).

parole.significato: Bent sharply back, so as to appear broken.
parole.testo: retro- + Latin fractus, past participle of frangere (“to break”).

parole.significato: To return to an earlier, simpler or worse condition; to regress.
parole.testo: From Latin retrōgressus, perfect active participle of retrōgradior (“retrograde”).

parole.significato: An animal that urinates backwards, such as the camel, hippo or raccoon.
parole.testo: From retro- (“backwards”) + past participle of Latin mingō (“to urinate”).

parole.significato: That drives or forces back; repelling or repellant.
parole.testo: From retro- + Latin pellere, pulsum (“to impel”).

parole.significato: Curved, pointed or oriented backward or downward.
