parole.significato: Consideration of past times.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin retrōspectum, from retrōspicio (“to look back at”), equivalent to retro- + -spect. Compare review.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or contemplating the past.
parole.testo: From retrospect + -ive. From Latin retrōspectus, perfect passive participle of retrōspiciō (“to look back at”).

parole.significato: Arranged in a backwards or reverse manner.
parole.testo: From Latin retroversus (“turned back”), from retro (“back”) + versum (“turned”). By surface analysis, retro- + -verse. Doublet of retrorse.

parole.significato: To turn back; to return to a previous state.
parole.testo: From retro- + Latin vertere, versum (“to turn”). Compare retrorse.

parole.significato: To thrust back.
parole.testo: From Latin retrudere; re- + trudere (“to thrust”).

parole.significato: Thrust backward; retruding.
parole.testo: From Latin retrusus (“concealed”), past participle of retrudere.

parole.significato: The act of retruding, or the state of being retruded.
parole.testo: From Latin retrūsiō, from retrūdō (“to push back”).

parole.significato: To blunt; to make less sharp.
parole.testo: From Latin retundere, retusum, from re- (“re-”) + tundere (“to beat”).

parole.significato: To draw back; to retract.
parole.testo: From Latin revellere, from re- + vellere (“to pluck, pull”).

parole.significato: To reveal.
parole.testo: Latin revēlātus, perfect passive participle of revēlō. By surface analysis this English verb can be interpreted as a back-formation from such words as revelation, revelator, and revelatory.

parole.significato: A person or personified agent who reveals; especially, one who makes a divine revelation.
parole.testo: From Middle English revelator, from Latin revēlātor; by surface analysis, revelate + -or.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or in the nature of a revelation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin revēlātōrius. By surface analysis, revelat(e) + -ory.

parole.significato: Causing revulsion; revulsive.
parole.testo: From Latin revellens.

parole.significato: To cause (a sound) to be (repeatedly) bounced against one or more surfaces; to re-echo.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin reverberātus, perfect passive participle of reverberō (“to rebound; to reflect; to repel”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), whence Middle French reverberer (French réverbérer) and Middle English reverberen (“to send back”)), from re- (prefix meaning ‘again’) and verberō (“to bea

parole.significato: Synonym of reverberant (“that tends to reverberate (“(repeatedly) bounce against one or more surfaces”) or has reverber…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin reverberātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more. etymology 2, adjective sense 2 (“ringing or vibrating with many echoing sounds”) was popularized by its use in Twelfth Night (written c. 1601–1602; published 1623) by the English playwright William Shakes

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or employing reverberation or deflection.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin reverberatorius; by surface analysis, reverberate + -ory.

parole.significato: Reverence.
parole.testo: From Latin reverentia.

parole.significato: Showing or characterized by reverence; respectful.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin reverentiālis, from Latin reverentia (“reverence”) + -ālis (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: The storage space or room in a church or temple where the vestments etc. are kept.
parole.testo: From Latin revestiarium: compare French revestiaire. See revest.

parole.significato: revival (return to life, usually figuratively)
parole.testo: From Latin revivere, revictum (“to live again”), from re- (“re-”) + vivere (“to live”).

parole.significato: To give new vigour to.
parole.testo: From Latin re- + vigoratus.

parole.significato: To overcome.
parole.testo: From Latin revincō.

parole.significato: A growing green or fresh again
parole.testo: From Latin revirescens, present participle of revirescere (“to grow green again”).

parole.significato: To revive; to revivify.
parole.testo: From Latin revīvificātus, past participle of revīvificō. Compare revivify. By surface analysis, re- + vivificate.

parole.significato: Able or disposed to revive; reviving.
parole.testo: From Latin reviviscens, present participle of reviviscere (“to revive”), from re- (“re-”) + viviscere, verb inchoate from vivere (“to live”).

parole.significato: To recall (troops, objects, etc)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin revoco, revocatus. Doublet of revoke.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to revocation; revocative; tending to revoke or recall.
parole.testo: Latin revocatorius: compare French révocatoire.

parole.significato: Capable of revolving.
parole.testo: From Latin revolubilis (“that may be rolled back”). See revolve.

parole.significato: Rolled or recurved on itself.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin revolūtus, perfect passive participle of revolvō (“roll back”).

parole.significato: To pull back with force.
parole.testo: From Latin revulsus (“revulsed”), past participle of revello (“to revulse”).

parole.significato: A king, particularly in ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin rēx (“king”). Doublet of rajah and roy. Noun sense 2 originally referred to rabbits of the Belgian "castorrex" breed, so named because their fur was similar to that of beavers, and entered English around 1920.

parole.significato: A righteous king, whose power is regarded as stemming from his piety etc.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rēx iūstus.

parole.significato: A senatorial priesthood in Ancient Rome, reserved for patricians.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rex (“king”) + sacrorum (“of the sacred”).

parole.significato: Divination with wands or rods, especially to use a divining rod to find things below the ground.
parole.testo: From rhabdo- + -mancy, first attested in 1646. From Latin rhabdomantīa, from Ancient Greek ῥαβδομαντεία (rhabdomanteía), from ῥάβδος (rhábdos, “rod”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).

parole.significato: A simple, straight spicule.
parole.testo: From a New Latin form of Ancient Greek ῥάβδος (rhábdos, “rod”).

parole.significato: A strict and just judge.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek Ῥαδάμανθυς (Rhadámanthus).

parole.significato: A variety of the mineral kyanite.
parole.testo: So called from Latin Rhaetia, Raetia (“the Rhetian Alps”), where it is found, + -ite.

parole.significato: The false rhubarb (Rheum rhaponticum)
parole.testo: From Latin rhaponticum, literally rha (“rhubarb”) ponticum (“Pontic; of the Black Sea”), from Ancient Greek ῥῆον (rhêon, “rhubarb”) and Ancient Greek Πόντος (Póntos, “Black Sea”).

parole.significato: chrysophanic acid
parole.testo: From Latin rhaponticum (“rhubarb”). See rhubarb.

parole.significato: An epic poem, or part of one, suitable for uninterrupted recitation.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Latin rhapsōdia (“part of an epic poem suitable for uninterrupted recitation”), from Koine Greek ῥαψῳδία (rhapsōidía, “part of an epic poem suitable for uninterrupted recitation; rigmarole”), Ancient Greek ῥαψῳδία (rhapsōidía, “composition or recitation of Epic poetry”), fro

parole.significato: A structure used for storage, sale, or manufacture of horse-drawn carriages.
parole.testo: From Latin rheda (“carriages”) + -arium, by analogy with aquarium.

parole.significato: An acid found in rhubarb; rhein.
parole.testo: From Latin rheum (“rhubarb”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A metallic chemical element with the atomic number 75: a heavy, silvery-gray transition metal.
parole.testo: From Latin Rhenus (“Rhine”), + -ium.

parole.significato: Part of or similar to rhetoric, the use of language as a means to persuade.
parole.testo: From Middle English rethorycal, rethoricalle, rethorycall, from rethorik, rhetoric (noun) or Latin rēthoricus, rhētoricus, from Ancient Greek ῥητορικός (rhētorikós, “concerning public speaking”). By surface analysis, rhetoric + -al.

parole.significato: To use rhetorical tropes or embellishments.
parole.testo: From Latin rhetoricari. See rhetoric.

parole.significato: A type of discourse that has a characteristic configuration of topics, themes, and arguments.
parole.testo: From Latin rhētorica from Ancient Greek ῥήτωρ (rhḗtōr, “public speaker”) + from Latin lectus, form of Latin legō (“to read”).

parole.significato: Any disorder of the muscles, tendons, joints, bones, nerves, characterized by pain, discomfort and disability.
parole.testo: First attested 1601, from Latin rheumatismus (“rheum”), from Ancient Greek ῥευματισμός (rheumatismós, “humour, discharge, rheum”) from ῥευματίζομαι (rheumatízomai, “to suffer from a rheum”) from ῥεῦμα (rheûma, “stream, flow”) from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”)

parole.significato: Inflammation of the nasal mucosa caused by the overuse of topical nasal decongestants.
parole.testo: From rhinitis + Latin medicamentosa (“medication”).

parole.significato: A type of chronic nasal inflammation where there is little to no nasal secretion, causing discomfort in breathing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin rhinitis sicca (“dry rhinitis”).

parole.significato: Any large herbivorous ungulate mammal native to Africa and Asia of the family Rhinocerotidae, with thick, gray skin and…
parole.testo: From Latin rhīnocerōs, from Ancient Greek ῥῑνόκερως (rhīnókerōs, “nose-horned”), composed of ῥῑ́ς, ῥῑνός (rhī́s, rhīnós, “nose, of (the) nose”) + κέρας (kéras, “horn”).

parole.significato: The rhinoceros.
parole.testo: From the inflected stem of Latin rhinoceros. Compare Middle French rhinocerote, obsolete Italian rinocerote.

parole.significato: a disorder that causes abnormal resonance in a human's voice due to increased airflow through the nose during speech
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The act or habit of nose-picking.
parole.testo: From rhino- + Latin tillexis.

parole.significato: Compulsive nose-picking; the insertion of a finger into one's nose.
parole.testo: From rhino- (“nose, nasal”) + Latin tillexis (“habit of plucking”, see below) + -o- + -mania (“obsession”). The tillexis stem is seemingly a New Latin borrowing from Ancient Greek τίλλω (tíllō, “to pluck or pull”). There is a divergence regarding the exo affix. It is suggested it may derive from ἔξω

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Rhipsalis, epiphytic flowering plants in the cactus family, often known as mistletoe cacti.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ῥίψ (rhíps, “wickerwork”) + Latin -alis (“-al”).

parole.significato: A rare, hard, silvery-white, inert metallic chemical element (symbol Rh) with an atomic number of 45.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin rhodium, from Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”), because of the colour of its salts' solutions.

parole.significato: Oleander (Nerium oleander).
parole.testo: The obsolete sense derives from Latin rhododendron (“oleander”), from Ancient Greek ῥοδόδενδρον (rhodódendron, “oleander”), from ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”) + δένδρον (déndron, “tree”). The modern sense comes through the intermediary of the genus name Rhododendron, not closely related taxonomically, but

parole.significato: A deciduous flowering shrub of species Rhododendron canadense, native to northeastern North America.
parole.testo: From Latin rhodōra.

parole.significato: An Archimedean solid with 62 regular faces (20 triangles, 30 squares, and 12 pentagons), 60 vertices and 120 edges.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin rhombicosidodecaēdron (coined by the German astronomer and mathematician Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) in his work Harmonices Mundi Libri V (The Harmony of the World in Five Books, 1619)), a blend of Latin rhomb(us) + īcos(aedron) + -i- + dodecaēdron. The English word

parole.significato: An Archimedean solid with eight triangular and eighteen square faces; the small rhombicuboctahedron.
parole.testo: From Latin rhombicuboctahaedron, referring to the fact that the twelve of the square faces lie in the same planes as the twelve faces of the rhombic dodecahedron, the dual of the cuboctahedron. (See rhombicuboctahedron on Wikipedia.Wikipedia )

parole.significato: A rhomboid.
parole.testo: From the Latin rhomboīdēs.

parole.significato: The ligament that joins the sternal end of the clavicle with the cartilage of the first rib.
parole.testo: From Latin rhomboideum.

parole.significato: Any of the rhomboid muscles.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A parallelogram having all sides of equal length.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rhombus, from Ancient Greek ῥόμβος (rhómbos, “rhombus, spinning top”). Doublet of rhomb and rhumb.

parole.significato: Making a snorting noise; snorting.
parole.testo: From Latin rhonchus, and sonans, the past participial of Latin sonare.

parole.significato: A dry rattling sound heard during breathing, due to deposits in the bronchial tubes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rhonchus (“snoring”), from Ancient Greek ῥόγχος (rhónkhos) (Caelius Aurelianus), of imitative origin.

parole.significato: Having each successive word longer by a letter or syllable.
parole.testo: From Latin rhopalicus, from Ancient Greek ῥόπαλον (rhópalon, “club, bat”).

parole.significato: One of the small sensory tentacular structures of various jellyfish species.
parole.testo: From New Latin rhopalium, from Ancient Greek ῥοπαλιον (rhopalion), diminutive of ῥόπαλον (rhópalon, “club”).

parole.significato: Having a series of fleshy lobes or filaments.
parole.testo: From New Latin rhopalium, from Ancient Greek ῥοπαλιον (rhopalion), diminutive of ῥόπαλον (rhópalon, “club”) + -cercous.

parole.significato: An exaggerated use of the sound of the letter R.
parole.testo: From New Latin rhōtacismus, from Ancient Greek *ῥωτακισμός (*rhōtakismós), from ῥωτακίζω (rhōtakízō, “to incorrectly use rho”), from ῥῶ (rhô, “rho (the Greek equivalent of r)”) in analogy with ἰωτακίζω (iōtakízō, “to incorrectly use iota”); itself from ἰῶτα (iôta) in analogy with ἀττικίζω (attikízō,

parole.significato: The variation of strong and weak elements (such as duration, accent) of sounds, notably in speech or music, over time;…
parole.testo: First coined in 1557, from Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós, “any measured flow or movement, symmetry, rhythm”), from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow, run, stream, gush”).

parole.significato: Someone who believes King Richard III was a just king, misrepresented by Tudor propaganda; a supporter of Richard III.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Ricardus (Latin form of Richard) + -ian.

parole.significato: An extremely toxic lectin extracted from the castor bean.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ricinus.

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or derived from, castor oil.
parole.testo: Latin ricinus (“castor-oil plant”).

parole.significato: An alkaloid extracted from the seeds of the castor oil plant, chemical formula C₈H₈N₂O₂
parole.testo: From Latin ricinus (“castor oil plant”) + -ine.

parole.significato: A mantle worn, mainly by women, in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin ricinium.

parole.significato: The glyceride of ricinoleic acid, present in castor oil.
parole.testo: From Latin ricinus (“castor-oil plant”) + oleum (“oil”).

parole.significato: A bird’s gaping mouth.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rictus.

parole.significato: laughing
parole.testo: From Latin ridens, present participle of ridere (“to laugh”).

parole.significato: Deserving of ridicule; foolish, absurd.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rīdiculus (“laughable, ridiculous”); Equivalent to ridicule + -ous.

parole.significato: irrigation
parole.testo: From Latin rigatio, from rigare (“to water”).

parole.significato: Becoming stiff or numb.
parole.testo: From Latin rigescens, present participle from rigescere (“to grow stiff”).

parole.significato: Half of the angle formed by a single straight line, equivalent to 90 degrees.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin angulus rectus.

parole.significato: Stiff, rather than flexible.
parole.testo: From Middle English rigide, from Latin rigidus (“stiff”), from rigeō (“to be stiff”). Compare rigor. Merged with Middle English rigged, rygged, rugged (“upright like a spine, rigid”, literally “ridged”).

parole.significato: The quality or state of being rigid; lack of pliability; the quality of resisting change of physical shape.
parole.testo: From rigid + -ity, from Latin rigiditas.

parole.significato: A heat-induced form of rigor mortis
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Temporary stiffness of the body's muscles and joints following death.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin rigor mortis (literally “stiffness of death”). First attested in 1842.

parole.significato: Someone who takes the strictest interpretation of a law, religious injunction etc.
parole.testo: From rigour, or its source, Latin rigor, + -ist.

parole.significato: A cleft or gap between two symmetrical parts, particularly between the vocal folds.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Latin rīma (“a cleft, crack, fissure, chink”).

parole.significato: The passage in the glottis between the true vocal cords.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin rīma glōttidis (“the cleft of the glottis”).

parole.significato: A narrow aperture or opening; a chink, a crack, a fissure; a rent, a rip.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English rim (“cleft, crack, fissure”), from Latin rīma (“chink, cleft, crack, fissure”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)reyH- (“to cut; to tear”). Doublet of rima. The verb is derived from Latin rīmārī, the present active infinitive of rīmor (“to explore

parole.significato: Having a surface covered with cracks, fissures, or crevices.
parole.testo: From Latin rimosus, from rima (“fissure”).

parole.significato: crack-shaped
parole.testo: From Latin rimula (“little crack”) + -iform.

parole.significato: A type of water snake formerly thought to poison water.
parole.testo: From Late Latin rinatrix (in Bartholomaeus Anglicus), apparently a misreading of Lucan 9.720 et natrix (“and the water snake”).

parole.significato: Having the semblance of lips parted wide, such as may be observed in certain flowers.
parole.testo: Latin ringens, from the verb ringi (“to open wide”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the bank of a river or stream.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rīpārius (“relating to a riverbank”) + -an.

parole.significato: Growing or living along the banks of rivers
parole.testo: Latin riparius.

parole.significato: The bank of a river.
parole.testo: From Middle English ripe, from Latin ripa.

parole.significato: Designating a range of mountains once thought to be located in northern Europe, later considered mythological or identi…
parole.testo: From Latin Rīphaeus + -an. Compare Rhipaean.

parole.significato: Any of the Ripuarian tribal section of the Frank people (comprising several tribes), who after some migration inhabited…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Ripuarius (perhaps from Latin ripa (“river bank”)) + -an.

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or producing, laughter.
parole.testo: From Latin risorius + -al.

parole.significato: A narrow band of facial muscle arising from the fascia over the masseter and inserting into the tissues at the corner o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin rīsōrius (“ridiculous, laughing”), clipping of mūsculus rīsōrius (“laughing muscle”).

parole.significato: A rictus grin; an abnormal sustained spasm of the facial muscles that appears to produce grinning, characteristic of te…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Related to a rite or repeated set of actions.
parole.testo: From Latin rītuālis (adjective), from rītus (“rite”) + -ālis. Displaced native Old English ġewuna and wuna.

parole.significato: A competitor (person, team, company, etc.) with the same goal as another, or striving to attain the same thing. Defeati…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rīvālis (literally “person using the same stream as another”). By surface analysis, Latin rīvus + -al.

parole.significato: rivalry; competition
parole.testo: From rival + -ity, from Latin rivalitas: compare French rivalité.

parole.significato: An anticoagulant drug C₁₉H₁₈ClN₃O₅S (trademark Xarelto) that inhibits the activity of factor X and is taken orally espe…
parole.testo: From rivaro- + -xaban (“blood coagulation factor Xa inhibitor”). The prefix is probably from Latin rīvārō, conjugation of rīvō (“to draw off, to withdraw”).

parole.significato: Marked with sinuate and irregular furrows.
parole.testo: From Latin rivus (“a brook, channel”).

parole.significato: Marked by thin, winding or crooked lines.
parole.testo: From Latin rivulus (“rivulet”) + -ose.

parole.significato: Scolding; brawling.
parole.testo: From Latin rīxārī (“to quarrel”).

parole.significato: quarrelsome
parole.testo: From Latin rixa + -y.

parole.significato: A syrup made of evaporating fruit juice over a fire, usually mixed with sugar or honey, and especially used for medicin…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rob, from Arabic ربّ (“thickened fruit juice”). Compare French rob, Spanish rob, Italian rob, robbo, Portuguese robe, arrobe, Persian ربودن (present stem: robâ).

parole.significato: Synonym of strengthening or restorative.
parole.testo: From Latin rōborāns (“strengthening”) directly and via Medieval Latin roborantia (“strengthening medicine”), from rōborāre (“to strengthen, to confirm”), from rōbur (“reddish oak; hardness, strength”) + -āre (“forming verbs”). Equivalent to roborate + -ant.

parole.significato: Synonym of confirm, to verify, to establish.
parole.testo: From Latin rōborāre (“to strengthen, to confirm”) + -ate (“forming verbs”), from rōbur (“reddish oak; hardness, strength”) + -āre (“forming verbs”).

parole.significato: Synonym of confirmation or ratification.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rōborātiō (“strengthening, confirmation, validity”), from rōborāre (“to strengthen, to confirm”) + -tiō (“-tion: forming abstract nouns”), from rōbur (“reddish oak; hardness, strength”) + -āre (“forming verbs”). Equivalent to roborate + -tion.

parole.significato: Synonym of roborant: strengthening, invigorating, or restorative.
parole.testo: From Latin rōborāre (“to strengthen, to invigorate”) + -ive (“forming adjectives”) directly and via French roboratif, from rōbur (“reddish oak; hardness, strength”) + -āre (“forming verbs”). Equivalent to roborate + -ive.

parole.significato: Synonym of oaken, made of oak or similar wood.
parole.testo: From Latin rōboreus (“oaken, sturdy”) + -an (“forming adjectives”), from robur (“reddish oak; strength, hardness”) + -eus (“-eous: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Synonym of oaken, made of oak wood.
parole.testo: From Latin roboreus (“oak, oaken, sturdy”), from robur (“reddish oak; strength, hardness”) + -eus (“-eous: forming adjectives”). Equivalent to roborate + -eous.

parole.significato: Able to withstand adverse conditions.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rōbustus.

parole.significato: Any plant of the species Coffea canephora of coffee plants, native to Africa, cultivated widely in Brazil.
parole.testo: From New Latin Coffea robusta, from Latin rōbusta, feminine of rōbustus (“strong”).

parole.significato: The lethal toxin from the Sydney funnel-web spider.
parole.testo: From New Latin Atrax robusta (“robust Atrax, the Sydney funnel-web spider”) + toxin.

parole.significato: Naphtha (liquid petroleum).
parole.testo: From rock + oil, a literal rendering of Latin petroleum (literally “rock oil”).

parole.significato: A mammal of the order Rodentia, characterized by long incisors that grow continuously and are worn down by gnawing.
parole.testo: From Latin rōdēns, rōdent- (“gnawer; one who gnaws”), present participle of rōdō (“to gnaw”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Rodentia.
parole.testo: From Latin stem of rodens (“gnawing”), + -ine.

parole.significato: A deeply serious and somber prayer or entreaty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rogātiō, from rogō (“request”). By surface analysis, Latin rog- + -ate + -ion.

parole.significato: To ask a question repeatedly.
parole.testo: From Latin rogitātus (“inquired”), past participle of rogitō (“inquire”).

parole.significato: A variety of tomato.
parole.testo: From Latin and Italian Roma (“Rome”). Doublet of Rome and Rum.

parole.parola: Roma locuta est, causa finita est
parole.significato: The discussion is at an end.
parole.testo: From Latin, literally "Rome has spoken, the case is closed".

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Eastern Roman Empire, that is, to the Byzantine Empire.
parole.testo: From post-Classical Latin Rōmaeus [calque of Ancient Greek Ῥωμαῖος (Rhōmaîos)] + -an. By surface analysis, Rome + -ean.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Rome or its people, especially Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rōmānicus. See Romance.

parole.significato: A person with romantic character (a character like those of the knights in a mythic romance).
parole.testo: From romant + -ic, or borrowed from Late Latin romanticus (“(of a poem) having qualities of a romance”). Compare French romantique, which is borrowed from English. Also compare Spanish romántico, Portuguese romântico, Italian romantico, Dutch romantisch, and German romantisch and Romantiker (“a comp

parole.significato: One of a particular English breed of small sheep with long wool and horns.
parole.testo: From a name of a village in Kent (see Old Romney), from a compound of Latin rumen (“gullet”) and Old English ēa (“river”).

parole.significato: Relating to dew; dewy.
parole.testo: From Latin rōs, rōris (“dew”).

parole.significato: Synonym of dewfall.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rōrātio (“dewfall”).

parole.significato: dew
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rōs, rōris (“dew, moisture”).

parole.significato: Resembling, pertaining to, or containing dew; dewy.
parole.testo: From Latin ros, roris (“dew”).

parole.significato: Dewy; containing dew.
parole.testo: From Latin rōridus, from rōs, rōris (“dew”).

parole.significato: Producing or generating dew.
parole.testo: From Latin rōrifer, from rōs (“dew, moisture”) + ferō (“carry, bear”), + -ous.

parole.significato: flowing with dew
parole.testo: From Latin ros, roris (“dew”) + fluens, present participle of fluere (“to flow”).

parole.significato: Full of dew.
parole.testo: From Latin rōrulentus (“full of dew, dewy”), from oblique stem of rōs, rōris (“dew”) + -ulentus (“full of, abounding in”) (whence -ule and -ent).

parole.significato: Covered by dew.
parole.testo: From Latin rōs / rōris (“dew”).

parole.significato: A chronic condition characterized by redness of the face.
parole.testo: Clipping of acne rosacea, from New Latin acnē (“acne”) + rosācea, feminine of rosāceus (“rose-colored”).

parole.testo: From Latin satispassiō, a compound of satis (“enough”) and passio (“suffering, or sufferance”). Compare passion.

parole.significato: Sown or planted; propagated by seed, shoot, or root; cultivated, not wild.
parole.testo: From Latin satīvus (“that may be sown or planted”).

parole.significato: A governor of a Persian province.
parole.testo: From Middle English satrape, from Latin satrapēs (“governor”), from Ancient Greek σατράπης (satrápēs), from Old Median *xšaθrapāvan (literally “kingdom-protector”), which is cognate with Old Persian 𐎧𐏁𐏂𐎱𐎠𐎺𐎠 (xšaçapāvā); see there for more.

parole.significato: Capable of being saturated, of achieving saturation
parole.testo: From Latin saturabilis: compare French saturable.

parole.significato: To cause to become completely permeated with, or soaked (especially with a liquid).
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in the second part of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English, the verb in 1538, the noun in 1921; inherited from Middle English saturat(e) (“satiated, satisfied”), borrowed from Latin saturātus, perfect passive participle of saturō (“to fill, satisfy, quench”) (see -ate

parole.significato: The act of saturating or the process of being saturated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin saturatio, saturationem.

parole.significato: The state of being satiated; fullness, repletion.
parole.testo: From Latin saturitas.

parole.significato: Sable (black), in the postmedieval practice of blazoning the tinctures in the arms of certain sovereign people and plac…
parole.testo: From Old English Sætern, from Latin Sāturnus, probably from Etruscan 𐌔𐌀𐌕𐌓𐌄 (satre), plausibly influenced by Latin satus, past participle of serere (“to sow”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Ancient Roman god Saturn or to the corresponding planetary entity in astrology.
parole.testo: From Latin saturnalis, itself from the Roman god Saturnus + -alis '-al'.

parole.significato: Excessive sexual desire, found in a man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin satyriasis, from Ancient Greek σατυρίασις (saturíasis).

parole.significato: Any of various kinds of orchids.
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek σατύριον (satúrion, “a kind of orchid”) from Σάτυρος (Sáturos, “a Satyr”).

parole.significato: Any of several Mediterranean herbs, of the genus Satureja, grown as culinary flavourings.
parole.testo: From Middle English saverey, possibly from Old English sæþerie, from Latin satureia, influenced by or via Old French savereie.

parole.significato: Living among rocks.
parole.testo: From Latin saxatilis, from saxum (“a rock”).

parole.significato: Boring or hollowing out rocks.
parole.testo: Latin saxum (“rock”) + cavare (“to make hollow”), from cavus (“hollow”): compare French saxicave.

parole.significato: Growing on, or living among, rocks or stones.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin saxum (“a rock”) + Latin colere (“to dwell”) + -ous.

parole.significato: Dissolving bladder stones.
parole.testo: Latin saxifragus (“stone-breaking”), from saxum (“stone”) + frangere (“to break”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the Anglo-Saxons or the Old English language.
parole.testo: From medieval Latin Saxonicus (“Saxon”) + -al. Compare Saxonic.

parole.significato: A fine soft woollen fabric.
parole.testo: From Middle English Saxonie, from Latin Saxōnia, from Saxō (stem Saxōn-) + -ia. By surface analysis, Saxon + -y.

parole.significato: A kind of percussion instrument played by the foot, used in dramatic performances.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scabellum.

parole.testo: From Middle English scabies, scabiez, from Latin scabiēs (“scurf; scab, mange, itch”), from scabō (“scratch, scrape”, verb).

parole.significato: Having scabs.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin scabiōsus (“scabious”), from Latin scabiēs (see scabies); partly reinterpretable as scab + -ious.

parole.significato: Any of various herbaceous plants of the genus Scabiosa.
parole.testo: ] From Medieval Latin scabiōsa, substantivized from scabiōsus (“scabious”), see Etymology 1; the name comes from their medical use in the Middle Ages to cure scabies and leprosy.

parole.significato: Roughness (of a surface).
parole.testo: From Latin scabrēdō (“roughness of the skin, scabbiness”) + -ity.

parole.significato: Covered with scales or scabs; hence, very coarse or rough.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scaber (“scabrous, rough; scabby, mangy, itchy”) (from scabō (“to scratch, scrape, abrade”), from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scratch”)) + English -ous; compare French scabreux, Late Latin scabrōsus.

parole.significato: Short, stiff projections or hairs which give a stem or leaf a rough texture, at least in one direction.

parole.significato: unluckiness
parole.testo: From Latin scaevitas, obsolete, 1623-1658, from scaevus.

parole.significato: Ladder; sequence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scāla (“ladder”). Doublet of scale.

parole.significato: Having magnitude but not direction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scālāris, adjectival form from scāla (“a flight of steps, stairs, staircase, ladder, scale”), for *scadla, from scandere (“to climb”); compare scale. The mathematics sense was coined by Irish mathematician and astronomer William Rowan Hamilton in 1846.

parole.significato: Having the form of a ladder
parole.testo: Latin scala (“ladder”), + -form.

parole.significato: Like a ladder; formed with steps.
parole.testo: Latin scalaris, from scale, plural scala (“staircase, ladder”).

parole.significato: A ladder; a series of steps; a means of ascending.
parole.testo: From Middle English scale, from Latin scāla, usually in plural scālae (“a flight of steps, stairs, staircase, ladder”), for *skand-slā, from scandō (“to climb”); see scan, ascend, descend, etc. Doublet of scala.

parole.significato: Having sides all unequal in length.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin scalēnus (“of unequal sides”), from Ancient Greek σκᾰληνός (skălēnós, “uneven, unequal”).

parole.significato: A small straight knife with a very sharp blade used for surgery, dissection and craftwork.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scalpellum, from scalprum (“knife”), from scalpere (“to cut”). Doublet of scalpellum.

parole.significato: One of the four filamentous organs in the proboscis of hemipterous insects.
parole.testo: From Latin scalpellum. Doublet of scalpel.

parole.significato: Shaped like a chisel.
parole.testo: From Latin scalprum (“chisel, knife”) + -form.

parole.significato: A toothed raspatory used in trephining and in removing carious bone.
parole.testo: From Latin scalprum.

parole.testo: From Latin [Term?] (“a little bench”), from scamnum (“bench, stool”).

parole.significato: To examine sequentially, carefully, or critically; to scrutinize; to behold closely.

parole.significato: To cause great offense to (someone); to shock with something scandalous.
parole.testo: From Latin scandalizō, from Ancient Greek σκανδαλίζω (skandalízō). By surface analysis, scandal + -ize.

parole.significato: defamation of a Great Officer of State or member of the peerage.

parole.significato: Climbing, without obvious morphological adaptations.

parole.significato: The rhythm or meter of a line or verse.

parole.significato: Adapted to or specialised for climbing
parole.testo: From Latin scansarius, from scansus, past participle of scandere (“to climb”).

parole.significato: Formed for climbing.
parole.testo: From Latin scansorius (“climbing”) + -ous, from scansus + -torius.

parole.significato: A muscle passing from the ilium to the femur in some vertebrates.
parole.testo: From Latin scansorius (“climbing”), from scansus + -torius.

parole.significato: A leafless stalk growing directly out of a root, bulb, or subterranean structure.
parole.testo: From Latin scāpus, from Doric Greek σκᾶπος (skâpos). Doublet of native English shaft.

parole.significato: The scaphoid fossa of the helix of the ear.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scapha (“light boat; skiff”).

parole.significato: The carina or keel of papilionaceous flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scaphium, from Ancient Greek σκάφιον (skáphion).

parole.significato: Shaped like a boat.
parole.testo: From Latin scaphoides, from Ancient Greek σκᾰφοειδής (skăphoeidḗs, “like a bowl, hollow”), from σκᾰ́φη (skắphē, “boat, trough, bowl”).

parole.significato: To work roughly, or shape without finishing, as stone before leaving the quarry.
parole.testo: Compare Old French eskaper, eschapler (“to cut, hew”), Late Latin scapello. Compare scabble.

parole.significato: Either of the two large, flat, bones forming the back of the shoulder.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the scapula.

parole.significato: scapular
parole.testo: From Middle English scapelarie, from Latin scapulārium, scapulāre.

parole.significato: A scape.
parole.testo: From Latin scapus (“shaft”).

parole.significato: A marine food fish, the scarus or parrotfish (family Scaridae).
parole.testo: From Latin scarus (“a kind of fish”), from Ancient Greek σκάρος (skáros, “parrot wrasse, Sparisoma cretense, syn. Scarus cretensis”).

parole.significato: An instrument, principally used in cupping, containing several lancets that are moved simultaneously by a spring, used…

parole.significato: A parrotfish, a Mediterranean food fish (any of various Scaridae species).

Equivalent to scato- + -phage. In particular reference to dungflies, an anglicization o

parole.significato: Abundant; overflowing.

parole.significato: A limping satiric meter in classical verse.

parole.significato: Wicked; villainous.

parole.significato: evil; wicked; atrocious
parole.testo: From Latin scelestus, from scelus (“wickedness”).

parole.significato: The design of theatrical sets.

parole.significato: A written paper.

parole.testo: From late Middle English scheame, from Medieval Latin schēma (“figure, form”), from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”), from ἔχω (ékhō, “to hold”). Doublet of schema. Compare sketch.

parole.significato: An Egyptian or Persian measure of length, varying from thirty-two to sixty stadia.
parole.testo: From Latin schoenus, from Ancient Greek σχοῖνος (skhoînos, “a rush, a reed, a land measure”).

parole.significato: A hard swelling of a gland or other organ.

parole.significato: A very small interval equal to half a comma.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin schisma, from Ancient Greek σχίσμα (skhísma, “cleft, division”), whence the orthographic borrowing skhisma. Doublet of schism.

parole.significato: An ancient unit of length and area based on the knotted cords first used in Egyptian surveying.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Originally, a musical school attached to a monastery or church. Also known as a schola cantorum.
parole.testo: From Latin schola. Doublet of school and shul.

parole.significato: A student; one who studies at school or college, typically having a scholarship.
parole.testo: From Middle English scolar, scolare, scoler, scolere (also scholer), from Old English scōlere (“scholar, learner”), from Late Latin scholāris, from schola (“school”), from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ, “spare time, leisure", later, "conversations and the knowledge gained through them during free time

parole.significato: A scholar who writes commentary on the works of an author, especially one of the ancient commentators on classical auth…
parole.testo: From Late Latin scholiasta, from Byzantine Greek σχολιαστής (skholiastḗs), from σχολιάζειν (skholiázein), from Ancient Greek σχόλιον (skhólion).

parole.significato: scholastic; academic
parole.testo: From Latin scholicus. See school.

parole.significato: A scholium.

parole.significato: A note added to a text as an explanation, criticism or commentary.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek σχόλιον (skhólion, “comment”), from σχολή (skholḗ, “discussion”).

parole.significato: A vowel formerly reconstructed for Proto-Indo-European; now generally held to be a syllabic laryngeal consonant.

parole.significato: An anaptyctic vowel inserted to break up illicit word-initial consonant clusters in Proto-Indo-European, particularly w…

parole.significato: Any of several nocturnal fish, of the genus Sciaena, from the Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean Sea and Black Sea; a croa…

parole.significato: shadow-boxing; fighting that is futile or make-believe
parole.testo: From Late Latin sciamachia, and its source, Hellenistic Ancient Greek σκιαμαχία (skiamakhía), from σκιά (skiá, “shadow”) + μάχη (mákhē, “battle”).

parole.significato: Neuralgia of the sciatic nerve, characterised by pain radiating down through the buttocks and the back of the thigh.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Late Latin sciatica, feminine of sciaticus, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιαδικός (iskhiadikós), the adjective of ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip”).

parole.significato: The sum of all the political, economic, technological, scientific, military, geographical, and psychological knowledge…
parole.testo: From Latin scienda (“things which ought to be known”), the nominative neuter plural of sciendus (“which ought to be known”), the gerundive of sciō (“to know”).

parole.significato: Knowing; aware; knowledgeable.
parole.testo: From Latin sciēns (“knowing”), from sciō (“know”).

parole.significato: deliberately, knowingly
parole.testo: From Latin scienter (“knowingly”), from sciō (“know”).

parole.significato: Knowledge is power; with knowledge or education, one's potential or abilities in life will certainly increase.
parole.testo: From Latin scientia potentia est (“knowledge is power”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to science or to knowledge.
parole.testo: Latin scientia (“knowledge”) + suffix -al.

parole.significato: The belief that the scientific method and the assumptions and research methods of the physical sciences are applicable…
parole.testo: From scient- (in either Classical Latin scientia or scientific) + -ism. Compare scientist.

parole.testo: Coined by English philosopher and historian of science William Whewell in March 1834 in an anonymous review of Mary Somerville's book On the Connexion of the Physical Sciences in the Quarterly Review as a suggested replacement for, and later seriously introduced by him in 1840 (see the quotation) as

parole.significato: Namely, to wit, as follows.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scīlicet.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Scilla; a squill.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scilla, from Ancient Greek σκίλλα (skílla). Doublet of squill.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the family Scincidae, or skinks.
parole.testo: Latin scincus a kind of lizard, from Ancient Greek σκίγγος (skíngos), σκίγκος (skínkos), + -oid. Compare skink.

parole.significato: A kind of stinging or biting insect; a flea, gnat, sandfly, or the like.
parole.testo: From Latin scinifes, cinifes or ciniphes, plural, from Ancient Greek σκνίψ (skníps, “gnat, small fly(, flea?)”), plural σκνῖφες (sknîphes) or σκνῖπες (sknîpes).

parole.significato: A small spark or flash.
parole.testo: Existing in English since the 17th century; borrowed from Latin scintilla (“spark”).

parole.significato: To give off sparks; to shine as if emanating sparks; to twinkle or glow.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scintillātus, past participle of scintillāre (“to sparkle, glitter, gleam, flash”), from scintilla (“a spark”).

parole.significato: One who exhibits only superficial knowledge; a self-proclaimed expert with little real understanding.
parole.testo: From Late Latin sciolus + -ist. First attested at the beginning of the 17th century.

parole.significato: Knowing superficially or imperfectly.
parole.testo: From Latin scīlus, sciolus, diminutive of scius (“knowing”), from sciō (“to know”). See science.

parole.significato: divination using shadows
parole.testo: From Late Latin sciomantia, from Ancient Greek σκιά (skiá, “shadow”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).

parole.significato: A judicial writ directing the sheriff to make the record known to a specified party, and requiring that defendant to sh…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scīre faciās (“let them know”).

parole.significato: The act of inquiring; inquiry; demand.
parole.testo: From Latin sciscitatio, from sciscere (“to seek to know”), verb inchoate from scire (“to know”).

parole.significato: To cut; to penetrate.
parole.testo: From Latin scindere, scissum (“to cut, split”); form influenced by the unrelated excise.

parole.significato: Capable of being cut by a sharp instrument.

parole.significato: Readily cut or split.

parole.testo: From Latin scissus, past participle of scindere (“to split”) + parere (“to bring forth”). Compare French scissiparité.

parole.significato: A longitudinal opening made by cutting; a cleft; a fissure.
parole.testo: From Late Latin scissura (“fissure”), from Latin scissurus (“about to split”), from scindo (“to split”).

parole.significato: The sum of all the political, economic, technological, scientific, military, geographical, and psychological knowledge…

parole.significato: A pleasant dish or delicacy.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or characteristic of squirrels.

parole.significato: The white of the eye; the tough outer coat of the eye that covers the eyeball except for the cornea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin sclera, from Ancient Greek σκληρός (sklērós, “hard”).

parole.significato: Resembling sawdust, filings or shavings.

parole.significato: The pedicle of the spikelets of grasses.

parole.significato: Raspings of wood, ivory, hartshorn, metals, or other hard substance.

parole.significato: The abnormal lateral curvature of the spine.

parole.significato: Resembling a snipe.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Scolopacidae, or sandpipers.

parole.significato: A mythical sea-creature, reputed to be able to disgorge its bowels to dislodge any fishing-hook.
parole.testo: From Latin scolopendra, from Ancient Greek σκολόπενδρα (skolópendra).

parole.significato: A fish of the genus Scomber.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scomber.

parole.significato: Of or relating to mackerel.

parole.significato: An idiot: a buffoon.

parole.significato: A small European migratory owl, Otus scops, that winters in sub-Saharran Africa.

parole.significato: A dense tuft of hair, as on the legs of certain insects.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or suffering from scurvy.
