parole.significato: The disease scurvy.
parole.testo: From New Latin scorbūtus, from French scorbut. Doublet of scorbut and scurvy.

parole.significato: The slag or dross that remains after the smelting of metal from an ore.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English, from Latin scōria, from Ancient Greek σκωρία (skōría), from σκῶρ (skôr, “dung”).

parole.significato: Someone with a Scorpio star sign
parole.testo: From Latin scorpiō (“scorpion”), from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos), calque of Akkadian 𒀯𒄈𒋰 (zuqaqīpu, “scorpion; constellation name”), calque of Sumerian 𒀯𒄈𒋰 (ᴹᵁᴸGIR₂.TAB). Doublet of scorpion.

parole.significato: Someone with the Scorpio star sign.
parole.testo: From the animal scorpion, from Latin scorpio (“scorpion”).

parole.significato: Any of the order Scorpiones of arachnids related to spiders, characterised by two large front pincers and a curved tail…
parole.testo: From Middle English scorpioun, skorpioun, schorpion, schorpiun, partly from Old English sċorpio and partly from Anglo-Norman scorpïun, Old French scorpïon, escorpïon; all from Latin scorpiō, ultimately from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos). The cheerleading move is so called because of the resembla

parole.significato: lewdness, fornication
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scortātiō, from scortārī.

parole.significato: Pertaining to scortation; fornicatory, lewd.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scortātōrius, from scortātor.

parole.significato: A person born in or native to Scotland.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Scot, from Old English Sċottas (“people from Ireland, Irishmen”), from Late Latin Scōttī (see Scōtī for more). See Scoti.

parole.significato: A concave molding with a lower edge projecting beyond the top.
parole.testo: From Latin scotia, from Ancient Greek σκοτία (skotía, “dark, shadowy”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to ancient Scotland.
parole.testo: From Latin Scōticus. By surface analysis, Scot + -ic.

parole.significato: A combining form relating to Scotland or Scottish people.
parole.testo: From Latin Scōto-, from Scōtus (“Scottish; a Scot”).

parole.significato: An area of impaired or lost vision within a visual field otherwise in a good (or at least healthy) state.
parole.testo: From Late Latin scotoma, from Ancient Greek σκότωμα (skótōma), from σκότος (skótos, “darkness”). By surface analysis, scot- + -oma. The figurative sense is an extension from the literal sense, as if the mind, like an eye, cannot "see" certain things.

parole.significato: To write or draw carelessly and in a hurry.
parole.testo: From Middle English scriblen, from (1) scrīben + -le and/or (2) Latin scrībillō (found in conscrībillō), from cōnscrībō, from scrībō (“write”), equivalent to scribe + -le (frequentative suffix).

parole.significato: To write.
parole.testo: From Middle English scryben (“to write”), from Latin scrībō (“to write”). Doublet of shrive. The carpentry sense comes from the way a workman uses a compass to mark a line before cutting.

parole.significato: An inscription indicating the identity of the person who wrote something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scrīpsit.

parole.significato: Synonym of scriptio continua.
parole.testo: From Latin scrīpta + continua.

parole.significato: A style of writing without spacing between the words of the text, particularly writing without any punctuation at all.
parole.testo: From Latin scrīptiō (“writing”) + continua (“continuous, held together”).

parole.significato: A writer, regarded as producing a work but not as providing its explanation (which is instead determined by the reader)…
parole.testo: From Latin scrīptor, to avoid the etymological link between author and authority.

parole.significato: One who is familiar with scripture or sacred writing, or who refers back to it frequently.
parole.testo: Derived from scripture, from Latin scrīptūra (“a writing, scripture”), from scrīptum, the supine of scrībō (“to write”), by analogy with terms such as historian.

parole.significato: A room set aside for the copying, writing, or illuminating of manuscripts and records, especially such a room in a mona…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin scrīptōrium, from Latin scrīptōrius (“pertaining to writing”). Doublet of escritoire.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to writing; expressed or used in writing; written.
parole.testo: From Latin scriptorius, from scribo (“to write”).

parole.significato: Synonym of scriptio continua.
parole.testo: From Latin scrīptūra + continua.

parole.significato: The foundational text of a given religion, or a text considered especially holy.
parole.testo: From Latin scrīptūra (“a writing, scripture”), from scrīptum, the supine of scrībō (“to write”).

parole.significato: A sacred writing or holy book.
parole.testo: From Middle English scripture, from Latin scrīptūra (“a writing, scripture”), from scrīptum, the supine of scrībō (“to write”). By surface analysis, script + -ure.

parole.significato: A trench.
parole.testo: From Latin scrobis (“ditch, dike, trench”).

parole.significato: A small groove, slit, or pit, commonly referring to roughness in the shell, or other firm surface, of an organism. cf.…
parole.testo: From New Latin scrobicula, alteration of Latin scrobiculus (“little trench”), from scrobis + -culus (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: A form of tuberculosis, most common in women 30-40 years of age, tending to cause enlarged and degenerated lymph nodes,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scrōfulae, a diminutive form of scrōfa (“breeding sow”), because swine were supposed to be subject to the complaint; or by fanciful comparison of the glandular swellings to little pigs.

parole.significato: Any affliction of the skin dependent on scrofula.
parole.testo: Latin diminutive of scrōfa (“a breeding sow”), because swine were supposed to be subject to the complaint; or by fanciful comparison of the glandular swellings to little pigs.

parole.significato: Of, related to, or suffering from scrofula (form of tuberculosis tending to cause enlarged lymph nodes and skin inflamm…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin scrōfulōsus. By surface analysis, scrofula + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the scrotum.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin scrōtālis. Equivalent to scrotum + -al.

parole.significato: The sac of skin and muscle that contains and protects the testicles in most placental mammals.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin scrōtum.

parole.significato: The property of being scrupulous; excessive attention to scruples.
parole.testo: From scrupulo(u)s + -ity, from Latin scrupulositas.

parole.significato: To scrutinize, peruse, inspect, investigate (something).
parole.testo: From Latin scrūtātus, perfect passive participle of scrūtor (“to search”).

parole.significato: Search; scrutiny.
parole.testo: Latin scrutatio.

parole.significato: A person who scrutinizes or investigates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scrūtātor.

parole.significato: To examine (something) carefully; to scrutinize.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scrūtor, scrūtārī (“to search carefully; to seek for”). Now often reanalyzed from inscrutable.

parole.significato: Intense study of someone or something.
parole.testo: From Middle English scrutiny, from Medieval Latin scrūtinium (“a search, an inquiry”), from Vulgar Latin scrūtor (“to search or examine thoroughly”), from Late Latin scrūta (“rubbish, broken trash”), from an extension of Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”).

parole.significato: A small fish of the family Cottidae, usually lacking scales. Often found on river bottoms and in tidal pools.
parole.testo: From earlier scorpene, from Latin scorpaena, from Ancient Greek σκόρπαινα (skórpaina, “kind of fish”), diminutive of σκορπίος (skorpíos). Compare scorpionfish.

parole.significato: An inscription indicating the identity of the person who created a sculpture.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Formed by carving; graven.
parole.testo: From Latin sculptilis.

parole.significato: A person who sculpts; an artist who produces sculpture.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sculptor, equivalent to sculpt + -or.

parole.significato: A woman who sculpts; a female sculptor; a sculptress.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sculptrīx. By surface analysis, sculpt + -trix.

parole.significato: Something that is scurrilous.
parole.testo: From scurril(ous) + -ity, from Latin scurrilitas.

parole.significato: Of a person, given to vulgar verbal abuse; foul-mouthed.
parole.testo: From Latin scurrīlis (“buffoon-like”) + -ous, from scurra (“a buffoon”).

parole.significato: A tax, paid in lieu of military service, that was a significant source of revenue in England in the twelfth and thirtee…
parole.testo: From Middle English scutage, from Medieval Latin scutagium, from Latin scutum (“shield”).

parole.significato: Shaped like a shield or buckler.
parole.testo: From Latin scutātus, from scutum (“shield”).

parole.significato: A horny, chitinous, or bony external plate or scale, as on the shell of a turtle, the skin of crocodiles, or the feet a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scutum (“shield”). Compare scutum, escudo, scudo, and écu.

parole.significato: saucer-shaped
parole.testo: Latin scutella (“a dish, salver”). Compare English scuttle (“a basket”).

parole.significato: scutellate, saucer-shaped
parole.testo: From Latin scutella (“a dish”) + -form.

parole.significato: Having thick scutella on the front, and small scales on the posterior side, of the tarsus.
parole.testo: From Latin scutellus (“a shield”) + planta (“foot”).

parole.significato: Any of several shield-shaped structures in insects, grasses etc
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin scūtellum, diminutive of Latin scūtum (“shield”).

parole.significato: Having a scute.
parole.testo: From Latin scutum (“shield”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Having the shape of a shield; scutate.
parole.testo: Latin scutum (“shield”) + -form

parole.significato: A container like an open bucket (usually to hold and carry coal).
parole.testo: From Middle English scuttel, scutel, from Old English scutel (“dish, platter”), from Latin scutella, diminutive form of Latin scutra (“flat tray, dish”), perhaps related to Latin scutum (“shield”); compare Dutch schotel and German Schüssel.

parole.significato: A yellow perifollicular saucer- or cup-shaped crust with a cheesy odour, composed of dense mats of mycelia and epitheli…
parole.testo: From Latin scutulum, diminutive of scutum (“shield”).

parole.significato: An oblong shield made of boards or wickerwork covered with leather, with sometimes an iron rim; carried chiefly by the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scūtum (“shield”). Doublet of escudo, scudo, scute, and écu.

parole.significato: Concave or cup-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin scyphātus, erroneously interpreted as scyphus (“cup, goblet”) + -ātus; in reality, probably derives from Arabic شَفَة (šafa, “edge, rim”), and refers to the distinctive and conspicuous border of the early histamena gold coins.

parole.significato: Shaped like a cup.
parole.testo: From Latin scyphus (“a cup”) + -iform.

parole.significato: A kind of large drinking cup used in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome, especially by poor people.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scyphus (“cup”), from Ancient Greek σκῠ́φος (skŭ́phos).

parole.significato: A cylinder with a strip of parchment wound around it on which a message is written, used for cryptography by the ancien…
parole.testo: From Latin scytale (“cylinder used for encoding and decoding”), from Ancient Greek σκυτάλη (skutálē, “club, baton, cylinder used for encoding and decoding”).

parole.significato: Any member of the family Scytalinidae of very slender burrowing fish called graveldivers.
parole.testo: From Latin Scytalinidae, from Ancient Greek σκυτάλη (skutálē, “club”) + -ινος (-inos, “-ine”) + -ίδης (-ídēs, “-id”). Equivalent to scytale + -ine + -id.

parole.significato: A tetralone derivative involved in certain redox reactions.
parole.testo: From scytale + -one, from Latin scytale, from Ancient Greek σκυτάλη (skutálē, “club”).

parole.significato: A Scythian.
parole.testo: From Latin Scytha, from Ancient Greek Σκύθης (Skúthēs). Doublet of Saca, Saka, and Shaka.

parole.significato: Scythian
parole.testo: From Latin scythicus.

parole.significato: A plea of self-defense.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Synonym of common seal (Phoca vitulina).
parole.testo: From Middle English see calf, ultimately a calque of Latin vitulus marīnus (literally “sea calf”). Compare French veau marin and German Seekalb. See also Latin porcus marīnus (“porpoise”, literally “sea pork”), rāna marīna (“anglerfish”, literally “sea frog”), bōs marīna (“sea cow, dugong”), caballu

parole.significato: Any of various birds which may be found at sea or along the coast, especially those of a size or color similar to a cro…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin corvus maritimus (“cormorant”).

parole.significato: An old English measure of grain, containing eight bushels.
parole.testo: From Old English sēam (“a burden”), from Latin sagma (“saddle”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to fat, sebum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sebaceus (whence -aceous), from Latin sebum, from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out”), which Proto-Germanic *saipǭ ("soap") is also derived from.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to sebacic acid or its derivatives
parole.testo: From Latin sēbāceus + -ic, from sēbum (“tallow”).

parole.significato: A medium-sized deciduous tree of species Cordia myxa or, less often, Cordia latifolia, Cordia sebestena, or other speci…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sebesten, from Arabic سِبِسْتَان (sibistān), from Persian سگپستان (sag-pestân, literally “dog teat”), from سگ (sag, “dog”) + پستان (pestân, “teat”).

parole.significato: Producing sebum; sebaceous.
parole.testo: Latin sebum (“tallow”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: sebaceous
parole.testo: Latin sebum (“tallow”) + parere (“to bring forth”).

parole.significato: A thick oily substance, secreted by the sebaceous glands of the skin, that consists of fat, keratin and cellular debris.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sēbum (“tallow, grease; suet”).

parole.significato: The capability of being divided.
parole.testo: From Latin secabilitas, from Latin secare (“to cut”) + -ability.

parole.significato: A straight line that intersects a curve at two or more points.
parole.testo: From Latin secāns, present participle of secō (“to cut”).

parole.significato: To split from or to withdraw from membership of a political union, an alliance or an organisation.
parole.testo: From Latin secedere, from se- (“apart”) + cēdō (“to go”).

parole.significato: To separate or set apart (someone or something from other persons or things).
parole.testo: PIE word  *swé Learned borrowing from Latin sēcernere, the present active infinitive of sēcernō (“to put apart, divide, separate, sever, sunder; (figuratively) to disjoin, dissociate, part; to discern, distinguish; to exclude, pull aside, set aside, reject”), from sē- (prefix meaning ‘apart; aside;

parole.significato: To secern.
parole.testo: From Latin secerno (“to sever”).

parole.significato: That which promotes secretion.
parole.testo: From Latin secernens.

parole.significato: retirement; retreat; secession
parole.testo: From Latin secessus. See secede.

parole.significato: The act of seceding.
parole.testo: From Latin sēcessiō (“a withdrawing”).

parole.significato: A century.
parole.testo: From Latin saeculum. Compare French siècle. See secular. Doublet of saeculum.

parole.significato: To shut off or keep apart, as from company, society, etc.; withdraw (oneself) from society or into solitude.
parole.testo: From Latin secludo.

parole.significato: Secluded.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēclūsus. Compare with Spanish secluso (now obsolete).

parole.significato: The act of secluding, shutting out or keeping apart.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin, from Latin seclusio, from secludere.

parole.significato: Serving or tending to seclude (oneself); affecting seclusion.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from *sēclūsīvus, a combination of sēclūdō (“to seclude”) + -īvus (“-ive”), whence the native Latin sēclūsus. Equivalent to seclude + -ive.

parole.significato: Next in order to the first or primary; of second place in origin, rank, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English secundarie, from Latin secundārius (“of the second class or quality”), from secundus (whence the English second) + -ārius (whence the English suffix -ary), equivalent to second + -ary; compare the French secondaire, the Italian secondario, the Occitan secundari, the Portuguese se

parole.significato: A piece of knowledge that is hidden and intended to be kept hidden.
parole.testo: The noun is from Middle English secret, from Latin sēcrētum. Doublet of secretum. Displaced Old English dēagolnes (“a secret”). The verb is from the noun.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a secretary.
parole.testo: From a Latin-type formation *sēcrētāriālis, from Medieval Latin sēcrētārius + Latin -ālis. By surface analysis, secretary + -al.

parole.significato: A person who keeps records, takes notes and handles general clerical work.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin secrētārius (“one entrusted with secrets”), from Latin secrētus (“private, secret”), past participle of secernere (“to separate, set apart”), from se- (“apart”) + cernere (“to separate”).

parole.significato: Separated; discrete.
parole.testo: First attested in 1678: from Latin sēcrētus (“[having been] separated”).

parole.significato: To extract a substance from blood, sap, or similar to produce and emit waste for excretion or for the fulfilling of a p…
parole.testo: First directly attested in 1728; attested as the past-participial adjective secreted in 1707: from Latin sēcrētus, perfect passive participle of sēcernō (“to separate”); reinforced by back-formation from secretion; compare secern; cognate with French sécréter and the Spanish secretar.

parole.significato: A special seal used for private correspondence.
parole.testo: From Latin sēcrētum. Doublet of secret.

parole.significato: One of the portions of space bounded by the three coordinate planes.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sectāns.

parole.significato: A follower, a disciple; someone who follows a particular school; partisan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sectātor, from sector, frequentative of sequor (“follow”).

parole.significato: Capable of being cut; easily cut.
parole.testo: From Latin sectilis.

parole.significato: A section or cutting; a subdivision or segment.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sectiō. Doublet of section.

parole.significato: A section.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sector.

parole.significato: The lay or temporal authority of a secular court to pronounce punishment (particularly capital punishment) of an offend…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English seculer arm, seculer arme (“civil authority or power”), a calque of Medieval Latin bracchium saeculāre (“(figurative) civil or lay power”), from Latin bracchium (“arm”) + saeculāre (neuter singular form of saeculāris (“profane, temporal, worldly”)).

parole.significato: One of two branches of the clergy, composed of deacons and priests who are not monastics and do not belong to religious…
parole.testo: secular + clergy, learned borrowing from Latin clerici saeculares, clēricī + saeculārēs

parole.significato: Arranged on one side only, as flowers or leaves on a stalk; unilateral.
parole.testo: From Latin secundus (“following the course or current of wind or water”). Doublet of second and secundo.

parole.significato: A lay vicar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin secundarius.

parole.significato: The second coat, or integument, of an ovule, lying within the primine.
parole.testo: From Late Latin secundinae (“afterbirth”), from Latin secundae (“the afterbirth”), shortened from secundae membranae "the second membranes", from secundus (“following, coming next”). See second.

parole.significato: A woman during or after her second pregnancy
parole.testo: From Latin secundipara.

parole.significato: Pregnant for the second time.
parole.testo: From Latin secundiparus. By surface analysis, from Latin secund(us) + -i- + -parous.

parole.significato: The condition of being secondborn
parole.testo: From New Latin secundōgenitūra.

parole.significato: according to
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin secundum.

parole.significato: Artificially.
parole.testo: From Latin secundum artem.

parole.significato: Naturally.
parole.testo: From Latin secundum naturam.

parole.significato: In certain respects only.
parole.testo: From Latin secundum quid.

parole.significato: Free from attack or danger; protected.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēcūrus (“of persons, free from care, quiet, easy; in a bad sense, careless, reckless; of things, tranquil, also free from danger, safe, secure”), from sē- (“without”) + cūra (“care”); see cure. Doublet of sure and the now obsolete or dialectal sicker (“certain, safe”).

parole.significato: A little axe, or a votive offering in that form.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin secūricula.

parole.significato: Having the form of an axe or hatchet.
parole.testo: Latin securis (“an axe or hatchet”) + -form: compare French sécuriforme.

parole.significato: otherwise, to the contrary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin secus.

parole.significato: Of a person or animal, or their behaviour: calm and composed (often in a dignified manner), and avoiding or unaffected…
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English sedate (“not painful or sore”), and directly from its etymon Latin sēdātus (“calm, quiet, composed”), participial adjective from sēdō (“to allay, appease, calm, settle; to end, stop”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”). Compare Eng

parole.significato: During the vacancy of an episcopal see.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēde vacante.

parole.significato: Having sixteen joints.
parole.testo: From Latin sedecim + articulate.

parole.significato: Sixteenfold.
parole.testo: First attested in 1744–1749; from the Latin sēdecuplus (“sixteenfold”); compare decuple.

parole.significato: sitting; inactive or still
parole.testo: From Latin sedentis. Doublet of sejant.

parole.significato: The school of thought, in Roman Catholicism, that the popes of the new religion of Vatican II council have been defecti…
parole.testo: From Latin sede + prīvātō + -ism. Probably modelled on sedevacantism.

parole.significato: A formal meeting, especially of a judicial or ecclesiastical body.
parole.testo: From Latin sederunt (“there were sitting”).

parole.significato: The position a word or phrase occupies within the meter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēdēs (“seat”). Doublet of see.

parole.significato: A papal or episcopal see when there is a partial cessation by the incumbent of his episcopal duties.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A papal or episcopal see when vacant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēdēs vacāns.

parole.significato: A series of seats, typically three, often recessed into the wall, on the south side of the chancel or choir, reserved f…
parole.testo: Latin, plural of sedile (“seat, bench”).

parole.significato: One of a row of seats in an Ancient Roman amphitheatre.
parole.testo: From Latin sedilium.

parole.significato: To beguile or lure (someone) away from duty, accepted principles, or proper conduct; to lead astray.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēdūcō (“to lead apart or astray”), from sē- (“aside, away, astray”) + dūcō (“to lead”); see duct. Compare adduce, conduce, deduce, etc. and Middle English seduct.

parole.significato: Attractive, alluring, tempting.
parole.testo: From Latin sēduct-, past-participle stem of sēdūcere, + -ive.

parole.significato: diligence, persistence
parole.testo: From sedul(ous) + -ity, from Latin sedulitas.

parole.significato: Of a person: diligent in application or pursuit; constant and persevering in business or in endeavours to effect a goal…
parole.testo: From Latin sēdulus (“diligent, industrious, sedulous; solicitous; unremitting; zealous”) + English -ous. Sēdulus is probably derived from sēdulō (“diligently; carefully; purposely; zealously”) (possibly from sē- (prefix meaning ‘without’) + dolō (ablative singular of dolus (“deceit, deception; evil

parole.significato: Any of various succulent plants, of the genus Sedum, native to temperate zones; the stonecrop.
parole.testo: From Middle English cedum, from Latin sedum (“houseleek”). Modern usage is a semantic loan from translingual Sedum.

parole.parola: seek a knot in a bulrush
parole.significato: To find problems where none exist.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin nōdum in scirpō quaerō.

parole.significato: A castrated farm animal.
parole.testo: Probably from the root of Latin secāre (“to cut”).

parole.significato: A length of some object.
parole.testo: From Latin segmentum (“a piece cut off, a strip, segment of the earth, a strip of tinsel”), from secāre (“to cut”).

parole.significato: Sluggishness or inactivity.
parole.testo: From Latin segnitas, from segnis (“slow, sluggish”).

parole.significato: An ancient tribe which dwelt in the region of Massalia (present-day Marseille, France).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Segobrigiī.

parole.significato: Separate; select.
parole.testo: From Latin sēgregātus, perfect passive participle of sēgregō (“to separate”), from sē- (“apart”) + gregō (“to flock or group”), from grex (“flock”). Compare gregarious, aggregate.

parole.significato: The act of setting apart and organizing things based upon their characteristics.
parole.testo: 1555. From Latin segregatio. Morphologically segregate + -ion.

parole.significato: Something peculiar to oneself; personal peculiarity; individuality.
parole.testo: Latin se (“oneself”).

parole.significato: To enjoy the present and not worry about the future; to live for the moment.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin carpe diem, originally meaning "enjoy the day", literally "pluck (or harvest) the day", from a poem by the ancient poet Horace. In Latin, it was common to use carpo (“to pluck something, pick off”) metaphorically to express enjoying a period of time. The use of seize is a traditional

parole.significato: To separate.
parole.testo: Latin sejungere; prefix se- (“aside”) + jungere (“to join”). See join.

parole.significato: separated, disjoined
parole.testo: From Latin seiunctus.

parole.significato: Separate; separated.
parole.testo: From Latin sēiūnctus, past participle of sēiungō (“separate”); from sē (“without”) + iungō (“to join”).

parole.significato: The act of disjoining, or the state of being disjoined.
parole.testo: From Latin sejunctio. See sejoin, sejunct.

parole.significato: Pertaining to (what is now classified as) the superorder Selachimorpha or division Selachii, comprising the sharks; or,…
parole.testo: From the (disused) genus name Selache, from Latin selachē, from the plural of Ancient Greek σέλαχος (sélakhos, “shark”).

parole.significato: Privileged, specially selected.
parole.testo: From Latin sēlēctus, perfect passive participle of sēligō (“choose out, select”), from sē- (“without; apart”) + legō (“gather, select”).

parole.significato: Relating to the Greek-Macedonian dynasty which ruled (312–63 BCE) an empire created by Seleucus out of the eastern conq…
parole.testo: From Latin Seleucides, from Ancient Greek Σελευκίδης (Seleukídēs), named after Seleucus I Nicator. Equivalent to Seleucus + -id.

parole.significato: A saddle-shaped depression in the sphenoid bone of the skull in humans and other hominids.
parole.testo: Latin: sella + turcica = literally “Turkish chair”.

parole.significato: Relating to the sella turcica.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sellāris.

parole.significato: A male prostitute.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sellārius.

parole.significato: That denotes a momentary or punctiliar action.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin semelfactīvus, from to Latin semel (“once, a single time”) + factum (“event, occurrence”) + adjectival suffix -īvus.

parole.significato: Reproducing only once in a lifetime.
parole.testo: From Latin semel (“once, a single time”) + pariō (“give birth, produce, bring forth”). Coined by Lamont Cole in 1954.

parole.significato: A sticky, milky fluid produced in male reproductive organs that contains the reproductive cells.
parole.testo: From Middle English semen, from Latin sēmen (“seed”), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“to sow; plant”).

parole.significato: santonica
parole.testo: Probably from Latin semen + ? (cf. original taxonomic name Artemisia cina), so meaning something like "cina seed"

parole.significato: Half-eaten.
parole.testo: From the Latin sēmēsus; from sēm- (“half-”) + ēsus (“eaten”), the perfect passive participle of edō (“to eat”).

parole.significato: half
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin semi- (“half”), from Proto-Indo-European *sēmi/*sēmi-. Cognate to English sam, and to hemi- (via Ancient Greek).

parole.significato: Somewhat or partially cordate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēmicordātus. By surface analysis, semi- + cordate.

parole.significato: A half bath, or one that covers only the lower extremities and the hips; a sitz bath.
parole.testo: From Latin semi (“half”) + cupa (“tub, cask”).

parole.significato: The apparent radius of a star etc, when viewed from Earth.
parole.testo: From Middle English semidiametre, semydiametre, from Medieval Latin sēmidiameter, equivalent to semi- + diameter.

parole.significato: A playoff in the round with only four players or teams left, the stage before the final.
parole.testo: From Latin semifinalis, equivalent to semi- + final.

parole.significato: A partial or imperfect form.
parole.testo: From Latin sēmifōrmis, equivalent to semi- + form.

parole.significato: Partially mature
parole.testo: From Middle English semimature, semymature, from Latin semimātūrus (“half-ripe”), equivalent to semi- + mature.

parole.significato: A muscle in the back of the thigh; the most medial of the three hamstring muscles (meaning it is more to the inner of t…
parole.testo: From Latin sēmimembrānōsus.

parole.significato: A theological school for the training of rabbis, priests, or ministers.
parole.testo: From Latin sēminārium, from sēmen (“seed”). Compare seminar. In the ground sense, from Middle English semynair, semynary.

parole.significato: To disseminate
parole.testo: From Latin seminat-, perfect passive participial stem of seminō (“to plant, sow”). Doublet of semé and semined.

parole.significato: The act of sowing or spreading.
parole.testo: Latin seminatio: compare French sémination.

parole.significato: Thickly covered or sown, as if with seeds.
parole.testo: As if from a verb *semine, ultimately from Latin sēminō (“to plant, sow”), from sēmen (“seed”, whence English semen) + -ō. Doublet of semé and seminate.

parole.significato: producing seed
parole.testo: From Late Latin sēminifer (“carrying semen”).

parole.significato: Forming or producing semen; seminiferous.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: The old theory that the newly created being is formed by the mixture of the seed of the male with the supposed seed of…
parole.testo: From Latin sēmen (“seed”) + -ism.

parole.significato: A believer in the theory of seminism.
parole.testo: From Latin sēmen (“seed”) + -ist.

parole.significato: seed-eating
parole.testo: From Latin sēmen (“seed”) + -vorous.

parole.significato: A form of testicular cancer
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin sēmen, sēminis (“seed”) + -oma.

parole.significato: A carbohydrate of the glucose group found in the thickened endosperm of certain seeds, and extracted as yellow syrup; D…
parole.testo: Latin semen seed + glucose.

parole.significato: Semiotics, the study of signs.
parole.testo: From New Latin semaeologia, from Ancient Greek σημεῖον (sēmeîon, “sign”) + -logia (“-logy”). By surface analysis, semio- + -logy.

parole.significato: Half of a metrical foot.
parole.testo: From Latin semipes, semipedis, from semi- (“half”) + pes, pedis (“a foot”).

parole.significato: A small bronze coin minted during the Roman Republic, valued at half an as.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēmis.

parole.significato: A chronic state of low-grade exhaustion caused by too little or fitful sleep.
parole.testo: From Latin semi- (“half”) + somnus (“sleep”) + -ia. Compare with insomnia. Coined by British sleep expert Neil Stanley in 2007.

parole.significato: A fasciole of a spatangoid sea urchin.
parole.testo: From Latin semita (“a path”).

parole.significato: A member of a modern people that speak a Semitic language.
parole.testo: From Sem, Shem + -ite, from Late Latin Sēm, from Ancient Greek Σήμ (Sḗm), from Biblical Hebrew שם (šēm). Compare German Semit, New Latin Sēmīta, French sémite.

parole.significato: always the same
parole.testo: From Latin semper idem.

parole.significato: Perpetual virgin. (Refers to the belief that Saint Mary remained a virgin her whole life.)
parole.testo: From Latin semper virgo (“ever virgin”).

parole.significato: always, unvarying
parole.testo: From the Latin adverb semper (“always”).

parole.significato: Evergreen.
parole.testo: From Latin semper (“always”) + virēns, present participle of vireō (“be green”).

parole.significato: A succulent plant, the houseleek.
parole.testo: From Latin semperviva, sempervivum, from sempervivus (“ever-living”), from semper (“always”) + vivus (“living”).

parole.significato: Existence within time but infinitely into the future, as opposed to eternity, understood as existence outside time.
parole.testo: From sempitern(al) + -ity, from Latin sempiternitas.

parole.significato: A durable twilled woollen material.
parole.testo: From Latin sempiternum.

parole.significato: A verse having six metric feet.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sēnārius. Doublet of senary.

parole.significato: Of sixth rank or order.
parole.testo: From the Latin sēnārius (“consisting of six each”), from sēnī (“six each, six at a time”) + -ārius (whence the English suffix -ary). Doublet of senarius.

parole.significato: A member, normally elected, in the house or chamber of a legislature called a senate, as, for instance, the legislature…
parole.testo: From Latin senātor, ultimately from senex (“old”), equivalent to senate + -or.

parole.significato: A female senator (a female member of a senate)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin senātrīx. By surface analysis, senator + -trix.

parole.significato: A governing body in certain universities.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin senatus.

parole.significato: The governing body of a Scottish university, consisting of the principal and professors.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin senātus acadēmicus.

parole.significato: A decree written by the Roman Senate.
parole.testo: From Latin senātūs cōnsultum.

parole.significato: groundsel
parole.testo: Corruption of Latin seneciō (“groundsel”).

parole.significato: old age
parole.testo: From Latin senectus (“aged, old age”), senex (“old”). Compare senescent.

parole.significato: To grow older; to reach maturity.
parole.testo: From Latin senēscere (“to grow old”).

parole.significato: Growing old; decaying with the lapse of time.
parole.testo: From Latin senescens, present participle of senescere (“to grow old”), from senere (“to be old”), from senex (“old”).

parole.significato: An older or old man, chiefly as a stock character.
parole.testo: From Latin senex.

parole.significato: The killing of an elderly person.
parole.testo: From Latin senex (“old”) + -cide.

parole.significato: Killing of old people, especially to conserve resources for younger people.
parole.testo: From Latin senilis + -cida or cognates.

parole.significato: Older.
parole.testo: From Middle English senior, from Latin senior (“older”), comparative form of senex (“old”); see senate. Doublet of seigneur, seignior, senhor, señor, senyor, signore, sir, and sire.

parole.significato: A measure of the amount of time a person has been a member of an organization, as compared to other members, and with a…
parole.testo: From Middle English senyoryte, from Medieval Latin senioritas, from Latin senior (“elder”).

parole.significato: Having six eyes.
parole.testo: From Latin sēnī (“six each”), from sex (“six”) + oculus (“eye”).

parole.significato: A Gaulish tribe in the Roman period.
parole.testo: Via Latin from Ancient Greek Σήνωνες (Sḗnōnes), originally the capital of the Gaulish people of the same name.

parole.significato: Perceived by one or more of the senses.
parole.testo: From Middle English sensat, from Late Latin sensatus (“able to sense”), from sensus (“sense”).

parole.significato: Acting with or showing good sense; able to make good judgements based on reason or wisdom, or reflecting such ability.
parole.testo: From Latin sēnsibilis (“perceptible by the senses, having feeling, sensible”), from sentiō (“to feel, perceive”).

parole.significato: converting into sensation
parole.testo: From Latin sensus (“sense”) + facere (“to make”).

parole.significato: Exciting or conveying sensation.
parole.testo: Latin sensifer; sensus (“sense”) + ferre (“to bear”). By surface analysis, sense + -i- + -fer + -ous.

parole.significato: Exciting sensation; causing something to be felt.
parole.testo: Latin sensificus; sensus (“sense”) + facere (“to make”).

parole.significato: A device or organ that detects certain external stimuli and responds in a distinctive manner.
parole.testo: Originated 1925–30, formed as a Latin loanword from sentiō (“to feel”) + -tor (“-er”). By surface analysis, sense + -or.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to sensation or the senses; sensory.
parole.testo: Either sensorium + -al or sensory + -al. Ultimately from Latin sentiō.

parole.significato: The entire sensory apparatus of an organism.
parole.testo: From Late Latin sensōrium, from Latin sentiō (“feel, perceive”) + Latin -ōrium (suffix denoting a place for a particular function).

parole.significato: in the sense of
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sensu.

parole.significato: Inducing pleasurable or erotic sensations.
parole.testo: From Late Latin sensualis (“endowed with feeling, sensual”), from Latin sensus (“feeling, sense”).

parole.significato: Appealing to the senses, or to sensual gratification.
parole.testo: From Latin sensus (“sense”) + English -ous.

parole.significato: Relating to a sentence.
parole.testo: From Latin sententialis.

parole.significato: Someone who studied, read lectures on, or made commentaries on, The Sentences by Peter Lombard.
parole.testo: Latin sententiarius.

parole.significato: Using as few words as possible; pithy and concise.
parole.testo: From Latin sententiōsus, from sententia (“opinion, purpose”).

parole.significato: Experiencing sensation, thought, or feeling.
parole.testo: From Latin sentiēns (“feeling, perceiving”), present active participle of sentiō.

parole.significato: A place for dregs and dirt; a sink; a sewer.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sentina (“bilge water, hold of a ship, dregs”).

parole.significato: painful vivisection, without the use of anesthetic
parole.testo: From Latin sentire (“to feel”) + English section.

parole.significato: To divide (a thing) into separate parts.
parole.testo: From Middle English separaten (“to separate”), from separat (“separated”) + -en, from Latin sēparātus, perfect passive participle of sēparō (“to separate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from sē- (“apart”) + parō (“prepare”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“produce, procure, bring for

parole.significato: Serving to separate.
parole.testo: Latin separativus.

parole.significato: An object located between two or more things and hence separating them.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēparātor.

parole.significato: The ⟨L⟩ or pipe ⟨|⟩ mark formerly used to divide integers from decimals.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sēparātrīx, the feminine form of separator (originally owing to an implied līnea (“line”)), from sēparāre (“to divide; to separate”) + -trix (forming female agents). By surface analysis, separate + -trix. First developed as a decimal mark among the medieval Arab mathemat

parole.significato: A dark brown pigment made from the secretions of the cuttlefish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēpia (“cuttlefish”), from Ancient Greek σηπία (sēpía). Cognate with Italian seppia, Portuguese siba, and Spanish sepia.

parole.significato: Something that separates; a hedge; a fence.
parole.testo: From Latin sepimentum, saepimentum, from sepire, saepire (“to hedge in”).

parole.significato: A hydrated magnesium silicate, clay mineral used for carving into decorative articles and smoking pipes.
parole.testo: From Latin sepia (“cuttlefish”) + -lite, from its resemblance to cuttlebone.

parole.significato: To set apart.
parole.testo: Latin se- (“aside”) + English pose.

parole.significato: A clan, tribe, or family, proceeding from a common progenitor; especially, one of the ancient clans of Ireland.
parole.testo: A corruption of sect, influenced by Latin saeptum (“fence, enclosure”).

parole.significato: Seven: forming words relating to seven.
parole.testo: From Latin septem (“seven”).

parole.significato: seven
parole.testo: From Latin septem.

parole.significato: Synonym of septicemia.
parole.testo: From New Latin septaemia, from Ancient Greek σηπτός (sēptós), verbal adjective of σήπω (sḗpō, “make rotten”), + αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + -ia.

parole.significato: Synonym of heptagon (“a polygon with seven sides and seven angles”).
parole.testo: From Latin septagōnus. By surface analysis, septa- + -gon.

parole.significato: Synonym of heptagonal.
parole.testo: From Renaissance Latin septangulāris. By surface analysis, sept- + -angular.

parole.significato: A flattened concretionary nodule, usually of limestone, intersected within by cracks which are often filled with calcit…
parole.testo: From Latin saeptum (“inclosure, partition”) + -arium.

parole.significato: Seven.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin septem (“seven”).

parole.significato: Cleft into seven.
parole.testo: From septem- + -fid, after Renaissance Latin septemfidus.

parole.significato: Having seven leaves or leaflets.
parole.testo: From septem- + foliate, after New Latin septemfoliātus.

parole.significato: A member of a septemvirate; one of seven people associated in some office.
parole.testo: From Latin septemvir.

parole.significato: Of or belonging to the septemviri or the septemvirate.
parole.testo: From Latin septemvirālis.

parole.significato: A group of seven people, especially (politics) a council of seven men who share office or rule.
parole.testo: From Latin septemvirātus, from septemvir + -ātus (“-ate”).

parole.significato: Synonym of septenarius.
parole.testo: From Classical Latin septēnārius; compare -ar. By surface analysis, septen- + -ar. Doublet of septenarius and septenary.

parole.significato: A verse having seven metrical feet.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin septēnārius (“a verse having seven metrical feet”), nominalized from the masculine forms of septēnārius (“septenary”). Doublet of septenar and septenary.

parole.significato: Consisting of or containing seven.
parole.testo: From Middle English septenarie, septenary, from Classical Latin septēnārius (“consisting of seven each”), from septēnus (“seven each; seven at a time”) + -ārius (whence the English suffix -ary). With use as noun compare septēnārius (“line of seven feet; unit of seven parts; period of seven years”).

parole.significato: Having seven parts.
parole.testo: From New Latin septēnātus, from Classical Latin septēnus (“seven each”) + -ātus (“having”). By surface analysis, septen- + -ate.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a 7 year period.
parole.testo: From septennium + -al, from Latin septennis (“7-year”), q.v.

parole.significato: A period of seven years.
parole.testo: From Late Latin septennium, from septennis (“7-year”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: The north or northern regions.
parole.testo: From Middle English septentrion, septentrione, septemtryones, septemtrioun, from Latin septentriō, septentriōnem (“the northern regions, the north”) directly and through Old French septentrïon, septemtrion, from septentriōnēs (“the seven stars near the north pole”) (called Charles's Wain, or the Gre

parole.significato: Pertaining to the north; northern.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin septentriōnālis, from septentriōnēs (“seven plow oxen”), a name for the constellations now known as Ursa Major and Ursa Minor, which appear in the northern sky.

parole.significato: A group of seven, particularly
parole.testo: PIE word  *septḿ̥ From Latin septem (“seven”).

parole.significato: seven
parole.testo: Latin septem (“seven”).

parole.significato: A mathematical object (function, curve, surface, etc.) of degree seven.
parole.testo: From Latin septem (“seven”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A disease caused by the presence of pathogenic organisms, especially bacteria, or their toxins, in the bloodstream, cha…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin sēpticaemia, from Latin sēpticus + -aemia.

parole.significato: Exhibiting or relating to a method of dehiscence in which a pod splits through the partitions and is divided into its c…
parole.testo: From septum + Latin caedere (“to cut”). Compare French septicide.

parole.significato: Breaking from the partitions; said of a method of dehiscence in which the valves of a pod break away from the partition…
parole.testo: From septum + Latin frangere, fractum (“to break”).

parole.significato: Relating to the number seven.
parole.testo: From both Latin septimus + -al and By surface analysis, sept- + -ime + -al.

parole.significato: Submit (someone or something) to septimation; reduce by one seventh.
parole.testo: Latin septimus (“seventh”) + English -ate, after decimate; compare septimation

parole.significato: The loss, seizure, destruction, or killing of one seventh (of something or of a group).
parole.testo: From Latin septimus (“seventh”) + -ation, after decimation; compare septimate.

parole.significato: A group of seven notes to be played in the time of four or six.
parole.testo: Latin septem (“seven”).

parole.significato: A heavy ancient Greek warship.
parole.testo: From Latin septirēmis (“having seven banks of oars”), from septem (“seven”) + rēmus (“oar”).

parole.significato: Of or coming from northern regions.
parole.testo: From Latin septem triōnēs, the seven stars of the Great Bear, from septem (“seven”) + triōnēs (plural of triō (“plow ox, plough ox”)).

parole.significato: Seven.
parole.testo: From a form of Latin septem (“seven”) used in septuāgintā (“seventy”).

parole.significato: A Sunday in the Christian calendar nine weeks before Easter Sunday.
parole.testo: From Latin septuagesima dies (“70th day”).

parole.significato: A group of 70 people or a collection of 70 things.
parole.testo: From Latin septuaginta (“seven tens, 70”), chiefly under the influence of the Septuagint and the story of its team of translators, q.v.

parole.significato: Being seven in number.
parole.testo: Latin septem (“seven”).

parole.significato: A little septum; a division between small cavities or parts.
parole.testo: Diminutive of Latin septum (“septum”).

parole.significato: A thin triangular vertical membrane separating the anterior horns of the left and right lateral ventricles of the brain…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Seven times as much; sevenfold.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin septuplus.

parole.significato: Sevenfold; made up of seven parts.
parole.testo: From Latin septem (“seven”) + plico (“fold together”).

parole.significato: Having seven nerves.
parole.testo: By surface analysis, septuple (“seven times, sevenfold”, from Latin septuplus) + -i- (Latinate interfix) + nerved (“having nerves”). Compare translingual septuplinervis, the specific epithet of Miconia septuplinervis.

parole.significato: Relating to a grave or to death; funereal.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sepulcralis.

parole.significato: buried.
parole.testo: From Latin sepultus.

parole.significato: Likely to follow or yield to physical pressure; easily shaped or molded.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin sequāx (“a follower”), from sequī (“to follow”), + -acious (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Quality or state of being sequacious.
parole.testo: From Latin sequācitās (whence -acity), from sequāx + -tās.

parole.significato: An early name for the element neptunium, based on a discredited claim of discovery.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Sequana (“the river Seine”) + -ium. Horia Hulubei, who thought he had discovered element 93, worked near the river at that time.

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sequēla (“aftermath, sequel; consequence, result”), from sequor (“to follow; to come or go after, pursue”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”)) + -ēla (suffix forming abstract nouns from verbs). Doublet of sequel. The plural form is a learned borrow

parole.significato: Synonym of consecutio temporum.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin cōnsecūtiō temporum.

parole.significato: A logical conclusion or consequence of facts.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sequitur (“it follows”), the third person form of sequor (“to follow”).

parole.significato: A temple or other religious institution dedicated to the syncretic Greco-Egyptian deity Serapis.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek Σεραπεῖον (Serapeîon).

parole.significato: A burning serpent, often winged, with human hands and sometimes feet; one of God's entourage. On Earth, they strike wit…
parole.testo: Back-formation of singular from plural seraphim, from Latin seraphim, from Biblical Hebrew שְׂרָפִים (sərāp̄īm), plural form of שָׂרָף (sārāp̄). The plural "seraphims" occurs in the King James Bible (Isaiah chapter 6). According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the singular "seraph" may have origin

parole.significato: Of or relating to a seraph or the seraphim.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin seraphicus, from Late Latin seraphīm, seraphīn, from Hebrew שָׂרָף (saráf, “seraph”). By surface analysis, seraph + -ic.

parole.significato: Any member of the species Lobophora halterata of geometrid moths.
parole.testo: From Latin seraphim, from Koine Greek σεραφείμ (serapheím), from Biblical Hebrew שְׂרָפִים (śərāp̄îm), plural of שָׂרָף (śārāp̄) (often translated as "fiery ones" although meaning is uncertain); perhaps related to the root שרף (“to burn”).

parole.significato: A natural succession community of organisms in an ecosystem, especially a series of communities succeeding one another…
parole.testo: From Latin serere, present active infinitive of serō (“to entwine, interlace, link together; to join in a series, string together”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind, tie together; to thread”).

parole.significato: Calm, peaceful, unruffled.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Latin serēnus (“clear, cloudless, untroubled”).

parole.significato: Having to do with or arranged in a series.
parole.testo: Formed as series + -al, on model of Latin seriālis, from seriēs + -ālis. Cognate to Italian seriale. First use appears c. 1823. See cite below.

parole.significato: Synonym of Chinese or Northern Chinese, chiefly in the context of ancient Greco-Roman knowledge of China and its role a…
parole.testo: From Seres + -ian, from Latin Seres (“the ancient northern Chinese”), from Ancient Greek, possibly from the Old Chinese word for silk.

parole.significato: Arranged in serial order.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin seriātus.

parole.significato: One after another, in order; taking one topic or subject at a time in an order; sequentially.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin seriatim, from Latin seriēs (“row, chain”) + -ātim, adverbial suffix.

parole.significato: a series, a sequence
parole.testo: From Latin seriatum, neuter of Medieval Latin or New Latin seriatus (“arranged in serial order”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Chinese or Northern Chinese, in the context of ancient Greco-Roman knowledge of China.
parole.testo: From Latin Sēricus, from Ancient Greek Σηρικός (Sērikós), from Σῆρες (Sêres, “Seres”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”), from σήρ (sḗr, “silkworm”), possibly from Old Chinese 絲 (*sə, “silk”). Equivalent to Seres + -ic. Doublet of Serican.

parole.significato: Synonym of silken, made of silk.
parole.testo: From Latin sēricus, from Ancient Greek σηρῐκός (sērĭkós), from σήρ (sḗr, “silkworm”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”), possibly ultimately from the Old Chinese word for silk. Doublet of silk and serge.

parole.significato: Synonym of Chinese or Northern Chinese, chiefly in the context of ancient Greco-Roman knowledge of China.
parole.testo: From Latin Sēricānus, from Sērica (“Serica, China, ancient northern China”) + -ānus (“-an”), from Ancient Greek Σηρικά (Sēriká), from σήρ (sḗr, “silkworm”), and possibly ultimately from Old Chinese 絲 (*sə, “silk”). Equivalent to Serica + -an. Doublet of Seric.

parole.significato: Of or relating to silk; consisting of, or resembling silk; silky.
parole.testo: From Latin sēricus (“silken”), sēricum (“Seric material; silk”), from Sēricus (“belonging to the Seres”): Sērēs, Ancient Greek Σῆρες (Sêres, “a people of Eastern Asia, the modern Chinese, celebrated for their silken fabrics”). Compare silk, serge.

parole.significato: A water-soluble glycoprotein that binds the two fibroin filaments of a silk fibre.
parole.testo: From a derivative of Latin sēricus.

parole.significato: A silk gland, as in the silkworms.
parole.testo: Late Latin sericterium, from Ancient Greek σηρικόν (sērikón, “silk”).

parole.significato: A number of things that follow on one after the other or are connected one after the other.
parole.testo: Attested from the 1610s; borrowed from Latin seriēs, from serere (“to join together, bind”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind, put together, to line up”). Related to desert, insert, sermon, and sorcerer.

parole.significato: a silkscreen print made by serigraphy
parole.testo: From Latin sericum (“silk”) + -graph.

parole.significato: A nonessential amino acid, CH₂OH.CH(NH₂)COOH, found in most animal proteins, notably silk.
parole.testo: From Latin sericus (“silken”). The compound was first obtained from silk protein, a particularly rich source, in 1865. See also serge.

parole.significato: Seriousness, especially self-seriousness.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from serious + -itude, with the spelling changed to suggest a pseudo-Latin derivation.

parole.significato: Synonym of seriousness.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin sēriōsitās, from Late Latin sēriōsus (“serious”) + Latin -itās (“-ity”).

parole.significato: The making of speeches or sermons; sermonizing.
parole.testo: From Latin sermocinatio. See sermon.

parole.significato: One who makes sermons or speeches; a preacher.
parole.testo: From Latin sermocinor (“to preach a sermon”).

parole.significato: A fatty substance found in the blood, probably a mixture of fats, cholesterol, etc.
parole.testo: From serum + Latin oleum (“oil”) + -in.

parole.significato: Developing at a later time or later in a season, especially than is customary with allied species; specifically (botany…

parole.significato: Synonym of serotine (“developing at a later time or later in a season, especially than is customary with allied species…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sērōtinus (“late (in ripening, etc.); relating to the evening”) (see further at serotine) + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives denoting pertinence or relation to something).

parole.significato: The fibrous aromatic root of the Virginia snakeroot (Aristolochia serpentaria).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin serpentāria.

parole.significato: Having the form of a snake.
parole.testo: Latin serpens (“serpent”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Bred of a serpent
parole.testo: From Latin serpens + -entis (“a serpent”) + -genous. Compare Latin serpentigena.

parole.significato: creeping, advancing
parole.testo: Latin serpigio (“creeping and spreading skin disease”).

parole.significato: A dry, scaly eruption on the skin; especially, a ringworm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin serpīgō.

parole.significato: Any of numerous species of tubicolous annelids of the genus Serpula and allied genera of the family Serpulidae that sec…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin serpula. See serpent.

parole.significato: A saw, or saw-like part.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin serra.

parole.significato: Having tooth-like projections on one side, as in a saw.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin serrātus, past participle of serrō.

parole.significato: Saw-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin serrātus (“saw”) + -iform.

parole.significato: A notching, like that between the teeth of a saw, in the edge of anything.
parole.testo: From Latin serratura (“a sawing”).

parole.significato: Any of several muscles of the vertebral or costal region that produce a serrated border.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin serratus.

parole.significato: Like the teeth of a saw; jagged.
parole.testo: Latin serra (“a saw”), + -ous.

parole.significato: A kind of tooth found in spiders.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin serrula (“a little saw”).

parole.significato: I shall keep faith (motto of various groups).
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Service tree.
parole.testo: Properly, the tree that bears sorb fruit, from Middle English serves, plural of serve (“sorb apple, serviceberry”), from Old English syrfe, from Vulgar Latin *sorbea, from Latin sorbus (“service tree”). See sorb.

parole.significato: Either of two rare Old World deciduous trees, Sorbus domestica or Sorbus torminalis.
parole.testo: Properly, the tree that bears sorb fruit, from Middle English serves, plural of serve (“sorb apple, serviceberry”), from Old English syrfe, from Vulgar Latin *sorbea, from Latin sorbus (“service tree”). See sorb. Not related to service, though it influenced its spelling

parole.significato: Several species of trees in the genus Sorbus, especially Sorbus domestica and Sorbus torminalis.
parole.testo: Compound of service (“sorb tree”) + berry. (The first part is from Latin sorbus, not English service (“assistance”).)

parole.significato: subordinate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin serviēns, servientis. Doublet of servant and sergeant.

parole.significato: Training or education that focuses on utilitarian skills, aimed towards employability rather than the development of a…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin artēs servīlēs.

parole.significato: One who performs the duties of a servant.
parole.testo: From Middle English servitour, borrowed from Latin servītor, from servīre (“to serve”).

parole.significato: A female servitor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin servītrīx. By surface analysis, servitor + -trix.

parole.significato: Of or relating to servitude.
parole.testo: From Latin servitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin servitūdō, from servus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, servitude + -al.

parole.significato: controlled
parole.testo: Derived from Latin servus (“slave”).

parole.significato: sesame
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin sēsamum. Doublet of sesame.

parole.significato: 1½; 1½ times
parole.testo: From Latin sēsqui- (“1½ times; increased by 50%”), from semi- (“half”) and -que (“and; also”).

parole.significato: Synonym of sesquialterate, 1½ times.
parole.testo: From Latin sēsquialter, from sēsqui- (“a half and a”) + alter (“another, a second”).

parole.significato: A ratio of 3 to 2 or 1½ to 1.
parole.testo: From Latin sesquialtera, form of sesquialtera, from sesqui- (“a half and a”) + alter (“another, a second”).

parole.significato: Synonym of sesquialterate, 1½ times.
parole.testo: From Latin sesquialter + English -al, from sesqui (“a half and a”) + alter (“another, a second”).

parole.significato: Synonym of sesquialterate, in the proportion of 3 to 2 or 1½ to 1.
parole.testo: From Latin sesquialter + English -an, from sesqui- (“a half and a”) + alter (“another, a second”). Equivalent to sesquialtera + -an.

parole.significato: Synonym of sesquialteral, having a band or dot occupying a third of a wing.
parole.testo: From Latin sesquialter + English -ous, from sesqui- (“a half and a”) + alter (“another, a second”).

parole.significato: Based on a cycle of 36 hours (one-and-a-half days)
parole.testo: From New Latin sēsquidiurnus + English -al. Equivalent to sesqui- + diurnal.

parole.significato: Occurring once every one and a half years (i.e. once every 18 months, or twice every three years); sesquiannual.
parole.testo: From Latin sesquiennium (compare sesqui- and biennial).

parole.significato: Measuring or containing a foot and a half.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sesquipedalis; equivalent to sesqui- (“one and a half”) + pedal (“foot, of the foot”).

parole.significato: Long; polysyllabic.
parole.testo: From sesquipedal + -ian (adjective- and noun-forming suffix), root from Latin sēsquipedālis (literally “a foot and a half long”), from Latin sēsqui (“one and a half times”) + Latin pedālis (“measuring a foot, foot (relational)”) (an adjective from pēs (“foot”)).

parole.significato: The practice of using long, sometimes obscure, words in speech or writing.
parole.testo: Surface form analyzed as sesquipedalian + -ism, from sesqui- (“one and a half”) + pedalian (“of the foot”). From Latin sēsquipedālis (“a foot and a half long; in metaphorical use, “of an unnatural length, huge, big””), from sēsqui (“one and a half times as great”) + pedālis (“foot”).

parole.significato: Having the ratio of one and one third to one (as 4:3).

parole.significato: Permanently attached to a substrate; not free to move about.

parole.significato: A money of account equal to 1000 sestertii.
parole.testo: From Latin sēstertium.

parole.testo: From Latin sēstertius (“that is two-and-a-half”), from sēmis (“half”) + tertius (“third”), in which “third” refers to the third as: the sestertius was worth two full asses and half of a third.

parole.significato: A bristle or hair.

parole.significato: An annelid having setae; a chaetopod.
parole.testo: From Latin saetiger.

parole.significato: Producing setae.

parole.significato: An oar-like swimming leg of an insect) having a fringe of hairs on the margin.

parole.significato: A few silk threads or horsehairs, or a strip of linen etc., introduced beneath the skin by a knife or needle, so as to…

parole.significato: Thickly set with bristles or bristly hairs.
parole.testo: Latin setosus, saetosus, from seta (“bristle”), saeta (“bristle”).

parole.significato: A small, short hair or bristle; a small seta
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin setula, saetula, diminutive of seta, saeta (“bristle”).

parole.significato: benzoinated suet
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A form of sexa-, meaning six.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sex- (“six”).

parole.significato: Six.

parole.significato: In the Christian calendar the Sunday two weeks before Lent, eight before Easter Sunday.
parole.testo: from Latin sexagesima dies, from the feminine of sexagesimus '60th' + dies 'day'

parole.significato: In the Catholic liturgical year, the eighth Sunday (i.e. the sixtieth—minus one—day) before Easter (and the second befo…
parole.testo: Latin sexagesima, the feminine inflection of sexagesimus 'the sixtieth' + Sunday

parole.significato: Of, related to, or based on the number sixty.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin sexagesimalis, from sexāgēsimus (“sixtieth”) + -ālis (“-al”), from sexāgintā (“sixty”). Cognate with sexagenary and sexagenarian. Cf. sextal.

parole.significato: A paper size, (1.87"-2.5" x 2.5"-3.125"), one sixty-fourth of a standard uncut flat sheet.
parole.testo: From Latin ablatives of sexāgēsimus (“sixtieth”) and quartus (“fourth”).

parole.significato: Synonym of sexagesimal: a sixtieth part of something.
parole.testo: From Latin sexāgēsima (“sixtieth”), either directly or via French.

parole.significato: Synonym of hexagon (“a polygon with six sides and six angles”).
parole.testo: From Latin sexangulus (“sexangular”), from sex (“six”) + angulus (“angle”). Compare French sexangle and English hexangular. By surface analysis, sex- + -angle. Piecewise doublet of hexangle.

parole.significato: Having six angles; hexagonal.
parole.testo: From Late Latin sexangulāris, from sexangulus. By surface analysis, sex- + -angular. Piecewise doublet of hexangular.

parole.significato: 10⁵¹.
parole.testo: From Latin sēdec(im), sexdec(im) (“sixteen”) + English -illion. By surface analysis, sex- (“six”) + decillion.

parole.significato: senary (proceeding by sixes or in a base of six)
parole.testo: Reshaping of senary, from Latin sēnārius.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a period of six years; taking place once every six years.
parole.testo: From New Latin sexennialis (16th century), equivalent to sexennium + -al.

parole.significato: A period of six years.
parole.testo: From Latin sexennium, from sexennis (“6-year”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: cleft into six
parole.testo: From Latin sexifidus, from sex (“six”) + -fidus, related to findere (“to split”).

parole.significato: Noon, reckoned as the sixth hour of daylight.
parole.testo: From Latin sexta (“sixth; sixth hour”). Doublet of siesta.

parole.significato: A stanza of six lines; a sestine or sestina.
parole.testo: From Latin sextus (“sixth”), from sex (“six”). Compare Italian sestina. Doublet of sestina.

parole.significato: A Roman coin worth one sixth of an as.
parole.testo: From Latin sextāns, from sex (“six”).

parole.significato: A navigational device for deriving angular distances between objects so as to determine latitude and longitude.
parole.testo: From Latin sextāns.

parole.testo: From Latin sextārius (“one-sixth”), from sextus (“sixth”) + -ārius (“-ary: forming adj.”). Doublet of sextary.

parole.significato: Synonym of sextarius, an ancient Roman unit of volume
parole.testo: From Middle English sextarie, sextary, anglicized from Latin sextārius (“pint”). Doublet of sextarius.

parole.significato: Reduce by one sixth.
parole.testo: Latin sextus (“sixth”) + English -ate; compare quintate, septimate, and decimate

parole.significato: Lasting or continuing six years.

parole.significato: Of or denoting the aspect or position of any two celestial bodies separated by 60°.
parole.testo: From Latin sextīlis (“one sixth”), from sextus (“sixth”) + īlis (“-ile”).

parole.significato: A book consisting of sheets each of which is folded into six leaves.
parole.testo: From Latin sextus (“sixth”).

parole.significato: A size of a sheet of paper resulting from folding and cutting a sheet of paper into sixteenths (3.25"–5" x 5"–6.25").
parole.testo: From Latin ablative of sextusdecimus (“sixteenth”).

parole.significato: a sixfold amount
parole.testo: Formed (in imitation of quadruple) from Latin sextus (“sixth”): compare French sextuple.

parole.significato: Six times the number, volume, length, etc. (of something else).
parole.testo: From Latin sextuplicātus, past participle form of sextuplicāre (“to sextuple”), from sextuplus (“sixfold”), from sextus (“sixth”) (from sex (“six”)) + -plus (“-fold”) (from plicare (“to fold”)).

parole.significato: Arising from the fact of being male or female; pertaining to sex or gender, or to the social relations between the sexe…

parole.significato: One who believes that plants reproduce by sexual reproduction, especially one who accepts the sexual classification met…

parole.significato: The quality of being sexual; that which is characterized or distinguished by sex.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin sexuālitās. By surface analysis, sexual + -ity.

parole.significato: Of or concerning sexuality.
parole.testo: Latin sexus

parole.significato: Any member of a group of six officials.

parole.significato: Either of a pair of prime numbers that differ by six.

parole.significato: Objects or texts relating to George Bernard Shaw.

parole.significato: Herpes zoster, caused by Human herpes virus 3, in genus Varicellovirus.

parole.significato: To hiss.

parole.significato: Having a hissing sound; sibilant.

parole.significato: A pagan female oracle or prophetess, especially the Cumaean sibyl.
parole.testo: From Latin Sibylla, from Ancient Greek Σίβυλλα (Síbulla).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to or resembling a sibyl or female oracle, especially the Cumaean Sibyl and the Sibylline Books.
parole.testo: From Latin sibyllinus, Sibillinus, from Sibylla. By surface analysis, sibyl + -ine.

parole.significato: Thus; as written; used to indicate, for example, that text is being quoted as it is from the source.

parole.significato: A curved dagger used in Ancient Roman times, associated with the Thracian and Illyrians, gladiators, and Sicarii.

parole.significato: Any of a group of Jews who attempted to expel the Romans from Judea using concealed daggers.

parole.significato: Synonym of Sjögren's syndrome

parole.significato: The Sicels.

parole.significato: The state of being suddenly paralysed; consternation.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the stars.

parole.significato: sidereal (relating to stars)

parole.significato: Of, from, or relating to Side, an ancient city on the Mediterranean coast of Anatolia (modern Turkey).

parole.significato: A seal, signature or signet.

parole.testo: A calque translation of Latin signum crucis.

parole.significato: Having definite colour markings; bearing spots resembling letters.
parole.testo: From Latin signatus.

parole.significato: A sign given, especially of a cross
parole.testo: Latin signātiō. See sign (verb).

parole.significato: A signatory: someone who signs something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin signātor.

parole.significato: One who signs or has signed something.
parole.testo: From Latin signatorius.

parole.significato: Bearing signs.
parole.testo: From Latin signifer, from signum (“sign”) + ferō (“to bear”).

parole.significato: Significance.
parole.testo: From Latin significantia + -ancy.

parole.significato: Signifying something; carrying meaning.
parole.testo: From Latin significans, present participle of significare, from signum (“sign”) + ficare (“do, make”), variant of facere.

parole.significato: One of several things signified by a common term.
parole.testo: From Latin significatus, past participle of significare.

parole.significato: That tends to signify or indicate; indicative
parole.testo: Latin sīgnificātīvus: compare French significatif.

parole.significato: significant; meaningful; having signification
parole.testo: Latin significatorius.

parole.significato: A female significator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin significātrīx. By surface analysis, significator + -trix.

parole.significato: A writ issuing out of chancery, upon certificate given by the ordinary, of a man's standing excommunicate by the space…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin significāvit (“he has signified”), from significāre (“to signify”).

parole.significato: A sign, mark, or symbol.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin signum. Doublet of sign.

parole.significato: A yellowish pigment used by painters in ancient times.
parole.testo: From Latin sil (“a kind of yellow earth, ochre”).

parole.significato: The section sign, or §.
parole.testo: Either a blend of section + pilcrow or a blend of pilcrow and Latin signum sectiōnis (“section sign”), or a derived form thereof.

parole.significato: Peace and quiet have great value.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin silentium est aureum (“silence is golden”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Silenus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Sīlēnicus, from Ancient Greek Σῑληνῐκός (Sīlēnĭkós). By surface analysis, Silenus + -ic.

parole.significato: Free from sound or noise; absolutely still; perfectly quiet.
parole.testo: From Latin silēns (“silent”), present participle of sileō (“be silent”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyl- (“still, windless, quiet, slow”). Related to Gothic 𐌰𐌽𐌰𐍃𐌹𐌻𐌰𐌽 (anasilan, “to cease, grow still, be silent”), Old English sālnes (“silence”).

parole.significato: A person who keeps silent, especially from religious motives.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Late Latin silentiarius.

parole.significato: Habitually taciturn; prone to silence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin silentiōsus. By surface analysis, silence + -ous.

parole.significato: Flint.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin silex.

parole.significato: Silicon dioxide.
parole.testo: From New Latin silica, from Latin silex (“hard stone, flint”), on model of alumina, soda.

parole.significato: of, related to, or derived from silica
parole.testo: From Latin silex, silicis (“a flint”). Compare French silicique.

parole.significato: The chemical element silicon.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin silicium, from Latin silex (“flint”) + -ium. Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1808.

parole.significato: A nonmetallic element (symbol Si) with an atomic number of 14 and atomic weight of 28.0855.
parole.testo: Coined by Scottish chemist Thomas Thomson as a modification of the earlier name silicium, from the stem of Latin silex (“flint, silica”) + -on from carbon.

parole.significato: A disease of the lungs caused by the inhalation of crystalline silica dust.
parole.testo: From Late Latin silica + -osis.

parole.significato: Bearing silicles.
parole.testo: From Latin silicula.

parole.significato: A fine fiber excreted by the silkworm or other arthropod (such as a spider).
parole.testo: From Middle English silk, sylk, selk, selc, from Old English sioloc, seoloc, seolc (“silk”). parole.significato: A plant, thought to be extinct, used in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome in cooking and as a contraceptive.
parole.testo: From Latin silphium, from Ancient Greek σίλφιον (sílphion).

parole.significato: A fish of the genus Silurus, such as the sheatfish.
parole.testo: From Latin silurus (“a sort of river fish”), from Ancient Greek σίλουρος (sílouros, “a very large sort of river fish”).

parole.significato: The forest trees of a particular area
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin silva. Doublet of selva.

parole.significato: Related to forests or woods.
parole.testo: From Latin sliva (“forest, wood; grove, orchard”) + -i-

parole.significato: Growing in woodlands.
parole.testo: From Latin silva (“forest”) + -colous.

parole.significato: The study of the characteristics of trees, including especially their role in the ecology of their forest habitats; suc…
parole.testo: From silva (“forest”) + -ics, from Latin silva.

parole.significato: The care and development of forests in order to obtain a product or provide a benefit.
parole.testo: From silvi- + culture. From Latin silva (“forest”) + cultūra (“cultivation”).

parole.significato: The scientific study of forests.
parole.testo: From silva + -o- + -logy. From Latin silva (“forest”) + Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “study of”). Coined by Roeloff Oldeman in 1990 in his book Forests: elements of silvology.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to apes and monkeys.
parole.testo: From Latin sīmia (“ape, monkey”), from Ancient Greek σιμός (simós, “snub-nosed”).

parole.significato: A member of the Simiidae; a monkey or ape excluding lemurs and humans.
parole.testo: From the taxonomic New Latin Simiidae.

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which one thing is explicitly compared to another, using e.g. like or as.
parole.testo: From Latin simile (“comparison, likeness, parallel”) (first attested 1393), originally from simile, neuter form of similis (“like, similar, resembling”). Compare English similar.

parole.significato: The form by which either party, in pleading, accepts the issue tendered by his/her opponent; a joinder in issue.
parole.testo: From Latin similiter (“similarly”).

parole.significato: Involving or expressing similitude.
parole.testo: From Latin similitūdin- + -ary, from oblique stem of Latin similitūdō, from similis + -tūdō. By surface analysis, similitude + -ary.

parole.significato: A remedy selected because it causes symptoms similar to those that the practitioner wishes to treat.
parole.testo: From Latin simillimum.

parole.significato: Simian; resembling a monkey.
parole.testo: From Latin simia (“ape”) + -ous.

parole.significato: snub or snub-nosed
parole.testo: From Latin simus, from Ancient Greek σιμός (simós, “flat-nosed, snub-nosed”).

parole.significato: Having a single structure; not composite or complex; undivided, unitary.
parole.testo: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin simplex (“plain, simple; single”). The first part, sim-, comes from Proto-Indo-European *sem-, *sm̥- (“one; together”). parole.significato: Simply, absolutely; without any qualification or condition.
parole.testo: From the Latin simpliciter (“simply”, “plainly”), from simplex (“simple”).

parole.significato: A physical image or representation of a deity, person, or thing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin simulācrum (“image, likeness”), from simul(ā) + -crum (a variant of -culum, from Proto-Indo-European *-tlom, a suffix forming instrument nouns), from similis (“similar (to)”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one; together”).

parole.significato: A thing to be simulated.
parole.testo: From the supine of Latin simulare. (The construction is parallel to dividend, operand, subtrahend, etc.)

parole.significato: false; specious; counterfeit
parole.testo: From Latin simulārius, from simulō (“to simulate”).

parole.significato: To model, replicate, duplicate the behavior, appearance or properties of.
parole.testo: First attested in 1652; Borrowed from Latin simulātus, perfect passive participle of simulō (“make like, imitate, copy, represent, feign”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from similis (“like”). See similar.

parole.significato: Feigned; pretended.
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1425, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English symulat(e), simulat(e), similat(e) (“feigned; similar”), borrowed from Latin simulātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: Happening at the same moment.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin simultaneus, from simultim (“at the same time, extended”), from Latin simul (“together, at the same time”); compare similar.

parole.significato: A simultaneous occurrence of unrelated events.
parole.testo: From New Latin simultaneum, from simul (“at the same time”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Chinese.

parole.significato: A glucosinolate found in the seeds of white mustard and in many wild plant species

parole.significato: Allyl cyanamide derived from oil of mustard.
parole.testo: From Latin sinapi (“mustard”).

parole.significato: An alkaloidal amine found in seeds of black mustard (Brassica nigra, syns. Rhamphospermum nigrum, Sinapis erysimoides,…
parole.testo: Latin sinapi, sinapis (“mustard”), Ancient Greek: compare French sinapine.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to sinapinic acid or its derivatives
parole.testo: From Latin sināpi (“mustard”), + -ic.

parole.significato: A substance extracted from mustard seed, probably identical with sinalbin.
parole.testo: From Latin sinapis (“mustard”) + -in.

parole.significato: A mustard plaster.
parole.testo: From Latin sināpi (“mustard”) + -ism.

parole.significato: In a sincere or earnest manner; honestly.

parole.significato: The front part of the head or skull (as contradistinct from occiput).

parole.significato: A fine thin linen muslin or cambric cloth.
