parole.significato: In a right triangle, the ratio of the length of the side opposite an angle to the length of the hypotenuse.

parole.significato: Without specifying a date (for a future event); indefinitely.

parole.significato: An essential or indispensable element, condition, or ingredient.

parole.significato: A position that requires little to no work, or easy work, but still gives an ample payment; a cushy job.

parole.significato: Synonym of Sinitic, of or related to the family of Chinese languages.
parole.testo: From Latin Sinensis (“Chinese”) + -ian, from Sinae (“Southern Chinese; Southern China”) + -ensis (“-ese”), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A noun (in any specific sense) that has no plural form and is only used with singular verbs. Frequently for mass nouns.
parole.testo: From Latin singulāre tantum (“singular as such; singular only”), from singulāre + tantum.

parole.significato: A sob.
parole.testo: From Latin singultus.

parole.significato: A fit of gasping or convulsive breathing.

parole.significato: Chinese.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Sinicus, from Sina (“China”) + -icus (“-ic”), from Late Latin Sinae (“the Southern Chinese; Southern China”), from Ancient Greek Σῖναι (Sînai), q.v. Equivalent to Sino- + -ic.

parole.significato: A slimy polysaccharide extracted from squill.
parole.testo: Latin sinister (“left”), because it is levorotatory.

parole.significato: Left; on the left; toward the left.
parole.testo: From Latin sinister (“left”).

parole.significato: Rising spirally from right to left (of the observer)
parole.testo: From Latin sinistrorsus, sinistroversus (“turned toward the left side”), from sinister (“left”) + vertere, vortere, versum, vorsum (“to turn”).

parole.significato: An inhabitant of the city of Šianu (identified with modern Siano on the coast of Syria).
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin Sineum, from Ancient Greek Ασενναῖον (Asennaîon), from Biblical Hebrew סִינִי (sînî).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Chinese languages
parole.testo: From Latin Sīna (“China”) + -itic, as in Semitic.

parole.significato: To advance in wavy or curvy manner, to bend, to curve, to wind in and out
parole.testo: From Latin sinuatus, past participle of sinuare (“to wind, bend”), from sinus (“a bend”). See also sine, from Latin sinus.

parole.significato: Having curves in alternate directions; meandering.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sinuōsus.

parole.significato: A pouch or cavity in a bone or other tissue, especially one in the bones of the face or skull connecting with the nasal…

parole.significato: The first chamber of the heart in fish, amphibians, and reptiles, emptying into the right atrium.

parole.significato: A siphon bottle.
parole.testo: Latin sipho (“a siphon”) + -oid.

parole.significato: A strand of tissue passing longitudinally through the shell of a cephalopod, used primarily in emptying water from new…

parole.significato: A tube that connects adjacent chambers in the shells of some cephalopods.
parole.testo: From Latin sīphunculus (“little tube”), from sīphō (“tube, pipe”) + -culus (diminutive suffix), from Ancient Greek σίφων (síphōn), of uncertain and possibly non-Indo-European Mediterranean substrate origin.

parole.significato: sunstroke
parole.testo: From Latin sīriāsis, from Ancient Greek σειρίᾱσις (seiríāsis, “heatstroke”)

parole.significato: To stay (e.g. judicial proceedings); to delay or suspend; to stop

parole.significato: Synonym of Poor Clare: a nun of the Order of Saint Clare.
parole.testo: Calque of Medieval Latin sorores minores (“lesser sisters”) and its variants in Norman, Middle French, and Italian. Doublet of Sister Minoress.

parole.significato: A sister born of the same parents
parole.testo: From Middle English sister germain, equivalent to sister + german, after Anglo-Norman and Middle French suer germaine and its etymon Classical Latin germāna soror.

parole.significato: An ancient Egyptian musical instrument, to be shaken, consisting of a metal frame holding percussive metal beads.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sīstrum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σεῖστρον (seîstron), from σείω (seíō, “shake”).

parole.significato: Thirsty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sitiēns (“thirsting, thirsty”).

parole.significato: A small passerine bird of the genus Daphoenositta, found in Australasia.
parole.testo: From New Latin (genus name), diminutive of Latin sitta (“nuthatch”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the family Sittidae, or nuthatches.
parole.testo: From New Latin sitta (“the nuthatch”), from Ancient Greek σίττη (síttē, “nuthatch”) + -ine.

parole.significato: Positional, relating to position or location.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin situalis, from situs (“site”) + -alis (“-al”).

parole.significato: To place on or into a physical location.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin situātus, past participle of Medieval Latin situō (“to locate, place”), from Latin situs (“a site”).

parole.significato: A deep ceramic vase with a wide opening.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin situla.

parole.significato: The position, especially the usual, normal position, of a body part or part of a plant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin situs (“position, site”). Doublet of site and sitio.

parole.testo: From the Latin Sixtō-Clēmentīnus.

parole.significato: A skeleton.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin sceletus, from Ancient Greek σκελετός (skeletós).

parole.significato: To reduce to a skeleton; to skin; to skeletonize.
parole.testo: From New Latin sceleton, from Ancient Greek σκελετόν (skeletón), the neuter of σκελετός (skeletós, “dried up, withered, dried body, parched, mummy”), from σκέλλω (skéllō, “dry, dry up, make dry, parch”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to parch, wither”); compare Ancient Greek σκληρός (sklērós

parole.significato: The practice or philosophy of being a skeptic.
parole.testo: From New Latin scepticismus; equivalent to skeptic + -ism.

parole.significato: A member of any of the peoples of Europe who speak the Slavic languages.
parole.testo: From Middle English Sclave, borrowed from Medieval Latin Sclavus, from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos); see that entry for more. Doublet of slave and ciao. Displaced native Old English Wined.

parole.significato: Of, denoting, or relating to the people who speak these languages, their languages, or cultures.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Slavonicus, Sclavonicus, from Slavonia, Sclavonia.

parole.significato: A mistake in speech.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin lapsus linguae.

parole.significato: An emerald.
parole.testo: From Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), μάραγδος (máragdos), from a Semitic language.

parole.significato: Emerald.
parole.testo: From Latin smaragdinus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδινος (smáragdinos), from σμάραγδος (smáragdos). See emerald for more.

parole.significato: Cleansing.
parole.testo: From Latin smecticus, from Ancient Greek σμηκτικός (smēktikós), from σμήχειν (smḗkhein, “to wipe, to cleanse”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”).

parole.significato: A whitish sebaceous secretion that collects between the glans penis and foreskin or in the vulva.
parole.testo: From Latin, borrowed from Ancient Greek σμῆγμα (smêgma), alternative form of σμῆμα (smêma, “soap, detergent”), from σμάω (smáō, “to wipe, clean”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or containing smegma.
parole.testo: From Latin smēgmaticus.

parole.significato: The lack of aspiration on a vowel or semivowel in Ancient Greek.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin spīritus lēnis, from Ancient Greek ψιλὸν πνεῦμα (psilòn pneûma).

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of (ancient) Smyrna. Contrast Smyrniot.
parole.testo: From Latin Smyrnaeus + English -an.

parole.significato: A hidden enemy.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin latet anguis in herbā (literally “a snake hides in the grass”), from Eclogue III by the Roman poet Virgil (traditionally 70 – 19 B.C.E.). Compare Dutch addertje onder het gras.

parole.significato: A shoot that runs along underground and forms new plants at short distances.
parole.testo: From Latin sobolēs.

parole.significato: The killing of a cousin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sobrīnicidium (“cousin-killing”)

parole.significato: To associate.
parole.testo: From Latin sociatus.

parole.significato: An organization that is supposedly a partnership but in which one partner claims the lion's share.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A social philosophy that promotes the well-being of the group without sacrificing the significance of the individual.
parole.testo: From the Latin societās + -ism.

parole.significato: A member of a particular nontrinitarian Christian denomination founded in the late 16th century.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Sociniānus.

parole.significato: society
parole.testo: From Latin socius (“associated, allied; partner, companion, ally”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-yo- (“companion”), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”).

parole.significato: Any of the autonomous tribes and city states of the Italian Peninsula in permanent military alliance with the Roman Rep…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin socius.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of the philosopher Socrates or his philosophy or methods.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Sōcratic(us). By surface analysis, Socrat(es) + -ic.

parole.significato: Engaging in sodomy; characterised by or involving sodomy.
parole.testo: From Latin Sodomiticus.

parole.significato: A soc (a medieval right to hold a court or to receive fines).
parole.testo: From Middle English soke, from Medieval Latin (Anglo-Latin) sōca "right of jurisdiction", from Old English sōcn (“jurisdiction, prosecution”, literally “act of seeking”), from Proto-West Germanic *sōkni, from Proto-Germanic *sōkniz (“seeking, inquiry”), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂g- (“to track”).

parole.significato: Or (gold), in the postmedieval practice of blazoning the tinctures of certain sovereigns' (especially British monarchs'…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Sōl.

parole.significato: A solar day on the planet Mars (equivalent to 24 hours, 39 minutes, 35 seconds).
parole.testo: From Latin sōl (“sun”); see further at etymology 3. Doublet of sol from Spanish.

parole.significato: The doctrine that the Church, and not Scripture alone, is the ultimate source of authority for Christian doctrine.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sōla ecclēsia (literally “the church alone”).

parole.significato: The doctrine that salvation is conveyed by the grace and goodwill of God, as a free gift, without merit on the part of…
parole.testo: Latin, meaning "solely grace".

parole.significato: The Protestant Christian doctrine that the Bible is the supreme authority in all matters of doctrine and practice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sōlā scrīptūrā (“by scripture alone”) (ablative).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the family Solanaceae, which includes the nightshades.
parole.testo: From modern Latin Solanaceae, from Latin solanum (“nightshade”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the sun; proceeding from the sun.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English solar, from Latin sōlāris, from sōl (“sun”), from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥ (“sun”).

parole.significato: A loft or upper chamber forming the private accommodation of the head of the household in a medieval hall; a garret roo…
parole.testo: From Middle English solar, soler; from a conflation of Old English soler, solere (“raised platform; loft, upper room, upper part of a house, soler”), from Latin sōlārium; and Old English solor, salor (“residence, dwelling; hall; palace”), from Proto-West Germanic *salaʀ, from Proto-Germanic *salaz,

parole.significato: A room, rooftop, balcony, or terrace, used for its abundant sunlight, especially when used as a medical treatment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sōlārium (“sundial, place for enjoying sunlight”), from sōl (“sun”) + -ārium (“-arium: indicating related places or devices”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the sun; solar.
parole.testo: From Latin solaris + -ary.

parole.significato: A form of compensation for emotional rather than physical or financial harm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin solatium.

parole.significato: Slipper-shaped; calceolate.
parole.testo: From Latin solea (“sandal”) + -iform.

parole.significato: skillful; clever; crafty
parole.testo: From Latin solers.

parole.significato: A broad, flat muscle that extends behind the gastrocnemius along the back of the calf.
parole.testo: Clipping of musculus soleus, a relative adjective to Latin solum.

parole.significato: One who solicits.
parole.testo: Latin solicitans, present participle of sollicitō.

parole.significato: solicitous
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sollicitātus, perfect passive participle of sollicitō (“to solicit, disturb, rouse”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Compare French solliciter.

parole.significato: To solicit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sollicitātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: Disposed to solicit; eager to obtain something desirable, or to avoid anything evil.
parole.testo: From Latin sōlicitus, sollicitus (“thoroughly disturbed, anxious”), from sollus (“whole, entire”) + cieō (“move, disturb”). By surface analysis, solicit + -ous.

parole.significato: Expressing solicitude.
parole.testo: From Latin sol(l)icitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin sollicitūdō, from sollicitus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, solicitude + -ous.

parole.significato: To make solid or firm; to solidify.
parole.testo: From Latin solidatus, past participle of solidare. See solder, consolidate.

parole.significato: The die of a pedestal.
parole.testo: From Latin solidum. Doublet of solid.

parole.significato: Various medieval and early modern coins or units of account
parole.testo: From Middle English solidus, from classical Latin solidus (“solid”), see below. Doublet of sol, sold, soldo, solid, sou, and xu. In numismatic and weight senses, via medieval Latin solidus (“various coins”), from Late Latin solidus (“a gold coin of the Roman Empire”). In chemical sense, via German S

parole.significato: An ancient Iberian heavy iron javelin. It was designed to be thrown a short distance of up to 30 meters.
parole.testo: From Latin soliferrum, from solus (“only”) + ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: A person who believes that faith alone (as opposed to good deeds) brings salvation.
parole.testo: From Latin sōlā fidē (“only by faith”) + -ian.

parole.significato: Soil creep caused by waterlogged soil slowly moving downhill on top of an impermeable layer.
parole.testo: From Latin solum (“soil”) + -i- + fluctiō (“act of flowing”).

parole.significato: Like the sun in appearance or nature.
parole.testo: From Latin sol (“sun”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Moving away from the sun.
parole.testo: From Latin sōl (“sun”) + fugiō (“to flee”) + -al.

parole.significato: Synonym of camel spider.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin solifuga.

parole.significato: The act of a character speaking to themselves so as to reveal their thoughts to the audience.
parole.testo: 1595–1605; From Late Latin sōliloquium in the title of St. Augustine's Soliloquiorum libri duo ("Two Books of Soliloquies"), from sōlus (“only, sole”) + loquor (“to speak”).

parole.significato: Relating to, or due to the influence of, both the sun and the moon.
parole.testo: From Latin sol (“sun”) and Latin luna (“moon”).

parole.significato: A mammal having a single hoof on each foot; a solidungulate.
parole.testo: From Latin sōliped-, sōlipēs.

parole.significato: Moving towards the sun.
parole.testo: From Latin sōl (“sun”) + petō, petere (“seek, aim”) + -al.

parole.significato: The idea that the self is all that exists or that can be proven to exist.
parole.testo: From Latin sōlus (“alone”) + ipse (“self”) + -ism.

parole.significato: Following the sun.
parole.testo: From Latin sol (“sun”) + sequor (“to follow”) + -ous.

parole.significato: Living or being by oneself; alone; having no companion present
parole.testo: From Middle English solitarie, borrowed from Latin sōlitārius. Doublet of solitaire.

parole.significato: One who remains solitary.
parole.testo: From Latin sōlitūdin- + -arian, from oblique stem of Latin sōlitūdō, from sōlus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, solitude + -arian.

parole.significato: Characterised by solitude
parole.testo: From Latin sōlitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin sōlitūdō, from sōlus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, solitude + -ous.

parole.significato: Wandering alone.
parole.testo: From Latin sōlivagāns, from sōlus (“alone”) + vagāns, present participle of vagō (“wander”).

parole.significato: solivagant; wandering alone
parole.testo: From Latin solivagus.

parole.significato: A person of unusual wisdom.
parole.testo: From Latin Solomōn (variant of Salomon), from Ancient Greek Σολομών (Solomṓn), from Biblical Hebrew שְׁלֹמֹה (šĕlōmōʰ), from שָׁלוֹם (šālōm, “peace”). Doublet of Shlomo and Suleiman.

parole.significato: Any flowering plant of the genus Polygonatum, especially Polygonatuym multiflorum.
parole.testo: From genitive form of Solomon (king of ancient Israel) + seal, translating Medieval Latin sigillum Solomōnis.

parole.significato: The act, practice, or quality of being sexual with oneself.
parole.testo: From Latin sōlus (“alone”) + sexuality.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a solstice.
parole.testo: From Latin sōlstitiālis.

parole.significato: Within a soil profile, a set of related soil horizons that share the same cycle of pedogenic processes; the upper layer…
parole.testo: From Latin solum (“base, bottom; soil”). Doublet of soil.

parole.significato: alone, unaccompanied (as a stage direction)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sōlus.

parole.significato: Free; liberal; loose.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin solutus, past participle of solvo.

parole.significato: Tending to produce relaxation (as of the bowels); having laxative properties.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin solutivus, from Latin solutus (the past participle of solvere) + -ive (from the Latin suffix -ivus). Compare French solutif.

parole.significato: To find an answer or solution to a problem or question; to work out.
parole.testo: From Middle English solven, from Latin solvō.

parole.significato: A substance to be dissolved.
parole.testo: From Latin solvendus (“to be loosened or dissolved”), from solvere. See solution.

parole.significato: The whole axial portion of an animal, including the head, neck, trunk, and tail.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek σῶμα (sôma, “body”).

parole.significato: Relating to sleep.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin somnus (“sleep”).

parole.significato: Walking as if, or while, asleep; sleepwalking.
parole.testo: From Latin somnus (“sleep”) + ambulō (“to walk”) + -ant.

parole.significato: The phenomenon of sleepwalking.
parole.testo: From Latin somnus (“sleep”) + ambulatio (“a walking about”), from ambulare (“to walk”). See somnolent, amble.

parole.significato: To sleepwalk; to somnambulate.
parole.testo: From Latin somnus (“sleep”) + ambulo (“to walk”), + -ize.

parole.significato: drowsy; sleepy.
parole.testo: Latin somniculosus.

parole.significato: Inducing or causing sleep.
parole.testo: From Latin somnus (“sleep”) + facio (“to make”).

parole.significato: causing or inducing sleep, normally with harmful overtones.
parole.testo: From Latin somnifer + -ous, from somnus (“sleep”) + ferre (“to bring”).

parole.significato: Causing sleep; somniferous.
parole.testo: From Latin somnificus, from somnus (“sleep”) + facere (“to make”). By surface analysis, somn- + -ific.

parole.significato: Talkative in one’s sleep.
parole.testo: From Latin somnus (“sleep”) + loquacious.

parole.significato: Talking while asleep.
parole.testo: Coined based on Latin somnus (“sleep”) + loquor (“to talk”).

parole.significato: Any sleep disorder.
parole.testo: From Latin somnus (“sleep”) + -pathy.

parole.significato: Having a desire to sleep.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin somnus + -i- + volēns; see also volition.

parole.significato: A hypnotic and sedative drug containing chloral hydrate.
parole.testo: From a proprietary name, from Latin somnos (“sleep”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to sound; sounding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sonāns, sonantis. By surface analysis, Latin son(ō) + -ant.

parole.significato: Producing or conveying sound; sonorous.
parole.testo: From Latin sonus (“sound”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Of or relating to sound.
parole.testo: From Latin sonus (“sound”).

parole.significato: Producing sound.
parole.testo: From Latin sonor (“a sound”), -oris + facere (“to make”). See sonorous.

parole.significato: Capable of giving out a deep, resonant sound.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sonōrus, from sonor (“sound”), early 17th century.

parole.significato: A high central vowel occurring in the Latin language, [ɨ] or possibly [ʉ], that developed from earlier /u/ in non-initi…
parole.testo: From Latin sonus medius (“intermediate sound”).

parole.significato: A device produced by Sony.
parole.testo: A combination of Latin sonus (“sound”) and sonny (“boy”, diminutive).

parole.significato: Wise men; sages.
parole.testo: From the Latin sophī, the nominative plural form of sophus, from the Ancient Greek σοφός (sophós).

parole.significato: Synonym of sophistical, of or related to the ancient Sophists, characterized by fallacious reasoning.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sophisticus, borrowing of Ancient Greek σοφιστικός (sophistikós). Equivalent to sophist + -ic and sophism + -istic.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a sophist or sophistry.
parole.testo: From Middle English sophistical, sophisticale, sophisticall, from Anglo-Latin sophisticālis, equivalent to sophist + -ical.

parole.significato: To make (something) less innocent or natural; to artificialize.
parole.testo: From Middle English sophisticaten (“to mix (something) with a foreign or inferior substance, adulterate”), from Medieval Latin sophisticātus, the perfect passive participle of sophisticāre (“to disguise; to tamper with; to trick using words”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more). Sophisticāre i

parole.significato: Of a person: having obtained worldly experience, and lacking naiveté; cosmopolitan, worldly-wise.
parole.testo: First English usage circa 1601. From Medieval Latin sophisticatus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Sophocles or his works.
parole.testo: From Latin Sophoclēus + English -an.

parole.significato: wisdom, knowledge, learning
parole.testo: From the Middle English sophie, from the Latin sophia, from the Ancient Greek σοφῐ́ᾱ (sophĭ́ā, “high knowledge”: “learning”, “wisdom”); compare Sophia.

parole.significato: A wise man; a sage.
parole.testo: A back-formation from sophies, originally plurale tantum, but later attested in singular use (see the 1678 quotation), itself an irregular Anglicisation of the Latin sophī, whence the English sophi; compare sophy.

parole.significato: To put to sleep, or to quieten.
parole.testo: From Latin sopitus, past participle of sopire (“to put to sleep”).

parole.significato: The act of putting to sleep.
parole.testo: From Latin sōpītiō, from sōpiō (“to put to sleep”).

parole.significato: An unnaturally deep sleep.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sopor (“sleep”).

parole.significato: To lay or put to sleep; to stupefy.
parole.testo: From Latin soporatus, past participle of soporare (“to put to sleep”), from sopor (“a heavy sleep”).

parole.significato: The awkward or humorous use of different languages mixed together, often using a foreign term incorrectly or in an inap…
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: To absorb or adsorb.
parole.testo: Back-formation from absorb and adsorb; ultimately from Latin sorbeō.

parole.significato: Producing absorption.
parole.testo: From Latin sorbere (“to suck in, absorb”) + faciens, p.pr. of facere (“to make”).

parole.significato: an unsaturated aliphatic carboxylic acid, CH₃.CH:CH.CH:CH.COOH, found in Rowan berries, and used as a preservative
parole.testo: Latin sorbum (“the rowan or serviceberry”).

parole.significato: Fit to be drunk or sipped.
parole.testo: From Latin sorbilis, from sorbere (“to suck in, to drink down”).

parole.significato: Deposits of dirt or bacteria on the body, discharges; bacterial deposits on the teeth or tongue.
parole.testo: From Latin sordes, related to sordere.

parole.significato: sordidness
parole.testo: Possibly from an unattested Latin *sordor, or by back-formation of a noun from sordidus (“dirty, vile”).

parole.significato: A cereal, Sorghum genus and species, the grains of which are cultivated to make flour and feed cattle. Almost all culti…
parole.testo: From New Latin genus name Sorghum, from Italian sorgo, from Vulgar Latin *syricum (“Syrian”), from Sȳricus. Doublet of the synonyms sorgho (via French) and sorgo (via Italian).

parole.significato: Copper sulphate, especially combined with other impurities, particularly in the context of the Roman Empire.
parole.testo: . Latin [Term?]?

parole.significato: Of or relating to the shrew family (Soricidae); resembling a shrew in form or habits.
parole.testo: From Latin soricinus, from sorex (“a shrew”).

parole.significato: A series of propositions whereby each conclusion is taken as the subject of the next.
parole.testo: From the Latin sōrītēs, from the Ancient Greek σωρῑ́της (sōrī́tēs, “fallacy of the heap”), from σωρός (sōrós, “heap”).

parole.significato: A member of Soroptimist International (founded 1921), a worldwide volunteer service organization for professional women…
parole.testo: From Latin soror (“sister”) and optima (“best”). See also -ist.

parole.significato: A sorority sister; a fellow member of one's sorority.
parole.testo: PIE word  *swésōr Shortening; also from Latin soror (“sister”), akin to frater from Latin frāter (“brother”). Doublet of sister.

parole.significato: Synonym of sororal (“of, pertaining to, or characteristic of a sister or sisters”).
parole.testo: PIE word  *swésōr Learned borrowing from Latin sorōrius (“sisterly”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Sorōrius is derived from soror (“sister”) + -ius (suffix meaning ‘belonging to’ forming adjectives).

parole.significato: The killing of one's sister.
parole.testo: From Latin sorōricīdium (“killing of one’s sister”), from soror (“sister”) + -cīdium (“killing”). Equivalent to Latin soror (“sister”) + -cide (“killing”).

parole.significato: A person who kills his or her sister.
parole.testo: From Latin sorōricīda (“one who kills his sister”), from soror (“sister”) + -cīda (“killer”). Equivalent to Latin soror (“sister”) + -cide (“killer”).

parole.significato: A group of girls or women associated for a common purpose; a sisterhood.
parole.testo: PIE word  *swésōr From Renaissance Latin sorōritās, from Latin soror (“sister”), from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr. Akin to Spanish sororidad, Portuguese sororidade, French sororité.

parole.significato: To associate, or have a relationship, as or as if sisters; to have sisterly feelings or bonds.
parole.testo: From Latin soror, sororis (“a sister”).

parole.significato: Either of the processes of absorption and adsorption; sorbing.
parole.testo: Back-formation from absorption; representing Latin sorbeō (“to suck in”).

parole.significato: divination, or the seeking of guidance, by chance selection of a passage in the Bible or another text regarded as autho…
parole.testo: From Latin plural of sors (“lot, fate, oracular response”).

parole.significato: Selection by drawing lots.
parole.testo: From Latin sortītiō.

parole.significato: Any reproductive structure, in some lichens and fungi, that produces spores.
parole.testo: From New Latin sōrus, from Ancient Greek σωρός (sōrós, “heap”).

parole.significato: iron(II) sulfate, or some earth impregnated with it
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sory, from Ancient Greek σῶρυ (sôru, “a kind of ore”).

parole.significato: Stupid person; fool.
parole.testo: From Middle English sot, from Old English sot, sott (“foolish, stupid”), from Medieval Latin sottus (“foolish”), of obscure origin and relation. parole.significato: A shoemaker or cobbler.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English soutere, from Old English sūtere, from Latin sūtor (“shoemaker, cobbler”).

parole.significato: new species
parole.testo: From Latin species nova.

parole.significato: The property of being spacious.
parole.testo: From Latin spatiōsitās, modified after spacious; compare Middle English spaciosite, spaciositee, Middle French spaciosite (“hollow space or cavity”), and modern French spaciosité (“spaciousness, extensiveness”, 1842).

parole.significato: Of a bright clear brown or chestnut colour.
parole.testo: From Latin spadix, spadicis (“a date-brown or nut-brown color”). See spadix.

parole.significato: A fleshy spike (inflorescence) with reduced flowers, usually enclosed by a spathe, characteristic of aroids.
parole.testo: Via Latin spādīx from Ancient Greek σπᾱ́δῑξ (spā́dīx, “palm branch”).

parole.significato: Someone who has been castrated; a eunuch or castrato.
parole.testo: From Latin spadō, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Pertaining to alchemy; alchemical, especially regarding medicine.
parole.testo: From Late Latin spagyricus, from Ancient Greek σπάω (spáō, “I draw, pull”) + ἀγείρω (ageírō, “I assemble”).

parole.significato: An alchemist, especially one who tried to discover remedies for diseases.
parole.testo: From modern Latin spagirista, from spagiricus (“alchemy”) (probably invented by Paracelsus).

parole.significato: The act of sprinkling.
parole.testo: From Latin spargere (“to strew”) + facere, factum (“to make”).

parole.significato: Any of several perciform fishes of the family Sparidae
parole.testo: From Latin sparus (“bream”) + -id.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the family, Sparidae, of deep-bodied, spinous-finned marine fish, including the sea bream, porgy, s…
parole.testo: From Latin sparus (“gilt-head, a certain kind of fish”) + -oid (“resembling”, suffix forming an adjective).

parole.significato: Having widely spaced intervals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sparsus.

parole.significato: A citizen of Sparta; a native or inhabitant of Sparta.
parole.testo: From Middle English Spartan, Spertan, from Latin Spartānus, from Sparta + -ānus, equivalent to Sparta + -an.

parole.significato: A Spartan, especially a full citizen.
parole.testo: From Middle English Sparciate, from Latin Spartiātēs, from Ancient Greek Σπᾰρτῐᾱ́της (Spărtĭā́tēs), from Σπᾰ́ρτη (Spắrtē) + -ᾱ́της (-ā́tēs).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a spasm; resembling a sudden contraction of the muscles.
parole.testo: From New Latin spasmōdicus, from Ancient Greek σπασμώδης (spasmṓdēs, “spasmodic”), from σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm”).

parole.significato: A syndrome characterised by the symptom triad of head nodding, ocular oscillations and anomalous head position (tortico…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spasmus nutans (literally “nodding spasm”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or affected by spasm.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin spasticus, from Ancient Greek σπαστικός (spastikós, “drawing in”). By surface analysis, spasm + -tic. Cf. French spastique and see also spasm.

parole.significato: An obsolete unit of distance in astronomy (symbol S), equal to one billion kilometres.
parole.testo: From Latin spatium (“space”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Spathiphyllum of peace lilies.
parole.testo: From New Latin, shortening of the genus name Spathiphyllum, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “blade”) + φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”).

parole.significato: A type of straight sword originating from the first-century Roman Empire. It was worn typically by cavalry officers and…
parole.testo: From Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “any broad blade, of wood or metal”). Doublet of spade, spathe, and epee.

parole.significato: A large bract that envelops or subtends a whole inflorescence, typically a spadix.
parole.testo: From Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “blade”). Doublet of epee, spatha, and spade.

parole.significato: lymph-filled spaces between the fibers of the ciliary zonule at the equator of the lens of the eye
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Pertaining to (the dimension of) space.
parole.testo: From Latin spatium + -al.

parole.significato: To rove or ramble.
parole.testo: From Latin spatiātus, past participle of spatior (“walk around, spread out”), from spatium (“space, room”). Compare Italian spaziare, German spazieren.

parole.significato: A kitchen utensil consisting of a flat surface attached to a long handle, used for turning, lifting, or stirring food.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spatula (“a flat piece”), the diminutive form of spatha (“broad or flat tool”), from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “a broad wood or metal blade”). Doublet of spauld; compare spatha and spathe.

parole.significato: divination using the shoulder blade of an animal
parole.testo: Latin spatula (“shoulder blade”) + -mancy

parole.significato: Type or kind, in various uses of the phrase in specie.
parole.testo: Originally in the phrase in specie; from Latin speciē, ablative singular of species. Compare in kind.

parole.significato: A type or kind. (Compare race.)
parole.testo: From Latin speciēs (“appearance; quality”), from speciō (“see”) + -iēs suffix signifying abstract noun. Doublet of spice.

parole.significato: Synonym of specific.
parole.testo: From Middle English specificalle, from Latin specificus + -al.

parole.significato: A surgical probe.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin specillum.

parole.significato: An individual instance that represents a class; an example.
parole.testo: From Latin specimen (“mark, sign, example”), from speciō (“observe, watch”).

parole.significato: The state or quality of being specious; speciousness.
parole.testo: From Middle English speciouste (“attractiveness”), from Latin speciōsitās (“beauty”), from speciēs (“appearance”). By surface analysis, speci(ous) + -osity.

parole.significato: Amazing or worthy of special notice.
parole.testo: From Latin spectaculum (“a sight, show”) + -ar.

parole.significato: A spectacle.
parole.testo: From Latin spectāculum. Doublet of spectacle.

parole.significato: Looking forward.
parole.testo: From Latin spectans, present participle of spectare (“to look at”).

parole.significato: Regard; aspect; appearance.
parole.testo: From Latin spectatio.

parole.significato: One who watches an event; especially, an event held outdoors.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spectātor, from frequentative verb spectō (“watch”), from speciō (“look at”). Equivalent to spectate + -or. Doublet of speculator.

parole.significato: A female spectator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin spectātrīx. By surface analysis, spectator + -trix.

parole.significato: A range; a continuous, infinite, one-dimensional set, possibly bounded by extremes.
parole.testo: From Latin spectrum (“appearance, image, apparition”), from speciō (“look at, view”). Doublet of specter. See also scope.

parole.significato: That can be the subject of speculation.
parole.testo: From Latin speculābilis; compare Middle English speculable.

parole.significato: Pertaining to mirrors; mirror-like, reflective.
parole.testo: From Latin speculāris, from speculum; and in some senses from speculārī (“to watch, observe”). Some later senses via French spéculaire.

parole.significato: To think, meditate or reflect on a subject; to consider, to deliberate or cogitate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin speculātus, perfect active participle of speculor (“to watch, observe, examine, spy”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from specula (“a watchtower”), ultimately from speciō (“to look at”).

parole.significato: One who speculates; an observer; a contemplator.
parole.testo: From Latin speculātor (“spy, explorer, investigator”), from speculor (“to watch, to observe”) + -tor (“-er: forming agent nouns”), from specula (“watchtower”), from speciō (“to watch, to observe”), q.v. In some senses, an agent noun formed within English from speculate. Doublet of spectator.

parole.significato: Intended or adapted for viewing or looking out.
parole.testo: From Latin speculātōrius (“of or pertaining to spies or scouts”).

parole.significato: A female speculator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin speculātrīx. By surface analysis, speculate + -trix.

parole.significato: A medical instrument used during an examination to dilate an orifice.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin speculum.

parole.significato: A medieval literary genre, popular from the 12th through the 16th centuries, inspired by the urge to encompass encyclop…
parole.testo: From Latin speculum (“mirror”) in the title of these works.

parole.significato: cave-dwelling
parole.testo: From Latin spelaeum (“cave”).

parole.significato: hopeful or hoped for
parole.testo: From Latin sperabilis. Compare esperance and see -ible.

parole.significato: hoped for
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin speratus, past participle of sperare (“to hope”).

parole.significato: The reproductive cell or gamete of the male; a spermatozoon.
parole.testo: From Middle English sperme, from Latin sperma, from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma, “seed, semen”). Compare also Old French esperme, sparme.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling sperm.
parole.testo: From Middle English spermatik, from Latin spermaticus, from Ancient Greek σπερματικός (spermatikós). By surface analysis, spermat- + -ic.

parole.significato: To produce or emit sperm.
parole.testo: From Latin spermatizare (“to spermatize”), possibly via French spermatiser, from Ancient Greek σπερματίζειν (spermatízein, “to sow, spread seed upon”), from σπέρμα (spérma, “seed, sperm”). By surface analysis, spermat- + -ize.

parole.significato: A spermatozoon.

parole.significato: The principle of following judicial precedent.

parole.significato: A receipt given by Jews on payment of debt.

parole.significato: Unchanging; that cannot or does not change.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a station.

parole.significato: A supporter of the status quo; one who believes that society is in an acceptable state and should not be changed.

parole.significato: A person who makes or deals in statues.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or characteristic of statues.

parole.significato: Soapstone. (often synonymous; more information at soapstone § Terminology).

parole.significato: An obelisk or upright stone pillar, usually as a primitive commemoration or gravestone.

parole.significato: A serving of Stella Artois, a brand of beer.

parole.significato: Shaped like a star, having points, or rays radiating from a center.

parole.significato: A person with a powerful or stentorian voice.

parole.significato: Relating to the sternum and the thyroid cartilage.

parole.significato: The breastbone, consisting of the manubrium, gladiolus, and xiphoid process.

parole.significato: To expel air as a reflex induced by an irritation in the nose.

parole.significato: An indication of infamy or disgrace.

parole.significato: A device for distilling liquids.

parole.significato: Pressed together; crowded.

parole.significato: Receiving a stipend.

parole.significato: To provide (someone) with a stipend, or salary; to pay, support or fund.

parole.significato: The act of stipulating; a contracting or bargaining; an agreement.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Strabo.

parole.significato: Sudden; suddenly done or made.

parole.significato: Lying beneath or at a lower level; underlying.

parole.significato: To cause (someone or something) to undergo a particular experience, especially one that is unpleasant or unwanted.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin subiectō, iterative of subiciō (“throw, lay, place”), from sub (“under, at the foot of”) + iaciō (“throw, hurl”).

parole.testo: From Late Middle English subiugate, subjugaten (“to conquer; to subdue”), from Latin subiugātus, subjugātus (“subjugated”): see further at etymology 1. The verb is attested slightly later than the adjective.

parole.significato: The act of subjugating.
parole.testo: From Latin subiugātiō, from Latin subiugō (“to subjugate”). By surface analysis, subjugate + -ion.

parole.significato: A person who subjugates or conquers.

parole.significato: A female subjugator.

parole.significato: Mood expressing an action or state which is hypothetical or anticipated rather than actual, including wishes and comman…
parole.testo: From subjunctive (from Latin subjunctivus, from sub- (“under”) + junctus (“joined”), perfect passive participle of jungere (“to join”) + adjective suffix -ivus) + mood (from Latin modus).

parole.significato: To negate, deny or contradict.
parole.testo: From Latin sublatum, past participle of suffero.

parole.significato: A kind of underwear worn in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subligāculum.

parole.significato: An intricately folded cloth used as underwear by both men and women in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subligaria.

parole.significato: The act of binding underneath.
parole.testo: Latin subligatio, from subligare to bind below; sub (“under”) + ligare (“to bind”).

parole.testo: From Middle English sublimacioun, sublimacion, from Medieval Latin sublīmātiō, from Latin sublīmō (“to raise, to elevate”, verb). Synchronically, sublimate + -ion.

parole.significato: A vessel or device used for sublimation.
parole.testo: From Middle English sublymatories pl, from Medieval Latin sublīmātōrium, from Latin sublīmātus (see sublime) + -ōrium.

parole.significato: The act of making sublime
parole.testo: From Latin sublimis (“sublime”) + -ification.

parole.testo: From sub- (“beneath, under”) + liminal (“of or pertaining to an entrance or threshold”) (from Latin līminālis, from līmen (“doorstep, threshold; doorway, entrance; beginning, commencement”); possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃l- (“to bend, bow; elbow”)) + *-mn̥ (suffix forming action

parole.significato: A muscular secondary tongue found below the primary tongue in prosimian primates.

parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin sublinguālis, from sub- (“under, below, beneath”) + linguālis (“relating to the tongue”); equivalent to sub- + lingual.

parole.significato: Partly lobate, having a somewhat lobey shape.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sublobātus. By surface analysis, sub- + lobate.

parole.significato: Synonym of subluxate: to partially dislocate or displace.
parole.testo: From New Latin subluxāre (“to subluxate”), q.v. Also parsed as a clipping of subluxate and equivalent to sub- + lux.

parole.significato: To cause the subluxation of something: to partially dislocate or displace.
parole.testo: From New Latin sublūxātus (“subluxated”), perfect active participle of subluxare (“to subluxate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from sub- (“under, below, lesser”) + lūxō (“to dislocate”). Equivalent to sub- + luxate.

parole.significato: Almost or imperfectly membranaceous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin submembrānāceus. By surface analysis, sub- + membranaceous.

parole.significato: To sink out of sight.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin submergere, from sub (“under”) + mergere (“to plunge”). By surface analysis, sub- + merge.

parole.significato: To submerge.
parole.testo: From Latin submersus, past participle of submergo.

parole.significato: The act of submerging, or the state of being submerged; immersion
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin summersio, summersionem.

parole.significato: to supply; to administer
parole.testo: From the Latin subministrō, sumministrō (equivalent to English sub- + minister).

parole.significato: subordinate or subservient
parole.testo: From Latin subministrans.

parole.significato: The act of subministering.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subministratio.

parole.significato: Submissive.

parole.significato: To yield or give way to another.
parole.testo: From Middle English submitten, borrowed from Latin submittere, infinitive of submittō (“place under, yield”), from sub (“under, from below, up”) + mitto (“to send”). Compare upsend.

parole.significato: To suggest; to prompt.
parole.testo: From Latin submonere, equivalent to summon + -ish.

parole.significato: suggestion; prompting
parole.testo: Latin submonitio.

parole.significato: Growing underneath.
parole.testo: Latin subnascens, present participle of subnasci (“to grow under”), from sub (“under”) + nasci (“to be born”).

parole.significato: To (literally) tie or fasten beneath, or to (figuratively) join beneath, i.e. as an addendum.
parole.testo: From Latin subnecto, from sub (“under”) + necto (“to tie”).

parole.significato: The seasonal microenvironment beneath the snow.
parole.testo: From sub- (“under”) + Latin nix (“snow”) + -ium.

parole.significato: A rescript
parole.testo: From Latin subnotatio (“a signing underneath”).

parole.significato: Placed in a lower class, rank, or position.
parole.testo: From Middle English subordinat, from Medieval Latin subōrdinātus, past participle of subōrdināre, from sub- + ōrdināre (“to order”).

parole.significato: Synonym of suborder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subōrdō.

parole.significato: Only somewhat characteristic of a prism; not quite prismatic.

parole.significato: Nearly or imperfectly quadrangular.

parole.significato: A subkingdom.
parole.testo: From New Latin subrēgnum.

parole.significato: Under Roman law, the act of giving false testimony.
parole.testo: From Latin subreptio, from subripere, subreptum (“to snatch or take away secretly”). Compare French subreption. See surreptitious, surreptition.

parole.significato: Surreptitious.
parole.testo: Latin subreptivus.

parole.significato: Characterized by a smile; smiling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin subrīdēns, subrīdentem (“smiling”), from Latin subrīdeō (“to smile”).

parole.significato: An act of smiling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin subrisio (“smile”), from Latin subrīdeō (“to smile”).

parole.significato: Playful, tongue-in-cheek.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin subrisivus (“amusing”), from Latin subrīdeō (“to smile”).

parole.significato: To replace one person or thing with another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subrogātus, perfect passive participle of subrogō, from sub (“under”) + rogō (“to ask, request”). A variant of surrogate.

parole.significato: Substitution of a different person in place of a creditor or claimant with respect to certain rights and duties.
parole.testo: From Late Latin subrogātiō, from sub- + rogātiō (“inquiry, request”); equivalent to sub- + rogation.

parole.significato: derision; mockery

parole.significato: A certain large, triangular muscle near the shoulder that plays a key role in rotating the arm

parole.significato: To write (one’s name) at the bottom of a document; to sign (one's name).
parole.testo: From Middle English subscriben, subskryben, from Latin subscrībere (“write beneath”). By surface analysis, sub- + scribe. Compare its native English equivalent underwrite.

parole.significato: Access to a resource for a period of time, generally for payment.
parole.testo: From Latin subscriptiō; by surface analysis, sub- + script + -ion. All senses reflect (either literally or figuratively) the notion of signing one's own name beneath some promise or description to indicate that one agrees with it or agrees to it.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a subscription, or signature.
parole.testo: From Latin subscrīptus (perfect passive participle of subscrībō) + -ive. By surface analysis, subscript (literally “underwrite”) + -ive.

parole.significato: Remaining; extra; spare.
parole.testo: From Latin subsecivus, from sub (“under”) and secare (“to cut”).

parole.significato: To follow closely, or so as to overtake; to pursue.
parole.testo: From Latin subsecūtus, past participle of subsequor (“follow close after”). See subsequent.

parole.significato: To be subservient to.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subservire; by surface analysis, sub- + serve.

parole.significato: Useful in an inferior capacity.
parole.testo: From Latin subserviens, present active of subservio (“to serve under”).

parole.significato: A low-growing woody shrub or perennial with a woody base.
parole.testo: Formed by the combination of sub- + shrub after the scientific Latin suffrutex. Compare the earlier undershrub.

parole.significato: To sink or fall to the bottom; to settle, as lees.
parole.testo: From Latin subsīdō (“to settle, subside”).

parole.significato: The process of becoming less active or severe.

parole.significato: Something that subsists.

parole.significato: A substitute; something that substitutes for another.

parole.significato: Something to be substituted or replaced.

parole.significato: To use in place of something else, with the same function.

parole.significato: A layer that lies underneath another.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin substrātum, nominalisation of the neuter of Latin substrātus, perfect passive participle of substernō. By surface analysis, sub- + stratum.

parole.significato: underbuilding; substructure
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin substructio, from substruere, substructum (“to build beneath”), from sub (“under”) + struere (“to build”).

parole.significato: Bounding; leaping; moving by sudden leaps or starts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin subsultōrius, as subsultim (“with leaps”) from subsilire (“to spring up”), from sub (“under”) + salire (“to leap”).

parole.significato: A twitching, or convulsive motion.
parole.testo: From New Latin subsultus. See subsultory.

parole.significato: To place (any one cognition) under another as belonging to it; to include or contain something else.

parole.significato: The act of subsuming.
parole.testo: From sub- + Latin sūmptus + -ion, from past participle of sūmō (“to take”).

parole.significato: Relating to, or containing, a subsumption.
parole.testo: From sub- + Latin sūmptus + -ive, from past participle of sūmō (“to take”).

parole.significato: To make thin or rare; to rarefy.

parole.significato: To remove or reduce; especially to reduce a quantity or number.

parole.significato: The process of subtracting a number from another.

parole.significato: A number or quantity to be subtracted from another.

parole.significato: A tribe making up part of a larger tribe.

parole.significato: Synonym of subtribe.

parole.significato: To place under; to insert below.

parole.significato: A man's undergarment or shirt.

parole.significato: Awl-shaped; tapering into a sharp point from a broader base.

parole.significato: The quality of being suburban.

parole.significato: A subordinate warden, a lower-ranking warden.

parole.significato: A substitute, replacement for something else, particularly of a medicine used in place of another.

parole.significato: Describing a small lobe that is sometimes attached to a placenta
parole.testo: From Latin succenturiātus, perfect passive participle of succenturiō (“to add soldiers to fill up a century; to substitute”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from sub- (“under”) + centuriō.

parole.significato: The achievement of one's aim or goal.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin successus, from succēdō (“succeed”), from sub- (“next to”) + cēdō (“go, move”).

parole.significato: Coming one after the other in a series.
parole.testo: From Latin succedere (“to succeed in”).

parole.significato: Relating to or derived from succinic acid.
parole.testo: From Latin succinum (“amber”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to succinic acid
parole.testo: From Latin succin(um) (“amber”) + -ic.

parole.significato: succinic
parole.testo: From Latin succinum (“amber”).

parole.significato: An outward growth from underneath.

parole.significato: Growing out from underneath.

parole.significato: A female demon or fiend; a succubus.

parole.significato: A bare axis or cylinder with staves or levers in it to turn it round, but without any drum.
parole.testo: From Latin sucula (“a winch, windlass, capstan”).

parole.significato: submissive; yielding
parole.testo: From Latin succumbens, present participle.

parole.significato: The expressed juice or sap of a plant, often for medicinal use
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin succus (“juice”).

parole.significato: Intestinal juice: the clear to pale yellow watery secretions from the glands lining the small intestine walls.

parole.significato: To shake with vigor.
parole.testo: From Latin succutere (“to shake up”), from sub- + quatere (“to shake”).

parole.significato: Violent shaking or jolting.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin succussatio, from the past participle stem of Latin succussare, frequentative of succutere, from sub- + quatere (“shake”).

parole.significato: The act of succussing or shaking; a shake.
parole.testo: From Latin succussio, from succutere.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to suckitude.
parole.testo: From suckitude + -al by analogy with other adjectives ending in -tudinal, from Latin -tūdin- + -al, the oblique stem of -tūdō.

parole.significato: A force which pushes matter from one space into another because the pressure inside the second space is lower than the…
parole.testo: From Latin sūctiō, sūctiōnem (whence -ion), attested since Late Latin and derived from sūctus, past participle of sūgō (“to suck”). Attested in English since the early 17th century.

parole.significato: Adapted for sucking; living by sucking.
parole.testo: From Latin sūctus + -ory + -al, from past participle of sūgō (“to suck”).

parole.significato: A small blister beneath the skin due to retention of fluid in a sweat follicle, or in the epidermis
parole.testo: From Latin sudare (“to sweat”).

parole.significato: A napkin or handkerchief.

parole.significato: A napkin or handkerchief.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin sudarium. Doublet of sudarium.

parole.significato: To perspire, to sweat.

parole.significato: Perspiration; sweat (fluid).

parole.significato: A sudatorium; a hot room used to induce sweating.
parole.testo: From Latin sūdatorius, from sūdāre (“to sweat”).

parole.significato: Of, from, constituting, inhabiting, or pertaining to the Sudetes or the Sudetenland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Sūdēticus, but with pronunciation influenced by German Sudeten and sudetisch.

parole.significato: Relating to stimulation of the sweat glands.
parole.testo: From Latin sudor (“sweat”), and motor.

parole.significato: Sweat; the salty fluid excreted by the sweat glands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sūdor.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to sweat; caused by sweat; characterised by the production of sweat.
parole.testo: From sudor + -al, from Latin sudor.
