parole.significato: In a state of perspiration; covered in sweat; sudoriferous, sweaty.
parole.testo: From New Latin sudorificus, from sūdor (“sweat”) (from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd- (“sweat; to sweat”)) + -ificus (from Proto-Italic *-fakos (suffix forming adjectives that denote bringing or making), ultimately related to Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put, place”)).

parole.significato: sudoriferous
parole.testo: Latin sudor (“sweat”) + parere (“to produce”).

parole.significato: Consisting of, or relating to, sweat.
parole.testo: From Latin sudorus, from sudor (“sweat”).

parole.significato: A group of Germanic tribes living mostly near Elbe in what is now central Germany around the first century BCE.
parole.testo: From Latin Suēbī

parole.significato: pertaining to Sweden or Swedish
parole.testo: From Latin Suecia.

parole.significato: An additional Roman consul elected during the official year, especially in order to replace a retiring one
parole.testo: From Latin suffectio (“replace, substitute”).

parole.significato: One of the chief magistrates who ruled ancient Carthage.
parole.testo: From Latin suffes, from Late Punic 𐤔𐤐𐤈 (špṭ, “judge”). Doublet of shophet.

parole.significato: Synonym of suffixal.
parole.testo: From the present stem of Latin suffīgō (“I fasten onto”) + -al. The formation on the Latin present stem is unusual; perhaps originally an innovation in German.

parole.significato: Synonym of suffixation.
parole.testo: From the present stem of Latin suffīgō (“to fasten onto”) + -ation. The formation on the Latin present stem is unusual; perhaps originally an innovation in German.

parole.significato: A morpheme added at the end of a word to modify the word's meaning.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin suffīxus (“suffix”), from sub- (“under”) + fīxus (perfect passive participle of fīgere (“to fasten, fix”)), equivalent to sub- + -fix.

parole.significato: To obstruct.
parole.testo: From Latin sufflāminō (“clog, block”).

parole.significato: To inflate; to blow up.
parole.testo: From Latin sufflare, from sub- + flare (“to blow”).

parole.significato: To suffer, or cause someone to suffer, from severely reduced oxygen intake to the body.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in the 1420s, the verb in 1526; from Middle English suffocat(e) (“deprived of air, suffocated”), borrowed from Latin suffōcātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin suffōcō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from sub- (“under, up

parole.significato: Internal erosion by liquid percolating through clay, sand, or silt.
parole.testo: From Latin suffossio, from suffodere, suffossum (“to dig under”), from sub (“under”) + fodere (“to dig”).

parole.significato: To vote.
parole.testo: From Latin suffragatus.

parole.significato: Someone who votes.
parole.testo: From Latin suffrāgātor (“voter”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the hock of an animal.
parole.testo: From Latin suffraginosus (“diseased in the hock”), from suffrago (“the pastern, or hock”).

parole.significato: The joint between the tibia and tarsus, such as the hock of a horse's hind leg or the heel of a bird.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin suffrāgō.

parole.significato: Slightly woody or shrubby at the base.
parole.testo: From Latin suffrutescens. For more, see sub- + frutescent.

parole.significato: A subshrub.
parole.testo: From the scientific Latin suffrutex. Cognate with the Italian suffrutice and the Spanish sufrútice.

parole.significato: Gradually blending into another colour.
parole.testo: From Latin suffulcire, suffultum (“to support”).

parole.significato: To fumigate from below.
parole.testo: From Latin suffumigatus, past participle of suffumigare (“to fumigate from below”). See sub-, and fumigate.

parole.significato: A medical fume.
parole.testo: Latin suffumigium.

parole.significato: To spread through or over (something), especially as a liquid, colour or light; to bathe.
parole.testo: From Latin suffundō.

parole.significato: Of or relating to sucking.
parole.testo: Latin sugere (“to suck”).

parole.significato: To imply but stop short of explicitly stating (something).
parole.testo: Coined based on Latin suggestus, perfect passive participle of suggerō (“bring up, bring under, lay beneath, furnish, supply, excite, advise, suggest”, verb), from sub (“from below, under”) + gerō (“bear, carry”, verb).

parole.significato: A misrepresentation of the truth brought about by implying a falsehood to be true; a lie of implication. Compare suppre…
parole.testo: Latin: suggestiō (“suggestion”) + falsī (“of a falsehood”, genitive singular form of falsum, “an untruth”, “falsehood”) = “a suggestion of an untruth” ≈ “suggestion of deceit”.

parole.significato: A raised platform.
parole.testo: From Latin suggestum, from suggerō (“to put under”).

parole.significato: To beat until bruised.
parole.testo: From Latin suggillo (“to beat until bruised”).

parole.significato: A livid mark; a blow; a bruise.
parole.testo: From Latin suggillatio, ultimately from suggillo. Compare French suggillation.

parole.significato: In a class of its own; one of a kind.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin suī generis (literally “of its own kind/class”).

parole.significato: Having the right and the capability to manage one's own affairs
parole.testo: Latin, meaning "of one's own right".

parole.significato: Of or relating to the suborder Suina of (especially) pigs, peccaries, and hippopotami.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin suīllīnus.

parole.significato: A selfish person
parole.testo: Latin suus (“belonging to himself or oneself”) + -ist.

parole.significato: The belief that one is a god.
parole.testo: Coined by American occultists David Michael Cunningham and Traeonna A. R. Wagener, from Latin sui (“of oneself”) and theism.

parole.significato: Having deep, narrow sulci, grooves or furrows.
parole.testo: From Latin sulcātus, perfect passive participle of sulcō (“to plough, furrow”).

parole.significato: Having the form of a sulcus.
parole.testo: From Latin sulcus (“groove”) + -form.

parole.significato: A furrow or groove in an organ or a tissue, especially that marking the convolutions of the surface of the brain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sulcus (“a furrow made by a plow”). Doublet of sullow ("plough").

parole.significato: A sulfide.
parole.testo: From Latin sulphuretum (“relating to sulphur; sulphide”), coined in 1788 as sulphuret by the translator of de Morveau, Lavoisier et al.'s 1787 book Méthode de nomenclature chimique James St. John as a translation of French sulfure. By surface analysis, sulfur + -uret.

parole.significato: Containing sulfur.
parole.testo: From Latin sulphurōsus. By surface analysis, sulfur + -ous.

parole.significato: A furrow.
parole.testo: From Latin sulcus.

parole.significato: ethylsulphuric acid
parole.testo: From sulpho- + Latin vinum (“wine”). Compare French sulfovinique.

parole.significato: Sulphurous.
parole.testo: From Latin sulphureus, sulfureus.

parole.significato: A comprehensive summary of, or treatise on a subject, especially theology or philosophy.
parole.testo: From Latin summa.

parole.significato: With highest (of three degrees of) praise; as noted, as an honor, on diplomas and degrees for work that is considered t…
parole.testo: From Latin summā cum laude (“with the greatest praise”).

parole.significato: Concise, brief, or presented in a condensed form; presenting information in such a form.
parole.testo: From Middle English summary, from Medieval Latin summārius, from Latin summa (“total, sum”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives).

parole.significato: An abstract or a condensed presentation of the substance of a body of material.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin summārium, from Latin summa (“total, sum”) + -ārium (suffix forming nouns of purpose).

parole.significato: The height or top of anything.
parole.testo: From summ + -ity, from Latin summitas, from summus (“highest”). Compare French sommité. See sum.

parole.significato: The greatest good; the ultimate importance; the singular end which human beings ought to pursue.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin summum bonum.

parole.significato: The highest, most all-inclusive genus; the one that is not a species of any other genus.
parole.testo: From Latin. Literally “highest genus”.

parole.significato: Adherence to or persistence in using a strictly correct term in rejection of a more common (but technically incorrect)…
parole.testo: From Latin sumpsimus, c. 1540–50. See mumpsimus for details.

parole.significato: A taking.
parole.testo: From Latin sumptio, from sumo (“to take”).

parole.significato: Relating to expenditure or expense, especially on luxury goods.
parole.testo: From Latin sūmptuārius (“of or relating to expenditure, sumptuary; person in charge of household expenses”) + English -ary (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Sūmptuārius is derived from sūmptus (“charge, cost, expense”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives); and sūmptus from s

parole.significato: The state or quality of being sumptuous; wealth; high price
parole.testo: From sumptuo(u)s + -ity, from Latin sumptuositas: compare French somptuosité.

parole.significato: A solstice.
parole.testo: From sun + stead (“place, point, spot, position”), a calque of Latin sōlstitium. Compare Old English sunnstede.

parole.significato: Synonym of sua sponte.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin suo motu.

parole.significato: A religious rite of Ancient Rome, the triple sacrifice of a pig, a ram, and a bull to the deity Mars in order to bless…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin suovetaurīlia.

parole.significato: Of excellent quality, superfine.
parole.testo: From super- (prefix), from Middle English super-, from Latin super-, from super (“above”). Doublet of over and hyper.

parole.significato: located above; (anatomy) superior in position
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin super-. Doublet of sur-, over-, and hyper-.

parole.significato: Capable of being overcome or surmounted; surmountable or conquerable.
parole.testo: From Latin superabilis (“that may be surmounted”), from superare (“to go over, rise above, surmount”), from super (“over”).

parole.significato: Obsolete, antiquated.
parole.testo: From the Latin superannuatus (“more than one year old”), from super (“over”) (English super-) + annus (“year”) (English annual).

parole.significato: To rise above; to overtop; to cover.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin superātus, perfect passive participle of superō (“to surmount, exceed, better”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: First-rate; of the highest quality; exceptionally good.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin superbus.

parole.significato: A toxic alkaloid found in Gloriosa superba.
parole.testo: From translingual (Gloriosa) superba + -ine, from Latin superbus (“superb”).

parole.significato: proud, overbearing
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin *superbiosus (“haughty, proud, arrogant”) (attested only in its adverbial form superbiose (“haughtily, proudly, arrogantly”)), from superbia (“pride, arrogance”) + -osus, from superbus (“haughty, proud”).

parole.significato: Faster-than-light travelling speed.
parole.testo: Presumed super- + cee, a respelling of the physics symbol c (denoting the speed of light in a vacuum; an abbreviation of both English constant and Latin celeritas (“swiftness”)).

parole.significato: Arrogantly superior; showing contemptuous indifference; haughty.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin superciliōsus (“haughty”).

parole.significato: The eyebrow (arch of hair above each eye).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin supercilium (“eyebrow; brow, ridge; pride, arrogance”).

parole.significato: Growing on some other growing thing.
parole.testo: From Latin supercrescens, present participle of supercrescere.

parole.significato: The quality of being supereminent.
parole.testo: From Latin supereminentia.

parole.significato: supererogatory
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Supererogatory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin supererogare. See supererogation.

parole.significato: An act of doing more than is required.
parole.testo: From Late Latin superērogātiō (“payment in addition”), from superērogāre (“to pay in addition”), from super (“in addition to”) + ērogāre (“to pay, pay out, expend, disburse”), equivalent to supererogate + -ion.

parole.significato: Pertaining to supererogation; doing more than is required.
parole.testo: From Latin superērogātōrius (“supererogatory”), from superērogātiō (“payment in addition”), from superērogō (“pay out over and above”), from super (“above”) + ērogō (“pay out, expend”); from ex (“out of, from”) + rogō (“ask; request”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the superessive case.
parole.testo: From Latin superesse (“to be over and above”).

parole.significato: To conceive after a prior conception, but before the birth of the offspring.
parole.testo: From Latin superfetare, from super (“above, over”) + fetare (“to bring forth”).

parole.significato: The formation of a fetus while another fetus is already present in the uterus.
parole.testo: From Latin superfetare (“conceive while pregnant”), from super- + fetus.

parole.significato: Existing, occurring, or located on the surface.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Late Latin superficiālis (“of or belonging to the surface”), from superficiēs (“top, surface”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: A two-dimensional magnitude that has length and breadth; especially such a surface that forms the boundary of a solid.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Latin superficiēs (“top, surface”), from super- (“above, over”) + faciēs (“form, configuration, shape”). Doublet of surface.

parole.significato: superfluity
parole.testo: From Latin superfluens, present active participle of superfluo (“to flow or run over”). See superfluous.

parole.significato: Floating on the surface.
parole.testo: From Middle English superfluent, from Latin superfluens, present participle of superfluere (“to overflow, run over”).

parole.significato: Floating above or on the surface.
parole.testo: Latin super (“above”) + fluitans, present participle of fluitare, intensive from fluere (“to flow”).

parole.significato: In excess of what is required or sufficient.
parole.testo: From Middle English superfluous, from Latin superfluus (“superfluous”) + -ous, from superfluō (“overflow”), from super (“above, more than, over”) + fluō (“flow”). Compare mellifluous and fluid, also from Latin. Literally corresponds to overflow, which is from Germanic, rather than Latin.

parole.significato: An overabundance; a great amount
parole.testo: From Latin superfluxus, from superfluō (“overflow”).

parole.significato: excess, exaltation
parole.testo: From Latin supergressio.

parole.significato: Beyond what is possible for a human being.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin superhūmānus. By surface analysis, super- + human.

parole.significato: Lying or resting on something else; overlying.
parole.testo: From Latin superincumbentem, present participle of superincumbere. By surface analysis, super- + incumbent.

parole.significato: To replace (someone) with someone else; to bring into another's position; especially, to take (a second wife) quickly a…
parole.testo: From late Latin superindūcere.

parole.significato: To oversee the work of others; to supervise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin superintendō.

parole.significato: A person who is authorized to supervise, direct or administer something.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin superintendens, a calque of Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos); thence being distantly related to English bishop.

parole.significato: The highest voice or part in early polyphony.
parole.testo: From Latin superius.

parole.significato: Positioned immediately above or on top of something else; overlying.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Latin superjacēns, present participle of superjacēre, from super- + jacēre (“to lie”).

parole.significato: excessive exaltation.
parole.testo: From Latin superlatio. See superlative.

parole.significato: Excessive or extraordinary gain.
parole.testo: From super- + Latin lucratio (“gain”).

parole.significato: According to the rules of an old drinking game in which the drinker upturned the empty cup and had to drink more if the…
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism from super- + naculum, nagulum, Latinized form of German Nagel, intended to mean “upon the nail”, after the German phrase auf den Nagel (trinken).

parole.significato: A person who works in a group, association, or public office without forming part of the regular staff (the numerary).
parole.testo: From Late Latin supernumerarius (“extra soldier added to a legion; supernumerary”), from super (“above; beyond”) + numerus (“number; collection, quantity”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns or numerals). The word is analysable as super- + numeral + -ary.

parole.significato: Of a natural number, being larger than another natural number by a unit fraction of that smaller number.
parole.testo: From Late Latin superparticulāris.

parole.significato: Being or relating to a ratio where the larger value exceeds the smaller by more than one unit, as in 3 to 5.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin superpartiens, from super (“over”) + partiens, the past participle of partire (“to divide”).

parole.significato: surplus
parole.testo: From super- + Latin plus (“more”). See surplus.

parole.significato: A rank in the classification of organisms: a superkingdom or domain.
parole.testo: From Latin above and rēgnum (“kingdom”).

parole.significato: Extremely salient.
parole.testo: super- + Latin saliens, participle of salire (“to leap”).

parole.significato: to write on the exterior of, the surface of, or above.
parole.testo: From Latin superscrībo (“write over”). By surface analysis, super- + scribe.

parole.significato: A type of surety bond that a court requires from an appellant who wants to delay payment of a judgement until the appea…
parole.testo: From Latin supersedeās.

parole.significato: A creditor's voluntary surcease of personal execution in behalf of a debtor.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The act of superseding; the fact of having been superseded.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin supersessiō, supersessiōnem, from supersedeō (“supersede”).

parole.significato: Someone or something that supersedes another.
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Latin supersedēre (“to supersede”).

parole.significato: To build over or upon (another structure); to erect upon (a foundation).
parole.testo: Latin superstrūctus, past participle of superstruō (“to build upon”); super (“over”) + struō (“to build”). See super- and structure.

parole.significato: More than substantial, transcending all substance; spiritual.
parole.testo: From super- + substantial, after Latin supersubstantialis used by Jerome to render Ancient Greek ἐπιούσιος (epioúsios) in the Lord's Prayer. Introduced in English (where ἐπιούσιος is otherwise rendered as "daily") by Thomas More in order to make a connection of the "daily bread" of the Lord's Prayer

parole.significato: Added above what is needed or necessary; superfluous, redundant.
parole.testo: From Latin supervacāneus; compare Italian supervacaneo, Portuguese supervacâneo, Spanish supervacáneo.

parole.significato: superfluous, more than needed
parole.testo: From Latin supervacuus (“more than needed”), from super (“above”) + vacuus (“vacant”), equivalent to super- + vacuous.

parole.significato: To follow (something) closely, either as a consequence or in contrast.
parole.testo: From Latin supervenīre (“come over or upon, overtake”), from super (“above”) + veniō (“come”).

parole.significato: In a relationship with another set such that membership in the other set implies membership in the present set
parole.testo: From Latin supervenient-, stem of superveniens, present participle of supervenio (“to come to or in addition to, to overtake”).

parole.significato: To oversee or direct (a task or organization).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin supervisus, from supervidere, from Latin super + videre. Doublet of survey.

parole.significato: The act or instance of supervising.
parole.testo: From Latin supervisiō.

parole.significato: A person with the official task of overseeing the work of a person or group, or of other operations and activities.
parole.testo: Attested since the 15th century C.E.; from Middle English supervisor, supervisour, supervysor, supervysour, from Latin supervīsor, from supervideō, in turn from super + videō. By surface analysis, supervise + -or.

parole.significato: To survive; to outlive.
parole.testo: From Latin supervivere. Doublet of survive.

parole.significato: Having a plaited and convolute arrangement in the bud, as in the morning glory.
parole.testo: From Latin supervolutus, past participle of supervolvere (“to roll over”), from super (“over”) + volvere (“to roll”).

parole.significato: To twist the forearm so as to turn the palm of the hand backwards if the forearm is pointing up, upwards if the forearm…
parole.testo: From Latin supīnō (“turn up, turn over”).

parole.significato: Lying on its back.
parole.testo: The adjective is borrowed from Latin supīnus, from *sup- (see sub (“under”)) + -īnus (“of, pertaining to”). The word is cognate with Catalan supí, Italian supino, Old French sovin, Middle French souvin, Anglo-Norman supin, Old Occitan sobin, sopin, Portuguese supino, Spanish supino. Partly displaced

parole.significato: The quality of being supine; negligence; laziness; heedlessness.
parole.testo: From supine + -ity, from Latin supinitas.

parole.significato: Beneath the feet, or supporting the feet.
parole.testo: From sub- + Latin pes, pedis (“a foot”). Compare Latin suppedaneum (“a footstool”).

parole.significato: a foot-support for a crucified person, projecting from the base of the cross
parole.testo: From Late Latin suppedāneum, neuter of suppedāneus (“under the feet”), composed of sup- (“under”) + ped- (“foot”) + -aneus (“-aneous”).

parole.significato: To supply; to furnish.
parole.testo: From Latin suppeditatus, past participle of suppeditare (“to supply”).

parole.significato: supply, or aid given.
parole.testo: From Latin suppeditatio.

parole.significato: Something added; especially, such an addition added to make up for a deficiency.
parole.testo: From Latin supplementum (“that which is added to supply a shortage”), from supplere (“to provide something”).

parole.significato: Making up for deficiencies; supplementary; suppletory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin suppletīvus.

parole.significato: A source of supply.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin suppletorius.

parole.significato: begging, pleading, supplicating
parole.testo: From Latin supplicans (“supplicating, bowing down”), from supplicō (“kneel, bow down, request”), from sub- (“lower”) + plicō (“fold”).

parole.significato: A petition, especially onewritten, with a certificate that the conditions have been complied with.
parole.testo: Latin, he supplicates.

parole.significato: To make a humble request to (someone, especially a person in authority); to beg, to beseech, to entreat.
parole.testo: PIE word  *upó From Late Middle English supplicaten (“to request (that someone do something)”) [and other forms], borrowed from Latin supplicātus (“prayed”) + Middle English -en (suffix forming the infinitive of verbs). Supplicātus is the perfect passive participle of supplicō (“to pray, supplicate;

parole.significato: A writ issued by the King's Bench or Chancery for taking the surety of the peace against a person.
parole.testo: From Latin supplicāvit.

parole.significato: The interpretation given to a term in a specific context.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin suppositiō.

parole.significato: The use of a word autonymously, or as a name for itself
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin suppositio materialis.

parole.significato: Spurious; substituted for the genuine, counterfeit; fake.
parole.testo: From New Latin suppositius, from Latin suppositīcius.

parole.significato: Spurious; substituted for the genuine, counterfeit; fake.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin suppositīcius.

parole.significato: Something supposed to be true; an assumption
parole.testo: From the past participle of Latin supponere (“to suppose”).

parole.significato: To put an end to, especially with force, to crush, do away with; to prohibit, subdue.
parole.testo: From Latin suppressus, perfect passive participle of supprimō (“press down or under”), from sub (“under”) + premō (“press”).

parole.significato: A misrepresentation of the truth by the omission or suppression of certain key facts; a lie of omission. Compare sugges…
parole.testo: Latin: suppressiō (“a pressing down”, “suppression”) + vērī (“of reality”, genitive singular form of vērum, “reality”, “fact”) = “a pressing down of reality” ≈ “suppression of the truth”

parole.significato: The act or instance of suppressing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin suppressiō.

parole.significato: A suppurative.
parole.testo: At least superficially suppure + -ant. Ultimately from Latin suppūrō.

parole.significato: To form or discharge pus.
parole.testo: From Latin suppūrātus, past participle of suppūrō, from pūr-, stem of pūs.

parole.significato: The decay in tissue producing pus, or the pus itself.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1425. From Latin suppūrātiō.

parole.significato: Of a disease or medical condition, causing suppuration: producing, or causing the production of, pus.
parole.testo: From suppurate + -ive, from Modern Latin suppūrātīvus, from suppūrō.

parole.significato: To suppurate.
parole.testo: From Latin suppūrō.

parole.significato: Used to indicate that the current citation is from a source cited earlier in the text.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin suprā.

parole.significato: Above, over, on top; (anatomy, medicine) superior
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin supra- (“above, over, beyond”).

parole.significato: Located above the chelicerae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin suprachēlicerālis. By surface analysis, supra- + chelicera + -al.

parole.significato: A pair of muscles that raise the wings of birds in flapping flight.
parole.testo: Latin; see supra-, coracoid, and -eus.

parole.significato: Supremacy.
parole.testo: From supreme + -ity, compare Latin suprēmitās.

parole.significato: (real analysis): Given a subset X of R, the smallest real number that is ≥ every element of X; (order theory): given a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin supremum.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the calf of the leg.
parole.testo: From Latin sura (“the calf of the leg”). Compare French sural.

parole.significato: A little shoot or branch; a twig; a sucker.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin surculus. Doublet of surculus.

parole.significato: Producing suckers or sucker-like shoots.
parole.testo: From Latin surculōsus, from surculus + -ōsus, from sūrus (“post, stake, branch”) + -culus (“diminutive suffix”). See surcle. By surface analysis, Latin sur- + -ule + -ose.

parole.significato: A shoot from a rootstock; a sucker.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin surculus. Doublet of surcle.

parole.significato: An irrational number, especially one expressed using the √ symbol.
parole.testo: First attested in the mid 16th century from Latin surdus (“deaf, mute”), used in mathematics for “irrational,” reflecting ἄλογος (álogos, “irrational, speechless”) as found in Euclid, apparently transmitted via Arabic جِذْر أَصَمّ (jiḏr ʔaṣamm, “deaf root”). The phonetic sense, “voiceless,” emerged

parole.significato: Deafness
parole.testo: From surd + -ity, from Latin surditas.

parole.significato: An erect penis; an erection.
parole.testo: Latin surgo (“to rise”).

parole.significato: Surging; rising.
parole.testo: From Latin surgens, present participle of surgo (“rise, get up”).

parole.significato: To form or to undergo surjection
parole.testo: From Latin superiaciō.

parole.significato: A surplus; a superabundance.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin surplusagium, from surplus.

parole.significato: upright
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin surrectus (“arisen”), the perfect passive participle of surgō (“to arise”).

parole.significato: A rising.
parole.testo: From Latin surrēctiō. Obsolete except as nonce word after resurrection. Compare Middle English surreccion (“insurrection, rebellion”).

parole.significato: The obtaining of something in a surreptitious manner, or by craft or stealth.
parole.testo: From Latin surreptio, or subreptio. Compare subreption.

parole.significato: Stealthy, furtive, well hidden, covert (especially movements).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin surrēptīcius (“furtive, clandestine”), from surrēpō (“to creep along”).

parole.significato: Of, concerning, relating to or acting as a substitute.
parole.testo: From Latin surrogātus, perfect passive participle of surrogō (“to choose someone as a substitute”); a variant of subrogō, from sub (“under”) + rogō (“ask”).

parole.significato: A thing put in the place of another; a substitute.
parole.testo: 1800s. Latin, neuter singular of surrogatus

parole.significato: The opening dialogue to the Preface of the Eucharistic Prayer or Anaphora in the liturgies of the Christian Church.
parole.testo: Latin, meaning "lift up your hearts".

parole.significato: In an upwards direction.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin sursum (“upwards”)

parole.significato: Of a person, to continue to live; to remain alive.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman survivre, Old French survivre, from Late Latin supervīvere (“to outlive”), from Latin super (“over”) + vivere (“to live”), akin to vita (“life”). See vivid. Compare devive, revive.

parole.significato: Likely to be affected by something.
parole.testo: From Late Latin susceptibilis, from Latin susceptus, from suscipiō.

parole.significato: The act of taking, or taking up; reception.
parole.testo: From Latin susceptio. Compare French susception. See susceptible.

parole.significato: One who undertakes anything; specifically, a godfather; a sponsor; a guardian.
parole.testo: From Latin susceptor. See susceptible.

parole.significato: Receiving; admitting.
parole.testo: From Latin suscipiens.

parole.significato: To rouse; to excite; to call into life and action.
parole.testo: From Latin suscitatus, past participle of suscitare (“to lift up, to rouse”), from sub- + citare (“to rouse, excite”). Compare excite, incite, and resuscitate.

parole.significato: The act of raising or exciting.
parole.testo: Latin suscitatio: compare French suscitation.

parole.significato: A toxic basic substance obtained from cultures of the swine fever bacillus.
parole.testo: From Latin sūs (“pig”) + toxin.

parole.significato: suspicion
parole.testo: From Middle English suspeccion, suspeccioun, suspeccyon, suspectyon, susspeccioun, from Latin suspectiō and Middle French suspeccion, suspection. Doublet of soupçon. By surface analysis, suspect + -ion.

parole.significato: The act of suspending, or the state of being suspended.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin suspensiōnem (“arching, vaulting; suspension”), from suspendēre (“to hang up, to suspend”), from sub- (“under”) + pendere (“to hang, to suspend”), from Proto-Italic *pendō (“to hang, to put in a hanging position”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pénd-e-ti, from *(s)pend- (“to

parole.significato: That suspends, temporarily stops.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin suspēnsīvus. First attested in 1557. By surface analysis, suspense + -ive.

parole.significato: Anything that suspends or holds up a part, especially the mandibular suspensorium, a series of bones or cartilages conn…
parole.testo: From New Latin

parole.significato: Liable to suspicion; suspicious or suspected.
parole.testo: From Latin suspicābilis, from suspicor (“to suspect”), akin to suspiciō. See suspect (verb).

parole.significato: The act of suspecting something or someone, especially of something wrong.
parole.testo: From Middle English suspecioun, borrowed from Latin suspīciō, suspīciōnem, from suspicere, from sub- (“up to”) with specere (“to look at”). Perhaps partly through the influence of Old French sospeçon (or rather the Anglo-Norman form suspecioun). Equivalent to suspect + -ion.

parole.significato: The act of breathing, not necessarily for a sustained period (compare respiration, which is sustained).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin suspīrātiō, suspīrātiōnem (“sighing”).

parole.significato: To breathe, especially to exhale
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Latin suspīrāre. Cognate with Old French sospirer (modern soupirer) and Spanish suspirar.

parole.significato: Suspiring; sighing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin suspīriōsus.

parole.significato: sustenance or substance.
parole.testo: From Latin sustentaculum. See sustentation.

parole.significato: A supporting structure, a body part that supports one or more other parts.
parole.testo: From Latin sustentaculum; compare sustentate. Attested since the eighteenth century.

parole.significato: Suspense.
parole.testo: From Latin sustentātiō. Doublet of sustentation.

parole.significato: A murmur or whisper.
parole.testo: From Latin susurrans, p.pr. of susurrare (“to whisper”).

parole.significato: Murmured, soft.
parole.testo: From Latin susurrāns (whence -ant), from susurrō (“to whisper”), from susurrus (“whisper, murmur”).

parole.significato: To whisper.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin susurrō, susurrātus (whence -ate).

parole.significato: A low and indistinct whispering sound; a murmur.
parole.testo: From Latin susurratio.

parole.significato: Having whispering or rustling sounds.
parole.testo: Latin susurrus + -ous.

parole.significato: A whispering or rustling sound; a murmur.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin susurrus (“a humming, whispering”); reduplication of imitative Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to buzz, hum”).

parole.significato: Done by stitching.
parole.testo: From Latin sūtilis.

parole.significato: shoemaker; cobbler.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sūtor.

parole.significato: Pertaining to shoemakers or shoemaking.
parole.testo: From Latin sūtōrius (“of a shoemaker”).

parole.significato: A seam formed by sewing two edges together, especially to join pieces of skin in surgically treating a wound.
parole.testo: From Middle English suture, from Latin sūtūra (“suture”), from suere (“sew, join or tack together”) + -tūra (forms action nouns).

parole.significato: A court held before the verderers of the forest as judges, by the steward of the court, three times a year, the swains…
parole.testo: From swain + mote. Compare Latin swanimotum.

parole.significato: A person devoted to luxury and pleasure; a hedonist.
parole.testo: The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin Sybarīta + English -ite (suffix forming demonyms). Sybarīta is derived from Ancient Greek Σῠβᾰρῑ́της (Sŭbărī́tēs, “(noun) inhabitant of Sybaris; (adjective) decadent; self-indulgent”), from Σῠ́βᾰρῐς (Sŭ́bărĭs, “Sybaris”) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs, suffix forming dem

parole.significato: Of or having the qualities of a sybarite (“a person devoted to luxury and pleasure”); dedicated to excessive comfort an…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Sybarīticus (“of or pertaining to Sybaris or its inhabitants”) + English -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, forming adjectives from nouns). Sybarīticus is derived from Ancient Greek Συβαρῑτικός (Subarītikós), from Σῠβᾰρῑ́της (Sŭbărī́tēs, “(noun) inhabitant of Syb

parole.significato: A tree, mentioned in Luke's Gospel, and thought to be the black mulberry.
parole.testo: From Latin sȳcamīnus, from Ancient Greek σῡκάμῑνος (sūkámīnos), from Hebrew שִׁקְמָה (shikmá, “sycamore”) (with assimilation to σῦκον (sûkon, “fig”)).

parole.significato: A collective fleshy fruit, in which the ovaries are hidden within a hollow receptacle, as in the fig; a hollow ball wit…
parole.testo: From New Latin sȳconium, from Ancient Greek σῦκον (sûkon, “fig”) + -ium.

parole.significato: The fawning behavior of a sycophant; servile flattery; fawningness.
parole.testo: From Latin sȳcophantia, from Ancient Greek σῡκοφᾰντῐ́ᾱ (sūkophăntĭ́ā), equivalent to sycophant + -cy.

parole.significato: One who uses obsequious compliments to gain self-serving favour or advantage from another; a servile flatterer.
parole.testo: First attested in 1537. From Latin sȳcophanta (“informer, trickster”), from Ancient Greek συκοφάντης (sukophántēs), itself from σῦκον (sûkon, “fig”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to show, demonstrate”). The gesture of "showing the fig" was a vulgar one, which was made by sticking the thumb between two fingers,

parole.significato: Granite.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Syēnītēs, from Syēnē (“Aswan”), because it was anciently quarried there.

parole.significato: A syllable of unfixed or undecided weight.
parole.testo: Latin: syllaba (“syllable”) + anceps (“double-headed, uncertain”)

parole.significato: A table or list of syllabic letters or syllables.
parole.testo: From New Latin syllabārium, from syllaba.

parole.significato: syllabification
parole.testo: First attested in 1829; formed as the Latin syllaba (“syllable”) + the English -ation; compare the French syllabation and the Medieval Latin syllabō.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or consisting of a syllable or syllables.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin syllabicus, from Ancient Greek συλλαβικός (sullabikós), from συλλαβή (sullabḗ, “syllable”).

parole.significato: The act of syllabifying; syllabification.
parole.testo: First attested in 1631; from the Medieval Latin sillabicātio, syllabicātio, noun of action of the verb syllabicō, from syllaba (“syllable”).

parole.significato: The division of a word into syllables.
parole.testo: First attested in 1764; a regular Anglicisation (see -fication) of a hypothetical etymon of the form *syllabificātiō, *syllabificātiōn-, formed regularly on the base of the Latin syllabificō, itself from syllaba (“syllable”).

parole.significato: To syllabify.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin syllabizō, from Ancient Greek σῠλλᾰβῐ́ζω (sŭllăbĭ́zō), from σῠλλᾰβή (sŭllăbḗ, “syllable”) + -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō, “-ize”).

parole.significato: A summary of topics which will be covered during an academic course, or a text or lecture.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin syllabus (“list”), which arose from accusative plural syllabōs appearing as a corruption of sittybās (accusative plural of sittyba, from Ancient Greek σιττύβα (sittúba, “parchment label; table of contents”)) in a 1470s edition of Cicero's “Ad Atticum” IV.5 and 8, influen

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which one word simultaneously modifies two or more other words such that the modification must be…
parole.testo: From Latin syllepsis, from Ancient Greek σύλληψις (súllēpsis), from συλλαμβάνω (sullambánō).

parole.significato: Omission of the conclusion of a syllogistic argument.
parole.testo: From Latin syllogismus (“syllogism”), from Ancient Greek συλλογισμός (sullogismós). Doublet of syllogism.

parole.significato: An invisible being of the air.
parole.testo: First attested in 1657. From New Latin sylphes, coined by Paracelsus in the 16th century. The coinage may derive from Latin sylvestris (“of the woods”) and nympha (“nymph”). Ultimately from the root silva (“woods, forest”). Related to sylvan. More at Wikipedia.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the forest, or woodlands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin sylvanus, possibly via Middle French sylvain, from Latin silvanus, cognate with Latin Silvānus (“Roman god of the woods”), from silva (“forest”), from Proto-Indo-European *sel-, *swel- (“beam, board, frame, threshold”). The ⟨y⟩ in sylvanus and its descendants is due to i

parole.significato: tellurium
parole.testo: From New Latin silvānium, so called from Transylvania, where it was first found, + -ium.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to woods or woodland organisms; sylvan
parole.testo: From Latin sylvāticus. See sylvan. Doublet of savage.

parole.significato: sylvan; woody or woodlike
parole.testo: Latin sylvestris, better silvestris.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Sylvicolinae or Sylvicolidae, former names for the family Parulidae, the New World warblers.
parole.testo: From Latin sylva, silva (“forest”) + colere (“to inhabit”).

parole.significato: Of, belonging to, or pertaining to Syme.
parole.testo: From Latin Sȳmaeus + English -an.

parole.significato: commensurable; symmetrical
parole.testo: Partly from Latin symmetros and partly from Ancient Greek σύμμετρος (súmmetros), + -al.

parole.significato: Synonym of symmetrical
parole.testo: From symmetry + -ic, from Latin symmetria, from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría).

parole.significato: Exact correspondence on either side of a dividing line, plane, center or axis.
parole.testo: From Latin symmetria, from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría), from σύμμετρος (súmmetros, “symmetrical”), from σύν (sún, “with”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”). By surface analysis, sym- + -metry.

parole.significato: Of, related to, feeling, showing, or characterized by sympathy.
parole.testo: Mid 17th century in the sense “relating to an affinity or paranormal influence”, from Latin sympathēticus. By surface analysis, sympathy + -etic (“pertaining to”); compare pathetic. Displaced native Old English efnþrōwiende.

parole.significato: The process of two originally separate bones growing together as the subject matures, as with the pubic bones or lower…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin symphysis.

parole.significato: The midline cartilaginous joint uniting the superior rami of the left and right pubic bones (pubis), also known as the…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a symposium.
parole.testo: From Latin symposiacus.

parole.significato: A conference or other meeting for discussion of a topic, especially one in which the participants make presentations.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin symposium, from Ancient Greek συμπόσιον (sumpósion, “drinking party”) from συμπίνω (sumpínō, “drink together”), from συν- (sun-, “together-”) + πίνω (pínō, “drink”). Morphologically compare compotation.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Ancient Greek symposium.
parole.testo: From Latin sympoticus or Ancient Greek συμποτικός (sumpotikós).

parole.significato: Synonym of sympotic.
parole.testo: From Latin sympoticus or Ancient Greek συμποτικός (sumpotikós) + -al.

parole.significato: A perceived change in some function, sensation or appearance of a person that indicates a disease or disorder, such as…
parole.testo: From Middle English sinthoma, from Medieval Latin sinthoma, altered by Late Latin symptoma, from Ancient Greek σύμπτωμα (súmptōma, “a happening, accident, symptom of disease”), from stem of συμπίπτω (sumpíptō, “Ι befall”), from συν- (sun-, “together”) + πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”). See also syn-, -oma,

parole.significato: The divided part beyond the pylangium in the aortic trunk of the amphibian heart.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from syn- + Ancient Greek ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “a vessel”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a synapse—the junction between the terminal of a neuron and another cell.
parole.testo: From New Latin synapticus, from Ancient Greek συναπτικός (sunaptikós, “capable of adjusting”).

parole.significato: Piling up of terms, especially adjectives, often as invective.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek συναθροισμός (sunathroismós, “collection, union, rhetorical grouping of diverse words”).

parole.significato: A congregation.
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek σύναξις (súnaxis, “gathering”), from συνάγω (sunágō, “to gather”). See synagogue.

parole.significato: A kind of aggregate fruit in which the ovaries cohere in a solid mass, with a slender receptacle, as in the magnolia.
parole.testo: From syn- + -carp, New Latin syncarpium. See syncarpous.

parole.significato: One who holds an office in an Eastern Catholic or Orthodox Church roughly equivalent to that of an episcopal vicar in t…
parole.testo: From Latin syncellus, from Ancient Greek σύγκελλος (súnkellos).

parole.significato: A form of only slightly moveable articulation between bones joined by hyaline cartilage, as in the spinal vertebrae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin synchondrōsis, equivalent to syn- + chondro- + -osis.

parole.significato: A complicated, interlocking word-order pattern in early Latin verse, demonstrated by Virgil and his contemporaries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin synchysis, from Ancient Greek σύγχυσις (súnkhusis, “a mixing”).

parole.significato: to omit a vocalic or consonantal sound or a syllable from a word; to use syncope
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin syncopātus, past participle of syncopō, from Late Latin syncopa, from Ancient Greek σύν (sún, “with”) + κόπτω (kóptō, “cut”).

parole.significato: The elision or loss of a sound from the interior of a word, especially of a vowel sound with loss of a syllable.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin syncopē, from Ancient Greek συγκοπή (sunkopḗ), from συγκόπτω (sunkóptō, “cut up”) + -η (-ē, nominalization suffix), from σύν (sún, “beside, with”) + κόπτω (kóptō, “strike, cut off”). Partly continues the (near-)doublets syncopis and sincopin, both from the Old Frenc

parole.significato: The reconciliation or fusion of different systems or beliefs (religious, cultural, or otherwise cosmologic or ontologic…
parole.testo: From Latin syncretismus, from Ancient Greek συγκρητισμός (sunkrētismós, “federation of Cretan cities”), from συγκρητίζω (sunkrētízō, “to unite against a common enemy”), from σύν (sún, “together”) (see English syn-) + Κρῆτες (Krêtes, “Cretans”). By surface analysis, syn- + Crete + -ism (“Crete joinin

parole.significato: A slightly movable articulation or joint where the contiguous bony surfaces are rough and are united by an interosseous…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin syndesmōsis.

parole.significato: Relating to syndesmosis
parole.testo: From New Latin syndesmōticus.

parole.significato: Of or related to syndeton, the use of a conjunction.
parole.testo: From Latin syndeticus, from Ancient Greek συνδετικός (sundetikós), from σύνδεσις (súndesis, “binding”) + -κός (-kós, “-ic: forming adjectives”), from συνδεῖν (sundeîn, “to join, to bind”), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “together”) + δεῖν (deîn, “to bind, to tie”).

parole.significato: A recognizable pattern of signs, symptoms and/or behaviours, especially of a disease or medical or psychological condit…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin syndrome, from Ancient Greek συνδρομή (sundromḗ, “concurrence of symptoms, concourse”), from σύνδρομος (súndromos, “running together”), from συν- (sun-, “with”) + δρόμος (drómos, “running, course”).

parole.significato: A figure of speech that uses the name of a part of something to represent the whole, or the whole to represent a part,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin synecdochē, from Ancient Greek συνεκδοχή (sunekdokhḗ, “receiving together”) from σύν (sún, “with”) + ἐκ (ek, “out of”) + δέχεσθαι (dékhesthai, “to accept”), this last element related to δοκέω (dokéō, “to think, suppose, seem”).

parole.significato: A document signed by both or all of the parties to a contract or bond.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin syngrapha.

parole.significato: A monetary tribute formerly paid to the bishop or archdeacon, at the time of his Easter visitation, by every parish pri…
parole.testo: From Middle English synodal, synodall, from Latin synodālis. By surface analysis, synod + -al.

parole.significato: Of, related to or produced by a synod; synodal.
parole.testo: From Latin synodicus, from Ancient Greek συνοδικός (sunodikós, “of or related to an assembly or meeting”). Equivalent to synod + -ic.

parole.significato: A term (word or phrase) which is synonymous with others.
parole.testo: From Middle English sinonyme, from Latin synōnymum, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμον (sunṓnumon), neuter singular form of συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “synonymous”), from σύν (sún, “with”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”). By surface analysis, syn- + -onym.

parole.significato: synonyms
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The use of two or more synonyms together to amplify or explain a given subject or term. A kind of repetition that adds…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin synōnymia, from Ancient Greek συνωνυμία (sunōnumía). Doublet of synonymy.

parole.significato: Synonym of thesaurus.
parole.testo: From New Latin synōnymicon, from Ancient Greek συνωνυμία (sunōnumía, “synonym”).

parole.significato: Having a similar (sometimes identical) meaning. (See Usage notes below)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin synōnymus, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos). By surface analysis, synonym + -ous.

parole.significato: A brief summary of the major points of a written work, either as prose or as a table; an abridgment or condensation of…
parole.testo: From Late Latin synopsis, itself from Ancient Greek σύνοψις (súnopsis), from σύν (sún, “with or whole”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view”) meaning whole view.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a synopsis.
parole.testo: From New Latin synopticus, from Ancient Greek συνοπτικός (sunoptikós, “seeing the whole together or at a glance”), from σύνοψις (súnopsis, “a general view, synopsis”), from συν- (sun-, “with”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view”).

parole.significato: Synonym of synovial fluid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin synovia.

parole.significato: Relating to or denoting a type of joint which is surrounded by a thick flexible membrane forming a sac into which is se…
parole.testo: From synovia + -al, related to New Latin synoviālis.

parole.significato: Of, related to or connected with syntax.
parole.testo: From New Latin syntacticus, from Ancient Greek συντακτικός (suntaktikós).

parole.significato: A constituent segment within a text, such as a word or a phrase that forms a syntactic unit.
parole.testo: From Late Latin syntagma, from Ancient Greek σύνταγμα (súntagma, “orderly arrangement”), from συντάσσω (suntássō, “arrange together”, “to order”).

parole.significato: A square formation of 256 soldiers arranged into sixteen files, sixteen ranks deep, led by a syntagmatarch; a syntagma.
parole.testo: First attested in 1670–1 and then once per century since; from the Latin syntagmatarchia, from the Ancient Greek συνταγματαρχία (suntagmatarkhía), from σύνταγμα (súntagma), whence the English syntagma.

parole.significato: A set of rules that govern how words are combined to form phrases and sentences.
parole.testo: Partly from Late Latin syntaxis and partly from its etymon, Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis), from σύν (sún, “together”) + τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”), from τάσσω (tássō, “to arrange”). Doublet of syntaxis.

parole.significato: Syntax.
parole.testo: From the Late Latin syntaxis, from the Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis). Doublet of syntax.

parole.significato: An aspect of one's conscience by which one can judge wrong from right and decide on what makes good conduct (as disting…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin syntērēsis (in Thomas Aquinas), from Ancient Greek συντήρησις (suntḗrēsis, “careful watching”), from συντηρεῖν (suntēreîn, “to keep guard”).

parole.significato: A change in the structure of magma by melting or the assimilation of a different type of rock.
parole.testo: From New Latin syntēxis, from Ancient Greek σύντηξις (súntēxis, “a melting”).

parole.significato: The formation of something complex or coherent by combining simpler things.
parole.testo: From Latin synthesis, from Ancient Greek σύνθεσις (súnthesis, “a putting together; composition”), from συντίθημι (suntíthēmi, “put together, combine”), from συν- (sun-, “together”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “set, place”). Doublet of sandhi.

parole.significato: A disease spread via sexual activity, caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum.
parole.testo: From New Latin syphilis, originally the title of a poem, circa 1530, by Girolamo Fracastoro concerning “Syphilus”, a shepherd boy who insulted the Greek god Apollo and was punished by that god with a horrible disease. Syphilis in the Old World began circa 1495. More in Wikipedia at History of syphil

parole.significato: A speaker of the Syriac language (see above).

parole.significato: The chief priest in the Roman province of Syria.

parole.significato: syrinx: Of or pertaining to a tube or tuboid structure, such as a fistula.

parole.significato: A set of panpipes.

parole.significato: A long dress that trailed on the floor, worn by tragic actors.

parole.significato: Synonym of quicksand.

parole.significato: Capable of, or taking place by, alternate contraction and dilatation.

parole.significato: The combination of different elements; synthesis.

parole.significato: Carried out according to a planned, ordered procedure.

parole.significato: The rhythmic contraction of the heart, by which blood is driven through the arteries.

parole.significato: Having a space equal to two diameters or four modules between two columns; said of a portico or building.

parole.significato: A medieval schematic map of the world, representing the three known continents surrounded by the Ocean Sea.

parole.significato: A second-person pronoun used in informal situations, to address friends, family, and sometimes inferiors.

parole.significato: The distinction between a formal and an informal second-person pronoun in some languages.
parole.testo: From Latin tū (“thou, singular you”) and vōs (“ye, plural you”).

parole.significato: A student of Cambridge University.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to species of the horsefly family, Tabanidae.

parole.significato: A medicated lozenge or hard electuary.

parole.significato: A membranous layer of tissue.

parole.testo: From French tarsi(er) + -oid, from Latin tarsus, from Ancient Greek ταρσός (tarsós, “wickerwork mat"; "broad, flat surface"”).

parole.significato: The part between the main part of the hindlimb and the metatarsus in terrestrial vertebrates.
