parole.significato: An enclosure wherein small animals are displayed, usually with some plants, in a naturalistic setting.
parole.testo: From Latin terra (“earth”) + -arium, by analogy with aquarium.

parole.significato: A small magnetized model ball representing the Earth, used in investigating magnetism.
parole.testo: From Latin terra (“Earth”) + -ella, meaning "little Earth". A modern formation: compare classical Latin terrula (“small field”).

parole.significato: An inhabitant of the planet Earth.
parole.testo: From Latin terrestris, from terra (“land, earth, ground”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Earth or its (native) inhabitants.
parole.testo: From Middle English terrestrialle, from terrestre or Latin terrestris, from terra (“land, earth, ground”), with the suffix -al.

parole.significato: Ground-dwelling or growing close to the ground.
parole.testo: From Latin terricolus (“ground-dwelling”). Equivalent to Latin terra (“earth”) + -cole.

parole.significato: A source of unnecessary or uncontrollable fear.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin terriculāmentum.

parole.significato: Produced by the earth.
parole.testo: Latin terrigena (“land-born”) + -ous

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or restricted to a specific geographic area, or territory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin territorialis, from Latin territorium; equivalent to territory + -al.

parole.significato: A large extent or tract of land; for example a region, country or district.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English territorie, from Latin territōrium.

parole.significato: Of speech or style: brief, concise, to the point.
parole.testo: From Latin tersus (“clean, cleansed, rubbed or wiped off; neat, spruce; terse”), perfect passive participle of Latin tergeō, tergō (“to clean, cleanse, rub, wipe, wipe off”).

parole.significato: tertiary form.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin tertius (“third”).

parole.significato: Third.
parole.testo: From Latin tertius (“third”).

parole.significato: Any flight feather attached to the humerus (upper arm) of a bird.
parole.testo: From Latin tertius (“third”); the tertial feathers are the third row of feathers. By surface analysis, terti- + -al.

parole.significato: Characterised by paroxysms recurring every other day (that is, every third day by inclusive reckoning).
parole.testo: From Middle English tertiān, terciān, terciāne (adjective and noun), originally often as part of the collocation fever cum terciane, after Latin febris cum tertiānā. Compare the "third" essence of tertiary. By surface analysis, terti- + -an.

parole.significato: Of third rank or order; subsequent.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes Borrowed from the Latin tertiārius (“of the third part or rank”), from tertius (“third”) (from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥tyós, whence English third) + -ārius (whence the English suffix -ary); compare the French tertiaire. By surface analysis, terti- + -ary.

parole.significato: To reduce by one third; especially, kill one third of (a group of people).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tertiāt-, the perfect passive participial stem of Latin tertiō, from tertius (“third”). By surface analysis, terti- + -ate.

parole.significato: Pregnant for the third time.
parole.testo: From Latin tertiparus. By surface analysis, from Terti- as in tertiary, Latin tertiō (“to do for the third time”) + -parous.

parole.significato: For every proposition, either it is true or its negation is true.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tertium non datur. Literally, “A third thing is not given.”.

parole.significato: Something intermediate between two classifications.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tertium quid (“third thing”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or in the style or manner of Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus from Carthage.
parole.testo: Anglicized from Latin Tertullianus.

parole.significato: An ancient Roman coin worth one quarter of an as.
parole.testo: From Latin teruncius.

parole.significato: Formed of tesserae, like a mosaic.
parole.testo: From Latin tessella (“a small square piece, a little cube”), diminutive of tessera (“a square piece of stone, wood, etc., a die”).

parole.significato: A small tessera.
parole.testo: From Latin tessella.

parole.significato: tessellated
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tessellātus, from tessella, diminutive of tessera; from Ancient Greek τέσσαρες (téssares), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.

parole.significato: A small square piece of stone, wood, ivory or glass used for making a mosaic.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tessera (“a cube, a die with numbers on all six sides”), from Ancient Greek τέσσαρες (téssares, “four”).

parole.significato: tesseral
parole.testo: From (assumed) New Latin tessula (diminutive of Latin tessera) + English -ar.

parole.significato: A seed coat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin testa.

parole.significato: Any of various shellfish, especially those of the obsolete orders Vermes or Acephala, or the suborder Thecosomata.
parole.testo: From Latin testāceus (“covered with a shell”).

parole.significato: Covered with or having a shell.
parole.testo: From Latin testaceus (“having a shell”) + -an.

parole.significato: Pertaining to earthenware or baked clay.
parole.testo: From Latin testāceus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a testament; testamentary.
parole.testo: Latin testamentalis.

parole.significato: The legal capacity to participate in a testamentum (will), be it as a testator, a heres (heir), or a signator (witness).
parole.testo: From Latin testāmentī factiō (“right of participating in a will”).

parole.significato: A certificate of successful completion of an examination.
parole.testo: From Latin testāmur (“we testify”).

parole.significato: having left a legally valid last will and testament (of one who has died).
parole.testo: From Latin testātus (“testified”), perfect passive participle of testor (“to be witness, testify, attest; to make a will”), from testis (“witness”).

parole.significato: One who makes or has made a legally valid will.
parole.testo: From Latin testator (“one who makes a will, in Late Latin also one who bears witness”), from testari (“to bear witness, make a will”). See testament.

parole.significato: A female testator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin testātrīx. By surface analysis, testator + -trix.

parole.significato: One of the clauses of an English deed, enumerating the operative words of transfer, statement of consideration, money,…
parole.testo: From Latin testatum.

parole.significato: A witness.
parole.testo: So called from Latin teste, ablative of testis (“a witness”), because this was formerly the initial word in the clause.

parole.significato: A testis: the male sex and endocrine gland, found in most types of animals, that produces sperm and male sex hormones,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin testiculus, diminutive of testis.

parole.significato: Having the testicles naturally concealed within the abdomen, such as in the case of the cetaceans.
parole.testo: From Latin testis (“testis”) + condere (“to hide”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to one or more testicles; of the testicle(s).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin testicularis, from Latin testiculum (“testicle”), diminutive of testis.

parole.significato: A certificate of good character that was required to allow travel between parishes in the 18th and early 19th centuries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin testificātus.

parole.significato: The act of testifying, or giving testimony or evidence.
parole.testo: From Latin testificātiō. Compare Old French testification. See testify.

parole.significato: A testifier.
parole.testo: From New Latin testificātor (“testifier”), from Latin testificor + -ātor.

parole.significato: A testicle of a vertebrate.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin testis.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to, tortoises.
parole.testo: From Latin testūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: Resembling or pertaining to the shell of a tortoise.
parole.testo: From Latin testūdin- + -ary + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: Of, like or relating to a tortoise.
parole.testo: From Latin testūdin- + -ate, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: A turtle.
parole.testo: From a substantivation of the above adjective. Equivalent toLatin testūdin- + -ate, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: Characteristic of a tortoise, or the shell of a tortoise.
parole.testo: From Latin testūdin- + -eous, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: Any member of the Testudinidae, the tortoises.
parole.testo: From Latin testūdin- + -id, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: Any turtle of the superfamily Testudinoidea.
parole.testo: Clipping of taxonomic name Testudinoidea. From Latin testūdin- + -oid, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: A shelter formed by a body of troops holding their shields or targets close together over their heads.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin testūdō (“tortoise, turtle, lyre, type of military shelter”).

parole.significato: A serious and often fatal disease caused by the infection of an open wound with the anaerobic bacterium Clostridium tet…
parole.testo: From Latin tetanus, from Ancient Greek τέτανος (tétanos), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”).

parole.significato: Extremely foul or ugly; horrible; terrible.
parole.testo: From Latin teterrima (“most foul, most ugly”).

parole.significato: Synonym of quadrennium: A four-year period, particularly (historical) those used in ancient Egyptian and Greek astronom…
parole.testo: From Late Latin tetraeteris, from Ancient Greek τετραετηρίς (tetraetērís), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + ἔτος (étos, “year”).

parole.significato: A bird belonging to the tribe Tetraonini, of which the genus Tetrao is the type.
parole.testo: Latin tetrao (“a heath cock, grouse”), from Ancient Greek. Compare French tétraonide.

parole.significato: A combination of wax, resin, lard, and pitch, composing an ointment.
parole.testo: See tetra- (“four”) and Latin pharmacum (“drug”).

parole.significato: In or of four identical experiments.
parole.testo: From Latin plicō (“to fold”) + Ancient Greek τετράς (tetrás, “four”).

parole.significato: A noun that has four cases.
parole.testo: From Latin tetraptōtum, from Ancient Greek τετράπτωτος (tetráptōtos).

parole.significato: A governor or ruler of a quarter of a country, especially of a fourth part of a province in or client state of Ancient…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tetrarchēs, from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “ruler, leader”).

parole.significato: A government where power is shared by four people, especially (historical) the Herodian tetrarchy established in Judea…
parole.testo: From Latin tetrarchia, from Ancient Greek τετραρχία (tetrarkhía), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “-archy: rule”), equivalent to tetra- + -archy.

parole.significato: A four-line stanza.
parole.testo: From Latin tetrastichon, from neuter of Ancient Greek τετράστιχον (tetrástikhon, “having four rows”), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + στίχος (stíkhos, “row”).

parole.significato: A collection of the four Gospels
parole.testo: From tetra- + ecclesiastical Latin evangelium (“evangel”).

parole.significato: Morose, bitter.
parole.testo: From Latin tetricus (“stern, severe, gloomy”).

parole.significato: The quality of being tetric: crabbedness, harshness, bitterness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tetricitas, taetricitas. By surface analysis, tetric + -ity.

parole.significato: One of the ancient Trojans.
parole.testo: From Latin Teucrus, from plural Teucri (“the Trojans”), from Teucer, the name of the first king of Troy.

parole.significato: Any of the genus Teucrium of lamiaceous plants; a germander.
parole.testo: From the genus name (New Latin Teucrium).

parole.significato: A member of an early Germanic tribe living in Jutland noted in historical writings by Greek and Roman authors.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tewtéh₂ Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂der. Latin Teutonēsbor. English Teuton Borrowed from Latin Teutonēs, Teutonī (“the Teutons”) (compare Ancient Greek Τεύτονες (Teútones)), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂ (“people”). First attested in the early 1700s.

parole.significato: Relating to the ancient Germanic people, the Teutons.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tewtéh₂ 1580, from Latin Teutonicus, from Teutonēs, Teutonī (“the Teutons”, name of a Germanic tribe that inhabited coastal Germany and devastated Gaul between 113–101 B.C.), equivalent to Teuton + -ic.

parole.significato: Any material made of interlacing or matted fibres, including carpeting and geotextiles, woven or nonwoven.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin textile, substantive use of textilis (“woven”), from texō (“weave”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to weaving.
parole.testo: From Latin textorius, from textor (“a weaver”), from texere, textum (“to weave”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to weaving
parole.testo: Latin textrīnus, for textōrīnus, from textor (“a weaver”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to text.
parole.testo: From Middle English textewell, textueel, textuel, textuele, tixtuel (“learned in texts, bookish”), possibly from Latin textuālis; also compare Middle French textuele; or perhaps a coinage by Chaucer from Latin textus and Middle English -el. English spelling conformed to Latin from late 15c. By surfa

parole.significato: The succession of printed Greek texts of the New Testament which constituted the translation base for various early ver…
parole.testo: From Latin textus receptus (“received text”).

parole.significato: Either of two large, ovoid structures of grey matter within the forebrain that relay sensory impulses to the cerebral c…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin thalamus, from Ancient Greek θάλαμος (thálamos, “an inner chamber, a bedroom, a bed”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Thalictrum; meadowrue.
parole.testo: From Latin thalictrum.

parole.significato: The presentation of something as a marvel rather than in a neutrally descriptive way.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek θαυμασμός (thaumasmós, “a wondering”).

parole.significato: A performer of thaumaturgy; a performer of miracles; a magician.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin thaumatūrgus, from Ancient Greek θαυματουργός (thaumatourgós), from θαύματο- (thaúmato-, “marvel”) + -ουργός (-ourgós, “worker, maker”). Doublet of thaumaturgus.

parole.significato: A miracle worker.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin thaumaturgus, from Ancient Greek θαυματουργός (thaumatourgós). Doublet of thaumaturge.

parole.parola: the cure is worse than the disease
parole.significato: The medical treatment for an illness produces a worse net result than the illness does (or threatens a non-negligible r…
parole.testo: From Latin aegrescit medendo (literally “it worsens with healing”) attributed to Virgil in book XII of the Aeneid.

parole.significato: A conclusive action has been taken, so events will proceed in an irreversible manner; the point of no return has been p…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin iacta ālea est, which is grammatically, and thereby semantically, an incorrect translation by the Roman historian Suetonius (c. 69 – p. 122 C.E.) in his work Vīta Dīvī Iūlī (On the Life of the Caesars, 121 C.E.) of the Ancient Greek ἀνερρίφθω κύβος (anerrhíphthō kúbos), which was sai

parole.parola: the voice of the people, the voice of God
parole.significato: The voice of the people should be heard.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin vōx populī, vōx Deī (“the voice of the people [is] the voice of God”).

parole.significato: god or deity
parole.testo: From Latin theo- (“god”), combining form of theos (“god”); from Ancient Greek θεο- (theo-, “god”), combining form of θεός (theós, “god”).

parole.significato: theatrical
parole.testo: From Latin theātrālis.

parole.significato: Relating to acting or the theater, theatrical.
parole.testo: From Late Latin theātricus, equivalent to theatre + -ic.

parole.significato: Theban; of or pertaining to Thebes, especially in the context of the Coptic scriptures.
parole.testo: From Latin Thēbaicus, from Ancient Greek Θηϐαϊκός (Thēbaïkós).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Thebes
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Thēbānus, from Thēb(ae) + -ānus. By surface analysis, Theb(es) + -an.

parole.significato: Any of several external cases or sheaths.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin thēca, from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē, “a case, box, receptacle”), from τίθημι (títhēmi, “put, set, place”). Doublet of tay.

parole.significato: The hymenium
parole.testo: From New Latin thēcium, from Ancient Greek θήκιον (thḗkion), diminutive of θήκη (thḗkē, “sheath”).

parole.significato: A morbid condition resulting from excessive consumption of tea.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin thea (“tea”, noun) + English -ism.

parole.significato: The tip or peak of a nipple.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek θηλή (thēlḗ, “nipple”) + -ion. By surface analysis, thel- + -ion.

parole.significato: A nipple or papilla.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek θηλή (thēlḗ, “nipple”). By surface analysis, thel- + -ium.

parole.significato: A toll or custom required from travelling merchants as a tax on doing business.
parole.testo: From Latin telōnium, from Ancient Greek τελώνῐον (telṓnĭon, “custom house”), from τέλος (télos, “due, tax, toll”).

parole.significato: god; deity
parole.testo: From Latin theo- (“god”), combining form of theos (“god”); from Ancient Greek θεο- (theo-, “god”), combining form of θεός (theós, “god”).

parole.significato: A surveying instrument, consisting of a small mounted telescope, used to measure horizontal and vertical angles.
parole.testo: From New Latin theodolitus (1571), perhaps containing Ancient Greek θέᾱ (théā, “sight, view”) and Arabic العِضَادَة (al-ʕiḍāda, “astrolabe, alidade”); if so, doublet of alidade.

parole.significato: A fiador.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Theodōrus, borrowed from Ancient Greek Θεόδωρος (Theódōros), from θεός (theós, “god”) + δῶρον (dôron, “gift”). The name was popularized in reference to the prominent St Theodore of Amasea. Unrelated to Theodoric.

parole.significato: A poor theologian; someone who merely pretends to be a theologian.
parole.testo: From Latin theologus + -aster.

parole.significato: A theologian.
parole.testo: From the stem of Latin theologus or English theology + -er; see -loger.

parole.significato: One who is skilled in, professes or practices that which relates or pertains to God.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin theologista.

parole.significato: To discuss or speculate about theological subjects.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin theologizāre, with the transitive sense possibly being formed by theology + -ize.

parole.significato: A student of theology
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin theologus, from Ancient Greek θεολόγος (theológos). Equivalent to theo- + -logue.

parole.significato: Synonym of theologian (“Roman Catholic lecturer”).
parole.testo: From Latin theologus.

parole.significato: A manifestation of a deity to a person.
parole.testo: From Late Latin theophania, corresponding to theo- + -phany, from θεός (theós, “God”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, appear”).

parole.significato: Concerned with theories or hypotheses rather than with practical matters.
parole.testo: English theory + -etic, from Latin theōrēticus, from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós).

parole.significato: Of or relating to theory; abstract; not empirical.
parole.testo: From Middle English theorothycall, probably from Latin theōrēticus + -al, from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós).

parole.significato: Relating to, or skilled in, theory; theoretical.
parole.testo: From Middle English theoryk, from Latin theōricus and Middle French theorique. By surface analysis, theory + -ic.

parole.significato: theoretical
parole.testo: From Middle English theorycall, from Latin theōricus + -al. By surface analysis, theory + -ical.

parole.significato: The likeness to or union with God; deification.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin theōsis, from Koine Greek θέωσις (théōsis).

parole.significato: A theosophist.
parole.testo: Attested circa 1835. From Medieval Latin theosophus (“a theologian”, noun), from Koine Greek θεόσοφος (theósophos, “wise in things concerning god”, adjective), from Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god”) + σοφός (sophós, “wise”). Cognate with French théosophe and Spanish teósofo.

parole.significato: Any doctrine of religious philosophy and mysticism claiming that knowledge of God can be attained through mystical insi…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin theosophia, from Ancient Greek θεοσοφῐ́ᾱ (theosophĭ́ā, “knowledge of things divine”, from θεός (theós, “god”) + σοφῐ́ᾱ (sophĭ́ā, “wisdom”)); By surface analysis, theo- + -sophy.

parole.significato: A Jewish sect which flourished in Alexandria and other parts of the Diaspora of Hellenistic Judaism in the final years…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek θερᾰπευταί (therăpeutaí), plural of θερᾰπευτής (therăpeutḗs, “one who serves the gods, worshipper”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to therapy.
parole.testo: From Middle English terapeucia, from New Latin therapeuticus (“curing, healing”), from Ancient Greek θεραπευτικός (therapeutikós, “attentive, helpful, obliging, curative”), from θεραπευτής (therapeutḗs, “one who waits on another, an attendant”), from θεραπεύω (therapeúō, “I wait on, attend, serve, c

parole.significato: Attempted remediation of a health problem following a diagnosis, usually synonymous with treatment.
parole.testo: From New Latin therapīa, from Ancient Greek θεραπεία (therapeía, “service, medical treatment”), from θεραπεύω (therapeúō, “to serve, treat medically”) + -ία (-ía, suffix for forming abstract nouns).

parole.parola: there is nothing new under the sun
parole.significato: There is nothing truly novel in existence; every new idea has some sort of precedent or echo from the past.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin nihil sub sōle novum, itself a calque from the Hebrew אֵין כָּל חָדָשׁ תַּחַת הַשָּׁמֶשׁ (en kol chadásh táchat hashámesh, “there is nothing new under the sun”) found in Ecclesiastes 1:9.

parole.significato: In subjective matters of taste, people have wildly different opinions; disagreements about matters of taste cannot be o…
parole.testo: Adaptation of Latin de gustibus non est disputandum.

parole.significato: A universal antidote against all poisons, particularly medicines considered to derive from a recipe of the Roman physic…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin theriacum, from Ancient Greek θηριακὸν (thēriakòn) and Late Latin theriaca, from Ancient Greek θηριακὴ (thēriakḕ, “of or related to poisonous reptiles”), from θηρίον (thēríon, “little beast”) + -κός (-kós), from θήρ (thḗr, “beast”) + -ίον (-íon, diminutive suffix). Doublet of the

parole.significato: Roman-style spring or baths with warm or hot water.
parole.testo: From Latin thermae, plural of therma. See thermal.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the city of Therma.
parole.testo: From Therma + -ean, modelled after Latin Thermaeus, from Ancient Greek Θερμαῖος (Thermaîos).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the city of Therma.
parole.testo: From Latin Thermaicus, from Ancient Greek Θερμαϊκός (Thermaïkós).

parole.significato: A place where food and hot drinks were sold.
parole.testo: From Latin thermopōlium.

parole.significato: A publication that provides synonyms (and sometimes antonyms and other semantic relations) for the words of a given lan…
parole.testo: 16th century, borrowed from Latin thēsaurus, from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse, treasure”); its current English usage/meaning was established soon after the publication of Peter Roget's Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases in 1852. Doublet of treasure.

parole.significato: This document (formerly used in official documents and decrees; now mainly confined to university diplomas).
parole.testo: Calque of Latin hae presentes [litterae], literally "these present [letters]" but idiomatically "this present [document]."

parole.significato: Senses relating to logic, rhetoric, etc.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English thesis (“lowering of the voice”) and also borrowed directly from its etymon Latin thesis (“proposition, thesis; lowering of the voice”), from Ancient Greek θέσῐς (thésĭs, “arrangement, placement, setting; conclusion, position, thesis; lowering of the voice”), from τῐ́θημῐ (t

parole.significato: Of, or relating to drama and acting; dramatic, theatrical.
parole.testo: From Latin Thespis, from the name of the Ancient Greek actor Thespis (fl. 6th century BCE), from Θέσπις (Théspis) + -ian.

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to, theurgy.
parole.testo: From Latin theurgicus. By surface analysis, theurgy + -ic.

parole.significato: A form of magic designed to allow for worship or conjuration of, or communication with spirits or deities.
parole.testo: From Late Latin theūrgia, from Ancient Greek θεουργίᾱ (theourgíā, “sorcery”), from θεός (theós, “god”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). By surface analysis, the- + -urgy.

parole.significato: A group of singers and dancers assembled to celebrate the festival of one of the gods.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek θίασος (thíasos).

parole.significato: Compression, especially constriction of vessels by an external cause.
parole.testo: From New Latin thlipsis, from Ancient Greek θλῖψις (thlîpsis, “pressure”).

parole.significato: A cupola, a dome, a rotunda; a tholus.
parole.testo: Anglicization of Latin tholus (“cupola, dome, rotunda”), from Ancient Greek θόλος (thólos, “dome, vault”), further etymology uncertain but possibly cognate with θᾰ́λᾰμος (thắlămos, “bedroom; inner chamber”) and/or English dale. Doublet of tholus and tholos.

parole.significato: A small domical mountain or hill.
parole.testo: From Latin tholus (“dome, rotunda”). Doublet of tholos.

parole.significato: An infidel or doubter.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Thomas, from Latin Thōmās m (as in the Vulgate), from Ancient Greek Θωμᾶς m (Thōmâs), the Biblical Greek transcription of Aramaic תאומא or תאמא (“twin”), the nickname of one of the Twelve Apostles. In the gospel of John (11:16, 20:24), the Aramaic nickname is also trans

parole.significato: A follower or advocate of Thomism.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin Thōmista.

parole.significato: nuptial
parole.testo: From Latin t(h)orus (“marriage”, literally “(marriage) bed”).

parole.significato: The region of the mammalian body between the neck and abdomen as well as the cavity containing the heart and lungs.
parole.testo: From Latin thorax, from Ancient Greek θώραξ (thṓrax, “a breastplate, cuirass, corslet”).

parole.significato: The rare earth thorium oxide.
parole.testo: From New Latin [Term?]. See thorite.

parole.significato: Boastful, bragging, vainglorious.
parole.testo: From Latin Thrasō, Thrason-, the name of a boastful soldier in the play Eunuchus by Terence. The name is derived from Ancient Greek θρασύς (thrasús, “bold, audacious”).

parole.significato: a dirge or lamentation
parole.testo: From Latin threnus, from Ancient Greek θρῆνος (thrênos, “funeral lament”).

parole.significato: A hymn to Dionysus, sung in processions in his honour.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin thriambus, from Ancient Greek θρίαμβος (thríambos), of Pre-Greek origin. Doublet of triumph and trump.

parole.significato: thrombus
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Greek the Ancient Greek θρόμβος (thrómbos, “lump”, “piece”, “blood clot”, “milk curd”).

parole.significato: A blood clot formed from platelets and other elements that forms in a blood vessel in a living organism, and causes thr…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin thrombus, from the Ancient Greek θρόμβος (thrómbos, “lump, piece, blood clot, milk curd”); compare thrombo-.

parole.significato: A tree of the genus Thuja.
parole.testo: From taxonomic New Latin Thuja, from Ancient Greek θυία (thuía).

parole.significato: The rare earth thulium oxide, Tm₂O₃.
parole.testo: From New Latin thūlia. Named in 1879 by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve.

parole.significato: Resembling a tuna.
parole.testo: From Latin thunnus (“tuna”) + -iform.

parole.significato: related to incense
parole.testo: From Latin thūrālis (adjective), from thūs (“incense”).

parole.significato: A censer, especially one hanging on a chain.
parole.testo: Originated 1400–50 from late Middle English turrible, from thoryble, from Latin thūribulum (“censer”), equivalent to thūs (“incense”) (root: thūr-) (from Ancient Greek θύος (thúos, “burnt offering”)) + -bulum (“instrumental suffix”).

parole.significato: A thurifer.
parole.testo: From unattested Latin *thūribulārius, *thūribulāriorum, ultimately from thūribulum.

parole.significato: An acolyte who carries a thurible.
parole.testo: Originated 1850–55 from New Latin thūrifer (“incense-bearing”), tūrifer, from Latin thūs, tūs (“incense”) + -fer (“bearing”)

parole.significato: The fragrant wood of a North African tree (Tetraclinis articulata) in the family Cupressaceae.
parole.testo: From Latin thȳinus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to thynnic acid or its derivatives
parole.testo: From Latin thynnus (“tuna”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A spot in the wing veins of Neuroptera, Hymenoptera and Trichoptera.
parole.testo: From Latin thyridium, from Ancient Greek θυρίδιον (thurídion), diminutive of θύρᾱ (thúrā, “door”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to both the thyroid and arytenoid cartilages of the larynx.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin thyreoarytaenoīdēs, from thyreoīdēs (“shield-shaped”) + arytaenoīdēs (“ladle-shaped”); equivalent to thyro- + arytenoid. Doublet of thyroarytenoideus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the thyroglossal duct
parole.testo: From thyro- + glossal. Back-formation from "thyroglossal duct", from New Latin ductus thyroglossalis.

parole.significato: An embryonic anatomical structure which connects the initial area of development of the thyroid gland to its final posi…
parole.testo: Calque of New Latin ductus thyroglossalis

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the thyroid cartilage of the larynx and the hyoid arch.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin thyreohȳoīdēs, from thyreoīdēs (“shield-shaped”) + hȳoīdēs (“U-shaped”); equivalent to thyro- + hyoid. Doublet of thyrohyoideus.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or being the thyroid cartilage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin thyreoīdēs, from Ancient Greek θῠρεοειδής (thŭreoeidḗs, “shield-shaped”), from θῠρεός (thŭreós, “an oblong shield”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-form, -like”).

parole.significato: A large butterfly-shaped endocrine gland situated on the front of the neck that produces various hormones.
parole.testo: From New Latin glandula thyreoidea, coined by Thomas Wharton in 1656.

parole.significato: A form of thyrotoxicosis caused by the ingestion of exogenous thyroid hormone
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: A staff topped with a conical ornament, carried by Bacchus or his followers.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos). Doublet of thyrse, torse, and torso.

parole.significato: The three-tiered papal crown.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tiāra, from Ancient Greek τιάρα (tiára), of unknown ultimate origin.

parole.significato: The inner and usually the larger of the two bones of the leg or hind limb below the knee, the shinbone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tībia (“shin bone, leg”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a tibia or a structure associated with a tibia.
parole.testo: From Latin tībiālis, equivalent to tibia + -al.

parole.significato: A flute-player; a piper, flautist.
parole.testo: From the Latin tībīcen (“piper, flautist”).

parole.significato: thrice per day, consumed three times per day
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ter in diē.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of the tiger.
parole.testo: From Latin tigrīnus.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling the family Tiliaceae (now principally subfamily Tilioideae in family Malvaceae) of flo…
parole.testo: From translingual Tiliaceae + -ous, from Latin tilia (“linden tree”).

parole.significato: Time passes quickly.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin tempus fugit.

parole.significato: A contemporary.
parole.testo: Likely a calque of Medieval Latin contemporārius.

parole.significato: The dyeing poison dart frog (Dendrobates tinctorius).
parole.testo: Probably from the Latin specific epithet tinctorius.

parole.significato: A tint or colour.
parole.testo: From Middle English tynct (noun) and tincten, tyncten, tynkten (verb), borrowed from Latin tīnctus, past participle of tingō (“to tinge”). Doublet of tint.

parole.significato: A stain; a preparation for staining.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tinctiō (“a soaking, dipping”).

parole.significato: tincture
parole.testo: From Latin tīnctūra. Doublet of tainture, teinture, and tincture.

parole.significato: A preparation made by macerating or digesting myrrh with alcohol and filtering.
parole.testo: From Latin tīnctūra myrrhae.

parole.significato: Senses relating to colour, and to dipping something into a liquid.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English tincture (“a dye, pigment; a colour, hue, tint; process of colouring or dyeing; medicinal ointment or salve (perhaps one discolouring the skin); use of a medicinal tincture; (alchemy) transmutation of base metals into gold; ability to cause such transmuta

parole.significato: A fungal infection of the skin, known generally as ringworm.
parole.testo: From Latin tinea (“moth; bookworm”).

parole.significato: Jock itch.
parole.testo: From Latin tinea crūris (literally “leg (ring)worm”).

parole.significato: athlete’s foot
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Ringworm (any of certain fungal infections) of a fingernail or toenail.
parole.testo: From Latin tinea (“worm, moth”) unguis (“fingernail, toenail, claw, hoof”).

parole.significato: A small added amount of colour; (by extension) a small added amount of some other thing.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Latin tingere, present active infinitive of tingō (“to dip; to moisten; to colour, dye, tinge”). The noun is derived from the verb.

parole.significato: Having the power to tinge (dye).
parole.testo: From Latin tingens, present participle of tingere (“to tinge”). See tinge.

parole.significato: Capable of being stained.
parole.testo: Latin tingere (“to dye”).

parole.significato: Having a ringing or clinking sound.
parole.testo: From Latin tinnīo + -ent.

parole.significato: Synonym of tintinnabulum.
parole.testo: From Latin tinniolum.

parole.significato: The experience of auditory sensations, such as a ringing or pulsating sound, occurring in the absence of any external s…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tinnītus (“a jingling, ringing”).

parole.significato: Of or related to bells; of the nature of a bell.
parole.testo: From Latin tintinnabulum (“little bell”) + -ar (“forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: A bell-ringer.
parole.testo: From tintinnabular + -ary. Noun sense possibly also under the influence of Latin tintinnabularius (“bell-ringer”).

parole.significato: To ring, tinkle, toll, or otherwise sound like bells.
parole.testo: From Latin tintinnabulatus (“furnished with a bell or bells”), from tintinnabulum ("a bell"). Akin to tinnitus.

parole.significato: A tinkling sound, as of a bell or of breaking glass.
parole.testo: Noun of action from tintinnabulate, from Latin tintinnabulum (“a bell”), from tintinō, a reduplicated form of tinniō (“ring, jingle”).

parole.significato: A compositional style characterized by two types of voice, the first of which (the "tintinnabular voice") arpeggiates t…
parole.testo: From Latin tintinnābulum (“a small monastic bell”).

parole.significato: A small clinking bell, particularly (historical) a small bell used to call monks to certain tasks.
parole.testo: From Latin tintinnābulum (“a small monastic bell”).

parole.significato: A shoulder covering, typically the fur of a fox, with long ends that dangle in front.
parole.testo: From Middle English tippet, Old English tæppet, from Latin tapete (“cloth”).

parole.significato: Any of many species of long-legged dipterous insects belonging to Tipula and allied genera; a common crane fly.
parole.testo: Related to Latin tippula (“water spider”).

parole.significato: Schooling, apprenticeship; novitiate.
parole.testo: From Latin tirocinium (“first military campaign; raw recruit; inexperience; first attempt”), from tīro (“beginner, recruit, novice”) + -cinor (“forming verbs: to be a ...”) + -ium (“forming nouns: the state of ...”), used in the title of William Cowper's 1784 poem on schools Tirocinium, or A Review

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Marcus Tullius Tiro (died circa 4 BCE), scribe of Cicero and inventor of an early shorthand.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Tīrōniānus.

parole.significato: Any one of thousands of signs in a system of shorthand developed in the 60s BC by Cicero’s scribe Marcus Tullius Tiro.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin nota Tīrōniāna

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Titans, a race of giant gods in Greek mythology.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Titanicus, or its etymon Ancient Greek Τιτανικός (Titanikós, “of or relating to the Titans”), from Τιτᾶνες (Titânes, “Titans”) + -ικός (-ikós, “suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives”). parole.significato: Any one of Uranus and Gaia's daughters; a female Titan.
parole.testo: From Latin Titanis, from Ancient Greek Τιτανίς (Titanís). By surface analysis, Titan + -id.

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Ti), atomic number 22; it is a strong, corrosion-resistant transition metal, used to make li…
parole.testo: From Latin titanium.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or denoting those rays of light which produce chemical effects; actinic.
parole.testo: Latin Tithonius (“belonging to Tithonus, the consort of Aurora”), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Any kind of spurge, especially Euphorbia cyparissias.
parole.testo: From Latin tithymalus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Titus Tatius, a king of the Sabines according to the Roman foundation myth.
parole.testo: From Latin Titiānus (“of or relating to Titus; a male given name”), from Titus + -iānus. By surface analysis, Titus + -ian.

parole.significato: To stimulate or excite sensually.
parole.testo: From Latin tītillātus, from tītillāre (“to tickle”).

parole.significato: A pleasurable or sexually exciting sensation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tītillātiō, tītillātiōnem.

parole.significato: The name of a film, musical piece, painting, or other work of art.
parole.testo: From Middle English title, titel, from Old English titul (“title, heading, superscription”), from Latin titulus (“title, inscription”). Doublet of tilde, titer/titre, titlo, tittle, and titulus.

parole.significato: stammering in speech
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin titubantia.

parole.significato: To stagger
parole.testo: From Latin titubatus, past participle of titubare (“to stagger, totter”).

parole.significato: A caption, title or other inscription, especially an Ancient Roman type.
parole.testo: From Latin titulus. Doublet of tilde, titer/titre, title, titlo, and tittle.

parole.significato: The insertion of one or more words between the components of a compound word.
parole.testo: From Late Latin tmēsis, from Ancient Greek τμῆσις (tmêsis, “a cutting”), from τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”). First attested in 1586.

parole.significato: Every person is entitled to their personal preferences and tastes.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin suum cuique, short for suum cuique pulchrum est (“to each his own is beautiful”).

parole.significato: Everyone makes mistakes.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin errāre hūmānum est.

parole.significato: An ancient people of Bactria.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Tocharī pl, from Ancient Greek Τόχαροι pl (Tókharoi).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Tochari (people of Bactria).
parole.testo: From Latin Tocharī + -ian, the first element deriving from Ancient Greek Τόχαροι (Tókharoi, “Tochari/Tukharas (an ancient people of Bactria)”), plural of Τόχαρος (Tókharos), probably from an Indo-Iranian source (Old Persian [script needed] (tuxāri-), Khotanese [script needed] (ttahvāra)); compare Sa

parole.significato: A loose outer garment worn by the citizens of Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed directly from Latin toga, from tegō (“to clothe”). Doublet of toge. The Philippine (and Indonesian) senses are due to the resemblance of the white ceremonial gowns worn by graduates of institutions to the loose outer garment worn by the citizens of Ancient Rome.

parole.significato: Clad in a toga; represented in art as wearing a toga.
parole.testo: From the Latin togātus (“wearing a toga”).

parole.significato: Dressed in a toga or gown; wearing a gown; gowned.
parole.testo: Latin togatus, from toga (“a toga”).

parole.significato: Any of the virus family Togaviridae.
parole.testo: From Latin toga (“loose outer garment worn in Roman Empire”) + virus

parole.significato: To allow or permit without explicit approval, usually if it is perceived as negative.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tolerātus, the perfect passive participle of tolerō (“to endure”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with Old English þolian (“to tolerate, suffer, bear”) and French tolérer. More at thole.

parole.significato: To take away; to vacate; to annul.
parole.testo: From Latin tollō (“to lift up”).

parole.significato: A toll or tribute of a sextary of ale, paid to the lords of some manors by their tenants in exchange for permission to…
parole.testo: From Latin tolsestrum. Compare toll (“a tax”).

parole.significato: A writ by which a cause pending in a court baron was removed into a county court.
parole.testo: From Latin tolta, from tollere (“to take away”).

parole.significato: A pacing or ambling.
parole.testo: From Latin tolutim (“on a trot, properly, lifting up the feet”), akin to tollere (“to lift up”). Compare Icelandic tölt.

parole.significato: A way of speaking characterized by nimbleness and volubility.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tolūtiloquentia.

parole.significato: covered in (often matted) hair.
parole.testo: From New Latin tōmentōsus of like application, from tōmentum + -ōsus.

parole.significato: The cutting edge of the bill of a bird.
parole.testo: From New Latin tomium, from Ancient Greek τομός (tomós, “sharp”) + -ium. See -tome.

parole.significato: A specific pitch.
parole.testo: From Middle English ton, tone, from Latin tonus (“sound, tone”) (possibly through Old French ton), from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, “strain, tension, pitch”), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”). Doublet of tune, ton, tonos, and tonus.

parole.significato: An explosive compound; a preparation of guncotton.
parole.testo: Compare Latin tonare (“to thunder”).

parole.significato: thundering
parole.testo: From Latin tonitruāns, present participle of tonitruō (“to thunder”), from Latin tonitrus (“thunder”) + -ant.

parole.significato: To thunder.
parole.testo: From the past participle stem of Latin tonitruare (“to thunder”), from tonitrus (“thunder”) + -ate.

parole.significato: thundering
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin tonitruōsus, from tonitrus (“thunder”) + -ōsus (“full of”).

parole.significato: Capable of being clipped.
parole.testo: From Latin tonsilis, from tondere, tonsum (“to shear, clip”). See tonsure.

parole.significato: Synonym of barber.
parole.testo: From Latin tōnsor (“barber, hairdresser”), from the supine root of tondēre (“to shave, to shear”) + -or (“-or: forming agent nouns”).

parole.significato: Relating to barbering, shaving, or hairdressing.
parole.testo: From Latin tonsor (“barber”).

parole.significato: tonicity; tone
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tonus (“strain, tension”). Doublet of tone, tune, and ton (fashion/style).

parole.significato: A small state, consisting of a few cities or towns; a petty country governed by a toparch.
parole.testo: From Latin toparchia, from Ancient Greek τοπαρχία (toparkhía), from τόπος (tópos, “place”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”).

parole.significato: A kind of sandstone.
parole.testo: From Latin tophus, tofus (“tufa, or tuff”). Doublet of tophus, tufa, and tuff.

parole.significato: gravelly; sandy; rough; stony
parole.testo: From Latin tophaceus, tofaceus.

parole.significato: A deposit of monosodium urate crystals in the body, caused by high levels of uric acid in the blood.
parole.testo: From Latin tophus (“stone”).

parole.significato: A kind of mural decoration common in Ancient Roman houses, usually featuring landscapes.
parole.testo: From Latin topia, from Ancient Greek τόπια (tópia), ultimately from Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos, “place”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to art of topiaries.
parole.testo: From Latin topiarius (“of or relating to ornamental gardening; an ornamental garden, an ornamental gardener”), from Latin topia (“ornamental gardening, landscape painting”), from Ancient Greek τόπια (tópia, “artistic representation in which natural or artificial features of a place are used as the m

parole.significato: topical
parole.testo: From Latin topica, from Ancient Greek τοπικός (topikós, “pertaining to a place, local, pertaining to a common place, or topic, topical”), from τόπος (tópos, “a place”).

parole.significato: A precise description of a place.
parole.testo: First attested in 1432. From Middle English topographye, from Latin topographia, from Ancient Greek τοπογραφία (topographía), from τόπος (tópos, “place”) + γράφω (gráphō, “to write”).

parole.significato: The branch of mathematics dealing with those properties of a geometrical object (of arbitrary dimensionality) that are…
parole.testo: From Late Latin topologia, from By surface analysis, topo- (“place”) + -logy (“study of, a branch of knowledge”).

parole.significato: The description of an imaginable or nonexistent place.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin topothesia.

parole.significato: winepress
parole.testo: From Latin torculō (“to press”).

parole.significato: A tourniquet.
parole.testo: From Latin torcular.

parole.significato: Synonym of confluence of sinuses.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin torcular Hērophilī (“Herophilos' winepress”), named after Greek physician Herophilos, while torcular was the Latin calque of Ancient Greek ληνός (lēnós, “anything shaped like a tub or trough; wine vat”), originally described by Herophilos.

parole.significato: Of or belonging to a (wine or oil) press.
parole.testo: From the Latin torculārius.

parole.significato: A neume denoting a set of three tones which first rise from the original tone, then fall.
parole.testo: From Latin torculus, from torqueō (“to twist, wind”).

parole.significato: A low-growing herb (Potentilla erecta, syn. Potentilla tormentilla).

parole.significato: An ancient engine for hurling missiles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tormentum.

parole.significato: acute pain in the abdomen; colic, gripes
parole.testo: From Latin tormina, ultimately from torqueō (“twist, turn”).

parole.significato: The free-swimming larva of various hemichordates, such as in Balanoglossus.
parole.testo: From Latin tornare (“to turn”).

parole.significato: Cylindrical with alternate swellings and contractions; having the surface covered with rounded prominences; having the…
parole.testo: From Latin torosus (“full of muscle, brawny, fleshy”). See torus.

parole.significato: stupefying; dull; torpid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin torpēdinōsus, from torpēdō + -ōsus.

parole.significato: An electric ray of the genus Torpedo.
parole.testo: * Borrowed from Latin torpēdō (“a torpedo fish; numbness, torpidity, electric ray”), from torpeō (“to be stiff, numb, torpid; to be astounded; to be inactive”) + -ēdō (noun suffix), from Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“stiff”). parole.significato: Having no motion or activity; benumbed; torpid.
parole.testo: From Latin torpens, present participle of torpere (“to be numb”).

parole.significato: Becoming torpid or numb.
parole.testo: From Latin torpescens.

parole.significato: unmoving
parole.testo: From Latin torpidus (“tired, numb”).

parole.significato: To make torpid; to benumb, to paralyse.
parole.testo: From Latin torpere (“to be torpid”) + -fy.

parole.significato: A state of being inactive or stuporous.
parole.testo: From Latin torpor (“numbness”), from torpeō (“to be numb”).

parole.significato: A rotational or twisting effect of a force; a moment of force, defined for measurement purposes as an equivalent straig…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin torqueō (“to twist”).

parole.significato: Synonym of torque (“collar or necklace of twisted metal”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin torquēs.

parole.significato: Drying or roasting; especially an anaerobic heat treatment to make wood waterproof.
parole.testo: Latin torrefaciō.

parole.significato: To subject to intense heat; to parch, to roast.

parole.significato: Very hot and dry.

parole.significato: Twisted, winding, contorted.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tortilis, from the participle stem of torqueō (“twist, turn”).

parole.significato: Twisted; wreathed.

parole.significato: Of, caused by, or causing trauma.
parole.testo: From the Latin traumaticus, from the Ancient Greek τραυματικός (traumatikós), from τραῦμα (traûma). By surface analysis, trauma + -tic.

parole.significato: A medicine for wounds; a vulnerary.
parole.testo: From the Latin [medicāmentum] traumaticum, from traumaticus.

parole.significato: Used for forming names of large numbers as the third in the sequence in the Conway–Guy system.
parole.testo: From a form of Latin trēs (“three”) used in trēdecim (“thirteen”).

parole.significato: A truce.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin treuga, from Gothic 𐍄𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌲𐍅𐌰 (triggwa, “treaty, covenant”), from Proto-Germanic *trewwō (“fidelity; pledge”). More at true, truce.

parole.significato: A period of thirteen years.
parole.testo: Latin trēdecennium + English -al or Latin trēdecim + English -ennial

parole.significato: Manna from the cocoons of the insects Larinus maculatus and Larinus nidificans.
parole.testo: From New Latin trehāla, from Turkish tıgala, from Classical Persian تیغال (tīġāl, “a kind of manna”).

parole.significato: Any fungus of the genus Tremella.
parole.testo: From the genus name. Derived from Latin tremulus, from the verb tremere (“to tremble”).

parole.significato: Resembling or characteristic of jelly.
parole.testo: From Latin tremulus (“shaking; trembling; quivering”) + -ose. See also English tremulous.

parole.significato: Synonym of tremendous.
parole.testo: From Latin tremendus. Doublet of tremendous.

parole.significato: Trembling, tremulous.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin tremulāns (“trembling, shaking”), ultimately from Latin tremēre (“to tremble, shake”).

parole.significato: A trembling, quivering.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin tremulātus (past participle of tremulāre) + -ion.

parole.significato: Trembling, quivering, or shaking.
parole.testo: From Latin tremulus, from tremō (“to tremble, shake”) + -ulus. Doublet of tremor and tremble. By surface analysis, tremulate + -ous.

parole.significato: A set of 30 requiem masses, said once a day for a month or all in one day.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin trentāle directly or via Old French trentel, from the neuter substantive of *Vulgar Latin trenta + -ālis (“-al: forming adjectives”), from Latin trīgintā (“thirty”).

parole.significato: The practice of drilling a hole in the skull as a physical, mental, or spiritual treatment.
parole.testo: From New Latin trepanatio, formed from French trépan (“a drill”), itself from Latin trepanum, ultimately from Ancient Greek τρύπανον (trúpanon, “an auger, a drill”).

parole.significato: Timid, timorous, fearful.
parole.testo: From Latin trepidus (“anxious”).

parole.significato: Trembling with fear or emotion.
parole.testo: From Latin trepidantem.

parole.significato: Anxiety over the uncertain future or possible ill-occurrence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trepidātiō, from trepidō (“be agitated”).

parole.significato: Three.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Latin tri- (“three”) and Ancient Greek τρι- (tri-, “three”).

parole.significato: The three names borne by free male Roman citizens, consisting of the praenomen, nomen, and cognomen.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tria nōmina, from tria (neuter of trēs (“three”)) + nōmina (plural of nōmen (“name”)), literally “three names”.

parole.significato: A grouping of three.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Latin triad-, stem of trias (“three, triad”), from Ancient Greek τριάς (triás). By surface analysis, tri- + -ad. parole.significato: Characterized by having three (usually equivalent) components.
parole.testo: From Latin tri- (stem of trēs (“three”)) + -al, on the pattern of dual.

parole.significato: To locate by means of triangulation.
parole.testo: From Latin triangulum + -ate or Medieval Latin *triangulāt-, the past participial stem of *triangulō. Compare French trianguler.

parole.significato: Synonym of triangular.
parole.testo: From Latin triangulātus. By surface analysis, tri- + angulate.

parole.significato: A technique in which distances and directions are estimated from an accurately measured baseline and the principles of…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin triangulātiō (“triangulation”), from triangulō (“to triangulate”) + -tiō (noun-forming suffix). Triangulō is derived from triangulus (“triangular; triangle”), from trēs (“three”) + angulus (“angle; corner”). By surface analysis, triangulate + ion; cognate with French triangulatio

parole.significato: Occupying the third post or rank.
parole.testo: Latin triarii (plural), a class of Roman soldiers who formed the third rank from the front, from tres, tria (“three”).

parole.significato: Relating to tribadism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tribadicus. By surface analysis, tribade + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to tribes.
parole.testo: From Latin tribālis. By surface analysis, tribe + -al, first attested in the 1630s. parole.significato: A metrical foot consisting of three short syllables.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From the Latin tribrachys, from the Ancient Greek τρῐ́βρᾰχῠς (trĭ́brăkhŭs), from τρῐ- (trĭ-, “tri-”) + βρᾰχῠ́ς (brăkhŭ́s, “short”). Compare the French tribraque.

parole.significato: The state or office of a tribune.
parole.testo: From Latin tribūnātus, from tribūnus (“tribune, tribal leader”) + -ātus (“-ate”, forming adjectives), from tribus (“tribe”). Compare French tribunat.

parole.significato: The first office of the Roman state that was open to the plebeians, with the power to convene and preside over the Conc…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin tribūnus plēbis.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a Roman tribune.
parole.testo: From Latin tribunicius + -an.

parole.significato: Synonym of tribe.
parole.testo: From Latin tribus. Doublet of tribe.

parole.significato: A natural water stream that flows into a larger river or other body of water.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Middle English tributarie (“paying tribute”), from Latin tribūtārius, from tribūtum (“tribute”).

parole.significato: An apothecium in certain lichens, having a spherical surface marked with spiral or concentric ridges and furrows.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin trica, coined by Erik Acharius in his 1803 work Methodus qua omnes detectos Lichenes. Perhaps connected to Latin trīcae, although the semantic relationship is unclear.

parole.significato: Having three tails.
parole.testo: From tri- + caudal, from Latin cauda (“tail”).

parole.significato: The highest rank and pay grade for prefectures in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin trīcēnārius, equivalent to tricenary + -an.

parole.significato: Of or related to the number thirty.
parole.testo: From Latin trīcēnārius, from trīcēnus (“thirty each”) + -ārius (“-ary: forming adjectives and related nouns”).

parole.significato: Synonym of trental, a set of 30 requiem masses.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin trīcēnārium, from Latin trīcēnārius + -ium.

parole.significato: Synonym of trental, set of 30 requiem masses, the payment for such services.
parole.testo: From mistaken use of Medieval Latin trīcennāle, neuter substantive of Latin trīcennālis (“tricennial”), from trīcennium (“30-year period”) + -ālis (“-al: forming adjectives”), from trīcennis (“30-year”) + -ium (“-ium: forming abstract nouns”), from trīciēs (“30 times”) + annus (“year”) + -is (“formi

parole.significato: The festival and religious rituals celebrating a Roman emperor's 30th year of rule.
parole.testo: From Latin trīcennālia, from trīcennium (“30-year period”) + -ālia (“-alia: forming the names of festivals”), from trīcennis (“30-year”) + -ium (“forming abstract nouns”), from trīciēs (“thirty each”) + annus (“year”) + -is (“forming compound adjectives”). Equivalent to tricennium + -alia.

parole.significato: Of, related to, lasting, or occurring once every thirty years.
parole.testo: From Latin trīcennium (“30-year period”) + -al, from trīcennis (“30-year”) + -ium, from trīciēs (“30 times”) + annus (“year”) + -is. Compare Latin tricennalis. Equivalent to tri- + decennial. Doublet of tricennal.

parole.significato: A period of thirty years.
parole.testo: From Latin trīcennium, from trīcennis (“30-year”) + -ium, from trīciēs (“30 times”) + annus (“year”) + -is (“forming compound adjectives”). Equivalent to tricennial + -ium.

parole.significato: Any muscle having three heads.
parole.testo: From Latin triceps (“triple-headed”), from trēs (“three”) + caput (“head”). See there for more details.

parole.significato: Any of several parasitic roundworms, of the genus Trichinella, that infect the intestines and cause trichinosis
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek τρίχινος (tríkhinos, “of hair”), from θρίξ (thríx, “hair”).

parole.significato: A disease characterized by headache, chills, fever, and soreness of muscles, caused by the presence of nematodes of gen…
parole.testo: From New Latin trichinōsis. By surface analysis, trichina + -osis.

parole.significato: Ingrown eyelash; trichiasis.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek τρίχωμα (tríkhōma), from θρίξ (thríx, “hair”) + -μα (-ma). Doublet of trichome.

parole.significato: The belief that three nails were used in the crucifixion of Jesus Christ.
parole.testo: From tri- + Latin clavus (“nail”) + -ian + -ism, coined by George Stanley Faber in 1838.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or using a triclinium, or to the ancient mode of reclining while eating.
parole.testo: From Latin tricliniaris. See triclinium.

parole.significato: A couch for reclining at mealtimes, extending round three sides of a table, and usually in three parts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trīclīnium, from Ancient Greek τρικλίνιον (triklínion).

parole.significato: A "rising" tricolon, its parts increasing in magnitude or intensity towards a climax on the third part
parole.testo: From tricolon (“a rhetorical device”) and Latin crēscēns (“increasing, growing, rising”).

parole.significato: A "diminishing" tricolon, its parts decreasing in magnitude or intensity
parole.testo: From tricolon (“a rhetorical device”) and Latin dīminuēns (“decreasing, diminishing”).

parole.significato: A three-cornered hat, with the brim turned up.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tricornis (“three-horned; three-pronged”). By surface analysis, tri- + corn(er). Compare French tricorne (“three-cornered hat”). Doublet of tricorne.

parole.significato: A three-pronged spear somewhat resembling a pitchfork.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Latin tridēns, from tri- (“three”) + dēns (“tooth”).

parole.significato: Relating to Trent, Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin Tridentīnus (“pertaining to Trent”).

parole.significato: Lasting three days.
parole.testo: From Latin triduanus, from triduum (“space of three days”).

parole.significato: A period of three days (especially in Roman Catholic liturgy).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trīduum, from trēs (“three”) + diēs (“day”).

parole.significato: Happening every three years.
parole.testo: From Latin triennium (“three-year period”), from tres (“three”) + annus (“year”). By surface analysis, tri- + -ennial.

parole.significato: A period of three years.
parole.testo: From Latin triennium, from triennis (“3-year”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: A bronze coin minted during the Roman Republic valued at 4 unciae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin triēns.

parole.significato: The captain of a trireme.
parole.testo: From Latin trierarchus.

parole.significato: Triennial: occurring once in three years.
parole.testo: From Latin trietericus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Facing three ways; arranged in three vertical ranks, like the leaves of veratrum.
parole.testo: From Latin trifarius (“of three sorts or ways, threefold”). Compare bifarious.

parole.significato: Divided into three lobes.
parole.testo: From Latin trifidus, from tri- (“three”) + -fidus, form of findere (“to split”).

parole.significato: Bifid, divided into two main parts.
parole.testo: From Latin trifidus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, trifid + -ate.

parole.significato: Having or comprising three leaves, or (loosely) trifoliolate (with three leaflets) or having leaves with three parts, a…
parole.testo: tri- (“three”) + Latin foliātus (“leaved”) Doublet of tréflé.

parole.significato: Melilot; sweet clover
parole.testo: From Latin trifolium. See trifoliate, trefoil.

parole.significato: The gallery of arches above the side-aisle vaulting in the nave of a church.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin triforium, from tria (“three”) + for (“opening”) + -ium.

parole.significato: Having three different forms
parole.testo: From Latin trifōrmis.

parole.significato: The state of being triform, or having three different shapes.
parole.testo: From triform + -ity, from Latin triformitas.

parole.significato: Forked, with three tines or points.
parole.testo: From Latin trifurcus, from tri- (“three”) + furca (“fork”).

parole.significato: A three-horse chariot used by the Ancient Romans.
parole.testo: From Latin triga, a contraction of ter or tri- (“thrice”) + iuga (“yoked”).

parole.significato: born three together; being one of three born at the same birth
parole.testo: From Latin trigeminus (“born three together”), from tri- + geminus (“twin”). Compare tergeminous.

parole.significato: Thirtieth.
parole.testo: From Latin trigesimus (“thirtieth”) + -al (“forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: A paper size, (3.75"–5" × 2.5"–3.125"), one thirty-second of a standard uncut flat sheet.
parole.testo: From Latin ablatives of trīgēsimus (“thirtieth”) and secundus (“second”).

parole.significato: A trental (various senses)
parole.testo: Latin trigintate, from Latin triginta thirty.

parole.significato: Synonym of tricennial, once every thirty years.
parole.testo: From Latin triginta (“thirty”) + -ennial, combining adjectival form of annus (“year”). Compare the actual Latin term tricennium.

parole.significato: 10⁹³.
parole.testo: From Latin trīgintā (“thirty”) + -illion.

parole.significato: Having three angles and three sides, triangular.
parole.testo: From Latin trigōnālis (“triangular”), equivalent to trigon + -al.

parole.significato: The branch of mathematics that deals with the relationships between the sides and angles of (in particular) right-angle…
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From 1610s, from New Latin trigōnometria, from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (trígōnon, “triangle”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”), equivalent to trigono- + -metry.

parole.significato: trigonal; triangular
parole.testo: Latin trigonus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: trijugate.
parole.testo: From Latin trijugus (“threefold”), from tri- + jugum (“a yoke”).

parole.significato: Having three sides
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin trilaterālis or from tri- + lateral.

parole.significato: A set of three connected works—usually dramas, literary pieces, films, or musical compositions—all related by theme, ch…
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes Learned borrowing from Latin trilogia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τριλογία (trilogía, “trilogy”). Morphologically from tri- + -logy.

parole.significato: A nouveau riche.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Trimalchiō, a wealthy freedman in the 1st century CE Roman work of fiction Satyricon.

parole.significato: A silver coin worth three cents, minted in the US from 1851 to 1873.
parole.testo: From Latin trēs (“three”), likely by analogy with dime.

parole.significato: trimellitic acid
parole.testo: From tri- + mellis (“honey”), genitive of Latin mel.

parole.significato: Having, or consisting of, three members.
parole.testo: Latin trimembris (“triple-membered”). See tri- and member.

parole.significato: The 3,000th anniversary of an event or happening.
parole.testo: From Latin trimillennialis, from tri- + mill- (“thousand”) + Latin enni(us) (“year”) + -al.

parole.significato: Having three parts; triple.
parole.testo: From the Medieval Latin trīnālis.

parole.significato: A trinary star.
parole.testo: From Late Latin trīnārius (“consisting of three”), from Latin trīni (“triple, three each”) + -ārius.

parole.significato: Having three ribs or nerves extending unbranched from the base to the apex.
parole.testo: From Latin trinervatus, from tri- + nervus (“nerve”).

parole.significato: Relating to a trinity or set of three, especially the Holy Trinity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trīnitārius.

parole.significato: trinkum-trankum
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from trinket + Latin -um.

parole.significato: A trinket.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from a humorous reduplication of trinket with Latin -um.

parole.significato: Lasting for three nights.
parole.testo: from Latin trinoctialis (“for three nights”), from tri- + nox, noctis (“night”).

parole.significato: A threefold tax in Anglo-Saxon times, by which subjects of the king were required to repair bridges and roads (bridge-b…
parole.testo: Latin [Term?] (literally “three-knotted obligation”)

parole.significato: trinomial
parole.testo: From tri- + oblique stem of Latin nōmen, nōminis + -al.

parole.significato: Mean; worthless.
parole.testo: From Late Latin triobolaris, from Latin triobolus (“a coin worth three oboli”), from Ancient Greek τρῐώβολον (trĭṓbolon). Literally, "having the value of three oboli".

parole.significato: The seven principal stars in the constellation Ursa Major
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin triōnēs, plural of triō; compare septentrion.

parole.significato: In three parts.
parole.testo: From Latin tripartītus.

parole.significato: Having three feet.
parole.testo: From Latin tripedalis, from tri- + pes, pedis (“a foot”). By surface analysis, tri- + -pedal.

parole.significato: Made up of three related elements, often matching

parole.significato: Having three parts; triple or threefold.
parole.testo: From Latin triplex. Analyzable as tri- + -plex.

parole.significato: Made thrice as much; threefold; tripled.
parole.testo: Early 15th century. From Latin triplicātus, perfect passive participle of triplicō (“to triple”) (see -ate), from tri- (“three”) + plicō (“to fold”). By surface analysis, tri- (“three”) + plicate, analogous with duplicate.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being triple or threefold; trebleness.
parole.testo: From triplic(ate) + -ity, from Latin triplicitas, from Latin triplex, triplicis (“threefold”). Compare French triplicité. See triplicate.

parole.significato: A three-legged stand or mount.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Tripoli
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Tripolitānus, from Tripolis + -itānus. By surface analysis, Tripolis + -itan.

parole.significato: trituration
parole.testo: From New Latin trīpsis, from Ancient Greek τρῖψις (trîpsis, “rubbing, friction”), from τρῑ́βω (trī́bō, “I rub”).

parole.significato: A noun which has three cases.
parole.testo: From Latin triptōtum, from Ancient Greek τρίπτωτος (tríptōtos), from τρι- (tri-, “three”) + πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”) + -τος (-tos, verbal adjective–forming suffix), influenced by the verbal noun πτῶσις (ptôsis, “inflection”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to dancing.
parole.testo: Latin tripudium (“a measured stamping, a leaping, a solemn religious dance”).

parole.significato: To dance with joy or exultation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tripudiō.

parole.significato: The act of dancing.
parole.testo: Latin tripudiatio.

parole.significato: A solemn religious dance of the Ancient Romans, performed in triple time.
parole.testo: From Latin tripudium.

parole.significato: A vessel (usually a pot or cauldron) resting on three legs, often given as an ornament, a prize, or as an offering at a…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin tripūs, from Ancient Greek τρίπους (trípous); doublet of tripod, tripos, and teapoy. In the sense associated with Cambridge University, the Tripus is named after the three-legged stool on which he sat during the degree-awarding ceremony.

parole.significato: A shape formed of three vesicae piscium, sometimes with an additional circle, a symbol of things and persons that are t…
parole.testo: From Latin triquētrus (“having three corners”).

parole.significato: Triangular; especially (in natural sciences), having a triangular cross-section.
parole.testo: From Latin triquetrus.

parole.significato: The triquetral bone
parole.testo: From Latin triquetrus.

parole.significato: A galley with three banks of oars, one above the other, used mainly as a warship.
parole.testo: From Latin trirēmis, from tri- + rēmus (“oar”).

parole.significato: A liturgical prayer that runs “Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us” in English, typically sung befor…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin trisagion, from Byzantine Greek τρισάγιον (triságion), from τρίς (trís, “thrice”) + ἅγιον (hágion, “holy”).

parole.significato: The inability to open the mouth normally, typically as a result of disease.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin trismus, from Ancient Greek τρισμός (trismós, “a grinding, rasping, scream”), from Ancient Greek τρίζω (trízō).

parole.significato: To sadden.
parole.testo: From Latin tristitia (“sadness”), from tristis (“sad”).

parole.significato: Something having three forks or prongs, especially a trident.
parole.testo: Latin trisulcus; tri- (“three”) + sulcus (“a furrow”).

parole.significato: used so many times that it is commonplace, or no longer interesting or effective; worn out, hackneyed.
parole.testo: From Latin trītus (“worn out”), perfect passive participle of terō (“to wear away, wear out”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek musical theory, the lower-pitched of the two movable notes in the farther tetrachord on a lyre, pitche…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin tritē, from Ancient Greek τρίτη (trítē, literally “third [string]”).

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Triticum (wheat and related cereals).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin trīticum.

parole.significato: A radioactive isotope of the element hydrogen (symbol T, ³H or 31H) having one proton and two neutrons.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin tritium, from Ancient Greek τρίτος (trítos, “third”) + New Latin -ium. By surface analysis, trit- + -ium.

parole.significato: An interval of three whole tones.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin tritonus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τρίτονος (trítonos). By surface analysis, tri- + tone.

parole.significato: An amphiploid cereal derived from the cross between a South American wild barley (Hordeum chilense) and durum wheat.
parole.testo: From the genus name, New Latin Tritordeum, apparently a blend of Triticum (“wheat”) + Hordeum (“barley”).

parole.significato: A vessel for separating liquids of different densities.
parole.testo: Compare Latin terere, tritum (“to rub”).

parole.significato: An embryonic insect which has twice cast its skin before hatching from the egg, such as some mites of Myobia
parole.testo: From trit- + Latin ovum (“egg”).

parole.significato: To grind to a fine powder, to pulverize.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trītūrāre (“thresh”).

parole.significato: A rubbing or grinding; trituration.
parole.testo: From Latin tritura.

parole.significato: To celebrate victory with pomp; to rejoice over success; to exult in an advantage gained; to exhibit exultation.
parole.testo: From Latin triumphō.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or being a triumph.
parole.testo: From Middle English triumphal, triumphall, tryumphal, from Latin triumphālis and Old French trionfal, triumphal.

parole.significato: One granted a triumph.
parole.testo: From Latin triumphātor. Compare Middle English tryumphatour.

parole.significato: One member of a triumvirate.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin triumvir. Compare Middle English triumvir (“committee of three magistrates”).

parole.significato: Of or belonging to the triumviri or the triumvirate.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin triumvirālis. By surface analysis, triumvir + -al.
