parole.significato: A female Tyrannosaurus rex.
parole.testo: By replacing rex (Latin rēx (“king”)) of Tyrannosaurus rex with Latin rēgīna (“queen”).

parole.significato: A beginner; a novice.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin tyro, and from its etymon Latin tīrō (“beginner, novice; young apprentice; (Roman military) recruit”); further etymology unknown, possibly from an unattested Etruscan word.

parole.significato: The condition of being a tyro or beginner; apprenticeship.
parole.testo: From Latin tirocinium (“first service, trial”). Doublet of tirocinium.

parole.significato: diazobenzol
parole.testo: From New Latin tyrotoxicon, from tyro- + Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón).

parole.significato: Synonym of Tyrrhenian.
parole.testo: From Latin Tyrrhēnus, from Ancient Greek Τυρρηνός (Turrhēnós).

parole.significato: Fruitful.
parole.testo: Formed from Latin uber (“full, fruitful, fertile, abundant, plentiful, copious, productive”) and the suffix -ous.

parole.significato: To find and specify the location of (someone or something); to locate.
parole.testo: Probably a back-formation from ubication (“condition or fact of being in, or occupying, a certain place or position”) on the basis of -ate (suffix forming verbs). Ubication is borrowed from New Latin ubicātiō (“location”) (compare the inflected forms ubicātiōnis, ubicātiōnī, etc.), from Latin ubicāt

parole.significato: The condition or fact of being in, or occupying, a certain place or position; whereness, ubiety; also, a location.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ubicātiō (“location”) (whence Portuguese ubicação and Spanish ubicación; compare the inflected forms ubicātiōnis, ubicātiōnī, etc.) + -ion. Ubicātiō is derived from Latin ubicātus (“located”) + -iō (suffix forming abstract nouns); while ubicātus is a past participial form of

parole.significato: whereabouts, location
parole.testo: From Latin ubi (“where”) + -icity.

parole.significato: The state of existing in a specific point in space, thereness.
parole.testo: From Latin ubi (“where”) + -iety.

parole.significato: Ubiquitous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ubīquitārius.

parole.significato: A microorganism that can be found in most types of environment.
parole.testo: From Latin ubique (“everywhere”) + -er.

parole.significato: The belief that the human nature of Christ is omnipresent.
parole.testo: From Latin ubique (“everywhere”) + -ism.

parole.significato: Widespread; ubiquitous.
parole.testo: From Latin ubique (“everywhere”) + -ist.

parole.significato: Being everywhere at once: omnipresent.
parole.testo: From ubiquity + -ous, from Medieval Latin ubīquitās, from Latin ubīque (“everywhere”), from ubī̆ (“where”) + -que (“each, ever”). Compare ubiety.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being, or appearing to be, everywhere at once; actual or perceived omnipresence.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ubīquitās, from Latin ubīque.

parole.significato: A neighbor whose house is on fire or has burned down.
parole.testo: From Latin Ūcalegōn, from Ancient Greek Οὐκαλέγων (Oukalégōn). He was one of the Elders of Troy, whose house was set on fire by the Achaeans when they sacked the city. He is one of Priam's friends in the Iliad (3.148) and the destruction of his house is referred to in the Aeneid (2.312).

parole.significato: A rain gauge.
parole.testo: Formed from Latin ūdus (“wet”) + -meter.

parole.significato: Relating to udometry.
parole.testo: From Latin ūdus (“wet”) + -metric.

parole.significato: rainfall measurement
parole.testo: From Latin ūdus (“wet”) + -metry.

parole.significato: Having an ulcus, a rounded pore-like aperture, at one or both poles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ulcerātus.

parole.significato: To cause an ulcer to develop.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ulcerō.

parole.significato: A rounded, pore-like aperture at either pole of a pollen grain.
parole.testo: From Latin ulcus (“sore”). Doublet of ulcer.

parole.significato: A small ulcer.
parole.testo: From Latin ulcusculum; compare corpuscle.

parole.significato: A little ulcer.
parole.testo: From Latin ulcusculum, diminutive of ulcus.

parole.significato: Slimy.
parole.testo: From Latin ūlīginōsus (“swampy”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to ulmin; designating an acid obtained from ulmin.
parole.testo: Formed from the root of Latin ulmus (“an elm”), with the suffix -ic: compare French ulmique.

parole.significato: A brown amorphous substance found in decaying vegetation.
parole.testo: Latin ulmus (“elm”), + -in: compare French ulmine.

parole.significato: The bone of the forearm that extends from the elbow to the wrist on the side opposite to the thumb, corresponding to th…
parole.testo: From Latin ulna (“elbow”). Doublet of ell.

parole.significato: ulna
parole.testo: From English ulna, from Latin ulna.

parole.significato: Situated beyond, or on the farther side.
parole.testo: From Latin ulterior (“further, more distant”), from ulter (“that is beyond”) + -ior (“more”).

parole.significato: The final syllable of a word.
parole.testo: From the Latin feminine of ultimus (“last”).

parole.significato: legal philosophy under which penal redress to crime should only be used as a measure of last resort
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A place beyond the borders of the known world.
parole.testo: From Latin ultima Thūlē, nominative feminine singular of ultimus (“furthest”) + Thule, from mediaeval geography; originally from the Ancient Greek Θούλη (Thoúlē), a (possibly mythical) island to the north of Britain.

parole.significato: Final; last in a series.
parole.testo: * From Medieval Latin ultimātus (“furthest, last”), perfect passive participle of ultimō (“to come to an end”) (see -ate (1,2 and 3)), from ultimus (“last, final”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See ultra-. * (ultimate frisbee): The sport was renamed to avoid the use of the Frisbee trademark.

parole.significato: A final statement of terms or conditions made by one party to another, especially one that expresses a threat of repris…
parole.testo: From Latin ultimatus (“late, last final”), from Latin ultimus (“extreme, last, furthest, farthest, final”).

parole.significato: The final stage or consequence; finality.
parole.testo: Latin ultimatus extremity, from Latin ultimus the last.

parole.significato: On the last day (of a specified month).
parole.testo: First attested in 1582; from Latin ultimō (elliptically for ultimō diē or ultimō mēnse), masculine ablative singular form of ultimus (“last”); cognate with Dutch ultimo, the German ultimo, the Swedish ultimo, etc.

parole.significato: A last resort.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: The process whereby the estate of a deceased person with no will or traceable blood relatives goes to the Crown.
parole.testo: From Latin ultimus haeres (“ultimate heir”).

parole.significato: A soil that has a weathered clay horizon as a result of argilluviation.
parole.testo: From Latin ultimus (“final”) and solum (“soil”).

parole.significato: Extreme; far beyond the norm; fanatical; uncompromising.
parole.testo: From Latin ultra.

parole.significato: beyond the legal power or authority of a person or body
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ultra vires (“beyond the power”).

parole.significato: Greater than normal quantity or importance, as in ultrasecret.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ultrā (“beyond”).

parole.significato: Beyond the sea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ultrāmarīnus, from Latin ultrā (“beyond”) + marīnus (“of or relating to the sea, marine”). By surface analysis, ultra + marine. Noun sense 1 (“pigment”) refers to the fact that lapis lazuli was obtained from foreign countries and hence “beyond the sea”.

parole.significato: extraordinary; abnormal
parole.testo: From Latin ultrāmundānus.

parole.significato: The quality of being ultroneous.
parole.testo: From ultrone(ous) + -ity, from Latin ultroneitas.

parole.significato: spontaneous; voluntary
parole.testo: From Latin ultroneus, from ultro (“to the further side, on his part, of one's own accord”). See ultra-.

parole.significato: Howling; wailing.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin ululāns, present participle of ululō (“to howl”).

parole.significato: To howl loudly or prolongedly in lamentation or joy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ululō, ululātus, of imitative origin. Cognate with Spanish aullar (“to howl”) and ulular (“to hoot”), and French ululer (“to howl”).

parole.significato: The act of ululating; a long, loud, wavering cry or howl.
parole.testo: ] Borrowed from Latin ululātiō, from ululō (“to howl, shriek, yell”) (from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root) + -ātiō (suffix forming nouns relating to some action or the result of an action) (from Proto-Indo-European *-tis (suffix forming abstract or action nouns from verb roots)).

parole.significato: Being or relating to a ululation.
parole.testo: From ululation + -ory, from Latin ululō (“to howl, shriek, yell”).

parole.significato: A flat-topped or rounded flower-cluster (= inflorescence) in which the individual flower stalks arise from the same poi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbella (“umbrella”). Compare umbrella, composed of the same etymological elements but formed independently.

parole.significato: umbellar
parole.testo: From Latin umbella (“a sunshade, parasol, umbrella”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Having a navel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin umbilicātus, from umbilicus (“navel”) + -ātus. By surface analysis, umbilic- + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A small, navel-shaped depression, or dimple, at the centre of a rounded body.
parole.testo: From Latin umbilicatus. By surface analysis, umbilic- + -ation.

parole.significato: A navel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbilīcus (“navel”).

parole.significato: The boss of a shield, at or near the middle and usually projecting, sometimes in a sharp spike.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbō (“a shield boss”). Doublet of umbone.

parole.significato: Having an umbo
parole.testo: From New Latin umbōnātus, from Latin umbō.

parole.significato: The fully shaded inner region of a shadow cast by an opaque object.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbra (“shadow”). Doublet of umber.

parole.significato: On a shadow in the shape of a right triangle, the length of the shadow's edge adjacent to a measured angle.
parole.testo: First attested in Modern English in 1688, although the phrase was also used in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) in his Treatise on the Astrolabe; Latin: umbra (“shadow”) + rēcta (feminine nominative singular of rēctus, “straight”) = “straight shadow”; compare umbra versa.

parole.significato: On a shadow in the shape of a right triangle, the length of the shadow's edge opposite to a measured angle.
parole.testo: First attested in Modern English in 1688, although the phrase was also used in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) in his Treatise on the Astrolabe; Latin: umbra (“shadow”) + versa (feminine nominative singular of versus, “turned”) = “turned shadow”; compare umbra recta.

parole.significato: Bearing something like an open umbrella.
parole.testo: From Latin umbraculum (“umbrella”), diminutive of umbra (“shade”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Having the form of something that offers shade, such as a treetop or especially an umbrella.
parole.testo: From Latin umbraculum (“anything that furnishes shade, a bower, umbrella”), diminutive of umbra (“a shade”) + -form.

parole.significato: Any umbrella-shaped appendage, such as the cap borne on the seta of Marchantia.
parole.testo: From Latin umbrāculum.

parole.significato: Magical control over shadows.
parole.testo: From Latin umbra (“shadow”) + -mancy (“divination of”), from Latin -mantia, ultimately from Ancient Greek μᾰντείᾱ (mănteíā, “divination”).

parole.significato: To shade; to shadow.
parole.testo: Latin umbratus, past participle of umbrare (“to shade”), from umbra (“a shade”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the shade or darkness; shadowy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbraticus, from umbra (“shade”). See umbrage.

parole.significato: Shady, shadowy.
parole.testo: From Latin umbratilis, from umbra.

parole.significato: Shadowy; faint; secluded; indistinct; vague; latent; indeterminate.
parole.testo: From Latin umbra (“shade, shadow”).

parole.significato: An Italic tribe of ancient Italy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbrī. Also called Ombrii in some Roman sources. Many Roman writers thought the Umbri to be Celtic; Cornelius Bocchus wrote that they descended from an ancient Gaulish tribe. Plutarch wrote that the name might be a different way of writing the name of the Celtic tribe Ambrones, w

parole.significato: providing or making shade; umbrageous.
parole.testo: From Latin umbrifer, from umbra (“a shade”) + ferre (“to bear”).

parole.significato: A kind of soil with a dark topsoil and having organic matter accumulated within the mineral surface soil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbra (“shadow”) + -sol

parole.significato: Shady; umbrageous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbrōsus, from umbra (“a shade”).

parole.significato: Shade, shadiness.
parole.testo: From umbrose + -ity, or borrowed from Latin umbrōsitās.

parole.significato: Used for the digit one to form systematic element names of elements whose existence has been predicted, and which have…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ūnus.

parole.significato: A churchman who holds only one benefice.
parole.testo: Latin unus one.

parole.significato: Based on unanimity, assent or agreement.
parole.testo: From Latin ūnanimus (“of one mind”), from ūnus (“one”) + animus (“mind”). Displaced native Old English ānmōd (literally “one-minded”).

parole.significato: Consisting of or involving a single element or component.
parole.testo: From Latin ūnus (“one”) + -ary, on the pattern of binary, ternary, etc.

parole.significato: The Roman ounce, 1/12 of a Roman pound.
parole.testo: From Latin ū̆ncia (“various Roman units”). Doublet of ounce, inch, onça, onza, oka, ouguiya, and awqiyyah.

parole.significato: Of or relating to an ounce, or an inch, especially to letters printed an inch high.
parole.testo: Attested 1650, from Latin ū̆ncia (“a twelfth part, ounce, inch”) + -al.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a majuscule style of writing with unjoined, rounded letters, originally used in the 4th–9th centuries.
parole.testo: Attested 1712, from Late Latin unciales (“uncials”), unciales litterae (“uncial letters”) (Jerome), plural of uncialis (“pertaining to one twelfth part, ounce, or inch”), from uncia (“one twelfth part, ounce, inch”). The literal meaning is unclear: some references indicate "inch-high letters", but s

parole.significato: Of the shape of a hook; hook-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin uncus (“hook”) + -form.

parole.significato: Hooked at the end.
parole.testo: From Latin uncīnātus, from uncīnus (“hook, barb”).

parole.significato: The hamate bone.
parole.testo: From New Latin [Term?], from Latin uncinatus (“hooked”). Compare uncinate.

parole.significato: A cloud species which consists of fine hair-like strands, with hooked terminations. Associated only with cirrus formati…
parole.testo: From Latin uncīnus (“hook”).

parole.significato: Curved or hook-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin uncus.

parole.significato: To anoint, especially a monarch or other patriarchal leader.
parole.testo: First appears in Middle English circa 1425, derived from Latin unctus (“anointed”) and related terms. Ayurvedic sense is one of several competing translations of Sanskrit snehana.

parole.significato: An ointment or salve.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin unctiō.

parole.significato: Having the nature or properties of an unguent or ointment; greasy, oily.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English unctuous [and other forms], borrowed from Medieval Latin ūnctuōsus (“greasy, oily, unctuous”), from Latin ūnctum (“ointment; rich banquet; rich savoury dish”) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of; overly’ forming adjectives from nouns). Ūnctum is a noun use of the perfect passiv

parole.significato: Not cultivated; rude; illiterate.
parole.testo: From un- (“not”) + Latin cultus, past participle of colere (“to cultivate”). Compare incult.

parole.significato: A hook or claw.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin uncus (“hook”).

parole.significato: An organ stop similar to the voix céleste, but typically using a dulciana or a softer-scale string (or even flutes).
parole.testo: From Latin unda maris (literally “sea wave”).

parole.significato: undated; rising and falling in waves
parole.testo: From Latin undātus.

parole.significato: Rising and falling in waves toward the margin, as a leaf; waved.
parole.testo: From Latin undatus, past participle of undare (“to rise in waves, to wave, to undulate”).

parole.significato: eleven
parole.testo: From Latin ūndecim.

parole.significato: A group of eleven musicians; a piece of music written for such a group
parole.testo: From decet on the model of Latin undecim (“eleven”).

parole.significato: Having eleven joints.
parole.testo: From Latin undecim + articulate.

parole.significato: Any member of a group of eleven officials.
parole.testo: From Latin ūndecimvir.

parole.significato: A group of eleven people, especially (politics) a council of eleven men sharing office or power and particularly (histo…
parole.testo: From Latin ūndecimvirātus, from ūndecimvirī (“undecimvirs”) + -ātus (“-ate”).

parole.significato: In base (radix) eleven.
parole.testo: From Latin ūndēnī (“eleven each, eleventh”) + -ary, from ūndēnus.

parole.significato: In secret; secretly, privately.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin sub rosā.

parole.significato: Based upon the number nineteen.
parole.testo: From Latin ūndēvīcēsimus (“nineteenth”) + -al.

parole.significato: To cause to move in a wavelike motion.
parole.testo: First attested in 1664; borrowed from New Latin undulātus, the perfect passive participle of undulō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from an unattested *undula (“small wave”), diminutive of Latin unda (“wave”).

parole.significato: Wavy in appearance or form.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin undulātus (“undulated”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: An instance or act of undulating.
parole.testo: From undulate + -ion, or borrowed from Medieval Latin undulātiō; compare French ondulation.

parole.significato: That doesn't have a known or readily available explanation.
parole.testo: From un- + explainable. from explain + -able. from Latin explanō (“to flatten, spread out, make plain or clear, explain”).

parole.significato: The surgical removal of a fingernail or toenail.
parole.testo: From Latin unguis (“nail, claw, hoof”) + -ectomy.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or resembling a creature's nail, claw or hoof; unguinal.
parole.testo: From Latin unguis (“nail, claw, hoof”) + -al .

parole.significato: Any cream containing medicinal ingredients applied to the skin for therapeutic purposes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin unguentum (“ointment”), from unguō (“to smear with ointment”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“to salve, anoint”). Cognates include Old Prussian anctan, Old High German ancho (German Anke (“butter”)), Welsh ymenyn (“butter”).

parole.significato: A small bottle used to store balms or scented oils
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin unguentarium.

parole.significato: Like, or containing, an unguent.
parole.testo: Latin unguentarius.

parole.significato: ungual
parole.testo: Latin unguis (“a nail or claw”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a claw or nail; ungual.
parole.testo: Latin unguiculus, diminutive of unguis (“a nail”).

parole.significato: Having nails or claws, as distinguished from hoofs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin unguiculātus.

parole.significato: A diminutive claw or similar appendage at the end of an insect's foot.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin unguiculus.

parole.significato: Producing, having, or supporting nails or claws.
parole.testo: Latin unguis (“nail, claw”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Consisting of, or resembling, fat or oil; unctuous; oleaginous.
parole.testo: From Latin unguinosus, from unguinis, from unguen (“fat, ointment”).

parole.significato: The nail, claw, talon, or hoof of a finger, toe, or other appendage.
parole.testo: From Latin unguis (“nail, claw, hoof”). Doublet of onyx.

parole.significato: A hoof, claw, or talon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ungula (“claw, hoof”), from unguis (“nail, claw, hoof”).

parole.significato: Having hooves.
parole.testo: From Late Latin ungulātus, from Latin ungula (“hoof”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). The noun was substantivized from the adjective through the associated taxon's name (Ungulata), see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Having hoofs of a tincture different from the body.
parole.testo: Latin ungula (“a claw”), + -ed.

parole.significato: That walks on hooves.
parole.testo: From Latin ungula (“claw, hoof”) + -grade (“means of walking”) (from Latin gradus). Compare French ongulograde.

parole.significato: one, single
parole.testo: From Latin uni-, combining form of unus (“one”).

parole.significato: A unique example or specimen of something
parole.testo: From the Latin ūnicum, the neuter nominative singular form of ūnicus (“unique”). Compare Dutch unicum, German Unicum. See unique.

parole.significato: The state of being the sole begotten.
parole.testo: From Latin unigenitus (“only-begotten”), from unus (“one”) + genitum (“to beget”).

parole.significato: Of a single type, or genus.
parole.testo: From Latin unigena, from unus (“one”) + genere, gignere (“to beget”), + -ous.

parole.significato: Done by one side only.
parole.testo: A modern creation (circa 1802), from New Latin ūnilaterālis (“one-sided”), from Latin ūnus (“one”) + laterālis (“sided, lateral”), equivalent to uni- + lateral.

parole.significato: Any of the genus Unio of freshwater mussels
parole.testo: From the genus name, Unio, from Latin ūniō (“large pearl”). Doublet of union.

parole.significato: Having a single line or series
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ūniseriātus. By surface analysis, uni- + seriate.

parole.significato: Pertaining to Unitarianism.
parole.testo: Related to New Latin ūnitārius (from Latin ūnitās (“unity”)) -an. First documented as unitaria religio, in a decree of the Diet of Lécfalva (1600). In English since 1687 By surface analysis, unitary + -ian.

parole.significato: To bring together as one.
parole.testo: From Middle English uniten, from Latin ūnītus, perfect passive participle of ūniō.

parole.significato: Union; the act of uniting, or the state of being united.
parole.testo: From Late Latin unitio, from Latin unire.

parole.significato: Of, causing, or involving unity or union.
parole.testo: From Late Latin unitīvus.

parole.significato: Having only one possible meaning.
parole.testo: From Late Latin ūnivocus + -al. By surface analysis, uni- + vocal.

parole.significato: The state or essence of being univocal.
parole.testo: From Late Latin ūnivocitās, from ūnivocus (“univocal”).

parole.significato: One over all.
parole.testo: Latin, or rather dog Latin, from uno (“one”) + ab (“from”) + alto (“height”), thus literally from one height.

parole.significato: At once, at one blast, at the same moment, contemporaneously, simultaneously.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ūnō flātū (“in one breath”, “at one blast”), ablative of time-within-which of ūnus flātus (“a single blast of wind or expulsion of breath”).

parole.significato: improbably
parole.testo: From un- + Latin probabilis (“approvable”), from probare (“to approve”). Compare probable.

parole.significato: Without the ability to reason; unreasoning.
parole.testo: From Middle English unresonable, equivalent to un- + reasonable, originally partly after Latin irratiōnābilis.

parole.significato: In an unreasonable manner.
parole.testo: From Middle English unresonably, equivalent to unreasonable + -ly, after resonably (whence reasonably) and (originally) Late Latin irratiōnābiliter.

parole.significato: Incessant; never slackening.
parole.testo: un- + remitting, from remit (in now rare sense of “diminish, abate”), from Middle English remitten, from Latin remittere (“to send, send back”). Compare Old French remettre, remetre, remitter. Not from nonexistent unremit. First attested in 1728.

parole.significato: To remove a veil from; to uncover; to reveal something hidden.
parole.testo: From Middle English *unveilen (suggested by past participle unveiled, vnueylyd (“unveiled”)). Equivalent to un- + veil. Ultimately from Latin velum (whence also English voile, English reveal, Russian вуа́ль (vuálʹ), Russian завуали́ровать (zavualírovatʹ) (compare typologically)). Also compare typolo

parole.significato: Synonym of inviolate.
parole.testo: From un- + violate (adjective), after Latin inviolātus.

parole.significato: A band of fibrous tissue extending from the bladder to the umbilicus.
parole.testo: From New Latin ūrachus, from Ancient Greek οὐραχός (ourakhós).

parole.significato: A representation of the sacred asp, symbolising supreme power in ancient Egypt.
parole.testo: From Latin uraeus, from Ancient Greek οὐραῖος (ouraîos). parole.significato: Celestial, heavenly; uranic.

parole.significato: Itchy, swollen, red areas of the skin which can appear quickly in response to an allergen or other conditions.

parole.significato: To have or produce a stinging sensation, as of nettles or urticating hair.

parole.significato: The act of beating or whipping.

parole.significato: An instrument used to measure variations in a magnetic field.

parole.significato: The capillaries that supply blood to vessels larger than 1 mm. They supply blood to the adventitia and middle tunicae.

parole.significato: Relating to the flow of fluids, such as blood, lymph, or sap, through the body of an animal or plant, or to the vessels…

parole.significato: The blood vessels or their arrangement in the body, or within an organ.

parole.significato: Vessel: Relating to blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, or both.

parole.significato: A container used by botanists to store newly-collected samples.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vāsculum (“small vessel”).

parole.significato: vastness; immensity

parole.significato: One of the great muscles upon the front of the thigh.
parole.testo: From Latin vastus (“vast, immense, enormous, huge, monstrous”). Doublet of vast.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a prophet; prophetic, oracular.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a prophet; prophetic.

parole.significato: The murder of a prophet.
parole.testo: From Latin; the first element is vātēs. Equivalent to + -cide.

parole.significato: To predict or foretell future events; to prophesy or presage.

parole.significato: Someone who vaticinates; a prophet.

parole.significato: A prediction; a vaticination.

parole.significato: A fictional prophecy that has been written after the supposedly predicted event but is presented as a genuine predictio…

parole.significato: Transport.

parole.significato: The act of carrying; conveyance; carriage.

parole.significato: Capable of growth and reproduction, but not feeling or reason (often opposed to sensible and rational).

parole.significato: lively; active; sprightly; vigorous.

parole.significato: vigorous; lively; active; energetic.

parole.significato: Vehemence.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a vehicle or vehicles, usually specifically cars and trucks; involving a vehicle.

parole.significato: The ∨ symbol used to represent the inclusive or, which is a logical connective.

parole.significato: or not; used when discussing the existence or nonexistence of a condition, circumstance, etc

parole.significato: Or the like; or similar.

parole.significato: A covering membrane or velum

parole.significato: Veil-like.

parole.significato: Articulated at the velum or soft palate.

parole.significato: The marginal membrane of certain medusae belonging to the Discophora.
parole.testo: From Latin vēlārium, from vēlum + -ārium. Doublet of veghar.

parole.significato: Having a veil; veiled.

parole.significato: A veiling; concealment; mystery.

parole.significato: A type of Roman infantryman who worked as a skirmisher.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a velum, usually the velum palatinum (soft palate, palatum molle)

parole.significato: The arrangement of veins in a leaf, wing, or similar structure.

parole.significato: The hunting of wild animals.

parole.significato: Salable; able to be bought, sold, or traded.

parole.significato: To exhibit, as though for sale; to show off.

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Venedotia or Gwynedd.

parole.significato: The act or practice of poisoning.

parole.significato: Synonym of venom.

parole.significato: Venomous; poisonous.

parole.significato: The qualities of being venerable; great age, respectability, infirmity, etc.

parole.significato: venial; pardonable

parole.significato: Indicating motion to or toward a thing.

parole.significato: A woman with offspring.

parole.significato: To replace stale or noxious air with fresh.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a ventricle or ventriculus.
parole.testo: From New Latin *ventricularis, from ventriculus (“belly, stomach, ventricle”), diminutive of venter (“belly, stomach, womb”). Equivalent to ventricle + -ar; See ventricle.

parole.significato: Somewhat distended in the middle.
parole.testo: Latin ventriculosus (“of the belly”).

parole.significato: A digestive cavity such as a gizzard or stomach.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ventriculus (“the belly”), diminutive of venter (“the belly”). Doublet of ventricle.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a ventriloquist or ventriloquism.

parole.significato: Ventriloquism.
parole.testo: From Latin ventriloquium, from venter (“stomach”) + loquī (“to speak”). By surface analysis, ventri- + -loquy.

parole.significato: abdomen, belly (especially of an animal)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin venter (“belly”), with the ending possibly changed by backformation from ventral and/or by analogy to dorsum (“back”).

parole.significato: A venule.
parole.testo: From Latin venula.

parole.significato: Sexual activity or intercourse; sex; lust, love.

parole.significato: Elegance; physical beauty.

parole.significato: The true or real cause of something.

parole.significato: veratrine

parole.significato: A word that indicates an action, event, or state of being.

parole.significato: A word game in which the players are given a set of letters and must form as many words as possible from subsets of tho…
parole.testo: From Latin verbum (“word”) + -arium.

parole.significato: Word for word; in exactly the same words as were used originally.
parole.testo: Attested in English since 1481 (therefore considered a Middle English derivation by some): from Medieval Latin verbātim (“word for word”), from Latin verbum (“word”) + -ātim (adverbial suffix).

parole.significato: Word-for-word and to the letter.
parole.testo: Latin verbātim (“word-for-word”) + et (“and”) + līterātim (“letter-for-letter”).

parole.significato: Verbena, a genus of herbaceous plants of which several species are extensively cultivated for the great beauty of their…

parole.significato: To hit; to beat; to strike

parole.significato: The act of verberating; a beating or striking.

parole.significato: A person whose mental imagery consists of words.

parole.significato: A fear of words.

parole.significato: Used to bring something to a conclusion, implying that further comment is unadvisable or unneeded.

parole.significato: Freshly green; verdant; covered with verdure, or consisting of it.

parole.significato: modest
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin verēcundus (“shy, modest”).

parole.significato: A written document in Old English law detailing the facts presented as true at a trial.
parole.testo: From Latin veredictum. Doublet of verdict.

parole.significato: To be or come very close; to border; to approach.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vergō (“to bend, turn, tend toward, incline”), from Proto-Indo-European *werg- (“to turn”), from a root *wer- (“to turn, bend”) (compare versus); strongly influenced by the above noun.

parole.significato: The metal bar with two pallets that drive the crown wheel in a verge escapement.
parole.testo: Originally just verge (from Latin virga (“staff, rod”)); it acquired the extra staff for clarity.

parole.significato: A magistrate in ancient Gaul who held the highest office in many Gallic cities, especially among the Aedui.
parole.testo: From Latin vergobretus (“chief magistrate amongst the Aedui”), from Gaulish uercobretos.

parole.significato: veridical
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin veridicus.

parole.significato: True.
parole.testo: From Latin veridicus (“truly said”), from verus (“true”) and dīcō (“to say”).

parole.significato: Synonym of verify.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vērificāt-, past participial stem of vērificō. Also an independent back-formation from verification. For its use by non-native speakers, compare Catalan, Galician, Occitan, Portuguese, and Spanish verificar and Italian verificare.

parole.significato: Serving to verify or authenticate.
parole.testo: From the past participial stem vērificāt- of Latin vērificō (in English verification) + -ory. By surface analysis, verificate + -ive.

parole.significato: Serving to verify something.
parole.testo: From the past participial stem vērificāt- of Latin vērificō (in English verification) + -ory. By surface analysis, verificate + -ory.

parole.significato: Speaking truth; truthful; corresponding to facts.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin vērācitās, semantically equivalent to Latin vērāc- (etymological inchoation of vērāx) "true" > ver + -iloquent.

parole.significato: Appearing to be true or real; probable; likely.
parole.testo: From Latin vērisimilis, prop. vērī similis (“having the appearance of truth”), from vērī (genitive of vērus (“true”)) + similis (“like, similar”); see very and similar.

parole.significato: Appearing to be verisimilar; exhibiting verisimilitude, in either a neutral or a dubious sense.
parole.testo: From Latin vērisimilitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin vērisimilitūdō, from vērī (genitive of vērus) + similitūdō, from similis + -tūdō. By surface analysis, verisimilitude + -ous.

parole.significato: Truth, particularly of a transcendent character.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēritās. Doublet of verity.

parole.significato: Relating to the vermis
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, from a supposed *vermalis, whereas Latin vermiculātus. From vermis + -al.

parole.significato: Related to worms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vermis (“worm”).

parole.significato: Any substance used to kill worms, especially parasitic intestinal worms
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”) + -cide.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of worms.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”).

parole.significato: To decorate with lines resembling the tracks of worms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vermiculatus (“inlaid in wavy lines”), past participle of vermiculor (“to be full of worms or worm-eaten”), from vermiculus (“little worm”).

parole.significato: The process of being turned into a worm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vermiculātiōnem, from vermiculor (“to be worm-eaten, to be wormy”) + -tiō (suffix forming nouns relating to actions or the results of actions) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-tis (suffix forming abstract or action nouns from verb roots)). The Latin verb is from vermis (“wo

parole.significato: A small worm or worm-like organism.
parole.testo: From Latin vermiculus, diminutive of vermis (“a worm”). See vermicular. Doublet of vermeil.

parole.significato: A hydrated silicate mineral which expands on heating; it is used in insulation and as a medium for planting.
parole.testo: From Latin vermiculus (“wormlet”), for its fibrous nature and tendency to expand into worm-like shapes when heated.

parole.significato: Containing, or full of, worms; resembling worms; wormy.
parole.testo: From Latin vermiculosus. See vermicule.

parole.significato: In the shape of a worm.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”) + -form.

parole.significato: Tending to prevent, destroy, or expel worms or vermin; anthelmintic.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“a worm”) + fugare (“to drive away”), from fugere (“to flee”). See worm, and fugitive.

parole.significato: Acting as a drug to cause the expulsion or death of intestinal worms.
parole.testo: Attested since about 1720, from Latin vermis (“worm”) + fugāre (“to cause to flee”). Compare -fuge.

parole.significato: To breed vermin.
parole.testo: From the Latin verminare (“to have worms”), from vermis (“worm”).

parole.significato: The generation or breeding of vermin.
parole.testo: Latin verminatio the worms, a disease of animals, a crawling, itching pain.

parole.significato: Giving birth to worms or grubs, such as various insects.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“a worm”) + parere (“to bring forth”), + -ous.

parole.significato: An abnormal or irrational fear of worms or being infected by worms.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”) + -phobia: Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: A narrow, worm-like structure found in animal brains between the hemispheres of the cerebellum; it is the site of termi…
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”), from Proto-Italic *wormis, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis. Doublet of worm.

parole.significato: A kind of soil subject to worm activity.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”) + -sol.

parole.significato: The language of a people or a national language.
parole.testo: From Latin vernāculus (“domestic, indigenous, of or pertaining to home-born slaves”), from verna (“a native, a home-born slave (one born in his master's house)”).

parole.significato: vernacular (of everyday language)
parole.testo: Latin vernaculus. See vernacular.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or occurring in spring.
parole.testo: PIE word  *wósr̥ From Latin vernālis (“(rare) of or pertaining to spring; vernal”), from vērnus (“of or pertaining to spring; vernal”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship). Vērnus is derived from vēr (“season of spring”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wósr̥ (“spring”)) + -nus (

parole.significato: The quality of being vernal or spring-like.
parole.testo: From vernal + -ity, from Latin vernalis (“pertainig to spring”).

parole.significato: Flourishing, as in spring; vernal.
parole.testo: From Latin vernans, present participle vernare (“to flourish”), from ver (“spring”).

parole.significato: The appearance of new leaves.
parole.testo: From New Latin vernātiō, from Latin vernāre (“to be verdant, to flourish”) + -tiō (“-tion”, suffix forming abstract nouns), from vernus (“springlike”) + -āre (verb-forming suffix), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wósr̥. Equivalent to vernal + -tion.

parole.significato: Suiting a slave; servile; obsequious.
parole.testo: From Latin vernilis (“servile”). See vernacular.

parole.significato: Fawning or obsequious behaviour; servility.
parole.testo: From vernile + -ity, from Latin vernilitas.

parole.significato: Vernix caseosa; a fatty deposit covering the skin of newborn babies.
parole.testo: Derived from Medieval Latin vernix (“varnish”).

parole.significato: The waxy or "cheesy" white substance found coating the skin of newborn humans.
parole.testo: From Latin vernix (“varnish”) + caseosa (“cheesy”).

parole.significato: Having verricules (thick tufts of parallel hairs, bristles, or branches).
parole.testo: Latin verriculum a net, seine.

parole.significato: A tuft of upright hairs.
parole.testo: From Latin verriculum (“a net”).

parole.significato: A wart, especially one that grows on the foot, caused by a human papilloma virus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin verrūca. Doublet of wart.

parole.significato: Covered in warts; warty
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin verrūcōsus, from Latin verrūca (“wart”). By surface analysis, verruca + -ose. Doublet of verrucous.

parole.significato: wart-like, resembling a verruca; verrucose
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin verrūcōsus, from Latin verrūca (“wart”). By surface analysis, verruca + -ous. Doublet of verrucose.

parole.significato: Capable of being turned; flexible, changeable, or inconsistent.
parole.testo: From Latin versabilis. Compare French versable. See versatile.

parole.significato: Capable of doing many things competently.
parole.testo: From Latin versātilis (“turning easily”), from versātus, past participle of versō (“to turn, change”), frequentative of vertō (“to turn”).

parole.significato: Having changing or varied colours.
parole.testo: From Latin versicolor.

parole.significato: Synonym of versicle.
parole.testo: From Latin versiculus.

parole.significato: Someone who writes verse; a poet.
parole.testo: From Latin versificator.

parole.significato: A female poet.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin versificātrīx. By surface analysis, versificator + -trix.

parole.significato: The back side of a flat object which is to be examined visually, as for reading, such as a sheet, leaf, coin or medal;
parole.testo: From Latin in versō foliō (“on the turned leaf, on the turned page”), the ablative case of the Latin versus (“turned, changed”) from the perfect passive participle of vertō (“turn”). Compare rēctus (“right”).

parole.significato: A quaternion of norm one.
parole.testo: From Latin vertere, versus (“to turn”). See version.

parole.significato: A true species, neither subspecies nor superspecies.
parole.testo: From Latin vērus (“true”) and species

parole.significato: Against; in opposition to.
parole.testo: From Middle English versus, borrowed from Latin versus (“facing”), past participle of vertere (“to turn, change, overthrow, destroy”).

parole.significato: To face in competition
parole.testo: From Middle English versus, borrowed from Latin versus (“facing”), past participle of vertere (“to turn, change, overthrow, destroy”).

parole.significato: crafty; wily; artful
parole.testo: From Latin versūtus, from vertö, versum (“to turn”).

parole.significato: To turn.
parole.testo: From Latin vertere (“to turn, overturn”).

parole.significato: Any of the bony or cartilaginous segments which make up the backbone, consisting in some lower vertebrates of several d…
parole.testo: Borrowing from Latin vertebra (“a joint”), from vertō (“to turn”) + -bra (instrumental nominal suffix). Having multiple vertebrae (plural of vertebra) in one's backbone instead of having a single bone or solid spine, allows for the movement of the body with bends and turns. Hence meaning 1.

parole.significato: Having a backbone.
parole.testo: Adapted borrowing of French vertébré, from Latin vertebrātus (“jointed”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

parole.significato: The formation of vertebrae.
parole.testo: From New Latin vertebrātiō. By surface analysis, vertebra + -ation.

parole.significato: The highest point, top or apex of something.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin vertex (“whirl, eddy; top, crown, peak, summit”). Doublet of vortex.

parole.significato: A whorl, a group of similar parts such as leaves radiating from a shared axis
parole.testo: From Latin verticillum.

parole.significato: A whorl of flowers apparently of one cluster, but composed of two opposite axillary cymes, as in mint.
parole.testo: Latin verticillus (“a whirl”) + aster (“a star”).

parole.significato: Forming or having whorls
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin verticillātus.

parole.significato: A whorl; a verticil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin verticillus.

parole.significato: A sensation of whirling and loss of balance, caused by looking down from a great height or by disease affecting the inn…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vertīgō.

parole.significato: A clay soil, containing a high content of montmorillonite, that forms deep cracks in drier conditions.
parole.testo: From Latin vertere (“turn”) + -i- + sol (“soil”).

parole.significato: A monoclinic-prismatic colorless mineral containing aluminum, calcium, hydrogen, oxygen, silicon, and strontium.
parole.testo: From Latin Vertumn(us) + -ite.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the English city of St Albans.
parole.testo: From Latin Verulamium (“an ancient British city near the site of St Albans”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Verulae.
parole.testo: From Latin Verulānus, from Verulae + -ānus. By surface analysis, Verulae + -an.

parole.significato: An elevation or crest in the wall of the urethra where the seminal ducts enter it.
parole.testo: From New Latin veru montānum (literally “mountainous javelin”).

parole.significato: Madness, insanity, mental derangement.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vēsānia, derived from vēsānus (“mad, insane”).

parole.significato: A supposed rare metallic element extracted from Vesuvian lava. Later tests showed it to be a composite.
parole.testo: From Latin Vesuvius, contracted to Vesbius, -ium.

parole.significato: A bladder, especially the urinary bladder or the gall bladder.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vēsīca (“bladder”).

parole.significato: Synonym of gall bladder.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin vesica biliaris.

parole.significato: Synonym of gall bladder.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin vesica fellea.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the urinary bladder.
parole.testo: From Latin vesica (“bladder”). By surface analysis, vesic- + -al.

parole.significato: Causing blistering to the skin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin vēsīcāns, present participle of vēsīcō. By surface analysis, vesic- + -ant.

parole.significato: bladder, as
parole.testo: From Latin vēsīca (“bladder, sac”) + -o-.

parole.significato: Synonym of vesicle (small blister).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēsīcula. By surface analysis, vesic- + -ula. Doublet of vesicle.

parole.significato: vesicula (vesicle) (cutaneous or mucosal); blister.
parole.testo: From Latin vēsīcula. By surface analysis, vesic- + -ule + -o-.

parole.significato: bladdery; vesicular; vesiculate; composed of, or covered with, vesicles
parole.testo: From Latin vesiculosus.

parole.significato: To darken as at the beginning of night
parole.testo: From Latin vesper.

parole.significato: westward; moving toward the setting sun.
parole.testo: From Latin vesper.

parole.significato: of, pertaining to, or characteristic of bats.
parole.testo: From Latin vespertīliō (“bat”) + -ian.

parole.significato: Of or related to the evening; that occurs in the evening.
parole.testo: From Middle English vespertyne, from Latin vespertīnus (“evening”).

parole.significato: A nest built by a social wasp species.
parole.testo: From Latin vespa (“wasp”), formed in imitation of apiary (a similar structure for bees).

parole.significato: One who carried out the dead bodies of the poor at night for burial.
parole.testo: From Latin vespillo.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Vesta, the virgin goddess of the hearth.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Vestālis.

parole.significato: A virgin dedicated to the service of the goddess Vesta.
parole.testo: From Latin; virgines Vestales referred to the priestesses in charge of the sacred fire in the temple of Vesta in Rome.

parole.significato: vestry
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin vestiārium.

parole.significato: Pertaining to clothes or clothing.
parole.testo: From Latin vestiarius, from vestis as Etymology 1, above.

parole.significato: A cavity into which, in certain bryozoans, the esophagus and anus open.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin vestibulum (“a forecourt, entrance court; an entrance”). Doublet of vestibule.

parole.significato: To investigate.
parole.testo: From Latin vestigatus, past participle of vestigare. See vestige.

parole.significato: A vestige.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vestīgium. Doublet of vestige.

parole.significato: Clothing, clothes, especially ecclesiastical.
parole.testo: A variant of vestment influenced by its etymon Latin vestīmentum (from vestiō (“to clothe”)).

parole.significato: The hairs of plants, invertebrates and other non-mammalian organisms, taken as a whole.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin vestitura, from Latin vestire.

parole.significato: Your fault, due to your error; you are to blame.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from the Latin phrase vestrā culpā (“through your (plural) fault”), ablative case of vestra culpa (“your fault, guilt”), used in English by analogy with mea culpa and nostra culpa.

parole.significato: A kind of firework supposed to resemble a volcano eruption.
parole.testo: From Latin Vesuvius, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Growing old.
parole.testo: From Latin veterāscēns.

parole.significato: Of long standing, experienced, seasoned.
parole.testo: From Latin veterātus.

parole.significato: aging
parole.testo: From Latin vetero (“to age”).

parole.significato: A medical doctor who treats non-human animals.
parole.testo: From Latin veterīnārius (“cattle doctor”) + -an, from veterīnae (“beasts of burden, draught-”), probably from vehō (“to convey, draw”), or from vetus (“old”). By surface analysis, veterinary + -an.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the medical or surgical treatment of non-human animals, especially domestic and farm animals.
parole.testo: From Latin veterīnārius, from veterīnus and veterīnae (“cattle;"beasts of burden/of draught"”); compare with veterinarian.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Old Testament of the Bible.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Latin vetus, veteris (“ancient, old”) + English testamentary (“pertaining to a testament or will”).

parole.significato: Expressing a wish that something will not happen, as in "May we never experience such hardship".
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from **vetitīvus (“prohibitive”), an unattested adjective formed from Classical Latin vetitus (“prohibited”, perfect passive participle of vetō (“to prohibit”)) + -īvus (relational adjective suffix), by analogy with English vetative, from Ecclesiastical Latin vetātīvus (“pro

parole.significato: A political right to disapprove of (and thereby stop) the process of a decision, a law etc.
parole.testo: From Latin vetō (“to forbid”).

parole.significato: antique; ancient; old, in a positive way
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vetustus (“old, ancient”).

parole.significato: The state of being old; old age.
parole.testo: From Latin vetustās (“old age”) + -ity, from vetus (“old”).

parole.significato: antiquity; great age
parole.testo: From Latin vetustās.

parole.significato: A vexed, unresolved, or intractable question.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vexāta quaestiō.

parole.significato: Creating a partition.
parole.testo: From Latin vexillarius: compare French vexillaire.

parole.significato: A company of soldiers (especially in ancient Rome) grouped under the same flag.
parole.testo: From Latin vexillatio, from vexillum.

parole.significato: A flag, banner, or standard.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēxillum (“flag, banner”).

parole.significato: By force, violently; specifically, causing damage to a person or property.
parole.testo: From Latin vi et armis (“with force and arms”).

parole.significato: A main road or highway, especially in ancient Rome. (Mainly used in set phrases, below.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin via (“road”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. Possible doublet of way. The sense in electronics is also explained as vertical interconnect access.

parole.significato: By way of; passing through.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin viā (“by the way (of)”), ablative singular of via (“way, road”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. Compare typologically Polish drogą, Russian путём (putjóm).

parole.significato: A kind of Ancient Roman road, made from earth with gravel on top.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A third way; a middle course, a compromise.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin via media (“a middle way”).

parole.significato: A kind of Ancient Roman road, paved with stone blocks.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A kind of Ancient Roman road, made from levelled earth.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A bridge with several spans that carries rail or road traffic over a valley or other obstacles.
parole.testo: Coined in 1816, from Latin via (“highway; road”) + English -duct, on the basis of aqueduct.

parole.significato: An early type of odometer.
parole.testo: Latin via (“a way”) + -meter.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to roads, or occurring on roads.
parole.testo: From Latin viarius, from via (“a way, road”).

parole.significato: The art of making roads or other patha travelling, including the construction of bridges, canals, viaducts, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin via (“way”) + -tecture, as in architecture.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to traveling or a journey.
parole.testo: Latin viaticus (“relating to a journey”), from via (“road”).

parole.significato: Life insurance policies which are sold at a discount to the face amount, or death benefit, of people who have been medi…
parole.testo: From Latin viaticum (“provisions for a long journey”).

parole.significato: The Eucharist, when given to a person who is dying or one in danger of death.
parole.testo: From Latin viāticum (“travelling-money, provisions for a journey”), from viāticus (“of a road or journey”), from via (“road”). Doublet of voyage.

parole.significato: A wayfarer, traveler.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin viātor (“traveler”).

parole.significato: A narrow streak of subcutaneous extravasation of blood, often one of many in a patch of such streaks, which may be exte…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vībex (“the mark of a blow”).

parole.significato: Characteristic of a vibraculum
parole.testo: From Latin vibrō + -acule + -oid.

parole.significato: A long, whiplike, modified zooid on the surface of certain colonies of bryozoa
parole.testo: From Latin vibrō + -aculum.

parole.significato: The quality of being vibrant.
parole.testo: From Latin vibrans, present participle of vibrare, equivalent to vibrant + -cy.

parole.significato: To shake with small, rapid movements to and fro.
parole.testo: The adjective (then also used as a participle) is first attested in 1420, in Middle English, the verb in 1620; partly from Middle English vibrat(e) (“reverberant”), partly directly borrowed from Latin vibrātus, perfect passive participle of vibrō (“to agitate, set in tremulous motion”) (see -ate (et

parole.significato: A minuscule or slight vibration; specifically, a vibration in brain tissue caused by the comparatively greater vibratio…
parole.testo: From modern Latin vibratiuncula, diminutive form of Latin vibrātio (“vibration”).

parole.significato: A device that vibrates or causes vibration.
parole.testo: From New Latin vibrātor, from Latin vibrō (“to vibrate”). By surface analysis, vibrate + -or.

parole.significato: Any of the tactile whiskers on the nose of an animal such as a cat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vibrissae.

parole.significato: Vibrant.
parole.testo: From Latin vibrissāns, present participle of vibrissō, from vibrō (“to vibrate”) + -issō.

parole.significato: The way an organism responds to mechanical (physical) vibrations.
parole.testo: From vibro-, from Latin vibrāre (“vibrate”) + Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”)

parole.significato: Any of many shrubs and trees, of the genus Viburnum, native to the Northern Hemisphere that have showy clusters of flow…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vīburnum.

parole.significato: Someone who walks or wanders streets.
parole.testo: From Latin vīcus (“street”) + -ambulist (“walker”). Later popularized by its inclusion in the Oxford English Dictionary and thence various "rare word" lists.

parole.significato: A priest entrusted by the bishop with a certain degree of leadership in a territorial division of a diocese or a pastor…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vicārius forāneus. See forane.

parole.significato: The Pope.
parole.testo: Calque of Ecclesiastical Latin vicārius Christī.

parole.significato: The quality of understanding or experiencing something vicariously.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin vicārietās and/or vicarious + -ity; compare precarity.

parole.significato: in place of; subordinate to; designating a person below another in rank
parole.testo: From Latin vice (“in place of”), ablative form of vicis. Compare French fois (“time”) and Spanish vez (“time, turn”).

parole.significato: The same but with the two items mentioned reversed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ablative absolute vice versā (“the position having been reversed”), from feminine third declension noun vicis (“arrangement, order, position”) + feminine ablative singular of perfect passive participle versus, from vertō (“to turn, to reverse”).

parole.significato: Taking the place or rank of (another person); deputy.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin vice (“in place of”), ablative form of vicis (“alternation, turn”). Compare viscount.

parole.significato: A viscount.
parole.testo: From Latin vicecomes. Doublet of vicomte and viscount.

parole.significato: The official administrative deputy of a ruler, head of state, or church official.
parole.testo: From Latin vicegerens.

parole.significato: A person whose age is between twenty and twenty-nine years, inclusive; someone in their twenties.
parole.testo: From vicenary + -ian, from Latin vīcēnārius (“vicenary”), from vīcēnus (“twenty each”) + -ārius (“-ary: forming adjectives and related nouns”).

parole.significato: Synonym of vicenary: of, pertaining to, or based on the number twenty.
parole.testo: From Latin vīcēnārius, from vīcēnus (“twenty each”) + -ārius (“-ary: forming adjectives and related nouns”). Doublet of vicenary. Ultimately cognate with English vigenary.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or based on the number twenty.
parole.testo: From Latin vīcēnārius, from vīcēnus (“twenty each”) + -ārius (“-ary: forming adjectives and related nouns”). Doublet of vicenarious. Ultimately cognate with English vigenary.

parole.significato: The festival and religious rituals celebrating a Roman emperor's 20th year of rule.
parole.testo: From Latin vīcennālia, from vīcennium (“20-year period”) + -ālia (“-alia: forming the names of festivals”), from vicennis (“20-year”) + -ium (“forming abstract nouns”), from vīciēs (“twenty each”) + annus (“year”) + -is (“forming compound adjectives”). Equivalent to vicennium + -alia.

parole.significato: Synonym of vicennalia: the festival and religious ritual held on the 20th anniversary of a Roman emperor's reign.
parole.testo: From Latin vīcennālia, from vīcennis (“20-year”) + -ālia (“-alia: forming festival names”), from vīciēs (“twenty times”) + annus (“year”) + -is (“forming compound adjectives”).

parole.significato: Occurring once every twenty years.
parole.testo: From vicennium + -al or directly from Latin vīcenniālis, from vīcennium (“20-year span”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjective-forming suffix), from vīcennis (“20-year”) + -ium (“-ium”, suffix forming abstract nouns), from vīciēs (“20 times”) + annus (“year”) + -is (suffix forming compound adjectives). Equivale

parole.significato: A period of twenty years.
parole.testo: From Latin vicennium, from vīcennis (“20-year”) + -ium, from vīciēs (“20 times”) + annus (“year”) + -is (suffix forming compound adjectives). Equivalent to vicennial + -ium.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city or province of Vicenza in the Veneto region in northeastern Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin Vīcentīnus, by-form of Vīcētīnus.

parole.significato: The destruction of one-twentieth of something; especially, the killing or putting to death of every twentieth person, e…

parole.significato: A paper size, (2.5"–3.3" x 5"–6.25"), one twenty-fourth of a standard uncut flat sheet.
parole.testo: From Latin ablatives of vīcēsimus (“twentieth”) and quartus (“fourth”).

parole.significato: By turns; in succession; alternatim.
parole.testo: From the Latin vicibus, the ablative plural form of vicis (“change”, “alternation”, “turn”; “succession”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a neighborhood; neighboring.

parole.significato: Nearby; neighbouring; vicinal.

parole.significato: An organic compound from Lathyrus sativus.

parole.significato: Proximity; the state of being near.

parole.significato: Viciousness.

parole.significato: pertaining to change, alteration, or mutation.
parole.testo: From Latin vicissitūdin- + -ary, from oblique stem of Latin vicissitūdō, from vicis + -tūdō. By surface analysis, vicissitude + -ary.

parole.significato: Characterized by or filled with vicissitudes.
parole.testo: From Latin vicissitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin vicissitūdō, from vicis + -tūdō. By surface analysis, vicissitude + -ous.

parole.significato: A change, as of fortune.
parole.testo: From viciss(itous) + -ity, from Latin vicissitas. Mentioned since at least 1717, in Elisha Coles's An English Dictionary.

parole.significato: A kind of police commandant in Ancient Rome, responsible for a vicus.
parole.testo: From Latin vic(us) + -o- + magister.

parole.significato: To make a victim of; to sacrifice; to immolate.
parole.testo: From Latin victimatus, past participle of victimare (“to sacrifice”).

parole.significato: radiotelephony clear-code word for the letter V.
parole.testo: From a Late Latin personal name Victor, borne by several saints, from victor (“conqueror”). Doublet of victor.

parole.significato: The overall champion in a sports contest, typically at a public school
parole.testo: From Latin, "winner of the games".

parole.significato: One of an American breed of medium-sized white pigs with a slightly dished face and very erect ears.
parole.testo: From Latin Victōria, from victōria (“victory”). Doublet of Vitória. The given name can also be analyzed as the male name Victor + -ia. The places were named in honour of Queen Victoria of Great Britain.

parole.significato: A silver coin, stamped with an image of Victory, minted during the Roman Republic, and valued at half a denarius.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin victōriātus.

parole.significato: Being the winner in a contest, struggle, war, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin victōriōsus, from victōria (“victory”), from victor (“conqueror”). Displaced native Old English siġefæst.

parole.significato: A female victor; a victress.
parole.testo: From Middle English victrice, from Latin victrīx.

parole.significato: victor (female); victress.

parole.significato: A small civilian settlement outside a Roman fort.

parole.significato: A remark directing the reader to look to the specified place for epexegesis; see; consult; refer to.

parole.significato: Namely, to wit, that is to say (used when clarifying or naming the preceding item or topic)

parole.significato: That which is to be seen.

parole.significato: Transient visual content or media, processed with technology, especially electronic.

parole.significato: See; consult; refer to—a remark directing the readers to look to the specified place for epexegesis.
parole.testo: From Latin vidēte (“see!”), second-person plural present active imperative form of videō (“to see”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Italian anatomist Guido Guidi (latinized name Vidus Vidius).
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Vidianus. By surface analysis, Vidius + an. Named after Italian surgeon and anatomist Vidus Vidius (1509–1569).

parole.significato: A group of observers.
parole.testo: From Latin vidēre (“to see”), by analogy with audience from Latin audīre (“to hear”).

parole.significato: A preliminary drawing of something to be designed and constructed.
parole.testo: Latin vidimus (“we have seen”).

parole.significato: Relating to widowhood, or widowed.

parole.significato: the state of being a widow; widowhood
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin viduitās, from vidua (“widow”).

parole.significato: Synonym of vicenary, of, pertaining to, or based on the number twenty.

parole.significato: Occurring in intervals of twenty.

parole.significato: Vigilance.

parole.significato: Synonym of vicennial, occurring every twenty years.

parole.significato: To say defamatory things about someone or something; to speak ill of.

parole.significato: The quality of being vile or base.

parole.significato: A country house, with farm buildings around a courtyard.

parole.significato: Having villi; having the shape of villi or small hairs.

parole.significato: A small projection from a membrane, particularly those found in the mucous membranes of the intestines.

parole.significato: life force

parole.significato: A long flexible shoot or branch of a plant.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, consisting of, or producing twigs.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to twigs.

parole.significato: Capable of being defeated or overcome; assailable or vulnerable.

parole.significato: A bond or tie that unifies.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the harvesting of grapes.

parole.significato: The gathering of grapes or honeycomb.

parole.significato: An official who supervised tax collection in the ancient Roman Empire.

parole.significato: able to be vindicated; justifiable

parole.significato: Eager to punish; vindicative.
parole.testo: From the Medieval Latin vindicālis (“avenging, punishing, vengeful, vindictive”), from the Classical Latin vindex (“avenger, punisher, revenger”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship).

parole.significato: To clear of an accusation, suspicion or criticism.

parole.significato: A person who vindicates.

parole.significato: A vindicatress.

parole.significato: Having a tendency to seek revenge when wronged, vengeful.

parole.testo: Calque of Latin vītis (“vine; vine staff”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, bearing, or containing, vines.
parole.testo: Latin vīneālis.

parole.significato: Synonym of viticulture, the cultivation of grape vines for producing wine.

parole.significato: Yielding wine.

parole.significato: To convert fruit juice—particularly grape juice—into wine by fermentation.

parole.significato: Drunkenness.

parole.significato: fond of drinking wine, especially to excess

parole.significato: Soaked with wine.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being vinous, or of having some essential characteristic of wine.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or having the characteristics of wine.

parole.significato: To make wine from fruit.

parole.significato: The univalent radical CH₂=CH−, derived from ethylene.

parole.significato: Any of several flowering plants, of the genus Viola, including the violets and pansies.

parole.significato: Violet-colored.

parole.significato: Subject to violation.

parole.significato: One who violates (a rule, a boundary, another person's body, etc.); offender

parole.significato: The condition or disease of having a virus in the bloodstream.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a virago; having the qualities of a virago.

parole.significato: Resembling an overbearing woman; shrew-like.

parole.significato: In mediaeval times, an outlaw; one who may be slain without judicial enquiry.

parole.significato: The chemical element wolfram or tungsten.

parole.significato: A single, unifying spirit believed by some to animate every living being in the world and to underlie the value of ever…

parole.significato: Any of the genus Xanthomonas of proteobacteria.

parole.significato: The concept of hospitality to strangers.

parole.significato: A room (or separate guesthouse) in a monastery for the temporary accommodation of guests or pilgrims.

parole.significato: The condition of being xenoparous.

parole.significato: A pigment found in Boletales fungi; the oxidized form of isoxerocomic acid.

parole.significato: Any of several North American plants, of the genus Xyris, resembling sedges.

parole.significato: The officer in charge of a xystus in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin xystarchēs, from Ancient Greek ξυστάρχης (xustárkhēs).

parole.significato: A miscellaneous thing or whimsical contraption; a thingamajig.

parole.significato: One who believed that maize was the cause of pellagra.

parole.significato: Characteristic of zealots, especially those that were part of rebellious movements in biblical times.

parole.significato: A zenaida dove (Zenaida spp.).

parole.significato: Pertaining to any of various people named Zeno or Zenon, or to their philosophies.
